Name: Abortion, Incomplete
Description: Incomplete abortion is a form of early pregnancy loss in which partial expulsion of products of conception occurs while retained intrauterine tissue persists, producing persistent uterine bleeding, crampy lower abdominal pain, an open cervical os, and often passage of tissue; subtypes are commonly described as spontaneous versus induced/unsafe, septic versus nonseptic, and first- versus second-trimester presentations. Its biology is usually multifactorial rather than monogenic, with many cases reflecting embryonic chromosomal abnormalities such as aneuploidy from meiotic nondisjunction, while recurrent miscarriage susceptibility has been linked in some patients to thrombophilia and placentation-related genes or variants including F5 Leiden, F2 G20210A, MTHFR, and occasionally immune or endocrine contributors; relevant molecular pathways include progesterone-receptor signaling required for decidual maintenance, prostaglandin EP receptor–calcium signaling and oxytocin-mediated myometrial contraction, matrix metalloproteinase-driven cervical remodeling, trophoblast invasion and angiogenic pathways involving VEGF, placental hCG signaling, and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6, especially in septic cases. Management centers on uterine evacuation and hemorrhage control: misoprostol, a PGE1 analog, stimulates cervical ripening and uterine contractions; mifepristone, a progesterone-receptor antagonist, enhances decidual breakdown and sensitizes the uterus to prostaglandins; oxytocin, an oxytocin-receptor agonist, promotes myometrial contraction; and when infection is suspected, broad-spectrum antibiotics such as doxycycline, metronidazole, and gentamicin are used via inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis or anaerobic DNA damage pathways. Major complications and comorbidities include acute hemorrhage, anemia, endometritis/sepsis, retained products, disseminated intravascular coagulation, infertility from intrauterine adhesions, and coexistence with ectopic pregnancy or gestational trophoblastic disease. Diagnosis relies on history and pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasonography showing retained products and nonviable pregnancy, serial quantitative beta-hCG trends, CBC and blood type/Rh testing with Rh immunoglobulin when indicated, and pathologic evaluation of evacuated tissue when diagnosis is uncertain.

Name: Acidosis, Renal Tubular
Description: Renal tubular acidosis is a group of disorders characterized by normal anion gap, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis caused by impaired renal tubular acid secretion, bicarbonate reclamation, or both, in the absence of major reduction in glomerular filtration. Major subtypes include distal RTA (type 1), proximal RTA (type 2), hyperkalemic RTA (type 4), and mixed forms such as carbonic anhydrase II deficiency. Distal RTA is linked to defects in acid-secretory machinery, including SLC4A1 encoding AE1, ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4 encoding vacuolar H+-ATPase subunits, and FOXI1; proximal RTA involves impaired bicarbonate transport via SLC4A4 or generalized Fanconi syndrome, while inherited type 4 RTA may involve aldosterone pathway genes such as NR3C2, SCNN1A, SCNN1B, and SCNN1G, or WNK1/WNK4 signaling affecting distal sodium handling and potassium-proton secretion. Key pathophysiology centers on intercalated-cell proton transport, carbonic anhydrase activity, bicarbonate transport, epithelial sodium channel function, and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, as with some SLC4A1-related disease, or autosomal recessive, as with ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4, CA2, and SLC4A4 mutations; acquired forms occur with autoimmune disease, especially Sjögren syndrome, drugs, obstructive uropathy, and diabetic hypoaldosteronism. Clinical features include fatigue, polyuria, dehydration, growth failure, rickets or osteomalacia, muscle weakness, hypokalemia in types 1 and 2 or hyperkalemia in type 4, nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis particularly in distal RTA, and sensorineural hearing loss in some proton pump defects. Diagnosis relies on persistent metabolic acidosis with inappropriately high urine pH in distal RTA, low serum bicarbonate, electrolyte patterns, urine anion gap, acid-loading or bicarbonate-infusion tests, assessment for Fanconi syndrome or aldosterone deficiency, renal imaging, and genetic testing in suspected inherited cases. Treatment commonly uses sodium bicarbonate or potassium citrate to replace alkali and raise systemic bicarbonate

Name: Acinetobacter infectious disease
Description: Acinetobacter infections, most often caused by the opportunistic Gram-negative coccobacillus Acinetobacter baumannii, are typically healthcare-associated syndromes that include ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infection, wound and burn infection, urinary tract infection, and meningitis, with presentations ranging from fever, purulent secretions, leukocytosis, hypoxemia, dysuria, cellulitis, or sepsis to septic shock and multiorgan failure. Major virulence and resistance determinants include outer membrane protein A (OmpA), phospholipases, the biofilm-associated protein Bap, capsular polysaccharide loci, the AdeABC, AdeIJK, and AdeFGH efflux systems, porins such as CarO, penicillin-binding proteins, and acquired resistance genes or mutations such as blaOXA-23, blaOXA-24/40, blaOXA-58, blaNDM, blaVIM, ampC/ADC, armA, and pmrA/pmrB or lpxA/lpxC/lpxD alterations linked to colistin resistance. Relevant pathways include lipopolysaccharide and capsule biosynthesis, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, iron acquisition, two-component regulatory systems including BfmRS and PmrAB, envelope stress responses, and host innate immune signaling through TLR4-, NF-kB-, cytokine-, complement-, and neutrophil-mediated pathways. Treatment depends on susceptibility testing and often uses ampicillin-sulbactam, in which sulbactam directly inhibits Acinetobacter PBPs in addition to beta-lactamase inhibition, carbapenems such as meropenem that block cell-wall synthesis when active, polymyxins such as colistin that disrupt the outer membrane by binding lipopolysaccharide, tetracycline derivatives such as minocycline or tigecycline that inhibit the 30S ribosomal subunit, and cefiderocol, a siderophore cephalosporin exploiting iron transport to inhibit PBPs. Important comorbidities and risk factors include mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU stay, trauma, burns, indwelling devices, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, diabetes, chronic lung disease, renal failure, malignancy, and immunosuppression. Name: Acne Vulgaris
Description: Acne vulgaris (MeSH D000152) is a common chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous unit driven by follicular hyperkeratinization, excess sebum production, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and innate and adaptive immune activation, typically presenting with open and closed comedones, inflammatory papules, pustules, nodules, cysts, seborrhea, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and scarring on the face, chest, and back. Major implicated pathways include androgen receptor signaling with increased sebaceous lipogenesis, IGF-1/insulin–PI3K-AKT-mTORC1 and FOXO1 dysregulation, abnormal keratinocyte differentiation, and inflammatory signaling through TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, AP-1, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1beta, IL-8, IL-17, TNF-alpha, and matrix metalloproteinases. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, supported by familial clustering and variants affecting androgen metabolism and inflammation; representative examples include CYP17A1, CYP19A1, SRD5A1/2, AR, TNF, IL1A, IL6, TLR2, and IGF1, while severe syndromic acne may occur in autoinflammatory disorders with PSTPIP1 mutations, such as PAPA/PASH-related phenotypes. Clinical subtypes include comedonal, papulopustular, nodulocystic/conglobata, fulminans, and adult female acne. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on lesion morphology, distribution, and severity grading; endocrine evaluation, serum total/free testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH, or pelvic ultrasound are reserved for hyperandrogenic features, and microbiologic testing is uncommon except in refractory or atypical cases. Common treatments include topical retinoids such as tretinoin or adapalene, which normalize desquamation and reduce comedogenesis; benzoyl peroxide, which is bactericidal via oxidative free radicals and limits antibiotic resistance; systemic or topical antibiotics such as doxycycline or clindamycin, which suppress C. acnes and inflammation; hormonal therapies including combined oral contraceptives and spironolactone, which reduce androgenic drive; and isotretinoin, which profoundly decreases sebaceous gland size, sebum output, comedogenesis, and inflammation

Name: Acromegaly
Description: Acromegaly is a chronic endocrine disorder caused in most cases by a growth hormone (GH)-secreting pituitary somatotroph adenoma, leading to excess insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and progressive somatic overgrowth; rarely it results from ectopic growth hormone-releasing hormone or GH secretion. Key molecular associations include dysregulation of the GHRH receptor–cAMP–PKA pathway, activating GNAS mutations in a subset of somatotroph adenomas, and inherited predisposition involving AIP mutations, MEN1, CDKN1B in MEN4, PRKAR1A in Carney complex, and Xq26.3 microduplication with GPR101 in X-linked acrogigantism; excess GH signals through the GH receptor, JAK2-STAT, MAPK, and PI3K-AKT pathways to stimulate hepatic and peripheral IGF-1 production. Clinically, patients develop enlarged hands and feet, coarse facial features, prognathism, interdental spacing, soft-tissue swelling, hyperhidrosis, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome, headaches, visual field defects, fatigue, and frequently menstrual disturbance, hypogonadism, or erectile dysfunction. Major complications and comorbidities include hypertension, insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, colonic polyps, osteoarthritis, vertebral fractures, and increased mortality if uncontrolled. Disease subtypes include sporadic versus familial forms, microadenoma versus macroadenoma, densely versus sparsely granulated somatotroph tumors, and gigantism when GH excess occurs before epiphyseal closure. Diagnosis is based on elevated age-adjusted IGF-1 with failure of GH suppression during oral glucose tolerance testing, followed by pituitary MRI and assessment of visual fields and pituitary function; histopathology and somatostatin receptor profiling may further classify tumors. Treatment centers on transsphenoidal surgery and drugs such as octreotide or lanreotide, somatostatin receptor ligands that inhibit GH secretion, pegvisomant, a GH receptor antagonist that normalizes IGF-1, and cabergoline, a dopamine D2 agonist that suppresses GH in selected tumors.

Name: Hypersomatotropic gigantism
Description: Hypersomatotropic gigantism is a rare endocrine overgrowth disorder caused by excess growth hormone (GH) secretion before epiphyseal closure, usually from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma or hyperplasia, leading to excessive linear growth and elevated insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). Genetic causes include germline AIP mutations in familial isolated pituitary adenoma, X-linked acrogigantism due to GPR101 microduplication, and syndromic associations such as MEN1, CDKN1B/MEN4, PRKAR1A in Carney complex, and mosaic GNAS activation in McCune-Albright syndrome; somatic GNAS mutations are also found in some GH-secreting adenomas. Pathobiology centers on hypothalamic GHRH-GHRH receptor signaling, pituitary GH synthesis and secretion, hepatic and peripheral JAK2-STAT5-mediated IGF-1 production, and downstream PI3K-AKT-mTOR and MAPK pathways promoting growth and soft-tissue proliferation. Patients typically present with accelerated height velocity, enlarged hands and feet, coarse facial features, prognathism, headaches, hyperhidrosis, visual field defects, delayed puberty or hypogonadism, and glucose intolerance. Major complications include cardiomyopathy, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, insulin resistance or diabetes mellitus, arthropathy, scoliosis, colonic polyps, and mass effects from macroadenomas. Subtypes include pituitary gigantism from adenoma, pituitary hyperplasia or ectopic GHRH excess, and genetic or syndromic forms. Inheritance depends on cause and may be autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, as in AIP or MEN1-related disease, X-linked in GPR101-associated disease, or sporadic from somatic mutation. Diagnosis relies on elevated age-adjusted IGF-1, failure of GH suppression during oral glucose tolerance testing, pituitary MRI, formal visual field testing when indicated, and confirmatory genetic testing in early-onset, familial, or syndromic cases. Treatment commonly combines transsphenoidal surgery with somatostatin analogs such as octreotide, lanreotide, or pasireotide, which inhibit GH secretion via somatostatin receptors, the GH receptor antagonist pegvisomant, which blocks IGF-1 generation, and dopamine agonists such as cabergoline, which suppress pituitary hormone secretion.

Name: Actinomycosis
Description: Actinomycosis (MeSH D000196) is a chronic, suppurative, granulomatous invasive bacterial infection caused most often by Actinomyces israelii and related anaerobic or microaerophilic Actinomyces species that are normal commensals of the oral, gastrointestinal, and female genital tracts; it is not an inherited disorder and has no disease-defining germline mutation, although host susceptibility is shaped by mucosal barrier disruption and immune-response genes and proteins involved in innate and adaptive defense, with representative components including TLR2/TLR4, NOD2, MYD88, NF-kB, TNF, IL1B, IL6, IL17, IFNG, and neutrophil/macrophage antimicrobial pathways. Pathobiology centers on polymicrobial synergy, biofilm-like aggregates, abscess formation, fibrosis, and sinus-tract development through activation of pattern-recognition receptor signaling, cytokine cascades, and fibroinflammatory tissue remodeling. Major clinical forms include cervicofacial, thoracic, abdominopelvic, pelvic/uterine-device-associated, central nervous system, and disseminated disease; typical findings are indurated masses, chronic pain, fever, weight loss, draining sinuses, sulfur granules, jaw or dental infection, pulmonary infiltrates or chest wall extension, bowel or pelvic masses, and occasional brain abscess. Common comorbidities and predisposing factors include poor dentition, recent dental procedures, aspiration, bowel perforation or surgery, diverticulitis, appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease, prolonged intrauterine-device use, diabetes, malnutrition, alcoholism, malignancy, and immunosuppression; complications include osteomyelitis, fistulas, empyema, mediastinal spread, bowel obstruction, and intracranial abscess. Diagnosis relies on compatible chronic invasive disease plus demonstration of branching Gram-positive filamentous organisms and sulfur granules in pus or tissue, anaerobic culture or 16S rRNA-based identification, and imaging such as CT or MRI to define extent, while histology helps distinguish it from cancer, nocardiosis, and tuberculosis. Name: Actinomycosis, Cervicofacial
Description: Cervicofacial actinomycosis (UMLS C0001264) is a chronic, locally invasive, suppurative and granulomatous bacterial infection—classically the “lumpy jaw” form of actinomycosis—most often caused by endogenous oral Actinomyces species, especially Actinomyces israelii, with A. gerencseriae, A. naeslundii, A. viscosus, and polymicrobial copathogens such as Aggregatibacter, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, and Streptococcus frequently contributing. It is an acquired infectious disease rather than a Mendelian disorder, so no specific inheritance pattern, driver mutation, or disease-defining gene is established; host susceptibility is instead linked to impaired mucosal barrier integrity after dental disease, extraction, trauma, irradiation, or surgery, and to immunologic factors involving neutrophil/macrophage dysfunction and inflammatory signaling through pattern-recognition pathways such as TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6. Clinically it presents as a slowly progressive, indurated mandibular or submandibular mass with pain that may be mild, firm “woody” swelling, abscesses, draining sinus tracts, trismus, fistulae, and sulfur granules; subtypes are usually categorized by site, with cervicofacial disease being the commonest, and extension may involve osteomyelitis of the jaw, deep neck spaces, or rarely contiguous intracranial spread. Common comorbidities and predisposing conditions include poor dentition, periodontal disease, diabetes, malnutrition, alcoholism, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical findings plus demonstration of branching filamentous Gram-positive organisms and sulfur granules in pus or tissue, anaerobic culture or increasingly 16S rRNA/MALDI-TOF identification, histopathology, and CT or MRI to define abscesses and bony invasion while excluding malignancy, nocardiosis, or tuberculosis. Name: Addison Disease
Description: Addison disease is a chronic primary adrenal insufficiency caused by destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, leading to deficient glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and often adrenal androgen production; in industrialized settings it is most often autoimmune, whereas infectious, infiltrative, hemorrhagic, metastatic, or genetic etiologies are less common. Key genetic associations include autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 due to biallelic AIRE mutations, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy caused by ABCD1 variants, and congenital adrenal hypoplasia from NR0B1/DAX1 mutations; susceptibility to autoimmune Addison disease is also linked to HLA-DR3/DR4, CTLA4, PTPN22, and CYP27B1, while steroidogenic defects involving CYP11A1, STAR, CYP21A2, MC2R, or MRAP can produce related primary adrenal failure phenotypes. Central molecular features include impaired ACTH-MC2R-cAMP-PKA signaling in some inherited forms, autoimmune T-cell-mediated adrenalitis with 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2) autoantibodies, disrupted cholesterol transport and steroidogenesis, and in adrenoleukodystrophy, peroxisomal very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation causing adrenal injury. Typical manifestations are fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, orthostatic hypotension, salt craving, hyperpigmentation from excess POMC-derived ACTH/MSH, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia; adrenal crisis may cause shock. Common comorbidities include autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, celiac disease, vitiligo, hypogonadism, and osteoporosis. Diagnosis rests on low morning cortisol with elevated ACTH, inadequate cortisol rise on cosyntropin stimulation, low aldosterone with high plasma renin in primary disease, electrolyte abnormalities, 21-hydroxylase antibodies, and etiology-directed testing such as adrenal CT, very-long-chain fatty acids, or genetic analysis. Name: Adrenocortical Hyperfunction
Description: Adrenocortical hyperfunction is a functional disorder of the adrenal cortex characterized by excessive secretion of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and/or adrenal androgens, most commonly manifesting as Cushing syndrome, primary hyperaldosteronism, or virilizing/feminizing adrenal disease; major subtypes include ACTH-dependent bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, ACTH-independent unilateral adenoma or adrenocortical carcinoma, and familial bilateral micronodular or macronodular hyperplasia. Its molecular basis often involves dysregulated cAMP/PKA signaling and steroidogenic pathways, with representative genetic lesions including PRKAR1A mutations in primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, ARMC5 variants in primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia, KCNJ5, CACNA1D, ATP1A1, and ATP2B3 mutations in aldosterone-producing adenomas, and less commonly TP53, CTNNB1, MEN1, APC, GNAS, PDE11A, PDE8B, or MC2R-related abnormalities; key proteins include steroidogenic acute regulatory protein, CYP11B1, CYP11B2, CYP17A1, and 11β-hydroxylase/aldosterone synthase. Clinical features reflect hormone excess: central obesity, moon facies, proximal myopathy, purple striae, hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, hypokalemic alkalosis, hirsutism, menstrual irregularity, acne, osteoporosis, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and in severe cases infections and thromboembolism. Common comorbidities and complications include cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, nephropathy, fractures, infertility, and adrenocortical carcinoma progression. Inheritance is usually sporadic, but autosomal dominant forms occur in Carney complex, MEN1, familial hyperaldosteronism, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Diagnosis relies on biochemical confirmation of autonomous steroid excess using late-night salivary or serum cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, dexamethasone suppression testing, plasma ACTH, aldosterone-renin ratio, serum DHEAS, electrolytes, and adrenal/ pituitary imaging, with adrenal venous sampling for subtype classification in hyperaldosteronism and histopathology when resected. Name: Adrenal Hyperplasia, Congenital
Description: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a group of inherited disorders of adrenal steroidogenesis, usually autosomal recessive, characterized by impaired cortisol biosynthesis with compensatory ACTH excess, adrenal hyperplasia, and variable deficiencies of aldosterone and/or excess adrenal androgens; the commonest form is 21-hydroxylase deficiency caused by biallelic CYP21A2 mutations or gene conversions/deletions, while rarer subtypes include 11β-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP11B1), 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency (CYP17A1), 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency (HSD3B2), steroidogenic acute regulatory protein deficiency/lipoid CAH (STAR), P450 oxidoreductase deficiency (POR), and aldosterone synthase defects (CYP11B2); the relevant pathway is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and adrenal cortical steroidogenic cascade involving cholesterol transport by StAR, CYP11A1-mediated pregnenolone formation, CYP17A1, HSD3B2, CYP21A2, CYP11B1, and mineralocorticoid receptor signaling, with ACTH-driven adrenal androgen overproduction when cortisol feedback fails. Clinical phenotypes include classic salt-wasting and simple virilizing disease and nonclassic late-onset disease, presenting with ambiguous genitalia in 46,XX infants, precocious puberty, hyperpigmentation, vomiting, dehydration, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, failure to thrive, accelerated growth with advanced bone age, hirsutism, acne, menstrual irregularity, infertility, or in 11β-hydroxylase deficiency hypertension from 11-deoxycorticosterone excess. Complications include adrenal crisis, short adult stature, metabolic syndrome, osteoporosis, testicular adrenal rest tumors, polycystic ovarian features, and psychosocial morbidity. Diagnosis relies on newborn screening with elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, confirmatory serum steroid profiling, electrolytes, plasma renin, ACTH stimulation testing, urinary steroid metabolomics, and molecular testing of genes such as CYP21A2. Name: Primary Myelofibrosis
Description: Primary myelofibrosis is a chronic clonal Philadelphia chromosome–negative myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by aberrant hematopoietic stem cell proliferation, progressive bone marrow fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, cytopenias or sometimes leukocytosis/thrombocytosis, and risk of evolution to acute myeloid leukemia. The disease is driven in most cases by mutually exclusive driver lesions activating JAK-STAT signaling, notably JAK2 V617F, CALR exon 9 frameshift mutations, and MPL W515 variants, with additional high-risk mutations such as ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, IDH1/2, TET2, and DNMT3A influencing prognosis; downstream pathways include JAK-STAT, MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT, inflammatory cytokine networks including TGF-β, and stromal fibroblast activation that promotes reticulin and collagen deposition. It may arise de novo as primary disease or less commonly evolve from polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia, and it is usually acquired rather than inherited, although familial clustering and inherited predisposition to myeloproliferative neoplasms can occur. Typical manifestations include fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, pruritus, abdominal fullness from massive splenomegaly, bone pain, early satiety, anemia, leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop cells, and cachexia; complications include portal hypertension, thrombosis, bleeding, infections, gout, severe transfusion dependence, iron overload, and leukemic transformation. Diagnosis relies on WHO/ICC clinicopathologic criteria integrating CBC and smear findings, bone marrow biopsy showing megakaryocytic atypia with reticulin or collagen fibrosis, exclusion of BCR-ABL1-positive chronic myeloid leukemia and other myeloid neoplasms, and molecular testing for JAK2, CALR, and MPL, with cytogenetics and next-generation sequencing aiding classification and risk stratification. Name: Alcohol Withdrawal Delirium
Description: Alcohol withdrawal delirium, or delirium tremens, is an acute, life-threatening neuropsychiatric syndrome that typically appears 48–96 hours after abrupt cessation or major reduction of prolonged heavy alcohol use and represents the severe end of the alcohol withdrawal spectrum, distinct from uncomplicated withdrawal and withdrawal seizures. Its pathobiology reflects chronic ethanol-induced neuroadaptation, with downregulated inhibitory GABA-A signaling and upregulated excitatory glutamatergic NMDA activity, plus catecholaminergic hyperactivity involving norepinephrine, dopamine, cortisol, and autonomic pathways; implicated genetic contributors to alcohol dependence and withdrawal susceptibility include variants in GABRA2 and other GABA-A receptor subunits, GRIN2A/GRIN2B in NMDA signaling, SLC6A4, DRD2, COMT, OPRM1, and alcohol-metabolizing genes ADH1B and ALDH2, but inheritance is complex, polygenic, and non-Mendelian rather than disease-specific. Clinically, patients develop fluctuating delirium, profound agitation, tremor, anxiety, insomnia, disorientation, visual or tactile hallucinations, fever, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, and sometimes generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Diagnosis is clinical, based on recent alcohol cessation, delirium with autonomic overactivity, and exclusion of mimics; CIWA-Ar may help in earlier withdrawal, while laboratory testing typically assesses electrolytes, glucose, magnesium, phosphate, liver and renal function, CBC, toxicology, ECG, and sometimes EEG or neuroimaging to rule out infection, trauma, hepatic encephalopathy, or intracranial disease. First-line treatment is benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam, and chlordiazepoxide, which are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors; refractory cases may require phenobarbital, a barbiturate that enhances GABA-A signaling, dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 agonist that blunts sympathetic outflow, or propofol, which potentiates GABA-A and inhibits NMDA receptors, alongside thiamine, fluids, and electrolyte correction. Name: Alcoholism
Description: Alcoholism, now generally termed alcohol use disorder (AUD), is a chronic relapsing neurobehavioral disease characterized by compulsive alcohol seeking and use despite harm, with subtypes ranging from hazardous use to mild, moderate, and severe AUD and clinical states including intoxication, withdrawal, and dependence. It is multifactorial and moderately heritable, with genetic liability commonly involving alcohol-metabolizing enzymes such as ADH1B and ALDH2, whose functional variants alter acetaldehyde handling and risk, and neurobiologic genes including GABRA2, OPRM1, SLC6A4, DRD2, and KCNJ6 that influence reward, stress responsivity, and impulsivity; inheritance is complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. Core pathophysiology centers on mesolimbic dopaminergic reward circuitry, glutamatergic NMDA signaling, GABAergic inhibition, endogenous opioid pathways, corticotropin-releasing factor and HPA-axis stress signaling, and neuroimmune/inflammatory mechanisms. Typical manifestations include craving, loss of control, tolerance, withdrawal tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, anxiety, insomnia, seizures or delirium tremens in severe withdrawal, and chronic complications such as cognitive impairment, peripheral neuropathy, alcoholic liver disease, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, malnutrition, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, trauma, and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders; frequent comorbidities include depression, anxiety, PTSD, other substance use, hypertension, and hepatitis. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 criteria, screening tools such as AUDIT or CAGE, collateral history, and laboratory evaluation including liver enzymes, gamma-glutamyl transferase, carbohydrate-deficient transferrin, mean corpuscular volume, phosphatidylethanol, and toxicology when relevant. Common pharmacotherapies include naltrexone, a mu-opioid receptor antagonist that reduces alcohol reward and heavy drinking; acamprosate, which modulates glutamatergic hyperexcitability and supports abstinence; and disulfiram, which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase to produce an aversive acetaldehyde reaction after alcohol exposure; adjuncts such as benzodiazepines are standard for acute withdrawal management.

Name: Alopecia
Description: Alopecia (MeSH D000505) is a heterogeneous disorder of hair loss that may be non-scarring or scarring, congenital or acquired, with major subtypes including androgenetic alopecia, alopecia areata, telogen effluvium, traction alopecia, cicatricial alopecias, and inherited hair-shaft or follicular disorders. Clinically it presents with patchy, diffuse, or patterned scalp hair loss, bitemporal recession or vertex thinning, exclamation-mark hairs in alopecia areata, reduced hair density, positive hair-pull test, and in scarring forms perifollicular erythema, scale, pustules, and irreversible follicular destruction; eyebrow, eyelash, beard, and body hair may also be affected. Genetic contributors vary by subtype: androgenetic alopecia is strongly polygenic with androgen receptor AR variants and loci involving EDA2R and WNT-related genes; alopecia areata is linked to immune-regulatory loci including HLA genes, CTLA4, IL2/IL21, and ULBP3; congenital hypotrichosis may reflect mutations in HR, DSG4, LIPH, LPAR6, or KRT genes, with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or complex inheritance patterns depending on the entity. Key pathways include androgen metabolism with testosterone conversion by 5-alpha-reductase to dihydrotestosterone acting via the androgen receptor, Wnt/beta-catenin and Sonic hedgehog signaling in follicle cycling, and in alopecia areata a collapse of follicular immune privilege with IFN-gamma, IL-15, NKG2D+ cytotoxic T cells, and JAK-STAT signaling. Common treatments include topical or oral minoxidil, a potassium-channel opener that prolongs anagen; finasteride or dutasteride, which inhibit 5-alpha-reductase and lower dihydrotestosterone; and corticosteroids, which suppress perifollicular inflammation, while JAK inhibitors such as baricitinib or ritlecitinib target cytokine signaling in severe alopecia areata. Comorbidities include autoimmune thyroid disease, vitiligo, atopy, psoriasis, iron deficiency, androgen excess states such as polycystic ovary syndrome, anxiety and depression, and complications include secondary infection, sun damage, and permanent scarring. Name: Altitude Sickness
Description: Altitude sickness, or high-altitude illness, is an acquired hypobaric hypoxia syndrome that includes acute mountain sickness (AMS), high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE), and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE); it is not classically inherited, but susceptibility is partly genetically influenced by variation in hypoxia-response and vascular genes, with representative associations reported in EPAS1/HIF2A, EGLN1/PHD2, HIF1A, VEGFA, NOS3/eNOS, ACE, EDN1, and components of the renin-angiotensin and nitric oxide pathways. Its core pathobiology involves alveolar hypoxia triggering HIF signaling, sympathetic activation, hyperventilation, cerebral vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, inflammatory mediators, endothelial dysfunction, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, endothelin-1 excess, and in HAPE, exaggerated hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with uneven pulmonary artery pressures and alveolar-capillary stress failure. Typical manifestations begin within hours after ascent and include headache, nausea, anorexia, fatigue, dizziness, poor sleep, tachycardia, and dyspnea on exertion; severe disease produces ataxia, confusion, altered consciousness, papilledema, cough, cyanosis, rales, and severe hypoxemia. Important complications and linked conditions include dehydration, pulmonary hypertension, right-heart strain, cerebral edema, retinal hemorrhage, and death, with higher risk in those with prior altitude illness, cardiopulmonary disease, or obstructive sleep apnea. Diagnosis is chiefly clinical in the setting of recent ascent, using symptom-based criteria such as the Lake Louise Score for AMS and neurologic dysfunction for HACE, supported by pulse oximetry, arterial blood gases, chest radiography for HAPE, and brain imaging when cerebral edema or alternative diagnoses are considered. Treatment relies on descent and oxygen, with acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that induces metabolic acidosis and augments ventilation; dexamethasone, a glucocorticoid that reduces cerebral edema and inflammation; nifedipine, a calcium-channel blocker that lowers pulmonary artery pressure in HAPE; and in selected cases phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil or tadalafil, or inhaled beta-agonists, to improve pulmonary vascular and alveolar fluid handling.

Name: Alveolitis, Extrinsic Allergic
Description: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis, or hypersensitivity pneumonitis, is an immune-mediated interstitial and small-airway lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of organic antigens such as thermophilic actinomycetes, avian proteins, molds, or isocyanates, and is classically divided into acute, subacute, and chronic fibrotic forms. Pathobiology reflects antigen-driven type III and type IV hypersensitivity with immune-complex formation, lymphocytic alveolitis, poorly formed noncaseating granulomas, and, in progressive disease, aberrant repair and fibrosis; key pathways include antigen presentation by HLA class II molecules, Th1/Th17 polarization, macrophage activation, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IFN-γ, CXCL9/CXCL10, and fibrogenic TGF-β signaling. Genetic susceptibility is incompletely penetrant but includes associations with HLA-DR and HLA-DQ alleles, MUC5B promoter variant rs35705950 in fibrotic disease, and telomere-related genes such as TERT and TERC in some patients; familial transmission is uncommon and no simple Mendelian inheritance pattern is typical. Symptoms usually include episodic fever, chills, cough, chest tightness, malaise, and dyspnea hours after exposure in acute disease, while chronic disease presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, weight loss, bibasilar crackles, and sometimes clubbing. Diagnosis integrates a convincing exposure history, serum precipitating IgG to suspected antigens, high-resolution CT showing ground-glass opacities, centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation or fibrosis, bronchoalveolar lavage lymphocytosis, restrictive physiology with reduced DLCO, and, when needed, lung biopsy demonstrating bronchiolocentric interstitial inflammation and granulomas. Main treatment is antigen avoidance plus corticosteroids such as prednisone, which suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription; steroid-sparing immunosuppressants including azathioprine, a purine synthesis inhibitor, and mycophenolate mofetil, an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor, are used in selected cases, while antifibrotics such as nintedanib, a multikinase inhibitor targeting PDGFR/FGFR/VEGFR, may slow chronic fibrosing progression. Name: Alzheimer Disease
Description: Alzheimer disease (MeSH D000544) is a progressive neurodegenerative dementia characterized pathologically by extracellular amyloid-β plaques, intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles, synaptic failure, neuronal loss, and cerebral atrophy, most prominently in the hippocampus and association cortex. Major genetic contributors include APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2 mutations causing autosomal dominant early-onset disease, and APOE ε4 as the strongest common risk allele for late-onset disease; additional susceptibility genes include TREM2, SORL1, ABCA7, CLU, PICALM, and BIN1. Core pathogenic pathways involve amyloidogenic APP processing by β-secretase BACE1 and γ-secretase, tau phosphorylation and aggregation mediated in part by GSK3β and CDK5, impaired cholinergic neurotransmission, glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity through NMDA receptors, microglial activation and neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, lysosomal-autophagic failure, and cerebrovascular amyloid deposition. Clinically, patients develop insidious episodic memory impairment followed by deficits in language, visuospatial and executive function, behavioral and neuropsychiatric symptoms such as apathy, depression, agitation, psychosis, and ultimately loss of activities of daily living, gait dysfunction, dysphagia, and seizures in some cases. Subtypes include sporadic late-onset, familial early-onset, and atypical variants such as posterior cortical atrophy and logopenic aphasia. Standard symptomatic treatments include donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, which inhibit acetylcholinesterase to enhance central cholinergic signaling, and memantine, a low-affinity NMDA receptor antagonist that reduces excitotoxicity; anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies such as lecanemab may reduce aggregated amyloid burden in selected early-stage patients. Common comorbidities and complications include cerebrovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, frailty, falls, malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia, delirium, and sleep disturbance. Diagnosis is based on characteristic progressive cognitive decline with functional impairment, neuropsychological testing, MRI or CT showing cortical and hippocampal atrophy, FDG-PET hypometabolism, amyloid or tau PET, CSF biomarkers including reduced Aβ42 with elevated total and phosphorylated tau, and confirmatory genetic testing when familial disease is suspected.

Name: Amebiasis
Description: Amebiasis (MeSH D000562) is a protozoal infection caused mainly by Entamoeba histolytica, typically acquired by the fecal-oral route and ranging from asymptomatic colonization to invasive colitis and extraintestinal disease, especially amebic liver abscess. Key parasite virulence determinants include the Gal/GalNAc lectin complex (heavy and light subunits; adhesion), cysteine proteases such as EhCP1, EhCP2, and EhCP5 (mucosal invasion and tissue destruction), amoebapores (pore-forming peptides), and host-interacting enzymes including peroxiredoxin; representative host susceptibility factors include HLA class II variants, leptin receptor polymorphisms such as Q223R, and innate immune mediators including TNF, IL-10, IFNG, and TLR signaling genes, although the disorder is infectious rather than Mendelian and has no classical inheritance pattern. Pathobiology involves epithelial adherence, MUC2 mucus degradation, contact-dependent cytotoxicity, complement evasion, neutrophil and macrophage activation, and NF-kB-, inflammasome-, TNF-alpha-, IL-1/IL-8-, and IFN-gamma-associated inflammatory pathways that drive ulceration. Clinical manifestations include abdominal pain, watery or bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, fever, weight loss, and flask-shaped colonic ulcers; extraintestinal spread may cause right upper quadrant pain, fever, hepatomegaly, and rarely pleuropulmonary or cerebral abscesses. Major forms are asymptomatic intestinal carriage, acute amebic colitis or dysentery, chronic colitis, fulminant necrotizing colitis, ameboma, and extraintestinal amebiasis. Comorbidities and complications include malnutrition, pregnancy, corticosteroid exposure, HIV-related vulnerability, toxic megacolon, perforation, hemorrhage, and liver abscess. Diagnosis relies on stool NAAT/PCR or antigen detection to distinguish E. histolytica from E. dispar, stool microscopy for cysts or trophozoites, serology for invasive disease, colonoscopy with biopsy when needed, and ultrasonography or CT for hepatic abscess. Treatment commonly uses metronidazole or tinidazole, nitroimidazoles that generate toxic free-radical intermediates damaging parasite DNA and proteins, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomy

Name: Amenorrhea
Description: Amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation, classified as primary when menses have not begun by about age 15 years despite secondary sexual development or by 13 years without it, and as secondary when established menses cease for at least 3 months, reflecting disruption anywhere along the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian-uterine axis. Common causes include functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, polycystic ovary syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, primary ovarian insufficiency, thyroid disease, congenital outflow tract anomalies, and pregnancy; typical findings include absent or infrequent bleeding, infertility, hot flashes, galactorrhea, hirsutism, acne, pelvic pain, low bone density, or pubertal delay depending on etiology. Genetic contributors are well recognized in gonadal dysgenesis and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, including X-chromosome abnormalities such as monosomy X in Turner syndrome, FMR1 premutation-associated primary ovarian insufficiency, and variants in ANOS1, FGFR1, GNRHR, KISS1R, TAC3/TACR3, FSHR, LHCGR, CYP17A1, CYP19A1, and NR5A1; altered proteins include GnRH receptor, FSH/LH receptors, aromatase, and steroidogenic enzymes. Key pathways involve pulsatile GnRH signaling, pituitary LH/FSH secretion, ovarian folliculogenesis and estradiol/progesterone feedback, prolactin-dopamine regulation, insulin and PI3K-AKT signaling in PCOS, and leptin-KISS1 neuroendocrine control of energy-dependent reproduction. Treatment is cause-specific and commonly includes combined estrogen-progestin therapy to replace sex steroids and protect bone/endometrium, cyclic progesterone to induce withdrawal bleeding and prevent endometrial hyperplasia, bromocriptine or cabergoline as dopamine D2 agonists for hyperprolactinemia, levothyroxine for hypothyroid-related amenorrhea, pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins for ovulation induction, and metformin to improve insulin sensitivity in PCOS. Important comorbidities and complications include infertility, osteoporosis, endometrial hyperplasia/cancer in chronic anovulation, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular risk, and psychological distress. Name: Amyloidosis
Description: Amyloidosis is a heterogeneous group of protein-misfolding disorders characterized by extracellular deposition of insoluble, beta-pleated fibrillar proteins that disrupt tissue architecture and cause progressive organ dysfunction; major subtypes include AL amyloidosis from monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains, AA amyloidosis from serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation, ATTR amyloidosis from transthyretin, including hereditary and wild-type forms, and less common Abeta2M, ALECT2, and organ-limited variants. Genetic components are subtype-specific: hereditary ATTR is usually autosomal dominant and caused by TTR mutations such as Val30Met and Val122Ile, while rarer familial forms involve APOA1, GSN, FGA, or lysozyme genes; AL instead reflects a plasma-cell clone rather than Mendelian inheritance. Pathobiology centers on protein destabilization, misfolding, oligomer formation, fibrillogenesis, proteotoxic stress, macrophage and inflammasome activation, NF-kappaB and cytokine signaling, and tissue injury with oxidative stress and apoptosis. Clinical manifestations depend on organ involvement and commonly include nephrotic-range proteinuria, progressive renal insufficiency, restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy with heart failure and arrhythmias, hepatomegaly, peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, orthostatic hypotension, diarrhea or constipation, weight loss, macroglossia, purpura, and carpal tunnel syndrome. Important comorbidities and complications include multiple myeloma or MGUS in AL, chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease in AA, chronic kidney disease, thromboembolism, and sudden cardiac death. Diagnosis requires demonstration and typing of amyloid by Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence, ideally confirmed by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry, with supportive testing including serum and urine immunofixation and free light chains, SAP or nuclear scintigraphy for ATTR, echocardiography, cardiac MRI, organ biopsy, and genetic testing when hereditary disease is suspected. Treatment is subtype-directed: bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone, and daratumumab suppress pathogenic plasma cells in AL; tafamidis stabilizes TTR tetramers, patisiran silences hepatic TTR via RNA interference, and inotersen is an antisense inhibitor for ATTR; colchicine and IL-6 blockade or other

Name: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Description: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; MeSH D000690) is a progressive, fatal adult-onset neurodegenerative motor neuron disease characterized by degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons in the motor cortex, brainstem, and spinal cord, producing asymmetric limb weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, spasticity, hyperreflexia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and ultimately respiratory failure, with frontotemporal cognitive or behavioral impairment in a subset. Major clinical subtypes include limb-onset and bulbar-onset ALS, familial versus sporadic ALS, and overlap syndromes such as ALS-frontotemporal dementia. Approximately 5–10% of cases are familial, most often autosomal dominant, with important genes including C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion, SOD1, TARDBP encoding TDP-43, and FUS; less common contributors include OPTN, TBK1, VCP, UBQLN2, SQSTM1, ANG, and PFN1, with rare X-linked and recessive forms. Core pathogenic pathways include toxic protein misfolding and aggregation of TDP-43 or mutant SOD1, impaired RNA processing, defective autophagy-proteostasis and ubiquitin-proteasome function, glutamate excitotoxicity involving EAAT2 and AMPA/NMDA signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, axonal transport defects, oxidative stress, ER stress, neuroinflammation mediated by microglia and astrocytes, and altered nucleocytoplasmic transport, particularly in C9orf72-related disease. Standard therapies include riluzole, which reduces glutamatergic neurotransmission and modestly prolongs survival, edaravone, a free-radical scavenger that may slow functional decline, sodium phenylbutyrate/taurursodiol, targeting ER and mitochondrial stress, and tofersen for SOD1-associated ALS, an antisense oligonucleotide that lowers SOD1 expression. Comorbidities and complications include malnutrition, sialorrhea, pseudobulbar affect, depression, venous thromboembolism, aspiration pneumonia, and chronic ventilatory insufficiency. Name: anaphylaxis
Description: Anaphylaxis (MeSH D000707) is an acute, potentially fatal systemic hypersensitivity reaction, most often IgE mediated, in which allergen cross-linking of FcεRI-bound IgE on mast cells and basophils triggers rapid degranulation and synthesis of mediators including histamine, tryptase, prostaglandin D2, leukotrienes, platelet-activating factor, and cytokines, with signaling through Lyn/Syk, PI3K, PLCγ, calcium flux, and MAPK pathways; non-IgE mechanisms also occur, including complement-mediated and direct mast-cell activation, notably via MRGPRX2. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex rather than Mendelian, but representative associations include KIT variants in clonal mast-cell disease, TPSAB1 copy gain in hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, and occasional links involving IL4, IL13, FCER1A, HLA alleles, and PAF acetylhydrolase deficiency; familial clustering is recognized, and inherited disorders such as mastocytosis-related syndromes can increase risk. Clinical manifestations begin abruptly and include pruritus, flushing, urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, abdominal cramping, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, syncope, and hypotension progressing to distributive shock. Major subtypes include food-, drug-, and venom-induced anaphylaxis, exercise- or cofactor-dependent anaphylaxis, perioperative anaphylaxis, idiopathic anaphylaxis, and biphasic reactions. Common comorbidities and risk modifiers include asthma, atopy, mastocytosis, cardiovascular disease, and use of beta-blockers or ACE inhibitors; complications include airway obstruction, arrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, hypoxic injury, and death. Diagnosis is clinical, based on acute illness with typical skin-mucosal, respiratory, cardiovascular, or persistent gastrointestinal involvement after likely exposure, supported by elevated acute serum tryptase relative to baseline, allergen-specific IgE testing, skin prick or intradermal testing, and selected challenge testing. First-line treatment is intramuscular epinephrine, an alpha- and beta-adrenergic agonist that reverses vasodilation, edema, and bronchospasm; adjuncts include H1 antihistamines such as diphenhydramine or cetirizine, H2 blockers such as famotidine, inhaled

Name: Ancylostomiasis
Description: Ancylostomiasis (MeSH D000724) is a soil-transmitted helminthiasis caused mainly by the hookworms Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus, with less common zoonotic cutaneous disease from A. braziliense and A. caninum; it is an acquired infectious disease rather than a Mendelian disorder, although host genetic susceptibility and severity are influenced by immune and hematologic loci, with representative associations involving HLA class II variants, cytokine genes such as IL4, IL13, IL10, TNF, and IFNG, eosinophil/Th2-response mediators, and iron-regulatory or erythrocyte-related genes including HAMP, TMPRSS6, HFE, and globin variants that can modify anemia risk. Pathobiology centers on skin invasion, pulmonary migration, and intestinal blood feeding, activating epithelial alarmins and Th2-polarized pathways with IL-4/IL-5/IL-13, IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, alternatively activated macrophages, TGF-β–mediated immunoregulation, and hepcidin-linked iron homeostasis disruption. Typical manifestations include pruritic ground itch at penetration sites, cough and wheeze during larval migration, abdominal pain, diarrhea, anorexia, pica, fatigue, pallor, eosinophilia, iron-deficiency anemia, hypoproteinemia, growth and cognitive impairment in children, and adverse pregnancy outcomes; major complications include severe anemia, heart failure in extreme cases, malnutrition, and coinfection-related morbidity. Diagnosis is usually based on exposure history and stool ova-and-parasite microscopy demonstrating characteristic hookworm eggs, with species differentiation by larval culture or PCR when needed, plus CBC showing eosinophilia or microcytic anemia and iron studies; endoscopy is rarely required. Treatment relies on benzimidazoles, especially albendazole and mebendazole, which bind parasite β-tubulin and inhibit microtubule-dependent glucose uptake, and pyrantel pamoate, a depolarizing nicotinic agonist that causes spastic paralysis; iron supplementation and nutritional support are often necessary.

Name: Anemia, Aplastic
Description: Aplastic anemia is a bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by hypocellular marrow and peripheral pancytopenia, most often acquired through immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, but also inherited in subsets such as Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and GATA2 deficiency. Key genetic and molecular associations include HLA-DR15 enrichment, somatic mutations in PIGA, BCOR, BCORL1, DNMT3A, ASXL1, and occasionally TERT, TERC, DKC1, FANCA/FANCC, SBDS, or GATA2, with proteins and pathways implicating telomere maintenance, DNA interstrand crosslink repair, ribosome biogenesis, and stem-cell survival. Central pathogenic pathways include oligoclonal cytotoxic T-cell activation, Th1 cytokines such as interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, Fas-mediated apoptosis, reduced thrombopoietin/MPL signaling, and clonal evolution affecting hematopoiesis. Patients typically present with fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, infections, fever, mucosal ulceration, easy bruising, petechiae, epistaxis, or menorrhagia, while lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are usually absent. Major subtypes include acquired severe and very severe aplastic anemia, non-severe aplastic anemia, and constitutional marrow failure syndromes; severity is commonly defined by marrow cellularity below 25 percent plus cytopenias, including neutrophils below 0.5 × 10^9/L, platelets below 20 × 10^9/L, and reticulocytopenia. Diagnosis relies on CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing hypocellularity, cytogenetics and myeloid NGS panels, flow cytometry for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria clones, and testing for inherited predisposition including chromosome breakage assays and telomere length studies when indicated. Standard treatments include antithymocyte globulin, which depletes pathogenic T cells, cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor that suppresses IL-2–dependent T-cell activation, eltrombopag, a thrombopoietin receptor agonist that stimulates residual stem-cell hematopoiesis, and allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; complications include life-threatening infection,

Name: Anemia, Hemolytic, Autoimmune
Description: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA; MeSH D000744) is an acquired immune-mediated hemolytic disorder in which autoantibodies against red blood cell antigens cause premature erythrocyte destruction, classically classified into warm AIHA (usually IgG-mediated), cold agglutinin disease/syndrome (usually IgM-mediated), and mixed forms; less commonly, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is driven by Donath-Landsteiner antibodies. The central molecular pathology involves B-cell activation, loss of immune tolerance, Fc gamma receptor-mediated splenic macrophage phagocytosis, classical complement pathway activation with C1q, C3, and sometimes terminal complement components, and cytokine signaling involving BAFF, IL-6, and other immune-regulatory pathways; genetic contributors are usually predisposing rather than Mendelian, with reported associations involving HLA class II alleles, immune-dysregulation genes such as CTLA4, TNFRSF6/FAS, KMT2D, CARD11, and PIK3CD in syndromic or secondary cases, and clonal lymphoid disease genes such as MYD88 in some cold agglutinin cases. Patients typically present with fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dyspnea, tachycardia, dark urine, splenomegaly, acrocyanosis or Raynaud-type symptoms in cold-reactive disease, and severe cases may cause syncope or heart failure. AIHA is commonly associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, common variable immunodeficiency, autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, infections including Mycoplasma pneumoniae and EBV, and drugs; complications include severe anemia, bilirubin gallstones, thrombosis, and Evans syndrome. Diagnosis rests on hemolysis evidence with reticulocytosis, elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and a positive direct antiglobulin test for IgG and/or C3, supported by eluate studies, cold agglutinin titer, thermal amplitude testing, peripheral smear, and evaluation for secondary causes. Name: Anemia, Megaloblastic
Description: Megaloblastic anemia is a macrocytic anemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis with nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony in hematopoietic precursors, most often due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, but also occurring in inherited defects of cobalamin or folate metabolism and marrow disorders. Genetic contributors include intrinsic factor deficiency from GIF variants, Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome due to CUBN or AMN mutations, transcobalamin II deficiency from TCN2, defects in intracellular cobalamin processing such as MMACHC and related cbl genes, folate transporter defects including SLC46A1 and FOLR1, and classic pernicious anemia linked to autoimmune loss of gastric parietal cells and intrinsic factor rather than simple Mendelian inheritance. Pathobiologically, disrupted one-carbon/folate and methionine synthase pathways, involving MTHFR, thymidylate synthase, methionine synthase, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, reduce dTMP and purine synthesis, activate ineffective erythropoiesis, and elevate homocysteine, with methylmalonic acid accumulation in B12 deficiency. Clinical features include fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, glossitis, jaundice, weight loss, and gastrointestinal symptoms; B12 deficiency may additionally cause peripheral neuropathy, gait ataxia, cognitive change, and subacute combined degeneration. Major subtypes include B12-deficient, folate-deficient, pernicious, congenital intrinsic-factor related, malabsorption-associated, drug-induced, and myelodysplasia-associated megaloblastic states. Comorbidities and complications include autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, Crohn disease, alcoholism, pregnancy-related folate depletion, infertility, pancytopenia, heart failure from severe anemia, thrombosis with hyperhomocysteinemia, and irreversible neurologic injury if untreated. Diagnosis relies on macrocytosis with high MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, low reticulocyte response, low serum B12 or folate, elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine patterns, anti-intrinsic factor and antiparietal cell antibodies, and selected genetic or absorption studies. Name: Angina Pectoris
Description: Angina pectoris is a clinical syndrome of transient myocardial ischemia, usually due to obstructive epicardial coronary atherosclerosis, but also caused by coronary vasospasm or coronary microvascular dysfunction; it presents as stable effort angina, unstable angina, variant (Prinzmetal) angina, and microvascular angina. Typical symptoms are substernal pressure, tightness, or burning precipitated by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin, often radiating to the arm, neck, jaw, or back, with dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, or fatigue; signs may be minimal between episodes. Its biology centers on endothelial dysfunction, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, inflammation, platelet activation, and imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, involving the NO-sGC-cGMP pathway, endothelin-1 signaling, adrenergic signaling, calcium handling, thromboxane A2, and atherosclerotic pathways linked to LDL metabolism and oxidative stress. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations involving LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, LPA, APOE, NOS3, CETP, MTHFR, and 9p21/CDKN2B-AS1; familial hypercholesterolemia and elevated lipoprotein(a) markedly increase risk. Common comorbidities include hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, obesity, chronic kidney disease, smoking, peripheral and cerebrovascular atherosclerotic disease, and heart failure; major complications are acute coronary syndrome, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, and sudden cardiac death. Diagnosis relies on ischemic symptoms, cardiovascular risk assessment, ECG during pain or stress, troponin testing to exclude infarction, stress testing with imaging, coronary CT angiography, invasive coronary angiography, and in selected cases vasospasm provocation or coronary flow reserve/microvascular testing. Treatment commonly includes nitrates such as nitroglycerin, which donate NO and increase cGMP to reduce preload and relieve spasm; beta-blockers such as metoprolol, which lower heart rate and contractility; calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine or diltiazem, which reduce afterload and vasoconstriction; plus antiplatelet therapy, statins, and sometimes ranolazine, which inhibits late sodium current.

Name: Angina Pectoris, Variant
Description: Variant angina pectoris, or Prinzmetal angina, is a vasospastic ischemic heart disease characterized by transient focal spasm of epicardial coronary arteries causing episodic myocardial ischemia, typically at rest and often nocturnally, with chest pressure or pain, transient ST-segment elevation or depression, palpitations, diaphoresis, and occasionally syncope, ventricular tachyarrhythmias, myocardial infarction, or sudden cardiac death. Its pathobiology centers on endothelial dysfunction and coronary smooth-muscle hyperreactivity, with impaired nitric oxide bioavailability and excess vasoconstrictor signaling through RhoA/ROCK, phospholipase C, intracellular Ca2+ influx, protein kinase C, endothelin-1, adrenergic pathways, oxidative stress, and inflammation. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex rather than Mendelian, but reported associations include endothelial nitric oxide synthase NOS3 variants, ALDH2 deficiency common in East Asian populations, and polymorphisms affecting ROCK2, endothelin signaling, adrenergic receptors, or inflammatory mediators; rare familial clustering suggests polygenic inheritance with gene-environment interaction, especially smoking. Diagnosis relies on compatible anginal episodes, transient ischemic ECG changes during symptoms, demonstration of reversible coronary spasm on invasive angiography, and when needed provocative testing with intracoronary acetylcholine or ergonovine showing nitrate-responsive vasoconstriction; ambulatory ECG, stress testing to exclude fixed obstructive disease, and coronary CT or invasive imaging help define anatomy. Major comorbidities include smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, migraine, Raynaud phenomenon, insulin resistance, anxiety, and concomitant atherosclerotic coronary disease, while microvascular spasm may represent a related subtype alongside classic epicardial spasm, with mixed vasospastic-angina/obstructive CAD phenotypes also recognized. Treatment is centered on calcium-channel blockers such as diltiazem, amlodipine, or nifedipine, which reduce L-type calcium entry and smooth-muscle contraction, and nitrates such as nitroglycerin or isosorbide mononitrate, which donate nitric oxide and increase cGMP-mediated vasodilation; nicorandil, where available, adds nitrate action and KATP-channel opening, whereas nonselective beta-blockers may aggravate spasm.

Name: Fabry Disease
Description: Fabry disease (UMLS C0002986) is a rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in GLA on Xq22.1, which encodes the lysosomal hydrolase alpha-galactosidase A; representative mutations include missense, nonsense, splice-site, and small deletion variants that reduce or abolish enzyme activity, leading to progressive accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and lyso-Gb3 in vascular endothelium, podocytes, cardiomyocytes, neurons, and smooth muscle. Disease biology centers on lysosomal dysfunction with downstream endothelial injury, oxidative stress, nitric oxide dysregulation, inflammation, fibrosis, autophagy impairment, and signaling through TGF-beta, NF-kappaB, MAPK/ERK, and profibrotic pathways. Classic Fabry disease presents in childhood or adolescence with acroparesthesias, burning neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, heat and exercise intolerance, corneal verticillata, gastrointestinal dysmotility, tinnitus, and fatigue, whereas later-onset or predominantly cardiac, renal, or cerebrovascular variants may present in adulthood. Major complications include proteinuric chronic kidney disease progressing to renal failure, left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmias, heart failure, valvular disease, transient ischemic attack, stroke, hearing loss, depression, and reduced survival. Inheritance is X-linked, but heterozygous females may be significantly affected because of random X-inactivation. Diagnosis relies on low alpha-galactosidase A activity in males, confirmatory GLA molecular testing in both sexes, elevated plasma or urine lyso-Gb3, and organ assessment with urinalysis, eGFR, ECG, echocardiography, cardiac MRI, brain MRI, and occasionally biopsy showing zebra bodies. Treatment includes enzyme replacement therapy with agalsidase beta or agalsidase alfa, which supplies recombinant alpha-galactosidase A to clear substrate, migalastat, a pharmacologic chaperone that stabilizes amenable mutant enzyme, and supportive renoprotective or cardioprotective therapy such as ACE inhibitors or ARBs for proteinuria and standard antiarrhythmic or heart failure management.

Name: Angioedema
Description: Angioedema is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by transient, localized edema of the deep dermis, subcutis, or submucosa caused either by mast-cell/histamine-mediated vascular leakage or by bradykinin-mediated excess permeability; clinically it presents with recurrent nonpitting swelling of the face, lips, tongue, extremities, genitalia, and bowel wall, with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, and may progress to life-threatening laryngeal edema. Major subtypes include allergic or idiopathic histaminergic angioedema, ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema, acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency, and hereditary angioedema (HAE), most often autosomal dominant. The best-established genetic causes are SERPING1 mutations causing HAE type I/II with quantitative or functional C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, and F12, PLG, ANGPT1, KNG1, MYOF, and HS3ST6 variants in HAE with normal C1 inhibitor; relevant proteins include C1-INH, factor XII, plasma kallikrein, high-molecular-weight kininogen, plasminogen, and bradykinin. Core pathways involve complement and contact activation, factor XIIa-driven prekallikrein-to-kallikrein conversion, cleavage of kininogen to bradykinin, and signaling through bradykinin B2 receptors on endothelium, whereas histaminergic disease involves IgE, mast cells, histamine, leukotrienes, and platelet-activating factor. Comorbid associations include urticaria and atopy in histaminergic disease, autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disorders in acquired C1-INH deficiency, and medication exposure such as ACE inhibitors or estrogens; major complications are airway obstruction, dehydration, and unnecessary abdominal surgery. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern, family and drug history, response to antihistamines, and laboratory testing including serum C4, C1-INH antigenic level and function, C1q for acquired forms, and targeted genetic testing when indicated. Treatment includes antihistamines such as cetirizine or diphenhydramine blocking H1 receptors, corticosteroids reducing inflammatory mediator transcription, epinephrine for anaphylaxis, and for bradykinin-mediated disease C1-INH concentrate replacing deficient inhibitor, icatibant antagonizing bradykinin B2 receptors, ecallantide inhibiting plasma kall

Name: Anthrax
Description: Anthrax is an acute, nonhereditary zoonotic infection caused by the spore-forming Gram-positive bacillus Bacillus anthracis, whose virulence is determined chiefly by the plasmid-encoded toxin genes pagA, cya, and lef, which produce protective antigen, edema factor, and lethal factor, together with the capsule biosynthesis operon capBCADE on pXO2; host susceptibility and inflammatory response are influenced by factors such as ANTXR1/TEM8 and ANTXR2/CMG2, the cellular anthrax toxin receptors, and innate immune pathways including TLR2/TLR4, NLRP1 inflammasome signaling, MAPK/MEK cleavage by lethal factor, cAMP-mediated signaling driven by edema factor, and macrophage dysfunction with cytokine dysregulation. Clinical forms include cutaneous, inhalational, gastrointestinal, injectional, and meningeal anthrax; typical findings are painless papule progressing to a vesicle and black eschar with marked edema in cutaneous disease, and fever, malaise, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, diaphoresis, sepsis, and shock in inhalational disease, often with hemorrhagic mediastinitis or pleural effusions. Major complications include bacteremia, hemorrhagic meningitis, respiratory failure, septic shock, coagulopathy, and death. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus compatible syndrome, supported by culture or PCR from blood, lesion, CSF, pleural fluid, or stool, immunohistochemistry, serology to protective antigen, and imaging such as widened mediastinum on chest radiography or CT in inhalational cases. Treatment typically combines ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, or doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit, with additional agents such as clindamycin, a 50S protein synthesis inhibitor with toxin-suppressive effects, or linezolid; severe systemic disease may also warrant beta-lactams such as meropenem for cell-wall inhibition and antitoxin therapy such as raxibacumab or obiltoxaximab, monoclonal antibodies that neutralize protective antigen.

Name: Cutaneous anthrax
Description: Cutaneous anthrax is an acute zoonotic infection of the skin caused by Bacillus anthracis, usually after inoculation of spores through disrupted skin, and is the most common, typically noninherited clinical form of anthrax; it classically progresses from a pruritic papule to a vesicle and then a painless ulcer with a characteristic black eschar, marked nonpitting edema, and regional lymphadenopathy, with fever and malaise variably present and systemic spread causing bacteremia, toxemia, meningitis, or sepsis in complicated cases. Disease severity is driven by bacterial virulence genes on plasmids pXO1 and pXO2, including pagA encoding protective antigen, lef encoding lethal factor, cya encoding edema factor, and cap genes for the poly-D-glutamate capsule; host susceptibility is not Mendelian, but variation in toxin receptors ANTXR1/TEM8 and ANTXR2/CMG2, innate immune pathways such as TLR2/TLR4, NLRP1 inflammasome signaling, and macrophage responses may modulate outcome. Key molecular pathways involve protective antigen binding to ANTXR1/ANTXR2, endocytosis and furin cleavage, translocation of lethal factor, a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves MAPKKs and suppresses MAPK signaling, and edema factor, a calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase that raises cAMP, disrupts barrier function, and impairs phagocyte activity, alongside inflammatory cytokine and vascular leak pathways. Major subtypes of anthrax are cutaneous, inhalational, gastrointestinal, injectional, and oropharyngeal. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure history and lesion morphology supported by Gram stain and culture, PCR for B. anthracis, immunohistochemistry or serology, and blood cultures if systemic illness is suspected. First-line therapy includes ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; doxycycline, a tetracycline blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit; and penicillin G or amoxicillin, beta-lactams inhibiting cell-wall transpeptidation when susceptibility is confirmed; severe disease may require combination therapy and antitoxin such as raxibacumab or obiltoxaximab targeting protective antigen.
