Name: Anxiety
Description: Anxiety is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by excessive fear, worry, and hyperarousal, encompassing generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, specific phobias, separation anxiety, and agoraphobia, with symptoms such as persistent apprehension, restlessness, irritability, impaired concentration, insomnia, muscle tension, autonomic activation, palpitations, dyspnea, tremor, gastrointestinal distress, and in panic attacks abrupt surges of intense fear with chest discomfort and paresthesias. Its biology is polygenic and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with modest heritability and risk variants reported in genes affecting serotonergic, catecholaminergic, neurotrophic, and stress-response systems, including SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR, HTR1A, COMT Val158Met, MAOA, BDNF Val66Met, FKBP5, CRHR1, NPY, and RGS2; implicated proteins and pathways include serotonin and norepinephrine signaling, GABAergic inhibition, glutamatergic transmission, CRH-ACTH-cortisol hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation, amygdala-prefrontal-hippocampal circuit dysregulation, neuroinflammatory mediators, and altered BDNF-TrkB plasticity. Common treatments include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as sertraline or escitalopram, which block SLC6A4 to enhance synaptic serotonin; serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors such as venlafaxine or duloxetine, which inhibit SLC6A4 and SLC6A2; benzodiazepines such as lorazepam or clonazepam, which are positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors; buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist; and pregabalin, which binds the alpha2delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels to reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release. Anxiety commonly co-occurs with major depressive disorder, substance use disorders, insomnia, chronic pain, irritable bowel syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and PTSD, and may lead to functional impairment, suicidality, medication dependence, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 or ICD criteria, supported by structured interviews and scales such as GAD-7, with laboratory testing, ECG, and thyroid or metabolic evaluation used

Name: Anxiety Disorders
Description: Anxiety disorders (MeSH D001008) are common, heterogeneous psychiatric illnesses characterized by excessive fear, worry, and avoidance with autonomic hyperarousal, and include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, specific phobias, separation anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and selective mutism. Symptoms typically include persistent apprehension, restlessness, irritability, impaired concentration, insomnia, muscle tension, palpitations, tremor, dyspnea, sweating, gastrointestinal distress, and in panic attacks abrupt surges of intense fear with chest discomfort and dizziness. They are multifactorial disorders with moderate heritability, usually polygenic rather than Mendelian, although rare high-impact variants may contribute; implicated genes and proteins include SLC6A4 and the serotonin transporter, HTR1A and HTR2A, COMT, MAOA, BDNF including the Val66Met variant, FKBP5, CRHR1, NPY, GAD1, RGS2, and catecholaminergic, GABAergic, and glutamatergic components. Pathophysiology centers on dysregulation of corticolimbic fear circuitry involving the amygdala, hippocampus, medial prefrontal cortex, locus coeruleus, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, with altered serotonergic, noradrenergic, GABA-A, glutamatergic, neuropeptide Y, and BDNF-TrkB signaling. Common treatments include SSRIs such as sertraline or escitalopram, which inhibit serotonin reuptake; SNRIs such as venlafaxine or duloxetine, which inhibit serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; benzodiazepines such as alprazolam or lorazepam, positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors; and buspirone, a partial 5-HT1A agonist. Frequent comorbidities include major depressive disorder, substance use disorders, PTSD, OCD, chronic pain, irritable bowel syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and sleep disorders, while complications include functional impairment, suicidality, medication dependence, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 criteria, severity scales such as GAD-7 or HAM-A, structured psychiatric interview, and targeted laboratory or cardiopulmonary testing to exclude mimics such as hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, or pheoch

Name: Aortic Coarctation
Description: Aortic coarctation is a congenital narrowing of the thoracic aorta, usually at the juxtaductal isthmus near the ductus arteriosus, producing fixed left ventricular afterload and upper-body hypertension; recognized forms include preductal/infantile and postductal/adult patterns, as well as native and recurrent coarctation. Its genetics are heterogeneous and often syndromic, with strong links to Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve, and representative variants in NOTCH1, MYH6, ACTA2, SMAD6, NKX2-5, and other genes involved in cardiovascular morphogenesis; inheritance is usually multifactorial but autosomal dominant transmission with variable penetrance is reported in some familial left-sided obstructive lesion syndromes. Pathobiology centers on abnormal neural crest-derived arch remodeling, ductal tissue extension into the aortic wall, altered extracellular matrix and smooth-muscle differentiation, and dysregulation of Notch, TGF-β/BMP-SMAD, VEGF, nitric oxide, and renin-angiotensin signaling pathways. Typical findings are diminished or delayed femoral pulses, arm-leg systolic pressure gradient, upper-extremity hypertension, systolic murmur over the back, headaches, epistaxis, claudication, exertional dyspnea, heart failure or shock in neonates after ductal closure, and rib notching in older patients. Common comorbidities and complications include bicuspid aortic valve, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, intracranial aneurysm, aortic aneurysm/dissection, premature coronary disease, persistent hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, endarteritis, stroke, and recoarctation. Diagnosis relies on examination plus echocardiography with Doppler gradients and arch anatomy, confirmed or complemented by CT or MR angiography, catheter angiography/hemodynamics, pulse oximetry and four-limb blood pressures in neonates, and genetic evaluation when syndromic features are present. Management is primarily surgical repair or balloon angioplasty/stenting, while drugs are adjunctive: prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency in critically ill neonates, beta-blockers such as esmolol or propranolol reduce heart rate and afterload, ACE inhibitors such as enalapril lower angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction, and nitropruss

Name: Appendicitis
Description: Appendicitis (MeSH D001064) is an acute inflammatory disorder of the vermiform appendix, usually triggered by luminal obstruction from fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, parasites, or, less often, neoplasia, and it is commonly classified as uncomplicated or complicated, the latter including gangrenous, perforated, phlegmonous, or abscess-forming disease. It is typically sporadic rather than classically inherited, but familial clustering and polygenic susceptibility have been reported, with inflammatory and innate immunity genes such as IL6, TNF, IL1B, TLR4, NOD2, and cytokine-regulatory variants proposed as contributors, although no single mutation is diagnostic. Pathobiologically, mucosal ischemia, bacterial overgrowth, neutrophil recruitment, and activation of NF-kB, Toll-like receptor, inflammasome, and cytokine pathways drive production of IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, prostaglandins, chemokines, and acute-phase reactants such as CRP. Patients usually present with periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fever, guarding, rebound tenderness, and leukocytosis, with atypical presentations in children, pregnancy, and older adults. Diagnosis is based on clinical assessment supported by scoring systems such as Alvarado or AIR, laboratory testing including CBC and CRP, urinalysis and pregnancy testing when relevant, and imaging, especially graded-compression ultrasonography or contrast-enhanced CT, with MRI useful in pregnancy. Standard treatment is appendectomy, but antibiotics are central in nonoperative management and perioperative prophylaxis; common examples include ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis; metronidazole, which generates free-radical intermediates that damage anaerobic DNA; piperacillin-tazobactam, combining cell-wall inhibition with beta-lactamase blockade; and analgesics such as ketorolac, a COX inhibitor that reduces prostaglandin-mediated pain. Important comorbid associations and complications include obesity, appendicolithiasis, inflammatory bowel disease, cystic fibrosis, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, intra-abdominal abscess, bowel obstruction, and postoperative wound infection.

Name: Arteriosclerosis
Description: Arteriosclerosis (MeSH D001161) is a chronic, progressive hardening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls that encompasses atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, and Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis; clinically important disease is driven by endothelial injury, lipid retention, inflammation, fibrosis, and calcification. Key molecular contributors include APOE, LDLR, PCSK9, LPA, APOB, CETP, MTHFR, NOS3, IL6, TNF, CRP, MMPs, and coagulation-related genes, while monogenic dyslipidemias such as familial hypercholesterolemia from LDLR, APOB, or gain-of-function PCSK9 variants markedly accelerate disease risk; inheritance is usually complex polygenic with strong environmental modification, although rare Mendelian lipid disorders occur. Central pathways include oxidized LDL uptake by macrophage scavenger receptors, foam-cell formation, NF-κB–mediated inflammatory signaling, endothelial nitric oxide dysfunction, renin-angiotensin signaling, platelet activation, smooth-muscle migration/proliferation via PDGF and TGF-β, and osteogenic calcification pathways involving BMP2/RUNX2. Major comorbidities and complications include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obesity, chronic kidney disease, dyslipidemia, smoking-related vascular injury, coronary artery disease, carotid stenosis, peripheral arterial disease, aortic aneurysm, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, limb ischemia, and heart failure. Symptoms vary by vascular bed and may be absent for years; when present they include angina, exertional dyspnea, claudication, diminished pulses, bruits, transient neurologic deficits, erectile dysfunction, and refractory hypertension. Diagnosis relies on risk-factor assessment plus evidence of vascular injury by lipid profile, glucose/HbA1c, inflammatory markers when appropriate, ankle-brachial index, duplex ultrasonography, coronary artery calcium scoring, CT/MR angiography, stress testing, and invasive angiography for selected cases. Treatment commonly includes statins such as atorvastatin, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and upregulate hepatic LDL receptors; ezetimibe, which blocks intestinal NPC1L1 cholesterol absorption; PCSK9 inhibitors such as evolocumab, which prevent LDL-receptor degradation; antiplatelet agents such as aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits COX-1 thromboxane synthesis; and

Name: Arthralgia
Description: Arthralgia (MeSH D018771) is joint pain, a symptom complex rather than a single disease, arising from inflammatory, degenerative, infectious, autoimmune, crystal-induced, traumatic, metabolic, or neuropathic disorders; common subtypes include acute versus chronic, monoarticular versus oligoarticular versus polyarticular, inflammatory versus noninflammatory, and localized versus generalized pain syndromes. Clinical features include pain with movement or at rest, tenderness, stiffness, swelling, warmth, reduced range of motion, and sometimes systemic findings such as fever, rash, fatigue, sicca symptoms, or morning stiffness, depending on cause. Genetic contributors are usually those of the underlying disorder rather than isolated arthralgia and include HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles and PTPN22 in rheumatoid arthritis, HLA-B27 in spondyloarthritis, IL23R variants in psoriatic disease, and NLRP3 mutations in autoinflammatory syndromes; relevant proteins and pathways include TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17/IL-23, JAK-STAT, NF-kB, COX/prostaglandin signaling, RANKL-mediated osteoclast activation, complement, and innate immune inflammasome pathways. Inheritance is therefore often complex polygenic with environmental triggers, although some monogenic periodic fever syndromes are autosomal dominant or recessive. Comorbidities and complications depend on etiology and include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, gout, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, viral infection, fibromyalgia, disability, sleep disturbance, depression, deformity, and functional decline. Diagnosis relies on history and examination to define inflammatory pattern and joint distribution, supported by ESR/CRP, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, ANA, uric acid, CBC, metabolic and infectious testing, synovial fluid analysis for crystals, cell count, Gram stain and culture, and imaging such as radiography, ultrasound, or MRI. Treatment is cause-directed and symptomatic, commonly using acetaminophen for central analgesia, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen via COX-1/COX-2 inhibition to reduce prostaglandins, glucocorticoids such as prednisone through broad cytokine suppression, and in selected inflammatory diseases DMARDs or biologics such as methotrexate, TNF inhibitors, or IL-6/JAK inhibitors.

Name: Arthritis, Gouty
Description: Gouty arthritis is an inflammatory crystal arthropathy caused by persistent hyperuricemia with supersaturation of monosodium urate, leading to acute synovitis, intercritical disease, chronic tophaceous gout, and uric acid nephrolithiasis; it is typically multifactorial rather than Mendelian, but heritability is substantial and involves renal and intestinal urate transport genes such as SLC2A9/GLUT9, ABCG2, SLC22A12/URAT1, and SLC17A1, with rarer monogenic contributors including HPRT1 deficiency and PRPS1 overactivity that increase urate production. Pathobiology centers on crystal phagocytosis by macrophages, activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1 cleavage, and IL-1β release, with amplification through TLR signaling, neutrophil recruitment, NET formation, complement, prostaglandins, and TNF-α/IL-6. Clinically, gout presents with abrupt, intensely painful, erythematous, warm, swollen monoarthritis classically affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint, but also ankles, midfoot, knees, wrists, and elbows; fever may occur, and chronic disease causes tophi, erosive damage, deformity, and reduced function. Major comorbidities include chronic kidney disease, hypertension, obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, nephrolithiasis, and increased risk of infection-mimicking presentations. Diagnosis is established by identification of negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid or tophus aspirate; supportive tools include serum urate, inflammatory markers, ultrasound double-contour sign, and dual-energy CT, while classification often follows 2015 ACR/EULAR criteria. Treatment includes NSAIDs such as indomethacin, which inhibit cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin synthesis; colchicine, which disrupts microtubules and neutrophil inflammasome-driven trafficking; corticosteroids, which broadly suppress cytokine transcription; and urate-lowering therapy such as allopurinol or febuxostat, xanthine oxidase inhibitors, and probenecid, a uricosuric that inhibits URAT1, with pegloticase reserved for refractory tophaceous disease by enzymatically converting urate

Name: Arthritis, Psoriatic
Description: Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory musculoskeletal disease within the spondyloarthritis spectrum, characterized by synovitis, enthesitis, dactylitis, and axial or peripheral joint inflammation occurring in association with psoriasis; major clinical patterns include oligoarticular and polyarticular peripheral disease, distal interphalangeal-predominant arthritis, axial disease/sacroiliitis, arthritis mutilans, and predominant enthesitis. Pathogenesis reflects polygenic susceptibility and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity rather than simple Mendelian inheritance, with familial aggregation and associations involving HLA-C*06:02, HLA-B27, HLA-B38, HLA-B39, IL23R, IL12B, TNIP1, TRAF3IP2, TYK2, and TNFAIP3; implicated proteins and cytokines include TNF-α, IL-23, IL-17A/F, IL-22, NF-κB pathway mediators, JAK-STAT components, and RANKL-driven osteoclast pathways that contribute to both erosive damage and aberrant new bone formation. Typical manifestations include inflammatory joint pain and stiffness, especially morning stiffness, swollen tender joints, dactylitis, heel pain from enthesitis, reduced spinal mobility, nail pitting or onycholysis, and cutaneous psoriatic plaques. Diagnosis is clinical and radiographic, commonly supported by CASPAR criteria, inflammatory markers such as ESR/CRP, exclusion of rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP positivity in many cases, and imaging with radiographs, ultrasound, or MRI showing erosions, periostitis, pencil-in-cup deformity, enthesitis, or sacroiliitis. Common comorbidities and complications include uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, metabolic syndrome, obesity, cardiovascular disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, depression, osteoporosis, and progressive joint destruction with disability. Treatment includes NSAIDs for symptom control, methotrexate as an antimetabolite DMARD, TNF inhibitors such as adalimumab or etanercept that neutralize TNF signaling, IL-17 inhibitors such as secukinumab, IL-12/23 or IL-23 blockers such as ustekinumab or guselkumab, and targeted synthetic agents including apremilast, a PDE4 inhibitor, and tofacitinib, a JAK inhibitor.

Name: Arthritis, Rheumatoid
Description: Rheumatoid arthritis (MeSH D001172) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis characterized by symmetric, erosive synovitis and extra-articular disease, usually affecting the small joints of the hands, wrists, and feet with morning stiffness, pain, swelling, warmth, reduced grip strength, fatigue, low-grade fever, rheumatoid nodules, and progressive deformity; major subtypes include seropositive and seronegative RA, early versus established disease, and juvenile forms are distinct entities. Its genetic architecture is complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with strongest susceptibility in HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles, and additional risk loci including PTPN22, STAT4, CTLA4, TNFAIP3, TRAF1/C5, PADI4, and IL6R, interacting with environmental triggers such as smoking to promote loss of tolerance to citrullinated proteins. Central pathogenic pathways involve antigen presentation, T- and B-cell activation, TNF, IL-6, IL-1, GM-CSF, JAK-STAT, NF-kB, and RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis, with autoantibodies including rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide driving immune complex formation, complement activation, pannus formation, cartilage destruction, and bone erosion. Common treatments include methotrexate, a folate antagonist and anchor csDMARD that increases adenosine-mediated anti-inflammatory effects; TNF inhibitors such as etanercept, adalimumab, or infliximab; IL-6 pathway blockade with tocilizumab; JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib or baricitinib; abatacept, which inhibits CD80/86-CD28 costimulation; rituximab, which depletes CD20-positive B cells; and glucocorticoids or NSAIDs for symptomatic control. RA is associated with osteoporosis, interstitial lung disease, vasculitis, Felty syndrome, anemia, cardiovascular disease, infection risk, depression, and AA amyloidosis. Diagnosis is based on clinical synovitis plus 2010 ACR/EULAR classification domains including joint involvement, serology, acute-phase reactants, and symptom duration, supported by ESR/CRP, RF, anti-CCP testing, and imaging with radiography, ultrasound, or MRI to detect synovitis and erosions.

Name: Ascariasis
Description: Ascariasis is a nonhereditary intestinal and hepatopulmonary helminthiasis caused mainly by Ascaris lumbricoides, with zoonotic overlap from A. suum, and ranges from asymptomatic infection to heavy-burden disease; major clinical forms include intestinal, pulmonary larval migration, and hepatobiliary or pancreatic ascariasis. Disease biology is driven less by parasite-specific human mutations than by host immune-response genes and proteins, with representative associations involving Th2-polarization and eosinophilic pathways such as IL4, IL5, IL13, STAT6, FCER1A, TLR2, TLR4, HLA class II loci, IgE, eosinophil peroxidase, and eotaxin/CCR3, alongside epithelial alarmins IL-25, IL-33, and TSLP. These converge on type 2 immune signaling, mast-cell activation, goblet-cell hyperplasia, mucus production, and alternatively activated macrophages, while tissue migration can trigger transient inflammatory injury. Typical symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, malnutrition, growth impairment, cough, wheeze, fever, urticaria, and eosinophilia; heavy infection may cause intestinal obstruction, volvulus, perforation, appendicitis, biliary colic, cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, hepatic abscess, and Löffler syndrome. Comorbidities commonly reflect poverty-associated polyparasitism, undernutrition, anemia, and coexisting enteric infections. Inheritance is not Mendelian, but familial clustering reflects exposure and host susceptibility variants influencing IgE and cytokine responses. Diagnosis rests on identification of characteristic ova on stool microscopy, with concentration methods or Kato-Katz for burden estimation, visualization of expelled adult worms, eosinophilia during larval migration, and ultrasonography, endoscopy, ERCP, or cross-sectional imaging for ectopic or obstructive disease; PCR-based speciation is occasionally used. Standard treatment includes albendazole and mebendazole, benzimidazoles that bind parasite beta-tubulin and inhibit microtubule-dependent glucose uptake, and ivermectin, which activates glutamate-gated chloride channels causing nematode paralysis; pyrantel pamoate, a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker via nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonism, is another common option.

Name: Ascorbic Acid Deficiency
Description: Ascorbic acid deficiency (vitamin C deficiency, scurvy; UMLS C0003969) is a nutritional deficiency disorder caused by inadequate intake, absorption, or increased metabolic loss of ascorbate, rather than a classic monogenic disease, although host genetic factors can modify susceptibility; representative candidates include SLC23A1 and SLC23A2, encoding the sodium-dependent vitamin C transporters SVCT1 and SVCT2, and variants in glutathione S-transferases or haptoglobin that may influence vitamin C homeostasis or oxidative stress handling. Pathobiologically, ascorbate is an essential reducing cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in collagen maturation, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, carnitine biosynthesis enzymes, and HIF prolyl hydroxylases, so deficiency disrupts extracellular matrix integrity, catecholamine and energy metabolism, antioxidant defense, and hypoxia signaling. Clinically, patients develop fatigue, weakness, irritability, myalgias, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, ecchymoses, gingival swelling and bleeding, poor wound healing, anemia, bone pain, and in children impaired osteoid formation with pseudoparalysis; severe cases may cause edema, hemarthroses, infection susceptibility, and rarely fatal hemorrhage. Common comorbid settings include malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, eating disorders, autism spectrum disorder with restricted diet, malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease, cancer, and smoking. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical findings, dietary history, and low plasma or leukocyte ascorbate, with supportive anemia studies and radiographs in pediatric disease. There are no true disease subtypes beyond dietary, malabsorptive, and secondary deficiency states, and inheritance is generally non-Mendelian, except that inherited transporter variation may predispose. Treatment is straightforward replacement: ascorbic acid orally or intravenously replenishes tissue stores and restores hydroxylation reactions; multivitamin preparations provide broader nutritional repletion; and iron supplementation, when concurrent iron deficiency exists, is aided by vitamin C–mediated reduction of ferric to ferrous iron to enhance absorption.

Name: Aspergillosis
Description: Aspergillosis (MeSH D001228) is a spectrum of opportunistic and allergic diseases caused predominantly by Aspergillus fumigatus, ranging from allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and aspergilloma to invasive aspergillosis, especially in neutropenic, transplant, corticosteroid-exposed, or advanced COPD patients. Disease expression reflects both fungal virulence and host immune genetics: impaired phagocyte and pattern-recognition pathways involving CYBB/NOX2 and other chronic granulomatous disease genes, STAT3, CARD9, CLEC7A encoding dectin-1, TLR2/TLR4, PTX3, and CFTR increase susceptibility, while ABPA is linked to atopic immune polarization with IL4/IL13 signaling and HLA associations. Key pathogenic pathways include β-glucan recognition through dectin-1/SYK/CARD9, TLR-NF-κB activation, Th1/Th17 versus Th2 skewing, neutrophil oxidative killing, complement, and angioinvasion with tissue necrosis in invasive disease. Typical manifestations include fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, wheeze, hemoptysis, weight loss, sinus symptoms, and in ABPA asthma exacerbations, mucus plugging, eosinophilia, and bronchiectasis; complications include respiratory failure, massive hemoptysis, dissemination to brain or other organs, and coexistence with tuberculosis cavities, cystic fibrosis, asthma, hematologic malignancy, or post-transplant immunosuppression. Diagnosis integrates host risk factors, compatible imaging such as nodules with halo sign, cavitary lesions or fungus ball, microbiology and pathology showing septate acute-angle branching hyphae, culture or PCR from respiratory or tissue samples, bronchoalveolar lavage or serum galactomannan, serum β-D-glucan, and in ABPA elevated total and Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG. Treatment centers on voriconazole, an azole that inhibits fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; isavuconazole or posaconazole with the same target; amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and disrupts membranes; and echinocandins such as caspofungin, which inhibit β-1,3-D-glucan synthase

Name: Asthma
Description: Asthma (MeSH D001249) is a chronic, heterogeneous inflammatory disease of the airways characterized by variable airflow obstruction, airway hyperresponsiveness, and, in some patients, structural remodeling; it commonly presents with episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnea, prolonged expiration, and reversible reductions in FEV1 or peak expiratory flow, often triggered by allergens, viral infections, exercise, cold air, or irritants. Major subtypes include allergic or atopic asthma, eosinophilic type 2-high disease, non-allergic or neutrophilic asthma, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, occupational asthma, and severe steroid-resistant asthma. Its genetic architecture is complex and usually polygenic rather than Mendelian, with heritable risk linked to loci such as IL4, IL13, IL4R, TSLP, IL33, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, ADAM33, FLG, and the beta2-adrenergic receptor gene ADRB2; these influence epithelial barrier function, IgE responses, eosinophilic inflammation, and bronchodilator responsiveness. Core pathways involve Th2 lymphocytes, ILC2 cells, dendritic cells, mast cells, eosinophils, and cytokines including IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, TSLP, and IL-33, with additional roles for leukotrienes, prostaglandins, IgE-FcεRI signaling, airway smooth-muscle contraction, and in some cases Th17/neutrophilic pathways. Standard therapy includes inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide or fluticasone, which suppress NF-kB-driven airway inflammation; short-acting beta2-agonists such as albuterol, which activate ADRB2 to increase cAMP and relax bronchial smooth muscle; long-acting beta2-agonists such as salmeterol, typically combined with inhaled corticosteroids; leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, which block CysLT1-mediated bronchoconstriction; and biologics including omalizumab, mepolizumab, and dupilumab targeting IgE, IL-5, or IL-4Rα. Common comorbidities and complications include allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, gastroesophageal reflux, obesity, anxiety, sleep disturbance,

Name: Atrial Fibrillation
Description: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, characterized by disorganized atrial electrical activity and ineffective atrial contraction, presenting as paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing persistent, or permanent disease and clinically causing palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse, dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, dizziness, chest discomfort, or sometimes no symptoms. It arises through electrical and structural atrial remodeling involving ion-channel dysfunction, abnormal calcium handling, fibrosis, inflammation, autonomic imbalance, and reentry/ectopic firing, especially from the pulmonary veins; implicated pathways include TGF-β/SMAD and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling promoting fibrosis, CaMKII- and calcium-handling networks involving RYR2 and ATP2A2/SERCA2a, and gap-junction and sodium/potassium channel components such as GJA5, SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNE2, and KCNA5. Genetic susceptibility is often complex and polygenic, but familial and monogenic forms occur, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance and variable penetrance; representative variants involve TTN, MYH7, LMNA, NPPA, PITX2, PRRX1, ZFHX3, SCN5A, KCNQ1, and GJA5, while RYR2 mutations may link atrial arrhythmia with catecholaminergic phenotypes. Major comorbidities and risk factors include hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, hyperthyroidism, chronic kidney disease, alcohol use, and aging; major complications are thromboembolic stroke, systemic embolism, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, heart failure exacerbation, and cognitive decline. Diagnosis is established by ECG showing absent discrete P waves and irregularly irregular RR intervals, supported by ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography, thyroid and electrolyte testing, and stroke-risk assessment. Treatment commonly includes rate control with beta-blockers such as metoprolol, nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as diltiazem, or digoxin via AV nodal slowing; rhythm control with amiodarone, flecainide, or dofetilide through potassium or sodium channel effects; and anticoagulation with apixaban, rivaroxaban, or

Name: Atrial Flutter
Description: Atrial flutter is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by rapid, organized atrial depolarization, most often due to a macroreentrant circuit in the right atrium traversing the cavotricuspid isthmus; typical flutter is counterclockwise or clockwise isthmus-dependent, whereas atypical flutter arises from left atrial or scar-related circuits after surgery or ablation. It commonly presents with palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, dizziness, reduced exercise tolerance, or syncope, and examination may show a rapid regular tachycardia, usually near 150 beats/min with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction. Diagnosis is established by ECG showing sawtooth flutter waves, best in inferior leads, often with atrial rates of 240-340/min, supplemented by ambulatory monitoring, transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography to assess structural disease and atrial thrombus before cardioversion, and electrophysiologic study for mechanism definition and ablation planning. Major associated pathways involve atrial electrical remodeling, conduction slowing, fibrosis, calcium handling, and ion-channel dysfunction, including abnormalities in sodium, potassium, and gap-junction signaling; implicated genes and proteins include SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNE2, MYH6, NPPA, GJA5 encoding connexin 40, and fibrosis-related mediators such as TGF-β, with overlap with familial atrial fibrillation genetics that is usually autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance when inherited. Atrial flutter is strongly linked to atrial fibrillation, hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, hyperthyroidism, chronic lung disease, obesity, sleep apnea, and alcohol use, and may lead to tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, thromboembolism, and stroke. Treatment includes rate control with beta-blockers such as metoprolol, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem, and rhythm control with class III agents such as ibutilide or dofetilide that prolong repolarization, class IC agents such as flecainide that block fast sodium channels in selected patients, plus anticoagulation with apixaban or warfarin to reduce embolic risk; catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus is highly effective definitive therapy for typical flutter.

Name: Autistic Disorder
Description: Autistic disorder, historically the prototypic condition within autism spectrum disorder, is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by early-onset deficits in social communication and reciprocal interaction together with restricted, repetitive behaviors, stereotypies, insistence on sameness, and atypical sensory responses, often accompanied by language delay, intellectual disability, irritability, sleep disturbance, and impaired adaptive functioning. Its biology is strongly genetic but multifactorial, with both syndromic and nonsyndromic forms; implicated genes include synaptic and chromatin regulators such as SHANK3, NRXN1, NLGN3, NLGN4X, CNTNAP2, CHD8, ADNP, PTEN, SCN2A, and FMR1, as well as copy-number variants at 16p11.2 and 22q11.2, with inheritance that may be de novo autosomal dominant, inherited dominant, X-linked, or polygenic with variable penetrance. Pathophysiologic themes include altered synaptogenesis and synaptic plasticity, excitation-inhibition imbalance involving glutamatergic and GABAergic circuits, mTOR/PI3K-AKT signaling, Wnt/β-catenin, MAPK, calcium-channel and sodium-channel signaling, oxytocin and serotonin pathways, and microglial or immune dysregulation. Common comorbidities include epilepsy, ADHD, anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, gastrointestinal dysfunction, sleep disorders, and motor coordination problems, with complications such as self-injury and severe behavioral dysregulation. Treatment is primarily behavioral and educational, but drugs are used symptomatically: risperidone and aripiprazole, dopamine-serotonin receptor modulators, are widely used for irritability and aggression, while selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine may target anxiety or repetitive symptoms; stimulants such as methylphenidate can help comorbid ADHD by blocking dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake. Diagnosis is clinical, based on persistent social-communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors beginning in early development and causing functional impairment, supported by developmental history, standardized instruments such as ADOS-2 and ADI-R, cognitive and language assessment, hearing evaluation, and when indicated genetic testing including chromosomal microarray, Fragile X testing, and increasingly exome sequencing.

Name: Autoimmune Diseases
Description: Autoimmune diseases are a heterogeneous group of chronic disorders in which loss of self-tolerance leads to adaptive and innate immune attack on host tissues, either organ-specific, as in type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and myasthenia gravis, or systemic, as in rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren syndrome, and ANCA-associated vasculitis. Genetic susceptibility is typically complex and polygenic, with strong HLA associations such as HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles in rheumatoid arthritis, HLA-B27 in spondyloarthritis, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 in celiac disease, and non-HLA loci including PTPN22, CTLA4, IL23R, STAT4, TNFAIP3, NOD2, and AIRE or FOXP3 mutations in rare monogenic autoimmunity; inheritance is therefore usually multifactorial, though Mendelian forms occur. Central pathogenic pathways include defective central and peripheral tolerance, autoreactive B and T cells, antigen presentation, complement activation, and cytokine networks involving TNF, type I interferons, IL-6, IL-17/IL-23, JAK-STAT, NF-kB, T-cell co-stimulation, and regulatory T-cell dysfunction. Clinical features vary by target organ but commonly include fatigue, fever, arthralgia or arthritis, rash, sicca symptoms, weakness, cytopenias, endocrinopathy, gastrointestinal inflammation, and relapsing-remitting or progressive organ damage. Frequent comorbidities and complications include cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, infection related to immunosuppression, interstitial lung disease, renal failure, thrombosis, malignancy risk in selected disorders, and overlap syndromes. Treatment often uses glucocorticoids, which broadly suppress NF-kB-dependent inflammatory gene transcription; methotrexate, a folate antagonist with anti-inflammatory effects partly via adenosine signaling; hydroxychloroquine, which impairs endosomal TLR signaling; TNF inhibitors such as infliximab or etanercept; rituximab, which depletes CD20-positive B cells; and JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib. Diagnosis integrates clinical criteria, family history, autoantibody testing such as ANA, anti-dsDNA, RF, anti-CCP, ANCA, anti-TPO, inflammatory markers, complement

Name: Back Pain
Description: Back pain (MeSH D001416) is a highly prevalent symptom complex rather than a single disease, arising from mechanical, degenerative, inflammatory, neuropathic, visceral, infectious, or neoplastic causes, and commonly classified as acute, subacute, or chronic, and as axial neck/thoracic/lumbar pain with or without radiculopathy; typical manifestations include localized or radiating pain, paraspinal tenderness, muscle spasm, stiffness, reduced range of motion, sensory change, weakness, and, in severe cases, cauda equina features or constitutional signs. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic and cause-specific: lumbar disc degeneration and chronic back pain have been associated with variants in COL9A2, COL11A1, ACAN, ASPN, CILP, MMP3, IL1A/IL6, GDF5, VDR, and COMT, while inflammatory back pain in ankylosing spondylitis is strongly linked to HLA-B27 with ERAP1 and IL23R contributions; relevant proteins and pathways include extracellular-matrix collagen/aggrecan homeostasis, matrix metalloproteinase-mediated disc breakdown, NF-kB, TNF-alpha, IL-1/IL-6, IL-17/IL-23, prostaglandin-COX signaling, TGF-beta/Wnt, nerve growth factor sensitization, and glial/central sensitization mechanisms. Most cases are multifactorial rather than Mendelian, although inherited disorders such as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasias, osteogenesis imperfecta, or familial spondyloarthritis can present with back pain. Common comorbidities include obesity, osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, fibromyalgia, diabetes, and smoking-related disease; complications include chronic disability, opioid dependence, falls, neurologic deficit, and impaired quality of life. Treatment depends on etiology and often includes acetaminophen, which acts centrally to reduce pain; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis; skeletal muscle relaxants such as cyclobenzaprine, which reduce tonic somatic motor activity; and for neuropathic or refractory pain, duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, or gabapentin, which binds alpha2delta calcium-channel subunits. Name: Pneumonia, Bacterial
Description: Bacterial pneumonia (MeSH D018410) is an acute infection of the lower respiratory tract characterized by microbial invasion of alveoli and distal airways, producing suppurative inflammation and consolidation, most commonly as community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration-related, lobar, bronchopneumonia, or necrotizing forms. Typical pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Gram-negative bacilli; host susceptibility is influenced by genetic components of innate immunity and mucosal defense, including variants in TLR2, TLR4, TLR9, NOD2, MBL2, FCGR2A, CFTR, SFTPA1/SFTPA2, SFTPD, and cytokine genes such as TNF, IL6, and IL10, while primary immunodeficiencies affecting BTK, CYBB, or complement genes can confer Mendelian predisposition rather than direct inheritance of pneumonia itself. Central pathways include pattern-recognition receptor signaling through TLR/MyD88/NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, complement, neutrophil recruitment via CXCL8/IL-8, JAK/STAT-mediated cytokine responses, and impaired surfactant and epithelial barrier function. Clinical manifestations typically include fever, chills, productive cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia, crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and radiographic infiltrates, with severe disease causing sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, empyema, lung abscess, bacteremia, and respiratory failure. Major comorbidities include COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, diabetes, alcoholism, chronic heart, liver, or kidney disease, malignancy, advanced age, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms and examination plus chest radiography or CT, pulse oximetry, CBC and inflammatory markers, sputum Gram stain and culture, blood cultures in severe illness, urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella, and PCR-based pathogen testing when indicated. Name: Bartonella Infections
Description: Bartonella infections are zoonotic, vector-borne bacterial diseases caused mainly by Bartonella henselae, B. quintana, and B. bacilliformis, producing clinical syndromes such as cat-scratch disease, trench fever, bacillary angiomatosis, peliosis hepatis, bacteremia, endocarditis, and Carrion disease. These are acquired rather than inherited disorders, but host genetic susceptibility influences severity; impaired cell-mediated immunity, especially HIV/AIDS, transplantation, or other immunodeficiencies, strongly predisposes to disseminated infection, and variants affecting IFN-γ/IL-12 axis signaling, TLR-mediated innate sensing, or angiogenic and inflammatory responses have been proposed as relevant host factors. Important bacterial virulence genes and proteins include the adhesin BadA, VirB/VirD4 type IV secretion system effectors, deformin, hemin-binding proteins, and Bartonella bacilliformis flagellar components, which promote erythrocyte and endothelial infection, immune evasion, and vasoproliferation. Pathobiology prominently involves endothelial activation, NF-κB signaling, HIF-1/VEGF-driven angiogenesis, and cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α. Typical manifestations include fever, malaise, tender regional lymphadenopathy, papules at inoculation sites, hepatosplenic lesions, vasoproliferative skin lesions, anemia, and culture-negative endocarditis; severe complications include encephalopathy, neuroretinitis, osteomyelitis, prolonged bacteremia, heart failure from valvular infection, and hemorrhagic or hemolytic complications in Carrion disease. Commonly used therapies include azithromycin, a macrolide that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; doxycycline, a tetracycline that inhibits 30S protein synthesis; rifampin, which inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; and in severe endocarditis or neuroretinitis, gentamicin, an aminoglycoside causing 30S-mediated mistranslation, often combined with doxycycline. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure history and syndrome, serology by indirect immunofluorescence, PCR or other nucleic acid amplification from blood or tissue, histopathology with Warthin-Starry staining in tissue lesions, echocardiography for endocarditis, and prolonged specialized culture when bacteremia is suspected.

Name: Behcet Syndrome
Description: Behçet syndrome is a chronic, relapsing, multisystem autoinflammatory vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all calibers, classically marked by recurrent oral aphthae, genital ulcers, uveitis, and diverse cutaneous, articular, neurologic, gastrointestinal, and vascular manifestations; common signs include erythema nodosum–like lesions, papulopustular eruptions, retinal vasculitis, arthritis, thrombophlebitis, and pathergy, while major complications include vision loss, cerebral venous thrombosis, stroke-like neuro-Behçet disease, pulmonary artery aneurysm, bowel perforation, and venous thromboembolism. It is usually sporadic with complex polygenic susceptibility rather than Mendelian inheritance, but strong genetic associations include HLA-B*51, and variants in ERAP1, IL10, IL23R-IL12RB2, STAT4, CCR1, KLRC4, TNFAIP3, and MEFV, implicating aberrant antigen processing, neutrophil hyperreactivity, Th1/Th17 polarization, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-17 signaling, endothelial activation, and innate immune dysregulation. Recognized phenotypic subtypes include mucocutaneous-dominant, ocular, vascular, intestinal, and neurologic disease. Diagnosis is clinical, commonly based on the International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease or older International Study Group criteria, supported by ophthalmologic examination, skin pathergy testing, inflammatory markers, and targeted imaging or endoscopy for organ involvement; no single diagnostic biomarker is definitive, although HLA-B51 may support risk stratification. Treatment is tailored to severity: colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization and neutrophil chemotaxis and is widely used for mucocutaneous and articular disease; corticosteroids suppress broad cytokine-driven inflammation for acute flares; azathioprine inhibits purine synthesis to control ocular and systemic disease; cyclosporine blocks calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation; TNF inhibitors such as infliximab or adalimumab neutralize TNF-α in refractory ocular, vascular, and intestinal disease; and apremilast, a phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor, reduces oral ulcer burden.

Name: Bejel
Description: Bejel, or endemic syphilis, is a chronic nonvenereal treponemal infection caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum, a spirochete whose pathogenicity is driven more by bacterial surface lipoproteins and antigenic variation, particularly Tpr family proteins and outer-membrane components, than by a well-defined host germline genetic basis; accordingly, no Mendelian inheritance pattern is recognized, although host susceptibility likely reflects complex immune-response variation involving innate and adaptive pathways such as TLR1/2-mediated recognition, NF-κB activation, macrophage and dendritic-cell signaling, and Th1 cytokines including IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-12. The disease is transmitted mainly by close household contact in children living in arid, resource-limited settings and classically progresses through early mucous patches and shallow oral or pharyngeal lesions, followed by generalized rash, condyloma-like lesions, and later destructive gummatous or periosteal disease with osteoperiostitis, bone pain, tibial bowing, and nasopharyngeal or palatal damage; clinically it is often described as early and late bejel rather than sharply distinct subtypes. Diagnosis relies on epidemiology and examination plus serologic testing analogous to syphilis, with nontreponemal assays such as VDRL or RPR for screening and activity assessment and treponemal tests such as TPPA, FTA-ABS, or EIA for confirmation, while dark-field microscopy or PCR from lesions can provide direct evidence where available, and differentiation from venereal syphilis, yaws, and pinta requires clinical and geographic context because serology cross-reacts. First-line therapy is benzathine penicillin G, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins; alternatives include doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, tetracycline, also a 30S inhibitor, and azithromycin, a macrolide that blocks 50S-mediated protein synthesis, though resistance concerns limit reliance. Complications include secondary bacterial superinfection, chronic osteitis, disfigurement, functional impairment, and social morbidity, with malnutrition, poor hygiene, and crowding as common linked comorbid conditions.

Name: C0004945
Description: C0004945, in the context of UMLS C0005138, corresponds to asthma, a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable expiratory airflow limitation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and episodic reversible obstruction driven by complex gene-environment interactions. Common symptoms include recurrent wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnea, nocturnal awakening, and prolonged expiration, with severe attacks causing hypoxemia and status asthmaticus. Major endotypes include type 2-high eosinophilic/allergic asthma and non-type 2 phenotypes, with clinical subtypes such as allergic, nonallergic, exercise-induced, occupational, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and severe refractory asthma. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic, with representative associations involving IL4, IL13, IL4RA, TSLP, ADAM33, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, FLG, and HLA-region variants; inheritance is complex familial rather than Mendelian. Key pathways include epithelial alarmins TSLP, IL-33, and IL-25; Th2 and ILC2 activation; IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation; eosinophilic inflammation via IL-5; goblet-cell metaplasia and mucus hypersecretion; leukotriene and prostaglandin signaling; and airway remodeling involving TGF-β, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, and subepithelial fibrosis. Treatment commonly includes inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide or fluticasone, which suppress NF-κB-dependent inflammatory gene transcription; short-acting β2-agonists such as albuterol, which relax bronchial smooth muscle via cAMP; long-acting β2-agonists such as salmeterol or formoterol, used with inhaled steroids; leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, which block CysLT1 signaling; antimuscarinics such as tiotropium; and biologics including omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, and dupilumab targeting IgE, IL-5/IL-5R, or IL-4Rα. Name: beta Thalassemia
Description: Beta thalassemia (UMLS C0005283) is an inherited hemoglobinopathy caused by reduced or absent β-globin synthesis, most often due to autosomal recessive pathogenic variants in HBB on chromosome 11, including promoter, splice-site, nonsense, frameshift, and missense mutations that produce β+ or β0 alleles; phenotype is further modified by coinherited variants in HBA1/HBA2, HBG2/HBS1L-MYB, and BCL11A that alter globin balance or fetal hemoglobin expression. The core pathobiology is imbalance between excess free α-globin chains and deficient β chains, driving oxidative stress, heme toxicity, erythroid apoptosis, ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, iron dysregulation through suppression of the BMP6-SMAD-hepcidin axis by erythroferrone, and compensatory EPO/JAK2-STAT signaling with marrow expansion and extramedullary hematopoiesis. Clinical forms include β-thalassemia major, intermedia, and minor/trait, with symptoms ranging from asymptomatic microcytosis to severe transfusion-dependent anemia presenting in infancy with pallor, jaundice, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, bone deformities, growth delay, and fatigue. Major complications include transfusional and secondary iron overload causing cardiomyopathy, liver disease, endocrinopathies, osteoporosis, gallstones, thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension, infection risk, leg ulcers, and splenectomy-related sequelae. Treatment commonly includes regular red-cell transfusion to suppress ineffective erythropoiesis, iron chelation with deferasirox, deferoxamine, or deferiprone to bind excess iron and promote excretion, hydroxyurea to increase HbF, and luspatercept, an activin receptor ligand trap that enhances late-stage erythroid maturation; selected patients may undergo allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation or receive gene therapy such as betibeglogene autotemcel. Diagnosis rests on CBC showing microcytic hypochromic anemia with elevated RBC count relative to iron deficiency, smear abnormalities, reticulocyte and hemolysis markers, hemoglobin analysis by HPLC or electrophoresis showing increased HbA2 and often HbF, molecular testing of HBB and modifiers, family studies, and iron studies to distinguish concomitant iron deficiency.

Name: Disease or Syndrome
Description: UMLS C0005424 corresponds to cancer, a heterogeneous group of malignant neoplasms characterized by uncontrolled cellular proliferation, invasion, and metastatic potential arising through accumulated genetic and epigenetic alterations. Commonly implicated genes and proteins include tumor suppressors TP53, RB1, APC, PTEN, and CDKN2A, oncogenes such as KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MYC, EGFR, ERBB2/HER2, ALK, and PIK3CA, and DNA-repair genes including BRCA1, BRCA2, MLH1, MSH2, and ATM; representative pathogenic events include KRAS codon 12 mutations, BRAF V600E, EGFR exon 19 deletions/L858R, HER2 amplification, BCR-ABL1 fusion, and loss-of-function TP53 variants. Dysregulated pathways prominently involve receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, WNT/β-catenin, p53-mediated DNA-damage response, cell-cycle control via cyclin D-CDK4/6-RB, TGF-β, JAK/STAT, angiogenesis through VEGF, apoptosis, and immune-checkpoint pathways such as PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4. Treatment depends on histology and stage and commonly includes cytotoxic agents such as cisplatin, which forms DNA crosslinks, doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor that intercalates DNA and generates free radicals, and paclitaxel, which stabilizes microtubules, as well as targeted or biologic therapies such as imatinib, a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor, trastuzumab, a HER2-directed monoclonal antibody, and pembrolizumab, a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor. Clinical manifestations vary by site but often include weight loss, fatigue, pain, bleeding, mass effect, anemia, cachexia, and organ-specific dysfunction; major types include carcinomas, sarcomas, leukemias, lymphomas, melanomas, and CNS tumors. Name: Bipolar Disorder
Description: Bipolar disorder (MeSH D001714) is a chronic, recurrent mood disorder characterized by pathologic oscillation between mania or hypomania and major depression, with subtypes including bipolar I disorder, bipolar II disorder, and cyclothymic disorder, and it presents clinically with elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased energy, pressured speech, grandiosity, impulsivity, psychomotor agitation, and during depressive phases, anhedonia, psychomotor slowing, guilt, suicidality, and cognitive impairment; psychotic features may occur in severe episodes. It is genetically complex and highly heritable, usually showing polygenic, non-Mendelian inheritance with familial aggregation; risk loci and representative genes include CACNA1C, ANK3, ODZ4/TENM4, NCAN, TRANK1, and clock-related genes such as CLOCK and ARNTL, while altered proteins and pathways implicate voltage-gated calcium channels, sodium channel-anchoring proteins, circadian rhythm regulation, synaptic plasticity, mitochondrial energetics, GSK3 signaling, PKC, BDNF-TrkB, glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission, second-messenger cascades, neuroinflammation, and HPA-axis dysregulation. Common treatments include lithium, which modulates inositol signaling and inhibits GSK3 with anti-suicidal and mood-stabilizing effects; valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and affects sodium channels and histone deacetylase activity; lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-sensitive sodium channels and reduces glutamate release; and atypical antipsychotics such as quetiapine, olanzapine, lurasidone, and cariprazine, which primarily modulate dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A/5-HT1A signaling. Important comorbidities and complications include anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, ADHD, migraine, obesity, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, thyroid dysfunction, sleep disorders, impaired functioning, and high suicide risk. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 or ICD criteria documenting distinct manic, hypomanic, and depressive episodes, supplemented by psychiatric interview, collateral history, rating scales, and laboratory testing or toxicology to exclude secondary or medication-induced causes; no single diagnostic biomarker is established.

Name: Urinary bladder stone (disorder)
Description: Urinary bladder stone disorder, or vesical calculosis, is a crystalline concretion disease of the lower urinary tract characterized by supersaturation of urine, crystal nucleation, aggregation, and retention within the bladder, most often secondary to urinary stasis, infection, foreign bodies, neurogenic bladder, or bladder outlet obstruction. Major subtypes include primary endemic childhood stones, usually ammonium acid urate or calcium oxalate in low-protein/dehydration settings, and secondary adult stones, commonly uric acid, calcium oxalate/phosphate, struvite, or mixed calculi associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia, catheterization, or reconstruction. Although most bladder stones are acquired rather than Mendelian, genetic contributors overlap with urolithiasis and include SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 in cystinuria, AGXT, GRHPR, and HOGA1 in primary hyperoxaluria, APRT deficiency causing 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stones, and UMOD or CASR variants that influence urinary mineral handling; relevant proteins include uromodulin, calcium-sensing receptor, Tamm-Horsfall protein, osteopontin, and matrix modulators of crystal adhesion. Pathobiology involves urinary pH dysregulation, urease-producing bacteria generating ammonia and alkalinization, inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress, and crystal-cell interaction pathways involving NF-kB, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, IL-1beta, ROS, and epithelial injury. Clinical manifestations include suprapubic pain, dysuria, frequency, urgency, interrupted stream, terminal hematuria, penile pain, recurrent urinary tract infection, and acute retention. Complications include obstruction, hydronephrosis, recurrent infection, bladder mucosal ulceration, fistula, and rarely squamous cell carcinoma in chronically irritated bladders; common comorbidities are BPH, neurogenic bladder, spinal cord injury, diabetes, dehydration, and chronic bacteriuria. Diagnosis relies on symptoms, urinalysis with pH/crystals/hematuria, urine culture, stone analysis, metabolic evaluation, cystoscopy, and imaging with ultrasound, KUB radiography for radiopaque stones, or noncontrast CT for confirmation. Name: Cancer of Bladder
Description: Urinary bladder neoplasms are predominantly urothelial carcinomas arising from the bladder mucosa, biologically heterogeneous and classically divided into non-muscle-invasive papillary tumors, carcinoma in situ, muscle-invasive disease, and less common variant histologies such as squamous, adenocarcinoma, micropapillary, plasmacytoid, and small-cell neuroendocrine tumors. Common molecular alterations include FGFR3, TERT promoter, PIK3CA, HRAS, KDM6A, and STAG2 mutations in low-grade papillary tumors, and TP53, RB1, CDKN2A loss, ERBB2/HER2 amplification, PTEN loss, and defects in DNA damage repair genes such as ERCC2, ATM, BRCA1/2, and MSH2 in aggressive disease; Lynch syndrome and rare hereditary retinoblastoma-related predisposition illustrate germline contributions, although most cases are sporadic. Key pathways involve RTK-RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, p53/RB cell-cycle control, chromatin remodeling, angiogenesis via VEGF, and immune evasion through PD-1/PD-L1 signaling. Typical presentation includes painless gross or microscopic hematuria, irritative voiding symptoms, dysuria, frequency, urgency, pelvic pain, recurrent urinary infection, hydronephrosis, or symptoms from nodal or distant metastases. Diagnosis relies on cystoscopy with transurethral resection and histopathology for grade and stage, urine cytology, adjunct urinary biomarkers in selected settings, and CT or MR urography plus cross-sectional staging imaging; muscle invasion and nodal status determine management. Standard therapies include intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, which induces local antitumor immune activation; cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy, which forms DNA cross-links; pembrolizumab or nivolumab, which block PD-1-mediated immune suppression; enfortumab vedotin, a nectin-4-directed antibody-drug conjugate delivering microtubule toxin MMAE; and erdafitinib, an FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor for susceptible tumors. Important comorbidities and complications include tobacco exposure, occupational aromatic amine exposure, chronic cystitis or schistosomiasis, upper tract urothelial carcinoma, obstruction, bleeding, recurrence, progression, and metastatic spread to lymph nodes, bone, liver, and lung

Name: Urinary Bladder, Neurogenic
Description: Neurogenic bladder is a functional disorder of urine storage and voiding caused by impaired central or peripheral neural control of the lower urinary tract, most often from spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, stroke, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, cauda equina lesions, or congenital neural tube defects such as spina bifida. It is not usually a primary Mendelian bladder disease, but genetic contributors are recognized through the underlying neurologic disorders, including LRRK2, SNCA, and PARK2 in parkinsonism, SOD1 and C9orf72 in motor neuron disease, and HLA-DRB1-linked susceptibility in multiple sclerosis; congenital syndromic forms may accompany MEN2B due to RET mutations or hereditary neuropathies such as PMP22-related Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Pathobiology centers on disrupted pontine micturition center–sacral reflex circuitry, altered parasympathetic cholinergic M3 signaling, sympathetic beta3-adrenergic and alpha1-adrenergic pathways, and sensory afferent mediators including ATP, TRPV1, and NGF, leading to detrusor overactivity, areflexia, or detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia. Clinical phenotypes include overactive/spastic suprasacral bladder and underactive/flaccid sacral or peripheral bladder, presenting with urgency, frequency, urge or overflow incontinence, hesitancy, weak stream, retention, elevated post-void residual, recurrent urinary tract infection, and autonomic dysreflexia in high spinal lesions. Major complications include vesicoureteral reflux, hydronephrosis, nephrolithiasis, renal insufficiency, bladder trabeculation, and upper tract damage. Treatment commonly includes antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin or tolterodine, which inhibit M3-mediated detrusor contraction; mirabegron, a beta3-adrenergic agonist that enhances storage by relaxing detrusor smooth muscle; alpha1-blockers such as tamsulosin to reduce outlet resistance; and intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA, which blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release. Name: Blast Crisis
Description: Blast crisis, the terminal transformation phase of chronic myeloid leukemia, is an aggressive myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by progression from chronic or accelerated phase to acute leukemia, usually when blasts comprise at least 20% of blood or marrow cells or when extramedullary blast proliferation develops; it is most often driven by the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) creating BCR::ABL1, with additional genetic lesions such as TP53, RUNX1, IKZF1, ASXL1, TET2, WT1, BCOR, and RAS-pathway mutations, ABL1 kinase-domain mutations including T315I, and cytogenetic evolution such as a second Ph chromosome, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q, or trisomy 19. Central signaling abnormalities include constitutive ABL1 tyrosine kinase activity with activation of JAK/STAT, RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, SRC-family kinases, MYC, and antiapoptotic programs. Blast crisis may be myeloid, lymphoid, or mixed phenotype, with myeloid disease predominating. Clinical features resemble acute leukemia and include fever, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, pallor, bruising or bleeding, infections, bone pain, marked leukocytosis or cytopenias, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and occasional CNS or other extramedullary involvement. Major complications include severe infection, hemorrhage, leukostasis, thrombosis, tumor lysis, marrow failure, and transformation-associated organ infiltration; comorbid hyperuricemia and treatment-related myelosuppression are common. It is generally acquired rather than inherited, although rare predisposition variants affecting DNA repair or hematopoietic regulation may influence risk. Diagnosis requires CBC and smear, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy with blast count, flow cytometry immunophenotyping, conventional cytogenetics, FISH for BCR::ABL1, quantitative RT-PCR transcript monitoring, and mutation testing for ABL1 and cooperating genes. Name: Blastomycosis
Description: Blastomycosis (MeSH D001759) is a systemic pyogranulomatous mycosis caused predominantly by the thermally dimorphic fungi Blastomyces dermatitidis and Blastomyces gilchristii, with less common disease from related species, acquired by inhalation of conidia from endemic environmental sources rather than by Mendelian inheritance; host genetic susceptibility is incompletely defined but appears to involve innate and cell-mediated immune determinants, with representative associations in pathways containing Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, Toll-like receptors, IL-12/IFN-γ, TNF-α, and Th1/Th17 cytokines such as IL-17, while fungal virulence proteins including BAD1 promote adhesion and immune evasion. The dominant molecular pathology reflects alveolar macrophage and neutrophil recognition of fungal cell-wall components through pattern-recognition receptors, activation of NF-κB and inflammasome-linked inflammatory signaling, and granulomatous or suppurative tissue responses. Clinical syndromes include acute or chronic pulmonary blastomycosis and disseminated disease involving skin, bone, genitourinary tract, and central nervous system; symptoms commonly include fever, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, night sweats, verrucous or ulcerative skin lesions, osteoarticular pain, and prostatitis or epididymo-orchitis. Major comorbidities and risk factors include immunosuppression, solid-organ transplantation, corticosteroid exposure, HIV infection, diabetes, chronic lung disease, and pregnancy, with complications such as acute respiratory distress syndrome, respiratory failure, osteomyelitis, CNS abscess or meningitis, and relapse. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure history and clinical-radiographic findings with confirmation by direct microscopy or histopathology showing broad-based budding yeasts, fungal culture, antigen detection in urine or serum with cross-reactivity limitations, serology of lesser sensitivity, and molecular assays where available. Standard therapy includes itraconazole, which inhibits fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis, amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores, and voriconazole or posaconazole, triazoles that also inhibit 14α-demethylase, with amphotericin B favored for severe, disseminated, pregnant, or CNS disease.

Name: Blepharoconjunctivitis
Description: Blepharoconjunctivitis (UMLS C0005743) is an inflammatory disorder involving both the eyelid margins and conjunctiva, most often chronic and multifactorial, arising from anterior blepharitis due to staphylococcal colonization or seborrhea, or posterior blepharitis driven by meibomian gland dysfunction; common subtypes include staphylococcal, seborrheic, meibomian gland dysfunction–associated, allergic, rosacea-associated, and angular forms. Typical findings are red, irritated, burning, gritty, pruritic eyes with tearing, photophobia, crusting of lashes, collarettes, conjunctival injection, lid margin telangiectasia, meibomian plugging, frothy tear film, and fluctuating vision, while complications include recurrent chalazia, hordeola, dry eye, punctate keratopathy, marginal keratitis, corneal ulceration, scarring, and rarely visual impairment. Pathobiology involves dysregulated innate immunity and tear-film instability, with bacterial lipases, Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, matrix metalloproteinases, and altered meibum composition promoting ocular-surface inflammation; in rosacea-associated disease, cathelicidin LL-37 processing, Demodex-related inflammation, and VEGF-linked vascular changes may contribute. No single causative gene is established for most cases, which are usually non-Mendelian, but genetic susceptibility is inferred in syndromic or associated conditions, including filaggrin variants in atopy, cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator mutations affecting meibomian secretions, and rosacea-related immune pathway variation; inheritance therefore depends on the underlying disorder rather than blepharoconjunctivitis itself. Treatment commonly combines lid hygiene with topical azithromycin, which suppresses bacterial protein synthesis and has anti-inflammatory effects; erythromycin or bacitracin ointment, which inhibit bacterial translation or cell-wall synthesis; doxycycline, which inhibits 30S ribosomal function and reduces meibomian inflammation and matrix metalloproteinases; and short courses of topical corticosteroids such as loteprednol, which inhibit phospholipase A2-mediated inflammatory cascades. Comorbidities include acne rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, atopy, psoriasis, dry eye disease, and Demodex infestation

Name: Boutonneuse Fever
Description: Boutonneuse fever (Mediterranean spotted fever) is an acute zoonotic tick-borne rickettsiosis caused predominantly by Rickettsia conorii conorii, with related spotted-fever group rickettsiae producing closely related subtypes such as Israeli spotted fever and Astrakhan fever; it is an infectious, non-Mendelian disease with no established host inheritance pattern, although severity may be influenced by host immune-response variation in genes regulating interferon, TNF, TLR4/NF-κB, and endothelial inflammatory signaling. The organism invades vascular endothelial cells through outer-membrane proteins including OmpA and OmpB and uses host actin-polymerization machinery via RickA/Arp2/3, driving NF-κB-, MAPK-, and cytokine-mediated inflammation, vasculitis, and increased vascular permeability. Typical features are abrupt fever, headache, myalgia, malaise, a maculopapular or petechial rash often involving palms and soles, and a dark inoculation eschar (tache noire); laboratory findings may include thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and mild transaminitis. Complications arise from disseminated vasculitis and include encephalitis, pneumonitis, acute kidney injury, myocarditis, shock, purpura fulminans, and multiorgan failure, with worse outcomes in older adults, diabetes, alcoholism, G6PD deficiency, immunosuppression, and delayed therapy. Diagnosis is primarily clinical-epidemiologic in a patient with compatible illness after tick exposure in an endemic area, supported by serology with indirect immunofluorescence showing paired acute/convalescent rising titers, PCR on eschar swab, biopsy, or blood, and occasionally immunohistochemistry or culture in specialized laboratories. Treatment is centered on doxycycline, which inhibits the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit; alternatives include tetracycline with the same mechanism, chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S peptidyl-transferase center, and azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S subunit and is used especially when tetracyclines are unsuitable.

Name: Brain Abscess
Description: Brain abscess (UMLS C0006105) is a focal, life-threatening intracerebral infection characterized by localized cerebritis that evolves into a pus-filled cavity surrounded by a vascularized capsule, most often arising from contiguous spread from otitis, mastoiditis, sinusitis, dental infection, or hematogenous seeding from endocarditis or pulmonary infection, and less often after trauma or neurosurgery. It is not a classic inherited disease, but host genetic susceptibility to pyogenic infection has been linked to defects in innate and adaptive immunity, including chronic granulomatous disease genes CYBB, CYBA, NCF1 and NCF2 affecting the NADPH oxidase complex, and rarer IL12RB1 or TLR pathway defects; key inflammatory proteins include TNF, IL1B, IL6, CXCL8, MMPs, complement, and neutrophil oxidative burst machinery. Pathobiology centers on blood-brain barrier disruption, microglial and astrocytic activation, leukocyte recruitment, and cytokine signaling through TLR/NF-kB and JAK/STAT pathways, with angiogenesis and fibroblast activation contributing to capsule formation. Typical symptoms are headache, fever, focal neurologic deficits, altered mental status, seizures, nausea, papilledema, and signs of raised intracranial pressure, while subtypes are classified by route of infection, stage, and location. Common pathogens include streptococci, anaerobes, Staphylococcus aureus, gram-negative bacilli, and in immunocompromised hosts Nocardia, Aspergillus, Toxoplasma gondii, or fungi. Major comorbidities and complications include congenital cyanotic heart disease, diabetes, HIV/immunosuppression, malignancy, ventriculitis, meningitis, intraventricular rupture, hydrocephalus, herniation, and persistent epilepsy. Diagnosis relies on contrast-enhanced MRI or CT showing ring-enhancing lesions with diffusion restriction, microbiologic evaluation of aspirate or blood cultures, inflammatory markers, and search for a primary focus; lumbar puncture is often avoided when mass effect is present. Name: Edema, Cerebral
Description: Brain edema is a pathophysiologic state of excess water accumulation within the brain parenchyma that raises intracranial pressure and compromises cerebral perfusion; it is classically subdivided into vasogenic edema from blood-brain barrier disruption, cytotoxic edema from cellular energy failure and ionic pump dysfunction, interstitial edema associated with hydrocephalus, and osmotic edema. Key molecular contributors include aquaporin-4 encoded by AQP4 on astrocytic endfeet, SUR1-TRPM4 channels involving ABCC8 and TRPM4, VEGF-mediated vascular permeability, matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP9, inflammatory cytokines including TNF, IL1B, and IL6, glutamate-NMDA receptor excitotoxicity, Na+/K+-ATPase failure, and hypoxia-inducible and NF-kappaB signaling; representative genetic associations are strongest in monogenic syndromes predisposing to edema, such as cerebral cavernous malformations due to KRIT1, CCM2, or PDCD10, and inherited metabolic or mitochondrial disorders, although most brain edema is acquired rather than inherited. Common causes and comorbidities include ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, traumatic brain injury, brain tumors, CNS infection, hepatic failure with hyperammonemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, hyponatremia, hydrocephalus, high-altitude cerebral edema, and seizures; complications include herniation, coma, ischemia, and death. Patients typically present with headache, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, papilledema, focal deficits, cranial nerve abnormalities, seizures, and Cushing response in severe cases. Treatment commonly includes mannitol, an osmotic diuretic that increases plasma osmolality; hypertonic saline, which draws water from brain tissue and may improve hemodynamics; dexamethasone, which reduces tumor-related vasogenic edema by stabilizing the blood-brain barrier; and condition-specific measures such as acetazolamide in selected settings. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion with urgent CT or MRI demonstrating edema patterns, mass effect, midline shift, or hydrocephalus, plus laboratory evaluation of sodium, osmolality, renal and hepatic function, and cause-directed testing; invasive intracranial pressure monitoring is used in selected severe cases.

Name: Brain Neoplasms
Description: Brain neoplasms comprise a heterogeneous group of primary and metastatic intracranial tumors arising from glial, meningeal, neuronal, embryonal, pituitary, or other CNS-associated cells, ranging from indolent lesions to highly aggressive malignancies; major subtypes include diffuse astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma, ependymoma, medulloblastoma, meningioma, schwannoma, and brain metastases. Their molecular landscape commonly involves alterations in IDH1/IDH2, TP53, ATRX, TERT promoter, EGFR amplification or EGFRvIII, PTEN loss, CDKN2A/B deletion, PDGFRA, BRAF V600E, H3 K27M, 1p/19q codeletion, MGMT promoter methylation, and NF2, with inherited predisposition in syndromes such as neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and APC-associated Turcot syndrome, although most cases are sporadic. Dysregulated signaling often centers on RTK/RAS/RAF/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53, RB cell-cycle, WNT/β-catenin, SHH, Notch, angiogenic VEGF, and epigenetic programs. Typical manifestations include headache, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, cognitive or personality change, aphasia, visual disturbance, gait imbalance, nausea/vomiting from raised intracranial pressure, and endocrine symptoms in sellar tumors. Common complications and comorbidities include cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, epilepsy, neurocognitive decline, endocrinopathies, depression, and treatment-related radionecrosis or myelosuppression. Diagnosis relies on contrast-enhanced MRI, sometimes CT for hemorrhage or calcification, advanced imaging such as perfusion or spectroscopy, histopathology integrated with molecular testing per WHO CNS classification, including immunohistochemistry, FISH, PCR, and next-generation sequencing; CSF cytology is useful in select leptomeningeal or embryonal tumors.
