Name: Brill-Zinsser Disease
Description: Brill-Zinsser disease is a recrudescent, usually milder form of epidemic typhus caused by reactivation of latent Rickettsia prowazekii years to decades after primary infection, rather than a Mendelian genetic disorder, so no human inheritance pattern is recognized and no disease-defining host mutations are established; instead, the key microbial determinants are rickettsial outer-membrane and surface antigens, including OmpB and lipopolysaccharide-associated epitopes used in serologic recognition, with pathobiology centered on endothelial cell invasion, phagosome escape, intracellular replication, and host inflammatory signaling through NF-kB, TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, interferon responses, chemokine-driven leukocyte recruitment, oxidative stress, and vascular injury leading to systemic vasculitis. Clinically, patients typically present with abrupt fever, severe headache, malaise, myalgias, chills, and sometimes a truncal maculopapular rash, with cough, delirium, or hypotension in more severe cases; compared with primary epidemic typhus, neurologic and multisystem involvement are often less intense, but complications can include pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, acute kidney injury, secondary bacterial infection, and, epidemiologically, renewed louse-mediated transmission during outbreaks. The principal subtype distinction is primary epidemic typhus versus recrudescent Brill-Zinsser disease. Diagnosis relies on compatible history, prior typhus exposure, and exclusion of other febrile exanthems, supported by indirect immunofluorescence or other serologic assays showing antibodies to typhus-group rickettsiae, PCR on blood or tissue when available, and occasionally immunohistochemistry; culture is rarely performed because of biosafety constraints. Treatment is centered on doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks bacterial protein synthesis; alternatives include tetracycline, with the same mechanism, chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S peptidyl-transferase activity, and in some settings azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S subunit, alongside supportive care and vector control.

Name: Bronchial Spasm
Description: Bronchial spasm, or acute reversible constriction of bronchial smooth muscle causing airflow limitation, is a clinical manifestation most often seen in asthma, COPD, anaphylaxis, respiratory infection, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, and irritant exposure rather than a single inherited disease entity. It is driven by airway hyperresponsiveness, vagal cholinergic tone, mast-cell and eosinophil activation, and inflammatory pathways involving IgE-FcεRI signaling, histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, TNF, and downstream calcium-dependent smooth-muscle contraction through Gq-PLC-IP3 and Rho kinase pathways; β2-adrenergic signaling via ADCY and cAMP normally promotes relaxation. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and polygenic, with representative associations in ADRB2, IL4, IL13, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, FCER1B, and the leukotriene pathway genes ALOX5 and LTC4S; rare monogenic inheritance is not typical, though familial atopy/asthma predisposition is common. Symptoms and signs include episodic wheeze, dyspnea, chest tightness, cough, prolonged expiration, reduced peak expiratory flow, and in severe attacks tachypnea, hypoxemia, accessory-muscle use, and silent chest. Clinically it may be allergic, nonallergic, exercise-induced, nocturnal, occupational, or medication-triggered, and may occur as mild intermittent episodes or life-threatening status asthmaticus. Common treatments include inhaled short-acting β2-agonists such as albuterol, which increase cAMP-mediated bronchodilation; antimuscarinics such as ipratropium or tiotropium, which block M3 receptor-mediated vagal bronchoconstriction; and corticosteroids such as prednisone or inhaled budesonide, which suppress eosinophilic and cytokine-driven airway inflammation; leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast are also used. Important comorbidities and complications include allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, GERD, obesity, atopic dermatitis, anxiety, respiratory failure, mucus plugging, and pneumothorax. Name: Bronchiectasis
Description: Bronchiectasis is a chronic suppurative airway disease defined by irreversible dilatation and distortion of medium-sized bronchi due to a vicious cycle of impaired mucociliary clearance, persistent infection, neutrophilic inflammation, and airway-wall destruction. It may be focal or diffuse and morphologically cylindrical, varicose, or cystic; major etiologic subtypes include post-infectious, cystic fibrosis–related, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency-associated, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis–associated, traction bronchiectasis, aspiration-related, and non-CF idiopathic disease. Genetic contributors are best established in CFTR mutations causing cystic fibrosis, DNAH5, DNAI1, CCDC39, and CCDC40 variants in primary ciliary dyskinesia, and immunologic defects such as TNFRSF13B/TACI or BTK in selected antibody deficiencies; SERPINA1 mutations may contribute when emphysema coexists. Pathobiology centers on CFTR-mediated ion transport, ciliary assembly and dynein-arm function, TLR/NF-κB and inflammasome signaling, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinases, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-α, IL-1β, and chronic colonization by organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Haemophilus influenzae, and nontuberculous mycobacteria. Typical manifestations are chronic daily productive cough, mucopurulent sputum, recurrent infective exacerbations, dyspnea, wheeze, fatigue, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, crackles, rhonchi, and sometimes digital clubbing. Common comorbidities and complications include COPD, asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, GERD, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, infertility in ciliopathies, massive hemoptysis, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, and cor pulmonale. Diagnosis is established primarily by high-resolution chest CT showing bronchial dilatation, lack of tapering, and bronchi visible near the pleura, supported by sputum microbiology, spirometry, CBC and inflammatory markers, serum immunoglobulins, total IgE and Aspergillus testing, sweat chloride or CFTR genotyping, nasal nitric oxide and ciliary studies, and bronchoscopy when obstruction is suspected. Name: Bronchitis
Description: Bronchitis is an inflammatory disorder of the bronchial airways, most often acute and infectious, usually viral, but also chronic when productive cough persists for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, typically as part of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; clinical hallmarks include cough, sputum production, wheeze, rhonchi, chest discomfort, dyspnea, and sometimes fever, with acute forms occasionally progressing to secondary bacterial infection or pneumonia and chronic disease complicated by airflow limitation, recurrent exacerbations, pulmonary hypertension, and cor pulmonale. Its biology is dominated by innate immune and mucosal injury pathways, including epithelial activation of NF-kB, MAPK, and JAK/STAT signaling, increased IL-1B, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF, TGF-beta, EGFR, and mucin genes such as MUC5AC, with neutrophils, macrophages, oxidative stress, protease-antiprotease imbalance involving MMP9 and alpha-1 antitrypsin, and impaired ciliary clearance contributing to airway remodeling. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, influenced by variants affecting host defense and COPD risk, with representative examples including SERPINA1 mutations causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, GSTM1/GSTP1 and TNF polymorphisms, and mucociliary disorders such as CFTR-related cystic fibrosis or primary ciliary dyskinesia genes that predispose to recurrent bronchitic illness. Common treatments include short-acting beta2-agonists such as albuterol, which relax bronchial smooth muscle via beta2-adrenergic receptor-mediated cyclic AMP elevation; antimuscarinics such as ipratropium, which block muscarinic M3-mediated bronchoconstriction; inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide, which suppress NF-kB-driven airway inflammation; and, when bacterial infection or COPD exacerbation is suspected, antibiotics such as azithromycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit. Important comorbidities include asthma, COPD, smoking-related cardiovascular disease, sinusitis, gastroesophageal reflux, and bronchiectasis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and examination, supported when indicated by pulse oximetry, chest radiography to exclude pneumonia, sputum testing in selected cases, and spirometry showing obstructive physiology in chronic bronchitis.

Name: Brucellosis
Description: Brucellosis (MeSH D002006) is a zoonotic, non-Mendelian infectious disease caused by intracellular Gram-negative coccobacilli of the genus Brucella, chiefly B. melitensis, B. abortus, B. suis, and B. canis, and it presents as acute, subacute, chronic, localized, or relapsing disease. Human susceptibility and severity are influenced by host immune genes rather than a single causative mutation; representative associations include polymorphisms in SLC11A1/NRAMP1, TLR2, TLR4, TLR9, NOD2, IFNG, TNF, IL10, IL12B, and HLA class II loci, while key proteins include Brucella lipopolysaccharide, outer membrane proteins, and the VirB type IV secretion system that promote macrophage survival. Pathogenesis centers on innate immune recognition and intracellular persistence, with TLR-NF-κB, JAK/STAT, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-12/Th1, inflammasome, and apoptotic/autophagic pathways shaping granulomatous inflammation and bacterial control. Typical manifestations are undulating fever, night sweats, malaise, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, arthralgia, myalgia, back pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and elevated inflammatory markers; focal disease may involve spondylitis, sacroiliitis, arthritis, epididymo-orchitis, hepatitis, neurobrucellosis, or endocarditis, the latter being the major cause of mortality. Common complications and comorbid associations include osteoarticular disease, chronic fatigue-like syndromes, depression, pregnancy loss, and coincident livestock exposure-related occupational illness. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure history and clinical syndrome plus blood or bone marrow culture, serology such as Rose Bengal, standard tube agglutination, Coombs, or ELISA for Brucella IgM/IgG, and PCR where available; imaging supports focal complications. Treatment typically combines doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, with rifampin, an RNA polymerase inhibitor, or streptomycin/gentamicin, aminoglycosides that irreversibly inhibit 30S translation; alternatives include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks folate synthesis, often in

Name: Bruxism
Description: Bruxism (UMLS C0006325) is a multifactorial jaw-muscle activity disorder characterized by repetitive clenching or grinding of the teeth and/or mandibular bracing or thrusting, occurring as awake bruxism or sleep bruxism, with primary idiopathic and secondary forms linked to medications, neurologic disease, or sleep-disordered breathing. It is not a classic Mendelian disease, but genetic susceptibility is supported by familial aggregation and candidate associations involving dopaminergic, serotonergic, and catecholaminergic genes and proteins, including DRD2, DRD3, SLC6A4, HTR2A, COMT, and occasionally CLOCK-related circadian regulators, consistent with implicated pathways in central dopamine signaling, serotonin modulation, arousal-autonomic activation, stress-response circuits, and sleep microarousal mechanisms involving basal ganglia, trigeminal motor nuclei, and masticatory muscle activity. Typical manifestations include tooth wear, fractured restorations, jaw-muscle pain or fatigue, morning headaches, masseter hypertrophy, temporomandibular joint pain or clicking, and disturbed sleep or bed-partner reports of grinding; complications include severe dental attrition, cracked teeth, temporomandibular disorders, myofascial pain, and reduced oral-health quality of life. Common comorbidities include anxiety, depression, stress-related disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, gastroesophageal reflux, movement disorders such as Parkinson disease, and stimulant or SSRI exposure. Diagnosis is clinical and graded as possible, probable, or definite using self-report/partner report, oral and facial examination for wear facets and muscle tenderness, questionnaires, electromyography, and for sleep bruxism the reference standard of polysomnography with audio-video and rhythmic masticatory muscle activity recording; imaging is used mainly to assess dental or TMJ damage. Treatment is symptomatic and cause-directed: occlusal splints protect dentition; clonazepam, a GABAA-positive allosteric modulator, may reduce sleep-related motor activity; botulinum toxin type A inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release to weaken overactive masseter/temporalis muscles; and clonidine, an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, can attenuate sympathetic arousal, while selected cases may use buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist, especially for SSRI-associated bruxism.

Name: Burkitt Lymphoma
Description: Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive, mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized biologically by deregulation of MYC, most often through t(8;14)(q24;q32) involving IGH, or less commonly t(2;8) or t(8;22) involving IGK or IGL; cooperating alterations can include ID3, TCF3, CCND3, TP53, and occasionally BCL6 pathway abnormalities, with tumor cells expressing surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, BCL6, and a nearly 100% Ki-67 proliferation index. Major pathogenic pathways include MYC-driven cell-cycle progression and metabolic reprogramming, tonic B-cell receptor/PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling, cyclin D3–CDK activity, and apoptosis dysregulation; endemic cases are strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus, while immunodeficiency-associated disease may arise in HIV or post-transplant settings. Clinically, it presents with rapidly enlarging extranodal or nodal masses and very short doubling time: endemic Burkitt lymphoma often involves the jaw or facial bones, sporadic disease more often affects the ileocecal region with abdominal pain, distension, bowel obstruction, or intussusception, and all forms may show fever, weight loss, night sweats, bulky adenopathy, bone marrow involvement, or central nervous system spread. Subtypes include endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated Burkitt lymphoma. It is usually sporadic rather than inherited, although constitutional cancer-predisposition syndromes such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome from germline TP53 variants can increase risk. Diagnosis rests on excisional biopsy with diffuse monomorphic medium-sized cells, starry-sky histology, immunophenotyping, and demonstration of MYC rearrangement by FISH or conventional cytogenetics, with flow cytometry, EBV testing, bone marrow and cerebrospinal fluid evaluation, PET/CT, LDH, uric acid, and renal function assessment for staging and tumor lysis risk. Treatment uses intensive short-course multiagent chemotherapy such as cyclophosphamide, an alkylating DNA cross-linker; doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor and free-radical generator; vincristine, a microtubule polymerization inhibitor; methotrexate, a folate antagonist; cytarabine, a DNA polymerase

Name: Burns
Description: Burns are acute thermal, chemical, electrical, or radiation-induced injuries to skin and sometimes deeper tissues, classified by depth as superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness, and by extent and mechanism including inhalation injury; they are primarily acquired rather than inherited, although host genetic variation can influence susceptibility to hypertrophic scarring, infection, and inflammation, with representative associations reported for TGFB1, MMP1, COL1A1, HLA loci, and cytokine genes such as TNF, IL6, and IL10, while proteins central to pathobiology include TGF-β1, VEGF, NF-κB, p53, HSP70, collagen, and matrix metalloproteinases. Key pathways include damage-associated molecular pattern signaling through TLRs, NF-κB-driven cytokine cascades, JAK/STAT, MAPK, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, oxidative-stress responses, coagulation-complement pathways, angiogenesis, and fibroblast/myofibroblast TGF-β/SMAD signaling underlying wound repair and fibrosis. Typical findings are pain, erythema, blistering, edema, eschar, impaired sensation in deep burns, fluid loss, and systemic inflammatory response, with complications including hypovolemic shock, inhalation injury, sepsis, acute kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, contractures, hypertrophic scars, chronic pain, and psychological morbidity; common comorbidities that worsen outcome include diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, malnutrition, and chronic lung disease. Diagnosis is clinical, based on mechanism, burn depth, and total body surface area estimation by the Rule of Nines or Lund-Browder chart, supplemented as needed by bronchoscopy or carboxyhemoglobin for smoke inhalation, laboratory monitoring, wound cultures when infection is suspected, and occasionally laser Doppler or indocyanine-green perfusion assessment for depth. Treatment centers on resuscitation and wound care, with representative drugs including silver sulfadiazine, which releases silver ions and inhibits bacterial folate metabolism; mafenide acetate, a sulfonamide that penetrates eschar and inhibits carbonic anhydrase-sensitive bacterial growth; bacitracin, which blocks cell-wall synthesis by interfering with bactoprenol recycling; opioids such as morphine, a μ-opioid receptor agonist for analgesia; and tetanus toxoid for immunoprophylaxis

Name: Bursitis
Description: Bursitis (MeSH D002062) is a localized inflammatory disorder of a synovial bursa, most often affecting the subacromial, olecranon, prepatellar, trochanteric, and pes anserine bursae, and may be acute traumatic, chronic repetitive/occupational, crystal-induced, inflammatory, or septic. Its biology is driven largely by innate immune and stromal-cell responses rather than a single causative gene, with increased expression of inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL1B, IL6, PTGS2/COX-2, CXCL8, MMPs, and VEGF in inflamed bursal tissue or fluid; key pathways include NF-kappaB, MAPK, arachidonic acid–prostaglandin signaling, NLRP3 inflammasome activation in crystal disease, and in some chronic shoulder bursitides, TGF-beta–mediated fibrosis and matrix remodeling. Inheritance is usually non-Mendelian and indirect, reflecting genetic susceptibility to associated disorders rather than primary bursitis itself; representative examples include HLA-B27 in spondyloarthritis, HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles and PTPN22 in rheumatoid arthritis, and MEFV or NLRP3 variants in autoinflammatory states that can include periarticular inflammation. Patients typically present with focal pain, swelling, tenderness, warmth, reduced range of motion, and pain with pressure or movement; septic bursitis more often causes erythema, marked warmth, fever, and purulent aspirate. Common comorbidities include gout, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, rheumatoid arthritis, seronegative spondyloarthropathies, diabetes, obesity, osteoarthritis, tendon disorders, and skin trauma, while complications include chronic pain, recurrence, calcification, fibrosis, restricted motion, and spread of infection. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by ultrasonography or MRI when needed; aspiration with cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis is central when infection or crystal bursitis is suspected, and inflammatory markers or serologies are adjunctive. Name: Candidiasis
Description: Candidiasis (MeSH D002177) is an opportunistic fungal infection caused predominantly by Candida albicans, but also by C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, and C. auris, ranging from superficial mucocutaneous disease to invasive candidemia and deep-organ candidiasis. Typical manifestations include oral thrush with white plaques, angular cheilitis, esophagitis with odynophagia, vulvovaginitis with pruritus and discharge, intertrigo, paronychia, and in invasive disease fever, sepsis, endophthalmitis, hepatosplenic lesions, and multiorgan dysfunction. Major host defense pathways involve epithelial and myeloid recognition through Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2/TLR4, CARD9, SYK, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, complement, neutrophil oxidative killing, and IL-17/IL-22-mediated mucosal immunity; representative human susceptibility genes include AIRE in autoimmune polyendocrinopathy with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, STAT1 gain-of-function, IL17F, IL17RA, ACT1/TRAF3IP2, CARD9, CLEC7A, and defects affecting Th17 differentiation such as RORC, with inheritance varying by disorder and including autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked patterns. Candida virulence factors include adhesins and biofilm-related proteins such as ALS3, HWP1, SAP proteases, and the hypha-associated toxin candidalysin encoded by ECE1. Common comorbidities and risk states include diabetes mellitus, HIV/AIDS, neutropenia, pregnancy, broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, corticosteroid or biologic immunosuppression, central venous catheters, intensive care, and malignancy; complications include candidemia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, renal microabscesses, and dissemination. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical findings plus microscopy with budding yeast or pseudohyphae, KOH prep, fungal culture, blood culture for invasive disease, histopathology, species identification by chromogenic media or MALDI-TOF, and adjunctive β-D-glucan or PCR assays. Treatment commonly includes fluconazole, which inhibits fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; echinocandins

Name: Candidiasis, Cutaneous
Description: Cutaneous candidiasis is a superficial to occasionally chronic mucocutaneous fungal infection of keratinized and intertriginous skin caused predominantly by Candida albicans, but also C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, and other Candida spp., producing erythematous, macerated, pruritic or burning plaques with satellite papules or pustules in skin folds, diaper area, periungual skin, and occasionally diffuse involvement in chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis; major subtypes include intertrigo, diaper dermatitis, paronychia/onychomycosis, perianal candidiasis, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Host defense depends on epithelial barrier integrity and innate/adaptive antifungal immunity, especially pattern-recognition via Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, TLR2/TLR4, IL-17RA/IL-17F, ACT1/TRAF3IP2, STAT1, STAT3, AIRE, and Th17-axis cytokines IL-17 and IL-22, while fungal adhesion, hyphal transition, and biofilm formation involve adhesins and secreted aspartyl proteinases; representative genetic predisposition includes autosomal recessive CARD9 or IL17RA deficiency, CLEC7A variants, autosomal dominant gain-of-function STAT1 mutations, AIRE mutations in APECED, and hyper-IgE syndromes with STAT3 defects, which underlie familial or syndromic chronic/recurrent disease. Common comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, obesity, occlusion, hyperhidrosis, pregnancy, infancy, immunosuppression including HIV, corticosteroid exposure, antibiotic use, malignancy, and primary immunodeficiency, with complications such as recurrent infection, fissuring, secondary bacterial superinfection, nail dystrophy, and disseminated candidiasis in severely immunocompromised hosts. Diagnosis is usually clinical and supported by potassium hydroxide microscopy showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae, fungal culture, periodic acid-Schiff histopathology when needed, and in refractory or early-onset recurrent cases by HIV/endocrine evaluation and genetic or immunologic testing. Treatment typically includes topical azoles such as clotrimazole or miconazole, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; nystatin, which binds ergosterol and disrupts membrane permeability; and for extensive or refractory disease

Name: Candidiasis, Oral
Description: Oral candidiasis is a mucosal fungal infection, usually caused by Candida albicans, that ranges from superficial commensal overgrowth to invasive mucosal disease and classically presents as pseudomembranous thrush with removable white plaques, erythematous or atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, burning mouth, dysgeusia, soreness, and dysphagia when extension occurs. Major clinical subtypes include pseudomembranous, erythematous/atrophic, hyperplastic, denture-associated stomatitis, and angular cheilitis. Pathobiology reflects fungal adhesion, hyphal transition, and biofilm formation, interacting with host epithelial and innate immune pathways centered on pattern-recognition receptors and IL-17 immunity, including Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, Th17 cytokines IL17A, IL17F, IL22, and STAT3 signaling; genetic susceptibility is best established in chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and related syndromes, with variants in AIRE, STAT1 gain-of-function, STAT3, CARD9, CLEC7A, IL17RA, IL17RC, ACT1/TRAF3IP2, and DECTIN-pathway components predisposing to persistent or recurrent oral disease, typically in Mendelian or syndromic patterns rather than classic inheritance for routine thrush. Important comorbidities include HIV/AIDS, diabetes mellitus, xerostomia, denture use, inhaled corticosteroids, broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, chemotherapy, malnutrition, extremes of age, and immunodeficiency; complications include recurrent infection, pain with poor oral intake, esophageal candidiasis, and rarely disseminated candidiasis in profoundly immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported when needed by potassium hydroxide preparation, Gram stain or cytology showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae, fungal culture, biopsy for chronic hyperplastic lesions to exclude dysplasia, and evaluation for predisposing systemic disease. Treatment commonly uses topical nystatin, a polyene that binds ergosterol; clotrimazole, an azole inhibiting fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase; and systemic fluconazole, which has the same azole target and is preferred for moderate, recurrent, or refractory disease, while miconazole or itraconazole are alternatives.

Name: Vaginitis, Monilial
Description: Vulvovaginal candidiasis is a common mucosal fungal infection, usually caused by Candida albicans but also by non-albicans species such as C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, and C. krusei, presenting with vulvar pruritus, burning, soreness, dyspareunia, dysuria, and thick adherent vaginal discharge with erythema and edema; complicated disease includes severe infection, recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, non-albicans infection, or disease in pregnancy or immunocompromised hosts. Pathogenesis reflects fungal adhesion and hyphal transformation mediated by adhesins and virulence proteins such as ALS family proteins, HWP1, SAP proteases, and candidalysin encoded by ECE1, interacting with host innate immune pathways involving TLR2/TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, MyD88, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1β, IL-17/Th17 signaling, and epithelial neutrophil recruitment; genetic susceptibility is usually complex rather than Mendelian, but recurrent disease has been associated with variants in CLEC7A, CARD9, TLR2, TLR4, NLRP3, IL17A, IL17F, IL17RA, and mannose-binding lectin gene MBL2, while rare IL-17 pathway defects predispose to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use, estrogen exposure, HIV or other immunosuppression, obesity, and atopy; complications include recurrent infection, fissuring, excoriation, secondary bacterial infection, and impaired quality of life. Diagnosis is based on compatible symptoms plus demonstration of yeast, pseudohyphae, or hyphae by saline or 10 percent KOH microscopy, acidic to normal vaginal pH usually below 4.5, culture or speciation for recurrent or refractory cases, and increasingly nucleic acid amplification tests. Standard treatment includes azoles such as fluconazole, clotrimazole, and miconazole, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase to impair ergosterol synthesis, and for selected refractory or non-albicans cases boric acid, which exerts direct fungistatic and fungicidal intravaginal activity.

Name: Cancer of Colon
Description: Colonic neoplasms are benign or malignant epithelial, neuroendocrine, mesenchymal, or lymphoid tumors of the colon, most commonly adenomatous polyps and colorectal adenocarcinoma, arising through the conventional adenoma-carcinoma sequence or the serrated pathway. Key genetic alterations include APC loss with WNT/beta-catenin activation, KRAS or NRAS mutations, TP53 inactivation, SMAD4/TGF-beta pathway disruption, PIK3CA activation, and mismatch-repair deficiency involving MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM, causing microsatellite instability; BRAF V600E is characteristic of many serrated lesions, whereas ERBB2 amplification and NTRK fusions occur in subsets. Major pathways implicated are WNT, EGFR-RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, TGF-beta, p53, VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, and immune-checkpoint signaling in MSI-high tumors. Hereditary predisposition is important, especially autosomal dominant familial adenomatous polyposis due to APC mutations and Lynch syndrome due to germline mismatch-repair defects, with additional risk in MUTYH-associated polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and juvenile polyposis. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with occult or overt rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, change in bowel habits, abdominal pain, weight loss, obstruction, perforation, or metastatic disease, particularly to liver and lung; comorbidities and complications include inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, diabetes, thrombosis, and treatment-related neuropathy or myelosuppression. Diagnosis relies on colonoscopy with biopsy and histopathology, polypectomy when feasible, TNM staging by CT or MRI, carcinoembryonic antigen monitoring, and molecular testing for MMR/MSI status and RAS, BRAF, HER2, or NTRK alterations to guide therapy. Treatment commonly includes 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine, which inhibit thymidylate synthase, oxaliplatin, a DNA crosslinking platinum, irinotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor, and selected biologics such as bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF antibody, cetuximab or panitumumab, anti-EGFR antibodies for RAS wild-type disease, and pembroliz

Name: Malignant neoplasm of thyroid
Description: Malignant neoplasm of the thyroid comprises a heterogeneous group of epithelial and neuroendocrine cancers, principally papillary thyroid carcinoma, follicular thyroid carcinoma, poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma, anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, and medullary thyroid carcinoma, arising from follicular cells except for medullary tumors, which derive from parafollicular C cells. Key molecular drivers include BRAF V600E, RAS mutations, RET/PTC rearrangements, NTRK and ALK fusions, TERT promoter mutations, TP53 alterations in aggressive/anaplastic disease, and RET activating mutations in hereditary and sporadic medullary carcinoma; relevant proteins include MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway components, RET tyrosine kinase, VEGFR, EGFR, and sodium-iodide symporter. These tumors commonly signal through MAPK and PI3K cascades, with dysregulated cell-cycle control, angiogenesis, dedifferentiation, and impaired iodine handling. Treatment depends on subtype and stage and commonly includes radioactive iodine, which exploits iodide uptake in differentiated tumors; levothyroxine for TSH suppression; and targeted agents such as sorafenib and lenvatinib, multikinase inhibitors of VEGFR and other kinases, vandetanib and cabozantinib for medullary disease targeting RET/VEGFR/MET, and selective RET inhibitors such as selpercatinib or pralsetinib. Patients often present with a thyroid nodule, cervical lymphadenopathy, hoarseness, dysphagia, neck pain, airway symptoms, or incidentally detected lesions, while medullary carcinoma may cause diarrhea or flushing via calcitonin-related secretion. Important complications and comorbidities include local invasion, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, hypocalcemia after surgery, pulmonary or osseous metastases, and association with multinodular goiter, autoimmune thyroid disease, MEN2 syndrome, or prior neck irradiation. Inheritance is usually sporadic, but germline RET mutations underlie MEN2-associated medullary carcinoma; rarer predisposition involves PTEN hamartoma syndrome, DICER1, APC/FAP, or CHEK2. Diagnosis relies on ultrasound risk stratification, fine-needle aspiration cytology using Bethesda criteria, serum TSH, calcitonin and CEA for suspected medullary carcinoma, thyroglobulin in surveillance, molecular testing for actionable alterations

Name: Basal Cell Cancer
Description: Basal cell cancer, or basal cell carcinoma, is the most common human malignancy and a slow-growing keratinocyte cancer arising from basal cells of the epidermis or follicular structures, driven predominantly by aberrant Hedgehog signaling; in sporadic tumors this most often reflects UV-induced loss-of-function mutations in PTCH1 or SUFU or activating mutations in SMO, with additional recurrent alterations in TP53, TERT promoter, MYCN, PPP6C, and CDKN2A, and overexpression of GLI transcription factors and antiapoptotic proteins such as BCL2. Major pathway biology centers on PTCH1-SMO-GLI signaling, with crosstalk involving p53, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, EGFR/RAS/MAPK, WNT, and DNA damage response pathways. Clinically, lesions usually present on chronically sun-exposed skin as pearly or translucent papules or nodules with rolled borders, arborizing telangiectasia, ulceration, bleeding, crusting, or superficial erythematous scaly plaques; subtypes include nodular, superficial, infiltrative, micronodular, morpheaform/sclerosing, pigmented, and basosquamous forms, the latter and deeply infiltrative variants carrying higher recurrence risk. Although usually locally destructive with rare metastasis, complications include tissue invasion, perineural spread, disfigurement, recurrence, and associations with other skin cancers; comorbid risk is increased with chronic UV exposure, fair skin, older age, immunosuppression, prior ionizing radiation, arsenic exposure, and genetic syndromes such as autosomal dominant nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) caused mainly by germline PTCH1, less often SUFU, mutations, as well as xeroderma pigmentosum. Diagnosis is based on clinical morphology plus dermoscopy and confirmed by shave, punch, or excisional biopsy with histopathology showing basaloid nests with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction; high-risk cases may require margin assessment by Mohs surgery and selective imaging for deep invasion. Treatment commonly includes vismodegib and sonidegib, SMO inhibitors that suppress Hedgehog signaling, and cemiplimab, a PD-1 inhibitor that restores antitumor immunity, with topical imiquimod, a TLR7 agonist, and 5-fluorouracil

Name: Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung
Description: Non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) is a heterogeneous epithelial malignancy of the lung, comprising mainly adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large-cell carcinoma, characterized by invasive growth, early regional or distant metastasis, and strong environmental causation, especially tobacco smoke, although major oncogenic drivers are well defined. Recurrent genetic alterations include activating EGFR mutations (for example exon 19 deletions and L858R), KRAS mutations, ALK, ROS1, and RET rearrangements, BRAF V600E, MET exon 14 skipping, ERBB2/HER2 mutations, and inactivation of TP53, STK11, KEAP1, LKB1, CDKN2A, and RB1; these perturb EGFR/RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, MET, HER2, ALK, ROS1, RET, and NRF2/KEAP1 signaling, promoting proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, immune evasion, and resistance. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited susceptibility is recognized, including rare germline EGFR T790M, TP53 in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and polymorphic risk loci such as 15q25 nicotinic receptor genes. Typical symptoms and signs include persistent cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, fatigue, recurrent pneumonia, pleural effusion, hoarseness, and symptoms from brain, bone, liver, or adrenal metastases; complications include respiratory failure, malignant effusions, venous thromboembolism, superior vena cava syndrome, paraneoplastic syndromes, and coexistence with COPD, emphysema, cardiovascular disease, and other smoking-related cancers. Diagnosis rests on imaging with chest CT and PET/CT, histopathology from bronchoscopy, needle biopsy, or surgical specimens, immunohistochemistry such as TTF-1, p40, and napsin A for subtype assignment, TNM staging, and comprehensive molecular testing by PCR or next-generation sequencing plus PD-L1 assessment. Common treatments include platinum agents such as cisplatin or carboplatin causing DNA crosslinking, pemetrexed inhibiting folate-dependent thymidylate and purine synthesis, paclitaxel stabilizing microtubules, EGFR inhibitors such as osimertinib, ALK inhibitors such as alect

Name: Carcinoma, Renal Cell
Description: Renal cell carcinoma is a malignant epithelial neoplasm arising from the renal tubular epithelium, most often in adults, and comprises several histologic subtypes, chiefly clear cell RCC, papillary RCC, chromophobe RCC, collecting duct carcinoma, and rarer translocation-associated tumors. Clear cell RCC is strongly linked to biallelic inactivation of VHL on chromosome 3p, causing HIF-1α/HIF-2α stabilization and upregulation of VEGF, PDGF, CAIX, and angiogenic signaling; other recurrent genetic alterations include PBRM1, SETD2, BAP1, KDM5C, and MTOR in clear cell disease, MET activation in hereditary and sporadic papillary RCC, FH mutations in hereditary leiomyomatosis-associated RCC, FLCN in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, and TSC1/TSC2 alterations affecting PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndromes include von Hippel-Lindau disease, hereditary papillary RCC, Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, hereditary leiomyomatosis and RCC, and tuberous sclerosis complex. Typical manifestations include hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass, constitutional symptoms, anemia, weight loss, fever, and paraneoplastic syndromes such as erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, hypertension, hepatic dysfunction, and amyloidosis; complications include venous invasion into the renal vein or inferior vena cava, metastases to lung, bone, liver, brain, and chronic kidney disease. Risk is increased by smoking, obesity, hypertension, and acquired cystic kidney disease. Diagnosis relies on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to define an enhancing renal mass and stage disease, with histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirming subtype when needed; biopsy is often used for indeterminate or metastatic lesions, and molecular or germline testing is indicated in early-onset, bilateral, multifocal, or syndromic cases. Treatment commonly includes surgery for localized disease and systemic therapy for advanced disease, such as sunitinib or pazopanib, multitarget VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors; cabozantinib, which inhibits VEGFR, MET, and AXL; everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor; and immune checkpoint inhibitors including nivolumab, a PD-1 blocker, and ipil

Name: Carcinoma, Squamous Cell
Description: Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant epithelial neoplasm showing keratinizing or nonkeratinizing squamous differentiation that arises most often in skin, head and neck mucosa, lung, esophagus, cervix, and anogenital sites, with major subtypes defined by anatomic site, HPV status, and histologic grade. Its molecular landscape commonly includes TP53 mutation or loss, CDKN2A inactivation, EGFR amplification or overexpression, CCND1/SOX2/PIK3CA amplification, NOTCH1 mutations, FAT1 loss, and, in HPV-driven tumors, viral E6/E7-mediated functional inactivation of p53 and RB1; altered proteins may include p63, PD-L1, and cytokeratins. Key dysregulated pathways include EGFR-RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, p53/cell-cycle, RB-cyclin D-CDK4/6, squamous differentiation/NOTCH signaling, oxidative stress responses, angiogenesis via VEGF, and immune-checkpoint signaling through PD-1/PD-L1. Treatment depends on site and stage but commonly uses cisplatin or carboplatin, DNA-crosslinking platinum agents; 5-fluorouracil, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor; paclitaxel or docetaxel, microtubule-stabilizing taxanes; cetuximab, an EGFR-blocking monoclonal antibody; and pembrolizumab or nivolumab, PD-1 inhibitors that restore antitumor T-cell activity. Clinical manifestations vary by organ but typically include enlarging ulcerated or exophytic lesions, pain, bleeding, dysphagia, hoarseness, cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, nonhealing plaques or nodules, and regional lymphadenopathy. Important risk factors and comorbidities include tobacco and alcohol use, chronic sun exposure, HPV infection, immunosuppression, chronic inflammation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and field cancerization with second primary tumors; complications include local tissue destruction, nodal and distant metastases, airway or esophageal obstruction, infection, and treatment-related mucositis or fibrosis. Name: Carcinoma, Transitional Cell
Description: Transitional cell carcinoma, now usually termed urothelial carcinoma, is a malignant epithelial neoplasm arising most often in the bladder but also in the renal pelvis, ureter, and urethra, with major clinicopathologic subtypes including non–muscle-invasive papillary carcinoma, carcinoma in situ, and muscle-invasive or metastatic disease. It is typically sporadic rather than Mendelian, but genetic susceptibility and somatic alterations are important: low-grade papillary tumors commonly harbor FGFR3, HRAS, PIK3CA, TERT promoter, and KDM6A mutations, whereas high-grade invasive tumors more often show TP53, RB1, CDKN2A, ERCC2, ARID1A, PTEN, and ERBB2 alterations; Lynch syndrome with MSH2 or other mismatch-repair defects particularly predisposes to upper tract urothelial carcinoma. Key dysregulated pathways include RTK/RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53/RB cell-cycle control, DNA-damage repair, chromatin remodeling, angiogenesis via VEGF, and immune evasion through PD-1/PD-L1 signaling. Patients classically present with painless gross or microscopic hematuria, irritative voiding symptoms, dysuria, frequency, urgency, flank pain in upper tract disease, and later weight loss, pelvic pain, or hydronephrosis. Major risk factors and linked comorbidities include tobacco exposure, aromatic amines, chronic cystitis, schistosomiasis in some regions, and association with hydronephrosis, recurrent urinary tract infection, obstruction, anemia, renal insufficiency, and metastases to lymph nodes, liver, lung, and bone. Diagnosis relies on cystoscopy with biopsy and histopathology, urine cytology, urinary biomarkers such as NMP22 or UroVysion FISH in selected settings, staging by CT urography or cross-sectional imaging, and molecular testing for FGFR alterations or PD-L1 when therapeutically relevant. Treatment commonly includes cisplatin, which forms DNA cross-links; gemcitabine, a nucleoside analog inhibiting DNA synthesis; and pembrolizumab, a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor, with additional use of intravesical BCG to stimulate antitumor immunity, enfortumab vedotin targeting nectin-4, and erdafitinib inhibiting FGFR2/3-altered tumors.

Name: Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic
Description: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a primary myocardial disease defined by otherwise unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, usually asymmetric and often involving the interventricular septum, with myocyte hypertrophy, disarray, and interstitial fibrosis; it includes obstructive and nonobstructive forms, apical and midventricular variants, and infantile or syndromic phenotypes. It is most commonly inherited as an autosomal dominant sarcomeric disorder with variable penetrance and expressivity, caused by pathogenic variants in genes such as MYH7, MYBPC3, TNNT2, TNNI3, TPM1, ACTC1, and MYL2/MYL3, while phenocopies arise in PRKAG2, GLA, LAMP2, and mitochondrial disorders. Disease mechanisms center on abnormal sarcomere force generation and calcium sensitivity, energetic inefficiency, and activation of hypertrophic and profibrotic signaling pathways including β-adrenergic signaling, calcineurin-NFAT, MAPK/ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, TGF-β, and altered CaMKII-mediated calcium handling. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with exertional dyspnea, angina, palpitations, presyncope or syncope, exercise intolerance, harsh systolic murmur from dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmia. Common complications and comorbidities include atrial fibrillation, heart failure with preserved or later reduced ejection fraction, myocardial ischemia, mitral regurgitation from systolic anterior motion, apical aneurysm, thromboembolism, and stroke. Diagnosis relies on echocardiography or cardiac MRI showing maximal left ventricular wall thickness at least 15 mm, or at least 13 mm in first-degree relatives, in the absence of another loading condition; ECG abnormalities, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, exercise testing, family screening, and genetic testing support diagnosis and risk stratification. Treatment commonly includes β-blockers such as metoprolol, which reduce heart rate and contractility; non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as verapamil, which improve diastolic filling; disopyramide, a negative inotrope that lowers outflow gradients; and in selected obstructive disease mavacamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor that reduces actin-myosin cross-bridge formation.

Name: Cerebral Embolism
Description: Cerebral embolism (UMLS C0007780) is an acute ischemic cerebrovascular disorder caused by embolic occlusion of an intracranial artery, most often from cardiac thromboemboli or artery-to-artery atheroemboli, producing sudden focal brain infarction; major subtypes include cardioembolic stroke, atheroembolic stroke, paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale, septic embolism, and less commonly tumor, fat, or air embolism. Typical manifestations are abrupt hemiparesis, facial droop, aphasia, dysarthria, visual field loss, hemisensory deficit, ataxia, neglect, altered consciousness, and sometimes seizures. Molecular contributors are largely those predisposing to thrombosis, arrhythmia, or atherosclerosis rather than single-gene causation: representative genetic factors include F5 Leiden, F2 G20210A, MTHFR variants, SERPINC1, PROC, and PROS1 deficiencies, ABO non-O blood group, and AF-related loci such as PITX2 and ZFHX3; proteins of interest include tissue factor, thrombin, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, platelet P2Y12, factor Xa, and inflammatory mediators such as IL-6 and CRP. Key pathways include the coagulation cascade, platelet activation and aggregation, endothelial dysfunction, atherosclerotic plaque inflammation, and ischemic glutamate-calcium excitotoxicity with oxidative stress. Commonly linked comorbidities are atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, recent myocardial infarction, infective endocarditis, carotid atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, malignancy, smoking, and heart failure; complications include cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, recurrent embolization, aspiration pneumonia, venous thromboembolism, and persistent cognitive or motor disability. Treatment commonly uses alteplase, a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin for thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion, aspirin as an irreversible COX-1 inhibitor reducing thromboxane A2, clopidogrel as a P2Y12 receptor antagonist, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, or apixaban/rivaroxaban, direct factor Xa inhibitors, especially for cardioembolic sources. Name: Cerebrovascular Disorders
Description: Cerebrovascular disorders comprise a heterogeneous group of diseases affecting cerebral arteries, arterioles, capillaries, and veins, producing ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury, most commonly ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, transient ischemic attack, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and hereditary small-vessel vasculopathies. Their pathobiology centers on atherosclerosis and thromboembolism, endothelial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier disruption, and coagulation/fibrinolytic imbalance, involving pathways such as platelet activation through COX-1/thromboxane A2 and ADP-P2Y12 signaling, the coagulation cascade with thrombin and factor Xa, nitric oxide and endothelin vascular tone regulation, matrix metalloproteinases, VEGF, and inflammatory mediators including IL-6, TNF, and NF-kB. Genetic contributors are strongest in monogenic and susceptibility syndromes, with representative genes including NOTCH3 in CADASIL, HTRA1 in CARASIL and autosomal dominant small-vessel disease, COL4A1/COL4A2 in familial hemorrhagic stroke and leukoencephalopathy, TREX1, KRIT1/CCM1, CCM2, PDCD10, and APOE, particularly the epsilon4 allele, associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy and lobar hemorrhage; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, recessive, or multifactorial depending on subtype. Common symptoms include abrupt focal weakness, aphasia, facial droop, hemisensory loss, visual field deficit, ataxia, vertigo, severe headache, altered consciousness, or seizures. Major comorbidities and complications include hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, dyslipidemia, smoking, coronary and peripheral vascular disease, vascular dementia, depression, aspiration pneumonia, cerebral edema, recurrent stroke, and epilepsy. Treatment commonly includes alteplase, a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin for thrombolysis; aspirin, an irreversible COX-1 inhibitor that suppresses platelet thromboxane A2; clopidogrel, an irreversible P2Y12 antagonist; anticoagulants such as apixaban, a direct factor Xa inhibitor, for cardioembolic prevention; and statins such as atorvastatin, an HMG-CoA reductase

Name: Malignant Tumor of Cervix
Description: Malignant tumor of the cervix, usually cervical carcinoma, is a predominantly HPV-driven epithelial malignancy arising in the transformation zone, most commonly as squamous cell carcinoma and less often adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, or other rare histologies. Its pathogenesis is strongly linked to persistent high-risk HPV infection, especially types 16 and 18, whose E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate TP53 and RB1, promote genomic instability, and alter cell-cycle regulators including CDKN2A/p16; recurrent molecular abnormalities may include PIK3CA, PTEN, KRAS, FBXW7, ERBB2, and STK11 alterations, with overexpression of EGFR, VEGF, and PD-L1 in subsets. Key pathways include p53 and Rb disruption, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, WNT/beta-catenin, angiogenesis via VEGF, apoptosis evasion, and immune-checkpoint signaling through PD-1/PD-L1. Typical symptoms and signs include postcoital, intermenstrual, or postmenopausal bleeding, watery or malodorous vaginal discharge, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and in advanced disease urinary or rectal symptoms, hydronephrosis, fistula, or weight loss. Common complications and comorbidities include anemia, infection, obstructive uropathy, renal failure, thromboembolism, HIV-related immunosuppression, smoking-related disease, and treatment-related infertility or premature menopause. Inheritance is usually not Mendelian, but host genetic susceptibility involving HLA loci, TP53 pathway variants, and rare syndromic associations such as Peutz-Jeghers syndrome due to STK11 mutations can modify risk. Diagnosis relies on cervical cytology and high-risk HPV testing, colposcopy with directed biopsy, histopathology, and staging by pelvic examination and imaging such as MRI, CT, or PET/CT. Standard therapies include cisplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum; paclitaxel, a microtubule-stabilizing mitotic inhibitor; topotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor; bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody; and pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor for selected PD-L1-positive or biomarker-defined recurrent or metastatic disease.

Name: Chancroid
Description: Chancroid is an acute sexually transmitted genital ulcer disease caused by the fastidious Gram-negative coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi, classically presenting with one or more painful, nonindurated genital ulcers with ragged undermined edges, a necrotic or purulent base, marked tenderness, and frequently painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenitis or fluctuant buboes that may suppurate; extragenital lesions and, rarely, autoinoculation or chronic ulcers can occur. The disorder is infectious rather than inherited, with no Mendelian transmission or established host germline mutation syndrome, although host susceptibility is influenced by innate and adaptive immune pathways; bacterial virulence determinants include the cytolethal distending toxin genes cdtA, cdtB, and cdtC, outer membrane and serum-resistance proteins such as DsrA, hemoglobin receptor HgbA, and Flp/Tad pili mediating adherence, microcolony formation, and immune evasion. Pathobiology centers on epithelial invasion, complement resistance, neutrophil- and macrophage-rich inflammation, and activation of cytokine networks including TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and NF-kappaB signaling, with tissue injury amplified by CDT-mediated DNA damage and cell-cycle arrest. Major complications and comorbidities include HIV acquisition and transmission, coinfection with syphilis, herpes simplex virus, gonorrhea, and chlamydia, as well as phimosis, fistula formation, scarring, and painful abscessed nodes. Clinical variants include transient papular, pustular, ulcerative, and bubonic forms. Diagnosis is usually clinical plus exclusion of other genital ulcer diseases, supported by epidemiologic exposure; definitive testing relies on culture on specialized media or nucleic acid amplification testing where available, while recommended evaluation includes syphilis serology, HSV testing, and HIV screening. First-line therapy commonly includes azithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis, ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis, ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, and erythromycin, another 50S inhibitor.

Name: Chickenpox
Description: Chickenpox, or primary varicella due to varicella-zoster virus (VZV; human herpesvirus 3), is an acute, highly contagious viral exanthem characterized by fever, malaise, pruritic crops of vesicles on an erythematous base evolving to pustules and crusts, and occasionally mucosal lesions; clinical variants include uncomplicated varicella, hemorrhagic or disseminated disease, congenital and neonatal varicella, and severe visceral infection in immunocompromised hosts. As an infectious disease it is not inherited in a Mendelian manner, but host genetic susceptibility influences severity, with defects in cell-mediated and innate antiviral immunity involving genes such as IFNG, IL10, TLR3, TICAM1/TRIF, IRF3, POLR3A, and HLA class I/II alleles reported in severe herpesvirus phenotypes; relevant viral proteins include envelope glycoproteins gE and gB and thymidine kinase. Pathobiology centers on viral entry, replication, latency in sensory ganglia, and immune evasion, engaging interferon/JAK-STAT signaling, TLR3–IRF3 innate sensing, NF-kB, and T-cell/NK-cell responses. Diagnosis is usually clinical from the characteristic asynchronous lesions in different stages, but confirmation uses PCR of vesicle fluid or scabs, direct fluorescent antibody testing, serology for VZV IgM/IgG or seroconversion, and occasionally histopathology or viral culture. Treatment is mainly supportive, with acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir as key antivirals that, after phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, inhibit viral DNA polymerase and terminate or impair DNA synthesis; varicella-zoster immune globulin provides passive immunization after high-risk exposure, while antipyretics and antipruritics are adjunctive, and aspirin is avoided because of Reye syndrome risk. Important complications and comorbid associations include secondary bacterial skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis, cerebellitis, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, dehydration, invasive group A streptococcal disease, pregnancy-related fetal malformations, and later herpes zoster from latent VZV reactivation.

Name: Chlamydia Infections
Description: Chlamydia infections are communicable bacterial diseases caused mainly by obligate intracellular Chlamydia trachomatis serovars, classically divided into urogenital serovars D–K, ocular serovars A–C causing trachoma, and invasive L1–L3 causing lymphogranuloma venereum; less commonly, C. psittaci and C. pneumoniae cause systemic or respiratory syndromes. Pathogenesis depends on the biphasic elementary body–reticulate body developmental cycle and chlamydial proteins such as major outer membrane protein OmpA, polymorphic membrane proteins, type III secretion effectors including Tarp, CPAF, and heat-shock protein 60, which drive host-cell entry, cytoskeletal remodeling, intracellular inclusion formation, and immune injury. Host susceptibility and severity are influenced by genetic components rather than Mendelian inheritance, with representative associations involving HLA class I/II alleles, TLR2/TLR4, NOD1, IFNG, IL10, TNFA, CXCR5, and matrix-remodeling genes such as MMP9. Key pathways include TLR2/4-MyD88-NF-κB signaling, NOD and inflammasome activation, IFN-γ–JAK/STAT antimicrobial responses, MAPK, PI3K/AKT, apoptosis modulation, and Th1-skewed cytokine networks involving IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and CXCL chemokines. Typical manifestations include asymptomatic infection, cervicitis, urethritis, dysuria, mucopurulent discharge, postcoital bleeding, epididymitis, proctitis, conjunctivitis, pelvic pain, and inguinal buboes in LGV. Major complications and comorbidities include pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, tubal-factor infertility, chronic pelvic pain, Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome, adverse pregnancy outcomes, neonatal conjunctivitis or pneumonia, reactive arthritis, and increased HIV acquisition/transmission risk. Diagnosis is primarily by nucleic acid amplification testing on vaginal, cervical, urine, rectal, or pharyngeal specimens; culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing, and serology are adjunctive in selected ocular, neonatal, psittacosis, or LGV settings. Name: Cholangitis
Description: Cholangitis is an inflammatory and usually infectious disorder of the biliary tree, classically arising from ductal obstruction and bacterial ascent in acute cholangitis, but also encompassing immune-mediated forms such as primary sclerosing cholangitis and primary biliary cholangitis; common symptoms and signs include fever, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, fatigue, and, in severe cases, hypotension and confusion. Acute disease is most often triggered by choledocholithiasis, benign or malignant strictures, or instrumentation, with enteric pathogens such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and their endotoxin-driven activation of TLR4, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, neutrophil recruitment, cholestatic injury, and fibrogenic TGF-β signaling; cholangiocyte-secretin, bile acid-FXR/TGR5, and HLA-linked immune pathways are particularly relevant in chronic cholangitides. Genetic associations are strongest in chronic subtypes, including HLA-B8, DRB1, DQA1, IL12A, IL12RB2, SPIB, IRF5, and TNFSF15 in primary biliary cholangitis, and HLA-B8, DRB1*03, DRB1*13, MST1, FUT2, and MMP3 in primary sclerosing cholangitis; rare monogenic mimics or predispositions include ABCB4 and CFTR variants, while inheritance is generally complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. Major comorbidities and complications include inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis in primary sclerosing cholangitis, gallstones, pancreatitis, hepatic abscess, sepsis, biliary cirrhosis, portal hypertension, cholangiocarcinoma, and liver failure. Diagnosis relies on cholestatic liver tests with elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, inflammatory markers, blood cultures in acute infection, ultrasound or CT for obstruction, MRCP or ERCP for ductal abnormalities and drainage, and autoimmune serologies such as antimitochondrial antibody and IgM in primary biliary cholangitis. Name: Biliary Cholangitides, Primary
Description: Biliary cirrhosis refers to chronic cholestatic liver disease caused by immune-mediated or obstructive injury to intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts, classically encompassing primary biliary cholangitis and advanced biliary fibrosis from primary sclerosing cholangitis or congenital cholangiopathies; it is characterized by progressive duct loss, portal inflammation, fibrosis, and eventual cirrhosis with jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort, hepatomegaly, xanthelasma, steatorrhea, and signs of portal hypertension or liver failure in late stages. In primary biliary cholangitis, hallmark serology is antimitochondrial antibody against the E2 subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase, with genetic susceptibility linked to HLA-DRB1, IL12A, IL12RB2, STAT4, SPIB, IRF5, and CTLA4, implicating IL-12/JAK-STAT, T-cell costimulatory, cytokine, and cholangiocyte apoptotic pathways; primary sclerosing cholangitis shows associations with HLA-B8, DR3, DRB1*1501 and inflammatory signaling involving TNF-α, TGF-β, NF-κB, bile acid–FXR/FGF19 signaling, and fibrogenic activation of hepatic stellate cells. Heritable causes of biliary cirrhosis include autosomal recessive ABCB4 deficiency, ATP8B1 or ABCB11-related cholestasis, and JAG1 or NOTCH2 mutations in Alagille syndrome, whereas most adult autoimmune forms are complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. Common treatments include ursodeoxycholic acid, a hydrophilic bile acid that improves bile flow and reduces bile acid toxicity; obeticholic acid, an FXR agonist that suppresses bile acid synthesis; cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant for pruritus; and, in selected cases, bezafibrate, rifampin, or liver transplantation for decompensated disease. Major comorbidities and complications include autoimmune thyroid disease, Sjögren syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, osteoporosis, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, hyperlipidemia, recurrent cholangitis, dominant strictures, portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma, and cholangiocarcinoma.
