Name: Cholecystitis
Description: Cholecystitis (UMLS C0008325) is an acute or chronic inflammatory disorder of the gallbladder, most often caused by cystic duct obstruction from cholesterol or pigment gallstones, with less common acalculous forms arising in critical illness, sepsis, trauma, burns, total parenteral nutrition, or ischemia. It is not classically inherited, but genetic susceptibility to cholelithiasis and biliary inflammation is influenced by variants in genes regulating cholesterol transport and bile composition, including ABCG5/ABCG8, ABCB4, APOE, UGT1A1, and CYP7A1, while inflammatory mediators and proteins such as IL6, TNF, CRP, TLR4, and COX-2 are implicated in disease activity. Key pathogenic pathways include bile supersaturation and gallbladder dysmotility, epithelial injury, ischemia-reperfusion, bacterial translocation, and innate immune signaling through TLR/NF-κB, cytokine cascades, prostaglandin synthesis, neutrophil recruitment, and in severe cases inflammasome-associated tissue damage. Typical features are right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, leukocytosis, and a positive Murphy sign, sometimes with mild jaundice; complications include empyema, gangrene, perforation, pericholecystic abscess, ascending cholangitis, pancreatitis, sepsis, and recurrent chronic cholecystitis. Major subtypes are acute calculous, acute acalculous, chronic, emphysematous, and gangrenous cholecystitis. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation plus inflammatory markers and cholestatic liver tests, with ultrasonography showing gallstones, wall thickening, sonographic Murphy sign, and pericholecystic fluid; hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scanning demonstrates cystic duct obstruction, and CT or MRI/MRCP can define complications or alternative diagnoses. Treatment commonly includes ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, metronidazole, which generates DNA-damaging radicals against anaerobes, piperacillin-tazobactam, combining cell-wall inhibition with beta-lactamase blockade, and analgesics such as NSAIDs that inhibit COX-mediated prostaglandin production, with definitive management usually by cholecystectomy.

Name: Cholelithiasis
Description: Cholelithiasis (MeSH D002769) is the formation of calculi within the gallbladder or biliary tree, usually classified as cholesterol stones, black pigment stones, or brown pigment stones, and it commonly presents with episodic right upper quadrant or epigastric pain after meals, nausea, vomiting, bloating, and, when complicated, fever, jaundice, or pancreatitis. Its pathobiology centers on cholesterol supersaturation of bile, impaired bile acid homeostasis, mucin hypersecretion, gallbladder hypomotility, and inflammation, with key pathways involving hepatic cholesterol transport and bile acid signaling through ABCG5/ABCG8, ABCB4, ABCB11, CYP7A1, FXR/NR1H4, LXR, and the FGF19-FGFR4 axis; inflammatory mediators and mucin genes also contribute to crystal nucleation. Genetic susceptibility is typically complex and polygenic, but clearly established examples include ABCG8 p.D19H, ABCB4 deficiency or mutation predisposing to low-phospholipid-associated cholelithiasis, UGT1A1 variants that increase bilirubin load in pigment stones, and hemolytic disorders such as sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis that promote black pigment stones; rare familial clustering occurs, but most cases are multifactorial rather than Mendelian. Major comorbidities and risk states include obesity, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, pregnancy, cirrhosis, Crohn disease with ileal dysfunction, rapid weight loss, and hemolysis, while complications include acute and chronic cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, ascending cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, and increased gallbladder carcinoma risk. Diagnosis is based on compatible symptoms plus imaging, with transabdominal ultrasonography as first line, liver tests and bilirubin for obstruction, endoscopic ultrasound or MRCP for suspected common bile duct stones, and ERCP when diagnosis and therapy are both needed. Treatment commonly includes ursodeoxycholic acid, which reduces biliary cholesterol saturation and improves bile flow, chenodeoxycholic acid, which suppresses hepatic cholesterol secretion and dissolves selected cholesterol stones, and NSAIDs such as diclofenac or ketorolac for biliary colic via cyclooxygenase inhibition; definitive management for symptomatic disease is

Name: Cholera
Description: Cholera is an acute secretory diarrheal disease caused by toxigenic Vibrio cholerae, classically serogroups O1 and O139, and is characterized by abrupt onset of profuse watery “rice-water” diarrhea, vomiting, leg cramps, rapid dehydration, metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, and potentially hypovolemic shock and death if untreated; clinically recognized biotypes and subtypes include classical and El Tor strains and severe versus mild or asymptomatic infection. Its central molecular pathology is mediated by cholera toxin encoded by ctxAB and coordinated by virulence regulators such as toxR, toxT, tcpA, and the toxin-coregulated pilus, which enable colonization and toxin production; the A subunit ADP-ribosylates the GNAS-encoded Gs alpha protein, causing persistent adenylate cyclase activation, elevated cAMP, protein kinase A signaling, phosphorylation of CFTR, and massive chloride and water secretion with relative inhibition of sodium absorption. Host susceptibility is not Mendelian, but genetic influences are recognized, including increased severity in blood group O individuals and potential modulation by variants affecting CFTR, innate immunity, and intestinal barrier function. Diagnosis rests on compatible acute watery diarrhea in an epidemiologic setting, assessment of dehydration, and laboratory confirmation by stool culture on selective media, rapid antigen or dipstick assays, PCR for toxigenic genes such as ctxA, and sometimes dark-field microscopy or serotyping. Treatment is primarily prompt oral or intravenous rehydration; antimicrobial therapy shortens illness and shedding, with doxycycline inhibiting the 30S ribosomal subunit, azithromycin binding the 50S subunit to block bacterial protein synthesis, and ciprofloxacin inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; tetracycline is another classic option. Important complications and comorbid associations include acute kidney injury, severe electrolyte disturbances, arrhythmias, pregnancy loss, malnutrition-related worse outcomes, and higher mortality in children and vulnerable adults.

Name: Cholestasis
Description: Cholestasis is a syndrome of impaired bile formation or bile flow that may be intrahepatic or extrahepatic, acute or chronic, and manifests clinically with jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, dark urine, pale stools, steatorrhea, xanthomas, hepatomegaly, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; laboratory diagnosis typically shows a cholestatic pattern with elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase, often with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, followed by etiologic evaluation using bile acids, autoimmune serologies, viral testing, abdominal ultrasonography or MRCP/ERCP to detect obstruction, liver biopsy when needed, and genetic testing in early-onset or familial cases. Major inherited forms include progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis and benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis, caused by variants in ATP8B1, ABCB11 encoding the bile salt export pump, ABCB4 encoding MDR3, TJP2, NR1H4/FXR, MYO5B, and JAG1 or NOTCH2 in Alagille syndrome, with autosomal recessive inheritance predominating in PFIC and autosomal dominant inheritance in some ductal plate disorders. Core molecular pathways involve hepatocellular bile acid synthesis and transport regulated by FXR, SHP, FGF19-FGFR4 signaling, canalicular transporters BSEP, MDR3, and MRP2, inflammatory cytokines, and cholangiocyte injury/ductular reaction leading to fibrosis. Common causes and comorbid settings include gallstones, biliary strictures, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, viral hepatitis, sepsis, pregnancy, total parenteral nutrition, cystic fibrosis, and drug-induced liver injury. Treatment targets cause and bile acid toxicity: ursodeoxycholic acid replaces hydrophobic bile acids and promotes choleresis, obeticholic acid is an FXR agonist that suppresses bile acid synthesis, cholestyramine binds intestinal bile acids to reduce pruritus, while rifampin induces detoxification pathways, naltrexone counteracts opioid-mediated itch, and advanced disease may require endoscopic or surgical decompression or liver transplantation. Complications include recurrent cholangitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, osteoporosis, malnutrition, and hepatobiliary malignancy.

Name: Choroiditis
Description: Choroiditis is an inflammatory disorder of the choroid, usually presenting as posterior uveitis or chorioretinitis, with blurred vision, floaters, photopsias, scotomas, metamorphopsia, ocular pain, redness, and reduced visual acuity, and it may be focal, multifocal, serpiginous, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot chorioretinopathy, or part of panuveitis. Its pathobiology is typically immune mediated or infectious, involving T-cell activation, antigen presentation, macrophage and microglial recruitment, and cytokine networks centered on TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-17, IFN-gamma, JAK-STAT, NF-kappaB, and complement signaling; VEGF-driven neovascular pathways are important in complications such as choroidal neovascularization. Genetic associations are strongest in specific subtypes rather than choroiditis as a whole, including HLA-A29 in birdshot chorioretinopathy, ERAP2 and other antigen-processing loci, and susceptibility variants in IL23R or other immune-regulatory genes in some posterior uveitis phenotypes; inheritance is usually complex, multifactorial, and non-Mendelian, although rare syndromic inflammatory disorders may show familial clustering. Infectious causes include Toxoplasma gondii, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Treponema pallidum, herpesviruses, and fungi, with relevant microbial proteins and host immune responses shaping disease expression. Common treatments include corticosteroids such as prednisone or intravitreal triamcinolone, which suppress NF-kappaB-dependent inflammatory transcription; methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil, which inhibit lymphocyte proliferation; cyclosporine or tacrolimus, which block calcineurin-mediated T-cell activation; and biologics such as adalimumab, an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody; antimicrobials are used when infection is identified, for example pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis. Important comorbidities and complications include cataract, glaucoma, cystoid macular edema, epiretinal membrane, retinal vasculitis, optic nerve involvement, and irreversible chorioretinal scarring with vision loss; diagnosis relies on ophthalmic examination, dilated funduscopy, OCT, fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography, fundus autof

Name: Chromoblastomycosis
Description: Chromoblastomycosis (MeSH D002862) is a chronic, slowly progressive subcutaneous mycosis caused by traumatic implantation of melanized dematiaceous fungi, most commonly Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa, and occasionally Rhinocladiella species, producing verrucous, nodular, plaque-like, tumoral, cicatricial, or ulcerative lesions, typically on the lower extremities, with pruritus, pain, crusting, lymphedema, secondary bacterial infection, fibrosis, and long-standing risk of disability and rare squamous cell carcinoma. It is an acquired infectious disease rather than an inherited disorder, and no Mendelian inheritance pattern is established; however, host susceptibility is shaped by immune-response genes and proteins, with representative associations involving pattern-recognition and inflammatory pathways such as TLR2, TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, MyD88, TNF, IL1B, IL6, IL10, IL17, IFNG, and macrophage nitric oxide and inflammasome responses, while fungal virulence relates to melanin biosynthesis and cell-wall components that impair phagocytic killing. Key pathogenic pathways include innate fungal recognition through C-type lectin and Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB activation, Th1/Th17 versus regulatory cytokine polarization, granulomatous inflammation, and defective macrophage clearance of muriform cells. Diagnosis rests on compatible chronic verrucous cutaneous lesions plus demonstration of characteristic pigmented sclerotic or muriform bodies on direct KOH examination or histopathology, supported by fungal culture and increasingly PCR or sequencing for species identification. Standard therapy includes itraconazole, an azole that inhibits fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; terbinafine, which inhibits squalene epoxidase; and posaconazole or voriconazole, broader triazoles with the same ergosterol-pathway target; adjunctive cryotherapy, thermotherapy, or surgical excision may be used for localized disease. Important comorbidities and worse outcomes occur with diabetes, malnutrition, immunosuppression, chronic lymphedema, and occupational trauma exposure.

Name: Bronchitis, Chronic
Description: Chronic bronchitis (UMLS C0008677) is a chronic inflammatory airway disease, classically defined clinically by productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years after exclusion of other causes, and is a major phenotype within chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, with simple and obstructive forms and overlap with emphysema or asthma-COPD overlap. It is driven predominantly by cigarette smoke, biomass exposure, and recurrent irritant injury, causing mucus gland and goblet-cell hyperplasia, impaired mucociliary clearance, airway wall remodeling, and recurrent infection. Molecularly, disease susceptibility and progression have been linked to variants affecting protease-antiprotease balance, xenobiotic response, and inflammation, including SERPINA1 mutations causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, GSTM1/GSTP1, MMP9, TGFB1, TNF, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, CHRNA3/5, HHIP, and FAM13A; implicated pathways include NF-kappaB, MAPK, TGF-beta/SMAD, EGFR-mediated mucin induction, oxidative stress–Nrf2 signaling, protease networks involving neutrophil elastase and matrix metalloproteinases, and cytokine signaling through TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-17. Typical manifestations are chronic sputum production, cough, wheeze, exertional dyspnea, prolonged expiration, rhonchi, frequent infective exacerbations, and in advanced disease hypoxemia, cyanosis, and signs of cor pulmonale. Common comorbidities and complications include emphysema, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, cardiovascular disease, lung cancer, anxiety, depression, and cachexia. Treatment centers on smoking cessation and inhaled bronchodilators such as albuterol, a short-acting beta2-agonist increasing cAMP-mediated smooth-muscle relaxation, tiotropium, a long-acting muscarinic M3 antagonist reducing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction, and salmeterol or formoterol, long-acting beta2-agonists; inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone suppress airway inflammatory gene transcription, while roflumilast inhibits phosphodiesterase-4 to reduce inflammatory signaling, and antibiotics are used for bacterial exacerbations. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, spirometry demonstrating persistent airflow limitation

Name: Cluster Headache
Description: Cluster headache is a primary trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia characterized by recurrent attacks of excruciating, strictly unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain lasting about 15–180 minutes, often accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features such as lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, eyelid edema, facial sweating, miosis, or ptosis, with marked restlessness or agitation; major subtypes are episodic and chronic cluster headache. Its biology implicates hypothalamic circadian dysfunction and activation of the trigeminovascular and trigeminal-autonomic reflex pathways, with key mediators including calcitonin gene-related peptide encoded by CALCA, pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, vasoactive intestinal peptide, substance P, serotoninergic signaling, orexin/hypocretin pathways including HCRTR2, nitric oxide signaling, and parasympathetic outflow via the superior salivatory nucleus and sphenopalatine ganglion. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, but familial aggregation is recognized; representative candidate genes include HCRTR2, CLOCK, ADCYAP1R1, and CACNA1A, and rare channelopathy overlap has been reported, although no single highly penetrant mutation explains most cases. Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD criteria requiring the typical unilateral severe attacks with autonomic signs or restlessness and characteristic frequency, while MRI of the brain and pituitary and targeted testing are used to exclude secondary mimics such as pituitary lesions, carotid dissection, or sinus disease. Acute treatment commonly includes high-flow oxygen, which likely suppresses trigeminovascular activation, subcutaneous or intranasal sumatriptan or zolmitriptan, 5-HT1B/1D agonists that inhibit neuropeptide release and cranial vasodilation, and preventive therapy with verapamil, a calcium-channel blocker, lithium, corticosteroids as transitional therapy, topiramate, and CGRP-targeted galcanezumab. Important comorbidities include tobacco use, sleep and circadian disorders, depression, anxiety, migraine, and increased suicidality; complications include medication adverse effects and profound functional impairment.

Name: Coccidioidomycosis
Description: Coccidioidomycosis (MeSH D003047) is a dimorphic fungal infection caused by inhalation of arthroconidia of Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii, producing a spectrum from asymptomatic infection and self-limited primary pulmonary disease to chronic cavitary pneumonia, cutaneous or osteoarticular disease, and disseminated meningeal infection. Typical manifestations include fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, fatigue, dyspnea, night sweats, weight loss, erythema nodosum, and sometimes eosinophilia; complications include pulmonary nodules or cavities, hemoptysis, respiratory failure, meningitis, osteomyelitis, and dissemination, especially in pregnancy, HIV/AIDS, transplantation, diabetes, and patients receiving corticosteroids or TNF-alpha inhibitors. Host genetic susceptibility is increasingly linked to defects in IL-12/IFN-gamma axis and cell-mediated immunity, including variants in IFNGR1, IFNGR2, STAT1, STAT3, IL12RB1, IL12B, TYK2, PLCG2, and HLA-associated risk, with rare Mendelian predisposition patterns usually autosomal recessive or dominant depending on the gene; fungal virulence proteins include the spherule outer wall glycoprotein and urease. Key pathways involve innate recognition through TLR2, TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, macrophage and neutrophil activation, and Th1/Th17 cytokine signaling with IL-12, IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, IL-17, and granuloma formation. Diagnosis relies on epidemiologic exposure plus compatible clinical and radiographic findings, supported by serology for IgM and IgG by enzyme immunoassay, immunodiffusion, and complement fixation titers, culture or histopathology showing spherules with endospores, antigen detection, PCR where available, and CSF studies in suspected meningitis. Treatment commonly uses fluconazole, an azole inhibiting fungal 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; itraconazole, with the same core azole mechanism and utility in bone or soft-tissue disease; and amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes, with voriconazole, posaconazole, or isavuconazole used in refractory disease.

Name: Colitis, Ulcerative
Description: Ulcerative colitis (MeSH D003093) is a chronic relapsing inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and extending proximally through the colon, classically classified as ulcerative proctitis, left-sided colitis, or extensive/pancolitis. It arises from polygenic susceptibility interacting with environmental and microbial factors rather than simple Mendelian inheritance, with familial clustering and risk variants in immune and epithelial barrier genes such as HLA class II loci, IL23R, ECM1, JAK2, STAT3, GNA12, and variants affecting mucosal defense and tight-junction integrity; unlike Crohn disease, NOD2 has less consistent association. Pathobiology involves dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, epithelial barrier failure, and altered microbiota, with prominent TNF, IL-13, IL-23/Th17, JAK-STAT, NF-kB, integrin-mediated leukocyte trafficking, and prostaglandin pathways, as well as oxidative stress and neutrophil recruitment. Patients typically present with bloody diarrhea, urgency, tenesmus, mucus per rectum, abdominal cramping, nocturnal stools, fatigue, weight loss, and fever in severe disease; endoscopy shows continuous erythematous friable mucosa with superficial ulceration, and histology demonstrates chronic active colitis with crypt architectural distortion, basal plasmacytosis, and crypt abscesses. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, colonoscopy with biopsy, exclusion of infection by stool testing including Clostridioides difficile, inflammatory markers such as CRP and fecal calprotectin, and imaging when complications are suspected. Standard therapy includes 5-aminosalicylates such as mesalamine, which inhibit cyclooxygenase/lipoxygenase-mediated inflammatory signaling; corticosteroids such as prednisone or budesonide, which suppress NF-kB-dependent cytokine transcription; immunomodulators such as azathioprine, a purine synthesis inhibitor; biologics including infliximab, an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, and vedolizumab, an anti-a4b7 integrin blocker; and JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib. Important comorbidities and complications include primary sclerosing cholangitis, venous thromboembolism, anemia, osteoporosis, toxic megacolon, perforation, severe hemorrhage, extraintestinal manifestations including arthritis, uveitis

Name: Common Cold
Description: Common cold (MeSH D003139) is an acute, usually self-limited viral upper respiratory tract infection caused predominantly by rhinoviruses, but also seasonal coronaviruses, adenoviruses, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, and others, with clinical subtypes often defined by causative virus or by syndromes such as coryza, nasopharyngitis, or viral rhinosinusitis. Its pathobiology centers on infection of nasal epithelial cells via receptors such as ICAM1 for major-group rhinoviruses and LDLR family members for minor-group strains, with downstream innate immune activation through TLR3, TLR7, RIG-I/MDA5, NF-κB, and IRF3/7 signaling, inducing type I/III interferons, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, and other mediators that drive mucus production, vascular leak, and neutrophilic inflammation. Host genetic susceptibility is modest and polygenic rather than Mendelian; representative components include variants affecting ICAM1, IFIH1, TLR pathways, interferon responses, mucin genes, and 17q21 asthma-risk loci such as ORMDL3/GSDMB that may influence severity or wheeze during viral colds. Typical manifestations are rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, cough, malaise, low-grade fever, and hoarseness, with examination showing erythematous nasal mucosa and pharynx. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on acute upper respiratory symptoms without features suggesting influenza, streptococcal pharyngitis, pneumonia, or bacterial sinusitis; multiplex PCR or rapid viral testing is reserved for selected settings. Treatment is supportive, including acetaminophen or ibuprofen, which inhibit cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin synthesis for analgesic-antipyretic effects, intranasal oxymetazoline, an alpha-adrenergic agonist causing vasoconstrictive decongestion, and ipratropium nasal spray, a muscarinic antagonist that reduces rhinorrhea; antihistamines and guaifenesin are also used symptomatically, whereas antibiotics are not indicated absent bacterial complication. Common comorbidities and complications include asthma and COPD exacerbations, otitis media, acute bacterial sinusitis, viral-triggered wheezing, and occasionally lower respiratory tract infection in vulnerable patients.

Name: Condylomata Acuminata
Description: Condylomata acuminata are benign but contagious anogenital epithelial proliferations caused primarily by sexually transmitted human papillomavirus, most often low-risk HPV-6 and HPV-11, with occasional coinfection by high-risk HPV-16, HPV-18, 31, or 33 that increases dysplasia and cancer risk. Viral pathobiology is driven by infection of basal keratinocytes and expression of E6 and E7 oncoproteins, which perturb TP53 and RB1 tumor-suppressor pathways, promote cell-cycle entry through E2F, and engage PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MAPK, and innate immune signaling networks; local cytokine responses and impaired cell-mediated immunity, including in HIV infection, strongly influence persistence and recurrence. The disease is not classically inherited, but host susceptibility has genetic components involving HLA variation and immune-regulatory genes, and it is more frequent or severe in individuals with acquired or inherited immunodeficiency. Clinically, lesions are soft, flesh-colored to hyperpigmented papules or cauliflower-like exophytic warts on the vulva, penis, perineum, perianal skin, urethra, vagina, or cervix, sometimes causing pruritus, irritation, bleeding, discharge, dyspareunia, or urinary obstruction; subtypes include acuminate, papular, keratotic, flat, giant condyloma of Buschke-Lowenstein, and intraepithelial neoplasia-associated lesions. Major comorbidities and complications include other sexually transmitted infections, cervical, vulvar, penile, or anal intraepithelial neoplasia, psychological distress, pregnancy-related enlargement, and rare malignant transformation. Diagnosis is usually clinical, aided when needed by acetic acid whitening, anoscopy/colposcopy, biopsy for atypia or refractory lesions showing koilocytosis, and HPV DNA testing mainly for cervical risk stratification rather than routine wart diagnosis. Common treatments include imiquimod, a TLR7 agonist that induces interferon-mediated antiviral immunity; podofilox or podophyllotoxin, which inhibits microtubule assembly and causes wart necrosis; sinecatechins, which exert immunomodulatory and antiproliferative effects; and provider-applied trichloroacetic acid, cryotherapy, electrosurgery, laser ablation, or excision for tissue destruction.

Name: Conjunctivitis, Allergic
Description: Allergic conjunctivitis is a noninfectious, IgE-mediated inflammatory disease of the conjunctiva, usually triggered by aeroallergens and classically divided into seasonal and perennial forms, with more severe chronic subtypes including vernal keratoconjunctivitis and atopic keratoconjunctivitis; giant papillary conjunctivitis is often grouped clinically but is largely mechanical with immune contribution. It commonly presents with intense ocular itching, tearing, hyperemia, chemosis, eyelid edema, ropy or watery discharge, papillary conjunctival reaction, and, in severe disease, photophobia, punctate keratopathy, corneal shield ulcers, or vision disturbance. Pathobiology centers on allergen-driven Th2 polarization and mast-cell degranulation, with IL4, IL5, IL13, TSLP, IL33, FCER1, histamine H1 receptor signaling, eosinophil recruitment via CCL11/eotaxin and CCR3, and epithelial barrier and remodeling pathways involving filaggrin and matrix metalloproteinases; representative genetic susceptibility signals overlap with atopy, including variants near IL13, IL4R, TSLP, FLG, HLA class II loci, and FCER1A, though inheritance is typically complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. It is strongly associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis, food allergy, and keratoconus, and complications include chronic ocular surface inflammation, corneal scarring, secondary infection, and corticosteroid-induced glaucoma or cataract. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on bilateral itching plus allergen exposure history and slit-lamp evidence of papillae, chemosis, and conjunctival injection, while supportive tests include skin-prick or serum specific-IgE testing, tear eosinophils, conjunctival cytology, and occasional differential diagnosis to exclude infectious, toxic, dry-eye, or autoimmune conjunctivitis. Treatment includes topical antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizers such as olopatadine and ketotifen, which block H1 receptors and inhibit mast-cell mediator release, cromolyn sodium, which stabilizes mast cells, and short courses of topical corticosteroids such as loteprednol, which suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription; adjuncts include artificial tears, dual-action agents like azelastine, and in refractory disease topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus to inhibit calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation.

Name: Conjunctivitis, Bacterial
Description: Bacterial conjunctivitis (MeSH D003234) is an acute or chronic infectious inflammation of the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva caused most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and, in hyperacute disease, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with Chlamydia trachomatis producing a related inclusion conjunctivitis; clinically it presents with conjunctival injection, mucopurulent discharge, eyelid matting, chemosis, foreign-body sensation, tearing, and sometimes mild photophobia, while severe pain, corneal opacity, or vision loss suggest keratitis or orbital extension rather than uncomplicated disease. Pathobiology is dominated by innate immune activation rather than Mendelian inheritance, with epithelial pattern-recognition receptors including TLR2, TLR4, and NOD-like pathways sensing bacterial products and driving NF-κB, MAPK, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-α, complement, neutrophil recruitment, mucin alteration, and barrier disruption; host susceptibility has been linked more to immune and surface-defense variation than to a single causative mutation, with representative components including DEFB1, MUC1/MUC16, TLR4, and cytokine genes, but no established inheritance pattern for routine disease. Important subtypes include acute purulent, hyperacute gonococcal, chronic staphylococcal, angular, neonatal ophthalmia neonatorum, and chlamydial conjunctivitis. Diagnosis is usually clinical, based on red eye with purulent discharge and lack of prominent itching, but Gram stain, bacterial culture, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and nucleic acid amplification tests are indicated in neonates, contact-lens wearers, immunocompromised patients, recurrent or refractory cases, and suspected gonococcal or chlamydial infection. Treatment commonly includes topical erythromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit; trimethoprim-polymyxin B, which inhibits folate metabolism and disrupts the bacterial outer membrane; and fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin or ciprofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, while gonococcal disease requires systemic ceftriaxone targeting penicillin-binding proteins. Name: Conjunctivitis, Giant Papillary
Description: Allergic conjunctivitis is a noninfectious, IgE-mediated inflammatory disease of the conjunctiva, usually triggered by aeroallergens and classically divided into seasonal and perennial forms, with more severe chronic subtypes including vernal keratoconjunctivitis and atopic keratoconjunctivitis; giant papillary conjunctivitis is often grouped clinically but is largely mechanical with immune contribution. It commonly presents with intense ocular itching, tearing, hyperemia, chemosis, eyelid edema, ropy or watery discharge, papillary conjunctival reaction, and, in severe disease, photophobia, punctate keratopathy, corneal shield ulcers, or vision disturbance. Pathobiology centers on allergen-driven Th2 polarization and mast-cell degranulation, with IL4, IL5, IL13, TSLP, IL33, FCER1, histamine H1 receptor signaling, eosinophil recruitment via CCL11/eotaxin and CCR3, and epithelial barrier and remodeling pathways involving filaggrin and matrix metalloproteinases; representative genetic susceptibility signals overlap with atopy, including variants near IL13, IL4R, TSLP, FLG, HLA class II loci, and FCER1A, though inheritance is typically complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. It is strongly associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis, food allergy, and keratoconus, and complications include chronic ocular surface inflammation, corneal scarring, secondary infection, and corticosteroid-induced glaucoma or cataract. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on bilateral itching plus allergen exposure history and slit-lamp evidence of papillae, chemosis, and conjunctival injection, while supportive tests include skin-prick or serum specific-IgE testing, tear eosinophils, conjunctival cytology, and occasional differential diagnosis to exclude infectious, toxic, dry-eye, or autoimmune conjunctivitis. Treatment includes topical antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizers such as olopatadine and ketotifen, which block H1 receptors and inhibit mast-cell mediator release, cromolyn sodium, which stabilizes mast cells, and short courses of topical corticosteroids such as loteprednol, which suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription; adjuncts include artificial tears, dual-action agents like azelastine, and in refractory disease topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus to inhibit calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation.

Name: Conjunctivitis, Inclusion
Description: Inclusion conjunctivitis is an infectious mucopurulent follicular conjunctivitis caused by ocular infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, most often serovars D–K in adults and by vertical transmission in neonates; it is therefore not a classic inherited disorder, although host susceptibility and severity may be influenced by immune-response genes such as HLA class II variants and polymorphisms in cytokine pathways including TNF, IFNG, IL10, and pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR2/TLR4. Its pathobiology reflects the chlamydial biphasic developmental cycle with elementary and reticulate bodies in conjunctival epithelial cells, activation of innate immune signaling through TLRs, NF-κB, MAPK, and inflammasome-related pathways, and recruitment of neutrophils, macrophages, and Th1 cells with interferon-γ–driven responses; persistent inflammation can promote epithelial damage and scarring. Clinically, patients develop unilateral or bilateral conjunctival injection, mucopurulent discharge, marked tarsal follicular reaction, papillary hypertrophy, chemosis, preauricular lymphadenopathy, foreign-body sensation, tearing, and in neonates eyelid swelling and discharge appearing days to weeks after birth; corneal punctate keratitis or superior pannus may occur. Major subtypes include adult inclusion conjunctivitis and neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum due to C. trachomatis). Diagnosis is based on compatible follicular conjunctivitis, sexual or perinatal exposure history, and laboratory confirmation by nucleic acid amplification testing on conjunctival swabs, with Giemsa cytology, direct fluorescent antibody testing, culture, or concurrent genital-site NAAT as adjuncts. Standard therapy includes azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks the 30S subunit; and erythromycin, another 50S inhibitor commonly used in neonates; levofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, is less typical but active. Important comorbidities and complications include concurrent urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, neonatal pneumonia, keratitis, conjunctival scarring, and persistent or recurrent infection if sexual partners or maternal genital infection are untreated.

Name: Constipation
Description: Constipation (MeSH D003248) is a common gastrointestinal disorder defined by infrequent, difficult, or incomplete defecation and is usually classified as functional constipation, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, opioid-induced constipation, or secondary constipation due to neurologic, endocrine, metabolic, structural, or medication-related causes; clinically it presents with fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements weekly, hard stools, excessive straining, bloating, abdominal discomfort, anorectal blockage, and a sense of incomplete evacuation, while complications include fecal impaction, hemorrhoids, anal fissures, rectal prolapse, megacolon, and impaired quality of life, and comorbidities commonly include IBS, pelvic floor dyssynergia, Parkinson disease, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, depression, and chronic opioid exposure. Pathobiology involves disordered colonic motility, altered enteric neuromuscular transmission, impaired rectoanal coordination, and disturbed epithelial fluid secretion, with relevant pathways including serotonergic 5-HT4 signaling, cholinergic and nitrergic enteric pathways, guanylate cyclase-C/cGMP/CFTR-mediated chloride and water secretion, prostaglandin-mediated chloride channel activation, and peripheral mu-opioid receptor signaling that suppresses propulsive motility. Genetic contributions are usually complex and non-Mendelian in ordinary functional constipation, but rare inherited forms occur, particularly Hirschsprung disease, caused by defective enteric nervous system development involving RET, EDNRB, EDN3, GDNF, SOX10, PHOX2B, or ZEB2 mutations, often with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance or recessive patterns in some families; channelopathies and connective-tissue disorders may also predispose. Diagnosis is primarily clinical using Rome IV criteria, Bristol stool form assessment, medication and alarm-feature review, digital rectal examination, and selective testing with thyroid and metabolic studies, colonoscopy when indicated, colonic transit studies, radiopaque marker or scintigraphic testing, anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion testing, and defecography. Name: Corneal Abrasions
Description: Corneal abrasion (UMLS C0010032) is an acute superficial epithelial defect of the cornea, usually traumatic or contact lens related rather than a primary genetic disease, characterized clinically by sudden ocular pain, foreign-body sensation, tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm, conjunctival injection, and reduced vision, with diagnosis based on history, slit-lamp examination, and fluorescein staining showing a well-demarcated epithelial defect, often supplemented by eyelid eversion to detect a retained foreign body, Seidel testing when perforation is suspected, and microbiologic cultures if infectious keratitis is a concern. Although most cases are acquired, genetic contributors are relevant through disorders that predispose to recurrent epithelial breakdown, particularly corneal dystrophies involving TGFBI mutations and epithelial adhesion abnormalities linked to KRT3, KRT12, COL17A1, or laminin-integrin hemidesmosomal components; inheritance in these settings is commonly autosomal dominant for TGFBI-related dystrophies, while other epithelial fragility syndromes may be dominant or recessive. Pathobiology centers on epithelial injury, cell migration, and basement membrane repair, involving EGFR, TGF-β, IL-1, TNF-α, matrix metalloproteinases, integrins, and focal adhesion signaling, with neutrophilic inflammation and, in healing, limbal stem-cell and keratocyte responses. Major subtypes include traumatic, foreign-body, contact lens-associated, recurrent corneal erosion-related, and chemical or UV-associated abrasions. Common treatments include topical erythromycin, a macrolide that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, or polymyxin B/trimethoprim, which disrupts bacterial membranes and inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, for prophylaxis in uncomplicated cases; fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, are preferred when Pseudomonas risk is present in contact lens wearers; cyclopentolate or homatropine, muscarinic antagonists, may relieve ciliary spasm, and oral NSAIDs reduce cyclooxygenase-mediated pain. Important comorbidities and complications include dry eye disease, diabetes, blepharitis, epithelial basement membrane dystrophy, recurrent erosions, infectious keratitis, corneal ulceration, scarring, and rarely vision-threatening perforation.

Name: Corneal Ulcer
Description: Corneal ulcer is an inflammatory, usually infectious, epithelial-stromal defect of the cornea that constitutes an ophthalmic emergency; it most often follows bacterial, fungal, viral, or protozoal keratitis, but may also arise in sterile neurotrophic, autoimmune, exposure, or peripheral ulcerative forms. Typical symptoms include severe ocular pain, foreign-body sensation, photophobia, redness, tearing, discharge, blurred vision, and reduced visual acuity, while signs include a fluorescein-staining epithelial defect with stromal infiltrate, edema, anterior chamber reaction, hypopyon, and in severe cases thinning or perforation. Molecularly, host susceptibility and tissue destruction are linked to inflammatory and wound-healing pathways involving TLR2/TLR4, IL1B, IL6, TNF, CXCL8/IL-8, NF-κB, MAPK, VEGF, MMP-2, MMP-9, and neutrophil recruitment; representative genetic contributors include PAX6 in aniridia-related keratopathy, TGFBI in stromal dystrophies predisposing to recurrent breakdown, and NTRK1/NGF-pathway defects in congenital corneal anesthesia, whereas inheritance of ulcer itself is generally not Mendelian except through such predisposing disorders. Common pathogens and virulence-associated host interactions include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Fusarium, Aspergillus, Candida, herpes simplex virus, and Acanthamoeba. Comorbidities and risk factors include contact lens wear, trauma, dry eye, blepharitis, lagophthalmos, diabetes, vitamin A deficiency, rheumatoid arthritis, and immunosuppression; complications include scarring, astigmatism, endophthalmitis, descemetocele, perforation, and blindness. Diagnosis is based on slit-lamp examination, fluorescein staining, corneal sensation assessment, and when infectious disease is suspected, corneal scraping for Gram stain, KOH, Giemsa, culture, and increasingly PCR or confocal microscopy for Acanthamoeba/fungal disease. Name: Cough
Description: Cough is a protective airway reflex rather than a single disease, arising from stimulation or hypersensitization of vagal sensory afferents in the larynx, trachea, and bronchi; clinically it is classified as acute, subacute, or chronic, and mechanistically may be productive or nonproductive, with common symptoms including throat irritation, paroxysms of expiratory effort, sputum production, wheeze, chest discomfort, hoarseness, and sleep disruption. Key molecular components include airway sensory neurons expressing TRPV1, TRPA1, P2X3, neurokinin-1 signaling, and inflammatory mediators such as substance P, prostaglandins, histamine, bradykinin, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and eosinophil-associated pathways; representative genes implicated in cough susceptibility or endotypes include P2RX3, TRPV1, TRPA1, TACR1, NGF, ADRB2, IL13, and eosinophilic/asthmatic cough-related variants in TSLP and GATA3, although inheritance is usually not Mendelian and genetic contributions are polygenic and context dependent. Major causes and comorbidities include viral upper respiratory infection, asthma and cough-variant asthma, eosinophilic bronchitis, COPD, gastroesophageal reflux disease, upper airway cough syndrome, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, heart failure, tuberculosis, lung cancer, and ACE inhibitor exposure; complications include syncope, rib fracture, urinary incontinence, vomiting, and impaired quality of life. Diagnosis relies on history and physical examination, duration of symptoms, medication review, red-flag assessment, chest radiography, spirometry with bronchodilator testing, and selected tests such as methacholine challenge, FeNO, sputum eosinophils, reflux evaluation, CT, bronchoscopy, or microbiology when indicated. Name: Cowpox
Description: Cowpox is a rare zoonotic orthopoxvirus infection caused by cowpox virus, a double-stranded DNA virus in the Poxviridae family, typically acquired from infected cats, rodents, or other animals and usually presenting as a localized cutaneous disease in humans rather than an inherited disorder. Viral pathogenicity is mediated by orthopoxvirus genes encoding immune-evasion and host-range proteins, with representative examples including viral hemagglutinin, serpins such as crmA/SPI-2 that inhibit caspase-1–dependent inflammatory responses, complement-control proteins, and ankyrin-repeat host-range factors; host antiviral determinants relevant to susceptibility and severity include interferon pathway components such as IFNAR1, STAT1, TLR3, and cellular entry or replication factors, although no specific Mendelian inheritance pattern is established for cowpox itself. Disease biology involves epithelial infection, cytoplasmic viral replication, and modulation of NF-κB, type I interferon/JAK-STAT, TNF, chemokine, and inflammasome-related pathways, with macrophages, dendritic cells, keratinocytes, and T cells contributing to lesion evolution. Patients classically develop a painful papule progressing to vesicle, pustule, ulcer, and black eschar with surrounding erythema, often with fever, malaise, regional lymphadenopathy, and occasionally ocular or generalized disease. Clinical forms include localized cutaneous cowpox, ocular cowpox, and disseminated or severe infection in immunocompromised hosts or those with atopic dermatitis. Important complications and comorbid associations include secondary bacterial infection, cellulitis, keratitis, pneumonia, encephalitis, extensive necrosis, eczema vaccinatum-like disease, and severe disease in transplant recipients or patients with hematologic malignancy. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus characteristic lesions, confirmed by orthopoxvirus PCR from lesion material, electron microscopy, viral culture in specialized laboratories, histopathology showing ballooning degeneration and eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions, serology, and sequencing for species-level identification. Treatment is mainly supportive, but severe cases may be treated with tecovirimat, which inhibits the viral VP37 protein and blocks virion egress, brincidofovir or cidofovir, nucleotide analog inhibitors of viral DNA polymerase, and vaccinia immune globulin for passive orthopoxvirus antibody-mediated neutralization.

Name: Congenital Hypothyroidism
Description: Congenital hypothyroidism (C0010308) is a neonatal endocrine disorder caused by deficient thyroid hormone production or action present at birth, most commonly from thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, ectopy, hypoplasia) or dyshormonogenesis, and more rarely from central hypothyroidism, thyroid hormone transport defects, or resistance; primary genetic contributors include developmental transcription factors and signaling genes such as PAX8, NKX2-1/TTF1, FOXE1/TTF2, NKX2-5, TSHR, and GLIS3, and biosynthetic genes including SLC5A5/NIS, SLC26A4, TG, TPO, DUOX2, DUOXA2, IYD, and SECISBP2, while central forms involve TSHB, TRHR, IGSF1, TBL1X, and IRS4. Disease biology centers on the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis, with TRH-TSH signaling through the TSH receptor–Gs–cAMP pathway stimulating iodide uptake, thyroglobulin iodination, and T4/T3 synthesis; disruption of deiodinase-mediated hormone activation and nuclear thyroid hormone receptor signaling impairs brain maturation, growth, myelination, and skeletal development. Most cases are sporadic, whereas dyshormonogenesis is often autosomal recessive; PAX8, TSHR, NKX2-1, and FOXE1 defects may show autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance, and some central forms are X-linked. Typical findings include prolonged jaundice, lethargy, feeding difficulty, constipation, hypotonia, macroglossia, large fontanelles, umbilical hernia, hoarse cry, hypothermia, dry skin, and poor growth, though many infants are initially asymptomatic. Major complications include irreversible intellectual disability, hearing impairment, developmental delay, short stature, and cardiometabolic effects if treatment is delayed; associated disorders may include congenital heart disease, cleft palate, choanal atresia, and neurologic or pulmonary disease in syndromic cases. Diagnosis relies on newborn screening showing elevated TSH with low free T4 in primary disease or low free T4 with low/normal TSH in central disease, confirmed by serum thyroid tests, thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide scan, thyroglobulin and perchlorate discharge testing in selected cases

Name: Crohn Disease
Description: Crohn disease (MeSH D003424) is a chronic, relapsing, transmural inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, most often the terminal ileum and colon, and is commonly classified by location and behavior into ileal, colonic, ileocolonic, and upper GI forms, and into inflammatory, stricturing, or penetrating subtypes. It arises from polygenic susceptibility interacting with environmental and microbial factors; key genetic associations include NOD2/CARD15 variants, ATG16L1, IRGM, IL23R, JAK2, STAT3, TNFSF15, and genes involved in epithelial barrier and autophagy, with familial clustering showing complex, non-Mendelian inheritance. Pathobiology features dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, defective bacterial sensing and autophagy, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and activation of TNF, IL-12/IL-23, Th1/Th17, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, integrin-mediated leukocyte trafficking, and MAPK-related inflammatory pathways. Typical manifestations include chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, fever, growth failure in children, perianal disease, and extraintestinal findings such as arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, and hepatobiliary disease. Important complications include strictures, fistulas, abscesses, bowel obstruction, malabsorption, anemia, osteoporosis, venous thromboembolism, and increased colorectal and small-bowel adenocarcinoma risk. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical presentation with ileocolonoscopy and histology showing chronic active, often patchy inflammation, aphthous or deep linear ulcers, and sometimes noncaseating granulomas, supported by fecal calprotectin, CRP/ESR, stool studies to exclude infection, CT or MR enterography, capsule endoscopy in selected patients, and serologies such as ASCA with limited specificity. Common treatments include corticosteroids for broad anti-inflammatory suppression, azathioprine or methotrexate as immunomodulators, anti-TNF agents such as infliximab or adalimumab that neutralize TNF-alpha, ustekinumab targeting IL-12/23 p40, and vedolizumab blocking alpha4beta7 integrin-dependent gut lymphocyte trafficking.

Name: Cryptococcus neoformans Infections
Description: Cryptococcosis (MeSH D003453) is an opportunistic invasive mycosis caused mainly by Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii, acquired by inhalation with primary pulmonary infection and potential hematogenous dissemination, especially to the central nervous system, producing pulmonary cryptococcosis, cryptococcemia, and meningoencephalitis. Disease risk is strongly shaped by host immune genetics rather than Mendelian inheritance, with susceptibility linked to defects in CD4 T-cell immunity and variants or deficiencies affecting IFN-γ/IL-12 signaling, CSF2/GM-CSF, Fcγ receptors, mannose-binding lectin, GATA2, STAT1 gain-of-function, and X-linked CD40LG, alongside acquired states such as HIV/AIDS, solid-organ transplantation, corticosteroid use, sarcoidosis, hematologic malignancy, and anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies. Key pathogenic pathways include fungal polysaccharide capsule and melanin-mediated immune evasion, macrophage and microglial interactions, Th1/Th17 responses, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-12/STAT4 signaling, complement activation, and cryptococcal traversal of the blood-brain barrier. Typical manifestations include fever, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, headache, vomiting, cranial neuropathies, visual changes, altered mental status, meningismus, and raised intracranial pressure; complications include hydrocephalus, stroke, blindness, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, respiratory failure, and death. Diagnosis relies on serum and cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen testing, India ink or histopathology demonstrating encapsulated budding yeasts, fungal culture, CSF opening pressure and chemistry, blood cultures, neuroimaging, and speciation when needed. Treatment commonly uses amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores, plus flucytosine, a pyrimidine analogue that inhibits fungal DNA and RNA synthesis, for induction, followed by fluconazole, a triazole that inhibits lanosterol 14-α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; alternatives or adjuncts include voriconazole or itraconazole for selected pulmonary or refractory cases.

Name: Cryptorchidism
Description: Cryptorchidism (UMLS C0010417) is a common congenital disorder of testicular descent, defined by absence of one or both testes from the scrotum because of arrested abdominal, inguinal, or ectopic migration, and it is classified as unilateral or bilateral, palpable or nonpalpable, congenital or acquired/ascending. Its pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving disturbed hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal signaling and abnormal gubernacular development, with implicated genes and proteins including INSL3 and its receptor RXFP2, androgen receptor signaling, CYP17A1, SRD5A2, HOXA10, WT1, NR5A1, AMH and AMHR2, and variants in genes causing disorders of sex development; endocrine-disrupting influences may also contribute. Key pathways include androgen biosynthesis and AR-mediated signaling, INSL3-RXFP2 signaling required for transabdominal descent, anti-Müllerian hormone pathways, and gonadotropin regulation by LH and hCG acting on Leydig cells to support testosterone production. Clinical findings are an empty or underdeveloped hemiscrotum and absent, high, or ectopic testis on examination, sometimes with associated inguinal hernia; bilateral cases may raise concern for hypogonadism or a syndromic/DSD etiology. Important complications and comorbidities include subfertility or infertility, impaired spermatogenesis, testicular torsion, trauma, inguinal hernia, testicular atrophy, and increased risk of testicular germ cell tumor, particularly seminoma. Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering occurs with complex/polygenic inheritance, and cryptorchidism can appear in syndromes such as Kallmann, Prader-Willi, Noonan, and various 46,XY DSDs. Diagnosis is primarily clinical by repeated careful physical examination; ultrasound has limited value for nonpalpable testes, while diagnostic laparoscopy is the reference standard when localization is unclear; hormonal evaluation, karyotype, and targeted genetic testing are indicated in bilateral nonpalpable testes or suspected DSD. Name: Cryptosporidiosis
Description: Cryptosporidiosis is a protozoal enteric infection caused mainly by Cryptosporidium hominis and C. parvum, producing a self-limited to severe diarrheal disease depending on host immunity; it is not a classic inherited disorder, but susceptibility and severity are influenced by host genetic factors, with reported associations involving immune genes such as IFNG, TNF, IL10, TLR2, TLR4, MBL2, HLA class II loci, and defects in CD40LG or IFN-γ/IL-12 axis function in primary immunodeficiency, while the parasite’s virulence is linked to surface glycoproteins including gp40/15 and Cp23. Pathogenesis centers on attachment and intracellular-extracytoplasmic residence in intestinal epithelial cells, triggering innate and adaptive signaling through Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, interferon-γ, IL-12/STAT4, and chemokine-mediated pathways, with CD4+ T-cell immunity being critical for clearance. Typical manifestations are profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, anorexia, weight loss, and dehydration; chronic infection can cause malabsorption, failure to thrive, and wasting, especially in children, people with AIDS, transplant recipients, and patients with hypogammaglobulinemia or severe combined immunodeficiency. Major complications include persistent cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, sclerosing cholangitis, and extraintestinal biliary disease. Clinical forms include acute, persistent, chronic, intestinal, and extraintestinal disease. Diagnosis is established by stool detection of oocysts using modified acid-fast stain, direct fluorescent antibody testing, enzyme immunoassay for antigen, or PCR-based panels, with repeated stool examinations often improving sensitivity; small-bowel biopsy may show organisms on the brush border in difficult cases. Treatment relies on nitazoxanide, which interferes with pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase-dependent anaerobic energy metabolism, with supportive oral or intravenous rehydration and electrolyte replacement; in HIV, immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy is essential, while paromomycin, a nonabsorbed aminoglycoside that inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit, and azithromycin, a macrolide that inhibits 50S ribosomal protein synthesis, are sometimes used with variable efficacy.

Name: Cyclitis
Description: Cyclitis (UMLS C0010543) is inflammation of the ciliary body and is usually classified within anterior or intermediate uveitis, occurring as acute, recurrent, or chronic nongranulomatous or granulomatous disease, and less often as part of panuveitis. It is typically immune mediated rather than a monogenic inherited disorder, although genetic susceptibility is well recognized, especially HLA-B27 in acute anterior uveitis and HLA-DRB1, IL23R, ERAP1, TNF, and CTLA4 variants in broader uveitic phenotypes; in specific syndromic or posterior-associated entities, mutations in NOD2, CAPN5, or genes causing Behçet disease susceptibility may be relevant. Pathobiology centers on breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier with activation of innate and adaptive immunity, including antigen-presenting cells, Th1 and Th17 lymphocytes, TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-17, IL-23, interferon-gamma, NF-kappaB, JAK/STAT, and complement-related inflammatory cascades. Patients present with ocular pain, photophobia, redness, blurred vision, lacrimation, ciliary flush, cells and flare in the anterior chamber, keratic precipitates, vitreous cells if pars planitis overlaps, and sometimes decreased accommodation or hypotony. Common associations include ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis, Behçet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, herpes simplex or zoster, tuberculosis, and syphilis; complications include posterior synechiae, cataract, band keratopathy, cystoid macular edema, glaucoma, hypotony, and vision loss. Diagnosis is clinical, based on slit-lamp examination and grading of anterior chamber inflammation, intraocular pressure assessment, dilated fundus examination, and targeted testing such as OCT, fluorescein angiography, ultrasound, HLA-B27 typing, ACE, syphilis and TB studies, and aqueous or vitreous PCR when infection is suspected. Treatment commonly includes prednisolone acetate or difluprednate eye drops, which suppress glucocorticoid-responsive cytokine transcription, cycloplegics such as atropine or cyclopentolate to relieve ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae, and systemic or local immunomodulators including methotrexate, adalimumab, or

Name: Cystic Fibrosis
Description: Cystic fibrosis is a multisystem autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in CFTR on chromosome 7q31, encoding the ATP-binding cassette chloride and bicarbonate channel CFTR; representative mutations include F508del, G551D, G542X, and N1303K, with disease subtypes often defined by pancreatic sufficiency versus insufficiency and by mutation class causing defective protein production, processing, gating, conductance, or stability. Impaired CFTR function disrupts epithelial ion and water transport, with secondary ENaC hyperactivity, airway surface dehydration, defective mucociliary clearance, abnormal innate immune signaling, neutrophil-dominant inflammation, chronic biofilm infection, and progressive bronchiectatic lung injury. Typical manifestations include chronic cough, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, wheeze, nasal polyposis, failure to thrive, steatorrhea, meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstruction, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, male infertility from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, and later CF-related diabetes, liver disease, and osteoporosis. Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and especially Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Major complications and comorbidities include bronchiectasis, hemoptysis, pneumothorax, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, chronic rhinosinusitis, pancreatitis, and depression/anxiety. Treatment includes CFTR modulators such as ivacaftor, a potentiator that increases channel opening; lumacaftor or tezacaftor, correctors that improve folding and trafficking of F508del CFTR; and elexacaftor, a next-generation corrector used in triple therapy with tezacaftor/ivacaftor, plus dornase alfa, which cleaves extracellular DNA to reduce sputum viscosity, inhaled hypertonic saline to rehydrate airway secretions, azithromycin for anti-inflammatory and anti-biofilm effects, and inhaled tobramycin for antipseudomonal therapy. Diagnosis relies on compatible phenotype or newborn screening with elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen, confirmed by sweat chloride testing, CFTR genotyping, and when needed nasal potential difference or intestinal current measurements.

Name: Cystinuria
Description: Cystinuria is a hereditary renal tubular transport disorder and classic inborn error of amino acid handling characterized by defective proximal tubular and intestinal reabsorption of cystine and the dibasic amino acids ornithine, lysine, and arginine, causing recurrent cystine urolithiasis. It is most commonly due to biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC3A1, encoding the heavy chain rBAT, or SLC7A9, encoding the light chain b0,+AT, which together form the apical heteromeric cystine/dibasic amino acid transporter of proximal tubular cells; representative mutations include missense, nonsense, splice-site, and deletion variants such as SLC3A1 p.Met467Thr and SLC7A9 p.Gly105Arg. The key pathogenic pathway is failure of epithelial amino acid transport across the brush-border membrane, leading to high urinary cystine supersaturation, crystal nucleation, and stone formation rather than a canonical inflammatory signaling cascade. Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive, although SLC7A9-related disease may show variable penetrance or apparent dominant transmission in some families; traditional phenotypic subtypes include type A, type B, and mixed AB cystinuria. Typical manifestations are childhood to early-adult recurrent nephrolithiasis, renal colic, hematuria, dysuria, urinary obstruction, gravel passage, and recurrent urinary tract infection, with complications including hydronephrosis, chronic kidney disease, renal scarring, and reduced quality of life; hypertension and infection-related morbidity may occur as comorbidities. Diagnosis rests on recurrent cystine stones, hexagonal cystine crystals on urine microscopy, elevated 24-hour urinary cystine or cystine capacity testing, positive cyanide-nitroprusside screening, stone analysis, and confirmation by molecular testing of SLC3A1/SLC7A9. Treatment centers on high fluid intake and dietary sodium reduction, plus urinary alkalinization with potassium citrate or potassium bicarbonate to increase cystine solubility; thiol drugs such as tiopronin, D-penicillamine, and captopril reduce free cystine by forming more soluble disulfide complexes, while procedures including lithotripsy or ureteroscopy are used for established stones.

Name: Cystitis
Description: Cystitis (MeSH D003556) is an inflammatory disorder of the urinary bladder, most often acute bacterial lower urinary tract infection caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli, but also occurring as recurrent uncomplicated cystitis, complicated cystitis, catheter-associated cystitis, radiation- or drug-induced hemorrhagic cystitis, eosinophilic cystitis, and interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome. Clinically it presents with dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain or pressure, nocturia, cloudy or malodorous urine, and sometimes hematuria, while fever, flank pain, or systemic toxicity suggest extension beyond isolated bladder disease. Pathobiology centers on urothelial adherence and invasion mediated by bacterial fimbriae binding uroplakins and host receptors, with activation of TLR4-, NF-κB-, IL-6/IL-8-, CXCL8-, and neutrophil-driven innate immune pathways; epithelial barrier and sensory signaling abnormalities involving GAG-layer disruption, mast cells, NGF, substance P, TRPV1, purinergic signaling, and cytokines such as TNF and IL1B are emphasized in interstitial cystitis. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex rather than Mendelian, with reported associations involving TLR4, CXCR1/CXCR2, IL8, VEGFA, NGF, HLA variants, and uroplakin-related host defense biology; rare inherited anatomic or voiding disorders may secondarily predispose. Common treatments include nitrofurantoin, which is reduced by bacterial nitroreductases to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which sequentially inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and dihydropteroate synthase; fosfomycin, which inhibits MurA and cell-wall synthesis; and, for symptom relief, phenazopyridine, a urinary tract analgesic. Diagnosis relies on symptoms plus urinalysis showing pyuria, bacteriuria, leukocyte esterase or nitrites, with urine culture for complicated, recurrent, male, pregnant, or treatment-failure cases; cystoscopy, imaging, urine cytology, or biopsy are reserved for hematuria, obstruction, suspected interstitial cystitis, stones, tumor, or other alternative diagnoses. Name: Cytomegalovirus Infections
Description: Cytomegalovirus infection is a common opportunistic disease caused by human herpesvirus 5, a double-stranded DNA beta-herpesvirus that establishes lifelong latency in monocytes, myeloid progenitors, and endothelial cells with reactivation during impaired cellular immunity. Viral pathogenicity involves immediate-early regulators IE1/IE2 (UL123/UL122), entry glycoproteins gB/UL55 and the gH/gL/UL128-131 pentamer, tegument phosphoprotein pp65/UL83, DNA polymerase UL54, kinase UL97, and immune-evasion genes including UL16, UL18, UL40, and UL111A; host susceptibility is influenced by T-cell, NK-cell, and interferon pathways, with examples including TLR2, TLR9, IFNAR1, STAT1, IL10, NKG2C/KLRC2, HLA variation, and severe Mendelian predisposition in primary immunodeficiencies affecting SCID-related genes or GATA2. Key signaling pathways include viral activation of NF-kappaB, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MAPK/ERK, JAK-STAT interferon signaling, apoptosis/autophagy control, and antigen-presentation suppression. Disease ranges from asymptomatic infection or heterophile-negative mononucleosis in immunocompetent hosts to congenital CMV, perinatal infection, and severe tissue-invasive disease in transplant recipients and people with advanced HIV, causing fever, malaise, hepatitis, cytopenias, pneumonitis, colitis, esophagitis, retinitis, encephalitis, and congenital sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, jaundice, petechiae, and growth restriction. Major complications include graft rejection, secondary bacterial or fungal infection, neurodevelopmental delay, and vision loss, with important comorbid settings including prematurity, transplantation, HIV/AIDS, and other immunosuppressive states. Diagnosis relies on clinical context plus quantitative CMV PCR or nucleic acid testing in blood or CSF, pp65 antigenemia, culture less commonly, histopathology showing cytomegalic cells with intranuclear inclusions, and serology for primary infection; congenital disease is established by PCR from saliva or urine within 21 days of life. Name: Dacryocystitis
Description: Dacryocystitis (UMLS C0010930) is an inflammatory, usually infectious disorder of the lacrimal sac that most often results from nasolacrimal duct obstruction, producing tear stasis and secondary bacterial overgrowth; acute disease is typically pyogenic, whereas chronic dacryocystitis is characterized by persistent low-grade inflammation and epiphora. Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, beta-hemolytic streptococci, Haemophilus influenzae, and in chronic cases mixed flora including anaerobes; the relevant molecular biology is largely inflammatory rather than disease-specific, with activation of innate immune pathways such as TLR/NF-kB signaling, neutrophil and macrophage recruitment, and cytokine mediators including IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and chemokines driving edema, pain, and mucopurulent secretion. No single Mendelian genetic cause is established for typical acquired dacryocystitis, and inheritance is generally absent, but congenital cases reflect developmental anomalies of the lacrimal drainage system that may occur sporadically or with craniofacial syndromes involving genes such as FGFR2, TCOF1, or TP63 in selected syndromic contexts. Clinical findings include epiphora, painful erythematous swelling below the medial canthus, tenderness over the lacrimal sac, reflux of purulent material on pressure, fever in severe cases, and chronic tearing with recurrent conjunctivitis in longstanding disease; major subtypes are congenital versus acquired and acute versus chronic. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by lacrimal sac expression and culture, slit-lamp and nasal examination, fluorescein dye disappearance testing in infants, probing and irrigation to confirm obstruction, and when complicated, CT or MRI to assess abscess, sinus disease, orbital spread, or tumor. Treatment commonly includes amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and extends beta-lactam coverage through beta-lactamase inhibition, cephalexin or cefazolin, also cell-wall synthesis inhibitors, and clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; topical fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, while definitive management of obstructive disease is often dacryocystorhinostomy.
