Name: Senile Dementia
Description: Senile dementia, a historical umbrella term now largely encompassed by major neurocognitive disorders of late life, most commonly reflects Alzheimer disease pathology but may also include vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, or mixed dementias; it is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative syndrome characterized by decline in memory and at least one other cognitive domain severe enough to impair independence, with typical symptoms including episodic memory loss, disorientation, executive dysfunction, aphasia, visuospatial impairment, apathy, agitation, sleep disturbance, gait instability, hallucinations in Lewy body disease, and later dysphagia and incontinence. Key molecular associations are most established for Alzheimer-type senile dementia and include APP, PSEN1, PSEN2, and APOE, especially APOE e4, with proteins and lesions involving amyloid-beta, tau/MAPT, cholinergic neuronal loss, alpha-synuclein in Lewy body cases, TDP-43 in some mixed phenotypes, and vascular injury pathways; implicated signaling mechanisms include amyloidogenic APP processing by beta-secretase and gamma-secretase, tau hyperphosphorylation via GSK3beta/CDK5, glutamatergic excitotoxicity through NMDA receptors, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation involving microglia, complement, and cytokines, and cerebrovascular endothelial dysfunction. Most cases are sporadic and multifactorial, while early-onset familial forms are usually autosomal dominant through APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2 mutations; risk is also modified by APOE and other loci such as TREM2. Common treatments are donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors that enhance central cholinergic transmission, and memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist that reduces excitotoxicity; antipsychotics or SSRIs are sometimes used symptomatically with caution. Frequent comorbidities and complications include depression, delirium, falls, frailty, malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia, urinary tract infection, stroke, and caregiver burden. Diagnosis relies on history, informant report, cognitive testing such as MMSE or MoCA, functional assessment, neurologic examination, laboratory exclusion of reversible causes, MRI or CT for atrophy or vascular disease, and selected biomarker testing with CSF amyloid-beta/tau or amyloid/tau PET when etiology is uncertain.

Name: Depressive Disorder
Description: Depressive disorder (MeSH D003866) is a heterogeneous, multifactorial mood disorder that includes major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), melancholic, atypical, psychotic, seasonal, peripartum, and bipolar-depression phenotypes, characterized clinically by persistent low mood or anhedonia with changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, psychomotor activity, guilt, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation, often accompanied by cognitive impairment and somatic symptoms. Its pathobiology is polygenic and environmentally modulated, with heritability typically around 30–40% for major depression; implicated genes and proteins include SLC6A4/5-HTT, BDNF, FKBP5, CRHR1, TPH2, HTR2A, COMT, MAOA, and circadian genes such as CLOCK, with representative variants including the SLC6A4 5-HTTLPR and BDNF Val66Met polymorphisms, although no single mutation is determinative and inheritance is generally complex rather than Mendelian. Key pathways involve monoaminergic neurotransmission in serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine circuits, dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis with cortisol excess, impaired BDNF-TrkB neuroplasticity, glutamatergic/NMDA signaling, GABAergic deficits, inflammatory cytokine pathways including IL-6 and TNF-α, and altered intracellular cAMP-CREB and MAPK signaling. Common treatments include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine and sertraline, which inhibit SERT; serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors such as venlafaxine, which blocks SERT and NET; bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor; mirtazapine, an α2-adrenergic antagonist enhancing noradrenergic and serotonergic transmission; and esketamine, an NMDA receptor antagonist with rapid antidepressant effects. Frequent comorbidities include anxiety disorders, substance use, chronic pain, cardiovascular and metabolic disease, sleep disorders, and increased risk of suicide and functional disability. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 or ICD criteria requiring symptom clusters and functional impairment over time, supported by standardized scales such as PHQ-9 or HAM-D, psychiatric assessment, suicide risk evaluation, and laboratory testing to exclude mimics

Name: Dermatitis, Exfoliative
Description: Exfoliative dermatitis (erythroderma) is a severe inflammatory reaction pattern rather than a single disease, defined by diffuse erythema and scaling involving most of the body surface area, often with pruritus, pain, edema, chills, fever, lymphadenopathy, nail and hair changes, and risk of dehydration, hypothermia, high-output cardiac failure, and secondary infection. It arises most commonly from psoriasis, atopic or contact dermatitis, drug hypersensitivity, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, or idiopathic causes, and subtypes are therefore classified by underlying etiology, including psoriatic erythroderma, eczematous erythroderma, drug-induced erythroderma, and malignancy-associated erythroderma. Molecular drivers reflect the cause and include T-cell–mediated cytokine networks with TNF, IL-17, IL-23, IL-4, IL-13, IFN-gamma, and NF-kappaB/JAK-STAT signaling; representative genetic associations are PSORS1/HLA-C*06:02 in psoriasis, FLG loss-of-function variants in atopic dermatitis, and occasional CARD14, IL36RN, or DSG1 abnormalities in pustular or barrier-disruption phenotypes that may exfoliate. Inheritance is usually complex and polygenic, although rare genodermatoses presenting with generalized exfoliation may be autosomal dominant or recessive depending on the causative gene. Diagnosis is clinical, based on generalized erythema and desquamation, with evaluation for triggers by history, medication review, CBC with eosinophils, metabolic panel, albumin, inflammatory markers, cultures when infection is suspected, skin biopsy to identify psoriasis, eczema, drug eruption, or cutaneous lymphoma, and sometimes T-cell receptor clonality or flow cytometry. Treatment centers on supportive care and therapy of the cause: topical corticosteroids suppress inflammatory gene transcription, cyclosporine inhibits calcineurin and T-cell activation, methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and lymphocyte proliferation, systemic retinoids normalize keratinocyte differentiation, and biologics such as infliximab or ustekinumab block TNF or IL-12/23 pathways; common comorbidities include psoriasis, atopy, malignancy, drug reactions, sepsis, electrolyte imbalance, and protein loss.

Name: Dermatitis Herpetiformis
Description: Dermatitis herpetiformis (MeSH D003874) is a chronic, intensely pruritic autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder regarded as the specific cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy/celiac disease, characterized clinically by symmetric grouped papules, urticarial plaques, vesicles, and excoriations on extensor surfaces such as the elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp, and back, with burning and severe itch often exceeding visible blistering. Its strongest genetic associations are HLA class II alleles involved in gluten antigen presentation, especially HLA-DQ2.5 encoded by DQA1*05:01 and DQB1*02:01 and HLA-DQ8 encoded by DQA1*03 and DQB1*03:02, while autoantigenic proteins include tissue transglutaminase/TGM2 in the gut and epidermal transglutaminase/TGM3 in skin; inheritance is complex polygenic rather than Mendelian, with familial clustering and overlap with celiac disease. Pathogenesis centers on gluten-driven adaptive immunity, deamidation of gliadin by TGM2, HLA-DQ2/DQ8-restricted T-cell activation, IgA autoantibody formation against TGM2 and TGM3, granular IgA deposition in dermal papillae, complement activation, neutrophil chemotaxis with microabscess formation, and protease-mediated dermal-epidermal separation. Common treatment includes dapsone, which rapidly suppresses neutrophil-mediated inflammation through inhibition of myeloperoxidase-dependent oxidative injury and chemotaxis; sulfapyridine and sulfasalazine, alternative sulfonamides with anti-inflammatory effects on neutrophils; and a strict gluten-free diet, which removes the antigenic trigger and gradually clears skin and enteropathy. Linked comorbidities include celiac disease, iron/folate/B12 deficiency, osteoporosis, autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, and rarely enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma if untreated. Diagnosis relies on compatible phenotype plus direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showing granular IgA at dermal papillae/basement membrane, supportive serology for IgA anti-endomysial, anti-TGM2, and anti-TGM3 antibodies, HLA typing when needed, and small-bowel biopsy in selected cases; recognized variants are mainly classic generalized dermatitis

Name: Dermatitis, Atopic
Description: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing, intensely pruritic inflammatory dermatosis driven by epidermal barrier dysfunction and type 2-skewed immune activation, typically beginning in childhood but occurring at any age; hallmark findings include xerosis, eczematous erythematous papules and plaques, excoriations, lichenification, sleep disturbance, and age-dependent flexural, facial, hand, or extensor involvement, with recognized intrinsic and extrinsic forms and infantile, childhood, and adult subtypes. Its genetic architecture is complex and polygenic, with the strongest replicated risk conferred by loss-of-function FLG mutations affecting filaggrin, and additional associations involving SPINK5, CLDN1, KIF3A, OVOL1, TSLP, IL4, IL13, IL4R, STAT6, and genes in epidermal differentiation and immune regulation; inheritance is not Mendelian in most cases but shows familial clustering with multifactorial susceptibility. Central pathways include barrier injury with reduced ceramides and tight-junction integrity, keratinocyte alarmins such as TSLP, IL-25, and IL-33, Th2 cytokine signaling through IL-4/IL-13-JAK-STAT, contributions from Th22, Th17, and Th1 axes in chronic or subtype-specific disease, eosinophilic and mast-cell inflammation, pruritus mediated partly by IL-31 and sensory nerve activation, and frequent Staphylococcus aureus dysbiosis. Common comorbidities include asthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergy, eosinophilic esophagitis, chronic hand eczema, cutaneous infections including eczema herpeticum, and increased psychiatric burden; complications include bacterial superinfection, sleep loss, and impaired quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, usually based on pruritus plus chronic or relapsing typical morphology and distribution with personal or family atopy, supported when needed by serum IgE, eosinophil count, patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis, skin biopsy to exclude mimics, and severity scores such as SCORAD or EASI. Treatment commonly includes topical corticosteroids, which broadly suppress inflammatory gene transcription; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus, which inhibit T-cell activation via calcineurin blockade; dupilumab, which blocks IL-4Rα and inhibits IL-4/IL-13

Name: Dermatitis, Contact
Description: Contact dermatitis is a common inflammatory skin disorder caused by either irritant injury or, in allergic contact dermatitis, a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to low-molecular-weight haptens such as nickel, fragrances, preservatives, rubber accelerators, or urushiol; protein and genetic factors that modify susceptibility include epidermal barrier genes such as FLG and other cornified-envelope components, immune-regulatory loci involving HLA variants, TLR2/TLR4, TNF, IL1A/IL1B, IL6, IL10, IFNG, and GST detoxification enzymes, although inheritance is usually complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian. Pathobiologically, keratinocyte damage and hapten presentation activate innate and adaptive pathways including NF-kB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, dendritic-cell maturation, and Th1/Th17- and sometimes Th2-skewed cytokine networks with TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, and IFN-gamma as key mediators. Clinically, patients develop pruritic, burning, erythematous, edematous, sharply localized patches or plaques that may vesiculate, ooze, fissure, lichenify, or scale, with acute, subacute, and chronic forms and the major subtypes being allergic and irritant contact dermatitis, plus photocontact variants and occupational disease. Common comorbidities and complications include atopic dermatitis, asthma or allergic rhinitis, secondary bacterial infection, sleep disturbance, chronic hand eczema, and significant occupational impairment. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on exposure distribution and morphology, supported by patch testing for allergic triggers, repeat open application or photopatch testing in selected cases, and exclusion of mimics such as psoriasis, tinea, or scabies; biopsy is nonspecific but may show spongiotic dermatitis. Treatment centers on allergen or irritant avoidance and topical corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone, triamcinolone, or clobetasol, which suppress glucocorticoid-responsive inflammatory transcription; topical calcineurin inhibitors tacrolimus and pimecrolimus inhibit calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation; and severe disease may require systemic prednisone, while antihistamines mainly reduce pruritus.

Name: Dermatomycoses
Description: Dermatomycoses (UMLS C0011630) are superficial to occasionally deeper fungal infections of keratinized tissues, most commonly caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton, and clinically include tinea pedis, corporis, cruris, capitis, unguium/onychomycosis, and less often Majocchi granuloma; disease is usually acquired rather than inherited, but host genetic susceptibility is recognized, with representative defects involving innate and adaptive antifungal immunity, including CARD9 deficiency, CLEC7A encoding dectin-1, STAT1 gain-of-function, and IL17/IL17R pathway abnormalities that impair Th17-mediated responses. Pathobiology centers on fungal adhesion and keratinase/protease-mediated invasion of stratum corneum, hair, or nails, with activation of pattern-recognition pathways such as dectin-1/SYK/CARD9/NF-κB, Toll-like receptor signaling, and IL-23/IL-17 immune circuits involving neutrophils, macrophages, keratinocytes, and antimicrobial peptides. Typical findings are pruritic annular scaly plaques with central clearing, interdigital maceration, erythema, vesiculation, scalp scaling with alopecia or black dots, and nail thickening, discoloration, and subungual debris. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, obesity, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression including HIV or corticosteroid use, atopy, hyperhidrosis, and occlusive footwear; complications include bacterial superinfection, cellulitis, chronic recurrent infection, scarring alopecia in inflammatory tinea capitis, and widespread disease in immunodeficient patients. Diagnosis is primarily clinical but should be confirmed by potassium hydroxide microscopy, fungal culture, histopathology with PAS or GMS stains, dermoscopy, and increasingly PCR-based assays, with Wood lamp examination useful for selected Microsporum infections. Treatment commonly uses terbinafine, a squalene epoxidase inhibitor; azoles such as clotrimazole, itraconazole, or fluconazole, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; and griseofulvin, which disrupts fungal microtubules and mitosis, with drug choice guided by site, severity, organism, and host factors.

Name: Dermatomyositis
Description: Dermatomyositis (MeSH D003882) is a heterogeneous idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by immune-mediated injury of skin and skeletal muscle, and in some patients lung and other organs, presenting with symmetric proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, myalgias, elevated creatine kinase, and characteristic cutaneous findings such as heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl or V signs, periungual telangiectasia, and in juvenile disease calcinosis. Major subtypes include classic dermatomyositis, amyopathic or hypomyopathic dermatomyositis, juvenile dermatomyositis, antisynthetase-overlap phenotypes, and cancer-associated dermatomyositis. Its molecular basis is usually polygenic and autoimmune rather than Mendelian, but strong genetic associations involve HLA class I and II alleles, particularly HLA-DRB1 and DQA1 haplotypes; disease-defining autoantibody targets include proteins encoded by TIF1 genes such as TRIM33/TIF1-gamma, NXP2/MORC3, MDA5/IFIH1, Mi-2/CHD4, SAE1, and HMGCR, with rare monogenic interferonopathy-like presentations linked to genes regulating innate immunity. Pathobiology prominently features type I interferon signaling, complement-mediated microangiopathy with C5b-9 deposition, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, B- and T-cell activation, endothelial injury, and cytokine pathways including TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and JAK-STAT signaling. Common treatments include corticosteroids such as prednisone, which broadly suppress NF-kB-dependent inflammatory transcription; methotrexate, a folate antagonist that increases adenosine-mediated immunosuppression; azathioprine, a purine synthesis inhibitor that reduces lymphocyte proliferation; intravenous immunoglobulin, which modulates Fc receptors and complement; and rituximab, which depletes CD20-positive B cells. Important comorbidities and complications include interstitial lung disease, dysphagia with aspiration, myocarditis, vasculopathy, malignancy, especially with anti-TIF1-gamma, and osteoporosis or infection related to therapy. Name: Dermatosclerosis
Description: Dermatosclerosis, most often used clinically to denote sclerotic skin disease such as localized or systemic cutaneous sclerosis and, in some settings, lipodermatosclerosis of venous insufficiency, is a chronic fibroinflammatory disorder characterized by excessive dermal and subcutaneous collagen deposition, induration, and impaired tissue remodeling. Molecularly, fibrosis is driven predominantly by TGF-β/SMAD, PDGF, connective tissue growth factor, endothelin-1, Wnt/β-catenin, IL-4/IL-13, and JAK/STAT signaling, with activation of fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, endothelial cells, and macrophages; representative associated factors include COL1A1/COL1A2, TGFB1, CTGF, FBN1, HLA class II risk alleles, and autoantibody-defined subsets with centromere, topoisomerase I, or RNA polymerase III reactivity, although inheritance is usually complex and non-Mendelian rather than a single-gene trait. Clinical findings include woody or bound-down skin thickening, edema progressing to induration, pigmentary change, pain or pruritus, reduced mobility, digital tightening or contractures, and in lipodermatosclerosis, lower-leg hyperpigmentation, inverted champagne-bottle deformity, and venous ulceration. Important subtypes include localized morphea, diffuse and limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, and secondary sclerosing dermatoses linked to chronic venous disease. Comorbidities and complications include Raynaud phenomenon, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, gastroesophageal dysmotility, renal crisis, calcinosis, chronic venous insufficiency, ulceration, and secondary infection. Treatment depends on subtype and severity and commonly includes methotrexate, a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor that suppresses lymphocyte-driven inflammation; mycophenolate mofetil, an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor that reduces lymphocyte proliferation and fibrosis; systemic corticosteroids, which inhibit NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling; and for selected systemic disease, nintedanib, a multikinase inhibitor targeting PDGFR/FGFR/VEGFR, or endothelin receptor antagonists such as bosentan for digital ulcers. Name: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1
Description: Diabetes mellitus type 1 (MeSH D003922) is a chronic autoimmune endocrinopathy characterized by T-cell–mediated destruction of pancreatic β cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency; it includes classic immune-mediated type 1A diabetes and the less common idiopathic type 1B, with fulminant forms described in some populations. Genetic susceptibility is strongly polygenic, dominated by HLA class II haplotypes DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8, with additional risk loci in INS, PTPN22, CTLA4, IL2RA, and IFIH1; monogenic or syndromic autoimmune predisposition can involve AIRE or FOXP3 variants, but most cases are complex rather than Mendelian, with familial clustering and markedly increased sibling risk. Pathogenesis centers on antigen presentation, autoreactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, B-cell/autoantibody responses to insulin, GAD65, IA-2, and ZnT8, and cytokine-driven inflammatory pathways including IL-1, interferon signaling, NF-κB, JAK-STAT, and apoptotic/ER-stress mechanisms within β cells. Typical presentation includes polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, nocturia, and sometimes diabetic ketoacidosis with abdominal pain, vomiting, Kussmaul respirations, and altered sensorium. Diagnosis is based on ADA glycemic criteria—fasting plasma glucose at least 126 mg/dL, 2-hour glucose at least 200 mg/dL during OGTT, HbA1c at least 6.5%, or random glucose at least 200 mg/dL with symptoms—supported by low or absent C-peptide and islet autoantibodies. Treatment requires insulin replacement, commonly rapid-acting insulin lispro or aspart to activate insulin receptors for prandial glucose disposal, long-acting insulin glargine or degludec for basal suppression of hepatic glucose output, and regular insulin intravenously in ketoacidosis; adjunctive pramlintide, an amylin analog, slows gastric emptying and suppresses glucagon. Important comorbidities and complications include autoimmune thyroid disease, celiac disease, Addison disease, dyslipidemia, nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy, cardiovascular disease, severe hypoglycemia, and recurrent ketoacidosis.

Name: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2
Description: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (MeSH D003924) is a chronic, heterogeneous metabolic disease characterized by insulin resistance in liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue together with progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction, resulting in persistent hyperglycemia; it typically presents in adults but increasingly affects younger individuals with obesity. Its genetic architecture is complex and predominantly polygenic rather than Mendelian, with common susceptibility variants in genes such as TCF7L2, PPARG, KCNJ11, SLC30A8, FTO, and IRS1, while rare monogenic forms that can phenocopy type 2 diabetes include HNF1A, HNF4A, and GCK defects; family clustering is strong and inheritance is multifactorial, modified by obesity, diet, and physical inactivity. Key pathogenic pathways include impaired insulin receptor/IRS-1/PI3K-AKT signaling, reduced GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake, dysregulated AMPK and mTOR signaling, adipokine and inflammatory pathways involving TNF, IL-6, and NF-kB, altered incretin signaling through GLP-1, excess hepatic gluconeogenesis, glucolipotoxicity, oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress, and islet amyloid polypeptide deposition. Clinical features include polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, blurred vision, recurrent infections, poor wound healing, and sometimes acanthosis nigricans, although many patients are initially asymptomatic. Diagnosis is established by HbA1c 6.5% or greater, fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL or greater, 2-hour plasma glucose 200 mg/dL or greater during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, or random glucose 200 mg/dL or greater with classic symptoms, with repeat confirmation when asymptomatic; evaluation also includes urine albumin, serum creatinine, lipid profile, retinal and foot assessment. Major subtypes include obesity-associated and lean phenotypes and ketosis-prone variants. Standard therapy includes metformin, which suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis largely via AMPK-related effects; sulfonylureas such as glipizide, which close beta-cell KATP channels to stimulate insulin secretion; SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin, which increase urinary glucose excretion; GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, which enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion and promote weight loss; and insulin when needed. Name: Diabetic Nephropathies
Description: Diabetic nephropathy, or diabetic kidney disease, is a chronic microvascular complication of type 1 and type 2 diabetes characterized by progressive glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury driven by persistent hyperglycemia, intraglomerular hypertension, oxidative stress, and inflammation, classically progressing from hyperfiltration to moderately increased albuminuria, overt proteinuria, declining estimated glomerular filtration rate, and eventually end-stage kidney disease. Key molecular pathways include activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, TGF-β/SMAD profibrotic signaling, AGE-RAGE signaling, PKC, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, VEGFA-mediated endothelial dysfunction, and dysregulated podocyte and mesangial cell responses involving ACE, AGT, NOS3, SLC2A1, EPO, TGFB1, CNDP1, APOL1 in some ancestries, and proteins such as nephrin NPHS1, podocin NPHS2, collagen IV, and inflammatory cytokines; susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with familial clustering and risk variants modifying progression rather than causing classic inheritance. Major comorbidities and complications include hypertension, retinopathy, neuropathy, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, anemia, hyperkalemia, and increased risk of acute kidney injury. Typical findings are persistent albuminuria, edema, worsening blood pressure control, reduced eGFR, and sometimes nephrotic-range proteinuria, although many patients are initially asymptomatic. Subtypes are often described by diabetes type, albuminuric versus non-albuminuric phenotypes, and histologic classes ranging from glomerular basement membrane thickening and mesangial expansion to nodular glomerulosclerosis Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions. Diagnosis relies on repeated urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio testing, serum creatinine-based eGFR, urinalysis, blood pressure assessment, and diabetic retinopathy correlation, with kidney biopsy reserved for atypical presentations such as active sediment, rapid decline, short diabetes duration, or absence of retinopathy. Name: Diabetic Neuropathies
Description: Diabetic neuropathies are a heterogeneous group of acquired, usually length-dependent peripheral and autonomic nerve disorders caused by chronic diabetes mellitus and related metabolic injury rather than classic Mendelian inheritance, although genetic susceptibility modifies risk; representative implicated genes and proteins include AKR1B1 encoding aldose reductase, NOS3, ACE, APOE, VEGFA, SOD2, TNF, IL6, MTHFR, and ion-channel genes affecting pain sensitivity such as SCN9A, while altered insulin signaling, reduced neurotrophic support including NGF and BDNF, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dyslipidemia contribute. Core pathogenic pathways include hyperglycemia-driven polyol flux, advanced glycation end-product formation with RAGE activation, PKC and hexosamine pathway activation, oxidative and nitrosative stress, PARP activation, microvascular ischemia, inflammation mediated by NF-κB, TNF-α and IL-6, and Schwann-cell and axonal injury. Major forms include distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy, small-fiber neuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, radiculoplexus neuropathy, focal mononeuropathies, and entrapment neuropathies. Patients typically develop stocking-glove numbness, burning pain, paresthesias, allodynia, loss of vibration and pinprick, reduced ankle reflexes, weakness in advanced disease, gait instability, and autonomic features such as orthostatic hypotension, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis, diarrhea, bladder and sexual dysfunction, and sudomotor failure. Diagnosis is based on diabetes plus compatible symptoms and signs, exclusion of alternative causes, bedside sensory testing with monofilament, vibration, temperature and reflex examination, nerve-conduction studies for large-fiber disease, skin biopsy or quantitative sudomotor/sensory testing for small-fiber disease, and autonomic reflex testing when indicated. Commonly linked complications and comorbidities include foot ulceration, Charcot arthropathy, falls, infections, nephropathy, retinopathy, cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction, depression, sleep disturbance, and chronic kidney disease. Treatment emphasizes glycemic control and risk-factor reduction, with symptomatic drugs such as duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; pregabalin or gabapentin, α2δ calcium-channel ligands that reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release; and tricyclic antidepress

Name: Diaper Rash
Description: Diaper rash, or diaper dermatitis (UMLS C0011974), is a common inflammatory disorder of infant skin in the occluded diaper area, usually caused by prolonged exposure to moisture, friction, urine and feces, with irritant contact dermatitis predominating, but with important subtypes including candidal diaper dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, atopic or allergic contact dermatitis, and rarer bacterial or psoriasiform variants. Pathobiology centers on epidermal barrier disruption with increased transepidermal water loss, pH elevation, fecal lipase and protease activation, keratinocyte release of IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-8, and innate immune signaling through NF-κB, MAPK, and, in Candida-associated disease, pattern-recognition pathways involving TLR2, TLR4, dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, and IL-17/Th17 responses; genetic susceptibility is not usually Mendelian, but barrier and inflammatory genes such as FLG, SPINK5, KRT genes, and immune-pathway defects affecting STAT3, DOCK8, CARD9, or IL17RA may predispose severe, recurrent, or unusual cases, typically with complex rather than simple inheritance. Clinically, patients develop erythematous patches or plaques on convex surfaces of the buttocks, perineum, lower abdomen, and thighs, sometimes with scaling, maceration, papules, erosions, discomfort, and in candidiasis the classic beefy-red plaques with satellite pustules and involvement of skin folds. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on morphology and distribution, while KOH preparation or fungal culture can confirm Candida, bacterial culture is used when secondary infection is suspected, and patch testing, biopsy, or immunologic/genetic workup is reserved for refractory, atypical, or recurrent disease. Treatment relies on barrier agents such as zinc oxide and petrolatum, which reduce irritant contact and water loss, antifungals including nystatin or clotrimazole that disrupt fungal membrane function, and low-potency hydrocortisone to suppress local inflammatory cytokine signaling; complications include secondary Candida or bacterial infection, ulceration, pain, sleep disturbance, and associations with diarrhea, antibiotic exposure, atopy, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, and immunodeficiency.

Name: Diarrhea
Description: Diarrhea (MeSH D003967) is a clinical syndrome rather than a single disease, defined by increased stool frequency, liquidity, or volume due to impaired intestinal absorption, increased secretion, dysmotility, or inflammation, and is commonly classified as acute infectious, persistent, chronic, osmotic, secretory, inflammatory/exudative, fatty/malabsorptive, or functional. Typical manifestations include loose or watery stools, urgency, abdominal cramping, bloating, nausea, fever, tenesmus, and signs of dehydration or electrolyte loss; severe cases may cause hypovolemia, acute kidney injury, metabolic acidosis, malnutrition, or growth failure. Molecular contributors include epithelial transport and barrier genes and host-defense pathways, with representative examples such as CFTR, whose activating mutations enhance chloride and water secretion, SLC26A3 in congenital chloride diarrhea, GUCY2C activating variants in familial secretory diarrhea, DGAT1 deficiency causing protein-losing enteropathy with diarrhea, and IL10, IL10RA, XIAP, TTC7A, or EPCAM defects predisposing to very-early-onset inflammatory diarrheal disease. Key pathways include cAMP/CFTR and cGMP/GUCY2C-mediated chloride secretion, calcium-dependent secretory signaling, sodium-hydrogen exchange and epithelial sodium transport, tight-junction and mucosal barrier regulation, bile acid-FXR/TGR5 signaling, enteric nervous system and serotonin-mediated motility, and inflammatory cascades involving TNF, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, and prostaglandins. Common treatments include oral rehydration solution, which exploits intact sodium-glucose cotransport via SGLT1; loperamide, a peripheral mu-opioid receptor agonist that slows transit and enhances absorption; bismuth subsalicylate, which has antisecretory and antimicrobial effects; racecadotril, an enkephalinase inhibitor that reduces hypersecretion; and pathogen-directed antibiotics such as azithromycin when indicated. Important comorbidities include inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, irritable bowel syndrome, pancreatic insufficiency, hyperthyroidism, diabetes-related autonomic neuropathy, HIV, and colorectal neoplasia. Name: Diphtheria
Description: Diphtheria (UMLS C0012546) is an acute, toxin-mediated bacterial infection caused predominantly by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae and less often C. ulcerans or C. pseudotuberculosis, in which disease severity depends on carriage of a lysogenic corynephage bearing the tox gene encoding diphtheria toxin; expression is regulated by the iron-dependent DtxR repressor, and the toxin is synthesized as a precursor that is proteolytically nicked into A and B fragments, with the B domain binding heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor precursor on host cells and the A domain ADP-ribosylating elongation factor 2, thereby shutting off protein synthesis, triggering cell death, local pseudomembrane formation, and inflammatory signaling. It is generally not an inherited disease, although host susceptibility and vaccine responsiveness may be modified by immune-response genes such as HLA variation, and there is no Mendelian subtype; recognized clinical forms include respiratory/nasopharyngeal, laryngeal, cutaneous, and rarely systemic disease. Typical findings are fever, sore throat, malaise, cervical lymphadenopathy with bull-neck swelling, hoarseness, and an adherent gray pharyngeal pseudomembrane that may bleed on removal, while cutaneous diphtheria causes chronic ulcerative lesions. Major complications include airway obstruction, myocarditis with arrhythmias or heart failure, cranial and peripheral neuropathy, renal injury, and secondary pneumonia; comorbid risk is increased in undervaccinated persons, crowded settings, alcoholism, malnutrition, and chronic skin disease. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical syndrome plus microbiologic confirmation by culture on selective media, identification of C. diphtheriae, toxigenicity testing by Elek immunoprecipitation or PCR for tox, and ECG/cardiac biomarker monitoring when severe. Treatment requires prompt diphtheria antitoxin to neutralize circulating toxin, erythromycin or penicillin G/procaine penicillin to inhibit bacterial growth by blocking protein synthesis or cell-wall transpeptidation, and alternatives such as azithromycin or rifampin in selected cases, together with airway support and vaccination after recovery.

Name: Disruptive Behavior Disorder
Description: Attention deficit and disruptive behavior disorders (MeSH D019958) comprise a neurodevelopmental and behavioral spectrum centered on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), oppositional defiant disorder, and conduct disorder, characterized by developmentally inappropriate inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, irritability, defiance, aggression, rule-breaking, and impaired academic, social, and family functioning. ADHD subtypes include predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined presentations, while disruptive disorders range from oppositional symptoms to more severe conduct pathology. The disorders are multifactorial, highly heritable, and typically polygenic rather than Mendelian, with twin studies supporting substantial genetic contribution; implicated genes include dopaminergic and noradrenergic regulators such as DRD4, DRD5, SLC6A3/DAT1, SNAP25, COMT, ADRA2A, and SLC6A2, with occasional contribution from rare copy-number variants or deleterious mutations affecting synaptic development. Pathophysiology emphasizes dysregulation of catecholamine signaling within frontostriatal, frontocerebellar, and limbic circuits, involving dopamine and norepinephrine transporters and receptors, vesicular release machinery, cyclic AMP signaling, and executive-control networks in prefrontal cortex. Common comorbidities include anxiety, depressive disorders, learning disorders, autism spectrum disorder, tic disorders, sleep disturbance, substance use, and increased risk of accidental injury, academic failure, and antisocial outcomes. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria requiring persistent symptoms across settings with functional impairment and age-of-onset requirements, supported by developmental history, standardized rating scales from parents and teachers, psychiatric and educational assessment, and exclusion of mimics; neuropsychological testing is adjunctive, and no biomarker is diagnostic. Standard treatments include methylphenidate and amphetamine preparations, which block dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake and, for amphetamines, also promote presynaptic release; atomoxetine, a selective norepinephrine transporter inhibitor; and alpha-2A agonists such as guanfacine or clonidine, which strengthen prefrontal cortical regulation, often combined with behavioral therapy and parent-management interventions.

Name: Dry Eye Syndromes
Description: Dry eye syndromes (MeSH D015352) are a multifactorial ocular surface disorder characterized by loss of tear-film homeostasis, hyperosmolarity, inflammation, and neurosensory abnormalities, broadly classified into aqueous-deficient dry eye, including Sjögren-related and non-Sjögren forms, and evaporative dry eye, most often due to meibomian gland dysfunction. Patients typically report burning, stinging, foreign-body sensation, fluctuating or blurred vision, photophobia, redness, reflex tearing, and contact lens intolerance, while signs include reduced tear break-up time, punctate epithelial erosions, low Schirmer scores, lid margin disease, and elevated tear osmolarity. Pathobiology involves lacrimal functional unit failure with activation of MAPK and NF-κB signaling, increased IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ, MMP-9, and chemokine pathways, goblet-cell loss, mucin abnormalities such as altered MUC1, MUC4, and MUC5AC, and meibomian lipid disturbances; representative associated genes/proteins include AQP5, CFTR, lacritin (LACRT), HLA-DR, and inflammatory mediators, while familial predisposition is usually complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, although inherited disorders such as ectodermal dysplasia, familial dysautonomia, and some connective-tissue or autoimmune susceptibility backgrounds can feature dry eye. Important comorbidities include Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, rosacea, thyroid eye disease, diabetes, graft-versus-host disease, blepharitis, depression, neuropathic pain, and complications such as filamentary keratitis, corneal ulceration, infection, and visual impairment. Diagnosis relies on symptom questionnaires such as OSDI or DEQ-5 plus examination with tear break-up time, corneal/conjunctival fluorescein or lissamine staining, Schirmer testing, tear osmolarity, meibography, and sometimes tear MMP-9 or autoimmune serologies. Common treatments include artificial tears and lubricants that supplement tear volume and reduce friction, topical cyclosporine which inhibits calcineurin-mediated T-cell activation and ocular surface inflammation, lifitegrast which blocks LFA-1/ICAM-1-mediated T-cell adhesion, and varenicline

Name: Muscular Dystrophy, Duchenne
Description: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe X-linked recessive dystrophinopathy caused by pathogenic variants in DMD on Xp21, most often out-of-frame deletions or duplications and nonsense mutations that abolish dystrophin, the sarcolemmal cytoskeletal protein linking F-actin to the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex, including dystroglycans and sarcoglycans; in-frame DMD variants more often underlie the milder Becker subtype, while rare manifesting female carriers can occur. Loss of dystrophin destabilizes the muscle membrane, causing calcium influx, myofiber necrosis, chronic inflammation, NF-kB, TGF-beta, MAPK, PI3K-Akt-mTOR, and myostatin-related signaling dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, fibrosis, and failed regeneration. Boys typically present in early childhood with delayed motor milestones, waddling gait, frequent falls, difficulty running or climbing stairs, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, progressive proximal weakness, contractures, scoliosis, and later respiratory insufficiency and dilated cardiomyopathy with arrhythmias; common complications and comorbidities include restrictive lung disease, osteoporosis and fractures, obesity or steroid-related growth suppression, cognitive or behavioral impairment, and anesthesia-related rhabdomyolysis risk. Diagnosis relies on characteristic clinical phenotype, markedly elevated serum creatine kinase, confirmatory molecular testing of DMD by deletion/duplication analysis and sequencing, and, when needed, muscle biopsy showing absent dystrophin by immunohistochemistry or Western blot, with cardiac and pulmonary assessment used for staging. Standard therapy includes glucocorticoids such as prednisone, prednisolone, and deflazacort, which slow muscle degeneration largely through anti-inflammatory effects and preservation of muscle strength; mutation-specific agents include eteplirsen or golodirsen for exon skipping to restore the reading frame and ataluren for nonsense-mutation readthrough where approved. Supportive treatment commonly includes ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril and beta-blockers for cardiomyopathy, along with physiotherapy, ventilatory support, and orthopedic management.

Name: Ductus Arteriosus, Patent
Description: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA; MeSH D004374) is a congenital cardiovascular malformation in which the fetal ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth, producing a persistent left-to-right shunt between the aorta and pulmonary artery; it may occur as an isolated lesion, in preterm infants, or as part of syndromic disease. Genetic contributors include TFAP2B mutations in Char syndrome, and associations with MYH11, ACTA2, TBX1/22q11.2 deletion, NKX2-5, GATA4, and chromosomal disorders such as trisomy 21, although inheritance is often multifactorial and can be autosomal dominant in defined syndromes. Molecular regulation centers on prostaglandin E2–EP4 signaling, cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin synthesis, oxygen-sensitive constriction pathways involving calcium influx, endothelin, nitric oxide, potassium-channel remodeling, and smooth-muscle/extracellular-matrix programs. Clinical findings range from asymptomatic small PDA to tachypnea, poor feeding, failure to thrive, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, hyperdynamic precordium, and a continuous machinery murmur; large shunts can cause pulmonary overcirculation, cardiomegaly, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger physiology, arrhythmias, and infective endarteritis, with common comorbidities including prematurity, respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Subtypes are commonly defined by hemodynamic significance, size, morphology, and the silent versus symptomatic, term versus preterm, and isolated versus syndromic forms. Diagnosis is established primarily by echocardiography with Doppler demonstrating ductal patency, shunt direction, chamber enlargement, and flow burden, supported by clinical examination, pulse oximetry, chest radiography, and ECG; cardiac catheterization is reserved for hemodynamic clarification or closure planning. Pharmacologic closure is commonly attempted with indomethacin and ibuprofen, nonselective COX inhibitors that reduce prostaglandin synthesis, or acetaminophen, which inhibits the peroxidase activity of prostaglandin H2 synthase, while prostaglandin E1 analogs such as alprostadil are used conversely to maintain ductal patency in duct-dependent lesions until definitive intervention.

Name: Duodenal Ulcer
Description: Duodenal ulcer (MeSH D004381) is a common form of peptic ulcer disease characterized by a mucosal break in the proximal duodenum, usually caused by an imbalance between aggressive factors, especially Helicobacter pylori infection and gastric acid-pepsin secretion, and mucosal defenses such as bicarbonate, mucus, prostaglandins, and epithelial restitution. Core molecular processes involve H. pylori virulence factors including CagA and VacA, host inflammatory signaling through NF-kB, IL1B, TNF, IL8/CXCL8, TLR pathways, COX-1/COX-2–prostaglandin signaling, EGF/EGFR-mediated repair, and the gastrin-histamine-acetylcholine axis regulating parietal-cell H+/K+-ATPase activity; representative genetic associations include polymorphisms in IL1B, IL1RN, TNFA, TLR4, MUC1, PTGS1/PTGS2, and CYP2C19, which may influence susceptibility, inflammation, or drug response, although inheritance is generally complex and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with familial clustering and occasional association with hypersecretory states such as MEN1-related Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Typical symptoms are burning or gnawing epigastric pain classically relieved by meals, nocturnal pain, dyspepsia, bloating, nausea, and sometimes occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding; major complications include hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, gastric outlet obstruction, anemia, and recurrent disease, with comorbid links to chronic gastritis, NSAID exposure, smoking, and less commonly Crohn disease or severe physiologic stress. Subtypes include H. pylori-associated, NSAID-associated, stress-related, and hypersecretory ulcers. Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion plus upper endoscopy, with testing for H. pylori by urea breath test, stool antigen, rapid urease test, histology, or culture, and adjunctive CBC or fecal occult blood testing when bleeding is suspected. Standard treatment includes proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase, H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine, which reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion, and mucosal protective or eradication regimens including sucralfate, bismuth, amoxicillin, clarithromycin,

Name: Dysentery
Description: Dysentery (MeSH D004403) is an acute inflammatory infectious colitis characterized by frequent passage of small-volume stools containing blood and mucus, abdominal cramping, tenesmus, fever, dehydration, and systemic toxicity, and it is classically divided into bacillary dysentery, most often caused by Shigella spp. or enteroinvasive Escherichia coli, and amoebic dysentery caused by Entamoeba histolytica. Its pathobiology is driven largely by microbial virulence factors rather than Mendelian inheritance: Shigella invasion plasmid antigens and the type III secretion system, E. histolytica Gal/GalNAc lectin, cysteine proteases, and amoebapores promote epithelial invasion and cytotoxicity, while host pathways include TLR4- and NOD-mediated innate sensing, NF-kB activation, IL-1beta, IL-8, TNF-alpha, neutrophil recruitment, inflammasome signaling, prostaglandin-mediated secretion, and epithelial barrier disruption. Human genetic susceptibility is not usually inherited in a simple pattern, but variants affecting mucosal immunity and inflammation, including HLA loci, TLR4, NOD2, IL8, TNF, LEP, and MUC2, have been associated in representative studies with altered risk or severity. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical syndrome plus stool microscopy for fecal leukocytes and erythrocytes, stool culture or multiplex PCR for Shigella/EIEC and other enteropathogens, ova-and-parasite examination or antigen/PCR testing for E. histolytica, and in selected severe cases endoscopy or imaging to assess colitis or complications. Treatment centers on rehydration and targeted antimicrobials, commonly ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, azithromycin, a macrolide that blocks the 50S ribosomal subunit, ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, and for amoebiasis metronidazole, which generates nitro radical intermediates damaging protozoal DNA, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin, an aminoglycoside that inhibits 30S translation. Name: Shigella Infection
Description: Bacillary dysentery is an acute invasive inflammatory colitis caused predominantly by Shigella species, especially S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri, S. sonnei, and S. boydii, and is therefore an infectious rather than inherited disease; host genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations reported for HLA class II loci, TLR4, CD14, IL8, IL10, TNF, and genes affecting epithelial barrier and innate immune responses, while key bacterial virulence determinants include the invasion plasmid antigens ipaB, ipaC, and ipaD, the type III secretion system, virG/icsA for intracellular actin-based spread, and Shiga toxin stx in S. dysenteriae type 1. Pathogenesis centers on colonic epithelial invasion and macrophage pyroptotic death, with activation of TLR/NF-kB and MAPK signaling, inflammasome-caspase-1 pathways, massive IL-1beta, IL-8, and TNF release, and neutrophil-rich mucosal injury. Patients typically present with fever, crampy abdominal pain, tenesmus, frequent small-volume stools containing blood and mucus, urgency, and dehydration; severe disease may cause seizures in children, toxic megacolon, intestinal perforation, sepsis, hemolytic-uremic syndrome, leukemoid reaction, and postinfectious reactive arthritis, and common comorbid contexts include malnutrition, HIV infection, and other causes of immunosuppression. Clinical subtypes are usually classified by species and severity, including toxin-mediated severe dysentery due to S. dysenteriae 1. Diagnosis relies on compatible inflammatory diarrhea plus stool culture or multiplex PCR/culture-independent NAAT for Shigella, with fecal leukocytes or lactoferrin/calprotectin, blood tests for dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, and susceptibility testing to guide therapy. Treatment combines rehydration with antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit; and ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, with pivmecillinam or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole used selectively according to resistance patterns.

Name: Dysmenorrhea
Description: Dysmenorrhea (MeSH D004412) is a common gynecologic pain disorder characterized by recurrent cramping pelvic pain during menstruation, often accompanied by low back pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, fatigue, and occasionally syncope; it is broadly classified as primary dysmenorrhea, in which no pelvic pathology is identified, and secondary dysmenorrhea, which is linked to conditions such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, leiomyomas, pelvic inflammatory disease, or congenital outflow obstruction. The core biology of primary dysmenorrhea involves exaggerated endometrial prostaglandin production, especially PTGS2/COX-2-driven synthesis of PGF2α and PGE2 from arachidonic acid, causing uterine hypercontractility, vasoconstriction, ischemia, and pain, with contributions from leukotrienes, vasopressin signaling, inflammatory cytokines including TNF and IL1B, nitric oxide pathways, and ion channel–mediated nociception. Genetic susceptibility is complex and non-Mendelian, with representative associations reported in PTGS2, OPRM1, COMT, ESR1, and cytokine-related loci, but no single highly penetrant mutation is established. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on cyclic pain beginning around menses and a normal pelvic evaluation in primary disease; pregnancy testing, pelvic examination, STI testing, pelvic ultrasonography, and sometimes laparoscopy are used to exclude secondary causes when symptoms are severe, progressive, or refractory. First-line treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and mefenamic acid, which inhibit COX enzymes and reduce prostaglandin synthesis; hormonal suppression with combined oral contraceptives or progestins decreases ovulation and endometrial proliferation, lowering prostaglandin generation, and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems can also help. Important comorbidities and complications include chronic pelvic pain, absenteeism, impaired quality of life, anxiety, depression, and reduced daily functioning, especially when secondary dysmenorrhea reflects underlying pelvic disease.

Name: Dyspepsia
Description: Dyspepsia (MeSH D004415) is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease, defined by chronic or recurrent epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating, belching, nausea, and sometimes vomiting, with physical examination often unrevealing unless an organic cause is present. It is commonly divided into functional dyspepsia, now subclassified into postprandial distress syndrome and epigastric pain syndrome, and organic dyspepsia related to peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux, Helicobacter pylori infection, medication injury, biliary or pancreatic disease, or malignancy. Pathobiology is heterogeneous and includes altered gastric accommodation and emptying, visceral hypersensitivity, low-grade duodenal inflammation, impaired mucosal barrier function, microbiologic effects of H. pylori virulence proteins such as CagA and VacA, and dysregulated brain-gut signaling involving vagal pathways, serotonin, acetylcholine, histamine, gastrin, cholecystokinin, prostaglandins, cyclooxygenase, acid-secretory H+/K+-ATPase, TRPV1, cytokines including IL6 and TNF, and occasionally GNB3 C825T, SLC6A4, IL10, TNF, and NOS1 polymorphisms as modest genetic susceptibility factors; no simple Mendelian inheritance is established, though familial aggregation occurs. Common comorbidities include anxiety, depression, irritable bowel syndrome, GERD, gastroparesis, peptic ulcer disease, and in selected patients celiac disease, eosinophilic gastroenteritis, or gastric cancer; complications are usually those of the underlying cause, such as ulcer bleeding, iron deficiency, weight loss, or obstruction. Diagnosis is clinical after history, medication review, and exclusion of alarm features including dysphagia, anemia, gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting, weight loss, or older age at onset; testing may include noninvasive H. pylori stool antigen or urea breath test, CBC, celiac serology, liver and pancreatic chemistries, and upper endoscopy with biopsy when indicated. Name: Dyspnea
Description: Dyspnea (MeSH D004417) is a subjective sensation of difficult or uncomfortable breathing rather than a single disease, arising from disordered respiratory, cardiac, neuromuscular, hematologic, metabolic, or psychogenic processes; common subtypes include acute versus chronic dyspnea and exertional, orthopneic, paroxysmal nocturnal, and rest dyspnea. Its biology reflects airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, pulmonary vascular remodeling, impaired gas exchange, reduced cardiac output, and altered central perception of breathlessness, with pathways involving beta2-adrenergic/cAMP signaling, cholinergic muscarinic M3 signaling, leukotriene and histamine pathways, nitric oxide–cGMP signaling, hypoxia-inducible factor, endothelin, inflammatory cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, TNF-alpha, and neurohumoral mediators including natriuretic peptides. Genetic contributors are usually indirect through underlying disorders, with representative examples including ADRB2, IL4RA, and ORMDL3 in asthma, SERPINA1 in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency–related COPD, BMPR2 in heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension, TTN and MYH7 in cardiomyopathy, and HBB in sickle cell disease; inheritance therefore depends on the cause and may be autosomal dominant, recessive, or complex polygenic. Symptoms and signs include air hunger, tachypnea, wheeze, cough, chest tightness, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, hypoxemia, crackles, stridor, edema, or exercise intolerance. Major comorbidities and complications include asthma, COPD, heart failure, coronary disease, pneumonia, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary embolism, anemia, obesity, anxiety, sleep apnea, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, and death. Treatment targets etiology and symptom relief: albuterol activates beta2 receptors to cause bronchodilation, ipratropium blocks muscarinic receptors, corticosteroids such as prednisone suppress airway and systemic inflammation, furosemide reduces pulmonary congestion via loop diuresis, nitrates donate nitric oxide to reduce preload, and opioids such as morphine can lessen central perception of breathlessness. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, integrating history, examination, pulse oximetry, arterial blood gas, chest radiography, ECG, spirometry

Name: Dysuria
Description: Dysuria (UMLS C0013428) is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease, defined by pain, burning, or discomfort during micturition and most commonly arising from lower urinary tract infection, urethritis, vaginitis, prostatitis, bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis, urolithiasis, or obstructive/inflammatory lesions of the urethra or bladder. Typical manifestations include burning with urination, urinary frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain, hesitancy, urethral discharge, hematuria, cloudy or malodorous urine, and sometimes fever, flank pain, or pelvic pain depending on cause; clinical subtypes are often categorized as infectious versus noninfectious, and lower versus upper tract or male, female, and catheter-associated presentations. Molecular associations are etiology-specific: uropathogenic Escherichia coli commonly engage TLR4-dependent innate immune signaling with downstream NF-kB, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, and neutrophil recruitment, while host susceptibility has been linked to variants affecting TLR4, CXCR1, DEFB1, HSPA1B, and innate mucosal defense pathways; sexually transmitted urethritis may involve inflammatory signaling triggered by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for dysuria itself, but genetic predisposition exists through infection susceptibility, stone disease genes, or interstitial cystitis-related pain and inflammatory pathways. Common treatments depend on etiology and include nitrofurantoin, which is reduced by bacterial nitroreductases to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which sequentially inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase; fosfomycin, which inhibits MurA and bacterial cell-wall synthesis; phenazopyridine for symptomatic urinary analgesia; and alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin when outlet obstruction contributes. Comorbidities and complications include recurrent UTI, pyelonephritis, sepsis, urethral stricture, urinary retention, nephrolithiasis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and chronic pelvic pain. Diagnosis relies on history and examination plus urinalysis, urine culture, leukocyte esterase and nitrite testing, microscopy for pyuria or hematuria, nucleic acid amplification testing for STIs, pregnancy

Name: Eczema
Description: Eczema, most commonly referring to atopic dermatitis but encompassing related eczematous disorders such as nummular, dyshidrotic, seborrheic, contact, and hand eczema, is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease characterized by epidermal barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and intense pruritus, typically presenting with xerosis, erythematous papules and plaques, excoriations, lichenification, oozing, and crusting, with age-dependent flexural or extensor distribution. Its genetic architecture is polygenic, with the strongest and most replicated risk factor being loss-of-function mutations in FLG encoding filaggrin; additional implicated genes include SPINK5, CLDN1, KRT family genes, TSLP, IL4, IL13, IL31, STAT6, OVOL1, and CARD11, supporting impaired barrier integrity and type 2 immune activation. Core pathogenic pathways include Th2-skewed cytokine signaling through IL-4/IL-13–JAK-STAT, epithelial alarmins such as TSLP, IL-25, and IL-33, pruritogenic IL-31 signaling, dendritic cell and eosinophil recruitment, microbiome dysbiosis with Staphylococcus aureus colonization, and in chronic lesions additional Th1/Th17/Th22 activity. Inheritance is usually complex and multifactorial, although familial aggregation is common and rare syndromic forms may show Mendelian patterns. Diagnosis is primarily clinical using standard criteria such as pruritus plus chronic or relapsing typical morphology and distribution, often supported by personal or family atopy; testing may include serum IgE, eosinophil count, skin biopsy when atypical, microbial studies for superinfection, and patch testing to exclude allergic contact dermatitis. Common treatments include topical corticosteroids, which suppress NF-kB-driven inflammatory gene expression; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus, which block T-cell activation; dupilumab, which inhibits IL-4Rα and thereby IL-4/IL-13 signaling; JAK inhibitors such as upadacitinib; and emollients to restore barrier function. Major comorbidities and complications include asthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergy, sleep disturbance, anxiety/depression, eczema herpeticum, and bacterial skin infection.

Name: Edema
Description: Edema (MeSH D004487) is the abnormal accumulation of fluid within the interstitial space or serous cavities and may be localized or generalized, pitting or nonpitting, with major subtypes including peripheral edema, pulmonary edema, cerebral edema, lymphedema, angioedema, and myxedematous edema. Its pathobiology reflects altered Starling forces, endothelial permeability, lymphatic dysfunction, and renal sodium retention, involving the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, vasopressin signaling, natriuretic peptide pathways, VEGF- and bradykinin-mediated vascular leak, inflammatory cytokines, aquaporins, and lymphangiogenic VEGFC/VEGFR3 signaling. Genetic contributors are best defined in inherited edema syndromes: FLT4/VEGFR3, FOXC2, GJC2, CCBE1, FAT4, and PIEZO1 in primary lymphedema, and SERPING1, F12, PLG, ANGPT1, or KNG1 variants in hereditary angioedema, with predominantly autosomal dominant inheritance for many of these disorders, while edema in heart, liver, or kidney disease is usually acquired and polygenic. Common causes and comorbidities include heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, venous insufficiency, deep vein thrombosis, hypothyroidism, infection, malignancy, pregnancy, and drug exposure; complications include skin breakdown, cellulitis, impaired wound healing, compartment syndromes, respiratory failure in pulmonary edema, and intracranial hypertension in cerebral edema. Typical findings are swelling, rapid weight gain, dependent pitting, dyspnea, orthopnea, ascites, pleural effusions, or nonpitting fibrotic limb enlargement. Treatment targets cause and fluid balance: loop diuretics such as furosemide inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, thiazides such as hydrochlorothiazide inhibit NCC in the distal convoluted tubule, and spironolactone antagonizes the mineralocorticoid receptor; angioedema may require C1 esterase inhibitor replacement or icatibant, a bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, integrating examination for pitting and distribution with serum creatinine, albumin, liver tests, urinalysis/proteinuria, BNP

Name: Elephantiasis
Description: Elephantiasis refers to end-stage massive enlargement and fibrosis of skin and subcutaneous tissues caused by chronic lymphatic obstruction, classically in lymphatic filariasis due to Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, or B. timori, but also in nonfilarial forms such as podoconiosis, postsurgical/postirradiation secondary lymphedema, and primary hereditary lymphedema. Its pathobiology centers on lymphatic vessel injury and remodeling, driven by inflammatory and lymphangiogenic pathways involving VEGFC/VEGFR3 (FLT4), FOXC2, GJC2, SOX18, CCBE1, FAT4, PIEZO1, and GATA2, with cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, IL-6, TGF-β, and macrophage-mediated fibrosis contributing; in filarial disease, Wolbachia endosymbionts and parasite antigens amplify innate and adaptive immune responses. Clinically, patients develop chronic nonpitting edema progressing to peau d’orange skin, hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, limb or genital enlargement, recurrent adenolymphangitis, pain, heaviness, and reduced mobility. Complications include cellulitis/erysipelas, fungal superinfection, hydrocele, verrucous change, ulceration, psychosocial disability, and rarely lymphangiosarcoma in longstanding lymphedema. Treatment depends on cause and includes diethylcarbamazine, which is microfilaricidal and partly macrofilaricidal via parasite membrane/arachidonic acid pathway effects and host immune enhancement; ivermectin, which activates parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels causing paralysis of microfilariae; albendazole, a β-tubulin inhibitor impairing helminth microtubules and glucose uptake; and doxycycline, which depletes Wolbachia, reducing embryogenesis and adult worm viability. Diagnosis is based on characteristic chronic lymphedema with exposure or familial history, exclusion of venous or malignant obstruction, demonstration of filarial infection by nocturnal blood smear, circulating filarial antigen or antibody assays, PCR, or ultrasound, and assessment of lymphatic dysfunction by lymphoscintigraphy or indocyanine green lymphography.
