Name: Embolism
Description: Embolism is an acute vascular occlusive disorder caused by intravascular migration of material such as thrombus, fat, air, cholesterol, tumor, or amniotic fluid, most often manifesting clinically as pulmonary embolism, systemic arterial embolism, or paradoxical embolism through a right-to-left shunt. Its biology is dominated by coagulation, platelet, endothelial, and fibrinolytic pathways, including tissue factor–factor VIIa activation of thrombin and fibrin, platelet P2Y12 and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa signaling, vWF-mediated adhesion, and impaired protein C/protein S/antithrombin regulation; representative genetic contributors include F5 Factor V Leiden, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1, PROC, PROS1, ABO non-O blood group, and occasionally MTHFR variants of limited clinical significance, with mostly multifactorial inheritance but autosomal dominant thrombophilias in some families. Major risk-associated proteins and markers include D-dimer, fibrinogen, factor VIII, P-selectin, and antiphospholipid antibodies. Common comorbidities and predisposing states include deep venous thrombosis, atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, malignancy, pregnancy, trauma, surgery, prolonged immobility, obesity, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, and inherited or acquired thrombophilia; complications include infarction, pulmonary hypertension, right-heart strain, stroke, limb ischemia, and sudden death. Symptoms and signs vary by site but classically include abrupt dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, syncope, unilateral leg swelling, or acute focal neurologic or ischemic limb deficits. Diagnosis integrates clinical probability scores, D-dimer testing, CT pulmonary angiography or ventilation-perfusion scanning for pulmonary embolism, Doppler ultrasonography for DVT, ECG, echocardiography, angiography, and selective thrombophilia testing. Treatment commonly includes heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin, which potentiate antithrombin; direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban or rivaroxaban, which inhibit factor Xa; warfarin, which suppresses vitamin K–dependent clotting factors; and in unstable cases alteplase, a tissue plasminogen activator that promotes fibrinolysis

Name: Empyema, Pleural
Description: Pleural empyema (UMLS C0014013) is a loculated collection of purulent infected fluid within the pleural space, usually arising as a complication of bacterial pneumonia, thoracic surgery, chest trauma, esophageal rupture, or hematogenous infection, and is best viewed as an acquired infectious-inflammatory disorder rather than a primary genetic disease. Its pathobiology evolves from an exudative stage to fibrinopurulent and organizing stages, driven by innate immune and coagulation-fibrinolytic pathways involving neutrophils, macrophages, IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, TGF-β, VEGF, NF-κB signaling, and impaired plasminogen activation with increased PAI-1 and fibrin deposition causing septation and pleural peel formation. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern, although host susceptibility to severe infection may be modified by variants in immune-response genes such as TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, CRP, and cytokine-related loci; pathogen factors are more central, with common organisms including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus including PVL-positive strains, Streptococcus anginosus group, anaerobes, and gram-negative bacilli. Typical manifestations are fever, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, cough, malaise, sepsis, reduced breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and persistent leukocytosis despite pneumonia treatment. Major comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes, alcoholism, chronic lung disease, bronchiectasis, aspiration, immunosuppression, malignancy, and rheumatoid disease; complications include loculation, trapped lung, fibrothorax, bronchopleural fistula, respiratory failure, and septic shock. Subtypes include parapneumonic empyema, postoperative or post-traumatic empyema, tuberculous empyema, and chronic organizing empyema. Diagnosis relies on imaging with chest radiography, ultrasound, and contrast CT plus thoracentesis showing frank pus or pleural infection with low pH below 7.20, low glucose, high LDH, neutrophilic predominance, and positive Gram stain or culture. Treatment combines drainage and antimicrobials such as ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis; vancomycin, a glycopeptide blocking peptidoglycan polymerization for MRSA

Name: Endocarditis, Bacterial
Description: Bacterial endocarditis, usually classified as infective endocarditis, is a microbial infection of the native or prosthetic endocardial surface, most often involving cardiac valves, with major subtypes including acute and subacute disease and native-valve, prosthetic-valve, and right-sided endocarditis. It is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci, enterococci, and coagulase-negative staphylococci; pathobiology centers on endothelial injury, platelet-fibrin thrombus formation, and bacterial adhesion through microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules, with host pathways involving tissue factor–coagulation, complement, TLR2/NF-κB-driven innate immune signaling, cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF, and matrix remodeling enzymes. Relevant microbial genes/proteins include S. aureus adhesins and biofilm factors such as fnbA/fnbB, clfA, cna, ica, and mecA in methicillin-resistant strains, while host genetic predisposition is not classically Mendelian but is influenced by structural heart disease and occasional variants affecting immunity or congenital valve defects; inherited risk examples include bicuspid aortic valve and some congenital heart disease genes such as NOTCH1. Clinical features typically include fever, new or changing murmur, malaise, weight loss, embolic phenomena, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, heart failure, and conduction abnormalities. Major complications include valvular destruction, abscess, stroke, systemic emboli, glomerulonephritis, mycotic aneurysm, and sepsis; important comorbidities include prosthetic valves, rheumatic or degenerative valve disease, congenital heart disease, intracardiac devices, injection drug use, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis relies on Duke or modified Duke criteria integrating repeated blood cultures, echocardiography, especially transesophageal imaging, and supportive inflammatory or microbiologic testing, with PCR or valve sequencing in culture-negative cases. Treatment uses prolonged bactericidal antibiotics such as vancomycin, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala, ceftriaxone or nafcillin, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins, and gentamicin, an aminoglycoside that blocks 30S ribosomal function; daptomycin,

Name: Endometriosis
Description: Endometriosis (MeSH D004715) is a chronic, estrogen-dependent inflammatory disorder defined by ectopic implantation of endometrial-like glands and stroma, classically presenting as superficial peritoneal disease, ovarian endometrioma, or deep infiltrating endometriosis. It commonly causes dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, dysuria, abnormal uterine bleeding, infertility, pelvic tenderness, and adnexal masses, with complications including adhesions, tubo-ovarian distortion, reduced ovarian reserve, bowel or urinary tract involvement, and increased risk of endometrioid and clear-cell ovarian carcinoma. Its pathobiology involves retrograde menstruation acting on a genetically susceptible host, with aberrant estrogen biosynthesis and progesterone resistance; implicated genes and proteins include ESR1/ESR2, PGR, CYP19A1 aromatase, KRAS, PIK3CA, PTEN, ARID1A, VEGFA, IL1B, IL6, TNF, MMPs, HOXA10, WNT4, and GREB1, while somatic mutations such as KRAS, PIK3CA, and ARID1A are particularly described in endometriomas and deep lesions. Key pathways include estrogen receptor signaling, progesterone signaling failure, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MAPK/ERK, NF-kB, TGF-beta, Wnt/beta-catenin, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, neuroangiogenesis, and immune dysfunction involving macrophages, prostaglandins, cytokines, and COX-2. Familial aggregation is well recognized, typically polygenic and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with increased risk in first-degree relatives and susceptibility loci from GWAS including WNT4, VEZT, GREB1, CDKN2B-AS1, and FN1. Diagnosis is based on compatible symptoms, pelvic examination, and imaging, especially transvaginal ultrasound for endometrioma/deep disease and MRI for mapping, with laparoscopy plus histologic confirmation as the traditional reference standard. Common treatments include NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit COX and prostaglandin synthesis; combined oral contraceptives, which suppress ovulation and induce decidualization; progestins such as dienogest or medroxyprogesterone, which antagonize estrogen-driven proliferation; Gn

Name: Endometritis
Description: Endometritis (UMLS C0014179) is an inflammatory, usually infectious disorder of the endometrial lining that may present acutely, most often postpartum or after miscarriage, instrumentation, or sexually transmitted infection, or chronically, often with plasma-cell–predominant inflammation and links to infertility or abnormal uterine bleeding. Common pathogens include polymicrobial vaginal flora, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and in postpartum disease anaerobes, streptococci, enterococci, and Gram-negative rods; host-response genes rather than Mendelian inheritance dominate susceptibility, with representative immune components including TLR2, TLR4, NOD1/2, IL1B, IL6, TNF, CXCL8/IL8, and NF-κB pathway activation, alongside leukocyte recruitment, prostaglandin synthesis, and in chronic disease aberrant B-cell/plasma-cell infiltration marked by CD138 positivity. Symptoms and signs typically include fever, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia or discharge, dyspareunia, intermenstrual bleeding, and sometimes infertility; major subtypes are acute puerperal/postabortal endometritis and chronic endometritis. Complications include pelvic inflammatory disease, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian abscess, bacteremia or sepsis, adhesions, recurrent implantation failure, miscarriage, and chronic pelvic pain, with comorbidities such as retained products of conception, bacterial vaginosis, endometriosis, and intrauterine device use in selected settings. Diagnosis is clinical in acute postpartum disease but supported by pelvic examination, CBC and inflammatory markers, cervical NAAT testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia, endometrial biopsy showing plasma cells for chronic disease, transvaginal ultrasound to assess retained products or abscess, and cultures when severe infection is suspected. Treatment commonly includes clindamycin, a lincosamide that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; gentamicin, an aminoglycoside causing 30S-mediated mistranslation; doxycycline, a tetracycline blocking 30S tRNA binding; with ampicillin or metronidazole added in selected polymicrobial or enterococcal settings.

Name: Enterobacteriaceae Infections
Description: Enterobacteriaceae infections are bacterial diseases caused by Gram-negative members of the Enterobacteriaceae family, chiefly Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae complex, Proteus, Serratia, Shigella, Salmonella, and Yersinia, producing syndromes that range from urinary tract infection, gastroenteritis, enteric fever, pneumonia, cholangitis, and intra-abdominal infection to bacteremia and sepsis. Disease expression reflects both host and microbial genetics: representative virulence determinants include E. coli type 1 fimbriae encoded by fimH, P fimbriae pap genes, shiga toxins stx1/stx2, heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins, K. pneumoniae capsule regulators rmpA/rmpA2 and siderophore systems, while resistance genes such as blaTEM, blaSHV, blaCTX-M, blaKPC, blaNDM, and mcr-1 are clinically pivotal; host susceptibility is influenced by innate immune pathways involving TLR4-CD14-MD2 recognition of lipopolysaccharide, NF-kB, complement, inflammasome signaling, and cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6, with rare Mendelian predispositions in TLR, IRAK4, or MYD88 pathway defects increasing risk for invasive Gram-negative infection. Typical findings include fever, dysuria, frequency, flank pain, abdominal cramps, diarrhea that may be bloody, vomiting, cough, hypotension, and altered mental status in sepsis. Major subtypes include diarrheagenic E. coli pathotypes, invasive nontyphoidal salmonellosis, typhoid/paratyphoid fever, healthcare-associated multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales infection, and toxin-mediated hemolytic-uremic syndrome. Common comorbidities and complications include diabetes, urinary obstruction, malignancy, cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, immunosuppression, dehydration, renal abscess, septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, and HUS. Diagnosis relies on syndrome-specific cultures of urine, blood, stool, sputum, or other sterile sites with identification and susceptibility testing, often supplemented by PCR or multiplex NAATs for toxin and resistance genes, and inflammatory markers and imaging when deep infection is suspected. Treatment depends on site and resistance profile and commonly includes ceftriaxone

Name: Enterocolitis
Description: Enterocolitis is an inflammatory disorder of the small intestine and colon that may be acute infectious, antibiotic-associated, ischemic, immune-mediated, or neonatal necrotizing, and is characterized clinically by diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, abdominal distension, rectal bleeding, and in severe cases ileus, sepsis, toxic megacolon, perforation, or shock. Its biology reflects epithelial barrier failure, dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, microbial toxins, and cytokine-driven injury, with major pathways involving TLR4/NF-kB signaling, TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6, IL-17, JAK/STAT, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, VEGF-mediated ischemic responses, and apoptosis/autophagy networks; in necrotizing enterocolitis, exaggerated TLR4 signaling in immature enterocytes is especially implicated. Genetic contributions are usually complex and non-Mendelian, but susceptibility has been linked to variants affecting mucosal immunity and barrier integrity, including NOD2, ATG16L1, IL23R, TNFSF15, CARD15, FUT2, TLR4, and genes in the IBD spectrum; rare monogenic immune dysregulation disorders can present with severe enterocolitis, including IL10, IL10RA, IL10RB, TTC7A, FOXP3, XIAP, and CYBB defects, which may show autosomal recessive, X-linked, or other inheritance patterns depending on the gene. Important comorbidities and complications include dehydration, electrolyte derangement, malnutrition, bacteremia, inflammatory bowel disease, Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, short-bowel sequelae, and postoperative adhesions. Treatment depends on cause and severity and commonly includes metronidazole, which damages anaerobic microbial DNA; oral vancomycin, which inhibits Gram-positive cell-wall synthesis and is central in Clostridioides difficile enterocolitis; fidaxomicin, a macrocyclic RNA polymerase inhibitor; broad-spectrum beta-lactams such as piperacillin-tazobactam for severe polymicrobial disease; and anti-inflammatory agents such as corticosteroids that suppress NF-kB-driven cytokine transcription in immune-mediated enterocolitis. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment plus stool culture or multiplex PCR, C. difficile toxin/PCR testing, CBC, CRP, electrolytes, blood cultures when septic, abdominal radiography or CT

Name: Enterocolitis, Pseudomembranous
Description: Pseudomembranous enterocolitis is an acute inflammatory colitis, usually antibiotic-associated and most often caused by toxigenic Clostridioides difficile, in which mucosal necrosis and fibrinoleukocytic pseudomembranes develop after disruption of the normal intestinal microbiota. Its core molecular determinants are the bacterial toxin genes tcdA and tcdB, and in hypervirulent strains binary toxin genes cdtA/cdtB, whose protein products TcdA and especially TcdB glucosylate Rho-family GTPases such as RHOA, RAC1, and CDC42, disrupting actin cytoskeleton, tight junctions, and epithelial barrier integrity while activating NF-kB, inflammasome-mediated IL-1beta release, TNF, IL-8/CXCL8, neutrophil recruitment, apoptosis, and Wnt/epithelial repair pathways; host susceptibility is influenced by immune and epithelial factors rather than classic Mendelian inheritance, although polymorphisms affecting innate immunity and toxin response, including IL8, NLRP3, TLR4, and FUT2, have been associated in some studies. Clinically it ranges from mild antibiotic-associated diarrhea to fulminant colitis, with watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, ileus, and toxic megacolon; recognized forms include non-severe, severe, fulminant, recurrent disease, and less commonly small-bowel enteritis after colectomy. Major comorbidities and risk factors include recent exposure to clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, or broad-spectrum beta-lactams, hospitalization, advanced age, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, transplantation, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, and proton-pump inhibitor use; complications include dehydration, sepsis, perforation, shock, and death. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms plus stool testing for C. difficile by NAAT/PCR for toxin genes, glutamate dehydrogenase antigen with toxin enzyme immunoassay in multistep algorithms, and occasionally toxigenic culture or cell cytotoxicity assay, with colonoscopy or CT showing pseudomembranes or colitis when diagnosis is uncertain or fulminant disease is suspected. Standard therapy includes oral vancomycin, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis; fidaxomicin, a macrocyclic inhibitor of the sigma

Name: Elbow Tendinopathy
Description: Elbow tendinopathy (UMLS C0014488), most commonly lateral epicondylitis and less often medial epicondylitis, is a degenerative overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor or flexor-pronator origin characterized more by failed tendon healing and angiofibroblastic change than by acute inflammation. Patients typically present with activity-related lateral or medial elbow pain, focal epicondylar tenderness, reduced grip strength, pain with resisted wrist extension or middle-finger extension in lateral disease, and pain with resisted wrist flexion or forearm pronation in medial disease. Pathobiology involves extracellular matrix disruption with altered type I/III collagen balance, tenocyte apoptosis/proliferation, neovascularization, glutamate and substance P signaling, and matrix remodeling driven by TGF-β, VEGF, IGF-1, IL-1β, TNF-α, COX-2/PGE2, and MMPs such as MMP3; representative genetic associations reported for tendinopathy susceptibility include variants in COL5A1, COL1A1, TNC, MMP3, TIMP2, and GDF5, although inheritance is not Mendelian and is best viewed as multifactorial/polygenic with biomechanical loading as the dominant environmental trigger. Common comorbidities include rotator cuff tendinopathy, shoulder or cervical pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, obesity, diabetes, smoking, and occupational or racquet-sport overuse; complications include chronic pain, work disability, tendon microtearing, and rarely rupture or persistent postoperative symptoms. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by provocative maneuvers such as Cozen, Mill, and Maudsley tests, with ultrasound or MRI used to show tendon thickening, hypoechogenicity, partial tearing, or neovascularity and to exclude radial tunnel syndrome, osteochondral disease, arthritis, or ligament injury. Treatment commonly includes NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or diclofenac, which inhibit COX and reduce prostaglandin synthesis, topical nitroglycerin, which donates nitric oxide and may enhance collagen synthesis, and corticosteroid injections such as triamcinolone, which suppress phospholipase A2-driven inflammatory signaling, although recurrence after injection is common.

Name: Epilepsy
Description: Epilepsy (MeSH D004827) is a heterogeneous group of chronic brain disorders defined by an enduring predisposition to generate unprovoked seizures, diagnosed clinically after at least two unprovoked seizures separated by more than 24 hours, one unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk, or an epilepsy syndrome, and classified as focal, generalized, combined generalized and focal, or unknown, with syndromic subtypes such as childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, temporal lobe epilepsy, and developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Its pathobiology reflects neuronal hyperexcitability and hypersynchrony involving altered voltage-gated sodium, potassium, and calcium channels, impaired GABAergic inhibition, excessive glutamatergic transmission, and mTOR and synaptic vesicle signaling; representative genetic contributors include SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNQ3, CACNA1H, GABRA1, GABRG2, SLC2A1, STXBP1, DEPDC5, TSC1, and TSC2, with pathogenic variants causing monogenic epilepsies through autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, de novo, and mitochondrial inheritance patterns. Typical manifestations include recurrent seizures with loss of awareness, convulsions, staring spells, myoclonus, sensory or autonomic auras, tongue biting, incontinence, and postictal confusion, while complications include status epilepticus, injury, cognitive impairment, depression, anxiety, migraine, sleep disorders, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Diagnosis relies on detailed history and witness accounts, neurologic examination, EEG or video-EEG demonstrating epileptiform discharges, brain MRI to detect structural lesions, and targeted genetic, metabolic, or autoimmune testing when indicated. Common treatments include valproate, which increases brain GABA and modulates sodium and calcium currents; lamotrigine and carbamazepine, which primarily inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels; levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to reduce synaptic neurotransmitter release; and ethosuximide, which blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels in absence epilepsy.

Name: Epilepsies, Partial
Description: Epilepsies, partial, now more commonly termed focal epilepsies, are disorders in which seizures arise from a localized cortical network and may remain focal or evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures; clinical manifestations depend on the involved lobe and include focal aware or impaired-awareness episodes with aura, automatisms, behavioral arrest, unilateral sensory or motor symptoms, autonomic or psychic phenomena, postictal confusion, and sometimes Todd paralysis. Etiologies are heterogeneous and include structural, infectious, immune, metabolic, and genetic causes; important genetic contributors include ion-channel and synaptic genes such as SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNQ3, KCNT1, DEPDC5, NPRL2, NPRL3, LGI1, GRIN2A, GABRA1, GABRG2, and CHRNA4, with pathogenic variants altering sodium, potassium, GABAergic, glutamatergic, cholinergic, or mTOR-related signaling. Key pathways involve excitation-inhibition imbalance, voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channel dysfunction, impaired GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition, NMDA/AMPA receptor hyperexcitability, synaptic vesicle release, neuroinflammation, and mTOR pathway activation, particularly in focal cortical dysplasia. Common subtypes include temporal, frontal, parietal, and occipital lobe epilepsy, mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis, sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy, and familial focal epilepsies; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or de novo depending on the gene, with examples including autosomal dominant CHRNA4- or LGI1-related focal epilepsy and DEPDC5-related familial focal epilepsy with variable foci. Treatment commonly uses antiseizure drugs such as carbamazepine or lamotrigine, which inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels, levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to modulate neurotransmitter release, and lacosamide, which enhances slow sodium-channel inactivation; valproate, topiramate, and oxcarbazepine are also used. Comorbidities and complications include depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, sleep disorders, injury, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Diagnosis requires history and witness description, focal epileptiform discharges or seizures on EEG or video-EEG

Name: Epilepsy, Tonic-Clonic
Description: Tonic-clonic epilepsy is a seizure disorder characterized by recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures, either primary generalized or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic, reflecting hypersynchronous cortical network firing with an initial tonic stiffening phase followed by clonic rhythmic jerking, loss of consciousness, tongue biting, cyanosis, autonomic changes, and postictal confusion, headache, or myalgia. Genetic contributions are prominent in idiopathic or developmental epilepsies and include pathogenic variants in ion-channel and synaptic genes such as SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, GABRA1, GABRG2, SLC2A1, STXBP1, and CACNA1H, with proteins affecting voltage-gated sodium, potassium, calcium, and GABA-A receptor function; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, de novo, X-linked, or complex/polygenic depending on syndrome. Core pathophysiology involves imbalance between excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic signaling, altered sodium, calcium, and potassium channel conductance, synaptic vesicle release, thalamocortical oscillatory circuits, and mTOR-related pathways in some developmental epilepsies. Commonly used antiseizure drugs include valproate, which increases GABAergic tone and modulates sodium and T-type calcium channels, levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to reduce synaptic neurotransmitter release, lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and glutamate release, and alternatives such as topiramate or carbamazepine in selected cases. Important comorbidities and complications include depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, sleep disorders, trauma, aspiration, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Diagnosis requires at least two unprovoked seizures or one seizure with high recurrence risk, supported by detailed history, witness description, neurologic examination, EEG showing generalized spike-wave or other epileptiform discharges, brain MRI to detect structural causes, and when indicated metabolic studies, toxicology, or epilepsy gene testing to define subtype and guide counseling and therapy.

Name: Epilepsies, Myoclonic
Description: Myoclonic epilepsies are a heterogeneous group of epileptic disorders defined by brief, shock-like myoclonic jerks arising from cortical hyperexcitability, ranging from genetic generalized epilepsies such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies including Dravet syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut spectrum cases with myoclonus, progressive myoclonic epilepsies such as Unverricht-Lundborg disease, Lafora disease, and mitochondrial forms such as MERRF. Their molecular basis commonly involves ion-channel and synaptic genes, with representative examples including SCN1A, GABRA1, GABRD, CACNB4, EFHC1, CSTB, EPM2A, NHLRC1, SLC2A1, CHD2, and mitochondrial MT-TK mutations; implicated pathways include impaired GABAergic inhibition, altered voltage-gated sodium and calcium channel signaling, synaptic vesicle release, glutamatergic excitation, glycogen metabolism with polyglucosan accumulation in Lafora disease, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation dysfunction. Clinical features typically include myoclonic jerks, often after awakening, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, sometimes absence or atonic seizures, photosensitivity, and in severe forms developmental delay, ataxia, cognitive regression, and stimulus sensitivity. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, mitochondrial, or complex/polygenic depending on subtype; for example, SCN1A-related disease is usually de novo dominant, CSTB and EPM2A/NHLRC1 disorders are recessive, and MERRF is maternally inherited. Common comorbidities and complications include intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, depression and anxiety, injuries, status epilepticus, SUDEP, gait impairment, and progressive neurodegeneration in PME. Diagnosis rests on seizure semiology, family history, neurologic examination, EEG showing generalized spike- or polyspike-wave discharges, photoparoxysmal response or background slowing, brain MRI to exclude structural causes, metabolic and mitochondrial testing when indicated, and targeted gene panels, exome sequencing, or specific assays such as skin biopsy for Lafora bodies. Treatment commonly includes valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and modulates sodium channels, levetiracetam via SV2A binding, clonazepam through GABAA receptor potentiation, and also topiramate or zonisamide;

Name: Epilepsy, Absence
Description: Absence epilepsy is a generalized nonconvulsive epilepsy characterized by brief, abrupt lapses of awareness caused by abnormal oscillatory activity within thalamocortical networks, typically presenting in childhood as frequent staring spells, behavioral arrest, unresponsiveness, eyelid flutter, automatisms, and immediate recovery without postictal confusion; electroencephalography classically shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges in childhood absence epilepsy, with faster 3.5–4-Hz patterns often seen in juvenile absence epilepsy, and hyperventilation commonly provokes events. The disorder includes childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile absence epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy with absence seizures, and less commonly myoclonic absence epilepsy, and may occur as an isolated genetic generalized epilepsy or within developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Genetic susceptibility is often complex and polygenic, but pathogenic variants have been reported in ion channel and synaptic genes including CACNA1H, CACNA1G, CACNA2D2, GABRG2, GABRA1, GABRB3, SLC2A1, HCN1, STX1B, and occasionally SCN1A; inheritance is frequently autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance in familial forms, although de novo and multifactorial patterns also occur. Pathophysiology centers on T-type calcium currents, GABAergic inhibition, glutamatergic corticothalamic excitation, and hyperpolarization-activated currents involving thalamic relay neurons and the reticular thalamic nucleus. First-line treatment is ethosuximide, which suppresses thalamic T-type calcium channels; valproate, which increases GABA availability and modulates sodium and calcium channels; and lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and reduces glutamate release, while selected refractory cases may receive levetiracetam or benzodiazepines. Important comorbidities and complications include attention and executive dysfunction, learning difficulties, anxiety, depression, injury risk, rare progression to generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and treatment adverse effects. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, video-EEG with provocation, neurologic examination typically normal between seizures, and selected genetic testing or neuroimaging when atypical features, developmental delay, or focal findings suggest an alternative syndrome.

Name: Erysipelas
Description: Erysipelas (UMLS C0014733) is an acute, non-necrotizing bacterial infection of the superficial dermis and dermal lymphatics, classically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus), with less common involvement of groups B, C, or G streptococci and, rarely, Staphylococcus aureus. It presents with abrupt fever, chills, malaise, and a painful, bright-red, edematous, warm plaque with a sharply demarcated, raised border, most often on the face or lower extremities; bullous, hemorrhagic, facial, neonatal, and recurrent forms are recognized. Pathobiology is driven more by pathogen virulence factors and host innate immunity than by Mendelian inheritance: streptococcal M proteins encoded by emm genes, hyaluronidase, streptolysins, and superantigens promote adhesion, tissue spread, and cytokine release, while host TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, complement, neutrophils, and lymphatic endothelium are central molecular and cellular components; rare susceptibility associations involve immune-regulatory variants such as HLA class II and mannose-binding lectin deficiency rather than a defined inheritance pattern. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by leukocytosis, elevated CRP or ESR, and when indicated blood cultures in systemic toxicity, culture or PCR from bullae or wounds, and ultrasonography to exclude abscess or deep venous thrombosis; biopsy is seldom required except to rule out cellulitis mimics or necrotizing fasciitis. First-line treatment is penicillin, which inhibits streptococcal cell-wall transpeptidation via penicillin-binding proteins; alternatives include cephalexin or cefazolin, beta-lactams with the same mechanism, clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit and suppresses toxin production, and in selected settings vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini to block cell-wall synthesis. Name: Erythema Multiforme
Description: Erythema multiforme (MeSH D004892) is an acute, usually self-limited, immune-mediated mucocutaneous hypersensitivity disorder characterized by symmetrically distributed targetoid papules or plaques, often acrally predominant, with variable mucosal erosions; it is classically divided into erythema multiforme minor and major, the latter involving one or more mucosal surfaces and greater systemic symptoms. The disease most often follows infection, especially herpes simplex virus type 1 or 2 and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, but can also be drug triggered; pathobiologically it reflects a cytotoxic T-cell response directed against keratinocytes, with prominent IFN-γ, TNF-α, Fas-FasL, perforin/granzyme, and chemokine-driven pathways involving CD8+ lymphocytes, NK cells, ICAM-1, and apoptotic signaling. Genetic predisposition is incompletely defined and inheritance is not typically Mendelian, but susceptibility has been linked in some populations to HLA class I and II alleles, particularly HLA-DQB1*0301, with occasional recurrent familial cases suggesting polygenic immune susceptibility rather than a single causative mutation. Histology and direct clinicopathologic correlation support diagnosis, showing interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes; evaluation includes history of recent HSV, respiratory infection, or new drugs, skin biopsy when uncertain, HSV or Mycoplasma testing in selected cases, and distinction from Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis by limited epidermal detachment and typical target lesions. Common comorbidities and complications include recurrent herpes labialis, pneumonia, dehydration, ocular inflammation, secondary infection, postinflammatory dyspigmentation, and rarely severe mucosal scarring. Treatment centers on trigger control and supportive care; topical or systemic corticosteroids suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription, acyclovir or valacyclovir inhibit viral DNA polymerase and are especially used in HSV-associated recurrent disease, and antihistamines such as cetirizine reduce pruritus via H1-receptor blockade, while severe refractory cases may prompt immunomodulators such as azathioprine or dapsone.

Name: Erythrasma
Description: Erythrasma (MeSH D004894) is a superficial bacterial infection of the stratum corneum caused predominantly by Corynebacterium minutissimum, producing a chronic intertriginous dermatosis rather than a primary genetic disease. It typically presents as well-demarcated red-brown to tan patches or thin plaques with fine scale and mild pruritus, most often in toe webs, groin, axillae, inframammary folds, and other occluded sites; interdigital disease may fissure or macerate. The condition is favored by moisture, hyperhidrosis, obesity, diabetes mellitus, advanced age, poor hygiene, and immunosuppression, and common comorbidities include tinea pedis, candidal intertrigo, diabetic foot problems, and secondary bacterial superinfection. Its key pathogenic feature is colonization by corynebacteria that produce porphyrins, especially coproporphyrin III, accounting for the characteristic coral-red fluorescence under Wood lamp examination; disease biology otherwise reflects superficial bacterial adherence, biofilm formation, and innate immune interactions rather than a defined oncogenic or monogenic signaling pathway, although local barrier dysfunction, inflammatory cytokine signaling, and altered skin microbiome ecology are relevant. No established Mendelian inheritance pattern, recurrent causal mutation, or disease-defining gene is known, though host susceptibility may be influenced by genetic determinants of epidermal barrier and immune function. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by Wood lamp fluorescence, potassium hydroxide preparation to exclude dermatophyte or Candida infection, Gram stain or culture showing gram-positive diphtheroid organisms, and histology only rarely. Localized and generalized forms are recognized, with interdigital and classic intertriginous subtypes. Treatment commonly includes topical erythromycin or clindamycin, which inhibit the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and suppress protein synthesis, fusidic acid, which blocks elongation factor G, or benzoyl peroxide, which exerts oxidative antibacterial effects; more extensive disease may be treated with oral macrolides such as erythromycin or clarithromycin.

Name: Escherichia coli Infections
Description: Escherichia coli infections are predominantly acquired bacterial diseases caused by diverse pathogenic E. coli pathotypes, including enterotoxigenic, enterohemorrhagic or Shiga toxin-producing, enteropathogenic, enteroaggregative, enteroinvasive, uropathogenic, and neonatal meningitis-associated strains, producing syndromes that range from self-limited diarrhea and hemorrhagic colitis to urinary tract infection, sepsis, and meningitis. Virulence is linked to microbial genes and proteins such as stx1/stx2 encoding Shiga toxins, elt/est encoding heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins, eae encoding intimin, tir, fimH and P fimbriae adhesins, hemolysin, K1 capsule, lipopolysaccharide, and siderophore systems, while host susceptibility is influenced by genes affecting innate immunity and receptors, including TLR4, CD14, FUT2, CFTR, and complement regulators; inheritance is therefore not Mendelian for infection itself, but host genetic predisposition can modify risk and severity. Key pathogenic pathways include adherence to intestinal or uroepithelial cells, TLR4-NF-κB and inflammasome activation by LPS, cAMP and cGMP signaling triggered by enterotoxins, type III secretion-mediated actin remodeling, complement activation, and in Shiga toxin disease inhibition of ribosomal function with endothelial injury. Clinical features include watery or bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, dysuria, frequency, flank pain, bacteremia, hypotension, and in severe cases hemolytic uremic syndrome, acute kidney injury, thrombotic microangiopathy, and meningitis; common comorbidities include dehydration, malnutrition, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes, urinary obstruction, pregnancy, immunosuppression, and chronic kidney disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical syndrome plus stool culture and Shiga toxin PCR or immunoassay for diarrheagenic disease, urine culture for UTI, blood cultures for sepsis, CSF analysis and culture for meningitis, with susceptibility testing and molecular typing when needed. Treatment depends on syndrome and resistance profile; commonly used agents include ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis, ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole,

Name: Esophagitis, Peptic
Description: Peptic esophagitis is an acid- and pepsin-mediated inflammatory injury of the esophageal squamous mucosa, usually representing the erosive end of gastroesophageal reflux disease, and ranges from nonerosive inflammation to erosive, ulcerative, hemorrhagic, and chronic fibrosing/stricture-forming disease, sometimes in the setting of Barrett esophagus. Typical manifestations include heartburn, acid regurgitation, retrosternal chest pain, odynophagia, dysphagia, water brash, and, in severe cases, bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia. Its pathobiology reflects impaired antireflux barrier and mucosal defense with cytokine-driven epithelial injury; implicated molecular components include IL1B, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, PTGS2/COX-2, EGFR, NF-κB, and oxidative stress pathways, while genes influencing reflux susceptibility or mucosal response such as IL1B, IL10, TNFA, MMPs, and Barrett-associated alterations including TP53 and CDKN2A may be encountered in complicated chronic disease, although classic Mendelian inheritance is not established and familial clustering is generally multifactorial/polygenic. Common comorbidities include obesity, hiatal hernia, delayed gastric emptying, pregnancy, asthma, chronic cough, laryngitis, peptic ulcer disease, and Barrett esophagus; major complications are ulceration, peptic stricture, aspiration, and progression from Barrett metaplasia to dysplasia and esophageal adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis is primarily clinical when typical reflux symptoms respond to empiric acid suppression, but upper endoscopy with biopsy is indicated for alarm features or refractory symptoms, using erosive grading such as the Los Angeles classification and histology to exclude eosinophilic, infectious, pill-induced, or malignant causes; ambulatory pH or pH-impedance monitoring and esophageal manometry help confirm pathologic reflux and define motility disorders. Standard therapy includes proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, and pantoprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion; and alginate-antacid or sucralfate therapy provides luminal neutralization and mucosal protection.

Name: Exanthema
Description: Exanthema is a descriptive clinical syndrome rather than a single inherited disease, referring to a widespread eruptive rash, usually maculopapular, morbilliform, vesicular, or scarlatiniform, caused most often by viral infection or drug hypersensitivity; common subtypes include viral exanthems such as measles, rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum, varicella, and nonspecific enteroviral eruptions, as well as drug-induced exanthems and toxin-mediated eruptions. Its molecular basis therefore varies by cause: representative infectious determinants include measles virus proteins acting through SLAMF1/CD150 and nectin-4 entry pathways, rubella virus structural proteins, parvovirus B19 capsid proteins with P antigen tropism, HHV-6 latency/reactivation programs, and varicella-zoster glycoproteins; host response pathways prominently involve innate interferon signaling, T-cell activation, Th1/Th2 cytokines, TNF, IL-6, and keratinocyte apoptosis, while drug exanthems may involve HLA-restricted immune recognition, exemplified by associations such as HLA-B*57:01 with abacavir hypersensitivity and HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine-related severe cutaneous reactions. Typical findings are fever, malaise, diffuse erythematous rash, pruritus, enanthem, conjunctivitis, lymphadenopathy, and, in some etiologies, Koplik spots or vesicles; complications include dehydration, secondary bacterial infection, pneumonia, encephalitis, hepatitis, myocarditis, and severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or DRESS. Inheritance is generally non-Mendelian, but genetic susceptibility reflects immune-response loci including HLA alleles and occasionally variants in interferon-pathway genes. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, integrating rash morphology, distribution, timing, medication exposure, vaccination and travel history, and associated systemic signs, with confirmation by PCR, viral serology, CBC and liver tests, skin biopsy when needed, and allergy evaluation or patch testing in selected drug eruptions. Treatment is cause-directed and supportive: acetaminophen inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis for fever, cetirizine blocks H1 receptors for pruritus, and topical or systemic corticosteroids suppress NF-κB– and cytokine-mediated inflammation in inflammatory or drug-related exanthems, while

Name: Radiation Exposure
Description: Radiation exposure is an acquired toxic injury caused by ionizing or, less often, nonionizing radiation, with acute radiation syndrome, localized radiation injury, and delayed stochastic effects such as carcinogenesis as major clinical subtypes; severity depends on dose, dose rate, field, and tissue susceptibility. Its biology is dominated by DNA double-strand breaks and reactive oxygen species, activating ATM-ATR, TP53, CHEK2, BRCA1/2, DNA-PK, PARP, NF-kappaB, TGF-beta/SMAD, MAPK, and apoptotic pathways, with cytokine mediators including IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CSF3. Genetic susceptibility is usually non-Mendelian, but inherited defects in DNA damage response or repair, such as ATM mutations in ataxia-telangiectasia, TP53 in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, NBN, BRCA1/2, XRCC genes, and Fanconi anemia genes, confer marked radiosensitivity and higher cancer risk. Typical manifestations include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, anorexia, transient or persistent erythema, epilation, mucositis, diarrhea, marrow failure with lymphopenia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, infection, bleeding, neurovascular collapse at extreme doses, and chronic fibrosis, cataracts, infertility, thyroid dysfunction, and secondary leukemia or solid tumors. Important comorbidities and complications include burns, sepsis, pancytopenia, gastrointestinal ulceration, radiation pneumonitis, enteritis, osteoradionecrosis, cardiovascular disease, and malignancy. Treatment is mainly supportive and exposure-specific: potassium iodide blocks thyroid uptake of radioactive iodine, Prussian blue binds cesium and thallium in the gut to enhance fecal elimination, and Ca-DTPA or Zn-DTPA chelate transuranics such as plutonium and americium; additional commonly used agents include filgrastim or sargramostim to stimulate granulopoiesis and broad-spectrum antiinfectives, antiemetics, fluids, and transfusions. Diagnosis relies on exposure history, serial time-to-emesis assessment, contamination surveys, CBCs with absolute lymphocyte depletion kinetics, cytogenetic biodosimetry such as dicentric chromosome assay or micronucleus testing, organ-specific laboratory and imaging evaluation, and dosimetry when available.

Name: Extrapyramidal Disorders
Description: Basal ganglia diseases comprise a heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative, metabolic, vascular, infectious, toxic, and inherited disorders affecting the caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and substantia nigra, and are clinically defined by abnormalities of movement, tone, and behavior, most often parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea, tremor, tics, bradykinesia, rigidity, gait disturbance, dysarthria, and neuropsychiatric or cognitive impairment. Major subtypes include Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonian syndromes, Huntington disease, Wilson disease, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, dystonia syndromes, and secondary basal ganglia injury from stroke or toxins. Key molecular associations include SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN, PINK1, and PARK7 in parkinsonian disorders; HTT CAG-repeat expansion in Huntington disease; ATP7B in Wilson disease; and PANK2, PLA2G6, and TOR1A in NBIA and dystonia, involving dopaminergic nigrostriatal signaling, basal ganglia direct and indirect GABAergic pathways, glutamatergic corticostriatal transmission, mitochondrial quality-control and oxidative-stress pathways, lysosomal-autophagic dysfunction, iron and copper homeostasis, and protein aggregation, particularly alpha-synuclein. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, as with HTT, LRRK2, SNCA, and TOR1A, autosomal recessive, as with PRKN, PINK1, DJ-1, ATP7B, and PANK2, or sporadic. Common therapies include levodopa, a dopamine precursor that restores striatal dopamine; dopamine agonists such as pramipexole or ropinirole, which stimulate dopamine receptors; anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl, which reduce cholinergic overactivity; tetrabenazine, a VMAT2 inhibitor for chorea; and botulinum toxin for focal dystonia by blocking acetylcholine release. Frequent comorbidities and complications include depression, psychosis, dementia, dysphagia, falls, aspiration pneumonia, autonomic dysfunction, hepatic disease in Wilson disease, and disability. Name: Eye Diseases
Description: Eye diseases comprise a heterogeneous group of inherited, degenerative, inflammatory, vascular, infectious, and neoplastic disorders affecting the cornea, lens, retina, uvea, optic nerve, and ocular surface; major subtypes include refractive and surface disease, cataract, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, inherited retinal dystrophies, uveitis, and retinal vascular occlusions. Clinical manifestations vary by structure involved but commonly include reduced visual acuity, metamorphopsia, photophobia, pain, redness, floaters, field loss, diplopia, impaired dark adaptation, and elevated intraocular pressure. Genetic contributors are well established in many entities, including ABCA4 in Stargardt disease, RHO and RPGR in retinitis pigmentosa, CFH and ARMS2/HTRA1 in macular degeneration susceptibility, MYOC and OPTN in primary open-angle glaucoma, PAX6 in aniridia, and crystallin genes such as CRYAA/CRYBB2 in congenital cataract; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial, or complex multifactorial depending on subtype. Pathobiology frequently involves VEGF-driven angiogenesis and vascular leakage, complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, TGF-β and Wnt signaling, phototransduction defects, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammasome activation, and apoptosis of retinal ganglion cells or photoreceptors. Common therapies include latanoprost, a prostaglandin F2α analog that increases uveoscleral outflow in glaucoma, timolol, a β-adrenergic blocker that reduces aqueous humor production, acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that lowers intraocular pressure, and intravitreal anti-VEGF agents such as ranibizumab or aflibercept that inhibit neovascularization; corticosteroids suppress ocular inflammation, and antimicrobial agents are used for infectious causes. Eye diseases are commonly linked with diabetes, hypertension, autoimmune disorders, atopy, and systemic infections, and complications include blindness, retinal detachment, corneal scarring, macular edema, neovascularization, and optic atrophy. Diagnosis relies on history and slit-lamp/fundus examination, tonometry, optical coherence tomography, fluorescein angiography, perimetry, electroretinography, ocular ultrasound, microbiologic studies, and targeted or panel-based genetic testing when hereditary disease

Name: Fascioliasis
Description: Fascioliasis (MeSH D005211) is a foodborne zoonotic trematode infection caused mainly by Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, with acute hepatic migratory and chronic biliary forms; it is acquired rather than inherited, and no human Mendelian predisposition is established, although host immunogenetic factors such as HLA variation and cytokine-related polymorphisms in IL4, IL10, IFNG, TLR2, and TLR4 have been implicated in differential susceptibility or inflammatory severity, while parasite-associated molecules including cathepsin L proteases, glutathione S-transferases, fatty acid-binding proteins, and tegumental antigens are important diagnostic and immunobiologic targets. Pathobiology is dominated by Th2-skewed and eosinophilic immune signaling involving IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, TGF-β, IgE, mast cells, macrophages, eosinophils, and hepatobiliary fibrogenic pathways. Patients typically present with fever, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, malaise, urticaria, weight loss, marked eosinophilia, and abnormal liver enzymes in the acute phase, followed in chronic disease by biliary colic, cholangitis, obstructive jaundice, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or recurrent abdominal pain. Major complications include biliary obstruction, secondary bacterial infection, liver abscess-like lesions, fibrosis, anemia, and occasional ectopic disease affecting lung, skin, or central nervous system; comorbidities may include gallstone disease, chronic hepatobiliary inflammation, and malnutrition in endemic settings. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus eosinophilia, stool microscopy for eggs in chronic infection, serology such as ELISA or immunoblot to parasite excretory-secretory antigens, coproantigen assays, and hepatobiliary imaging by ultrasound, CT, MRI, or ERCP when obstruction is suspected. Triclabendazole is first-line, acting by binding parasite β-tubulin and disrupting microtubule-dependent tegumental and metabolic processes; bithionol is an alternative with flukicidal effects on parasite oxidative metabolism; nitazoxanide inhibits pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase-dependent anaerobic energy metabolism, though efficacy is variable, and endoscopic or surgical intervention may be required for complicated

Name: Fever
Description: Fever (MeSH D005334) is a regulated elevation of core body temperature, usually >38.0°C, caused by a hypothalamic set-point increase in response to infection, inflammation, malignancy, drug exposure, or autoimmune/autoinflammatory disease, and is best viewed as a clinical sign and physiologic syndrome rather than a single inherited disease. Its molecular basis centers on pyrogen-driven innate immune signaling, especially IL1B, IL6, TNF, IFNG, PTGS2/COX-2, TLR4, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and prostaglandin E2 signaling through EP3 receptors in the preoptic hypothalamus; representative genetic causes are most relevant in periodic fever syndromes, including MEFV mutations in familial Mediterranean fever, TNFRSF1A in TRAPS, MVK in mevalonate kinase deficiency, and NLRP3 gain-of-function variants in cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, typically inherited in autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant patterns depending on the disorder. Clinical manifestations include elevated temperature, chills, rigors, sweats, malaise, myalgias, headache, tachycardia, dehydration, and, in severe cases, delirium or febrile seizures; patterns include intermittent, remittent, sustained, relapsing, hyperpyrexia, and periodic fever. Common comorbidities and complications include sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis, dehydration, acute kidney injury, shock, and exacerbation of underlying cardiovascular or neurologic disease. Treatment targets the cause and symptoms: acetaminophen inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis to lower the hypothalamic set point, ibuprofen and aspirin inhibit COX enzymes and reduce PGE2-mediated pyresis, and in selected inflammatory or periodic fever syndromes corticosteroids suppress NF-κB-dependent cytokine transcription, while colchicine or IL-1 blockers such as anakinra may be used when autoinflammation is confirmed. Diagnosis relies on documented temperature elevation plus history and examination, followed by targeted testing such as CBC, CRP/ESR, blood and urine cultures, viral PCR, imaging, and, when recurrent unexplained fevers suggest heritable syndromes, genetic testing for MEFV, TNFRSF1A, MVK, or NLRP3.

Name: Breast Fibrocystic Disease
Description: Fibrocystic breast disease, more accurately termed fibrocystic breast change, is a common benign, non-neoplastic disorder of the breast characterized by hormonally responsive cyst formation, stromal fibrosis, and varying degrees of epithelial hyperplasia, often classified into nonproliferative change, proliferative disease without atypia, and atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia, the latter conferring a modestly increased future breast cancer risk. It is not usually inherited in a Mendelian pattern, but susceptibility reflects hormonal milieu and polygenic influences; representative molecular associations include estrogen receptor ESR1, progesterone receptor PGR, prolactin signaling components, growth-factor pathways such as EGFR/HER family members, cyclin D1/CCND1, and occasional overlap with hereditary breast cancer predisposition genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 when atypia or strong family history is present, although no single causative mutation defines typical disease. Pathobiology centers on estrogen- and progesterone-driven epithelial proliferation, fluid secretion, and stromal remodeling, with MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT, TGF-β, and prolactin/JAK-STAT signaling implicated. Clinical features include cyclic mastalgia, breast fullness, nodularity, tenderness, and palpable mobile cystic areas, usually fluctuating with the menstrual cycle. Diagnosis is based on history and breast examination, complemented by ultrasound for cystic lesions, mammography when age-appropriate, aspiration of symptomatic cysts, and core needle biopsy when imaging or examination suggests a solid, complex, persistent, or atypical lesion; pathology excludes malignancy and characterizes proliferative change. Commonly used treatments are symptomatic rather than disease-specific and include acetaminophen, a central analgesic; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or topical diclofenac, which inhibit cyclooxygenase and reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain; and danazol, a pituitary gonadotropin suppressor that reduces ovarian estrogen production. Selected refractory cases may use tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, or bromocriptine, a dopamine D2 agonist that lowers prolactin. Comorbidities include anxiety about cancer, recurrent breast cysts, mastitis-like discomfort, and coexistence with benign breast lesions such as fibroadenoma.

Name: Fibromyalgia
Description: Fibromyalgia (MeSH D005356) is a chronic centralized pain syndrome characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, nonrestorative sleep, cognitive dysfunction, and somatic symptom burden, often accompanied by tenderness, stiffness, headache, irritable bowel symptoms, and mood disturbance. Its pathobiology is multifactorial rather than monogenic, with genetic susceptibility supported by familial aggregation and low-to-moderate heritability; implicated genes include SLC6A4 and HTR2A in serotonergic signaling, COMT and MAOA in catecholamine metabolism, DRD4, TACR1, TRPV1, and adrenergic receptor variants, although no single mutation is diagnostic. Core mechanisms involve central sensitization with augmented nociceptive processing, impaired descending inhibitory pathways using serotonin and norepinephrine, glutamatergic and substance P excess, altered dopamine signaling, neuroinflammation with cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation, and small-fiber neuropathy in a subset. Commonly linked comorbidities include depression, anxiety, migraine, temporomandibular disorder, chronic fatigue syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, interstitial cystitis, dysautonomia, obesity, and sleep disorders; complications include functional impairment, disability, and medication adverse effects. Recognized subtypes are primary fibromyalgia and secondary fibromyalgia occurring with rheumatic or other chronic disorders. Inheritance is complex polygenic and non-Mendelian, influenced by environmental triggers such as trauma, infection, and psychosocial stress. Diagnosis is clinical, based on the American College of Rheumatology criteria using widespread pain index and symptom severity scores, with generalized pain present for at least 3 months; laboratory testing, inflammatory markers, thyroid studies, and selective rheumatologic evaluation are mainly used to exclude mimicking conditions, while tender point examination is now supportive rather than required. Treatment commonly includes duloxetine and milnacipran, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors that enhance descending analgesic inhibition, and pregabalin, an α2δ calcium-channel ligand that reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release; amitriptyline, cyclobenzaprine, and gabapentin are also frequently used.

Name: Flatulence
Description: Flatulence (UMLS C0016204) is a symptom complex rather than a primary inherited disease, characterized by excessive intestinal gas production or impaired gas transit, leading to increased passage of flatus, abdominal bloating, borborygmi, pressure, and sometimes crampy pain; clinically it may be physiologic, diet related, dysbiotic, or secondary to gastrointestinal disorders such as lactose intolerance, fructose or FODMAP malabsorption, celiac disease, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, inflammatory bowel disease, or gastrointestinal motility disorders. Genetic contributions are usually indirect and disease specific, with representative examples including LCT regulatory variants causing adult-type hypolactasia, sucrase-isomaltase (SI) defects causing carbohydrate maldigestion, CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis, and genes affecting enteric neuromuscular function or visceral sensitivity in subsets of IBS; inheritance therefore depends on the underlying disorder, ranging from common complex polygenic susceptibility to autosomal recessive enzyme or transporter defects. Pathophysiologically, excess gas arises from colonic microbial fermentation and host-microbe interactions involving methane- and hydrogen-producing archaea and bacteria, epithelial transport, short-chain fatty acid signaling, serotonin-mediated motility pathways, bile acid handling, low-grade mucosal immune activation, and gut-brain axis dysregulation. Common treatments include simethicone, an anti-foaming agent that coalesces gas bubbles; alpha-galactosidase, which hydrolyzes nonabsorbable oligosaccharides before fermentation; lactase enzyme replacement for lactose maldigestion; rifaximin, a poorly absorbed antibiotic used particularly when SIBO or IBS is suspected; and probiotics that modulate microbial composition and fermentation. Comorbidities include functional dyspepsia, anxiety, depression, pelvic floor dysfunction, and chronic constipation; complications are usually limited to impaired quality of life, though persistent symptoms may signal malabsorption, weight loss, anemia, or serious structural disease. Diagnosis is clinical but guided by alarm features, dietary history, stool pattern, and symptom burden, with targeted testing such as lactose hydrogen breath testing, celiac serologies, SIBO breath tests, stool studies, fecal elastase, endoscopy, or imaging when indicated.

Name: Folliculitis
Description: Folliculitis (UMLS C0016436) is a usually acquired inflammatory disorder of the hair follicle, most often infectious but also irritant, occlusive, eosinophilic, or drug induced, characterized clinically by pruritic or tender follicular papules and pustules centered on hairs, sometimes with perifollicular erythema, crusting, pain, or postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and, in deeper forms such as sycosis barbae or furunculosis, nodules, abscesses, and scarring alopecia. Common subtypes include superficial bacterial folliculitis, hot-tub folliculitis due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Malassezia folliculitis, gram-negative folliculitis, pseudofolliculitis barbae, eosinophilic folliculitis, and dissecting or decalvans forms of the scalp. Pathobiology centers on follicular barrier disruption, microbial overgrowth, neutrophilic or eosinophilic inflammation, and innate immune signaling through Toll-like receptors, NF-kB, inflammasome/IL-1, TNF-alpha, IL-8/CXCL8, IL-17, and Th2 cytokines in eosinophilic disease; complement, keratinization pathways, and biofilm formation may contribute in chronic scarring variants. Genetic factors are usually indirect rather than Mendelian, but susceptibility is increased by immunodeficiency or barrier defects, with representative associations including HIV in eosinophilic folliculitis, CYBB-related chronic granulomatous disease, STAT3 deficiency, and keratinization-related disorders; recurrent staphylococcal disease can involve host variation affecting filaggrin, TLR2, or DEFB4-mediated antimicrobial defense. Treatment depends on cause and commonly includes topical or oral antibiotics such as mupirocin, which inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase, clindamycin, which blocks the 50S ribosomal subunit, and doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S subunit and also suppresses neutrophilic inflammation; other options include benzoyl peroxide, azoles such as ketoconazole for Malassezia, and isotretinoin, which reduces sebaceous activity and follicular occlusion. Comorbidities include diabetes, obesity, hidradenitis suppurativa, atopic dermatitis, acne, shaving trauma, and immunosuppression, while

Name: Furunculosis
Description: Furunculosis (UMLS C0016867) is a usually acute, sometimes recurrent, deep bacterial infection of the hair follicle and perifollicular dermis that produces painful erythematous nodules evolving to pustular or fluctuant abscesses, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including community-acquired MRSA, with common symptoms and signs of localized pain, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, surrounding cellulitis, and occasionally fever or regional lymphadenitis; carbuncles represent a deeper, coalescent subtype, and chronic or recurrent furunculosis is recognized clinically. Its pathobiology centers on bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation, neutrophil recruitment, and innate immune signaling through TLR2, NF-κB, inflammasome/IL-1 and IL-17 axes, with virulence factors such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin and alpha-toxin contributing to tissue necrosis, while host susceptibility is increased by impaired skin barrier and immune dysfunction. Genetic contributions are generally predispositional rather than Mendelian, but recurrent disease may occur with variants affecting innate immunity, including MYD88, IRAK4, NCF1/NCF2/CYBB in chronic granulomatous disease, STAT3 in hyper-IgE syndrome, and FLG-mediated barrier dysfunction; inheritance therefore depends on the underlying disorder and may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked. Important comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, obesity, hidradenitis suppurativa, atopic dermatitis, nasal S. aureus carriage, immunodeficiency, scarring, bacteremia, osteomyelitis, and rarely sepsis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by examination for fluctuance, bacterial culture and susceptibility testing of drainage, MRSA screening, blood glucose/HbA1c, CBC, and immunologic or genetic evaluation in severe, early-onset, or recurrent cases. Treatment combines incision and drainage with anti-staphylococcal agents such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins, clindamycin, which inhibits 50S ribosomal protein synthesis, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline, which inhibit folate synthesis and the 30S ribosome respectively; mupirocin and chlorhexidine are often used for decolonization.

Name: Gastritis
Description: Gastritis (MeSH D005756) is an inflammatory and often erosive or atrophic disorder of the gastric mucosa that may be acute or chronic and is classically subdivided into Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis, autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis, reactive/chemical gastritis from bile reflux or NSAIDs, eosinophilic gastritis, and stress-related hemorrhagic gastritis. Its pathobiology centers on epithelial injury and immune activation, with H. pylori virulence factors such as CagA and VacA driving NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, TLR, NLRP3 inflammasome, and cytokine pathways involving IL1B, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, IFNG, PTGS2/COX-2, and CDH1-related epithelial integrity; host susceptibility has been linked to polymorphisms in IL1B, IL10, TNFA, TLR4, and other inflammatory genes, while autoimmune disease features antibodies to ATP4A/ATP4B and intrinsic factor targeting parietal cells. Most cases are acquired rather than inherited, but familial clustering reflects polygenic inflammatory predisposition and, rarely, syndromic risk for diffuse gastric cancer in CDH1 mutation carriers with chronic gastritic change. Typical manifestations include epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness, nausea, vomiting, bloating, anorexia, occult or overt upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and in chronic atrophic forms iron deficiency or vitamin B12 deficiency with pernicious anemia. Important comorbidities and complications include peptic ulcer disease, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, gastric adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma, GI hemorrhage, and association with autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, and other autoimmune disorders. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, medication and alcohol review, H. pylori testing by urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy, upper endoscopy with histology for inflammation, activity, atrophy, metaplasia, or eosinophilia, CBC and iron/B12 studies, and serologies for parietal cell or intrinsic factor antibodies when autoimmune gastritis is suspected. Treatment commonly includes proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase, H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine, which suppress histamine-mediated acid

Name: Gastroesophageal Reflux
Description: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD; MeSH D005764) is a common multifactorial disorder in which reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus causes troublesome symptoms or mucosal injury, driven primarily by transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations, hypotensive lower esophageal sphincter tone, impaired esophageal clearance, delayed gastric emptying, hiatal hernia, and increased intra-abdominal pressure. Typical symptoms and signs include heartburn, acid regurgitation, sour taste, chest discomfort, dysphagia, odynophagia, chronic cough, hoarseness, throat clearing, laryngitis, and enamel erosion; major subtypes include nonerosive reflux disease, erosive reflux esophagitis, extraesophageal reflux, and Barrett-associated reflux. Molecular contributors are incompletely defined but include familial susceptibility and variants in genes influencing epithelial integrity, inflammation, and visceral sensation, with representative associations reported for GNB3, IL1B, IL10, COX2/PTGS2, MMP9, and collagen-related loci, while Barrett progression involves TP53 and CDKN2A alterations rather than uncomplicated GERD itself; inheritance is therefore complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. Relevant pathways include vagovagal and nitric oxide-mediated lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, inflammatory signaling through NF-kB, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, cyclooxygenase-prostaglandin pathways, oxidative stress responses, and epithelial barrier dysfunction involving tight-junction proteins such as claudins and occludin. Treatment commonly uses proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, and pantoprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the parietal-cell H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine, which reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion; alginate-antacids, which neutralize acid and form a raft barrier; and prokinetics such as metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist that enhances gastric emptying and lower esophageal sphincter tone. GERD is linked to obesity, pregnancy, asthma, chronic laryngitis, obstructive sleep apnea, and scleroderma, and complications include erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, ulceration, bleeding, Barrett esophagus, and esophageal adenocarcinoma.
