Name: Gaucher Disease
Description: Gaucher disease (MeSH D005776) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused predominantly by autosomal recessive pathogenic variants in GBA1, which encodes the lysosomal hydrolase acid beta-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase), leading to impaired degradation of glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine and accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages (Gaucher cells); common mutations include N370S (p.Asn409Ser) and L444P (p.Leu483Pro), while saposin C deficiency due to PSAP variants is a rare phenocopy. The central pathobiology involves lysosomal dysfunction, macrophage activation, cytokine-driven inflammation, ER stress, autophagy impairment, and disturbed sphingolipid metabolism, with downstream effects on osteoclast/osteoblast balance, spleen and liver reticuloendothelial compartments, and in neuronopathic forms the central nervous system. Type 1 disease is non-neuronopathic, whereas types 2 and 3 are acute and chronic neuronopathic forms. Typical manifestations include splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, easy bruising, fatigue, growth delay, delayed puberty, bone pain, osteopenia, osteonecrosis, fractures, and marrow infiltration; neurologic signs such as gaze palsy, seizures, bulbar dysfunction, spasticity, and developmental regression characterize types 2 and 3. Important complications and comorbidities include hypersplenism, pulmonary hypertension, interstitial lung disease, gallstones, Parkinson disease risk in GBA1 carriers and patients, monoclonal gammopathy, and multiple myeloma. Diagnosis rests on low leukocyte or fibroblast glucocerebrosidase enzymatic activity, confirmatory GBA1 molecular testing, and supportive biomarkers such as elevated chitotriosidase, CCL18, and glucosylsphingosine, with MRI and bone evaluation used for staging. Treatment includes enzyme replacement therapy with imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa, or taliglucerase alfa, which supply functional glucocerebrosidase to macrophages, and substrate reduction therapy with eliglustat or miglustat, which inhibit glucosylceramide synthase and reduce sphingolipid production.

Name: Genital chancre
Description: Genital chancre is the classic primary lesion of sexually acquired syphilis, an infectious ulcerative disease caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum, usually presenting as a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer with a clean base and associated non-tender regional lymphadenopathy, although lesions may be multiple, painful if secondarily infected, or atypical in immunocompromised hosts. It is not an inherited disorder and has no Mendelian transmission pattern; host genetic susceptibility is incompletely defined, but variability in innate and adaptive immune response genes, particularly HLA class II loci and cytokine-related pathways, may influence susceptibility and severity, while the pathogen’s relevant molecular determinants include outer membrane proteins such as TprK, which undergoes antigenic variation, fibronectin-binding proteins, and Tp47/TpN47 and other lipoproteins that stimulate host immunity. Pathobiology centers on spirochetal adhesion, tissue invasion, endothelial interaction, and a Th1-skewed inflammatory response involving macrophages, dendritic cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, and NF-kB/TLR1-TLR2 signaling. Important subtypes are syphilitic chancres of primary syphilis, including genital, anal, and oral inoculation lesions, with progression to secondary, latent, tertiary, or neurosyphilitic disease if untreated. Standard therapy includes benzathine penicillin G, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; doxycycline, a tetracycline that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks protein synthesis; ceftriaxone, a cephalosporin that also inhibits cell wall synthesis; and, less commonly in selected situations, azithromycin, a macrolide targeting the 50S ribosomal subunit, though resistance can occur via 23S rRNA mutations such as A2058G. Major comorbidities and complications include HIV coinfection, other sexually transmitted infections, secondary bacterial superinfection, progression to disseminated syphilis, vertical transmission causing congenital syphilis, and, later, cardiovascular or neurologic involvement. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical findings plus direct detection by dark-field microscopy, PCR, or direct fluorescent antibody testing from lesion exudate, together with serologic confirmation using nontreponemal tests such as RPR

Name: Giardiasis
Description: Giardiasis (MeSH D005873) is a noninvasive protozoal infection of the upper small intestine caused by Giardia duodenalis (syn. G. lamblia, G. intestinalis), typically transmitted by the fecal-oral route through contaminated water, food, or person-to-person spread, and clinically ranging from asymptomatic carriage to acute or chronic diarrheal disease. Major assemblages infecting humans are A and B, with parasite virulence and host susceptibility influenced by giardial variant-specific surface proteins, giardins, arginine deiminase, cysteine proteases, and host immune genes affecting mucosal defense, including IgA production and HLA-linked responses; increased risk is seen in primary humoral immunodeficiencies such as common variable immunodeficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and selective IgA deficiency, but the infection itself is not inherited. Pathobiology involves epithelial adherence by the ventral disc, disruption of tight-junction and brush-border function, mast-cell and T-cell responses, IL-6/IL-17- and nitric oxide-related pathways, and malabsorption driven by enterocyte injury and altered bile acid and electrolyte handling. Typical findings are foul-smelling greasy diarrhea, steatorrhea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramps, nausea, weight loss, fatigue, and failure to thrive in children; complications include chronic malabsorption, lactose intolerance, micronutrient deficiency, post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome, growth impairment, and occasionally reactive arthritis or urticaria. Diagnosis is established by stool antigen or nucleic acid amplification testing, ova-and-parasite microscopy on serial stool specimens demonstrating cysts or trophozoites, or duodenal aspirate/biopsy when stool tests are negative but suspicion remains. Standard therapy includes metronidazole, tinidazole, and nitazoxanide; nitroimidazoles are reduced in anaerobic metabolism to DNA-damaging radicals, whereas nitazoxanide inhibits pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase-dependent electron transfer. Albendazole, which disrupts parasite microtubules by binding beta-tubulin, is an alternative, and refractory disease may require combination therapy and evaluation for underlying immunodeficiency or reinfection.

Name: Gingivitis
Description: Gingivitis (UMLS C0017574) is a common, usually reversible inflammatory disease of the gingiva caused primarily by dental plaque biofilm, with subtypes including plaque-induced gingivitis and non–plaque-induced forms related to hormonal changes, drugs, allergy, infection, or systemic disease. It typically presents with erythema, edema, tenderness, halitosis, and bleeding on brushing or probing, while attachment loss and alveolar bone destruction are absent, distinguishing it from periodontitis. Pathobiology is driven by host-microbial interactions involving dysbiotic organisms and activation of innate and adaptive immune pathways, particularly Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB, MAPK, inflammasome activity, and cytokine networks centered on IL1B, IL6, TNF, CXCL8, PTGS2/COX-2, matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP8 and MMP9, and RANKL/OPG balance; salivary or tissue biomarkers may reflect these processes. Genetic contribution is modest and usually complex rather than Mendelian, but susceptibility has been linked to variants in IL1A/IL1B, TNF, IL6, TLR4, VDR, DEFB1, and Fc gamma receptor genes, while rare syndromic backgrounds with severe gingival inflammation can occur in immune dysfunction states; inheritance therefore is generally multifactorial with gene-environment interaction. Important comorbidities and modifiers include diabetes mellitus, smoking, pregnancy, puberty, malnutrition, immunodeficiency, leukemia, and poor oral hygiene, and complications include progression to periodontitis, gingival enlargement, ulceration, and tooth-supporting tissue damage if persistent. Diagnosis is clinical, based on visible inflammation and bleeding on probing without clinical attachment loss, supported by periodontal charting, plaque and bleeding indices, radiographs to exclude bone loss, and selective microbiologic, hematologic, or biopsy evaluation when atypical disease is suspected. Treatment centers on plaque control and professional debridement, with adjunctive drugs such as chlorhexidine, a broad-spectrum membrane-disrupting bisbiguanide antiseptic; metronidazole, which damages anaerobic bacterial DNA after intracellular reduction; doxycycline, a tetracycline that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and, at subantimicrobial dosing, suppresses MMP activity; and for symptom relief, ibuprofen, a COX inhibitor that reduces prostaglandin-mediated inflammation.

Name: Glaucoma
Description: Glaucoma (MeSH D005901) is a heterogeneous group of progressive optic neuropathies characterized by retinal ganglion cell loss, optic nerve head cupping, and corresponding visual field defects, usually but not invariably associated with elevated intraocular pressure from impaired aqueous humor outflow. Major subtypes include primary open-angle glaucoma, normal-tension glaucoma, primary angle-closure glaucoma, congenital/juvenile glaucoma, and secondary glaucomas such as pseudoexfoliative, pigmentary, uveitic, neovascular, and steroid-induced disease. Clinical features include initially asymptomatic peripheral field loss, progressive tunnel vision, increased cup-to-disc ratio, retinal nerve fiber layer thinning, and in acute angle closure severe ocular pain, halos, headache, nausea, corneal edema, and a mid-dilated fixed pupil. Genetic contributors include MYOC mutations causing juvenile/adult-onset open-angle glaucoma, CYP1B1 and TEK/ANGPT1 in congenital glaucoma, OPTN and TBK1 in normal-tension glaucoma, and LOXL1 in exfoliation syndrome; inheritance is often complex polygenic, although autosomal dominant MYOC- or OPTN-related disease and autosomal recessive CYP1B1-related disease are recognized. Pathobiology involves trabecular meshwork dysfunction, extracellular matrix remodeling, TGF-β, Wnt, Rho kinase, myocilin-induced ER stress, vascular dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, glutamate excitotoxicity, neuroinflammation, and apoptosis. Treatment aims to lower intraocular pressure: prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost increase uveoscleral outflow; beta-blockers such as timolol reduce aqueous production; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dorzolamide or acetazolamide reduce bicarbonate-dependent secretion; alpha2-agonists such as brimonidine decrease production and increase outflow; pilocarpine enhances trabecular outflow; and rho-kinase inhibitors such as netarsudil increase conventional outflow and lower episcleral venous pressure. Comorbidities and complications include cataract, myopia or hyperopia depending on subtype, diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea, migraine, uveitis, retinal vein occlusion, and irreversible blindness. Name: Glaucoma, Angle-Closure
Description: Angle-closure glaucoma is a vision-threatening ocular disorder in which mechanical obstruction of aqueous humor outflow at the iridocorneal angle, usually from pupillary block, plateau iris configuration, or lens-related crowding, causes abrupt or chronic elevation of intraocular pressure and optic neuropathy; major subtypes include primary angle-closure suspect, primary angle closure, acute primary angle-closure crisis, chronic angle-closure glaucoma, and secondary forms due to neovascularization, uveitis, lens intumescence, or drugs. Genetic susceptibility is complex and usually multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with associations reported for PLEKHA7, COL11A1, PCMTD1-ST18, EPDR1, FERMT2, and matrix-remodeling genes such as MMP9, while rare familial clustering reflects inherited ocular biometry including short axial length and shallow anterior chamber. Relevant molecular pathways include extracellular matrix and scleral/corneal remodeling, TGF-β signaling, MMP-mediated tissue turnover, iris stromal and ciliary body anatomy, aqueous humor dynamics involving carbonic anhydrase, Na+/K+-ATPase, and adrenergic/cholinergic regulation, and in secondary disease VEGF-driven neovascular angle closure. Patients typically present with severe ocular pain, blurred vision, halos, headache, nausea, vomiting, conjunctival injection, corneal edema, mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, shallow anterior chamber, and markedly elevated intraocular pressure, whereas chronic disease may be insidious with peripheral anterior synechiae, glaucomatous cupping, and visual field loss. Diagnosis relies on tonometry, gonioscopy demonstrating appositional or synechial angle closure, slit-lamp examination, optic nerve and retinal nerve fiber layer assessment, automated perimetry, anterior-segment OCT or ultrasound biomicroscopy, and biometric evaluation. Treatment commonly includes acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces aqueous production; topical timolol, a β-adrenergic blocker that decreases aqueous secretion; pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist producing miosis and opening the angle; and often brimonidine, an α2-agonist reducing production and increasing uveoscleral outflow, with laser peripheral iridotomy or lens extraction definitive in many cases. Important comorbidities and complications include cataract, hyperopia, diabetes, vascular disease, recurrent attacks, syne

Name: Glaucoma, Open-Angle
Description: Open-angle glaucoma is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy, usually bilateral and often asymmetrical, characterized by retinal ganglion cell loss, optic nerve head cupping, and corresponding visual field defects, most commonly primary open-angle glaucoma but including normal-tension, juvenile-onset, and secondary open-angle forms such as pseudoexfoliative and pigmentary glaucoma. Its pathobiology centers on impaired aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal, extracellular matrix remodeling, TGF-β signaling, MYOC-associated endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and glutamate-mediated or other apoptotic pathways affecting retinal ganglion cells. Genetic contributors include MYOC mutations, especially in juvenile and some adult familial cases, OPTN and TBK1 in normal-tension glaucoma, CYP1B1 in early-onset disease, and common risk loci such as CDKN2B-AS1, CAV1/CAV2, TMCO1, SIX6, and LOXL1 in pseudoexfoliation-related disease; inheritance is often complex and multifactorial, although autosomal dominant transmission is seen with some MYOC pedigrees and copy-number variation involving TBK1. Patients are frequently asymptomatic until peripheral visual field loss develops; signs include elevated intraocular pressure in many but not all cases, open anterior chamber angles on gonioscopy, increased cup-to-disc ratio, retinal nerve fiber layer thinning, optic disc hemorrhages, and arcuate, nasal step, or paracentral defects on perimetry. Diagnosis relies on tonometry, pachymetry, gonioscopy, dilated optic nerve examination, automated visual field testing, and optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer and ganglion cell complex, with risk stratification aided selectively by family history and genetic testing. Major comorbidities and complications include cataract, myopia, diabetes, hypertension, vascular dysregulation, sleep apnea, and irreversible blindness. Standard treatments lower intraocular pressure: prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost increase uveoscleral outflow, topical beta-blockers such as timolol reduce aqueous production, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dorzolamide decrease bicarbonate-dependent aqueous secretion, and alpha2-agonists such as brimonidine both reduce production and enhance uveoscleral outflow.

Name: Goiter
Description: Goiter (MeSH D006042) is an enlargement of the thyroid gland that may be diffuse or nodular and occur in euthyroid, hypothyroid, or hyperthyroid states, most commonly from iodine deficiency, autoimmune disease, or autonomous nodular growth. Genetic contributors include germline defects in thyroid hormone synthesis and thyroid development genes such as TSHR, TG, TPO, SLC5A5/NIS, SLC26A4, DUOX2, DUOXA2, IYD, PAX8, NKX2-1, FOXE1, and TSHB, while somatic activating mutations in TSHR or GNAS are classic in toxic adenoma and toxic multinodular goiter. Key biology involves the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis, especially TSH-TSHR signaling through cAMP/PKA and growth-promoting PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways, as well as iodide transport, organification, thyroglobulin iodination, and autoimmune inflammatory pathways in Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis. Clinical features include visible or palpable neck swelling, pressure symptoms such as dysphagia, dyspnea, cough, hoarseness, and manifestations of thyroid dysfunction including weight change, heat or cold intolerance, tremor, palpitations, constipation, and fatigue. Major subtypes are diffuse nontoxic goiter, multinodular goiter, toxic multinodular goiter, endemic goiter, sporadic goiter, and congenital dyshormonogenetic goiter. Inheritance is often multifactorial, but congenital forms may be autosomal recessive, whereas susceptibility variants in transcription-factor genes can be familial. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, serum TSH with free T4 and T3, thyroid autoantibodies when autoimmune disease is suspected, ultrasonography to define size and nodules, radionuclide uptake scanning for functional autonomy, urinary iodine in population assessment, and fine-needle aspiration for suspicious nodules. Treatment depends on cause and physiology and commonly includes levothyroxine to replace hormone and suppress TSH in selected hypothyroid or diffuse goiters, methimazole or propylthiouracil to inhibit thyroid peroxidase-mediated hormone synthesis, radioactive iodine to ablate hyperfunctioning tissue, iodine supplementation in deficiency, and surgery for compressive symptoms or malignancy concern; complications include airway or esophageal compression, arr

Name: Gonorrhea
Description: Gonorrhea (MeSH D006069) is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the Gram-negative diplococcus Neisseria gonorrhoeae, producing localized mucosal disease or disseminated infection and classically presenting with urethritis, cervicitis, purulent urethral or vaginal discharge, dysuria, pelvic pain, intermenstrual bleeding, proctitis, pharyngitis, or conjunctivitis, although many infections, especially cervical and pharyngeal, are asymptomatic. Disease phenotypes include uncomplicated urogenital, rectal, and pharyngeal gonorrhea, ophthalmia neonatorum, pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymo-orchitis, and disseminated gonococcal infection with dermatitis, tenosynovitis, and septic arthritis. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial pili and Opa/PorB adhesins, lipooligosaccharide, IgA protease, and marked antigenic variation involving pilE/pilS and opa genes, while antimicrobial resistance is linked to mosaic penA encoding altered PBP2, mtrR and the MtrCDE efflux system, porB penB variants, ponA, gyrA/parC, and 23S rRNA or rplD/rplV mutations. Host interaction prominently activates TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and epithelial cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF. Treatment relies on antibiotics, most commonly ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits cell-wall transpeptidation via penicillin-binding proteins, often with doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, if Chlamydia trachomatis has not been excluded; alternatives in selected settings include azithromycin, a 50S macrolide inhibitor, cefixime, and gentamicin, an aminoglycoside causing mistranslation. Major complications include infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, adverse pregnancy outcomes, neonatal blindness, HIV acquisition/transmission, and invasive arthritis or rarely endocarditis/meningitis. Gonorrhea is infectious rather than inherited, but susceptibility is modified by host genetics such as complement deficiencies predisposing to disseminated disease and polymorphisms affecting innate immunity. Diagnosis is established by nucleic acid amplification testing of urine

Name: Gout
Description: Gout (MeSH D006073) is a common inflammatory crystal arthropathy caused by sustained hyperuricemia leading to deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues, and it presents with abrupt, intensely painful attacks of monoarthritis, classically podagra, with erythema, warmth, swelling, exquisite tenderness, and in chronic disease tophi, bursitis, nephrolithiasis, and urate nephropathy. It comprises asymptomatic hyperuricemia, acute gout flares, intercritical gout, and chronic tophaceous gout. Pathobiologically, urate overproduction or more often impaired renal or intestinal excretion is influenced by genes encoding urate transporters and purine-metabolic proteins, notably SLC2A9/GLUT9, ABCG2, SLC22A12/URAT1, SLC17A1, and less commonly PRPS1 and HPRT1; familial juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy due to UMOD-related renal handling defects can predispose to gout, and inheritance is usually complex polygenic, although rare monogenic forms occur. MSU crystals activate innate immunity through phagocytosis, lysosomal injury, TLR2/TLR4 priming, NF-κB signaling, and especially the NLRP3 inflammasome with caspase-1-mediated IL-1β and IL-18 release, driving neutrophil recruitment and acute synovitis. Major comorbidities include obesity, metabolic syndrome, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and alcohol overuse. Diagnosis is definitive by identification of negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals in synovial fluid or tophus aspirate; classification commonly uses the 2015 ACR/EULAR criteria, supported by serum urate measurement, inflammatory markers, ultrasound double-contour sign, and dual-energy CT. Treatment includes NSAIDs such as indomethacin, colchicine, which inhibits microtubule-dependent neutrophil inflammasome responses, corticosteroids for flare suppression, allopurinol and febuxostat, xanthine oxidase inhibitors that reduce urate synthesis, probenecid, a uricosuric inhibiting URAT1-mediated reabsorption, and pegloticase, a recombinant uricase that enzymatically degrades uric acid.

Name: Graft vs Host Disease
Description: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a non-inherited, immune-mediated complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and less often solid-organ transplantation or transfusion, in which donor T lymphocytes recognize recipient alloantigens and induce tissue injury; it is classically divided into acute and chronic forms, with overlap syndromes. Its biology centers on HLA disparity and minor histocompatibility antigens, donor T-cell receptor activation, host and donor antigen-presenting cells, and inflammatory pathways involving IL-2, IL-6, TNF, IFN-γ, JAK/STAT, NF-κB, chemokine trafficking, B-cell activation including BAFF, and regulatory T-cell dysfunction; representative genetic contributors to susceptibility or severity include donor-recipient HLA class I/II mismatching, and polymorphisms in CTLA4, IL10, TNF, NOD2/CARD15, and cytokine-related loci. Acute GVHD typically affects skin, gastrointestinal tract, and liver, causing maculopapular rash, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, ileus, and cholestatic hepatitis with hyperbilirubinemia; chronic GVHD resembles autoimmune/fibrosing disease, with lichenoid or sclerodermatous skin changes, sicca syndrome, oral ulcers, bronchiolitis obliterans, fasciitis, cholestasis, genital involvement, and weight loss. Major complications include opportunistic infection, malnutrition, liver dysfunction, pulmonary impairment, fibrosis, relapse interactions with graft-versus-leukemia effects, and treatment-related metabolic and cardiovascular morbidity. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical features after transplant, organ staging and grading, exclusion of mimics such as infection or drug toxicity, laboratory liver tests, endoscopy with biopsy for GI disease, skin or liver biopsy when needed, pulmonary function testing and imaging for chronic lung involvement, and histopathology showing epithelial apoptosis or interface injury. Standard therapy includes corticosteroids, which broadly suppress cytokine transcription and lymphocyte activation; calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or cyclosporine, which block NFAT-dependent IL-2 signaling; ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor that dampens cytokine signaling; mycophenolate mofetil, an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor that impairs lymphocyte purine synthesis; and extracorporeal photopheresis

Name: Granuloma Inguinale
Description: Granuloma inguinale (donovanosis; MeSH D006100) is a chronic, sexually transmitted, ulcerative bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella granulomatis, a Gram-negative intracellular bacillus formerly termed Calymmatobacterium granulomatis, and is not a Mendelian genetic disorder; accordingly, no disease-defining inherited mutations or subtypes based on host genotype are established, although susceptibility and lesion biology likely reflect host immune-response genes and macrophage pathways rather than specific heritable variants. The organism invades mononuclear phagocytes, forming characteristic Donovan bodies within macrophages, and disease pathobiology centers on innate immune activation, macrophage phagolysosomal interactions, NF-κB-driven inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6, and local angiogenic and granulation-tissue responses that produce beefy-red, friable lesions. Clinically, it presents with slowly progressive, painless papules or nodules that evolve into exuberant, easily bleeding genital, perineal, or inguinal ulcers, sometimes with hypertrophic, ulcerovegetative, necrotic, or sclerotic/cicatricial forms; true lymphadenopathy is uncommon, though pseudobuboes may occur. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion in endemic settings and laboratory confirmation by tissue smear, crush preparation, or biopsy demonstrating Donovan bodies on Wright-Giemsa, Leishman, or silver stains; culture is difficult, so histopathology and increasingly PCR-based detection are used, while syphilis, chancroid, lymphogranuloma venereum, herpes simplex, and malignancy must be excluded. Standard therapy includes azithromycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks 30S-mediated protein synthesis; and erythromycin, another 50S inhibitor; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone are alternatives, with prolonged treatment until complete re-epithelialization. Important comorbidities and complications include HIV coinfection, secondary bacterial superinfection, extensive tissue destruction, scarring, genital lymphedema, urethral or anal stenosis, and increased susceptibility to other sexually transmitted infections.

Name: Graves Disease
Description: Graves disease (MeSH D006111) is an autoimmune organ-specific cause of hyperthyroidism characterized by loss of tolerance to the thyrotropin receptor, with stimulatory TSHR autoantibodies driving diffuse thyroid hyperplasia and excess thyroid hormone synthesis; it often occurs as classic hyperthyroid Graves disease and less commonly with extrathyroidal-predominant ophthalmopathy or dermopathy. Genetic susceptibility is typically complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with associations involving HLA-DR3, HLA-DQA1, CTLA4, PTPN22, CD40, FCRL3, IL2RA, thyroglobulin, and especially TSHR variants, while familial clustering and concordance in twins support heritability. Pathobiology centers on TSHR-cAMP-protein kinase A signaling in thyrocytes, activation of iodide uptake via SLC5A5/NIS, thyroid peroxidase-mediated organification, and immune pathways involving antigen presentation, Th1/Th2/Th17 cells, B cells, cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and orbital fibroblast IGF-1R signaling with hyaluronan production in ophthalmopathy. Typical manifestations include weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, proximal myopathy, goiter, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, lid retraction, stare, and sometimes pretibial myxedema or thyroid storm. Major comorbidities and complications include Graves orbitopathy, osteoporosis, heart failure, arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and coexistence with other autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, vitiligo, pernicious anemia, and myasthenia gravis. Diagnosis relies on suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 and/or T3, positive TSHR antibodies or thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, and when needed diffuse increased radioactive iodine uptake or hypervascularity on Doppler ultrasound; supportive findings include anti-TPO antibodies. Standard therapy includes methimazole and propylthiouracil, which inhibit thyroid peroxidase-mediated hormone synthesis, with propylthiouracil also reducing peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; beta-blockers such as propranolol provide adrenergic symptom control and modestly reduce T4-to-T3 conversion,

Name: Rhinitis, Allergic, Seasonal
Description: Seasonal allergic rhinitis (UMLS C0018621) is a common IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity disorder of the nasal mucosa triggered by seasonal aeroallens, especially tree, grass, and weed pollens, and is characterized by episodic sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal pruritus, congestion, and often ocular itching and tearing; examination may show pale edematous turbinates, clear secretions, conjunctival injection, and allergic shiners. Its pathobiology reflects epithelial barrier dysfunction and Th2-skewed immunity, with genetic susceptibility involving variants in IL4, IL13, IL4RA, FCER1A, HLA class II loci, TSLP, FLG, and ORMDL3, which influence IgE production, mast-cell and basophil activation, and mucosal inflammation rather than following a simple Mendelian inheritance pattern; familial aggregation is typical as part of atopy. Key pathways include allergen presentation by dendritic cells, Th2 polarization, B-cell class switching to IgE, FcεRI-mediated mast-cell degranulation, and cytokine signaling through IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, TSLP, eosinophil recruitment, histamine release, leukotriene synthesis, and chemokines such as eotaxin. Major subtypes are intermittent versus persistent and mild versus moderate-severe disease, with seasonal forms distinguished from perennial allergic rhinitis. Common comorbidities include allergic conjunctivitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media with eustachian tube dysfunction, sleep disturbance, and impaired cognition or school/work performance; complications may include sinus obstruction and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by temporal correlation with pollen exposure and personal or family atopy, and confirmed by skin-prick testing or serum allergen-specific IgE assays; nasal eosinophils may support the diagnosis, while total IgE is nonspecific. Treatment commonly includes intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress local inflammatory gene transcription; oral or intranasal H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine and azelastine, which block histamine signaling; and leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, which inhibit cysteinyl leukotriene-mediated congestion, with allergen immunotherapy used for selected refractory patients.

Name: Heart Arrest
Description: Heart arrest, more precisely cardiac arrest, is an abrupt cessation of effective cardiac mechanical activity causing loss of pulse, apnea or agonal respirations, and unconsciousness, usually arising from malignant ventricular arrhythmias, pulseless electrical activity, or asystole; it is a clinical syndrome rather than a single inherited disease, but genetic susceptibility is well recognized, especially in sudden arrhythmic arrest linked to ion-channel and cardiomyopathy genes such as KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A, RYR2, CASQ2, LMNA, DSP, MYH7, and TTN, whose protein products govern sodium, potassium, calcium handling, desmosomal integrity, and sarcomeric function. Key pathobiologic pathways include myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury, autonomic dysregulation, oxidative stress, calcium-overload signaling, mitochondrial failure, and disordered conduction involving the cardiac action-potential machinery, gap junctions such as connexin-43, and adrenergic signaling through beta-1 receptors. Major comorbidities and precipitants include coronary artery disease, prior myocardial infarction, heart failure, cardiomyopathies, electrolyte disturbances, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism, drug toxicity, and inherited arrhythmia syndromes; complications include anoxic brain injury, recurrent arrest, shock, multiorgan failure, and death. Subtypes are commonly classified by rhythm as ventricular fibrillation/pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity, and asystole, and by context as in-hospital versus out-of-hospital arrest. Treatment is emergent and includes epinephrine, an alpha- and beta-adrenergic agonist that augments coronary and cerebral perfusion during CPR; amiodarone, a predominantly class III antiarrhythmic that prolongs repolarization and also blocks sodium, calcium, and beta-adrenergic currents; lidocaine, a class Ib sodium-channel blocker used for refractory ventricular arrhythmias; and magnesium sulfate for torsades de pointes by stabilizing repolarization. Diagnosis is clinical, based on absent pulse and unresponsiveness, with ECG rhythm assessment, defibrillator monitoring, post-resuscitation troponin and electrolyte testing, toxicology, echocardiography, coronary evaluation, and, when inherited disease is suspected, family history, provocative ECG testing, and targeted or panel-based genetic testing, most often

Name: Heart Failure
Description: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which structural or functional cardiac impairment prevents adequate ventricular filling or ejection, producing reduced or preserved ejection fraction phenotypes, including left-, right-, and biventricular failure, and acute or chronic forms. It commonly arises from ischemic heart disease, hypertension, valvular disease, myocarditis, or primary cardiomyopathies, and manifests with dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, exercise intolerance, elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary rales, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, and S3 gallop. Molecular contributors include sarcomeric and cytoskeletal genes such as TTN truncating variants, MYH7, MYBPC3, LMNA, PLN, and SCN5A, as well as natriuretic peptide and neurohormonal proteins including BNP/NT-proBNP, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone, neprilysin, and beta-adrenergic signaling components; inheritance is often complex but familial dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may show autosomal dominant transmission, with X-linked or mitochondrial causes less commonly recognized. Central pathways include chronic activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sympathetic nervous system, maladaptive TGF-beta, calcium-handling and cAMP signaling, natriuretic peptide signaling, inflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, fibrosis, and ventricular remodeling. Core therapies include ACE inhibitors such as enalapril, which reduce angiotensin II generation; beta-blockers such as carvedilol or metoprolol succinate, which blunt adrenergic toxicity; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone, which inhibit aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and fibrosis; additionally, loop diuretics like furosemide relieve congestion, SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin improve cardiorenal outcomes, and sacubitril/valsartan augments natriuretic peptides while blocking AT1 receptors. Common comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, anemia, sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, cardiorenal syndrome, and sudden cardiac death. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, elevated BNP or NT-proBNP, ECG, chest radiography, echocardiographic evidence

Name: Heartburn
Description: Heartburn (MeSH D006356) is a symptom complex, most often reflecting gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), in which retrograde exposure of the esophageal squamous mucosa to gastric acid, pepsin, and sometimes bile produces substernal burning, postprandial or recumbent discomfort, sour regurgitation, water brash, chest pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, chronic cough, hoarseness, or nocturnal symptoms; clinically it includes nonerosive reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, and extraesophageal reflux phenotypes. Its pathobiology centers on transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations, hypotensive sphincter tone, impaired esophageal clearance, delayed gastric emptying, hiatal hernia, and mucosal inflammatory signaling involving epithelial barrier dysfunction, TRPV1-mediated chemosensation, cytokines such as IL-8, and acid-sensing pathways; genetic susceptibility is modest but supported by familial clustering and twin studies, with representative associations reported near FOXF1, MHC loci, and genes influencing obesity or connective tissue traits, although no single Mendelian mutation explains most cases. Major comorbidities include obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, asthma, chronic laryngitis, obstructive sleep apnea, anxiety, and functional dyspepsia; complications include erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, ulceration, Barrett esophagus, and esophageal adenocarcinoma. Treatment relies on proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, pantoprazole, and esomeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine reduce histamine-stimulated acid secretion; and alginate-antacid formulations such as sodium alginate with calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide neutralize acid and form a raft barrier, while baclofen may reduce transient sphincter relaxations. Diagnosis is usually clinical when typical symptoms respond to empiric acid suppression, but alarm features prompt upper endoscopy; ambulatory 24-hour pH or pH-impedance monitoring, esophageal manometry, and selective biopsy are used to confirm reflux, assess motility, and exclude eosinophilic esophagitis, malignancy, or other mimics.

Name: Hemangioma
Description: Hemangioma is a benign vascular neoplasm or malformation spectrum, most often represented by infantile hemangioma, a GLUT1-positive endothelial tumor that typically appears in early infancy, proliferates rapidly, and then involutes, whereas congenital hemangiomas are fully formed at birth and include rapidly involuting and non-involuting subtypes; vascular malformations such as cavernous or venous lesions may overlap clinically but differ biologically. Its pathobiology centers on dysregulated angiogenesis involving VEGFA/VEGFR2, bFGF, HIF-1α, angiopoietin-TIE2, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, and Notch signaling, with endothelial markers including CD31 and CD34; representative genetic associations include somatic GNAQ and GNA11 mutations in some vascular lesions, TEK/TIE2 and PIK3CA variants in venous malformation–hemangioma overlap syndromes, and familial cerebral cavernous malformation genes KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10 in related cavernous lesions, while most infantile hemangiomas are sporadic and non-Mendelian. Clinically, lesions present as superficial bright-red papules or plaques, deep blue compressible masses, or mixed tumors, and may ulcerate, bleed, cause pain, disfigurement, visual axis obstruction, airway compromise, high-output cardiac failure, consumptive hypothyroidism, or Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon in specific vascular tumors. Important comorbid associations include PHACE syndrome, LUMBAR/PELVIS syndromes, and, for hepatic lesions, arteriovenous shunting and heart failure. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by Doppler ultrasonography and MRI to define extent and flow characteristics; biopsy with GLUT1 immunostaining is reserved for atypical cases, and molecular testing may be useful in syndromic or diagnostically ambiguous lesions. Treatment commonly includes propranolol, a nonselective β-adrenergic blocker that causes vasoconstriction and suppresses VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, topical timolol for small superficial lesions via similar β-blockade, corticosteroids that reduce endothelial proliferation and inflammatory signaling, and in refractory or syndromic cases sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor targeting PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling.

Name: Hemorrhoids
Description: Hemorrhoids are a common anorectal vascular-connective tissue disorder characterized by symptomatic enlargement and distal displacement of the normal anal cushions, producing internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line and external hemorrhoids below it, with mixed forms and graded internal disease from I to IV based on prolapse. Pathobiology is dominated less by a single Mendelian cause than by degeneration of supporting connective tissue, venous dilation, local inflammation, and mechanical strain from constipation, prolonged straining, pregnancy, obesity, aging, and portal hypertension; genetic influences are incompletely defined but likely involve susceptibility in extracellular-matrix and vascular-remodeling pathways, with representative candidate genes/proteins including COL1A1, COL3A1, ELN, MMP9, VEGFA, NOS3, and inflammatory mediators such as TNF and IL6 rather than recurrent disease-specific mutations or a clear inheritance pattern, although familial clustering is reported. Relevant signaling processes include matrix turnover and weakening through MMP/TIMP imbalance, angiogenesis via VEGF signaling, endothelial nitric oxide and vascular tone pathways, TGF-β-mediated connective tissue remodeling, and cytokine-driven inflammatory cascades involving NF-κB. Typical symptoms are painless bright red rectal bleeding, prolapse, mucus soiling, pruritus, discomfort, swelling, and, in thrombosed external hemorrhoids, acute severe pain with a tender perianal bluish nodule; complications include iron-deficiency anemia, thrombosis, strangulation, ulceration, and coexistence with anal fissure or pelvic floor dysfunction. Commonly used treatments include fiber/bulk agents such as psyllium, which increase stool bulk and reduce straining; topical or oral flavonoids such as diosmin-hesperidin, which improve venous tone, capillary permeability, and inflammation; local anesthetics such as lidocaine, which block voltage-gated sodium channels for symptomatic relief; corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory signaling; and osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol, which retain water in stool. Diagnosis is primarily clinical by history and inspection, digital rectal examination, and anoscopy or proctoscopy, with colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy when bleeding is atypical, age or risk factors warrant exclusion of colorectal neoplasia, or alarm features are present.

Name: Comas, Hepatic
Description: Hepatic encephalopathy (MeSH D006501) is a potentially reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by acute or chronic liver failure and/or portosystemic shunting, most commonly in cirrhosis, and is clinically classified as covert or overt and by etiology as type A from acute liver failure, type B from portosystemic bypass, and type C from cirrhosis. Its pathobiology is dominated by hyperammonemia with impaired hepatic urea-cycle detoxification; ammonia handling involves CPS1, OTC, ASS1, ASL, ARG1, GLS, and glutamine synthetase, while representative genetic modifiers linked to susceptibility or severity include variants in glutaminase, aquaporin-4, manganese transport and inflammatory genes, though hepatic encephalopathy is generally acquired rather than inherited. Key signaling mechanisms include astrocyte glutamine accumulation causing osmotic swelling and low-grade cerebral edema, GABAergic/neurosteroid tone, manganese deposition, oxidative and nitrosative stress, microglial activation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, altered benzodiazepine receptor signaling, and systemic inflammation mediated by TNF, IL-1β, and IL-6, often amplified by gut dysbiosis. Typical manifestations range from sleep-wake disturbance, impaired attention, psychomotor slowing, asterixis, disorientation, and personality change to somnolence, stupor, coma, and occasionally hyperreflexia or fetor hepaticus. Common precipitants and comorbidities include gastrointestinal bleeding, infection or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, constipation, dehydration, renal failure, hyponatremia, sarcopenia, alcohol-related liver disease, and hepatocellular carcinoma; complications include falls, aspiration, recurrent hospitalization, and increased mortality. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by West Haven grading, psychometric or critical flicker testing for minimal disease, EEG slowing, exclusion of competing causes of altered mental status, serum ammonia as an adjunct rather than a definitive test, and imaging mainly to rule out structural lesions or identify shunts. Name: Hepatolenticular Degeneration
Description: Hepatolenticular degeneration, or Wilson disease, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused predominantly by biallelic pathogenic variants in ATP7B on chromosome 13, which encodes a hepatocellular P-type ATPase required for copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and biliary copper excretion; representative mutations include H1069Q in many European populations and R778L in East Asians, while ATP7A, ATOX1, COMMD1, metallothioneins, and ceruloplasmin participate in related copper-trafficking networks rather than being primary causes. The central pathogenic pathway is failure of ATP7B-mediated trans-Golgi and canalicular copper transport, leading to impaired ceruloplasmin loading, toxic hepatic copper accumulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial injury, proteostasis disturbance, and secondary deposition in basal ganglia, cornea, kidney, and heart. Clinical phenotypes include hepatic, neurologic, psychiatric, and mixed forms, with presentations ranging from asymptomatic transaminitis to hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis, tremor, dystonia, parkinsonism, dysarthria, ataxia, personality change, depression, and cognitive decline; Kayser-Fleischer rings and sunflower cataracts are classic signs. Major complications include portal hypertension, liver failure, renal tubular dysfunction, nephrolithiasis, osteopenia, arthropathy, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, infertility, and treatment-related neurologic worsening. Diagnosis integrates low serum ceruloplasmin, elevated 24-hour urinary copper, increased hepatic copper on biopsy, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination, characteristic brain MRI abnormalities, ATP7B molecular testing, and Leipzig scoring, with family screening essential. Standard therapy relies on copper chelation and reduction of intestinal absorption: D-penicillamine and trientine bind copper to enhance urinary excretion, zinc salts induce enterocyte metallothionein to block copper uptake, and tetrathiomolybdate forms complexes with copper and albumin to lower bioavailable copper; liver transplantation is indicated for fulminant failure or end-stage disease.

Name: Angioedemas, Hereditary
Description: Hereditary angioedemas are rare, usually autosomal dominant disorders characterized by recurrent, nonpruritic, nonpitting episodes of subcutaneous and submucosal edema caused most often by dysregulation of the kallikrein-kinin system and excess bradykinin rather than histamine. The classic forms are HAE type I, due to SERPING1 mutations causing quantitative C1 inhibitor deficiency, and type II, due to dysfunctional C1 inhibitor; additional inherited forms with normal C1 inhibitor include variants in F12, PLG, ANGPT1, KNG1, MYOF, and HS3ST6, with factor XII, plasminogen, angiopoietin-1, high-molecular-weight kininogen, myoferlin, and heparan sulfate biosynthetic pathways implicated. Core molecular events involve factor XII activation, prekallikrein-to-kallikrein conversion, cleavage of kininogen to bradykinin, and signaling through the bradykinin B2 receptor to increase endothelial permeability; complement abnormalities include persistently low C4 and, in C1 inhibitor deficiency, reduced C1-INH level or function. Patients develop recurrent swelling of the extremities, face, genitals, bowel wall, and upper airway, with severe crampy abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potentially fatal laryngeal edema; attacks may be triggered by trauma, stress, infection, estrogen exposure, or ACE inhibitors. Important complications and linked conditions include asphyxia, dehydration or unnecessary abdominal surgery from misdiagnosis, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is based on compatible recurrent angioedema without urticaria, family history, low C4, C1-INH antigenic and functional assays, and, when indicated, genetic testing for SERPING1 or other causative genes. Treatment includes plasma-derived or recombinant C1-INH replacement to restore inhibitor activity, icatibant to block bradykinin B2 receptors, ecallantide to inhibit plasma kallikrein, and lanadelumab or berotralstat for prophylaxis by suppressing kallikrein; antihistamines, corticosteroids, and epinephrine are typically ineffective.

Name: Herpes Genitalis
Description: Herpes genitalis (MeSH D006558) is a common sexually transmitted mucocutaneous infection caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) and increasingly by HSV-1, characterized by primary lytic infection of genital epithelium followed by lifelong latency in sacral sensory ganglia and recurrent reactivation. Disease expression is shaped more by host and viral factors than Mendelian inheritance; relevant genetic components include variation in innate antiviral pathways such as TLR2, TLR3, IFNL3/IFNL4, HLA class I/II alleles, and, in severe HSV susceptibility, rare defects affecting TLR3-TRIF-IRF3/type I interferon signaling, while viral glycoproteins gB, gC, gD, gH/gL and proteins including thymidine kinase and DNA polymerase are central functional targets. Key pathways include viral attachment to heparan sulfate and nectin-1/HVEM entry receptors, membrane fusion, nuclear replication, latency-associated transcript biology, and host NF-kB, interferon alpha/beta, JAK-STAT, NK-cell and CD8+ T-cell responses. Typical manifestations are painful grouped vesicles evolving to ulcers on the vulva, penis, perineum, cervix, or perianal skin, with burning, pruritus, dysuria, tender inguinal adenopathy, fever and malaise in primary disease, and milder recurrent episodes or asymptomatic shedding thereafter; subtypes include primary first-episode, nonprimary first-episode, recurrent, and neonatal/disseminated infection. Important comorbidities and complications include increased HIV acquisition and transmission, secondary bacterial superinfection, aseptic meningitis, radiculitis, urinary retention, proctitis, psychological distress, and severe neonatal herpes in pregnancy-associated transmission. Diagnosis is based on compatible lesions plus laboratory confirmation, preferably lesion NAAT/PCR with typing, while viral culture is less sensitive; type-specific serology to glycoprotein G supports diagnosis when lesions are absent, and direct fluorescent antibody or Tzanck smear are now limited. Standard treatments include acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, nucleoside analogs activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit HSV DNA polymerase and terminate or impair DNA synthesis; foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analog that directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase, is used for resistant infection

Name: Herpes Labialis
Description: Herpes labialis (MeSH D006560) is a common, usually recurrent mucocutaneous infection of the lips and perioral skin caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 1, and less often HSV-2, characterized by lifelong latency in trigeminal ganglia with periodic reactivation. Disease expression reflects viral factors and host genetics rather than simple Mendelian inheritance; susceptibility and recurrence have been associated with variation in immune-response genes such as TLR2, TLR3, IFNL3/IL28B, HLA class I/II loci, and other innate antiviral components, while viral proteins including glycoproteins gB, gC, gD, gH/gL, thymidine kinase, and DNA polymerase are central pathogenic and therapeutic targets. Key pathways include viral attachment and entry via heparan sulfate and nectin-1/HVEM, intracellular replication, latency-associated transcript-mediated persistence, and host interferon, NF-κB, JAK-STAT, TLR, and CD8+ T-cell responses that constrain replication but also shape recurrence. Typical symptoms are prodromal tingling, burning, or pain followed by clustered vesicles on an erythematous base, ulceration, crusting, and spontaneous healing; primary infection may cause gingivostomatitis, fever, and cervical adenopathy. Clinical subtypes include primary versus recurrent herpes labialis and occasional severe, disseminated, or chronic ulcerative disease in immunocompromised hosts. Diagnosis is often clinical, supported when needed by HSV PCR from lesion swabs, viral culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing, Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells, or type-specific serology in selected cases. Standard treatment includes acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, which are guanosine analog prodrugs activated by viral thymidine kinase and then inhibit viral DNA polymerase; penciclovir cream and docosanol, which impairs viral-envelope fusion with host membranes, are also used. Important comorbidities and complications include atopic dermatitis with eczema herpeticum, immunosuppression, dehydration from painful oral lesions, secondary bacterial superinfection, herpetic whitlow, keratitis, and rarely encephalitis.

Name: Herpes Simplex
Description: Herpes simplex is a common mucocutaneous and neurotropic viral disease caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 or type 2, with primary, latent, and recurrent forms that include orolabial herpes, genital herpes, herpetic whitlow, keratitis, eczema herpeticum, neonatal herpes, and herpes simplex encephalitis. Clinical manifestations typically include grouped painful vesicles on an erythematous base that evolve to erosions or crusts, burning or tingling prodromes, fever and tender lymphadenopathy in primary infection, and in severe disease keratitis, urinary retention, meningitis, or encephalitis. Disease susceptibility and severity are strongly influenced by host genetics rather than Mendelian inheritance of the infection itself; representative defects include TLR3, UNC93B1, TRIF/TICAM1, TBK1, IRF3, STAT1, and NEMO/IKBKG, which impair type I interferon immunity and predispose particularly to herpes simplex encephalitis, while variants affecting MHC/HLA and NK-cell function may modify recurrence risk. Major pathogenic pathways involve viral entry through glycoproteins gB, gD, gH/gL engaging receptors such as Nectin-1/PVRL1 and HVEM/TNFRSF14, neuronal latency with LAT transcripts, and host sensing through TLR, cGAS-STING, JAK-STAT interferon signaling, NF-kB activation, and CD8 T-cell and NK-cell antiviral responses. Standard therapy includes acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, guanosine analog prodrugs activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit viral DNA polymerase and terminate or impair DNA synthesis; intravenous acyclovir is standard for encephalitis and severe neonatal disease, while foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase in acyclovir-resistant, often thymidine-kinase-deficient strains. Important comorbidities and complications include HIV infection, immunosuppression, atopic dermatitis, bacterial superinfection, corneal scarring, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and disseminated neonatal infection. Diagnosis relies on characteristic lesions supported by PCR or other nucleic acid amplification from lesion swabs, CSF PCR for encephalitis, viral culture in selected cases, direct fluorescent antigen testing less commonly, and type-specific HSV-1/HSV-2 serology when lesions are absent or exposure

Name: Keratitis, Herpetic
Description: Herpetic keratitis is an infectious, often recurrent corneal disease caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 1, less often HSV-2, in which latent neurotropic virus in the trigeminal ganglion reactivates to involve corneal epithelium, stroma, or endothelium; major clinical subtypes include epithelial dendritic or geographic keratitis, stromal immune or necrotizing keratitis, endothelial disciform keratitis, and neurotrophic keratopathy. Patients typically present with unilateral ocular pain, redness, photophobia, tearing, blurred vision, foreign-body sensation, and reduced corneal sensitivity, with slit-lamp findings such as fluorescein-staining dendrites with terminal bulbs, stromal haze, edema, keratic precipitates, or anterior uveitis. Pathobiology reflects viral entry and immune injury involving viral glycoproteins gB, gD, gH/gL and host receptors such as nectin-1/PVRL1 and HVEM/TNFRSF14, with innate and adaptive pathways including TLR2, TLR3, cGAS-STING, type I interferons, NF-κB, and cytokines/chemokines such as IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ, CXCL10, plus VEGF-driven corneal neovascularization and matrix metalloproteinases contributing to stromal damage. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, but variation in C21orf91, TLR3, IFNL3/IL28B, HLA loci, and other immune-response genes has been associated with recurrent or severe disease; rare monogenic defects in antiviral immunity may predispose to severe HSV infection. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by slit-lamp examination, corneal sensitivity testing, fluorescein or rose bengal staining, and when needed corneal scrapings for HSV PCR, viral culture, or direct immunofluorescence. Standard therapy includes acyclovir or valacyclovir, guanosine analogs activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit viral DNA polymerase, topical ganciclovir with the same polymerase-targeting principle, and trifluridine, a nucleoside analog impairing viral DNA synthesis; topical corticosteroids are used cautiously for stromal or endothelial immune disease, while complications include corneal scarring, thinning or perforation, secondary bacterial infection

Name: Herpes Zoster
Description: Herpes zoster (MeSH D006562) is a neurocutaneous disease caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV, human herpesvirus 3) in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia, producing a unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption and neuropathic pain; major clinical features include prodromal burning, tingling or allodynia, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, fever, pruritus, and in severe cases motor weakness or cranial neuropathies, with subtypes including localized zoster, disseminated zoster, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, oticus/Ramsay Hunt syndrome, and recurrent zoster. Host genetic susceptibility is not Mendelian in most cases, but impaired cell-mediated immunity is central, and rare monogenic predisposition to severe VZV disease involves defects in interferon and innate sensing pathways such as TLR3, IFNAR1, STAT1, STAT2, POLR3A, and RNA polymerase III-related signaling; HLA variation and immunosenescence also influence risk. Relevant pathways include viral entry and replication, cGAS-STING and TLR sensing, type I interferon signaling through JAK-STAT, NF-kB activation, and T-cell-mediated control involving CD4+, CD8+, and NK cells. Common comorbidities and risk settings include advanced age, HIV infection, malignancy, transplantation, corticosteroid or JAK inhibitor use, diabetes, and autoimmune disease; important complications include postherpetic neuralgia, bacterial superinfection, keratitis, uveitis, retinal necrosis, stroke, meningitis, encephalitis, myelitis, and disseminated visceral infection. Diagnosis is usually clinical based on a painful unilateral dermatomal rash, but confirmation is by VZV PCR from vesicle fluid, scab, CSF, or tissue; direct fluorescent antibody testing, serology for selected contexts, and ophthalmologic or neurologic evaluation are used when indicated. Standard therapy includes acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, nucleoside analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit viral DNA polymerase; analgesics, gabapentin or pregabalin for neuralgia, and selected corticosteroid use may be adjunctive.

Name: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome
Description: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (UMLS C0019562) is a rare autosomal dominant hereditary cancer-predisposition disorder caused by germline pathogenic variants or deletions in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p25, with somatic second-hit inactivation in tumors; representative abnormalities include missense, truncating, splice-site, and large deletion mutations that disrupt the pVHL E3 ubiquitin ligase complex with elongin B/C, cullin-2, and RBX1. Loss of pVHL prevents normoxic degradation of HIF-1α and HIF-2α, activating hypoxia-signaling pathways and downstream VEGF, PDGF, TGF-α, EPO, GLUT1, and angiogenic, metabolic, and proliferative programs; additional relevance has been shown for mTOR and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. Clinically, VHL causes multisystem benign and malignant neoplasia, classically retinal, cerebellar, brainstem, and spinal hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma and renal cysts, pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma, pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumors, endolymphatic sac tumors, epididymal or broad ligament cystadenomas, with symptoms including headache, ataxia, visual loss, hearing loss, vertigo, hypertension, catecholamine spells, hematuria, abdominal pain, and neurologic deficits. Major subtypes include type 1 VHL with low pheochromocytoma risk and type 2A, 2B, and 2C with increasing pheochromocytoma and renal carcinoma associations. Important complications include metastatic renal cancer, retinal detachment, hydrocephalus, spinal cord compression, hemorrhage, and chronic kidney disease. Diagnosis is based on characteristic lesions with family history or identification of a pathogenic VHL variant by sequencing and deletion/duplication testing, supported by ophthalmologic examination, MRI of brain/spine and abdomen, renal imaging, audiology, and biochemical screening for catecholamine excess. Treatment centers on surveillance and lesion-directed therapy; commonly used drugs include belzutifan, an oral HIF-2α inhibitor, and anti-VEGF agents such as sunitinib and pazopanib, multitarget VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, with additional use of axitinib, cabozantinib, or pembrol

Name: Histoplasmosis
Description: Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic organism Histoplasma capsulatum, acquired mainly by inhalation of microconidia from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings, and it ranges from asymptomatic or self-limited pulmonary disease to severe disseminated infection. Clinical forms include acute pulmonary, chronic cavitary pulmonary, mediastinal granulomatous or fibrosing disease, and progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; typical manifestations are fever, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, malaise, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, mucocutaneous lesions, and in severe cases adrenal, central nervous system, or bone marrow involvement. Host defense is dominated by macrophage and T-cell immunity, especially IL12B/IL12RB1-IFNG/IFNGR1-STAT1 signaling, TNF-mediated granuloma formation, and pattern-recognition pathways involving Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2, and NF-kB; susceptibility is increased by defects or variants affecting IFN-gamma/IL-12 axis genes, STAT3, GATA2, NEMO/IKBKG, CD40LG, and by anti-TNF therapy or advanced HIV with low CD4 counts. Fungal virulence-associated proteins include HSP60, which promotes macrophage binding via CD11/CD18, and CBP1 and alpha-(1,3)-glucan, which facilitate intracellular survival and immune evasion. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology and syndrome plus Histoplasma urine or serum antigen testing, serology by complement fixation or immunodiffusion, fungal culture, histopathology showing small intracellular budding yeasts in macrophages, molecular assays when available, and imaging such as chest radiography or CT. Treatment commonly includes itraconazole, which inhibits fungal 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes; and fluconazole or posaconazole as azole alternatives with the same ergosterol-pathway target. Important comorbidities and complications include chronic lung disease, AIDS, solid organ transplantation, hematologic malignancy, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, respiratory failure, mediastinal fibrosis, relapse, and death.

Name: HIV Infections
Description: HIV infection is a chronic, transmissible retroviral disease caused by HIV-1 or HIV-2, characterized by progressive immune dysfunction through infection of CD4+ T cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells via viral gp120 binding to CD4 and the coreceptors CCR5 or CXCR4, followed by reverse transcription, integration, and persistent replication; key viral genes and proteins include gag, pol, and env, as well as Tat, Rev, Nef, Vif, Vpr, and Vpu, while clinically relevant host genetic factors include CCR5-Δ32, which confers resistance to R5-tropic strains, HLA class I variants such as HLA-B57/B27 associated with better viral control, and polymorphisms in CCR2 or APOBEC3G. Major pathogenic pathways involve CD4 receptor signaling, chemokine-receptor entry pathways, reverse-transcriptase and integrase-dependent replication, NF-κB activation, chronic interferon and cytokine signaling, T-cell exhaustion through PD-1, and inflammasome-mediated immune activation. Typical manifestations range from an acute retroviral syndrome with fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and myalgias to chronic infection with weight loss, persistent generalized lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhea, and ultimately AIDS, defined by severe immunosuppression and opportunistic infections or malignancies. Important comorbidities and complications include tuberculosis, viral hepatitis B/C, HPV-related disease, pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcosis, CMV disease, Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, nephropathy, and cardiovascular disease. Treatment relies on combination antiretroviral therapy, commonly including tenofovir, a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor; emtricitabine or lamivudine, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; dolutegravir or bictegravir, integrase strand transfer inhibitors; and in some regimens darunavir, a protease inhibitor, or maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist. Disease types include HIV-1 versus HIV-2, acute, chronic, and advanced/AIDS stages, and CCR5- versus CXCR4-tropic variants. It is not inherited in a Mendelian manner, though host susceptibility is partly genetic. Diagnosis is based on risk assessment plus laboratory testing with fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody assays,

Name: Hodgkin Disease
Description: Hodgkin disease, or Hodgkin lymphoma, is a malignant B-cell lymphoid neoplasm defined by rare Reed-Sternberg and related Hodgkin cells within a prominent inflammatory microenvironment; it comprises classical Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted—and the distinct nodular lymphocyte-predominant form. Pathobiology commonly involves constitutive NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling, immune-evasion through PD-1/PD-L1 activation, and, in a subset, Epstein-Barr virus-driven programs; recurrent molecular abnormalities include 9p24.1 copy gain/amplification with PD-L1/PD-L2 and JAK2 overexpression, REL amplification, TNFAIP3/A20 loss, SOCS1, STAT6, B2M, CIITA, and XPO1 alterations, with CD30 and often CD15 expression in classical disease and CD20/BCL6 in nodular lymphocyte-predominant cases. Most cases are sporadic, but familial aggregation and polygenic susceptibility involving HLA loci and immune-regulatory genes are recognized rather than simple Mendelian inheritance. Patients typically present with painless cervical or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, B symptoms of fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss, pruritus, fatigue, alcohol-induced node pain, or cough/dyspnea from mediastinal masses. Diagnosis requires excisional lymph node biopsy with histopathology and immunophenotyping, supported by PET-CT for Ann Arbor/Cotswolds staging, CBC, ESR, chemistry panels, and bone marrow evaluation in selected cases. Standard therapy includes doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor and DNA intercalator; bleomycin, which induces free radical-mediated DNA strand breaks; vinblastine, a microtubule polymerization inhibitor; dacarbazine, an alkylating methylating agent; brentuximab vedotin, an anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate delivering MMAE; and PD-1 inhibitors such as nivolumab or pembrolizumab, which restore antitumor T-cell activity. Important comorbidities and complications include immunosuppression with infection risk, secondary leukemias and solid tumors, infertility, pulmonary fibrosis, cardiomyopathy, hypothyroidism after radiation, venous thromboembolism, and transformation or relapse.

Name: Hordeolum
Description: Hordeolum (UMLS C0019917) is an acute, usually self-limited, localized suppurative inflammation of the eyelid margin caused most often by bacterial infection, classically Staphylococcus aureus, involving the glands of Zeis or Moll in external hordeolum and the meibomian glands in internal hordeolum; it is therefore primarily an infectious and inflammatory disorder rather than a mendelian genetic disease. Molecularly, host-pathogen interactions engage innate immune pathways including Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB activation, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, CXCL8/IL-8, neutrophil recruitment, and in meibomian dysfunction, altered lipid metabolism and keratinization pathways; no single causative mutation is established, although susceptibility may be influenced by genes relevant to barrier and inflammatory responses such as TLR2, NFKB1, IL1B, and factors predisposing to rosacea or atopy. Clinically, patients present with acute focal eyelid pain, tenderness, erythema, edema, warmth, and a pustular or nodular lesion near the lash line or tarsal plate, sometimes with tearing, foreign-body sensation, and mild photophobia. Diagnosis is usually clinical by eyelid examination, with culture of expressed material or biopsy reserved for recurrent, atypical, or treatment-refractory lesions to exclude resistant infection, chalazion, sebaceous carcinoma, or other masqueraders. Commonly linked comorbidities include blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, acne rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, diabetes mellitus, and immunosuppression; complications include preseptal cellulitis, abscess formation, and progression to chalazion. Treatment relies on warm compresses and lid hygiene, with erythromycin or bacitracin topical ointment, tetracyclines such as doxycycline that inhibit the 30S ribosomal subunit and also reduce matrix metalloproteinase-driven inflammation, and when needed antistaphylococcal agents such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis; inheritance is not characteristic, though recurrent disease can cluster through inherited predisposition to atopy, rosacea, or gland dysfunction.

Name: Hyperaldosteronism
Description: Hyperaldosteronism is a disorder of autonomous or excessive aldosterone production by the adrenal zona glomerulosa, causing mineralocorticoid excess with renal sodium retention, potassium and hydrogen ion wasting, suppressed renin in primary forms, and consequent hypertension; major subtypes include primary hyperaldosteronism, most commonly aldosterone-producing adenoma and bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia, and less often familial hyperaldosteronism, unilateral hyperplasia, or adrenal carcinoma, whereas secondary hyperaldosteronism reflects renin-driven states such as renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, or diuretic use. Key molecular drivers involve dysregulated calcium signaling and membrane depolarization in adrenal cells, with recurrent somatic or germline variants in KCNJ5, CACNA1D, ATP1A1, ATP2B3, and CLCN2, and rare inherited forms involving CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimerism in glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, often autosomal dominant; these abnormalities increase intracellular Ca2+, activate calmodulin-dependent pathways and steroidogenic enzymes including CYP11B2 aldosterone synthase, and enhance the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system’s downstream mineralocorticoid receptor signaling. Typical manifestations are resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, muscle weakness, cramps, paresthesias, headache, polyuria, polydipsia, and sometimes arrhythmias, although many patients are normokalemic. Important complications and comorbidities include cardiovascular and renal injury disproportionate to blood pressure level, especially atrial fibrillation, left ventricular hypertrophy, stroke, myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease, and impaired glucose metabolism. Diagnosis relies on elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio with confirmatory suppression testing such as saline infusion, oral sodium loading, fludrocortisone suppression, or captopril challenge, followed by adrenal CT and often adrenal venous sampling to distinguish unilateral from bilateral disease; treatment includes mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone and eplerenone, the epithelial sodium channel blocker amiloride, and adrenalectomy for unilateral disease, while glucocorticoids can suppress ACTH-driven aldosterone production in familial type I disease.

Name: Hypercalcemia
Description: Hypercalcemia is a biochemical disorder characterized by elevated serum calcium, most often caused by primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy, and less commonly by vitamin D excess, granulomatous disease, medications, endocrine disorders, or inherited defects in calcium sensing; major subtypes therefore include PTH-dependent and PTH-independent hypercalcemia, as well as familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia and hypercalcemic crisis. Its molecular basis centers on the PTH/PTH1R, calcium-sensing receptor, vitamin D receptor, and RANK/RANKL/OPG axes that regulate bone resorption, renal tubular calcium handling, and intestinal absorption; representative genetic contributors include CASR loss-of-function mutations in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, MEN1 and CDC73 alterations in hereditary primary hyperparathyroidism, RET mutations in MEN2A, CYP24A1 defects causing impaired vitamin D catabolism, and PTHLH overexpression or osteolytic cytokine signaling in cancer. Clinical manifestations range from fatigue, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, nephrolithiasis, bone pain, muscle weakness, and neurocognitive changes to dehydration, arrhythmia, pancreatitis, and coma in severe cases; common comorbidities and complications include osteoporosis, fractures, chronic kidney disease, peptic ulcer disease, and recurrent renal stones. Diagnosis relies on confirmed elevated total calcium corrected for albumin or ionized calcium, followed by intact PTH to distinguish etiologies, with adjunctive phosphate, creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, PTHrP, urinary calcium excretion or calcium/creatinine clearance ratio, ECG, and targeted imaging or genetic testing when indicated. Treatment depends on cause and severity: isotonic saline restores intravascular volume and promotes calciuresis, calcitonin rapidly inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, intravenous bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid or pamidronate suppress osteoclasts, denosumab blocks RANKL, cinacalcet allosterically activates CaSR to reduce PTH secretion, and glucocorticoids decrease vitamin D-mediated intestinal calcium absorption.

Name: Hypercholesterolemia
Description: Hypercholesterolemia is a disorder of lipid metabolism characterized by persistently elevated plasma total and especially LDL cholesterol, most often due to impaired hepatic LDL clearance or increased apoB-containing lipoprotein production, and it may be primary or secondary; primary forms include familial hypercholesterolemia, familial defective apolipoprotein B-100, polygenic hypercholesterolemia, and rare autosomal recessive hypercholesterolemia. Major genetic determinants include pathogenic variants in LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, and LDLRAP1, with less common contributions from APOE and genes affecting cholesterol synthesis or trafficking; inheritance is usually autosomal dominant for LDLR, APOB, and gain-of-function PCSK9 variants, and autosomal recessive for LDLRAP1-related disease. Key pathogenic pathways involve LDL receptor endocytosis and recycling, apoB-100–mediated lipoprotein binding, PCSK9-driven lysosomal degradation of LDLR, hepatic cholesterol synthesis through HMG-CoA reductase, bile acid homeostasis, and regulation by SREBP2. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic biochemical elevation to tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, corneal arcus, and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, particularly coronary artery disease, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease; comorbidities and complications include obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, hypertension, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, pancreatitis when mixed dyslipidemia is present, and aortic valve disease in severe familial cases. Diagnosis is based on fasting or nonfasting lipid profile showing elevated LDL-C, exclusion of secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestatic liver disease, and drugs, plus family history and physical findings; Dutch Lipid Clinic Network or Simon Broome criteria and confirmatory genetic testing are used for suspected familial disease, and cascade screening is recommended. Treatment centers on statins such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and upregulate LDLR; ezetimibe, which blocks intestinal NPC1L1-mediated cholesterol absorption; PCSK9 inhibitors such as evolocumab or alirocumab, which increase LDLR recycling; and selected use of bile acid sequestrants, bempedoic acid, inclisiran, lomitapide, evinacumab, or lipoprotein apheresis in refractory or homozyg

Name: Hyperhidrosis
Description: Hyperhidrosis is a disorder of eccrine sweat overproduction beyond thermoregulatory needs, most often presenting as primary focal hyperhidrosis involving the axillae, palms, soles, or craniofacial regions, and less often as secondary generalized hyperhidrosis due to endocrine, infectious, neurologic, malignant, or drug-related causes.
