Clinically it is characterized by visible, excessive, usually symmetric sweating causing skin maceration, bromhidrosis, dyshidrosis, social embarrassment, occupational impairment, anxiety, and reduced quality of life, with complications including secondary bacterial or fungal infection and association with mood disorders; secondary forms may accompany diabetes, hyperthyroidism, obesity, menopause, Parkinson disease, and pheochromocytoma. Primary disease is thought to reflect hyperexcitability of sympathetic cholinergic sudomotor pathways rather than gland hyperplasia, with signaling centered on hypothalamic and autonomic circuits, acetylcholine release from postganglionic sympathetic fibers, and M3 muscarinic receptor activation, alongside ionic and water transport through channels such as aquaporin-5 and CFTR in secretory coils; genetic susceptibility is supported by frequent familial clustering, commonly compatible with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance, although no single causative gene is established and linkage studies have implicated loci including 14q11.2-q13 and 2q31.1. Diagnosis is primarily clinical using criteria such as focal visible sweating for at least 6 months without apparent cause plus typical features including bilateral symmetry, onset before age 25, weekly episodes, cessation during sleep, family history, and functional impairment; testing may include gravimetric measurement, Minor starch-iodine testing, Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale, and laboratory evaluation for secondary causes. Common treatments include topical aluminum chloride, which obstructs eccrine ducts; oral or topical anticholinergics such as glycopyrrolate or oxybutynin, which inhibit muscarinic signaling; botulinum toxin A, which blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release; and iontophoresis, with refractory cases sometimes treated by endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy.

Name: Hyperinsulinism
Description: Hyperinsulinism is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by inappropriate insulin secretion despite low plasma glucose, causing recurrent hypoketotic hypoglycemia that is most often congenital but may also be transient neonatal, syndromic, or acquired, including insulinoma-related disease. The commonest genetic forms involve dysregulation of the pancreatic beta-cell KATP channel, especially biallelic or dominant mutations in ABCC8 and KCNJ11 encoding SUR1 and Kir6.2, while other implicated genes include GLUD1, GCK, HADH, HNF4A, HNF1A, UCP2, SLC16A1, HK1, PGM1, PMM2, FOXA2, CACNA1D, and mitochondrial UCP2-related mechanisms; focal disease often reflects a paternally inherited ABCC8/KCNJ11 mutation with somatic loss of maternal 11p15. Key pathways include glucose sensing and oxidative metabolism, ATP-mediated closure of KATP channels, beta-cell membrane depolarization, opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium-triggered insulin exocytosis, and modulatory amino acid and mTOR-linked signaling, with GLUD1 mutations enhancing leucine-sensitive glutamate dehydrogenase activity and ammoniagenesis. Clinically, infants present with jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures, apnea, cyanosis, or coma, and persistent disease risks developmental delay, epilepsy, and permanent brain injury; associated findings may include macrosomia, hyperammonemia, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and later diabetes in some HNF4A/HNF1A families. Major subtypes are diffuse and focal congenital hyperinsulinism and atypical or syndromic forms. Inheritance is commonly autosomal recessive or dominant depending on the gene, with occasional de novo and mosaic mechanisms. Diagnosis rests on documented hypoglycemia with inappropriately detectable insulin or C-peptide, suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate and free fatty acids, glycemic response to glucagon, high glucose infusion requirements, genetic testing, and lesion localization by 18F-DOPA PET/CT when focal disease is suspected. Treatment includes diazoxide, a KATP channel opener; octreotide or lanreotide, somatostatin receptor agonists that suppress insulin release; glucagon, which promotes hepatic glycogenolysis; and refractory cases may require sirolimus or pancreatectomy

Name: Hyperkalemia
Description: Hyperkalemia is a potentially life-threatening electrolyte disorder defined by elevated serum potassium, typically >5.0–5.5 mmol/L, that reflects impaired renal potassium excretion, transcellular potassium shift, or excess intake, and is commonly classified as mild, moderate, or severe and as acute or chronic. It most often accompanies chronic kidney disease, acute kidney injury, hypoaldosteronism, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, and adrenal insufficiency, and may cause fatal complications including ventricular arrhythmias, bradycardia, conduction block, and cardiac arrest. Symptoms range from none to weakness, fatigue, paresthesias, flaccid paralysis, nausea, and palpitations; classic signs include peaked T waves, PR prolongation, QRS widening, and sine-wave ECG changes. Core molecular determinants include the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis and distal nephron potassium handling through mineralocorticoid receptor signaling, epithelial sodium channel ENaC subunits encoded by SCNN1A, SCNN1B, and SCNN1G, the renal outer medullary potassium channel ROMK/KCNJ1, WNK1 and WNK4-SPAK/OSR1 signaling, NCC/SLC12A3, and the Na+/K+-ATPase ATP1A1; insulin-PI3K-AKT and beta2-adrenergic-cAMP pathways also regulate cellular potassium uptake. Genetic forms include pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 due to NR3C2 or ENaC mutations and Gordon syndrome, or pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2, due to WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, or CUL3 variants, with autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance depending on the gene. Diagnosis relies on serum potassium measurement, exclusion of pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis, assessment of renal function, acid-base status, glucose, renin and aldosterone, urinary potassium indices, medication review, and ECG. Treatment commonly includes intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize cardiac membranes, insulin with dextrose and inhaled albuterol to shift potassium intracellularly, loop diuretics to enhance renal excretion, potassium binders such as sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer to increase gastrointestinal elimination, and dialysis for refractory or severe cases.

Name: Hyperlipidemias
Description: Hyperlipidemias are a heterogeneous group of inherited and acquired disorders characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol, triglycerides, or both, caused by overproduction or impaired clearance of lipoproteins and classically subdivided into familial hypercholesterolemia, familial combined hyperlipidemia, familial chylomicronemia, dysbetalipoproteinemia, and mixed or secondary hyperlipidemias. Key genetic determinants include LDLR, APOB, and gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations in autosomal dominant familial hypercholesterolemia; biallelic LDLRAP1 defects in recessive disease; LPL, APOC2, APOA5, GPIHBP1, and LMF1 variants in severe hypertriglyceridemia/chylomicronemia; and APOE, especially APOE2 homozygosity, in dysbetalipoproteinemia. Pathobiology centers on hepatic LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis, PCSK9-directed LDLR degradation, lipoprotein lipase hydrolysis of triglyceride-rich particles, apoB-containing VLDL production, reverse cholesterol transport, and regulatory pathways involving SREBP, HMG-CoA reductase, PPAR-alpha, and ANGPTL3/4 inhibition of LPL. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with xanthelasma, tendon or eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal pain from pancreatitis, or premature corneal arcus; major complications include accelerated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral arterial disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and acute pancreatitis. Common comorbidities include obesity, insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, cholestatic liver disease, and alcohol excess. Diagnosis relies on a fasting or nonfasting lipid profile showing elevated LDL-C and/or triglycerides, apolipoprotein measurements, exclusion of secondary causes, family history, physical stigmata, and selected testing such as genetic analysis, lipoprotein electrophoresis, or ultracentrifugation; familial hypercholesterolemia is often assessed using Dutch Lipid Clinic or Simon Broome criteria. Treatment includes statins, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and upregulate LDLR; ezetimibe, which blocks intestinal NPC1L1-mediated cholesterol absorption; fibrates, which activate

Name: Hyperlipidemia, Familial Combined
Description: Familial combined hyperlipidemia is a common, genetically complex primary dyslipidemia characterized by hepatic overproduction of apolipoprotein B–containing lipoproteins, producing variable elevations of LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, or both, often with increased VLDL, small dense LDL, and reduced HDL; it is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant–like familial pattern with multigenic susceptibility rather than a single Mendelian defect. Genetic contributors include variants affecting apoB lipoprotein assembly and metabolism, with representative associations in USF1, APOA1/C3/A4/A5, APOB, LDLR, LPL, CETP, and PCSK9, although no single mutation explains most cases. Pathobiologically, the disorder involves dysregulation of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein production and clearance through apoB/VLDL secretion pathways, lipoprotein lipase-mediated hydrolysis, LDL receptor uptake, and related insulin resistance, SREBP, PPAR-alpha, and PCSK9 signaling networks. Clinically, patients may be asymptomatic or present with mixed hyperlipidemia on screening, premature coronary artery disease, central obesity, hypertension, or features of metabolic syndrome; xanthomas are less typical than in familial hypercholesterolemia, but tendon xanthomas are generally absent, and complications include atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral arterial disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and pancreatitis when triglycerides are markedly elevated. Subtypes are often expressed phenotypically as hypercholesterolemic, hypertriglyceridemic, or mixed forms within the same family over time. Diagnosis is based on persistent elevation of total cholesterol and/or triglycerides in at least two family members, elevated apoB, increased non-HDL cholesterol, exclusion of secondary causes such as diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, alcohol excess, and medications, and lipid profiling with apoB measurement; genetic testing may support risk stratification but is not usually definitive. Treatment centers on lifestyle measures plus statins such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and upregulate LDL receptors, fibrates such as fenofibrate, which activate PPAR-alpha to enhance triglyceride clearance, ezetimibe, which inhibits intestinal NPC1L1-mediated cholesterol absorption, and in selected cases omega-3 fatty acids or PCSK9 inhibitors.

Name: Hyperlipoproteinemia Type III
Description: Hyperlipoproteinemia type III, or familial dysbetalipoproteinemia, is an inherited remnant lipoprotein clearance disorder characterized by accumulation of cholesterol- and triglyceride-rich chylomicron and VLDL remnants (beta-VLDL) and classically presents with mixed hyperlipidemia, palmar xanthoma striatum, tuberous or tuberoeruptive xanthomas, premature atherosclerosis, and sometimes hepatosplenomegaly or peripheral vascular disease. The major genetic determinant is APOE, which encodes apolipoprotein E, the ligand mediating hepatic uptake of remnant particles through the LDL receptor, LDL receptor-related protein 1, and heparan sulfate proteoglycan pathways; most affected patients are homozygous for APOE epsilon2 (Arg158Cys), which has reduced receptor binding, although rare dominant APOE variants such as apoE2(Lys146Gln), apoE3-Leiden, and other APOE mutations can cause similar phenotypes, often with additional contributions from secondary factors including obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, estrogen deficiency, renal disease, or alcohol use. Pathobiologically, impaired remnant receptor binding disrupts lipoprotein trafficking within the apoE-LDLR/LRP1 axis, alters lipolysis coordinated by lipoprotein lipase and hepatic lipase, and promotes foam-cell formation and vascular inflammation. Diagnosis is based on combined elevation of total cholesterol and triglycerides, excess remnant lipoproteins, characteristic electrophoretic broad-beta band, elevated VLDL cholesterol-to-triglyceride ratio, apoE genotyping or phenotyping, and exclusion of secondary dyslipidemia. Type III may occur in classic recessive APOE epsilon2/epsilon2-associated disease or rarer autosomal dominant apoE variant forms. Common comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, carotid and peripheral arterial disease, pancreatitis less commonly than in severe chylomicronemia, metabolic syndrome, and fatty liver. Treatment relies on diet, weight loss, correction of secondary causes, and lipid-lowering therapy such as fibrates including fenofibrate or gemfibrozil, which activate PPAR-alpha to increase lipoprotein lipase activity and remnant catabolism; statins such as atorvastatin, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and upregulate hepatic LDL receptors; and niacin, which reduces hepatic V

Name: Hyperoxaluria, Primary
Description: Primary hyperoxaluria is a rare inherited hepatic glyoxylate metabolism disorder characterized by endogenous oxalate overproduction, recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis, and progressive kidney injury; the major subtypes are primary hyperoxaluria type 1, caused by biallelic AGXT mutations encoding the peroxisomal enzyme alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT), type 2 due to GRHPR mutations encoding glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase, and type 3 due to HOGA1 mutations encoding 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate aldolase, with mostly autosomal recessive inheritance and representative AGXT variants including p.Gly170Arg and p.Phe152Ile, some of which are pyridoxine responsive. Pathobiologically, defective detoxification of glyoxylate drives excess oxalate generation, involving peroxisomal, cytosolic, and mitochondrial glyoxylate-handling pathways and resulting in calcium oxalate crystal formation, tubular injury, inflammation, fibrosis, and, in advanced disease, systemic oxalosis affecting bone, retina, skin, heart, vessels, and bone marrow. Typical manifestations include childhood or adult-onset recurrent renal colic, hematuria, crystalluria, urinary tract obstruction, nephrocalcinosis, reduced glomerular filtration rate, chronic kidney disease, and end-stage kidney disease; complications include recurrent urolithiasis, pyelonephritis, hypertension, anemia, fractures, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and visual impairment. Diagnosis relies on high urinary or plasma oxalate, stone analysis showing calcium oxalate, urine glycolate elevation in PH1 or L-glycerate elevation in PH2, renal imaging for stones/nephrocalcinosis, genetic confirmation by AGXT, GRHPR, or HOGA1 testing, and, less commonly now, liver enzyme assay or biopsy. Treatment includes high fluid intake and crystallization inhibitors such as potassium citrate, which raises urinary citrate and alkalinizes urine, pyridoxine to enhance residual AGT activity in responsive PH1, and RNA interference therapies such as lumasiran, which suppresses hepatic glycolate oxidase (HAO1), and nedosiran, which suppresses hepatic lactate dehydrogenase A, thereby reducing oxalate

Name: Hyperparathyroidism
Description: Hyperparathyroidism is a disorder of inappropriate excess parathyroid hormone secretion causing disordered calcium-phosphate homeostasis, classically divided into primary disease from a parathyroid adenoma, multigland hyperplasia, or rarely carcinoma, secondary disease driven by chronic hypocalcemic stimuli such as chronic kidney disease or vitamin D deficiency, and tertiary disease with autonomous secretion after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism. Key genetic associations include MEN1, RET in MEN2A, CDC73/HRPT2 in hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome and parathyroid carcinoma, CASR loss-of-function variants, GCM2 activation, and cyclin D1/CCND1 overexpression; relevant proteins and pathways include the calcium-sensing receptor–G protein–phospholipase C–IP3 signaling axis, PTH/PTH1R–cAMP/PKA signaling, vitamin D receptor feedback, FGF23-Klotho phosphate regulation, and RANKL-mediated osteoclast activation. Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually sporadic but may be autosomal dominant in familial isolated hyperparathyroidism, MEN1, MEN2A, and CDC73-related syndromes; CASR defects can overlap with familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, an important mimic. Typical manifestations include hypercalcemia, nephrolithiasis, polyuria, polydipsia, constipation, abdominal pain, neurocognitive symptoms, fatigue, myalgias, bone pain, osteoporosis, fragility fractures, and in severe cases osteitis fibrosa cystica. Complications include renal impairment, pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease, hypertension, arrhythmias, and vascular or soft-tissue calcification, especially in renal secondary disease. Diagnosis rests on elevated or inappropriately normal PTH in the setting of hypercalcemia for primary disease, or elevated PTH with hypocalcemia/normocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia in secondary renal disease, supported by serum and ionized calcium, phosphate, creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 24-hour urinary calcium or calcium-creatinine clearance ratio, bone density testing, renal imaging, and localization studies such as neck ultrasound or sestamibi scanning. Medical therapy includes cinacalcet, a positive allosteric CASR modulator that suppresses PTH; calcitriol or paricalcitol, vitamin D receptor agonists that reduce PTH synthesis; and bisph

Name: Hyperparathyroidism, Secondary
Description: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a usually acquired, compensatory disorder characterized by diffuse parathyroid hyperplasia and excess parathyroid hormone secretion in response to chronic hypocalcemic or phosphate-retaining stimuli, most commonly chronic kidney disease and, less often, vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, or resistance to vitamin D. Its molecular basis prominently involves reduced calcium-sensing receptor CASR signaling, impaired vitamin D receptor VDR activation, disordered FGF23-FGFR1/Klotho signaling, and altered phosphate handling through PTH1R-mediated cAMP/PKA and phospholipase C pathways; representative genes/proteins implicated in susceptibility or parathyroid biology include PTH, CASR, VDR, FGF23, KL, FGFR1, GCM2, MEN1, and cyclin D1/CCND1, although classic Mendelian inheritance is not typical and familial forms are uncommon, arising mainly through inherited renal or vitamin D metabolism disorders or rare variants affecting parathyroid set-point regulation. Patients commonly present with CKD-mineral and bone disorder, bone pain, pruritus, muscle weakness, fractures, osteitis fibrosa, and biochemical abnormalities of elevated PTH with hyperphosphatemia and low or low-normal calcium in renal disease; chronic disease may progress to nodular hyperplasia and tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Important complications and comorbidities include renal osteodystrophy, vascular and valvular calcification, calciphylaxis, anemia, left ventricular hypertrophy, cardiovascular events, and increased mortality. Diagnosis relies on the clinical context plus laboratory testing showing persistently elevated intact PTH, calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and renal function, with adjunctive bone density assessment, skeletal imaging, and occasional parathyroid ultrasound or sestamibi scanning when surgery is considered. Treatment targets the underlying cause and includes calcitriol, paricalcitol, and doxercalciferol, which activate VDR to suppress PTH transcription; cinacalcet and etelcalcetide, calcimimetics that allosterically activate CASR and lower PTH; and phosphate binders such as sevelamer, calcium acetate, or lanthanum carbonate, which reduce intestinal phosphate absorption.

Name: Hyperprolactinemia
Description: Hyperprolactinemia is an endocrine disorder defined by persistently elevated serum prolactin, most commonly caused by prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas, reduced hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition, medications, primary hypothyroidism, pregnancy, or renal failure; major subtypes include physiologic, pharmacologic, pathologic, and idiopathic forms, as well as pituitary microprolactinoma and macroprolactinoma. Its molecular basis centers on lactotroph dysregulation of dopamine D2 receptor signaling and stimulatory TRH, estrogen receptor, JAK2-STAT5, MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, and cAMP pathways; implicated genes in familial or syndromic cases include MEN1, AIP, CDKN1B, PRKAR1A, and rarely SDHx-related genes, while DRD2 and PRL/PRLR axis abnormalities have functional relevance. Inheritance is usually absent in sporadic disease, but autosomal dominant predisposition occurs in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 and familial isolated pituitary adenoma, with representative MEN1 or AIP mutations. Clinical manifestations reflect hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and mass effect: women commonly present with amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, decreased libido, and bone loss, whereas men more often have decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility, gynecomastia, and delayed diagnosis; headaches and bitemporal visual field defects suggest macroadenoma. Important comorbidities and complications include osteoporosis, osteopenia, metabolic dysfunction, mood symptoms, sexual dysfunction, and tumor expansion with optic chiasm compression or, rarely, pituitary apoplexy. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms plus elevated fasting serum prolactin on repeat testing, exclusion of pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal or hepatic disease, and drug causes, recognition of macroprolactin, assessment of other pituitary hormones, and pituitary MRI when appropriate. Treatment is primarily with dopamine agonists such as cabergoline and bromocriptine, which stimulate D2 receptors to suppress prolactin synthesis and secretion and shrink adenomas, or quinagolide, another D2 agonist; resistant or compressive tumors may require transsphenoidal surgery, radiotherapy, or management of the underlying cause.

Name: Hypertension
Description: Hypertension (MeSH D006973) is a chronic, multifactorial cardiovascular disorder defined by persistently elevated systemic arterial pressure, most often essential (primary) hypertension but also secondary forms due to renal parenchymal or renovascular disease, primary aldosteronism, endocrine disorders such as pheochromocytoma or Cushing syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, and monogenic syndromes. Its pathobiology centers on dysregulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system, renal sodium handling, vascular smooth muscle tone, endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide and increased endothelin-1, inflammation, oxidative stress, and vascular remodeling; implicated genes and proteins include ACE, AGT, AGTR1, REN, NOS3, ADD1, CYP11B2, SCNN1B/SCNN1G and WNK1/WNK4-KLHL3-CUL3 in inherited salt-sensitive hypertension, with mutations in KCNJ5, CACNA1D, ATP1A1, or ATP2B3 in some aldosterone-producing adenomas. Most patients are asymptomatic, but headache, dizziness, palpitations, epistaxis, and visual blurring may occur, while signs and sequelae include left ventricular hypertrophy, retinopathy, nephropathy, and vascular disease. Major comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke, chronic kidney disease, peripheral arterial disease, aortic aneurysm/dissection, diabetes, obesity, and metabolic syndrome. Genetic risk is usually polygenic with familial aggregation, although Mendelian forms show autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance, exemplified by Liddle syndrome, Gordon syndrome, and apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Diagnosis relies on repeated standardized office blood pressure measurement, ideally confirmed by ambulatory or home monitoring; typical thresholds are at least 130/80 mmHg by ACC/AHA or at least 140/90 mmHg by many other guidelines, followed by evaluation for target-organ damage and secondary causes using serum creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, aldosterone-renin testing, ECG, echocardiography, and retinal examination. Treatment commonly includes thiazide-type diuretics such as chlorthalidone, which inhibit the distal Na+/Cl− cotransporter, ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril, which reduce angiotensin II and aldosterone formation

Name: Hypertension, Pulmonary
Description: Pulmonary hypertension is a progressive cardiopulmonary vascular disorder defined hemodynamically by elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure on right-heart catheterization, now typically >20 mmHg at rest, and characterized by pulmonary vasoconstriction, endothelial dysfunction, vascular remodeling, thrombosis in situ, and eventual right ventricular failure. Major subtypes include pulmonary arterial hypertension, PH due to left heart disease, lung disease or hypoxemia, chronic thromboembolic PH, and multifactorial or unclear mechanisms. Heritable and idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension are strongly linked to pathogenic variants in BMPR2, with additional genes including ACVRL1, ENG, SMAD9, CAV1, KCNK3, SOX17, TBX4, ATP13A3, and EIF2AK4, the latter classically causing autosomal recessive pulmonary veno-occlusive disease; inheritance is often autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance for BMPR2-related disease. Dysregulated pathways include BMP/TGF-β-SMAD signaling, endothelin-1, nitric oxide–soluble guanylate cyclase–cGMP, prostacyclin–cAMP, serotonin, Rho kinase, inflammation, and growth-promoting pathways involving PDGF and VEGF. Patients commonly present with exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, syncope, palpitations, loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, jugular venous distention, edema, cyanosis, and signs of right heart strain. Important comorbidities and complications include connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease, portal hypertension, HIV infection, schistosomiasis, obstructive sleep apnea, interstitial lung disease, chronic thromboembolism, arrhythmias, hemoptysis, and progressive cor pulmonale. Diagnosis relies on echocardiographic suspicion, ECG, chest imaging, pulmonary function tests, V/Q scanning for thromboembolic disease, CT angiography, BNP or NT-proBNP, serologic and genetic testing in selected patients, and confirmation with hemodynamic profiling by right-heart catheterization. Common therapies include endothelin receptor antagonists such as bosentan or ambrisentan, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil or tadalafil that augment cGMP signaling, prostacyclin analogs or receptor agonists such as epoprostenol, treprostinil, or selexipag that promote vas

Name: Hyperthyroidism
Description: Hyperthyroidism is a clinical state of excessive thyroid hormone action, most commonly caused by Graves disease, but also by toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis, TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, and rare causes such as activating germline or somatic TSHR mutations or GNAS-related autonomous nodules. Central molecular drivers include the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and thyroid follicular cell signaling through the TSH receptor, a Gs protein-coupled receptor that activates cAMP-PKA and downstream thyroid hormone synthesis pathways involving thyroglobulin, thyroid peroxidase, the sodium-iodide symporter SLC5A5, pendrin SLC26A4, and deiodinases; in Graves disease, stimulatory antibodies to TSHR predominate, with genetic susceptibility linked to HLA-DR, CTLA4, PTPN22, CD40, TG, and TSHR, typically in a complex polygenic autoimmune pattern, while familial nonautoimmune hyperthyroidism may be autosomal dominant via activating TSHR variants. Patients usually present with weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, hyperdefecation, proximal myopathy, goiter, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, and sometimes ophthalmopathy and dermopathy in Graves disease. Major complications include osteoporosis, heart failure, thromboembolism, thyroid storm, menstrual disturbance, infertility, and adverse pregnancy outcomes; common comorbidities include other autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, vitiligo, and pernicious anemia. Diagnosis rests on suppressed serum TSH with elevated free T4 and/or T3, supported by TSHR antibodies or thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, radioactive iodine uptake and scan to distinguish diffuse increased uptake from nodular autonomy or low-uptake thyroiditis, and thyroid ultrasonography with Doppler when needed. Standard therapies include methimazole and propylthiouracil, which inhibit thyroid peroxidase-mediated organification and coupling, with propylthiouracil also reducing peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, beta-blockers such as propranolol for adrenergic symptom control and partial T4-to-T3 inhibition, radioactive iodine ablation, and thyroidectomy.

Name: Hypertriglyceridemia
Description: Hypertriglyceridemia is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder defined by elevated fasting or nonfasting plasma triglycerides due to excess triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, especially chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoproteins, and may be primary, secondary, or multifactorial, ranging from mild/moderate disease to severe hypertriglyceridemia and familial chylomicronemia syndrome. Monogenic forms classically involve biallelic defects in the lipolytic pathway, including LPL, APOC2, APOA5, GPIHBP1, and LMF1, whereas polygenic susceptibility and familial combined hyperlipidemia may involve variants in APOE, GCKR, ANGPTL3, and ANGPTL4; inheritance is often autosomal recessive in familial chylomicronemia and more commonly complex/polygenic or autosomal dominant with variable penetrance in familial forms. The core pathogenic pathway centers on hepatic VLDL production, insulin signaling and resistance, lipoprotein lipase-mediated hydrolysis, apolipoprotein regulation, and ANGPTL3/4/8 inhibition of LPL, with impaired remnant clearance contributing. Common secondary contributors include diabetes mellitus, obesity, metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy, alcohol use, and triglyceride-raising drugs such as estrogens, retinoids, corticosteroids, protease inhibitors, and atypical antipsychotics. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal pain, and recurrent acute pancreatitis, while long-term complications include pancreatitis, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and increased atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, particularly with remnant-rich states. Diagnosis relies on lipid profiling, usually fasting when triglycerides are markedly elevated, repeated confirmation, evaluation for secondary causes, and sometimes apolipoprotein B, non-HDL cholesterol, thyroid, renal, hepatic, and glycemic testing; severe levels, commonly at least 500 mg/dL and especially at least 1000 mg/dL, raise pancreatitis risk, and genetic testing is considered in early-onset or refractory cases. Treatment includes fibrates such as fenofibrate and gemfibrozil, which activate PPAR-alpha to increase LPL activity and fatty acid oxidation; omega-3 fatty acids including icosapent ethyl, which reduce

Name: Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder
Description: Psychological sexual dysfunctions comprise a heterogeneous group of disorders in which disturbed desire, arousal, orgasm, or pain during sexual activity is driven predominantly by cognitive, affective, relational, or learned factors rather than a primary structural lesion; major subtypes include male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, female sexual interest/arousal disorder, erectile disorder with psychogenic predominance, delayed ejaculation, premature ejaculation with prominent psychobehavioral contributors, female orgasmic disorder, genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, and substance- or medication-associated presentations. Symptoms include low libido, impaired arousal or lubrication, situational erectile failure, anorgasmia, rapid or delayed ejaculation, avoidance, anticipatory anxiety, distress, and interpersonal dysfunction. Comorbid depression, anxiety, PTSD, obsessive traits, relationship conflict, chronic pain, endocrine disease, cardiovascular disease, and adverse effects of SSRIs, antipsychotics, antihypertensives, and alcohol are common, with complications including infertility, reduced quality of life, and partnership instability. Genetic contribution is complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with heritable influences reported for sexual desire, arousal, and ejaculation latency; representative candidate genes include SLC6A4 and HTR2A in serotonergic signaling, DRD2 and COMT in dopaminergic reward pathways, OXTR, ESR1, AR, NOS3, PDE5A, and androgen receptor CAG-repeat variation, although effects are modest and non-diagnostic. Relevant pathways include central dopaminergic mesolimbic reward, serotonergic inhibitory circuits, oxytocinergic bonding, hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal steroid signaling, nitric oxide–guanylate cyclase–cGMP vascular smooth muscle relaxation, sympathetic-parasympathetic autonomic balance, and stress-axis activation. Treatment is individualized and typically combines psychotherapy with drugs such as sildenafil, tadalafil, or vardenafil, which inhibit PDE5 to enhance NO-cGMP signaling; flibanserin, a 5-HT1A agonist/5-HT2A antagonist that modulates serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine; bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor used especially for antidepressant-associated dysfunction; and dapoxetine or other SSRIs for premature ejaculation via serotonergic delay of orgasm. Diagnosis relies on DSM-5 style criteria requiring persistent symptoms, clinically significant distress, contextual assessment, medication

Name: Hypocalcemia
Description: Hypocalcemia is a biochemical and clinical disorder defined by low total or ionized serum calcium, usually reflecting impaired parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion or action, vitamin D deficiency or resistance, renal disease, magnesium disturbance, or calcium complexation, and it may present acutely or chronically as neonatal, postsurgical, hypoparathyroid, pseudohypoparathyroid, vitamin D–related, or chronic kidney disease–associated forms. Key genetic causes include loss-of-function variants in PTH, GCM2, TBCE, and the 22q11.2 deletion causing DiGeorge syndrome with parathyroid hypoplasia, activating CASR mutations causing autosomal dominant hypocalcemia, and GNAS defects producing PTH resistance in pseudohypoparathyroidism; vitamin D pathway genes such as CYP27B1 and VDR are implicated in inherited rickets/osteomalacia syndromes. Central pathways involve the calcium-sensing receptor in parathyroid and kidney, PTH signaling through PTH1R and Gs alpha/cAMP, vitamin D activation and VDR-mediated intestinal calcium transport, and bone-kidney-intestine cross-talk regulating calcium-phosphate homeostasis. Typical manifestations include perioral numbness, paresthesias, cramps, tetany, carpopedal spasm, seizures, laryngospasm, prolonged QT interval, arrhythmias, fatigue, cataracts, dry skin, and neuropsychiatric symptoms; Chvostek and Trousseau signs may be present. Important comorbidities and complications include hyperphosphatemia, chronic kidney disease, nephrocalcinosis in treated or CASR-related disease, basal ganglia calcifications, dental abnormalities, osteomalacia/rickets, heart failure, and postoperative endocrine disorders. Diagnosis rests on low corrected total or ionized calcium with albumin assessment, plus PTH, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and sometimes 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, urinary calcium, ECG, and genetic testing when hereditary disease is suspected. Treatment commonly includes calcium salts such as calcium gluconate intravenously for symptomatic acute hypocalcemia and oral calcium carbonate or citrate for maintenance, cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol for deficiency, calcitriol to bypass impaired renal activation or absent PTH, magnesium repletion when deficient, and recombinant PTH in

Name: Hypokalemia
Description: Hypokalemia (MeSH D007008) is a biochemical and clinical disorder defined by a serum potassium concentration below 3.5 mmol/L, reflecting total-body potassium deficit, transcellular shift, or both, and it is commonly classified as mild, moderate, or severe, and as renal versus extrarenal potassium loss or redistribution states. Clinically it causes fatigue, muscle weakness, cramps, ileus, constipation, polyuria, rhabdomyolysis, paresthesias, and, in severe cases, paralysis and characteristic ECG changes with U waves, ST depression, QT prolongation, and ventricular or atrial arrhythmias. Major molecular determinants include renal transport genes and proteins such as SLC12A3 encoding the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter in Gitelman syndrome, CLCNKB in Bartter syndrome, KCNJ1/ROMK, SLC12A1/NKCC2, BSND/barttin, WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, and CUL3 in familial hyperaldosteronism-related or Gordon-spectrum tubulopathies, HSD11B2 in apparent mineralocorticoid excess, NR3C2 encoding the mineralocorticoid receptor, and CACNA1S, SCN4A, and KCNJ2 in hypokalemic periodic paralysis; inheritance may be autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, X-linked, or mitochondrial depending on the cause. Pathophysiology centers on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, mineralocorticoid receptor signaling, ENaC-mediated distal sodium absorption coupled to ROMK/BK potassium secretion, WNK-SPAK/OSR1 kinase regulation of NCC, and Na+/K+-ATPase-driven intracellular potassium shifts promoted by insulin or beta-adrenergic stimulation. Common treatments include potassium chloride replacement to restore extracellular potassium, potassium-sparing agents such as spironolactone or eplerenone, which antagonize the mineralocorticoid receptor, and amiloride, which blocks ENaC; magnesium repletion is important when deficiency coexists. Frequent comorbidities and complications include hypertension, hyperaldosteronism, diuretic exposure, vomiting or diarrhea, renal tubular disorders, magnesium deficiency, nephropathy, and sudden cardiac death. Diagnosis relies on serum potassium level, acid-base status, magnesium, urinary potassium excretion

Name: Hyponatremia
Description: Hyponatremia (MeSH D007010) is a common electrolyte disorder defined by a serum sodium concentration below 135 mmol/L, usually reflecting excess free water relative to body sodium rather than absolute sodium deficiency, and is clinically classified as hypovolemic, euvolemic, or hypervolemic and as acute or chronic; symptoms range from nausea, headache, gait instability, cramps, and confusion to seizures, coma, respiratory arrest, and cerebral edema, while overly rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination. Central molecular mechanisms involve arginine vasopressin (AVP/ADH) signaling through AVPR2 in collecting-duct principal cells, Gs-cAMP-PKA activation, aquaporin-2 trafficking, and renal medullary sodium handling, with additional roles for NKCC2/SLC12A1, NCC/SLC12A3, ENaC subunits SCNN1A/SCNN1B/SCNN1G, mineralocorticoid receptor NR3C2, and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis; natriuretic peptides and inflammatory or ectopic tumor pathways also contribute in SIADH. Genetic forms are uncommon but include X-linked gain-of-function AVPR2 mutations causing nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, activating GNAS variants, and inherited salt-wasting tubulopathies such as SLC12A1 or KCNJ1 defects in Bartter syndrome and SLC12A3 defects in Gitelman syndrome, typically showing Mendelian inheritance depending on the gene. Important comorbid associations include heart failure, cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, pneumonia, CNS disease, malignancy, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and thiazide or SSRI exposure. Diagnosis integrates serum sodium with measured serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium, assessment of extracellular volume status, renal function, glucose, cortisol, and thyroid testing, with targeted imaging or medication review when SIADH or endocrine/CNS causes are suspected. Treatment depends on cause and chronicity and includes hypertonic saline to raise extracellular tonicity in severe symptomatic cases, fluid restriction to reduce free-water intake, loop diuretics such as furosemide to increase electrolyte-free water excretion, vasopressin receptor antagonists such as tolvaptan or conivaptan to block V2-mediated water reabsorption

Name: Hypoparathyroidism
Description: Hypoparathyroidism is a disorder of deficient parathyroid hormone secretion or action causing hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, most often acquired after neck surgery or from autoimmune destruction, but also inherited in isolated or syndromic forms. Key genetic causes include loss-of-function variants in PTH, GCM2, TBCE, SOX3, and GNA11, activating variants in CASR that suppress PTH release, and syndromic defects such as 22q11.2 deletion involving TBX1 in DiGeorge spectrum, AIRE mutations in autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1, and GNAS abnormalities in pseudohypoparathyroidism, a PTH-resistance subtype typically showing elevated rather than low PTH. Core biology centers on the calcium-sensing receptor–G protein pathway in parathyroid chief cells, PTH/PTH1R signaling via Gs alpha, cAMP/PKA and phospholipase C, renal tubular calcium and phosphate handling, bone remodeling, and vitamin D activation through renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase. Patients develop perioral numbness, paresthesias, cramps, tetany, carpopedal spasm, seizures, laryngospasm, fatigue, anxiety, prolonged QT, cataracts, basal ganglia calcifications, nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis, and reduced bone turnover; comorbid autoimmune endocrinopathies, especially adrenal insufficiency and candidiasis in APS-1, may coexist. Diagnosis relies on low corrected or ionized calcium with inappropriately low or normal PTH, elevated phosphate, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, assessment of magnesium, urinary calcium, renal function, ECG, and when indicated genetic testing, autoimmune evaluation, or imaging for calcifications. Treatment classically combines oral calcium salts with active vitamin D analogs such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol to raise intestinal calcium absorption, magnesium repletion when deficient, and thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide to reduce calciuria; recombinant human PTH, including PTH(1-84) or teriparatide, replaces deficient hormone in selected chronic cases.

Name: Hypopituitarism
Description: Hypopituitarism is a clinical syndrome of partial or complete deficiency of anterior and sometimes posterior pituitary hormones caused by congenital developmental defects, genetic mutations, pituitary or hypothalamic tumors, surgery, irradiation, infarction, trauma, inflammation, or infiltrative disease. Genetic forms include mutations in PROP1, POU1F1/PIT1, HESX1, LHX3, LHX4, SOX2, SOX3, OTX2, GH1, GHRHR, TBX19, and IGSF1, producing isolated growth hormone deficiency or combined pituitary hormone deficiency; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked, depending on the gene. Pathobiology centers on disrupted hypothalamic-pituitary signaling, including GHRH-GHRHR-cAMP/PKA signaling in somatotrophs, CRH-ACTH-melanocortin signaling, TRH-TSH-thyroid axis, GnRH-LH/FSH-gonadal axis, dopamine inhibition of prolactin, and vasopressin pathways when the posterior pituitary is involved. Subtypes are often defined as isolated versus combined hormone deficiency, anterior versus panhypopituitarism, and congenital versus acquired disease. Clinical manifestations reflect the deficient axis and include fatigue, weakness, growth failure, delayed puberty, amenorrhea, infertility, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, hypothyroid symptoms, secondary adrenal insufficiency with hypotension or hyponatremia, and occasionally diabetes insipidus; major complications include adrenal crisis, severe hypoglycemia, osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular risk, and impaired quality of life. Commonly linked conditions include pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, Sheehan syndrome, lymphocytic hypophysitis, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, traumatic brain injury, and empty sella. Diagnosis relies on low target hormones with inappropriately low or normal pituitary trophic hormones, dynamic testing such as insulin tolerance, ACTH stimulation, GnRH or GHRH-based tests, pituitary MRI, visual field assessment when mass lesions are suspected, and selected genetic testing in familial or early-onset cases. Treatment is primarily hormone replacement, including hydrocortisone or prednisone, glucocorticoid receptor agonists replacing cortisol; levothyroxine, a synthetic T4 converted to T3; sex

Name: Hypotension
Description: Hypotension (MeSH D007022) is a hemodynamic disorder defined by abnormally low arterial pressure, often operationally as systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure insufficient to maintain organ perfusion, and it may be acute or chronic, primary or secondary, with major subtypes including orthostatic hypotension, neurally mediated syncope, postprandial hypotension, and shock-related hypotension. Clinical manifestations reflect cerebral and systemic hypoperfusion and include dizziness, lightheadedness, blurred vision, weakness, fatigue, nausea, presyncope or syncope, cold clammy skin, tachycardia or, in neurogenic forms, inadequate heart-rate compensation. Pathobiology involves impaired autonomic reflexes, reduced intravascular volume, cardiac pump failure, venous pooling, and dysregulated vascular tone mediated through baroreflex pathways, sympathetic adrenergic signaling, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, vasopressin signaling, nitric oxide-cGMP pathways, and inflammatory cytokine networks in sepsis. Genetic contributions are usually complex and secondary but are clearer in familial dysautonomias and connective-tissue disorders; representative genes include IKBKAP/ELP1 in familial dysautonomia, DBH causing dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency with severe orthostatic hypotension, and autonomic neuropathy-associated variants in transthyretin (TTR), while mutations affecting norepinephrine transport or baroreflex pathways have also been described. Common treatments include fludrocortisone, a mineralocorticoid that expands plasma volume; midodrine, an alpha1-adrenergic agonist that increases peripheral vasoconstriction; and droxidopa, a norepinephrine precursor that augments sympathetic tone; vasopressors such as norepinephrine are used in shock, and underlying causes such as hemorrhage, adrenal insufficiency, sepsis, arrhythmia, diabetes, Parkinson disease, or medication effects should be corrected. Important comorbidities and complications include falls, fractures, cognitive impairment, myocardial or renal hypoperfusion, stroke in severe cases, and recurrent syncope. Diagnosis relies on history, medication review, orthostatic vital signs with a sustained blood pressure drop of at least 20/10 mmHg on standing, ECG, laboratory assessment for anemia, endocrine or metabolic causes, tilt-table testing, autonomic reflex testing

Name: Hypotension, Orthostatic
Description: Orthostatic hypotension is a hemodynamic autonomic disorder defined by a sustained fall in blood pressure on standing, classically at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes, caused by failure of compensatory vasoconstriction, hypovolemia, medication effects, or impaired cardiac output; symptoms and signs include dizziness, lightheadedness, visual dimming, neck or shoulder “coat-hanger” pain, weakness, cognitive slowing, presyncope, syncope, and falls, sometimes with supine hypertension. Major subtypes include neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, non-neurogenic/volume-depletion or drug-induced orthostatic hypotension, and delayed orthostatic hypotension. Genetic associations are strongest in inherited autonomic and neurodegenerative syndromes rather than isolated disease, with examples including DBH deficiency causing norepinephrine deficiency, NTRK1 mutations in hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy, IKBKAP/ELP1 in familial dysautonomia, and SNCA, LRRK2, GBA, or PRNP in synucleinopathies or related disorders that can manifest neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; implicated proteins and pathways include norepinephrine synthesis and signaling via dopamine beta-hydroxylase, adrenergic receptors, baroreflex afferent signaling, sympathetic ganglionic transmission, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, vasopressin, and vascular smooth-muscle vasoconstrictor pathways. It is commonly linked to Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, pure autonomic failure, diabetes, amyloidosis, peripheral neuropathies, adrenal insufficiency, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, anemia, and frailty, with complications including recurrent syncope, traumatic injury, cerebral hypoperfusion, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis relies on orthostatic vital signs or tilt-table testing, review of heart-rate response to distinguish neurogenic from non-neurogenic forms, autonomic reflex testing, ECG, and evaluation for volume depletion, anemia, endocrine disease, neuropathy, and offending drugs. Common treatments include midodrine, an alpha1-adrenergic agonist that increases peripheral vascular resistance; fludrocortisone, a mineralocorticoid that expands plasma volume; droxidopa, a norepinephrine prodrug; and sometimes pyridostigmine, which aug

Name: Hypothyroidism
Description: Hypothyroidism (MeSH D007037) is a clinical state of deficient thyroid hormone action, most often primary from autoimmune thyroid failure but also central from pituitary or hypothalamic disease, and less commonly congenital, transient, subclinical, or consumptive. Key genetic and molecular associations include autoimmune susceptibility loci such as HLA-DR, CTLA4, PTPN22, and TG/TSHR-related thyroid autoimmunity, and monogenic forms caused by variants in TSHR, TPO, TG, DUOX2, DUOXA2, SLC5A5/NIS, SLC26A4, IYD, PAX8, NKX2-1, FOXE1, TSHB, TRHR, IGSF1, TBL1X, and IRS4; representative defects impair thyroid development, iodide transport, thyroglobulin synthesis, or hormone biosynthesis. Pathobiology centers on the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis, TSH receptor–Gs-cAMP signaling in thyrocytes, iodide uptake via NIS, organification by thyroid peroxidase with H2O2 generated by DUOX2, coupling on thyroglobulin to form T4/T3, and nuclear thyroid hormone receptor signaling that regulates metabolic, cardiovascular, neurologic, and developmental gene expression. Common treatment is thyroid hormone replacement, principally levothyroxine, a synthetic T4 converted peripherally to T3; liothyronine, synthetic T3 with direct receptor agonism; and, less commonly, liotrix or desiccated thyroid extract providing mixed T4/T3. Symptoms and signs include fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, depression, menorrhagia, delayed reflex relaxation, myxedema, hyperlipidemia, infertility, and in infants prolonged jaundice and neurodevelopmental delay. Major comorbidities and complications include Hashimoto thyroiditis, goiter, dyslipidemia, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, hyponatremia, anemia, peripheral neuropathy, pregnancy loss, and myxedema coma. Diagnosis relies on elevated serum TSH with low free T4 in primary disease, low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4 in central disease, thyroid peroxidase or thyroglobulin antibodies for autoimmune etiology, newborn screening, and

Name: Hypovolemic Shock
Description: Shock is an acute, life-threatening syndrome of circulatory failure causing inadequate tissue oxygen delivery and cellular hypoxia, classically divided into septic/distributive, hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and obstructive subtypes, with anaphylactic and neurogenic forms often included clinically. Its molecular biology is most defined in septic and inflammatory shock, in which pathogen sensing through TLR4/CD14, TNF, IL1B, IL6, NFKB, MAPK, JAK-STAT, complement, coagulation, and endothelial nitric oxide pathways drives vasodilation, capillary leak, mitochondrial dysfunction, and microvascular thrombosis; representative associated genes or proteins include NOS2, ACE, TNF, IL6, TLR4, NFKB1, VEGFA, SERPINE1, F5, F2, and adrenergic receptors such as ADRB1, although inherited causes are usually indirect and reflect predisposition or an underlying disorder rather than Mendelian transmission of shock itself. Genetic contributors may include thrombophilia variants such as factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A predisposing to obstructive shock via pulmonary embolism, and cardiomyopathy genes such as TTN or MYH7 predisposing to cardiogenic shock. Common manifestations are hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status, cold clammy or warm flushed skin depending on subtype, oliguria, tachypnea, elevated lactate, metabolic acidosis, and signs of end-organ hypoperfusion. Major comorbidities and complications include sepsis, trauma, myocardial infarction, heart failure, hemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, adrenal insufficiency, acute kidney injury, ARDS, DIC, hepatic injury, mesenteric ischemia, and multiorgan failure. Treatment is cause-directed and hemodynamic: norepinephrine, an alpha-1 greater than beta-1 agonist, is first-line for vasodilatory shock; vasopressin acts at V1 receptors to raise vascular tone; dobutamine, a beta-1 agonist, augments cardiac output; epinephrine provides mixed alpha/beta support and is essential in anaphylaxis; crystalloid fluids restore preload; and broad-spectrum antibiotics treat septic sources. Diagnosis relies on clinical evidence of hypoperfusion with blood pressure abnormalities, serum lactate, arterial blood gas, CBC, metabolic panel, cultures, ECG, troponin, coagulation studies,

Name: Impacted wax
Description: Impacted wax (cerumen impaction; UMLS C0021092) is a common external auditory canal disorder caused by retained desquamated keratin, sebum, and apocrine ceruminous secretions that accumulate when normal epithelial migration and self-cleaning fail; it is generally multifactorial rather than a classic monogenic disease, although cerumen phenotype has a known genetic component through ABCC11, in which the 538G>A variant strongly influences wet versus dry earwax and may alter secretion characteristics, while keratinization and glandular proteins such as keratins, mucins, and antimicrobial lipids contribute to wax composition. Relevant biologic processes include epithelial turnover and migration, apocrine and sebaceous secretion, local innate immune signaling, and inflammatory pathways involving cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF when secondary otitis externa develops, rather than a single canonical signaling pathway. Clinical manifestations include conductive hearing loss, aural fullness, otalgia, itching, tinnitus, cough via vagal stimulation, hearing-aid dysfunction, and sometimes dizziness; major subtypes are partial versus complete impaction, soft versus hard/dry impaction, and primary impaction versus secondary impaction associated with devices or canal abnormalities. Comorbidities and risk factors include older age, hearing-aid or earplug use, narrow or tortuous canals, exostoses, excessive hair, dermatologic disease such as eczema or psoriasis, diabetes, cognitive impairment, and recurrent otitis externa; complications include canal trauma, tympanic membrane injury, secondary infection, and transient vertigo during irrigation. Inheritance is not Mendelian for impaction itself, but familial cerumen traits related to ABCC11 and anatomic predisposition are recognized. Diagnosis is clinical, based on symptoms or inability to visualize the tympanic membrane with otoscopic or microscopic confirmation of obstructing cerumen; audiometry is used when hearing loss persists, and irrigation is avoided if perforation is suspected. Treatment relies on cerumenolytics such as carbamide peroxide, which releases oxygen and softens debris, hydrogen peroxide, which effervesces and breaks up wax, docusate sodium, a surfactant that penetrates and loosens cerumen, and mineral or olive oil, which lubricate and soften wax, often followed by irrigation or manual removal.

Name: Impetigo
Description: Impetigo (MeSH D007169) is a common, highly contagious superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis, classically caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes, presenting as nonbullous impetigo with vesicles that rupture into honey-colored crusts or as bullous impetigo caused by exfoliative toxin-producing S. aureus, with flaccid bullae and erosions; ecthyma is a deeper ulcerative variant. Its pathobiology is driven less by inherited host mutations than by microbial virulence factors and innate immune responses, including staphylococcal exfoliative toxins A and B targeting desmoglein 1, streptococcal M protein and pyrogenic exotoxins, and activation of keratinocyte Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, cytokine, complement, and neutrophil pathways; recognized host susceptibility factors include skin-barrier defects and inflammatory dermatoses, with genes such as FLG and immune-response loci occasionally implicated indirectly through predisposition to colonization or atopic dermatitis rather than Mendelian inheritance, so no consistent inheritance pattern is established. Diagnosis is usually clinical, based on characteristic lesions, distribution, and epidemiology, with bacterial culture and susceptibility testing from exudate or crusts used in recurrent, extensive, outbreak-associated, or treatment-refractory disease; PCR is rarely needed, and biopsy is uncommon. Standard therapy includes topical mupirocin, which inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase; retapamulin, a pleuromutilin that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; fusidic acid, which blocks elongation factor G; and for more extensive disease oral dicloxacillin or cephalexin, which inhibit cell-wall synthesis, or clindamycin, doxycycline, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole when MRSA is suspected. Important comorbidities and predisposing conditions include atopic dermatitis, scabies, pediculosis, diabetes, malnutrition, and poor hygiene; complications include cellulitis, lymphangitis, bacteremia, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, and particularly post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, whereas acute rheumatic fever is not typically linked.

Name: Inappropriate ADH Syndrome
Description: Inappropriate ADH syndrome, or syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH; MeSH D007177), is a disorder of impaired free-water excretion caused by persistent arginine vasopressin (AVP, ADH) activity despite hypo-osmolality and euvolemia, producing dilutional hyponatremia and inappropriately concentrated urine. It is usually acquired rather than inherited, most often linked to ectopic AVP production by small-cell lung carcinoma, pulmonary or CNS disease, postoperative stress, pain, nausea, and drugs; rare genetic forms include gain-of-function AVPR2 mutations causing nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and less commonly dysregulated AVP processing involving the AVP-neurophysin II precursor. The core pathway is AVP binding the renal collecting-duct V2 receptor (AVPR2), activating Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cAMP–PKA signaling, increasing aquaporin-2 trafficking and expression, with water retention; V1a signaling may contribute to vasoconstrictive effects, and natriuresis is influenced by suppression of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and relative increases in atrial natriuretic peptide. Clinical manifestations reflect severity and chronicity of hyponatremia and include anorexia, nausea, headache, gait instability, muscle cramps, confusion, lethargy, seizures, and coma, while examination typically shows euvolemia. Major complications include cerebral edema, falls, osteoporosis or fracture risk in chronic hyponatremia, and osmotic demyelination if sodium is corrected too rapidly; common comorbid associations include malignancy, pneumonia, meningitis, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and heart failure or cirrhosis as important differentials. Diagnosis rests on hypotonic hyponatremia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately elevated urine osmolality and urine sodium, clinical euvolemia, normal adrenal and thyroid function, and exclusion of diuretics and other causes; supporting tests include serum uric acid, BUN, cortisol, TSH, and response to fluid restriction. Treatment includes fluid restriction, hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic cases, oral urea to increase osmotic water excretion, demeclocycline to induce nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, loop diuretics such as furosemide to reduce medullary concentrating

Name: Swimmer's ear
Description: Swimmer’s ear, or acute otitis externa (UMLS C0021355), is an inflammatory and usually infectious disorder of the external auditory canal, most often precipitated by retained moisture, local trauma, hearing aids, dermatologic barrier disease, or canal obstruction; the dominant pathogens are Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, with fungal subtypes such as otomycosis due to Aspergillus or Candida and more severe necrotizing otitis externa occurring particularly in older adults with diabetes or immunocompromise. Its biology is driven less by Mendelian inheritance than by epithelial barrier disruption and innate immune activation, including Toll-like receptor and NF-κB signaling, neutrophil recruitment, cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, and bacterial quorum sensing and biofilm programs in P. aeruginosa; no disease-defining germline mutation is established, although host factors affecting immunity or diabetes susceptibility may increase risk. Typical findings are otalgia, pruritus, aural fullness, pain with tragal manipulation or pinna traction, erythematous edematous canal skin, otorrhea, conductive hearing reduction, and debris; malignant disease may add granulation tissue, severe nocturnal pain, cranial neuropathies, and skull-base osteomyelitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical by otoscopic examination showing diffuse canal inflammation with tenderness, while culture is reserved for recurrent, resistant, fungal, or necrotizing cases; glucose testing and inflammatory markers may support evaluation, and CT or MRI is used when invasive extension is suspected. Standard therapy includes topical acetic acid, which acidifies the canal and inhibits microbial growth; ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; neomycin or gentamicin, aminoglycosides that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit; polymyxin B, which disrupts gram-negative membranes; hydrocortisone or dexamethasone, which suppress inflammatory gene transcription; and clotrimazole, which inhibits ergosterol synthesis in fungal disease. Important comorbidities and complications include eczema, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, cellulitis, canal stenosis, recurrent infection, tympanic membrane injury, and, rarely, skull-base osteomyelitis.

Name: Female infertility
Description: Female infertility is a heterogeneous disorder defined by failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse, or after 6 months in women aged 35 years or older, and may result from ovulatory dysfunction, diminished ovarian reserve or primary ovarian insufficiency, tubal or peritoneal disease, uterine or cervical factors, endometriosis, or unexplained causes. Common symptoms and signs include inability to conceive, irregular or absent menses, oligo-ovulation, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, hirsutism, galactorrhea, and clinical features of estrogen deficiency in ovarian failure. Genetic contributors include FMR1 premutation, BMP15, GDF9, NOBOX, FIGLA, FOXL2, STAG3, MCM8/MCM9, EIF4ENIF1, and FSHR or LHCGR variants affecting folliculogenesis and gonadotropin signaling; chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner syndrome mosaicism and Xq deletions are classic, while thrombophilia, CFTR-related congenital absence of reproductive tract structures, and genes implicated in endometriosis or PCOS, including CYP19A1, INSR, and DENND1A, may contribute in selected phenotypes. Key pathways involve the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis with GnRH, FSH, LH, estrogen, progesterone, inhibin, and anti-Müllerian hormone, as well as insulin/PI3K-AKT signaling, TGF-β family signaling, steroidogenesis, folliculogenesis, inflammation, and aberrant angiogenesis in endometriosis. Important comorbidities and complications include polycystic ovary syndrome, obesity, insulin resistance, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, uterine fibroids, recurrent pregnancy loss, osteoporosis in hypoestrogenism, and psychological distress. Treatment depends on etiology and commonly includes clomiphene citrate, a selective estrogen receptor modulator that increases pituitary FSH secretion; letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor that lowers estrogen and augments follicular recruitment; metformin, which improves insulin sensitivity in PCOS; exogenous gonadotropins to stimulate ovulation; and dopamine agonists such as cabergoline for hyperprolactinemia. Diagnosis relies on history, timed intercourse assessment, semen analysis of the partner, ovulation testing, day-3 F

Name: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
Description: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic, relapsing immune-mediated disorders of the gastrointestinal tract comprising mainly Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, and indeterminate colitis; Crohn disease is transmural and may affect any GI segment, whereas ulcerative colitis is typically continuous and confined to the colonic mucosa. IBD arises from polygenic susceptibility interacting with environmental and microbial triggers, with familial clustering and complex non-Mendelian inheritance; representative genetic factors include NOD2/CARD15, IL23R, ATG16L1, IRGM, JAK2, HLA alleles, and variants affecting epithelial barrier and innate immunity, while proteins such as TNF, IL-12/23, integrins, and JAK-STAT mediators are central to pathobiology. Key pathways include dysregulated mucosal innate and adaptive immunity, Th1/Th17 polarization, TNF/NF-kB signaling, IL-23/IL-17 and JAK-STAT cascades, defective autophagy, impaired epithelial tight-junction/barrier function, and altered host-microbiome interactions. Typical manifestations are chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, urgency, weight loss, fatigue, fever, growth failure in children, and extraintestinal signs such as arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Major complications include strictures, fistulas, abscesses, toxic megacolon, malnutrition, venous thromboembolism, osteoporosis, and increased colorectal cancer risk, especially with long-standing colitis. Diagnosis integrates clinical presentation with inflammatory markers, stool fecal calprotectin or lactoferrin, colonoscopy with ileoscopy and histopathology, cross-sectional imaging such as MR or CT enterography, and exclusion of infection; serologies including pANCA and ASCA may support classification. Common treatments include 5-aminosalicylates such as mesalamine, which inhibit prostaglandin/leukotriene-mediated mucosal inflammation; corticosteroids such as prednisone, which broadly suppress NF-kB-driven cytokine transcription; thiopurines such as azathioprine, which impair purine synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation; biologics including infliximab or adalimumab targeting TNF, vedolizumab blocking alpha4beta7-integrin-mediated gut lymphocyte trafficking, ustekinumab inhibiting

Name: Influenza, Human
Description: Human influenza is an acute, contagious viral respiratory disease caused primarily by influenza A and B viruses, with influenza A further subtyped by hemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface proteins (for example H1N1 and H3N2), and less commonly influenza C causing milder illness; pathogenesis is driven by viral hemagglutinin binding to sialylated airway epithelial receptors, endosomal uncoating via the M2 ion channel, RNA replication by the PB1, PB2, PA polymerase complex and NP, and neuraminidase-mediated virion release, while host-response pathways prominently include RIG-I/MAVS, TLR3 and TLR7, JAK-STAT type I interferon signaling, NF-kB, inflammasome activation, and cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF that contribute to symptoms and severe inflammatory lung injury. Host genetic susceptibility is not Mendelian in most cases, but rare deleterious variants in IFITM3, IRF7, IRF9, GATA2, TLR3, and related interferon-pathway genes can predispose to severe influenza, and viral mutations such as neuraminidase H275Y or M2 S31N confer antiviral resistance. Typical manifestations include abrupt fever, myalgia, headache, malaise, nonproductive cough, sore throat, and rhinorrhea, with severe cases developing dyspnea, hypoxemia, primary viral pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia, ARDS, myocarditis, encephalopathy, myositis, rhabdomyolysis, or sepsis-like multiorgan dysfunction; important comorbidities include asthma, COPD, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, pregnancy, immunosuppression, and extremes of age. Diagnosis is based on compatible seasonal acute respiratory illness plus laboratory confirmation, preferably nucleic acid amplification testing such as RT-PCR, with rapid antigen tests less sensitive and viral culture or sequencing used selectively. Common treatments include oseltamivir and zanamivir, neuraminidase inhibitors that block viral release, peramivir, an intravenous neuraminidase inhibitor, and baloxavir marboxil, a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor that targets polymerase PA; supportive care remains essential.

Name: Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders
Description: Sleep initiation and maintenance disorders, broadly corresponding to chronic insomnia disorder and related phenotypes, are heterogeneous sleep-wake disorders characterized by persistent difficulty falling asleep, frequent nocturnal awakenings, early morning awakening, or nonrestorative sleep despite adequate opportunity for sleep, with resulting daytime fatigue, impaired attention, irritability, mood symptoms, and reduced function. Pathobiology is multifactorial, centering on hyperarousal and circadian dysregulation involving GABAergic inhibition, orexin/hypocretin signaling, melatonin pathways, and monoaminergic and HPA-axis activation; implicated molecular components include MTNR1A/MTNR1B, CLOCK, BMAL1/ARNTL, PER1-3, CRY1/2, ADA, COMT, SLC6A4, GABRA1, and orexin receptors HCRTR1/HCRTR2, with rare familial circadian-related sleep phenotypes linked to PER2 or CSNK1D variants and common insomnia susceptibility showing polygenic inheritance. Subtypes include short-term and chronic insomnia, psychophysiologic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, comorbid insomnia, and circadian-related sleep initiation complaints. Common comorbidities include depression, anxiety, PTSD, substance use disorders, chronic pain, cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes, GERD, and obstructive sleep apnea; complications include accidents, cognitive impairment, poorer cardiometabolic outcomes, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, typically using ICSD-3/DSM-5 criteria requiring nocturnal sleep difficulty with daytime consequences at least three times weekly for at least three months in chronic cases, supported by sleep history, sleep diary, actigraphy, insomnia severity scales, medication and psychiatric review, and polysomnography when sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder, parasomnia, or atypical features are suspected. Treatments include benzodiazepine receptor agonists such as zolpidem or eszopiclone, which positively modulate GABAA receptors; doxepin, which at low dose blocks histamine H1 receptors to improve sleep maintenance; melatonin agonists such as ramelteon acting at MT1/MT2 receptors to facilitate sleep onset; and dual orexin receptor antagonists such as suvorexant or lemborexant, which inhibit wake-promoting orexin signaling.

Name: Insulinoma
Description: Insulinoma is a usually small, well-differentiated functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor arising from beta cells that secretes insulin inappropriately and causes endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia; most cases are solitary and benign, while a minority are malignant or occur as multiple tumors, particularly in the setting of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Genetic drivers include MEN1 loss-of-function mutations and menin dysfunction, with less frequent alterations reported in YY1, DAXX/ATRX, and mTOR-pathway genes such as TSC2 or PTEN, implicating PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling, cell-cycle control, chromatin regulation, and beta-cell stimulus-secretion pathways involving KATP channels, calcium influx, and insulin granule exocytosis. Inheritance is usually sporadic, but MEN1-associated insulinoma follows an autosomal dominant pattern and may coexist with parathyroid and pituitary tumors; complications include recurrent neuroglycopenia, seizures, coma, traumatic injury, weight gain, and consequences of metastatic disease, most often to liver or lymph nodes. Typical symptoms are fasting or exertional hypoglycemia with adrenergic manifestations such as diaphoresis, tremor, palpitations, hunger, and anxiety, together with confusion, visual disturbance, behavioral change, weakness, or loss of consciousness. Diagnosis relies on Whipple triad and supervised fasting, typically up to 72 hours, showing inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin during hypoglycemia with suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate and negative sulfonylurea screen, followed by localization with contrast CT or MRI, endoscopic ultrasound, selective arterial calcium stimulation with hepatic venous sampling, and somatostatin receptor or GLP-1 receptor imaging in selected cases. Definitive treatment is surgical enucleation or pancreatectomy when feasible; medical therapy includes diazoxide, which opens KATP channels to inhibit insulin release, somatostatin analogs such as octreotide or lanreotide that suppress hormone secretion via somatostatin receptors, and everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor used particularly in advanced or unresectable disease, with additional options including glucocorticoids, streptozocin-based chemotherapy, sunitinib, or peptide receptor radionuclide therapy for malignant tumors.

Name: Intermittent Claudication
Description: Intermittent claudication is a symptom complex of peripheral artery disease, usually caused by atherosclerotic obstruction of lower-extremity arteries, in which reproducible exertional ischemic pain, cramping, fatigue, or weakness of the calf, thigh, or buttock resolves with rest; signs commonly include diminished pulses, cool skin, trophic change, bruits, and reduced walking distance. It is best regarded as a clinical manifestation rather than a single inherited disorder, with anatomic subtypes determined by aortoiliac, femoropopliteal, or infrapopliteal disease and pathophysiologic distinction from neurogenic claudication. Its biology reflects endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, thrombosis, and impaired angiogenesis involving nitric oxide and eNOS, VEGF signaling, HIF-1, TGF-β, NF-κB, cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α, matrix metalloproteinases, platelet activation, and lipid-handling pathways; associated genetic susceptibility is polygenic, with representative variants reported in APOE, LDLR, PCSK9, LPA, MTHFR, NOS3, ACE, IL6, and 9p21/CDKN2B-AS1, while rare monogenic dyslipidemias such as familial hypercholesterolemia markedly increase risk. Major comorbidities include smoking-related vascular disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, coronary and cerebrovascular disease, and complications such as critical limb ischemia, nonhealing ulcers, gangrene, acute limb ischemia, amputation, and excess cardiovascular mortality. Diagnosis relies on history and vascular examination plus an ankle-brachial index of 0.90 or less, with exercise ABI, toe-brachial index, duplex ultrasonography, CT or MR angiography, and catheter angiography used for confirmation and anatomical definition. Treatment combines risk-factor modification, supervised exercise, and antiplatelet and vasculoprotective drugs, including aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and thromboxane A2 synthesis, clopidogrel, a P2Y12 receptor antagonist, cilostazol, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor that raises cAMP to inhibit platelets and vasodilate, and statins, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and improve lipid-mediated vascular risk.

Name: Iridocyclitis
Description: Iridocyclitis is an anterior uveitis characterized by inflammation of the iris and ciliary body, usually immune mediated but sometimes infectious or traumatic, presenting with ocular pain, photophobia, circumlimbal injection, blurred vision, lacrimation, and cells and flare in the anterior chamber, often with keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae, and variable intraocular pressure; acute, recurrent, chronic, granulomatous, and nongranulomatous subtypes are recognized. Strong genetic associations include HLA-B27, especially in acute recurrent disease linked to spondyloarthritis, while HLA-DRB1 and other MHC variants may contribute in autoimmune forms; in syndromic or systemic inflammatory settings, variants affecting IL23R, ERAP1, NOD2, TNFAIP3, and CTLA4 are representative examples, although most cases are complex rather than Mendelian. Key pathways involve innate and adaptive immune activation with antigen presentation, Th1/Th17 polarization, and cytokine networks centered on TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-17, IL-23, IFN-gamma, NF-kappaB, JAK-STAT signaling, leukocyte adhesion, and breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier. Common comorbidities include ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, tuberculosis, syphilis, and herpesvirus infection; major complications are cataract, glaucoma, cystoid macular edema, band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, hypotony, and permanent visual loss. Treatment typically uses topical corticosteroids such as prednisolone acetate, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory gene expression, cycloplegic/mydriatic agents such as atropine or cyclopentolate, which block muscarinic receptors to relieve ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae, and systemic or topical NSAIDs such as diclofenac, which inhibit cyclooxygenase; refractory or steroid-dependent disease may require methotrexate, a folate antagonist immunomodulator, or biologics such as adalimumab, an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody. Diagnosis is clinical by slit-lamp demonstration of anterior chamber cells and flare, supplemented by tonometry, dilated fundus examination, optical coherence tomography when macular edema is suspected

Name: Iritis
