Description: Iritis, the anterior form of uveitis, is an intraocular inflammatory disease of the iris and often the ciliary body that may be acute, recurrent, chronic, granulomatous, or nongranulomatous, and typically presents with ocular pain, photophobia, circumlimbal redness, blurred vision, tearing, and consensual photophobia, with slit-lamp findings of anterior chamber cells and flare, keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae, and sometimes hypopyon or elevated intraocular pressure. It is usually complex rather than Mendelian, but strong genetic associations are recognized, especially HLA-B27 in acute recurrent nongranulomatous iritis, with additional links to HLA-DRB1 and immune regulatory genes such as IL23R, ERAP1, TNF, and CTLA4 in overlapping uveitic phenotypes; rare monogenic autoinflammatory disorders including NOD2-associated Blau syndrome can feature granulomatous iritis. Pathobiology centers on dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, including antigen presentation, Th1/Th17 polarization, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17, IL-23, interferon-γ, NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling, leukocyte trafficking, and breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier. Common comorbidities include ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthritides, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis, Behçet disease, and infections such as herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, syphilis, or tuberculosis; major complications include cataract, glaucoma, band keratopathy, cystoid macular edema, posterior synechiae, and permanent visual loss. Diagnosis is clinical but supported by slit-lamp biomicroscopy, tonometry, dilated fundus examination, optical coherence tomography when posterior involvement or macular edema is suspected, and targeted etiologic testing such as HLA-B27 typing, syphilis serology, chest imaging, ACE testing, TB assays, or aqueous PCR for viral DNA. Treatment usually includes topical corticosteroids such as prednisolone acetate, difluprednate, or dexamethasone, which suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription; cycloplegic/mydriatic agents such as atropine or cyclopentolate, which block muscarinic

Name: Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Description: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS; MeSH D043183) is a chronic disorder of gut–brain interaction, formerly classified as a functional gastrointestinal disorder, characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits in the absence of structural disease; major subtypes are IBS with constipation (IBS-C), diarrhea (IBS-D), mixed bowel pattern (IBS-M), and unclassified IBS. Pathobiology is multifactorial and includes heritable susceptibility, visceral hypersensitivity, dysmotility, altered intestinal permeability, immune activation, bile acid dysregulation, microbiome perturbation, and central stress-response abnormalities involving serotonergic signaling, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, enteric nervous system pathways, mast cells, cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, and ion/transport proteins. Genetic contributors are modest and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations reported for SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR, HTR3A and HTR3E, TPH1, SCN5A, TNFSF15, NPSR1, and cytokine variants including IL10; rare SCN5A channel dysfunction may influence motility. Symptoms include crampy abdominal pain, bloating, distension, constipation and/or diarrhea, urgency, mucus passage, and sensation of incomplete evacuation, often exacerbated by meals or stress. IBS commonly coexists with anxiety, depression, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, dyspepsia, gastroesophageal reflux, interstitial cystitis, migraine, and pelvic pain, and complications mainly reflect reduced quality of life, unnecessary procedures, and in some patients malnutrition or medication adverse effects rather than progression to inflammatory bowel disease or cancer. Diagnosis is clinical using Rome IV criteria, supported by normal basic evaluation and selective testing such as CBC, CRP or fecal calprotectin, celiac serology, stool studies, breath testing for lactose intolerance or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth when indicated, and colonoscopy only for alarm features. Common treatments include loperamide, a peripheral μ-opioid receptor agonist that slows transit; linaclotide, a guanylate cyclase-C agonist that increases cGMP-mediated chloride and fluid secretion; rifaximin, a minimally absorbed antibiotic that modulates gut microbiota; and alosetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist that reduces visceral pain and diarrhea in severe IBS-D.

Name: Keloid
Description: Keloid is a benign fibroproliferative scar disorder characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and persistent inflammation, producing firm, shiny, pruritic or painful scars that extend beyond the original wound margins and commonly follow acne, burns, surgery, piercing, or trauma; major subtypes include earlobe, presternal, deltoid, and post-surgical keloids, sometimes distinguished from hypertrophic scars by their growth beyond the initial injury and low tendency to regress. Its pathobiology centers on hyperactive fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, increased collagen I/III, fibronectin, and connective tissue growth factor, with dysregulation of TGF-β/SMAD, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MAPK/ERK, Wnt/β-catenin, JAK/STAT, VEGF, and inflammatory signaling involving IL-6, TNF-α, and mast cells; representative associated genes or proteins include TGFB1, TGFBR1/2, SMAD2/3, COL1A1, COL3A1, CTGF, VEGFA, MMPs, TIMPs, HIF1A, and p53 pathway components, while susceptibility loci such as 2q23 and variants near NEDD4, FOXL2, and MYO1E have been reported. Inheritance is usually complex and polygenic with familial clustering, higher prevalence in individuals of African, Asian, or Hispanic ancestry, and occasional apparent autosomal dominant transmission with incomplete penetrance. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by dermoscopy or histopathology showing broad hyalinized collagen bundles, and by exclusion of hypertrophic scar, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, and scleroderma; recurrence after excision supports the diagnosis. Common treatments include intralesional triamcinolone, which suppresses inflammation, fibroblast proliferation, and collagen synthesis; 5-fluorouracil, an antimetabolite that inhibits rapidly proliferating fibroblasts; bleomycin, which reduces collagen production and induces fibroblast apoptosis; and adjunctive silicone sheeting, cryotherapy, pressure therapy, laser therapy, or surgery often combined with corticosteroid or radiotherapy. Comorbidities and complications include acne, wound tension, infection, pregnancy-related worsening, cosmetic disfigurement, contracture, limited mobility, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, and frequent recurrence

Name: Keratitis
Description: Keratitis is an inflammatory, often vision-threatening disorder of the cornea that may be infectious or noninfectious, with major subtypes including bacterial, वायरल, fungal, Acanthamoeba, neurotrophic, exposure-related, and immune-mediated peripheral ulcerative keratitis. Patients typically present with ocular pain, photophobia, foreign-body sensation, tearing, conjunctival hyperemia, reduced vision, blepharospasm, and corneal epithelial defect, infiltrate, edema, ulceration, stromal haze, or hypopyon on slit-lamp examination. Pathobiology involves epithelial barrier failure and innate and adaptive immune activation, with TLR2/TLR4-, NF-κB-, MAPK-, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, CXCL8/IL-8, MMP-9, VEGF, and neutrophil-driven pathways central to tissue damage and repair; HSV keratitis additionally reflects viral latency/reactivation pathways involving herpes simplex virus proteins, while fungal and Acanthamoeba keratitis engage pattern-recognition receptors and inflammasome signaling. Genetic contributions are usually complex rather than Mendelian, but susceptibility or severity has been linked to variants in TLR4, IL1B, CXCL8, MMP9, DEFB1, and HLA alleles; keratitis may also occur in inherited corneal disease or predisposition states such as TGFBI-related corneal dystrophy, PAX6-associated aniridia, and familial dry-eye or atopy traits, though most cases are acquired. Important comorbidities include contact lens wear, dry eye, blepharitis, diabetes, trauma, autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and complications include corneal perforation, scarring, neovascularization, endophthalmitis, and permanent visual loss. Diagnosis relies on history and slit-lamp findings with fluorescein staining, corneal sensation testing when HSV is suspected, and microbiologic workup including corneal scraping for Gram stain, KOH, culture, PCR, or confocal microscopy. Treatment depends on cause and commonly includes fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin, which inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV; acyclovir or ganciclovir, which inhibit herpesviral DNA polymerase after phosphorylation; natamycin, which binds ergosterol in fungal membranes; and adjunct

Name: Keratitis, Dendritic
Description: Dendritic keratitis is a superficial ulcerative keratitis classically caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 reactivation in the corneal epithelium, producing branching epithelial ulcers with terminal bulbs; less commonly zoster pseudodendrites occur in varicella-zoster infection. It is an infectious inflammatory disease of the ocular surface characterized by pain, photophobia, tearing, foreign-body sensation, reduced corneal sensitivity, conjunctival injection, and blurred vision, with fluorescein- and rose-bengal/lissamine-green–staining dendrites on slit-lamp examination as a key diagnostic sign. HSV latency and recurrence are shaped by host and viral genetic factors, including HSV glycoproteins gB, gD, and thymidine kinase/UL23 and DNA polymerase/UL30, while human susceptibility and severity have been linked to innate immune genes and proteins such as TLR3, UNC93B1, TRIF/TICAM1, TRAF3, IFNAR1, and interferon-mediated antiviral pathways; HLA associations and immune dysregulation may also influence recurrence. Relevant signaling involves corneal epithelial infection triggering TLR and cGAS-STING sensing, type I interferon, NF-κB, MAPK, and cytokine networks including IL-1, TNF-α, and chemokines, with VEGF- and matrix metalloproteinase–related pathways contributing to stromal damage and neovascularization in recurrent disease. Standard therapy includes topical or oral acyclovir and valacyclovir, guanosine analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit viral DNA polymerase, and topical ganciclovir, another nucleoside analogue blocking HSV DNA synthesis; trifluridine, a fluorinated pyrimidine nucleoside interfering with viral DNA replication, is also commonly used, while topical corticosteroids are reserved for stromal or immune keratitis under antiviral cover. Important subtypes include epithelial dendritic/geographic keratitis, stromal keratitis, endothelitis, and neurotrophic keratopathy. Complications include recurrent keratitis, corneal scarring, thinning or perforation, secondary bacterial infection, uveitis, glaucoma, and permanent visual loss; comorbidities include atopy, immunosuppression, fever, UV exposure, and ocular surface disease. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by corneal scraping PCR, viral culture, cytology,

Name: Keratoconjunctivitis
Description: Keratoconjunctivitis (UMLS C0022573) is an inflammatory disorder of the cornea and conjunctiva that may be acute or chronic, infectious, allergic, toxic, or autoimmune, with major subtypes including epidemic adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis, vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis, and keratoconjunctivitis sicca/dry-eye disease. Its pathobiology is dominated by epithelial injury and tear-film instability with activation of innate and adaptive immune pathways, notably NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, Th2 cytokine signaling via IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 in allergic disease, and Th1/Th17 mediators including IFN-γ, IL-17, TNF-α, and matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP-9 in dry-eye and autoimmune forms; HLA associations and inflammatory regulators including TNF, IL1, IL6, and MUC1/MUC4-related mucins have been implicated, while inherited predisposition is usually complex except in syndromic dry-eye states such as ectodermal dysplasia or familial alacrima. Symptoms and signs typically include ocular pain or burning, foreign-body sensation, redness, tearing or dryness, photophobia, itching, blurred vision, discharge, punctate epithelial erosions, follicles or papillae, superficial keratitis, and in severe cases corneal ulceration, scarring, neovascularization, or vision loss. Common comorbidities include allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis, Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, and contact lens-related disease. Diagnosis relies on history and slit-lamp examination, fluorescein or lissamine staining, tear breakup time, Schirmer testing, corneal sensitivity when neurotrophic disease is suspected, microbiologic testing when infection is possible, and adjunctive assays such as conjunctival cytology, serum autoantibodies, and tear osmolarity or MMP-9 testing. Treatment depends on cause and commonly includes lubricating artificial tears that restore tear-film volume, topical cyclosporine which inhibits calcineurin-mediated T-cell activation, lifitegrast which blocks LFA-1/ICAM-1 interaction and lymphocyte trafficking, topical antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizers such as olopatadine, short-course corticosteroids

Name: Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca
Description: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye disease) is a multifactorial disorder of the tear film and ocular surface characterized by tear deficiency and/or excessive evaporation, producing hyperosmolarity, epithelial injury, and chronic inflammation; major subtypes include aqueous-deficient disease, particularly Sjögren-related and non-Sjögren forms, and evaporative disease dominated by meibomian gland dysfunction. Symptoms include ocular dryness, burning, foreign-body sensation, fluctuating or blurred vision, photophobia, redness, mucus strands, and reflex tearing, while signs include reduced tear meniscus, punctate epithelial erosions, filamentary keratitis, conjunctival injection, and, in severe cases, corneal ulceration or scarring. Pathobiology centers on lacrimal functional unit dysfunction, innate and adaptive immune activation, MAPK and NF-κB signaling, increased IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ, matrix metalloproteinase-9, apoptosis pathways, and altered mucin and secretory proteins such as MUC1, MUC4, MUC5AC, aquaporin-5, lactoferrin, lysozyme, and lipocalin; in Sjögren-associated cases, susceptibility genes and autoimmunity-related loci including HLA class II, IRF5, STAT4, BLK, and CXCL13 are implicated, with complex non-Mendelian inheritance rather than a simple hereditary pattern. Commonly linked comorbidities include Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroid disease, diabetes, rosacea, blepharitis, graft-versus-host disease, androgen deficiency, and medication effects. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by symptom questionnaires such as OSDI, tear breakup time, Schirmer testing, ocular surface staining with fluorescein or lissamine green, tear osmolarity, meibomian gland assessment, and sometimes inflammatory biomarkers such as tear MMP-9, with Sjögren evaluation including anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, and salivary or lacrimal testing. Treatment commonly includes cyclosporine ophthalmic, a calcineurin inhibitor that suppresses T-cell-mediated inflammation and improves tear production; lifitegrast, an LFA-1 antagonist that blocks T-cell adhesion via ICAM-1; corticosteroid eye drops that inhibit phospholipase

Name: Keratoconjunctivitis, Vernal
Description: Allergic conjunctivitis is a noninfectious, IgE-mediated inflammatory disease of the conjunctiva, usually triggered by aeroallergens and classically divided into seasonal and perennial forms, with more severe chronic subtypes including vernal keratoconjunctivitis and atopic keratoconjunctivitis; giant papillary conjunctivitis is often grouped clinically but is largely mechanical with immune contribution. It commonly presents with intense ocular itching, tearing, hyperemia, chemosis, eyelid edema, ropy or watery discharge, papillary conjunctival reaction, and, in severe disease, photophobia, punctate keratopathy, corneal shield ulcers, or vision disturbance. Pathobiology centers on allergen-driven Th2 polarization and mast-cell degranulation, with IL4, IL5, IL13, TSLP, IL33, FCER1, histamine H1 receptor signaling, eosinophil recruitment via CCL11/eotaxin and CCR3, and epithelial barrier and remodeling pathways involving filaggrin and matrix metalloproteinases; representative genetic susceptibility signals overlap with atopy, including variants near IL13, IL4R, TSLP, FLG, HLA class II loci, and FCER1A, though inheritance is typically complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. It is strongly associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis, food allergy, and keratoconus, and complications include chronic ocular surface inflammation, corneal scarring, secondary infection, and corticosteroid-induced glaucoma or cataract. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on bilateral itching plus allergen exposure history and slit-lamp evidence of papillae, chemosis, and conjunctival injection, while supportive tests include skin-prick or serum specific-IgE testing, tear eosinophils, conjunctival cytology, and occasional differential diagnosis to exclude infectious, toxic, dry-eye, or autoimmune conjunctivitis. Treatment includes topical antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizers such as olopatadine and ketotifen, which block H1 receptors and inhibit mast-cell mediator release, cromolyn sodium, which stabilizes mast cells, and short courses of topical corticosteroids such as loteprednol, which suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription; adjuncts include artificial tears, dual-action agents like azelastine, and in refractory disease topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus to inhibit calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation.

Name: Keratosis, Actinic
Description: Actinic keratosis is a common ultraviolet radiation–induced intraepidermal keratinocytic neoplasia and precursor to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, typically arising on chronically sun-exposed skin of fair-skinned older adults as rough, adherent, erythematous to skin-colored scaly macules, papules, or plaques, often tender or easier felt than seen; variants include hypertrophic, atrophic, pigmented, lichenoid, bowenoid, and actinic cheilitis involving the lip. Its molecular pathogenesis is dominated by cumulative UVB/UVA DNA damage with frequent TP53 mutation or p53 protein dysregulation, and additional abnormalities in CDKN2A/p16, NOTCH1/2, TERT promoter, HRAS/KRAS, EGFR, cyclin D1, COX-2, MMPs, and DNA-repair genes such as XPC in highly susceptible patients, leading to genomic instability, impaired apoptosis, and abnormal keratinocyte differentiation. Key pathways include p53-mediated DNA-damage response, MAPK/RAS/RAF, EGFR, NF-kB, COX-2/prostaglandin signaling, telomerase activation, oxidative stress, and local immune evasion. Inheritance is usually not Mendelian, but genetic susceptibility is influenced by pigment and DNA-repair genes, and risk is markedly increased in xeroderma pigmentosum and other rare repair disorders. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by dermoscopy showing a facial strawberry pattern, scale, rosettes, and perifollicular keratosis; biopsy is indicated for induration, ulceration, rapid growth, treatment resistance, or suspected invasive squamous cell carcinoma, with histology demonstrating atypical basal/suprabasal keratinocytes, parakeratosis, solar elastosis, and variable epidermal dysplasia. Common therapies include cryotherapy causing cellular ice-crystal injury, topical 5-fluorouracil inhibiting thymidylate synthase and DNA synthesis, imiquimod activating TLR7 to enhance interferon-mediated antitumor immunity, diclofenac inhibiting COX pathways, and photodynamic therapy with aminolevulinic acid or methyl aminolevulinate generating reactive oxygen species. Important comorbidities and complications include chronic photodamage, field cancerization, nonmelanoma skin cancer, immunosuppression, and progression to invasive

Name: Klebsiella Infections
Description: Klebsiella infections are opportunistic, usually non-Mendelian bacterial diseases caused predominantly by Klebsiella pneumoniae, but also K. oxytoca and hypervirulent K. variicola-related strains, producing community- or healthcare-associated pneumonia, urinary tract infection, bacteremia, liver abscess, wound infection, and neonatal sepsis. Pathogenesis is driven by microbial virulence determinants including the capsular polysaccharide loci with hypermucoviscosity regulators rmpA/rmpA2, siderophore systems such as aerobactin iuc, yersiniabactin ybt, and salmochelin iro, adhesins including type 1 and type 3 fimbriae genes fimH and mrkD, lipopolysaccharide, and beta-lactam resistance enzymes such as blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48-like, blaCTX-M, and blaSHV; host susceptibility is influenced by inflammatory and innate immune pathways involving TLR4-CD14 recognition of LPS, MyD88/NF-kB, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, and IL-6, with risk-modifying human variants reported in genes affecting TLR signaling, mannose-binding lectin, and neutrophil function rather than classic inheritance. Clinical features depend on site and may include fever, cough, purulent or currant-jelly sputum, dyspnea, dysuria, flank pain, abdominal pain, sepsis, and metastatic infection; major comorbidities and complications include diabetes, alcoholism, chronic lung disease, malignancy, transplantation, intensive care exposure, abscess formation, respiratory failure, septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death. Subtypes include classical versus hypervirulent strains and multidrug-resistant, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing, or carbapenem-resistant isolates. Diagnosis relies on culture of blood, sputum, urine, or sterile-site specimens with species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, with adjunctive PCR or other molecular assays for resistance genes, string test in hypermucoviscous isolates, imaging for pneumonia or abscess, and standard sepsis markers. Treatment commonly includes ceftriaxone or cefepime, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis; meropenem for severe ESBL infection, also a PBP-binding beta-lactam

Name: Klinefelter Syndrome
Description: Klinefelter syndrome (UMLS C0022735) is a sex-chromosome aneuploidy disorder caused most often by a 47,XXY karyotype, with mosaic 46,XY/47,XXY and higher-grade variants such as 48,XXXY or 48,XXYY producing variable severity; it is usually sporadic, arising from meiotic or postzygotic nondisjunction rather than Mendelian inheritance, although phenotype reflects gene-dosage effects from X-chromosome escape genes such as SHOX and androgen receptor pathway variation, including CAG repeat length in AR, with downstream perturbation of hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal signaling, Sertoli and Leydig cell dysfunction, reduced testosterone biosynthesis, elevated LH and FSH, impaired inhibin B/AMH regulation, and altered androgen-responsive cellular programs. The disorder is a primary testicular failure syndrome characterized clinically by tall stature with eunuchoid habitus, small firm testes, infertility or azoospermia, delayed or incomplete puberty, gynecomastia, sparse facial and body hair, decreased muscle mass, low libido, erectile dysfunction, and frequent language, learning, executive, or psychosocial difficulties. Important comorbidities and complications include metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, venous thromboembolism, autoimmune disease, obstructive sleep apnea, breast cancer, extragonadal germ cell tumors, and cardiovascular morbidity. Diagnosis is suggested by hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and semen abnormalities and confirmed by karyotyping, with chromosomal microarray or FISH useful in mosaic cases; adjunctive evaluation includes serum testosterone, LH, FSH, inhibin B, AMH, bone density testing, and testicular ultrasound when indicated. Treatment is supportive and endocrine-based: testosterone esters such as testosterone cypionate or enanthate, and transdermal testosterone gel, act as androgen receptor agonists to restore virilization, bone and muscle anabolism, and sexual function; anastrozole inhibits aromatase to reduce estrogen excess in selected patients, and bisphosphonates such as alendronate inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption for osteoporosis, while fertility options may include micro-TESE with intracytoplasmic sperm injection.

Name: Lactose Intolerance
Description: Lactose intolerance (UMLS C0022951) is a common gastrointestinal disorder caused by impaired hydrolysis of lactose due to reduced activity of lactase-phlorizin hydrolase, the brush-border enzyme encoded by LCT on chromosome 2, leading to osmotic malabsorption and colonic bacterial fermentation rather than a primary inflammatory signaling disease; the best-established genetic determinants are cis-regulatory variants upstream of LCT within MCM6, particularly the −13910C>T and related enhancer polymorphisms that underlie lactase persistence or non-persistence, with primary adult-type hypolactasia typically showing an autosomal recessive-like population pattern for low-expression haplotypes, while congenital lactase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic LCT variants. Key pathophysiologic components include undigested luminal lactose, epithelial brush-border deficiency, osmotic water retention, and microbiota-generated hydrogen, methane, and short-chain fatty acids that drive bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, borborygmi, and osmotic diarrhea after dairy ingestion; nausea is common, whereas weight loss or malnutrition suggests severe or secondary disease. Subtypes include primary genetic lactase non-persistence, congenital lactase deficiency, developmental deficiency in premature infants, and secondary lactose intolerance due to mucosal injury from celiac disease, Crohn disease, infectious gastroenteritis, chemotherapy, or other enteropathies. Management is mainly noncurative and dietary, but commonly used agents include oral lactase enzyme supplements such as lactase tablets or drops, which hydrolyze lactose into glucose and galactose before absorption, probiotic preparations such as Lactobacillus acidophilus or Bifidobacterium species, which may enhance bacterial lactose metabolism and symptom tolerance, and simethicone, which reduces surface tension of gas bubbles to lessen bloating; calcium and vitamin D supplementation are often added to prevent deficiency when dairy intake is restricted. Diagnosis relies on symptom provocation with lactose exposure plus improvement on restriction, hydrogen breath testing, lactose tolerance testing, stool acidity in infants, and, when needed, small-bowel biopsy or testing for secondary causes and LCT/MCM6-associated genotypes.

Name: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome
Description: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS; UMLS C0022972) is a rare autoimmune disorder of the presynaptic neuromuscular junction characterized by impaired acetylcholine release, most often caused by IgG autoantibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels composed chiefly of CACNA1A-encoded Cav2.1 subunits, with less frequent reactivity to related presynaptic proteins such as synaptotagmin or SOX1 in paraneoplastic cases; it is usually acquired rather than inherited, although HLA-linked immune susceptibility, especially HLA-B8, DR3, and DQ2, has been reported, and no Mendelian inheritance pattern defines classic disease. The central pathogenic pathway involves antibody-mediated reduction of presynaptic calcium influx, disruption of depolarization-secretion coupling, and secondary failure of quantal acetylcholine release, often in the setting of anti-tumor immunity, particularly with small-cell lung carcinoma. Clinically, LEMS causes proximal leg-predominant weakness, fatigability, autonomic dysfunction including dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction, and hyporeflexia or areflexia with post-exercise facilitation; ocular and bulbar symptoms may occur but are usually less prominent than in myasthenia gravis. Major subtypes are paraneoplastic LEMS, most commonly associated with small-cell lung cancer, and non-paraneoplastic autoimmune LEMS; complications include falls, respiratory or bulbar compromise, and morbidity from associated malignancy or other autoimmune diseases such as thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, and pernicious anemia. Diagnosis relies on the clinical phenotype, electrodiagnostic testing showing low compound muscle action potential amplitudes with incremental response after brief exercise or high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation, and serologic detection of P/Q-type VGCC antibodies, with cancer screening integral to evaluation. Treatment commonly includes amifampridine, a presynaptic potassium-channel blocker that prolongs depolarization and enhances calcium-dependent acetylcholine release, pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, and immunomodulatory therapy such as prednisone, azathioprine, intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange; definitive management of an underlying tumor can also improve neurologic symptoms.

Name: Laryngeal Edema
Description: Laryngeal edema is an acute or subacute swelling of the supraglottic, glottic, or subglottic laryngeal tissues that may rapidly compromise the airway; it is best viewed as a clinical syndrome rather than a single disease and includes allergic or anaphylactic edema, infectious/inflammatory edema, traumatic or post-intubation edema, radiation-related edema, and bradykinin-mediated angioedema. Molecular associations depend on subtype: hereditary angioedema is classically linked to SERPING1 variants causing C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction, with less common pathogenic variants in F12, PLG, ANGPT1, KNG1, MYOF, or HS3ST6; key proteins include C1-INH, factor XII, kallikrein, high-molecular-weight kininogen, bradykinin, and the bradykinin B2 receptor, whereas histamine-mediated forms involve IgE/FcεRI signaling, mast-cell degranulation, histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and cytokines. Common treatments include intramuscular epinephrine, an alpha/beta-adrenergic agonist that reverses vasodilation, reduces mucosal edema, and relieves bronchospasm; corticosteroids such as dexamethasone or methylprednisolone, which suppress NF-κB-driven inflammation and capillary leak; H1-antihistamines such as diphenhydramine or cetirizine, which block histamine H1 receptors; and, for bradykinin-mediated disease, icatibant, a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist, C1-INH concentrate replacement, ecallantide, a plasma kallikrein inhibitor, and in selected hereditary cases lanadelumab prophylaxis. Clinical features include hoarseness, muffled voice, odynophagia, dysphagia, throat tightness, stridor, dyspnea, drooling, and hypoxemia. Important comorbidities and precipitants include anaphylaxis, asthma, urticaria, ACE-inhibitor exposure, hereditary angioedema, upper-airway infection, GERD, trauma, and head-and-neck cancer therapy; complications include difficult intubation, respiratory failure, and death. Diagnosis is primarily clinical with urgent airway assessment, flexible laryngoscopy, pulse oximetry, and consideration of neck imaging

Name: Legionnaires' Disease
Description: Legionnaires disease (MeSH D007877) is an acute, severe, non-hereditary atypical pneumonia caused predominantly by Legionella pneumophila, especially serogroup 1, with less common disease from other Legionella species; a milder non-pneumonic form is Pontiac fever. Pathogenesis centers on bacterial entry into alveolar macrophages via complement receptors and pattern-recognition pathways, with host inflammatory signaling through TLR2/TLR5, MyD88, NF-κB, MAPK, and inflammasome/caspase-1 axes driving cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and IFN-γ, while the bacterial Dot/Icm type IV secretion system and effectors manipulate Rab1, ER trafficking, PI3K/Akt, and autophagy-related processes to create a replication vacuole. Genetic susceptibility is not Mendelian, but host factors in innate immunity have been implicated, including TLR polymorphisms and defects in interferon-pathway or anti-GM-CSF signaling in selected immunocompromised patients; no single mutation is diagnostic. Clinical features typically include high fever, nonproductive cough, dyspnea, myalgias, headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, confusion, hyponatremia, and rapidly progressive multilobar pneumonia. Major comorbidities and risk factors include smoking, COPD, chronic lung disease, advanced age, diabetes, malignancy, transplantation, corticosteroid or other immunosuppressive exposure, and chronic kidney disease; complications include respiratory failure, ARDS, sepsis, shock, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and multiorgan dysfunction. Diagnosis relies on compatible pneumonia plus microbiologic confirmation, most commonly urinary antigen testing for L. pneumophila serogroup 1, respiratory PCR, and culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract media, supported by paired serology and characteristic laboratory abnormalities. Treatment requires intracellularly active antibiotics, especially azithromycin, a macrolide that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, fluoroquinolones that inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; and doxycycline, a tetracycline that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, with rifampin, an RNA polymerase inhibitor, occasionally used adjunctively in severe disease.

Name: Leishmaniasis
Description: Leishmaniasis (MeSH D007896) is a vector-borne protozoal disease caused by Leishmania species transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies, classically presenting as cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral disease; clinical findings range from papules, nodules, ulcerative skin lesions, and destructive naso-oropharyngeal inflammation to prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia in visceral leishmaniasis. Disease expression is strongly shaped by host immunogenetics rather than Mendelian inheritance, with susceptibility associations reported for SLC11A1/NRAMP1, HLA class II alleles, IFNG, IL10, TNF, TLR2, TLR4, and CXCR3, while parasite virulence factors such as GP63, lipophosphoglycan, and A2 proteins promote macrophage invasion and survival. Key pathways include macrophage phagolysosomal infection, TLR-mediated innate sensing, IL-12/IFN-γ-driven Th1 responses and nitric oxide killing, counterbalanced by IL-10, TGF-β, PD-1/immune exhaustion, and parasite manipulation of JAK/STAT, MAPK, NF-κB, and arginine metabolism. Common treatments include pentavalent antimonials such as sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate, which impair parasite bioenergetics and thiol redox systems; amphotericin B, especially liposomal, which binds ergosterol-like membrane sterols causing pore formation; miltefosine, which disrupts membrane phospholipid metabolism and signaling; and paromomycin, an aminoglycoside that inhibits protein synthesis. Major complications include secondary bacterial infection, scarring, mucosal destruction, severe anemia, hemorrhage, malnutrition, and relapse, especially with HIV coinfection or other immunosuppression; post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis may follow visceral infection. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology and syndrome plus demonstration of amastigotes on tissue smear, histopathology, or culture, PCR-based species identification, and in visceral disease serology such as rK39 or direct agglutination, with Montenegro skin testing supporting exposure mainly outside active visceral disease.

Name: Leishmaniasis, Cutaneous
Description: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a vector-borne protozoal skin infection caused by Leishmania species transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies, most commonly Old World L. major, L. tropica, and L. aethiopica and New World L. mexicana, L. braziliensis, and related species, producing localized, diffuse, or mucocutaneous-prone forms characterized by papules that enlarge into nodules, plaques, or painless ulcers with raised indurated borders, sometimes with satellite lesions, lymphangitis, regional adenopathy, and chronic scarring. Disease expression is strongly shaped by host immunogenetics rather than Mendelian inheritance; susceptibility and severity have been associated with variants affecting SLC11A1/NRAMP1, IFNG, TNF, IL10, IL4, CXCR2, and HLA class I/II loci, while diffuse cutaneous disease is linked to impaired cell-mediated immunity. Central pathogenic pathways include macrophage phagocytosis via complement receptors, intracellular survival in phagolysosomes, Th1/Th2 polarization, IL-12–IFN-γ–STAT1–inducible nitric oxide synthase antimicrobial signaling, TNF-mediated granulomatous inflammation, and regulatory IL-10/TGF-β pathways that permit parasite persistence. Diagnosis is based on compatible travel or endemic exposure plus demonstration of amastigotes on smear, histopathology, or culture, with PCR and species typing increasingly important for prognosis and treatment selection; Montenegro skin testing and serology may support but do not reliably confirm active disease. Standard therapies include pentavalent antimonials such as sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate, which disrupt parasite bioenergetics and thiol-redox metabolism; amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol-like membrane sterols causing parasite membrane leakage; miltefosine, an alkylphosphocholine that alters membrane lipid metabolism and signaling; and paromomycin, an aminoglycoside that inhibits protein synthesis. Important complications and comorbid associations include bacterial superinfection, destructive mucosal dissemination especially with Viannia species, relapse, disfiguring scar-related psychosocial morbidity, and more severe or atypical disease in HIV infection, malnutrition, or other immunosuppressed states.

Name: Leishmaniasis, Visceral
Description: Visceral leishmaniasis, or kala-azar, is a life-threatening systemic protozoal infection caused mainly by the Leishmania donovani complex, especially L. donovani and L. infantum/chagasi, in which amastigotes parasitize macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system; clinically it presents with prolonged irregular fever, weight loss, profound splenomegaly often with hepatomegaly, pancytopenia, weakness, hypergammaglobulinemia, and darkening of the skin, and may be complicated by bleeding, severe bacterial superinfection, malnutrition, hemophagocytic syndrome, post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, and death, with particularly severe disease in HIV coinfection. Host susceptibility is complex and non-Mendelian, with representative genetic associations involving SLC11A1/NRAMP1, IFNG, IL10, IL4, TNF, HLA class II loci, CXCR2, and TLR polymorphisms, while parasite virulence factors include lipophosphoglycan, gp63 metalloprotease, and A2 proteins. Pathobiology centers on macrophage invasion and survival within phagolysosomes, dysregulated Th1/Th2 balance, impaired IL-12 and IFN-γ–driven macrophage activation, excess IL-10 and TGF-β signaling, JAK-STAT, NF-κB, Toll-like receptor, complement, nitric oxide/reactive oxygen, and PD-1–associated T-cell exhaustion pathways. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology and syndrome plus demonstration of amastigotes in splenic, bone marrow, or lymph node aspirates, supported by culture or PCR, and by serology such as rK39 immunochromatographic testing or direct agglutination; hematologic abnormalities and liver function changes are common ancillary findings. Major treatment options include liposomal amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol-like parasite membrane sterols causing membrane disruption; pentavalent antimonials such as sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate, which impair parasite bioenergetics and thiol redox metabolism; miltefosine, which perturbs membrane phospholipid metabolism and signaling; and paromomycin, an aminoglycoside that inhibits parasite protein synthesis.

Name: Leprosy
Description: Leprosy, or Hansen disease (MeSH D007918), is a chronic granulomatous infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae and, less commonly, M. lepromatosis, with tropism for skin, peripheral nerves, and cooler tissues; clinical manifestations range across a host immune spectrum from paucibacillary tuberculoid disease to multibacillary lepromatous disease, with borderline forms and pure neuritic variants. Typical signs include hypopigmented or erythematous anesthetic patches, peripheral nerve enlargement, sensory loss, weakness, trophic ulcers, leonine facies, nodules, madarosis, and nasal or ocular involvement. Pathobiology is strongly shaped by innate and adaptive immune signaling, notably TLR1/TLR2-, NOD2-, vitamin D receptor–cathelicidin, TNF, IFN-γ/IL-12 Th1, and IL-4/IL-10 Th2 pathways, as well as Schwann-cell interaction and macrophage granuloma biology; representative susceptibility genes include HLA-DR/DQ, LTA, TNF, PRKN/PACRG, LRRK2, NOD2, TLR1, SLC11A1, IL10, and VDR, with common risk polymorphisms rather than Mendelian inheritance predominating. Diagnosis is based on cardinal features such as anesthetic skin lesions, thickened peripheral nerves with sensory or motor deficit, and demonstration of acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear or biopsy; histopathology, Fite-Faraco staining, PCR for mycobacterial DNA, and nerve conduction testing support classification and confirmation. Standard therapy is multidrug treatment with rifampicin, which inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; dapsone, a folate synthesis inhibitor targeting dihydropteroate synthase; and clofazimine, a riminophenazine with antimycobacterial and anti-inflammatory effects that disrupts mycobacterial redox/membrane function; alternatives or adjuncts include ofloxacin, minocycline, and clarithromycin. Major complications include type 1 reversal reactions, type 2 erythema nodosum leprosum, neuritis, deformity, blindness, secondary infections, and disability, with linked comorbidities including malnutrition, tuberculosis coinfection, and psychosocial morbidity.

Name: Leukemia
Description: Leukemia (MeSH D007938) is a heterogeneous group of clonal hematopoietic malignancies arising from transformed myeloid or lymphoid progenitors, broadly classified as acute or chronic and as lymphoblastic/lymphocytic or myeloid, with major subtypes including acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and chronic myeloid leukemia. Its biology is driven by recurrent genetic lesions such as BCR::ABL1 from t(9;22) in CML and some ALL, PML::RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia, FLT3, NPM1, CEBPA, IDH1/2, RUNX1, TP53, DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, JAK2, and in CLL del(13q), trisomy 12, del(11q/ATM), del(17p/TP53), NOTCH1, and SF3B1 abnormalities; dysregulated pathways commonly involve tyrosine kinase signaling, JAK-STAT, RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, B-cell receptor signaling, apoptosis control via BCL2, cell-cycle and epigenetic regulation, and altered differentiation. Most cases are sporadic, but predisposition may be inherited in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Down syndrome, GATA2, RUNX1, CEBPA, DDX41, ETV6, and ANKRD26-related syndromes, typically with autosomal dominant patterns in familial myeloid neoplasia. Patients often present with marrow failure and leukemic infiltration causing fatigue, pallor, fever, infections, bleeding, bruising, bone pain, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and occasionally leukostasis, CNS disease, or mediastinal mass. Complications include severe infection, tumor lysis syndrome, coagulopathy including DIC in APL, thrombosis, anemia, relapse, and transformation such as Richter syndrome. Diagnosis relies on CBC with differential, peripheral smear, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy with blast quantification, immunophenotyping by flow cytometry, cytogenetics/FISH, PCR or next-generation sequencing, and disease-specific criteria such as WHO/ICC classifications. Treatments include cytarabine, a nucleoside analog that inhibits DNA synthesis; anthracy

Name: Leukemia, Lymphocytic, Chronic, B-Cell
Description: Chronic B-cell lymphocytic leukemia (CLL; MeSH D015451) is an indolent mature B-cell neoplasm, closely related to small lymphocytic lymphoma, characterized by clonal accumulation of CD5-positive, CD19-positive, CD20dim, CD23-positive B lymphocytes in blood, marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen. Recurrent genetic lesions include del(13q14) involving loss of miR-15a/miR-16-1, trisomy 12, del(11q) affecting ATM, del(17p) with TP53 loss, and less often NOTCH1, SF3B1, BIRC3, POT1, MYD88, and BTK/PLCG2 mutations; IGHV mutation status is a major biologic and prognostic marker, with unmutated IGHV associated with more aggressive disease. Pathobiology centers on chronic B-cell receptor signaling, with SYK, LYN, BTK, PI3K-delta, PLCgamma2, NF-kappaB, MAPK/ERK, JAK/STAT, and antiapoptotic BCL2 pathways, together with microenvironmental support from stromal cells, CXCR4/CXCL12, and CD40 signaling. Patients often present with asymptomatic lymphocytosis, fatigue, night sweats, weight loss, painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, recurrent infections, or cytopenias. Major complications include hypogammaglobulinemia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, marrow failure, Richter transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and increased risk of secondary malignancies and infection. Diagnosis requires persistent peripheral blood monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis of at least 5 × 10^9/L, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, blood smear showing small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells, and supportive cytogenetic or molecular testing by FISH, karyotype, TP53 and IGHV analysis; marrow biopsy is not always required. Clinical entities include CLL, small lymphocytic lymphoma, and monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis. Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering indicates inherited susceptibility with polygenic risk, including loci such as IRF4 and BCL2. Name: Leukemia, Erythroblastic, Acute
Description: Acute erythroblastic leukemia, usually classified within acute erythroid leukemia in the AML spectrum, is a rare, aggressive myeloid neoplasm characterized by predominant immature erythroid precursors in bone marrow and often a high burden of genomic instability rather than a single pathognomonic lesion. Recurrent molecular abnormalities include TP53 mutations or biallelic loss, complex karyotypes with deletions of 5q and 7q, monosomy 5 or 7, abnormalities of 17p, and less commonly mutations seen in AML such as NPM1, FLT3, DNMT3A, TET2, IDH1/2, RUNX1, or ASXL1; erythroid differentiation is also governed by GATA1, GATA2, KLF1, TAL1, EPOR/JAK2, and BCL2-related survival programs. Relevant pathways include dysregulated p53-mediated DNA-damage response, JAK-STAT and erythropoietin receptor signaling, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, apoptosis control, and epigenetic regulation of hematopoietic differentiation. Patients typically present with marrow failure causing fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, fever, infections, bleeding, bruising, petechiae, and sometimes hepatosplenomegaly; complications include severe anemia, transfusion dependence, neutropenic sepsis, hemorrhage, disseminated intravascular coagulation, iron overload, and progression or overlap with myelodysplastic syndrome or therapy-related AML. Historic subtypes include erythroleukemia and pure erythroid leukemia, although current classification emphasizes AML genetic features and blast criteria. Most cases are sporadic rather than inherited, but predisposition may occur in germline TP53 (Li-Fraumeni), RUNX1, CEBPA, DDX41, GATA2, or Fanconi-anemia-related syndromes. Diagnosis relies on CBC and smear, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy showing marked erythroid predominance with increased proerythroblasts or myeloblasts, multiparameter flow cytometry, cytochemistry, and cytogenetic/molecular testing by karyotype, FISH, and NGS. Name: Leukemia, Hairy Cell
Description: Hairy cell leukemia is an indolent mature B-cell neoplasm characterized by clonal accumulation of small to medium lymphoid cells with circumferential cytoplasmic projections in bone marrow, spleen, and peripheral blood, classically causing pancytopenia, monocytopenia, massive splenomegaly, fatigue, recurrent infections, bleeding, and sometimes constitutional symptoms; a variant form, hairy cell leukemia-variant, is biologically distinct and more aggressive. The molecular hallmark of classic hairy cell leukemia is the activating BRAF V600E mutation, with downstream MAPK/ERK signaling central to pathogenesis; additional abnormalities may involve CDKN1B, KLF2, and epigenetic regulators, while the variant form more often shows MAP2K1 mutations and usually lacks BRAF V600E. The leukemic cells express pan-B-cell markers with a characteristic immunophenotype including CD11c, CD25, CD103, CD123, annexin A1, and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positivity, and signal dependence may also involve B-cell receptor, CXCR4-CXCL12, and microenvironmental interactions that support survival. The disease is generally sporadic rather than inherited, with no established Mendelian transmission, although its genetic basis resides in acquired somatic driver mutations. Diagnosis relies on blood counts, peripheral smear, bone marrow biopsy and aspirate, flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, TRAP staining, splenic findings, and molecular testing for BRAF or MAP2K1 mutations to distinguish subtypes and from splenic marginal zone lymphoma. Standard therapy includes purine analogs such as cladribine and pentostatin, which impair DNA synthesis and induce apoptosis; rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody; interferon-alpha, an immunomodulator; and in relapsed disease vemurafenib or dabrafenib, which inhibit mutant BRAF, as well as moxetumomab pasudotox, an anti-CD22 immunotoxin that blocks protein synthesis. Important complications and comorbidities include severe bacterial or opportunistic infections, marrow failure, autoimmune vasculitis or cytopenias, secondary malignancies, and treatment-related prolonged immunosuppression.

Name: Acute lymphocytic leukaemia
Description: Acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL; UMLS C0023449) is an aggressive hematologic malignancy of lymphoid progenitors, most often B-cell precursor disease and less commonly T-cell ALL, characterized by clonal accumulation of lymphoblasts in marrow, blood, and extramedullary sites. Recurrent genetic lesions include aneuploidy such as hyperdiploidy, ETV6-RUNX1, BCR-ABL1 from t(9;22), TCF3-PBX1, KMT2A rearrangements, intrachromosomal amplification of chromosome 21, and alterations in PAX5, IKZF1, CDKN2A/B, CRLF2, JAK1/2, NOTCH1, FBXW7, and TP53; inherited predisposition is usually not Mendelian but is increased in syndromes such as Down syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, and germline PAX5, ETV6, or IKZF1 variants. Leukemogenesis commonly engages aberrant B-cell receptor precursor programs, JAK-STAT, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, ABL/SRC kinase signaling, and in T-ALL, NOTCH1-driven transcriptional networks. Patients typically present with marrow failure causing fatigue, pallor, fever, infection, bruising or bleeding, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and sometimes mediastinal mass, testicular enlargement, or central nervous system involvement. Major complications and comorbidities include severe infection, tumor lysis syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombosis, relapse, and treatment-related cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and endocrinopathies. Diagnosis relies on complete blood count and smear, bone marrow examination showing at least 20% lymphoblasts, immunophenotyping by flow cytometry to define B- or T-lineage, cytogenetics, FISH, and molecular assays including RT-PCR or next-generation sequencing for risk stratification and minimal residual disease monitoring. Name: Leukemia, Mast-Cell
Description: Mast-cell leukemia is a rare, highly aggressive leukemic variant of systemic mastocytosis characterized by diffuse marrow and often blood involvement by neoplastic mast cells, most commonly arising from activating KIT mutations, especially KIT D816V, with additional lesions such as SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1, TET2, CBL, JAK2, NRAS/KRAS, or NPM1 in some cases that influence prognosis and clonal evolution. Its biology is driven principally by constitutive KIT signaling through PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, JAK/STAT, and SRC-family pathways, with mast-cell activation causing release of histamine, tryptase, heparin, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes. Clinically, patients present with constitutional symptoms, flushing, pruritus, urticaria, abdominal pain, diarrhea, peptic symptoms, hypotension or anaphylactoid episodes, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, cytopenias, bone pain, osteolysis or osteoporosis, ascites, and organ damage; major complications include liver dysfunction, malabsorption, bleeding, infections, and multiorgan failure. It is classified as acute when circulating mast cells are at least 10% of leukocytes and aleukemic when peripheral blood involvement is lower, and may occur de novo or with an associated hematologic neoplasm. Most cases are sporadic rather than inherited, although rare familial mastocytosis implicates germline KIT alterations. Diagnosis requires integration of bone marrow morphology showing at least 20% atypical or immature mast cells, immunophenotyping with CD117 and tryptase plus aberrant CD25 and/or CD2 or CD30, elevated serum tryptase, KIT mutation testing by PCR or sequencing, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and imaging for organ involvement. Treatment commonly includes midostaurin, a multikinase inhibitor active against KIT D816V; avapritinib, a potent KIT D816V inhibitor; cladribine, a purine analog cytoreductive agent; and in selected KIT wild-type or non-D816V cases imatinib, a KIT/ABL/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, with supportive antimediator therapy and allogeneic transplantation considered in eligible patients.

Name: Leukemia, Monocytic, Acute
Description: Acute monocytic leukemia, a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia corresponding largely to FAB M5 and divided into M5a poorly differentiated monoblastic and M5b differentiated monocytic forms, is an aggressive clonal neoplasm of monoblasts/promonocytes characterized by marrow failure and frequent extramedullary infiltration, especially gingiva, skin, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and central nervous system. Recurrent genetic lesions include KMT2A rearrangements such as t(9;11)/KMT2A-MLLT3, NPM1 mutation, FLT3-ITD or TKD, NRAS/KRAS, KIT, IDH1/2, DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, RUNX1, TP53, and less commonly core-binding factor abnormalities; altered proteins and pathways commonly involve FLT3, RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, HOXA/MEIS1 programs downstream of KMT2A, epigenetic dysregulation, and antiapoptotic BCL2 signaling. Most cases are acquired rather than inherited, but predisposition may occur in germline RUNX1, CEBPA, GATA2, DDX41, TP53, or Fanconi-anemia-related syndromes. Typical manifestations include fatigue, pallor, fever, infections, bleeding, bruising, disseminated intravascular coagulation, bone pain, leukocytosis with circulating blasts, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and tissue infiltration causing gingival hypertrophy, cutaneous leukemia, hepatosplenomegaly, or CNS symptoms. Important complications and comorbidities include sepsis, tumor lysis syndrome, hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis, coagulopathy, organ infiltration, relapse, and treatment-related cytopenias or cardiotoxicity. Diagnosis relies on CBC and smear, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy showing 20% or more blasts or defining AML genetics, cytochemistry with nonspecific esterase positivity, flow cytometry demonstrating myeloid/monocytic markers such as CD33, CD13, CD64, CD14, CD11b, CD11c, lysozyme, and often HLA-DR, plus cytogenetics, FISH, PCR, and next-generation sequencing for risk stratification. Name: Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute
Description: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive clonal hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell malignancy defined by impaired myeloid differentiation and accumulation of blasts in bone marrow, blood, and sometimes extramedullary tissues. Recurrent genetic lesions include FLT3 internal tandem duplication or tyrosine kinase domain mutations, NPM1, DNMT3A, IDH1/IDH2, RUNX1, CEBPA, TP53, KIT, WT1, TET2, ASXL1, and KMT2A rearrangements, while acute promyelocytic leukemia is characterized by PML-RARA from t(15;17); these lesions perturb transcriptional control, epigenetic regulation, apoptosis, and proliferation through pathways such as FLT3/RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK-STAT, BCL2-mediated survival, and aberrant retinoic acid signaling. AML comprises genetically defined subtypes, therapy-related AML, AML with myelodysplasia-related changes, and morphologic variants including APL; inheritance is usually not Mendelian, but germline predisposition occurs with CEBPA, DDX41, RUNX1, GATA2, and TP53 variants and in syndromes such as Fanconi anemia. Patients typically present with marrow failure causing fatigue, pallor, fever, recurrent infection, mucosal bleeding, petechiae, bruising, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, gingival hypertrophy, leukostasis, and occasionally chloromas. Major complications include severe infection, disseminated intravascular coagulation especially in APL, tumor lysis, anemia, hemorrhage, relapse, and progression from antecedent myelodysplastic neoplasms. Diagnosis requires CBC and smear, bone marrow examination usually showing at least 20% myeloid blasts unless defining cytogenetic abnormalities are present, multiparameter flow cytometry, cytogenetics/FISH, and molecular testing by PCR or next-generation sequencing for risk stratification and measurable residual disease. Standard treatments include cytarabine, a pyrimidine analog inhibiting DNA synthesis; anthracyclines such as daunorubicin or idarubicin, topoisomerase II inhibitors causing DNA damage; azacitidine or decitabine, hypomethylating agents; venetoclax, a BCL2 inhibitor; midostaurin or gilteritin

Name: Myeloid Leukemia, Chronic / Chronic myeloid leukemia
Description: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm of hematopoietic stem cells characterized in most cases by the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)(q34;q11.2), which creates the BCR::ABL1 fusion oncogene encoding a constitutively active ABL1 tyrosine kinase; common transcript variants include e13a2 and e14a2, and kinase-domain mutations such as T315I, E255K, and Y253H are major mechanisms of resistance. BCR::ABL1 drives leukemogenesis through RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, SRC-family kinase, MYC, and anti-apoptotic signaling, promoting uncontrolled granulocytic proliferation, reduced apoptosis, abnormal adhesion, and genomic instability. CML classically evolves through chronic phase, accelerated phase, and blast phase, the latter resembling acute leukemia. It is usually acquired rather than inherited, with no Mendelian transmission pattern, although rare familial clustering and additional somatic lesions such as ASXL1, RUNX1, IKZF1, or TP53 abnormalities may influence progression. Typical manifestations include fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, early satiety from splenomegaly, abdominal fullness, leukocytosis often with basophilia and eosinophilia, anemia, thrombocytosis or thrombocytopenia, and sometimes bone pain or gout from hyperuricemia. Major complications include massive splenomegaly, thrombosis or bleeding, infection, tumor lysis, transformation to blast crisis, and comorbid anemia and cardiovascular risk that may affect therapy choice. Diagnosis rests on CBC and smear showing myeloid left shift, bone marrow hypercellularity, and definitive demonstration of BCR::ABL1 by karyotyping, FISH, or quantitative RT-PCR, which is also central to molecular monitoring using international scale response milestones. Standard treatment is tyrosine kinase inhibition with imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib, asciminib, or ponatinib; these agents inhibit BCR::ABL1 signaling, with ponatinib active against T315I and asciminib targeting the ABL1 myristoyl pocket, while allogeneic stem-cell transplantation remains an option for refractory or advanced disease.

Name: Leukemia, Myeloid, Chronic-Phase
Description: Chronic-phase myeloid leukemia, usually referring to chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase, is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm of hematopoietic stem cells defined in most cases by the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11.2), which creates the BCR::ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase; p210 BCR::ABL1 is the classic protein product, while additional lesions such as ASXL1, RUNX1, IKZF1, TET2, DNMT3A, and ABL1 kinase domain mutations may influence progression or drug resistance rather than primary causation. Constitutive BCR::ABL1 signaling activates RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, SRC-family kinase, MYC, and antiapoptotic pathways, driving granulocytic proliferation, reduced apoptosis, altered adhesion, and splenic extramedullary hematopoiesis. Standard therapy centers on tyrosine kinase inhibitors: imatinib inhibits the ATP-binding site of BCR::ABL1, dasatinib inhibits BCR::ABL1 and SRC-family kinases, nilotinib is a more potent selective BCR::ABL1 inhibitor, and bosutinib or ponatinib may be used in resistant disease, with ponatinib active against T315I; allogeneic stem cell transplantation is reserved for select advanced or refractory cases. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, low-grade fever, early satiety, abdominal fullness from splenomegaly, bone pain, bruising, or symptoms of hyperleukocytosis. Chronic phase is distinguished from accelerated and blast phases by lower blast counts and lesser biologic instability; complications include anemia, thrombocytosis or thrombocytopenia, infections, bleeding, gout/hyperuricemia, thrombosis, splenic infarction, leukostasis, and transformation to blast crisis. The disease is typically acquired rather than inherited, with no Mendelian transmission, though rare familial predisposition to myeloid neoplasia may reflect germline variants such as DDX41 or RUNX1 in broader contexts. Name: Leukemia, Myelomonocytic, Acute
Description: Acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML-M4; UMLS C0023479) is an aggressive acute myeloid leukemia characterized by clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts showing both granulocytic and monocytic differentiation, classically involving blood, marrow, and sometimes extramedullary sites such as gingiva, skin, and the CNS. Recurrent genetic lesions include KMT2A rearrangements, inv(16)/t(16;16) creating CBFB::MYH11, FLT3-ITD/TKD, NPM1, RAS-pathway mutations including NRAS and KRAS, KIT, CEBPA, DNMT3A, TET2, IDH1/2, and less commonly TP53; the leukemic phenotype reflects dysregulation of transcriptional control, epigenetic programming, apoptosis, and proliferative signaling through RAS/MAPK, FLT3-STAT5/PI3K-AKT/mTOR, JAK-STAT, and core-binding-factor pathways. Typical manifestations include fatigue, pallor, fever, infections, bruising or bleeding from thrombocytopenia, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, leukostasis with dyspnea or neurologic symptoms, and monocytic tissue infiltration causing gingival hypertrophy or cutaneous leukemia; major complications include severe infection, DIC, tumor lysis, hyperleukocytosis, and relapse. Diagnosis is based on marrow or blood blasts meeting AML criteria, morphologic and cytochemical evidence of myelomonocytic differentiation, flow cytometry with markers such as CD13, CD33, CD117, MPO, CD14, CD64, CD11b, and HLA-DR, and confirmation by karyotyping, FISH, PCR, and next-generation sequencing. Treatment commonly uses cytarabine, a deoxycytidine analog that inhibits DNA synthesis, plus an anthracycline such as daunorubicin or idarubicin, which inhibit topoisomerase II and generate DNA damage; additional options include azacitidine or decitabine, hypomethylating agents, venetoclax, a BCL2 inhibitor, gemtuzumab ozogamicin targeting CD33, and targeted agents such as midostaurin or gilteritinib for FLT3-mutated disease and ivosidenib or enasidenib for IDH1/2

Name: Leukemia, Myelomonocytic, Chronic
Description: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML; historically termed chronic myelomonocytic leukemia/myelomonocytic leukemia, chronic) is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell neoplasm with overlapping myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features, characterized by persistent peripheral blood monocytosis and dysregulated myelomonocytic differentiation. Recurrent genetic lesions commonly involve epigenetic and signaling regulators, notably TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, SETBP1, RUNX1, CBL, NRAS, KRAS, JAK2, EZH2, and less often FLT3 or IDH1/2; corresponding pathogenic mechanisms include altered DNA methylation, RNA splicing, chromatin regulation, and hyperactive RAS/MAPK, JAK/STAT, and GM-CSF–responsive signaling, with downstream effects on ERK, PI3K/AKT, and inflammatory cytokine networks. CMML is usually sporadic rather than inherited, although rare familial predisposition can occur in syndromes involving germline RUNX1, GATA2, DDX41, ANKRD26, or CBL variants. Clinically, patients often present with fatigue, weight loss, fever, night sweats, pallor, easy bruising or bleeding, recurrent infections, leukocytosis or cytopenias, absolute monocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly, and sometimes extramedullary infiltrates or skin lesions. Recognized forms include dysplastic and proliferative CMML, and CMML-0, CMML-1, and CMML-2 based on blast burden; major complications include severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, infection, hemorrhage, autoimmune phenomena, splenomegaly-related symptoms, and progression to acute myeloid leukemia. Diagnosis relies on sustained absolute monocyte count at least 0.5 x 10^9/L with monocytes at least 10 percent of leukocytes, exclusion of BCR::ABL1-positive chronic myeloid leukemia and other myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia-associated kinase fusions, bone marrow morphology showing dysplasia or clonal cytogenetic/molecular abnormalities, blast quantification, flow cytometric monocyte repartitioning, cytogenetics, and next-generation sequencing. Name: Leukemia, Promyelocytic, Acute
Description: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a distinct, highly curable subtype of acute myeloid leukemia characterized by malignant accumulation of abnormal promyelocytes due in most cases to the balanced translocation t(15;17)(q24;q21), creating the PML-RARA fusion protein, which aberrantly recruits corepressor complexes and blocks retinoic acid–dependent myeloid differentiation; less common RARA fusion partners such as PLZF/ZBTB16, NPM1, NuMA, STAT5B, and rare RARB or RARG rearrangements define variant forms with differing retinoid sensitivity. Cooperating lesions often include FLT3-ITD or TKD mutations and occasionally WT1, NRAS, or KRAS alterations, affecting MAPK, PI3K/AKT, JAK/STAT, p53, apoptosis, and differentiation pathways, while degradation of PML-RARA by arsenic trioxide restores PML nuclear bodies and promotes apoptosis. Clinically, APL presents abruptly with fatigue, pallor, fever, infections, bruising, mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, menorrhagia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hyperfibrinolysis, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and sometimes leukocytosis or differentiation syndrome during therapy. Morphologic subtypes include hypergranular/classic APL and microgranular/hypogranular APL, the latter often associated with high leukocyte counts. Standard therapy includes all-trans retinoic acid, which relieves transcriptional repression and induces terminal differentiation; arsenic trioxide, which targets and degrades PML-RARA and triggers apoptosis; and anthracyclines such as idarubicin or daunorubicin, topoisomerase II inhibitors used in induction or consolidation, with gemtuzumab ozogamicin sometimes added in selected CD33-positive disease. Major complications include catastrophic hemorrhage, thrombosis, infection, differentiation syndrome, and relapse. APL is usually sporadic rather than inherited, with no Mendelian transmission pattern, although rare familial clustering of myeloid neoplasia may reflect predisposition genes rather than direct inheritance of PML-RARA. Name: Lichen Planus
Description: Lichen planus (MeSH D008010) is a chronic inflammatory mucocutaneous disease, usually sporadic and immune mediated rather than Mendelian, characterized by a T-cell-driven interface dermatitis targeting basal keratinocytes; genetic susceptibility is supported by HLA associations such as HLA-DR1, HLA-DR10, HLA-B7, and HLA-DQB1 variants, with inflammatory mediators including TNF, IFNG, IL6, IL17, CXCL9/CXCL10, ICAM1, and p53 upregulation reported in lesional tissue, but no single recurrent causal mutation is established. Pathobiology centers on antigen presentation, CD8+ cytotoxic lymphocyte activation, Th1/Th17 polarization, JAK/STAT, NF-kB, and TNF-alpha signaling, with keratinocyte apoptosis mediated through Fas/FasL, perforin-granzyme, and oxidative stress pathways. Clinically it presents with intensely pruritic, polygonal, planar, purple papules and plaques with Wickham striae on flexor wrists, ankles, and trunk, or with oral, genital, scalp, nail, and esophageal involvement causing reticular white plaques, erosions, pain, scarring alopecia, or nail dystrophy; major subtypes include cutaneous, oral, hypertrophic, atrophic, annular, actinic, bullous, erosive/ulcerative, lichen planopilaris, and nail lichen planus. Important comorbidities include hepatitis C infection, other autoimmune disease, metabolic syndrome, anxiety/depression, and, particularly in chronic erosive oral disease, a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma; complications include secondary infection, dyspigmentation, cicatricial alopecia, and permanent nail loss. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and supported by biopsy showing lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate, saw-tooth acanthosis, hypergranulosis, civatte bodies, and basal vacuolar change; direct immunofluorescence may show shaggy fibrinogen along the basement membrane, and testing may include hepatitis C screening and clinicopathologic exclusion of lichenoid drug eruption. Name: Liposarcoma
Description: Liposarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm showing adipocytic differentiation, typically arising in deep soft tissues of the extremities or retroperitoneum, and comprises biologically distinct subtypes including well-differentiated/atypical lipomatous tumor, dedifferentiated, myxoid, round cell, and pleomorphic liposarcoma. Its molecular pathology is subtype-specific: well-differentiated and dedifferentiated tumors characteristically harbor 12q13-15 amplification with MDM2 and CDK4 overexpression, often with HMGA2 and YEATS4 co-amplification, driving p53 suppression and cell-cycle progression through the RB-CDK4/6 axis; myxoid/round cell liposarcoma is defined by FUS::DDIT3, less often EWSR1::DDIT3, fusion oncogenes that alter adipocytic differentiation and transcriptional programs; pleomorphic tumors have complex karyotypes with TP53, RB1, and PTEN pathway abnormalities. Relevant signaling networks include p53, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, apoptosis, adipogenesis/PPAR-gamma, and angiogenic pathways involving VEGF. Most cases are sporadic rather than inherited, although rare cancer predisposition syndromes such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome with germline TP53 variants may increase risk. Patients usually present with a slowly enlarging, often painless deep mass, while retroperitoneal disease may cause abdominal distension, pain, early satiety, bowel or urinary compression, and weight loss; complications include local recurrence, dedifferentiation, pulmonary or extrapulmonary metastasis, cachexia, and organ compromise. Diagnosis relies on imaging with MRI for extremity lesions and CT for retroperitoneal disease, followed by core-needle biopsy and histopathology demonstrating lipoblasts and subtype-specific morphology, supported by immunohistochemistry and molecular testing such as MDM2 amplification by FISH or PCR and DDIT3 rearrangement assays. Treatment centers on surgical resection with radiotherapy in selected cases and systemic agents including doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II poison that intercalates DNA; ifosfamide, an alkylating DNA cross-linker; trabectedin, which binds the minor groove of DNA and is active in translocation-related sarcomas; eribulin, a microtubule dynamics inhibitor

Name: Listeriosis
Description: Listeriosis (MeSH D008088) is an invasive foodborne infection caused predominantly by Listeria monocytogenes, a facultative intracellular Gram-positive bacillus whose virulence depends on bacterial factors such as internalins InlA/InlB, listeriolysin O encoded by hly, ActA, and phospholipases plcA/plcB that mediate epithelial entry, phagosomal escape, actin-based intracellular spread, and placental and central nervous system tropism. Host susceptibility is strongly shaped by cell-mediated immunity, with genetic or acquired defects in IFN-γ/IL-12–STAT1 signaling, TNF-mediated macrophage activation, and pattern-recognition pathways including TLR2/NF-κB increasing risk; representative inherited predispositions include IL12RB1, IFNGR1, STAT1, GATA2, and NEMO/IKBKG defects. Major pathways engaged include E-cadherin–InlA and c-Met–InlB entry signaling, inflammasome activation, and Th1 macrophage bactericidal responses. Disease ranges from self-limited febrile gastroenteritis to invasive listeremia, meningoencephalitis, rhombencephalitis, brain abscess, and maternofetal infection causing chorioamnionitis, miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, or neonatal early- and late-onset sepsis/meningitis; typical symptoms include fever, myalgias, diarrhea, bacteremia, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits. Important comorbid risk states are pregnancy, neonates, older age, hematologic malignancy, solid-organ transplantation, cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, HIV infection, corticosteroid or anti-TNF therapy, and iron overload. Diagnosis relies on compatible syndrome plus isolation of Listeria from blood, CSF, placental, or sterile-site culture, with CSF showing bacterial meningitis features; PCR or 16S molecular testing may support diagnosis, and susceptibility testing is useful when resistance or allergy is relevant. Name: Liver Abscess
Description: Liver abscess (UMLS C0023885) is a focal suppurative or necrotic infection of the hepatic parenchyma, classically divided into pyogenic, amebic, and less commonly fungal abscesses, arising most often from biliary infection, portal venous spread, hematogenous seeding, or direct extension. It is not an inherited disorder, but host genetic influences on susceptibility to invasive infection and sepsis have been described, including variation in innate immune genes such as TLR4, NOD2, IL6, TNF, and HLA-related loci; in hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess, relevant microbial virulence determinants include magA, rmpA, siderophore systems, and capsular K1/K2 serotypes rather than patient germline mutations. Pathobiology is dominated by innate immune and inflammatory signaling, particularly LPS-TLR4, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and in amebiasis, parasite-induced cytotoxicity and hepatocyte apoptosis. Typical manifestations include fever, right upper quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly, chills, malaise, anorexia, nausea, and sometimes jaundice or sepsis; laboratory findings often show leukocytosis, elevated CRP/ESR, cholestatic or mixed liver enzyme abnormalities, and positive blood cultures in pyogenic disease. Major comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, biliary tract disease, colorectal or intra-abdominal infection, cirrhosis, malignancy, immunosuppression, and chronic alcoholism, while complications include rupture into the peritoneum or pleura, empyema, endophthalmitis, brain abscess, septic shock, and portal vein thrombosis. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus ultrasound or contrast CT demonstrating a hepatic fluid collection, microbiologic confirmation by blood culture and aspirate Gram stain/culture, and serology or stool testing when Entamoeba histolytica is suspected.
