Name: Liver Abscess, Amebic
Description: Amebic liver abscess is an invasive extraintestinal manifestation of Entamoeba histolytica infection, usually arising after colonic invasion and portal venous spread to the liver, where trophozoites cause necrotic abscesses, most often solitary and in the right lobe; disease may be uncomplicated or complicated by rupture into the pleura, lung, peritoneum, or pericardium, and is associated with colitis, malnutrition, alcohol use, pregnancy, diabetes, and immunosuppression. Its molecular pathobiology is driven primarily by parasite rather than inherited host genetics, with key virulence factors including the Gal/GalNAc lectin complex for adherence, cysteine proteases such as EhCP1 and EhCP5, amoebapores, and the surface antigen KERP1; involved host-parasite pathways include epithelial adhesion, extracellular matrix degradation, complement resistance, neutrophil killing, and inflammatory signaling through TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-8, IFN-γ, NF-κB, and matrix metalloproteinases. No Mendelian inheritance pattern is established, but host susceptibility may be modified by immune-response polymorphisms, including associations reported for HLA class II alleles, leptin receptor variants, and cytokine genes. Typical presentation includes fever, right upper quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly, malaise, anorexia, weight loss, and sometimes cough, pleuritic pain, diarrhea, or jaundice. Diagnosis rests on compatible epidemiology and imaging showing a hepatic abscess on ultrasound or CT, plus positive serology for anti-amebic antibodies, stool or abscess PCR/antigen testing when available, and exclusion of pyogenic abscess; aspirate classically contains sterile anchovy-paste material and is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, left-lobe lesions, or risk of rupture. Standard therapy includes metronidazole or tinidazole, nitroimidazoles that are reduced in anaerobic metabolism to radicals causing DNA damage, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin, which inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit, or iodoquinol, a poorly absorbed intraluminal amebicide; diloxanide furoate may also be used where available.

Name: Lung Abscess
Description: Lung abscess (UMLS C0024110) is a necrotizing, suppurative infection of the pulmonary parenchyma characterized by a cavitary lesion containing pus, most often arising after aspiration of oropharyngeal contents, polymicrobial anaerobic infection, or secondary infection distal to bronchial obstruction; primary abscesses occur in otherwise normal lungs, whereas secondary abscesses complicate malignancy, immunosuppression, septic emboli, or structural lung disease. It is not classically an inherited disorder, but host susceptibility may be influenced by genetic defects in innate and adaptive immunity, including variants affecting NADPH oxidase in chronic granulomatous disease (CYBB, NCF1), neutrophil and cytokine signaling, and humoral immunity, while microbial virulence factors such as Staphylococcus aureus Panton-Valentine leukocidin and adhesins may contribute. Pathobiology centers on intense neutrophilic inflammation, tissue necrosis, hypoxia, and cavitation mediated through TLR/NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, complement, and matrix metalloproteinase pathways. Typical symptoms include fever, productive cough with foul-smelling or purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, malaise, and night sweats, with examination variably showing crackles, bronchial breath sounds, or clubbing in chronic cases. Common comorbidities include alcoholism, poor dentition, dysphagia, altered consciousness, gastroesophageal reflux, diabetes, COPD, bronchiectasis, lung cancer, HIV infection, and post-obstructive lesions; complications include empyema, bronchopleural fistula, massive hemoptysis, sepsis, and chronic cavitary destruction. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical features plus imaging showing a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level, usually on chest radiograph or CT, supported by CBC and inflammatory markers, sputum and blood cultures, bronchoscopy when obstruction or unusual pathogens are suspected, and exclusion of tuberculosis, fungal infection, and cavitary cancer. Name: Lung Diseases
Description: Lung diseases comprise a heterogeneous group of disorders affecting the airways, alveoli, interstitium, pulmonary vasculature, pleura, or inherited structural defenses, and include obstructive diseases such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, infectious pneumonias, cystic fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, and neoplastic conditions. Clinical manifestations commonly include cough, dyspnea, wheeze, chest tightness or pain, sputum production, hemoptysis, hypoxemia, crackles, and reduced exercise tolerance, with complications including respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, recurrent infection, bronchiectasis, fibrosis, and increased cardiovascular and thromboembolic risk; common comorbidities include smoking-related vascular disease, gastroesophageal reflux, obesity, anxiety/depression, and sleep apnea. Molecular contributors vary by subtype but include CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis, SERPINA1 deficiency in hereditary emphysema, MUC5B promoter variants, TERT/TERC and surfactant genes SFTPA1, SFTPA2, SFTPC, ABCA3 in familial fibrotic lung disease, and EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, and TP53 alterations in lung cancer; corresponding proteins include CFTR chloride channel, alpha-1 antitrypsin, surfactant proteins, mucins, and receptor tyrosine kinases. Central pathways include NF-kB, TNF-alpha, IL-4/IL-5/IL-13, TGF-beta/SMAD, JAK/STAT, EGFR-MAPK-PI3K/AKT, oxidative stress, protease-antiprotease imbalance, fibroblast activation, and aberrant innate and adaptive immune signaling. Treatment depends on subtype and commonly includes albuterol, a beta2-agonist bronchodilator; inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress inflammatory gene transcription; tiotropium, a muscarinic M3 antagonist; pirfenidone or nintedanib, which slow fibrogenic signaling; antibiotics when infection is present; and targeted anticancer agents such as osimertinib for EGFR-mutant tumors. Name: Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive
Description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common, preventable, and treatable heterogeneous chronic inflammatory lung disease characterized by persistent, usually progressive airflow limitation caused by small-airway disease and emphysema, most often from cigarette smoke or biomass exposure. Clinically it presents with chronic dyspnea, cough, sputum production, wheeze, prolonged expiration, reduced exercise tolerance, recurrent exacerbations, and in advanced cases weight loss, cyanosis, hyperinflation, cor pulmonale, and respiratory failure; major subtypes include emphysema-predominant and chronic bronchitis-predominant disease, with frequent overlap with asthma. Genetic susceptibility is exemplified by SERPINA1 mutations causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, classically severe early emphysema, while additional associated loci include CHRNA3/5, HHIP, FAM13A, MMP12, TGFB1, GSTM1, and TNF; inheritance is usually complex polygenic with strong environmental interaction, except the codominant Mendelian SERPINA1 deficiency. Pathobiology involves neutrophilic and macrophage-driven inflammation, CD8+ T cells, oxidative stress, protease-antiprotease imbalance involving neutrophil elastase and matrix metalloproteinases, mucus hypersecretion, apoptosis, and dysregulated NF-kB, TGF-beta, PI3K-Akt, MAPK, EGFR, and Nrf2 pathways. Diagnosis rests on compatible exposure and symptoms plus post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1/FVC less than 0.70, with severity staged by FEV1 and symptom/exacerbation burden; adjunctive testing includes bronchodilator response, DLCO, chest radiography or CT for emphysema, pulse oximetry, arterial blood gases, eosinophil count, and alpha-1 antitrypsin testing in selected patients. Treatment commonly includes inhaled beta2-agonists such as albuterol or salmeterol, which activate beta2 receptors to relax airway smooth muscle; muscarinic antagonists such as tiotropium, which block M3-mediated bronchoconstriction; inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress airway inflammation; and in selected cases roflumilast, a PDE4 inhibitor that reduces inflammatory signaling. Name: Lupus Erythematosus, Discoid
Description: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE; MeSH D008179) is a chronic cutaneous autoimmune lupus subtype, usually skin-limited but occasionally associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, characterized by well-demarcated erythematous to violaceous discoid plaques with adherent scale, follicular plugging, dyspigmentation, telangiectasia, atrophy, and scarring alopecia on sun-exposed sites, especially the face, scalp, and ears. Its pathobiology reflects genetic susceptibility and ultraviolet-triggered innate and adaptive immune activation, with associations reported in HLA class II alleles such as HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQA1, complement pathway variants including C2 and C4 deficiency, and lupus-risk polymorphisms affecting IRF5, STAT4, TNFAIP3, ITGAM, and TYK2; lesional skin shows keratinocyte apoptosis, plasmacytoid dendritic cell activation, and increased interferon-stimulated genes and proteins such as IFN-alpha, CXCL10, TNF, BAFF, and complement deposition along the dermoepidermal junction. Key pathways include type I interferon/JAK-STAT signaling, TLR7/9 nucleic acid sensing, B-cell activation, T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and immune-complex/complement injury. Most cases are sporadic with complex polygenic inheritance rather than Mendelian transmission. Important comorbidities and complications include photosensitivity, secondary infection, permanent scarring and pigmentary change, cicatricial alopecia, smoking-associated refractory disease, and progression to systemic lupus in a minority. Diagnosis is based on characteristic morphology and chronicity, supported by skin biopsy showing interface dermatitis, basement membrane thickening, follicular plugging, periadnexal/perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and dermal mucin, direct immunofluorescence demonstrating a lupus band, and serologies such as ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro/SSA, complement levels, and CBC/urinalysis to assess systemic involvement. Treatment commonly includes topical or intralesional corticosteroids, which suppress NF-kB-driven cytokine transcription; hydroxychloroquine, which inhibits endosomal TLR signaling and antigen presentation; and calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, which block T-cell activation, with refractory disease sometimes treated with methotrexate, mycophen

Name: Lupus Nephritis
Description: Lupus nephritis (MeSH D008181) is an immune complex-mediated, inflammatory glomerular and tubulointerstitial manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus characterized by loss of self-tolerance, autoantibody production, complement activation, and progressive renal injury. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative risk loci in HLA-DR2/HLA-DR3, IRF5, STAT4, TNFSF4, BLK, BANK1, FCGR2A/FCGR3A, ITGAM, TREX1, complement genes such as C1q, C2, and C4, and APOL1 risk variants that worsen outcomes in some African ancestry populations; monogenic complement deficiencies can produce highly penetrant lupus-spectrum disease. Core pathways include type I interferon signaling, TLR7/TLR9 activation by nucleic acid-containing immune complexes, B-cell receptor and BAFF-mediated B-cell survival, T-cell costimulation, NETosis, cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF, and classical complement cascade activation with glomerular deposition of IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, and C1q. Patients typically present with proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, red cell casts, hypertension, edema, declining eGFR, and sometimes nephrotic syndrome or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, often accompanied by extrarenal SLE features such as rash, arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, and antiphospholipid syndrome. Disease is classified histologically by ISN/RPS classes I-VI, including mesangial, focal, diffuse, membranous, and advanced sclerosing forms. Diagnosis relies on SLE serologies including ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, complement consumption, urinalysis with protein quantification, serum creatinine, and kidney biopsy for class, activity, and chronicity indices. Name: Lyme Disease
Description: Lyme disease (MeSH D008193) is a multisystem zoonotic infection caused predominantly by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, including B. burgdorferi sensu stricto, B. afzelii, and B. garinii, transmitted by Ixodes ticks; it is not a Mendelian disorder, but host genetic susceptibility influences severity, with associations reported for HLA-DRB1 alleles, TLR1 and TLR2 variants, CD14, and cytokine genes such as IL6 and TNF, while key bacterial virulence proteins include outer surface proteins OspA, OspC, VlsE, and decorin-binding proteins DbpA/DbpB. Pathobiology centers on innate and adaptive immune activation through TLR1/2-NF-κB signaling, type I interferon responses, chemokine networks including CXCL13, complement interaction, and inflammatory pathways involving IL-6, TNF-α, and Th1/Th17 cells. Clinically, disease is classically divided into early localized, early disseminated, and late Lyme disease; typical manifestations include erythema migrans, fever, fatigue, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, regional lymphadenopathy, cranial neuropathy especially facial palsy, meningitis, radiculoneuritis, carditis with atrioventricular block, and later intermittent or persistent oligoarthritis and, less commonly, encephalopathy or peripheral neuropathy. Important complications and comorbidities include Lyme arthritis, neuroborreliosis, carditis, post-treatment Lyme disease symptoms, and coinfections such as babesiosis or anaplasmosis. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure and clinical findings, especially erythema migrans, supported by two-tier serology with EIA or ELISA followed by immunoblot, or modified two-EIA algorithms; PCR may aid selected synovial fluid or cerebrospinal fluid evaluation, and CSF antibody index supports neuroborreliosis. Standard therapy includes doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit; amoxicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; cefuroxime or ceftriaxone, cephalosporins that also inhibit cell-wall synthesis, with intravenous ceftriaxone favored for severe neurologic or cardiac disease.

Name: Lymphangiectasis
Description: Lymphangiectasis is a disorder characterized by pathological dilatation of intestinal, pulmonary, or systemic lymphatic vessels, causing impaired lymph drainage and protein-rich lymph loss; it may be primary/congenital, often presenting as primary intestinal lymphangiectasia or part of generalized lymphatic anomaly syndromes, or secondary to lymphatic obstruction from constrictive pericarditis, right-sided heart failure, lymphoma, inflammatory bowel disease, infections, or postoperative/radiation fibrosis. Genetic forms are increasingly linked to dysregulated lymphangiogenesis, with representative genes including FLT4/VEGFR3, FOXC2, CCBE1, FAT4, PIEZO1, ADAMTS3, GATA2, SOX18, PTPN14, and EPHB4; the relevant biology centers on the VEGF-C/VEGFR3 axis, Prox1-driven lymphatic endothelial differentiation, Angiopoietin/TIE, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, and mechanotransduction pathways controlling lymphatic valve formation and vessel maturation. Typical manifestations include peripheral edema, chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, ascites, pleural or pericardial effusions, chylothorax, failure to thrive, lymphedema, recurrent infections, and laboratory evidence of hypoproteinemia, hypoalbuminemia, lymphopenia, and hypogammaglobulinemia. Major complications include malnutrition, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, immunodeficiency, thromboembolism, and serosal fluid collections; associated disorders include Noonan-spectrum disease, Hennekam syndrome, yellow nail syndrome, and congenital heart disease. Most primary cases are sporadic, but autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance are recognized depending on the gene. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus low serum proteins, stool alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance for enteric protein loss, endoscopy showing white villi with biopsy-confirmed dilated mucosal/submucosal lacteals, and imaging such as lymphoscintigraphy, MR lymphangiography, CT, or echocardiography to define extent and exclude secondary causes; genetic testing is appropriate in syndromic or familial disease. Treatment is mainly supportive and etiologic: a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides reduces intestinal lymph flow, octreotide decreases splanchnic secretion and lymph production, sirolimus inhibits mTOR

Name: Lymphangioma
Description: Lymphangioma (often termed lymphatic malformation) is a benign developmental anomaly of lymphatic vessels rather than a true neoplasm, characterized by congenital sequestration and dilation of lymphatic channels, most commonly presenting as macrocystic, microcystic, or mixed lesions, including the classic cystic hygroma of the neck. Its molecular basis is heterogeneous but increasingly linked to dysregulated lymphangiogenesis, with somatic activating variants in PIK3CA and less often alterations affecting the PI3K-AKT-mTOR axis, RAS/MAPK signaling, and genes important for lymphatic endothelial identity such as FLT4/VEGFR3, VEGFC, FOXC2, SOX18, and CCBE1 in syndromic or familial lymphatic disorders; implicated proteins include VEGF-C, VEGFR-3, PROX1, and downstream AKT and mTOR effectors. Most cases are sporadic and non-Mendelian, although familial clustering can occur in inherited lymphedema-lymphatic dysplasia syndromes with autosomal dominant or recessive patterns depending on the gene. Clinically, lesions are soft, compressible, transilluminant masses, typically in the head and neck or axilla, causing swelling, pain, recurrent infection, hemorrhage, cosmetic deformity, dysphagia, or airway compromise; prenatal large nuchal lesions may associate with Turner syndrome, trisomies, hydrops fetalis, and congenital heart disease. Important complications include cellulitis, leakage, intralesional bleeding, compression of adjacent structures, and functional impairment. Diagnosis is based on clinical examination and imaging, especially ultrasound and MRI to define cystic architecture and extent, with CT used selectively; histopathology shows endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces, and immunostains such as D2-40/podoplanin, PROX1, LYVE1, and VEGFR3 help confirm lymphatic origin, while molecular testing may identify actionable somatic variants in complex cases. Treatment is individualized and includes sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor that suppresses abnormal lymphatic endothelial growth; sclerosing agents such as bleomycin, doxycycline, or OK-432/picibanil, which induce endothelial injury and fibrosis; and surgery or laser therapy for selected lesions.

Name: Lymphogranuloma Venereum
Description: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV; MeSH D008219) is an invasive sexually transmitted infection caused by the obligate intracellular bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, specifically the L1, L2, and L3 serovars, rather than a Mendelian genetic disorder, so no human inheritance pattern is recognized; instead, pathogenicity is linked to microbial factors including the major outer membrane protein encoded by ompA, polymorphic membrane proteins, lipopolysaccharide, and type III secretion effectors, while host susceptibility and severity are influenced by immune-response genes and proteins such as HLA variants, TLR2/TLR4, NOD1/NOD2, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and Th1-cell responses. Disease biology centers on epithelial invasion, intracellular survival in reticulate and elementary body forms, and activation of NF-κB, MAPK, and JAK/STAT-linked inflammatory pathways, with macrophages, dendritic cells, and lymphatics driving granulomatous lymphangitis. Clinically, LGV usually begins with a transient genital papule, pustule, or ulcer followed by painful inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy with buboes, fever, malaise, and in rectal exposure severe proctitis or proctocolitis causing rectal pain, bleeding, discharge, tenesmus, and constipation; subtypes are defined by serovars L1-L3 and by anogenital versus anorectal presentations. Major complications include abscesses, fistulas, strictures, chronic colorectal inflammation, genital elephantiasis, infertility, and facilitation of HIV acquisition/transmission, with frequent comorbidity with HIV and other sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea, syphilis, and hepatitis viruses in high-risk populations. Diagnosis relies on compatible syndrome plus detection of C. trachomatis by nucleic acid amplification testing from lesion, rectal, or lymph node specimens, with LGV-specific genotyping when available; serology is supportive but nonspecific, and imaging or aspiration may aid evaluation of buboes. Recommended therapy includes doxycycline, a tetracycline that inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit; erythromycin, a macrolide that blocks 50S-mediated protein synthesis; and azithromycin, another 50S inhibitor sometimes used as an alternative.

Name: Lymphoma
Description: Lymphoma (MeSH D008223) is a heterogeneous group of malignant neoplasms of lymphoid cells arising in lymph nodes or extranodal lymphoid tissues and broadly divided into Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by Reed–Sternberg cells, and non-Hodgkin lymphomas including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and peripheral or cutaneous T-cell lymphomas. Its pathobiology commonly involves dysregulated B-cell receptor, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, apoptotic, and cell-cycle pathways, with recurrent genetic lesions such as BCL2 translocation t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, MYC rearrangement in Burkitt lymphoma, BCL6 alterations in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, CCND1 t(11;14) in mantle cell lymphoma, and TP53, EZH2, MYD88, CD79B, and NOTCH pathway mutations in selected subtypes; EBV, HHV-8, chronic Helicobacter pylori infection, immunodeficiency, and autoimmune disease may contribute in specific settings. Most cases are sporadic, although familial clustering and inherited predisposition syndromes involving ATM, TP53, and other DNA-repair or immune-regulatory genes are recognized. Typical manifestations include painless lymphadenopathy, B symptoms such as fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss, fatigue, pruritus, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, mediastinal mass, or extranodal organ dysfunction. Diagnosis relies on excisional tissue biopsy with histopathology, immunophenotyping by flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics and FISH for hallmark rearrangements, molecular testing, PET/CT-based Ann Arbor staging, bone marrow evaluation in selected cases, and laboratory markers including LDH and viral serologies. Standard therapies include rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody; cyclophosphamide, an alkylating DNA-crosslinking agent; doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor; vincristine, a microtubule inhibitor; prednisone, a lymphocytotoxic glucocorticoid; and in Hodgkin lymphoma, brentuximab vedotin targeting CD30 and PD-1 inhibitors such as nivolumab. Name: Lymphoma, Follicular
Description: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma derived from germinal-center B cells, classically characterized by the t(14;18)(q32;q21) IGH-BCL2 translocation causing BCL2 overexpression and apoptosis resistance; additional recurrent genetic lesions include KMT2D, CREBBP, EZH2, TNFRSF14, EP300, ARID1A, BCL6, CARD11, STAT6, and mutations affecting chromatin remodeling, immune evasion, and B-cell receptor signaling. Its biology involves constitutive survival signaling through the B-cell receptor, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, NF-kB, JAK/STAT, and antiapoptotic BCL2 pathways, with critical support from the follicular microenvironment including follicular helper T cells, stromal cells, CXCR4/CXCL12, and CD20-positive neoplastic B cells. Patients typically present with painless generalized lymphadenopathy, waxing and waning nodal enlargement, splenomegaly, fatigue, B symptoms in a minority, cytopenias from marrow involvement, and less commonly extranodal disease. Major subtypes include grades 1-2, grade 3A, and grade 3B, as well as in situ follicular neoplasia and transformed disease, most often to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The disease is usually sporadic rather than Mendelian, though familial clustering and inherited immune-regulatory susceptibility loci are recognized; the defining alterations are predominantly acquired somatic events. Diagnosis relies on excisional lymph node biopsy showing a follicular growth pattern of centrocytes and centroblasts, immunophenotype positive for CD19, CD20, CD10, BCL6, and usually BCL2, low to intermediate Ki-67, flow cytometry demonstrating a clonal light-chain-restricted B-cell population, and cytogenetic or molecular confirmation of IGH-BCL2 by FISH or PCR, with PET/CT and bone marrow biopsy used for staging. Standard therapies include rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody; obinutuzumab, a glycoengineered anti-CD20 antibody; bendamustine, an alkylating cytotoxic agent; CHOP components such as cyclophosphamide and doxorubicin; lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory cereblon-binding agent; PI3K

Name: Lymphoma, Non-Hodgkin
Description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a heterogeneous group of malignant lymphoid neoplasms, usually of B-cell origin but also arising from T cells or NK cells, characterized by clonal proliferation in lymph nodes or extranodal sites and including major subtypes such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and peripheral T-cell lymphomas. Its molecular basis commonly involves dysregulation of B-cell receptor, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, apoptosis, and germinal-center differentiation pathways, with representative genetic lesions including BCL2 overexpression from t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, MYC rearrangement in Burkitt lymphoma, CCND1 overexpression from t(11;14) in mantle cell lymphoma, and recurrent alterations of BCL6, TP53, EZH2, CD79A/CD79B, CARD11, MYD88, and NOTCH1/2. Most cases are sporadic, although inherited susceptibility is suggested by familial clustering and rare germline defects in immune-regulatory or DNA-repair genes; risk is increased with congenital or acquired immunodeficiency, autoimmune disease, Epstein-Barr virus, HTLV-1, hepatitis C, and Helicobacter pylori in some marginal zone lymphomas. Patients typically present with painless lymphadenopathy, B symptoms such as fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss, fatigue, pruritus, recurrent infections, or organ-specific manifestations including splenomegaly, marrow failure, gastrointestinal, cutaneous, or CNS involvement. Diagnosis relies on excisional biopsy with histopathology, immunophenotyping by flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics/FISH, molecular clonality or mutation testing, bone marrow evaluation, and staging with PET/CT or CT, integrated with WHO/ICC classification criteria. Treatment commonly includes rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody mediating B-cell depletion; cyclophosphamide, an alkylating DNA cross-linker; doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor; vincristine, a microtubule inhibitor; prednisone, a lymphocytotoxic glucocorticoid; and in selected subtypes BTK inhibitors such as ibrutinib. Name: Waldenstrom Macroglobulinemia
Description: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (WM; lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with bone marrow involvement and an IgM monoclonal gammopathy) is an indolent mature B-cell neoplasm characterized biologically by recurrent MYD88 L265P mutation in most cases and CXCR4 WHIM-like mutations in a substantial subset, with less frequent abnormalities affecting ARID1A, TP53, and 6q deletion; these lesions drive NF-kB, BTK/TLR, JAK-STAT, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, CXCR4-CXCL12, and B-cell receptor signaling, promoting survival of CD19+, CD20+, surface IgM+ lymphoplasmacytic cells and secretion of monoclonal IgM. Clinically, WM causes fatigue from anemia, constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, neuropathy, cryoglobulinemia, cold agglutinin disease, hyperviscosity with headaches, visual disturbance and mucosal bleeding, and may be complicated by Bing-Neel syndrome, amyloidosis, infections, and transformation to aggressive lymphoma. It includes asymptomatic/smoldering WM and symptomatic WM, and overlaps with IgM MGUS as a precursor state. Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering indicates inherited susceptibility in some kindreds; WM itself is not classically Mendelian, though germline predisposition affecting B-cell regulatory pathways has been described. Diagnosis requires demonstration of a serum IgM monoclonal protein, usually by serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, plus bone marrow infiltration by small lymphocytes with plasmacytoid/plasma cell differentiation, supported by flow cytometry, MYD88/CXCR4 molecular testing, quantitative IgM, serum viscosity, beta-2 microglobulin, and imaging when extramedullary disease is suspected, while excluding IgM myeloma and marginal zone lymphoma. Common therapies include rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody; ibrutinib or zanubrutinib, BTK inhibitors that block B-cell receptor/MYD88 signaling; and bendamustine, an alkylating cytotoxic agent, with proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax used in selected patients.

Name: Malaria
Description: Malaria (MeSH D008288) is a mosquito-borne protozoal infection caused by Plasmodium species, principally P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi, with clinical syndromes ranging from uncomplicated febrile illness to severe cerebral, placental, or multiorgan malaria. Disease biology centers on hepatocyte invasion and erythrocytic replication mediated by parasite ligands and host receptors such as PfEMP1 encoded by var genes, EBA-175, AMA1, MSP1, and host glycophorins, basigin/CD147, Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines (ACKR1/DARC), ATP2B4, G6PD, HBB, and HBA variants; protective human polymorphisms include sickle trait HbS, thalassemias, G6PD deficiency, ovalocytosis due to SLC4A1, and Duffy negativity against many P. vivax infections. Key pathogenic pathways include merozoite invasion, cytoadherence and sequestration via endothelial ICAM1 and CD36, inflammatory cytokine signaling with TNF, IFN-γ, IL-1 and nitric oxide, hemolysis, complement activation, coagulation dysregulation, and hemozoin-driven innate immune activation. Typical symptoms are periodic fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly; severe disease may cause altered consciousness, seizures, acidosis, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, shock, and severe anemia. Common treatments include artemisinin derivatives such as artesunate, which generate toxic free radicals after heme activation; chloroquine, which blocks heme detoxification in the food vacuole; atovaquone-proguanil, which inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome bc1 and dihydrofolate reductase; and primaquine or tafenoquine, which eradicate latent hepatic hypnozoites in vivax and ovale malaria. Important complications and comorbidities include pregnancy, malnutrition, HIV coinfection, bacterial sepsis, and blackwater fever. Diagnosis relies on compatible travel or exposure history plus microscopy of thick and thin blood smears with species identification and parasitemia assessment, rapid antigen tests such as HRP2 or pLDH, and PCR for confirmation

Name: Malaria, Falciparum
Description: Falciparum malaria (MeSH D016778) is a severe, non-Mendelian infectious disease caused by the apicomplexan protozoan Plasmodium falciparum, whose virulence reflects erythrocyte invasion and cytoadherence mediated by parasite proteins such as PfEMP1 encoded by var genes, erythrocyte-binding antigens and RH proteins, while major antimalarial resistance determinants include pfcrt, pfmdr1, pfdhfr, pfdhps, kelch13, and occasional plasmepsin 2/3 amplification; host genetic components that modify susceptibility or severity include HBB variants causing sickle trait, G6PD deficiency, ABO blood group, Duffy-related pathways to a lesser extent than in vivax malaria, and polymorphisms in TNF, IFN-γ, ICAM1, CD36, TLRs, and NOS2. Key pathogenic pathways include merozoite invasion through receptor-ligand interactions, heme detoxification to hemozoin within the food vacuole, parasite folate synthesis, mitochondrial electron transport, endothelial activation, cytokine signaling, rosetting, sequestration via ICAM-1, EPCR, and CD36, and nitric oxide and coagulation dysregulation. Typical manifestations are cyclical or irregular fever, chills, headache, malaise, myalgia, anemia, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and gastrointestinal symptoms; severe subtypes include cerebral malaria, severe malarial anemia, algid malaria, blackwater fever, placental malaria, and multiorgan failure. Complications include hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, ARDS, shock, DIC, secondary bacterial sepsis, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Treatment commonly uses artemisinin derivatives such as artesunate, which generate toxic radical species after heme activation, often in artemisinin-based combination regimens with lumefantrine or mefloquine; atovaquone-proguanil inhibits cytochrome bc1 and dihydrofolate reductase, quinine interferes with heme detoxification, and chloroquine, though limited by resistance, acts similarly. Diagnosis rests on compatible febrile illness with travel or exposure history and confirmation by Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood smears, rapid antigen tests such as HRP2 or pLDH, and PCR for species identification,

Name: Quartan malaria
Description: Quartan malaria is a protozoal infectious disease caused by Plasmodium malariae, a non-Mendelian, vector-borne parasitosis transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes rather than an inherited disorder, although host genetic factors influence susceptibility and severity; representative examples include erythrocyte polymorphisms and immune-response genes such as HBB variants including sickle hemoglobin, G6PD deficiency, Duffy/ACKR1-related erythrocyte phenotypes, HLA loci, and cytokine genes including TNF and IFNG, while parasite proteins important to pathobiology include circumsporozoite protein, merozoite surface proteins, AMA1, and variant surface antigens involved in erythrocyte invasion and immune evasion. The disease is characterized by a 72-hour erythrocytic cycle producing the classic quartan fever pattern, with paroxysms of fever, chills, sweats, headache, malaise, myalgia, anemia, splenomegaly, and thrombocytopenia; subtypes are mainly uncomplicated versus chronic or severe infection, the latter less common than in falciparum malaria but notable for long persistence and recrudescence. Key pathogenic pathways include hepatocyte invasion followed by erythrocytic replication, hemozoin formation, innate immune activation through macrophages, dendritic cells, and TLR-mediated cytokine release such as TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and IFN-γ, splenic clearance of infected erythrocytes, endothelial activation, and immune-complex deposition, which helps explain the classic association with nephrotic syndrome or chronic glomerulopathy; other complications include severe anemia, splenomegaly, and rarely renal failure. Diagnosis rests on exposure history plus identification of parasites on Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood smears, supported by rapid antigen tests with lower sensitivity for P. malariae and PCR for species confirmation. Treatment commonly includes chloroquine, which inhibits heme polymerization in the parasite food vacuole; quinine, which similarly disrupts heme detoxification; and artemisinin-based combinations such as artemether-lumefantrine, in which artemisinin generates toxic free radicals and lumefantrine inhibits heme detoxification; atovaquone-proguanil may also be used by inhibiting parasite mitochondrial electron transport and dihydrofolate reductase, respectively.

Name: Malaria, Vivax
Description: Malaria, Vivax (MeSH D016780) is a mosquito-borne protozoal infection caused by Plasmodium vivax, characterized by invasion of reticulocytes, dormant hepatic hypnozoites that drive relapse, and blood-stage hemolytic infection producing cyclical febrile illness. Key parasite molecules include the Duffy binding protein DBP/PvDBP interacting with the human Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines encoded by ACKR1, merozoite surface proteins such as MSP1, circumsporozoite protein, and chloroquine-resistance transporter and multidrug-resistance loci including pvcrt-o and pvmdr1; host genetic components that modify susceptibility or treatment safety include the Duffy-negative ACKR1 phenotype, G6PD deficiency, and CYP2D6 variants affecting primaquine activation, with these traits showing Mendelian inheritance according to the underlying gene defect. Relevant pathways include hepatocyte invasion and hypnozoite persistence, erythrocyte invasion via DBP-ACKR1 binding, inflammatory cytokine signaling with TNF, IFN-gamma, and IL-6, splenic clearance, hemolysis, and heme-related oxidative stress. Typical manifestations are intermittent fever with chills and sweats, headache, malaise, myalgia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, jaundice, and splenomegaly; severe complications may include acute respiratory distress, severe anemia, splenic rupture, renal or hepatic dysfunction, and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and comorbidities such as malnutrition, pregnancy, hemoglobinopathies, and coinfections can worsen disease. Subtypes are commonly framed as uncomplicated versus severe vivax malaria and as primary, recrudescent, or relapsing infection. Diagnosis relies on compatible travel or exposure history plus detection of parasites by Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood smears, rapid antigen tests, or PCR, with species identification and parasitemia assessment guiding management. Standard therapy includes chloroquine, which inhibits heme detoxification in blood schizonts where susceptibility remains; artemisinin-based combinations such as artemether-lumefantrine, which generate toxic radical damage and provide partner-drug clearance of residual parasites; and primaquine or tafenoquine, 8-aminoquinolines that eradicate hypnozoites and gametocytes through oxidative mitochondrial injury, requiring G6PD testing before use.

Name: Malignant Carcinoid Syndrome
Description: Malignant carcinoid syndrome refers to the systemic paraneoplastic syndrome caused by metastatic, usually well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors of the midgut or occasionally bronchopulmonary or pancreatic origin, in which vasoactive products such as serotonin, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid precursors, tachykinins, histamine, kallikrein, and prostaglandins escape hepatic metabolism; biologically, these tumors commonly express neuroendocrine proteins including chromogranin A, synaptophysin, somatostatin receptors, especially SSTR2, and enzymes of serotonin synthesis such as tryptophan hydroxylase 1, while recurrent molecular abnormalities in neuroendocrine neoplasia include MEN1 alterations, CDKN1B mutations in some small-intestinal cases, and less often DAXX, ATRX, or mTOR-pathway genes, with hereditary predisposition most clearly seen in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, although most carcinoid syndrome cases are sporadic rather than Mendelian. Pathobiology involves serotonin biosynthesis and secretion, somatostatin receptor signaling, PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathways, angiogenic signaling including VEGF, and profibrotic TGF-beta–related mechanisms underlying carcinoid heart disease and mesenteric fibrosis. Hallmark manifestations are episodic flushing, secretory diarrhea, abdominal cramping, wheezing or bronchospasm, hypotension or labile hemodynamics, pellagra from tryptophan depletion, weight loss, and, in advanced disease, right-sided valvular fibrosis with tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis. Major subtypes are typical versus atypical pulmonary carcinoid and functional versus nonfunctional gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, with syndrome classically associated with metastatic midgut disease. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms plus elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA or plasma 5-HIAA, chromogranin A, cross-sectional imaging, somatostatin-receptor imaging such as Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT, echocardiography for cardiac involvement, and histologic confirmation with Ki-67 grading. Treatment commonly includes octreotide or lanreotide, somatostatin analogs that suppress hormone release via SSTR binding; telotristat ethyl, a peripheral tryptophan hydroxylase inhibitor that reduces serotonin production

Name: Malignant Essential Hypertension
Description: Malignant essential hypertension is a severe, rapidly progressive form of primary hypertension characterized by marked elevation of blood pressure, classically with diastolic pressure above 120 mmHg, acute target-organ injury, and retinal hemorrhages, exudates, or papilledema; it is now often framed within the hypertensive emergency spectrum. It arises from complex polygenic and environmental mechanisms rather than Mendelian inheritance, with heritable susceptibility involving variants in genes regulating renal sodium handling, vascular tone, and neurohormonal activation, including representative examples such as ACE, AGT, AGTR1, REN, ADD1, NOS3, CYP11B2, and UMOD, while proteins central to pathobiology include angiotensin II, aldosterone, endothelin-1, nitric oxide synthase, and sympathetic catecholamine signaling. Key pathways include the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic overactivity, endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide and increased oxidative stress, vascular smooth muscle remodeling, inflammation, and pressure-induced fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles. Typical manifestations include severe headache, visual disturbance, encephalopathy, confusion, chest pain, dyspnea, nausea, seizures, and signs of acute kidney injury, heart failure, or stroke. Major complications and linked comorbidities include chronic kidney disease, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, coronary artery disease, left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, aortic dissection, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, retinopathy, diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnea. Diagnosis relies on repeated blood-pressure measurement plus evidence of acute end-organ damage, with fundoscopy, serum creatinine and urinalysis, ECG, troponin, echocardiography, and brain or chest imaging as indicated; evaluation also excludes secondary causes such as renovascular disease, pheochromocytoma, and primary aldosteronism. Treatment requires controlled blood-pressure reduction using agents such as labetalol, a combined alpha1- and beta-adrenergic blocker, nicardipine, a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, and sodium nitroprusside, a nitric oxide donor, with additional use of clevidipine, nitroglycerin, or hydralazine in selected settings.

Name: Malignant Hyperthermia
Description: Malignant hyperthermia (MeSH D008305) is a rare, life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle calcium homeostasis, usually triggered by volatile halogenated anesthetics such as sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane, or by succinylcholine, and most often inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance; the principal genetic cause is pathogenic variation in RYR1, which encodes the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor, with less frequent involvement of CACNA1S encoding the α1S subunit of the dihydropyridine receptor, and rarer associations with STAC3 and other excitation-contraction coupling genes. The core pathobiology is dysregulated sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release in the triad junction, involving abnormal coupling between Cav1.1 and RyR1, excessive myoplasmic calcium, sustained actin-myosin contraction, ATP depletion, mitochondrial hypermetabolism, accelerated glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, heat generation, lactic acidosis, and cell membrane breakdown with potassium and creatine kinase release. Clinically, malignant hyperthermia susceptibility may remain silent until exposure, when patients develop rapidly rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, generalized or masseter rigidity, hyperthermia, mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria, and potentially disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, and death; related disorders and comorbid associations include exertional rhabdomyolysis, heat illness, central core disease, multiminicore myopathy, and other RYR1-related congenital myopathies. Recognition is primarily clinical during anesthesia, supported by blood gases, serum CK and potassium, urine myoglobin, and response to treatment; definitive evaluation uses the caffeine-halothane contracture test or in vitro contracture testing, with molecular genetic testing as an adjunct. Treatment requires immediate discontinuation of triggering agents, dantrolene as the specific RyR1 antagonist that suppresses sarcoplasmic calcium release, active cooling, sodium bicarbonate for acidosis, insulin with glucose or calcium for hyperkalemia and membrane stabilization, and supportive intensive care; susceptibility is broadly categorized as malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, fulminant anesthetic-triggered crisis, and allelic RYR1/CACNA1

Name: Gastric Cancer
Description: Stomach neoplasms, most commonly gastric adenocarcinomas, are malignant epithelial tumors of the stomach that include intestinal and diffuse Lauren subtypes, proximal/cardia and distal/non-cardia cancers, and less often hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, lymphoma, and neuroendocrine neoplasms; they arise through multifactorial interactions among Helicobacter pylori–driven chronic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, Epstein-Barr virus in a subset, environmental exposures, and genetic alterations involving TP53, CDH1/E-cadherin, APC, ARID1A, KRAS, PIK3CA, SMAD4, RNF43, and mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1 and MSH2, with protein overexpression or amplification of ERBB2/HER2, EGFR, MET, FGFR2, and Claudin 18.2 in selected cases. Key pathways include Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, TGF-β/SMAD, cell-cycle and p53 signaling, DNA damage repair, angiogenesis via VEGF/VEGFR, and immune evasion through PD-1/PD-L1. Typical manifestations are dyspepsia, epigastric pain, early satiety, nausea, weight loss, anorexia, iron-deficiency anemia, occult or overt bleeding, vomiting, dysphagia in proximal lesions, and advanced signs such as Virchow node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, ascites, or gastric outlet obstruction; complications include hemorrhage, perforation, obstruction, malnutrition, venous thromboembolism, and metastases to liver, peritoneum, lung, and bone. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited risk occurs in CDH1-associated autosomal dominant hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and juvenile polyposis. Diagnosis relies on upper endoscopy with multiple biopsies and histopathology, staging by endoscopic ultrasound and CT/PET, and biomarker testing for HER2, MMR/MSI, PD-L1, EBV, and sometimes CLDN18.2 or NTRK fusions. Treatment commonly includes fluorouracil or capecitabine, which inhibit thymidylate synthase; platinum agents

Name: Melanoma
Description: Melanoma (MeSH D008545) is a malignant neoplasm of melanocytes arising most often in the skin but also in mucosal, acral, or uveal sites, characterized by aggressive metastatic potential and marked molecular heterogeneity. Common driver alterations include activating BRAF mutations, especially V600E/K, NRAS mutations, KIT mutations in acral/mucosal disease, NF1 loss, TERT promoter mutations, and less often GNAQ or GNA11 in uveal melanoma; relevant proteins and tumor suppressors include BRAF, NRAS, KIT, PTEN, CDKN2A/p16INK4A, CDK4, TP53, and MITF. Major oncogenic pathways involve MAPK signaling through RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, cell-cycle dysregulation via CDKN2A-CDK4/6-RB, telomerase activation, and immune evasion through PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 checkpoints. Treatment commonly includes immune checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab or nivolumab, monoclonal antibodies blocking PD-1 to restore antitumor T-cell activity, and ipilimumab, which inhibits CTLA-4; for BRAF-mutant melanoma, targeted therapy with vemurafenib or dabrafenib, BRAF kinase inhibitors, often combined with MEK inhibitors such as trametinib, is standard, while KIT-mutant cases may respond to imatinib, a KIT tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Typical manifestations are an evolving pigmented lesion with ABCDE features, asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, diameter enlargement, ulceration, bleeding, pruritus, or regional lymphadenopathy; subtypes include superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous, desmoplastic, mucosal, and uveal melanoma. Risk is usually multifactorial, driven by ultraviolet exposure and fair-phenotype susceptibility, but familial cases show autosomal dominant predisposition involving CDKN2A, CDK4, BAP1, MITF, POT1, or TERT. Diagnosis relies on full-thickness excisional biopsy with histopathology, Breslow depth, ulceration and mitotic assessment, staging with sentinel lymph node biopsy and imaging when indicated, and molecular testing for actionable mutations; complications include local recurrence, nodal and visceral metastases

Name: Chloasmas
Description: Chloasma, more commonly termed melasma, is a chronic acquired disorder of facial hypermelanosis characterized by symmetric light- to dark-brown macules and patches, most often on the centrofacial, malar, or mandibular regions, with epidermal, dermal, or mixed subtypes and occasional extrafacial disease. It is driven by melanocyte hyperactivity rather than melanocyte proliferation and reflects interplay among ultraviolet and visible light exposure, hormonal influences, and genetic susceptibility; implicated molecular components include increased melanogenic signaling through MC1R, tyrosinase, TYRP1, DCT, MITF, endothelin-1, stem cell factor/KIT, α-MSH, Wnt/β-catenin, cAMP/PKA/CREB, MAPK, and estrogen/progesterone receptor pathways, with lesional overexpression of melanogenesis, vascular, and basement-membrane-remodeling mediators such as VEGF and MMPs. A familial tendency is common, but inheritance is typically complex polygenic rather than Mendelian; representative susceptibility associations have involved MC1R and pigmentary genes such as TYR, though no single causal mutation defines most cases. Common comorbid or precipitating factors include pregnancy, oral contraceptive or hormone therapy use, thyroid disease, photodamage, and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, while psychosocial distress and recurrence are major complications. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on characteristic distribution and chronic relapsing course, aided by Wood lamp examination to estimate pigment depth, dermoscopy, colorimetry, and occasionally biopsy showing increased basal melanin with variable melanophages. Treatment centers on photoprotection and topical depigmenting agents: hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase and melanosome formation, tretinoin accelerates keratinocyte turnover and enhances pigment dispersion, corticosteroids suppress inflammation and melanocyte metabolic activity, azelaic acid competitively inhibits tyrosinase, tranexamic acid reduces plasmin-mediated UV-induced melanogenesis and vascular signals, and cysteamine acts as an antioxidant and melanogenesis inhibitor; triple-combination hydroquinone/tretinoin/fluocinolone is widely used, with chemical peels or lasers reserved for selected refractory cases because they may trigger rebound or postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Name: Meniere Disease
Description: Meniere disease is a chronic inner-ear disorder, usually idiopathic, characterized pathologically by endolymphatic hydrops of the membranous labyrinth and clinically by recurrent spontaneous vertigo, fluctuating low- to mid-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness; attacks may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, imbalance, Tumarkin drop attacks, and progressive permanent hearing loss. It is commonly unilateral at onset but may become bilateral, and is classified as definite or probable disease by clinical criteria requiring episodic vertigo with documented sensorineural hearing loss and fluctuating aural symptoms, supported by audiometry, vestibular testing such as calorics, vHIT, VEMP, electrocochleography, and exclusion of alternative causes by MRI of the internal auditory canals and brain. Molecularly, implicated pathways include disturbed endolymph ion and water homeostasis, epithelial transport, inflammation, oxidative stress, and immune signaling, involving aquaporins, Na+/K+-ATPase, potassium recycling and calcium homeostasis in the stria vascularis and endolymphatic sac; genetic associations reported in familial and sporadic cases include FAM136A, DTNA, PRKCB, DPT, SEMA3D, OTOG, MYO7A, TECTA, and HMX2/HMX3, with some families showing autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity, while many cases remain polygenic or multifactorial. Common comorbidities include migraine, autoimmune thyroid disease and other autoimmune disorders, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, and increased fall risk. Treatment is symptomatic and preventive: betahistine, an H1 agonist/H3 antagonist, may improve labyrinthine microcirculation and vestibular compensation; thiazide-type diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide, often with triamterene, reduce fluid retention and are used to limit hydrops; meclizine or diazepam suppress acute vestibular symptoms via antihistaminic or GABA-A–mediated effects; and refractory disease may be treated with intratympanic gentamicin, which causes vestibular hair-cell ablation, or intratympanic corticosteroids such as dexamethasone, which reduce inner-ear inflammatory activity.

Name: Meningitis
Description: Meningitis (MeSH D008581) is an acute or chronic inflammatory disorder of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid, most often caused by bacterial, viral, fungal, or mycobacterial infection, but it may also be autoimmune, drug induced, or neoplastic. Key host genetic factors that influence susceptibility or severity include complement pathway defects, especially terminal complement components C5-C9 and properdin deficiency, TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, IRAK4, NFKBIA, and mannose-binding lectin variants, while pathogen-related determinants include Neisseria meningitidis capsule genes and pneumococcal virulence proteins such as pneumolysin. Central molecular pathways include pathogen recognition through TLR and NOD signaling, NF-kappaB activation, inflammasome/IL-1beta signaling, TNF-alpha, IL-6, chemokine-driven neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and coagulation-endothelial injury cascades. Typical symptoms and signs are fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, rash in meningococcemia, and in infants irritability, poor feeding, and bulging fontanelle. Major subtypes include acute bacterial meningitis, aseptic/viral meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, recurrent meningitis, and chronic meningitis. Diagnosis is based on urgent clinical suspicion with lumbar puncture and CSF analysis showing cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, and PCR/NAAT panels, with blood cultures, cryptococcal antigen or acid-fast testing when indicated, and neuroimaging before lumbar puncture in selected patients at risk of herniation. Standard treatments include ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins; vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala and blocks peptidoglycan assembly; ampicillin for Listeria via beta-lactam cell-wall inhibition; acyclovir, a viral DNA polymerase inhibitor, when HSV encephalitis is a concern; amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol, for fungal disease; and adjunctive dexamethasone, which suppresses cytokine-mediated inflammation. Name: Meningitis, Listeria
Description: Listeria meningitis (UMLS C0025293) is an invasive bacterial meningoencephalitis caused predominantly by Listeria monocytogenes, a facultative intracellular Gram-positive bacillus, classically affecting neonates, pregnant patients, older adults, and immunocompromised hosts; clinically it presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, seizures, focal deficits, ataxia, and sometimes rhombencephalitis or brainstem signs, while neonatal disease may occur as early- or late-onset sepsis/meningitis. Pathogenesis depends on bacterial virulence factors including internalins InlA and InlB, listeriolysin O encoded by hly, ActA, plcA/plcB, and the regulator PrfA, which mediate epithelial invasion, phagosomal escape, actin-based intracellular spread, and CNS invasion; host susceptibility is shaped by innate and cell-mediated immunity, particularly TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, TLR/MyD88, NF-κB, and JAK/STAT signaling, with rare predisposition from defects affecting IL12RB1, IFNGR1, STAT1, GATA2, NEMO/IKBKG, or anti–IFN-γ immunity. Diagnosis is based on compatible meningitis/meningoencephalitis plus microbiologic confirmation, typically CSF and blood cultures, CSF analysis showing pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, Gram stain sometimes revealing Gram-positive rods, and PCR/NAAT when available, with neuroimaging used to detect cerebritis, abscess, or hydrocephalus. Standard therapy is high-dose ampicillin, a beta-lactam that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and cell wall synthesis, usually with gentamicin, an aminoglycoside that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit for synergistic bactericidal activity; penicillin G is an alternative beta-lactam, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis via dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase inhibition, is used for beta-lactam allergy or salvage therapy, whereas cephalosporins are intrinsically ineffective. Name: Meningitis, Meningococcal
Description: Meningococcal meningitis is an acute, often rapidly progressive bacterial meningitis caused predominantly by Neisseria meningitidis, usually presenting as sporadic disease or outbreaks due to serogroups A, B, C, W, X, and Y, and clinically characterized by fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, and sometimes a petechial or purpuric rash with meningococcemia, septic shock, and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Disease pathogenesis reflects nasopharyngeal colonization followed by bloodstream invasion and blood-brain barrier penetration mediated by bacterial capsule genes, porA/porB outer membrane porins, fHbp and NHBA, Opc/Opa adhesins, and lipooligosaccharide endotoxin, which activates TLR4-, NF-kB-, TNF-, IL1-, IL6-, complement-, and coagulation-driven inflammatory pathways, leading to endothelial injury, capillary leak, and intracranial inflammation. Host genetic susceptibility is best established for terminal complement pathway and properdin defects, including C5, C6, C7, C8, C9, CFD, and CFP, with X-linked properdin deficiency and rare variants in CFH or TLR4 influencing risk; inheritance is therefore usually not Mendelian for the infection itself, but may follow the pattern of the underlying immune defect. Diagnosis is based on compatible acute meningitic illness with cerebrospinal fluid showing neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose, and microbiologic confirmation by CSF or blood culture, Gram stain showing gram-negative diplococci, PCR or antigen testing, with adjunctive CBC, coagulation studies, and neuroimaging when indicated. Standard therapy includes ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; high-dose penicillin G or ampicillin for susceptible isolates, also blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking; and chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, when beta-lactams cannot be used. Major complications include hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, cognitive impairment, stroke, disseminated intravascular coagulation, adrenal hemorrhage, and multiorgan failure.

Name: Meningitis, Pneumococcal
Description: Pneumococcal meningitis (MeSH D008586) is an acute, life-threatening bacterial infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, usually arising from nasopharyngeal colonization with hematogenous spread or contiguous extension from otitis, sinusitis, mastoiditis, or pneumonia; major virulence determinants include the capsular polysaccharide locus, pneumolysin (ply), autolysin LytA, neuraminidases, and surface proteins such as PspA and CbpA/PspC that promote blood-brain barrier invasion and immune evasion. Host susceptibility is influenced by innate-immune and splenic pathways, with reported associations involving TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, IRAK4, NFKB-related signaling, complement genes including C2, C3, CFH and properdin, MBL2, FCN2, and immunoglobulin defects, although inheritance is usually not Mendelian and reflects complex or syndromic predisposition; classical Mendelian examples include IRAK4 or MYD88 deficiency and terminal or alternative complement defects predisposing to invasive pneumococcal disease. Pathobiology is driven by pathogen-associated molecular pattern recognition, NF-kB activation, TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and CXCL8 release, complement activation, neutrophil influx, matrix metalloproteinases, endothelial injury, cerebral edema, vasculitis, and thrombosis. Patients typically present with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status, vomiting, seizures, and sometimes focal deficits or coma. Important subtypes include community-acquired, post-traumatic/post-neurosurgical, recurrent meningitis, and disease in asplenic, immunocompromised, or pediatric versus adult hosts. Diagnosis relies on urgent blood cultures, lumbar puncture showing neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low CSF glucose, Gram-positive diplococci on Gram stain, CSF culture, pneumococcal antigen testing, and PCR/NAAT, with neuroimaging when herniation risk is suspected. Name: Menorrhagia
Description: Menorrhagia, now often termed heavy menstrual bleeding, is a clinical syndrome of excessive cyclic uterine blood loss that interferes with physical, emotional, social, or material quality of life and may arise from structural uterine disease or nonstructural disorders classified within the PALM-COEIN framework, including leiomyoma, adenomyosis, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial causes, and coagulopathy. Patients typically present with prolonged or heavy menses, passage of clots, frequent pad or tampon changes, flooding, dysmenorrhea, fatigue, pallor, and iron-deficiency anemia; major complications include severe anemia, reduced fertility in some etiologies, and impaired daily functioning. Important comorbidities include uterine fibroids, endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, thyroid disease, obesity, and inherited bleeding disorders, especially von Willebrand disease and platelet function defects. Genetic contributors are usually indirect through underlying causes rather than a single Mendelian menorrhagia gene; representative examples include VWF mutations in von Willebrand disease, F8 and F9 in hemophilia carriers, and fibrinolytic pathway genes such as SERPINE1 and PLAT in rare hyperfibrinolytic states, while fibroid-associated somatic mutations such as MED12 may secondarily drive heavy bleeding. Pathobiology commonly involves dysregulated endometrial hemostasis, prostaglandin and cyclooxygenase signaling, local fibrinolysis with plasmin activation, estrogen and progesterone receptor signaling, angiogenesis including VEGF, and inflammatory mediators. Treatment depends on cause and includes tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic that inhibits plasminogen activation; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as mefenamic acid or ibuprofen, which inhibit COX-mediated prostaglandin synthesis; combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives, which suppress ovulation and stabilize endometrium; levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine therapy, which causes endometrial decidualization and atrophy; and in selected cases GnRH agonists or desmopressin. Diagnosis is based on menstrual history and impact, pelvic examination, pregnancy testing, CBC and ferritin, coagulation studies when indicated, thyroid testing, pelvic ultrasound, and endometrial sampling in patients at risk for hyperplasia or malignancy.

Name: Metrorrhagia
Description: Metrorrhagia, now generally classified within abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), is irregular uterine bleeding occurring between expected menses and is a clinical syndrome rather than a single inherited disease; it commonly reflects structural causes such as endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyomas, malignancy/hyperplasia, or nonstructural causes including ovulatory dysfunction, coagulopathy, endometrial hemostatic defects, iatrogenic hormonal effects, and pregnancy-related disorders. Symptoms include unpredictable intermenstrual bleeding, prolonged or heavy flow, pelvic pain or pressure when fibroids or adenomyosis are present, and complications such as iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, infertility, hemodynamic instability, and missed gynecologic cancer. Molecular associations are cause-specific: uterine leiomyomas frequently harbor MED12 mutations, HMGA2 rearrangements, and fumarate hydratase defects; endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma may involve PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, ARID1A, TP53, and mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 in Lynch syndrome; coagulation-related bleeding may reflect variants in VWF or F8. Relevant pathways include estrogen-progesterone receptor signaling, hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis dysregulation, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, TGF-β/SMAD and WNT/β-catenin signaling, angiogenesis via VEGF, and local prostaglandin, fibrinolytic, and matrix-remodeling pathways controlling endometrial shedding and repair. Treatment depends on etiology and often includes combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives to stabilize endometrium and suppress ovulation, progestins such as medroxyprogesterone to oppose estrogen and induce endometrial decidualization/atrophy, tranexamic acid as an antifibrinolytic blocking plasminogen activation, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or mefenamic acid to reduce prostaglandin synthesis and menstrual blood loss, and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine therapy for potent local endometrial suppression; GnRH agonists may be used short term for fibroid-associated bleeding. Inheritance is usually absent except through underlying disorders, including Lynch syndrome, hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer due to FH mutations, and inherited bleeding disorders

Name: Motion Sickness
Description: Motion sickness (MeSH D009041) is a common, usually self-limited neurovestibular disorder caused by sensory conflict or neural mismatch between visual, vestibular, and somatosensory inputs during passive or apparent motion; major subtypes include seasickness, carsickness, airsickness, space motion sickness, and visually induced motion sickness. Core symptoms are nausea, vomiting, pallor, cold sweating, dizziness, malaise, drowsiness, headache, and occasionally postural instability or “sopite” symptoms, with complications such as dehydration, functional impairment, falls, and provocation or worsening of vestibular migraine, anxiety, and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness; comorbid susceptibility is also seen with migraine, vestibular disorders, pregnancy, and autonomic lability. Pathophysiology centers on vestibular labyrinth and brainstem circuitry, including otolith and semicircular canal signaling to vestibular nuclei, cerebellum, nucleus tractus solitarius, and vomiting center, with prominent cholinergic muscarinic M1, histaminergic H1, and monoaminergic/autonomic pathways; genetic contributions are modest but heritable susceptibility has been reported, with representative associations involving adrenergic receptor genes such as ADRA2A, cholinergic and dopaminergic signaling genes, and variants influencing vestibular or migraine biology, though no single Mendelian mutation is established and inheritance is generally complex/polygenic. Diagnosis is clinical, based on a reproducible trigger of motion exposure with typical symptom constellation, supported when needed by vestibular examination, autonomic assessment, symptom questionnaires, and exclusion of alternative causes such as vestibular neuritis, Ménière disease, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, concussion, or central neurologic disease; routine genetic testing is not indicated. Common treatments include scopolamine, a muscarinic antagonist that suppresses vestibular cholinergic transmission; dimenhydrinate or meclizine, H1 antihistamines with central anticholinergic and vestibular suppressant effects; promethazine, an H1 antagonist with antiemetic sedative activity; and adjunctive ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist less effective for vestibular mechanisms but useful for nausea control.

Name: Mucormycosis
Description: Mucormycosis is an aggressive, opportunistic, angioinvasive fungal infection caused by molds of the order Mucorales, most commonly Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia, and Rhizomucor, classically presenting as rhino-orbito-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, renal, or disseminated disease with fever, facial pain, nasal congestion, black eschar, cranial neuropathies, cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, necrotic skin lesions, or sepsis. Its pathobiology centers on endothelial invasion and tissue infarction mediated by fungal CotH proteins binding host GRP78, with enhanced growth in hyperglycemia, ketoacidosis, and iron excess; innate immune pathways involving neutrophils, macrophages, Dectin-1/TLR signaling, oxidative burst, and cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6 are critical, and defects in these defenses increase risk. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for mucormycosis itself, but host genetic susceptibility has been linked to immunodeficiency-related genes and pathways, including GATA2, STAT1/STAT3, CARD9, CYBA/NCF1 in chronic granulomatous disease, and diabetes-associated metabolic dysregulation; representative fungal virulence genes include CotH family members and iron acquisition genes such as FTR1. Major comorbidities include uncontrolled diabetes, especially with ketoacidosis, hematologic malignancy, transplantation, prolonged neutropenia, corticosteroid or deferoxamine exposure, trauma or burns, iron overload, and severe viral illness including COVID-19; complications include orbital invasion, cavernous sinus thrombosis, cerebral abscess, massive hemoptysis, bowel perforation, and disseminated multiorgan failure. Diagnosis requires urgent clinicoradiologic suspicion plus tissue biopsy showing broad pauciseptate hyphae with right-angle branching and vascular invasion, supported by culture, histopathology, CT/MRI, and increasingly PCR or sequencing from tissue, while serum galactomannan and β-D-glucan are typically negative.
