Name: Multiple Myeloma
Description: Multiple myeloma (MeSH D009101) is a malignant plasma-cell neoplasm characterized by clonal expansion of immunoglobulin-secreting cells in the bone marrow and production of a monoclonal protein, usually evolving from monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance through smoldering myeloma to symptomatic disease; major biologic subtypes include hyperdiploid myeloma and non-hyperdiploid disease with recurrent IgH translocations such as t(11;14)(CCND1), t(4;14)(FGFR3/MMSET), and t(14;16)(MAF), while common secondary lesions involve KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, TP53 deletion/mutation, MYC activation, 1q gain, and del(17p). Pathogenesis is driven by bone marrow microenvironmental signaling, notably IL-6/JAK/STAT3, NF-κB, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, cyclin D dysregulation, and RANKL-mediated osteoclast activation with suppression of osteoblast function. It is usually sporadic rather than Mendelian, although familial clustering and inherited susceptibility loci are recognized. Typical manifestations include bone pain, lytic lesions, pathologic fractures, fatigue from normocytic anemia, recurrent infections, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, weight loss, and sometimes hyperviscosity, neuropathy, or amyloidosis; major complications include cast nephropathy, light-chain deposition disease, AL amyloidosis, venous thromboembolism, spinal cord compression, and treatment-related cytopenias. Diagnosis relies on serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light-chain assay, bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cells, and imaging by low-dose whole-body CT, PET-CT, or MRI, with current criteria requiring clonal marrow plasma cells of at least 10% or plasmacytoma plus myeloma-defining events such as CRAB features or biomarkers including at least 60% marrow plasma cells, free light-chain ratio at least 100, or more than one focal MRI lesion. Standard therapies include bortezomib, a proteasome inhibitor; lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory cereblon-binding agent; dexamethasone, a glucocorticoid cytotoxic to plasma cells; daratumumab,

Name: Multiple Sclerosis
Description: Multiple sclerosis (MeSH D009103) is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory demyelinating and neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system characterized by multifocal white and gray matter lesions, blood-brain barrier disruption, oligodendrocyte injury, axonal loss, and gliosis, most often presenting as relapsing-remitting disease but also as secondary progressive, primary progressive, and clinically isolated syndrome. Susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with the strongest association in HLA-DRB1*15:01 within the MHC, and additional risk variants in IL2RA, IL7R, TYK2, CD6, CD40, and TNFRSF1A; pathology involves autoreactive CD4+ Th1/Th17 and CD8+ T cells, B cells and plasma cells, macrophage/microglial activation, and cytokine networks including IL-2, IL-7, IL-17, IFN-gamma, GM-CSF, TNF, JAK-STAT, NF-kappaB, complement, and B-cell receptor signaling. Typical manifestations include optic neuritis, diplopia or internuclear ophthalmoplegia, sensory loss, limb weakness, spasticity, ataxia, bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction, fatigue, pain, and cognitive or mood impairment. Common comorbidities and complications include depression, anxiety, migraine, cardiovascular risk factors, autoimmune thyroid disease, osteoporosis, recurrent urinary tract infections, falls, and progressive disability. Diagnosis requires demonstration of dissemination in space and time, usually by the McDonald criteria, integrating characteristic MRI lesions in periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord regions, cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal IgG bands or elevated IgG index, and evoked potentials, while excluding mimics such as neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Disease-modifying therapy includes interferon-beta, which shifts cytokine balance and reduces lymphocyte trafficking; glatiramer acetate, which induces tolerogenic immune responses; fingolimod, an S1P receptor modulator that sequesters lymphocytes; natalizumab, an alpha4-integrin blocker that inhibits CNS leukocyte migration; ocrelizumab, an anti-CD20 B-cell-depleting antibody; and dimethyl fumarate, which activates Nrf2-mediated cytoprotective pathways.

Name: Muscle Spasticity
Description: Muscle spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone and exaggerated tendon reflexes caused by upper motor neuron dysfunction, most often after stroke, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, or hereditary spastic paraplegia; clinically it presents with stiffness, painful spasms, clonus, scissoring gait, hyperreflexia, weakness, reduced dexterity, contractures, and impaired mobility, speech, swallowing, hygiene, and sleep. It is commonly classified as focal, segmental, or generalized, and by etiology as cerebral or spinal spasticity. Pathobiologically, spasticity reflects loss of descending corticospinal and reticulospinal inhibition, spinal disinhibition of the stretch reflex, alpha-motor-neuron hyperexcitability, altered Ia afferent signaling, reduced GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition, glutamatergic/NMDA-mediated excitation, and maladaptive plasticity involving ion channels and persistent inward calcium and sodium currents. Genetic associations are best established in inherited syndromes that feature spasticity, especially hereditary spastic paraplegias caused by variants in SPAST, ATL1, KIF5A, CYP7B1, SPG11, REEP1, and CAPN1, with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, and occasionally mitochondrial inheritance; spasticity is also prominent in cerebral palsy linked in some cases to CTNNB1, COL4A1, or AP4 complex genes. Treatment commonly includes baclofen, a GABAB receptor agonist that suppresses spinal excitatory transmission; tizanidine, a central alpha2-adrenergic agonist that reduces presynaptic excitatory neurotransmitter release; diazepam, a GABAA positive allosteric modulator; dantrolene, which inhibits skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor-mediated calcium release; and botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Major comorbidities and complications include pain, falls, pressure injury, urinary dysfunction, constipation, hip dislocation, scoliosis, tendon shortening, and fixed deformity. Diagnosis is clinical, based on an upper motor neuron syndrome with velocity-dependent resistance to passive stretch, commonly quantified with the Modified Ashworth or Tardieu scales, gait and functional assessment, neuroimaging to define central lesions, and targeted electrophysiology or genetic

Name: Spinal Muscular Atrophy
Description: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA; UMLS C0026847) is a hereditary lower motor neuron disease characterized by degeneration of anterior horn cells and motor nuclei in the brainstem, causing progressive symmetric proximal weakness, hypotonia, areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, feeding difficulty, and restrictive respiratory insufficiency, with severity ranging from prenatal onset to mild adult disease. Most cases are autosomal recessive and result from biallelic loss or mutation of SMN1 on 5q13, most commonly homozygous exon 7 deletion, while SMN2 copy number is the major disease modifier because it predominantly produces unstable truncated survival motor neuron (SMN) protein through exon 7 skipping; rare non-5q SMA genes include UBA1, VAPB, and DYNC1H1. Pathobiology centers on SMN deficiency impairing snRNP assembly, pre-mRNA splicing, axonal mRNA trafficking, neuromuscular junction maturation, cytoskeletal dynamics, and motor neuron survival, with downstream involvement of RNA-processing pathways, ubiquitin-proteasome mechanisms, mitochondrial stress, and denervation-related muscle atrophy signaling. Clinical subtypes include type 0, type I (Werdnig-Hoffmann), type II, type III (Kugelberg-Welander), and type IV, often correlated inversely with SMN2 copy number. Major complications include aspiration, recurrent pneumonia, scoliosis, contractures, hip dislocation, malnutrition, sleep-disordered breathing, and chronic respiratory failure. Diagnosis is established primarily by molecular testing showing SMN1 deletion or pathogenic variants with SMN2 copy-number assessment; supportive studies may include newborn screening, carrier testing, prenatal diagnosis, electromyography showing denervation, and rarely muscle biopsy. Disease-modifying therapies include nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide that promotes SMN2 exon 7 inclusion; risdiplam, an oral SMN2 splicing modifier that increases full-length SMN protein; and onasemnogene abeparvovec, an AAV9-based SMN1 gene replacement therapy, alongside multidisciplinary supportive care including ventilatory, nutritional, and orthopedic management.

Name: Musculoskeletal Diseases
Description: Musculoskeletal diseases (MeSH D009140) comprise a heterogeneous group of disorders affecting bone, cartilage, muscle, tendon, ligament, synovium, and connective tissue, including inflammatory arthritides, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, muscular dystrophies, metabolic bone disease, and heritable connective-tissue disorders. Clinical manifestations commonly include pain, stiffness, swelling, weakness, fatigue, reduced range of motion, deformity, gait impairment, fractures, enthesitis, and loss of function, with major complications such as disability, falls, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, chronic pain syndromes, infection, and depression. Genetic contributors vary by subtype and include HLA-B27 in spondyloarthritis; HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, PTPN22, and STAT4 in rheumatoid arthritis; COL1A1/COL1A2 in osteogenesis imperfecta; DMD mutations causing dystrophin deficiency in Duchenne muscular dystrophy; and FBN1 in Marfan syndrome, with inheritance patterns ranging from multifactorial/polygenic to autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked. Key pathogenic pathways include TNF, IL-6, IL-17/IL-23, RANK/RANKL/OPG-mediated osteoclast activation, NF-κB, JAK-STAT, TGF-β, Wnt/β-catenin, myostatin, and matrix metalloproteinases, involving immune cells, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, chondrocytes, fibroblast-like synoviocytes, and myofibers. Common treatments include NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit COX enzymes and reduce prostaglandin synthesis; glucocorticoids such as prednisone, which suppress NF-κB-driven inflammation; methotrexate, a folate antagonist that increases adenosine and acts as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug; biologics such as adalimumab, a TNF inhibitor; tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor blocker; and alendronate, a bisphosphonate that inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Diagnosis integrates history and examination with inflammatory markers, autoantibodies including rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, creatine kinase, calcium/phosphate/vitamin D studies, genetic testing when indicated, and imaging such as radiography, ultrasound, MRI, DEXA

Name: Myasthenia Gravis
Description: Myasthenia gravis (MeSH D009157) is a chronic autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterized by fluctuating, fatigable skeletal muscle weakness caused most often by pathogenic IgG antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (CHRNA1, CHRNB1, CHRND, CHRNE subunit complex) and less commonly against muscle-specific kinase (MUSK), lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4), or related postsynaptic proteins; in contrast, rare congenital myasthenic syndromes are inherited, nonautoimmune disorders involving genes such as CHRNE, RAPSN, DOK7, COLQ, CHAT, and GFPT1, usually with autosomal recessive inheritance. Core pathogenic pathways include loss of neuromuscular transmission through antibody-mediated receptor blockade, cross-linking and internalization, and complement activation at the postsynaptic membrane, with T-cell/B-cell dysregulation, germinal-center activity, and thymic hyperplasia or thymoma contributing in many AChR-positive cases. Major subtypes include ocular, generalized, AChR-positive, MuSK-positive, LRP4-positive, seronegative, thymoma-associated, neonatal transient myasthenia from maternal antibodies, and congenital myasthenic syndromes. Typical manifestations are ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, facial and neck weakness, proximal limb weakness, and potentially life-threatening respiratory failure in myasthenic crisis. Common treatments include pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases synaptic acetylcholine; corticosteroids such as prednisone, which suppress pathogenic immune responses; steroid-sparing immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil, which inhibit lymphocyte proliferation; and in selected patients thymectomy, IVIG, plasma exchange, rituximab, complement inhibitors eculizumab or ravulizumab, and the FcRn antagonist efgartigimod. Important comorbidities and complications include thymoma, other autoimmune diseases such as autoimmune thyroid disease, lupus, and rheumatoid arthritis, treatment-related infections, aspiration, and respiratory insufficiency. Diagnosis rests on characteristic fatigable weakness, serum autoantibodies, electrophysiology with decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation or increased jitter on single-fiber EMG, bedside ice-pack testing for ptosis, and chest imaging to evaluate thymic disease

Name: Mycoses
Description: Mycoses are fungal infections caused by yeasts, molds, or dimorphic fungi that range from superficial disease of skin, hair, and nails to subcutaneous, allergic, and life-threatening invasive or systemic infection; major subtypes include dermatophytoses and candidiasis, aspergillosis, cryptococcosis, mucormycosis, endemic dimorphic mycoses such as histoplasmosis and coccidioidomycosis, and Pneumocystis pneumonia. Clinical manifestations depend on site and host immunity and include pruritic erythematous plaques, scaling, onychodystrophy, oral or vaginal thrush, fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, sinusitis, fungemia, meningitis, and necrotic tissue invasion. Pathobiology centers on fungal cell-wall and membrane integrity and host innate/adaptive immunity, notably ergosterol biosynthesis, β-1,3-D-glucan and chitin synthesis, biofilm formation, calcineurin and Hsp90 stress-response pathways, and immune recognition through Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, TLR signaling, IL-17/Th17, IFN-γ, and neutrophil/macrophage function. Although most mycoses are not inherited disorders, genetic susceptibility is well described, including CARD9 deficiency causing invasive candidiasis and dermatophytosis, CLEC7A variants, STAT1 gain-of-function and AIRE mutations in chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, and defects in IL17RA/IL17F, STAT3, CYBB, and GATA2 that predispose to specific fungal infections. Important microbial or molecular examples include Candida ALS adhesins and FKS1-mediated echinocandin resistance, Aspergillus cyp51A mutations conferring azole resistance, and Cryptococcus capsule and melanin as virulence factors. Treatment commonly uses azoles such as fluconazole or voriconazole, which inhibit fungal 14-α-demethylase; echinocandins such as caspofungin, which inhibit β-1,3-D-glucan synthase; and amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol to disrupt membranes, with terbinafine inhibiting squalene epoxidase and flucytosine inhibiting fungal nucleic acid synthesis in selected cases. Name: Mycosis Fungoides
Description: Mycosis fungoides (MeSH D009182) is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, an acquired, usually non-inherited mature skin-homing CD4+ memory T-cell neoplasm characterized by epidermotropism and clonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement; classic disease progresses from patch to plaque to tumor stages, with recognized variants including folliculotropic, pagetoid reticulosis, granulomatous slack skin, and large-cell transformation, and Sézary syndrome representing the leukemic erythrodermic end of the spectrum. Recurrent molecular abnormalities are heterogeneous rather than pathognomonic and include altered TCR/NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling, with examples such as STAT3, STAT5B, PLCG1, CARD11, TNFRSF1B, DNMT3A, TET2, TP53, FAS, and CDKN2A lesions, plus overexpression of TOX, GATA3, CCR4, and PD-1 in subsets; malignant cells typically produce Th2-skewed cytokines including IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13, contributing to immune dysregulation. Patients usually present with chronic pruritic erythematous patches or plaques on sun-protected sites, later developing tumors, ulceration, lymphadenopathy, alopecia, palmoplantar disease, or erythroderma, and advanced disease may involve blood, nodes, and viscera. Diagnosis rests on clinicopathologic correlation using repeated skin biopsies showing epidermotropic atypical cerebriform lymphocytes and Pautrier microabscesses, immunophenotyping that often shows CD3+, CD4+, loss of CD7 or CD26, TCR clonality testing by PCR or sequencing, and staging with blood studies, flow cytometry, and imaging when indicated. Important complications include secondary skin infections, severe pruritus, treatment-related immunosuppression, large-cell transformation, and increased risk of other lymphomas or internal malignancies. Common therapies include skin-directed corticosteroids, mechlorethamine causing DNA alkylation, bexarotene activating retinoid X receptors, interferon-α enhancing antitumor immunity, methotrexate inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, histone deacetylase inhibitors such as vorinostat or romidepsin, and targeted agents including brentuximab

Name: Mydriasis
Description: Mydriasis is a clinical sign rather than a single disease entity, defined as abnormal pupillary dilation due to physiological variation or disruption of the autonomic control of the iris, especially increased sympathetic activity or impaired parasympathetic cholinergic constriction of the sphincter pupillae. Key molecular components include muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, particularly CHRM3/M3, adrenergic signaling through α1-adrenergic receptors, postganglionic parasympathetic pathways from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus via the ciliary ganglion, and sympathetic pathways involving norepinephrine release; representative genetic associations are uncommon but include inherited autonomic neuropathies such as IKBKAP/ELP1-related familial dysautonomia, PHOX2B-related autonomic dysfunction, and rare congenital mydriasis reported with ACTA2 mutations affecting iris smooth muscle. Subtypes include physiologic, pharmacologic, paralytic, traumatic, unilateral, bilateral, congenital, and intermittent mydriasis. Typical findings are enlarged pupils, poor light reaction, blurred vision, glare, photophobia, impaired near response, anisocoria when unilateral, and in acute settings headache, ocular pain, ptosis, diplopia, or altered mental status if associated with third-nerve palsy or intracranial mass effect. Important comorbidities and complications include acute angle-closure glaucoma, Adie tonic pupil, autonomic neuropathy, diabetes, migraine, trauma, intoxication, aneurysm, stroke, and uncal herniation. Treatment targets the cause: pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist, can constrict the pupil in some parasympathetic lesions; dapiprazole, an α-adrenergic antagonist, reverses pharmacologic dilation; and apraclonidine, an α2-agonist with weak α1 activity, is mainly diagnostic and therapeutic in Horner-related anisocoria rather than true mydriasis; management may also require discontinuation of anticholinergics such as atropine or tropicamide, or urgent neurosurgical/ophthalmic intervention. Inheritance is usually absent except in rare congenital or syndromic autonomic disorders, which may be autosomal dominant or recessive depending on the gene. Diagnosis relies on pupillary examination in light and dark, anisocoria assessment, extraocular movement and neurologic evaluation, pharmacologic pupil testing, slit-lamp

Name: MYELOFIBROSIS
Description: Myelofibrosis (UMLS C0026987) is a chronic clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm, either primary or evolving secondarily from polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia, characterized by dysregulated hematopoiesis, progressive bone marrow reticulin/collagen fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, cytopenias, and risk of leukemic transformation to acute myeloid leukemia. Central molecular lesions typically involve constitutive JAK-STAT signaling driven by JAK2 mutations, especially JAK2 V617F, CALR exon 9 frameshift mutations, or MPL mutations, with frequent cooperating lesions in epigenetic, splicing, and tumor suppressor genes such as ASXL1, TET2, DNMT3A, EZH2, SRSF2, IDH1/2, and TP53; abnormal cytokine networks, including thrombopoietin/MPL, interleukin-6, TGF-beta, and NF-kappaB signaling, contribute to megakaryocytic atypia, fibroblast activation, and stromal remodeling. Most cases are acquired rather than inherited, although rare familial clustering and inherited predisposition to myeloproliferative neoplasms are recognized. Typical findings include fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, fever, early satiety, abdominal fullness from massive splenomegaly, bone pain, pruritus, pallor, hepatomegaly, anemia, leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop erythrocytes, thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis, and elevated LDH. Important complications and comorbidities include portal hypertension, thrombosis, bleeding, infections, cachexia, transfusion dependence, gout/hyperuricemia, pulmonary hypertension, and iron overload. Diagnosis relies on WHO/ICC clinicopathologic criteria integrating CBC and smear, bone marrow biopsy showing megakaryocytic proliferation with reticulin or collagen fibrosis, exclusion of other myeloid neoplasms, and molecular testing for JAK2, CALR, and MPL, with cytogenetics and next-generation sequencing aiding prognosis. Name: Myeloproliferative Disorders
Description: Myeloproliferative disorders, now commonly classified as myeloproliferative neoplasms, are clonal hematopoietic stem-cell diseases characterized by chronic overproduction of one or more myeloid lineages; major subtypes include chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis, with overlap or unclassifiable forms also recognized. Their molecular basis typically involves constitutive tyrosine kinase or cytokine-receptor signaling, most notably BCR-ABL1 from t(9;22) in chronic myeloid leukemia and JAK-STAT pathway activation through JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutations, CALR frameshift mutations, and MPL mutations in Philadelphia chromosome-negative disease; cooperating lesions such as TET2, ASXL1, DNMT3A, EZH2, IDH1/2, and SRSF2 may influence phenotype, prognosis, and leukemic transformation. Key pathways include JAK-STAT, MAPK/ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, cytokine signaling via thrombopoietin and erythropoietin receptors, and inflammatory/fibrogenic signaling involving megakaryocytes, TGF-β, and marrow stromal cells. Patients commonly present with fatigue, pruritus, night sweats, weight loss, headaches, erythromelalgia, splenomegaly, early satiety, thrombosis or hemorrhage, and abnormal blood counts, while complications include Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal or arterial thrombosis, gout, hyperuricemia, myelofibrosis, cytopenias, and progression to acute myeloid leukemia. Most cases are acquired and sporadic, although familial predisposition occurs, including inherited risk alleles such as JAK2 46/1 haplotype and rare germline variants in JAK2, MPL, TERT, or SH2B3. Diagnosis integrates CBC and smear findings, bone marrow morphology and fibrosis grading, serum erythropoietin, cytogenetics, and molecular testing for BCR-ABL1, JAK2, CALR, and MPL, using WHO/ICC criteria. Name: Myocardial Infarction
Description: Myocardial infarction (MI) is an acute ischemic necrosis of myocardium, usually caused by atherosclerotic plaque rupture or erosion with coronary thrombosis, and is classified clinically as ST-elevation MI, non-ST-elevation MI, and less commonly type 2 MI from supply-demand mismatch. Its pathobiology centers on endothelial dysfunction, lipid accumulation, inflammation, platelet activation, and myocyte death, involving pathways such as LDL oxidation, IL-1/TNF/NF-κB inflammatory signaling, coagulation and thrombin generation, platelet P2Y12 and thromboxane A2 signaling, calcium overload, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and ischemia-response pathways including HIF-1. Genetic susceptibility is typically polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative loci including 9p21 near CDKN2A/CDKN2B, LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, LPA, APOE, and genes affecting thrombosis or homocysteine metabolism such as F5 and MTHFR; rare inherited contributors include familial hypercholesterolemia from LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 variants. Relevant proteins include troponin I/T, CK-MB, CRP, fibrinogen, P-selectin, and lipoprotein(a). Common symptoms are crushing substernal chest pain or pressure radiating to the arm, neck, or jaw, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, and syncope, although atypical or silent presentations occur, especially in diabetes, women, and older adults. Diagnosis relies on the universal definition: a rise and/or fall in cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile plus evidence of ischemia from symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes or Q waves, imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or wall-motion abnormality, or angiographic thrombus; testing includes serial ECGs, high-sensitivity troponin, echocardiography, coronary angiography, and sometimes cardiac MRI. Standard treatment includes aspirin, an irreversible COX-1 inhibitor that suppresses thromboxane-mediated platelet aggregation, P2Y12 inhibitors such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor that block ADP-dependent platelet activation, anticoagulants such as heparin that potentiate antithrombin, beta-blockers that reduce myocardial oxygen demand, statins that inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and stabilize plaque, and reperfusion with

Name: Myxedema
Description: Myxedema denotes severe, advanced hypothyroidism, classically characterized by dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation causing nonpitting edema and, in its extreme form, myxedema coma; it is usually acquired from autoimmune thyroid failure such as Hashimoto thyroiditis but may also follow thyroidectomy, radioiodine, central hypothyroidism, iodine deficiency, or congenital defects in thyroid development or hormone synthesis. Genetic contributors include HLA-DR variants and immune-regulatory genes such as CTLA4 and PTPN22 in autoimmune disease, and rarer monogenic causes involving TSHR, TPO, TG, DUOX2, SLC5A5/NIS, IYD, PAX8, NKX2-1, FOXE1, and TSHB; inheritance is typically complex multifactorial in autoimmune cases but may be autosomal recessive or dominant in congenital hypothyroidism depending on the gene. Pathobiology centers on impaired thyroid hormone production and reduced T3 signaling through thyroid hormone receptors, with altered hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis feedback involving TRH and TSH, reduced mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, depressed adrenergic responsiveness, and fibroblast glycosaminoglycan deposition. Clinical features include fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, dry coarse skin, alopecia, hoarseness, delayed reflex relaxation, cognitive slowing, depression, menstrual disturbance, and in severe cases hypothermia, hypoventilation, hypotension, hyponatremia, and coma. Diagnosis relies on elevated TSH with low free T4 in primary disease, low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4 in central disease, anti-TPO or anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, lipid and sodium abnormalities, and selected thyroid ultrasound, pituitary imaging, or newborn screening. Major subtypes include primary, secondary, tertiary, congenital, and myxedema coma. Treatment is thyroid hormone replacement: levothyroxine, a synthetic T4 prohormone converted to T3; liothyronine, synthetic T3 acting directly at nuclear receptors; and intravenous levothyroxine or liothyronine for coma, often with empiric hydrocortisone to cover possible adrenal insufficiency. Comorbidities and complications include hyperlipidemia, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, pericardial effusion, infertility, pregnancy complications, anemia, neuropathy

Name: Narcolepsy
Description: Narcolepsy (MeSH D009290) is a chronic central disorder of hypersomnolence characterized by instability of sleep–wake regulation, classically presenting with excessive daytime sleepiness, irresistible sleep attacks, fragmented nocturnal sleep, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, and, in type 1 disease, cataplexy. Its core biology centers on loss or dysfunction of hypothalamic orexin/hypocretin neurons, with deficient hypocretin-1 signaling through orexin receptors OX1R and OX2R and downstream arousal networks involving histaminergic, noradrenergic, dopaminergic, serotonergic, and cholinergic pathways; autoimmune mechanisms are strongly implicated, particularly in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02, often with associations at T-cell receptor loci such as TCRA and other immune-related genes including P2RY11 and CTSH. Rare familial or syndromic cases involve variants affecting hypocretin signaling, including HCRT, HCRTR2, or broader neurologic disorders, but most cases are sporadic with complex polygenic risk rather than Mendelian inheritance. Major subtypes are narcolepsy type 1, defined by cataplexy and/or low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1, and type 2, in which cataplexy is absent and hypocretin is usually normal or unmeasured. Diagnosis relies on clinical history plus polysomnography followed by multiple sleep latency testing showing mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with at least two sleep-onset REM periods; CSF hypocretin-1 measurement and HLA typing can support diagnosis. Common comorbidities include obesity, depression, anxiety, attention and cognitive difficulties, obstructive sleep apnea, REM sleep behavior phenomena, and accident risk. Treatment is symptomatic: modafinil or armodafinil promote wakefulness partly via dopaminergic catecholamine effects; solriamfetol inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake; pitolisant is an H3-receptor inverse agonist enhancing histaminergic arousal; and sodium oxybate or low-sodium oxybate, acting through GABA-B–related mechanisms, improve daytime sleepiness and cataplexy, while antidepressants such as venlafaxine or clomipramine suppress cataplexy via monoaminergic REM inhibition.

Name: Congestion of nose
Description: Congestion of the nose (UMLS C0027424) is a common clinical manifestation rather than a single disease, reflecting mucosal inflammation, venous engorgement, edema, and/or excess secretions in disorders such as acute viral rhinitis, allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without nasal polyps, nonallergic/vasomotor rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, and structural obstruction. Typical symptoms include nasal blockage, rhinorrhea, sneezing, pruritus, hyposmia, facial pressure, mouth breathing, snoring, and postnasal drip, with exam findings of swollen turbinates, erythematous or pale boggy mucosa, and sometimes polyps or purulence. Molecular contributors are best defined in allergic and polypoid disease and include IgE-FcεRI signaling, mast-cell mediators, eosinophilic type 2 inflammation driven by IL4, IL5, IL13, TSLP, and eotaxins, leukotriene and histamine pathways, and epithelial barrier genes/proteins such as FLG, TLRs, and mucins; CRS with polyps may also involve CLC, periostin, and local IgE, while primary ciliary dyskinesia genes such as DNAH5 or DNAI1 and CFTR mutations can predispose to chronic sinonasal congestion. Inheritance is usually complex and polygenic, with familial atopy common; Mendelian associations are uncommon and mainly occur in syndromic or monogenic causes such as cystic fibrosis or primary ciliary dyskinesia. Treatment depends on etiology and commonly includes intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone or budesonide, which suppress NF-κB-mediated cytokine transcription and eosinophilic inflammation; antihistamines such as cetirizine, which block H1 receptors; and decongestants such as pseudoephedrine or oxymetazoline, alpha-adrenergic agonists that vasoconstrict nasal capacitance vessels. Saline irrigation, ipratropium, leukotriene antagonists, antibiotics for selected bacterial sinusitis, and biologics such as dupilumab may be used. Important comorbidities include asthma, atopic dermatitis, conjunctivitis, chronic sinusitis, otitis media, obstructive sleep apnea, and anosmia; complications include sleep disturbance, impaired quality of life

Name: Nausea
Description: Nausea (MeSH D009325) is a subjective, multifactorial symptom rather than a primary disease, defined by the unpleasant sensation of impending vomiting and arising from activation of central emetic networks in the area postrema, nucleus tractus solitarius, dorsal vagal complex, vestibular nuclei, cortex, and enteric-vagal afferents. Key molecular pathways include serotonergic 5-HT3 signaling from enterochromaffin cells, dopaminergic D2 transmission in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, histaminergic H1 and muscarinic M1 vestibular pathways, neurokinin-1 signaling mediated by substance P, cannabinoid CB1 pathways, and inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and cytokines. Although nausea is usually acquired, genetic susceptibility influences motion sickness, migraine-associated nausea, postoperative nausea and vomiting, and drug response; representative associations include polymorphisms in HTR3A/HTR3B, TACR1, DRD2, COMT, OPRM1, ABCB1, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4/5 affecting receptor sensitivity or antiemetic pharmacokinetics. Common clinical features include epigastric awareness, autonomic symptoms such as pallor, diaphoresis, hypersalivation, tachycardia, and often retching or vomiting; major subtypes include acute infectious or toxic nausea, postoperative, chemotherapy-induced, pregnancy-related, vestibular/motion-related, migraine-associated, gastroparetic, functional or chronic unexplained nausea, and psychogenic forms. Frequent comorbidities include gastroenteritis, GERD, peptic ulcer disease, gastroparesis, bowel obstruction, pancreatobiliary disease, pregnancy, vestibular disorders, migraine, anxiety, intracranial pathology, renal or hepatic failure, and adverse drug effects; complications include dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, malnutrition, aspiration, and reduced treatment adherence. Treatment targets cause and pathway: ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors, metoclopramide antagonizes D2 receptors and is prokinetic via 5-HT4 agonism, promethazine blocks H1 receptors with anticholinergic effects, scopolamine antagonizes M1 receptors, and aprepitant blocks NK1 receptors. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, based on history, medication review, examination, pregnancy testing when relevant, and selective testing such as CBC, electroly

Name: Vomiting and Nausea
Description: Vomiting and nausea (UMLS C0027498) are symptoms rather than a single inherited disease, arising from activation of the medullary vomiting center and chemoreceptor trigger zone through vagal and enteric inputs, vestibular pathways, and higher cortical circuits; key molecular mediators include serotonin acting at 5-HT3 receptors, dopamine at D2 receptors, histamine at H1 receptors, acetylcholine at muscarinic M1 receptors, substance P at neurokinin-1 receptors, and endocannabinoid signaling via CB1. Genetic contributors are best established in specific subtypes and treatment responses, including RYR2 and CACNA1A variants reported in cyclic vomiting syndrome and migraine-related emesis, SCN1A and POLG in epileptic or mitochondrial disorders with recurrent vomiting, and CYP2D6 or HTR3 family variation influencing antiemetic efficacy; inheritance is usually non-Mendelian unless vomiting occurs within monogenic neurologic, metabolic, or mitochondrial syndromes, which may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or maternal in mitochondrial disease. Major clinical forms include acute infectious or toxic vomiting, postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, motion sickness, pregnancy-related nausea including hyperemesis gravidarum, gastroparesis-related, vestibular, migraine-associated, and cyclic vomiting syndrome. Typical manifestations are queasiness, retching, emesis, pallor, diaphoresis, abdominal discomfort, dehydration, weight loss, electrolyte disturbance, and occasionally hematemesis or aspiration. Common treatments include ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist; metoclopramide, a D2 antagonist with prokinetic 5-HT4 agonist activity; promethazine, an H1 antihistamine with anticholinergic effects; scopolamine, an M1 antagonist; aprepitant, an NK1 antagonist; and in selected cases prochlorperazine or cannabinoid-based agents. Important comorbidities and complications include gastroenteritis, migraine, pregnancy, diabetes with gastroparesis, bowel obstruction, pancreatobiliary disease, intracranial pathology, anxiety, malnutrition, metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, Mallory-Weiss tear, and aspiration pneumonia. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, based on history, examination, medication review, pregnancy testing, serum electrolytes, renal and liver panels, glucose, lipase, ECG when QT-prolong

Name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia
Description: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN; UMLS C0027662) comprises inherited cancer-predisposition syndromes characterized by multifocal hyperplasia and neoplasia of endocrine tissues, principally MEN1, MEN2A, MEN2B, and related familial medullary thyroid cancer; MEN1 is caused by germline inactivating mutations of MEN1 encoding menin, a tumor-suppressor that regulates transcription, chromatin remodeling, DNA repair, and TGF-β/JunD and cell-cycle pathways, whereas MEN2 syndromes are usually due to activating RET proto-oncogene mutations, driving receptor tyrosine kinase signaling through RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, PLCγ, and JAK/STAT pathways, with subtype correlations such as RET codon 634 in MEN2A and M918T in MEN2B; rare MEN-like phenocopies involve CDKN1B and other cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor genes. MEN1 typically presents with parathyroid adenomas causing primary hyperparathyroidism, pancreaticoduodenal neuroendocrine tumors such as gastrinomas or insulinomas, and pituitary adenomas, while MEN2 features medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and in MEN2A hyperparathyroidism, or in MEN2B mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, and aggressive early thyroid cancer. Symptoms include nephrolithiasis, bone loss, peptic ulcer disease, hypoglycemia, diarrhea, headaches, visual changes, episodic hypertension, palpitations, and flushing; complications include metastatic endocrine malignancy, hypertensive crisis, severe hypercalcemia, and hormone-excess syndromes. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant with high penetrance. Diagnosis integrates family history, clinical criteria, biochemical testing such as calcium/PTH, prolactin, gastrin, insulin, calcitonin, metanephrines, and other hormone assays, anatomical and functional imaging, and confirmatory germline genetic testing with RET or MEN1 sequencing and genotype-guided surveillance. Treatment includes surgery as the mainstay, with calcimimetics such as cinacalcet activating the calcium-sensing receptor for hyperparathyroidism, proton pump inhibitors blocking gastric H+/K+-ATPase for gastrinoma-associated acid hypersecretion, somatostatin analogs such as octreotide inhibiting hormone release in neuroendocrine tumors, tyrosine kinase

Name: Wilms Tumor
Description: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma; MeSH D009396) is a malignant embryonal renal tumor of childhood arising from aberrant nephrogenesis, classically composed of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements and divided into favorable-histology and anaplastic/high-risk forms, with variants including bilateral or multifocal disease. Its molecular basis commonly involves alterations in WT1 on 11p13, IGF2/H19 imprinting abnormalities at 11p15, WTX/AMER1, CTNNB1, TP53 in diffuse anaplasia, and less often MYCN, DROSHA, DGCR8, SIX1, and SIX2, implicating WNT/β-catenin, p53-mediated DNA-damage control, IGF/PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and developmental kidney pathways. Most cases are sporadic, but predisposition may be germline and usually autosomal dominant with variable penetrance in syndromic settings such as WAGR syndrome, Denys-Drash and Frasier syndromes (WT1-related), Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15 imprinting defects), and Perlman syndrome; associated congenital anomalies and comorbidities include aniridia, hemihyperplasia, genitourinary malformations, cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and nephrogenic rests. Patients typically present with an asymptomatic enlarging abdominal mass, abdominal pain, hematuria, hypertension from renin secretion, fever, anemia, and occasionally tumor rupture; complications include pulmonary or hepatic metastases, renal insufficiency, treatment-related cardiomyopathy, infertility, and secondary malignancy. Diagnosis relies on renal ultrasound followed by contrast-enhanced CT or MRI for local staging and bilateral disease assessment, chest CT for lung metastases, urinalysis and renal function tests, and histopathologic confirmation after nephrectomy or biopsy depending on protocol, with molecular testing for 1p/16q loss, 11p15 changes, WT1/TP53 status, and germline evaluation when syndromic features are present. Standard therapy combines surgery with chemotherapy such as vincristine, which inhibits microtubule assembly, dactinomycin, which intercalates DNA and blocks RNA synthesis, and doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor that also generates free radicals; higher-risk disease may require cyclophosphamide,

Name: Nephrotic Syndrome
Description: Nephrotic syndrome is a clinicopathologic syndrome caused by glomerular filtration barrier injury, classically defined by heavy proteinuria exceeding 3.5 g/24 h, hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria; common symptoms and signs include periorbital or dependent edema, foamy urine, weight gain, fatigue, and sometimes hypertension, hematuria, or reduced kidney function. Major primary subtypes include minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, and congenital or hereditary nephrotic syndromes, while secondary forms occur with diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, infections, amyloidosis, malignancy, and drugs. Key molecular determinants involve podocyte slit-diaphragm and basement membrane genes and proteins such as NPHS1/nephrin, NPHS2/podocin, WT1, LAMB2, PLCE1, ACTN4, TRPC6, INF2, APOL1 risk alleles, and in membranous nephropathy PLA2R and THSD7A autoantigen pathways; pathogenic signaling includes podocyte actin-cytoskeleton dysregulation, RhoA/Rac1/Cdc42, TRPC6-calcium and calcineurin-NFAT signaling, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, TGF-beta, VEGF, complement activation, and immune cytokine pathways affecting permeability. Inheritance may be autosomal recessive, dominant, X-linked, or complex depending on etiology, with congenital nephrotic syndrome often recessive, for example NPHS1 or NPHS2 mutations. Diagnosis relies on urinalysis and urine protein quantification, serum albumin, creatinine and lipid levels, serologic testing for secondary causes, anti-PLA2R antibodies when relevant, renal ultrasound, genetic testing in early-onset or familial disease, and kidney biopsy to define histology except in selected children with presumed minimal change disease. Treatment commonly includes corticosteroids, which suppress inflammatory and lymphocyte-mediated permeability factors; calcineurin inhibitors such as cyclosporine or tacrolimus, which inhibit calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation and stabilize podocyte cytoskeleton; and renin-angiotensin system blockers such as ACE inhibitors or ARBs, which reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria; additional agents include rituximab, diuretics,

Name: Neuroblastoma
Description: Neuroblastoma (MeSH D009447) is a malignant embryonal tumor of the sympathetic nervous system arising from neural crest–derived precursors, usually in the adrenal medulla or paraspinal ganglia, and is the most common extracranial solid cancer of childhood. Its biology is strongly shaped by genomic alterations including MYCN amplification, ALK activating mutations or amplification, PHOX2B pathogenic variants, segmental chromosomal abnormalities such as 1p and 11q loss and 17q gain, ATRX mutation in older children, and TERT rearrangements; familial cases are uncommon and typically show autosomal dominant predisposition with incomplete penetrance involving ALK or PHOX2B. Dysregulated pathways prominently include ALK-RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53-MDM2, Trk neurotrophin signaling including NTRK1/TrkA and BDNF-NTRK2/TrkB, telomere maintenance, and angiogenic and differentiation programs. Clinical presentation varies from asymptomatic abdominal mass to abdominal pain, distension, weight loss, fever, bone pain, limp, anemia, periorbital ecchymoses, spinal cord compression, hypertension, diarrhea from vasoactive intestinal peptide, or opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome; common complications include marrow failure, metastatic bone and liver disease, Horner syndrome, treatment-related cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, hearing loss, infertility, and secondary malignancies. Subtypes are defined by risk and stage, including localized, metastatic, and the infantile MS/4S pattern with skin, liver, and marrow dissemination. Diagnosis relies on histopathology of tumor or marrow plus demonstration of catecholamine excess with urinary VMA/HVA, imaging with MRI or CT and metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy, marrow evaluation, and molecular risk stratification assessing MYCN, 11q, ploidy, and segmental aberrations. Treatment commonly uses vincristine, a microtubule inhibitor, cyclophosphamide, an alkylating DNA crosslinker, doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor and free radical generator, cisplatin, a platinum DNA crosslinker, etoposide, another topoisomerase II inhibitor, isotretinoin to induce differentiation, anti-GD2 immunotherapy such as dinutux

Name: Neurofibromatosis 1
Description: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1; UMLS C0027831) is a common autosomal dominant neurocutaneous tumor-predisposition disorder caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants or deletions of NF1 on 17q11.2, including truncating, splice-site, missense, whole-gene deletion, and mosaic mutations; NF1 encodes neurofibromin, a Ras GTPase-activating protein that negatively regulates RAS/MAPK and also influences PI3K-AKT-mTOR and cAMP signaling, so biallelic inactivation in tumors drives proliferation of Schwann cells, fibroblasts, mast cells, and other neural crest-derived elements. Major manifestations include multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, cutaneous, subcutaneous, and plexiform neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, distinctive osseous lesions such as sphenoid dysplasia or tibial pseudarthrosis, scoliosis, macrocephaly, short stature, chronic pain, pruritus, and frequent neurodevelopmental and behavioral problems including learning disability, ADHD, and autism-spectrum features; vascular disease, hypertension, epilepsy, and osteoporosis may occur. Important complications include disfigurement, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, other gliomas, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, pheochromocytoma, breast cancer risk, and compressive neurologic deficits. Phenotypic forms include generalized/classic NF1, segmental or mosaic NF1, spinal NF1, and microdeletion-associated severe disease. Diagnosis is clinical using NIH/updated international criteria, supported by molecular testing of NF1 and, when needed, SPRED1 to distinguish Legius syndrome; testing methods include sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis, RNA studies for splicing defects, ophthalmologic examination, MRI for optic or plexiform tumors, and targeted evaluation of skeletal or vascular lesions. Treatment is multidisciplinary and largely complication-directed; selumetinib, a MEK1/2 inhibitor, is used for symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, while trametinib has similar MAPK-pathway inhibition in selected cases, surgery debulks symptomatic tumors, and conventional agents such as carboplatin/vincristine for optic pathway glioma and antihypertensives for NF1-related hypertension are commonly employed.

Name: Neurosyphilis
Description: Neurosyphilis (MeSH D009494) is an acquired infection of the central nervous system caused by dissemination of Treponema pallidum after untreated or inadequately treated syphilis, classically manifesting as asymptomatic neurosyphilis, meningeal, meningovascular, parenchymatous disease including general paresis and tabes dorsalis, and ocular or otic syphilis. It is not a Mendelian disorder and has no established inheritance pattern, but host susceptibility and severity may be influenced by immune-response genes and proteins such as HLA class II alleles, TLR1/TLR2 signaling components, TNF, IL6, IL10, IFNG, CXCL13, and chemokines regulating B-cell and macrophage trafficking; treponemal lipoproteins activate innate immune pathways through TLR2/NF-kB, driving microglial activation, endothelial inflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and CSF pleocytosis. Typical features include headache, meningismus, cranial neuropathies, stroke in younger adults from obliterative endarteritis, cognitive decline, psychiatric change, sensory ataxia, lightning pains, Argyll Robertson pupils, hearing loss, and visual impairment. Major comorbidities and risk modifiers include HIV coinfection, other sexually transmitted infections, cardiovascular syphilis, pregnancy-associated vertical transmission risk, and complications such as ischemic stroke, dementia, blindness, deafness, and chronic neuropathic pain. Diagnosis relies on compatible neurologic, ocular, or auditory syndromes in a patient with reactive serum treponemal and nontreponemal tests, supported by CSF abnormalities including lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and reactive CSF-VDRL, with CSF FTA-ABS or TP-PA used when suspicion remains high despite a nonreactive CSF-VDRL; neuroimaging and ophthalmologic or audiologic evaluation help define subtype and exclude mimics. Standard treatment is intravenous aqueous penicillin G, a beta-lactam that inhibits treponemal cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; alternatives in selected cases include intramuscular procaine penicillin plus oral probenecid, which raises penicillin levels by blocking renal tubular secretion, and ceftriaxone, a cephalosporin beta-lactam with similar cell-wall inhibition, while doxycycline, a tetr

Name: Dependence, Nicotine
Description: Tobacco use disorder (MeSH D014029) is a chronic, relapsing substance-use disorder characterized by compulsive nicotine seeking and continued use despite harm, typically presenting with craving, tolerance, withdrawal, inability to cut down, irritability, anxiety, dysphoria, restlessness, impaired concentration, increased appetite, and strong cue-induced smoking behavior. It is commonly conceptualized as mild, moderate, or severe by DSM-5 criteria and may occur predominantly with combustible cigarettes, smokeless tobacco, cigars, or electronic nicotine delivery systems. Its biology centers on nicotine activation of neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, especially the α4β2 and α7 subtypes encoded by CHRNA4, CHRNB2, and CHRNA7, with strong genetic associations in the CHRNA5-CHRNA3-CHRNB4 cluster, notably CHRNA5 rs16969968; other implicated genes include CYP2A6, which influences nicotine metabolism, DRD2, SLC6A3, COMT, OPRM1, and BDNF. Key pathways involve mesolimbic dopaminergic reward signaling from the ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens, glutamatergic and GABAergic modulation, cAMP-CREB and MAPK signaling, and stress-axis mechanisms involving corticotropin-releasing hormone. Heritability is moderate, roughly 40-70%, with complex polygenic, non-Mendelian inheritance shaped by environmental exposure. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 substance-use criteria, nicotine dependence scales such as the Fagerström Test, and confirmation of recent exposure by cotinine testing in blood, saliva, or urine, exhaled carbon monoxide, or anabasine testing when nicotine replacement is used. First-line treatments include nicotine replacement therapy, a nicotinic receptor agonist/substitution strategy; varenicline, a partial agonist at α4β2 receptors that reduces withdrawal and blocks reward; and bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor and nicotinic antagonist; cytisinicline/cytisine is another partial nicotinic agonist. Common comorbidities and complications include depression, anxiety, alcohol and other substance use disorders, COPD, cardiovascular disease, stroke, multiple cancers, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and all-cause mortality.

Name: Nocardia Infections
Description: Nocardia infections are opportunistic, suppurative to granulomatous bacterial diseases caused by aerobic, weakly acid-fast, branching filamentous actinomycetes, most commonly members of the Nocardia asteroides complex, N. farcinica, N. brasiliensis, and N. otitidiscaviarum, presenting as pulmonary, cutaneous/lymphocutaneous, or disseminated, particularly CNS disease. Host susceptibility is strongly linked to impaired cell-mediated immunity rather than Mendelian inheritance, with genetic and protein defects reported in IFN-gamma/IL-12 axis and phagocyte function, including IL12RB1, IFNGR1, STAT1, CYBB/gp91phox and other chronic granulomatous disease genes, as well as GATA2 deficiency; these implicate macrophage activation, Th1 signaling, NADPH oxidase-dependent respiratory burst, TNF-alpha/NF-kappaB, and pattern-recognition pathways such as TLR2-mediated innate immune responses. Major comorbidities include corticosteroid exposure, solid-organ or hematopoietic transplantation, HIV/AIDS, malignancy, chronic lung disease including COPD and bronchiectasis, diabetes, and chronic granulomatous disease; complications include cavitary pneumonia, empyema, brain abscess, meningitis, bacteremia, and multisite dissemination. Typical manifestations are subacute fever, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, nodules or abscesses, cellulitis, draining sinuses, mycetoma, and focal neurologic deficits or seizures when the CNS is involved. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion in at-risk hosts, imaging such as chest CT or brain MRI, direct microscopy showing beaded branching Gram-positive weakly acid-fast organisms, culture with speciation, and increasingly 16S rRNA sequencing or MALDI-TOF; susceptibility testing is important because resistance patterns vary by species. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is standard therapy by sequential inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase; imipenem inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins; amikacin binds the 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; linezolid blocks 50S initiation complex formation, and minocycline inhibits 30S translation, with prolonged combination treatment often required for severe or disseminated disease.

Name: Noonan Syndrome
Description: Noonan syndrome (UMLS C0028326) is a genetically heterogeneous, usually autosomal dominant RASopathy characterized by dysregulation of the RAS-MAPK signaling cascade, most commonly due to pathogenic variants in PTPN11 encoding SHP2, and less often SOS1, RAF1, KRAS, RIT1, NRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1, SOS2, LZTR1, MRAS, RRAS2, or SHOC2; gain-of-function effects that enhance signaling through RAS, RAF, MEK, and ERK underlie abnormal growth, cardiac development, lymphatic function, and hematopoiesis. Typical features include distinctive facies with hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, webbed neck, short stature, pectus deformity, congenital heart disease, developmental delay, feeding difficulty, cryptorchidism, bleeding diathesis, scoliosis, and lymphatic abnormalities. Major subphenotypes include Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines, often linked to specific PTPN11 or RAF1 variants, and clinically overlapping forms such as Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair associated with SHOC2. Comorbidities and complications include pulmonary valve stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, atrial septal defects, arrhythmias, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia and other myeloproliferative disorders, hearing loss, infertility, and psychosocial impairment. Diagnosis is based on characteristic clinical criteria supported by echocardiography, growth and developmental assessment, coagulation studies, and molecular confirmation by targeted multigene RASopathy panels, single-gene testing when phenotype is suggestive, or exome sequencing; prenatal ultrasound may show increased nuchal translucency, cystic hygroma, or hydrops. Management is supportive and complication-directed: recombinant human growth hormone stimulates IGF-1 signaling to improve linear growth in selected children, propranolol or other beta-blockers reduce adrenergic drive for arrhythmia or hypertrophic obstructive physiology, furosemide inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter to treat heart failure-related congestion, and in severe refractory hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten may be considered.

Name: Nocturia
Description: Nocturia (UMLS C0028734) is a symptom-defined lower urinary tract disorder characterized by waking from sleep one or more times to void, with clinically significant disease often defined by bothersome episodes, commonly at least two nightly voids, and it is broadly classified into nocturnal polyuria, global polyuria, reduced nocturnal bladder capacity, mixed forms, and secondary nocturia due to sleep, endocrine, cardiovascular, renal, neurologic, or urologic disease. Typical manifestations include fragmented sleep, urgency, frequency, reduced quality of life, fatigue, falls, and fractures in older adults. Major comorbidities include benign prostatic hyperplasia, overactive bladder, urinary tract infection, diabetes mellitus or insipidus, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, peripheral edema, depression, and neurodegenerative disease. Its biology is heterogeneous rather than monogenic, but relevant molecular systems include arginine vasopressin signaling through AVPR2 and AQP2 in renal collecting ducts regulating nocturnal water reabsorption, circadian clock pathways involving CLOCK, BMAL1/ARNTL, PER, and CRY, natriuretic peptide signaling with ANP/BNP, and bladder sensory-contractile pathways involving muscarinic M3, beta3-adrenergic, and prostaglandin signaling; rare inherited contributors include AVP, AVPR2, or AQP2 defects causing diabetes insipidus and aquaporin dysregulation, and salt-handling gene defects such as SLC12A3 in Gitelman syndrome, which can present with nocturia. Diagnosis relies on history, physical examination, medication review, urinalysis, serum glucose, electrolytes and renal function, postvoid residual assessment, and especially a frequency-volume chart to distinguish nocturnal polyuria from reduced bladder capacity. Common treatments include desmopressin, a vasopressin V2-receptor agonist that increases collecting-duct water reabsorption; antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin or tolterodine, which inhibit M3-mediated detrusor overactivity; beta3-agonists such as mirabegron, which relax detrusor smooth muscle; and, when outlet obstruction contributes, alpha1-blockers such as tamsulosin, which reduce prostatic/bladder neck tone.

Name: Obesity
Description: Obesity (MeSH D009765) is a chronic, multifactorial, relapsing adiposity disease characterized by excess body fat sufficient to impair health, most commonly presenting with increased BMI and central adiposity, and clinically associated with weight gain, enlarged waist circumference, exertional dyspnea, fatigue, reduced mobility, osteoarticular pain, snoring, and acanthosis nigricans. It comprises polygenic common obesity and rarer monogenic or syndromic forms, including leptin deficiency, MC4R-related obesity, Prader-Willi syndrome, and Bardet-Biedl syndrome; heritability is substantial, with important genetic contributors including FTO, MC4R, LEP, LEPR, POMC, PCSK1, SIM1, BDNF, and SH2B1, inherited most often in complex polygenic fashion but sometimes as autosomal recessive or dominant defects. Core pathobiology involves dysregulation of hypothalamic leptin-melanocortin signaling, insulin/PI3K-AKT and AMPK-mTOR nutrient-sensing pathways, sympathetic and reward circuitry, adipokine and inflammatory mediators such as leptin, adiponectin, TNF-α, IL-6, and altered GLP-1 signaling, leading to increased intake, reduced satiety, insulin resistance, adipose expansion, and ectopic lipid deposition. Major comorbidities include type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, infertility, polycystic ovary syndrome, gastroesophageal reflux, osteoarthritis, depression, and increased risk of several cancers. Diagnosis is based on BMI, typically ≥30 kg/m2 in adults, waist circumference and obesity-related complications, with severity further assessed by metabolic profile, liver enzymes, HbA1c or fasting glucose, lipid testing, blood pressure, sleep apnea evaluation, and, when early-onset severe obesity, hyperphagia, developmental features, or family history suggest, targeted genetic testing. Treatment centers on lifestyle intervention plus anti-obesity pharmacotherapy such as orlistat, a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor; liraglutide or semaglutide, GLP-1 receptor agonists that enhance satiety and delay gastric emptying; phentermine/topiramate, combining sympathomimetic appetite suppression with central anticonvulsant

Name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
Description: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD; MeSH D009771) is a chronic, often disabling neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by intrusive obsessions and/or repetitive compulsions that are time-consuming, distressing, and recognized as excessive to variable degrees, with common symptom dimensions including contamination/cleaning, symmetry/ordering, taboo thoughts/checking, and hoarding-related features, the latter now often classified separately. Its pathobiology is strongly linked to dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits involving orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, caudate, and thalamus, with serotonergic, glutamatergic, dopaminergic, and GABAergic signaling implicated; representative genetic associations include SLC6A4, HTR2A, SLC1A1, DLGAP3, SAPAP3, GRIN2B, COMT, BDNF, and rare copy-number or synaptic variants, while PANDAS/PANS-like presentations suggest immune-mediated mechanisms involving basal ganglia inflammation. OCD is typically multifactorial with moderate heritability, often higher in early-onset cases, showing complex polygenic inheritance rather than Mendelian transmission, though familial aggregation is well established. Comorbidities commonly include major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety, tic disorders/Tourette syndrome, autism spectrum traits, ADHD, body dysmorphic disorder, eating disorders, and substance misuse, with complications such as severe functional impairment, social isolation, dermatologic injury from washing, and elevated suicidality. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 criteria, psychiatric interview, severity scales such as Y-BOCS, assessment of insight, and exclusion of substance-, medication-, or neurologic causes; testing may include neuropsychological evaluation and targeted laboratory or neurologic workup when atypical or abrupt pediatric onset is suspected. First-line pharmacotherapy includes selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine, sertraline, and fluvoxamine, which block SLC6A4-mediated serotonin reuptake, and clomipramine, a potent serotonin reuptake-inhibiting tricyclic; augmentation for resistant disease often uses antipsychotics such as risperidone or aripiprazole, which modulate dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2 signaling.

Name: Ocular Hypertension
Description: Ocular hypertension is a usually asymptomatic state defined by chronically elevated intraocular pressure (classically >21 mmHg on repeated measurements) without reproducible glaucomatous optic neuropathy, retinal nerve fiber layer loss, or characteristic visual field defects, and it is both a major risk factor and a common precursor state for primary open-angle glaucoma. It most often reflects impaired aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal, involving extracellular matrix remodeling, TGF-β/SMAD, RhoA/ROCK cytoskeletal signaling, nitric oxide signaling, myocilin-associated endoplasmic reticulum stress, and steroid-responsive glucocorticoid pathways; relevant genes and proteins include MYOC, OPTN, CYP1B1, FOXC1, LTBP2, ANGPT1/TEK, CAV1/CAV2, TMCO1, and matrix metalloproteinases, with MYOC mutations representing a classic inherited cause of juvenile or early-onset pressure elevation. Subtypes include primary ocular hypertension and secondary forms due to corticosteroid exposure, pseudoexfoliation, pigment dispersion, inflammation, trauma, uveitis, or angle closure mechanisms. When familial, inheritance is commonly autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, though most cases are complex polygenic traits influenced by age, African ancestry, thin central cornea, myopia, diabetes, and family history. Clinical signs are elevated tonometric pressure, open anterior chamber angles on gonioscopy in most cases, and sometimes increased cup-to-disc ratio without definite damage; symptoms are often absent, though intermittent blur, halos, or ocular discomfort may occur, especially with marked pressure elevation. Diagnosis relies on Goldmann applanation tonometry, pachymetry, gonioscopy, optic nerve examination, OCT of the retinal nerve fiber layer, standard automated perimetry, and exclusion of secondary causes. Treatment aims to reduce pressure and prevent conversion to glaucoma, commonly with prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost or travoprost, which increase uveoscleral outflow, beta-blockers such as timolol, which reduce aqueous production, alpha2-agonists such as brimonidine, which decrease production and increase uveoscleral outflow, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dorzolamide or acetazolamide, which suppress ciliary body aqueous secretion; complications are mainly progression to primary open-angle glaucoma with irreversible

Name: Onchocerciasis
Description: Onchocerciasis (river blindness; MeSH D009855) is a chronic vector-borne helminthiasis caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by Simulium blackflies, in which disease is driven largely by host inflammatory responses to microfilariae and their Wolbachia endosymbionts rather than a classic Mendelian inherited defect. Key molecular elements include parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels, the target of ivermectin; Wolbachia bacterial protein synthesis and heme/riboflavin metabolism, targeted by tetracyclines; and host innate/adaptive immune pathways involving TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, TNF-α, eosinophils, mast cells, macrophages, and Th2/Treg polarization, with corneal inflammation and fibrosis also linked to VEGF, matrix-remodeling enzymes, and keratitis-associated cytokine cascades. Human genetic susceptibility is polygenic, with reported associations in HLA loci and cytokine/immune-response genes such as IL13, IL10, TNF, and TLR variants that may influence infection intensity, dermatitis, or ocular damage, but no single causative mutation defines the disease. Clinically, patients develop pruritic papular dermatitis, lichenified or atrophic depigmented skin, subcutaneous onchocercomata, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and ocular disease ranging from punctate keratitis and uveitis to chorioretinitis, optic atrophy, and blindness; recognized phenotypes include generalized and hyperreactive sowda forms, and eye-predominant versus skin-predominant disease. Major complications include irreversible visual loss, secondary bacterial skin infection, chronic disability, stigma, epilepsy including onchocerciasis-associated epilepsy/nodding syndrome, and coinfection-related adverse events in Loa loa endemic areas. Diagnosis rests on compatible exposure plus demonstration of microfilariae by skin snip microscopy or PCR, slit-lamp detection in the eye, nodule palpation/excision, Ov16 serology, and sometimes ultrasonography.
