Name: Ophthalmia neonatorum
Description: Ophthalmia neonatorum (UMLS C0029076) is an acute conjunctivitis occurring in the first 28 days of life, usually acquired during passage through an infected birth canal or, less often, from postnatal exposure or chemical prophylaxis, and is best regarded as an infectious neonatal mucosal disease rather than a primary genetic disorder. Major etiologic subtypes include gonococcal, chlamydial, and other bacterial forms, viral disease such as herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis, and noninfectious chemical conjunctivitis. Its biology is driven more by host-pathogen interactions than inherited mutations: Neisseria gonorrhoeae uses pili, PorB, Opa proteins, lipooligosaccharide, and complement-evasion mechanisms; Chlamydia trachomatis relies on major outer membrane protein, type III secretion, and intracellular developmental cycling; herpes simplex virus uses glycoproteins and host entry receptors, with inflammation mediated through Toll-like receptor, NF-kB, MAPK, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, neutrophil recruitment, epithelial apoptosis, and complement pathways. Symptoms and signs include conjunctival injection, marked eyelid edema, chemosis, mucopurulent or purulent discharge, tearing, pseudomembranes, and in severe cases keratitis or corneal ulceration; timing may suggest cause, with gonococcal disease often hyperacute at 2-5 days, chlamydial disease at 5-14 days, and herpetic disease with vesicular skin lesions or keratitis. Complications include corneal perforation, endophthalmitis, blindness, neonatal sepsis, pneumonia especially with chlamydia, and disseminated HSV infection; linked maternal comorbidities include sexually transmitted infections and premature rupture of membranes. Diagnosis rests on neonatal conjunctivitis plus microbiologic testing, including Gram stain and culture for N. gonorrhoeae, NAAT for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae, HSV PCR or viral culture when suspected, and fluorescein examination for corneal involvement. Treatment is etiology-specific: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis for gonococcal infection, oral erythromycin or azithromycin inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit for chlamydial disease, and acyclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase for HSV,

Name: Ophthalmia, Sympathetic
Description: Sympathetic ophthalmia (UMLS C0029077) is a rare, bilateral granulomatous autoimmune panuveitis that follows penetrating ocular trauma or intraocular surgery to one eye, after which exposure of sequestered uveal and retinal antigens triggers a T-cell–mediated immune response against the injured exciting eye and the fellow sympathizing eye. Although it is not a classic Mendelian disorder, genetic susceptibility has been linked to HLA class II alleles, particularly HLA-DR4/DRB1*04 and related immune-regulatory loci, with melanocyte and retinal proteins such as retinal S-antigen, interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein, rhodopsin, and recoverin implicated as target autoantigens rather than primary mutations. The dominant pathogenic pathways involve antigen presentation by dendritic cells, Th1 and Th17 polarization, and cytokine networks including IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23, and chemokine-driven leukocyte recruitment, resulting in diffuse choroidal inflammation and Dalen-Fuchs nodules. Clinically, patients develop decreased vision, floaters, photophobia, pain, redness, lacrimation, headache, and impaired accommodation, with signs of bilateral anterior and posterior uveitis, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, vitritis, serous retinal detachment, choroiditis, papillitis, and later sunset-glow fundus; acute and chronic/recurrent forms are recognized. Diagnosis is based on a history of ocular injury or surgery plus bilateral granulomatous uveitis after exclusion of mimics such as Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, and syphilis, supported by slit-lamp and dilated fundus examination, optical coherence tomography, fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography, B-scan ultrasonography, and targeted laboratory testing. Treatment relies on high-dose corticosteroids such as prednisone or methylprednisolone, which suppress NF-κB–dependent cytokine transcription; steroid-sparing immunosuppressants including methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclosporine, which inhibit folate-dependent lymphocyte proliferation, purine synthesis, or calcineurin signaling; and biologics such as adalimumab or infliximab, which neutralize TNF-α.

Name: Opioid withdrawal
Description: Opioid withdrawal (UMLS C0029104) is an acquired neurobehavioral syndrome that follows abrupt cessation or reduction of prolonged opioid exposure, or administration of an antagonist, and reflects rebound hyperactivity of systems chronically suppressed by mu-opioid receptor signaling. Its biology centers on OPRM1-encoded mu-opioid receptors, with contributory genetic variation reported in OPRM1 (for example A118G), COMT, DRD2, SLC6A4, CYP2D6, CYP3A4, and ABCB1 that may influence dependence liability, withdrawal severity, and treatment response, although no Mendelian inheritance pattern exists and heritability is complex and polygenic. Key pathways include Gi/o-coupled inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and cAMP during opioid exposure, followed in withdrawal by locus coeruleus noradrenergic overactivation, increased cAMP-protein kinase A signaling, CREB-mediated transcription, glutamatergic NMDA signaling, dopaminergic reward-circuit dysregulation, and stress-axis activation involving corticotropin-releasing hormone. Typical manifestations include craving, anxiety, irritability, insomnia, mydriasis, yawning, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, piloerection, diaphoresis, tremor, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia, hypertension, and diffuse myalgias; major subtypes are spontaneous withdrawal, precipitated withdrawal, and neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Diagnosis is clinical, based on recent opioid reduction or antagonist exposure plus characteristic signs and symptoms, using DSM-5 opioid withdrawal criteria and severity scales such as COWS, with urine drug testing, medication history, toxicology, and targeted laboratory assessment to exclude mimics or complications. Standard treatments include methadone, a long-acting full mu-opioid receptor agonist; buprenorphine, a high-affinity partial mu agonist and kappa antagonist; clonidine or lofexidine, central alpha-2 adrenergic agonists that reduce sympathetic symptoms; and adjuncts such as antiemetics, loperamide, and NSAIDs. Important comorbidities and complications include opioid use disorder, polysubstance use, depression, anxiety, PTSD, chronic pain, dehydration, relapse, overdose risk after loss of tolerance, infectious complications related to injection drug use, and adverse pregnancy or neonatal outcomes.

Name: Opisthorchiasis
Description: Opisthorchiasis is a food-borne trematode infection caused mainly by Opisthorchis viverrini and O. felineus, acquired by ingestion of raw or undercooked freshwater fish, and is therefore an infectious parasitic disease rather than an inherited disorder, although host genetic susceptibility influences severity; reported associations include inflammatory, fibrogenic, and carcinogenesis-related genes and proteins such as IL6, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, TGFB1, IFNG, TLR2, TLR4, NF-kB, COX-2/PTGS2, iNOS/NOS2, p53/TP53, KRAS, and mucins, especially in patients progressing to periductal fibrosis or cholangiocarcinoma. Pathobiology is driven by chronic mechanical and secretory irritation of the biliary epithelium, with activation of innate immune and wound-healing pathways including TLR, NF-kB, MAPK/ERK, JAK/STAT, TGF-beta/SMAD, oxidative stress, and IL-6-mediated inflammatory signaling, with eosinophils, macrophages, cholangiocytes, and fibroblasts as key cellular effectors. Disease ranges from asymptomatic or mild intestinal-hepatobiliary infection to chronic biliary disease; common manifestations include dyspepsia, right upper quadrant pain, fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, fever, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia, and cholestatic liver enzyme abnormalities, while complications include recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, cholecystitis, gallstones, pancreatitis, obstructive jaundice, periductal fibrosis, and especially cholangiocarcinoma. Diagnosis relies on exposure history in endemic regions, identification of characteristic operculated eggs in stool or duodenal aspirate, serology or PCR when egg burden is low, eosinophilia and liver tests, and ultrasonography, CT, MRI, or ERCP to document biliary tract disease and exclude malignancy. Treatment is centered on praziquantel, which increases parasite tegumental calcium permeability causing spastic paralysis; albendazole, a beta-tubulin inhibitor that impairs microtubule-dependent glucose uptake; and tribendimidine, a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist producing helminth paralysis, with supportive management and endoscopic or surgical treatment for obstructive or neoplastic complications.

Name: Uses oral contraception
Description: Use of oral contraception, represented by UMLS C0029151, is not a disease in the classic inherited-pathobiologic sense but a pharmacologic exposure and reproductive health state defined by administration of combined estrogen-progestin or progestin-only oral agents for contraception, cycle regulation, dysmenorrhea, acne, endometriosis, and polycystic ovary syndrome; its biologic effects are mediated through ESR1 and ESR2 encoding estrogen receptors, PGR encoding the progesterone receptor, SHBG, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and CYP2D6 involved in steroid metabolism, and thrombosis-related genes such as F5 Leiden and F2 G20210A that modify risk, with rare influence from SERPINC1, PROC, and PROS1 deficiencies. Key pathways include hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis suppression through negative feedback on GnRH, LH, and FSH, inhibition of ovulation, progestin-induced cervical mucus thickening, and endometrial decidualization and atrophy, alongside hepatic modulation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, fibrinogen, and angiotensinogen. Common drugs include ethinyl estradiol/levonorgestrel, which suppresses gonadotropins and inhibits ovulation; ethinyl estradiol/drospirenone, which adds antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic activity; and norethindrone or desogestrel-only pills, which primarily alter cervical mucus and endometrium and variably suppress ovulation. Typical intended effects are anovulation and lighter, more regular menses, while common symptoms or adverse effects include breakthrough bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness, headache, mood change, and blood pressure elevation. Major subtypes are combined oral contraceptives, progestin-only pills, monophasic and multiphasic formulations. Important comorbidities and complications include venous thromboembolism, ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction in smokers or migraine with aura, cholestasis, hepatic adenoma, and drug interactions that reduce efficacy, whereas benefits include reduced risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for oral contraceptive use itself, but family history and thrombophilia genetics inform safety. Name: Psittacosis
Description: Psittacosis (MeSH D009956) is a zoonotic, usually sporadic atypical pneumonia caused by the obligate intracellular bacterium Chlamydia psittaci, most often acquired by inhalation of aerosolized secretions or feces from infected birds; it is therefore an infectious disease rather than an inherited disorder, and no Mendelian inheritance pattern is recognized, although host response variability may involve immune-related genes such as HLA loci and cytokine genes including TNF and IL6, while the pathogen’s virulence is linked to chlamydial outer membrane proteins, lipopolysaccharide, type III secretion effectors, and polymorphic membrane proteins. The organism invades respiratory epithelium and mononuclear phagocytes, trafficking through endosomal inclusion pathways and engaging innate immune signaling, particularly TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, MAPK, interferon-gamma, and inflammasome-associated responses that drive pulmonary and systemic inflammation. Clinical disease ranges from subclinical infection to fulminant systemic illness, classically presenting with abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgia, dry cough, malaise, and radiographic interstitial or lobar pneumonia; hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia, conjunctivitis, and gastrointestinal symptoms may occur. Major complications include acute respiratory failure, myocarditis, endocarditis, hepatitis, meningoencephalitis, sepsis, and multiorgan dysfunction, and comorbid chronic lung disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy, and advanced age may worsen outcome. Recognized forms include avian infection, human psittacosis, and occasionally severe disseminated disease. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus compatible pneumonia, supported by PCR on respiratory samples, serology showing species-specific microimmunofluorescence or a fourfold rise in antibody titers, culture only in specialized high-containment laboratories, and nonspecific findings such as elevated transaminases. First-line therapy is doxycycline, which inhibits bacterial protein synthesis via the 30S ribosomal subunit; tetracycline acts similarly; macrolides such as azithromycin inhibit the 50S subunit and are alternatives in pregnancy or tetracycline intolerance, while fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV but are generally second-line.

Name: Osteitis Deformans
Description: Osteitis deformans, or Paget disease of bone, is a chronic focal disorder of accelerated and disorganized bone remodeling characterized by excessive osteoclast-mediated resorption followed by chaotic osteoblastic bone formation, producing enlarged, hypervascular, mechanically weak bone. It is classically monostotic or polyostotic and usually presents in later adulthood with bone pain, skeletal deformity, increased warmth over affected bone, hearing loss when the skull is involved, headache, radiculopathy, pathologic fractures, secondary osteoarthritis, kyphosis, and bowing of long bones, although many patients are asymptomatic and identified by elevated alkaline phosphatase. Genetic susceptibility is well established, most notably SQSTM1/p62 mutations, with additional associations involving TNFRSF11A encoding RANK, TNFRSF11B encoding osteoprotegerin, VCP, OPTN, CSF1, and PFN1; inheritance in familial cases is typically autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance. Pathobiology centers on osteoclast differentiation and NF-κB signaling downstream of the RANK/RANKL/OPG axis, with contributions from sequestosome-mediated autophagy, IL-6, M-CSF, and, in some models, paramyxoviral nucleocapsid protein effects on osteoclast activity. Diagnosis is based on characteristic radiographic findings such as mixed lytic-sclerotic lesions, cortical thickening, bone enlargement, and coarsened trabeculae, supported by scintigraphy to define extent and biochemical markers including total or bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, with CT or MRI used for complications and biopsy reserved for atypical lesions or suspected sarcomatous transformation. Major complications include deformity, fracture, osteoarthritis, spinal stenosis, cranial neuropathies, high-output cardiac failure in extensive disease, nephrolithiasis from immobilization or hypercalcemia, and rare osteosarcoma or giant cell tumor. First-line therapy is with potent bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid, alendronate, and risedronate, which inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteoclasts to suppress bone resorption; pamidronate is another option, and calcitonin, which directly inhibits osteoclast function, is reserved when bisphosphonates are contraindicated.

Name: Osteoarthritis
Description: Osteoarthritis (MeSH D010003) is a common, usually slowly progressive degenerative and low-grade inflammatory joint disease characterized by articular cartilage loss, subchondral bone remodeling, osteophyte formation, synovitis, and varying periarticular muscle weakness; major phenotypes include primary idiopathic osteoarthritis and secondary forms related to trauma, obesity, malalignment, crystal disease, congenital abnormalities, or inflammatory/metabolic disorders, with erosive hand, generalized nodal, knee, hip, spine, and post-traumatic subtypes. Its genetic architecture is complex and largely polygenic rather than Mendelian, with heritability particularly strong for hand and hip disease; representative susceptibility genes include GDF5, SMAD3, COL2A1, ASPN, FRZB, and DVWA, while rare early-onset syndromic or familial forms may involve pathogenic variants affecting cartilage extracellular matrix such as COL2A1. Pathobiology centers on mechanical stress, chondrocyte senescence, extracellular matrix degradation, and innate inflammatory signaling, including IL-1β, TNF-α, NF-κB, TGF-β/SMAD, Wnt/β-catenin, MAPK, and MMP/ADAMTS pathways, with key mediators such as MMP-13, ADAMTS5, aggrecan, type II collagen, and lubricin. Patients typically present with activity-related joint pain, brief morning stiffness, crepitus, reduced range of motion, bony enlargement, tenderness, instability, and functional limitation; advanced disease can cause deformity, effusions, falls, disability, and need for arthroplasty. Common comorbidities include obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, depression, sleep disturbance, and chronic pain syndromes. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by plain radiography showing joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and cysts; MRI or ultrasound may detect earlier cartilage, meniscal, marrow, or synovial changes, while laboratory tests are usually noninflammatory and used mainly to exclude mimics. Treatment is symptomatic and multimodal, commonly including acetaminophen, which acts centrally to reduce pain, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX enzymes and prostaglandin synthesis, topical diclofenac with similar COX inhibition, duloxetine, a serotonin-norepine

Name: Massive Osteolyses
Description: Massive osteolysis, classically exemplified by Gorham-Stout disease and related idiopathic osteolysis syndromes, is a rare, usually nonmalignant disorder characterized by progressive destruction and resorption of bone accompanied by proliferation of lymphatic and/or vascular channels within bone and adjacent soft tissue. Molecular studies implicate dysregulated osteoclastogenesis and lymphangiogenesis, with reported involvement of RANK/RANKL/OPG, M-CSF, VEGF-A/VEGF-C/VEGFR-3, PDGF, IL-6, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, and occasionally MAPK signaling; in some patients, somatic activating mutations in KRAS or other genes in complex lymphatic anomaly spectra have been described, while hereditary multicentric osteolysis phenocopies may involve MMP2, MAFB, TNFRSF11A, LMNA, or PTH1R depending on subtype. Clinically, patients present with insidious pain, swelling, weakness, deformity, pathologic fractures, limited motion, and radiographic disappearance of part of a bone, most often affecting the shoulder girdle, ribs, spine, pelvis, or jaw; complications include spinal instability, neurologic compromise, pleural or pericardial effusions, especially chylothorax, respiratory failure, functional disability, and secondary infection. Subtypes include Gorham-Stout disease, Winchester syndrome, multicentric carpal-tarsal osteolysis, nodulosis-arthropathy-osteolysis, and other idiopathic multicentric osteolyses, with inheritance ranging from sporadic to autosomal dominant or recessive depending on the genetic syndrome. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical and imaging findings, progressive osteolysis on radiography, CT, or MRI, exclusion of malignancy, infection, inflammatory, endocrine, and metabolic causes, and biopsy showing angiomatous or lymphatic tissue without marked atypia. Treatment is largely empiric and multidisciplinary: bisphosphonates such as pamidronate, zoledronic acid, or alendronate inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; sirolimus suppresses mTOR-driven lymphangiogenesis; interferon alfa has antiangiogenic effects; and denosumab blocks RANKL, while surgery and radiotherapy are used selectively for stabilization or refractory disease.

Name: OM - osteomalacia
Description: Osteomalacia is an acquired or hereditary disorder of defective mineralization of mature osteoid in adults, most often caused by vitamin D deficiency or resistance, phosphate wasting, chronic kidney or liver disease, malabsorption, or drugs, and characterized clinically by diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, fragility fractures or pseudofractures, gait difficulty, skeletal tenderness, and sometimes hypocalcemic tetany. Important genetic forms include X-linked hypophosphatemic osteomalacia from PHEX mutations, autosomal dominant disease from FGF23 mutations, autosomal recessive forms involving DMP1 or ENPP1, and vitamin D–dependent/resistant osteomalacia due to CYP27B1, CYP2R1, VDR, or less commonly SLC34A3 defects; key proteins include FGF23, PHEX, DMP1, ENPP1, VDR, 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and sodium-phosphate cotransporters. Central pathobiology involves the vitamin D endocrine axis and phosphate homeostasis, including reduced 25-hydroxyvitamin D or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D signaling through VDR, impaired intestinal calcium-phosphate absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism via PTH, renal phosphate wasting mediated by excess FGF23 acting through FGFR1-Klotho, and defective alkaline phosphatase-dependent matrix mineralization. Common treatments include cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol, which replenish vitamin D stores; calcitriol or alfacalcidol, which directly activate vitamin D signaling and increase intestinal calcium/phosphate absorption; phosphate salts, which correct hypophosphatemia in renal phosphate-wasting states; calcium supplementation, which restores substrate for mineralization; and in FGF23-mediated hypophosphatemia burosumab, a monoclonal antibody that neutralizes FGF23 and increases renal phosphate reabsorption. Complications include fractures, Looser zones, deformity, osteopenia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, nephrocalcinosis in treated phosphate-wasting disease, and association with CKD-mineral bone disorder. Diagnosis rests on compatible symptoms, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D or phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, variable calcium, elevated PTH, low tubular phosphate reabsorption in renal wasting, radiographic pseudofractures, low bone mineral density, and when indicated genetic testing and bone

Name: Osteomyelitis
Description: Osteomyelitis (MeSH D010019) is an infection-driven inflammatory disease of bone and marrow, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA, but also streptococci, gram-negative bacilli, Salmonella in sickle cell disease, and polymicrobial diabetic foot infections; it may be acute, subacute, chronic, contiguous-focus, hematogenous, vertebral, or implant-associated. Its pathobiology is dominated by microbial adhesion and biofilm formation, neutrophil and macrophage activation, and cytokine networks involving TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, RANK/RANKL/OPG, and osteoclastogenic signaling that drives bone destruction, with proteins such as CRP and procalcitonin serving as inflammatory markers; representative host genetic associations are not usually Mendelian but include susceptibility signals in IL1B, IL6, TNF, TLR2, TLR4, VDR, and MMP genes, while inherited disorders predisposing to osteomyelitis include sickle cell disease from HBB mutations and chronic granulomatous disease involving CYBB or related NADPH oxidase genes. Typical manifestations are localized bone pain, tenderness, swelling, erythema, warmth, reduced function, fever, draining sinus tracts in chronic disease, and vertebral cases with back pain and possible neurologic deficits. Common comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression, trauma, pressure ulcers, prosthetic hardware, bacteremia, sepsis, abscess, sequestrum/involucrum, pathologic fracture, growth disturbance in children, and chronic recurrent infection. Diagnosis integrates clinical findings with elevated ESR/CRP, blood cultures, MRI as the most sensitive imaging test, radiographs or CT for structural change, nuclear imaging when needed, and definitive bone biopsy with histology and culture. Treatment relies on source control plus prolonged antimicrobials such as vancomycin, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala; cefazolin or nafcillin, β-lactams targeting penicillin-binding proteins for MSSA; and ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase/topoisomerase, with linezolid or rifampin-based biofilm-active combinations used in selected device-associated cases.

Name: Osteoporosis
Description: Osteoporosis (MeSH D010024) is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone, causing increased fragility and susceptibility to fracture, classically at the vertebrae, hip, and distal radius; it is often clinically silent until a fragility fracture occurs, but common manifestations include height loss, kyphosis, and chronic back pain from vertebral compression fractures. Major forms include primary osteoporosis, comprising postmenopausal type I and age-related/senile type II disease, and secondary osteoporosis due to glucocorticoid exposure, hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory disorders, alcohol misuse, or immobilization. Pathobiology centers on uncoupled bone remodeling, especially excess osteoclast activity relative to osteoblast formation, involving the RANK/RANKL/OPG axis, Wnt/β-catenin signaling, sclerostin, estrogen receptor signaling, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, TGF-β, and cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF. Genetic susceptibility is typically polygenic, with representative genes including LRP5, SOST, TNFRSF11B encoding osteoprotegerin, TNFSF11 encoding RANKL, ESR1, COL1A1, and VDR; rare monogenic disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta from COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations can present with severe osteoporosis, with inheritance patterns including multifactorial, autosomal dominant, or recessive forms depending on the gene. Important comorbidities and complications include frailty, falls, sarcopenia, chronic pain, disability, loss of independence, and increased mortality after hip fracture. Diagnosis is based on bone mineral density by DXA, with WHO criteria of T-score ≤ -2.5 for osteoporosis, osteopenia from -1.0 to -2.5, or the presence of a low-trauma hip or vertebral fracture; evaluation commonly includes FRAX risk estimation, vertebral imaging, and laboratory testing for calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, renal and thyroid function, PTH, and secondary causes. Name: Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal
Description: Postmenopausal osteoporosis is a common systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration caused primarily by estrogen deficiency after menopause, leading to increased bone resorption, reduced bone strength, and fragility fractures. It is typically polygenic rather than Mendelian, with susceptibility influenced by variants in genes regulating bone turnover and mineral metabolism, including ESR1, VDR, LRP5, WNT1, COL1A1, SOST, TNFRSF11B encoding osteoprotegerin, and the RANK/RANKL axis genes TNFSF11 and TNFRSF11A; rare high-impact mutations in LRP5 or WNT-pathway genes can markedly alter bone density. Central pathogenic pathways include estrogen signaling, RANKL-RANK-NF-κB-mediated osteoclastogenesis, osteoprotegerin antagonism of RANKL, Wnt/β-catenin signaling modulated by sclerostin, and cytokine networks involving IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α that amplify osteoclast activity. Patients are often asymptomatic until fracture, but typical manifestations include loss of height, thoracic kyphosis, back pain, vertebral compression fractures, and low-trauma fractures of the spine, hip, pelvis, proximal humerus, or distal radius. Major complications include chronic pain, disability, frailty, immobility, and excess mortality after hip fracture; common comorbidities include sarcopenia, vitamin D deficiency, falls, hyperparathyroidism, and other age-related cardiometabolic disorders. Subtypes are usually defined by severity, fracture status, or bone-turnover profile rather than discrete histologic classes. Diagnosis relies on DXA showing osteoporosis at the lumbar spine, total hip, or femoral neck with T-score ≤ -2.5, or osteopenia with fragility fracture/high FRAX risk, supported by vertebral imaging and laboratory evaluation to exclude secondary causes such as calcium, phosphate, creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, PTH, and thyroid testing. Standard treatments include bisphosphonates such as alendronate or zoledronic acid, which inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteoclasts; denosumab, a monoclonal antibody to RANKL; selective estrogen receptor modulators such as raloxifene; anabolic agents teriparatide or abaloparatide

Name: Otitis Externa
Description: Otitis externa (MeSH D010032) is an inflammatory disorder of the external auditory canal, usually infectious but also eczematous, allergic, traumatic, or invasive, and classically includes acute diffuse bacterial otitis externa, localized furunculosis, chronic eczematous otitis externa, fungal otomycosis, and necrotizing or malignant otitis externa. It presents with otalgia, pruritus, aural fullness, otorrhea, canal edema and erythema, tragal or pinna tenderness, conductive hearing loss, and sometimes debris or granulation tissue. The condition is most often driven by Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus, with fungi such as Aspergillus and Candida in otomycosis; relevant host-response molecules include TLR2, TLR4, NF-κB, IL1B, IL6, TNF, CXCL8, defensins, and epithelial barrier proteins such as filaggrin, and representative genetic susceptibility may be seen in atopic disease or ichthyosis with FLG-related barrier dysfunction, diabetes-linked immune impairment, or rare immunodeficiency states rather than a Mendelian otitis-externa gene. Pathobiology centers on moisture, maceration, elevated canal pH, microtrauma, biofilm formation, and innate immune activation, with cytokine-mediated neutrophilic inflammation; in malignant otitis externa, osteomyelitis of the skull base reflects invasive infection and exaggerated inflammatory injury. Common treatments include topical fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin, which inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; aminoglycosides such as neomycin, which bind the 30S ribosomal subunit; polymyxin B, which disrupts gram-negative bacterial membranes; azole antifungals such as clotrimazole, which inhibit ergosterol synthesis; and corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone or dexamethasone, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory signaling. Major comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, dermatologic disorders such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis, hearing-aid use, swimming exposure, and immunosuppression; complications include canal stenosis, abscess, perichondritis, cellulitis, tympanic membrane injury, and cranial neuropathies in necrotizing disease. Name: Pain
Description: Pain (MeSH D010146) is a complex sensory and emotional symptom rather than a single disease, arising from actual or threatened tissue injury or from lesions/dysfunction within the somatosensory system, and is commonly classified as nociceptive, inflammatory, neuropathic, or nociplastic, with acute and chronic forms. Key molecular contributors include ion channels and receptors in peripheral and central nociceptive pathways, notably SCN9A/Nav1.7, SCN10A/Nav1.8, TRPV1, TRPA1, CACNA2D1, OPRM1, COMT, and NGF/NTRK1; representative mutations include SCN9A loss-of-function causing congenital insensitivity to pain and gain-of-function variants causing erythromelalgia or paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, while NTRK1 mutations also impair pain perception. Major signaling pathways involve prostaglandin/COX-mediated sensitization, NGF-TrkA, bradykinin, substance P, CGRP, glutamate acting at NMDA/AMPA receptors, sodium and calcium channel hyperexcitability, spinal microglial and cytokine pathways including TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, and IL-6, and descending serotonergic and noradrenergic modulation. Common treatments include acetaminophen, which acts predominantly via central prostaglandin inhibition; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and reduce prostaglandin synthesis; opioids such as morphine, oxycodone, or fentanyl, which are mu-opioid receptor agonists; gabapentin or pregabalin, which bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels; duloxetine or amitriptyline, which enhance descending monoaminergic inhibition; and local anesthetics such as lidocaine, which block voltage-gated sodium channels. Pain commonly coexists with depression, anxiety, insomnia, migraine, osteoarthritis, diabetes, fibromyalgia, and cancer, and may lead to disability, opioid dependence, central sensitization, and impaired quality of life. Name: Postoperative Pain
Description: Postoperative pain is an acute nociceptive and inflammatory pain state arising after tissue injury from surgery, often with neuropathic features when nerves are stretched, transected, or inflamed; clinically it is characterized by incisional or deep visceral pain, tenderness, hyperalgesia, allodynia, guarding, impaired mobilization, tachycardia, hypertension, sleep disruption, and reduced pulmonary effort, and may be classified as somatic, visceral, neuropathic, acute versus persistent postsurgical pain, and procedure-specific syndromes. Its biology involves peripheral sensitization driven by prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P, CGRP, NGF, TNF, IL-1β, and IL-6, and central sensitization through glutamatergic NMDA receptor signaling, microglial activation, descending serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways, and ion channels including SCN9A/NaV1.7, SCN10A/NaV1.8, TRPV1, OPRM1, COMT, and CACNA2D1; representative genetic influences on pain sensitivity or analgesic response include OPRM1 A118G, COMT Val158Met, CYP2D6 variation affecting codeine or tramadol bioactivation, and rare SCN9A variants altering nociception, although postoperative pain itself is not inherited in a Mendelian pattern. Common treatments include acetaminophen, which acts centrally to reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or ketorolac, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis; opioids such as morphine, fentanyl, or oxycodone, which activate μ-opioid receptors; and adjuvants including local anesthetics such as bupivacaine, which block voltage-gated sodium channels, and gabapentin, which binds the α2δ calcium-channel subunit. Important comorbidities and complications include anxiety, depression, catastrophizing, sleep disturbance, obesity, diabetes, chronic pain disorders, opioid-related respiratory depression, ileus, nausea, delirium, infection risk from immobility, thromboembolism, and transition to chronic postsurgical pain. Diagnosis is clinical, based on recent surgery, pain intensity and functional impairment assessed with validated scales such as the Numeric Rating Scale or visual analog scale, focused examination for nociceptive versus

Name: Pancreatitis
Description: Pancreatitis is an inflammatory disorder of the exocrine pancreas that may present as acute, recurrent acute, or chronic disease, ranging from mild interstitial edema to necrotizing pancreatitis with systemic inflammatory response and organ failure; patients typically develop severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, abdominal tenderness, fever, tachycardia, ileus, and, in chronic disease, steatorrhea, weight loss, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and diabetes mellitus. Pathobiology centers on premature intrapancreatic trypsin activation, acinar-cell injury, calcium dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and endoplasmic-reticulum stress, NF-kB– and cytokine-driven inflammation, and pancreatic stellate-cell activation with TGF-beta–mediated fibrosis; key genes include PRSS1 gain-of-function mutations, SPINK1 loss-of-function variants, CFTR dysfunction, CTRC variants, CPA1, CASR, and CLDN2 risk alleles, with hereditary pancreatitis classically autosomal dominant in PRSS1, whereas CFTR-related and some SPINK1-associated disease show more complex or recessive inheritance. Major etiologies and comorbid associations include gallstones, alcohol use disorder, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, smoking, obesity, autoimmune pancreatitis, pancreatic divisum, trauma, ERCP, and drugs, while complications include pseudocyst, walled-off necrosis, infected necrosis, hemorrhage, splenic or portal vein thrombosis, ARDS, AKI, malnutrition, exocrine insufficiency, and increased pancreatic cancer risk in chronic/hereditary disease. Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis requires two of three criteria: characteristic pain, serum lipase or amylase at least three times normal, and imaging findings on contrast CT, MRI/MRCP, or ultrasound; chronic pancreatitis is assessed by CT, MRI/MRCP, EUS, pancreatic function tests, fecal elastase, and IgG4 when autoimmune disease is suspected, with genetic testing considered in early-onset or familial cases. Treatment is largely supportive with aggressive IV lactated Ringer’s, opioid analgesics such as morphine or hydromorphone acting at mu-opioid receptors, antiemetics such as ondansetron via 5-HT3 antagonism, and enteral nutrition; cause-specific therapy includes ERCP for biliary obstruction, insulin or

Name: Panic Disorder
Description: Panic disorder is an anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks and persistent concern about additional attacks or their consequences, often accompanied by maladaptive behavioral change; clinical manifestations include abrupt surges of intense fear with palpitations, chest discomfort, dyspnea, dizziness, tremor, sweating, paresthesias, gastrointestinal distress, derealization or depersonalization, and fear of dying or losing control, frequently with anticipatory anxiety and agoraphobia, and subtypes are commonly defined as panic disorder with or without agoraphobia. It is a complex, multifactorial illness with moderate heritability, usually showing polygenic rather than Mendelian inheritance, with representative associations reported in serotonergic, catecholaminergic, and stress-response genes including SLC6A4, HTR1A, HTR2A, COMT, MAOA, BDNF, NPY, CRHR1, and TMEM132D, although no single mutation is determinative. Pathophysiology implicates dysregulation of fear circuitry centered on the amygdala, hippocampus, insula, prefrontal cortex, locus coeruleus, and periaqueductal gray, involving serotonergic, noradrenergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, and HPA-axis signaling, with components such as CRH, cortisol, GABA-A receptors, and BDNF-related synaptic plasticity. Common comorbidities include major depressive disorder, other anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, migraine, irritable bowel syndrome, and cardiovascular or respiratory symptom syndromes; complications include functional impairment, avoidance behavior, suicidality, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria requiring recurrent unexpected panic attacks and at least 1 month of persistent worry or behavioral change, supported by psychiatric assessment and exclusion of medical mimics such as arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, seizure, asthma, stimulant use, and pheochromocytoma through targeted history, examination, ECG, thyroid testing, toxicology, or other studies as indicated. First-line drugs include SSRIs such as sertraline, paroxetine, and fluoxetine, which inhibit serotonin reuptake; SNRIs such as venlafaxine, which inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; and benzodiazepines such as clonazepam or alprazolam, which positively modulate GABA-A receptors

Name: Paralytic Ileus
Description: Paralytic ileus (UMLS C0030446) is a functional, nonmechanical cessation of propulsive intestinal motility, most often acute and postoperative, but also occurring with sepsis, peritonitis, trauma, electrolyte derangements, medications, and severe systemic illness; clinically it presents with abdominal distension, pain or discomfort, nausea, vomiting, obstipation or delayed passage of stool and flatus, hypoactive or absent bowel sounds, and intolerance of oral intake. Its pathobiology reflects neuroimmune and myogenic dysmotility rather than a single monogenic defect, with key pathways involving inhibition of enteric cholinergic signaling, increased sympathetic adrenergic tone, inflammatory activation of macrophages and neutrophils with cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-alpha, and nitric oxide synthase, opioid-mediated mu-opioid receptor signaling, prostaglandins, and interstitial cells of Cajal dysfunction; representative molecular contributors described in related dysmotility states include NOS1, SCN5A, ACTG2, FLNA, RET, GDNF, and EDNRB, although inherited causes are uncommon in typical postoperative ileus and are more relevant to chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Subtypes include postoperative ileus, adynamic ileus, medication-induced ileus, and generalized ileus associated with metabolic or inflammatory states. Important comorbidities and complications include abdominal surgery, opioid exposure, hypokalemia, uremia, pneumonia, pancreatitis, bowel ischemia, aspiration, dehydration, malnutrition, bacterial translocation, perforation, and prolonged hospitalization. Diagnosis is based on clinical evidence of bowel dysfunction without a mechanical transition point, supported by abdominal radiography or CT showing diffuse gaseous distension of small and large bowel, laboratory testing for electrolyte or inflammatory triggers, medication review, and exclusion of obstruction, ischemia, and toxic megacolon. Management is mainly supportive, but commonly used drugs include alvimopan, a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist that accelerates postoperative gastrointestinal recovery; metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist with 5-HT4 agonist prokinetic effects; erythromycin, a motilin receptor agonist; and neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used selectively to enhance colonic motility.

Name: Paratyphoid Fever
Description: Paratyphoid fever (MeSH D010284) is an acute systemic enteric fever caused predominantly by Salmonella enterica serovars Paratyphi A, B, or C, a non-Mendelian infectious disease in which host genetic susceptibility rather than inheritance of the disease itself may influence risk; representative host factors implicated in enteric salmonellosis include variants affecting TLR4, TLR5, NOD2, NRAMP1/SLC11A1, CFTR, HLA class II loci, and cytokine genes such as TNF and IL10, while key bacterial virulence determinants include lipopolysaccharide, flagellin, Vi-related capsular biology in some strains, and type III secretion system proteins encoded on Salmonella pathogenicity islands. Pathogenesis centers on intestinal epithelial invasion through M cells, macrophage survival, and dissemination via SPI-1/SPI-2 secretion systems, with activation of TLR-NF-κB, inflammasome, IL-1/IL-18, IFN-γ, TNF-α, and JAK-STAT signaling, leading to reticuloendothelial infection and bacteremia. Typical manifestations include stepwise or sustained fever, headache, malaise, abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia, and sometimes rose spots; major clinical forms correspond to infection by Paratyphi A, B, or C, with severity ranging from uncomplicated febrile illness to severe sepsis. Important complications include intestinal hemorrhage or perforation, encephalopathy, hepatitis, cholecystitis, myocarditis, relapse, chronic biliary carriage, and coinfection or worsened outcomes in malnutrition, HIV infection, hemoglobinopathies, or other immunocompromised states. Diagnosis relies on compatible travel or exposure history plus microbiologic confirmation, with blood culture as the standard early test and bone marrow, stool, or urine cultures as adjuncts; PCR and other nucleic acid tests may assist, whereas serology such as Widal is less specific. Name: Parkinson Disease
Description: Parkinson disease (MeSH D010300) is a progressive neurodegenerative synucleinopathy characterized pathologically by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein in Lewy bodies and neurites, producing bradykinesia with resting tremor, rigidity, postural instability, gait freezing, masked facies, hypophonia, micrographia, and prominent nonmotor features such as anosmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression, autonomic dysfunction, pain, and later cognitive impairment or dementia. Major molecular contributors include SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN/PARK2, PINK1, DJ-1/PARK7, GBA1, VPS35, and ATP13A2, with representative mutations such as SNCA multiplications, LRRK2 G2019S, parkin loss-of-function, and biallelic PINK1 variants; implicated pathways include alpha-synuclein proteostasis and aggregation, ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosomal systems, mitochondrial quality control/mitophagy, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, calcium handling, and basal ganglia dopaminergic signaling involving nigrostriatal dopamine, D1/D2 receptor circuits, MAO-B, COMT, and adenosine A2A pathways. Clinical subtypes include tremor-dominant, akinetic-rigid/postural instability-gait difficulty, early-onset, and forms with dementia or prominent autonomic failure; most cases are sporadic, but monogenic disease may be autosomal dominant, as with LRRK2 or SNCA, or autosomal recessive, as with PRKN, PINK1, and DJ-1, while GBA1 variants confer strong risk. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, requiring parkinsonism with bradykinesia plus tremor or rigidity, supported by levodopa responsiveness and exclusion of atypical features; testing may include DaTscan to document presynaptic dopaminergic deficit, brain MRI to exclude mimics, and genetic testing in early-onset or familial disease. Name: Parkinson Disease, Postencephalitic
Description: Postencephalitic Parkinson disease is a secondary, acquired parkinsonian syndrome classically emerging after epidemic encephalitis lethargica or other inflammatory encephalitic insults, characterized by degeneration of nigrostriatal dopaminergic circuitry and basal ganglia dysfunction rather than a primary Mendelian neurodegenerative disorder. Its molecular biology is incompletely defined, but implicated components include substantia nigra dopamine neurons, α-synuclein/SNCA-positive Lewy-type pathology in some cases, tau/MAPT-related neurofibrillary change, microglial activation, cytokine-driven neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and disturbed dopamine synthesis, vesicular handling, and D1/D2 receptor signaling within basal ganglia-thalamocortical pathways; unlike idiopathic Parkinson disease, causative inherited mutations are not established, although genes linked to parkinsonism susceptibility such as SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN, PINK1, DJ-1/PARK7, and GBA may be considered in the differential diagnosis when the presentation is atypical or familial. Clinically, patients develop bradykinesia, rigidity, masked facies, hypophonia, postural instability, gait freezing, tremor that may be less prominent than in idiopathic Parkinson disease, oculogyric crises, dystonia, sleep disturbance, autonomic symptoms, cognitive and behavioral changes, depression, and sometimes catatonic or ophthalmoplegic features. Common comorbidities and complications include dysphagia with aspiration, falls, pneumonia, dementia, psychosis, pressure injury, and treatment-induced dyskinesias. Subtypes are usually defined pragmatically as postencephalitic parkinsonism within secondary parkinsonism, with akinetic-rigid versus tremor-predominant phenotypes. Diagnosis is clinical, based on a history of prior encephalitis followed by persistent parkinsonian signs, exclusion of drug-induced, vascular, and genetic causes, neurologic examination, brain MRI to assess alternative structural etiologies, and functional imaging such as DAT-SPECT or PET when needed to document presynaptic dopaminergic deficit. Name: Paronychia
Description: Paronychia (UMLS C0030578) is an inflammatory and usually infectious disorder of the proximal or lateral nail folds, classically divided into acute paronychia, most often bacterial, and chronic paronychia, a multifactorial irritant dermatitis with secondary microbial colonization; patients typically present with painful periungual erythema, swelling, warmth, tenderness, throbbing, and sometimes fluctuance or purulent drainage, while chronic disease shows boggy swollen nail folds, loss of cuticle, nail dystrophy, onycholysis, and recurrent episodes. Its pathobiology is dominated by barrier disruption from trauma, nail biting, manicuring, ingrown nails, wet work, or irritants, with activation of innate immune pathways including keratinocyte NF-kB signaling, IL-1, TNF-alpha, and neutrophil recruitment; common microbes include Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, and in chronic cases Candida albicans, although Candida is often a colonizer rather than the primary driver. Genetic causation is not typical, and inheritance is generally absent, but susceptibility may be increased in Mendelian disorders affecting epidermal integrity or immunity, such as SPINK5-related Netherton syndrome or immune dysregulation states, and chronic paronychia can occur in psoriasis, eczema, diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, and immunosuppression. Drug-associated paronychia is well recognized with EGFR-pathway inhibitors such as cetuximab, erlotinib, and gefitinib, reflecting impaired epidermal growth factor signaling in periungual tissue; retinoids and taxanes are additional causes. Treatment depends on subtype and severity: topical or systemic antistaphylococcal antibiotics such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, clindamycin inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, and mupirocin inhibits isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase; abscesses require incision and drainage, while chronic disease is managed with irritant avoidance plus topical corticosteroids such as triamcinolone, which suppress NF-kB-mediated inflammation, and sometimes azoles such as clotrimazole, which inhibit fungal ergosterol synthesis. Name: Supraventricular Tachycardia, Paroxysmal
Description: Ventricular tachycardia is a potentially life-threatening tachyarrhythmia arising distal to the His bundle, defined clinically by three or more consecutive ventricular beats, usually at rates >100–120/min, and occurring as monomorphic, polymorphic, sustained, nonsustained, idiopathic outflow-tract/fascicular, scar-related reentrant, or inherited channelopathy-associated forms. Its molecular basis includes abnormalities in ion-channel and calcium-handling genes and structural cardiomyopathy genes, with representative examples including KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A, RYR2, CASQ2, LMNA, PKP2, DSP, DSG2, and TTN; these affect repolarization, sodium-current conduction, desmosomal integrity, and sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release. Key pathways involve reentry around ischemic or fibrotic scar, triggered activity from delayed afterdepolarizations mediated by catecholamine-sensitive Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent signaling, abnormal automaticity, and altered autonomic, β-adrenergic, sodium, potassium, and calcium-channel function. Common associated conditions include prior myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, dilated or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, electrolyte disturbances, long-QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; major complications are syncope, hemodynamic collapse, ventricular fibrillation, sudden cardiac death, and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Symptoms range from palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness, and presyncope to syncope or cardiac arrest, with signs including hypotension and wide-complex tachycardia on ECG. Inherited forms are often autosomal dominant, although autosomal recessive disease occurs, for example CASQ2-related catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Diagnosis relies on 12-lead ECG criteria for wide-complex VT, ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, echocardiography, cardiac MRI, ischemia evaluation, electrophysiology study, laboratory assessment including potassium and magnesium, and selective genetic testing. Treatment commonly includes amiodarone, a multichannel blocker; lidocaine, a class Ib sodium-channel blocker useful in ischemic VT; procainamide, a class Ia sodium-channel and potassium-current blocker; and β-blockers such as propranolol or nadolol

Name: Pasteurella Infections
Description: Pasteurella infections are acute zoonotic bacterial infections, most often caused by Pasteurella multocida after cat or dog bites, scratches, or saliva exposure, producing a pyogenic soft-tissue infection that may progress to invasive disease; major virulence-associated genes and proteins include the capsular biosynthesis loci (hyaD-hyaC in serogroup A), lipopolysaccharide outer-core biosynthesis genes, outer membrane adhesins and porins such as OmpA and Oma87, iron-acquisition systems, neuraminidase NanH, filamentous hemagglutinin PfhA, and in toxigenic strains the dermonecrotic Pasteurella multocida toxin encoded by toxA, which activates Rho/mitogen signaling. Host responses prominently involve Toll-like receptor 4 recognition of lipopolysaccharide with downstream NF-kB, MAPK, TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6 inflammatory pathways, neutrophil recruitment, and occasionally complement-mediated injury in sepsis. Clinically, patients typically develop rapidly evolving pain, erythema, swelling, warmth, purulent drainage, lymphangitis, and reduced range of motion within 24 hours, while pneumonia, bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, meningitis, endocarditis, and abscesses occur particularly in older adults or immunocompromised hosts. Common disease patterns include localized cellulitis, deep hand-space infection, respiratory infection, and disseminated/invasive pasteurellosis. Important comorbidities and risk factors include chronic lung disease, cirrhosis, diabetes, malignancy, asplenia, alcoholism, and immunosuppression. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for the infection itself, but host susceptibility may be modified by immune defects, including complement deficiency or impaired splenic function. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus compatible syndrome, Gram stain showing small Gram-negative coccobacilli, culture of wound, blood, respiratory, or joint specimens with species identification by biochemical methods or MALDI-TOF, and selected use of PCR/16S rRNA sequencing. Treatment commonly uses penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation; amoxicillin-clavulanate, adding beta-lactamase inhibition; doxycycline, which inhibits 30S ribosomal protein synthesis; and third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone

Name: Pediculosis capitis
Description: Pediculosis capitis (UMLS C0030757) is a superficial ectoparasitic infestation of the scalp and hair by the human head louse, Pediculus humanus capitis, characterized clinically by scalp pruritus, excoriations, visible live lice or viable nits near the scalp, and sometimes postauricular or occipital lymphadenopathy; major subtypes are active infestation versus nit-only carriage, and it is commonly classified with light or heavy burden and treatment-sensitive or treatment-resistant disease. The disorder is not a Mendelian genetic disease and shows no established inheritance pattern, although host susceptibility may be influenced by grooming practices, hair characteristics, exposure networks, and immune reactivity; the most clearly defined molecular genetics instead involve the parasite, particularly knockdown resistance mutations in the voltage-gated sodium channel gene such as T917I, T929I, and L920F, which alter the target protein for pyrethrins and permethrin and contribute to treatment failure. Relevant biologic pathways are therefore chiefly parasite neurophysiologic signaling pathways, including sodium channel-mediated axonal depolarization, glutamate-gated chloride channel signaling, and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor pathways. Common treatments include permethrin or pyrethrins, which prolong louse sodium channel opening and cause paralysis; malathion, an organophosphate acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; ivermectin, which activates glutamate-gated chloride channels causing neuromuscular paralysis; spinosad, which overstimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors; and benzyl alcohol, which kills lice by asphyxiation. Complications include impetiginization, eczematization, sleep disturbance, anxiety, social stigma, and rarely secondary bacterial infection from scratching. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, requiring demonstration of a live louse by careful scalp inspection, wet combing, or fine-toothed detection comb; dermoscopy can assist, while nits alone are insufficient for definitive active disease, and evaluation should include assessment of contacts, prior pediculicide exposure, and possible resistance when infestation persists despite correct treatment.

Name: Pediculosis corporis
Description: Pediculosis corporis (UMLS C0030758) is an ectoparasitic infestation by the body louse, Pediculus humanus humanus, acquired through close contact and poor hygienic conditions rather than inherited susceptibility, so no Mendelian pattern is recognized and no disease-defining human gene mutation is established, although host immune-response mediators such as IL4, IL13, IFNG, TNF, histamine-related pathways, and eosinophil/mast-cell activation influence pruritic hypersensitivity, while louse nervous-system targets including voltage-gated sodium channels and glutamate-gated chloride channels are central to pharmacologic response and resistance. Clinically, patients develop intense pruritus, excoriated erythematous papules or wheals, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, linear scratch marks, and lichenification concentrated on the trunk, waistline, axillae, and areas where clothing seams contact skin; heavy chronic infestation may produce vagabond’s disease with diffuse skin thickening and discoloration. Major subtypes are uncomplicated infestation and louse-borne infection-associated disease, because body lice are vectors for Bartonella quintana, Borrelia recurrentis, and Rickettsia prowazekii, linking infestation to trench fever, relapsing fever, epidemic typhus, secondary bacterial pyoderma, cellulitis, anemia, and systemic illness, especially in homeless, displaced, or debilitated populations. Diagnosis is usually clinical and confirmed by identification of lice or nits in clothing seams rather than scalp hair, aided by direct visual inspection, dermoscopy or light microscopy, and targeted testing for vector-borne pathogens when fever or systemic features are present. Treatment centers on decontamination by laundering or heat-treating clothing and bedding and improving hygiene, with adjunctive pediculicides such as permethrin, a synthetic pyrethroid that prolongs arthropod sodium-channel opening; malathion, an organophosphate acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; ivermectin, which activates parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels causing paralysis; and, less commonly, benzyl alcohol, which kills lice by asphyxiation.

Name: Crabs
Description: Crabs, more properly crab louse infestation or pediculosis pubis (UMLS C0030759), is an ectoparasitic sexually transmitted infestation caused by Phthirus pubis rather than a primary genetic disease, so no validated human disease-causing genes, proteins, mutations, inheritance pattern, or molecular subtypes are established; similarly, no specific host signaling pathway defines the disorder, although pruritus reflects local cutaneous immune and inflammatory activation with mast-cell degranulation, histamine release, and cytokine-mediated epidermal irritation in response to louse saliva and fecal antigens. The condition typically involves terminal hair of the pubic region but may affect axillary, chest, beard, and occasionally eyelashes, and presents with intense pruritus, visible lice or nits attached to hair shafts, excoriations, secondary eczematization, and sometimes blue-gray macules ceruleae; eyelash infestation can cause blepharitis and conjunctival irritation. Major complications include secondary bacterial skin infection, impetiginization, sleep disturbance, psychosocial distress, and coinfection with other sexually transmitted infections, especially gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, HIV, and trichomoniasis, warranting STI screening. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by direct visualization of adult lice, nymphs, or viable nits using careful inspection, magnification, dermoscopy, or microscopy of removed specimens; diagnostic criteria center on identification of the organism or attached ova in a compatible clinical setting. Treatment relies on topical pediculicides and environmental/partner management: permethrin 1% disrupts parasite sodium channel function causing paralysis, pyrethrins with piperonyl butoxide prolong neurotoxic effects by impairing louse detoxification pathways, and malathion inhibits acetylcholinesterase; oral ivermectin, which activates glutamate-gated chloride channels in arthropods, is used in selected or refractory cases, while petrolatum occlusion is commonly used for eyelash involvement. Simultaneous treatment of sexual partners, decontamination of clothing and bedding, and retreatment when needed are central to preventing reinfestation.

Name: Pellagra
Description: Pellagra (MeSH D010383) is a systemic nutritional deficiency disorder caused primarily by inadequate niacin (vitamin B3) or its precursor tryptophan, producing impaired formation of the essential redox cofactors NAD and NADP and consequent failure of energy metabolism, DNA repair, and oxidative stress responses in rapidly renewing tissues. It is usually acquired rather than inherited, but genetic contributors include disorders of tryptophan absorption or metabolism such as Hartnup disease due to SLC6A19 variants, and rare perturbations affecting kynurenine-pathway enzymes that reduce endogenous niacin synthesis; relevant proteins therefore include the neutral amino acid transporter B0AT1, indoleamine/tryptophan dioxygenase and downstream NAD biosynthetic enzymes. Pathobiologically, pellagra reflects disruption of tryptophan-kynurenine-NAD salvage pathways, with epithelial injury, neuroinflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Classic manifestations are the 4 Ds: photosensitive symmetric dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and, if untreated, death; additional findings include glossitis, stomatitis, abdominal pain, weight loss, depression, irritability, peripheral neuropathy, confusion, and delirium. Major causes and associated conditions include alcoholism, severe malnutrition, maize-based diets lacking bioavailable niacin, chronic diarrhea, malabsorption, carcinoid syndrome, HIV infection, anorexia nervosa, and drug-induced pellagra, especially from isoniazid, 5-fluorouracil, azathioprine, or prolonged anticonvulsant use. Subtypes are commonly described as primary dietary pellagra and secondary pellagra due to impaired absorption, metabolism, or increased consumption of tryptophan. Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by dietary and medication history, characteristic rash, and response to replacement; laboratory assessment may include low urinary N1-methylnicotinamide or low niacin metabolites, nutritional panels, and evaluation for underlying causes. Treatment centers on nicotinamide, which replenishes NAD without causing flushing, niacin/nicotinic acid, which restores NAD and also activates GPR109A to reduce adipose lipolysis, and tryptophan supplementation or balanced nutritional repletion to increase endogenous niacin synthesis, along with management of comorbid infection, alcoholism, or malabsorption.

Name: Pelvic abscess
Description: Pelvic abscess (UMLS C0030785) is a localized, walled-off purulent infection within the pelvic cavity, most often arising as a complication of pelvic inflammatory disease, appendicitis, diverticulitis, Crohn disease, postoperative or postpartum infection, or anastomotic leak, and is usually polymicrobial with enteric gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes. Its pathobiology is dominated by innate immune and inflammatory signaling rather than a Mendelian genetic basis, with activation of Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, chemokine, complement, coagulation, and neutrophil extracellular trap pathways; representative host susceptibility factors reported for complicated intra-abdominal or pelvic sepsis include variants affecting TLR4, NOD2/CARD15, IL6, TNF, MBL2, and CFTR in selected contexts, but no specific inheritance pattern is established for pelvic abscess itself. Clinically, patients typically present with fever, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, adnexal or rectal tenderness, leukocytosis, sepsis, vaginal discharge, ileus, diarrhea, dysuria, and occasionally a palpable mass; major subtypes include tubo-ovarian abscess, postoperative pelvic abscess, postpartum abscess, diverticular abscess, and abscess secondary to gastrointestinal perforation or inflammatory bowel disease. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical findings plus laboratory evidence of inflammation and imaging, especially transvaginal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced CT, with MRI used selectively; microbiologic confirmation may come from blood cultures or image-guided aspiration/drainage. Treatment centers on source control and broad-spectrum antimicrobials such as metronidazole, which generates free-radical intermediates that damage anaerobic DNA, ceftriaxone or other β-lactams that inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis, doxycycline that blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit, piperacillin-tazobactam combining cell-wall inhibition with β-lactamase blockade, or clindamycin inhibiting the 50S subunit and toxin production. Important comorbidities and complications include PID, diabetes, malignancy, immunosuppression, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, fistula, bowel obstruction, recurrent abscess, bacteremia, and septic shock.

Name: Pemphigoid, Bullous
Description: Bullous pemphigoid is an acquired, usually nonhereditary autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder of older adults characterized by intense pruritus, urticarial or eczematous plaques, and tense vesicles or bullae, sometimes with erosions and limited mucosal involvement; major subtypes include classic bullous pemphigoid, nonbullous/prodromal pemphigoid, localized forms, and variants overlapping with mucous membrane pemphigoid or pemphigoid gestationis. Its core molecular targets are hemidesmosomal basement-membrane proteins BP180/type XVII collagen encoded by COL17A1 and BP230/dystonin encoded by DST, with autoantibodies most often directed against the NC16A domain of BP180; although inherited epidermolysis bullosa due to COL17A1 mutations can phenocopy some features, bullous pemphigoid itself is typically sporadic, with genetic susceptibility linked mainly to HLA class II alleles such as HLA-DQB1*0301. Pathogenesis involves IgG and often IgE autoantibodies, complement activation with C3 deposition, mast-cell and eosinophil recruitment, Th2-skewed cytokines including IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, eosinophil proteases, and downstream dermal-epidermal separation. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinicopathologic findings, skin biopsy showing eosinophil-rich subepidermal blisters, direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin demonstrating linear IgG and/or C3 along the basement membrane zone, and serologic testing by indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split skin and ELISA for BP180 and BP230 autoantibodies. Common comorbidities include neurologic disease such as stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, and multiple sclerosis, as well as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and increased risks of secondary infection, fluid imbalance, and treatment toxicity. Standard therapy includes high-potency topical corticosteroids or systemic prednisone, which broadly suppress inflammatory cytokine transcription; doxycycline, which inhibits neutrophil/eosinophil-associated matrix metalloproteinases and has anti-inflammatory effects; azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil, which inhibit lymphocyte proliferation; and in refractory disease rituximab, which depletes CD20-positive B cells, or dupil

Name: Pemphigus
Description: Pemphigus (MeSH D010392) is a rare, potentially life-threatening autoimmune intraepidermal blistering disorder caused by loss of keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis), most often driven by IgG autoantibodies against desmosomal proteins, especially desmoglein 3 and desmoglein 1 (DSG3, DSG1), with additional targets such as desmocollins in some cases; genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian and is strongly linked to HLA class II alleles, particularly HLA-DRB1 and DQB1 haplotypes, with examples including DRB1*0402 and DQB1*0503. Major subtypes include pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus, paraneoplastic pemphigus, IgA pemphigus, and endemic fogo selvagem. Pathobiologically, autoantibody binding disrupts desmosomes and activates signaling pathways involving p38 MAPK, EGFR, Src, PLC/Ca2+ signaling, apoptotic caspases, and complement-independent internalization of desmogleins, culminating in suprabasal or subcorneal blister formation. Clinically, patients develop flaccid bullae and erosions of skin and mucous membranes, painful oral ulcers, crusted erosions, positive Nikolsky sign, and risk of dehydration, malnutrition, pain, and secondary bacterial, viral, or fungal infection; paraneoplastic pemphigus is associated with lymphoproliferative malignancies such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and Castleman disease. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinicopathologic findings, histology showing intraepidermal acantholysis, direct immunofluorescence demonstrating intercellular IgG/C3 in a net-like pattern, indirect immunofluorescence, and ELISA for anti-DSG1/anti-DSG3 antibodies. Treatment relies on immunosuppression: systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone suppress broad inflammatory and immune gene transcription; rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells and reduces pathogenic autoantibodies; azathioprine inhibits purine synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation; mycophenolate mofetil inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase; and intravenous immunoglobulin or cyclophosphamide may be used in refractory disease.
