Name: Penile Induration
Description: Penile induration most commonly refers to Peyronie disease, an acquired, localized fibrotic disorder of the tunica albuginea characterized by inelastic plaque formation that causes penile curvature, deformity, shortening, pain, and variable erectile dysfunction; less commonly, induration may reflect inflammatory, traumatic, or neoplastic processes. Its pathobiology is thought to involve repetitive microvascular injury with aberrant wound healing, myofibroblast activation, excess extracellular matrix deposition, and reduced collagen degradation, with implicated molecular mediators including TGF-β1, SMAD signaling, WNT/β-catenin, PDGF, FGF, TNF-α, ROS/NF-κB, MMP/TIMP imbalance, collagen types I and III, elastin abnormalities, and profibrotic proteins such as fibronectin; representative genetic associations reported in susceptibility or plaque biology include TGFB1, WNT2, MMPs, LOX, and HLA-linked immune factors, but inheritance is usually non-Mendelian and multifactorial, with familial clustering in some cases and overlap with fibrosing diatheses such as Dupuytren contracture. Clinical subtypes include acute/active inflammatory disease, marked by pain and evolving curvature, and chronic/stable disease with mature calcified plaque and fixed deformity. Common comorbidities include erectile dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, smoking-related vasculopathy, hypogonadism, depression, and Dupuytren contracture; complications include sexual dysfunction, penile instability, severe curvature preventing intercourse, and psychological distress. Diagnosis is primarily clinical by history and palpation of a tunical plaque, assessment of deformity and erectile function, and exclusion of malignancy or infection; standardized evaluation may include induced erection with goniometric measurement, penile duplex Doppler ultrasonography to define plaque and calcification, and occasional MRI in complex cases. Common treatments include collagenase clostridium histolyticum, which enzymatically degrades plaque collagen; phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as tadalafil or sildenafil, which enhance nitric oxide–cGMP signaling to improve erectile function and possibly tissue remodeling; and intralesional verapamil, which reduces fibroblast matrix synthesis, with interferon-α2b also used to inhibit fibroblast proliferation and collagen production.

Name: Peptic Ulcer
Description: Peptic ulcer disease is an acid-peptic injury disorder characterized by mucosal breaks extending through the muscularis mucosae in the stomach or proximal duodenum, classically subdivided into gastric and duodenal ulcers, with stress-related, NSAID-associated, and Helicobacter pylori–associated forms predominating. Its pathogenesis reflects imbalance between aggressive factors such as gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori virulence determinants including CagA and VacA, NSAID-mediated cyclooxygenase inhibition, and impaired mucosal defense involving mucus, bicarbonate, epithelial restitution, and prostaglandins; key pathways include COX-1/COX-2–prostaglandin E2 signaling, histamine-H2 receptor and gastrin/cholecystokinin-B receptor stimulation of parietal cells, vagal cholinergic M3 signaling, the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, NF-kB–driven inflammation, cytokines such as IL1B, TNF, and IL8, and nitric oxide and growth factor pathways involved in repair. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, with reported associations involving IL1B, IL1RN, TNF, TLR4, MUC1, PSCA, ABO blood group, and CYP2C19 variants that influence proton-pump inhibitor metabolism rather than causing disease directly. Typical manifestations include epigastric burning or gnawing pain, postprandial discomfort, nocturnal pain, nausea, bloating, occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, and sometimes weight loss; complications include hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, gastric outlet obstruction, and, in gastric ulcer patients, concern for underlying malignancy, while common comorbidities include H. pylori gastritis, NSAID use, smoking, cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, COPD, and critical illness. Diagnosis relies on upper endoscopy with biopsy for gastric ulcers or alarm features, H. pylori testing by urea breath test, stool antigen, histology, or rapid urease test, and selective laboratory evaluation for anemia or hypergastrinemia when Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is suspected. Treatment commonly includes proton-pump inhibitors such as omeprazole or pantoprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine, which block histamine

Name: Familial Mediterranean Fever
Description: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF; MeSH D010505) is a prototypic autoinflammatory disease characterized by recurrent, self-limited episodes of fever and sterile serositis, classically causing peritonitis with abdominal pain, pleuritis, synovitis/monoarthritis, and sometimes erysipelas-like erythema, scrotal pain, or myalgia; the major long-term complication is AA amyloidosis with proteinuria and progressive renal failure, and comorbid inflammatory disorders such as spondyloarthritis, vasculitides including IgA vasculitis and polyarteritis nodosa, and inflammatory bowel disease-like phenotypes may occur. FMF is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, although incomplete penetrance and dominant-like transmission are recognized, and is caused mainly by pathogenic variants in MEFV on 16p13.3 encoding pyrin/marenostrin, with representative mutations including M694V, M680I, V726A, and E148Q; severe disease and amyloidosis risk are particularly associated with homozygous M694V in some populations. Pathobiologically, pyrin dysregulation leads to excessive pyrin-inflammasome activation involving ASC/PYCARD, caspase-1, IL-1β and IL-18 maturation, neutrophil-driven inflammation, and signaling linked to RhoA GTPase perturbation and NF-κB-associated innate immune responses. Diagnosis is based on typical recurrent attacks, ethnicity/family history, elevated acute-phase reactants such as CRP and serum amyloid A during or between attacks, exclusion of mimics, and confirmation by MEFV molecular testing; Tel Hashomer and pediatric Yalçinkaya-Ozen criteria are commonly used, and amyloidosis surveillance includes urinalysis and renal assessment. Colchicine is first-line lifelong therapy, suppressing microtubule polymerization, neutrophil chemotaxis, and pyrin-inflammasome activity; for colchicine-resistant or intolerant disease, IL-1–targeted agents are standard, including anakinra, a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist, canakinumab, a monoclonal antibody to IL-1β, and rilonacept, an IL-1 trap fusion protein.

Name: Periodontitis
Description: Periodontitis (UMLS C0031099) is a common chronic polymicrobial inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting tissues characterized by dysbiotic subgingival biofilms and a host immune response that drives gingival inflammation, periodontal pocket formation, clinical attachment loss, alveolar bone resorption, tooth mobility, and eventual tooth loss; typical signs include bleeding on probing, erythematous or edematous gingiva, suppuration, halitosis, recession, and radiographic bone loss, although aggressive early-onset forms may show rapid destruction with limited plaque. Its pathobiology involves innate and adaptive immune pathways, especially TLR2/TLR4 recognition of organisms such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, NF-κB, MAPK, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, prostaglandin E2, matrix metalloproteinases including MMP8 and MMP9, and RANK/RANKL/OPG-mediated osteoclastogenesis. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian in most cases, with representative associations involving IL1A/IL1B, IL6, TNF, VDR, TLR4, FCGR2A, MMPs, and DEFB1; severe periodontitis may occur in monogenic syndromes such as Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome due to CTSC mutations, and risk is modified by epigenetic and environmental factors, especially smoking and diabetes. Recognized forms include plaque-induced chronic periodontitis, grade C/aggressive phenotypes, necrotizing periodontal disease, and periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease. Diagnosis is clinical and radiographic, based on interdental clinical attachment loss at nonadjacent teeth or buccal/oral attachment loss with pocketing, with full-mouth probing depths, bleeding indices, mobility assessment, and dental radiographs; adjuncts may include microbial testing and inflammatory biomarkers in gingival crevicular fluid. Treatment centers on mechanical debridement plus adjunctive drugs such as chlorhexidine, a membrane-disrupting antiseptic; doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic that also inhibits MMPs at subantimicrobial doses; metronidazole, which causes anaerobic bacterial DNA damage; and amoxicillin, a β-lactam cell-wall synthesis inhibitor. Important comorbidities and complications include type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, adverse pregnancy

Name: Peritonitis
Description: Peritonitis (MeSH D010538) is an acute or chronic inflammatory disorder of the peritoneum, most often infectious from gastrointestinal perforation, appendicitis, diverticulitis, biliary leakage, pelvic infection, or peritoneal dialysis contamination, but it may also be sterile/chemical or granulomatous, including tuberculous peritonitis and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis. Its biology is dominated by innate immune activation through pattern-recognition pathways such as TLR2/TLR4-CD14, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, complement, and cytokine networks involving TNF, IL1B, IL6, CXCL8/IL8, VEGF, and TGF-β, with neutrophil recruitment, mesothelial injury, fibrin deposition, and, in severe cases, sepsis-related coagulation dysfunction. No single germline cause defines most cases, but host susceptibility and severity can be influenced by variants in inflammatory genes such as TLR4, NOD2, TNF, IL6, and MBL2; inherited autoinflammatory disorders, especially MEFV mutations in familial Mediterranean fever, can produce recurrent sterile peritonitis. Typical manifestations include severe abdominal pain and tenderness, guarding, rebound, abdominal distension, fever, nausea, vomiting, ileus, altered bowel sounds, leukocytosis, and in advanced disease hypotension, lactic acidosis, and shock. Major subtypes are primary/spontaneous, secondary, and tertiary/recurrent peritonitis. Comorbidities and complications include cirrhosis with ascites, chronic kidney disease on peritoneal dialysis, diabetes, malignancy, adhesions, intra-abdominal abscess, bacteremia, sepsis, multiorgan failure, and death. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus CBC, CRP/procalcitonin, serum chemistries and lactate, blood cultures, abdominal CT or ultrasound, and source-specific testing such as paracentesis showing ascitic PMN count at least 250/µL with culture for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, or peritoneal dialysis effluent WBC elevation and culture. Name: Persistent Fetal Circulation Syndrome
Description: Persistent fetal circulation syndrome, more commonly termed persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), is a neonatal cardiopulmonary disorder in which failure of the normal postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance sustains right-to-left shunting through the ductus arteriosus and/or foramen ovale, producing severe hypoxemic respiratory failure and cyanosis; clinically it presents in term or near-term infants with tachypnea, labile hypoxemia, pre/postductal oxygen saturation differences, a loud second heart sound, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, and sometimes systemic hypotension. Major mechanistic pathways involve impaired endothelial nitric oxide–soluble guanylate cyclase–cGMP signaling, excess endothelin-1/ETA receptor vasoconstriction, prostacyclin–cAMP deficiency, altered serotonin and Rho kinase signaling, oxidative stress, and remodeling of smooth muscle and extracellular matrix. Genetic contributions are usually complex rather than Mendelian, but variants or altered expression in NOS3, EDN1/EDNRA, VEGFA, BMPR2, CPS1, ABCA3, CRHR1, and surfactant genes such as SFTPB and SFTPC have been reported in subsets, particularly when PPHN accompanies developmental lung disease or surfactant dysfunction; inheritance is therefore typically multifactorial, though rare syndromic or monogenic causes may follow autosomal dominant or recessive patterns depending on the underlying gene. Common subtypes include idiopathic PPHN, parenchymal lung disease-associated PPHN, hypoplastic pulmonary vasculature forms such as congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and maladaptation related to asphyxia, meconium aspiration, sepsis, or maternal drug exposure. Treatment commonly includes inhaled nitric oxide, which increases cGMP-mediated pulmonary vasodilation; sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that preserves cGMP; milrinone, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor that augments cAMP and improves cardiac output; and sometimes epoprostenol or bosentan. Important comorbidities and complications include meconium aspiration syndrome, respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia, sepsis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, pulmonary hypoplasia, neurodevelopmental impairment, hearing loss, shock, and death. Name: Pharyngitis
Description: Pharyngitis (MeSH D010612) is an acute or chronic inflammatory disorder of the pharyngeal mucosa, most often infectious and usually viral, but also caused by Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), Epstein–Barr virus, adenovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, Candida, irritants, allergy, or reflux; clinically it presents with sore throat, odynophagia, fever, pharyngeal erythema, tonsillar enlargement or exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and sometimes cough, coryza, hoarseness, palatal petechiae, or fatigue. Major subtypes include viral, streptococcal, non-streptococcal bacterial, fungal, chronic irritative/reflux-related, and ulcerative pharyngitis. Its biology is dominated by innate and adaptive immune activation, including epithelial toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB and MAPK pathway activation, inflammasome-mediated IL-1β release, and cytokines such as TNF, IL6, IFNG, CXCL8/IL-8, and C-reactive protein; in streptococcal disease, host-pathogen interactions involve streptococcal M protein encoded by emm genes, superantigen exotoxins such as SpeA/SpeC, and variable host susceptibility linked to HLA class II and other immune-response loci rather than a Mendelian inheritance pattern. Diagnosis is primarily clinical but is refined by Centor or McIsaac criteria, throat examination, rapid antigen detection testing for GAS, confirmatory throat culture when indicated, and selective nucleic acid amplification, viral testing, heterophile/EBV serology, or CBC/CRP in atypical cases. Treatment is usually supportive, with acetaminophen acting centrally to reduce pain and fever, ibuprofen inhibiting COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis, and topical benzocaine producing local sodium-channel blockade; confirmed streptococcal pharyngitis is treated with penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, or azithromycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor, in selected allergic patients. Name: Pheochromocytoma
Description: Pheochromocytoma (MeSH D010673) is a usually catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumor of chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, closely related to extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglioma, and may be sporadic or hereditary; major genetic drivers include germline or somatic alterations in RET, VHL, NF1, and the succinate dehydrogenase genes SDHB, SDHD, SDHC, and SDHA, with less frequent involvement of TMEM127, MAX, FH, EPAS1/HIF2A, EGLN1/PHD2, and HRAS. These lesions broadly segregate into pseudohypoxic tumors characterized by Krebs cycle dysfunction, succinate accumulation, HIF stabilization, angiogenic signaling, and epigenetic dysregulation, versus kinase-signaling tumors involving RAS/RAF/MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways; catecholamine synthesis depends on tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, and sometimes PNMT. Clinical manifestations reflect excess epinephrine and norepinephrine and include sustained or paroxysmal hypertension, headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, tremor, pallor, anxiety, orthostasis, hyperglycemia, and weight loss, while complications include hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, stroke, myocardial infarction, and metastatic disease, particularly with SDHB-mutated tumors. Syndromic associations include MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, and hereditary paraganglioma syndromes; inheritance is commonly autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, with parent-of-origin effects for SDHD and SDHAF2. Diagnosis rests on biochemical evidence of catecholamine excess, especially elevated plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines, followed by localization with CT or MRI and functional imaging such as 123I-MIBG, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET, or 18F-FDG PET in selected cases, plus histopathology and genetic testing. Definitive treatment is surgical adrenalectomy after alpha-adrenergic blockade, typically phenoxybenzamine, or selective alpha1 blockers such as doxazosin, to prevent perioperative crisis; beta-blockers such as propranolol or metoprolol are added only after adequate alpha blockade for tachyarr

Name: Phobia, Social
Description: Social phobia, or social anxiety disorder (UMLS C0031572), is a common anxiety disorder characterized by marked, persistent fear of social or performance situations in which scrutiny, embarrassment, or negative evaluation is anticipated, producing symptoms such as anticipatory anxiety, blushing, tremor, sweating, palpitations, gastrointestinal distress, cognitive self-focused rumination, avoidance, and functional impairment; generalized and performance-only subtypes are recognized. Its biology is polygenic and moderately heritable, with family and twin studies supporting complex inheritance rather than Mendelian transmission, and representative susceptibility signals implicate serotonergic, dopaminergic, and stress-response genes and proteins including SLC6A4/5-HTT, HTR1A, COMT, MAOA, DRD2, BDNF, CRHR1, RGS2, and FKBP5, although effect sizes are small and non-deterministic. Relevant pathways include amygdala-prefrontal fear circuitry, hyperreactive insula and anterior cingulate networks, serotonin and norepinephrine signaling, dopaminergic reward/social salience processing, GABAergic inhibition, glutamatergic modulation, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation with cortisol stress responses. Common comorbidities include major depressive disorder, other anxiety disorders, avoidant personality disorder, substance use disorders, especially alcohol misuse, and increased risk of social, academic, and occupational disability and suicidality. First-line pharmacotherapy includes SSRIs such as sertraline and paroxetine, which inhibit the serotonin transporter to enhance synaptic 5-HT, and the SNRI venlafaxine, which inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; additional agents include benzodiazepines such as clonazepam, a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptors, and performance-situation treatment with propranolol, a nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker that reduces peripheral autonomic symptoms. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 criteria requiring disproportionate fear, near-consistent provocation, avoidance or endurance with intense distress, duration typically at least 6 months, and impairment, supported by structured interview and rating scales such as the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, while laboratory or imaging tests are used mainly to exclude medical mimics.

Name: Pinta
Description: Pinta (UMLS C0031946) is a chronic, nonvenereal endemic treponematosis caused by the spirochete Treponema carateum, now generally regarded as closely related to, and possibly a variant within, the T. pallidum complex rather than a genetically defined inherited disorder; consequently, no human Mendelian inheritance pattern, disease-causing germline mutations, or validated host susceptibility genes are established, although spirochetal outer-membrane and flagellar proteins, TpN47/Tpp47-like lipoproteins, and other treponemal antigens are implicated in host interaction and immune recognition. Pathobiology centers on cutaneous inoculation, local replication, and a host inflammatory response involving innate immune cells, macrophages, T lymphocytes, endothelial activation, and cytokine networks such as TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-1, and IL-6, with downstream NF-kB–linked inflammatory signaling contributing to chronic dermal injury and pigmentary change rather than a single canonical molecular pathway. Clinically, pinta progresses through primary papular or scaly inoculation lesions to disseminated pintids and later dyschromic plaques with hyperkeratosis, pruritus, and characteristic hyperpigmented, hypopigmented, or achromic patches, usually without visceral, cardiovascular, or neurologic syphilis-like involvement. Subtypes are usually described by stage as primary, secondary, and late or tertiary pinta. Diagnosis is based on epidemiologic exposure in endemic rural settings, compatible skin findings, dark-field or microscopy being rarely useful, and positive treponemal and nontreponemal serology such as VDRL, RPR, FTA-ABS, or TPPA, while PCR or histopathology may support difficult cases; diagnosis also requires exclusion of vitiligo, tinea versicolor, leprosy, yaws, and syphilis. Standard treatment includes benzathine penicillin G, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit; azithromycin, a macrolide that inhibits 50S-mediated protein synthesis; and, in some settings, erythromycin with a similar 50S mechanism. Name: Pituitary Neoplasms
Description: Pituitary neoplasms are usually benign adenohypophyseal tumors, most commonly pituitary adenomas or pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, classified as functioning or nonfunctioning and by lineage into lactotroph, somatotroph, corticotroph, thyrotroph, gonadotroph, null-cell, and rare aggressive or metastatic pituitary carcinoma. Their biology involves dysregulated cAMP/PKA, MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, EGFR, cell-cycle, and hypothalamic dopamine-somatostatin signaling pathways; representative molecular alterations include GNAS mutations in somatotroph tumors, USP8 mutations in corticotroph adenomas, and less often MEN1, AIP, PRKAR1A, CDKN1B, SDHx, DICER1, or mismatch-repair defects in hereditary predisposition syndromes, with proteins such as PIT1, TPIT, SF1, prolactin, GH, ACTH, and SSTR2/SSTR5 aiding classification. Most cases are sporadic, but familial isolated pituitary adenoma is often autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, especially with AIP variants, and pituitary tumors also occur in MEN1, Carney complex, and MEN4. Clinical manifestations reflect hormone excess or mass effect: hyperprolactinemia causing galactorrhea, hypogonadism, infertility, and amenorrhea; GH excess causing acromegaly; ACTH excess causing Cushing disease; TSH excess causing thyrotoxicosis; and headache, bitemporal hemianopia, cranial neuropathies, pituitary apoplexy, or hypopituitarism from larger lesions. Important comorbidities and complications include diabetes, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, sleep apnea, osteoporosis, thromboembolic risk, visual loss, cerebrospinal fluid leak, and treatment-related endocrine deficits. Diagnosis relies on pituitary hormone testing and dynamic studies, visual field assessment, pituitary MRI with contrast, and pathology with immunohistochemistry and Ki-67 when resected; germline or somatic genetic testing is considered in early-onset, familial, syndromic, or aggressive disease. Name: Pityriasis
Description: Pityriasis is a descriptive group of papulosquamous disorders characterized by fine scaling eruptions, most commonly including pityriasis rosea, pityriasis alba, pityriasis rubra pilaris, and pityriasis versicolor, with clinical behavior ranging from self-limited inflammatory exanthem to chronic keratinization disorder or superficial fungal infection. Typical findings are oval or annular scaly patches or plaques, often pruritic, with pityriasis rosea classically showing a herald patch followed by cleavage-line distributed lesions, pityriasis alba causing hypopigmented facial patches, pityriasis rubra pilaris producing follicular hyperkeratotic papules with palmoplantar keratoderma, and pityriasis versicolor presenting with hypo- or hyperpigmented finely scaling macules on the trunk. Genetic and molecular associations are subtype-specific: familial pityriasis rubra pilaris is linked to autosomal dominant CARD14 gain-of-function variants with downstream NF-κB, IL-23/Th17, and keratinocyte inflammatory signaling; psoriasis-overlapping pathways involving TNF-α, IL-17A, IL-22, and STAT3 may be active in some cases, while pityriasis rosea has been associated with reactivation of human herpesviruses 6 and 7 rather than Mendelian inheritance, and pityriasis versicolor is associated with Malassezia species lipases and altered epidermal barrier and sebaceous microenvironment rather than a single causal mutation. Common treatments include topical corticosteroids, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory cytokine signaling and reduce pruritus; ketoconazole or selenium sulfide for pityriasis versicolor, which impair ergosterol-dependent fungal membrane function or reduce Malassezia burden; and acitretin for pityriasis rubra pilaris, which normalizes keratinocyte differentiation via retinoid receptor signaling; additional options include emollients, tacrolimus, methotrexate, or biologics targeting TNF-α or IL-17 in refractory inflammatory disease. Comorbidities and complications include atopy, pigmentary alteration, erythroderma, secondary infection, and psychosocial burden. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by KOH microscopy for versicolor, Wood lamp examination, skin biopsy showing subtype-specific histopathology, and targeted genetic testing for CARD14 in familial pityriasis rubra

Name: Plague
Description: Plague (MeSH D010930) is an acute, often fulminant zoonotic infection caused by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Yersinia pestis, transmitted mainly by flea bites or exposure to infected animals and, in pneumonic plague, by respiratory droplets; major clinical forms are bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic plague. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial virulence genes and proteins rather than host Mendelian inheritance, notably the pCD1/type III secretion system with Yops such as YopH, YopE, YopJ/P, and LcrV, the plasminogen activator Pla, the F1 capsular antigen encoded by caf1, and iron-acquisition systems including yersiniabactin, which disable innate immunity, promote lymphatic and hematogenous spread, and trigger dysregulated host signaling involving TLR2/TLR4 recognition, NF-κB and MAPK modulation, inflammasome and complement activation, cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and profound coagulation-endothelial injury responses. Typical features include abrupt fever, chills, severe malaise, painful suppurative regional lymphadenitis (buboes), headache, myalgia, abdominal symptoms, and in advanced disease hypotension, delirium, acral necrosis, DIC, shock, hemoptysis, and rapidly progressive pneumonia or ARDS. Important complications and comorbid associations include bacteremia, meningitis, secondary pneumonia, multiorgan failure, and worse outcomes with delayed treatment, malnutrition, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, or immunocompromise. There is no recognized hereditary inheritance pattern for plague susceptibility, although host genetic variation in innate immune pathways may modify risk. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology plus clinical syndrome and confirmatory testing by culture or PCR from bubo aspirate, blood, or sputum, direct fluorescent antibody or F1 antigen detection, and paired serology to F1 antibody. First-line therapy includes streptomycin or gentamicin, aminoglycosides that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause mistranslation; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding at 30S; and ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S pept

Name: Pneumococcal Infections
Description: Pneumococcal infections are acute mucosal or invasive diseases caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, classically presenting as noninvasive otitis media, sinusitis, and nonbacteremic pneumonia, or as invasive pneumococcal disease with bacteremia, sepsis, and meningitis; symptoms typically include fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, lobar consolidation, otalgia or sinus pain, and in meningitis headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, and sometimes shock. Pathogenesis is driven by pneumococcal virulence factors including the capsular polysaccharide, pneumolysin encoded by ply, autolysin LytA, neuraminidases NanA/NanB, and surface proteins such as PspA and CbpA/PspC that mediate epithelial adhesion, complement evasion, and blood-brain barrier invasion. Host susceptibility is strongly influenced by innate and adaptive immune pathways, notably TLR2/TLR4, MyD88, IRAK4, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1, IL-6, TNF, complement components C2/C3, and antibody-mediated opsonophagocytosis; representative genetic predisposition factors include inherited IRAK4 or MYD88 deficiency, terminal or early complement defects, and functional asplenia or hemoglobinopathies such as HBB-related sickle cell disease, while the infection itself is not inherited. Major comorbidities and risk states include extremes of age, COPD, influenza or other viral respiratory infections, diabetes, alcoholism, chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease, CSF leak, cochlear implant, HIV, malignancy, and immunosuppression; complications include empyema, respiratory failure, meningitis, hearing loss, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, and septic shock. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical syndrome plus microbiologic confirmation by blood, CSF, or sputum culture, Gram stain showing lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci, urinary pneumococcal antigen testing, PCR or multiplex respiratory panels, and susceptibility testing. Name: Pneumonia
Description: Pneumonia (MeSH D011014) is an acute inflammatory infection of the pulmonary parenchyma, most often caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi, and is clinically classified as community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration, atypical/interstitial, and opportunistic pneumonia. Its pathobiology centers on pathogen recognition and dysregulated host defense, with key involvement of TLR2/TLR4, NOD-like receptor and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, interferon, complement, and cytokine networks including TNF, IL1B, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, and IFNG, driving neutrophil and macrophage recruitment, alveolar-capillary injury, and impaired gas exchange. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, but variants in TLR4, MBL2, CFTR, SFTPA1/SFTPD, and immune genes affecting IL6 or TNF responses, as well as primary immunodeficiencies, can increase risk; monogenic inheritance is uncommon except in syndromic predisposition states. Common pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae with virulence proteins such as pneumolysin and PspA, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella, influenza virus, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2. Symptoms and signs typically include fever, cough with or without purulent sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia, crackles, and radiographic infiltrates. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical presentation plus chest radiography or CT, pulse oximetry, CBC and inflammatory markers, sputum and blood cultures, urinary pneumococcal or Legionella antigens, and PCR-based respiratory pathogen testing; severity tools such as CURB-65 are often used. Treatment depends on etiology and setting: amoxicillin or ceftriaxone inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, azithromycin inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, levofloxacin inhibits DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV, and oseltamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase. Name: Pneumonia, Aspiration
Description: Aspiration pneumonia (UMLS C0032290) is an infectious and inflammatory lung disease caused by inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents into the lower airways, producing a spectrum from chemical pneumonitis to polymicrobial bacterial pneumonia, classically involving dependent lung segments; subtypes include community-acquired, hospital-acquired, anaerobe-predominant, and aspiration associated with gastric acid injury. Its pathobiology is dominated by innate immune signaling, including Toll-like receptor and NF-κB activation, cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, epithelial-endothelial barrier injury, and in severe cases oxidative stress, alveolar macrophage dysfunction, and sepsis-related pathways. There is no single Mendelian cause, but genetic susceptibility may influence aspiration risk or inflammatory response, with representative associations involving TNF, IL6, TLR4, MUC genes, and genes underlying neurologic or swallowing disorders such as SCN1A, DMD, HTT, or APOE-linked stroke/neurodegeneration; inheritance therefore usually reflects the underlying predisposing condition rather than the pneumonia itself. Major comorbidities include stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, esophageal dysmotility, gastroesophageal reflux, alcoholism, poor dentition, tube feeding, sedation, seizures, and mechanical ventilation; complications include lung abscess, empyema, acute respiratory distress syndrome, respiratory failure, bacteremia, and death. Typical manifestations are cough, fever, dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, pleuritic chest discomfort, foul-smelling sputum, crackles, and altered mental status, although chemical aspiration may present abruptly after a witnessed event. Diagnosis is clinical-radiographic, supported by aspiration risk factors, infiltrates in dependent lobes on chest radiography or CT, pulse oximetry or arterial blood gas abnormalities, leukocytosis and inflammatory markers, sputum and blood cultures when severe, and swallowing evaluation by bedside assessment, videofluoroscopic swallow study, or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation. Name: Pneumonia, Mycoplasma
Description: Pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MeSH D011019) is a contagious atypical community-acquired pneumonia caused by a cell wall–deficient bacterium that adheres to respiratory epithelium through the P1 adhesin complex and accessory proteins such as P30, provoking ciliary dysfunction and host inflammation rather than extensive alveolar invasion; major host-response pathways include TLR2/TLR6- and NF-κB-mediated cytokine signaling, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, MAPK pathways, and adaptive immune responses with IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and Th1/Th17 components. Disease ranges from upper respiratory infection and tracheobronchitis to mild “walking pneumonia” and severe or fulminant pneumonia, sometimes with macrolide-resistant strains linked to 23S rRNA mutations, especially A2063G and A2064G. Common symptoms are persistent dry cough, fever, malaise, headache, sore throat, wheeze, and auscultatory findings often milder than radiographic infiltrates; extrapulmonary manifestations may include hemolytic anemia from cold agglutinins, rash, hepatitis, myocarditis, and encephalitis. Comorbidities and complications include asthma exacerbation, COPD, bronchiolitis obliterans, pleural effusion, respiratory failure, and secondary bacterial infection. Treatment commonly includes macrolides such as azithromycin or clarithromycin, which bind the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibit protein synthesis; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks the 30S subunit; and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical and radiographic features plus laboratory confirmation by NAAT/PCR of respiratory specimens, serology showing specific IgM or rising paired IgG titers, and less commonly culture; supportive findings can include cold agglutinins. It is not a Mendelian inherited disorder, but host susceptibility and severity may be modified by immune-related genes, with reported associations involving TLR2, TLR4, IL6, IL8, TNF, and HLA variants.

Name: Pneumonia, Staphylococcal
Description: Staphylococcal pneumonia is an acute bacterial infection of the lung parenchyma caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant strains, and is often necrotizing, abscess-forming, or post-influenza in nature; major virulence determinants include mecA/PBP2a in MRSA, the PVL genes lukS-PV/lukF-PV linked to severe necrotizing disease, agr quorum-sensing regulators, spa, coa, alpha-toxin hla, and protein A, while host susceptibility is influenced by immune genes and pathways such as TLR2, MYD88, NF-kappaB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1, IL-6, TNF, CXCL8/IL-8, complement, and neutrophil oxidative killing, with rare inherited predisposition in disorders such as chronic granulomatous disease involving CYBB or other NADPH oxidase genes, STAT3-related hyper-IgE syndrome, and IRAK4 or MYD88 deficiency. Typical presentations include fever, cough, purulent sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxemia, leukocytosis, multilobar or cavitary infiltrates, empyema, and rapid progression to sepsis or acute respiratory distress syndrome. Subtypes include community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, post-viral, necrotizing, and bacteremic pneumonia. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical and radiographic findings plus microbiologic confirmation by sputum or tracheal aspirate culture, blood cultures, bronchoalveolar lavage in selected cases, Gram stain showing gram-positive cocci in clusters, and susceptibility testing including cefoxitin or oxacillin testing or PCR for mecA/mecC; inflammatory markers and chest CT may help define complications. Standard therapy includes vancomycin, a glycopeptide that inhibits cell-wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala; linezolid, an oxazolidinone that blocks 50S initiation; and nafcillin or oxacillin, beta-lactams that inhibit PBPs in MSSA, with alternatives such as cefazolin, ceftaroline, or clindamycin, the latter also reducing toxin production. Name: Polycythemia Vera
Description: Polycythemia vera is a chronic BCR::ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal erythrocytosis, often with accompanying leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, arising most commonly from acquired activating mutations in JAK2, especially JAK2 V617F and less often exon 12 variants, which drive constitutive JAK-STAT signaling downstream of the erythropoietin receptor and related cytokine receptors; cooperating lesions in epigenetic regulators such as TET2, ASXL1, DNMT3A, EZH2, SF3B1, and IDH1/2 may influence phenotype, progression, and prognosis. The disease is usually sporadic rather than classically inherited, although familial predisposition occurs and rare germline contributors affecting JAK2 signaling, erythropoietin sensing, or clonal hematopoiesis susceptibility have been described. Clinically, patients present with hyperviscosity-related headache, dizziness, visual disturbance, aquagenic pruritus, facial plethora, erythromelalgia, hypertension, splenomegaly, fatigue, and vasomotor symptoms, while major complications include arterial and venous thrombosis, hemorrhage, gout, peptic ulcer disease, myelofibrotic transformation, and evolution to acute myeloid leukemia. Diagnostic evaluation relies on WHO/ICC-style criteria integrating elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit/red cell mass, bone marrow panmyelosis with pleomorphic mature megakaryocytes, presence of a JAK2 mutation, and subnormal serum erythropoietin, with confirmation by CBC, peripheral smear, marrow biopsy, molecular testing for JAK2 V617F or exon 12, and exclusion of secondary erythrocytosis. Recognized forms include classic overt polycythemia vera and masked or prodromal disease. Treatment aims to reduce thrombosis risk and control symptoms: phlebotomy lowers hematocrit, low-dose aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and thromboxane A2 production, hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase to provide cytoreduction, interferon alfa or ropeginterferon alfa modulates clonal hematopoiesis and suppresses JAK2-mutant burden, and ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, is used for hydroxyurea-resistant or intolerant disease.

Name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
Description: Polymyalgia rheumatica (MeSH D011111) is a common inflammatory rheumatic disorder of older adults, usually after age 50, characterized by abrupt or subacute bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain, marked morning stiffness, neck pain, constitutional symptoms, and elevated acute-phase reactants; it is closely linked to giant cell arteritis, which represents a major vascular complication requiring urgent recognition because of risks such as vision loss, stroke, and aortic aneurysm. The disease is generally considered multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with genetic susceptibility most consistently involving HLA class II alleles, especially HLA-DRB1 and related haplotypes, and inflammatory mediators including IL6, TNF, IL1B, and CRP; no single causal mutation is established, but immune dysregulation in innate and adaptive pathways, with monocyte/macrophage activation, Th17 and T-cell signaling, JAK-STAT, NF-kappaB, and IL-6-driven hepatic acute-phase responses, is central. Typical subtypes include isolated polymyalgia rheumatica and polymyalgia rheumatica associated with giant cell arteritis. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by elevated ESR and/or CRP, exclusion of mimics such as rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, infection, and malignancy, rapid response to low-dose glucocorticoids, and 2012 EULAR/ACR classification criteria; ultrasound showing bilateral subdeltoid bursitis, biceps tenosynovitis, or hip synovitis can increase specificity, while temporal artery assessment or vascular imaging is used if giant cell arteritis is suspected. First-line treatment is prednisone or prednisolone, which suppress glucocorticoid receptor-mediated transcription of proinflammatory cytokines; methotrexate is commonly used as a steroid-sparing antifolate that inhibits purine metabolism and dampens lymphocyte proliferation; tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist, is used particularly in refractory disease or when giant cell arteritis coexists. Important comorbidities and treatment-related complications include osteoporosis, diabetes, hypertension, infection, relapse, frailty, and glucocorticoid toxicity.

Name: Polyuria
Description: Polyuria is a clinical syndrome, not a single disease, defined in adults as urine output typically exceeding 3 L/day and reflecting either water diuresis or solute diuresis; it presents with frequent large-volume urination, nocturia, polydipsia, dehydration, orthostasis, and, depending on cause, hypernatremia or hyponatremia. Major subtypes include central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, primary polydipsia, osmotic diuresis from diabetes mellitus, and less commonly postobstructive or drug-induced polyuria. Key molecular determinants center on the arginine vasopressin pathway: AVP from the hypothalamic-pituitary axis binds AVPR2 on collecting duct principal cells, activating Gs-cAMP-PKA signaling to promote AQP2 trafficking to the apical membrane; defects in AVP, AVPR2, AQP2, or medullary concentrating mechanisms impair water reabsorption. Representative genetic causes include AVP mutations causing autosomal dominant central diabetes insipidus, AVPR2 mutations causing X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and AQP2 mutations causing autosomal recessive or dominant nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; polyuria also accompanies hereditary tubulopathies and cystic kidney disorders. Common treatments depend on etiology: desmopressin, a V2-receptor agonist, replaces vasopressin in central diabetes insipidus; thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide paradoxically reduce urine volume by inducing mild volume contraction and increasing proximal sodium-water reabsorption; amiloride blocks epithelial sodium channels and is especially useful in lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; indomethacin reduces renal prostaglandin-mediated antagonism of vasopressin; osmotic polyuria from diabetes mellitus is treated with insulin or other antihyperglycemics. Comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, electrolyte disturbances, nephrocalcinosis, growth failure in children, urinary tract dilation, and recurrent dehydration. Diagnosis relies on 24-hour urine volume, serum and urine osmolality, electrolytes, glucose and calcium testing, water-deprivation and desmopressin challenge, copeptin measurement, urinalysis, and targeted pituitary or renal imaging and genetic testing when hereditary disease is suspected.

Name: Neuralgia, Postherpetic
Description: Postherpetic neuralgia is a chronic neuropathic pain syndrome that persists, classically for 90 days or longer, after healing of herpes zoster rash and reflects varicella-zoster virus–induced injury to peripheral nerves, dorsal root ganglia, and central sensory pathways. It is not a Mendelian disorder, but host susceptibility is influenced by genetic components affecting pain processing and immunity, with reported associations involving voltage-gated sodium channel genes such as SCN9A and SCN10A, catechol-O-methyltransferase COMT, cytokine genes including IL6, TNF, and IL10, and HLA-related variation; relevant proteins include Nav1.7, Nav1.8, TRPV1, CGRP, substance P, and inflammatory mediators. Pathobiology involves neuroinflammation and maladaptive sensitization, including VZV-triggered activation of NF-kB, JAK/STAT, MAPK/ERK, toll-like receptor, and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, with contributions from sodium and calcium channel upregulation, ectopic discharges, microglial and astrocyte activation, and loss of inhibitory GABAergic tone. Patients typically present with persistent dermatomal burning, stabbing, or electric-shock pain with allodynia, hyperalgesia, dysesthesia, pruritus, sensory loss, and sleep or mood disturbance; subtypes are often described as irritable nociceptor versus deafferentation phenotypes, or by affected dermatome such as trigeminal involvement. Diagnosis is clinical, based on prior zoster in the same distribution and persistent neuropathic pain, supported when needed by sensory examination, pain questionnaires, quantitative sensory testing, nerve conduction studies in selected cases, or skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber loss. Common treatments include gabapentin and pregabalin, which bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels to reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release; tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline, which inhibit norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake and modulate sodium channels; topical lidocaine, which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels; and capsaicin, a TRPV1 agonist causing defunctionalization of nociceptors. Name: Postpartum Hemorrhage
Description: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH; MeSH D006473) is an acute obstetric emergency defined classically as blood loss ≥500 mL after vaginal delivery or ≥1000 mL after cesarean birth, with current practice emphasizing cumulative blood loss accompanied by hypovolemia within 24 hours for primary PPH and from 24 hours to 6–12 weeks for secondary PPH. It is not a Mendelian disease, but genetic susceptibility is recognized through inherited bleeding and uterotonic-response pathways, including coagulation factor defects such as F11, F8, F9, VWF, and F13A1 variants, platelet-function genes such as ITGA2B and ITGB3, and rare uterine contractility-related candidates involving oxytocin/prostaglandin signaling; representative protein abnormalities include reduced von Willebrand factor, factor XI deficiency, and impaired fibrin cross-linking. Core pathobiology is summarized by the four Ts: tone, tissue, trauma, and thrombin, with major molecular pathways involving oxytocin receptor–Gq/PLC/IP3/Ca2+-mediated myometrial contraction, prostaglandin FP/EP signaling, thromboxane-induced vasoconstriction and platelet activation, tissue factor–thrombin–fibrin hemostasis, and fibrinolysis regulated by plasmin. Clinical features include excessive vaginal bleeding, uterine atony, tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, dizziness, falling hemoglobin, and in severe cases hemorrhagic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Important subtypes include atonic, traumatic, retained products/placental, and coagulopathic PPH. Common treatments are oxytocin, a uterotonic that activates oxytocin receptors to increase intracellular calcium and uterine contraction; methylergonovine, an ergot alkaloid causing sustained myometrial and vascular smooth-muscle contraction via serotonergic/adrenergic pathways; carboprost, a PGF2α analog stimulating myometrial contraction; misoprostol, a PGE1 analog; and tranexamic acid, which inhibits plasminogen activation and fibrinolysis. Major comorbidities and risk factors include placenta previa/accreta spectrum, hypertensive disorders, prolonged labor, chorioamnionitis, multiple gestation, uterine fibroids, prior PPH, anemia, and inherited coagulopathies

Name: Prader-Willi Syndrome
Description: Prader-Willi syndrome (UMLS C0032897) is a multisystem neurodevelopmental and imprinting disorder caused by loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13, most commonly due to a paternal deletion, maternal uniparental disomy 15, or an imprinting center defect; key genes/transcripts implicated include SNORD116, MAGEL2, NDN, MKRN3, and SNRPN, with the phenotype reflecting absent paternal expression rather than classic Mendelian inheritance, although rare familial recurrence occurs with imprinting center mutations or chromosomal rearrangements. The disorder is characterized by hypothalamic dysfunction affecting leptin-melanocortin, ghrelin, oxytocin, growth hormone/IGF-1, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone pathways, contributing to neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding followed later by hyperphagia, impaired satiety, obesity, short stature, developmental delay, mild to moderate intellectual disability, behavioral dysregulation, sleep disturbance, hypogonadism, and characteristic facies, small hands and feet, and scoliosis. Major subtypes correspond to deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, and imprinting defect, with some genotype-phenotype differences including relatively higher psychosis risk in maternal UPD. Common comorbidities and complications include type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, cardiovascular disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, osteoporosis, cryptorchidism, infertility or subfertility, skin picking, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive traits, and occasionally psychosis. Treatment is supportive and multidisciplinary; somatropin, a recombinant growth hormone, improves linear growth, body composition, and motor function via GH receptor–JAK2/STAT5 signaling; sex steroid replacement such as testosterone or estrogen/progestin treats hypogonadism through nuclear hormone receptor activation; and topiramate, which modulates voltage-gated sodium channels, enhances GABAergic activity, and antagonizes AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors, is used for hyperphagia or behavioral symptoms, while SSRIs such as fluoxetine may help compulsive behaviors through serotonin reuptake inhibition. Diagnosis is established by DNA methylation testing of 15q11-q13, with chromosomal microarray, FISH, MLPA, or SNP-based studies distinguishing deletion, UPD, and imprinting defects; clinical suspicion arises from consensus criteria emphasizing age-dependent hypotonia

Name: Premature Ejaculation
Description: Premature ejaculation (UMLS C0033038) is a common male sexual dysfunction characterized by persistent or recurrent ejaculation occurring before or within about 1 minute of vaginal penetration in lifelong cases, or a clinically significant reduction in latency, often to 3 minutes or less, in acquired forms, accompanied by inability to delay ejaculation and marked personal distress, frustration, or avoidance of intimacy. It is typically classified as lifelong versus acquired, and as generalized versus situational. The disorder is multifactorial, involving dysregulation of central serotonergic pathways, especially 5-HT1A and 5-HT2C receptor signaling, with additional contributions from dopaminergic, oxytocinergic, adrenergic, and nitric oxide/cGMP pathways; representative genetic associations include polymorphisms in SLC6A4 encoding the serotonin transporter, HTR1A, HTR2C, and dopaminergic genes such as DRD2, although effects are modest and inheritance is complex, polygenic, and non-Mendelian, with familial clustering reported but no single causative mutation established. Symptoms center on consistently short intravaginal ejaculatory latency time, poor perceived ejaculatory control, and distress, while complications include relationship conflict, reduced quality of life, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sexual avoidance. Important comorbidities include erectile dysfunction, chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome, thyroid dysfunction, especially hyperthyroidism, metabolic and cardiovascular risk states, and other anxiety-related disorders. Diagnosis is clinical, based on sexual history, estimated or stopwatch-measured intravaginal ejaculatory latency time, validated instruments such as the Premature Ejaculation Diagnostic Tool, and evaluation for secondary causes with focused examination and selected testing, including thyroid studies or urologic assessment when indicated. Common treatments include dapoxetine, a short-acting selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor that enhances synaptic serotonin and delays ejaculatory reflexes; paroxetine, sertraline, fluoxetine, or clomipramine, which similarly prolong latency through serotonergic reuptake inhibition; topical lidocaine-prilocaine, which reduces penile sensory input via sodium-channel blockade; and tramadol, an opioid agonist with monoamine reuptake inhibition, used more selectively because of dependence and adverse-effect concerns.

Name: Proctitis
Description: Proctitis is inflammation of the rectal mucosa that may be acute or chronic and is most often infectious, inflammatory bowel disease-related, radiation-induced, ischemic, traumatic, medication-associated, or diversion-related rather than a primary inherited disorder. Clinically it presents with rectal pain, tenesmus, urgency, frequent small-volume stools, diarrhea, hematochezia, mucus discharge, anorectal burning, and sometimes fever or pelvic discomfort; ulcerative proctitis is a distal subtype of ulcerative colitis, while sexually transmitted infectious proctitis commonly reflects Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis including LGV serovars, herpes simplex virus, or Treponema pallidum, and radiation proctitis is classified as acute or chronic. Molecular associations are best defined when proctitis occurs within inflammatory bowel disease, where susceptibility genes such as NOD2, IL23R, ATG16L1, JAK2, HLA variants, and epithelial barrier or mucin-related factors may contribute, with proteins and pathways involving TNF, IL-12/IL-23, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, integrins, chemokines, T-cell trafficking, neutrophil recruitment, oxidative stress, and epithelial repair; infectious forms additionally engage innate immune sensing via TLRs and interferon signaling. Common treatments include topical or oral mesalamine, a 5-aminosalicylate that inhibits cyclooxygenase/lipoxygenase pathways and modulates NF-kB; corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone or budesonide, which suppress proinflammatory cytokine transcription; doxycycline for chlamydial/LGV disease via 30S ribosomal inhibition; ceftriaxone for gonorrhea by binding penicillin-binding proteins and inhibiting cell-wall synthesis; and acyclovir for HSV by inhibiting viral DNA polymerase after phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase. Comorbidities include ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, other sexually transmitted infections including HIV, pelvic malignancy after radiotherapy, and anorectal dysfunction; complications include ulceration, severe bleeding, stricture, fistula, abscess, perforation, anemia, and, in chronic inflammatory settings, dysplasia. Diagnosis relies on history and exposure assessment, digital rectal examination, anoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy, stool studies, rectal NAATs and cultures for pathogens,

Name: Prostatic Neoplasms
Description: Prostatic neoplasms, predominantly prostatic adenocarcinoma arising from glandular epithelium and less commonly including ductal adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine/small-cell carcinoma, and castration-resistant metastatic disease, are typically age-related malignant tumors driven by androgen receptor signaling and genomic alterations involving TMPRSS2-ERG fusion, PTEN loss with PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation, TP53 and RB1 inactivation, SPOP, FOXA1, ATM, CHEK2, CDK12, and DNA-repair defects such as BRCA1/2 mutations; inherited susceptibility is usually complex but is increased in familial cancer syndromes, especially autosomal dominant hereditary breast-ovarian/prostate cancer linked to BRCA2, and Lynch syndrome with mismatch-repair genes. Key pathways include androgen-AR transcriptional programs, PI3K/AKT, RAS/MAPK, WNT/beta-catenin, DNA-damage response, and neuroendocrine lineage plasticity. Common manifestations are often absent early, but may include urinary hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, hematuria, hematospermia, pelvic discomfort, erectile dysfunction, and, in advanced disease, weight loss, anemia, and bone pain from osteoblastic metastases. Major complications include bladder outlet obstruction, urinary retention, hydronephrosis, pathologic fractures, spinal cord compression, and thromboembolic disease; comorbidities commonly coexist with benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, and age-related cardiovascular or metabolic disease. Diagnosis relies on abnormal digital rectal examination, elevated or rising prostate-specific antigen, multiparametric MRI, and histopathologic confirmation by transrectal or transperineal biopsy with Gleason grade group/ISUP scoring, TNM staging, and immunohistochemistry; germline and somatic testing for homologous-recombination or mismatch-repair defects and PSMA-based PET imaging are increasingly used in advanced cases. Standard therapies include leuprolide, a GnRH agonist causing medical castration; enzalutamide, an androgen-receptor signaling inhibitor; docetaxel, a microtubule-stabilizing taxane; abiraterone, a CYP17 inhibitor that suppresses androgen synthesis; and in selected biomarker-defined tumors olaparib, a PARP inhibitor.

Name: Prostatitis
Description: Prostatitis (MeSH D011472) is a heterogeneous inflammatory disorder of the prostate encompassing acute bacterial prostatitis, chronic bacterial prostatitis, chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS; inflammatory and noninflammatory forms), and asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis. Its biology is multifactorial, involving microbial infection, intraprostatic urinary reflux, pelvic floor dysfunction, neuroimmune sensitization, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity; commonly implicated molecular components include Toll-like receptor/NF-κB signaling, inflammasome activation, and cytokines/chemokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, COX-2, iNOS, reactive oxygen species, and, in some studies, altered androgen receptor and PSA-related pathways. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian rather than inherited in a single-gene pattern; reported associations include polymorphisms in IL6, IL8, TNF, TLR4, and other immune-response genes, although no highly penetrant mutation is established for most cases. Typical manifestations are pelvic, perineal, suprapubic, testicular, penile, or low-back pain, dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, painful ejaculation, sexual dysfunction, obstructive voiding symptoms, and, in acute bacterial disease, fever, chills, malaise, and a tender boggy prostate. Common pathogens include Escherichia coli and other Enterobacterales, occasionally Enterococcus. Treatment depends on subtype: fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole inhibits sequential folate synthesis; doxycycline inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit; α1-blockers such as tamsulosin reduce bladder outlet and prostatic smooth-muscle tone; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen inhibit COX-mediated prostaglandin synthesis. Comorbidities include benign prostatic hyperplasia, recurrent urinary tract infection, epididymitis, infertility/subfertility, anxiety, depression, irritable bowel syndrome, and chronic pain syndromes; complications include urinary retention, prostatic abscess, bacteremia, and sepsis. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, urinalysis and urine culture, pre- and post-prostatic massage localization tests or semen culture in chronic infection, STI testing when indicated,

Name: Pruritus
Description: Pruritus (itch; MeSH D011537) is a symptom complex rather than a single disease, defined by an unpleasant sensation provoking the urge to scratch, and it may be acute or chronic (>6 weeks), localized or generalized, with major subtypes including dermatologic, systemic, neuropathic, psychogenic, and mixed itch. Its biology centers on cutaneous and neural pruriceptive pathways involving histamine H1/H4 receptors, protease-activated receptor-2, Mas-related G protein-coupled receptors, TRPV1/TRPA1 ion channels, opioid receptors, neurokinin-1 signaling, and cytokine axes such as IL-4/IL-13-JAK-STAT and IL-31/IL31RA-OSMR; representative genetic contributors are best established in itch-associated disorders, including FLG loss-of-function variants in atopic dermatitis, STAT3 mutations in hyper-IgE syndrome, and ATP2C1 mutations in Hailey-Hailey disease, while familial cholestatic pruritus may accompany ABCB11 or ATP8B1 defects. Common associated proteins include substance P, nerve growth factor, thymic stromal lymphopoietin, and bile acid-related mediators. Typical features are itching with excoriations, lichenification, prurigo nodules, sleep disturbance, anxiety, and impaired quality of life; complications include secondary infection, eczematization, depression, and in severe systemic disease, malnutrition or suicidality. Important comorbidities include atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, chronic kidney disease, cholestatic liver disease, hematologic malignancy, iron deficiency, diabetes, thyroid disease, HIV, and neuropathies. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, based on history, skin examination, medication review, assessment of itch severity, and directed testing such as CBC, renal and liver chemistries, thyroid studies, ferritin, glucose, hepatitis/HIV testing, skin scraping or biopsy, and imaging when malignancy is suspected. Treatment targets cause and pathways: antihistamines such as cetirizine reduce H1-mediated itch, topical corticosteroids suppress cutaneous inflammation, gabapentin attenuates neuropathic neuronal excitability, cholestyramine binds pruritogenic bile acids in cholestasis, nalfurafine or other opioid modulators rebalance opioid signaling, and dupilumab blocks IL-4Rα to inhibit IL-4/

Name: Pruritus Ani
Description: Pruritus ani (MeSH D011538) is a symptom-defined anorectal disorder characterized by intense itching, burning, soreness, and perianal irritation that may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to identifiable local or systemic disease; examination may show erythema, lichenification, excoriations, fissuring, moisture, or secondary infection. Its biology is usually inflammatory and neurocutaneous rather than monogenic, with itch signaling involving epidermal barrier dysfunction, mast-cell and eosinophil mediators, protease-activated receptor and histamine pathways, and cytokine networks such as IL-4/IL-13, IL-31, TNF, and nerve sensitization through TRPV1 and related sensory pathways; when secondary to dermatoses or inflammatory bowel disease, representative molecular associations include FLG barrier variants in atopic dermatitis, filaggrin-related epidermal proteins, and immune pathways centered on JAK-STAT, Th2, and NF-kB signaling. Common causes and comorbidities include hemorrhoids, anal fissures, fecal seepage or incontinence, obesity, diabetes, candidiasis, dermatophyte infection, pinworm infestation, psoriasis, atopic or contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, sexually transmitted infections, and less commonly anal intraepithelial neoplasia or carcinoma; complications include sleep disturbance, chronic excoriation, lichen simplex chronicus, bleeding, and superinfection. Treatment is directed at cause and skin protection, commonly including zinc oxide or petrolatum barrier preparations that reduce moisture and friction, topical hydrocortisone that suppresses local phospholipase A2-driven inflammatory signaling, topical azole antifungals such as clotrimazole that inhibit fungal ergosterol synthesis, and in selected cases capsaicin, which defunctionalizes TRPV1-expressing sensory fibers, or antihistamines for symptomatic relief. There is no established Mendelian inheritance for idiopathic pruritus ani, but genetic predisposition may reflect inherited atopy or inflammatory dermatoses. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, based on history, anorectal and dermatologic examination, digital rectal exam and anoscopy, review of irritants and hygiene practices, with stool testing for parasites, fungal or bacterial cultures, patch testing, biopsy of persistent or atypical lesions, and targeted testing for diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, or malignancy when indicated

Name: Pruritus of genital organs
Description: Pruritus of the genital organs (UMLS C0033777) is a symptom-defined disorder rather than a single inherited disease, characterized by localized vulvar, penile, scrotal, or perineal itch arising from dermatologic, infectious, inflammatory, neuropathic, allergic, endocrine, or neoplastic causes. Common symptoms include persistent or nocturnal itching, burning, soreness, excoriations, erythema, lichenification, fissures, dyspareunia, dysuria, and secondary infection; major subtypes include vulvar pruritus and male genital pruritus, with frequent etiologies such as candidiasis, contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus, lichen simplex chronicus, scabies, pinworm infestation, vulvodynia-associated itch, and premalignant or malignant lesions. Molecularly, disease associations depend on cause and include barrier and immune genes such as FLG in atopic dermatitis, HLA-DQ7 and autoimmune susceptibility in lichen sclerosus, and cytokine-driven pathways involving IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, JAK-STAT, Th2 signaling, histamine-H1 receptor activation, TRPV1/TRPA1 neuronal itch pathways, protease-activated receptors, and NF-kB-mediated inflammation; proteins such as filaggrin, thymic stromal lymphopoietin, nerve growth factor, and eosinophil/mast-cell mediators may be implicated. Inheritance is usually absent or multifactorial, though atopic predisposition and autoimmune tendency can cluster in families. Comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, obesity, immunosuppression, menopause-related atrophy, anxiety/depression, other atopic disease, sexually transmitted infections, and autoimmune disorders; complications include sleep disturbance, sexual dysfunction, lichenification, ulceration, and delayed diagnosis of vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia or squamous cell carcinoma. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, based on focused history, inspection, pH testing when relevant, wet mount/KOH microscopy, fungal culture or NAATs for infectious causes, patch testing for contact allergy, skin biopsy for lichen sclerosus or neoplasia, and selected glucose, liver, renal, or thyroid studies for systemic contributors. Name: Pseudotumor Cerebri
Description: Pseudotumor cerebri, more commonly termed idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), is a syndrome of chronically elevated intracranial pressure without mass lesion, hydrocephalus, central nervous system infection, or structural venous cause, classically affecting obese women of childbearing age and presenting with daily headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy, papilledema, and progressive visual field loss. It is usually sporadic rather than Mendelian, but genetic susceptibility is supported by familial clustering and associations involving obesity- and CSF-regulatory pathways, with representative candidates including FTO, MC4R, LEPR, aquaporin-1, and loci influencing steroid metabolism and venous/extracellular matrix biology; no single recurrent pathogenic mutation defines most cases. Pathobiology is multifactorial, centering on impaired CSF absorption or increased secretion at the choroid plexus, venous sinus outflow restriction, obesity-related endocrine inflammation, and altered glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid signaling, with key components including carbonic anhydrase, aquaporins, sodium transporters, 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, adipokines, and transverse sinus stenosis. Commonly linked comorbidities include obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, metabolic syndrome, iron deficiency anemia, and exposure to tetracyclines, hypervitaminosis A/retinoids, growth hormone, or steroid withdrawal; major complications are permanent optic neuropathy and chronic disabling headache. Recognized forms include primary/idiopathic IIH and secondary intracranial hypertension. Diagnosis relies on modified Dandy/Friedman criteria: symptoms and signs of raised intracranial pressure, papilledema with otherwise nonfocal examination except possible abducens palsy, normal brain MRI with MR venography excluding mass and venous sinus thrombosis, normal CSF composition, and elevated lumbar puncture opening pressure, typically at least 25 cm H2O in adults. Name: Psoriasis
Description: Psoriasis (MeSH D011565) is a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory skin disease with systemic manifestations, characterized by sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, commonly on the scalp, elbows, knees, lumbosacral area, and nails, often accompanied by pruritus, Auspitz sign, Koebner phenomenon, and in some patients arthritis. Major subtypes include chronic plaque psoriasis, guttate, inverse, pustular, and erythrodermic psoriasis, with psoriatic arthritis as a related inflammatory musculoskeletal phenotype. Its pathobiology reflects a polygenic predisposition interacting with environmental triggers such as streptococcal infection, trauma, obesity, smoking, and drugs, with strongest genetic association at PSORS1 within HLA-C*06:02 and additional susceptibility genes involving IL23R, IL12B, TNIP1, TRAF3IP2, CARD14, TYK2, STAT3, and deletions of LCE3B/LCE3C; rare pustular forms may involve IL36RN, CARD14, or AP1S3 mutations. Central pathways include dendritic-cell activation, TNF signaling, the IL-23/Th17 axis, IL-17A/F, IL-22, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, and keratinocyte hyperproliferation with aberrant differentiation and neutrophilic infiltration. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported when needed by skin biopsy showing acanthosis, parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, hypogranulosis, and Munro microabscesses; severity assessment uses body surface area, PASI, and DLQI, and evaluation may include nail examination and screening for psoriatic arthritis. Common treatments include topical corticosteroids, which suppress inflammatory gene transcription; methotrexate, a folate antagonist with antiproliferative and immunomodulatory effects; cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor that reduces T-cell activation; phototherapy; and biologics such as adalimumab or infliximab targeting TNF-alpha, ustekinumab targeting IL-12/23, secukinumab targeting IL-17A, and guselkumab targeting IL-23.
