Name: Tension-Type Headache
Description: Tension-type headache (UMLS C0033893) is a common primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent bilateral, pressing or tightening, nonpulsatile head pain of mild to moderate intensity, typically without aggravation by routine physical activity and with little or no nausea, although photophobia or phonophobia may occur singly; patients often report pericranial muscle tenderness, scalp tightness, and neck or shoulder discomfort. It is classified as infrequent episodic, frequent episodic, and chronic tension-type headache, the latter occurring on at least 15 days per month and carrying higher risk of medication overuse, disability, sleep disturbance, anxiety, and depression. The disorder is considered multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with modest heritability strongest in chronic forms; no single causal mutation is established, but candidate genetic influences have included serotonergic, catecholaminergic, and pain-modulatory genes such as SLC6A4, COMT, HTR2A, and BDNF, with relevant proteins including the serotonin transporter, catechol-O-methyltransferase, serotonin receptors, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Pathobiology involves peripheral myofascial nociception and central sensitization, with altered descending pain control and signaling through serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways, trigeminal and cervical nociceptive circuits, glutamatergic/NMDA mechanisms, GABAergic modulation, nitric oxide, CGRP, substance P, and inflammatory cytokines. Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD criteria, supported by history and neurologic examination; headache diaries help define frequency and triggers, while neuroimaging or laboratory testing is reserved for red flags or atypical features. Common treatments include acetaminophen, which acts centrally to inhibit prostaglandin synthesis; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and reduce prostaglandin-mediated nociception; and amitriptyline for prevention, which inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake and may reduce central sensitization; other preventive options include mirtazapine or venlafaxine.

Name: Psychotic Disorders
Description: Psychotic disorders are a heterogeneous group of severe mental illnesses characterized by impaired reality testing, most commonly delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought or speech, abnormal psychomotor behavior, and negative symptoms such as avolition, alogia, and affective blunting; major subtypes include schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, schizophreniform disorder, brief psychotic disorder, delusional disorder, and substance- or medical condition-induced psychosis. Their pathobiology is multifactorial, with strong but complex genetic contributions involving common and rare variants in genes such as DRD2, COMT, DISC1, NRG1, AKT1, CACNA1C, GRIN2A, and C4A, as well as copy-number variants including 22q11.2 deletion, indicating predominantly polygenic inheritance with occasional high-impact mutations or syndromic forms. Implicated pathways include dopaminergic signaling, particularly mesolimbic D2 receptor hyperactivity, mesocortical dopaminergic deficits, glutamatergic NMDA receptor hypofunction, GABAergic interneuron dysfunction, synaptic pruning and complement signaling, neurodevelopmental pathways, calcium-channel signaling, and intracellular cascades such as PI3K-AKT-mTOR. Common treatments are antipsychotics including haloperidol, a potent D2 receptor antagonist; risperidone, a D2 and 5-HT2A antagonist; olanzapine, a multi-receptor atypical antipsychotic with D2/5-HT2A blockade; and clozapine for treatment-resistant illness, with broad serotonergic and dopaminergic effects and unique efficacy against suicidality. Frequent comorbidities and complications include depression, anxiety, substance use disorders, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, cognitive impairment, suicide, aggression, social dysfunction, and medication adverse effects such as extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, agranulocytosis, and tardive dyskinesia. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 or ICD criteria incorporating symptom type, duration, functional decline, and exclusion of mood, substance, neurologic, and medical causes, supported by psychiatric assessment, mental status examination, toxicology, laboratory screening, neurocognitive testing, and selective neuroimaging or EEG when secondary psychosis is suspected.

Name: Puberty, Delayed
Description: Delayed puberty is a clinical syndrome defined by absent or incomplete sexual maturation beyond the expected age, classically no breast development by 13 years in girls, no testicular enlargement to at least 4 mL by 14 years in boys, or prolonged interval to completion, and it may reflect constitutional delay of growth and puberty, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, or functional suppression from chronic illness. Key genetic causes include defects in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis such as ANOS1/KAL1, FGFR1, FGF8, GNRHR, GNRH1, KISS1, KISS1R, TAC3, TACR3, LEP, LEPR, and PROKR2 in congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, often with X-linked, autosomal dominant, or autosomal recessive inheritance, while primary gonadal failure may involve Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, or variants in NR5A1, LH receptor, FSH receptor, or androgen receptor genes. Core pathways include pulsatile GnRH signaling to pituitary gonadotrophs, LH and FSH action on gonadal steroidogenesis and gametogenesis, kisspeptin-neurokinin B signaling, leptin-mediated metabolic gating, and downstream sex steroid receptor pathways. Clinical findings include short stature or slowed growth velocity, delayed thelarche, menarche, or testicular enlargement, sparse pubic hair, low libido, infertility, anosmia in Kallmann syndrome, and low bone mineral accrual; complications include osteoporosis, psychosocial distress, and adverse effects of underlying disorders such as malnutrition, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, pituitary lesions, or chronic renal disease. Diagnosis relies on history, growth and family patterns, Tanner staging, bone age radiography, serum LH, FSH, estradiol or testosterone, prolactin, thyroid studies, CBC and inflammatory or nutritional tests, karyotype when indicated, MRI for central causes, and targeted genetic testing. Treatment commonly uses testosterone esters or transdermal testosterone in boys to activate androgen receptor signaling, low-dose estradiol followed by cyclic progestin in girls to induce secondary sexual characteristics and endometrial protection, and pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins such as hCG and FSH to stimulate the gonads and fertility in hypogonadotropic states.

Name: Puberty, Precocious
Description: Precocious puberty is the pathologic onset of secondary sexual development before age 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys, caused either by premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in central precocious puberty or by gonadotropin-independent peripheral sex steroid excess. Central forms are often idiopathic in girls but may reflect monogenic defects involving MKRN3, DLK1, KISS1, KISS1R, PROKR2, and less commonly LIN28B, with loss-of-function MKRN3 mutations causing a relatively common paternally inherited familial form; syndromic associations include activating GNAS mutations in McCune-Albright syndrome and inactivating CYP21A2 variants in congenital adrenal hyperplasia as causes of peripheral precocity. Core signaling involves premature GnRH pulsatility, kisspeptin-KISS1R and neurokinin B/TAC3-TACR3 regulation, pituitary LH and FSH secretion, and downstream gonadal steroidogenesis through aromatase, estrogen receptor, and androgen receptor pathways. Clinical features include early thelarche, pubarche, menarche, testicular enlargement, accelerated linear growth, advanced bone age, acne, body odor, and psychosocial distress; complications include reduced adult height, obesity, insulin resistance, polycystic ovary syndrome risk, and occasionally intracranial lesions such as hypothalamic hamartoma, especially in boys or very early onset cases. Diagnosis relies on history, Tanner staging, growth velocity, bone-age radiography, basal and GnRH-stimulated LH/FSH testing, serum estradiol or testosterone, adrenal steroids, thyroid studies, pelvic ultrasonography, and brain MRI when central nervous system pathology is suspected. Treatment depends on subtype: leuprolide, triptorelin, and histrelin act as continuous GnRH receptor agonists that downregulate pituitary gonadotrophs in central disease, while ketoconazole inhibits steroidogenic CYP enzymes, letrozole blocks aromatase, and medroxyprogesterone suppresses sex steroid effects in selected peripheral forms.

Name: Pulmonary Edema
Description: Pulmonary edema (MeSH D011654) is a clinical syndrome defined by abnormal accumulation of fluid within the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli due either to increased hydrostatic pressure, most commonly from left-sided heart failure, acute coronary syndromes, valvular disease, or hypertensive crisis, or to increased alveolar-capillary permeability as in acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, high-altitude exposure, renal failure, or toxin/drug injury. Symptoms and signs typically include acute dyspnea, orthopnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, cough with frothy sometimes pink sputum, diffuse crackles, wheeze, cyanosis, and severe cases of respiratory failure. Molecularly, pulmonary edema reflects dysregulation of endothelial and epithelial barrier function, with VEGF, TNF, IL-1beta, IL-6, NF-kappaB, Angiopoietin-Tie2, nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species, and epithelial sodium and water transport mediated by ENaC, CFTR, Na+/K+-ATPase, and aquaporins as key components; hypoxia-inducible signaling is especially relevant in high-altitude pulmonary edema. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex rather than Mendelian, but variants in ACE, VEGFA, AQP5, SLC12A3, NOS3, and surfactant-related genes such as SFTPB or ABCA3 have been implicated in edema susceptibility or causative neonatal respiratory syndromes, while pulmonary veno-occlusive disease caused by autosomal recessive EIF2AK4 mutations can present with edema after vasodilator exposure. Major comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, COPD, pneumonia, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and secondary infection. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment plus pulse oximetry or arterial blood gases, chest radiography showing interstitial or alveolar opacities, lung ultrasound B-lines, echocardiography, ECG, BNP/NT-proBNP, and cause-directed testing; hemodynamic distinction may require catheterization. Treatment commonly includes loop diuretics such as furosemide, which inhibit NKCC2 to promote natriuresis and reduce preload, nitrates such as nitroglycerin, which donate nitric oxide causing venodilation and afterload reduction, and noninvasive or invasive positive-pressure ventilation to improve oxygenation and alveolar

Name: Pulmonary Embolism
Description: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is an acute or chronic thromboembolic disorder in which thrombus, usually arising from deep venous thrombosis of the legs or pelvis, obstructs the pulmonary arterial tree, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxemia, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, right ventricular strain, and in severe cases obstructive shock; major forms include massive/high-risk, submassive/intermediate-risk, low-risk, recurrent, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, and septic or fat embolic variants. Genetic susceptibility is most clearly linked to inherited thrombophilia, especially F5 factor V Leiden, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1 antithrombin deficiency, PROC protein C deficiency, PROS1 protein S deficiency, and occasionally elevated factor VIII, ABO non-O blood group, or dysregulated fibrinolysis involving PLG and SERPINE1; these defects are typically autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and predispose through excess thrombin generation. Core molecular pathways include tissue factor-FVIIa activation of the coagulation cascade, factor Xa and thrombin signaling, platelet activation, impaired protein C/protein S and antithrombin anticoagulant pathways, fibrin formation and plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis, with endothelial injury, inflammation, and hypoxia-induced vasoconstriction contributing. Common symptoms and signs are sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, cough, hemoptysis, syncope, hypoxemia, accentuated P2, and signs of DVT; comorbidities and risk states include cancer, surgery, trauma, immobilization, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, obesity, heart failure, COPD, prior VTE, and antiphospholipid syndrome, while complications include recurrent VTE, pulmonary infarction, right heart failure, and death. Diagnosis integrates clinical probability scores such as Wells or Geneva, D-dimer testing in low/intermediate-risk patients, CT pulmonary angiography as the principal imaging test, ventilation-perfusion scanning when CT is unsuitable, lower-extremity venous ultrasonography, echocardiographic evidence of RV dysfunction, and cardiac biomarkers such as troponin and BNP for risk stratification. Name: Pulmonary Emphysema
Description: Pulmonary emphysema (MeSH D011656) is a chronic obstructive lung disease defined by irreversible enlargement of distal airspaces with destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil, most often caused by cigarette smoke but also influenced by genetic susceptibility, notably SERPINA1 mutations causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, typically inherited in an autosomal codominant pattern, with severe PiZZ and related alleles predisposing especially to early-onset panacinar emphysema; additional implicated genes and proteins include MMP12, MMP9, ELANE, TGFB1, GSTP1, CHRNA3/5, HHIP, and SOD3, reflecting protease-antiprotease imbalance, oxidant injury, and abnormal repair. Central pathogenic pathways include chronic macrophage and neutrophil inflammation, TNF, IL-8/CXCL8, NF-kappaB, TGF-beta, oxidative stress/Nrf2 dysregulation, apoptosis, and extracellular matrix degradation by elastase and matrix metalloproteinases. Major subtypes are centriacinar, panacinar, paraseptal, and irregular emphysema. Typical manifestations include progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough with variable sputum, wheeze, prolonged expiration, diminished breath sounds, hyperinflation, barrel chest, weight loss, and reduced exercise tolerance. Common comorbidities and complications include chronic bronchitis/COPD overlap, recurrent infections, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, spontaneous pneumothorax, respiratory failure, lung cancer, osteoporosis, anxiety/depression, and cardiovascular disease. Diagnosis is supported by spirometry showing persistent airflow limitation, usually post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC less than 0.70, reduced diffusing capacity, and imaging with chest radiography or high-resolution CT demonstrating hyperlucency, bullae, and airspace destruction; alpha-1 antitrypsin level and genotype testing are indicated in selected patients. Treatment is symptomatic and preventive, using bronchodilators such as albuterol, a short-acting beta2-agonist, tiotropium, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, and salmeterol, a long-acting beta2-agonist, often with inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone to suppress airway inflammation, while roflumilast inhibits phosphodiesterase-4 and alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor

Name: Pulmonary Fibrosis
Description: Pulmonary fibrosis (MeSH D011658) is a chronic, progressive interstitial lung disease characterized by aberrant alveolar epithelial injury, fibroblast activation, myofibroblast accumulation, and excessive extracellular matrix deposition leading to irreversible scarring and restrictive ventilatory failure; major forms include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, connective tissue disease-associated, hypersensitivity pneumonitis-related, occupational/drug-induced, sarcoid-related, and familial pulmonary fibrosis. Pathobiology is driven by TGF-β/SMAD, PDGF, FGF, VEGF, Wnt/β-catenin, integrin, TNF-α, IL-13, and oxidative stress pathways, with key cellular participants including injured type II pneumocytes, macrophages, fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts. Genetic susceptibility is well established, especially in familial disease, with variants or mutations in MUC5B promoter, TERT, TERC, RTEL1, PARN, DKC1, SFTPA1, SFTPA2, SFTPC, ABCA3, and telomere-related genes; inheritance is often autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, while short telomere syndromes may underlie early-onset or syndromic cases. Patients typically present with progressive exertional dyspnea, persistent dry cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, fatigue, hypoxemia, and digital clubbing. Important comorbidities and complications include pulmonary hypertension, acute exacerbations, respiratory failure, lung cancer, gastroesophageal reflux, obstructive sleep apnea, venous thromboembolism, coronary disease, anxiety/depression, and increased infection risk. Diagnosis integrates history of exposures or autoimmune disease, pulmonary function tests showing restriction and reduced DLCO, high-resolution CT demonstrating reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and often usual interstitial pneumonia with subpleural basal honeycombing, serologies for connective tissue disease, bronchoalveolar lavage in selected cases, and surgical or cryobiopsy when imaging is indeterminate. Standard antifibrotic therapy includes pirfenidone, which suppresses TGF-β-driven collagen synthesis and inflammatory signaling, and nintedanib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting PDGFR, FGFR, and VEGFR to blunt fibroblast proliferation; additional management may include corticosteroids or mycophenolate mofetil in inflammatory or autoimmune-associated subtypes, supplemental oxygen,

Name: Pyelonephritis
Description: Pyelonephritis (MeSH D011704) is an acute or chronic bacterial infection of the renal pelvis and parenchyma, usually caused by ascending uropathogens, especially uropathogenic Escherichia coli, and less often Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, or hematogenous Staphylococcus aureus. Disease susceptibility and severity reflect host innate immune and anatomic factors, with representative genetic associations involving TLR4, CXCR1/CXCR2, IL6, IL8, HSPA1B, VEGFA, DEFB1, and uromodulin/UMOD; rare monogenic contributors are typically indirect, via vesicoureteral reflux or congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract linked to genes such as PAX2, ROBO2, RET, and UPK3A. Pathobiology centers on urothelial adherence by type 1 and P fimbriae, activation of TLR4-NF-κB and MAPK signaling, inflammasome-mediated IL-1β release, neutrophil recruitment through IL-8/CXCL8 and complement, and in chronic injury, TGF-β-driven fibrosis and tubular scarring. Patients commonly present with fever, chills, flank pain, costovertebral-angle tenderness, dysuria, frequency, urgency, nausea, vomiting, and pyuria, sometimes progressing to bacteremia or sepsis. Major forms include uncomplicated and complicated pyelonephritis, acute focal bacterial nephritis, emphysematous pyelonephritis, xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, chronic reflux-associated pyelonephritis, and pyonephrosis. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, nephrolithiasis, obstruction, neurogenic bladder, urinary catheterization, reflux, and immunosuppression; complications include renal abscess, papillary necrosis, acute kidney injury, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and scarring. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical syndrome plus urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase or nitrites, urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing, blood cultures in severe cases, and imaging such as renal ultrasound or contrast CT when obstruction, abscess, emphysematous disease, or treatment failure is suspected. Name: Q Fever
Description: Q fever (MeSH D011778) is a zoonotic infection caused by the obligate intracellular Gram-negative coccobacillus Coxiella burnetii, acquired mainly by inhalation of contaminated aerosols from sheep, goats, or cattle, and classically presenting as an acute febrile illness with severe headache, myalgia, atypical pneumonia, or hepatitis, while chronic or persistent focal infection most often manifests as endocarditis or vascular graft/aneurysm infection. Its pathobiology reflects survival of C. burnetii within monocytes/macrophages in an acidified parasitophorous vacuole, with major roles for phase I and phase II lipopolysaccharide antigens, type IV secretion system effectors, and host innate and adaptive immune pathways including TLR2/TLR4 recognition, NF-κB signaling, IFN-γ, TNF, IL-6, and granuloma formation; susceptibility and severity have been linked to host immune-genetic variation rather than Mendelian inheritance, with representative associations reported for HLA class II alleles and cytokine-pathway genes such as IFNG, TNF, IL10, and TLR polymorphisms. Important complications and comorbid associations include pre-existing valvular heart disease, prosthetic valves, aortic aneurysm or vascular prostheses, pregnancy, and immunosuppression, which increase risk of persistent infection, as well as osteomyelitis and chronic fatigue syndrome after acute disease. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus serology by indirect immunofluorescence showing phase II IgM/IgG predominance in acute infection and high phase I IgG titers in chronic disease, supported by PCR on blood or tissue, liver tests, inflammatory markers, and echocardiography or PET/CT when endocarditis or vascular infection is suspected. Treatment typically uses doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, for acute disease; doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine, which alkalinizes the phagolysosome and improves intracellular killing, for chronic Q fever; and alternatives such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, inhibiting folate synthesis, especially in pregnancy, with fluoroquinolones or rifampin sometimes used adjunctively.

Name: Rat-Bite Fever
Description: Rat-bite fever is an acute systemic zoonotic bacterial infection acquired after bites, scratches, or exposure to rodents or contaminated food or water, classically caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis in North America and Spirillum minus in Asia, with Haverhill fever representing the ingestion-associated streptobacillary form. It is not an inherited disorder, and no host germline mutation defines the disease, although interindividual susceptibility may plausibly be influenced by innate immune pathways involving TLR, NF-kappaB, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and acute-phase signaling; in the pathogen, virulence-related proteins such as Streptobacillus adhesins and lipopolysaccharide-like outer membrane components are implicated, but no single routinely used molecular biomarker is canonical in clinical practice. Patients typically develop fever, rigors, headache, myalgia, vomiting, and a migratory polyarthralgia or septic arthritis, often with a maculopapular, petechial, or pustular acral rash; an inoculation lesion and regional adenopathy are more typical of S. minus infection. Major complications include endocarditis, sepsis, meningitis, pneumonia, abscesses, osteomyelitis, and multiorgan failure, with higher risk in alcoholism, immunocompromise, pregnancy, and underlying valvular heart disease. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus compatible febrile rash-arthritis syndrome, supported by culture of blood, synovial fluid, or tissue for S. moniliformis using appropriate media because routine sodium polyanethol sulfonate blood culture systems may inhibit growth, or dark-field microscopy/PCR/16S rRNA sequencing when available, especially for S. minus, which is difficult to culture. Treatment is primarily penicillin G followed by oral penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins; ceftriaxone, another beta-lactam with the same core mechanism, is commonly used; doxycycline inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit and is a standard alternative in beta-lactam allergy, while streptomycin or other tetracyclines are less commonly used in selected cases.

Name: Raynaud Disease
Description: Raynaud disease (primary Raynaud phenomenon; MeSH D011928) is a vasospastic disorder of the digital arteries, arterioles, and cutaneous arteriovenous shunts characterized by episodic, cold- or emotion-triggered ischemia of the fingers and less often toes, nose, or ears, producing the classic triphasic color change of pallor, cyanosis, and reactive erythema with numbness, pain, paresthesia, and cold sensitivity; primary disease is typically benign, symmetric, and nonulcerative, whereas secondary Raynaud syndrome is associated with structural vasculopathy and tissue injury. Pathobiology centers on exaggerated vasoconstriction with increased alpha2C-adrenergic receptor signaling, endothelin-1 activity, impaired nitric oxide and prostacyclin-mediated vasodilation, oxidative stress, platelet activation, and abnormal RhoA/ROCK, serotonin, and neurovascular pathways; candidate genetic components include familial susceptibility and polymorphic associations in NOS3, EDN1, ADRA2A/ADRA2C, ACE, and genes influencing vascular tone, although no single Mendelian cause is established for typical primary disease. Secondary forms commonly accompany systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren syndrome, dermatomyositis, hypothyroidism, atherosclerosis, vibration injury, and drug exposure such as beta-blockers, bleomycin, cisplatin, interferons, or ergot alkaloids, and complications include digital ulcers, pitting scars, infection, and rarely gangrene or critical ischemia. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history of reversible attacks, examination, nailfold capillaroscopy, and laboratory testing to distinguish primary from secondary disease, including ANA, ESR/CRP, and disease-specific autoantibodies such as anticentromere or anti-Scl-70. Treatment emphasizes cold avoidance and smoking cessation; common drugs include dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine or amlodipine, which inhibit L-type calcium influx to reduce vasoconstriction, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil, which augment nitric oxide-cGMP signaling, and topical or systemic nitrates, which donate nitric oxide; refractory ischemia may be treated with prostacyclin analogs such as iloprost or endothelin-receptor antagonists such as bosentan, particularly in systemic sclerosis

Name: Rectal Pain
Description: Rectal pain (UMLS C0034886) is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease, arising from anorectal, neurologic, inflammatory, infectious, ischemic, or neoplastic disorders; major subtypes include acute pain from anal fissure, thrombosed external hemorrhoid, abscess, proctitis, or trauma, and chronic functional anorectal pain syndromes such as levator ani syndrome and proctalgia fugax. Clinical features include sharp or burning anal pain, tenesmus, pain with defecation, rectal fullness, bleeding, discharge, pruritus, constipation, diarrhea, fever, and pelvic floor spasm, with complications including urinary retention, sepsis from anorectal abscess, fistula formation, chronic opioid exposure, and impaired quality of life. Genetic associations are generally indirect and track underlying causes: inflammatory bowel disease-related rectal pain is linked to NOD2, IL23R, ATG16L1, and TNFSF15; colorectal neoplasia to APC, KRAS, TP53, SMAD4, mismatch-repair genes MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2, and occasionally BRAF; congenital aganglionosis causing obstructed defecation and pain involves RET, EDNRB, and SOX10. Relevant pathways therefore include TNF, IL-23/Th17, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, TGF-beta, Wnt/beta-catenin, EGFR-MAPK, VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, enteric neural crest migration signaling, and nociceptive TRPV1/substance P/CGRP pathways, with pelvic floor dyssynergia and internal anal sphincter hypertonia contributing in functional disease. Treatment is etiology-directed and commonly includes topical nitroglycerin, which donates nitric oxide to relax the internal anal sphincter in fissure; topical diltiazem or nifedipine, calcium-channel blockers that reduce sphincter tone; lidocaine, a sodium-channel blocker for local analgesia; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen via cyclooxygenase inhibition; antibiotics such as metronidazole or ciprofloxacin for infectious proctitis or abscess-associated infection; and biologics such as infliximab, an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, for Crohn-related proctitis. Name: Relapsing Fever
Description: Relapsing fever (MeSH D012061) is an acute, vector-borne spirochetal infection caused by Borrelia species, classically louse-borne B. recurrentis and tick-borne species such as B. hermsii, B. duttonii, and B. turicatae, characterized by recurrent febrile episodes resulting from antigenic variation rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder. The key molecular basis is sequential switching of Borrelia variable major proteins, especially variable large and small proteins encoded at vlp and vsp expression loci and related silent cassettes, enabling immune evasion; pathobiology also involves outer surface lipoproteins, Toll-like receptor 2-mediated innate recognition, NF-kB-driven cytokine release, complement interaction, and macrophage-neutrophil responses. Typical manifestations are abrupt high fever, rigors, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, nausea, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, cough, epistaxis, rash in some cases, and recurrent crises separated by afebrile intervals; severe disease may cause hypotension, myocarditis, acute respiratory distress, neurologic involvement including meningitis or cranial neuropathy, miscarriage, and multiorgan failure. Important complications and comorbid associations include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatitis, malnutrition, pregnancy, coinfection with other louse- or tick-borne pathogens, and a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after therapy. Diagnosis relies on epidemiologic exposure plus demonstration of spirochetemia on Giemsa- or Wright-stained peripheral blood smears during febrile periods, with dark-field microscopy, buffy coat examination, PCR targeting Borrelia 16S rRNA, flaB, or glpQ, and serology as adjuncts. Treatment commonly uses doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit; tetracycline, also a 30S inhibitor; erythromycin, a macrolide that blocks 50S-mediated translocation; or penicillin G/ceftriaxone, beta-lactams that inhibit cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis. Disease subtypes are broadly louse-borne and tick-borne relapsing fever, and host genetic predisposition is not established, although variation in innate immune and complement pathways may influence severity.

Name: Osteodystrophies, Renal
Description: Renal osteodystrophy is the skeletal manifestation of chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder, a largely acquired, multifactorial disease characterized by abnormal bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth, or strength due to disordered calcium-phosphate-homeostatic signaling rather than a classic Mendelian bone dysplasia, although rare genetic contributors to the CKD-MBD axis include FGF23, KL encoding Klotho, PTH, CASR, VDR, CYP27B1, and phosphate transporter genes such as SLC34A1/SLC34A3, with mutations in PHEX or DMP1 producing related phosphate-wasting phenotypes that inform pathobiology. Central pathways involve phosphate retention, reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity with calcitriol deficiency, hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, FGF23-Klotho signaling, PTH/PTH1R-cAMP signaling, vitamin D receptor signaling, calcium-sensing receptor activity, and altered RANKL/OPG-mediated osteoclast activation and Wnt-sclerostin regulation of osteoblasts. Major subtypes include high-turnover osteitis fibrosa from secondary hyperparathyroidism, low-turnover adynamic bone disease, osteomalacia with defective mineralization, mixed uremic osteodystrophy, and pediatric growth-related disease. Patients commonly present with bone pain, fragility fractures, skeletal deformity, muscle weakness, pruritus, and in children growth retardation; laboratory findings often include hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia or low-normal calcium, elevated PTH, elevated alkaline phosphatase in high-turnover states, and altered 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels. Important comorbidities and complications include cardiovascular and valvular calcification, calciphylaxis, anemia, sarcopenia, dialysis-related amyloidosis, and increased fracture-related mortality. Diagnosis rests on CKD context, serial serum phosphate, calcium, PTH, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D measurements, radiography or DXA when indicated, and definitive bone histomorphometry after tetracycline-labeled iliac crest biopsy in selected cases. Treatment commonly includes phosphate binders such as sevelamer or calcium acetate to reduce intestinal phosphate absorption, vitamin D analogs such as calcitriol or paricalcitol to suppress PTH

Name: Respiratory Distress Syndrome, Newborn
Description: Respiratory Distress Syndrome of the newborn is an acute neonatal lung disease, most often affecting premature infants, caused primarily by developmental deficiency of pulmonary surfactant and structural immaturity of the distal lung, leading to diffuse alveolar collapse, reduced compliance, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and hypoxemic respiratory failure with hyaline membrane formation. Clinically it presents within minutes to hours after birth with tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal and sternal retractions, cyanosis, and increasing oxygen requirement; chest radiography typically shows low lung volumes and a diffuse reticulogranular ground-glass pattern with air bronchograms, while blood gases demonstrate hypoxemia and sometimes hypercapnia. Major molecular determinants include surfactant proteins and phospholipid transport genes such as SFTPB, SFTPC, ABCA3, and NKX2-1, with rarer contributions from CSF2RA/CSF2RB, and severe monogenic forms may show autosomal recessive inheritance for SFTPB or ABCA3 variants, autosomal dominant or de novo disease for some SFTPC mutations, and variable thyroid-lung-neurologic syndrome with NKX2-1 defects. Relevant pathways include glucocorticoid-driven fetal lung maturation, surfactant synthesis and lamellar body trafficking, GM-CSF signaling in alveolar homeostasis, inflammatory cytokine cascades, and epithelial sodium channel-mediated alveolar fluid clearance. Standard therapy includes exogenous surfactants such as beractant, poractant alfa, or calfactant, which replenish deficient surface-active phospholipids and proteins to lower alveolar surface tension; antenatal betamethasone or dexamethasone accelerates type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant production; and caffeine citrate, often used in preterm infants, antagonizes adenosine receptors to improve respiratory drive and reduce apnea. Important complications and comorbidities include prematurity, patent ductus arteriosus, sepsis, pulmonary hemorrhage, air leak syndromes, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage, retinopathy of prematurity, and later chronic respiratory morbidity; diagnosis is based on prematurity risk, characteristic early respiratory distress, imaging, oxygen need, and exclusion of mimics such as neonatal pneumonia, transient tachypnea, meconium aspiration, and congenital heart disease.

Name: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections
Description: Respiratory syncytial virus infection is an acute contagious viral disease of the lower and upper respiratory tract caused mainly by human orthopneumovirus A and B subtypes, classically producing bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants but also serious disease in older adults and immunocompromised hosts. It typically presents with rhinorrhea, cough, wheeze, fever, tachypnea, crackles, chest retractions, apnea in young infants, and hypoxemia, and complications include bronchiolitis obliterans, secondary bacterial pneumonia, respiratory failure, recurrent wheezing or asthma exacerbation, and hospitalization risk amplified by prematurity, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, neuromuscular disease, and immunodeficiency. Key viral proteins include the fusion F protein, attachment G glycoprotein, SH protein, nucleoprotein N, phosphoprotein P, matrix protein M, and polymerase L; host susceptibility and severity have been linked to variants in TLR4, CX3CR1, IFIH1, IL4, IL13, IL10, TNF, surfactant protein genes SFTPA and SFTPD, and innate immune loci such as RIG-I/DDX58, although inheritance is not Mendelian and is instead complex polygenic predisposition interacting with age and environment. Major pathways include epithelial viral entry and syncytium formation via F protein, G protein interaction with CX3CR1, TLR3/TLR4 and RIG-I/MDA5 sensing, NF-kB and IRF3/IRF7 activation, type I and III interferon signaling, chemokine-driven neutrophilic and monocytic inflammation, and Th2-skewed cytokine responses in severe disease. Diagnosis relies on compatible seasonally clustered respiratory illness plus confirmation by RT-PCR or multiplex nucleic acid amplification from nasopharyngeal specimens; rapid antigen tests, viral culture, chest radiography, and pulse oximetry are adjuncts. Treatment is largely supportive with oxygen, hydration, and ventilatory support when needed; ribavirin inhibits viral RNA synthesis, palivizumab and nirsevimab target the prefusion F protein to prevent fusion and are used mainly for prophylaxis in high-risk populations, and bronchodilators or corticosteroids are not routinely effective except in selected comorbid airway disease.

Name: Respiratory Tract Infections
Description: Respiratory tract infections (MeSH D012141) comprise acute or chronic infections of the upper airways (rhinitis, sinusitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis, otitis-associated disease) and lower tract (tracheobronchitis, bronchiolitis, pneumonia), caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi and ranging from self-limited mucosal inflammation to invasive parenchymal disease and sepsis. Host susceptibility is strongly influenced by innate and adaptive immune genes, with representative examples including CFTR mutations predisposing to chronic sinopulmonary infection in cystic fibrosis, TLR2, TLR4, TLR3, IFIH1/MDA5, MAVS, IRF7, IFNAR1, STAT1, and MyD88 pathway defects impairing pathogen sensing or interferon signaling, and mucociliary or surfactant-related genes such as DNAH5, CCDC39, and SFTPA/SFTPD affecting airway defense; key proteins include ACE2 and TMPRSS2 for some viral entry, defensins, mucins, and inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF, CXCL8, and NF-κB. Pathobiology centers on epithelial invasion, PRR activation, inflammasome and JAK-STAT signaling, neutrophil/macrophage recruitment, mucus hypersecretion, and, in severe disease, alveolar-capillary injury. Common treatments include amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation; azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and may also dampen inflammation; ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin blocking cell-wall synthesis; oseltamivir, a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza; and, when indicated, antifungals such as voriconazole inhibiting ergosterol synthesis. Typical symptoms are fever, cough, coryza, sore throat, sputum, dyspnea, wheeze, pleuritic chest pain, and crackles or hypoxemia. Major comorbidities and complications include asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, heart failure, diabetes, immunodeficiency, otitis/sinusitis, respiratory failure, abscess, empyema, ARDS, and bacteremia. Name: Restless Legs Syndrome
Description: Restless legs syndrome (RLS; Willis-Ekbom disease) is a chronic sensorimotor neurologic disorder characterized by an urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by unpleasant deep paresthetic sensations, beginning or worsening during rest, relieved by movement, and showing a circadian pattern with evening or nocturnal predominance; major subtypes include primary or idiopathic/familial RLS and secondary RLS associated with iron deficiency, pregnancy, end-stage renal disease, or neuropathy. Pathobiology centers on brain iron dysregulation and dopaminergic dysfunction within nigrostriatal and spinal networks, with implicated pathways involving iron transport and storage, tyrosine hydroxylase-dependent dopamine synthesis, D2/D3 receptor signaling, adenosinergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and altered spinal excitability. Genetic susceptibility is often polygenic with frequent familial clustering and usually complex, often autosomal-dominant-like transmission with incomplete penetrance; representative risk loci include MEIS1, BTBD9, PTPRD, MAP2K5/SKOR1, TOX3, and iron-related genes such as HFE, while BTBD9 and MEIS1 have been linked to ferritin regulation and dopaminergic development. Common comorbidities include insomnia, periodic limb movement disorder, depression, anxiety, cardiovascular disease, migraine, Parkinson disease, peripheral neuropathy, and adverse pregnancy or renal disease associations; complications include sleep fragmentation, daytime fatigue, impaired cognition and quality of life, and augmentation from dopaminergic therapy. Diagnosis is clinical using International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group criteria, supported by history, family history, medication review, neurologic examination, ferritin and iron studies, renal function testing, pregnancy assessment when relevant, and selected polysomnography or immobilization testing to document periodic limb movements or exclude mimics. Treatment commonly includes dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole, which stimulate D2/D3 receptors, rotigotine transdermal therapy with similar receptor agonism, alpha-2-delta ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin, which reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release via voltage-gated calcium channels, and iron replacement when ferritin is low.

Name: Retinoblastoma
Description: Retinoblastoma is a rare, highly malignant embryonal tumor of the developing retina that usually presents in infancy or early childhood as heritable or nonheritable disease, classically driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on 13q14, with loss of pRB-mediated G1/S checkpoint control and dysregulation of E2F-dependent cell-cycle signaling; representative genetic events include germline or somatic RB1 nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, or deletion mutations, while a minority of RB1-wild-type cases harbor MYCN amplification. Key pathogenic pathways include cell-cycle deregulation involving cyclin D/CDK4/6, p53 pathway attenuation through MDM2/MDM4, epigenetic and apoptotic dysregulation, and proangiogenic signaling such as VEGF. Clinically, patients typically present with leukocoria, strabismus, decreased vision, nystagmus, painful red eye, glaucoma, hyphema, vitreous seeding, or proptosis in advanced extraocular disease. Major subtypes include unilateral versus bilateral disease, heritable versus sporadic retinoblastoma, and intraocular versus extraocular/metastatic forms. Heritable retinoblastoma follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with high penetrance at the familial predisposition level, although tumor formation requires a second hit; affected children are also predisposed to trilateral retinoblastoma with pineal or suprasellar primitive neuroectodermal tumors and to later second primary malignancies such as osteosarcoma and soft-tissue sarcoma, particularly after radiotherapy. Diagnosis is based on ophthalmologic examination under anesthesia with indirect ophthalmoscopy and fundus imaging, ocular ultrasonography showing calcification, and MRI of the orbits and brain to assess optic nerve, CNS extension, and trilateral disease; RB1 molecular testing, chromosomal analysis, and genetic counseling are central, while biopsy is generally avoided because of tumor-seeding risk. Treatment commonly includes vincristine, a microtubule polymerization inhibitor, etoposide, a topoisomerase II inhibitor, and carboplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum agent, with focal therapies and intravitreal or intra-arterial melphalan, an alkylating agent, used in selected cases.

Name: Rheumatism
Description: Rheumatic diseases (MeSH D012216) comprise a heterogeneous group of predominantly autoimmune and autoinflammatory disorders affecting joints, periarticular tissues, muscle, connective tissue, and systemic organs, including rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritides, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, inflammatory myopathies, vasculitides, crystal arthropathies, and pediatric forms such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis. They typically present with chronic arthralgia, inflammatory back pain, morning stiffness, synovitis, joint swelling, enthesitis, myalgia, muscle weakness, rash, sicca symptoms, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, fatigue, and progressive functional impairment; complications include erosive joint destruction, deformity, interstitial lung disease, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, renal involvement, infection, thrombosis, and amyloidosis. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and polygenic, with strong HLA associations such as HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles in rheumatoid arthritis, HLA-B27 in ankylosing spondylitis, and HLA-DR2/DR3 in lupus; representative non-HLA genes include PTPN22, STAT4, CTLA4, TNFAIP3, IL23R, and complement deficiencies, while rare monogenic autoinflammatory phenocopies involve MEFV, NLRP3, and TNFRSF1A variants, and inheritance is generally multifactorial rather than Mendelian. Central pathogenic pathways include loss of immune tolerance, B-cell autoantibody production, Th1/Th17 and type I interferon signaling, TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, IL-23, JAK-STAT, NF-kB, complement activation, inflammasome signaling, osteoclast activation via RANKL, and fibroblast-like synoviocyte proliferation. Diagnosis integrates clinical classification criteria, inflammatory markers, autoantibodies such as rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, ANCA, serum urate or complement levels, synovial fluid analysis, radiography, ultrasound, MRI, and organ-specific testing, with biopsy when needed. Common treatments include NSAIDs via cyclooxygenase inhibition, glucocorticoids via broad anti-inflammatory genomic effects, methotrexate via folate antagonism and adenosine-mediated immunomodulation, hydroxychloroquine via lysosomal

Name: Rheumatic Fever
Description: Rheumatic fever (MeSH D012213) is an acute, immune-mediated, non-Mendelian sequela of untreated pharyngeal infection with group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) in genetically susceptible hosts, characterized by molecular mimicry in which streptococcal M proteins and N-acetyl-β-D-glucosamine elicit cross-reactive antibodies and T cells against cardiac myosin, laminin, valvular endothelium, and neuronal tissue; implicated susceptibility loci include HLA class II alleles such as HLA-DR7, HLA-DQ8, and other immune-regulatory genes including TNF, IL6, IL1B, TLR2, TLR4, FCN2, and MBL2, although no single causative mutation is established and familial clustering suggests complex polygenic inheritance. Key pathogenic pathways involve adaptive and innate immune activation, B-cell autoantibody production, CD4+ Th1/Th17 responses, cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and IFN-γ, complement activation, endothelial adhesion signaling, and inflammatory injury leading to Aschoff bodies and chronic valvular fibrosis. Clinically, the disease presents with the Jones criteria manifestations: migratory polyarthritis, carditis/valvulitis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules, often accompanied by fever, elevated ESR or CRP, prolonged PR interval, and evidence of antecedent streptococcal infection by throat culture, rapid antigen testing, or elevated antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase B titers; echocardiography is central for detecting clinical or subclinical carditis. Major subtypes are acute rheumatic fever and chronic rheumatic heart disease, with complications including mitral or aortic regurgitation/stenosis, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, infective endocarditis, recurrent episodes, and neuropsychiatric sequelae. Treatment commonly includes penicillin or benzathine penicillin to eradicate streptococci by inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, aspirin or naproxen to inhibit cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin production for arthritis and inflammation, corticosteroids such as prednisone to suppress cytokine-driven inflammation in severe carditis, and long-term secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin.

Name: Rheumatic Heart Disease
Description: Rheumatic heart disease (UMLS C0035439) is a chronic immune-mediated valvular disorder that follows acute rheumatic fever after untreated group A Streptococcus pharyngitis, driven by molecular mimicry and inflammatory injury rather than simple Mendelian inheritance; genetic susceptibility is nevertheless supported by associations with HLA class II alleles such as HLA-DR7, DQA1, and DQB1, and immune/inflammatory genes including TNF, IL6, IL10, TLR2, TLR4, MBL2, and FCN2, while cross-reactive streptococcal M proteins and host cardiac proteins including myosin, laminin, vimentin, collagen, and valve endothelium-related targets are central antigenic mediators. Key pathways involve adaptive Th1/Th17 responses, B-cell autoantibody production, complement activation, endothelial activation, and profibrotic TGF-β signaling leading to leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, chordal shortening, calcification, and ultimately mitral-predominant stenosis or regurgitation; aortic, tricuspid, and mixed multivalvular disease are recognized subtypes. Typical manifestations include prior migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers, followed chronically by dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, fatigue, chest discomfort, murmur, atrial fibrillation, hemoptysis, right or left heart failure, and embolic events. Major complications and comorbidities include recurrent rheumatic fever, infective endocarditis, pulmonary hypertension, stroke, pregnancy-related decompensation, and chronic heart failure. Diagnosis relies on Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever, evidence of antecedent streptococcal infection by throat culture, rapid antigen testing, or elevated antistreptolysin O/anti-DNase B titers, and echocardiography with Doppler to define valvular morphology and severity; ECG and chest radiography provide supportive evidence. Treatment commonly includes benzathine penicillin G for eradication and secondary prophylaxis by inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, aspirin or naproxen to suppress cyclooxygenase-mediated inflammation, corticosteroids such as prednisone for severe carditis via broad cytokine inhibition, and when indicated diuretics, beta-blockers, anticoagulation, or valve intervention.

Name: Rhinitis
Description: Rhinitis is a heterogeneous inflammatory disorder of the nasal mucosa, classically divided into allergic rhinitis, infectious rhinitis, and nonallergic forms such as vasomotor, occupational, hormonal, drug-induced, gustatory, and atrophic rhinitis, and is characterized clinically by rhinorrhea, sneezing, nasal obstruction, itching, postnasal drip, and sometimes hyposmia, mucosal edema, pale or erythematous turbinates, and conjunctival symptoms. Allergic rhinitis is the best-defined molecular subtype, driven by IgE-mediated type 2 immunity with epithelial alarmins such as TSLP, IL-25, and IL-33 activating dendritic cells, Th2 cells, mast cells, eosinophils, and B cells, leading to IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 signaling, class-switch recombination, histamine release through H1 receptors, leukotriene production, and chemokine pathways involving CCL11 and other eosinophil attractants; representative susceptibility genes include IL4, IL13, IL4RA, FCER1A, TSLP, FLG, HLA class II loci, and variants affecting innate immunity such as TLR genes, although inheritance is typically complex polygenic with strong environmental interaction rather than Mendelian. Common comorbidities include asthma, atopic dermatitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media with effusion, sleep disturbance, and reduced quality of life, with complications including sinus infection and impaired school or work performance. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by temporal symptom pattern and trigger history, physical examination, nasal endoscopy when needed, and demonstration of allergen sensitization by skin-prick testing or serum allergen-specific IgE; adjunctive tests may include nasal smear eosinophils, acoustic rhinometry, or exclusion of structural and infectious causes. Treatment commonly includes intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone or budesonide, which suppress NF-κB-driven inflammatory gene transcription; oral or intranasal antihistamines such as cetirizine or azelastine, which block H1 receptors; and leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, which inhibit cysteinyl leukotriene signaling, with ipratropium for rhinorrhea and allergen immunotherapy as selected disease-modifying therapy.

Name: Rhinitis, Allergic, Perennial
Description: Perennial allergic rhinitis is a chronic IgE-mediated inflammatory disorder of the nasal mucosa triggered year-round by indoor allergens, especially house dust mites, animal dander, cockroach, and molds, and is phenotypically distinguished from seasonal disease by persistent symptoms that may be intermittent in intensity. Its pathobiology reflects epithelial barrier dysfunction and type 2 immune polarization, with genetic susceptibility involving variants in IL4, IL13, IL4RA, FCER1A, TSLP, FLG, HLA class II loci, and the 17q21 region, among others, promoting allergen sensitization, IgE class switching, mast-cell and basophil activation, and eosinophilic inflammation. Key pathways include allergen presentation by dendritic cells, Th2 differentiation, IL-4/IL-5/IL-13 signaling, FcεRI-mediated mast-cell degranulation, histamine, leukotriene, and prostaglandin release, and recruitment of eosinophils, innate lymphoid cells, and goblet-cell hyperplasia. Typical manifestations are chronic sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, nasal pruritus, congestion, postnasal drip, pale edematous turbinates, and often itchy, watery eyes, cough, sleep disturbance, fatigue, and impaired concentration. Common comorbidities include asthma, atopic dermatitis, allergic conjunctivitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media with effusion, eustachian tube dysfunction, and sleep-disordered breathing; complications include sinus obstruction and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is based on compatible chronic symptoms plus evidence of sensitization by skin-prick testing or serum allergen-specific IgE, with nasal endoscopy or rhinoscopy, eosinophil assessment, and selective use of total IgE or nasal provocation testing in difficult cases. Treatment commonly includes intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress local cytokine transcription and eosinophilic inflammation; oral or intranasal H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine or azelastine, which block histamine H1 receptors; and leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, which inhibit cysteinyl leukotriene signaling; allergen immunotherapy is used for persistent, sensitization-driven disease.

Name: Rhinitis, Vasomotor
Description: Vasomotor rhinitis, now commonly grouped within nonallergic, noninfectious rhinitis, is a chronic disorder of nasal mucosal hyperreactivity characterized by episodic rhinorrhea, congestion, postnasal drip, sneezing, and sometimes nasal burning or pressure triggered by temperature shifts, odors, smoke, alcohol, emotions, or irritants in the absence of IgE-mediated allergy or infection. Its pathobiology is thought to reflect dysregulated autonomic and neurogenic signaling rather than a single causal mutation, with representative molecular associations including sensory ion channels TRPV1 and TRPA1, cholinergic and adrenergic neural pathways, neuropeptides such as substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide, nitric oxide signaling, and inflammatory mediators including histamine and leukotrienes in some patients; epithelial barrier and innate immune contributors such as TLRs may also participate. Clear Mendelian inheritance is not established, but familial susceptibility to nasal hyperresponsiveness and atopy-related traits can occur, and genetic variation affecting neurogenic inflammation or receptor sensitivity is plausible rather than diagnostic. Subtypes include nonallergic rhinopathy, gustatory rhinitis, occupational/irritant-induced rhinitis, weather-induced rhinitis, and mixed rhinitis with concomitant allergic disease. Common comorbidities include chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, gastroesophageal reflux, migraine, sleep disturbance, and eustachian tube dysfunction, while complications include impaired quality of life, mouth breathing, and recurrent sinus symptoms. Diagnosis is clinical and one of exclusion, based on chronic symptoms with characteristic triggers, normal or nonspecific nasal examination, and negative allergy testing by skin-prick or serum specific IgE when allergic rhinitis is excluded; nasal endoscopy, sinus imaging, nasal cytology, or provocation testing may help rule out structural disease, chronic sinusitis, cerebrospinal fluid leak, or eosinophilic syndromes. Treatment commonly includes intranasal ipratropium, a muscarinic antagonist that reduces glandular secretions; intranasal azelastine, an H1-antihistamine with anti-inflammatory and neuroinhibitory effects; intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress mucosal cytokine signaling; and, in selected patients, capsaicin desensitization targeting TRPV1-mediated sensory hyperreactivity.

Name: Rhinoscleroma
Description: Rhinoscleroma (UMLS C0035468) is a chronic, slowly progressive granulomatous infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae subsp. rhinoscleromatis, classically involving the nasal cavity but potentially extending to the nasopharynx, larynx, trachea, and bronchi; it is not a Mendelian genetic disorder, and no reproducible host germline mutation defines susceptibility, although innate and cell-mediated immune response elements such as macrophage activation, IL-10, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and NF-κB-linked inflammatory signaling are implicated in pathogenesis, together with bacterial virulence factors including lipopolysaccharide and capsular polysaccharide that promote persistence within Mikulicz cells. Clinically, patients present with chronic rhinitis, fetid purulent rhinorrhea, nasal obstruction, crusting, epistaxis, hoarseness, cough, dyspnea, and deformity; disease is often described in catarrhal, granulomatous/proliferative, and cicatricial/sclerotic stages, the last associated with fibrosis and airway stenosis. Diagnosis rests on compatible chronic sinonasal or airway lesions, endoscopy and imaging to define extent, histopathology showing Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies, and microbiologic confirmation by culture or molecular identification of K. rhinoscleromatis; biopsy is essential to distinguish it from tuberculosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, leprosy, syphilis, fungal infection, and malignancy. Treatment relies on prolonged antibiotics with intracellular activity, commonly ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks 30S ribosomal protein synthesis; rifampin, an inhibitor of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; and sometimes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which inhibits sequential folate synthesis steps. Major complications include scarring, septal destruction, laryngotracheal stenosis, secondary bacterial infection, chronic sinusitis, hearing dysfunction from Eustachian involvement, and potentially life-threatening airway compromise; comorbidity is often linked more to overcrowding, poor sanitation, malnutrition, and immunologic vulnerability than to inherited predisposition.

Name: Rickets
Description: Rickets (UMLS C0035579) is a disorder of the growing skeleton caused by defective mineralization of epiphyseal growth plates and osteoid, classically due to vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate deficiency, but also occurring in inherited forms that disrupt mineral ion homeostasis. Major genetic causes include PHEX mutations in X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, FGF23 gain-of-function variants in autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets, biallelic DMP1 or ENPP1 defects, SLC34A3 and SLC34A1 renal phosphate transporter defects, CYP27B1 mutations causing vitamin D–dependent rickets type 1, CYP2R1 deficiency, and VDR mutations causing vitamin D–dependent rickets type 2; representative proteins include FGF23, 1alpha-hydroxylase, the vitamin D receptor, NaPi cotransporters, and alkaline phosphatase. The central pathways involve vitamin D synthesis and signaling, renal phosphate reabsorption, parathyroid hormone regulation, and the FGF23-Klotho-FGFR axis, culminating in impaired calcium-phosphate balance, defective chondrocyte maturation, and poor matrix mineralization. Clinical features typically include bone pain, delayed growth, craniotabes, frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, widened wrists, bowing of the legs, waddling gait, muscle weakness, and delayed dentition; complications include fractures, deformity, short stature, dental disease, nephrocalcinosis, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and in severe cases hypocalcemic seizures or cardiomyopathy. Subtypes include nutritional rickets, hypophosphatemic rickets, vitamin D–dependent/resistant rickets, renal rickets, and syndromic forms; inheritance may be X-linked dominant, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or acquired. Diagnosis rests on clinical and radiographic metaphyseal changes plus biochemical testing showing altered alkaline phosphatase, calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, with urinary phosphate indices, tubular maximum phosphate reabsorption, FGF23 levels, renal evaluation, and confirmatory genetic testing when hereditary disease is suspected. Name: Rickettsia Infections
Description: Rickettsia infections are acute, predominantly tick-, flea-, louse-, or mite-borne zoonotic diseases caused by obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacteria of the spotted fever group, typhus group, and scrub typhus–like illnesses, including Rocky Mountain spotted fever due to Rickettsia rickettsii, Mediterranean spotted fever due to R. conorii, epidemic typhus due to R. prowazekii, murine typhus due to R. typhi, and other related rickettsioses. Their pathobiology centers on endothelial cell invasion and injury, with bacterial outer membrane proteins such as OmpA, OmpB, Sca family adhesins, RickA, and phospholipase D promoting host-cell adhesion, actin-based motility, intracellular spread, and vasculitis; host responses prominently involve TLR4/TLR2 sensing, NF-κB, MAPK, JAK-STAT, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-1/IL-6 chemokine signaling, endothelial coagulation pathways, and cytotoxic T-cell/macrophage activation. No Mendelian inheritance pattern is established for the infection itself, but host genetic susceptibility is likely polygenic, with representative associations reported in immune-response genes such as TLR4, TLR2, HLA loci, IFNG, and TNF. Typical manifestations include abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgia, malaise, nausea, conjunctival injection, rash that may become petechial, and sometimes an inoculation eschar; complications reflect systemic vasculitis and include pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, acute kidney injury, hepatitis, myocarditis, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multiorgan failure, with comorbid risk heightened by older age, immunosuppression, G6PD deficiency in some settings, diabetes, and chronic cardiopulmonary disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus exposure history, supported by PCR on blood, eschar, or tissue, immunohistochemistry, culture in specialized laboratories, and serology, especially indirect immunofluorescence showing a fourfold rise in paired antibody titers; thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and transaminitis are common laboratory clues.
