Name: Rickettsia akari Infection
Description: Rickettsia akari infection, or rickettsialpox, is an acute zoonotic spotted-fever group rickettsiosis caused by the obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium Rickettsia akari, usually transmitted by the house-mouse mite Liponyssoides sanguineus; it is an infectious disease rather than an inherited disorder, so no Mendelian inheritance pattern is recognized, although host response genes influencing severity are biologically plausible, with immune pathways involving endothelial infection, actin-based intracellular motility mediated by RickA and Sca2, outer-membrane adhesins such as OmpB/Sca5, and activation of NF-kB, type I/II interferon, TNF-alpha, IL-1/IL-6, chemokine signaling, and CD8-positive T-cell/macrophage responses contributing to vasculitic injury. Typical illness begins with a papule at the mite bite that evolves into a black eschar, followed days later by abrupt fever, chills, headache, myalgias, and a generalized papulovesicular rash that can mimic varicella; nausea, photophobia, and regional lymphadenopathy may occur, while severe complications are uncommon but can include pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, dehydration, secondary bacterial skin infection, or diagnostic delay due to confusion with chickenpox, other spotted fever rickettsioses, or mpox. No major clinical subtypes are established beyond uncomplicated versus rare severe/systemic presentations. Diagnosis is based on compatible exposure history, eschar plus febrile vesicular exanthem, and laboratory confirmation by indirect immunofluorescence serology showing rising antibody titers, PCR amplification of R. akari DNA from eschar, skin lesion, or blood, immunohistochemistry, or culture in specialized laboratories; routine labs may show mild leukopenia or thrombocytopenia. Treatment is typically with doxycycline, which inhibits the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit; alternatives include tetracycline, also a 30S inhibitor, chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S peptidyl-transferase center, and sometimes azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S subunit, particularly when tetracyclines are unsuitable.

Name: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
Description: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (MeSH D012373) is an acute, potentially fatal tick-borne zoonosis caused by the obligate intracellular bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii, producing a systemic vasculitis through infection of vascular endothelial cells rather than a classic inherited disorder; thus no Mendelian inheritance pattern or recurrent human driver mutation is established, although host susceptibility and severity are plausibly influenced by innate and adaptive immune genes such as TLR4, IFNG, TNF, and HLA loci, while representative microbial virulence proteins include the outer-membrane adhesins OmpA and OmpB and actin-based motility factor RickA. Pathobiologically, endothelial invasion activates NF-kB, MAPK, JAK-STAT, inflammasome-related signaling, cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, and IFN-gamma, reactive oxygen species, coagulation pathways, and increased vascular permeability, culminating in edema, thrombosis, and multiorgan injury. Typical presentation after a 2-14 day incubation includes abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgia, malaise, nausea, abdominal pain, conjunctival injection, and a maculopapular rash that often begins on wrists and ankles and may become petechial with palm and sole involvement, though rash can be absent early. Disease is usually classified by severity or by spotted-fever group rickettsiosis context rather than molecular subtype. Major complications and comorbid associations include encephalitis, meningitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, myocarditis, acute kidney injury, hepatitis, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, gangrene, and death, with worse outcomes in delayed therapy, alcoholism, G6PD deficiency, older age, and immunocompromise. Diagnosis is primarily clinical in an appropriate epidemiologic setting because early serology is often negative; confirmatory tests include paired indirect immunofluorescence antibody titers, PCR on blood or skin biopsy, immunohistochemistry, and supportive laboratory findings such as thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and transaminitis. Treatment should not await confirmation: doxycycline, which binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis, is first line for adults and children; tetracycline acts similarly; chloramphenicol inhibits the 50S peptidyl-transferase center and is an alternative when tetracyclines cannot be used

Name: Rosacea
Description: Rosacea is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory dermatosis of the centrofacial skin characterized by dysregulated innate immunity, neurovascular hyperreactivity, and epidermal barrier dysfunction, presenting with persistent erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, papules, pustules, burning, stinging, edema, and, in some patients, phymatous tissue hypertrophy or ocular disease with blepharitis, conjunctival injection, and keratitis. Major clinical subtypes include erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous, and ocular rosacea, although overlap is common. Pathobiology implicates increased cathelicidin processing with KLK5 serine protease activity, Toll-like receptor 2 signaling, NF-κB-driven cytokines, mast cells, matrix metalloproteinases, vascular endothelial growth factor, transient receptor potential channels such as TRPV1/TRPA1, and microbial triggers including Demodex-associated Bacillus antigens; representative associated genes/proteins include CAMP, KLK5, TLR2, MMP9, TNF, IL1B, VEGFA, GSTT1/GSTM1, and HLA class II loci, with genetic susceptibility typically complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, although family clustering is recognized. Diagnosis is clinical, based on persistent centrofacial erythema with periodic intensification or phymatous change as diagnostic features, supported by major features such as flushing, papules/pustules, telangiectasia, and ocular findings; dermoscopy may aid vascular assessment, biopsy is reserved for atypical cases, and ophthalmologic examination is indicated when ocular involvement is suspected. Common treatments include topical metronidazole, which reduces reactive oxygen species and inflammatory signaling; azelaic acid, which has anti-inflammatory and keratinocyte-normalizing effects; topical ivermectin, which is anti-Demodex and anti-inflammatory; oral doxycycline, especially subantimicrobial dose, which inhibits neutrophil-mediated inflammation and matrix metalloproteinases; and brimonidine or oxymetazoline, α-adrenergic agonists that vasoconstrict superficial vessels. Important comorbidities and complications include migraine, gastrointestinal disorders, cardiovascular risk associations, anxiety/depression, rhinophyma, and sight-threatening corneal involvement.

Name: Salmonella Infections
Description: Salmonella infections are acute bacterial diseases caused by Salmonella enterica, classically divided into typhoidal disease due to S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi and non-typhoidal salmonellosis causing gastroenteritis, bacteremia, and focal invasive infection. Disease results from fecal-oral acquisition and intracellular invasion of intestinal epithelium and macrophages through type III secretion systems encoded in Salmonella pathogenicity islands, with key virulence factors including lipopolysaccharide, flagellin, Vi capsular antigen in S. Typhi, and proteins such as SipA, SopE, SopB, and SptP that manipulate host actin and inflammatory signaling. Host pathways prominently involve TLR4 and TLR5, NF-κB, MAPK, inflammasome and IL-1/IL-18 activation, IFN-γ/IL-12 axis, and NADPH oxidase-dependent killing; genetic susceptibility is increased by defects in IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, STAT1, CYBB, G6PD, HLA-related variation, and sickle cell disease, but infection itself is not inherited. Typical manifestations include fever, nausea, abdominal cramps, diarrhea that may be inflammatory, vomiting, headache, rose spots and relative bradycardia in enteric fever, and occasionally sepsis. Important complications and comorbid links include dehydration, intestinal hemorrhage or perforation, encephalopathy, osteomyelitis, endovascular infection, reactive arthritis, chronic carriage, and severe disease in infants, older adults, HIV infection, malaria, malnutrition, inflammatory bowel disease, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis relies on stool culture for enterocolitis, blood culture early in typhoid, bone marrow culture as the most sensitive test for enteric fever, with PCR or multiplex GI panels and serology such as Widal used adjunctively; antimicrobial susceptibility testing is essential because of multidrug resistance. Treatment commonly includes ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin blocking cell wall synthesis, and azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, with rehydration central to management.

Name: Salpingitis
Description: Salpingitis (UMLS C0036130) is an inflammatory, usually infectious disorder of the fallopian tubes and a major component of pelvic inflammatory disease, most often caused by ascending sexually transmitted pathogens such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, with polymicrobial contributions from anaerobes, Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and enteric organisms; clinically it presents with lower abdominal or pelvic pain, cervical motion and adnexal tenderness, fever, purulent vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, abnormal uterine bleeding, and sometimes nausea or dysuria. Acute, chronic, and recurrent forms are recognized, and severe variants include pyosalpinx and tubo-ovarian abscess. Pathobiology is dominated by innate and mucosal immune signaling rather than a Mendelian genetic basis, with activation of TLR2/TLR4-, NF-kB-, MAPK-, inflammasome-, and cytokine/chemokine-mediated pathways involving IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, interferon responses, neutrophils, macrophages, epithelial injury, fibrosis, and scarring; host susceptibility has been linked in some studies to variants in immune-response genes such as TLR2, TLR4, TNF, IL10, and HLA loci, but inheritance is not typically defined. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by pelvic examination showing uterine, adnexal, or cervical motion tenderness, pregnancy testing to exclude ectopic pregnancy, NAAT testing for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, vaginal microscopy, inflammatory markers, transvaginal ultrasonography, and when needed laparoscopy as a reference standard. Treatment is empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, commonly ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam cephalosporin that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, plus doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit, with metronidazole, which generates free-radical intermediates that damage anaerobic microbial DNA; alternatives include azithromycin, a macrolide 50S inhibitor. Important comorbidities and complications include cervicitis, endometritis, bacterial vaginosis, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, adhesions, sepsis, and tubo-ovarian abscess.

Name: Sarcoidosis
Description: Sarcoidosis (MeSH D012507) is a multisystem inflammatory granulomatous disease of unknown etiology characterized pathologically by noncaseating granulomas, most often affecting lung and intrathoracic lymph nodes but also skin, eyes, heart, liver, and nervous system; common manifestations include cough, dyspnea, chest pain, fatigue, fever, weight loss, erythema nodosum, uveitis, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, while major complications include pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias or cardiomyopathy from cardiac sarcoidosis, neurosarcoidosis, hypercalcemia/nephrolithiasis, and increased risk of chronic respiratory impairment, with comorbid autoimmune disease also reported. Its biology reflects exaggerated cell-mediated immunity with antigen presentation via HLA class II molecules, macrophage and Th1/Th17 activation, and cytokine networks involving TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-2, IL-12, IL-17, NF-kappaB, JAK-STAT, and mTOR signaling; genetic susceptibility is complex and usually non-Mendelian, with associations in HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQB1, BTNL2, ANXA11, and ACE, and phenotype-specific links such as HLA-DRB1 alleles in Löfgren syndrome, while rare familial clustering supports polygenic inheritance rather than a single causal mutation. Clinical subtypes include acute self-limited Löfgren syndrome, chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis, and organ-specific forms such as cardiac, ocular, cutaneous, and neurosarcoidosis. Diagnosis rests on a compatible clinical-radiologic picture, histologic demonstration of noncaseating granulomas, and exclusion of alternative granulomatous disorders including tuberculosis, fungal infection, berylliosis, and lymphoma; testing typically includes chest radiography or CT with Scadding staging, pulmonary function tests, bronchoscopy with transbronchial or EBUS-guided biopsy, BAL lymphocytosis with elevated CD4:CD8 ratio, serum ACE or soluble IL-2 receptor as supportive markers, ECG/cardiac MRI or FDG-PET for cardiac disease, and ophthalmologic examination. Treatment commonly uses corticosteroids, which broadly suppress NF-kappaB-driven cytokine transcription; methotrexate, a folate antagonist with steroid-sparing immunomodulatory effects; azathioprine, a purine

Name: Sarcoma, Kaposi
Description: Kaposi sarcoma is a multifocal angioproliferative low- to intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm driven by infection with Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus/human herpesvirus 8 (KSHV/HHV-8), arising most often in the setting of immune dysregulation such as HIV/AIDS, post-transplant immunosuppression, or endemic exposure; classic, endemic African, epidemic AIDS-related, and iatrogenic/post-transplant forms are recognized. The lesion is composed of HHV-8–infected spindle cells expressing latent nuclear antigen-1, with viral and host abnormalities involving LANA, vGPCR, vIL-6, cyclin D dysregulation, p53 and RB pathway interference, VEGF/VEGFR-driven angiogenesis, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MAPK, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, HIF-1α, PDGF, and inflammatory cytokines including IL-6 and TNF-α. It is generally not a Mendelian inherited cancer, but host genetic susceptibility and HLA/immune-response variation may modify risk; somatic recurrent driver mutations are less defining than viral oncogenesis. Patients typically present with painless violaceous macules, plaques, or nodules on skin or oral mucosa, with edema, lymphadenopathy, and possible gastrointestinal or pulmonary involvement causing bleeding, obstruction, cough, dyspnea, or effusions. Major comorbidities and complications include HIV infection, opportunistic infections, immune reconstitution inflammatory phenomena, chronic lymphedema, superinfection, visceral dissemination, and organ failure. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion confirmed by biopsy showing slit-like vascular spaces and spindle-cell proliferation with erythrocyte extravasation and hemosiderin, plus immunohistochemistry for HHV-8 LANA and endothelial/lymphatic markers such as CD31, CD34, and D2-40; HIV testing, CD4 count, HHV-8 studies, and CT, endoscopy, or bronchoscopy are used for staging visceral disease. Treatment includes antiretroviral therapy for HIV-associated disease, liposomal doxorubicin, which intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, paclitaxel, which stabilizes microtubules and blocks mitosis, and interferon-α, which exerts antiviral, antiproliferative, and immunomodulatory effects; selected cases may

Name: Scabies
Description: Scabies (MeSH D012532) is a contagious ectoparasitic dermatosis caused by infestation with the human itch mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, with classic and crusted (Norwegian) forms and occasional nodular or bullous variants; it is not a Mendelian genetic disease, but host susceptibility and severity are influenced by immune-related genes and proteins, with reported associations involving HLA class II loci, cytokines such as IL-4, IL-13, IL-17, IL-23, IFN-γ, TNF, and chemokines/eosinophil mediators, while mite proteins including proteases and serpins modulate complement and keratinocyte responses. Pathobiology centers on epidermal burrowing and a delayed hypersensitivity reaction engaging innate and adaptive pathways, including Th1/Th2/Th17 polarization, mast cells, eosinophils, dendritic cells, IgE production, complement activation, and skin-barrier dysfunction. Clinically, patients develop intense nocturnal pruritus, excoriated papules, burrows, vesicles, or nodules in finger webs, wrists, axillae, waistline, genitalia, and areolae; infants may show scalp, face, palm, and sole involvement, whereas crusted scabies presents with hyperkeratotic plaques and very high mite burden. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by contact history and demonstration of mites, eggs, or scybala by skin scraping with microscopy, dermoscopy showing the delta-wing/jet sign, adhesive tape testing, or biopsy in difficult cases. First-line therapy includes permethrin 5% cream, a synthetic pyrethroid that disrupts mite voltage-gated sodium channels; ivermectin, an oral macrocyclic lactone that activates glutamate-gated chloride channels causing parasite paralysis; and sulfur preparations, which are scabicidal and keratolytic; additional options include benzyl benzoate, crotamiton, and spinosad. Important comorbidities and complications include secondary impetigo, cellulitis, abscesses, sepsis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, possible rheumatic heart disease risk in endemic settings, eczematization, sleep disturbance, and outbreaks in immunosuppressed, elderly, or institutionalized patients.

Name: Scalp Dermatoses
Description: Scalp dermatoses comprise a heterogeneous group of inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, and inherited disorders affecting the hair-bearing scalp, most commonly including seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, tinea capitis, folliculitis decalvans, discoid lupus erythematosus, lichen planopilaris, and alopecia areata; they typically present with pruritus, erythema, scale, pustules, pain or burning, patchy or diffuse alopecia, broken hairs, and in cicatricial forms permanent scarring. Molecular associations vary by subtype: psoriasis is linked to HLA-C*06:02 and IL23R/IL12B, with TNF, IL-23/Th17, NF-kB, and JAK-STAT signaling driving keratinocyte hyperproliferation; atopic and seborrheic phenotypes involve epidermal barrier and immune genes such as FLG and TSLP, with Th2 cytokines IL-4/IL-13 and Malassezia-triggered innate responses; alopecia areata is associated with HLA loci, ULBP3, CTLA4, and IFN-gamma/JAK signaling; discoid lupus implicates type I interferon pathways; and inherited scalp fragility or keratinization disorders may involve KRT, DSP, or desmosomal genes, usually with Mendelian inheritance. Common treatments include topical corticosteroids, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory mediators and cytokine transcription; ketoconazole, which inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis and reduces Malassezia burden; and vitamin D analogs such as calcipotriol, which modulate keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation. Additional therapies include terbinafine for dermatophytes via squalene epoxidase inhibition, salicylic acid as a keratolytic, topical calcineurin inhibitors, systemic tetracyclines, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and JAK or biologic agents in selected immune-mediated disease. Comorbidities include psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, other atopic disease, bacterial superinfection, lymphadenopathy in tinea capitis, psychosocial distress, and irreversible cicatricial alopecia. Diagnosis relies on history and morphology, trichoscopy, fungal microscopy/culture or PCR, bacterial culture, dermoscopy, patch testing when contact dermatitis is suspected, scalp biopsy with histopathology

Name: Scarlet Fever
Description: Scarlet fever is an acute toxin-mediated exanthematous illness caused by infection with Group A Streptococcus, usually Streptococcus pyogenes, most often pharyngitis-associated, in which host genetics are not Mendelian determinants of disease but susceptibility and severity reflect immune-response variation, while the core microbial molecular drivers are streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins encoded by bacteriophage-associated genes such as speA, speC, and ssa, together with virulence factors including the emm-encoded M protein, superantigen activity, and inflammatory signaling through MHC class II–T-cell receptor interactions, NF-κB activation, cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6, and innate immune pathways involving Toll-like receptors. Clinically it presents after fever and sore throat with a diffuse blanching sandpaper-like erythematous rash, Pastia lines, circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, pharyngeal erythema or exudates, tender cervical adenopathy, and later desquamation; recognized forms include classic pharyngeal scarlet fever and less commonly wound- or puerperal-associated disease. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical findings plus microbiologic confirmation of GAS by rapid antigen detection test, throat culture, or nucleic acid amplification, with CBC and inflammatory markers being nonspecific; testing helps distinguish it from viral exanthems, Kawasaki disease, toxic shock syndromes, and drug eruptions. First-line therapy is penicillin V or amoxicillin, beta-lactams that inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins; alternatives include cephalexin, another cell-wall active beta-lactam, azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits protein synthesis, or clindamycin, which also inhibits 50S-mediated protein synthesis and may reduce toxin production. Important complications and linked sequelae include otitis media, sinusitis, peritonsillar abscess, invasive streptococcal infection, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and rarely streptococcal toxic shock or necrotizing fasciitis.

Name: Schistosomiasis
Description: Schistosomiasis (bilharziasis; MeSH D012552) is a chronic helminthic disease caused by trematodes of the genus Schistosoma, principally S. haematobium, S. mansoni, and S. japonicum, with intestinal, hepatosplenic, and urogenital subtypes determined by species and egg deposition sites. Disease manifestations reflect immune responses to parasite eggs rather than inherited host mutations, so it is acquired rather than Mendelian, although host genetic susceptibility and fibrosis risk have been linked to variants in immune and fibrogenic genes such as IL4, IL13, IFNG, TNF, STAT6, CTGF, TGFB1, HLA class II loci, and SLC11A1; parasite proteins of pathogenic and diagnostic relevance include circulating anodic and cathodic antigens, omega-1, IPSE/alpha-1, and glutathione S-transferases. Core pathways include Th2 polarization driven by IL-4/IL-5/IL-13, eosinophilic inflammation, IgE-mediated responses, alternatively activated macrophages, granuloma formation, TGF-beta/SMAD and hepatic stellate-cell activation causing periportal fibrosis, and modulation of NF-kB, JAK/STAT, and regulatory T-cell networks. Typical features include cercarial dermatitis, Katayama fever with fever, cough, eosinophilia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly, followed chronically by hematuria, dysuria, portal hypertension, ascites, anemia, growth impairment, infertility, and, in neuroschistosomiasis, seizures or myelopathy. Major complications include obstructive uropathy, bladder calcification, pulmonary hypertension, and increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, with comorbid anemia, malnutrition, chronic liver disease, and coinfections. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus ova detection in stool or urine, urine filtration or Kato-Katz methods, tissue biopsy when needed, serology, circulating antigen assays, eosinophilia, and ultrasound or endoscopy to stage organ damage. Treatment centers on praziquantel, which increases parasite tegumental calcium permeability causing spastic paralysis and death; oxamniquine, a DNA-binding schistosomicide used mainly for S. mansoni; and metrifonate, a cholinesterase-inhibiting prodrug active against S.

Name: Schizophrenia
Description: Schizophrenia (MeSH D012559) is a chronic, severe neurodevelopmental psychiatric disorder characterized by psychosis and cognitive-behavioral dysfunction, typically presenting in late adolescence or early adulthood with positive symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech or behavior, negative symptoms including avolition, alogia, anhedonia, and social withdrawal, and cognitive deficits affecting attention, working memory, and executive function. It is clinically heterogeneous, with traditional subtypes such as paranoid, disorganized, catatonic, undifferentiated, and residual now largely replaced by dimensional assessment; related syndromes include schizoaffective disorder and first-episode psychosis. The disorder is highly heritable, usually polygenic and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with risk linked to common and rare variants in genes such as DRD2, COMT, DISC1, NRG1, DTNBP1, CACNA1C, GRIN2A, and C4A within the MHC locus, as well as recurrent copy-number variants including 22q11.2 deletion. Implicated pathways include dopaminergic signaling, especially mesolimbic D2 hyperactivity and mesocortical hypofunction, glutamatergic NMDA receptor dysfunction, GABAergic interneuron abnormalities, synaptic pruning, calcium-channel signaling, neuroinflammatory and complement pathways, and downstream AKT1-GSK3 and cAMP-related signaling. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 or ICD criteria requiring characteristic psychotic symptoms with functional decline and duration criteria, supported by mental status examination, collateral history, toxicology and laboratory testing to exclude secondary causes, and brain imaging when indicated; no definitive biomarker exists. Treatment relies on antipsychotics such as haloperidol, a potent D2 receptor antagonist, risperidone, a D2 and 5-HT2A antagonist, olanzapine, a multireceptor atypical antipsychotic with strong 5-HT2A/D2 blockade, and clozapine for treatment-resistant illness via broad dopaminergic and serotonergic antagonism. Common comorbidities and complications include substance use disorders, depression, anxiety, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, suicide, and impaired social and occupational functioning.

Name: Scleroderma, Systemic
Description: Systemic scleroderma, or systemic sclerosis (MeSH D012595), is a chronic autoimmune connective-tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation, noninflammatory obliterative vasculopathy, and progressive fibrosis of skin and internal organs, classically divided into limited cutaneous, diffuse cutaneous, and sine scleroderma subsets, with overlap syndromes also recognized. It is usually sporadic with complex polygenic susceptibility rather than Mendelian inheritance; associated loci include HLA class II alleles such as HLA-DRB1 and DQB1, and immune-regulatory or fibrotic genes including IRF5, STAT4, PTPN22, BANK1, TNFSF4, TBX21, CTGF, and variants influencing TGF-β signaling, while disease-defining proteins/autoantibodies include anticentromere, anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70), and anti-RNA polymerase III. Pathobiology centers on endothelial injury, fibroblast activation, and excess extracellular matrix deposition through TGF-β/SMAD, PDGF, endothelin-1, IL-6/JAK-STAT, type I interferon, and connective tissue growth factor pathways, with myofibroblasts producing collagen I/III and other matrix proteins. Typical manifestations include Raynaud phenomenon, puffy fingers progressing to sclerodactyly, skin thickening, digital ulcers, telangiectasia, calcinosis, gastroesophageal reflux and dysmotility, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, inflammatory arthritis, myopathy, and renal crisis. Important complications and comorbidities include cardiac fibrosis/arrhythmia, malabsorption, infection, depression, and increased malignancy risk, especially with anti-RNA polymerase III. Diagnosis relies on 2013 ACR/EULAR classification criteria integrating skin thickening proximal to the MCP joints, fingertip lesions, telangiectasia, abnormal nailfold capillaries, PAH or ILD, Raynaud phenomenon, and disease-specific autoantibodies, supported by ANA serology, pulmonary function tests with DLCO, high-resolution chest CT, echocardiography/right-heart catheterization, capillaroscopy, and renal monitoring. Name: Scrub Typhus
Description: Scrub typhus (MeSH D012612) is an acute zoonotic mite-borne rickettsial infection caused by the obligate intracellular bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi, classically transmitted by chigger larvae and presenting as a systemic febrile vasculitic illness. Human disease is not inherited, but host genetic susceptibility has been linked to immune-response genes and inflammatory mediators, with representative associations reported for HLA alleles, TNF, IL10, TLR4, TLR2, IFNG, and VEGFA variants; major microbial antigens and proteins relevant to pathogenesis and diagnosis include the 56-kDa type-specific antigen, 47-kDa outer-membrane protein, GroEL, and Sca family proteins, while strain diversity underlies antigenic subtypes such as Karp, Gilliam, Kato, Boryong, and Kawasaki. Pathobiology centers on endothelial infection and macrophage activation with NF-kB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, interferon signaling, TLR-mediated innate immune pathways, cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8, and IFN-gamma, and resultant vascular leak and multiorgan inflammation. Typical features are acute fever, headache, myalgia, rash, regional or generalized lymphadenopathy, cough, gastrointestinal symptoms, and the characteristic eschar, although this may be absent; severe complications include pneumonitis/ARDS, hepatitis, acute kidney injury, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis, shock, DIC, and multiorgan failure, and comorbid diabetes, chronic liver or kidney disease, pregnancy, and advanced age increase risk. Diagnosis relies on epidemiologic exposure plus compatible illness, eschar identification, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis, confirmation by indirect immunofluorescence assay, ELISA, PCR targeting the 56-kDa or 47-kDa genes, or paired serology showing rising titers. Treatment is primarily doxycycline, which inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit; azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S subunit, is favored in pregnancy and children; chloramphenicol inhibits the 50S peptidyl transferase center; and rifampin, which inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, is active in some doxycycline-refractory settings.

Name: Dermatitis, Seborrheic
Description: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory dermatosis of sebaceous gland–rich skin that arises from interaction among Malassezia yeasts, epidermal barrier dysfunction, sebaceous lipids, and host immune susceptibility rather than a simple Mendelian disorder, although genetic contributors affecting barrier and inflammatory signaling have been implicated, including variants or altered expression in FLG, CLDN1, KRT and desmosomal proteins, and innate immune/inflammatory mediators such as TLR2, CARD9, IL17, IL4/IL13, TNF, and components of the NF-κB axis; rare susceptibility may be seen in immunodeficiency states with genetic bases, including HIV-related immunosuppression or CARD9-associated fungal dysregulation. Key pathways include Malassezia lipid metabolism with release of irritating fatty acids, keratinocyte activation through pattern-recognition receptors, Th1/Th17- and sometimes Th2-skewed cytokine responses, complement activation, and impaired barrier homeostasis. Clinically it presents as pruritic, erythematous patches and plaques with greasy yellow-white scale on the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears, beard, presternal chest, and intertriginous areas; subtypes include infantile seborrheic dermatitis or cradle cap and adult disease, with scalp-limited dandruff considered part of the spectrum. It is associated with Parkinson disease and other neurologic disorders, HIV/AIDS, mood stress, alcohol misuse, and occasionally secondary bacterial infection, erythroderma, or marked quality-of-life impairment. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on distribution and morphology, with KOH examination or fungal studies used mainly to exclude tinea, and biopsy reserved for atypical cases showing spongiotic and psoriasiform dermatitis. Treatment commonly includes ketoconazole, ciclopirox, or selenium sulfide and zinc pyrithione, which reduce Malassezia burden by impairing fungal membrane or metabolic function; low-potency topical corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone suppress NF-κB–mediated inflammation; and calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus block T-cell activation through calcineurin inhibition.

Name: Serum Sickness
Description: Serum sickness (UMLS C0036830) is an acquired, non-Mendelian, type III hypersensitivity disorder caused by circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes, classically after exposure to heterologous antiserum, monoclonal antibodies, antibiotics, or other biologics, with a related but distinct serum sickness-like reaction lacking the same degree of immune-complex formation. Its pathobiology centers on immunoglobulins, especially IgG and IgM, formation of soluble complexes, classical complement activation through C1q, C4, and C3, generation of C3a and C5a, Fc gamma receptor engagement on neutrophils and macrophages, endothelial injury, and cytokine release involving TNF, IL-1, and IL-6; representative implicated genetic components are not disease-defining but susceptibility may be modified by HLA variation, complement component deficiencies such as C2 or C4, and Fc receptor polymorphisms. Typical manifestations begin 1-2 weeks after exposure and include fever, urticarial or morbilliform rash, pruritus, arthralgia or arthritis, lymphadenopathy, malaise, and edema, with possible proteinuria, hematuria, vasculitis, nephritis, neuropathy, and rarely glomerulonephritis or systemic involvement; common comorbid associations are atopy, autoimmune disease, and exposure-related drug hypersensitivity. Diagnosis is clinical, based on a compatible exposure history and delayed symptom onset, supported by inflammatory markers, hypocomplementemia, eosinophilia or mild leukocytosis, urinalysis for renal involvement, and occasionally skin or renal biopsy showing immune-complex vasculitic injury; allergy testing is limited, and differential diagnosis includes anaphylaxis, urticaria, viral exanthem, lupus, and small-vessel vasculitis. Treatment is primarily withdrawal of the offending agent, with antihistamines such as diphenhydramine or cetirizine acting through H1-receptor blockade for pruritus and rash, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen inhibiting cyclooxygenase to reduce pain and inflammation, and corticosteroids such as prednisone suppressing NF-kB-dependent cytokine transcription and leukocyte activation in more severe cases.

Name: Shock, Cardiogenic
Description: Cardiogenic shock is an acute, life-threatening state of systemic hypoperfusion caused by primary cardiac pump failure, most often complicating acute myocardial infarction, but also decompensated heart failure, fulminant myocarditis, severe valvular disease, mechanical complications such as papillary muscle or septal rupture, and malignant arrhythmias; clinically it presents with persistent hypotension, typically systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg or need for vasopressors, cool clammy extremities, oliguria, altered mentation, elevated lactate, pulmonary edema, jugular venous distension, tachycardia, and signs of end-organ dysfunction. Major subtypes include left ventricular, right ventricular, biventricular, and mixed cardiogenic-distributive shock. Its molecular basis is heterogeneous and usually secondary rather than inherited, but genetic contributors to underlying cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia syndromes can predispose, with representative genes including TTN, LMNA, MYH7, MYBPC3, PLN, DSP, SCN5A, and desmosomal proteins, while ischemic susceptibility and inflammatory injury involve troponins, BNP/NT-proBNP, TNF, IL-6, nitric oxide, catecholamines, calcium-handling proteins, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Key pathways include adrenergic signaling, calcium cycling, RAAS activation, inflammatory cytokine and nitric oxide signaling, coagulation, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and impaired myocardial energetics. Treatment commonly uses norepinephrine, an alpha-1 predominant vasopressor that raises systemic vascular resistance, dobutamine, a beta-1 agonist that augments inotropy and cardiac output, and milrinone, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor that increases cAMP to provide inotropy and vasodilation; additional agents include dopamine, epinephrine, vasopressin, and diuretics, alongside urgent revascularization or mechanical circulatory support when indicated. Common comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, acute kidney injury, hepatic injury, respiratory failure, multiorgan failure, and death. Diagnosis relies on hemodynamic and clinical criteria supported by ECG, cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography, chest imaging, lactate and renal/hepatic panels, and sometimes pulmonary artery catheterization showing reduced cardiac index with elevated filling pressures.

Name: Short Bowel Syndrome
Description: Short bowel syndrome (SBS; UMLS C0036992) is an intestinal failure state caused by extensive congenital or acquired loss of functional small intestine, leading to malabsorption of წყater, electrolytes, macronutrients, and micronutrients; major subtypes are postsurgical SBS, congenital SBS, and SBS with intestinal failure, with severity influenced by residual bowel length, presence of colon, and ileocecal valve. Typical manifestations include chronic diarrhea or high-output stoma, steatorrhea, dehydration, weight loss, failure to thrive, fatigue, electrolyte disturbances, and vitamin and trace-element deficiencies, while complications include parenteral-nutrition dependence, catheter-related sepsis, intestinal failure–associated liver disease/cholestasis, nephrolithiasis, gallstones, D-lactic acidosis, bacterial overgrowth, metabolic bone disease, and renal dysfunction. Although most cases are non-Mendelian and secondary to surgery for Crohn disease, mesenteric ischemia, trauma, volvulus, or necrotizing enterocolitis, rare inherited forms are linked to genes such as CLMP and FLNA causing congenital short bowel, usually with autosomal recessive inheritance for CLMP and X-linked inheritance for FLNA-related disease. Adaptive and therapeutic biology centers on GLP-2 signaling through GLP2R, promoting crypt-cell proliferation, reduced apoptosis, enhanced mucosal blood flow, barrier integrity, and absorptive capacity, with downstream mediators including IGF-1, EGFR, PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and VEGF pathways; bile acid–FXR/FGF19 and nutrient transport processes also contribute. Treatment combines oral rehydration and nutrition support with drugs such as teduglutide, a GLP-2 analog that augments intestinal adaptation and reduces parenteral support; loperamide, a peripheral µ-opioid receptor agonist that slows transit; proton-pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, which decrease gastric hypersecretion; and sometimes octreotide, a somatostatin analog that reduces secretory losses. Diagnosis is clinical and anatomical, based on history of resection or congenital bowel shortening plus evidence of malabsorption or parenteral support need, supported by imaging, endoscopy when indicated, stool and serum nutrient/electrolyte testing, liver and renal assessment, D-xylose or fecal fat studies, and genetic testing in suspected congenital cases.

Name: Sialorrhea
Description: Sialorrhea (MeSH D012798) is excessive salivary loss, usually from impaired oral containment or swallowing rather than true hypersalivation, and is classically categorized as anterior drooling from the mouth or posterior drooling into the hypopharynx, with neurogenic, structural, medication-related, and rarely primary secretory subtypes. It is most often associated with cerebral palsy, Parkinson disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, stroke, intellectual disability, bulbar palsy, and oropharyngeal or esophageal disorders, and may lead to perioral dermatitis, dehydration, dysarthria, social stigmatization, aspiration, recurrent pneumonia, and sleep disturbance. Symptoms include persistent drooling, wet speech, choking, coughing, nocturnal pooling, and difficulty managing oral secretions. Molecularly, salivary secretion is driven chiefly by parasympathetic cholinergic signaling through acetylcholine acting at muscarinic M3 receptors encoded by CHRM3, engaging Gq/11, phospholipase C, IP3-mediated intracellular Ca2+ release, aquaporin-5 trafficking, and ion transporters such as CFTR and SLC12A2; adrenergic pathways and α-synuclein-related neurodegeneration in Parkinson disease can contribute indirectly by impairing oropharyngeal clearance, while rare congenital contexts reflect broader genetic disorders affecting neuromuscular control, such as SMN1-related spinal muscular atrophy or ATP7B-related Wilson disease, rather than a Mendelian drooling trait. Treatment commonly uses glycopyrrolate, a peripheral muscarinic antagonist; scopolamine, a nonselective antimuscarinic transdermal agent; atropine, another antimuscarinic often given sublingually; and botulinum toxin A or B injections into parotid and submandibular glands, which block presynaptic acetylcholine release by cleaving SNARE proteins. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on frequency, severity, skin and pulmonary consequences, and neurologic or swallowing assessment, supplemented by drooling scales, speech-language evaluation, videofluoroscopic or fiberoptic swallow testing, salivary flow assessment, medication review, and targeted neurologic, structural, or genetic workup when an underlying syndrome is suspected.

Name: Sinus headache
Description: Sinus headache refers to facial or frontal pain attributed to acute or chronic rhinosinusitis, although many self-diagnosed cases are actually migraine; it is therefore best viewed as a symptom complex arising from inflammatory disease of the paranasal sinuses rather than a primary genetic disorder. Typical manifestations include pressure-like pain over the maxillary, frontal, or ethmoid regions that worsens with bending forward, accompanied by nasal obstruction, purulent rhinorrhea, hyposmia, postnasal drip, fever, cough, and sinus tenderness, with acute, recurrent acute, chronic, and chronic-with-nasal-polyps forms recognized. Pathobiology centers on impaired sinus drainage and mucosal inflammation involving epithelial barrier dysfunction, edema, and innate/adaptive immune signaling, including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, NF-κB, eicosanoid, histamine, and, in chronic rhinosinusitis, Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 with eosinophilic inflammation, or alternatively neutrophilic pathways; TGF-β-mediated remodeling may contribute. Clear monogenic causation is uncommon, but genetic susceptibility is seen in disorders predisposing to sinus disease such as CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis and DNAH5, DNAI1, or other ciliary genes in primary ciliary dyskinesia; inflammatory associations with TAS2R38, IL33, and related mucosal immune genes have also been reported, with inheritance patterns therefore usually complex/polygenic except in those underlying syndromes, which are often autosomal recessive. Common treatments include acetaminophen or NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit central or peripheral prostaglandin synthesis for analgesia; intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone or mometasone, which suppress cytokine-driven mucosal inflammation; decongestants such as pseudoephedrine or oxymetazoline, which are α-adrenergic vasoconstrictors that reduce mucosal edema; and when bacterial sinusitis is likely, amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis and β-lactamases. Comorbidities include allergic rhinitis, asthma, migraine, nasal polyposis, immunodeficiency, cystic fibrosis, and ciliary dyskinesia; complications include chronic rhinosinusitis, orbital cellulitis/abscess, osteitis, and intracranial spread

Name: Sinusitis
Description: Sinusitis, more precisely rhinosinusitis, is an inflammatory disorder of the paranasal sinus and nasal mucosa that is usually infectious or allergy-driven and is classified as acute viral, acute bacterial, recurrent acute, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps; cardinal features include nasal obstruction, purulent rhinorrhea or postnasal drip, facial pain or pressure, hyposmia or anosmia, cough, fever, and endoscopic evidence of mucosal edema or polyps. Its pathobiology reflects impaired mucociliary clearance, ostial obstruction, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and dysregulated innate/type 2 immunity, involving TLR and NF-kappaB signaling, IL-4/IL-5/IL-13, eosinophils, mast cells, goblet-cell hyperplasia, leukotrienes, and remodeling mediators such as TGF-beta; representative molecular associations include CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis, DNAH5 and DNAI1 defects in primary ciliary dyskinesia, TAS2R38 bitter-taste receptor variants linked to host defense, and inflammatory proteins such as periostin, eosinophil cationic protein, IgE, and Staphylococcus aureus superantigen-responsive pathways, while CRS with polyps commonly shows type 2 inflammation and some non-polypoid disease shows neutrophilic IL-17-skewed responses. Common treatments include intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress glucocorticoid-responsive inflammatory gene transcription; amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis while clavulanate blocks beta-lactamases; doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit and may reduce matrix metalloproteinases; saline irrigation for mechanical clearance; and in selected severe eosinophilic polyp disease biologics such as dupilumab, which blocks IL-4Ralpha and inhibits IL-4/IL-13 signaling. Important comorbidities include allergic rhinitis, asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, gastroesophageal reflux, and odontogenic infection; complications include orbital cellulitis or abscess, osteitis, intracranial spread, and mucocele. Diagnosis is clinical for many acute cases, but chronic disease typically requires symptoms for at least 12 weeks plus objective evidence on nasal

Name: Skin Diseases
Description: Skin diseases (MeSH D012871) comprise a heterogeneous group of inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, keratinization, pigmentary, adnexal, and neoplastic disorders affecting the epidermis, dermis, and appendages, typically presenting with pruritus, pain, erythema, scale, papules, plaques, vesicles, pustules, nodules, ulceration, dyspigmentation, alopecia, or impaired barrier function. Molecularly, representative genetic contributors include FLG loss-of-function variants in atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris, KRT5/KRT14 mutations in epidermolysis bullosa simplex, COL7A1 in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, TGM1 in autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, TYR in albinism, and HLA-C*06:02, IL23R, and CARD14 as susceptibility factors in psoriasis; relevant proteins include keratins, filaggrin, type VII collagen, desmogleins, cytokines such as TNF, IL-4, IL-13, IL-17, and IL-23, and growth regulators in MAPK and EGFR signaling. Key pathways include Th2/JAK-STAT signaling in atopic dermatitis, TNF/IL-23/IL-17 axis and NF-kB activation in psoriasis, TGF-beta and wound-healing pathways in scarring disorders, complement and autoantibody-mediated mechanisms in blistering disease, and Hedgehog signaling in basal cell carcinoma. Common treatments include topical corticosteroids, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory gene expression; retinoids such as isotretinoin or acitretin, which modulate retinoic acid receptors to normalize keratinocyte differentiation; methotrexate, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and dampens T-cell-driven inflammation; and biologics including dupilumab blocking IL-4Ralpha and secukinumab neutralizing IL-17A. Comorbidities include asthma and allergic rhinitis, psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, infection, depression, scarring, and cutaneous malignancy. Disease types may be inherited or acquired, acute or chronic, localized or systemic, with autosomal dominant, recessive, X-linked, or complex polygenic inheritance. Diagnosis relies on history and morphologic examination, dermoscopy, skin biopsy with histopathology and direct immunofluorescence

Name: Smallpox
Description: Smallpox, caused by variola virus, is an acute, highly contagious Orthopoxvirus infection and not an inherited genetic disorder; accordingly, there is no Mendelian inheritance pattern, but host susceptibility and severity are influenced by immune-response genes and proteins, with representative associations described for HLA class I/II alleles, interferon pathway components such as IFNAR1, STAT1, TLR3, and antiviral restriction or inflammatory mediators including OAS1, MX1, TNF, and IL6. Its pathobiology centers on viral entry and replication in respiratory mucosa and lymphoreticular tissues, followed by viremia, with modulation of innate immune signaling through interferon, Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, JAK-STAT, cytokine/chemokine, complement, and apoptotic pathways; viral immune-evasion proteins can bind or neutralize host cytokines such as TNF and interferons and disrupt chemokine signaling. Clinically, smallpox presents after an incubation period with abrupt high fever, malaise, severe headache, back pain, vomiting, and then a centrifugal, synchronous rash evolving from macules to papules, vesicles, pustules, and crusts, often involving the face and extremities including palms and soles; major forms include ordinary, modified, flat/malignant, and hemorrhagic smallpox, with variola major and variola minor as principal disease types. Complications include secondary bacterial skin infection, keratitis and corneal scarring, pneumonia, encephalitis, sepsis, dehydration, shock, and death, and comorbid risk is heightened by pregnancy, immunosuppression, eczema, and malnutrition. Diagnosis historically relied on characteristic clinical syndrome and epidemiology, confirmed by PCR or other nucleic acid amplification from lesion material, electron microscopy, viral culture in specialized high-containment laboratories, histopathology, and serology. Treatment is primarily supportive, but targeted antivirals include tecovirimat, which inhibits the viral VP37 protein and blocks extracellular virion formation; brincidofovir, a lipid-conjugated cidofovir analog inhibiting viral DNA polymerase after intracellular activation; and cidofovir, a nucleotide analog that also inhibits viral DNA polymerase.

Name: Sneezing
Description: Sneezing (UMLS C0037383) is a protective brainstem-mediated expiratory reflex rather than a disease per se, most commonly arising in allergic rhinitis, viral upper respiratory infection, nonallergic/vasomotor rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, irritant exposure, or photic sneeze reflex. It is characterized by paroxysmal forceful nasal expiration preceded by nasal itching or irritation and often accompanied by rhinorrhea, congestion, lacrimation, and ocular pruritus; subtypes are therefore commonly classified as allergic, infectious, irritant-induced, gustatory, drug-induced, and photic sneezing. Molecular drivers are best defined in allergy, where sensitization to aeroallergens leads to IgE production and Fc epsilon RI-mediated mast-cell and basophil activation with release of histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and cytokines including IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, engaging Th2, JAK-STAT, eosinophilic, and neurogenic TRPA1/TRPV1 sensory pathways carried largely by the trigeminal nerve to the medullary sneeze center. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian in most patients, with representative associations involving IL4, IL13, FCER1B, TSLP, FLG, and HLA loci in atopy, while photic sneeze shows familial clustering consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance in some kindreds. Common treatments include intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress NF-kappaB-dependent inflammatory gene transcription; second-generation H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine or loratadine, which block histamine H1 receptors; and intranasal ipratropium, a muscarinic antagonist that reduces glandular secretion; adjuncts include montelukast, a cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonist, and allergen immunotherapy to induce immune tolerance. Important comorbidities include asthma, atopic dermatitis, conjunctivitis, nasal polyposis, sinusitis, otitis media, sleep disturbance, and reduced quality of life, while complications are usually minor but may include epistaxis, syncope, postoperative wound stress, or urinary leakage. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when indicated by allergen history, nasal examination, skin-prick or serum specific-IgE testing, nasal endoscopy, viral testing, and selective imaging to identify

Name: Spasms, Infantile
Description: Infantile spasms (West syndrome when accompanied by developmental arrest/regression and hypsarrhythmia) are a severe early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by clusters of brief flexor, extensor, or mixed axial and limb spasms, typically beginning between 3 and 12 months of age, often on awakening, with irritability, loss of milestones, and later cognitive, behavioral, and motor impairment. The disorder is etiologically heterogeneous, with structural, metabolic, infectious, immune, and genetic causes; recurrently implicated genes include TSC1/TSC2, ARX, CDKL5, STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A, DEPDC5, GRIN2B, KCNT1, and genes in trisomy 21, with X-linked, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and de novo patterns all recognized. Pathobiology commonly converges on dysregulated cortical network excitability involving GABAergic interneuron dysfunction, glutamatergic/NMDA signaling, voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, synaptic vesicle release, and mTOR/PI3K-AKT signaling, particularly in tuberous sclerosis complex. Major subtypes include symptomatic/structural-metabolic-genetic, cryptogenic, and idiopathic forms. Diagnosis rests on clinical recognition of epileptic spasm semiology plus EEG showing hypsarrhythmia or modified hypsarrhythmia, although spasms may occur without classic patterns; prolonged video-EEG, brain MRI, metabolic testing when indicated, and chromosomal microarray or epilepsy gene panels/exome sequencing help define etiology. First-line therapy commonly includes adrenocorticotropic hormone or high-dose prednisolone, which suppress neuroinflammatory and corticotropin-releasing hormone–related excitability, and vigabatrin, an irreversible GABA transaminase inhibitor that raises brain GABA and is especially effective in TSC-associated spasms; additional agents include valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and modulates sodium channels, topiramate, which blocks AMPA/kainate receptors and sodium channels and inhibits carbonic anhydrase, and ketogenic diet or epilepsy surgery in selected refractory cases. Common comorbidities and complications include autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy, persistent epilepsy including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, visual toxicity with vigabatrin, and substantial long-term neurodevelopmental disability

Name: Spondylitis, Ankylosing
Description: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory spondyloarthritis that primarily targets the sacroiliac joints and axial skeleton, causing inflammatory back pain beginning before age 45, prolonged morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, reduced spinal mobility, alternating buttock pain, enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, chest expansion limitation, and in advanced disease syndesmophytes and spinal ankylosis with kyphosis. Its strongest genetic association is with HLA-B27, while additional susceptibility genes include ERAP1, IL23R, RUNX3, TNFSF15, and STAT3; familial aggregation is typical, with a complex polygenic, non-Mendelian inheritance pattern in which HLA-B27 greatly increases risk but is neither necessary nor sufficient. Pathobiology centers on aberrant antigen presentation and misfolding-related stress, activation of the IL-23/IL-17 axis, TNF signaling, JAK-STAT pathways, Th17 cells, macrophages, osteoclasts, and osteoblast-driven pathologic new bone formation. Major subtypes include radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (classic ankylosing spondylitis) and non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, with juvenile-onset and axial disease associated with psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease also recognized. Common comorbidities and complications include acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis, Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, osteoporosis, vertebral fractures, atlantoaxial instability, restrictive lung disease from chest wall involvement, aortic root dilation with aortic regurgitation, conduction abnormalities, and functional disability. Diagnosis relies on clinical features plus elevated CRP or ESR, HLA-B27 testing, radiographic sacroiliitis under modified New York criteria, and MRI showing active sacroiliac inflammation for earlier disease under ASAS axial spondyloarthritis criteria. Treatment typically begins with NSAIDs such as indomethacin, naproxen, or celecoxib, which inhibit cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin synthesis; biologics include TNF inhibitors such as adalimumab or etanercept, and IL-17 inhibitors such as secukinumab, while JAK inhibitors such as upadacitinib suppress intracellular cytokine signaling.

Name: Staphylococcal enterocolitis
Description: Staphylococcal enterocolitis (UMLS C0038157) is an acute infectious and toxin-mediated inflammatory disease of the small intestine and colon caused predominantly by enterotoxigenic or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, usually arising after antibiotic-induced disruption of normal gut flora, hospitalization, abdominal surgery, or immunocompromise rather than from a Mendelian inherited defect. Its principal molecular determinants are bacterial genes and proteins, especially enterotoxins encoded by sea, seb, sec, sed, and related superantigen loci, toxic shock syndrome toxin-1, alpha-toxin (hla), Panton-Valentine leukocidin in some strains, and resistance determinants such as mecA encoding altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a; host susceptibility may be influenced by innate immune pathways involving TLR2, NFKB, inflammasome signaling, neutrophil recruitment, epithelial tight-junction injury, and cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-8. Clinically it presents with profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, leukocytosis, and sometimes pseudomembranous or hemorrhagic colitis, dehydration, ileus, sepsis, toxic megacolon, perforation, and shock; recognized forms include antibiotic-associated enterocolitis, postoperative enterocolitis, MRSA enterocolitis, and staphylococcal food-borne enteritis. Comorbid settings include inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, neutropenia, and coinfection or prior therapy for Clostridioides difficile. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical syndrome plus stool culture or multiplex PCR demonstrating heavy S. aureus, exclusion of alternative pathogens including C. difficile toxin/PCR, and when needed endoscopy or histopathology showing mucosal inflammation or pseudomembranes. Treatment centers on stopping precipitating antibiotics, fluid and electrolyte replacement, and anti-staphylococcal agents such as oral vancomycin, which inhibits cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis; linezolid, which blocks 50S-mediated protein synthesis; daptomycin, which depolarizes bacterial membranes but is generally not preferred intraluminally; and, for susceptible isolates, nafcillin or cefazolin targeting penicillin-binding proteins.

Name: Staphylococcal Infections
Description: Staphylococcal infections are acute or chronic bacterial diseases caused primarily by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant strains, and less virulent coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis, producing syndromes that range from impetigo, cellulitis, folliculitis, abscesses, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, bacteremia, endocarditis, food poisoning, toxic shock syndrome, and scalded skin syndrome to device-associated biofilm infections. Major microbial determinants include mecA or mecC encoding the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a that mediates methicillin resistance, blaZ beta-lactamase, the accessory gene regulator agr quorum-sensing system, staphylococcal protein A encoded by spa, Panton-Valentine leukocidin genes lukS-PV/lukF-PV, alpha-toxin hla, and exfoliative toxins eta/etb. Host susceptibility has genetic components, particularly defects in neutrophil and Th17/IL-17 immunity, including CYBB in chronic granulomatous disease, STAT3 in hyper-IgE syndrome, and IL6ST, DOCK8, or CARD9-related immunodeficiency. Pathobiology centers on TLR2/NF-kB activation by peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, complement and opsonophagocytic killing, cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and the IL-17/IL-23 axis, together with biofilm pathways involving icaADBC polysaccharide matrix production. Typical findings include painful erythematous purulent skin lesions, fever, drainage, hypotension in invasive disease, respiratory symptoms in pneumonia, and positive blood or site cultures. Diagnosis relies on Gram stain and culture, susceptibility testing, PCR for mecA/mecC or toxin genes, blood cultures, imaging for deep foci, and echocardiography when endocarditis is suspected. Treatment commonly includes nafcillin or oxacillin, beta-lactams that inhibit cell-wall transpeptidation, vancomycin, a glycopeptide blocking peptidoglycan synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala, and linezolid, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor; daptomycin depolarizes the bacterial membrane,

Name: Staphylococcal Skin Infections
Description: Staphylococcal skin infections are common bacterial infections of the epidermis, dermis, and adnexal structures, caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant strains, and less often by coagulase-negative staphylococci; clinically they range from impetigo, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, cellulitis, abscesses, and wound infections to toxin-mediated syndromes such as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Disease pathogenesis reflects both bacterial virulence and host susceptibility: key microbial determinants include mecA or mecC encoding PBP2a-mediated beta-lactam resistance, PVL genes lukS-PV/lukF-PV linked to necrotizing abscesses, exfoliative toxins ETA/ETB, alpha-toxin, protein A, clumping factors, fibronectin-binding proteins, and agr quorum-sensing regulators. Relevant host pathways include Toll-like receptor 2, MyD88, NF-kappaB, IL-1/IL-17, TNF, complement, neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocyte oxidative burst; inherited predisposition is usually not Mendelian for the infection itself, but susceptibility is increased by pathogenic variants affecting skin barrier or innate immunity, such as FLG, DOCK8, STAT3, CXCR2, CYBB, and MYD88, as well as diabetes, atopic dermatitis, HIV, obesity, and chronic kidney disease. Typical findings are erythema, warmth, tenderness, pustules, honey-colored crusts, fluctuance, purulent drainage, and sometimes fever or lymphangitis. Important complications include recurrent infection, bacteremia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, necrotizing pneumonia, sepsis, and scarring. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by Gram stain and culture with susceptibility testing from pus or wound material, blood cultures in systemic illness, and molecular assays for mecA/MRSA; biopsy is rarely required. Treatment commonly includes dicloxacillin or cephalexin, which inhibit cell-wall transpeptidation; clindamycin, which binds the 50S ribosome and may suppress toxin production; doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosome; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks folate synthesis; and vancomycin, which binds D-Ala

Name: Status Epilepticus
Description: Status epilepticus is a neurological emergency defined by prolonged seizure activity or recurrent seizures without recovery, operationally usually lasting at least 5 minutes for convulsive status epilepticus, and it comprises convulsive, nonconvulsive, focal, generalized, refractory, and super-refractory subtypes. Clinically it presents with persistent tonic-clonic movements or subtle motor phenomena, impaired awareness, aphasia, gaze deviation, autonomic instability, and postictal or ongoing coma; major complications include hypoxic brain injury, excitotoxic neuronal death, cerebral edema, rhabdomyolysis, aspiration pneumonia, metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, and death, with common comorbidities including epilepsy, stroke, CNS infection, traumatic brain injury, brain tumors, autoimmune encephalitis, alcohol withdrawal, and systemic metabolic derangements. Pathobiologically, status epilepticus reflects failure of seizure termination with excessive glutamatergic transmission and impaired GABAergic inhibition, involving NMDA and AMPA receptors, GABAA receptor internalization, voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, neuroinflammatory mediators such as IL-1beta and TNF, and mTOR-related network hyperexcitability. Although often acquired, genetic susceptibility is recognized, especially in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies and febrile seizure syndromes, with representative genes including SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, STXBP1, GABRG2, GABRA1, KCNQ2, KCNT1, PCDH19, and DEPDC5; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, X-linked as in PCDH19, or de novo. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and electroencephalographic, supported by urgent EEG for nonconvulsive cases, neuroimaging, serum glucose, electrolytes, renal and hepatic indices, toxicology, lumbar puncture when infection is suspected, and targeted genetic testing in recurrent, early-onset, or syndromic cases. First-line treatment is benzodiazepines such as lorazepam, diazepam, or midazolam, which positively modulate GABAA receptors; common second-line agents include fosphenytoin or phenytoin, which block voltage-gated sodium channels, valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and reduces sodium channel firing, and levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to reduce synaptic neurotransmitter release

Name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
Description: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS; MeSH D013262) is an acute, life-threatening, usually drug-triggered mucocutaneous hypersensitivity disorder on the erythema multiforme–toxic epidermal necrolysis spectrum, defined by epidermal necrosis and detachment involving less than 10% body surface area, with SJS/TEN overlap at 10–30% and TEN above 30%. It most often presents with fever, malaise, rapidly progressive atypical targetoid macules, blistering, painful erosive stomatitis, conjunctivitis, genital mucositis, and a positive Nikolsky sign, and may be complicated by sepsis, dehydration, pneumonia, hepatitis, multiorgan failure, and chronic ocular, cutaneous, and genital scarring. Pathobiology reflects a T-cell–mediated cytotoxic reaction in which HLA-restricted drug presentation activates CD8+ lymphocytes and NK cells, with key effectors including granulysin, perforin, granzyme B, Fas-FasL, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and apoptotic keratinocyte signaling through caspases and related immune pathways. Important genetic susceptibility factors are largely pharmacogenetic rather than Mendelian, notably HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine and phenytoin, HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol, and HLA-A*31:01 with carbamazepine; variants in CYP2C9, drug transport, and immune-regulatory genes have also been reported. Common precipitants include antiepileptics, sulfonamide antibiotics, allopurinol, NSAIDs, and nevirapine, while treatment is primarily immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug and intensive supportive burn-unit-style care; commonly used agents include corticosteroids, which suppress NF-κB–dependent inflammatory transcription and lymphocyte activation, intravenous immunoglobulin, which may inhibit Fas-mediated apoptosis, and cyclosporine, which blocks calcineurin-driven T-cell activation, with TNF-α inhibitors such as etanercept also used in some centers. Diagnosis is based on clinical morphology, extent of detachment, medication history, SCORTEN severity assessment, and skin biopsy showing full-thickness epidermal necrosis; direct immunofluorescence helps exclude autoimmune blistering disease.

Name: Stomach Ulcer
Description: Stomach ulcer, or gastric ulcer, is a peptic ulcer disease characterized by a mucosal break extending through the muscularis mucosae of the stomach, usually arising from an imbalance between aggressive factors such as gastric acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and mucosal defenses including mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, and epithelial restitution. Key molecular associations include H. pylori virulence factors CagA and VacA, host inflammatory genes such as IL1B, IL8, TNF, PTGS1 and PTGS2, and ulcer susceptibility variants reported in cytokine and mucosal repair pathways, although inheritance is generally complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian; rare familial clustering may reflect shared H. pylori exposure and genetic predisposition. Central pathways involve NF-kappaB activation, COX-prostaglandin signaling, EGFR-mediated mucosal repair, cytokine-driven neutrophilic inflammation, oxidative stress, and acid secretory regulation through histamine H2 receptors, acetylcholine M3 receptors, and gastrin-cholecystokinin B signaling to the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase. Typical symptoms are epigastric pain or burning, postprandial discomfort, nausea, bloating, early satiety, occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, melena, iron deficiency anemia, and sometimes weight loss, though some ulcers are silent. Major subtypes include H. pylori-associated, NSAID-associated, stress-related, malignant-appearing or cancer-associated ulceration, and less commonly hypersecretory ulcers such as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Important comorbidities and complications include chronic gastritis, duodenal ulcer disease, gastric outlet obstruction, perforation, hemorrhage, anemia, and gastric adenocarcinoma risk in the setting of chronic H. pylori infection. Diagnosis relies on upper endoscopy with biopsy to exclude malignancy and test for H. pylori, supported by urea breath test, stool antigen testing, histology, or rapid urease testing. Standard treatment includes proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase, H2 blockers such as famotidine, which reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion, and mucosal protective agents such as sucralfate or misoprostol, the latter a prostaglandin E1 analog;

Name: Stomatitis, Aphthous
Description: Stomatitis, aphthous, or recurrent aphthous stomatitis, is a common chronic inflammatory disorder of the nonkeratinized oral mucosa characterized by recurrent, painful, shallow round or oval ulcers with a yellow-gray fibrinous base and erythematous halo that impair eating, speaking, and swallowing; major clinical subtypes are minor, major, and herpetiform aphthae. Its pathobiology is multifactorial, dominated by T-cell–mediated mucosal immune dysregulation with increased TNF, IL-2, IL-6, IL-17, IFN-γ, and NF-κB signaling, neutrophil and keratinocyte activation, and altered epithelial barrier and oxidative stress responses; representative genetic associations include HLA class I and II alleles such as HLA-B12, HLA-B51, HLA-DR2, and HLA-DR7, cytokine variants in TNF and IL10, and occasional overlap with monogenic autoinflammatory disorders involving MEFV, MVK, TNFAIP3, or PSTPIP1, especially when oral ulcers occur in Behçet spectrum disease or PFAPA-like phenotypes. Inheritance is usually complex and polygenic with familial clustering rather than Mendelian transmission. Important comorbidities and mimics include Behçet disease, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, PFAPA, cyclic neutropenia, HIV infection, iron, folate, vitamin B12 or zinc deficiency, and complications such as dehydration, weight loss, secondary infection, and scarring in major aphthae. Diagnosis is clinical, based on recurrent typical ulcers and exclusion of trauma, herpes simplex, oral lichen planus, pemphigus, and malignancy; testing may include CBC, ferritin, folate, vitamin B12, celiac serologies, inflammatory markers, HIV testing, and biopsy only for atypical, persistent, or indurated lesions. Treatment is mainly anti-inflammatory and symptomatic: topical corticosteroids such as triamcinolone acetonide or clobetasol suppress cytokine transcription, chlorhexidine reduces microbial burden, topical lidocaine provides sodium-channel blockade analgesia, and refractory disease may require colchicine, dapsone, thalidomide, or short systemic corticosteroids.

Name: Streptococcal Infections
Description: Streptococcal infections are acute or invasive bacterial diseases caused by Gram-positive cocci of the genus Streptococcus, most commonly group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), and Streptococcus pneumoniae, producing syndromes ranging from pharyngitis, impetigo, cellulitis, erysipelas, pneumonia, otitis media, and neonatal sepsis to necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal toxic shock. Key microbial virulence determinants include the emm-encoded M protein, streptolysins O and S, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins SpeA/SpeC, hyaluronic acid capsule genes such as hasA, C5a peptidase ScpA, pneumococcal capsule loci, pneumolysin ply, and autolysin lytA; host susceptibility is partly influenced by variants in HLA class II, TLR2/TLR4, NOD2, complement components, and Fc-gamma receptor genes, but inheritance is not Mendelian and mainly reflects complex polygenic immune predisposition. Pathobiology centers on epithelial adherence, immune evasion, superantigen-driven T-cell activation, NF-kB and MAPK signaling, cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-17, complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, and, in post-streptococcal autoimmunity, molecular mimicry affecting heart, kidney, or CNS. Complications include scarlet fever, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, bacteremia, endocarditis, abscess, meningitis, and septic shock; important comorbid risks include diabetes, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy, and extremes of age. Diagnosis relies on syndrome-specific evaluation with throat culture or rapid antigen/PCR testing for pharyngitis, culture and susceptibility from blood, CSF, wounds, or sputum for invasive disease, urinary antigen for pneumococcus, imaging when deep infection is suspected, and serology such as ASO or anti-DNase B for recent infection. First-line treatment commonly includes penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; ceftriaxone, another beta-lactam with

Name: Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic
Description: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a trauma- and stressor-related psychiatric disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence and is characterized by intrusive recollections or nightmares, avoidance of trauma reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, hyperarousal, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep disturbance, dissociation in some patients, and functional impairment; recognized phenotypes include acute, chronic, delayed-expression, and dissociative subtypes, with complex trauma presentations often overlapping. Its biology is multifactorial and moderately heritable rather than Mendelian, with genetic susceptibility supported by variants in stress-response and neurotransmission genes such as FKBP5, NR3C1, CRHR1, SLC6A4 including the 5-HTTLPR promoter polymorphism, BDNF including Val66Met, COMT, ADCYAP1R1, and OPRL1, acting through gene-environment interaction and epigenetic regulation. Core pathophysiology involves dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and glucocorticoid signaling, corticotropin-releasing hormone pathways, noradrenergic and serotonergic circuits, dopaminergic and GABA/glutamate transmission, neuroinflammatory signaling, altered amygdala-prefrontal-hippocampal network function, and impaired fear extinction. Common comorbidities include major depressive disorder, substance use disorders, anxiety disorders, chronic pain, traumatic brain injury, cardiovascular and metabolic disease, and complications such as suicide risk, social dysfunction, and impaired occupational performance. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 or ICD criteria requiring symptom clusters persisting longer than 1 month after trauma, assessed with structured interviews or scales such as CAPS-5 and PCL-5; testing primarily excludes mimics and evaluates comorbidity, while biomarkers and neuroimaging remain investigational. First-line pharmacotherapy commonly includes sertraline and paroxetine, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors that enhance serotonergic neurotransmission, venlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, and prazosin, an alpha1-adrenergic antagonist often used for trauma-related nightmares; psychotherapy, especially trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy and prolonged exposure, remains central to management.

Name: Female urinary stress incontinence
Description: Female urinary stress incontinence (UMLS C0038437) is a common pelvic floor disorder defined by involuntary leakage of urine during effort, exertion, coughing, sneezing, or exercise because urethral closure pressure fails to exceed rises in intravesical pressure; major subtypes reflect urethral hypermobility from pelvic support failure and intrinsic sphincter deficiency, often coexisting. Symptoms include small-volume leakage with physical stress, pad use, activity limitation, and on examination a positive cough stress test, urethral mobility, and sometimes pelvic organ prolapse. The biology centers on connective-tissue remodeling, neuromuscular integrity, and estrogen-responsive trophic signaling, with implicated genes/proteins including COL1A1, COL3A1, ELN, FBLN5, LOXL1, MMP1, MMP9, LAMC1, ESR1, and ADRB3, affecting extracellular matrix elasticity, collagen cross-linking, smooth-muscle function, and pudendal/striated sphincter support; inheritance is usually complex and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, although familial clustering and associations with connective-tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome support genetic susceptibility. Relevant pathways include TGF-β/SMAD-mediated fibrosis and matrix turnover, matrix metalloproteinase activity, elastogenesis, estrogen receptor signaling, and adrenergic/cholinergic control of urethral smooth and striated muscle.
