Common comorbidities include obesity, pregnancy and vaginal childbirth history, menopause, chronic cough, constipation, diabetes, recurrent urinary tract infection, overactive bladder or mixed incontinence, and pelvic organ prolapse; complications include skin irritation, sleep and sexual dysfunction, falls in older adults, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history, bladder diary, urinalysis, pelvic examination, postvoid residual when indicated, validated questionnaires, pad testing, and selective urodynamics, cystoscopy, or imaging to distinguish stress from urge or overflow incontinence. Treatment commonly includes duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that augments pudendal motor neuron outflow and urethral sphincter contraction, topical vaginal estrogen to improve urethral mucosal coaptation in hypoestrogenic women, and periurethral bulking agents such as polyacrylamide hydrogel or calcium hydroxylapatite that increase outlet resistance.

Name: Stroke
Description: Stroke (MeSH D020521) is an acute cerebrovascular syndrome caused by interruption of cerebral blood flow or vessel rupture, broadly classified into ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and subarachnoid hemorrhage, with ischemic stroke further divided into large-artery atherosclerotic, cardioembolic, small-vessel (lacunar), and cryptogenic subtypes. Clinically it presents with sudden focal neurologic deficits such as hemiparesis, facial droop, aphasia, dysarthria, hemisensory loss, ataxia, visual field defects, neglect, severe headache, or depressed consciousness depending on vascular territory and hemorrhagic involvement. Pathobiology involves excitotoxic glutamate signaling, calcium influx, oxidative stress, mitochondrial failure, endothelial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, and thromboinflammatory pathways mediated by platelets, coagulation factors, cytokines, microglia, matrix metalloproteinases, and nitric oxide. Genetic contributors are usually complex and polygenic, but representative associations include APOE, MTHFR, ACE, PDE4D, HDAC9, PITX2 and ZFHX3 for cardioembolic/atrial fibrillation-related risk, and NOTCH3 mutations in CADASIL, HTRA1 in hereditary small-vessel disease, COL4A1/COL4A2 in hemorrhagic and ischemic vasculopathy, and sickle hemoglobin variants predisposing to childhood stroke; inheritance is generally multifactorial except in monogenic syndromes, which are often autosomal dominant. Major comorbidities and risk factors include hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, carotid atherosclerosis, obesity, chronic kidney disease, and prior transient ischemic attack; complications include cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, seizures, aspiration pneumonia, deep venous thrombosis, recurrent stroke, cognitive impairment, depression, and disability. Diagnosis relies on abrupt clinical onset plus neuroimaging with noncontrast CT to exclude hemorrhage, MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging for early ischemia, CT/MR angiography or carotid ultrasound for vascular lesions, ECG/telemetry and echocardiography for embolic sources, and laboratory coagulation/metabolic testing. Treatment commonly includes alteplase or tenecteplase, which activate plasminogen to dissolve fibrin thrombi, aspirin or clopidogrel

Name: Strongyloidiasis
Description: Strongyloidiasis (MeSH D013322) is a helminthic infection caused predominantly by Strongyloides stercoralis, characterized by chronic intestinal colonization with autoinfection and, in susceptible hosts, hyperinfection or disseminated disease. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic eosinophilia to pruritic serpiginous rash, urticaria, larva currens, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, cough, wheeze, and weight loss; severe disease may produce enterocolitis, pneumonitis, Gram-negative sepsis, meningitis, and multiorgan failure. Major subtypes are uncomplicated chronic infection, hyperinfection syndrome, and disseminated strongyloidiasis. Risk is strongly shaped by host immunity rather than Mendelian inheritance, but genetic and molecular correlates of susceptibility include Th2/IgE-eosinophil pathways with IL4, IL5, IL13, STAT6, GATA3, FCER1A, HLA class II variation, and impaired anti-helminth defense in HTLV-1 coinfection, corticosteroid exposure, malignancy, transplantation, malnutrition, and advanced HIV or other immunosuppression; eosinophils, mast cells, goblet cells, and alternatively activated macrophages are key cellular effectors. Relevant signaling networks include IL-4/IL-13–JAK-STAT6 signaling, IL-5-driven eosinophilopoiesis, IgE-FcεRI-mediated mast-cell activation, epithelial alarmins such as IL-33, and regulatory T-cell and glucocorticoid-mediated suppression that favors autoinfection. Diagnosis relies on epidemiologic exposure plus detection of larvae in serial stool microscopy or concentration/culture methods such as Baermann or agar plate, duodenal aspirate or biopsy when needed, serology for Strongyloides IgG, eosinophilia, and in severe cases identification in sputum or other body fluids; PCR is increasingly used where available. Treatment is centered on ivermectin, which binds parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels causing paralysis and death; albendazole, a β-tubulin inhibitor that blocks microtubule assembly and glucose uptake; and thiabendazole, another benzimidazole now less used because of toxicity; refractory hyperinfection may require prolonged or combination therapy and reduction of immunosuppression.

Name: Synovitis
Description: Synovitis is inflammation of the synovial membrane of diarthrodial joints, tendon sheaths, or bursae, occurring as an acute or chronic process in disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout, osteoarthritis, trauma, and infection; clinically it causes joint pain, swelling, warmth, effusion, morning stiffness, tenderness, and reduced range of motion, and in proliferative forms may produce pannus and progressive cartilage and bone damage. Molecularly, synovitis is driven by activation of innate and adaptive immune pathways, especially TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, MAPK, RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis, VEGF-dependent angiogenesis, matrix metalloproteinases, cyclooxygenase-2, and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, with representative associated genes and proteins including HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, PTPN22, STAT4, CTLA4, TNF, IL6, IL1B, MMP3, MMP9, and ACPA/RF-related autoimmunity in rheumatoid synovitis; inherited risk is usually complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, although crystal arthropathies may reflect variants affecting urate handling such as SLC2A9 or ABCG2. Major subtypes include inflammatory, infectious, crystal-induced, traumatic, pigmented villonodular/tenosynovial giant cell, and osteoarthritic synovitis. Common treatments include NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and reduce prostaglandin synthesis; glucocorticoids such as prednisone or intra-articular triamcinolone, which suppress NF-kB-dependent cytokine transcription; methotrexate, which augments adenosine-mediated anti-inflammatory effects; biologics such as adalimumab or infliximab targeting TNF-alpha, tocilizumab blocking the IL-6 receptor, and JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib reducing cytokine signaling. Important comorbidities and complications include joint destruction, tendon rupture, deformity, disability, osteoarthritis, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, and secondary infection. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, inflammatory markers, autoantibodies, serum urate when relevant, synovial fluid analysis with cell

Name: Syphilis
Description: Syphilis is a chronic, systemic sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum, notable for stage-specific manifestations and transplacental transmission in congenital disease rather than Mendelian inheritance; host genetic susceptibility is incompletely defined but appears to involve immune-response loci, with representative associations in HLA class II alleles and variation affecting TLR1, TLR2, TLR6, TLR4, CD14, TNF, IL10, IFNG, and CXCL8, while major treponemal virulence-related proteins include the TpN15, TpN17, and TpN47 antigens, TprK antigenic variation protein, and outer membrane lipoproteins that trigger innate and adaptive immunity. Pathobiology centers on Toll-like receptor and NF-kB signaling, macrophage and dendritic-cell activation, Th1-predominant cytokine responses with IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha, endothelial invasion, and plasma-cell-rich inflammation. Clinical subtypes include primary syphilis with a painless chancre and regional lymphadenopathy, secondary syphilis with diffuse rash involving palms and soles, mucous patches, condylomata lata, fever, and alopecia, latent syphilis, tertiary syphilis with gummatous, cardiovascular, and neurosyphilitic disease, plus congenital and neurosyphilis at any stage. Important complications and comorbidities include HIV coinfection, uveitis, stroke, tabes dorsalis, general paresis, aortitis, aneurysm, pregnancy loss, stillbirth, and neonatal multisystem disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical context plus serology using nontreponemal tests such as RPR or VDRL for screening and monitoring, confirmed by treponemal assays including FTA-ABS, TP-PA, or EIA/CIA; dark-field microscopy, PCR from lesions, and CSF VDRL with CSF pleocytosis or elevated protein support direct or neurosyphilis diagnosis. Treatment is centered on benzathine penicillin G, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins, aqueous crystalline penicillin G for neurosyphilis, and alternatives such as doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, or ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam cell-wall synthesis inhibitor

Name: Syphilis, Congenital
Description: Congenital syphilis (UMLS C0039131) is a vertically transmitted fetal and neonatal infection caused by transplacental or intrapartum exposure to Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum rather than a Mendelian genetic disorder, so no causal inherited mutation is established; host susceptibility and inflammatory severity may be modified by immune-response genes and proteins such as HLA class II alleles, TLR1/TLR2/TLR4, TNF, IL6, IL10, IFNG, and chemokines including CXCL8, while the pathogen’s major lipoproteins and adhesin-related antigens, exemplified by Tp47 and TmpA, engage innate immune signaling. Disease pathobiology is driven by spirochetal dissemination, endothelial invasion, placental inflammation, and activation of TLR-NF-kB, JAK-STAT, complement, macrophage, and Th1-skewed cytokine pathways, producing vasculitis and multisystem injury. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic infection to miscarriage, stillbirth, prematurity, hepatosplenomegaly, snuffles, jaundice, rash with desquamation, lymphadenopathy, anemia, thrombocytopenia, osteochondritis, periostitis, meningitis, and nephrotic syndrome; late disease includes interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness, and Hutchinson teeth, classically grouped into early and late congenital syphilis. Major complications and comorbidities include hydrops fetalis, growth restriction, neurosyphilis, skeletal deformity, developmental delay, and coinfection settings such as maternal HIV. Diagnosis rests on maternal risk assessment and serology plus infant evaluation using nontreponemal tests such as RPR or VDRL with comparison to maternal titers, confirmatory treponemal assays including TPPA, FTA-ABS, or EIA/CIA, dark-field or PCR when available, placental or lesion studies, and targeted assessment for dissemination with CSF VDRL, cell count and protein, CBC, liver tests, and long-bone radiographs. Treatment is centered on penicillins: aqueous crystalline penicillin G and procaine penicillin G, which are beta-lactams that bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking, and benzathine penicillin G for selected exposed infants or maternal infection; ceftriax

Name: Syphilis, Latent
Description: Latent syphilis (UMLS C0039133) is a sexually transmitted, systemic infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum in which seroreactivity persists despite the absence of overt clinical signs; it is classified as early latent (generally acquired within the preceding year) or late latent/latent of unknown duration, and may progress to tertiary cardiovascular or neurosyphilis or permit vertical transmission causing congenital syphilis. Unlike monogenic disorders, latent syphilis has no Mendelian inheritance pattern; host susceptibility and disease course are influenced by immune-response genes and proteins rather than pathogen-specific inherited mutations, with reported associations involving HLA class II loci, TLR1/TLR2-mediated innate sensing, CD14, TNF, IFNG, IL10, CXCL13, and macrophage- and T cell-driven responses, while T. pallidum lipoproteins activate NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and cytokine/chemokine signaling pathways that shape persistent infection and tissue injury. Typical latent disease is asymptomatic, although a history of prior chancre, rash, mucous patches, condylomata lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, or unexplained seroconversion may be elicited; complications include neurosyphilis, ocular or otic syphilis, aortitis, gummatous disease, HIV coinfection, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and congenital infection. Diagnosis relies on serology, usually a nontreponemal test such as RPR or VDRL with confirmatory treponemal assays including FTA-ABS, TP-PA, or EIA/CIA, interpreted with exposure history and prior treatment records; CSF examination with cell count, protein, and CSF-VDRL is reserved for neurologic, ocular, or otic involvement or selected treatment failures. First-line therapy is benzathine penicillin G, which releases penicillin slowly to inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins; alternatives for nonpregnant penicillin-allergic patients include doxycycline and tetracycline, which inhibit protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit, and ceftriaxone, a β-lactam that also blocks cell-wall synthesis.

Name: Tachycardia, Supraventricular
Description: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is a heterogeneous group of rapid atrial or atrioventricular junctional arrhythmias arising above the ventricles, most commonly atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia, atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia associated with accessory pathways as in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and focal or macroreentrant atrial tachycardias including atrial flutter. Its molecular basis reflects disordered impulse generation or re-entry involving ion-channel and conduction-system proteins; representative genetic associations include PRKAG2, RYR2, SCN5A, CACNA1C, KCNH2, KCNE1/2, ANK2, LMNA, NKX2-5, and accessory-pathway syndromes linked to familial WPW, with inheritance often autosomal dominant and variable penetrance in syndromic or familial cases, although most SVT is sporadic. Relevant pathways include cardiac action-potential regulation through sodium, L-type calcium, and potassium currents, cAMP/Ca2+-dependent signaling, ryanodine-receptor-mediated sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium handling, AV nodal conduction, and fibrotic or structural remodeling that stabilizes re-entry circuits. Typical manifestations are abrupt episodic palpitations, rapid regular heartbeat, chest discomfort, dyspnea, lightheadedness, anxiety, neck pounding, presyncope or syncope, and occasionally hypotension or heart failure in sustained episodes. Comorbidities and complications include congenital heart disease, cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, electrolyte disturbance, anxiety, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, thromboembolism particularly with atrial flutter, and rare sudden cardiac death in pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Diagnosis relies on ECG documentation of a narrow-complex tachycardia or pre-excitation, vagal response patterns, ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography to assess structural disease, laboratory testing for reversible triggers, and electrophysiology study for mechanism definition and ablation planning. Treatment commonly uses adenosine, which transiently blocks AV nodal conduction via A1-receptor-mediated suppression of cAMP; beta-blockers such as metoprolol, which reduce sympathetic drive and AV nodal conduction; nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil or diltiazem, which inhibit L-type calcium current in the

Name: Giant Cell Arteritis
Description: Giant cell arteritis (MeSH D013700) is a granulomatous large- and medium-vessel vasculitis of older adults, classically affecting the extracranial branches of the carotid artery, especially the temporal artery, and often overlapping with polymyalgia rheumatica; major subtypes include cranial GCA and large-vessel/aortic GCA. Its pathobiology reflects dendritic-cell activation in the arterial adventitia, Th1/Th17 polarization, macrophage infiltration, multinucleated giant cells, intimal hyperplasia, and ischemia, with key mediators including HLA-DRB1*04 alleles as the strongest genetic risk factors, plus associations near IL6, IL17A, PTPN22, and FCGR2A/FCGR3A; proteins and pathways implicated include IL-6/JAK-STAT, IL-12/IFN-gamma, IL-17, TNF, VEGF, PDGF, matrix metalloproteinases, and endothelial and smooth-muscle remodeling pathways. The disease is not Mendelian, shows complex polygenic susceptibility, and lacks a single causative mutation. Typical manifestations are new-onset temporal or occipital headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, constitutional symptoms, polymyalgic shoulder/hip pain, visual blurring or amaurosis fugax, diplopia, and reduced temporal artery pulse, while complications include irreversible anterior ischemic optic neuropathy and blindness, stroke, aortic aneurysm, dissection, and large-vessel stenosis; comorbidities include polymyalgia rheumatica, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, and glucocorticoid toxicity. Diagnosis relies on compatible age older than 50 years, elevated ESR and/or CRP, and the 1990 ACR classification features, supported by temporal artery biopsy showing transmural granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and elastic lamina fragmentation, or by color Doppler ultrasound halo sign, MRI, CT angiography, or FDG-PET for large-vessel involvement. Treatment centers on glucocorticoids such as prednisone or intravenous methylprednisolone, which broadly suppress NF-kappaB-driven cytokine transcription; tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist, is an effective steroid-sparing agent; methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate-dependent proliferation and dampens immune activation; and aspirin is often used to reduce thrombotic

Name: Tendinitis
Description: Tendinitis (UMLS C0039503) is a common painful disorder of tendon inflammation and, more often in chronic cases, failed tendon healing with degenerative tendinopathy caused by repetitive mechanical overload, acute strain, aging, or systemic disease. It typically presents with localized pain, tenderness, swelling, crepitus, and activity-related functional limitation at sites such as the rotator cuff, lateral epicondyle, patellar, Achilles, or wrist tendons; subtypes are generally classified by anatomic site and by acute inflammatory versus chronic degenerative forms. Its biology involves extracellular matrix disruption and tenocyte dysregulation, with altered collagen turnover and neovascularity driven by pathways centered on COL1A1/COL5A1, matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP3, cytokines including IL1B, IL6, and TNF, prostaglandin/COX-2 signaling, TGF-β, VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, and mechanotransduction pathways including NF-κB and MAPK. Genetic susceptibility is usually multifactorial rather than Mendelian, but variants in COL5A1, TNC, MMP3, and GDF5 have been associated with Achilles or other tendinopathies in some populations. Comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, obesity, hypercholesterolemia, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, chronic kidney disease, fluoroquinolone exposure, and corticosteroid use, while complications include tendon rupture, calcific change, and chronic pain-related disability. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on focal tendon pain reproducible with resisted movement or stretch and exclusion of tear or alternative causes; ultrasonography and MRI help identify tendon thickening, hypoechogenicity, partial tearing, or peritendinous fluid, and laboratory tests are reserved when infection, crystal disease, or inflammatory arthropathy is suspected. Common treatments include ibuprofen or naproxen, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit COX enzymes and reduce prostaglandin synthesis; diclofenac, another NSAID often used topically or orally; and corticosteroid injections such as triamcinolone, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory gene transcription, although repeated steroid exposure may weaken tendon tissue.

Name: Tenosynovitis
Description: Tenosynovitis (UMLS C0039520) is an inflammatory or fibroproliferative disorder of the synovial sheath surrounding a tendon, arising from repetitive mechanical overuse, autoimmune synovitis, crystalline or infectious causes, or stenosing entrapment such as trigger finger and de Quervain tenosynovitis. Molecularly, inflammatory forms are linked to cytokine- and matrix-remodeling networks rather than a single causative gene, with increased TNF, IL1B, IL6, COX-2/PTGS2, VEGFA, MMP1, MMP3, and MMP9, activation of NF-kB, JAK/STAT, MAPK, prostaglandin, and RANKL-mediated osteoclast pathways, and in rheumatoid disease associations with HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, PTPN22, and STAT4; tenosynovial giant cell tumor, a distinct proliferative subtype, is often driven by CSF1 overexpression from CSF1 rearrangements, recruiting CSF1R-positive macrophages. Clinical manifestations typically include localized pain, swelling, warmth, tenderness, crepitus, painful motion, triggering or locking, and impaired grip or function; infectious cases may show erythema, fusiform swelling, severe pain with passive stretch, and systemic features. Important comorbidities include rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout, diabetes mellitus, carpal tunnel syndrome, Dupuytren disease, and occupational overuse, while complications include tendon rupture, adhesions, chronic stiffness, nerve compression, and spread of infection. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by examination maneuvers such as Finkelstein testing for de Quervain disease, laboratory markers of inflammation or autoimmunity, urate analysis when indicated, microbiologic culture for suspected infection, and imaging with ultrasound showing sheath fluid or Doppler hyperemia, MRI for deep or proliferative disease, and radiographs to assess alternative pathology. Treatment commonly includes NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-mediated prostaglandin synthesis; corticosteroid injection or oral prednisone, which suppress NF-kB-driven inflammatory gene expression; and antibiotics for pyogenic disease, for example cefazolin or vancomycin targeting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, with surgery reserved for drainage or refractory stenosing disease.

Name: Tetanus
Description: Tetanus (MeSH D013742) is an acute, noncommunicable neurotoxic syndrome caused by infection of contaminated wounds, the umbilical stump, or devitalized tissue with Clostridium tetani, whose tetanospasmin protein (encoded by the plasmid-borne tetX gene in older nomenclature, more commonly TeNT) is the central virulence factor; unlike Mendelian disorders, tetanus has no established inheritance pattern, although host variation in immune-response genes such as HLA loci and immunoglobulin responsiveness may influence vaccine response rather than disease causation. The toxin binds peripheral nerve terminals via gangliosides and nidogen, undergoes retrograde axonal transport, and its zinc-dependent light-chain endopeptidase cleaves the synaptic vesicle SNARE protein VAMP/synaptobrevin, blocking release of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine from spinal interneurons, thereby disinhibiting motor and autonomic pathways. Clinically, generalized tetanus is most common and presents with trismus, risus sardonicus, neck and abdominal rigidity, painful stimulus-induced spasms, opisthotonus, dysphagia, and autonomic instability; localized, cephalic, and neonatal forms are recognized subtypes. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on compatible symptoms with incomplete immunization or a contaminated wound, because wound culture is insensitive and no routine laboratory test confirms disease; toxin detection, PCR for C. tetani genes, and electromyography may support atypical cases, while differential diagnosis includes strychnine poisoning, dystonic reactions, hypocalcemic tetany, meningitis, and seizures. Treatment combines human tetanus immune globulin, which neutralizes unbound toxin, metronidazole, which inhibits anaerobic bacterial DNA synthesis, and benzodiazepines such as diazepam or midazolam, which potentiate GABAA signaling to reduce spasm; penicillin, baclofen, magnesium sulfate, and neuromuscular blockers are also used when indicated. Major complications include laryngospasm, aspiration pneumonia, fractures, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure, pulmonary embolism, and dysautonomia, with important comorbid contexts including substance use, diabetes, chronic wounds, and inadequate vaccination.

Name: Tetany
Description: Tetany is a clinical syndrome of increased neuromuscular excitability rather than a single disease, most often caused by hypocalcemia, alkalosis, or hypomagnesemia, and characterized by perioral numbness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, muscle cramps, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, seizures, hyperreflexia, and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs; severe cases may produce arrhythmias and respiratory compromise. Major subtypes include hypocalcemic tetany, normocalcemic respiratory alkalosis–related tetany, hypomagnesemic tetany, and rare hereditary forms. Genetic contributors are best defined in disorders predisposing to electrolyte imbalance, including CASR gain-of-function variants causing autosomal dominant hypocalcemia, GNA11 and AP2S1 abnormalities affecting calcium-sensing receptor signaling, PTH mutations and GCM2 defects in familial hypoparathyroidism, and renal magnesium-handling genes such as TRPM6, CLDN16, and SLC12A3; these implicate the calcium-sensing receptor–parathyroid hormone–vitamin D axis, renal tubular calcium/magnesium transport, and membrane excitability pathways involving voltage-gated sodium channels. Common comorbidities and complications include hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, pancreatitis, malabsorption, diarrhea, alcoholism, postoperative thyroid/parathyroid injury, nephrocalcinosis, cataracts, basal ganglia calcifications, fractures, and prolonged QT. Treatment targets the underlying disturbance: intravenous calcium gluconate rapidly restores extracellular calcium to stabilize excitable membranes in acute tetany; oral calcium carbonate is used for maintenance replacement; calcitriol increases intestinal calcium absorption in hypoparathyroid states; magnesium sulfate corrects hypomagnesemia and reverses impaired PTH secretion/action; and ergocalciferol or cholecalciferol treat vitamin D deficiency. Diagnosis rests on compatible symptoms plus biochemical confirmation with ionized or total calcium corrected for albumin, magnesium, phosphate, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, renal function, and blood gas assessment for alkalosis, with ECG for QT prolongation, urinary calcium/magnesium studies, and targeted genetic testing when familial hypocalcemia, hypoparathyroidism, or inherited tubulopathies are suspected.

Name: Tetralogy of Fallot
Description: Tetralogy of Fallot is a conotruncal congenital cyanotic heart disease defined by the tetrad of ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction or pulmonary stenosis, and secondary right ventricular hypertrophy, with clinical expression ranging from classic cyanosis and hypoxic tet spells to murmur, clubbing, poor feeding, failure to thrive, dyspnea, squatting, and exercise intolerance. It arises from abnormal cardiac neural crest migration and outflow tract septation, and may occur as pulmonary atresia, absent pulmonary valve syndrome, or TOF with major aortopulmonary collateral arteries. Genetic contributors include 22q11.2 deletion involving TBX1, and variants in JAG1, NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, NOTCH1, FLT4, ZFPM2, and occasionally VEGF-related genes; inheritance is often sporadic but may be autosomal dominant with variable penetrance in syndromic or familial cases, including DiGeorge/velocardiofacial, Alagille, trisomy 21, and CHARGE associations. Relevant pathways include Notch-JAG1, TBX1/FGF8, NKX2-5/GATA transcriptional networks, VEGF-mediated vasculogenesis, and retinoic acid and cardiac neural crest developmental signaling. Common complications and comorbidities include arrhythmias, aortic root dilation, pulmonary regurgitation after repair, right heart failure, infective endocarditis, stroke or brain abscess from right-to-left shunting, and extracardiac anomalies such as thymic or parathyroid defects in 22q11.2 deletion. Diagnosis is based on echocardiographic demonstration of the four defining lesions, supported by pulse oximetry, ECG, chest radiography, fetal ultrasound, cardiac MRI/CT, and catheterization when anatomy or hemodynamics require clarification; genetic testing such as chromosomal microarray or targeted panels is recommended when syndromic features are present. Drug therapy is mainly supportive or perioperative, including propranolol to blunt infundibular spasm during tet spells via beta-adrenergic blockade, prostaglandin E1 to maintain ductal patency in duct-dependent neonates, phenylephrine to raise systemic vascular resistance and reduce right-to-left shunting, and diuretics such as furosemide for heart failure

Name: Thiamine Deficiency
Description: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1 deficiency; UMLS C0039841) is a nutritional and sometimes genetically influenced disorder that impairs carbohydrate metabolism and cellular energy production because thiamine pyrophosphate is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase; consequently, oxidative phosphorylation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, pentose phosphate pathway, mitochondrial ATP generation, and neural ion homeostasis are disrupted, with lactate accumulation and oxidative stress. Although most cases are acquired from alcoholism, malnutrition, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, dialysis, or prolonged diuretic use, genetic contributors include SLC19A2 and SLC19A3 mutations encoding thiamine transporters, TPK1 variants affecting thiamine pyrophosphokinase, and mitochondrial enzyme defects such as PDHA1-related pyruvate dehydrogenase dysfunction that can phenocopy or exacerbate deficiency states; inheritance is typically not Mendelian in acquired disease, but these transporter and metabolic defects are usually autosomal recessive, except PDHA1, which is X-linked. Clinical forms include dry beriberi with symmetric peripheral neuropathy, paresthesias, areflexia, and muscle wasting; wet beriberi with high-output heart failure, edema, and tachycardia; infantile beriberi; and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome characterized by confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, gait ataxia, and chronic amnesia. Common comorbidities and complications include alcohol use disorder, liver disease, malabsorption, heart failure, lactic acidosis, irreversible cognitive impairment, and death. Diagnosis is primarily clinical in at-risk patients, supported by low whole-blood thiamine diphosphate, reduced erythrocyte transketolase activity with stimulation by thiamine pyrophosphate, elevated lactate or pyruvate, and sometimes MRI showing typical Wernicke lesions; response to therapy is also diagnostically informative. Treatment centers on thiamine, usually parenteral initially, which replenishes intracellular thiamine pyrophosphate; benfotiamine, a lipid-soluble thiamine derivative, increases tissue delivery; and multivitamin or B-complex replacement, often with magnesium repletion because magnesium is required

Name: Thromboangiitis Obliterans
Description: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease; MeSH D013919) is a nonatherosclerotic, segmental inflammatory and thrombotic vasculopathy of small- and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities, seen predominantly in young to middle-aged tobacco users, in which highly tobacco-dependent immune-mediated endothelial injury leads to occlusive thrombosis with relative preservation of the internal elastic lamina. Its genetic contribution is complex and non-Mendelian, with susceptibility associations reported for HLA haplotypes such as HLA-B5, HLA-A9, HLA-B54, and polymorphisms in immune, endothelial, and coagulation-related genes including NOS3/eNOS, ICAM1, MMPs, CD14, and prothrombotic variants such as factor V Leiden in some cohorts, but no single causative mutation is established. Pathobiology implicates tobacco antigen hypersensitivity, T-cell and macrophage activation, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, platelet activation, cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, adhesion molecules, thromboxane signaling, and impaired nitric oxide and prostacyclin pathways, with sympathetic vasoconstriction further worsening ischemia. Patients typically present with distal ischemic pain, claudication of the feet, legs, hands, or forearms, Raynaud phenomenon, cold sensitivity, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis, ischemic ulcers, and digital gangrene; major complications include recurrent infection, osteomyelitis, critical limb ischemia, and amputation, while comorbidities include heavy cigarette or smokeless tobacco use and periodontal disease. Recognized phenotypes include distal extremity-predominant arterial disease with or without venous involvement. Diagnosis is clinical and angiographic, commonly based on Shionoya or Olin criteria: age usually under 45 to 50 years, current or recent tobacco exposure, distal infrapopliteal/infrabrachial ischemia, exclusion of diabetes, autoimmune disease, hypercoagulable states, and proximal embolic sources, and characteristic angiography showing segmental occlusions and corkscrew collaterals; testing includes ankle-brachial and digit pressures, duplex ultrasonography, catheter or CT/MR angiography, inflammatory and thrombophilia panels, and occasionally biopsy. Treatment centers on absolute tobacco cessation; adjunctive drugs include iloprost, a prostacyclin analog

Name: Thrombocytopenia
Description: Thrombocytopenia (MeSH D013921) is a heterogeneous disorder defined by a platelet count below 150 × 10^9/L due to decreased marrow production, increased peripheral destruction or consumption, splenic sequestration, or dilution, and it may be inherited or acquired. Clinically it presents with petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, easy bruising, and, in severe cases, gastrointestinal or intracranial hemorrhage. Major subtypes include immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), thrombotic microangiopathies such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, bone marrow failure or infiltrative thrombocytopenia, congenital thrombocytopenias, and consumptive states such as disseminated intravascular coagulation. Relevant genes and proteins include MPL, THPO, and JAK2 in thrombopoietin signaling; GP1BA, GP1BB, and GP9 in Bernard-Soulier syndrome; MYH9 in MYH9-related disease; WAS in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome; ANKRD26, ETV6, and RUNX1 in inherited thrombocytopenia with hematologic malignancy predisposition; and ADAMTS13 deficiency or autoantibodies in TTP. Key pathways involve thrombopoietin-MPL-JAK2-STAT signaling controlling megakaryopoiesis, Fcγ receptor-mediated splenic macrophage clearance and B-cell/T-cell immune dysregulation in ITP, platelet activation and von Willebrand factor-rich microthrombi in TTP, and thrombin-driven coagulation cascade activation in DIC. Treatments depend on cause and include corticosteroids, which suppress autoantibody production and reticuloendothelial platelet destruction; intravenous immunoglobulin, which blocks Fc receptor-mediated clearance; thrombopoietin receptor agonists such as romiplostim or eltrombopag, which stimulate megakaryocyte proliferation; rituximab, which depletes CD20-positive B cells; and caplacizumab in acquired TTP, which inhibits von Willebrand factor–platelet interaction. Important comorbidities and complications include autoimmune disease, viral infections, liver disease, pregnancy, malignancy, anemia, thrombosis paradoxically in HIT or TTP, and life-threatening bleeding. Diagnosis relies on CBC with smear, medication and infection

Name: Thromboembolism
Description: Thromboembolism is a vascular disorder in which a thrombus forms in the venous or arterial circulation and embolizes to obstruct downstream vessels, classically presenting as venous thromboembolism with deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, but also including arterial thromboembolism causing stroke, limb ischemia, or mesenteric ischemia. Its biology reflects Virchow triad and dysregulated coagulation, platelet activation, and fibrinolysis, with key pathways involving tissue factor–factor VIIa initiation, thrombin generation through factors II, V, VIII, IX, X, and XI, fibrin formation from fibrinogen, platelet P2Y12 and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa signaling, and impaired protein C/protein S/antithrombin anticoagulant and plasmin-mediated fibrinolytic systems. Genetic susceptibility is well established, especially for venous disease, with representative inherited thrombophilias including F5 Factor V Leiden, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1 antithrombin deficiency, PROC protein C deficiency, PROS1 protein S deficiency, and less commonly elevated factor VIII, dysfibrinogenemia, or variants affecting ABO and fibrinolytic genes; these are usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance. Common symptoms include unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema in DVT, and dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, cough, hemoptysis, syncope, or hypoxemia in pulmonary embolism. Major comorbidities and risk states include cancer, surgery, trauma, immobility, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, obesity, antiphospholipid syndrome, heart failure, and myeloproliferative neoplasms, while complications include recurrent embolism, post-thrombotic syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, right-heart strain, and sudden death. Diagnosis integrates clinical probability scores such as Wells, D-dimer testing, compression ultrasonography for DVT, CT pulmonary angiography or ventilation-perfusion scanning for PE, and selected thrombophilia testing. Standard treatment includes heparins that potentiate antithrombin, warfarin that inhibits vitamin K–dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X, and direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban or rivaroxaban that inhibit factor Xa

Name: Thrombosis
Description: Thrombosis (MeSH D013927) is the pathologic formation of an intravascular blood clot within arteries, veins, or the microcirculation, driven by Virchow’s triad of endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability. Major molecular determinants include platelet adhesion/activation pathways involving von Willebrand factor, glycoprotein Ib/IIbIIIa, thromboxane A2, ADP-P2Y12, and thrombin-PAR signaling, together with the coagulation cascade centered on tissue factor, factors II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI, fibrinogen, and natural anticoagulants protein C, protein S, and antithrombin. Well-established genetic contributors include Factor V Leiden (F5 p.Arg506Gln) causing activated protein C resistance, the prothrombin F2 G20210A variant, SERPINC1, PROC, and PROS1 deficiencies, and less commonly elevated homocysteine linked to MTHFR variants; thrombosis is usually multifactorial, although inherited thrombophilia often follows autosomal dominant transmission with variable penetrance. Clinical forms include venous thromboembolism such as deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, arterial thrombosis causing myocardial infarction or ischemic stroke, and microvascular thrombosis as seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation or antiphospholipid syndrome. Typical manifestations include limb swelling, pain, erythema, warmth, venous cord, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, hypoxemia, or acute ischemic neurologic/cardiac deficits, while complications include post-thrombotic syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, embolization, recurrent thrombosis, organ infarction, and death. Common comorbid associations include cancer, surgery, trauma, immobility, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, obesity, smoking, myeloproliferative neoplasms including JAK2-mutant disease, nephrotic syndrome, heart failure, and autoimmune disorders. Diagnosis relies on clinical probability assessment, D-dimer testing, duplex ultrasonography, CT pulmonary angiography, MR or conventional angiography when indicated, and selected thrombophilia testing. Treatment commonly includes unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin via antithrombin-mediated inhibition of factor Xa and thrombin, warfarin through vitamin K antagonism

Name: Thyroid Crisis
Description: Thyroid crisis, or thyroid storm, is a rare, life-threatening endocrine emergency representing the extreme decompensated form of thyrotoxicosis, most often arising in Graves disease but also toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis, or iodine- or amiodarone-related hyperthyroidism; it is not itself a Mendelian disorder, yet genetic susceptibility reflects the underlying hyperthyroid state, with Graves disease linked to HLA-DR3, CTLA4, PTPN22, TSHR, and thyroglobulin loci, and activating TSHR or GNAS mutations occurring in autonomous nodules. Its pathobiology centers on excess T3 and T4 signaling through thyroid hormone receptors TRalpha and TRbeta, amplified beta-adrenergic activity, increased cAMP signaling, mitochondrial oxygen consumption, thermogenesis, and systemic cytokine stress responses, often precipitated by infection, surgery, trauma, myocardial infarction, diabetic ketoacidosis, or parturition. Patients typically present with high fever, marked tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, heart failure, agitation, delirium, tremor, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, and may progress to jaundice, shock, seizures, or coma. Major complications include arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, hepatic injury, respiratory failure, thromboembolism, and death, with frequent comorbid autoimmune disease and cardiovascular disease. Diagnosis is clinical, commonly supported by severe biochemical thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH and elevated free T4 and/or T3, plus precipitation assessment and scoring systems such as Burch-Wartofsky or Japanese Thyroid Association criteria; testing also includes ECG, electrolytes, liver function, CBC, cultures, and imaging as indicated to identify triggers. Treatment combines propylthiouracil, which inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, or methimazole, which inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis, followed by iodine solutions that acutely block hormone release, beta-blockers such as propranolol or esmolol to blunt adrenergic effects and reduce T4-to-T3 conversion, and glucocorticoids such as hydrocortisone or dexamethasone to treat relative adrenal insufficiency and decrease peripheral conversion.

Name: Thyroiditis
Description: Thyroiditis (UMLS C0040147) comprises a heterogeneous group of inflammatory thyroid disorders, most commonly chronic autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis, subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, painless/silent and postpartum thyroiditis, acute suppurative thyroiditis, and drug- or radiation-induced forms, characterized clinically by transient or permanent thyrotoxicosis, euthyroidism, or hypothyroidism depending on stage and subtype. Autoimmune thyroiditis has the clearest genetic basis, with susceptibility linked to HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, HLA-DR5, CTLA4, PTPN22, TG, TSHR, FOXP3, IL2RA, and immune-regulatory variants; proteins central to pathogenesis include thyroid peroxidase, thyroglobulin, and the TSH receptor, with anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies as representative biomarkers, while postpartum thyroiditis shares autoimmune predisposition. Key pathways involve loss of self-tolerance, antigen presentation through HLA class II, T-cell and B-cell activation, cytokine signaling including IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, IL-6, and apoptosis of thyrocytes via Fas/FasL and related inflammatory cascades; subacute thyroiditis is often post-viral, with macrophage and giant-cell–mediated injury. Typical features include painless or tender goiter, anterior neck pain radiating to the jaw in subacute disease, fatigue, weight change, palpitations, tremor, heat or cold intolerance, constipation, menstrual irregularity, and later hypothyroid symptoms. Important comorbidities include type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, pernicious anemia, Addison disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus, with complications such as permanent hypothyroidism, transient atrial arrhythmias, and rarely thyroid abscess in suppurative disease. Diagnosis relies on TSH and free T4/free T3 patterns, anti-TPO/anti-Tg antibodies, ESR/CRP elevation in subacute disease, thyroid ultrasonography showing heterogeneous hypoechogenicity, low radioactive iodine uptake in destructive thyroiditis, and fine-needle aspiration or culture when abscess or malignancy is suspected. Treatment is etiology-specific: levothyroxine replaces deficient hormone via thyroid hormone receptor activation, propranolol ameliorates adrenergic symptoms through beta-adrenergic blockade,

Name: Tinea Capitis
Description: Tinea capitis is a contagious dermatophyte infection of the scalp hair shafts and follicles, seen predominantly in prepubertal children, most often caused by Trichophyton tonsurans, Microsporum canis, and related species, and classically divided into noninflammatory gray-patch and black-dot forms, inflammatory kerion, and favus. The disease is not a Mendelian disorder, but host susceptibility is influenced by immune genes and proteins involved in cutaneous antifungal defense, including pattern-recognition and cytokine pathways such as Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, toll-like receptors, IL-17/IL-22, TNF-α, and antimicrobial peptides; rare CARD9 deficiency and other primary immunodeficiencies can predispose to severe, recurrent, or invasive dermatophytosis. Pathobiologically, fungal adherence to keratinized tissue, secretion of keratinases and other proteases, and host innate and Th17-mediated inflammatory signaling are central. Typical findings are patchy alopecia with scale, broken hairs, black dots, pruritus, erythema, posterior cervical or occipital lymphadenopathy, and in kerion, painful boggy plaques with pustules; complications include scarring alopecia, bacterial superinfection, abscess formation, id reactions, and psychosocial distress, while comorbid associations include atopic dermatitis, household dermatophytosis, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis is based on characteristic examination plus confirmation by potassium hydroxide microscopy, fungal culture, trichoscopy showing comma or corkscrew hairs, Wood lamp fluorescence in some Microsporum infections, and occasionally PCR or histopathology. Treatment requires systemic antifungals: griseofulvin, which disrupts fungal mitotic microtubules and concentrates in keratin; terbinafine, a squalene epoxidase inhibitor that blocks ergosterol synthesis; itraconazole and fluconazole, azoles that inhibit fungal CYP51/14-α-demethylase; adjunctive selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo reduces spore shedding and transmission.

Name: Tinea Corporis
Description: Tinea (MeSH D014005) is a superficial dermatophyte infection of keratinized tissues caused mainly by Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton species, producing ringworm syndromes classified by site as tinea corporis, capitis, pedis, cruris, barbae, manuum, faciei, and unguium/onychomycosis. Disease expression reflects fungal keratin degradation and host defense rather than a simple Mendelian disorder; fungal virulence factors include secreted keratinases/subtilisins and metalloproteases, while host susceptibility has been linked to impaired epidermal barrier and innate/adaptive immunity, with representative genetic associations involving CARD9 deficiency causing severe or invasive dermatophytosis, and variants affecting DECTIN-1/CLEC7A, TLR2, IL-17/Th17 signaling, and antimicrobial peptide responses. Key pathways include pattern-recognition receptor activation by fungal cell-wall β-glucans and mannans, downstream SYK-CARD9-NF-κB signaling, Th17/IL-17 and IL-22-mediated neutrophil recruitment, and local inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. Clinically, tinea presents with pruritic, erythematous, annular scaly plaques with central clearing, interdigital maceration, plantar hyperkeratosis, scalp scaling with alopecia or black dots, or dystrophic thickened nails; diagnosis is based on compatible morphology plus potassium hydroxide microscopy of skin scrapings, hair, or nail material, fungal culture, histopathology with PAS/GMS stains, dermoscopy, and increasingly PCR-based identification. Common treatments include terbinafine, which inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase; azoles such as clotrimazole, miconazole, itraconazole, or fluconazole, which inhibit lanosterol 14-α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; and griseofulvin, which disrupts fungal microtubules and mitosis. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes, obesity, occlusive footwear, hyperhidrosis, atopic skin disease, immunosuppression including HIV or corticosteroid use, and household animal exposure; complications include bacterial superinfection, Majocchi granuloma, chronic/recurrent infection, scarring alopecia in inflammatory tinea capitis, and spread

Name: Tinea Pedis
Description: Tinea pedis (MeSH D014008) is a common superficial dermatophyte infection of the plantar and interdigital skin, caused predominantly by Trichophyton rubrum, T. interdigitale/mentagrophytes, and less often Epidermophyton floccosum, in which fungal keratinases, subtilisins, metalloproteases, and cell-wall components such as β-glucan and mannans interact with host innate and adaptive immunity. Host susceptibility has genetic components rather than a simple Mendelian pattern, with representative associations involving impaired epidermal barrier or antifungal immune pathways, including CARD9 deficiency, Dectin-1/CLEC7A signaling, TLR2/TLR4, IL-17/Th17 axis genes, and occasional contributions from filaggrin-related barrier dysfunction; familial clustering is recognized, especially in chronic or recurrent disease. Pathobiologically, fungal pathogen-associated molecular patterns activate keratinocyte and myeloid-cell pattern-recognition receptors, triggering NF-κB, MAPK, and IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, and TNF-mediated inflammatory pathways, while chronic infection may reflect ineffective cell-mediated immunity. Clinical subtypes include interdigital, hyperkeratotic/moccasin, vesiculobullous, and ulcerative tinea pedis, presenting with pruritus, scaling, erythema, maceration, fissuring, malodor, plantar hyperkeratosis, or vesicles/bullae. Major comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, obesity, hyperhidrosis, immunosuppression, onychomycosis, recurrent cellulitis/erysipelas, secondary bacterial infection, and spread to tinea manuum, cruris, or corporis. Diagnosis is usually clinical but is supported by potassium hydroxide microscopy of skin scrapings showing septate branching hyphae, fungal culture, periodic acid-Schiff histopathology when needed, and increasingly PCR-based assays; differential diagnosis includes eczema, psoriasis, and candidiasis. Treatment relies on topical or systemic antifungals such as terbinafine, which inhibits squalene epoxidase; azoles including clotrimazole or miconazole, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51) and impair ergosterol synthesis; and systemic itraconazole or fluconazole with the same azole mechanism,

Name: Onychomycosis
Description: Onychomycosis (MeSH D014009) is a chronic fungal infection of the nail unit, most often caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum and T. interdigitale, but also by Candida and non-dermatophyte molds, and it presents clinically with nail discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, thickening, brittleness, friability, and sometimes pain, impaired ambulation, or secondary bacterial infection. Major subtypes include distal lateral subungual, superficial white, proximal subungual, endonyx, and total dystrophic onychomycosis. Disease biology centers on fungal adhesion and keratin invasion, including secreted subtilisin-like proteases and fungal keratinases, ergosterol biosynthesis enzymes such as squalene epoxidase and lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, and host innate immune pathways involving pattern-recognition receptors including Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2 and TLR4, CARD9-dependent signaling, Th17/IL-17 and IL-22 responses, and defensins; genetic susceptibility has been linked to variants affecting antifungal immunity, including CARD9 deficiency and polymorphisms in DEFB4, CLEC7A, and HLA loci, although inheritance is usually multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with occasional familial clustering. Important comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, psoriasis, obesity, HIV/immunosuppression, advancing age, and tinea pedis; complications include cellulitis, diabetic foot ulcer risk, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis requires compatible nail changes plus mycologic confirmation by potassium hydroxide microscopy, fungal culture, histopathology of nail clippings with PAS stain, or PCR-based assays. Common treatments include terbinafine, which inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase; itraconazole and fluconazole, azoles that inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; and topical efinaconazole, tavaborole, or ciclopirox, which impair membrane synthesis or, for tavaborole, inhibit leucyl-tRNA synthetase. Resistance can involve SQLE mutations in dermatophytes, especially with terbinafine exposure.

Name: Tinea Versicolor
Description: Tinea versicolor (pityriasis versicolor; MeSH D014010) is a common, superficial, recurrent Malassezia-associated mycosis of the stratum corneum in which lipophilic yeasts, most often Malassezia globosa, M. furfur, and M. sympodialis, convert from commensal yeast to pathogenic hyphal forms, producing finely scaling hypo-, hyper-, or erythematous macules and patches, classically on the trunk, neck, and proximal arms, with mild pruritus or no symptoms. Disease expression reflects fungal lipase and phospholipase activity, indole metabolites and azelaic acid that alter melanocyte function, and host innate immune pathways involving keratinocytes, antimicrobial peptides, pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR2, and Th1/Th17-related cytokine signaling; no single causative human mutation or Mendelian inheritance pattern is established, but familial clustering and host susceptibility have been linked to polygenic influences on skin barrier, sebaceous activity, sweating, and immune response, while Malassezia allergens/proteins such as Mala s 1 may be immunologically relevant. Predisposing factors and comorbidities include hot humid climates, hyperhidrosis, oily skin, adolescence, pregnancy, malnutrition, corticosteroid exposure, diabetes mellitus, Cushing syndrome, and immunosuppression; complications are mainly cosmetic dyspigmentation and frequent relapse. Clinical subtypes are based on pigmentary pattern and distribution, including hypopigmented, hyperpigmented, and inverse forms, and diagnosis is usually clinical but is supported by Wood lamp yellow-gold or coppery fluorescence, potassium hydroxide microscopy showing short hyphae with clustered spores in a spaghetti and meatballs pattern, and, when needed, histopathology with PAS stain or dermoscopy. Standard therapy includes selenium sulfide, which is cytostatic to epidermis and toxic to fungal cells; ketoconazole, clotrimazole, or other azoles, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; terbinafine, which inhibits squalene epoxidase; and for extensive or refractory disease, oral itraconazole or fluconazole, which also impair ergosterol biosynthesis.

Name: Tonsillitis
Description: Tonsillitis (MeSH D014069) is an acute or recurrent inflammatory disorder of the palatine tonsils, most often infectious and usually caused by respiratory viruses or by Group A Streptococcus, with less common bacterial causes including Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and anaerobes; clinically it presents with sore throat, odynophagia, fever, tonsillar erythema and enlargement, purulent exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, halitosis, muffled voice, and sometimes airway obstruction. Disease forms include acute, recurrent, and chronic tonsillitis, and severe variants may overlap with peritonsillar cellulitis or abscess. Pathobiology centers on innate and adaptive mucosal immune activation, including Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB and MAPK pathways, inflammasome-related cytokine release, and Th1/Th17 responses, with key mediators such as IL1B, IL6, TNF, IFNG, CXCL8, CRP, and antimicrobial proteins in tonsillar epithelium and lymphoid tissue; host susceptibility is incompletely defined but immune-response polymorphisms in genes such as HLA class II, TLR4, IL1B, IL6, TNF, and MBL2 have been reported as representative associations rather than deterministic causes, and there is no simple Mendelian inheritance pattern, though familial clustering of recurrent tonsillitis suggests polygenic predisposition. Important comorbidities and complications include otitis media, sinusitis, obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, dehydration, cervical adenitis, rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in streptococcal infection, and peritonsillar or deep neck space abscess. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by Centor or McIsaac criteria, throat culture or rapid streptococcal antigen testing, and selective NAATs, CBC, EBV testing, or imaging when alternative diagnoses or abscess are suspected. Treatment is mainly supportive, while confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial disease is commonly treated with penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking, or macrolides such as azithromycin, which inhibit the 50S ribosomal subunit; ibuprofen or acetaminophen are used for analgesia and antipyresis via cyclooxygenase inhibition

Name: Toothache
Description: Toothache, or odontalgia, is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease, most commonly arising from dental caries with pulpal inflammation, apical periodontitis, dentin hypersensitivity, cracked tooth, or periodontal disease, and less often from pericoronitis, sinusitis, temporomandibular disorders, or neuropathic pain. Its biology is dominated by bacterial biofilm-driven inflammation and nociception, with key organisms including Streptococcus mutans and lactobacilli, and molecular mediators involving TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, COX-2, prostaglandin E2, bradykinin, TNF, IL1B, IL6, TRPV1, TRPA1, ASICs, voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN9A/NaV1.7, and neuropeptides including substance P and CGRP. Genetic contribution is usually polygenic and indirect, influencing susceptibility to caries, pain sensitivity, enamel defects, or dentin disorders; representative genes include AMELX, ENAM, MMP20, KLK4, DSPP, WNT10A, and SCN9A, while Mendelian conditions such as amelogenesis imperfecta and dentinogenesis imperfecta can predispose to severe tooth pain, with X-linked, autosomal dominant, or autosomal recessive inheritance depending on the gene. Typical features are spontaneous or stimulus-evoked sharp, throbbing, or lingering pain, thermal sensitivity, pain on biting, nocturnal worsening, localized swelling, percussion tenderness, and occasionally fever, trismus, or draining sinus when infection spreads. Important comorbidities and complications include dental abscess, cellulitis, osteomyelitis, maxillary sinusitis, malnutrition, sleep disturbance, and, rarely, deep neck space infection or sepsis. Diagnosis relies on history, oral examination, pulp vitality testing with cold, heat, or electric methods, percussion and bite tests, periodontal probing, and dental radiographs, with cone-beam CT reserved for selected cases. Treatment targets the cause and pain: ibuprofen inhibits COX-1/COX-2, acetaminophen acts centrally to reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain, lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels for local anesthesia, and when bacterial spread is evident, amoxicillin or metronidazole suppress susceptible oral anaerobes.

Name: Tourette Syndrome
Description: Tourette syndrome is a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental tic disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one phonic tic persisting for more than 1 year, usually beginning between ages 4 and 8, with waxing and waning severity, premonitory urges, suppressibility, and symptoms such as eye blinking, facial grimacing, shoulder shrugging, throat clearing, sniffing, grunting, echolalia, or coprolalia in a minority. It is clinically heterogeneous, ranging from simple to complex tic phenotypes and often considered within a spectrum that includes provisional tic disorder and persistent motor or vocal tic disorder. The disorder is highly heritable with a complex, predominantly polygenic architecture and occasional rare high-impact variants; implicated genes include SLITRK1, HDC, CNTNAP2, NRXN1, FLT3, and genes affected by copy-number variation such as 16p13.11 and 22q11.2, with generally multifactorial rather than Mendelian inheritance, though autosomal dominant transmission with reduced penetrance has been reported in some families. Pathobiology centers on cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit dysfunction involving dopaminergic hyperinnervation or supersensitivity, GABAergic interneuron deficits, glutamatergic and serotonergic modulation, histaminergic signaling, synaptic adhesion and neurodevelopmental pathways, and immune-related mechanisms. Common comorbidities include ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, depression, autism spectrum traits, sleep disturbance, rage attacks, and self-injurious behavior; complications include social impairment, educational difficulty, pain, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 criteria after excluding secondary tic causes by history, neurologic examination, and selective testing such as brain MRI, EEG, thyroid studies, Wilson disease testing, or genetic evaluation when atypical features are present. Treatment is symptomatic: behavioral therapy, especially CBIT, is first-line, while drugs include aripiprazole and risperidone, dopamine D2 receptor antagonists/partial agonists that reduce tic expression, haloperidol, a potent D2 antagonist, and alpha-2 adrenergic agonists such as clonidine or guanfacine, which reduce noradrenergic tone and are particularly useful with comorbid ADHD; tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine, VMAT2 inhibitors, may also be used.

Name: Toxocariasis
Description: Toxocariasis (MeSH D014120) is a zoonotic helminthic infection caused primarily by the dog and cat roundworms Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati; humans are accidental dead-end hosts in whom migrating larvae produce visceral larva migrans, ocular toxocariasis, covert/common toxocariasis, and less often neurotoxocariasis. Disease is not inherited, but host genetic susceptibility to Th2-skewed inflammation and eosinophilia has been linked in candidate studies to variants in cytokine and immune-response genes such as IL4, IL5, IL10, IFNG, HLA class II loci, and eosinophil-associated pathways, although no single causative mutation is established. Pathobiology is dominated by larval tissue migration and granulomatous inflammation driven by Th2/IgE signaling, with activation of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, STAT6, eosinophils, mast cells, macrophages, and chemokines such as eotaxin/CCR3; antibody responses to parasite excretory-secretory antigens are central. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic infection to fever, wheeze or asthma-like cough, abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, urticaria, marked eosinophilia, and hyper-IgE, while ocular disease may cause unilateral visual loss, retinal granuloma, endophthalmitis, or strabismus, and CNS involvement may lead to seizures or focal deficits. Important complications include chronic visual impairment, eosinophilic pneumonia, myocarditis, encephalitis, and overlap with allergic disease. Diagnosis relies on exposure history, eosinophilia, elevated total IgE, compatible organ findings, and serology, especially TES-ELISA with confirmatory Western blot; ophthalmic examination and retinal imaging support ocular cases, and ultrasound, CT, or MRI may show hepatic, pulmonary, or CNS lesions, whereas stool studies are not useful in humans. Treatment commonly includes albendazole, a benzimidazole that inhibits parasite β-tubulin and microtubule assembly, mebendazole with a similar mechanism, and thiabendazole, less often used, plus corticosteroids such as prednisone to suppress damaging ocular, neurologic, or severe inflammatory responses.

Name: Toxoplasmosis
Description: Toxoplasmosis (MeSH D014123) is a protozoal infection caused by Toxoplasma gondii, acquired congenitally or after ingestion of tissue cysts or oocysts, and presenting as acute acquired, congenital, ocular, cerebral, or disseminated disease, with severity determined largely by host cellular immunity rather than Mendelian inheritance. Key host genetic associations involve immune response genes such as HLA loci, IFNG, IL12B, IL12RB1, TNF, TLR2, TLR4, TLR9, NOD2, and P2RX7, while rare primary immunodeficiencies affecting the IL-12/IFN-γ axis can predispose to severe infection; parasite virulence is influenced by secreted rhoptry and dense granule proteins including ROP18, ROP16, GRA15, and SAG1. Pathobiology centers on dendritic cells and macrophages recognizing the parasite through Toll-like receptor and inflammasome pathways, driving IL-12 production, NK- and T-cell IFN-γ responses, STAT1 signaling, nitric oxide-mediated intracellular killing, and chronic bradyzoite cyst persistence in brain, retina, and muscle. Typical manifestations include asymptomatic seroconversion, fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, and in severe cases chorioretinitis, encephalitis, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, headache, and pneumonitis; congenital infection may cause miscarriage, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, developmental delay, and hearing or visual loss. Important comorbid contexts include HIV/AIDS, hematologic malignancy, transplantation, pregnancy, and immunosuppressive therapy, with complications such as blindness, recurrent ocular inflammation, and life-threatening CNS disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical context plus serology with Toxoplasma IgG, IgM, avidity testing, PCR of blood, CSF, amniotic fluid, or ocular fluid, neuroimaging for ring-enhancing brain lesions, ophthalmologic examination, and occasionally histopathology. Standard therapy includes pyrimethamine, a parasitic dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor, with sulfadiazine, a dihydropteroate synthase inhibitor, plus leucovorin rescue; alternatives include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin, atovaquone, or spiramy

Name: Toxoplasmosis, Congenital
Description: Congenital toxoplasmosis is a vertically acquired protozoal infection caused by transplacental transmission of Toxoplasma gondii during maternal primary infection, with severity generally greatest after early gestational infection and transmission risk highest later in pregnancy; recognized phenotypic forms include subclinical infection at birth, neonatal disseminated disease, and predominantly ocular or neurologic disease. Disease pathobiology reflects intracellular tachyzoite invasion and persistence of bradyzoite cysts, with host control driven by IL-12/IFN-γ, TNF, JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and Toll-like receptor signaling, and susceptibility influenced by immune genes such as IFNG, IL12B, TLR2, TLR4, HLA loci, and in some populations the purinergic receptor P2RX7, while parasite virulence correlates with strain effectors including ROP18, ROP5, and GRA15. Typical manifestations include the classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications, along with seizures, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, rash, lymphadenopathy, anemia, thrombocytopenia, developmental delay, and later visual or hearing impairment. Major complications include recurrent ocular toxoplasmosis, epilepsy, cognitive impairment, endocrine or growth sequelae from CNS injury, and coincident severe disease in immunocompromised hosts. The condition is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion, but host genetic variation may modify susceptibility and severity; rare inborn errors affecting IFN-γ/IL-12 axis immunity can predispose to severe toxoplasmosis. Diagnosis relies on maternal serology showing seroconversion or low-avidity IgG with IgM/IgA, fetal detection by PCR of amniotic fluid, and neonatal confirmation by Toxoplasma-specific IgM or IgA, persistent or rising IgG beyond infancy, plus cranial ultrasound or CT/MRI and ophthalmologic examination. Treatment commonly uses spiramycin to reduce transplacental spread in maternal infection before fetal infection is proven, and pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with folinic acid after confirmed fetal or neonatal infection; pyrimethamine inhibits parasitic dihydrofolate reductase, sulfadiazine inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, folinic acid limits marrow toxicity, and trimethoprim-sulfamethox

Name: Trachoma
Description: Trachoma is a chronic infectious keratoconjunctivitis caused by repeated ocular infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, classically serovars A, B, Ba, and C, and remains a leading preventable cause of blindness. Its pathobiology reflects epithelial infection and a host inflammatory-fibrotic response rather than Mendelian inheritance; no single causal germline mutation is established, although susceptibility has been linked to immune-response genes and proteins such as HLA class I/II alleles, TNF, IFNG, IL10, MMP9, and TLR4, with chlamydial antigens including major outer membrane protein and host mediators such as TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IFN-γ, CXCL8, matrix metalloproteinases, fibroblasts, and conjunctival epithelial cells participating in NF-κB, Toll-like receptor, JAK-STAT, and pro-fibrotic TGF-β signaling pathways that drive scarring. Clinically, active trachoma causes recurrent follicular conjunctivitis, papillary hypertrophy, conjunctival hyperemia, mucopurulent discharge, irritation, tearing, photophobia, and superior corneal pannus; chronic cicatricial disease leads to conjunctival scarring, entropion, trichiasis, corneal abrasion, ulceration, opacity, and visual loss. Disease forms include active inflammatory trachoma, cicatricial trachoma, trachomatous trichiasis, and corneal opacity, aligned with the WHO simplified grading scheme of TF, TI, TS, TT, and CO. Diagnosis is primarily clinical by eyelid eversion and grading in endemic settings, supported when needed by nucleic acid amplification testing or PCR for C. trachomatis, direct fluorescent antibody tests, antigen assays, cytology, and visual/corneal examination. Treatment centers on the SAFE strategy; commonly used drugs include azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis, tetracycline ophthalmic ointment, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, and erythromycin, another 50S inhibitor, while doxycycline may be used in selected cases. Important complications and linked conditions include secondary bacterial superinfection, dry eye, blepharitis, corneal scarring, blindness, and coexistence with poor sanitation, crowded living conditions, and recurrent

Name: Trichinellosis
Description: Trichinellosis (MeSH D014235) is a food-borne zoonotic helminthiasis caused by nematodes of the genus Trichinella, classically T. spiralis but also T. britovi, T. nativa, T. pseudospiralis, and related species, acquired by ingestion of raw or undercooked pork or wild game containing encysted larvae; it is an infectious, non-Mendelian disease with no recognized host inheritance pattern, although host genetic factors likely influence severity, with representative immune-response genes and proteins implicated in pathobiology including HLA variants, IL4, IL5, IL10, IFNG, TNF, NOS2, eosinophil cationic protein, IgE, and creatine kinase as a muscle-injury biomarker rather than a causal gene. Disease evolution reflects enteric invasion followed by larval dissemination to striated muscle, driven by Th2-polarized immune signaling pathways involving IL-4/IL-13–STAT6, IL-5–eosinophil activation, mast cells, alternatively activated macrophages, NF-kB-mediated inflammation, and chemokines promoting myositis. Clinical manifestations range from intestinal diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting to systemic fever, marked eosinophilia, myalgia, periorbital edema, conjunctival hemorrhage, weakness, and elevated muscle enzymes; severe complications include myocarditis, arrhythmias, heart failure, encephalitis, meningitis, pneumonitis, rhabdomyolysis, and rarely death. Intestinal, migratory, and muscular phases are recognized clinically, with severity varying by infecting species and larval burden. Diagnosis is based on exposure history plus eosinophilia, elevated CK/LDH, serology such as ELISA or immunoblot for anti-Trichinella antibodies, and confirmatory muscle biopsy showing encysted larvae when needed; PCR can identify species in tissue or food sources. Treatment relies on benzimidazoles, especially albendazole and mebendazole, which bind parasite beta-tubulin and inhibit microtubule-dependent glucose uptake, and thiabendazole historically with the same class mechanism; corticosteroids such as prednisone are added to suppress inflammatory reactions in severe myositis, neurologic disease, or cardiac involvement.

Name: Trichomonas Infections
Description: Trichomonas infection, classically trichomoniasis caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, is a sexually transmitted, non-Mendelian infectious disease of the urogenital tract rather than an inherited genetic disorder, although host susceptibility is influenced by immune and inflammatory genes; representative host factors include polymorphic variation in TLR2, TLR4, IL8, TNF, and HLA loci, while parasite virulence determinants include adhesins AP65, AP51, AP33 and AP23, cysteine proteinases, lipophosphoglycan, and variable surface immunogens. Pathobiology centers on epithelial adherence, cytotoxicity, neutrophilic inflammation, and signaling through TLR/NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome, and cytokine networks involving IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha, with disruption of the vaginal microbiome and synergy with HIV acquisition and shedding. Typical manifestations are asymptomatic infection or vaginitis with malodorous frothy yellow-green discharge, vulvovaginal irritation, dysuria, dyspareunia, pruritus, vaginal pH elevation, and strawberry cervix; men may have asymptomatic urethritis, dysuria, epididymitis, or prostatitis. Major clinical forms include female urogenital infection, male urethral/prostatic infection, and persistent or recurrent disease, sometimes linked to nitroimidazole resistance. Standard therapy includes metronidazole and tinidazole, both nitroimidazoles activated in anaerobic protozoa to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and other macromolecules, and secnidazole, a longer-acting 5-nitroimidazole with the same core mechanism; topical agents are generally ineffective. Important comorbidities and complications include bacterial vaginosis, other sexually transmitted infections, pelvic inflammatory disease, adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm birth and low birth weight, infertility associations, and increased cervical neoplasia risk. Diagnosis is established by nucleic acid amplification testing as the most sensitive method, with wet mount microscopy, culture, rapid antigen tests, and point-of-care molecular assays as alternatives; diagnosis is supported by compatible symptoms, elevated vaginal pH, and identification of motile trichomonads or organism-specific nucleic acid, with partner evaluation and retesting in recurrent cases.

Name: Trichuriasis
Description: Trichuriasis (MeSH D014257) is a soil-transmitted helminthiasis caused predominantly by the colonic nematode Trichuris trichiura, with disease severity ranging from asymptomatic light infection to heavy-burden inflammatory colitis and the classic Trichuris dysentery syndrome. Human genetic susceptibility is incompletely defined and there is no Mendelian inheritance pattern, but host immune-response genes and proteins influence burden and pathology, with representative associations involving IL4, IL5, IL13, IFNG, TNF, FOXP3, HLA class II loci, eosinophil granule proteins, mucins such as MUC2, and epithelial alarmin pathways including IL-25, IL-33, and TSLP; these converge on Th2-polarized signaling through JAK-STAT, especially STAT6, goblet-cell hyperplasia, IgE production, eosinophilia, and barrier remodeling, while chronic infection may also engage regulatory T-cell and NF-kB-mediated inflammatory pathways. Typical symptoms include abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, mucus or blood in stool, tenesmus, anorexia, growth retardation, iron-deficiency anemia, and in children rectal prolapse; major complications include severe colitis, malnutrition, cognitive impairment, and coinfection-related morbidity with other soil-transmitted helminths. Clinical subtypes are usually defined by intensity and manifestations, including uncomplicated intestinal infection and severe Trichuris dysentery syndrome. Diagnosis rests on stool ova-and-parasite microscopy demonstrating characteristic barrel- or lemon-shaped eggs with bipolar plugs, ideally with concentration or Kato-Katz quantification; colonoscopy may reveal embedded worms, and CBC may show eosinophilia or anemia. Standard therapy includes mebendazole, which inhibits parasite beta-tubulin polymerization and microtubule-dependent glucose uptake; albendazole, a related benzimidazole with the same core mechanism; and ivermectin, which enhances glutamate-gated chloride channel activity causing parasite neuromuscular paralysis; oxantel pamoate, a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist/depolarizing agent, is also used in some settings, especially in combination regimens for refractory or high-burden infection.

Name: Trigeminal Neuralgia
Description: Trigeminal neuralgia (MeSH D014277) is a neuropathic craniofacial pain disorder characterized by recurrent, brief, electric shock-like unilateral pain in one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve, often triggered by light tactile stimuli, chewing, speaking, or cold air, with examination typically normal between attacks except in secondary forms.
