It is classically divided into classical trigeminal neuralgia, usually caused by neurovascular compression at the root entry zone with focal demyelination, secondary trigeminal neuralgia due to disorders such as multiple sclerosis, tumors, or structural lesions, and idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia. Pathobiology centers on ectopic impulse generation and ephaptic transmission involving hyperexcitable sensory axons, altered sodium-channel signaling, and glial-neuronal interactions; implicated molecular components include voltage-gated sodium channels SCN9A/Nav1.7, SCN8A/Nav1.6, and SCN10A/Nav1.8, myelin-related proteins such as MPZ and PMP22 in rare hereditary neuropathic backgrounds, and inflammatory mediators including TNF-alpha and IL-6, with pathways involving demyelination, MAPK signaling, and central sensitization in the trigeminal nucleus. Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering suggests genetic susceptibility, occasionally with autosomal dominant patterns and rare associations with ion-channel variants or inherited neuropathies. Common comorbidities and complications include anxiety, depression, insomnia, weight loss, impaired oral intake, medication toxicity, and secondary causes such as multiple sclerosis. Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD-3 features of paroxysmal unilateral facial pain lasting fractions of a second to 2 minutes, severe intensity, and triggerability, supported by high-resolution MRI with and without contrast to identify vascular compression or exclude secondary lesions; trigeminal reflex testing and neurophysiology may help atypical cases. First-line treatment is carbamazepine, a use-dependent voltage-gated sodium-channel blocker; oxcarbazepine acts similarly with improved tolerability; baclofen, a GABAB agonist, reduces excitatory neurotransmission; lamotrigine inhibits sodium channels and glutamate release; and gabapentin or pregabalin modulate alpha2delta calcium-channel subunits, particularly in refractory or painful neuropathic variants.

Name: Trypanosomiasis, African
Description: African trypanosomiasis, or human African sleeping sickness, is a vector-borne protozoal infection caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, which produces a chronic West and Central African form, and T. brucei rhodesiense, which causes a more acute East and Southern African form; it is an acquired infectious disease rather than an inherited disorder, although host genetic susceptibility influences risk and severity, with representative associations involving APOL1, HLA loci, IL6, IL10, TNFA, IFNG, and innate immune pathways, while parasite virulence depends on variant surface glycoprotein genes mediating antigenic variation, serum-resistance associated protein in rhodesiense, and pathways involving trypanosome glycolysis, polyamine and trypanothione metabolism, RNA editing, and host macrophage, complement, cytokine, endothelial activation, and blood-brain barrier inflammatory signaling. Typical manifestations include a trypanosomal chancre, intermittent fever, headache, pruritus, lymphadenopathy including Winterbottom sign, myalgia, weight loss, anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, then meningoencephalitic disease with sleep-wake disturbance, behavioral change, confusion, ataxia, tremor, endocrine dysfunction, coma, and death if untreated. Major complications and comorbidities include severe malnutrition, secondary bacterial infection, myocarditis, nephropathy, seizures, aspiration, and coinfections such as HIV, malaria, and helminthiasis. Diagnosis relies on epidemiologic exposure, parasite detection in blood, lymph node aspirate, chancre fluid, or bone marrow, species-oriented serology such as CATT or rapid tests for gambiense disease, concentration techniques, PCR or LAMP where available, and staging by cerebrospinal fluid white-cell count and demonstration of trypanosomes in CSF. Treatment includes pentamidine for first-stage gambiense disease, which interferes with nucleic acid and mitochondrial function; suramin for first-stage rhodesiense disease, which inhibits parasite energy metabolism and enzymes; eflornithine, an ornithine decarboxylase inhibitor; nifurtimox, generating toxic nitro-radicals and used with eflornithine; melarsoprol, an arsenical that disrupts trypanothione-dependent metabolism for CNS disease; and oral fexinidazole, a nitroimidazole prodrug causing

Name: Chagas Disease
Description: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis; MeSH D014355) is a vector-borne protozoal infection caused by Trypanosoma cruzi that presents as acute, indeterminate, and chronic cardiac, digestive, or mixed forms. Acute infection is often asymptomatic or marked by fever, malaise, chagoma, Romaña sign, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, myocarditis, or meningoencephalitis, whereas chronic disease may manifest years later with conduction abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias, apical aneurysm, dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, thromboembolism, megaesophagus, and megacolon. Pathogenesis reflects persistent parasitism and host immune injury involving parasite surface molecules such as trans-sialidase, mucins, cruzipain, and GP85 family proteins, with activation of Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, TNF-α, IFN-γ, TGF-β, endothelin-1, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, fibrosis, and autonomic neuronal loss. Human genetic susceptibility is complex and non-Mendelian, with reported associations in immune and remodeling genes including HLA class I/II alleles, TNF, IFNG, IL10, CCR5, TLR2, TLR4, MMP2, MMP9, and TGFB1 variants that may influence infection control or cardiomyopathy risk. Diagnosis depends on the stage: acute disease is identified by direct microscopy of blood, microhematocrit, concentration methods, PCR, or occasionally hemoculture, while chronic infection requires two different positive serologic assays, typically ELISA, indirect immunofluorescence, or hemagglutination, with ECG, echocardiography, chest imaging, Holter monitoring, barium studies, and PCR used to assess organ involvement or reactivation. Antiparasitic treatment relies chiefly on benznidazole, a nitroimidazole prodrug generating reactive intermediates that damage parasite DNA and proteins, and nifurtimox, a nitrofuran producing toxic nitro-radicals and oxidative stress; adjunctive management includes amiodarone for ventricular arrhythmias via class III antiarrhythmic potassium-channel blockade, along with standard heart-failure therapy. Name: Tuberculosis, Meningeal
Description: Tuberculous meningitis is the most severe extrapulmonary form of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, caused by hematogenous dissemination or rupture of a subependymal or subpial Rich focus into the subarachnoid space, producing a granulomatous basilar meningitis with vasculitis, infarction, and obstructive or communicating hydrocephalus; clinically it typically presents subacutely with fever, persistent headache, malaise, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status, cranial neuropathies, seizures, and focal deficits, and is often classified as definite, probable, or possible disease, or by stage I to III severity based on neurologic impairment. Host susceptibility is influenced by immune genetic factors rather than Mendelian inheritance, with reported associations involving TLR2, TLR4, TIRAP, IFNG, IFNGR1, IL12B, IL12RB1, LTA4H, VDR, SLC11A1/NRAMP1, and HLA variants; rare monogenic defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ axis can predispose to severe mycobacterial disease. Pathobiology centers on macrophage and microglial activation, TLR/NF-κB signaling, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-12, IFN-γ, chemokines, matrix metalloproteinases, eicosanoid balance including LTA4H-mediated inflammation, and VEGF-linked blood-brain barrier disruption. Diagnosis relies on cerebrospinal fluid showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose, with confirmation by acid-fast smear, mycobacterial culture, or nucleic acid amplification such as Xpert MTB/RIF; supportive tests include CSF adenosine deaminase, brain MRI or CT demonstrating basilar enhancement, tuberculomas, infarcts, or hydrocephalus, and chest imaging. Standard treatment uses isoniazid, which inhibits mycolic acid synthesis; rifampin, which blocks DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; pyrazinamide, which disrupts membrane energetics in acidic compartments; and ethambutol, which inhibits arabinosyl transferases in the cell wall, often with adjunctive corticosteroids such as dexamethasone to blunt inflammation. Name: Tuberculosis, Miliary
Description: Miliary tuberculosis is a severe disseminated form of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection caused by hematogenous spread, producing innumerable millet seed–like granulomatous foci in the lungs and often liver, spleen, bone marrow, meninges, and other organs; it is usually considered a clinicopathologic subtype of active tuberculosis and may occur as acute fulminant disease or more indolent disseminated disease. Its pathobiology is dominated by macrophage infection, granuloma formation, and Th1 immune signaling, especially the IL-12/IFN-γ axis, TNF-α, TLR2/TLR4, JAK-STAT signaling, NF-κB activation, and vitamin D–dependent antimicrobial responses, while host susceptibility is influenced by genetic defects or polymorphisms in IFNG, IFNGR1, IL12B, IL12RB1, STAT1, TYK2, TLR2, SLC11A1/NRAMP1, and VDR, with rare Mendelian predisposition in primary immunodeficiencies rather than classic inheritance of the infection itself. Typical manifestations include prolonged fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, malaise, cough, dyspnea, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, choroidal tubercles, anemia, and laboratory evidence of systemic inflammation; complications include acute respiratory failure, ARDS, meningitis, adrenal insufficiency, sepsis-like multiorgan dysfunction, and bone marrow suppression. Major comorbid associations include HIV/AIDS, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, anti-TNF therapy, corticosteroid use, extremes of age, and other states of impaired cellular immunity. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical syndrome plus imaging showing diffuse 1–3 mm micronodules on chest radiograph or high-resolution CT, microbiologic confirmation by sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, blood, bone marrow, CSF, or tissue acid-fast smear, culture, and nucleic acid amplification testing, supported by histology demonstrating necrotizing or non-necrotizing granulomas. Standard treatment uses isoniazid, which inhibits mycolic acid synthesis; rifampin, which blocks DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; pyrazinamide, which disrupts mycobacterial energy metabolism in acidic compartments; and ethambutol, which inhibits arabinosyl transferases involved in cell wall synthesis.

Name: Tuberculosis, Pulmonary
Description: Pulmonary tuberculosis is a chronic airborne infectious granulomatous disease caused predominantly by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, most often involving the lung parenchyma and ranging from primary infection and latent tuberculosis infection to post-primary/reactivation disease, cavitary tuberculosis, miliary spread, and drug-susceptible, multidrug-resistant, or extensively drug-resistant forms. Host susceptibility is partly genetically determined, with variants affecting IFN-γ/IL-12 axis and macrophage immunity, including IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, TLR2, TLR4, SLC11A1/NRAMP1, VDR, TNF, HLA loci, and rare Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease genes; pathogen resistance commonly reflects katG or inhA mutations for isoniazid, rpoB for rifampin, pncA for pyrazinamide, embB for ethambutol, and gyrA/gyrB for fluoroquinolones. Central pathways include TLR2/4-mediated innate recognition, NF-κB and MAPK activation, TNF-α signaling, IL-12-driven Th1 differentiation, IFN-γ activation of macrophages, autophagy, phagolysosome maturation, granuloma formation, and immune-checkpoint and matrix metalloproteinase pathways contributing to tissue damage. Typical symptoms are chronic cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, chest pain, and apical or cavitary infiltrates on imaging. Major comorbidities and complications include HIV infection, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, silicosis, chronic kidney disease, smoking, alcoholism, COPD, bronchiectasis, massive hemoptysis, respiratory failure, pleural disease, and dissemination. Standard treatment uses isoniazid, which inhibits mycolic acid synthesis; rifampin, which inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; pyrazinamide, active in acidic intracellular environments and disrupting membrane energetics; and ethambutol, which inhibits arabinosyl transferases in the cell wall. Name: Tuberous Sclerosis
Description: Tuberous sclerosis, or tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), is a multisystem autosomal dominant hamartoma syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in TSC1 on 9q34 encoding hamartin or TSC2 on 16p13 encoding tuberin, with TSC2 mutations generally associated with more severe disease; many cases arise de novo, and mosaicism occurs. Loss of the hamartin-tuberin complex disables inhibition of RHEB and constitutively activates the PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 signaling axis, driving abnormal cell growth, proliferation, and differentiation. The disorder is characterized by benign tumors and dysplastic lesions in brain, skin, kidney, heart, lung, and eye, with major manifestations including cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, renal angiomyolipomas and cysts, cardiac rhabdomyomas, pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis, retinal hamartomas, and cutaneous findings such as facial angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patches, and ungual fibromas. Typical symptoms include epilepsy, infantile spasms, developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, behavioral and psychiatric problems, headache, hydrocephalus, hematuria, pneumothorax, and declining renal or pulmonary function. Important comorbidities and complications include chronic kidney disease, hemorrhage from angiomyolipomas, obstructive hydrocephalus from SEGA, refractory seizures, and TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders. Clinical subtypes are often framed by organ involvement, especially neurologic, renal, and pulmonary disease, rather than distinct molecular classes. Diagnosis relies on established major and minor clinical criteria plus molecular confirmation by identifying a pathogenic TSC1 or TSC2 variant; evaluation includes brain MRI, renal imaging, chest CT in at-risk adults, echocardiography, ophthalmologic and dermatologic examination, EEG when seizures are suspected, and genetic testing by sequencing with deletion-duplication analysis. Common treatments include everolimus and sirolimus, mTOR inhibitors that suppress mTORC1-driven tumor growth and can reduce SEGA, angiomyolipoma, and some seizure burden, and vigabatrin, an irreversible GABA transaminase inhibitor used especially for infantile spasms, with adjunct antiseizure drugs such as levetir

Name: Tubo-ovarian abscess
Description: Tubo-ovarian abscess (UMLS C0041343) is a severe, usually polymicrobial, suppurative subtype of complicated pelvic inflammatory disease in which infection extends from the upper genital tract to form an inflammatory mass involving the fallopian tube, ovary, and often adjacent pelvic structures; common microbiologic drivers include Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis as initiators, with mixed anaerobic and enteric flora such as Bacteroides, Escherichia coli, Peptostreptococcus, and streptococci sustaining abscess formation. Its biology is dominated by innate immune and inflammatory signaling rather than a Mendelian genetic basis, with activation of Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, and prostaglandin pathways, neutrophil recruitment, matrix metalloproteinases, and acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein; representative host susceptibility factors studied in PID include polymorphic variation in TLR4, TNF, IL10, and MBL2, but no specific inherited mutation is diagnostic or causative for most cases. Patients typically present with lower abdominal or pelvic pain, fever, adnexal tenderness or mass, cervical motion tenderness, vaginal discharge, leukocytosis, elevated ESR/CRP, and sometimes sepsis; major subtypes include unilateral versus bilateral abscess, ruptured versus unruptured disease, and pregnancy- or postpartum-associated cases. Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion in a patient with PID plus imaging evidence, most commonly transvaginal ultrasonography showing a complex multiloculated adnexal mass, with CT or MRI used when uncertain; pregnancy testing, CBC, inflammatory markers, NAATs for gonorrhea/chlamydia, and cultures when drainage occurs help define etiology and severity. Standard treatment uses broad-spectrum antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, a β-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit; metronidazole, which generates DNA-damaging radicals in anaerobes; and often clindamycin, a 50S inhibitor, with image-guided drainage or surgery for rupture, persistent sepsis, or treatment failure. Name: Tularemia
Description: Tularemia is an acute zoonotic infection caused by the highly infectious Gram-negative intracellular coccobacillus Francisella tularensis, classically divided into the more virulent type A subspecies tularensis and the less virulent type B subspecies holarctica, with clinical forms including ulceroglandular, glandular, oculoglandular, oropharyngeal, pneumonic, and typhoidal disease. Human susceptibility is not Mendelian, but host genetic components influencing innate immunity are implicated, including TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, NOD-like receptor, IFNG, TNF, IL6, IL12B, and SLC11A1 pathways; protective responses center on macrophage infection, dendritic-cell activation, inflammasome signaling, and Th1 immunity with IL-12, IFN-γ, and TNF-α driving intracellular killing, while Francisella virulence factors such as atypical lipopolysaccharide, the Francisella pathogenicity island, IglC, and type VI secretion-associated proteins promote phagosomal escape and immune evasion. Typical manifestations are abrupt fever, chills, malaise, headache, myalgia, painful regional lymphadenopathy, and, depending on portal of entry, a skin ulcer, conjunctivitis, exudative pharyngitis, cough, pleuritic chest pain, or pneumonia; complications include suppurative lymph nodes, sepsis, acute respiratory failure, meningitis, osteomyelitis, and relapse, with greater severity in older, immunocompromised, or chronic cardiopulmonary patients. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure history, characteristic syndrome, culture with biosafety precautions, PCR or other nucleic acid amplification from tissue or respiratory samples, serology showing seroconversion or a fourfold rise in antibody titer, and occasionally immunohistochemistry. First-line therapy commonly includes streptomycin or gentamicin, aminoglycosides that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the 30S subunit; and ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.

Name: Typhoid Fever
Description: Typhoid fever (MeSH D014435) is a systemic enteric infection caused primarily by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, with related paratyphoid syndromes caused by S. Paratyphi A, B, or C; it is an acquired infectious disease rather than a Mendelian disorder, although host genetic susceptibility influences risk and severity. Important microbial virulence determinants include the Vi capsular polysaccharide encoded in the viaB locus, lipopolysaccharide, flagellin, type III secretion systems in Salmonella pathogenicity islands SPI-1 and SPI-2, and regulators such as phoP/phoQ, while host susceptibility and inflammatory response have been linked to variants in TLR4, TLR5, NOD2, NRAMP1/SLC11A1, CFTR, HLA loci, TNF, IL6, and IFNG. Pathogenesis involves intestinal invasion through M cells, macrophage survival within Salmonella-containing vacuoles, and activation of TLR/NF-kappaB, inflammasome, JAK/STAT, MAPK, and cytokine pathways involving IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and interferon-gamma. Patients typically present after an incubation of 1 to 2 weeks with sustained high fever, headache, malaise, abdominal pain, relative bradycardia, constipation or diarrhea, dry cough, hepatosplenomegaly, and sometimes rose spots, leukopenia, and abnormal liver enzymes. Major complications include intestinal hemorrhage or perforation, encephalopathy, shock, hepatitis, cholecystitis, chronic gallbladder carriage, relapse, and coinfections or worsened outcomes with malnutrition, HIV, malaria, schistosomiasis, or hemoglobinopathies. Diagnosis rests on compatible febrile illness plus microbiologic confirmation, best by blood culture early and bone marrow culture when pretreated or culture-negative, with stool or urine cultures later, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and molecular assays such as PCR where available; Widal serology is nonspecific. Treatment commonly includes ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis; azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; and ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, although resistance mediated by gyrA/parC mutations,

Name: Typhus, Endemic Flea-Borne
Description: Endemic flea-borne typhus, or murine typhus, is an acute zoonotic rickettsiosis caused primarily by Rickettsia typhi and less commonly Rickettsia felis, transmitted by fleas, classically Xenopsylla cheopis from rats but also cat fleas; it is an infectious, non-Mendelian disease with no established host inheritance pattern, although severity may be influenced by host immune-response variation rather than recurrent pathogenic germline mutations. Key microbial factors include the rickettsial outer-membrane proteins OmpB and OmpA-like adhesins, the Sca family, lipopolysaccharide, phospholipase D, type IV secretion system components, and actin-based motility proteins such as RickA, which promote endothelial adhesion, invasion, intracellular survival, and dissemination. Pathobiology centers on infection of vascular endothelial cells and macrophages with activation of NF-κB, p38 MAPK, JAK/STAT, and inflammasome-related signaling, driving TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IFN-γ, chemokine release, vascular inflammation, and increased permeability. Typical presentation is abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgia, malaise, nausea, and a truncal maculopapular rash that may be absent, with cough, abdominal pain, or mild hepatitis; complications include pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, acute kidney injury, shock, thrombocytopenia, and multiorgan dysfunction, especially in older, pregnant, or immunocompromised patients, and comorbid diabetes, liver disease, or alcoholism may worsen outcome. Clinical subtypes are mainly classic murine typhus and flea-borne spotted fever due to R. felis. Diagnosis relies on compatible febrile illness plus exposure history, laboratory abnormalities such as elevated transaminases, hyponatremia, and thrombocytopenia, serology by indirect immunofluorescence with paired acute-convalescent titers, PCR on blood or tissue early in illness, and occasionally immunohistochemistry. Treatment is doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor and first-line therapy; tetracycline likewise inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; chloramphenicol inhibits the 50S peptidyl-transferase center and is an alternative when tetracyclines cannot be used, while azithromycin, a 50S macrolide inhibitor

Name: Typhus, Epidemic Louse-Borne
Description: Epidemic louse-borne typhus (UMLS C0041473) is an acute systemic febrile vasculitic infection caused by Rickettsia prowazekii, an obligate intracellular Gram-negative coccobacillus transmitted chiefly by the human body louse, with recrudescent disease termed Brill-Zinsser disease. Its pathobiology centers on infection of vascular endothelial cells, intracellular escape and actin-based spread mediated by rickettsial outer membrane proteins and adhesins such as OmpB, OmpA-like surface proteins, Sca family proteins, RickA, and phospholipase/hemolysin activities, leading to host NF-kB, MAPK, interferon, TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6 inflammatory signaling, endothelial injury, capillary leak, and multisystem vasculitis; however, no Mendelian inheritance pattern is known because this is an acquired infectious disease, although host susceptibility may be modified by immune-response genes without established diagnostic mutations. Clinically, patients typically develop abrupt high fever, severe headache, myalgia, malaise, cough, delirium, and a truncal maculopapular or petechial rash that may spread centrifugally, with severe cases progressing to hypotension, stupor, gangrene, myocarditis, pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, acute kidney injury, and shock; common complications and comorbid settings include malnutrition, homelessness, crowding, war, advanced age, alcoholism, HIV or other immunosuppression, and secondary bacterial infection. Diagnosis relies on epidemiologic exposure, compatible illness, and laboratory confirmation by PCR on blood or tissue, indirect immunofluorescence serology showing rising antibody titers, immunohistochemistry, or culture in specialized laboratories, with thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and transaminitis as supportive findings. Treatment is primarily doxycycline, which binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; alternatives include tetracycline with the same mechanism, chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S peptidyl transferase center, and occasionally azithromycin, a macrolide that blocks 50S-mediated translocation, although tetracyclines remain preferred.

Name: Infection by Uncinaria
Description: Infection by Uncinaria denotes a zoonotic hookworm infection caused primarily by dog and cat hookworms of the genus Uncinaria and, in related human hookworm disease, by other ancylostomatid nematodes; in humans it is typically an acquired parasitic disorder rather than an inherited disease, although host susceptibility and immune polarization are influenced by genetic variation in cytokine and barrier genes such as IL4, IL13, IFNG, TNF, TLR2, TLR4, HLA class II loci, and eosinophil/IgE-regulatory pathways. Pathobiology centers on larval tissue invasion and a type 2 immune response involving epithelial alarmins IL-25, IL-33, and TSLP, Th2 signaling through STAT6, eosinophils, mast cells, IgE, alternatively activated macrophages, and chemokines that drive pruritic inflammation; in intestinal infection, blood-feeding and anticoagulant secreted proteins contribute to iron deficiency. Clinical forms include cutaneous larva migrans and, less commonly, enteric or eosinophilic intestinal disease; typical findings are serpiginous intensely pruritic tracks, erythema, papules, localized swelling, cough or wheeze during larval migration, abdominal pain, diarrhea, eosinophilia, and occasionally occult or chronic blood loss with anemia. Comorbidities and complications include secondary bacterial cellulitis from excoriation, asthma/allergic disease exacerbation, malnutrition, iron-deficiency anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and rarely eosinophilic pneumonitis or enteritis. Diagnosis is usually clinical for cutaneous disease based on exposure to contaminated الرمل/soil or animal feces and characteristic migrating lesions, while enteric disease may require stool ova/parasite examination, endoscopy, histopathology, CBC showing eosinophilia or anemia, and species confirmation by PCR when available. Treatment relies on antihelminthics such as albendazole, which inhibits parasite beta-tubulin and microtubule assembly; mebendazole, with a similar benzimidazole mechanism impairing glucose uptake; and ivermectin, which activates glutamate-gated chloride channels causing parasite paralysis; topical thiabendazole or supportive antipruritics may also be used.

Name: Upper Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage
Description: Upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage (UMLS C0041909) is an acute, potentially life-threatening syndrome of bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, most commonly caused by peptic ulcer disease, erosive gastritis/esophagitis, Mallory-Weiss tear, or portal hypertensive varices, and it presents with hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, sometimes hematochezia if brisk, plus epigastric pain, orthostasis, tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, and anemia. Major subtypes are nonvariceal and variceal bleeding, with less common vascular causes such as Dieulafoy lesion or angiodysplasia. Its biology is usually acquired rather than inherited, but genetic contributors are recognized through etiologic predisposition: Helicobacter pylori-related disease engages IL1B, TNF, IL10, PTGS1/COX1, PTGS2/COX2, and MUC1-associated inflammatory and mucosal defense pathways; variceal hemorrhage reflects cirrhosis-related fibrogenic and vasoactive signaling involving TGFB1, PDGFR, VEGFA, endothelin, nitric oxide, and RAAS components; and rare inherited hemorrhagic syndromes such as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia from ENG, ACVRL1, or SMAD4 variants, or von Willebrand disease from VWF defects, can predispose to upper GI bleeding. Key pathways include prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection, acid secretion through the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, platelet adhesion/aggregation, coagulation cascades, angiogenesis, and portal-pressure regulation. Common treatments include proton pump inhibitors such as pantoprazole or omeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit gastric H+/K+-ATPase; octreotide, a somatostatin analog that reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure; nonselective beta-blockers such as propranolol for secondary variceal prophylaxis by lowering portal venous inflow; and adjunctive ceftriaxone in cirrhotics to prevent infection-triggered rebleeding. Important comorbidities and complications include H. pylori infection, NSAID or antithrombotic exposure, chronic liver disease, coagulopathy, renal failure, shock, rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, and death. Diagnosis relies on hemodynamic assessment

Name: Respiratory Infection, Upper
Description: Respiratory tract infections (MeSH D012141) comprise acute or chronic infections of the upper airways (rhinitis, sinusitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis, otitis-associated disease) and lower tract (tracheobronchitis, bronchiolitis, pneumonia), caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi and ranging from self-limited mucosal inflammation to invasive parenchymal disease and sepsis. Host susceptibility is strongly influenced by innate and adaptive immune genes, with representative examples including CFTR mutations predisposing to chronic sinopulmonary infection in cystic fibrosis, TLR2, TLR4, TLR3, IFIH1/MDA5, MAVS, IRF7, IFNAR1, STAT1, and MyD88 pathway defects impairing pathogen sensing or interferon signaling, and mucociliary or surfactant-related genes such as DNAH5, CCDC39, and SFTPA/SFTPD affecting airway defense; key proteins include ACE2 and TMPRSS2 for some viral entry, defensins, mucins, and inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF, CXCL8, and NF-κB. Pathobiology centers on epithelial invasion, PRR activation, inflammasome and JAK-STAT signaling, neutrophil/macrophage recruitment, mucus hypersecretion, and, in severe disease, alveolar-capillary injury. Common treatments include amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation; azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and may also dampen inflammation; ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin blocking cell-wall synthesis; oseltamivir, a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza; and, when indicated, antifungals such as voriconazole inhibiting ergosterol synthesis. Typical symptoms are fever, cough, coryza, sore throat, sputum, dyspnea, wheeze, pleuritic chest pain, and crackles or hypoxemia. Major comorbidities and complications include asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, heart failure, diabetes, immunodeficiency, otitis/sinusitis, respiratory failure, abscess, empyema, ARDS, and bacteremia.
