Name: Urinary Incontinence
Description: Urinary incontinence is a heterogeneous symptom complex defined by involuntary leakage of urine and arises from failure of bladder storage or outlet competence; major clinical subtypes include stress incontinence, urgency incontinence/overactive bladder, mixed incontinence, overflow incontinence, functional incontinence, and neurogenic incontinence. Typical manifestations are urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia, leakage with cough or exertion, enuresis, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, and recurrent urinary tract infection, with complications including skin breakdown, falls, sleep disturbance, depression, sexual dysfunction, and reduced quality of life. Its biology involves detrusor smooth-muscle excitability, urethral sphincter integrity, autonomic and somatic innervation, and extracellular matrix remodeling, with implicated pathways including parasympathetic cholinergic M3 receptor–Gq/PLC/Ca2+ signaling, sympathetic beta3-adrenergic receptor–cAMP relaxation, purinergic ATP signaling, TRPV1/TRPV4 mechanosensory pathways, serotonin/norepinephrine modulation of Onuf’s nucleus, and collagen/TGF-beta-related support of pelvic connective tissue. Genetic contributors are usually polygenic and subtype-specific rather than Mendelian, but associations have been reported for ADRB3, CHRM3, COL1A1, COL3A1, ELN, ESR1, MMP1/MMP9, LAMC1, and muscarinic or ion-channel genes; rare syndromic predisposition may occur in heritable connective-tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Comorbidities include pelvic organ prolapse, obesity, diabetes, pregnancy and vaginal childbirth, menopause, benign prostatic hyperplasia, neurologic disease such as stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, or spinal cord injury, and cognitive impairment. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history, bladder diary, urinalysis, medication review, pelvic and neurologic examination, stress test, postvoid residual measurement, and selected use of urodynamics, pad testing, cystoscopy, or imaging when diagnosis is uncertain or complicated. Common drug therapies include antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin, tolterodine, and solifenacin, which inhibit detrusor M3-mediated contractions; mirabegron, a beta3-adrenergic agonist that promotes bladder relaxation; duloxetine, which increases serotonergic and noradrenergic urethral

Name: Urinary Tract Infections
Description: Urinary tract infections (UTIs; MeSH D014552) are common, usually ascending bacterial infections of the urethra, bladder, ureters, or kidney, classically caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli, but also Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus; clinically they range from uncomplicated cystitis to pyelonephritis, catheter-associated UTI, recurrent UTI, and asymptomatic bacteriuria. Pathogenesis centers on microbial adhesion and innate immune activation, including type 1 fimbriae FimH binding to uroplakins, Toll-like receptor signaling, especially TLR4 and TLR5, CXCL8/IL-8–driven neutrophil recruitment, NF-κB activation, complement, and antimicrobial peptides such as defensins; host susceptibility has been linked to variants in TLR4, CXCR1, TLR1, HSPA1B, and secretor/FUT2 and ABO-related mucosal glycosylation, while severe recurrent pyelonephritis may rarely cluster in families in a complex, non-Mendelian manner rather than showing a single-gene inheritance pattern. Typical symptoms include dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, malodorous or cloudy urine, hematuria, and, in upper-tract disease, fever, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral-angle tenderness; older adults may present atypically. Major comorbidities and risk factors include female sex, pregnancy, diabetes, urinary obstruction, nephrolithiasis, vesicoureteral reflux, neurogenic bladder, benign prostatic hyperplasia, spinal cord injury, and urinary catheterization, with complications including renal scarring, abscess, emphysematous infection, bacteremia, sepsis, and preterm birth. Diagnosis relies on symptoms plus urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and sometimes hematuria, with urine culture and susceptibility testing for confirmation in complicated cases, recurrence, pregnancy, men, or pyelonephritis, and imaging when obstruction or abscess is suspected. Common treatments include nitrofurantoin, reduced by bacterial nitroreductases to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis via dihydropteroate synthase

Name: Urticaria
Description: Urticaria (MeSH D014581) is a heterogeneous mast cell–driven disorder characterized by transient pruritic wheals, erythema, and sometimes deeper angioedema caused by increased dermal vascular permeability; lesions usually resolve within 24 hours, whereas chronic urticaria persists for more than 6 weeks and includes chronic spontaneous urticaria and inducible forms such as cold, heat, cholinergic, pressure, solar, and dermographism, with urticarial vasculitis as an important mimic when lesions are painful or prolonged. Core molecular mechanisms involve IgE/FcεRI-mediated mast-cell and basophil activation, histamine, leukotriene, prostaglandin, platelet-activating factor, tryptase, and cytokine release, with contributions from complement, coagulation, neuroimmune signaling, TH2 pathways, and autoimmune endotypes including IgG autoantibodies to FcεRIα or IgE; genetic associations are usually complex rather than Mendelian, but variants affecting KIT, FCER1A, HNMT, IL4, IL13, TNF, and autoimmune loci have been reported, while hereditary angioedema due to SERPING1, F12, PLG, ANGPT1, or KNG1 mutations should be distinguished because it is typically nonurticarial and bradykinin mediated. Common comorbidities include autoimmune thyroid disease, asthma, atopy, chronic infections, anxiety/depression, metabolic syndrome, and less commonly systemic lupus, Sjögren syndrome, or celiac disease; complications include sleep disturbance, impaired quality of life, medication sedation, and rarely anaphylaxis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by history of trigger patterns and wheal duration, with selective testing such as CBC, ESR/CRP, thyroid antibodies, total or specific IgE, skin-prick or provocation tests for inducible disease, and biopsy when vasculitis is suspected. Treatment centers on second-generation H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine, fexofenadine, or loratadine, which block H1 receptors; omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody that downregulates FcεRI signaling; corticosteroids for short rescue via broad anti-inflammatory effects; and in refractory cases cyclosporine, which suppresses calcineurin-dependent T-cell and mast-cell activation.

Name: Fibroid, Uterine
Description: Uterine fibroid, or uterine leiomyoma, is a common benign monoclonal smooth-muscle neoplasm of the myometrium, typically classified by location as intramural, submucosal, or subserosal, with cervical and pedunculated variants, and it presents most often with heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure or pain, dysmenorrhea, urinary frequency, constipation, abdominal enlargement, infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss, or it may be asymptomatic. Its molecular pathogenesis is strongly hormone responsive, driven by estrogen and progesterone signaling and extracellular matrix accumulation, and frequently involves somatic MED12 mutations, HMGA2 overexpression or rearrangement, biallelic fumarate hydratase loss in hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome, and less commonly alterations involving COL4A5-COL4A6, RAD51B, or TERT; relevant proteins and pathways include estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, WNT/β-catenin, TGF-β/SMAD, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, IGF, and angiogenic mediators. Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering occurs, and inherited predisposition is best established for autosomal dominant FH mutation carriers, who may develop multiple early-onset leiomyomas. Important comorbidities and complications include iron-deficiency anemia, adverse obstetric outcomes, hydronephrosis or urinary symptoms from mass effect, degeneration or torsion, and the rare but critical differential diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma. Diagnosis is based on history and pelvic examination, confirmed primarily by pelvic ultrasonography, with MRI used for mapping or atypical cases; laboratory testing often includes pregnancy testing and complete blood count, while histopathology after myomectomy or hysterectomy confirms intersecting fascicles of benign smooth muscle and excludes malignancy. Common medical treatments include gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists such as leuprolide, which suppress pituitary gonadotropins and lower ovarian steroid production; GnRH antagonists such as elagolix or relugolix, which directly block GnRH receptors; levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems, which reduce endometrial bleeding; tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit cyclooxygenase; and selective progesterone receptor modulators such as uliprist

Name: Uterine Inertia
Description: Uterine inertia is an obstetric disorder of inadequate myometrial contractility during labor, classically divided into primary uterine inertia, in which contractions are weak from labor onset, and secondary uterine inertia, in which initially effective contractions become exhausted, resulting in hypotonic labor arrest. Its biology centers on impaired excitation-contraction coupling in uterine smooth muscle, including oxytocin–OXTR signaling, prostaglandin synthesis and receptor pathways, calcium influx through voltage-gated channels, gap-junction communication mediated by connexin-43 encoded by GJA1, and downstream actin-myosin activation via calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase; representative molecular contributors reported or plausibly implicated in dysfunctional labor include OXTR, PTGS2, GJA1, ESR1, PGR, and ion-channel or contractility-related genes such as CACNA1C and RYR2, although most cases are multifactorial rather than monogenic. Clinically, patients show infrequent, short, or weak contractions, prolonged latent or active labor, poor cervical dilation and fetal descent, maternal exhaustion, and increased risk of postpartum hemorrhage. Commonly linked complications and associations include cephalopelvic disproportion, fetal macrosomia, malpresentation, chorioamnionitis, multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, obesity, excessive uterine distention, and fetal distress, with obstructed labor, infection, uterine atony, and operative delivery as major sequelae. Treatment is primarily pharmacologic augmentation and supportive obstetric management: oxytocin stimulates OXTR to raise intracellular calcium and strengthen contractions; dinoprostone and misoprostol, prostaglandin E2 and E1 analogs, enhance cervical ripening and myometrial activity; ergometrine or methylergonovine increase uterine smooth-muscle tone via serotonergic and alpha-adrenergic effects, mainly postpartum; and tranexamic acid is used when hemorrhage complicates uterine atony. Inheritance is usually absent, though familial susceptibility to dysfunctional labor has been suggested through maternal-effect variation in contraction and hormone-response genes. Diagnosis is clinical, based on abnormal labor progress despite adequate time, contraction assessment by palpation or intrauterine pressure catheter, cervical change on serial examinations, fetal and maternal monitoring, and exclusion of mechanical causes before labeling uterine inertia.

Name: Uveitis
Description: Uveitis is a heterogeneous, predominantly immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the uveal tract and adjacent ocular tissues, classified anatomically into anterior, intermediate, posterior, and panuveitis and etiologically into infectious and noninfectious forms; typical manifestations include ocular pain, redness, photophobia, floaters, blurred vision, decreased visual acuity, and cells/flare in the anterior chamber or vitreous, with complications such as cataract, glaucoma, cystoid macular edema, synechiae, retinal vasculitis, and permanent vision loss. Its pathobiology involves dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity with Th1/Th17 polarization, TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-17, IL-23, IFN-gamma, JAK/STAT, NF-kappaB, and complement-related signaling, as well as breakdown of the blood-ocular barrier and activation of T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and retinal microglia. Genetic susceptibility is strongest for HLA loci, especially HLA-B27 in acute anterior uveitis, with additional associations including HLA-A29 in birdshot chorioretinopathy, HLA-B51 in Behcet disease, and variants in IL23R, ERAP1, TNF, and CTLA4; Mendelian autoinflammatory disorders such as NOD2 mutations in Blau syndrome and CAPN5 mutations in neovascular inflammatory vitreoretinopathy illustrate rarer inherited forms, while most cases show complex multifactorial inheritance. Uveitis is commonly linked to spondyloarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, multiple sclerosis, and infections such as herpes viruses, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, and syphilis. Diagnosis is based on ophthalmic examination with slit-lamp biomicroscopy, fundoscopy, optical coherence tomography, fluorescein or indocyanine angiography, ocular ultrasound when needed, and targeted laboratory testing including HLA-B27, syphilis and tuberculosis screening, serum ACE, and directed infectious PCR or aqueous/vitreous sampling. Treatment commonly includes corticosteroids, which suppress NF-kappaB-driven cytokine transcription; methotrexate, a folate antagonist used as a steroid-sparing immunomodulator; mycophenolate mofetil, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and lymphocyte proliferation; cyclosporine, a calcineurin

Name: Uveitis, Anterior
Description: Anterior uveitis is an intraocular inflammatory disorder primarily involving the iris and anterior ciliary body, usually immune mediated and often acute, recurrent, or chronic, with nongranulomatous and granulomatous subtypes; common symptoms and signs include ocular pain, photophobia, conjunctival or ciliary injection, blurred vision, lacrimation, consensual photophobia, keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells and flare, posterior synechiae, and variable intraocular pressure. It may be idiopathic or linked to systemic disease, especially HLA-B27-associated spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis, Behçet disease, and herpetic infection, and complications include cataract, band keratopathy, cystoid macular edema, glaucoma, hypotony, and vision loss. Genetic susceptibility is strongest for HLA-B27, with additional associations reported for HLA-DRB1, ERAP1, IL23R, TNF, and CTLA4 variants, supporting polygenic rather than Mendelian inheritance except in rare syndromic contexts. Pathobiology centers on breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier and activation of innate and adaptive immunity, including antigen presentation, Th1/Th17 polarization, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17, IL-23, IFN-γ, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and complement-related inflammatory cascades, with leukocyte trafficking and macrophage, dendritic cell, and T-cell effector responses in the uveal tract. Diagnosis is clinical by slit-lamp demonstration of anterior chamber inflammation graded by SUN criteria, supported by tonometry, dilated fundus examination, OCT when macular edema is suspected, and targeted testing such as HLA-B27 typing, ANA in children, syphilis and tuberculosis studies, ACE or chest imaging for sarcoidosis, and aqueous PCR for HSV or VZV when indicated. Treatment commonly includes topical corticosteroids such as prednisolone acetate, which suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription, cycloplegics such as atropine or cyclopentolate, which relieve ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae, and systemic or local immunomodulators including methotrexate, a folate antagonist that reduces lymphocyte proliferation, adalimumab or infliximab, anti-TNF biologics, and antiviral

Name: Varicose Veins
Description: Varicose veins are a chronic venous disease characterized by permanently dilated, elongated, tortuous superficial veins, most often of the lower limbs, caused by venous valve incompetence, venous hypertension, and maladaptive remodeling of the vein wall. They commonly present with visible bulging veins, leg heaviness, aching, burning, pruritus, nocturnal cramps, edema, and symptoms worsened by prolonged standing; advanced disease may lead to skin hyperpigmentation, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, superficial thrombophlebitis, bleeding, and venous ulceration, and they are frequently associated with chronic venous insufficiency, obesity, pregnancy, prior deep venous thrombosis, and reduced mobility. Primary and secondary forms are recognized, with truncal, reticular, and telangiectatic subtypes, and familial clustering supports a complex polygenic predisposition with examples including variants or altered expression in FOXC2, VEGFA, MMP2, MMP9, COL1A1, COL3A1, ELN, THBS1, NOTCH3, and genes affecting extracellular matrix integrity, angiogenesis, and smooth-muscle/valve development; rare syndromic venous valve failure can show autosomal dominant inheritance, but most cases are multifactorial rather than Mendelian. Pathobiology implicates endothelial dysfunction, leukocyte adhesion, inflammation, matrix metalloproteinase activation, TGF-β, VEGF, Notch, nitric oxide, hypoxia-inducible, and integrin-mediated mechanotransduction pathways, with loss of elastin-collagen balance and venous smooth muscle dysregulation. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by CEAP classification and duplex ultrasonography demonstrating reflux, venous dilation, obstruction, or perforator incompetence; additional testing may include plethysmography or venography in selected cases. Treatment is guided by symptoms and anatomy: compression therapy reduces ambulatory venous hypertension; polidocanol or sodium tetradecyl sulfate act as sclerosants by endothelial injury and fibrosis; venoactive drugs such as micronized purified flavonoid fraction and horse chestnut seed extract decrease capillary permeability and improve venous tone; pentoxifylline improves microcirculatory flow and is used particularly with venous ulcers.

Name: Vascular Diseases
Description: Vascular diseases comprise a heterogeneous group of arterial, venous, and microvascular disorders characterized by endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, thrombosis, vascular remodeling, and impaired tissue perfusion; major subtypes include atherosclerotic coronary, carotid, and peripheral arterial disease, aneurysmal disease, vasculitides, venous thromboembolism, chronic venous insufficiency, and hereditary arteriopathies. Genetic susceptibility is often polygenic, with representative contributors including LDLR, APOB, and PCSK9 in premature atherosclerosis, LPA in thrombogenic/atherogenic risk, MTHFR and F5 Leiden or F2 G20210A in venous thrombosis, FBN1 in aneurysmal disease, COL3A1 in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and NOTCH3 in CADASIL; inheritance may be multifactorial or autosomal dominant in defined syndromes. Key pathways include dyslipidemia-driven LDL retention and oxidation, nitric oxide deficiency, renin-angiotensin signaling, TGF-β and matrix metalloproteinase-mediated extracellular matrix turnover, VEGF-dependent angiogenesis, platelet activation via thromboxane A2 and P2Y12, and coagulation/cytokine networks involving tissue factor, thrombin, IL-6, TNF-α, and complement. Clinical manifestations vary by vascular bed and include hypertension, bruits, claudication, rest pain, ulceration, edema, varicosities, livedo, ischemic chest pain, transient ischemic attack or stroke, aneurysm rupture, and acute limb or organ ischemia. Common comorbidities and complications include diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, smoking-related lung disease, dyslipidemia, myocardial infarction, heart failure, stroke, critical limb ischemia, gangrene, and pulmonary embolism. Diagnosis relies on history and examination plus ankle-brachial index, duplex ultrasonography, CT or MR angiography, catheter angiography, echocardiography when indicated, inflammatory markers, lipid and coagulation testing, and targeted genetic testing in suspected inherited disorders. Treatment commonly includes statins, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and stabilize plaques; antiplatelet agents such as aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits COX-1, or clopidogrel, a P2Y12 antagonist; and anticoagulants such as heparin or direct oral factor Xa/throm

Name: Vascular Headaches
Description: Vascular headaches most commonly encompass migraine, cluster headache, and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, disorders now understood as neurovascular rather than purely vascular, characterized by recurrent attacks driven by activation of the trigeminovascular system, meningeal nociceptors, brainstem and hypothalamic networks, and release of calcitonin gene-related peptide, substance P, glutamate, nitric oxide, serotonin, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, with cortical spreading depression particularly implicated in migraine aura. Genetic susceptibility is often polygenic in common migraine, with representative genes including CACNA1A, ATP1A2, and SCN1A in familial hemiplegic migraine, KCNK18 and TRPM8 in some susceptibility studies, and HCRTR2 variants reported in cluster headache; inheritance is frequently complex multifactorial, although familial hemiplegic migraine is typically autosomal dominant. Clinically, migraine presents with unilateral or bilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes aura, whereas cluster headache causes excruciating unilateral orbital or temporal pain with lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, ptosis, or miosis; subtypes include migraine with or without aura, chronic migraine, hemiplegic migraine, retinal migraine, cluster headache, and paroxysmal hemicrania. Common comorbidities include depression, anxiety, epilepsy, sleep disorders, hypertension, obesity, stroke risk in migraine with aura, medication-overuse headache, and functional impairment. Treatment includes triptans such as sumatriptan, 5-HT1B/1D agonists that inhibit trigeminal neurotransmitter release and constrict cranial vessels; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit cyclooxygenase-mediated prostaglandin synthesis; verapamil for cluster prophylaxis via calcium-channel blockade; topiramate, which modulates sodium channels, GABA, and glutamate; beta-blockers such as propranolol; oxygen for cluster attacks; and CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies or gepants. Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD criteria, supported by attack pattern, neurologic examination, headache diaries, and selective MRI or CT, vascular imaging, or laboratory testing to exclude secondary causes.

Name: Venous Insufficiency
Description: Venous insufficiency (UMLS C0042485), most often chronic venous insufficiency of the lower extremities, is a multifactorial vascular disorder characterized by venous hypertension caused by valvular incompetence, venous outflow obstruction, or failure of the calf-muscle pump, leading to reflux, ambulatory venous pressure elevation, and progressive microvascular injury. Clinical subtypes include superficial, deep, and perforator venous insufficiency, primary versus secondary disease, and CEAP classes ranging from telangiectasias and varicose veins to edema, skin change, and active venous ulceration. Typical manifestations are leg heaviness, aching, fatigue, pruritus, swelling worse with dependency, varicosities, hyperpigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, eczema, and venous ulcers; complications include recurrent cellulitis, hemorrhage from varices, superficial thrombophlebitis, deep venous thrombosis, and chronic nonhealing wounds, with common comorbidities such as obesity, pregnancy, advanced age, immobility, heart failure, and post-thrombotic syndrome. Genetic susceptibility is usually polygenic rather than Mendelian, with reported associations involving FOXC2, GJC2/connexin-47, VEGFA, MMP2, MMP9, TIMP2, COL1A1, COL3A1, ELN, NOS3, and thrombophilia-related variants such as F5 Leiden and F2 prothrombin in secondary disease; rare familial varicose vein/lymphedema phenotypes may show autosomal dominant inheritance, especially with FOXC2 mutations. Pathobiology prominently involves endothelial dysfunction, leukocyte adhesion and inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, TGF-β, VEGF, MMP, nitric oxide, NF-κB, hypoxia/HIF-1, and coagulation-fibrinolytic pathways. Diagnosis is clinical and hemodynamic, anchored by duplex ultrasonography demonstrating reflux or obstruction, with adjunctive CEAP/Venous Clinical Severity Score staging, ankle-brachial index to exclude significant arterial disease before compression, and selected use of plethysmography, CT/MR venography, or intravascular ultrasound. Treatment commonly includes compression therapy; venoactive drugs such as micronized purified flavonoid fraction/diosmin-hesperidin, which reduce capillary permeability and leukocyte activation, pentoxifyll

Name: Venous Thrombosis
Description: Venous thrombosis is the pathologic formation of fibrin- and erythrocyte-rich thrombi within the venous circulation, most commonly presenting as deep vein thrombosis of the leg and potentially progressing to pulmonary embolism; major subtypes include provoked and unprovoked disease, distal or proximal deep vein thrombosis, upper-extremity thrombosis, splanchnic or cerebral venous thrombosis, and superficial venous thrombosis. It arises through Virchow triad mechanisms of stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability, with key molecular contributors including tissue factor–factor VIIa initiation, thrombin generation, fibrin formation, platelet-leukocyte interactions, P-selectin, NETosis, and impaired anticoagulant or fibrinolytic pathways involving antithrombin, protein C, protein S, plasminogen, and PAI-1. Genetic predisposition is often multifactorial but may be autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance in inherited thrombophilia, exemplified by F5 factor V Leiden, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1 antithrombin deficiency, PROC protein C deficiency, PROS1 protein S deficiency, and less commonly dysfibrinogenemia or elevated factor VIII; acquired associations include antiphospholipid syndrome and malignancy. Typical symptoms and signs are unilateral leg pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, tenderness, edema, and dilated superficial veins, while complications include post-thrombotic syndrome, recurrent venous thromboembolism, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, venous ulceration, and death from embolism; important comorbidities include cancer, recent surgery or trauma, immobility, obesity, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, and inflammatory disease. Diagnosis relies on pretest probability assessment, D-dimer testing, compression duplex ultrasonography for limb thrombosis, and CT pulmonary angiography, MR venography, or conventional venography in selected cases, with thrombophilia testing reserved for targeted scenarios. Treatment centers on anticoagulation with heparin or low-molecular-weight heparins that potentiate antithrombin against factor Xa and thrombin, warfarin that inhibits vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis, and direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, or dabigatran that directly inhibit factor Xa or

Name: Ventricular Fibrillation
Description: Ventricular fibrillation is a malignant ventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by chaotic, disorganized ventricular activation causing immediate loss of effective cardiac output and sudden cardiac arrest; it most often complicates acute myocardial ischemia or infarction, but also occurs in structurally normal hearts through inherited channelopathies and in cardiomyopathies. Genetic contributors include SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNH2, KCNE1/2, RYR2, CASQ2, LMNA, DSP, PKP2, PLN, and TTN, with representative pathogenic variants causing Brugada syndrome, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy; inheritance is commonly autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, although autosomal recessive forms occur, such as CASQ2-related disease. Core mechanisms involve reentry, triggered activity, and abnormal automaticity driven by impaired sodium, potassium, and calcium handling, gap-junction dysfunction, fibrosis, ischemia, and autonomic modulation, implicating ion-channel signaling, beta-adrenergic/cAMP-PKA pathways, calcium-calmodulin/CaMKII signaling, sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release via RyR2, and scar-related conduction heterogeneity. Patients present with palpitations, presyncope, syncope, agonal respirations, pulseless collapse, and sudden death; subtypes include primary VF, ischemic VF, idiopathic VF, and VF associated with inherited arrhythmia syndromes or cardiomyopathy. Major comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, electrolyte disturbances, myocarditis, hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, recurrent arrest, and death. Diagnosis is established by ECG or rhythm strip showing rapid irregular fibrillatory waves without organized QRS complexes, often supplemented by troponin testing, echocardiography, coronary evaluation, cardiac MRI, electrolyte and toxicology studies, ambulatory monitoring, provocative ECG testing, and genetic testing in suspected inherited cases. Treatment centers on immediate defibrillation and CPR; commonly used drugs include epinephrine, a beta-adrenergic agonist used during arrest to augment coronary perfusion, amiodarone, a multichannel antiarrhythmic prolonging repolarization and slowing conduction, lidocaine, a class Ib sodium-channel blocker that suppresses ventricular ectopy, and in selected synd

Name: Plantar warts
Description: Plantar warts (UMLS C0042548) are benign hyperkeratotic lesions of the sole caused by infection of keratinocytes with cutaneous human papillomaviruses, most often HPV-1, HPV-2, HPV-4, HPV-27, or HPV-57, and are classified clinically as solitary endophytic myrmecia, mosaic plantar warts, or multiple punctate lesions. Viral pathobiology centers on HPV early proteins E6 and E7, which perturb p53- and RB1-dependent cell-cycle control, promote keratinocyte proliferation, and interact with innate immune pathways, including interferon signaling, antigen presentation, and local cytokine responses; host susceptibility is increased by defects in epidermal barrier or immunity, with representative genetic associations including TMC6/EVER1 and TMC8/EVER2 in epidermodysplasia verruciformis, CXCR4 in WHIM syndrome, GATA2 deficiency, and other T-cell or NK-cell immunodeficiencies, although most cases are acquired rather than inherited. Patients typically present with rough, well-circumscribed, painful weight-bearing papules or plaques that interrupt dermatoglyphics, show thrombosed capillaries as black dots after paring, and cause tenderness with lateral compression; diagnosis is usually clinical, supported when needed by dermoscopy, histopathology showing papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, koilocytosis, and inward growth, and rarely HPV PCR typing or biopsy to exclude callus, corn, verruca plana, or squamous neoplasia. Common treatments include salicylic acid, a keratolytic that disrupts corneocyte cohesion; cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, which causes cellular ice injury and secondary immune activation; and cantharidin, a vesicant inducing intraepidermal blistering; additional options include imiquimod, a TLR7 agonist that enhances local interferon-mediated antiviral immunity, and intralesional bleomycin, a cytotoxic DNA-damaging agent. Plantar warts are linked to immunosuppression, atopy, and skin barrier disruption, and complications include pain, altered gait, recurrence, treatment-related scarring, and secondary bacterial infection.

Name: Vertigo
Description: Vertigo is a symptom complex rather than a single disease, defined by a false sensation of motion arising most often from peripheral vestibular disorders or less commonly from central brainstem and cerebellar disease; major subtypes include benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, Ménière disease, vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis, vestibular migraine, bilateral vestibulopathy, and central vertigo due to stroke, demyelination, tumor, or neurodegeneration. Patients typically report spinning dizziness, positional provocation, nausea, vomiting, gait imbalance, oscillopsia, nystagmus, motion intolerance, and sometimes hearing loss, tinnitus, or aural fullness. Molecular associations are strongest in specific syndromic or familial forms: recurrent vertigo with migraine may involve CACNA1A, ATP1A2, and SCN1A; Ménière-like or hereditary hearing-loss syndromes can involve COCH, FAM136A, DTNA, and ionic homeostasis genes such as SLC26A4, KCNQ4, or GJB2; episodic ataxia with vertigo is linked to CACNA1A or KCNA1. Relevant pathways include mechanotransduction in vestibular hair cells, glutamatergic synaptic transmission, voltage-gated calcium and potassium channel signaling, endolymph fluid and ion transport, neuroinflammatory signaling, and central vestibulo-cerebellar processing. Treatment is etiology-directed: meclizine or dimenhydrinate are H1-antihistaminic vestibular suppressants, benzodiazepines such as diazepam enhance GABA-A signaling, and scopolamine blocks muscarinic cholinergic transmission; ondansetron is used for nausea via 5-HT3 antagonism, while Ménière disease may be treated with diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide-triamterene to reduce endolymphatic hydrops, and vestibular migraine may respond to prophylaxis such as verapamil or topiramate. Comorbidities include migraine, anxiety, depression, hearing disorders, falls, dehydration, and stroke risk in central causes. Diagnosis rests on history, bedside oculomotor and positional testing including Dix-Hallpike and HINTS, audiometry, vestibular testing such as calorics or video head impulse testing, and MRI when central pathology is suspected; inheritance is usually multifactorial, but autosomal dominant

Name: Vitamin A Deficiency
Description: Vitamin A deficiency (MeSH D014802) is a nutritional deficiency disorder caused by inadequate intake, malabsorption, impaired hepatic storage, or defective retinoid transport/metabolism, leading to reduced retinol, retinal, and retinoic acid signaling; it may be primary from dietary lack or secondary to conditions such as fat-malabsorption, cholestatic liver disease, pancreatic insufficiency, inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery, alcoholism, or severe protein-energy malnutrition. Molecularly, disease biology centers on retinoid uptake and transport proteins and signaling genes including RBP4 and transthyretin, the STRA6 membrane receptor, LRAT and RPE65 in retinyl esterification and visual cycling, and nuclear retinoic acid receptors RAR/RXR that regulate epithelial differentiation, immunity, and phototransduction-related gene expression; rare inherited defects in RBP4, STRA6, RPE65, or related visual-cycle genes can produce familial hypovitaminosis A or phenocopies, typically with autosomal recessive inheritance, although most cases are acquired and non-Mendelian. Hallmark manifestations are nyctalopia, conjunctival and corneal xerosis, Bitot spots, keratomalacia, impaired dark adaptation, dry scaly skin, follicular hyperkeratosis, growth failure, infertility, and increased susceptibility to respiratory and diarrheal infections; major complications include corneal ulceration, permanent blindness, and heightened morbidity with measles and other infections, often coexisting with zinc deficiency and general malnutrition. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical findings plus low serum retinol, often <0.70 µmol/L, depressed retinol-binding protein, dose-response or isotope dilution tests where available, ocular examination, dark-adaptation testing, and evaluation for underlying malabsorptive or hepatic disease; genetic testing is reserved for suspected inherited retinoid-pathway disorders. Treatment is vitamin A replacement, usually retinyl palmitate or retinyl acetate, which replenish hepatic stores and restore retinoid-dependent transcription and visual pigment regeneration; beta-carotene serves as a provitamin A precursor converted by BCMO1; and in selected retinal dystrophy states, 9-cis-retinoids such as voretigene’s related retinoid approaches or experimental 9-cis-retinyl acetate can bypass visual-cycle defects, alongside correction of the underlying cause.

Name: Vitamin B 12 Deficiency
Description: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a nutritional, malabsorptive, or inherited disorder of cobalamin homeostasis that impairs the methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reactions, disrupting one-carbon metabolism, DNA synthesis, myelin maintenance, and mitochondrial fatty acid/amino acid metabolism; key molecular components include intrinsic factor encoded by GIF, the gastric parietal cell-intrinsic factor axis, the ileal cubam receptor complex CUBN/AMN, transcobalamin II encoded by TCN2, lysosomal cobalamin export via LMBRD1, and intracellular processing genes such as MMACHC, MMADHC, MMAA, MMAB, and MTR/MTRR, with pathogenic variants causing congenital selective cobalamin malabsorption, transcobalamin deficiency, or combined methylmalonic acidemia-homocystinuria syndromes, usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, whereas pernicious anemia reflects autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor/parietal cells rather than Mendelian inheritance. Clinical manifestations range from subclinical biochemical deficiency to megaloblastic anemia, glossitis, fatigue, pallor, jaundice, paresthesias, peripheral neuropathy, gait ataxia, loss of vibration/proprioception, cognitive or psychiatric change, optic neuropathy, infertility, and in infants developmental delay and failure to thrive; major subtypes include dietary deficiency, pernicious anemia, food-cobalamin malabsorption, post-gastrectomy or ileal disease-associated deficiency, medication-related disease, and inherited cobalamin disorders. Comorbidities and complications include autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, celiac or Crohn disease, metformin or proton-pump inhibitor exposure, hyperhomocysteinemia with thrombotic risk, reversible or permanent myeloneuropathy, and pancytopenia. Diagnosis relies on low serum B12 with supportive elevation of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, macrocytosis/megaloblastosis, anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, and targeted genetic testing when hereditary disease is suspected. Treatment consists primarily of cyanocobalamin, hydroxocobalamin, or methylcobalamin replacement, which restore intracellular cobalamin cofactors; folic acid may correct coexisting folate deficiency but does not treat neurologic injury, and betaine can lower homocysteine in inherited remethylation defects by serving as an alternative methyl donor

Name: Vitamin D Deficiency
Description: Vitamin D deficiency (UMLS C0042870) is a common nutritional-endocrine disorder characterized by inadequate 25-hydroxyvitamin D stores leading to impaired calcium-phosphate homeostasis, secondary hyperparathyroidism, defective bone mineralization, and, in severe cases, rickets in children or osteomalacia in adults; typical manifestations include bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, fragility fractures, growth delay, delayed fontanelle closure, genu varum/valgum, rachitic rosary, hypocalcemic tetany, and sometimes seizures. Major molecular components include cutaneous synthesis and hepatic and renal activation pathways involving DHCR7, CYP2R1, CYP27B1, and CYP24A1, transport by GC/DBP, and signaling through the vitamin D receptor VDR, which heterodimerizes with RXR to regulate intestinal TRPV6, calbindin, and other genes controlling calcium absorption, bone turnover, and immune function; PTH-FGF23-klotho signaling also modulates this axis. Genetic forms include vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A from biallelic CYP27B1 variants, type 1B from CYP2R1 defects, type 2A from VDR mutations, and rare transport defects involving GC, usually with autosomal recessive inheritance, whereas common deficiency is typically multifactorial, influenced by limited sun exposure, malabsorption, obesity, chronic kidney or liver disease, darker skin pigmentation, and anticonvulsant or glucocorticoid use. Diagnosis is primarily based on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration, with supportive findings of elevated PTH and alkaline phosphatase, low or normal calcium, low phosphate, reduced bone mineral density, and radiographic metaphyseal cupping/fraying in rickets; selected cases warrant 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D measurement or genetic testing. Treatment commonly uses cholecalciferol, which is converted to active metabolites to restore stores; ergocalciferol, another precursor used similarly; and calcitriol, the active VDR agonist used particularly in renal failure or genetic activation defects; calcium supplementation is often added. Linked comorbidities and complications include osteoporosis, falls, fractures, chronic kidney disease–mineral bone disorder, and persistent skeletal deformity.

Name: Vitamin E Deficiency
Description: Vitamin E deficiency is a fat-soluble vitamin deficiency disorder characterized by impaired antioxidant defense, most prominently affecting the nervous system, retina, erythrocytes, and skeletal muscle through unchecked lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated membrane lipids; it may be acquired from fat malabsorption or cholestatic liver disease, or hereditary, classically as autosomal recessive ataxia with vitamin E deficiency caused by biallelic TTPA mutations encoding alpha-tocopherol transfer protein, while related defects in lipid handling such as MTTP, APOB, SAR1B, NPC1L1, ABCA1, and genes causing cholestasis or pancreatic insufficiency can produce secondary deficiency. The relevant molecular pathway centers on intestinal absorption and hepatic trafficking of alpha-tocopherol via chylomicrons, VLDL secretion, and TTPA-mediated incorporation into circulating lipoproteins, with downstream protection against reactive oxygen species, ferroptotic membrane injury, and oxidative damage in neurons and red cells. Clinical manifestations include spinocerebellar ataxia, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, peripheral neuropathy, areflexia, dysarthria, retinopathy, ophthalmoparesis, proximal myopathy, and hemolytic anemia, especially in infants or severe malabsorption; complications include progressive disability, visual impairment, and worsening neuromuscular dysfunction, often with comorbid cystic fibrosis, abetalipoproteinemia, Crohn disease, chronic cholestasis, short-bowel syndrome, or pancreatic insufficiency. Major subtypes are primary genetic vitamin E deficiency and secondary deficiency due to impaired absorption or transport. Diagnosis rests on low serum alpha-tocopherol, ideally interpreted against total lipid or cholesterol levels, elevated alpha-tocopherol:lipid ratio abnormalities, evidence of hemolysis or neurophysiologic deficits, and etiologic testing such as fat absorption studies, liver and pancreatic evaluation, lipoprotein analysis, and molecular testing for TTPA or other causal genes. Treatment is centered on oral vitamin E replacement, usually alpha-tocopherol or water-miscible tocopheryl polyethylene glycol succinate, which restore antioxidant capacity, and management of underlying malabsorption with agents such as pancreatic enzyme replacement, ursodeoxycholic acid, or bile acid supplementation when indicated.

Name: Vitiligo
Description: Vitiligo (MeSH D014820) is an acquired, usually chronic autoimmune depigmenting disorder characterized by selective destruction of epidermal melanocytes, producing well-demarcated chalk-white macules and patches, often symmetrically distributed on the face, hands, periocular, perioral, acral, and genital sites, sometimes with leukotrichia, Koebner phenomenon, and psychosocial morbidity. It is classically divided into nonsegmental vitiligo, including generalized, acrofacial, mucosal, and universal forms, and segmental vitiligo, which is typically unilateral and earlier onset. Pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving genetic susceptibility, immune dysregulation, and oxidative stress; associated genes include HLA class I/II loci, PTPN22, NLRP1, TYR, TYRP1, MC1R, CTLA4, FOXP3, XBP1, and IL2RA, with mostly complex polygenic inheritance and familial aggregation rather than Mendelian transmission. Key pathways include IFN-gamma/CXCL9-CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling driving CD8+ T-cell recruitment, JAK-STAT activation, melanocyte oxidative stress with excess hydrogen peroxide, unfolded protein response, and reduced WNT/beta-catenin and melanogenic signaling. Vitiligo is strongly associated with autoimmune comorbidities, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, Addison disease, alopecia areata, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus; complications include sun sensitivity and marked quality-of-life impairment. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by Wood lamp accentuation, dermoscopy, assessment of lesion distribution and progression, and when needed skin biopsy showing absent melanocytes with little inflammation; laboratory screening commonly evaluates thyroid function and autoimmunity. Standard treatments include topical corticosteroids, which suppress cutaneous inflammation; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus, which inhibit T-cell activation via calcineurin blockade; narrowband UVB phototherapy, which promotes immunomodulation and melanocyte regeneration; and in selected patients excimer laser, systemic corticosteroid mini-pulse therapy, or topical ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor that counteracts IFN-gamma signaling.

Name: Vomiting
Description: Vomiting is a symptom complex rather than a single disease, defined as forceful expulsion of gastric contents through coordinated central and enteric reflexes; it may be acute or chronic and can be classified as infectious/toxic, gastrointestinal obstructive or inflammatory, metabolic/endocrine, vestibular, pregnancy-related, postoperative, drug-induced, psychogenic, cyclic vomiting syndrome, or raised-intracranial-pressure associated. Core pathobiology involves the medullary dorsal vagal complex, especially the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius, with vagal and enteric afferent input and signaling through serotonin 5-HT3, dopamine D2, neurokinin-1/substance P, histamine H1, muscarinic M1, cannabinoid CB1, and opioid pathways; representative molecular associations include HTR3A/B, TACR1, DRD2, SCN10A, and mitochondrial DNA variants reported in cyclic vomiting syndrome, which may also show maternal inheritance and overlap with migraine susceptibility, while familial gastrointestinal or neurologic disorders can secondarily predispose to vomiting. Typical features include nausea, retching, pallor, diaphoresis, abdominal pain, dehydration, orthostasis, electrolyte abnormalities, and weight loss, with complications such as aspiration, Mallory-Weiss tear, esophagitis, dental enamel erosion, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and acute kidney injury; common comorbidities include gastroenteritis, migraine, gastroparesis, GERD, peptic ulcer disease, bowel obstruction, pancreatobiliary disease, pregnancy, vestibular disorders, intracranial disease, anxiety, and eating disorders. Treatment is cause-directed and antiemetic: ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors, metoclopramide antagonizes D2 receptors and promotes gastric emptying via prokinetic effects, promethazine blocks H1 receptors with anticholinergic activity, scopolamine is an M1 antagonist, and aprepitant blocks NK1 receptors. Diagnosis is clinical but requires severity assessment and evaluation for red flags; testing may include serum electrolytes, renal and liver panels, pregnancy testing, lipase, toxicology, ECG when QT-prolonging drugs are used, and targeted imaging, endoscopy, gastric emptying studies, vestibular evaluation, or neuroimaging based on suspected etiology.

Name: Vulvovaginitis
Description: Vulvovaginitis (UMLS C0042998) is an inflammatory syndrome of the vulva and vagina, usually infectious but also irritant, allergic, atrophic, inflammatory, or dysbiotic in nature, presenting with pruritus, burning, erythema, edema, dysuria, dyspareunia, vulvar soreness, and abnormal discharge whose odor, pH, and appearance vary by subtype; major forms include candidal vulvovaginitis, bacterial vaginosis-associated vaginitis, trichomonal vaginitis, aerobic/desquamative inflammatory vaginitis, and atrophic vulvovaginitis. Its molecular basis is largely non-Mendelian and pathogen-host driven: Candida albicans virulence genes and proteins such as ALS3, HWP1, SAP family proteases, and candidalysin promote epithelial adhesion and damage; host innate immune components including TLR2, TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL1B, IL17A/IL22, TNF, and defensins mediate susceptibility and inflammation, with rare variants in CLEC7A or CARD9 predisposing to recurrent fungal disease. In bacterial vaginosis, loss of Lactobacillus dominance and Gardnerella vaginalis biofilm formation with sialidase and vaginolysin are important, while Trichomonas vaginalis triggers NF-kB-dependent cytokine responses. Key pathways include epithelial barrier disruption, pattern-recognition receptor signaling, Th17 immunity, inflammasome activation, and estrogen-dependent maintenance of glycogen-rich mucosa and lactobacillus homeostasis. Common therapies include metronidazole, which forms nitro-radicals that damage anaerobic and protozoal DNA; clindamycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor active against anaerobes; and fluconazole, an inhibitor of fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase that blocks ergosterol synthesis, with topical azoles such as clotrimazole similarly used. Comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, antibiotic exposure, immunosuppression including HIV, dermatologic disorders, pelvic inflammatory disease risk with trichomoniasis, adverse pregnancy outcomes, recurrent infection, fissuring, excoriation, and secondary bacterial superinfection. Diagnosis relies on history and pelvic examination, vaginal pH, microscopy with saline and KOH wet mount,

Name: Verrucous lesions
Description: Verrucous lesions are exophytic, hyperkeratotic, papillomatous epithelial proliferations that represent a morphologic pattern rather than a single disease entity, encompassing common viral warts, condyloma acuminata, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, verrucous carcinoma, and inflammatory or genodermatosis-associated verrucous plaques. They most often arise from HPV-driven keratinocyte infection or neoplastic transformation; representative viral and host molecular associations include HPV types 2, 4, 6, 11, 16, and 18, with E6/E7 oncoprotein-mediated disruption of TP53 and RB1, while inherited susceptibility is seen with TMC6/EVER1 and TMC8/EVER2 mutations in epidermodysplasia verruciformis, and occasionally defects affecting immune surveillance such as GATA2 or CXCR4. Relevant pathways include p53/Rb cell-cycle control, EGFR-MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling, keratinocyte differentiation, and local immune pathways involving interferon, T-cell, and dendritic-cell responses. Clinically, lesions are verrucous, rough, well-demarcated papules, plaques, or cauliflower-like masses that may fissure, bleed, itch, cause pain or malodor, and vary by subtype from plantar and periungual warts to anogenital lesions and slowly invasive verrucous carcinoma. Important comorbidities and complications include immunosuppression, HIV infection, diabetes, chronic lymphedema, tobacco exposure, secondary bacterial infection, functional impairment, cosmetic distress, recurrence, and in high-risk HPV-associated or long-standing lesions, dysplasia or malignant transformation. Treatment depends on cause and site and commonly includes salicylic acid, which causes keratolysis; cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, which induces cellular necrosis; imiquimod, a TLR7 agonist that enhances antiviral immunity; podophyllotoxin, a microtubule inhibitor; and 5-fluorouracil, an antimetabolite blocking thymidylate synthase. Name: Wheezings
Description: Wheezing, indexed in UMLS as C0043144, is not a single inherited disease but a clinical sign characterized by a high-pitched, predominantly expiratory musical sound caused by airflow limitation through narrowed intrathoracic airways; it most commonly reflects asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiolitis, anaphylaxis, heart failure, airway malacia, foreign-body aspiration, or focal obstruction from tumor or vocal cord dysfunction. In asthma-associated wheezing, genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations involving IL4, IL13, IL4R, ADRB2, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, TSLP, and ADAM33, and proteins such as IgE, eosinophil-derived mediators, leukotrienes, and cytokines including IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13; key pathways include Th2-driven airway inflammation, Fc epsilon RI–mast-cell signaling, JAK-STAT signaling, eosinophil recruitment, vagally mediated bronchoconstriction, and airway remodeling involving TGF-beta. Common treatments include short-acting beta2-agonists such as albuterol, which activate beta2-adrenergic receptors to increase cAMP and relax bronchial smooth muscle; inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide or fluticasone, which suppress NF-kappaB–dependent inflammatory gene transcription; antimuscarinics such as ipratropium or tiotropium, which block M3 receptor-mediated bronchoconstriction; and, in selected phenotypes, leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast. Wheezing may coexist with allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, gastroesophageal reflux, obesity, sinus disease, sleep apnea, and smoking-related lung disease, and complications include status asthmaticus, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, respiratory failure, recurrent exacerbations, and impaired quality of life. Clinical manifestations include episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnea, prolonged expiration, and accessory muscle use. Subtypes include diffuse versus localized, inspiratory versus expiratory, and recurrent viral, atopic, occupational, or exercise-induced patterns. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, supported by auscultation, spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, peak-flow variability, methacholine challenge, pulse oximetry, chest imaging when indicated, allergy testing

Name: Wounds
Description: Wounds are disruptions of skin or deeper tissue integrity caused by mechanical, thermal, chemical, ischemic, infectious, or surgical injury; they are commonly classified as acute or chronic and further subdivided into incisional, laceration, abrasion, puncture, burn, pressure, venous, arterial, and diabetic foot wounds. Their biology is governed by hemostatic, inflammatory, proliferative, and remodeling programs involving platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts, keratinocytes, endothelial cells, and extracellular matrix, with key pathways including coagulation and fibrinolysis, TGF-β/SMAD, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, PDGF/EGFR signaling, Wnt/β-catenin, HIF-1α hypoxia signaling, NF-κB/TNF/IL-1 inflammatory cascades, and matrix turnover mediated by MMP2, MMP9, TIMPs, COL1A1, COL3A1, FN1, TGFB1, VEGFA, FGF2, EGF, CTNNB1, TP53, NOS2, and integrins; impaired repair may reflect excessive protease activity, biofilm, ischemia, or inherited connective-tissue defects such as COL3A1-related vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, COL7A1 epidermolysis bullosa, or coagulation disorders including F8/F9 deficiency. Clinical features include pain, bleeding, erythema, edema, exudate, tissue loss, delayed granulation and epithelialization, necrosis, malodor, and impaired function, while diagnosis relies on history and examination of size, depth, undermining, perfusion, neuropathy, and infection, supplemented as indicated by ankle-brachial index, Doppler or vascular imaging, probe-to-bone testing, wound culture or tissue biopsy, inflammatory markers, glucose/HbA1c, and biopsy for atypical or malignant ulcers. Common comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease, chronic venous insufficiency, neuropathy, obesity, malnutrition, smoking, renal failure, infection, cellulitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis, gangrene, hypertrophic scar, and chronic pain. Name: Xerostomia
Description: Xerostomia is the subjective sensation of dry mouth, usually reflecting salivary gland hypofunction but sometimes occurring despite near-normal flow, and it may be primary, medication-induced, radiation-induced, autoimmune, metabolic, neurogenic, or age-associated. Core symptoms and signs include oral dryness, thirst, difficulty chewing, swallowing and speaking, nocturnal waking to drink, burning mouth, dysgeusia, stringy saliva, mucosal erythema, fissured tongue, angular cheilitis, and increased dental caries, candidiasis, periodontal disease, halitosis, and impaired denture retention. Major comorbidities include Sjögren syndrome, diabetes mellitus, depression and anxiety, Parkinson disease, head and neck cancer after radiotherapy, chronic kidney disease, hepatitis C, and HIV infection. Molecularly, xerostomia is most clearly linked to autoimmune and gland-injury pathways: lymphocytic infiltration with B-cell activation, interferon signaling, TNF, IL-6, BAFF, and NF-κB; cholinergic muscarinic M3 receptor signaling, AQP5-mediated water transport, and acinar calcium-dependent secretion are key components. Representative associated genes and proteins, especially in Sjögren-related xerostomia, include HLA-DR and HLA-DQ alleles, IRF5, STAT4, BLK, CXCR5, TNFAIP3, AQP5, MUC7, and autoantigens Ro/SSA and La/SSB; inheritance is usually complex polygenic susceptibility rather than Mendelian, although rare monogenic salivary gland developmental disorders can contribute to congenital hypofunction. Common treatments include pilocarpine, a muscarinic receptor agonist that stimulates residual exocrine secretion; cevimeline, an M1/M3-preferring muscarinic agonist; and saliva substitutes containing carboxymethylcellulose or glycerol that provide lubrication rather than gland stimulation; adjuncts may include topical fluoride and antifungals to prevent complications. Diagnosis is clinical but supported by medication and radiation history, oral examination, unstimulated and stimulated sialometry, salivary gland ultrasound or scintigraphy, and, when autoimmune disease is suspected, anti-SSA/SSB serology and minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.

Name: Yaws
Description: Yaws (MeSH D015001) is a chronic, relapsing, nonvenereal endemic treponematosis caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, a spirochete whose pathogenic repertoire overlaps with syphilis and includes outer membrane/adhesin proteins and immunogenic antigens such as Tp0136, Tp0751, and the highly variable Tpr family, while host susceptibility is shaped mainly by inflammatory and innate immune genes rather than Mendelian inheritance, with representative associations reported for HLA class II loci, TNF, IL10, TLR1/2, and IFNG pathways. Disease biology is dominated by spirochetal attachment, dissemination, and immune evasion, with activation of TLR2-mediated innate signaling, macrophage and dendritic-cell responses, Th1/Th17 cytokine networks, and plasma-cell-rich inflammation causing tissue injury. It is acquired by skin-to-skin contact, usually in children in tropical settings, and progresses through primary yaws, characterized by a papillomatous “mother yaw” or ulcer at the inoculation site, secondary yaws with multiple papillomas, hyperkeratosis, widespread skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, and painful periostitis/osteitis, and late destructive disease with gummatous lesions, gangosa, and sabre tibia. Important complications include chronic ulceration, secondary bacterial superinfection, osteoarticular deformity, disability, stigma, and coinfections common in endemic poverty-associated settings. Diagnosis rests on compatible epidemiology and examination plus serology, typically a reactive treponemal test such as TPPA/TPHA or rapid treponemal assay together with a nontreponemal test such as RPR or VDRL for activity and treatment response; dark-field microscopy is rarely used, and PCR targeting treponemal genes such as polA or tpr loci from lesions helps confirmation and distinction from Haemophilus ducreyi ulcers. Treatment is usually azithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis, or benzathine benzylpenicillin/penicillin G, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, may be used when macrolides or penicillin are unsuitable, and macrolide resistance can arise through 23S rRNA

Name: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome
Description: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a rare neuroendocrine disorder caused by gastrin-secreting tumors, usually duodenal or pancreatic gastrinomas, that drive marked gastric acid hypersecretion and severe peptic ulcer disease; it occurs sporadically or as an autosomal dominant manifestation of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 due to germline MEN1 mutations encoding menin, with less frequent association with alterations affecting cell-cycle and neuroendocrine tumor biology such as CDKN1B, ATRX, DAXX, and mTOR-pathway genes in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. Pathobiologically, excess gastrin activates the cholecystokinin B/gastrin receptor on enterochromaffin-like and parietal cells, stimulating histamine release, H+/K+-ATPase activity, and proliferative signaling through MAPK/ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, calcium, and cAMP-linked pathways. Clinically, patients present with refractory or multiple peptic ulcers, gastroesophageal reflux, abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, nausea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and weight loss; complications include ulcer perforation, strictures, malabsorption, esophagitis, and metastatic spread, especially to liver and lymph nodes. Major subtypes include sporadic versus MEN1-associated disease and localized versus metastatic gastrinoma. Diagnosis is based on fasting hypergastrinemia, typically with gastric pH 2 or less or elevated basal acid output, exclusion of proton pump inhibitor effect or achlorhydria, and provocative secretin testing showing a paradoxical rise in gastrin; chromogranin A may be elevated, and localization uses endoscopic ultrasound, multiphasic CT or MRI, somatostatin receptor imaging such as 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT, and sometimes selective arterial secretagogue testing. Treatment centers on proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, pantoprazole, or esomeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion; somatostatin analogs such as octreotide suppress gastrin release via somatostatin receptors; and selected patients may undergo surgical resection or receive targeted systemic therapy including everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor.

Name: Lymphoma, T-Cell, Cutaneous
Description: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL; MeSH D016410) is a heterogeneous group of primary skin-homing non-Hodgkin lymphomas, classically including mycosis fungoides, Sézary syndrome, primary cutaneous CD30-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, and rarer variants such as gamma-delta and subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma, characterized by malignant mature T cells, usually CD4-positive memory T cells, infiltrating the skin and sometimes blood, lymph nodes, and viscera. Recurrent molecular abnormalities involve T-cell receptor/NF-kB signaling, JAK/STAT activation, PI3K-AKT-mTOR and MAPK pathways, impaired apoptosis, and epigenetic dysregulation, with representative alterations in STAT3, STAT5B, PLCG1, CARD11, TNFRSF1B, DNMT3A, TET2, ARID1A, TP53, FAS, CDKN2A, and occasional PD-1/PD-L1 axis activation; overexpression of CCR4, KIR3DL2, TOX, GATA3, and IL2RA may support tumor survival and trafficking. Most cases are sporadic rather than inherited, although rare predisposition may reflect variants affecting immune regulation or DNA repair, and familial clustering is uncommon. Patients typically present with chronic pruritic patches, plaques, tumors, erythroderma, poikiloderma, alopecia, palmoplantar keratoderma, lymphadenopathy, or circulating Sézary cells, and complications include secondary skin infection, immunosuppression, large-cell transformation, extracutaneous dissemination, and increased risk of other hematologic malignancies. Diagnosis integrates clinicopathologic correlation, repeated skin biopsy showing epidermotropic atypical cerebriform T cells or dermal infiltrates, immunophenotyping with aberrant loss of pan-T-cell markers such as CD7 or CD26, flow cytometry of blood, T-cell receptor gene rearrangement clonality studies, and stage-defining imaging and hematologic assessment. Treatment commonly includes skin-directed therapy for limited disease and systemic agents for advanced disease, such as bexarotene, a retinoid X receptor agonist; methotrexate, an antifolate inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase; vorinostat or romidepsin, histone deacetylase inhibitors; mogamulizumab, an anti

Name: Lymphoma, T-Cell, Peripheral
Description: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) is a heterogeneous group of aggressive mature post-thymic non-Hodgkin lymphomas derived from peripheral T cells or NK/T-cell lineages, encompassing major subtypes such as PTCL, not otherwise specified, angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma including ALK-positive and ALK-negative forms, extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, and enteropathy-associated intestinal T-cell lymphoma. Recurrent genetic lesions involve T-cell receptor signaling and epigenetic regulation, with representative abnormalities including ALK rearrangements, especially NPM1-ALK, DUSP22 or TP63 rearrangements, RHOA G17V, TET2, DNMT3A, IDH2, PLCG1, CD28, VAV1, STAT3, STAT5B, JAK1, JAK3, TP53, and FAS; protein overexpression of CD30 is characteristic in many ALCLs. Key pathogenic pathways include aberrant TCR/NF-kB signaling, JAK/STAT activation, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, immune-checkpoint dysregulation, apoptosis escape, and epigenetic remodeling. Most cases are sporadic rather than Mendelian, although inherited predisposition is uncommon and may relate to immune dysregulation or celiac disease in enteropathy-associated forms; viral association is important in EBV-driven NK/T-cell lymphoma. Typical presentation includes generalized lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, extranodal disease involving skin, marrow, liver, spleen, gastrointestinal tract or nasal cavity, rash, pruritus, effusions, cytopenias, eosinophilia, and sometimes hemophagocytic syndrome; complications include infections, marrow failure, thromboembolism, intestinal perforation, and transformation or relapse. Diagnosis relies on excisional biopsy with histopathology, immunophenotyping by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry for markers such as CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD30, ALK, T-follicular helper markers, and Ki-67, supported by TCR gene rearrangement studies, FISH or PCR for rearrangements, next-generation sequencing, EBV testing, and PET/CT with marrow evaluation for staging. Treatment commonly includes CHOP-like chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone,

Name: Tachyarrhythmia
Description: Tachycardia (MeSH D013610) is a cardiac rhythm disorder defined by an abnormally rapid heart rate, generally exceeding 100 beats/min in adults, arising either physiologically or from dysregulation of impulse formation or conduction within the sinoatrial node, atria, atrioventricular node, or ventricles; major subtypes include sinus tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardias such as atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, AV nodal reentrant tachycardia and AV reentrant tachycardia, and ventricular tachycardia. Genetic susceptibility is best established in inherited arrhythmia syndromes and conduction disorders, with representative variants in SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNH2, RYR2, CASQ2, LMNA, and PKP2 affecting cardiac sodium, potassium, and calcium handling proteins, including NaV1.5, hERG, Kv7.1, ryanodine receptor 2, calsequestrin 2, lamin A/C, and plakophilin-2; inheritance may be autosomal dominant in long-QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, and autosomal recessive in some CASQ2-related disease. Key mechanisms involve sympathetic beta-adrenergic signaling, cAMP-PKA–mediated calcium cycling, abnormal automaticity, triggered activity from delayed afterdepolarizations, and reentry circuits dependent on AV nodal or myocardial conduction pathways. Patients typically present with palpitations, rapid pulse, chest discomfort, dyspnea, dizziness, anxiety, presyncope, or syncope, while complications include hypotension, heart failure, ischemia, thromboembolism and stroke in atrial tachyarrhythmias, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. Common comorbidities include coronary artery disease, structural heart disease, hypertension, hyperthyroidism, electrolyte disturbances, anemia, infection, and stimulant or drug exposure. Diagnosis relies on history, physical examination, ECG and rhythm-strip documentation, ambulatory monitoring, electrophysiology study when indicated, echocardiography, thyroid and electrolyte testing, troponin in selected cases, and genetic testing in suspected inherited syndromes. Name: Granuloma Annulare
Description: Granuloma annulare (UMLS C0085074) is a usually benign, noninfectious, inflammatory granulomatous dermatosis characterized clinically by flesh-colored to erythematous papules coalescing into annular plaques, most often on the dorsal hands, feet, wrists, or ankles, with localized, generalized/disseminated, subcutaneous, perforating, and patch variants recognized; lesions are often asymptomatic or mildly pruritic, whereas generalized disease may be persistent and cosmetically burdensome. Its pathobiology is incompletely defined but is thought to reflect a delayed-type, T cell/macrophage-mediated reaction with collagen degeneration and mucin deposition, involving TNF, IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-12/23, and JAK-STAT-related signaling, with activated histiocytes and matrix remodeling enzymes such as MMPs implicated; no single causative mutation is established, inheritance is not Mendelian, and most cases are sporadic, although occasional familial clustering and associations with HLA haplotypes and rare reports in monogenic immune dysregulation suggest a genetic susceptibility background rather than a defined inherited disorder. Reported comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, autoimmune thyroid disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and less consistently malignancy or chronic infections, while complications are mainly chronicity, recurrence, dyspigmentation, or scarring in perforating disease. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by skin biopsy showing palisading or interstitial granulomatous dermatitis with necrobiotic collagen and dermal mucin, highlighted by Alcian blue or colloidal iron stains; evaluation may include glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile, and selected screening for mimics such as tinea, sarcoidosis, or necrobiosis lipoidica. Treatment is often unnecessary for localized disease, but commonly used therapies include topical or intralesional corticosteroids, which suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription and leukocyte infiltration, hydroxychloroquine, which impairs lysosomal antigen processing and toll-like receptor signaling, and phototherapy such as NB-UVB or PUVA, which induces cutaneous immunomodulation and T-cell apoptosis; refractory generalized cases may respond to dapsone, retinoids, methotrexate, apremilast, or TNF inhibitors such as adalimumab.

Name: Peripheral Vascular Diseases
Description: Peripheral vascular diseases are a heterogeneous group of arterial, venous, and lymphatic disorders affecting the extracardiac circulation, most commonly peripheral arterial disease caused by atherosclerotic obstruction of lower-extremity arteries, but also including thromboangiitis obliterans, vasculitic occlusive disease, chronic venous insufficiency, deep venous thrombosis, lymphedema, aneurysmal disease, and hereditary arteriopathies. Their molecular basis is usually multifactorial, involving endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, thrombosis, and maladaptive vascular remodeling, with key pathways including nitric oxide/eNOS signaling, VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, hypoxia-inducible factor signaling, TGF-β, NF-κB, platelet activation through COX-1/thromboxane A2 and P2Y12, coagulation cascades, matrix metalloproteinases, and renin-angiotensin signaling; representative genetic contributors include variants in LPA, MTHFR, F5 Leiden, F2 G20210A, SERPINE1, NOS3, APOE, PCSK9, and LDLR, while specific inherited subtypes include vascular Ehlers-Danlos from COL3A1 mutations, Marfan syndrome from FBN1, CADASIL from NOTCH3, and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia from ENG or ACVRL1, with inheritance often complex/polygenic but sometimes autosomal dominant. Typical manifestations include intermittent claudication, rest pain, diminished pulses, cool extremities, bruits, nonhealing ulcers, color change, edema, varicosities, and in severe cases tissue loss or gangrene. Major comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking-related disease, coronary and cerebrovascular atherosclerosis, infection, acute limb ischemia, aneurysm rupture, venous thromboembolism, and amputation. Diagnosis relies on vascular history and examination plus ankle-brachial index, duplex ultrasonography, toe pressures, venous Doppler, CT or MR angiography, catheter angiography, pulse-volume recordings, and selected laboratory thrombophilia, inflammatory, lipid, and glucose testing.
