Name: Seasonal Affective Disorder
Description: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD; UMLS C0085159) is a recurrent mood disorder, usually considered a specifier or subtype of major depressive disorder or bipolar disorder, characterized by seasonal onset and remission, most commonly winter-pattern depression with atypical features, though a rarer summer-pattern form occurs. Its biology implicates circadian, serotonergic, dopaminergic, and melatonergic mechanisms, with genetic associations reported for clock and monoamine-related genes such as SLC6A4, HTR2A, TPH2, MAOA, COMT, PER2, ARNTL/BMAL1, CLOCK, and melatonin pathway genes including MTNR1A/MTNR1B, although no single mutation is determinative and inheritance appears complex, polygenic, and influenced by latitude and light exposure. Relevant pathways include retinal light input through melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, regulation of pineal melatonin secretion, circadian clock transcriptional feedback loops, and downstream serotonin and dopamine signaling affecting mood, sleep, appetite, and energy. Typical symptoms include depressed mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia, fatigue, psychomotor slowing, increased appetite, carbohydrate craving, weight gain, impaired concentration, and social withdrawal; complications include functional impairment, recurrent major depression, suicidal ideation, and bipolar switching. Comorbidities commonly include anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, substance misuse, obesity, and sleep-wake disorders. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 seasonal pattern criteria requiring a temporal relationship between mood episodes and a particular season for at least 2 years, seasonal remission, and a predominance of seasonal over nonseasonal episodes; assessment may be supported by structured psychiatric interview, depression scales such as the SIGH-SAD, sleep and circadian history, and exclusion of medical contributors such as hypothyroidism. Common treatments include bright light therapy, which phase-shifts circadian rhythms and suppresses melatonin; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as sertraline and fluoxetine, which increase synaptic serotonin; and bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor used both acutely and prophylactically.

Name: Vaginosis, Bacterial
Description: Bacterial vaginosis is a common, noninflammatory or only mildly inflammatory polymicrobial dysbiosis of the vagina characterized by loss of protective hydrogen peroxide- and lactic acid–producing Lactobacillus species, especially L. crispatus, and overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Atopobium vaginae, Mobiluncus, Prevotella, and BV-associated bacteria, often organized in adherent biofilm. Host susceptibility has no Mendelian inheritance pattern, but genetic components affecting innate immunity and mucosal defense have been associated, including variants or altered expression in TLR2, TLR4, IL1B, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, DEFB1, MBL2, and FCGR2A; corresponding proteins and pathways include Toll-like receptor–NF-κB signaling, inflammasome-linked cytokine release, chemokine-mediated neutrophil recruitment, defensin activity, and perturbation of epithelial barrier and vaginal glycogen/lactic acid homeostasis. Typical symptoms are thin homogeneous gray-white discharge, fishy amine odor often accentuated after intercourse or KOH testing, elevated vaginal pH greater than 4.5, and clue cells, although many patients are asymptomatic; pruritus, burning, and erythema are usually absent or mild. Clinical subtypes are commonly defined by symptomatic versus asymptomatic disease, recurrent BV, and biofilm-dominant or mixed anaerobic forms. Diagnosis is made by Amsel criteria, requiring at least 3 of 4 findings, or by Nugent Gram-stain scoring; adjunctive methods include NAAT panels for G. vaginalis, A. vaginae, BVAB, and Lactobacillus depletion. Standard therapy includes metronidazole, which after anaerobic reduction generates radicals that damage DNA; clindamycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor that suppresses bacterial protein synthesis; and tinidazole or secnidazole, nitroimidazoles with similar DNA-damaging mechanisms. BV is linked to recurrent vaginitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, post-gynecologic procedure infection, increased acquisition and transmission of HIV and other STIs, and adverse pregnancy outcomes including preterm birth, preterm premature rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, and postpartum endometritis.

Name: Alagille Syndrome
Description: Alagille syndrome (UMLS C0085280) is a multisystem, predominantly autosomal dominant developmental disorder characterized by paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts and chronic cholestasis, most commonly caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants or deletions in JAG1 and less often NOTCH2, implicating the Jagged1-Notch2 signaling pathway that regulates bile duct morphogenesis, vascular development, and cardiac, skeletal, ocular, and renal patterning through canonical Notch receptor cleavage and transcriptional activation. The phenotype includes neonatal or infantile jaundice, pruritus, xanthomas, hepatomegaly, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, growth failure, characteristic facies, posterior embryotoxon, butterfly vertebrae, and congenital heart disease, especially peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis and tetralogy of Fallot, with frequent renal anomalies and vascular abnormalities. Major complications include progressive liver fibrosis or cirrhosis, portal hypertension, intracranial or systemic bleeding from vascular malformations, chronic kidney disease, malnutrition, and reduced quality of life from severe pruritus. Classic and incomplete forms are recognized, with marked intrafamilial variability and occasional de novo mutations. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical features plus molecular confirmation of JAG1 or NOTCH2 variants by sequencing and deletion-duplication analysis, supported by liver biopsy showing bile duct paucity, cholestatic liver tests, echocardiography, spinal radiography, ophthalmologic examination, and renal and vascular imaging; historically, diagnosis often required bile duct paucity with at least three major extrahepatic features. Treatment is supportive and complication-directed: ursodeoxycholic acid increases hydrophilic bile acid flow to improve cholestasis; cholestyramine sequesters bile acids in the intestine to reduce pruritus; rifampin likely induces hepatic detoxification pathways and alters pruritogen handling; ileal bile acid transporter inhibitors such as maralixibat and odevixibat reduce enterohepatic bile acid reabsorption; and severe end-stage disease may require liver transplantation.

Name: Serratia Infections
Description: Serratia infections, classically caused by Serratia marcescens but also by S. liquefaciens and S. rubidaea, are opportunistic Gram-negative Enterobacterales infections that are predominantly healthcare-associated and manifest as catheter-associated urinary tract infection, pneumonia, bloodstream infection, wound and surgical-site infection, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and, less commonly, meningitis or neonatal sepsis. Disease severity reflects both bacterial virulence and host susceptibility: important bacterial determinants include chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase, outer-membrane porins, efflux systems, lipopolysaccharide, fimbriae, hemolysin ShlA/ShlB, phospholipase, prodigiosin, and biofilm-related genes such as fimA and bsmB; resistance mutations or acquired genes may involve ampC derepression, ESBLs including blaCTX-M and blaSHV, and carbapenemases such as blaKPC, blaNDM, or blaVIM. Relevant pathogenic pathways include TLR4/NF-kappaB-driven innate immune activation by LPS, complement and neutrophil responses, quorum sensing, adhesion and biofilm formation on indwelling devices, and beta-lactam resistance pathways mediated by AmpC induction or carbapenemase activity. Typical symptoms and signs depend on site of infection and include fever, leukocytosis, dysuria, flank pain, cough, dyspnea, purulent secretions, hypotension, and sepsis. Major comorbidities and risk factors include immunosuppression, diabetes, chronic lung disease, malignancy, renal failure, prematurity, prolonged hospitalization, ICU stay, prior broad-spectrum antibiotics, and urinary or vascular catheters, with complications including septic shock, abscess, metastatic infection, and multidrug resistance. Treatment is guided by susceptibility testing and commonly uses cefepime, a fourth-generation beta-lactam that inhibits cell-wall transpeptidases and is relatively stable to AmpC; meropenem, a carbapenem inhibiting penicillin-binding proteins with broad activity against resistant strains; piperacillin-tazobactam, combining cell-wall inhibition with beta-lactamase inhibition; or ciprofloxacin, which inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. These infections are not inherited disorders, but host genetic predisposition may influence risk, with examples including variants affecting TLR4

Name: POEMS Syndrome
Description: POEMS syndrome is a rare, multisystem paraneoplastic plasma-cell dyscrasia, usually considered a monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance rather than an inherited disorder, defined by the constellation of polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma-cell disorder, and skin changes. Its biology is driven less by recurrent germline mutations than by a clonal lambda-restricted plasma-cell population and marked cytokine dysregulation, particularly overproduction of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), with contributions from IL-6, TNF-α, and other inflammatory mediators that promote angiogenesis, microvascular permeability, edema, papilledema, thrombocytosis, and end-organ dysfunction; occasional plasma-cell neoplasia-associated events may involve immunoglobulin gene rearrangements and canonical myeloma lesions, but no specific inherited mutation is characteristic. Clinically, patients typically develop a progressive demyelinating sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with weakness and pain, extravascular volume overload, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, sclerotic bone lesions, endocrinopathies such as hypogonadism, thyroid dysfunction, glucose intolerance/diabetes, and adrenal abnormalities, along with hyperpigmentation, hemangiomas, clubbing, and white nails; Castleman disease may coexist, and complications include pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, thrombosis, renal impairment, and severe disability from neuropathy. Subtypes include classic POEMS and Castleman disease-associated variants, with isolated osteosclerotic plasmacytoma representing a related presentation. Diagnosis relies on established criteria requiring both mandatory features, polyneuropathy and a monoclonal plasma-cell proliferative disorder, plus additional major criteria such as elevated VEGF, sclerotic bone lesions, or Castleman disease, and minor criteria including organomegaly, edema, endocrinopathy, skin changes, papilledema, and thrombocytosis/polycythemia; evaluation uses serum and urine immunofixation, serum free light chains, VEGF measurement, nerve conduction studies, bone marrow biopsy, and CT/PET or skeletal imaging. Treatment commonly includes radiation for localized plasmacytoma, corticosteroids such as dexamethasone, alkylators such as melphalan or cyclophosphamide, immunomodulators such as lenalidomide or thalidomide, proteasome inhibition with bortezomib, and autolog

Name: Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant
Description: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD; UMLS C0085413) is a common inherited ciliopathy characterized by progressive bilateral renal cyst formation, kidney enlargement, and gradual loss of renal function, most often caused by pathogenic variants in PKD1 encoding polycystin-1 or PKD2 encoding polycystin-2, with rarer genetically similar phenotypes involving GANAB, DNAJB11, ALG9, ALG5, IFT140, or SEC63; disease severity is generally greater and earlier in PKD1 than PKD2. Defective polycystin signaling at the primary cilium disrupts intracellular calcium flux, increases cAMP, and promotes abnormal proliferation, chloride-driven fluid secretion, planar cell polarity defects, and fibrosis through pathways including vasopressin V2 receptor signaling, mTOR, MAPK/ERK, JAK/STAT, Wnt, AMPK, EGFR, and TGF-β. Typical manifestations include hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, hematuria, nephrolithiasis, recurrent urinary tract infection, declining estimated GFR, and palpable enlarged kidneys, with common extrarenal features such as hepatic cysts, pancreatic cysts, intracranial berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, abdominal wall hernia, and colonic diverticulosis; major complications include chronic kidney disease, end-stage kidney disease, cyst hemorrhage or infection, and cardiovascular morbidity. Subtypes are chiefly PKD1-ADPKD and PKD2-ADPKD, with allelic and modifier effects contributing to variable expressivity; inheritance is autosomal dominant, though de novo variants and occasional mosaicism occur. Diagnosis relies on family history, age-specific imaging criteria by ultrasound, with CT or MRI for greater sensitivity and total kidney volume assessment, plus molecular testing by multigene panels or targeted PKD1/PKD2 sequencing when imaging is equivocal or for at-risk relatives. Treatment is supportive and disease-modifying: tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, lowers cAMP and slows cyst growth; ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril and ARBs such as losartan control hypertension and reduce renin-angiotensin signaling; thiazide or loop diuretics may assist blood pressure and volume control; antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones are used for cyst infection.

Name: Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections
Description: Gram-negative bacterial infections are a heterogeneous group of infectious diseases caused by organisms with an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide, including Enterobacterales such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, nonfermenters such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii, and fastidious species such as Neisseria meningitidis; syndromic subtypes include urinary tract infection, pneumonia, intra-abdominal infection, bacteremia/sepsis, meningitis, and sexually transmitted infection. Clinical manifestations vary by focus but commonly include fever, chills, leukocytosis, dysuria, cough, purulent sputum, abdominal pain, hypotension, rash, and organ dysfunction, with major complications including septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, renal failure, and metastatic abscesses; common comorbidities are diabetes, chronic lung disease, cirrhosis, malignancy, neutropenia, indwelling devices, burns, and immunosuppression. Pathobiology centers on host recognition of LPS by LBP-CD14-TLR4-MD2, activation of MyD88/TRIF, NF-κB, MAPK, inflammasome and complement pathways, and cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6, while microbial virulence and resistance determinants include beta-lactamases blaTEM, blaSHV, blaCTX-M, carbapenemases blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48, P. aeruginosa exotoxin A, and porin or efflux alterations; host susceptibility is largely non-Mendelian, but variants in TLR4, CD14, MBL2, CFTR, and NADPH oxidase genes can modify risk or severity. Diagnosis relies on compatible syndrome plus microbiologic confirmation by Gram stain and culture from blood or site-specific specimens, susceptibility testing, and increasingly PCR or multiplex panels for pathogen and resistance genes, with inflammatory markers and imaging used to define extent. Treatment depends on source and resistance profile and commonly includes beta-lactams such as ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall cross-linking, carbapenems such as meropenem with broad PBP-mediated bactericidal activity, fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin inhibiting DNA gyrase/topoisomer

Name: Meningitis, Cryptococcal
Description: Cryptococcal meningitis is a life-threatening fungal infection of the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, usually caused by Cryptococcus neoformans and less often C. gattii, classically presenting as subacute or chronic meningoencephalitis with headache, fever, nausea, vomiting, malaise, photophobia, neck stiffness, cranial neuropathies, altered mental status, seizures, and raised intracranial pressure; pulmonary or disseminated cryptococcosis may coexist. Major disease subsets include HIV-associated disease, transplant- or corticosteroid-associated disease, other non-HIV immunocompromised cases, and relatively immunocompetent hosts, especially with C. gattii. Host susceptibility is strongly influenced by cell-mediated immunity and genetic defects rather than Mendelian inheritance of the infection itself; implicated genes and proteins include CD4, IFNG, IFNGR1, IL12RB1, STAT1 gain-of-function, GATA2, ADA2/CECR1, CSF2/GM-CSF with anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies, Fc gamma receptors, TLR2, TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, mannose-binding lectin, HLA variants, and HIV-mediated CD4 depletion. Key pathways involve Th1 and Th17 immunity, macrophage and microglial fungicidal activity, pattern-recognition receptor signaling, JAK-STAT responses to IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha and IL-12/IL-23 axes, complement and opsonophagocytosis, and in some cases damaging immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after antiretroviral initiation. Standard therapy uses amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores, plus flucytosine, a pyrimidine analogue that inhibits fungal DNA and RNA synthesis, followed by fluconazole, a CYP51/14-alpha-demethylase inhibitor that blocks ergosterol biosynthesis; alternatives include liposomal amphotericin B, voriconazole, and itraconazole. Important comorbidities and complications include AIDS, solid-organ transplantation, sarcoidosis, hematologic malignancy, diabetes, hydrocephalus, vision or hearing loss, stroke, persistent cognitive deficits, relapse, and death. Diagnosis rests on CSF cryptococcal antigen testing, India ink or fungal stain, culture, blood antigenemia, lumbar puncture with elevated opening pressure and lymph

Name: Meningitis, Bacterial
Description: Bacterial meningitis is an acute, life-threatening pyogenic infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae, group B Streptococcus, Listeria monocytogenes, and gram-negative bacilli; clinically it presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status, vomiting, seizures, and sometimes petechial or purpuric rash in meningococcemia, and major subtypes are classified by pathogen, age group, and community- versus healthcare-associated disease. Pathogenesis reflects bacterial adhesion and blood-brain barrier invasion followed by innate immune activation through TLR2, TLR4, and NOD signaling, NF-κB and MAPK pathway induction, complement activation, and cytokine release including TNF, IL1B, and IL6, with matrix metalloproteinases, endothelial injury, leukocyte influx, cerebral edema, vasculitis, and neuronal damage; representative host susceptibility genes/proteins include terminal complement components C5-C9 and properdin, CFH, MBL2, TLR4, NFKBIA, and cytokine variants, while MYD88 or IRAK4 defects predispose particularly to invasive pneumococcal disease, and asplenia or cochlear malformations are important non-Mendelian risk states. Treatment relies on rapid empiric antibiotics such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins, vancomycin, a glycopeptide blocking cell-wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala termini, and ampicillin, a beta-lactam added for Listeria coverage; meropenem and rifampin are additional options, and adjunctive dexamethasone suppresses inflammatory cytokine signaling. Complications include septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hydrocephalus, stroke, brain abscess, hearing loss, cranial neuropathies, cognitive impairment, and epilepsy; diagnosis is based on urgent lumbar puncture with CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose, Gram stain and culture, multiplex PCR/antigen testing, blood cultures, and neuroimaging when raised intracranial pressure or focal deficits are suspected.

Name: Meningitis, Fungal
Description: Fungal meningitis is an invasive infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid caused most commonly by Cryptococcus neoformans or C. gattii, but also by Candida, Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Aspergillus, and, rarely, Mucorales; major subtypes therefore include cryptococcal, coccidioidal, candidal, histoplasmal, and aspergillary meningitis, with acute, subacute, or chronic presentations. Disease pathobiology reflects impaired host antifungal immunity, especially defects in innate recognition and Th1/Th17 signaling pathways involving Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, IL-12/IFN-gamma, GM-CSF, TNF, IL-17, and JAK-STAT components; representative genetic susceptibility factors include HIV-associated CD4 depletion, anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies, and rare inherited variants in CARD9, STAT1 gain-of-function, IL12RB1, IFNGR1, GATA2, and CXCR4, although most cases are acquired rather than classically inherited. Typical symptoms are headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, cranial neuropathies, altered mental status, seizures, and signs of raised intracranial pressure, often with hydrocephalus in cryptococcosis. Important comorbidities include AIDS, transplantation, hematologic malignancy, corticosteroid or biologic immunosuppression, diabetes, cirrhosis, and pregnancy for coccidioidomycosis; complications include cerebral infarction, abscess, ventriculitis, vision or hearing loss, and death. Diagnosis relies on CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose, opening pressure elevation, fungal culture, cryptococcal antigen testing, India ink in selected settings, CSF/serum beta-D-glucan in some non-cryptococcal cases, Coccidioides or Histoplasma serology/antigen assays, PCR where available, and brain imaging before lumbar puncture when mass effect is suspected. Treatment commonly uses amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores, often with flucytosine, a pyrimidine analog inhibiting fungal DNA/RNA synthesis, followed by fluconazole, an azole that inhibits lanosterol

Name: Essential Hypertension
Description: Essential hypertension is a chronic, multifactorial elevation of systemic arterial pressure without a single identifiable secondary cause, typically classified into stage 1 and stage 2 disease and sometimes into low-renin, salt-sensitive, obesity-related, or isolated systolic phenotypes; it is usually asymptomatic for years, but patients may present with headache, dizziness, palpitations, epistaxis, or be identified by persistently elevated office, home, or ambulatory blood pressure. Its genetic architecture is predominantly complex and polygenic, with heritability commonly estimated at 30%–50%, arising from common variants and occasional rare variants affecting renal sodium handling, vascular tone, and neurohormonal regulation; representative genes include ACE, AGT, AGTR1, REN, NOS3, ADD1, CYP11B2, SCNN1B/SCNN1G, WNK1, and SLC12A3, while monogenic hypertensive syndromes with Mendelian inheritance, such as Liddle syndrome or glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, illustrate specific pathogenic mechanisms. Core pathways involve the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system activation, endothelial nitric oxide dysfunction, oxidative stress, vascular inflammation, calcium signaling in vascular smooth muscle, and renal pressure-natriuresis impairment. Common treatments include thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide, which inhibit the distal tubular Na+/Cl− cotransporter; ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril, which reduce angiotensin II generation; angiotensin receptor blockers such as losartan, which block AT1 receptors; calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine, which inhibit L-type calcium channels; and beta-blockers such as metoprolol, which reduce cardiac output and renin release. Major comorbidities and complications include obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke, peripheral arterial disease, retinopathy, and hypertensive nephrosclerosis. Diagnosis relies on repeated standardized blood pressure measurements, confirmation with ambulatory or home monitoring, and evaluation for target-organ damage and secondary causes using serum creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, glucose or HbA1c, lipids, ECG, and selected endocrine or renal testing when clinically indicated.

Name: Liver Failure
Description: Liver failure (MeSH D017093) is a life-threatening clinical syndrome of severe hepatocellular dysfunction causing loss of synthetic, detoxifying, and excretory capacity, occurring as acute liver failure, acute-on-chronic liver failure, or end-stage chronic liver failure/cirrhosis, with manifestations including jaundice, coagulopathy, hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, edema, fatigue, nausea, pruritus, fetor hepaticus, gastrointestinal bleeding, and hepatorenal or hepatopulmonary complications. Major causes include viral hepatitis, alcohol-associated and metabolic steatohepatitis, ischemic or toxic injury, autoimmune cholangiopathic disease, and inherited disorders; genetic contributors include HFE mutations in hereditary hemochromatosis, ATP7B in Wilson disease, SERPINA1 in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and variants in PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 that increase steatohepatitis and cirrhosis risk, while some pediatric or mitochondrial forms involve POLG or urea-cycle genes. Pathobiology centers on hepatocyte death, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, bile acid toxicity, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, with prominent TNF-alpha/NF-kB, IL-6/JAK-STAT, TGF-beta/SMAD, inflammasome, and stellate-cell fibrogenic pathways, plus impaired ammonia metabolism and cerebral astrocyte swelling in encephalopathy. Commonly used therapies are etiology- and complication-directed: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and improves redox balance, especially in acetaminophen toxicity; lactulose acidifies colonic contents and lowers systemic ammonia; rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria; diuretics such as spironolactone and furosemide promote natriuresis for ascites; and antivirals such as tenofovir suppress hepatitis B polymerase. Comorbidities and complications include portal hypertension, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, variceal hemorrhage, renal failure, sepsis, malnutrition, diabetes, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis relies on clinical context plus markedly abnormal aminotransferases or cholestatic tests, elevated bilirubin, prolonged INR, low albumin, hyperammonemia, thrombocytopenia, imaging for cirrhosis or vascular obstruction, etiologic serologies, toxicology, autoimmune and metabolic panels, and, when needed

Name: Urinary urgency
Description: Urinary urgency (UMLS C0085606) is a symptom complex characterized by a sudden compelling desire to void that is difficult to defer, most commonly reflecting overactive bladder or detrusor overactivity, but it may also occur with urinary tract infection, bladder outlet obstruction, interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, neurogenic bladder, and pelvic floor dysfunction. Clinically it presents with abrupt urgency, often accompanied by frequency, nocturia, urge incontinence, small voided volumes, and sometimes suprapubic discomfort, while complications include falls in older adults, sleep disturbance, recurrent infection, skin breakdown, anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life; common comorbidities include benign prostatic hyperplasia, diabetes, obesity, stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, and pelvic organ prolapse. Molecular contributors are heterogeneous rather than monogenic, but implicated genes and proteins include cholinergic signaling components CHRM2 and CHRM3, adrenergic receptor ADRB3, TRPV1 and TRPV4 mechanosensory channels, purinergic receptors such as P2RX3, nerve growth factor, TACR1/substance P pathways, connexins including GJA1, and contractile proteins such as ROCK and myosin light-chain kinase; rare inherited predisposition is polygenic and sometimes linked to neurologic disorders rather than isolated urgency. Relevant pathways include parasympathetic acetylcholine-M3 signaling, sympathetic beta3-adrenergic relaxation, urothelial ATP-purinergic afferent signaling, TRP-mediated sensory transduction, and central inhibitory circuits involving pontine and sacral micturition networks. Treatment commonly uses antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin, tolterodine, and solifenacin, which inhibit M3-predominant detrusor contraction; mirabegron and vibegron activate beta3 receptors to relax detrusor smooth muscle during storage; and onabotulinumtoxinA blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release in refractory cases. Diagnosis is clinical and etiologic, based on history, bladder diary, physical examination, urinalysis and culture, postvoid residual measurement, medication review, and targeted testing such as uroflowmetry, urodynamics, cystoscopy, pelvic examination, or neurologic evaluation when red flags, hematuria, pain, obstruction, or neurogenic disease are suspected.

Name: Sinus Bradycardia
Description: Sinus bradycardia (UMLS C0085610) is a cardiac rhythm disorder defined by reduced sinus node automaticity producing a resting sinus rate typically below 60 beats/min in adults, physiologic in athletes and sleep but pathologic when due to intrinsic sinus node dysfunction or extrinsic vagal, metabolic, toxic, or ischemic influences. Symptoms range from none to fatigue, exercise intolerance, dizziness, presyncope, syncope, dyspnea, chest discomfort, hypotension, and confusion; ECG shows a regular sinus rhythm with slow rate, upright P waves in lead II, and normal P-wave morphology, while ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, atropine response, electrophysiologic studies, echocardiography, thyroid and electrolyte testing, and medication review help confirm diagnosis and cause. Major subtypes include physiologic sinus bradycardia, drug-induced bradycardia, reflex/vagally mediated bradycardia, and sinus node dysfunction/sick sinus syndrome, including bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome. Molecularly, disease may involve impaired pacemaker “funny” current and calcium-clock signaling, with genes such as HCN4, SCN5A, CACNA1D, RYR2, ANK2, LMNA, MYH6, and GNB2 implicated in familial forms; relevant proteins and pathways include HCN4 channels, Nav1.5, L-type calcium channels, ryanodine receptor–mediated sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ cycling, autonomic muscarinic M2-Gi signaling, and cAMP/PKA regulation of sinoatrial nodal firing. Inheritance is most often sporadic, but autosomal dominant familial sinus node disease is well described, for example with HCN4 or SCN5A variants. Common associations include coronary artery disease, inferior myocardial infarction, myocarditis, hypothyroidism, sleep apnea, electrolyte disorders, increased intracranial pressure, aging-related fibrosis, and concomitant atrial fibrillation; complications include recurrent syncope, heart failure exacerbation, chronotropic incompetence, falls, and rarely sudden death when part of broader conduction disease. Acute treatment may use atropine, a muscarinic antagonist that reduces vagal inhibition, epinephrine or dopamine, beta-adrenergic agonists that increase chronotropy via cAMP, and definitive management for persistent symptomatic disease is often permanent pacemaker implantation after

Name: Ventricular Arrhythmia
Description: Ventricular arrhythmia is a heterogeneous group of rhythm disorders arising from abnormal impulse formation or reentry within the ventricular myocardium, ranging from isolated premature ventricular complexes to sustained ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, and it may occur in structurally normal hearts or with ischemic, inflammatory, inherited, or cardiomyopathic substrates. Typical manifestations include palpitations, presyncope or syncope, dizziness, chest discomfort, dyspnea, hemodynamic collapse, and sudden cardiac death; major complications include heart failure, recurrent arrest, thromboembolism in selected settings, and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Important genetic contributors include ion-channel and desmosomal genes such as KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A, RYR2, CASQ2, KCNE1/2, DSP, PKP2, DSG2, and LMNA, with representative syndromic associations including long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy; inheritance is commonly autosomal dominant, although autosomal recessive forms occur, for example with CASQ2-related CPVT or Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome. Pathobiology centers on altered sodium, potassium, and calcium handling, impaired repolarization, triggered activity from delayed afterdepolarizations, reentry through scar or fibrofatty replacement, beta-adrenergic signaling, CaMKII activation, gap-junction dysfunction involving connexin-43, and structural remodeling in ischemia or cardiomyopathy. Common treatments include beta-blockers such as propranolol or nadolol, which blunt sympathetic-triggered automaticity and calcium overload; amiodarone, which predominantly blocks potassium channels but also sodium and calcium channels and beta receptors; lidocaine or mexiletine, class Ib sodium-channel blockers; and sotalol, which combines beta blockade with class III potassium-channel blockade. Diagnosis relies on ECG criteria, ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, echocardiography, cardiac MRI, electrophysiology study, ischemia evaluation, serum electrolytes and troponin when appropriate, and targeted genetic testing in suspected inherited syndromes.

Name: Agitated
Description: Agitation, represented by UMLS C0085631, is a clinical syndrome or behavioral state rather than a single inherited disease, characterized by excessive psychomotor activity, inner tension, irritability, emotional dysregulation, aggression, restlessness, pressured speech, insomnia, autonomic arousal, and impaired impulse control; it occurs across subtypes such as acute undifferentiated agitation, psychotic agitation, manic agitation, delirium-related agitation, substance-induced agitation, dementia-related agitation, and agitation associated with autism or traumatic brain injury. Its biology is heterogeneous and commonly involves dysregulation of dopaminergic, serotonergic, noradrenergic, GABAergic, and glutamatergic signaling, with representative molecular contributors including DRD2, SLC6A4, COMT, MAOA, HTR2A, CACNA1C, BDNF, and inflammatory mediators such as IL6 and TNF; implicated pathways include mesolimbic dopamine signaling, 5-HT receptor signaling, NMDA/GABA excitation-inhibition balance, HPA-axis stress responses, and neuroinflammatory and circadian regulatory networks. Genetic liability is usually complex and polygenic, often reflecting the underlying disorder rather than agitation itself, although rare Mendelian neurodevelopmental syndromes may include agitation as a feature. Common comorbidities include schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, delirium, dementia, substance intoxication or withdrawal, PTSD, personality disorders, epilepsy, pain, infection, metabolic derangements, and endocrine disease; complications include violence, self-harm, falls, rhabdomyolysis, dehydration, hyperthermia, restraint-related injury, and cardiovascular events. Treatment commonly uses antipsychotics such as haloperidol, a D2 receptor antagonist, olanzapine, a D2/5-HT2A antagonist, and ziprasidone, a D2/5-HT2A antagonist with serotonergic reuptake effects, as well as benzodiazepines such as lorazepam, a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptors; valproate or dexmedetomidine may be used in selected settings. Diagnosis is clinical, based on observable agitation severity, mental-status examination, and etiology-focused assessment using tools such as the PANSS-EC, BARS, or RASS, supplemented by toxicology, CBC, electrolytes, renal/hepatic panels, ECG

Name: Edema, peripheral
Description: Peripheral edema is a clinical sign rather than a single disease, defined by excess interstitial fluid accumulation in dependent tissues, most often the legs, ankles, and feet, and it may be pitting or nonpitting, unilateral or bilateral, acute or chronic. Its biology reflects imbalance among capillary hydrostatic pressure, plasma oncotic pressure, endothelial permeability, lymphatic drainage, and renal sodium handling, with key pathways involving the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic activation, vasopressin, natriuretic peptides, VEGF-mediated vascular permeability, inflammatory cytokines, and lymphangiogenic VEGFC/VEGFR3 signaling. Genetic contributors are most clearly established in hereditary lymphedema and vascular permeability disorders, including FLT4/VEGFR3, FOXC2, GJC2, CCBE1, PIEZO1, PTPN14, EPHB4, RASA1, and FLCN, while SERPING1 mutations cause hereditary angioedema with episodic swelling; these are usually autosomal dominant, although recessive forms occur. Common causes and comorbidities include chronic venous insufficiency, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis with hypoalbuminemia, obesity, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, deep venous thrombosis, cellulitis, pulmonary hypertension, and medication effects such as calcium-channel blockers, NSAIDs, thiazolidinediones, corticosteroids, and estrogens. Typical findings are limb swelling, weight gain, tight skin, pitting, pain or heaviness, venous stasis changes, reduced mobility, and in lymphatic disease recurrent infection, fibrosis, and hyperkeratosis; major complications include venous ulceration, cellulitis, skin breakdown, compartment syndrome, and thromboembolism depending on etiology. Subtypes include venous edema, cardiac edema, renal edema, hepatic edema, lymphedema, lipedema-associated swelling, inflammatory edema, drug-induced edema, and angioedema. Diagnosis is clinical but etiologic evaluation uses examination, medication review, CBC, CMP, creatinine, albumin, urinalysis with protein quantification, BNP, liver and thyroid testing, venous duplex ultrasonography, echocardiography, lymphoscintigraphy or indocyanine green lymphography, and selective genetic testing. Name: Pyoderma Gangrenosum
Description: Pyoderma gangrenosum is an uncommon, noninfectious neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by dysregulated innate immunity and painful, rapidly progressive sterile skin ulceration, classically beginning as pustules, papules, or nodules that break down into necrotic ulcers with undermined violaceous borders and marked pathergy; major clinical variants include ulcerative, bullous, pustular, vegetative, and peristomal forms. It is usually sporadic, but genetic susceptibility is supported by syndromic and familial cases involving PSTPIP1 mutations in PAPA syndrome and related autoinflammatory disorders, with additional links to LPIN2, IL1RN, NLRP3, NOD2, MEFV, and occasionally JAK/STAT-related inflammatory signatures; key mediators include neutrophil chemotaxis and activation, overexpression of TNF, IL-1β, IL-8/CXCL8, IL-17, IL-23, IL-36, complement, and matrix metalloproteinases, implicating TNF/NF-κB, inflammasome, Th17, and JAK-STAT pathways. Strong comorbid associations include inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid and seronegative arthritis, hidradenitis suppurativa, hematologic disorders such as monoclonal gammopathy, myelodysplastic syndrome, and leukemia, and complications include secondary infection, severe pain, scarring, functional impairment, and rarely systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion, supported by skin biopsy showing sterile neutrophilic infiltrates and excluding vasculitis, infection, and malignancy; wound cultures, inflammatory markers, CBC, serum protein studies, and targeted evaluation for IBD, arthritis, and hematologic disease are commonly performed, and Delphi/PARACELSUS criteria are often applied. Treatment centers on immunosuppression and wound care: systemic corticosteroids suppress broad inflammatory gene transcription, cyclosporine inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation, and anti-TNF agents such as infliximab or adalimumab neutralize TNF; additional options include dapsone, colchicine, tacrolimus, methotrexate, mycophenolate, ustekinumab, and anakinra depending on severity and pathway involvement.

Name: Nummular eczema
Description: Nummular eczema (discoid eczema; UMLS C0085656) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory dermatosis characterized by intensely pruritic, coin-shaped eczematous plaques, usually on the extremities and trunk, with xerosis, erythema, papules, vesiculation, oozing, crusting, scaling, and later lichenification or postinflammatory pigment change; recognized patterns include exudative/acute, dry/xerotic, lichenified/chronic, and sometimes impetiginized lesions. It is generally considered a multifactorial, non-Mendelian disorder of skin-barrier dysfunction and immune dysregulation rather than a single-gene disease, but genetic susceptibility overlaps with atopic dermatitis, with representative associations involving FLG loss-of-function variants affecting filaggrin and epidermal barrier integrity, SPINK5 and CLDN1 in some eczematous phenotypes, and increased type 2 inflammatory mediators such as IL4, IL13, IL31, and TSLP; relevant pathways include keratinocyte barrier disruption, Th2-skewed cytokine signaling through JAK-STAT, pruritus neuroimmune signaling, and secondary activation of innate immunity with Staphylococcus aureus colonization. Comorbidities include atopy, asthma, allergic rhinitis, contact allergy, depression/anxiety, sleep disturbance, and bacterial superinfection/cellulitis as complications. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on characteristic morphology and distribution, with exclusion of mimics such as tinea corporis, psoriasis, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; testing may include KOH microscopy/fungal culture, bacterial culture if infected, patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis, dermoscopy, and biopsy showing spongiotic dermatitis when uncertain. Treatment commonly uses topical corticosteroids such as clobetasol or triamcinolone, which suppress NF-kB–driven inflammatory gene expression; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus, which inhibit calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation; and liberal emollients that restore barrier lipids and reduce transepidermal water loss; refractory disease may require phototherapy, short systemic corticosteroids, cyclosporine, methotrexate, or dupilumab, an IL-4Rα antagonist that blocks IL-4/IL-13 signaling.

Name: Hypophosphatemia
Description: Hypophosphatemia is a metabolic disorder defined by abnormally low serum phosphate due to reduced intestinal absorption, intracellular shifts, or, most commonly in chronic disease, renal phosphate wasting; it may be acute or chronic and includes inherited forms such as X-linked hypophosphatemia, autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets, autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rickets, hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria, and tumor-induced osteomalacia. Key genetic and molecular causes include PHEX loss-of-function mutations in X-linked hypophosphatemia, FGF23 gain-of-function variants in autosomal dominant disease, and pathogenic variants in DMP1, ENPP1, SLC34A3, SLC34A1, CYP27B1, and GALNT3; representative proteins include fibroblast growth factor 23, the renal sodium-phosphate cotransporters NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc, Klotho, and 1α-hydroxylase. Central pathways involve the FGF23-FGFR1/Klotho axis, which suppresses proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption and decreases calcitriol synthesis, as well as PTH-vitamin D signaling and proximal tubular transport mechanisms. Clinical manifestations include bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue, rickets or osteomalacia, impaired growth, bowed legs, fractures or pseudofractures, dental abscesses, and in severe acute cases rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, respiratory failure, or arrhythmia. Complications and comorbidities include secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism, nephrocalcinosis, chronic kidney disease, enthesopathy, hearing impairment, and skeletal deformity. Diagnosis relies on low serum phosphate adjusted for age, assessment of renal phosphate wasting by tubular maximum phosphate reabsorption or fractional excretion, alkaline phosphatase, calcium, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, FGF23 when appropriate, urinary phosphate, radiographs showing rickets or osteomalacia, and confirmatory genetic testing in familial cases. Name: Chronic gastritis
Description: Chronic gastritis (UMLS C0085695) is a persistent inflammatory disorder of the gastric mucosa, classically divided into Helicobacter pylori-associated antral-predominant gastritis, autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis involving the corpus/fundus, and reactive or chemical gastropathy related to bile reflux, alcohol, or NSAIDs. H. pylori disease is driven by bacterial virulence factors such as CagA and VacA and host inflammatory pathways including TLR/NF-kB activation, IL1B, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, IFNG, COX-2/PTGS2, and NF-kB-mediated cytokine signaling, while autoimmune gastritis features CD4+ T-cell-mediated destruction of parietal cells, antibodies to H+/K+-ATPase and intrinsic factor, achlorhydria, hypergastrinemia, ECL-cell hyperplasia, and increased risk of pernicious anemia. Genetic susceptibility is complex rather than Mendelian, with representative associations in IL1B, IL1RN, TNF, TLR4, and HLA class II loci influencing inflammation, atrophy, and cancer risk. Symptoms are often absent or nonspecific, but may include epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness, nausea, bloating, early satiety, dyspepsia, halitosis, and, in autoimmune disease, glossitis, fatigue, pallor, or neurologic findings from vitamin B12 deficiency. Major comorbidities and complications include peptic ulcer disease, iron deficiency, pernicious anemia, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, gastric adenocarcinoma, and gastric MALT lymphoma. Diagnosis relies on clinical context plus upper endoscopy with biopsies showing chronic inflammatory infiltrates, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, or H. pylori; testing includes histology, rapid urease test, stool antigen, urea breath test, serology when appropriate, CBC, iron studies, vitamin B12, gastrin, pepsinogen I/II, and parietal cell or intrinsic-factor antibodies. Treatment commonly includes proton-pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; amoxicillin or clarithromycin in eradication regimens, inhibiting bacterial cell-wall or protein synthesis; bismuth subsalicylate, which is antimicrobial and muc

Name: Chronic pyelonephritis
Description: Chronic pyelonephritis is a chronic tubulointerstitial renal disease characterized by recurrent or persistent bacterial infection and inflammation, usually superimposed on vesicoureteral reflux, urinary tract obstruction, or nephrolithiasis, leading to irregular cortical scarring, calyceal deformity, tubular atrophy, and progressive chronic kidney disease. It commonly presents with recurrent urinary tract infections, flank or loin pain, fever during exacerbations, dysuria, frequency, hypertension, polyuria from impaired concentrating ability, and gradually rising creatinine, although some patients are identified only after scarring or renal insufficiency is detected. Major forms include reflux nephropathy-associated chronic pyelonephritis, obstructive chronic pyelonephritis, and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. The molecular landscape is driven more by host susceptibility and inflammatory response than by recurrent somatic mutations; relevant inherited contributors include genes involved in congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract or reflux such as PAX2, HNF1B, ROBO2, RET, and UPK3A, while innate immune and fibrosis-related mediators including TLR4, IL6, CXCL8, TNF, TGFB1, NF-kB, JAK/STAT, complement, and renin-angiotensin signaling participate in bacterial recognition, leukocyte recruitment, interstitial fibrosis, and progression to renal scarring. Inheritance is therefore usually not Mendelian for the pyelonephritis itself, but familial predisposition may occur through inherited reflux or CAKUT. Common pathogens are uropathogenic Escherichia coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus. Treatment centers on eradication of infection and correction of the underlying anatomic cause; representative drugs include ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis, and ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, with amoxicillin-clavulanate or aminoglycosides used in selected cases. Important comorbidities and complications include vesicoureteral reflux, obstructive uropathy, stones, hypertension, proteinuria, renal abscess, papillary necrosis, and end-stage kidney disease. Name: Enterobiasis
Description: Enterobiasis (MeSH D017229) is a common intestinal helminthiasis caused by the human pinworm Enterobius vermicularis, usually transmitted by fecal-oral spread or autoinoculation, and is not an inherited disorder, although host susceptibility may be influenced by immune-response genes such as HLA class II loci and cytokine-related pathways including IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, and Th2 polarization; the parasite itself expresses structural and metabolic proteins such as tubulin and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits that serve as pharmacologic targets rather than validated routine diagnostic biomarkers. Disease is typically classified as uncomplicated intestinal enterobiasis or ectopic/genitourinary and appendiceal infection, with heavy-burden or recurrent household infection recognized clinically. Hallmark manifestations are nocturnal perianal pruritus, disturbed sleep, irritability, restlessness, bruxism, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and sometimes vulvovaginitis in girls or women; complications include secondary bacterial skin infection from scratching, recurrent vulvovaginitis, urinary tract irritation, appendiceal involvement, rare eosinophilic enterocolitis, and occasional pelvic or peritoneal granulomatous lesions. Diagnosis is based primarily on characteristic symptoms plus demonstration of ova or adult worms, most sensitively by early-morning perianal adhesive tape testing on 3 consecutive days; stool ova-and-parasite examination is relatively insensitive, while direct visualization and occasional microscopy of worms or eggs support confirmation. Standard treatment includes mebendazole, which binds parasite beta-tubulin and inhibits microtubule-dependent glucose uptake; albendazole, a related benzimidazole with similar beta-tubulin-mediated blockade of microtubule polymerization and energy depletion; and pyrantel pamoate, a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker acting at nicotinic receptors to cause spastic paralysis; repeated dosing after about 2 weeks and simultaneous treatment of close contacts, along with hygiene and laundering measures, are central to preventing reinfection.

Name: Acute cystitis
Description: Acute cystitis (UMLS C0149523) is an acute, usually ascending bacterial infection and inflammatory disorder of the urinary bladder mucosa, most often a lower urinary tract infection caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli, with other agents including Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, and Enterococcus faecalis. It typically presents with dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain or pressure, cloudy or malodorous urine, and sometimes hematuria, while fever, flank pain, or systemic toxicity suggest upper tract involvement rather than isolated cystitis. Pathobiologically, urothelial adherence and invasion are mediated by bacterial adhesins such as type 1 fimbriae with FimH and P fimbriae, and host responses involve TLR4-dependent innate immune signaling, NF-κB activation, IL-6/IL-8 production, neutrophil recruitment, and epithelial antimicrobial peptides. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian rather than inherited as a single-gene disorder; representative host factors linked to recurrent or severe infection include variants in TLR4, CXCR1/CXCR2, DEFB1, and secretor status determined by FUT2, while no pathognomonic somatic mutation defines the disease. Major subtypes include uncomplicated cystitis, complicated cystitis, recurrent cystitis, hemorrhagic cystitis, and catheter-associated cystitis. Common treatments include nitrofurantoin, which is reduced intracellularly to reactive intermediates that damage bacterial DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which sequentially inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and dihydropteroate synthase; fosfomycin, which inhibits MurA and early peptidoglycan synthesis; and selected beta-lactams that inhibit penicillin-binding proteins. Important comorbidities and risk factors include female sex, sexual activity, pregnancy, menopause, diabetes mellitus, urinary obstruction, neurogenic bladder, urolithiasis, and indwelling catheters; complications include recurrence, pyelonephritis, bacteremia, and, less commonly, renal scarring. Diagnosis is primarily clinical in symptomatic patients and is supported by urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and sometimes hematuria, with urine culture, susceptibility testing, and selective imaging or cystoscopy

Name: Allergic urticaria
Description: Allergic urticaria is an acute or recurrent mast cell–driven hypersensitivity disorder of the skin characterized by transient pruritic wheals, erythema, and sometimes angioedema, most often triggered by foods, drugs, insect venom, latex, infections, or aeroallergens; lesions usually resolve within 24 hours, but severe cases may accompany anaphylaxis with bronchospasm or hypotension. Its pathobiology is dominated by allergen-induced IgE cross-linking of FcεRI on mast cells and basophils, with downstream Lyn/Syk activation, phospholipase C/Ca2+ flux, PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and NF-κB signaling, leading to release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, platelet-activating factor, and cytokines including IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13; complement anaphylatoxins may amplify degranulation. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, with representative associations involving FCER1A, MS4A2/FCER1B, IL4, IL13, HLA class II alleles, HRH1, and KIT-related mast-cell biology, while rare monogenic urticaria-like syndromes in the differential include NLRP3-associated autoinflammatory disease. Clinical subtypes include acute allergic urticaria, recurrent/intermittent urticaria with identifiable allergens, and urticaria with angioedema. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on evanescent wheals and exposure history, supported when indicated by skin-prick or serum allergen-specific IgE testing, CBC/eosinophils, serum tryptase in systemic reactions, and selective oral or drug challenge; biopsy is reserved for atypical persistent lesions to exclude urticarial vasculitis. First-line therapy is with second-generation H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine, loratadine, or fexofenadine, which block H1 receptors; adjuncts include diphenhydramine as a sedating H1 blocker, corticosteroids such as prednisone to suppress inflammatory gene transcription, montelukast to antagonize cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1, and epinephrine for anaphylaxis via α/β-adrenergic effects. Name: Gingivostomatitis (disorder)
Description: Gingivostomatitis is an inflammatory disorder of the gingiva and oral mucosa, most often acute and infectious, classically presenting as primary herpetic gingivostomatitis caused by herpes simplex virus type 1, but it may also be aphthous, enteroviral, Candida-associated, drug related, or part of systemic inflammatory disease. Typical findings include fever, malaise, painful erythematous and edematous gingiva, vesicles that rupture into shallow oral ulcers, drooling, halitosis, dysphagia, cervical lymphadenopathy, and reduced oral intake with risk of dehydration; chronic or recurrent forms may reflect recurrent HSV infection, immunodeficiency, or autoimmune mucosal disease. Molecularly, HSV-associated disease depends on viral glycoproteins such as gB, gD, and gH/gL engaging epithelial receptors including NECTIN1/PVRL1 and HVEM/TNFRSF14, with host innate signaling through TLR2, TLR3, cGAS-STING, type I interferons, NF-kB, and cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF; rare severe mucocutaneous HSV susceptibility is linked to variants in TLR3 pathway genes including TLR3, TICAM1/TRIF, UNC93B1, TRAF3, and IRF3, while neutrophil dysfunction and immunosuppression are broader host risk factors. Treatment is mainly supportive, but acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir are commonly used antivirals that inhibit viral DNA polymerase after phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase; adjuncts include acetaminophen or ibuprofen for analgesia via central cyclooxygenase inhibition or peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibition, topical lidocaine as a sodium-channel blocker, and nystatin or fluconazole for fungal superinfection. Important comorbidities and complications include malnutrition, secondary bacterial infection, oral candidiasis, eczema herpeticum, keratitis, and more severe disease in HIV infection, hematologic malignancy, transplant recipients, Behcet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and PFAPA. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported when needed by HSV PCR from lesion swabs, viral culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing, Tzanck smear, fungal studies, CBC, inflammatory markers, and targeted immune or genetic testing in unusually severe, recurrent,

Name: Lower Respiratory Tract Infection
Description: Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI; UMLS C0149725) is a heterogeneous, usually acute infectious syndrome involving the bronchi, bronchioles, and lung parenchyma, encompassing acute bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and community- or hospital-acquired pneumonia caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi. Its pathobiology is driven by innate and adaptive immune signaling, notably Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, JAK-STAT, interferon, inflammasome, and cytokine pathways involving TNF, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, IFN-γ, complement, neutrophils, macrophages, and epithelial barrier dysfunction. Host susceptibility has genetic components rather than classic Mendelian inheritance in most cases, with representative associations involving TLR2, TLR4, IFIH1, MBL2, CFTR, SERPINA1, and cytokine genes such as IL6 and TNF; rare primary immunodeficiencies, including variants affecting BTK, CYBB, or STAT3, can predispose to recurrent or severe LRTI. Typical manifestations include fever, cough, sputum production, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia, wheeze or crackles, and systemic inflammatory features, while major complications include respiratory failure, sepsis, empyema, lung abscess, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and exacerbation of asthma, COPD, heart failure, or bronchiectasis; common comorbidities include extremes of age, smoking, diabetes, chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, aspiration risk, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis integrates history and examination with pulse oximetry, chest radiography or CT when needed, complete blood count, inflammatory markers, microbiologic testing such as sputum and blood cultures, urinary antigens, and viral PCR panels; severity tools such as CURB-65 or PSI guide management. Treatment depends on etiology and setting, with common agents including amoxicillin or other β-lactams, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation; azithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; ceftriaxone, another β-lactam; and, for influenza-associated LRTI, oseltamivir, a neuraminidase inhibitor that blocks viral release.

Name: Deep Vein Thromboses
Description: Venous thrombosis is the pathologic formation of fibrin- and erythrocyte-rich thrombi within the venous circulation, most commonly presenting as deep vein thrombosis of the leg and potentially progressing to pulmonary embolism; major subtypes include provoked and unprovoked disease, distal or proximal deep vein thrombosis, upper-extremity thrombosis, splanchnic or cerebral venous thrombosis, and superficial venous thrombosis. It arises through Virchow triad mechanisms of stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability, with key molecular contributors including tissue factor–factor VIIa initiation, thrombin generation, fibrin formation, platelet-leukocyte interactions, P-selectin, NETosis, and impaired anticoagulant or fibrinolytic pathways involving antithrombin, protein C, protein S, plasminogen, and PAI-1. Genetic predisposition is often multifactorial but may be autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance in inherited thrombophilia, exemplified by F5 factor V Leiden, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1 antithrombin deficiency, PROC protein C deficiency, PROS1 protein S deficiency, and less commonly dysfibrinogenemia or elevated factor VIII; acquired associations include antiphospholipid syndrome and malignancy. Typical symptoms and signs are unilateral leg pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, tenderness, edema, and dilated superficial veins, while complications include post-thrombotic syndrome, recurrent venous thromboembolism, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, venous ulceration, and death from embolism; important comorbidities include cancer, recent surgery or trauma, immobility, obesity, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, and inflammatory disease. Diagnosis relies on pretest probability assessment, D-dimer testing, compression duplex ultrasonography for limb thrombosis, and CT pulmonary angiography, MR venography, or conventional venography in selected cases, with thrombophilia testing reserved for targeted scenarios. Treatment centers on anticoagulation with heparin or low-molecular-weight heparins that potentiate antithrombin against factor Xa and thrombin, warfarin that inhibits vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis, and direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, or dabigatran that directly inhibit factor Xa or

Name: Secondary glaucoma
Description: Secondary glaucoma is a heterogeneous group of acquired or less commonly genetically predisposed glaucomas in which elevated intraocular pressure and optic neuropathy arise from an identifiable ocular or systemic cause, including pseudoexfoliative, pigmentary, neovascular, uveitic, steroid-induced, traumatic, lens-induced, aphakic/pseudophakic, and tumor-associated forms; patients typically present with ocular pain or pressure, blurred vision, halos, redness, headache, photophobia, or may be asymptomatic until visual field loss, optic disc cupping, and retinal nerve fiber layer thinning develop. Molecular contributors vary by subtype and include MYOC and CYP1B1 variants that can modify susceptibility, LOXL1 in pseudoexfoliation with abnormal fibrillar matrix deposition, and genes involved in angiogenesis or inflammation such as VEGFA, TGFB2, MMPs, IL6, and TNF; protein and pathway abnormalities commonly implicate TGF-β/SMAD-driven extracellular matrix remodeling of the trabecular meshwork, Rho kinase–mediated actomyosin contractility and outflow resistance, VEGF signaling in iris and angle neovascularization, oxidative stress, complement activation, and inflammatory cytokine/NF-κB pathways. Treatment targets the cause and intraocular pressure: prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost increase uveoscleral outflow, topical beta-blockers such as timolol reduce aqueous humor production, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dorzolamide or acetazolamide decrease bicarbonate-dependent aqueous secretion, alpha2-agonists such as brimonidine suppress aqueous production and enhance uveoscleral outflow, pilocarpine can increase trabecular outflow in selected mechanisms, corticosteroid withdrawal is essential in steroid glaucoma, and anti-VEGF agents such as bevacizumab are used in neovascular disease; surgery or laser, including trabeculectomy, drainage devices, or cyclodestructive procedures, is often required. Important comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, retinal vein occlusion, ocular ischemic syndrome, uveitis, trauma, cataract, and pseudoexfoliation syndrome, while complications include peripheral anterior synechiae, corneal edema, acute angle closure, and irreversible vision loss. Diagnosis rests on identifying an underlying cause together with elevated or fluctuating intraocular pressure, gonioscopy, slit-lamp examination, optic nerve assessment, pachym

Name: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (disorder)
Description: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy is an acquired paraneoplastic metabolic disorder in which systemic hypercalcemia results primarily from tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHLH/PTHrP), most often in squamous cell carcinomas of lung, head and neck, esophagus, renal and bladder cancers, ovarian and endometrial tumors, and adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma; less often it reflects excess calcitriol production or, rarely, ectopic PTH. The central molecular axis is PTHrP binding the PTH1 receptor (PTH1R) in bone and kidney, activating cAMP/PKA and phospholipase C signaling, increasing RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis, renal distal tubular calcium reabsorption, and phosphaturia, with frequent cooperation from osteolytic cytokines such as IL1, IL6, TNF, TGF-β, and prostaglandins; in calcitriol-mediated cases, CYP27B1-driven vitamin D activation is important. Genetic components are usually somatic and tumor-specific rather than inherited, with representative abnormalities including PTHLH overexpression, squamous lineage alterations such as TP53 or EGFR pathway dysregulation, and HTLV1-associated leukemogenesis in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma; there is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for the syndrome itself. Clinical manifestations reflect acute or subacute severe hypercalcemia and include weakness, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, confusion, lethargy, shortened QT interval, arrhythmia, and coma, with complications such as acute kidney injury, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, nephrolithiasis, pancreatitis, and poor prognosis from advanced cancer. Diagnosis rests on elevated albumin-corrected or ionized calcium, suppressed intact PTH, low or normal phosphate, often elevated PTHrP, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D except in lymphoma, and assessment for malignancy by imaging and pathology; subtypes include PTHrP-mediated humoral disease, local osteolytic hypercalcemia, calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia, and ectopic PTH secretion.
