Name: Neurodermatitis, Circumscribed
Description: Neurodermatitis, circumscribed, also called lichen simplex chronicus, is a chronic localized inflammatory dermatosis driven primarily by an itch–scratch cycle rather than a single Mendelian defect, characterized clinically by intense pruritus, well-demarcated lichenified plaques, excoriations, hyperpigmentation or erythema, and accentuated skin markings, typically on the nape, scalp, ankles, vulva, scrotum, or extensor surfaces; recognized variants are largely site-specific, including genital, scalp, and pretibial forms. Its biology overlaps with atopic dermatitis and chronic pruritus, with reported involvement of epidermal barrier and neuroimmune genes or proteins such as FLG, IL4, IL13, IL31, IL31RA, TSLP, NGF, TRPV1, and substance P/NK1R signaling, activating Th2-skewed cytokine networks, JAK-STAT pathways, mast cells, sensory nerves, keratinocytes, and impaired barrier responses, although these associations are often indirect and not disease-specific. Inheritance is usually complex or absent, but familial atopy and barrier dysfunction may confer susceptibility rather than deterministic transmission. Common comorbidities include atopic dermatitis, anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive traits, sleep disturbance, xerosis, contact dermatitis, and neuropathic or psychogenic pruritus; complications include secondary bacterial infection, impetiginization, fissuring, scarring, and rarely diagnostic confusion with psoriasis, lichen planus, tinea, or cutaneous lymphoma. Diagnosis is clinical, based on chronic localized pruritus with lichenification in accessible scratch areas, supported when needed by dermoscopy, skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and vertical collagen streaking, and targeted exclusion of mimics using KOH preparation, patch testing, or laboratory evaluation for systemic pruritus. Treatment relies on potent topical corticosteroids such as clobetasol, which suppress NF-kB-mediated cutaneous inflammation, topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus, which block T-cell activation via calcineurin inhibition, and sedating antihistamines such as hydroxyzine, which reduce histamine-mediated itch and nocturnal scratching; adjuncts may include capsaicin, gabapentin, or doxepin.

Name: Small Cell Lung Carcinoma
Description: Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is a high-grade, poorly differentiated pulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma, strongly linked to tobacco exposure, characterized by rapid growth, early hematogenous spread, and frequent paraneoplastic phenomena. Genetically, it is defined by near-universal inactivation of TP53 and RB1, with recurrent alterations in MYC family amplification, PTEN loss, CREBBP/EP300, NOTCH pathway genes, BCL2 overexpression, SOX2 amplification, and DNA damage response genes such as ATM; rare familial inheritance is not typical, although inherited susceptibility to lung cancer may be modified by variants affecting nicotine dependence, carcinogen metabolism, and DNA repair. Core oncogenic pathways include cell-cycle dysregulation through p53/Rb loss, PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, Notch neuroendocrine differentiation programs, anti-apoptotic BCL2 signaling, DLL3 expression, and angiogenic and immune-evasion pathways. Clinically, patients often present with cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, bulky mediastinal disease, and symptoms from metastases to brain, liver, bone, or adrenal glands; SIADH, ectopic ACTH/Cushing syndrome, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, and recurrent infection from airway obstruction are classic complications/comorbidities, along with COPD and cardiovascular disease related to smoking. Major disease categories are limited-stage and extensive-stage SCLC, with pure and combined histologic subtypes. Diagnosis rests on tissue biopsy or cytology showing small blue cells with scant cytoplasm, high mitotic rate, necrosis, and neuroendocrine marker expression such as synaptophysin, chromogranin, CD56, and often TTF-1, supported by CT/PET staging and brain MRI. Standard treatment includes platinum agents such as cisplatin or carboplatin, which form DNA crosslinks, plus etoposide, a topoisomerase II inhibitor, often combined with PD-L1 inhibitors such as atezolizumab or durvalumab that restore antitumor T-cell activity; other active drugs include irinotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor, and lurbinectedin, which inhibits oncogenic transcription and induces DNA damage.

Name: Migraine Disorders
Description: Migraine disorders are common, episodic or chronic primary neurovascular headache disorders characterized by genetically mediated neuronal hyperexcitability, trigeminovascular activation, and release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), substance P, glutamate, serotonin-related mediators, nitric oxide, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, with cortical spreading depression underlying many aura phenomena. Clinically, they cause recurrent unilateral or bilateral throbbing headache lasting 4–72 hours, often worsened by activity and accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, cutaneous allodynia, and in some patients transient visual, sensory, language, brainstem, or motor aura. Major subtypes include migraine without aura, migraine with aura, chronic migraine, hemiplegic migraine, vestibular migraine, menstrual migraine, retinal migraine, and migraine with brainstem aura. Genetic contribution is typically complex and polygenic, but monogenic forms are established in familial hemiplegic migraine, most notably involving CACNA1A, ATP1A2, and SCN1A; susceptibility loci and genes affecting glutamatergic transmission, ion channels, and vascular-neuronal signaling include TRPM8, KCNK18, LRP1, PRRT2, and CGRP-pathway components. Inheritance is usually multifactorial with familial aggregation, while hemiplegic migraine often shows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance. Diagnosis is clinical using International Classification of Headache Disorders criteria, supported by headache history, neurologic examination, and headache diaries; MRI or CT, vascular imaging, lumbar puncture, or genetic testing are reserved for red flags, atypical presentations, secondary headache exclusion, or suspected familial hemiplegic migraine. Common comorbidities include depression, anxiety, epilepsy, sleep disorders, asthma, obesity, fibromyalgia, temporomandibular disorder, and ischemic stroke risk, especially with aura; complications include status migrainosus, medication-overuse headache, persistent aura, migrainous infarction, and chronic daily headache. Treatment includes triptans such as sumatriptan, 5-HT1B/1D agonists that inhibit trigeminovascular neurotransmission and promote cranial vasoconstriction; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen via cyclooxygenase inhibition; topiramate, which reduces neuronal excitability through sodium-channel, GABA

Name: Acute otitis externa
Description: Acute otitis externa (UMLS C0149948) is an acute inflammatory and usually infectious disorder of the external auditory canal, most often caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus after moisture exposure, trauma, or breakdown of the cerumen-skin barrier; it presents with rapid-onset otalgia, marked tragal or pinna tenderness, pruritus, aural fullness, edema and erythema of the canal, otorrhea, and sometimes temporary conductive hearing loss. Molecularly, it is driven less by a single inherited lesion than by innate immune and epithelial-barrier responses involving Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB activation, proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF, and chemokines recruiting neutrophils, while bacterial virulence factors, biofilm pathways, and in some cases host factors affecting skin integrity or immunity modulate severity; representative host components implicated in susceptibility to recurrent or severe external ear/skin infection include filaggrin and other epidermal-barrier genes in atopic dermatitis, and immune defects affecting neutrophil or humoral function, although no Mendelian inheritance pattern is typical for uncomplicated acute disease. Subtypes include diffuse bacterial otitis externa, localized furunculosis, and fungal otitis externa, while necrotizing or malignant otitis externa is a severe invasive complication seen especially in diabetes or immunocompromise. Common comorbidities include eczema, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, diabetes mellitus, hearing-aid use, and immunosuppression; complications include canal stenosis, cellulitis, perichondritis, and skull-base osteomyelitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on acute symptoms plus signs of canal inflammation and tenderness on auricular manipulation, with otoscopy showing edema, debris, and discharge; culture is reserved for refractory, recurrent, or immunocompromised cases, and imaging such as CT or MRI is used when invasive disease is suspected. Treatment is mainly topical, with agents such as ciprofloxacin, an inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase fluoroquinolone; ofloxacin, a similar fluoroquinolone; and neomycin-polymyxin B-hydrocortisone, combining aminoglycoside ribosomal inhibition, polymyxin-mediated membrane disruption, and corticosteroid suppression of inflammatory gene transcription; acetic acid lowers canal pH and limits

Name: Gonorrhea of pharynx
Description: Pharyngeal gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted mucosal infection of the oropharynx caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, usually acquired through oral sexual exposure; it is not an inherited disorder, although host susceptibility may be influenced by immune-related genetic variation, while the principal microbial genetic determinants include pilE/pilC and opa adhesins, porB, lptA, and LOS biosynthesis genes that mediate epithelial adherence, invasion, immune evasion, and inflammation, together with resistance-associated mutations such as penA mosaic alleles affecting penicillin-binding protein 2, mtrR and the mtrCDE efflux pump, porB alterations, and gyrA/parC mutations linked to fluoroquinolone resistance. Pathobiology involves attachment to CEACAMs and complement-regulatory proteins, activation of TLR2/TLR4-, NF-kB-, MAPK-, inflammasome-, IL-1/IL-8-, and neutrophil-dominant signaling pathways, with biofilm formation and frequent asymptomatic colonization of the tonsillar and posterior pharyngeal mucosa. When symptomatic, patients may have sore throat, odynophagia, pharyngeal erythema, exudate, cervical lymphadenopathy, or fever, but many cases are detected only by screening. Recognized forms include uncomplicated localized pharyngeal infection and infection with dissemination or coinfection at urogenital, rectal, or conjunctival sites. Important comorbidities include concurrent Chlamydia trachomatis, syphilis, HIV, and other STIs; complications include persistent carriage, transmission, treatment failure from antimicrobial resistance, and rarely disseminated gonococcal infection with dermatitis, tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, or meningitis. Diagnosis relies on exposure history and detection by nucleic acid amplification testing on pharyngeal swabs, the preferred test, with culture used for antimicrobial susceptibility testing and confirmation when resistance or treatment failure is suspected. Standard treatment is ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, often with doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, if chlamydial infection is not excluded; azithromycin, a 50S inhibitor, and cefixime, an oral cephalosporin, are additional agents historically or selectively used, though resistance limits some regimens.

Name: Syphilis, secondary
Description: Secondary syphilis (UMLS C0149985) is a systemic, hematogenously disseminated stage of infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum that follows the primary chancre and is characterized by widespread mucocutaneous and lymphoreticular involvement rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder; accordingly, no causal human germline mutation defines the disease, although host susceptibility and severity are influenced by immune-response genes and proteins such as HLA class II alleles, TLR1/TLR2, TLR6, CD14, MYD88, TNF, IFNG, IL10, and CXCL8, while major pathogen-associated proteins include outer membrane and lipoprotein antigens such as Tp47, TmpA, TpN15, TpN17, and TpN47. Pathobiology centers on innate and adaptive immune activation through treponemal lipoprotein engagement of TLR2/TLR1 and TLR2/TLR6, NF-κB signaling, macrophage and dendritic-cell activation, Th1-skewed cytokine responses with IFN-γ and TNF-α, immune-complex formation, endothelial activation, and plasma-cell-rich inflammation. Clinically it presents with diffuse symmetric nonpruritic maculopapular rash often involving palms and soles, mucous patches, condylomata lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, sore throat, patchy alopecia, hepatitic or nephrotic manifestations, and occasional ocular, otic, or early neurologic involvement. It may be classified within early syphilis, including classic secondary, recurrent secondary, and overlap with early latent disease. Common comorbidities and complications include HIV coinfection, other sexually transmitted infections, neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, otosyphilis, hepatitis, glomerulonephritis, and progression to latent or tertiary syphilis if untreated. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical findings plus serology using nontreponemal tests such as RPR or VDRL with treponemal confirmation by TP-PA, FTA-ABS, or EIA/CIA, direct detection by dark-field microscopy or PCR from lesions when available, and CSF evaluation when neurologic or ocular disease is suspected. Name: Urinary Incontinence, Urge
Description: Urge urinary incontinence, usually a manifestation of overactive bladder, is a symptom-defined lower urinary tract disorder characterized by involuntary urine leakage accompanied or immediately preceded by urgency, typically with frequency and nocturia, and reflects detrusor overactivity that may be idiopathic or neurogenic. Pathobiology involves abnormal parasympathetic cholinergic signaling through acetylcholine at muscarinic M3 receptors encoded in part by CHRM3, altered purinergic ATP signaling via P2X3/P2X2-3 afferent pathways, β3-adrenergic relaxation mechanisms mediated by ADRB3, and sensory/inflammatory pathways involving TRPV1, nerve growth factor, and urothelial signaling; representative genetic associations, generally complex and non-Mendelian rather than deterministic, have been reported with ADRB3 variants such as Trp64Arg, muscarinic receptor genes, collagen/extracellular matrix genes, and ion-channel or connective-tissue loci, while rare familial clustering suggests polygenic susceptibility rather than a single inheritance pattern. Common subtypes include idiopathic urge incontinence, neurogenic urge incontinence due to stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, or diabetic neuropathy, and mixed urinary incontinence when stress leakage coexists. Frequent comorbidities include pelvic organ prolapse, recurrent urinary tract infection, benign prostatic hyperplasia or bladder outlet obstruction, obesity, constipation, sleep disturbance, depression, and frailty, with complications such as falls, skin breakdown, social isolation, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical after exclusion of infection and other causes, using history, bladder diary, physical examination, urinalysis, post-void residual measurement, and validated symptom questionnaires, with urodynamics, cystoscopy, or imaging reserved for refractory, complicated, or neurologically complex cases. Treatment commonly includes antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin, tolterodine, and solifenacin, which inhibit M3-predominant detrusor contraction, and the β3-agonist mirabegron, which promotes bladder relaxation; refractory cases may respond to intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA, which blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release.

Name: Chronic Pain
Description: Chronic pain (UMLS C0150055) is a multifactorial disorder defined as pain persisting or recurring for more than 3 months beyond expected tissue healing, encompassing nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic, and mixed phenotypes such as chronic low back pain, fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis pain, postsurgical pain, and peripheral neuropathic pain. Its biology involves peripheral and central sensitization with altered ion-channel excitability and neuroimmune signaling; implicated genes and proteins include SCN9A and SCN10A sodium channels, COMT, OPRM1, TRPV1, CACNA2D1, GCH1, BDNF, NGF, TNF, IL6, and glial mediators, while key pathways include prostaglandin/COX signaling, substance P and CGRP transmission, glutamatergic NMDA-receptor activation, descending serotonergic and noradrenergic modulation, voltage-gated calcium-channel signaling, and microglial/astrocytic MAPK, JAK-STAT, and NF-kB inflammatory cascades. Genetic contribution is usually polygenic and complex rather than Mendelian, although rare high-impact variants, especially in SCN9A, can strongly alter pain sensitivity; familial clustering is reported in fibromyalgia, migraine, and some neuropathic pain states. Common symptoms are persistent spontaneous or evoked pain, burning, aching, allodynia, hyperalgesia, sleep disturbance, fatigue, impaired function, cognitive complaints, anxiety, and depression, with complications including disability, opioid dependence, falls, and reduced quality of life; frequent comorbidities include mood disorders, insomnia, obesity, migraine, irritable bowel syndrome, and substance-use disorder. Diagnosis is clinical, based on duration, distribution, intensity, functional interference, neurologic and musculoskeletal examination, and identification of pain mechanism, supported when indicated by validated scales, quantitative sensory testing, nerve conduction studies/electromyography, imaging, laboratory evaluation for inflammatory or metabolic causes, and skin biopsy for small-fiber neuropathy. Treatment commonly includes NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit COX-mediated prostaglandin synthesis, duloxetine, which augments descending serotonin-norepinephrine inhibition, gabapentin or pregabalin, which bind the alpha2delta calcium-channel subunit to reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release, and in selected cases opioids such as morphine, a

Name: Addisonian Crisis
Description: Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal crisis; UMLS C0151467) is a life-threatening endocrine emergency caused by abrupt deficiency of glucocorticoids, often with mineralocorticoid deficiency, most commonly in primary adrenal insufficiency but also after secondary or tertiary adrenal failure or sudden withdrawal of chronic corticosteroids; it is not itself a Mendelian disorder, but important genetic substrates include autoimmune polyglandular syndromes linked to AIRE variants, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy due to ABCD1 mutations, congenital adrenal hyperplasia from CYP21A2 and less often CYP11B1, HSD3B2, STAR, or NR0B1 defects, and rare ACTH resistance involving MC2R or MRAP. Pathobiologically, impaired hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal signaling with reduced CRH-ACTH-MC2R activation leads to failure of adrenal steroidogenesis from cholesterol via StAR and cytochrome P450 enzymes, with loss of cortisol’s vascular permissive, gluconeogenic, and anti-inflammatory effects and, in primary disease, aldosterone deficiency causing renal sodium wasting, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemia. Typical features are profound weakness, hypotension or shock, dehydration, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, confusion, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and in primary disease hyperpigmentation; major precipitants include infection, surgery, trauma, and missed steroid doses. Key subtypes are primary adrenal crisis, secondary/tertiary crisis, and crisis associated with CAH or adrenal hemorrhage. Treatment centers on immediate parenteral hydrocortisone, a glucocorticoid that replaces cortisol and at stress doses provides mineralocorticoid activity, aggressive isotonic saline and dextrose resuscitation, and after stabilization fludrocortisone, a mineralocorticoid receptor agonist, for primary insufficiency; dexamethasone, a potent glucocorticoid with minimal mineralocorticoid effect, is an alternative when cortisol testing must be preserved. Comorbidities include autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, celiac disease, sepsis, and adrenal hemorrhage, while complications include arrhythmia, refractory shock, acute kidney injury, and death. Name: Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
Description: Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency (UMLS C0151482) is an acquired macrocytic anemia caused by impaired folate-dependent one-carbon transfer needed for thymidylate and purine synthesis, leading to defective DNA replication, ineffective erythropoiesis, and megaloblastic change in bone marrow. Key molecular components include folate transport and metabolism genes and proteins such as SLC19A1/RFC1, SLC46A1/PCFT, FOLR1, dihydrofolate reductase, methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), thymidylate synthase, and methionine synthase (MTR); rare inherited susceptibility can involve pathogenic variants in SLC46A1 causing hereditary folate malabsorption or MTHFR and other one-carbon pathway genes, usually with autosomal recessive inheritance in severe congenital disorders. Pathobiology centers on the folate cycle, methionine cycle, and nucleotide biosynthesis pathways, with secondary homocysteine elevation and relative preservation of methylmalonic acid, helping distinguish it from vitamin B12 deficiency. Common causes include poor intake, alcoholism, pregnancy, malabsorption such as celiac disease or tropical sprue, increased cellular turnover, and antifolate or folate-depleting drugs. Typical findings are fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, glossitis, angular cheilitis, gastrointestinal symptoms, macro-ovalocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils, elevated RDW, low serum and red-cell folate, increased homocysteine, and megaloblastic marrow; neurologic deficits are usually absent unless concurrent B12 deficiency exists. Subtypes include nutritional, malabsorptive, drug-induced, increased-requirement, and rare hereditary folate deficiency states. Treatment relies on folic acid, which replenishes reduced folate pools; folinic acid (leucovorin), which bypasses dihydrofolate reductase blockade and is used in antifolate toxicity; and hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin when B12 deficiency cannot be excluded, to prevent masking hematologic disease while neurologic injury progresses. Name: Ventricular Premature Complexes
Description: Ventricular premature complexes (VPCs, premature ventricular contractions) are common ectopic ventricular depolarizations arising from enhanced automaticity, triggered activity, or reentry within the His-Purkinje system or ventricular myocardium, occurring as isolated beats, couplets, bigeminy, multifocal PVCs, or nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. They may be idiopathic, often from the right or left ventricular outflow tract, or secondary to structural heart disease, ischemia, myocarditis, electrolyte disturbance, stimulant exposure, or inherited arrhythmia/cardiomyopathy syndromes. Genetic contributors are best defined when VPCs occur within broader inherited disorders, with representative genes including RYR2 and CASQ2 in catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNH2, and KCNE1/2 in channelopathies, and LMNA, PKP2, DSP, DSG2, DSC2, and FLNC in arrhythmogenic or dilated cardiomyopathy; inheritance is commonly autosomal dominant, though autosomal recessive forms such as CASQ2-related disease occur. Relevant pathways include cardiac sodium, potassium, and calcium channel signaling, abnormal sarcoplasmic-reticulum Ca2+ handling, cAMP/PKA- and β-adrenergic-mediated delayed afterdepolarizations, connexin-mediated conduction, fibrosis/inflammation, and ischemia-related reentry substrates. Symptoms range from none to palpitations, skipped beats, chest discomfort, dyspnea, dizziness, or presyncope, while high PVC burden can cause PVC-induced cardiomyopathy and rarely trigger sustained ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death in susceptible patients. Diagnosis relies on ECG showing premature wide QRS complexes without preceding P waves and usually with compensatory pause, ambulatory Holter or patch monitoring to quantify burden and morphology, echocardiography and often cardiac MRI to identify structural disease, exercise testing when adrenergic triggers are suspected, and laboratory evaluation for potassium, magnesium, and thyroid abnormalities; electrophysiology study is reserved for selected cases. Treatment commonly includes β-blockers such as metoprolol, which blunt sympathetic stimulation; non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil for some idiopathic outflow-tract foci; and antiarrhythmics including flecainide or propafenone, which block fast sodium channels,

Name: Hypermagnesaemia
Description: Hypermagnesaemia (UMLS C0151714) is an electrolyte disorder defined by abnormally elevated serum magnesium, most often acquired rather than primary, usually from reduced renal excretion in acute or chronic kidney disease or excessive magnesium intake from antacids, laxatives, bowel preparations, or obstetric magnesium sulfate therapy; rarer genetic contributors include disorders of tubular magnesium handling such as familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia due to inactivating CASR variants, and abnormalities affecting magnesium transport proteins including TRPM6, CNNM2, CLDN16, CLDN19, FXYD2, and SLC12A3, although these more commonly cause hypomagnesemic phenotypes than sustained hypermagnesaemia. Pathobiologically, magnesium acts through renal tubular reabsorption pathways in the thick ascending limb and distal convoluted tubule, calcium-sensing receptor signaling, paracellular claudin-mediated transport, and competition with calcium at voltage-gated channels and the neuromuscular junction, thereby suppressing acetylcholine release, reducing myocardial conduction, and causing vasodilation. Clinical manifestations correlate with severity and include nausea, flushing, lethargy, weakness, hyporeflexia or areflexia, hypotension, bradycardia, somnolence, ileus, urinary retention, respiratory depression, paralysis, heart block, and cardiac arrest; major complications include arrhythmia, coma, and death, with common comorbidities including chronic kidney disease, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, lithium exposure, and bowel disorders that increase magnesium absorption. Subtypes are often classified as mild, moderate, or severe by serum magnesium level and as iatrogenic, renal-retention, or genetic forms. Diagnosis relies on elevated serum magnesium, renal function assessment, ECG, medication and exposure review, and evaluation of associated electrolytes, especially calcium and potassium, with urinary magnesium excretion or fractional excretion helping distinguish renal retention from excess load. Treatment centers on stopping magnesium sources, intravenous calcium gluconate or calcium chloride to antagonize magnesium’s membrane effects, isotonic saline with loop diuretics such as furosemide to enhance renal magnesium excretion, and hemodialysis for severe toxicity or renal failure.

Name: Hypogonadism, Male
Description: Male hypogonadism is a clinical syndrome of impaired testicular testosterone production and/or spermatogenesis, classified as primary hypergonadotropic hypogonadism from testicular failure, secondary or central hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, or combined forms; congenital and acquired subtypes are recognized. Key genetic causes include AR mutations causing androgen insensitivity, KAL1/ANOS1, FGFR1, GNRHR, KISS1R, TACR3, PROKR2, CHD7, and LEP/LEPR defects in congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism/Kallmann spectrum, and testicular genes such as Klinefelter syndrome with 47,XXY, NR5A1, HSD17B3, SRD5A2, LHB, FSHB, and CYP17A1 abnormalities; inheritance may be X-linked, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, chromosomal, or sporadic. Pathobiology centers on disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, including GnRH pulsatility, kisspeptin/KISS1-KISS1R, neurokinin B/TAC3-TACR3, leptin signaling, LH/FSH action on Leydig and Sertoli cells, steroidogenesis through StAR, CYP11A1, CYP17A1, HSD17B3, aromatase, and androgen receptor signaling. Typical features include delayed or absent puberty, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility, low energy, depressed mood, reduced muscle mass and body hair, gynecomastia, small testes, and decreased bone density. Comorbidities and complications include osteoporosis, anemia, metabolic syndrome, obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular risk, sexual dysfunction, and psychosocial distress. Diagnosis requires consistent symptoms plus unequivocally low morning total testosterone on repeat testing, with free testosterone when SHBG is altered, followed by LH, FSH, prolactin, estradiol, iron studies, pituitary and thyroid assessment, semen analysis, karyotype or targeted genetic testing, olfactory evaluation, and pituitary MRI when central disease is suspected. Common treatments include testosterone replacement with testosterone enanthate, cypionate, or transdermal testosterone acting as androgen receptor agonists; human chorionic gonadotropin as an LH receptor agonist; pulsatile GnRH or

Name: Hypomagnesaemia
Description: Hypomagnesaemia (UMLS C0151723) is a biochemical and clinical disorder defined by abnormally low serum magnesium, usually reflecting gastrointestinal loss, renal wasting, poor intake, drug effects, or inherited defects in tubular or intestinal magnesium handling. It may be asymptomatic or present with neuromuscular hyperexcitability, tremor, muscle cramps, weakness, tetany, seizures, nystagmus, confusion, and cardiac manifestations including QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, and other arrhythmias, often with refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia due to impaired PTH secretion or action. Important genetic forms include isolated recessive hypomagnesaemia from TRPM6 mutations affecting epithelial Mg2+ influx, familial hypomagnesaemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis from CLDN16 or CLDN19 defects altering paracellular transport in the thick ascending limb, and renal magnesium wasting associated with CNNM2, FXYD2, HNF1B, SLC12A3 in Gitelman syndrome, and KCNA1 variants; inheritance may be autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, X-linked, or mitochondrial depending on the cause. Key pathways involve TRPM6/TRPM7-mediated transcellular uptake, claudin-16/19 tight-junction paracellular reabsorption, distal convoluted tubule NCC signaling, EGF-EGFR regulation of TRPM6, and calcium-sensing receptor–related modulation of tubular divalent cation transport. Common treatments include oral magnesium oxide, magnesium chloride, or magnesium lactate, which replenish body magnesium stores; intravenous magnesium sulfate for severe deficiency, seizures, or arrhythmia, supplying bioavailable Mg2+; and amiloride, which reduces distal renal magnesium wasting by blocking epithelial sodium channels and enhancing tubular magnesium conservation. Linked comorbidities and complications include alcoholism, malnutrition, diabetes mellitus, chronic diarrhea, pancreatitis, proton-pump inhibitor exposure, loop or thiazide diuretic use, nephrocalcinosis, chondrocalcinosis, and sudden cardiac death. Diagnosis rests on low serum magnesium, assessment of concurrent potassium and calcium abnormalities, ECG changes, urinary magnesium excretion or fractional excretion to distinguish renal from extrarenal loss, renal function testing, and targeted genetic testing when familial disease is suspected.

Name: Fungal infection of lung
Description: Fungal infection of the lung is an acquired, non-Mendelian infectious disease encompassing invasive, chronic, and allergic entities caused most often by Aspergillus, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Blastomyces, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, and Mucorales; major subtypes include invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis/aspergilloma, pulmonary mucormycosis, pneumocystis pneumonia, endemic pulmonary mycoses, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Host susceptibility is strongly shaped by immune genes and proteins, with representative defects involving NADPH oxidase components CYBB, NCF1, NCF2, and CYBA in chronic granulomatous disease, STAT1/STAT3, CARD9, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2/TLR4, IL12RB1, IFNGR1, and CFTR variants, which perturb fungal sensing and killing through Dectin-1–SYK–CARD9–NF-κB, Toll-like receptor, JAK-STAT interferon, Th1/Th17, IL-17/IL-23, TNF-α, and neutrophil oxidative burst pathways. Typical manifestations include fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, wheeze, hemoptysis, weight loss, and hypoxemia, with radiologic findings such as nodules, cavitation, halo or air-crescent signs, consolidations, or diffuse ground-glass opacities. Important comorbidities and complications include HIV/AIDS, neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, transplantation, corticosteroid or biologic immunosuppression, diabetes, COPD, tuberculosis cavities, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, and sarcoidosis, leading to respiratory failure, massive hemoptysis, dissemination to brain or blood, empyema, and death. Diagnosis integrates exposure and host risk, CT imaging, microscopy and culture of sputum or BAL, histopathology showing tissue invasion, fungal antigen tests such as galactomannan, β-D-glucan, cryptococcal antigen, and Histoplasma urine antigen, serology for endemic fungi and Aspergillus IgG/IgE, and PCR where available. Name: Discolouration of skin
Description: Discolouration of skin is a descriptive clinical sign rather than a single disease entity, encompassing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, depigmentation, erythematous, cyanotic, jaundiced, and vascular color changes caused by altered melanin synthesis or transfer, hemoglobin oxygenation, bilirubin deposition, inflammation, or dermal pigment/vascular abnormalities. Genetic contributors are best defined in inherited pigmentary disorders and include TYR, OCA2, TYRP1, SLC45A2, and MC1R in albinism and pigmentation phenotypes, KITLG and MITF in melanocyte biology, and autoimmune vitiligo susceptibility loci such as HLA variants, PTPN22, NLRP1, and TYR; key proteins and pathways include tyrosinase, melanocortin-1 receptor, c-KIT/MITF signaling, α-MSH/cAMP/PKA/CREB, Wnt/β-catenin, endothelin, and JAK-STAT and IFN-γ–CXCL9/10 pathways in vitiligo, with oxidative stress and T-cell-mediated melanocyte injury as central mechanisms. Common therapeutic agents include topical corticosteroids, which suppress inflammatory cytokine signaling; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, which inhibit T-cell activation via calcineurin blockade; hydroquinone, which inhibits tyrosinase to reduce hyperpigmentation; and, in selected cases, ruxolitinib cream, a JAK1/2 inhibitor that attenuates IFN-γ signaling. Associated comorbidities and complications depend on cause and include autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, Addison disease, hearing or ocular defects in albinism, photosensitivity, skin cancer risk, psychosocial distress, and secondary infection or scarring. Clinical findings include focal or diffuse macules, patches, mottling, pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, or post-inflammatory change; subtypes include vitiligo, melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, albinism, livedo, and systemic discoloration from hepatic, endocrine, vascular, or drug-related causes. Inheritance may be autosomal recessive in oculocutaneous albinism or complex polygenic in vitiligo. Diagnosis relies on history, examination, Wood lamp assessment, dermoscopy, skin biopsy when uncertain, and targeted laboratory or genetic testing guided

Name: Dry Skin
Description: Dry skin, or xerosis cutis (UMLS C0151908), is a common, multifactorial disorder of epidermal barrier function characterized by reduced stratum corneum water content and impaired lipid organization, presenting with roughness, scaling, fissuring, pruritus, dullness, and increased skin sensitivity, and ranging from simple age- or climate-related xerosis to inherited ichthyosiform phenotypes such as ichthyosis vulgaris. Key molecular determinants include loss-of-function or reduced-expression variants in FLG encoding filaggrin, which disrupt natural moisturizing factor generation, as well as abnormalities in SPINK5, TGM1, ALOX12B, ALOXE3, ABCA12, KRT1, and KRT10 in syndromic or severe keratinization disorders; relevant proteins include filaggrin, loricrin, involucrin, corneodesmosomal components, aquaporin-3, and epidermal ceramide-processing enzymes. Pathobiology centers on defective keratinocyte differentiation, diminished ceramide/cholesterol/free fatty acid lamellae, increased transepidermal water loss, altered calcium gradients, and inflammatory signaling involving Th2 cytokines such as IL-4 and IL-13, alarmins including TSLP, and PAR2-mediated itch and barrier injury pathways. Xerosis is associated with atopic dermatitis, ichthyosis, psoriasis, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, aging, and medication exposure, and complications include eczematization, secondary bacterial infection, excoriations, sleep disturbance, and impaired quality of life. Treatment relies primarily on barrier repair and anti-inflammatory therapy: emollients containing petrolatum act as occlusive moisturizers that reduce water loss, urea is a humectant and keratolytic, lactic acid or ammonium lactate promotes hydration and desquamation, ceramide-containing creams replenish barrier lipids, and topical corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone suppress cutaneous inflammation when dermatitis coexists. Inheritance is often complex in common xerosis but may be autosomal dominant in FLG-related ichthyosis vulgaris or autosomal recessive in several congenital ichthyoses. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history, examination of scale pattern and distribution, exclusion of systemic causes with targeted laboratory testing, and, when indicated, skin biopsy or genetic testing for keratinization disorders.

Name: Hypocalcemic tetany
Description: Hypocalcemic tetany is an acute neuromuscular hyperexcitability syndrome caused by low ionized calcium, most often arising from hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, pancreatitis, sepsis, alkalosis, or hypomagnesemia; clinically it presents with perioral numbness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, muscle cramps, laryngospasm, seizures, hyperreflexia, and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, with severe cases causing bronchospasm, arrhythmia, and QT prolongation. Genetic forms include isolated or syndromic hypoparathyroidism due to variants in CASR, GCM2, PTH, TBCE, GNA11, TRPM6, and autoimmune or developmental causes linked to AIRE, GATA3, and 22q11.2 deletion involving TBX1; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or de novo depending on the defect. Core molecular pathways involve parathyroid hormone signaling through PTH1R and Gs alpha/cAMP, calcium-sensing receptor signaling, vitamin D synthesis and VDR-mediated transcription, renal tubular calcium and magnesium handling, and bone-mineral axis components including FGF23-Klotho. Important subtypes include hypoparathyroid, pseudohypoparathyroid/PTH-resistant, vitamin D-deficient or resistant, renal, and hypomagnesemic hypocalcemic tetany. Treatment targets restoration of serum calcium and the underlying mechanism: intravenous calcium gluconate or calcium chloride directly increases extracellular calcium in emergencies, oral calcium carbonate or citrate provides ongoing replacement, calcitriol bypasses impaired renal activation of vitamin D to enhance intestinal calcium absorption, cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol correct deficiency, magnesium sulfate reverses hypocalcemia due to magnesium depletion, and recombinant human PTH may be used in chronic hypoparathyroidism. Common comorbidities and complications include nephrocalcinosis from therapy, cataracts, basal ganglia calcifications, dental enamel defects, osteoporosis or osteomalacia, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune endocrinopathies, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Diagnosis relies on low total and ionized calcium with ECG changes, plus measurement of PTH, magnesium, phosphate, creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and sometimes 1,25-dihydro

Name: Ulcer of oesophagus
Description: Ulcer of the oesophagus is a mucosal defect extending through the squamous or columnar epithelium of the esophageal wall, most often acquired rather than inherited, and usually reflects severe gastroesophageal reflux, pill-induced injury, infection, caustic exposure, radiation, or ischemic and inflammatory damage. Molecularly, no single causal gene defines the disorder, but susceptibility and healing are influenced by inflammatory and epithelial-repair pathways involving TNF, IL1B, IL6, PTGS2/COX-2, TGFB1, EGF/EGFR, VEGFA, MMPs, NF-kB signaling, oxidative-stress responses, and acid-sensing and tight-junction components; representative genetic associations are better established in related reflux phenotypes, including cytokine variants such as IL1B and TNFA and occasional epithelial barrier genes, while infectious ulcers may involve viral proteins from CMV or HSV rather than host mutations. Major subtypes include reflux-related peptic ulcer, drug-induced ulcer, infectious ulcer, eosinophilic or Crohn-related ulceration, malignant ulceration, and corrosive ulcer. Typical manifestations are odynophagia, dysphagia, retrosternal pain, heartburn, hematemesis or melena, iron-deficiency anemia, and weight loss. Common comorbidities include GERD, hiatal hernia, Barrett esophagus, immunosuppression, diabetes, connective-tissue disease, and malignancy; complications include hemorrhage, perforation, stricture, aspiration, fistula formation, and progression to Barrett-associated dysplasia or adenocarcinoma in chronic reflux settings. Diagnosis relies on upper endoscopy demonstrating a discrete ulcer crater with biopsy to exclude malignancy, eosinophilic esophagitis, CMV, HSV, or fungal infection, supported when appropriate by histopathology, viral immunostaining/PCR, barium swallow, ambulatory pH or impedance monitoring, and medication and caustic-exposure history. Treatment centers on proton-pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, pantoprazole, or esomeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion; and sucralfate forms a mucosal protective barrier, with antimicrobials or withdrawal of the offending drug when indicated.

Name: Gastroparesis
Description: Gastroparesis (MeSH D018589) is a chronic gastric neuromuscular motility disorder defined by objectively delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction, most often presenting with nausea, vomiting, early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating, epigastric pain, and weight loss or malnutrition. Major clinical subtypes include diabetic, idiopathic, postsurgical/vagal injury-related, medication-induced, connective tissue disease-associated, and less commonly pediatric or hereditary forms. Pathobiology centers on impaired fundic accommodation and antral-pyloroduodenal coordination involving autonomic and enteric neuropathy, loss or dysfunction of interstitial cells of Cajal, smooth-muscle abnormalities, and altered nitrergic signaling; key molecular components include KIT/CD117-positive ICC networks, neuronal nitric oxide synthase encoded by NOS1, heme oxygenase-1, ghrelin/GHSR, motilin pathways, and hyperglycemia-related oxidative and inflammatory injury. Genetic contributions are usually complex rather than Mendelian, but candidate associations include SCN5A variants affecting gastrointestinal pacemaker/conduction function, NOS1 polymorphisms, and rare syndromic mitochondrial or neuromuscular disorders; familial clustering is uncommon, and inheritance is generally not predictable except in underlying inherited diseases. Common comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, autonomic neuropathy, Parkinson disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, systemic sclerosis, hypothyroidism, chronic opioid use, anxiety/depression, and prior foregut surgery; complications include dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, bezoars, poor glycemic control, aspiration, and recurrent hospitalization. Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms plus exclusion of obstruction by upper endoscopy or imaging and demonstration of delayed emptying, classically by 4-hour gastric emptying scintigraphy, with wireless motility capsule or 13C breath testing as alternatives; antroduodenal manometry and electrogastrography may further characterize dysrhythmia. Treatment is largely symptomatic and prokinetic: metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist with 5-HT4 agonist activity, enhances acetylcholine release and gastric emptying; domperidone, a peripheral D2 antagonist, improves antral motility; erythromycin, a motilin receptor agonist, stimulates migrating motor complexes; additional options include antiemetics such as ondansetron, pyloric botulinum toxin in selected cases, gastric electrical stimulation

Name: Skin irritation
Description: Skin irritation is a nonspecific inflammatory reaction of the skin rather than a single inherited disease, encompassing irritant contact dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, frictional or chemical irritation, and symptom-predominant states seen in atopic dermatitis, xerosis, and barrier-disruption disorders; clinically it presents with pruritus, burning, stinging, erythema, dryness, scaling, edema, fissuring, papules or vesicles, and in chronic cases lichenification and excoriations. Its biology centers on epidermal barrier failure and innate/adaptive immune activation, with relevant genes and proteins including FLG loss-of-function variants, SPINK5, KRT1/KRT10, CLDN1, loricrin, involucrin, and cytokine mediators such as IL-1, TNF-α, TSLP, IL-4, IL-13, IL-17, IL-22, histamine, and mast-cell products; key pathways include NF-κB, JAK-STAT, Th2-skewed signaling, aryl hydrocarbon receptor responses, and keratinocyte stress pathways triggered by detergents, metals, solvents, allergens, or microbes. Although most cases are multifactorial and non-Mendelian, genetic susceptibility is well recognized, especially semidominant FLG-associated barrier dysfunction and familial atopy. Common comorbidities and complications include atopic disease (asthma, allergic rhinitis), secondary bacterial infection such as Staphylococcus aureus impetiginization, sleep disturbance, anxiety/depression, post-inflammatory pigment change, and chronic hand eczema. Treatment depends on subtype and trigger avoidance but commonly includes topical corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone or triamcinolone, which suppress phospholipase A2-driven cytokine transcription; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, which inhibit T-cell activation via calcineurin blockade; oral antihistamines such as cetirizine, which block H1 receptors to reduce itch; and emollients that restore barrier lipids. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by exposure history, distribution and morphology, with patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis, skin-prick or IgE testing when atopy is suspected, microbiologic testing if infection is present, and rarely biopsy to exclude psoriasis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, or other inflammatory dermatoses.

Name: Malaria by Plasmodium ovale
Description: Malaria due to Plasmodium ovale (UMLS C0152072) is a relapsing protozoal infection of humans caused by the erythrocytic and hepatic stages of P. ovale, now recognized as two closely related subtypes/species, P. ovale curtisi and P. ovale wallikeri, transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes and characterized by dormant liver hypnozoites that drive late relapse. Disease biology centers on hepatocyte invasion, merozoite egress, and reticulocyte-preferring erythrocyte invasion, with host inflammatory pathways involving TNF, IFN-γ, IL-6, macrophage activation, endothelial adhesion, splenic clearance, and heme-driven innate immune signaling contributing to fever and anemia; parasite proteins such as circumsporozoite protein, merozoite surface proteins, Duffy-binding-like/reticulocyte-binding ligands, lactate dehydrogenase, and cytochrome b are diagnostically or biologically relevant, while host genetic modifiers of malaria severity include G6PD deficiency, sickle hemoglobin, thalassemias, Southeast Asian ovalocytosis, and HLA-linked immune variation rather than Mendelian inheritance of the infection itself. Typical manifestations are intermittent fever, chills, sweats, headache, malaise, myalgia, pallor, thrombocytopenia, mild jaundice, and splenomegaly, usually with lower parasitemia than falciparum malaria but with complications including severe anemia, acute respiratory distress, splenic rupture, relapse, and heightened risk in pregnancy or immunocompromise; common comorbidities include malnutrition, HIV, bacterial coinfection, and other hemoglobinopathies. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus demonstration of parasites by Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films showing enlarged oval erythrocytes with fimbriated edges and Schüffner/James dots, supported by rapid antigen tests of limited sensitivity and confirmatory PCR or other nucleic-acid assays for speciation. Treatment commonly includes chloroquine, which inhibits heme detoxification in the parasite food vacuole where sensitivity persists, artemether-lumefantrine or other artemisinin-based combinations that generate toxic radicals and impair heme metabolism, and primaquine, an 8-aminoquinoline that eradicates hepatic hypnozoites and prevents relapse but requires prior G6PD testing because of hemol

Name: Pustular psoriasis (disorder)
Description: Pustular psoriasis is a rare, severe neutrophilic inflammatory psoriasis spectrum disorder characterized by sterile, recurrent eruptions of superficial pustules on erythematous skin, either generalized or localized, and clinically presents with painful burning erythema, sheets of pustules, scaling, fever, malaise, leukocytosis, elevated acute-phase reactants, and in palmoplantar forms disabling pustules and fissuring of the hands and feet; major subtypes include generalized pustular psoriasis, including acute von Zumbusch flares and impetigo herpetiformis of pregnancy, annular/circinate forms, palmoplantar pustulosis, and acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau. Its pathobiology is strongly linked to dysregulated innate immunity centered on the IL-36 axis, NF-kB/MAPK signaling, and the IL-23/Th17/TNF network, with keratinocyte and myeloid-cell production of IL-36, IL-1 family cytokines, CXCL8, IL-17, and TNF driving neutrophil recruitment; representative genetic associations include loss-of-function IL36RN mutations encoding the IL-36 receptor antagonist, AP1S3 variants affecting keratinocyte autophagy, CARD14 gain-of-function variants augmenting NF-kB activation, and less commonly MPO, SERPINA3, and TNIP1 variants, with inheritance often sporadic but sometimes autosomal recessive for IL36RN-related disease and autosomal dominant with variable penetrance for some CARD14-associated cases. Diagnosis is based on characteristic sterile pustules on erythematous skin, exclusion of infection and drug eruptions, biopsy showing spongiform pustules of Kogoj and psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, laboratory evidence of systemic inflammation, and supportive genetic testing in early-onset, familial, or atypical cases. Comorbidities and complications include psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, depression, secondary infection, electrolyte disturbances, and potentially life-threatening sepsis-like systemic inflammation. Treatment commonly uses acitretin, a retinoid normalizing keratinocyte differentiation; methotrexate, a folate antagonist with immunosuppressive effects; cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor blocking T-cell activation; and biologics such as TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, IL-23 inhibitors, or the IL-36 receptor blocker spesolim

Name: Posterior synechiae
Description: Posterior synechiae (UMLS C0152253) is an acquired ocular disorder defined by adhesion of the posterior iris surface to the anterior lens capsule, usually reflecting prior or ongoing anterior uveitis rather than a primary inherited disease, although genetic susceptibility is often mediated through immune-associated loci such as HLA-B27, HLA-DRB1, and, in specific uveitic syndromes, variants involving ERAP1, IL23R, NOD2, or TNFA pathways. Its pathobiology centers on breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier with leukocyte infiltration, fibrin exudation, and cytokine-driven inflammation involving TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-17/Th17, IL-23, NF-kappaB, JAK/STAT, prostaglandin, and TGF-beta-mediated fibrotic signaling, promoting persistent iris-lens apposition and scar formation. Posterior synechiae commonly complicates HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, tuberculosis, herpetic uveitis, Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis, and postoperative or traumatic iritis, and may lead to seclusio pupillae, iris bombe, secondary angle-closure or inflammatory glaucoma, cataract, irregular fixed pupil, and vision loss. Patients typically present with ocular pain, photophobia, redness, blurred vision, ciliary flush, decreased pupillary mobility, and an irregular or festooned pupil on slit-lamp examination. Patterns may be segmental or annular, recent and breakable or chronic fibrotic, and are often classified by extent or by underlying uveitic etiology rather than by a formal molecular subtype. Diagnosis is clinical, based on slit-lamp biomicroscopy after pupillary dilation, often supplemented by tonometry, gonioscopy, anterior-segment OCT or ultrasound biomicroscopy, and etiologic workup for uveitis including HLA-B27 typing, inflammatory markers, infectious serologies, and chest imaging when indicated. Treatment targets inflammation and synechial prevention with topical corticosteroids such as prednisolone acetate, which suppress NF-kappaB-dependent cytokine transcription; cycloplegic-mydriatics such as atropine, homatropine, or cyclopentolate, which block muscarinic receptors to dilate the pupil and reduce iris-l

Name: Salmonella Septicemia
Description: Salmonella septicemia (UMLS C0152486) is an invasive bloodstream infection caused mainly by Salmonella enterica, particularly typhoidal serovars Typhi and Paratyphi and invasive nontyphoidal strains such as S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis, in which bacterial virulence determinants rather than Mendelian inheritance define disease biology; key microbial genes and proteins include SPI-1/SPI-2 type III secretion system effectors, Vi capsular polysaccharide, lipopolysaccharide, flagellin, PhoP/PhoQ, and siderophore systems, while host susceptibility is influenced by variants affecting IFN-γ/IL-12 axis immunity, TLR4, NOD2, NRAMP1/SLC11A1, CYBB in chronic granulomatous disease, and sickle cell-associated splenic dysfunction. Pathogenesis centers on intestinal invasion, macrophage survival, and hematogenous dissemination driven by TLR4- and TLR5-triggered NF-κB, inflammasome, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and JAK-STAT signaling, with endotoxin-mediated sepsis and endothelial injury. Clinically, patients develop high fever, rigors, malaise, abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation, nausea, hepatosplenomegaly, hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, and sometimes rose spots, progressing to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, pneumonia, meningitis, osteomyelitis, or endovascular infection. Important comorbidities include HIV/AIDS, malaria, malnutrition, extremes of age, hemoglobinopathies, immunosuppressive therapy, malignancy, cirrhosis, and diabetes. Disease forms include typhoidal septicemia, invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia, recurrent disease, and focal metastatic infection. Diagnosis relies on blood culture as the standard, with culture of bone marrow, stool, urine, CSF, or focal sites when indicated, plus CBC, inflammatory markers, metabolic panels, susceptibility testing, and molecular assays such as PCR or serotyping to define strain and resistance. Treatment is prompt antimicrobial therapy guided by local resistance patterns, commonly ceftriaxone, a β-lactam inhibiting penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis, ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase/topoisomerase

Name: Acute amebiasis
Description: Acute amebiasis (UMLS C0152499) is an infectious protozoal disease caused by Entamoeba histolytica, usually presenting as acute intestinal amebic colitis and less commonly as invasive extraintestinal disease such as amebic liver abscess; clinical features include abdominal pain, cramping, tenesmus, watery or bloody diarrhea, fever, weight loss, and colonic tenderness, while severe cases may progress to fulminant necrotizing colitis, toxic megacolon, perforation, or hepatic abscess with right upper quadrant pain. Pathobiology is driven by parasite adherence and cytotoxicity mediated by the Gal/GalNAc lectin complex, cysteine proteases including EhCP1, EhCP2, and EhCP5, and amoebapores, with host-parasite interactions involving mucin depletion, epithelial apoptosis, complement resistance, and inflammatory signaling through NF-kB, MAPK, NLRP3 inflammasome, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-8, and IFN-gamma pathways. Genetic susceptibility is not Mendelian, but host variants affecting innate and mucosal immunity have been associated, including representative examples in leptin receptor LEPR Q223R, HLA class II loci, and polymorphisms influencing MBL2, TLR2, TLR4, and cytokine responses; there are no classic inheritance patterns, although malnutrition, pregnancy, corticosteroid exposure, and immunosuppression increase risk of invasive disease. Common comorbidities and complications include dehydration, anemia, malnutrition, HIV infection, inflammatory bowel disease mimicry, pyogenic superinfection, and pleuropulmonary spread from liver abscess. Diagnosis rests on compatible epidemiology and symptoms plus stool antigen testing or PCR to distinguish E. histolytica from nonpathogenic Entamoeba species, stool microscopy for trophozoites or cysts, serology especially in extraintestinal disease, colonoscopy with biopsy when needed, and imaging such as ultrasound or CT for hepatic involvement. Treatment typically uses metronidazole or tinidazole, nitroimidazoles that generate toxic radical intermediates damaging parasite DNA and proteins, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin, an aminoglycoside that inhibits 30S ribosomal protein synthesis, or iodoquinol, a luminal amebicide with metal-chelating and metabolic inhibitory effects

Name: Intestinal infection caused by Pseudomonas
Description: Intestinal infection caused by Pseudomonas, usually due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa and less often other Pseudomonas species, is an opportunistic gram-negative enteric infection ranging from self-limited gastroenteritis to invasive necrotizing enterocolitis, hemorrhagic colitis, or sepsis, particularly in neonates, critically ill, immunocompromised, or antibiotic-exposed patients. Bacterial virulence is driven by genes and proteins such as toxA encoding exotoxin A, the type III secretion effectors ExoS, ExoT, ExoU, and ExoY, elastases LasA/LasB, phospholipase C, alginate/biofilm pathways involving algD, quorum-sensing systems las, rhl, and pqs, and multidrug-resistance determinants including AmpC, OprD loss, and metallo-beta-lactamases such as VIM and IMP. Host susceptibility is not classically Mendelian, but genetic contributors include CFTR variants in cystic fibrosis, chronic granulomatous disease genes such as CYBB, neutropenia-associated states, and immunodeficiency pathways affecting TLR, NF-kappaB, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF signaling, which mediate epithelial injury, neutrophilic inflammation, and barrier disruption. Typical manifestations include fever, abdominal pain, watery or bloody diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal distension, ileus, and signs of dehydration or systemic toxicity; complications include bacteremia, perforation, toxic megacolon, septic shock, and death, with comorbidities such as inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, prematurity, diabetes, and prior broad-spectrum antibiotic use. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus stool culture or rectal swab with species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, blood cultures when invasive disease is suspected, and in selected severe cases PCR, colonoscopy, histopathology, or abdominal imaging to document colitis or necrosis. Treatment is guided by susceptibility testing and typically uses antipseudomonal agents such as piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis with beta-lactamase blockade, ceftazidime or cefepime, beta-lactams that bind penicillin-binding proteins, and ciprofloxacin, a DNA gyrase/topoisomerase inhibitor; carbapenems or aminoglycosides may be used in resistant or

Name: Septic enteritis
Description: Septic enteritis is an acute infectious and inflammatory disorder of the small intestine caused by invasive bacteria or their toxins, most often presenting as a severe form of infectious enteritis with systemic toxicity or sepsis; common etiologic subtypes include Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, enteroinvasive or shiga-toxin-producing Escherichia coli, Clostridioides difficile-associated enterocolitis, and neutropenic enterocolitis in immunocompromised hosts. Pathobiology centers on microbial adherence and invasion, epithelial barrier disruption, and activation of innate immune signaling, particularly TLR4-LPS, NOD-like receptor, NF-κB, MAPK, inflammasome, TNF, IL1B, IL6, CXCL8, IFNG, and complement/coagulation pathways; representative host susceptibility genes and proteins implicated in enteric infection severity include TLR4, NOD2, TNF, IL6, CFTR, MUC2, DEFA5, and HLA-linked immune response variation, although classic Mendelian inheritance is not typical and genetic contribution is usually complex and polygenic rather than deterministic. Patients typically develop fever, abdominal pain or cramping, nausea, vomiting, watery or bloody diarrhea, dehydration, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and in severe cases hypotension, ileus, toxic megacolon, bacteremia, or septic shock. Important comorbidities and risk states include extremes of age, malnutrition, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes, HIV/AIDS, malignancy, neutropenia, recent antibiotic exposure, and chronic liver or kidney disease; complications include electrolyte disturbances, acute kidney injury, bowel perforation, hemolytic uremic syndrome, and multiorgan failure. Diagnosis relies on clinical evidence of infectious enteritis plus systemic inflammatory response, supported by stool culture or multiplex PCR, C. difficile toxin/PCR testing when indicated, blood cultures in febrile or unstable patients, CBC, metabolic panel, lactate, inflammatory markers, and abdominal imaging or endoscopy selectively. Treatment is primarily rehydration and source-directed antimicrobials such as ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin blocking bacterial cell-wall synthesis, azithromycin, a macrolide inhibiting the 50S ribosomal subunit, and oral vancomycin for

Name: Black Death
Description: Plague (MeSH D010930) is an acute, often fulminant zoonotic infection caused by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Yersinia pestis, transmitted mainly by flea bites or exposure to infected animals and, in pneumonic plague, by respiratory droplets; major clinical forms are bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic plague. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial virulence genes and proteins rather than host Mendelian inheritance, notably the pCD1/type III secretion system with Yops such as YopH, YopE, YopJ/P, and LcrV, the plasminogen activator Pla, the F1 capsular antigen encoded by caf1, and iron-acquisition systems including yersiniabactin, which disable innate immunity, promote lymphatic and hematogenous spread, and trigger dysregulated host signaling involving TLR2/TLR4 recognition, NF-κB and MAPK modulation, inflammasome and complement activation, cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and profound coagulation-endothelial injury responses. Typical features include abrupt fever, chills, severe malaise, painful suppurative regional lymphadenitis (buboes), headache, myalgia, abdominal symptoms, and in advanced disease hypotension, delirium, acral necrosis, DIC, shock, hemoptysis, and rapidly progressive pneumonia or ARDS. Important complications and comorbid associations include bacteremia, meningitis, secondary pneumonia, multiorgan failure, and worse outcomes with delayed treatment, malnutrition, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, or immunocompromise. There is no recognized hereditary inheritance pattern for plague susceptibility, although host genetic variation in innate immune pathways may modify risk. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology plus clinical syndrome and confirmatory testing by culture or PCR from bubo aspirate, blood, or sputum, direct fluorescent antibody or F1 antigen detection, and paired serology to F1 antibody. First-line therapy includes streptomycin or gentamicin, aminoglycosides that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause mistranslation; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding at 30S; and ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S pept

Name: Gastrointestinal anthrax
Description: Gastrointestinal anthrax (UMLS C0152945) is an acute, often fulminant zoonotic infection caused by ingestion of Bacillus anthracis spores in contaminated meat, producing oropharyngeal or intestinal disease rather than a hereditary disorder; thus there is no Mendelian inheritance pattern, although host susceptibility may be influenced by variation in innate immune genes and toxin receptors, including ANTXR1/TEM8 and ANTXR2/CMG2, through which protective antigen mediates cellular entry of edema factor and lethal factor. The principal pathogenic proteins are protective antigen, edema factor, a calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase that raises intracellular cAMP, and lethal factor, a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves MAPKKs, disrupting MAPK signaling; disease severity is further shaped by macrophage and dendritic-cell responses, TNF, IL-1, NLRP1 inflammasome activation, endothelial dysfunction, and the antiphagocytic poly-D-glutamate capsule encoded on virulence plasmids. Clinically, patients develop severe abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, bloody diarrhea or hematemesis, dysphagia with cervical edema in oropharyngeal disease, ascites, ileus, and rapid progression to sepsis, shock, bowel necrosis, perforation, or meningitis; common complications and comorbid states include dehydration, peritonitis, bacteremia, multiorgan failure, and worse outcomes in malnutrition or immunocompromise. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure history plus culture or PCR from blood, stool, ascitic fluid, or lesion material, Gram stain, immunohistochemistry, serology for anti-protective antigen antibodies, and imaging or endoscopy when stable. Recommended treatment uses multidrug therapy such as ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks 30S ribosomal protein synthesis, and a beta-lactam such as meropenem or penicillin when susceptibility is known, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis; antitoxin agents including raxibacumab or obiltoxaximab neutralize protective antigen and are added in systemic disease.

Name: [X]Streptococcal septicaemia, unspecified
Description: Streptococcal septicaemia, unspecified (UMLS C0152964) is an acute invasive bloodstream infection caused by Streptococcus species, most commonly beta-hemolytic streptococci such as Streptococcus pyogenes or agalactiae and sometimes pneumococci or viridans streptococci, producing a sepsis syndrome driven more by pathogen virulence and host-response biology than by Mendelian inheritance. Key microbial factors include the M protein encoded by emm, streptolysins O and S, hyaluronic acid capsule synthesis genes such as hasA, C5a peptidase scpA, and superantigen exotoxins including speA and speC, while host susceptibility and severity have been associated with variants in innate and inflammatory genes including TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, NFKB-related pathways, TNF, IL6, and HLA class II loci. Pathobiology centers on pattern-recognition receptor activation by streptococcal cell-wall components, triggering NF-kB, MAPK, complement, coagulation, and cytokine networks with neutrophil, endothelial, and platelet activation, capillary leak, and possible toxic shock. Clinical manifestations include fever or hypothermia, chills, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, and focal findings from skin/soft-tissue, pulmonary, endometrial, or endovascular infection; complications include septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury, multiorgan failure, necrotizing fasciitis, endocarditis, and meningitis. Subtypes are usually defined by causative species or syndrome, including group A or B streptococcal bacteremia and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Diagnosis relies on sepsis criteria plus blood cultures with Gram stain, species identification and susceptibility testing, supported by CBC, inflammatory markers, serum lactate, organ-function tests, and imaging or echocardiography to identify the source. Treatment requires rapid source control and intravenous antibiotics such as penicillin G or ceftriaxone, which inhibit cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking, and clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit and suppresses toxin production; vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala cell

Name: Staphylococcal septicemia (disorder)
Description: Staphylococcal septicemia is an acute, life-threatening bloodstream infection caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant strains, and less often by coagulase-negative staphylococci in device-related disease; it is an infectious rather than inherited disorder, although host genetic susceptibility is influenced by variants in innate-immune genes such as TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, IL6, TNF, MBL2, and FCGR2A, while bacterial virulence and resistance determinants commonly include mecA or mecC encoding altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a, blaZ beta-lactamase, and toxins such as alpha-hemolysin encoded by hla, Panton-Valentine leukocidin genes lukS/lukF-PV, protein A spa, and agr quorum-sensing regulators. Pathobiology centers on activation of TLR2-NF-kappaB, complement, inflammasome, cytokine networks involving TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6, endothelial injury, coagulation, and biofilm formation on catheters or prostheses, driving sepsis, microvascular dysfunction, and metastatic infection. Typical manifestations include fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated inflammatory markers, and signs of a primary focus such as skin/soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, or infected intravascular hardware. Major complications and comorbid links include septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, acute respiratory distress syndrome, infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, abscesses, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, and indwelling devices. Diagnosis requires positive blood cultures, species identification and susceptibility testing, often with PCR for mecA/mecC or rapid MALDI-TOF methods, plus echocardiography and imaging to identify endocarditis or deep foci; clinical criteria follow sepsis definitions with organ dysfunction. Treatment depends on subtype, including uncomplicated bacteremia, complicated bacteremia, catheter-related infection, and MRSA septicemia; common drugs include nafcillin or oxacillin, which inhibit cell-wall transpeptidation in MSSA, vancomycin, a glycopeptide blocking peptidoglycan synthesis in MRSA, daptomycin

Name: Anaerobic septicemia (disorder)
Description: Anaerobic septicemia is a life-threatening bloodstream infection caused by obligate anaerobic bacteria, most commonly Bacteroides fragilis group, Clostridium species such as C. perfringens and C. septicum, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, and mixed anaerobic flora arising from intra-abdominal, pelvic, soft-tissue, dental, or ischemic sources; clinically it presents with fever, rigors, hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, lactic acidosis, and organ dysfunction, with subtype patterns including clostridial septicemia, bacteremic spread from abdominal or pelvic sepsis, and polymicrobial anaerobic bacteremia. Pathobiology is driven less by host inheritance than by microbial virulence determinants and host inflammatory pathways: examples include B. fragilis capsular polysaccharide and beta-lactamase, C. perfringens alpha-toxin encoded by plc, perfringolysin O encoded by pfoA, and Fusobacterium adhesins, which activate Toll-like receptor, NF-kappaB, inflammasome, complement, coagulation, and cytokine cascades involving TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6, leading to endothelial injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemolysis, and septic shock. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for the disorder itself, but susceptibility is increased by immunosuppression, neutropenia, malignancy, diabetes, bowel perforation, surgery, trauma, and mucosal barrier injury; notable associations include C. septicum bacteremia with occult colorectal cancer and hematologic malignancy. Common complications include abscess formation, liver abscess, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, acute kidney injury, acute respiratory distress syndrome, multiorgan failure, and death. Diagnosis relies on clinical sepsis criteria plus identification of anaerobes in properly collected blood cultures, source cultures under anaerobic conditions, Gram stain, imaging to find abscess or ischemic bowel, and laboratory markers such as lactate; molecular methods including 16S rRNA PCR or MALDI-TOF may aid speciation. Name: Septicemia due to Serratia (disorder)
Description: Septicemia due to Serratia is an acute, usually healthcare-associated Gram-negative bloodstream infection most often caused by Serratia marcescens, although other species such as S. liquefaciens and S. odorifera may occur; it is not an inherited disorder, but host genetic susceptibility to severe sepsis has been linked to variation in innate immune and inflammatory genes such as TLR4, CD14, NOD2, TNF, IL6, and mannose-binding lectin/MBL2, while bacterial virulence and resistance determinants commonly include lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis genes, porin alterations, AmpC beta-lactamase overexpression, extended-spectrum beta-lactamases such as CTX-M, and carbapenemases including KPC and metallo-beta-lactamases. Pathobiology centers on LPS-triggered TLR4-CD14-MD2 signaling, NF-kB and MAPK activation, inflammasome-mediated cytokine release, complement and coagulation cascade activation, endothelial injury, and dysregulated neutrophil responses leading to vasodilation, capillary leak, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and septic shock. Typical manifestations include fever or hypothermia, rigors, hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, and evidence of organ dysfunction, often arising from catheter-related infection, urinary tract infection, pneumonia, wound infection, or neonatal intensive care exposure. Important subtypes include uncomplicated bacteremia, catheter-associated bloodstream infection, neonatal sepsis, and multidrug-resistant or carbapenem-resistant Serratia septicemia. Comorbidities commonly include immunosuppression, malignancy, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, burns, prematurity, prolonged hospitalization, invasive devices, and prior broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure; complications include shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, metastatic abscesses, and death.
