Name: Herpes zoster with keratoconjunctivitis
Description: Herpes zoster with keratoconjunctivitis is an ocular manifestation of varicella-zoster virus reactivation, usually involving the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, in which latent human herpesvirus 3 resumes lytic replication in sensory ganglia and spreads to the cornea, conjunctiva, and periocular tissues, producing a painful unilateral vesicular dermatomal eruption with red eye, photophobia, tearing, blurred vision, foreign-body sensation, decreased corneal sensitivity, punctate or pseudodendritiform keratitis, conjunctivitis, and sometimes stromal keratitis or anterior uveitis. The disease is infectious rather than inherited, but host susceptibility is influenced by immune-response genes and pathways, with representative associations involving HLA class I and II loci, interferon signaling genes such as IFNAR1 and STAT1, innate viral sensing through TLR3 and cGAS-STING, and T-cell/IL-2, NF-kB, and JAK-STAT pathways that govern viral control and ocular inflammation; no single causal germline mutation defines typical cases, although immunodeficiency states can confer risk. Common subtypes include epithelial, stromal, endothelial, and neurotrophic keratitis within herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Standard therapy includes acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, which are guanosine analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase and inhibit viral DNA polymerase; adjunctive topical or systemic corticosteroids such as prednisolone reduce immune-mediated stromal keratitis or uveitis, and cycloplegics such as atropine relieve ciliary spasm. Important comorbidities and complications include older age, HIV infection, malignancy, transplantation, diabetes, postherpetic neuralgia, bacterial superinfection, cranial nerve palsies, glaucoma, cataract, chronic dry eye, neurotrophic ulceration, corneal scarring, retinal necrosis, and permanent vision loss. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining, corneal sensation testing, intraocular pressure assessment, and when needed PCR for VZV DNA from vesicle, tear, or ocular samples; diagnosis is strengthened by a typical unilateral V1 rash, Hutchinson sign, and characteristic ocular inflammation.

Name: Syphilis, tertiary
Description: Tertiary syphilis (UMLS C0153188) is a late, chronic, non-Mendelian infectious sequela of untreated Treponema pallidum infection characterized by persistent spirochetal infection and a host delayed-type hypersensitivity/plasma cell-rich inflammatory response rather than a defined inherited disorder; no single causative human gene is established, but susceptibility and severity have been linked to immune-response variation, including HLA class II alleles, TLR1/TLR2/TLR6, CD14, TNF, IL10, and IFNG pathways, while major treponemal antigens and proteins such as Tp47, TmpA, and outer membrane lipoproteins drive innate immune activation. Pathobiology involves TLR-NF-kB signaling, macrophage and Th1/Th17 cytokine networks, endothelial inflammation, obliterative endarteritis, and granulomatous tissue injury. Major clinical forms are gummatous syphilis, cardiovascular syphilis, and neurosyphilis, presenting years after primary infection with destructive gummas of skin, bone, or viscera, aortitis with ascending aortic aneurysm or aortic regurgitation, and neurologic syndromes including tabes dorsalis, meningovascular disease, general paresis, sensory ataxia, lightning pains, Argyll Robertson pupils, cognitive decline, and psychiatric change. Common comorbidities and complications include HIV coinfection, stroke, blindness, hearing loss, Charcot arthropathy, and heart failure. Diagnosis rests on compatible late manifestations plus serology, typically a treponemal test such as FTA-ABS or TP-PA with a non-treponemal test such as RPR or VDRL for activity, recognizing that titers may be lower in late disease; CSF VDRL, CSF cell count and protein, and neuroimaging support neurosyphilis, while echocardiography or CT/MR angiography assess cardiovascular involvement. Name: Acute gonococcal epididymo-orchitis
Description: Acute gonococcal epididymo-orchitis is an acute, sexually transmitted bacterial inflammation of the epididymis with variable extension to the testis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, typically representing ascending urethral infection in sexually active men; it is not a Mendelian genetic disease and has no defined inheritance pattern, although host susceptibility is influenced by immune-response variation rather than high-penetrance mutations, with representative host factors including complement terminal pathway deficiencies predisposing to invasive gonococcal disease and polymorphic innate immune genes affecting TNF, IL6, TLR2, TLR4, and CXCL8/IL-8 signaling. Pathobiology centers on gonococcal pili, Opa proteins, PorB, lipooligosaccharide, and IgA protease driving epithelial adhesion, neutrophilic inflammation, and cytokine activation through TLR/NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome, and complement pathways, with IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, C3, and C5b-9 as key components. Patients usually present with acute unilateral scrotal pain, swelling, epididymal tenderness, warmth, erythema, dysuria, urethral discharge, fever, and sometimes reactive hydrocele; subtypes are chiefly categorized by localization as epididymitis, epididymo-orchitis, or orchitis, and by uncomplicated versus abscess-forming or disseminated infection. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical findings plus microbiologic confirmation using nucleic acid amplification testing of urine or urethral specimens for N. gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, urethral Gram stain showing intracellular gram-negative diplococci in symptomatic men, and culture for antimicrobial susceptibility; scrotal ultrasonography helps exclude torsion and may show epididymal hyperemia. Standard therapy includes ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam cephalosporin that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, often combined with doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks 30S ribosomal protein synthesis for possible chlamydial coinfection, or azithromycin, a macrolide inhibiting 50S translocation; historical fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin inhibit DNA gyrase but are limited by resistance. Name: Acute gonococcal cervicitis
Description: Acute gonococcal cervicitis (UMLS C0153195) is an acute sexually transmitted mucopurulent inflammation of the endocervical epithelium caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, most often presenting with purulent endocervical discharge, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, dysuria, dyspareunia, pelvic discomfort, cervical friability, and many asymptomatic cases. Disease severity reflects bacterial adherence and immune evasion mediated by type IV pili, PorB porin, Opa opacity proteins, lipooligosaccharide, and the MtrCDE efflux pump; representative microbial genetic determinants include penA mosaic alleles, mtrR and porB mutations, and 23S rRNA or gyrA/parC variants that influence cephalosporin, macrolide, and fluoroquinolone susceptibility rather than host inheritance. Host responses prominently involve TLR2/TLR4-, NF-kB-, MAPK-, inflammasome-, and IL-1/IL-6/IL-8/TNF-alpha-driven neutrophilic inflammation, with complement interactions and occasional susceptibility contributions from terminal complement deficiency that also predisposes to disseminated gonococcal infection. Common subtypes include uncomplicated cervicitis, cervicitis with urethritis, and ascending infection associated with pelvic inflammatory disease; important complications and linked comorbidities include coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis, HIV acquisition/transmission, endometritis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian abscess, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and neonatal ophthalmia. The condition is non-Mendelian and not inherited in the usual sense, although host polymorphisms in innate immune or complement genes may modify risk. Diagnosis is established clinically in a sexually exposed patient with mucopurulent cervicitis and confirmed primarily by nucleic acid amplification testing on vaginal, endocervical, or urine specimens, with culture on selective media and antimicrobial susceptibility testing when treatment failure, resistance surveillance, or pharyngeal disease is suspected. Name: Acute gonococcal endometritis
Description: Acute gonococcal endometritis is an acute, sexually transmitted bacterial infection of the endometrial lining caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, usually as part of ascending gonococcal cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease, and is best regarded as an infectious inflammatory disorder rather than an inherited disease. Its pathobiology centers on gonococcal adherence and invasion mediated by type IV pili, Opa proteins, porin PorB, lipooligosaccharide, and IgA protease, with host innate immune activation through TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome-related IL-1beta signaling, and marked neutrophil-, TNF-alpha-, IL-6-, and IL-8/CXCL8-driven mucosal inflammation; variation in gonococcal penA, mtrR, porB, gyrA, parC, and 23S rRNA can influence antimicrobial resistance, while host susceptibility has been linked more broadly to immune-response polymorphisms than to a Mendelian inheritance pattern. Typical manifestations include lower abdominal or pelvic pain, fever, abnormal uterine bleeding, purulent cervical or vaginal discharge, cervical motion and uterine tenderness, dyspareunia, and sometimes concurrent urethritis or pharyngogenital infection. Recognized clinical forms include uncomplicated lower genital tract infection, acute endometritis within pelvic inflammatory disease, postpartum or post-procedural endometritis, and mixed infection with Chlamydia trachomatis or anaerobes. Major comorbidities and complications include cervicitis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian abscess, chronic pelvic pain, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, perihepatitis, bacteremia, and enhanced HIV acquisition and transmission. Diagnosis relies on clinical PID criteria in a sexually active patient with pelvic pain plus uterine, adnexal, or cervical motion tenderness, supported by nucleic acid amplification testing for N. gonorrhoeae from cervical or vaginal swabs or urine, pregnancy testing, microscopy and inflammatory markers, culture with susceptibility testing when resistance is a concern, and occasionally endometrial sampling or pelvic imaging to assess complications. Name: Gonococcal infection of joint
Description: Gonococcal infection of the joint, or gonococcal arthritis, is an acute septic arthritis caused by dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae from a mucosal genital, rectal, or pharyngeal focus and classically presents as either the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome or localized purulent monoarthritis, most often affecting knees, wrists, ankles, or small joints with fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular or vesiculopustular skin lesions, joint effusion, warmth, and restricted motion. Its pathobiology is driven by gonococcal pili, opacity proteins, PorB porin, lipooligosaccharide, and IgA1 protease, with host inflammatory activation through TLR2/TLR4, NF-kB, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-8; susceptibility is influenced more by host factors than Mendelian inheritance, notably terminal complement pathway defects involving C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9, and occasionally variants affecting innate immunity, while bacterial antimicrobial resistance determinants include penA alterations, mtrR dysregulation, porB mutations, and gyrA/parC mutations. Important comorbidities and risk settings include concomitant cervicitis, urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, HIV infection, pregnancy, menstruation, systemic lupus erythematosus, and complement deficiency, and complications include cartilage destruction, osteomyelitis, recurrent disseminated infection, infertility from associated genital disease, and rarely endocarditis or meningitis. Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion plus synovial fluid analysis showing inflammatory or purulent effusion, Gram stain and culture of synovial fluid, blood, and mucosal sites, and especially nucleic acid amplification testing from urogenital and extragenital specimens; culture also permits susceptibility testing. Standard treatment uses ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and bacterial cell wall synthesis, often with doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, or azithromycin, a 50S inhibitor, when Chlamydia trachomatis coinfection is not excluded; historical or alternative agents include cefotaxime and spectinomycin.

Name: Gonococcal meningitis
Description: Gonococcal meningitis (UMLS C0153225) is a rare, severe form of invasive Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection in which hematogenous dissemination from mucosal gonorrhea leads to meningeal invasion and acute bacterial meningitis; it is not a hereditary disease, but host susceptibility is influenced by genetic and immunologic factors, notably terminal complement pathway defects in C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9, properdin deficiency, and variants affecting innate recognition such as TLR4, while key bacterial virulence determinants include type IV pili, PorB, Opa proteins, lipooligosaccharide, Rmp, and transferrin-binding proteins, with frequent antimicrobial-resistance mutations in penA, porB, mtrR, and gyrA/parC. Pathobiologically, infection engages TLR2/TLR4-, NF-kB-, inflammasome-, and complement-mediated pathways, driving TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6, IL-8, neutrophil recruitment, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and purulent CSF inflammation. Patients typically present with fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, nausea or vomiting, altered mental status, and sometimes petechial rash, arthralgia, tenosynovitis, or concomitant urethritis/cervicitis as part of disseminated gonococcal infection; major complications include sepsis, septic arthritis, endocarditis, cerebral edema, cranial neuropathies, hearing loss, seizures, stroke, and death. Subtypes are best considered within disseminated gonococcal infection phenotypes, including arthritis-dermatitis syndrome and purulent focal infection with meningitis. Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion plus CSF analysis showing neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, with confirmation by CSF and blood culture or NAAT/PCR for N. gonorrhoeae from CSF or mucosal sites, Gram stain showing gram-negative diplococci, and susceptibility testing. Name: Gonococcal endocarditis
Description: Gonococcal endocarditis (UMLS C0153227) is a rare, severe form of infective endocarditis caused by hematogenous dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, usually arising from disseminated gonococcal infection rather than inherited host disease; accordingly, no Mendelian inheritance pattern is established, although bacterial virulence determinants such as type IV pili/pilE, opacity proteins Opa, porin PorB, lipooligosaccharide biosynthetic genes, and iron-acquisition proteins, together with resistance-associated mutations in penA, mtrR, porB, and gyrA/parC, can influence invasiveness and antibiotic susceptibility, while host susceptibility has been linked more broadly to terminal complement deficiency and occasionally SLE-related complement dysfunction. Pathobiology centers on adherence to endothelium, immune evasion, bacteremia, and intense innate immune activation through TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, complement, and neutrophil-driven inflammatory pathways, culminating in valvular destruction, most often of the aortic or mitral valve, with large friable vegetations. Patients typically present with fever, chills, malaise, new or changing murmur, tachycardia, embolic phenomena, heart failure, and often antecedent or concurrent migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, or genitourinary/pharyngeal infection; complications include acute severe valvular regurgitation, perivalvular abscess, systemic emboli, stroke, sepsis, and death. Disease may be classified clinically as native-valve versus prosthetic-valve infection or as part of disseminated gonococcal infection. Diagnosis relies on modified Duke criteria, repeated blood cultures with species identification and susceptibility testing, echocardiography—preferably transesophageal when suspicion is high—and sampling of genital, rectal, or pharyngeal sites by NAAT or culture; inflammatory markers and evaluation for complement deficiency or other STI coinfections may be useful adjuncts. Treatment is centered on ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis, often with doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, or azithromycin, a 50S macrolide, when Chlamydia trachomatis coinfection has

Name: Latent yaws
Description: Latent yaws (UMLS C0153240) is a nonvenereal, chronic treponemal infection caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, in which patients have no active skin lesions yet remain seroreactive after prior primary or secondary yaws; it is an infectious disease rather than an inherited disorder, so no human Mendelian inheritance pattern is recognized, although pathogen factors such as treponemal outer-membrane and immunogenic proteins including Tp47, TmpA, and variable tpr family antigens, and occasional macrolide-resistance 23S rRNA mutations such as A2058G or A2059G, are relevant examples. Pathobiology centers on host innate and adaptive immune activation, especially macrophages, dendritic cells, CD4+ T cells, plasma cells, and cytokine pathways involving TLR-mediated recognition, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-1, and IL-6, with endarteritis and chronic inflammatory tissue injury as key cellular processes. Typical latent disease is asymptomatic, but historical clues include prior papillomatous or ulcerative “mother yaw,” disseminated secondary papules, plantar hyperkeratosis, and regional lymphadenopathy; untreated infection may relapse to infectious lesions or progress to tertiary destructive complications such as gummatous skin and bone disease, osteoperiostitis, saber shin, juxta-articular nodules, and mutilating rhinopharyngitis, with frequent comorbidity from bacterial superinfection, anemia, malnutrition, and co-endemic tropical skin diseases. Subtypes are early latent and late latent yaws, distinguished by shorter versus longer duration since active disease and lower relapse risk in late infection. Diagnosis relies on epidemiologic exposure in endemic settings, compatible past clinical history, and positive serology using a treponemal test such as TPPA or FTA-ABS plus a nontreponemal test such as RPR or VDRL for activity and follow-up; dark-field microscopy and PCR from active lesions, when present, can confirm treponemal infection and help distinguish yaws from venereal syphilis. Name: tinea manus
Description: Tinea manus (UMLS C0153246) is a superficial dermatophyte infection of the palmar hand, most often caused by Trichophyton rubrum, followed by T. mentagrophytes/interdigitale and Epidermophyton floccosum, and it is typically acquired rather than inherited, although host susceptibility may be influenced by genetic variation in cutaneous antifungal immunity, including CARD9 deficiency and polymorphisms affecting Dectin-1/CLEC7A, toll-like receptor signaling, and IL-17/Th17 axis components that regulate keratinocyte responses, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-17. The disease reflects fungal adherence to and invasion of keratinized stratum corneum with protease- and keratinase-mediated tissue colonization; major clinical patterns include diffuse hyperkeratotic “moccasin-like” palmar scaling and unilateral or asymmetric annular inflammatory lesions, often occurring with tinea pedis as the classic “two-feet one-hand” syndrome. Symptoms and signs include dry scaling, erythema, pruritus, accentuated palmar creases, fissuring, and occasionally vesicles or pustules, while complications include secondary bacterial infection, chronic hand dermatitis, onychomycosis, spread to other body sites, and recurrence; common comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, atopy, and concomitant tinea pedis or unguium. Diagnosis is based on compatible morphology and exposure history, confirmed by potassium hydroxide microscopy showing septate hyphae, fungal culture, and increasingly PCR or other dermatophyte assays, with biopsy and PAS stain reserved for equivocal cases; important differentials are irritant or allergic contact dermatitis, psoriasis, dyshidrotic eczema, and candidiasis. Treatment relies on topical allylamines such as terbinafine, which inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, azoles such as clotrimazole or ketoconazole, which inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis, and for extensive or refractory disease oral terbinafine, itraconazole, or fluconazole.

Name: Systemic candidiasis
Description: Systemic candidiasis is an invasive fungal disease caused predominantly by Candida albicans, but also by C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, and C. krusei, in which bloodstream dissemination or deep-organ invasion occurs, most often in critically ill, neutropenic, postoperative, premature neonatal, or otherwise immunocompromised patients. Its pathobiology centers on fungal adhesion, hyphal transition, biofilm formation, and immune evasion, with virulence determinants including ALS adhesins, HWP1, SAP proteases, candidalysin encoded by ECE1, and ergosterol-biosynthetic enzymes such as ERG11; resistance-associated mutations include ERG11 alterations for azole resistance and FKS1/FKS2 hot-spot mutations for echinocandin resistance. Host susceptibility is influenced by innate and adaptive immune genes, including CARD9 deficiency, CLEC7A encoding dectin-1, TLR1/TLR2/TLR4, IL17RA/IL17F, STAT1 gain-of-function, and AIRE in syndromic contexts, although most cases are acquired rather than classically inherited; when genetic, inheritance may be autosomal recessive as in CARD9 deficiency or autosomal dominant in selected immune dysregulation syndromes. Key pathways include dectin-1/SYK/CARD9/NF-κB signaling, Toll-like receptor pathways, Th17/IL-17 and IL-22 immunity, neutrophil oxidative killing, complement, and inflammasome activation. Typical manifestations include persistent fever and sepsis despite antibacterials, candidemia, hypotension, multiorgan dysfunction, hepatosplenic lesions, endophthalmitis, renal microabscesses, and skin papules. Major subtypes include candidemia, acute disseminated candidiasis, chronic disseminated or hepatosplenic candidiasis, and deep-seated organ candidiasis. Important comorbidities and complications include central venous catheters, total parenteral nutrition, diabetes, malignancy, organ transplantation, HIV or steroid exposure, infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, meningitis, shock, and death. Diagnosis relies on blood or sterile-site culture, species identification with susceptibility testing, β-D-glucan, PCR or T2Candida assays, and targeted imaging plus ophthalmologic evaluation. Name: Candidal endocarditis
Description: Candidal endocarditis (UMLS C0153254) is a rare, life-threatening fungal infective endocarditis caused predominantly by Candida albicans, with non-albicans species such as C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, C. glabrata, and occasionally C. auris also implicated; it usually affects native or prosthetic valves and intracardiac devices through hematogenous seeding and biofilm formation rather than following a Mendelian inheritance pattern. Host susceptibility is influenced by genetic and immunologic factors in fungal recognition and innate immunity, including variants affecting CARD9, CLEC7A encoding dectin-1, TLR2/TLR4, and cytokine pathways such as IL17A/IL17RA, IL6, and TNF, while fungal virulence genes and proteins including ALS adhesins, HWP1, secreted aspartyl proteases, candidalysin from ECE1, and biofilm regulators contribute to endothelial adhesion and valve destruction. Key pathogenic pathways include pattern-recognition receptor signaling, NF-kB activation, Th17-mediated immunity, complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, endothelial invasion, and extracellular matrix interaction within biofilms. Major risk factors and comorbidities include prior valve disease, prosthetic valves, indwelling central venous catheters, intravenous drug use, prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, total parenteral nutrition, recent cardiac surgery, diabetes, malignancy, neutropenia, transplantation, and other immunosuppressed states; complications include large vegetations, systemic emboli, stroke, heart failure, myocardial abscess, persistent candidemia, and relapse. Typical findings are persistent fever, new or changing murmur, sepsis, embolic phenomena, and signs of heart failure, though presentation may be subacute. Diagnosis relies on repeated blood cultures for Candida, species identification and susceptibility testing, transthoracic and especially transesophageal echocardiography, and adjunctive serum biomarkers such as beta-D-glucan; Duke criteria are applied with microbiologic and echocardiographic evidence. Treatment commonly combines surgery with prolonged antifungal therapy, using liposomal amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes, often with flucytosine, a pyrimidine analog that inhibits fungal DNA/RNA synthesis, or an echinocandin such as caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulaf

Name: Candidal meningitis
Description: Candidal meningitis (UMLS C0153256) is an uncommon but severe invasive fungal infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid caused predominantly by Candida albicans, with C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. glabrata, and C. krusei also implicated, occurring most often in neonates, neurosurgical patients, and immunocompromised hosts. Pathobiology reflects fungal adhesion and biofilm programs and host innate immune signaling, notably Candida cell-wall mannan and beta-glucan recognition by Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2, TLR4, CARD9, MYD88, SYK, NF-kappaB, inflammasome/IL-1beta, and Th17-axis mediators including IL17RA, IL17F, STAT1, and STAT3; rare susceptibility variants in CARD9, CLEC7A, STAT1 gain-of-function, AIRE, and related primary immunodeficiency genes can predispose to invasive or chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, although candidal meningitis is usually acquired rather than classically inherited. Fungal virulence genes and proteins such as ALS adhesins, HWP1, SAP proteases, EFG1, and CPH1 support tissue invasion. Typical manifestations include fever, headache, vomiting, altered mental status, meningismus, cranial neuropathies, seizures, and signs of raised intracranial pressure, often with subacute onset. Important complications and comorbidities include candidemia, ventriculitis, hydrocephalus, cerebral abscess, vasculitic infarction, endophthalmitis, prematurity, malignancy, HIV infection, diabetes, organ transplantation, corticosteroid exposure, indwelling CNS devices, and broad-spectrum antibiotic use. Diagnosis rests on CSF analysis showing pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose, and definitive or supportive identification by CSF culture, blood culture, fungal stain, histopathology, Candida PCR, and occasionally beta-D-glucan, with MRI or CT to detect meningeal enhancement, ventriculitis, or abscess; disease may be categorized as neonatal, postoperative/device-associated, or disseminated hematogenous CNS candidiasis. Treatment commonly uses liposomal amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores, often with flucytosine, a pyrimidine analog that inhibits fungal DNA

Name: Echinococcus granulosus infection of liver
Description: Echinococcus granulosus infection of the liver, or hepatic cystic echinococcosis, is a zoonotic helminthic disease caused by larval cestodes that form slowly enlarging hydatid cysts, most often classified by imaging as WHO CE1–CE5 active, transitional, or inactive lesions; disease is acquired rather than inherited, although host susceptibility and immune response are influenced by genetic variation in cytokine and HLA loci, with reported associations involving HLA-DRB1, TNF, IFNG, IL10, and TLR polymorphisms rather than a Mendelian pattern. Its pathobiology centers on parasite laminated and germinal layers, protoscoleces, and host Th2-skewed immune signaling, including IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, eosinophils, IgE, and alternatively activated macrophages, with contributory innate pathways involving TLR2/TLR4, dendritic cells, complement, and fibrosis-related TGF-β signaling around the pericyst. Patients may be asymptomatic for years or present with right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, nausea, early satiety, cholestatic jaundice, fever if secondarily infected, or urticaria and anaphylaxis after leakage or rupture. Major complications include biliary communication, cholangitis, cyst rupture into the peritoneum or thorax, secondary bacterial abscess, portal compression, and recurrence; comorbidities can include other hepatobiliary disease and pulmonary echinococcosis. Diagnosis relies on exposure history, ultrasound as first-line test with CT or MRI for anatomy and complications, and serology such as Echinococcus IgG ELISA with immunoblot confirmation, while eosinophilia is variably present and definitive confirmation may come from visualization of daughter cysts, hydatid sand, or parasitic elements. Treatment commonly uses albendazole, a benzimidazole that binds parasite β-tubulin and inhibits microtubule-dependent glucose uptake, mebendazole with a similar mechanism, praziquantel, which increases parasite membrane calcium permeability and may aid protoscolex killing, plus selected PAIR drainage or surgery depending on cyst stage, size, and biliary involvement.

Name: Echinococcus granulosus infection of lung
Description: Echinococcus granulosus infection of the lung, or pulmonary cystic echinococcosis, is a zoonotic helminthic disease caused by larval-stage E. granulosus sensu lato that forms fluid-filled hydatid cysts in the lung, either as isolated pulmonary disease or with concurrent hepatic involvement; major clinical subtypes include uncomplicated intact cysts, ruptured or infected cysts, single versus multiple cysts, and unilateral versus bilateral disease. It is not an inherited disorder, but host susceptibility and immune response have genetic correlates, with representative associations reported for HLA class II alleles and cytokine-related genes such as IL10, TNF, IFNG, TLR2, and TLR4, while parasite antigens and proteins including antigen B and antigen 5 are central diagnostic and immunobiologic markers rather than somatic mutations. Pathobiology is dominated by Th2-skewed immunity and host-parasite interactions involving IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, IgE, eosinophils, macrophages, and regulatory T-cell pathways, with fibrosis and granulomatous inflammation around cysts. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with cough, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, fever, or expectoration of salty fluid or membranes after rupture; complications include secondary bacterial infection, pleural rupture, pneumothorax, hydropneumothorax, empyema, anaphylaxis, respiratory compromise, and recurrence, with comorbid liver cystic echinococcosis being most common. Diagnosis relies on exposure history in endemic settings, chest radiography and CT showing characteristic well-circumscribed cystic lesions or detached membranes, supplemented by ultrasonography for extrapulmonary disease, serology such as ELISA or immunoblot to antigen B/5, eosinophilia in some cases, and confirmatory histopathology or parasitologic examination when tissue is obtained. Treatment commonly includes albendazole, a benzimidazole that inhibits parasite beta-tubulin and microtubule assembly; mebendazole, with a similar mechanism; and praziquantel, which increases parasite membrane calcium permeability and may be used adjunctively, while definitive management often requires cyst-preserving surgery or resection depending on size, rupture, and complications.

Name: Mixed intestinal infection caused by Cestoda and/or Trematoda and/or Phylum Nematoda
Description: Mixed intestinal infection caused by Cestoda, Trematoda, and/or Nematoda (UMLS C0153303) is a polymicrobial helminthiasis in which concurrent intestinal tapeworm, fluke, and roundworm infections produce additive mucosal injury, nutrient theft, blood loss, and immune dysregulation rather than a single Mendelian disorder; accordingly, no consistent human causative germline mutation or inheritance pattern is defined, although host susceptibility and severity may be modified by immune-response genes and proteins such as HLA class II alleles, IL4, IL5, IL13, IL10, TNF, IFNG, TLR2, TLR4, STAT6, and eosinophil-derived mediators including major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein. Pathobiology is dominated by Th2-polarized and regulatory pathways, with epithelial alarmins IL-25, IL-33, and TSLP activating dendritic cells, ILC2 cells, mast cells, goblet-cell hyperplasia, IgE class switching, eosinophilia, and mucosal remodeling, while chronic infection may also involve TGF-β–driven immune tolerance and fibrosis. Patients commonly present with abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating, nausea, anorexia, weight loss, malnutrition, iron-deficiency anemia, eosinophilia, pruritus ani, and passage of worms or segments; severe disease can cause intestinal obstruction, biliary or pancreatic involvement, protein-losing enteropathy, growth impairment, and cognitive effects in children. Important subtypes are defined by the constituent parasites, for example ascariasis, trichuriasis, hookworm disease, enterobiasis, taeniasis, hymenolepiasis, diphyllobothriasis, and intestinal fluke infection, with frequent comorbidities including malnutrition, micronutrient deficiency, HIV-related immunosuppression, and other enteric infections. Diagnosis relies on exposure history and repeated stool ova-and-parasite microscopy with concentration techniques and species recognition, supplemented when needed by antigen assays, PCR, CBC showing eosinophilia or anemia, and imaging or endoscopy for complications. Treatment commonly uses albendazole or mebendazole, which bind parasite β-tubulin and inhibit microtubule-dependent glucose uptake; praziquantel, which increases tegumental calcium permeability causing spastic paralysis; and niclosamide

Name: Malignant Tumor of Small Intestine
Description: Malignant tumor of the small intestine is a heterogeneous group of aggressive epithelial, neuroendocrine, mesenchymal, and lymphoid neoplasms arising in the duodenum, jejunum, or ileum, most commonly including adenocarcinoma, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and primary intestinal lymphoma. Its molecular basis varies by subtype: small-bowel adenocarcinoma often shows APC, KRAS, TP53, SMAD4, ERBB2, and mismatch-repair gene alterations such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, with dysregulation of WNT/beta-catenin, RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, TGF-beta, EGFR/HER2, and microsatellite-instability immune pathways; GIST is characterized by KIT or PDGFRA activating mutations driving constitutive receptor tyrosine kinase signaling; neuroendocrine tumors may involve MEN1, DAXX, ATRX, and mTOR-pathway abnormalities. Predisposition is usually sporadic but may be inherited in Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with STK11 mutation, juvenile polyposis with SMAD4/BMPR1A, celiac disease, and Crohn disease, which also act as important comorbid risk states. Patients typically present with vague abdominal pain, occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, bowel obstruction, intussusception, perforation, or jaundice for duodenal lesions; neuroendocrine tumors may cause carcinoid syndrome. Complications include metastatic spread to liver or peritoneum, malabsorption, cachexia, and thromboembolism. Diagnosis relies on histopathologic confirmation from endoscopic or surgical biopsy, cross-sectional CT/MR enterography, capsule endoscopy or balloon enteroscopy, immunohistochemistry such as cytokeratins, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, CD117/DOG1, and lymphoma markers, plus molecular tests for MMR deficiency/MSI, KIT/PDGFRA, or other actionable variants. Treatment commonly includes surgical resection and systemic therapy tailored to subtype, with fluorouracil or capecitabine inhibiting thymidylate synthase, oxaliplatin causing DNA cross-link

Name: Malignant neoplasm of peritoneum
Description: Malignant neoplasm of the peritoneum most commonly refers to primary peritoneal carcinoma, malignant peritoneal mesothelioma, or secondary peritoneal carcinomatosis from ovarian, gastrointestinal, pancreatic, or appendiceal primaries; it is an aggressive serosal malignancy characterized by diffuse peritoneal implantation, ascites, omental caking, and progressive bowel and nutritional compromise. Molecular abnormalities vary by subtype: high-grade serous primary peritoneal carcinoma frequently shows TP53 mutation with homologous recombination defects involving BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, or RAD51-related genes and overexpression of PAX8, WT1, CA125/MUC16, and often folate receptor alpha, whereas mesothelioma is associated with BAP1 loss, CDKN2A deletion, NF2 alteration, and mesothelin expression; KRAS, GNAS, APC, PIK3CA, SMAD4, and mismatch-repair genes may be relevant in appendiceal or colorectal peritoneal spread. Key pathways include p53, DNA damage repair/homologous recombination, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, Hippo, angiogenesis via VEGF, and inflammatory mesothelial-stromal signaling. Symptoms typically include increasing abdominal girth, pain, bloating, early satiety, weight loss, nausea, altered bowel habit, and dyspnea from ascites or pleural extension. Important comorbidities and complications include malignant ascites, bowel obstruction, cachexia, venous thromboembolism, hydronephrosis, pleural effusion, and treatment-related myelosuppression or nephrotoxicity. Most cases are sporadic, but hereditary predisposition is recognized, especially autosomal dominant BRCA1/2-associated hereditary breast-ovarian cancer and Lynch syndrome in selected Müllerian or gastrointestinal-associated cases. Diagnosis relies on imaging with CT or MRI, serum markers such as CA125 or CEA depending on suspected origin, cytology of ascitic fluid, and definitive histopathology with immunohistochemistry distinguishing Müllerian carcinoma from mesothelioma or metastatic adenocarcinoma. Treatment commonly includes carboplatin, a platinum DNA crosslinker, paclitaxel, a microtubule stabilizer, and bevacizumab, a VEGF inhibitor; selected patients receive cisplatin-based HI

Name: Testicular Cancer
Description: Testicular neoplasms are predominantly malignant germ cell tumors of the testis, classically divided into seminoma and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors, including embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, and mixed forms, while less common subtypes include sex cord-stromal tumors such as Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors and primary testicular lymphoma in older men. They arise most often from germ cell neoplasia in situ and are characterized by chromosome 12p gain, especially i(12p), with frequent dysregulation of KIT/KITLG, KRAS/NRAS, MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, p53-mediated DNA-damage response, and pluripotency networks involving OCT3/4, NANOG, and SOX17/SOX2; representative molecular abnormalities include KIT mutations in a subset of seminomas and isochromosome 12p across many germ cell tumors. Risk is usually sporadic, but genetic susceptibility is supported by familial clustering and variants in KITLG, SPRY4, BAK1, DMRT1, TERT-CLPTM1L, and PDE11A; associated developmental disorders include cryptorchidism, gonadal dysgenesis, infertility, and testicular dysgenesis syndrome, with increased risk in Klinefelter syndrome for extragonadal germ cell tumors. Typical presentation is a painless unilateral testicular mass or enlargement, sometimes with heaviness or dull ache, while acute pain, gynecomastia, or symptoms from metastases to retroperitoneum, lung, brain, or liver may occur; complications include infertility, hypogonadism, treatment-related cardiovascular disease, neuropathy, ototoxicity, pulmonary toxicity, and secondary malignancies. Diagnosis relies on scrotal ultrasonography, serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH, radical inguinal orchiectomy for histopathology, and CT-based staging; seminoma typically lacks AFP elevation. Standard therapy includes cisplatin, which forms DNA cross-links, etoposide, a topoisomerase II inhibitor, and bleomycin, which induces free radical-mediated DNA strand breaks, with carboplatin used in selected seminoma cases and radiation historically used for radiosensitive seminoma.

Name: Penile Cancer
Description: Penile cancer is an uncommon malignant neoplasm of the penis, most often penile squamous cell carcinoma arising from the glans, coronal sulcus, or prepuce, with histologic subtypes including usual, basaloid, warty, verrucous, papillary, and sarcomatoid forms; clinically it typically presents as a persistent penile ulcer, exophytic or fungating mass, induration, bleeding, foul discharge, pain, phimosis, dysuria, or palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. Its pathogenesis is heterogeneous, with HPV-related tumors, especially those driven by HPV16 and HPV18 E6/E7 oncoproteins, causing TP53 and RB1 pathway disruption and p16 overexpression, while HPV-independent tumors more often show alterations in TP53, CDKN2A, PIK3CA, EGFR, CCND1, HRAS, NOTCH1, and TERT promoter regulation; implicated signaling networks include p53/Rb cell-cycle control, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, EGFR/RAS/RAF/MAPK, apoptosis, immune evasion via PD-1/PD-L1, and inflammatory pathways. Established risk factors and linked comorbidities include phimosis, lichen sclerosus, chronic balanitis, smoking, poor genital hygiene, immunosuppression including HIV, obesity, and HPV infection; major complications include local tissue destruction, urethral obstruction, nodal and distant metastases, sexual and urinary dysfunction, and treatment-related disfigurement. It is usually sporadic rather than classically inherited, although host susceptibility may reflect polymorphisms in immune-response and carcinogen-metabolism genes rather than Mendelian transmission. Diagnosis relies on physical examination and biopsy-confirmed histopathology, HPV testing or p16 immunohistochemistry in selected cases, imaging such as penile MRI and CT or PET/CT for local and nodal staging, and pathologic assessment of inguinal nodes by ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration or sentinel node techniques. Treatment commonly includes cisplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum; 5-fluorouracil, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor; paclitaxel, a microtubule stabilizer; and in selected advanced cases ifosfamide, an alkylating agent, or cetuximab, an EGFR-directed monoclonal antibody.

Name: Brain Malignant Neoplasm
Description: Brain neoplasms comprise a heterogeneous group of primary and metastatic intracranial tumors arising from glial, meningeal, neuronal, embryonal, pituitary, or other CNS-associated cells, ranging from indolent lesions to highly aggressive malignancies; major subtypes include diffuse astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma, ependymoma, medulloblastoma, meningioma, schwannoma, and brain metastases. Their molecular landscape commonly involves alterations in IDH1/IDH2, TP53, ATRX, TERT promoter, EGFR amplification or EGFRvIII, PTEN loss, CDKN2A/B deletion, PDGFRA, BRAF V600E, H3 K27M, 1p/19q codeletion, MGMT promoter methylation, and NF2, with inherited predisposition in syndromes such as neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and APC-associated Turcot syndrome, although most cases are sporadic. Dysregulated signaling often centers on RTK/RAS/RAF/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53, RB cell-cycle, WNT/β-catenin, SHH, Notch, angiogenic VEGF, and epigenetic programs. Typical manifestations include headache, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, cognitive or personality change, aphasia, visual disturbance, gait imbalance, nausea/vomiting from raised intracranial pressure, and endocrine symptoms in sellar tumors. Common complications and comorbidities include cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, epilepsy, neurocognitive decline, endocrinopathies, depression, and treatment-related radionecrosis or myelosuppression. Diagnosis relies on contrast-enhanced MRI, sometimes CT for hemorrhage or calcification, advanced imaging such as perfusion or spectroscopy, histopathology integrated with molecular testing per WHO CNS classification, including immunohistochemistry, FISH, PCR, and next-generation sequencing; CSF cytology is useful in select leptomeningeal or embryonal tumors. Treatment commonly includes temozolomide, an oral DNA-alkylating agent; lomustine, a nitrosourea causing DNA cross-linking; bevacizumab, a VEGF-neutralizing antiangi

Name: Metastatic malignant neoplasm to kidney
Description: Metastatic malignant neoplasm to the kidney is a secondary renal malignancy produced by hematogenous, lymphatic, or direct spread from a primary cancer, most often lung, breast, gastrointestinal tract, melanoma, or contralateral renal tumors, and is biologically defined by the molecular features of the primary neoplasm rather than a unique inherited renal cancer genotype. Accordingly, representative genetic alterations include TP53, KRAS, EGFR, ALK, BRAF, PIK3CA, APC, PTEN, HER2/ERBB2, and VHL abnormalities depending on origin, with proteins such as PD-L1, VEGF, MET, and EGFR often influencing behavior and therapy. Key pathways commonly implicated include RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, HIF-VEGF angiogenic signaling, EGFR/HER family signaling, MET, WNT/beta-catenin, and immune-checkpoint pathways involving PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with hematuria, flank pain, renal mass effect, constitutional symptoms, acute kidney injury, or less commonly hypertension; lesions may be solitary or multiple, unilateral or bilateral, and may coexist with widespread metastatic disease. Major complications include chronic kidney disease, obstruction, hemorrhage, infection, anemia, hypercalcemia, and poor performance status, with comorbidities typically reflecting advanced cancer burden. Treatment is usually directed by the primary tumor and extent of disease, using systemic agents such as pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor; nivolumab, another PD-1 inhibitor; sunitinib, a multikinase VEGFR/PDGFR inhibitor; trastuzumab, a HER2-targeted monoclonal antibody; erlotinib, an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor; or cytotoxic drugs such as platinum compounds that cause DNA cross-linking. Diagnosis relies on oncologic history, contrast-enhanced CT or MRI and sometimes PET/CT, with biopsy and immunohistochemistry or molecular profiling to distinguish metastasis from primary renal cell carcinoma; there is no classic Mendelian inheritance for renal metastasis itself, although hereditary cancer syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, hereditary breast-ovarian cancer, familial adenomatous polyposis, or VHL disease may underlie the primary malignancy.

Name: Urea Cycle Disorders, Inborn
Description: Urea cycle disorders are a heterogeneous group of inborn errors of hepatic nitrogen disposal caused by defects in enzymes or transporters of the urea cycle, leading to hyperammonemia and glutamine accumulation with secondary astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, mitochondrial dysfunction, altered nitric oxide and arginine metabolism, and impaired flux through the carbamoyl phosphate–ornithine–citrulline–argininosuccinate pathway. Major genetic causes include CPS1 deficiency, NAGS deficiency, OTC deficiency, ASS1 deficiency causing citrullinemia type I, ASL deficiency causing argininosuccinic aciduria, ARG1 deficiency causing argininemia, and transporter defects such as SLC25A15 in ornithine translocase deficiency and SLC25A13 in citrin deficiency; most are autosomal recessive, whereas OTC is X-linked, with pathogenic missense, nonsense, splice-site, deletion, and promoter variants reported. Clinical presentation ranges from catastrophic neonatal encephalopathy to late-onset episodic disease, with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, tachypnea from respiratory alkalosis, seizures, hypotonia, coma, developmental delay, behavioral or psychiatric symptoms, spasticity, liver dysfunction, and protein intolerance; complications include recurrent hyperammonemic crises, intellectual disability, cerebral edema, stroke-like injury, chronic liver disease, and death. Subtypes are defined by the affected enzyme or transporter and by neonatal versus late-onset phenotype. Diagnosis relies on elevated plasma ammonia, characteristic plasma amino acid and urine orotic acid patterns, liver function assessment, enzymatic studies in selected cases, and confirmatory molecular testing; newborn screening may detect citrulline abnormalities in some forms. Treatment combines protein restriction and acute ammonia-lowering therapy with sodium benzoate, which conjugates glycine for renal excretion, sodium phenylbutyrate or glycerol phenylbutyrate, which generate phenylacetate to scavenge glutamine as phenylacetylglutamine, arginine or citrulline supplementation to support residual cycle function, carglumic acid as an N-acetylglutamate analog in NAGS deficiency, and hemodialysis or liver transplantation in severe disease.

Name: Acquired thrombocytopenia
Description: Acquired thrombocytopenia is a heterogeneous, usually noninherited disorder defined by a reduced platelet count due to increased peripheral destruction, splenic sequestration, dilution, or impaired megakaryopoiesis, most commonly presenting with petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, easy bruising, and, in severe cases, gastrointestinal or intracranial hemorrhage; major acquired subtypes include immune thrombocytopenia, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, thrombotic microangiopathies such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, marrow failure or infiltration, infection-associated thrombocytopenia, and hypersplenism. Key molecular associations vary by subtype and include antiplatelet autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins GPIIb/IIIa and GPIb/IX, ADAMTS13 deficiency or inhibitory antibodies in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, platelet factor 4 in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and thrombopoietin-MPL-JAK2-STAT signaling in platelet production; immune effector pathways involve Fcγ receptor-mediated splenic macrophage clearance, complement activation, B-cell and T-cell dysregulation, and cytokines such as interleukin-2 and BAFF. Although acquired forms lack classic Mendelian inheritance, genetic predisposition may influence risk, with representative components including HLA alleles, FCGR2A/FCGR3A variants, and rare susceptibility in complement-regulatory genes in microangiopathy. Common comorbidities include systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, chronic liver disease, HIV, hepatitis C, Helicobacter pylori infection, lymphoproliferative disorders, pregnancy, sepsis, and autoimmune thyroid disease, while complications include major bleeding, thrombosis in HIT or TTP, and treatment-related infection. Treatment depends on cause and commonly includes corticosteroids, which suppress autoantibody production and reticuloendothelial clearance, intravenous immune globulin, which blocks Fc receptor-mediated platelet destruction, rituximab, which depletes CD20-positive B cells, and thrombopoietin receptor agonists such as eltrombopag or romiplostim, which stimulate megakaryopoiesis. Name: Streptococcal meningitis
Description: Streptococcal meningitis is an acute, usually non-inherited, pyogenic bacterial meningitis caused most often by Streptococcus pneumoniae and less commonly by group B streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae), S. pyogenes, or viridans streptococci, producing rapidly progressive meningeal and cerebral inflammation with high mortality and neurologic sequelae. Pathogenesis is driven by microbial factors such as the pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide, pneumolysin encoded by PLY, autolysin LytA, neuraminidases, and adhesins including CbpA/PspC, with host susceptibility influenced by variants in innate immune and barrier genes such as TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, IRAK4, CFH, MBL2, NFKBIA, and complement pathway components; inheritance is therefore generally absent except for rare Mendelian predisposition to invasive bacterial infection in complement deficiency or IRAK4/MYD88-related primary immunodeficiency. Key pathways include nasopharyngeal colonization, blood-brain barrier invasion, complement activation, TLR/NF-kB signaling, inflammasome and cytokine responses involving TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6, and neutrophil recruitment, leading to vasculitis, edema, raised intracranial pressure, and neuronal injury. Typical features are fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, focal deficits, and in neonates irritability, poor feeding, apnea, or bulging fontanelle. Important subtypes include neonatal group B streptococcal meningitis and adult pneumococcal meningitis. Diagnosis relies on urgent blood cultures and lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose, Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain, and confirmation by culture or PCR; CT or MRI is used when mass effect or complications are suspected. Standard treatment includes ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, beta-lactams that inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala to block cell-wall synthesis for resistant pneumococci; and ampicillin or penicillin G for susceptible isolates, often with adjunctive dexamethasone to blunt inflammatory injury. Name: Staphylococcal meningitis
Description: Staphylococcal meningitis (UMLS C0154640) is an acute, usually pyogenic bacterial infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant strains, and less often coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis, especially after neurosurgery, trauma, or CSF shunt placement. Disease biology is driven by bacterial adhesins and virulence determinants including mecA/PBP2a in MRSA, toxins such as alpha-hemolysin encoded by hla, Panton-Valentine leukocidin, biofilm-associated genes including icaADBC, and host innate immune pathways involving TLR2, NOD2, NF-kappaB, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, and IL-6; host susceptibility may be modified by rare defects or polymorphisms affecting TLR signaling, MyD88, IRAK4, complement, or immunoglobulin function, although the infection is not classically inherited. Typical manifestations include fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, altered mental status, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and sometimes sepsis; subtypes include community-acquired hematogenous disease and healthcare-associated post-neurosurgical, post-traumatic, or device-related meningitis. Major comorbidities and predisposing conditions include bacteremia, endocarditis, skin and soft-tissue infection, diabetes, renal failure, immunosuppression, cranial trauma, and intracranial devices, while complications include ventriculitis, brain abscess, stroke, hydrocephalus, hearing loss, and death. Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion plus CSF analysis showing neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose, and microbiologic confirmation by CSF Gram stain and culture, blood cultures, and increasingly PCR or multiplex meningitis panels, with neuroimaging when complications are suspected. Treatment typically includes vancomycin, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala; nafcillin or oxacillin for MSSA, which bind penicillin-binding proteins; linezolid, which blocks 50S ribosomal initiation; and sometimes rifampin, which inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, particularly for biofilm-associated device infection, alongside source control such as shunt removal

Name: Glossopharyngeal Neuralgia
Description: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia (UMLS C0154731) is a rare cranial neuropathic pain disorder characterized by recurrent, brief, severe, electric shock-like paroxysms in the sensory distribution of the glossopharyngeal nerve, typically involving the throat, tonsillar fossa, base of tongue, deep ear, and angle of the jaw, often triggered by swallowing, chewing, talking, coughing, or yawning; some patients develop vagal involvement with bradycardia, syncope, or asystole. It is usually classified as classical glossopharyngeal neuralgia, most often due to neurovascular compression of cranial nerve IX at the root entry zone, secondary glossopharyngeal neuralgia caused by structural lesions such as tumors, elongated styloid process in Eagle syndrome, multiple sclerosis, infection, trauma, or Chiari malformation, and idiopathic cases. Molecular genetics are far less defined than in trigeminal neuralgia, and most cases are sporadic without a Mendelian inheritance pattern, although demyelinating mechanisms and neuronal hyperexcitability involving voltage-gated sodium channels, ectopic impulse generation, ephaptic transmission, and altered calcium signaling are implicated; representative neuropathic pain genes and proteins of interest include SCN9A/Nav1.7, SCN10A/Nav1.8, SCN11A/Nav1.9, CACNA2D1, and myelin-related pathways in multiple sclerosis. Key pathobiologic pathways include focal demyelination, neuroinflammation, and abnormal afferent transmission within glossopharyngeal and nucleus tractus solitarius circuits. First-line treatment commonly uses carbamazepine, a use-dependent blocker of voltage-gated sodium channels, oxcarbazepine with a similar mechanism, and gabapentin or pregabalin, which bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of presynaptic calcium channels to reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release; baclofen, a GABAB agonist, and lamotrigine, which inhibits sodium channel-mediated glutamate release, are additional options. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by ICHD criteria, trigger history, neurologic examination, response to carbamazepine, and MRI with high-resolution cranial nerve sequences and vascular imaging to identify compression or exclude secondary causes; important comorbidities and complications include anxiety, depression, malnutrition from odynophagia, sleep disturbance, and

Name: Hypertrichosis of eyelid
Description: Hypertrichosis of the eyelid is an uncommon disorder characterized by excessive terminal hair growth on the upper and/or lower lids, occurring as a localized congenital anomaly or as an acquired manifestation of systemic disease or drug exposure; it may present as isolated ciliary hypertrichosis or as part of generalized hypertrichosis syndromes. Genetic contributors are heterogeneous and usually extrapolated from broader hypertrichosis biology, including congenital forms linked to chromosomal rearrangements at Xq24-q27.1, SOX3 regulatory alterations, and occasional associations with genes involved in hair-follicle development such as ABCA5, FGF5, or KRT-related pathways, while eyelash hypertrichosis is also pharmacologically induced through prostaglandin signaling at the PTGFR receptor. Relevant molecular pathways include Wnt/β-catenin, sonic hedgehog, EGFR, FGF, TGF-β/BMP, and prostaglandin-mediated anagen promotion, with key cellular actors being follicular keratinocytes, dermal papilla cells, melanocytes, and perifollicular fibroblasts. Commonly implicated drugs include bimatoprost, latanoprost, and travoprost, prostaglandin F2α analogs that prolong the anagen phase and enlarge follicles; less commonly, cyclosporine can induce periocular hypertrichosis through calcineurin-dependent effects on follicular cycling. Clinical findings include abnormally long, thick, pigmented eyelashes or ectopic lid hair, sometimes causing cosmetic concern, trichiasis, visual interference, blepharitis, corneal irritation, or recurrent conjunctivitis. Comorbidities may include generalized hypertrichosis, endocrine disorders, malnutrition, porphyria, mucopolysaccharidoses, fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, and congenital dysmorphism. Inheritance depends on the underlying syndrome and can be X-linked, autosomal dominant, sporadic, or secondary/nonhereditary. Diagnosis is clinical, based on excessive hair density or length relative to age, sex, and ethnicity, with slit-lamp examination, medication review, assessment for syndromic features, and targeted testing such as chromosomal microarray, gene panels, or endocrine/metabolic studies when a genetic or systemic cause is suspected.

Name: Chronic tubotympanic suppurative otitis media
Description: Chronic tubotympanic suppurative otitis media is the “safe,” mucosal subtype of chronic suppurative otitis media characterized by persistent inflammation and infection of the middle-ear cleft with a central tympanic membrane perforation and recurrent or continuous otorrhea, usually causing conductive hearing loss, aural fullness, and sometimes tinnitus, while otalgia and fever are typically minimal unless acutely exacerbated. It is usually polymicrobial, commonly involving Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Proteus species, and anaerobes, and pathobiology reflects dysregulated innate immunity and chronic biofilm formation, with inflammatory signaling through TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, MUC5AC, matrix metalloproteinases, and VEGF; host susceptibility has been linked more to complex genetic predisposition than Mendelian inheritance, with representative associations reported in cytokine and mucosal defense genes such as TNF, IL6, IL10, TLR4, MBL2, FUT2, and CFTR, especially where disease coexists with cystic fibrosis or primary ciliary dysfunction. Important comorbidities and risk factors include recurrent acute otitis media, Eustachian tube dysfunction, adenoid hypertrophy, allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, cleft palate, immunodeficiency, malnutrition, craniofacial anomalies, and poor environmental hygiene; complications include persistent hearing impairment, tympanosclerosis, ossicular erosion, mastoiditis, labyrinthitis, facial nerve palsy, and, less commonly in tubotympanic disease than atticoantral disease, intracranial spread such as meningitis or brain abscess. Diagnosis is clinical and microbiologic, based on chronic ear discharge through a central perforation for at least 6 weeks, otoscopy or otoendoscopy, aural microscopy, pure-tone audiometry, tympanometry when feasible, and culture of otorrhea in refractory cases, with CT of the temporal bone reserved for suspected complications or surgical planning. Treatment commonly includes topical ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; ofloxacin, with the same mechanism; amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis and β-lactamases when systemic therapy is needed; and met

Name: Arterial embolus and thrombosis
Description: Arterial embolus and thrombosis (UMLS C0155749) is an acute vascular occlusive disorder in which an artery is blocked either by in situ thrombus formation, usually on a ruptured or eroded atherosclerotic plaque, or by an embolus arising from the heart, proximal arteries, aneurysms, or paradoxical venous sources, leading to ischemia and infarction of downstream tissue. Major molecular contributors include platelet activation pathways involving GP1BA, ITGA2B/ITGB3, von Willebrand factor and fibrinogen, the coagulation cascade with F2, F5, FGA, FGB, FGG and SERPINC1, and fibrinolysis regulators such as PLG and SERPINE1; representative inherited risk variants include factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, deficiencies of protein C, protein S or antithrombin, and hyperhomocysteinemia related to MTHFR polymorphisms, although arterial events are more often multifactorial than Mendelian. Key signaling mechanisms include tissue factor–factor VIIa initiation of thrombin generation, thrombin-PAR signaling, ADP-P2Y12, thromboxane A2, cyclooxygenase-1, calcium-dependent platelet degranulation, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and NET-mediated thrombosis. Typical causes and subtypes include native artery thrombosis, cardioembolism, cholesterol or thromboembolism, and acute limb, mesenteric, renal, retinal, coronary, or cerebral arterial occlusion. Patients classically present with sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia in limb ischemia, or organ-specific deficits such as stroke, myocardial ischemia, visual loss or abdominal pain. Name: Acute maxillary sinusitis
Description: Acute maxillary sinusitis (UMLS C0155804) is an acute inflammatory infection of the maxillary paranasal sinus, usually viral after an upper respiratory tract infection but sometimes bacterial, most commonly involving Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Moraxella catarrhalis, with inflammation driven by innate immune pathways including Toll-like receptor activation, NF-κB signaling, and downstream cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-α, and neutrophil- and epithelial-derived mediators, while mucociliary dysfunction involving ciliary proteins and epithelial ion transport can contribute; although it is not a classic inherited disorder, genetic susceptibility is recognized in disorders affecting host defense or mucociliary clearance, including CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis, DNAH5 and DNAI1 defects in primary ciliary dyskinesia, and immune-related variation such as TLR pathway polymorphisms. Typical symptoms and signs include unilateral or bilateral facial pressure over the cheeks, purulent nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, hyposmia, maxillary tooth pain, postnasal drip, fever, and tenderness over the maxillary sinus; clinical subtypes include viral acute rhinosinusitis and acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, with recurrent acute disease as a related phenotype. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by persistence beyond 10 days, severe fever and purulent discharge or facial pain for at least 3 to 4 days, or double worsening after initial improvement; nasal endoscopy, sinus CT when complications or alternative diagnoses are suspected, and rarely culture from sinus aspirate help confirm etiology. Treatment is mainly symptomatic, but when bacterial infection is likely, amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis and β-lactamases, doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, are commonly used; intranasal corticosteroids reduce inflammatory cytokine signaling. Comorbidities include allergic rhinitis, asthma, viral URI, dental infection, smoking exposure, immunodeficiency, and anatomic obstruction, while complications include chronic rhinosinusitis, orbital cellulitis, osteitis, abscess, and rarely intracranial spread.

Name: Acute epiglottitis
Description: Acute epiglottitis is an acute, rapidly progressive supraglottic cellulitis, usually infectious and potentially life-threatening because edema of the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds can abruptly obstruct the airway; it classically presents with high fever, severe odynophagia, dysphagia, muffled “hot-potato” voice, drooling, inspiratory stridor, anxiety, tripod positioning, and respiratory distress, while adults may have a more indolent course than children. Historically it was most strongly linked to Haemophilus influenzae type b, but Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, and occasionally viral or fungal pathogens are also implicated; disease biology is dominated by innate immune activation through pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4 and downstream NF-κB signaling, with cytokines including TNF, IL-1β, and IL-6 driving mucosal inflammation, vascular leak, and neutrophil recruitment. No Mendelian inheritance pattern is established, but susceptibility may be modified by host immune genes and proteins relevant to encapsulated bacteria, with representative examples including HLA class II variation, TLR4, MYD88, IRAK4, NFKB1, and complement pathway components; recognized genetic risk is strongest in rare primary immunodeficiencies rather than in the disease itself. Common treatment centers on airway stabilization plus empiric intravenous antibiotics such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, and vancomycin, a glycopeptide that blocks peptidoglycan polymerization, with ampicillin-sulbactam as another option combining a β-lactam and β-lactamase inhibitor; dexamethasone is often added to reduce inflammatory edema via glucocorticoid receptor-mediated transcriptional suppression. Important comorbidities and risk states include diabetes, immunosuppression, incomplete Hib vaccination, upper respiratory infection, and local trauma, while complications include sudden airway occlusion, hypoxemia, epiglottic abscess, bacteremia, and sepsis. Name: Pneumonia caused by Pseudomonas
Description: Pneumonia caused by Pseudomonas, usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa, is an acute bacterial lower respiratory tract infection classically presenting as hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, or opportunistic pneumonia in structurally diseased or immunocompromised lungs rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder; host genetic susceptibility is instead polygenic and context dependent, with representative associations involving CFTR in cystic fibrosis, TLR4 and TLR5 in innate recognition of lipopolysaccharide and flagellin, and inflammatory mediators such as IL6, TNF, and CXCL8/IL8, while bacterial virulence and resistance determinants commonly include alginate biosynthesis genes in mucoid strains, type III secretion effectors ExoS and ExoU, quorum-sensing regulators Las and Rhl, porin OprD loss, AmpC derepression, and acquired metallo-beta-lactamases such as VIM or IMP. Pathobiology centers on adhesion, biofilm formation, epithelial injury, neutrophilic inflammation, and signaling through TLR-LPS/MyD88-NF-kappaB, inflammasome, complement, and oxidative stress pathways. Typical features include fever, purulent sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxemia, leukocytosis, and new or progressive infiltrates, often with severe necrotizing disease, abscess, bacteremia, or sepsis. Major risk states and linked comorbidities include COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, mechanical ventilation, burns, neutropenia, malignancy, diabetes, and prior broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure; complications include respiratory failure, empyema, septic shock, and multidrug resistance. Clinical subtypes include community-acquired disease in high-risk hosts, hospital-acquired pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and chronic colonization with recurrent infectious exacerbations in bronchiectasis or cystic fibrosis. Diagnosis relies on compatible syndrome plus imaging, microbiologic confirmation from sputum, endotracheal aspirate, BAL, or blood cultures with susceptibility testing, and in selected cases PCR or other rapid resistance assays. Name: Pneumonia, Pneumococcal
Description: Pneumococcal pneumonia is an acute bacterial infection of the lung parenchyma caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, classically presenting as community-acquired lobar pneumonia but also occurring as bronchopneumonia or severe invasive disease with bacteremia and empyema. Its pathobiology is driven by pneumococcal virulence factors including capsular polysaccharide, pneumolysin encoded by ply, the autolysin LytA, and surface adhesins such as PspA and PspC/CbpA, which interact with host innate-immune pathways involving TLR2, TLR4, MyD88, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, complement components C3 and factor H, neutrophil recruitment through IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, and CXCL8/IL-8, and platelet-activating factor receptor-mediated epithelial invasion. Host susceptibility is multifactorial rather than Mendelian in most cases, but increased risk is associated with variants or deficiencies in TLR signaling, IRAK4, MyD88, MBL2, FCGR2A, CRP, and terminal complement or splenic dysfunction states; inherited predisposition is therefore usually complex, with rare primary immunodeficiencies showing autosomal recessive or other Mendelian patterns. Typical symptoms and signs include abrupt fever, chills, productive cough with purulent or rusty sputum, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and lobar consolidation on examination or imaging. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical and radiographic findings plus microbiologic confirmation by sputum Gram stain and culture, blood cultures, urinary pneumococcal antigen testing, and increasingly PCR from respiratory samples; severity is commonly assessed with CURB-65 or PSI. Standard therapy includes beta-lactams such as amoxicillin or ceftriaxone, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and bacterial cell-wall synthesis, macrolides such as azithromycin, which bind the 50S ribosomal subunit to block protein synthesis, and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Name: Inhalation anthrax
Description: Inhalation anthrax (UMLS C0155866) is an acute, often fulminant zoonotic infection caused by inhalation of Bacillus anthracis spores, classically producing a biphasic illness that begins with fever, malaise, myalgia, nonproductive cough, chest discomfort, and dyspnea and may rapidly progress to severe respiratory distress, widened mediastinum from hemorrhagic mediastinitis, pleural effusions, sepsis, shock, meningitis, and multiorgan failure. Its principal molecular determinants are microbial rather than inherited host defects: the pXO1 plasmid encodes protective antigen (pagA), lethal factor (lef), and edema factor (cya), while pXO2 encodes capsule biosynthesis genes such as capA, capB, and capC; protective antigen mediates cellular entry through ANTXR1/TEM8 and ANTXR2/CMG2 receptors, edema factor is a calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase that raises cAMP, and lethal factor is a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves MAPKKs, disrupting MAPK signaling, inflammasome-linked innate responses, endothelial integrity, and macrophage function. Disease subtypes are usually inhalational, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, injectional, and anthrax meningitis, with inhalation anthrax representing the most lethal systemic form. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for the disease itself, although host susceptibility may be modified by variation in toxin receptor genes and immune-response pathways; no routine genetic testing is used clinically. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus compatible syndrome, blood or pleural fluid culture, PCR for B. anthracis targets, immunohistochemistry or direct fluorescent testing, serology to protective antigen, and chest imaging showing mediastinal widening or effusions. Standard therapy combines bactericidal agents such as ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV, or doxycycline, a tetracycline blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit, with additional protein-synthesis inhibitors such as clindamycin or linezolid to reduce toxin production; beta-lactams such as meropenem may be added, and antitoxins including raxibacumab, obiltoxaximab, or anthrax immune globulin neutralize protective antigen. Name: Allergic asthma (disorder)
Description: Allergic asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder, usually representing a type 2 high endotype, characterized by variable airflow obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and reversible wheeze triggered by aeroallergen sensitization; clinically it presents with episodic wheezing, cough, chest tightness, dyspnea, nocturnal symptoms, and reduced peak flow or FEV1, and may range from intermittent to persistent, mild to severe, including eosinophilic and childhood-onset allergic subtypes. Its pathobiology is driven by allergen-specific IgE, mast cells, eosinophils, dendritic cells, basophils, and Th2/ILC2 responses, with key signaling pathways involving IL-4/IL-13 through JAK-STAT6, IL-5-mediated eosinophil survival, Fc epsilon RI signaling, epithelial alarmins such as TSLP, IL-33, and IL-25, and leukotriene and prostaglandin networks. Genetic susceptibility is complex and usually multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with replicated associations in IL4, IL13, IL4R, STAT6, TSLP, ADAM33, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, FCER1B, FLG, and HLA loci; polymorphisms affecting IgE regulation, epithelial barrier function, and airway remodeling contribute, and family clustering supports heritable risk. Common comorbidities include allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without nasal polyps, food allergy, obesity, gastroesophageal reflux, anxiety, and obstructive sleep symptoms; complications include recurrent exacerbations, airway remodeling, mucus plugging, and rarely respiratory failure. Diagnosis relies on compatible history plus demonstration of variable expiratory airflow limitation by spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, peak-flow variability, or bronchoprovocation, alongside evidence of atopy by skin-prick or serum specific IgE testing, with blood or sputum eosinophils and exhaled nitric oxide supporting type 2 inflammation.
