Name: Asthma due to internal immunological process
Description: Asthma due to an internal immunological process is a chronic, heterogeneous inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable expiratory airflow limitation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, mucus hypersecretion, and recurrent, usually reversible, airway obstruction driven most often by type 2 immune mechanisms, although non-type 2 phenotypes also occur. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic, with representative associations involving IL4, IL13, IL4RA, TSLP, GSDMB/ORMDL3 at 17q21, ADAM33, FLG, HLA loci, and the beta-2 adrenergic receptor gene ADRB2; rare severe eosinophilic forms may show marked cytokine pathway activation rather than single-gene causation, and familial clustering is common with complex, non-Mendelian inheritance influenced by atopy. Core pathways include epithelial alarmins TSLP, IL-33, and IL-25 activating dendritic cells and ILC2/Th2 responses, leading to IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 signaling, IgE class switching, mast-cell and eosinophil recruitment, leukotriene production, and airway remodeling; non-type 2 disease may involve Th17 cells, neutrophils, and IL-17. Typical symptoms are episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, nocturnal or exercise-induced dyspnea, prolonged expiration, and variable peak-flow reduction. Major subtypes include allergic/extrinsic, nonallergic/intrinsic, eosinophilic, neutrophilic, exercise-induced, occupational, cough-variant, and severe refractory asthma. Common comorbidities and complications include allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, atopic dermatitis, gastroesophageal reflux, obesity, anxiety, sleep disturbance, status asthmaticus, and fixed airflow remodeling. Diagnosis relies on characteristic symptom variability plus objective evidence of reversible airflow obstruction by spirometry showing reduced FEV1/FVC with bronchodilator reversibility, peak expiratory flow variability, methacholine challenge when spirometry is nondiagnostic, and supportive testing such as eosinophils, total/specific IgE, FeNO, and allergy testing. Name: Acute pulmonary edema
Description: Acute pulmonary edema is a rapidly developing syndrome of fluid accumulation in the alveoli and interstitium that is usually cardiogenic from abrupt elevation of pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure in acute left ventricular failure, but may also be noncardiogenic from increased alveolar-capillary permeability as in acute respiratory distress syndrome, sepsis, aspiration, high-altitude pulmonary edema, or neurogenic injury. Genetic contributions are generally indirect and reflect predisposition to underlying causes or permeability responses rather than simple Mendelian inheritance; representative examples include cardiomyopathy genes such as TTN, MYH7, LMNA, and MYBPC3, arrhythmia genes such as SCN5A, and variants in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and vascular pathways including ACE, AGT, AGTR1, NOS3, VEGFA, AQP5, and the epithelial sodium channel genes SCNN1A/SCNN1B/SCNN1G, while rare familial susceptibility to high-altitude pulmonary edema has been linked to exaggerated hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction involving endothelin and nitric oxide signaling. Key pathways include sympathetic and RAAS activation, natriuretic peptide signaling, endothelial barrier disruption mediated by VEGF, inflammatory cytokines including TNF, IL6, and IL1B, oxidative stress, and impaired alveolar fluid clearance through ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase. Typical features are acute dyspnea, orthopnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, pink frothy sputum, diffuse crackles, diaphoresis, hypertension or hypotension, and respiratory distress. Commonly used treatments include furosemide, a loop diuretic inhibiting NKCC2 to reduce preload; nitroglycerin, a nitric oxide donor causing venodilation and reduced filling pressures; and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation or oxygen to improve gas exchange, with morphine now used selectively and inotropes such as dobutamine, a beta-1 agonist, reserved for low-output states. Comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, cardiogenic shock, and respiratory failure. Name: Atrophic vulvitis
Description: Atrophic vulvitis is a largely non-neoplastic, usually hypoestrogenic inflammatory-atrophic disorder of the vulvar epithelium, most often occurring after menopause, during lactation, or with anti-estrogen therapy, and clinically characterized by vulvar dryness, burning, pruritus, dyspareunia, fissuring, irritation, pallor, smooth shiny thinned mucosa, introital narrowing, and contact bleeding or recurrent urinary discomfort. Its biology is driven primarily by estrogen deficiency rather than a Mendelian genetic lesion, with reduced ESR1/ESR2-mediated signaling leading to diminished epithelial proliferation, lower glycogen, impaired lactobacillary support, reduced collagen and elastin maintenance, decreased vascularity, and altered TGF-β, inflammatory cytokine, and extracellular-matrix remodeling pathways; in some patients, overlap with chronic inflammatory vulvar dermatoses implicates immune mediators such as NF-κB, IL-1, IL-6, TNF, and matrix metalloproteinases. No specific inherited mutation defines isolated atrophic vulvitis, and inheritance is generally not established, although genetic influences on age at menopause, estrogen metabolism, and susceptibility to vulvar dermatoses may modify risk. Important differential subtypes or overlapping entities include postmenopausal vulvovaginal atrophy/genitourinary syndrome of menopause, lactational atrophy, and atrophy secondary to endocrine suppression or radiation. Comorbidities include atrophic vaginitis, recurrent urinary tract infection, dyspareunia with sexual dysfunction, secondary candidiasis or bacterial infection, contact dermatitis, and diagnostic confusion with lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, or vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by pelvic examination, vaginal/vulvar pH elevation, microscopy when infection is suspected, and biopsy when lesions are atypical, ulcerative, pigmented, indurated, or refractory, to exclude neoplasia and specific dermatoses. Treatment commonly includes topical estradiol, conjugated estrogens, or estriol, which restore estrogen receptor signaling and epithelial maturation; nonhormonal moisturizers/lubricants for barrier support; and intravaginal prasterone or the selective estrogen receptor modulator ospemifene in appropriate patients, with topical corticosteroids reserved when concomitant inflammatory dermatosis is present.

Name: Abortion
Description: Abortion, in medical usage, refers to termination or loss of pregnancy before fetal viability and includes spontaneous abortion (miscarriage), threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed, septic, and recurrent abortion, as well as induced medical or surgical abortion; clinically it typically presents with vaginal bleeding, cramping pelvic pain, passage of tissue, cervical dilation in progressive cases, and on ultrasound absence of expected embryonic or fetal cardiac activity or retained products of conception. Its biology is heterogeneous: many spontaneous first-trimester losses are caused by embryonic chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomies, monosomy X, triploidy, and structural rearrangements, while recurrent abortion may involve parental balanced translocations and variants affecting thrombosis, implantation, or placentation, with representative genes including F5 (Factor V Leiden), F2, MTHFR, ANXA5, and immune tolerance or placental genes; relevant proteins and pathways include coagulation and fibrin formation, trophoblast invasion and angiogenesis mediated by VEGF, TGF-β, integrins, matrix metalloproteinases, progesterone receptor signaling, hCG support of the corpus luteum, inflammatory cytokine networks such as TNF-α and IL-6, and apoptotic pathways. Important comorbidities and risk factors include antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine anomalies, cervical insufficiency, endocrine disease such as diabetes or thyroid dysfunction, polycystic ovary syndrome, infection, advanced maternal age, and prior pregnancy loss; complications include hemorrhage, anemia, retained products, endometritis or sepsis, infertility-related distress, and in unsafe induced abortion, uterine perforation and shock. Management depends on type and context: misoprostol, a PGE1 analog, induces uterine contractions and cervical ripening; mifepristone, a progesterone receptor antagonist, causes decidual breakdown and sensitizes the myometrium; methotrexate, a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor, is used mainly for ectopic gestation; prophylactic or therapeutic antibiotics such as doxycycline, metronidazole, or clindamycin reduce infectious complications. Diagnosis relies on history, pelvic examination, serial quantitative β-hCG, transvaginal ultrasonography, CBC and blood type/Rh testing, pathologic examination of tissue, and in recurrent cases parental karyotyping, fetal genetic testing, uterine imaging, and antiphospholipid

Name: Eclampsia in pregnancy
Description: Eclampsia in pregnancy (UMLS C0156677) is a severe hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, usually regarded as the convulsive end of the preeclampsia spectrum, defined by new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with preeclampsia or related gestational hypertension, most often after 20 weeks’ gestation, intrapartum, or postpartum. Its pathobiology centers on abnormal placentation with shallow trophoblast invasion and uteroplacental ischemia, leading to maternal endothelial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier injury, vasospasm, and systemic inflammation; implicated molecular pathways include excess antiangiogenic signaling through sFlt-1/FLT1 and soluble endoglin with relative VEGF and PlGF deficiency, nitric oxide and endothelin imbalance, oxidative stress, complement activation, coagulation activation, and dysregulated renin-angiotensin signaling. Genetic susceptibility is complex and non-Mendelian, with maternal and fetal contributions; representative associations include FLT1, ENG, VEGFA, NOS3, ACE, AGT, AGTR1, STOX1, ERAP2, HLA-G, and thrombophilia-related variants such as F5 Leiden and F2 G20210A in selected populations. Typical manifestations include severe hypertension, headache, visual disturbance, hyperreflexia, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, edema, proteinuria, and seizures, with complications including HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, stroke, DIC, liver hematoma, fetal growth restriction, prematurity, and fetal or maternal death. Subtypes are commonly antepartum, intrapartum, and postpartum eclampsia, often arising from preeclampsia with severe features. Diagnosis is clinical after excluding other seizure causes, supported by blood pressure measurement, urine protein assessment, CBC with platelets, creatinine, liver enzymes, LDH, uric acid, coagulation studies when indicated, and fetal surveillance; neuroimaging is used for atypical presentations or suspected PRES. Core treatment includes magnesium sulfate, which blocks NMDA-mediated excitotoxicity and stabilizes neuronal and vascular membranes; labetalol, a combined alpha1/beta-adrenergic blocker; hydralazine, a direct arteriolar vasodilator; and nifedipine, an L-type calcium-channel blocker, with definitive management by prompt delivery.

Name: Infectious arthropathy
Description: Infectious arthropathy is a heterogeneous group of joint disorders caused by direct microbial invasion of synovium or periarticular tissues, most often presenting as acute septic arthritis but also including gonococcal arthritis, Lyme arthritis, tuberculous arthritis, viral arthritides, and prosthetic-joint infection; clinically it usually manifests with rapid-onset monoarthritis or oligoarthritis, severe pain, warmth, swelling, erythema, restricted range of motion, effusion, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers, although indolent forms such as mycobacterial or Borrelia burgdorferi infection may be subacute. Pathobiology is dominated by innate immune activation through pattern-recognition pathways including TLR2, TLR4, NOD-like receptors, NF-κB, inflammasome signaling, and cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and complement, with neutrophil recruitment, matrix metalloproteinases, RANKL-mediated osteoclast activation, and bacterial virulence factors such as Staphylococcus aureus adhesins and Panton-Valentine leukocidin contributing to cartilage and bone destruction; representative pathogen-related molecular determinants include mecA in methicillin-resistant S. aureus, penA alterations in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Borrelia outer surface proteins, and mycobacterial ESAT-6/CFP-10. The condition is generally acquired rather than inherited, but host susceptibility is influenced by immune and inflammatory genes, with reported associations involving HLA alleles, TLR polymorphisms, and cytokine gene variants, especially in reactive or postinfectious phenotypes such as HLA-B27-associated disease. Diagnosis relies on urgent arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, Gram stain, crystal analysis, culture, and increasingly PCR or 16S rRNA testing, plus blood cultures and imaging; Lyme serology and mycobacterial studies are used selectively. Treatment centers on drainage and targeted antimicrobials, commonly vancomycin, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis in resistant gram-positive organisms, ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin that blocks bacterial cell-wall crosslinking, and doxycycline, a tetracycline that inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit; other examples include antituberculous rifampin-based regimens and azithromycin. Name: Acute osteomyelitis (disorder)
Description: Acute osteomyelitis is an acute pyogenic infection of bone and marrow, usually caused by hematogenous seeding or contiguous spread after trauma, surgery, diabetic foot infection, or vascular insufficiency, and is most often due to Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA; other pathogens include Streptococcus pyogenes, Salmonella spp. in sickle cell disease, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in puncture wounds or injection drug use. Its pathobiology is dominated by innate immune activation through TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and chemokine signaling, with osteoclastogenesis driven by the RANK/RANKL/OPG axis and bone destruction amplified by matrix metalloproteinases; bacterial virulence factors such as S. aureus protein A, fibronectin-binding proteins, Panton-Valentine leukocidin, and mecA-mediated PBP2a in MRSA are representative molecular determinants. Genetic susceptibility is not typically Mendelian, but host variation in immune and bone-remodeling genes such as TLR2, TLR4, IL1B, IL6, TNF, VDR, RANKL, and OPG has been associated in some studies, while inherited conditions including sickle cell disease and chronic granulomatous disease increase risk. Clinical features include localized bone pain, tenderness, swelling, warmth, erythema, fever, reduced limb use or inability to bear weight, and in vertebral disease, back pain. Major subtypes are hematogenous, contiguous-focus, and vascular insufficiency-associated acute osteomyelitis, affecting long bones in children and vertebrae, pelvis, or feet in adults. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus elevated ESR/CRP, leukocytosis, positive blood cultures, MRI as the most sensitive imaging test, radiographs for later bony change, and definitive pathogen identification by bone biopsy with culture and histopathology. Treatment usually combines source control with antibiotics such as vancomycin, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala, cefazolin or nafcillin, β-lactams that inhibit penicillin-binding proteins, and clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; alternatives include linezolid, daptomycin, or fluoroquinolones when indicated. Name: Anemia of Prematurity
Description: Anemia of prematurity (UMLS C0158996) is an acquired, typically normocytic-normochromic hyporegenerative anemia of preterm infants caused by developmental immaturity of erythropoiesis rather than a classic Mendelian disorder, although genetic modifiers of red-cell production and iron handling may influence severity; representative implicated genes/proteins include EPO and the erythropoietin receptor EPOR, hypoxia-sensing pathway components HIF1A, HIF2A/EPAS1, VHL, and EGLN1/PHD2, iron-regulatory mediators HAMP/hepcidin, ferroportin SLC40A1, transferrin and transferrin receptor TF/TFR1, and globin or membrane genes such as HBB, HBA, G6PD, and PKLR when alternative or coexisting causes of anemia are considered. Pathobiologically, blunted renal/hepatic erythropoietin response to anemia, rapid postnatal growth, shortened neonatal erythrocyte lifespan, iron-restricted erythropoiesis, inflammatory cytokine signaling, and iatrogenic phlebotomy dominate, with key pathways involving HIF-EPO-EPOR/JAK2-STAT5 signaling, iron sensing through hepcidin-ferroportin, and erythroid proliferation/differentiation in marrow. Clinical features include pallor, tachycardia, poor weight gain, feeding intolerance, lethargy, apnea, bradycardia, increased oxygen requirement, and diminished reticulocytosis; severity is often stratified by gestational age and transfusion dependence. Commonly linked comorbidities and complications include respiratory distress syndrome, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, retinopathy of prematurity, heart failure in severe cases, and risks related to repeated transfusions such as iron overload and alloimmunization. Treatment commonly includes packed red blood cell transfusion to restore oxygen-carrying capacity, iron supplementation such as ferrous sulfate or iron sucrose to support hemoglobin synthesis, and recombinant human erythropoietin or darbepoetin alfa, which activate EPOR to stimulate erythroid progenitors; folate and vitamin E are sometimes used adjunctively. Name: Anemia, Iron-Deficiency
Description: Iron-deficiency anemia is an acquired microcytic, hypochromic anemia caused by insufficient iron for hemoglobin synthesis, most often from chronic blood loss, inadequate intake, malabsorption, or increased demand, and it commonly presents with fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea, tachycardia, weakness, headache, pica, restless legs, glossitis, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, and, in severe or prolonged cases, cognitive impairment, heart failure exacerbation, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and impaired child neurodevelopment. Core molecular determinants involve iron homeostasis genes and proteins, including HAMP-hepcidin, SLC40A1-ferroportin, TF and TFRC, DMT1/SLC11A2, DCYTB/CYBRD1, ferritin, TMPRSS6, HFE, TFR2, HJV, and occasional rare mutations such as TMPRSS6 loss-of-function causing iron-refractory iron-deficiency anemia with inappropriately high hepcidin and poor oral iron response; anemia may also accompany hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia or celiac disease susceptibility. Key pathways include the hepcidin-ferroportin axis, intestinal iron uptake in duodenal enterocytes, transferrin-mediated transport, ferritin storage, erythropoietin-driven erythropoiesis, and inflammatory IL-6/BMP-SMAD signaling that increases hepcidin and limits iron availability. Major subtypes include absolute iron deficiency, functional iron deficiency, iron-refractory iron-deficiency anemia, and etiologic categories related to bleeding, malabsorption, diet, or pregnancy. It is usually non-Mendelian, but genetic predisposition exists through variants affecting iron absorption or regulation, while rare monogenic forms are typically autosomal recessive, exemplified by TMPRSS6-associated disease. Diagnosis relies on CBC showing low hemoglobin with low MCV and MCH, iron studies demonstrating low ferritin, low serum iron, high transferrin or TIBC, and low transferrin saturation, with reticulocyte indices, peripheral smear, soluble transferrin receptor, stool occult blood testing, endoscopy, celiac testing, or marrow iron assessment when needed. Name: Porphyria, Acute Intermittent
Description: Acute intermittent porphyria is an acute hepatic porphyria, classically an autosomal dominant disorder with low penetrance caused by pathogenic variants in HMBS, which encodes hydroxymethylbilane synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase), with representative missense, nonsense, splice-site, and small deletion mutations producing partial enzyme deficiency; rare homozygous or compound heterozygous states cause severe childhood disease. The central pathogenic pathway is dysregulated hepatic heme biosynthesis: reduced HMBS activity, coupled with induction of ALAS1, leads to overproduction of the neurotoxic precursors delta-aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen, while heme deficiency perturbs cytochrome P450-dependent signaling; attacks are precipitated by porphyrinogenic drugs, alcohol, fasting, infection, smoking, and progesterone. Clinically, AIP presents with episodic severe diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension, dark urine, peripheral motor neuropathy, paresthesias, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, and hyponatremia from SIADH, usually without cutaneous photosensitivity. Major complications include respiratory paralysis, chronic neuropathic pain, chronic kidney disease, hepatocellular carcinoma, and recurrent depression or anxiety; comorbid associations include epilepsy, particularly when treated with unsafe anticonvulsants, and other acute hepatic porphyrias in the differential such as hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria. Diagnosis is established during attacks by markedly increased urinary porphobilinogen and delta-aminolevulinic acid, with confirmatory erythrocyte HMBS activity in many cases and molecular testing of HMBS for familial screening; plasma and fecal porphyrin patterns help exclude other porphyrias. Treatment centers on withdrawal of triggers and carbohydrate loading or intravenous glucose to suppress ALAS1, intravenous hemin or heme arginate to replenish hepatic heme and downregulate ALAS1, and givosiran, an siRNA targeting hepatic ALAS1 mRNA, for prevention of recurrent attacks; supportive therapy includes analgesics, antiemetics, correction of electrolyte disturbances, and careful use of porphyria-safe medications.

Name: Protoporphyria, Erythropoietic
Description: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is a hereditary cutaneous porphyria caused by impaired heme biosynthesis, most often from partial ferrochelatase deficiency due to biallelic FECH defects or, classically, a loss-of-function FECH variant in trans with the common low-expression IVS3-48C allele; a less common X-linked subtype, X-linked protoporphyria, results from gain-of-function ALAS2 mutations that increase erythroid 5-aminolevulinate synthase activity and protoporphyrin production. The central pathogenic pathway is the erythroid heme synthesis cascade, in which excess metal-free protoporphyrin IX accumulates in erythrocytes, plasma, skin, and hepatobiliary tissue, generating reactive oxygen species after visible-light exposure and causing hepatocellular and biliary injury through protoporphyrin precipitation. Patients typically present in childhood with immediate, painful nonblistering photosensitivity, burning, erythema, edema, waxy scarring or lichenification over exposed skin, and avoidance of sunlight; complications include cholelithiasis, chronic liver disease, cholestatic liver failure, mild microcytic or iron-deficiency anemia, and vitamin D deficiency, with hepatopathy representing the major serious comorbidity. Management includes afamelanotide, an α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone analog that activates MC1R to increase eumelanin and photoprotection; dersimelagon, an oral MC1R agonist with similar melanogenic effects; and bile acid sequestrants such as cholestyramine or activated charcoal, which interrupt enterohepatic recirculation of protoporphyrin to reduce hepatic burden; severe hepatic disease may require ursodeoxycholic acid, hemin support, plasmapheresis or exchange transfusion, and liver transplantation, sometimes followed by hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation to correct the erythroid source. Diagnosis relies on markedly increased total and metal-free erythrocyte protoporphyrin, plasma fluorescence peaking near 634 nm, normal or minimally increased urine porphyrins, FECH enzyme or molecular testing, ALAS2 sequencing when indicated, and assessment of liver function and biliary involvement.

Name: Skin Diseases, Bacterial
Description: Skin diseases, bacterial comprise a heterogeneous group of infectious dermatoses caused most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant strains carrying mecA/PBP2a and virulence factors such as PVL, and by Streptococcus pyogenes, with additional forms due to Corynebacterium, Pseudomonas, and Mycobacterium species; major clinical subtypes include impetigo, ecthyma, folliculitis, furuncles/carbuncles, cellulitis, erysipelas, erythrasma, and secondary bacterial infection of wounds or eczematous skin. Pathobiology centers on epidermal barrier disruption and innate immune activation, with TLR2-NF-κB, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and, in recurrent or severe disease, host susceptibility genes affecting barrier and immunity such as FLG, DEFB4, TLR2, NCF1/NCF2/CYBB in chronic granulomatous disease, and STAT3 in hyper-IgE syndrome; inheritance is therefore usually non-Mendelian and pathogen-acquired, but Mendelian immunodeficiency or barrier disorders can confer predisposition. Patients typically present with erythema, warmth, tenderness, edema, pustules, crusted erosions, honey-colored crusts, fluctuance, lymphangitis, pain, and sometimes fever or malaise. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by Gram stain and culture of pus or tissue, blood cultures in systemic illness, biopsy for atypical or mycobacterial infection, and susceptibility testing; recurrent disease may warrant screening for diabetes, neutrophil defects, or nasal staphylococcal carriage. Standard therapy includes beta-lactams such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation; clindamycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and suppresses toxin production; doxycycline, a 30S inhibitor useful for community MRSA; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks folate synthesis; topical mupirocin, an isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase inhibitor; and vancomycin for severe MRSA. Important comorbidities and complications include atopic dermatitis, venous or diabetic ulcers, obesity, lymphedema, abscess, bacteremia, osteomy

Name: MELAS Syndrome
Description: MELAS syndrome, a mitochondrial encephalomyopathy characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes, is most often caused by maternally inherited pathogenic mtDNA variants, classically the MT-TL1 m.3243A>G mutation encoding mitochondrial tRNALeu(UUR), with other cases due to MT-ND5, MT-ND1, MT-TH, MT-TV, MT-TS1, or POLG-related defects; heteroplasmy, replicative segregation, and tissue-specific mutant load strongly influence phenotype, and rare nuclear gene causes can produce MELAS-like disease. The core pathobiology involves impaired oxidative phosphorylation, especially respiratory chain complex I deficiency, reduced ATP generation, excess reactive oxygen species, disturbed mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy, nitric oxide deficiency with endothelial dysfunction, and excitotoxic and metabolic injury within neurovascular units. Clinically, patients typically present in childhood or early adulthood with recurrent stroke-like episodes not confined to vascular territories, seizures, migraine-like headache, encephalopathy, vomiting, exercise intolerance, proximal myopathy, hearing loss, short stature, diabetes, and elevated blood and CSF lactate; complications include status epilepticus, cognitive decline, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, renal disease, retinopathy, psychiatric symptoms, and endocrine dysfunction. MELAS is considered a multisystem mitochondrial disorder, with classic and MELAS-overlap phenotypes. Diagnosis relies on clinical features plus biochemical and genetic confirmation: serum/CSF lactate, neuroimaging showing cortical stroke-like lesions, EEG, audiology, echocardiography, muscle biopsy with ragged-red and cytochrome c oxidase-negative fibers and respiratory chain studies, and mtDNA sequencing with heteroplasmy quantification from blood, urine, or muscle. Treatment is supportive and complication-directed; commonly used agents include L-arginine or citrulline to augment nitric oxide production and potentially improve stroke-like episodes, coenzyme Q10 to facilitate electron transport in the respiratory chain, levetiracetam for seizure control via synaptic vesicle protein SV2A modulation, and sometimes riboflavin or L-carnitine as mitochondrial cofactors, while valproate is generally avoided because of mitochondrial toxicity.

Name: Acneiform Eruptions
Description: Acneiform eruptions (UMLS C0175167) are inflammatory papulopustular follicular disorders that resemble acne vulgaris but are often monomorphic, abrupt in onset, and triggered by medications, endocrine states, infections, or mechanical/occlusive exposures rather than primary comedonal acne. Pathobiology centers on altered follicular keratinization and neutrophil-rich perifollicular inflammation involving EGFR/MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling, androgen receptor–driven sebaceous activity, innate immune mediators such as IL-1, IL-8, TNF-α, and Toll-like receptor pathways, with representative genetic contributors in acne-prone phenotypes including AR, CYP21A2, FGFR2, NCSTN, and occasionally defects affecting keratinization or autoinflammation; inherited predisposition is usually complex/polygenic, although syndromic acneiform disease may occur in autosomal dominant or recessive settings. Important subtypes include drug-induced eruptions from corticosteroids, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin, androgens, and especially EGFR inhibitors or MEK inhibitors; chloracne from halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons; Malassezia folliculitis; steroid acne; and acneiform lesions in hidradenitis suppurativa-related spectra. Typical findings are follicular papules and pustules on the face, chest, back, scalp, or proximal extremities, sometimes with pruritus, tenderness, erythema, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and less often nodules or scarring; comorbidities and complications depend on cause and include endocrine hyperandrogenism, hidradenitis suppurativa, secondary bacterial infection, psychosocial distress, and permanent scarring. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, emphasizing morphology, absence or paucity of comedones in many cases, lesion distribution, and temporal relation to culprit exposure, supported when indicated by medication review, bacterial or fungal studies, endocrine testing, skin biopsy showing suppurative folliculitis, or patch/exposure history for chloracne. Treatment targets the trigger and inflammation, with topical benzoyl peroxide generating reactive oxygen species, topical or oral retinoids such as adapalene or isotretinoin normalizing keratinization and reducing sebaceous activity, tetracyclines such as doxycycline inhibiting Cutibacterium acnes and neutrophilic inflammation, and adjunctive topical clind

Name: Anemia, Hypoplastic
Description: Aplastic anemia is a bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by hypocellular marrow and peripheral pancytopenia, most often acquired through immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, but also inherited in subsets such as Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and GATA2 deficiency. Key genetic and molecular associations include HLA-DR15 enrichment, somatic mutations in PIGA, BCOR, BCORL1, DNMT3A, ASXL1, and occasionally TERT, TERC, DKC1, FANCA/FANCC, SBDS, or GATA2, with proteins and pathways implicating telomere maintenance, DNA interstrand crosslink repair, ribosome biogenesis, and stem-cell survival. Central pathogenic pathways include oligoclonal cytotoxic T-cell activation, Th1 cytokines such as interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, Fas-mediated apoptosis, reduced thrombopoietin/MPL signaling, and clonal evolution affecting hematopoiesis. Patients typically present with fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, infections, fever, mucosal ulceration, easy bruising, petechiae, epistaxis, or menorrhagia, while lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are usually absent. Major subtypes include acquired severe and very severe aplastic anemia, non-severe aplastic anemia, and constitutional marrow failure syndromes; severity is commonly defined by marrow cellularity below 25 percent plus cytopenias, including neutrophils below 0.5 × 10^9/L, platelets below 20 × 10^9/L, and reticulocytopenia. Diagnosis relies on CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing hypocellularity, cytogenetics and myeloid NGS panels, flow cytometry for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria clones, and testing for inherited predisposition including chromosome breakage assays and telomere length studies when indicated. Standard treatments include antithymocyte globulin, which depletes pathogenic T cells, cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor that suppresses IL-2–dependent T-cell activation, eltrombopag, a thrombopoietin receptor agonist that stimulates residual stem-cell hematopoiesis, and allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; complications include life-threatening infection,

Name: Epithelioid Sarcomas
Description: Sarcoma is a heterogeneous group of malignant mesenchymal neoplasms arising in soft tissue, bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, vascular, or fibrous connective tissues, with major subtypes including osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, liposarcoma, synovial sarcoma, angiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Its molecular basis varies by subtype and includes complex karyotypic tumors with TP53, RB1, ATRX, CDKN2A, PTEN, MDM2, and NF1 alterations, as well as translocation-driven sarcomas such as EWSR1-FLI1 in Ewing sarcoma, SS18-SSX in synovial sarcoma, FUS-DDIT3 in myxoid liposarcoma, and KIT or PDGFRA mutations in GIST; germline predisposition occurs in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, hereditary retinoblastoma, neurofibromatosis type 1, familial adenomatous polyposis, and SDH-deficient syndromes, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance. Key pathways include p53 and RB cell-cycle control, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, IGF signaling, VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, Wnt/beta-catenin, and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling through KIT, PDGFRA, ALK, NTRK, and MET. Patients typically present with a painless enlarging mass, local pain, swelling, reduced function, pathologic fracture in bone sarcoma, constitutional symptoms in advanced disease, and pulmonary metastases as a common complication; treatment-related morbidity, local recurrence, thromboembolism, and cardiotoxicity may also occur. Diagnosis relies on imaging with MRI for soft tissue and CT or radiography for bone and staging, followed by core needle or incisional biopsy, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing by FISH, RT-PCR, or next-generation sequencing to define subtype and actionable alterations. Name: Lung Diseases, Interstitial
Description: Interstitial lung diseases are a heterogeneous group of diffuse parenchymal lung disorders characterized by varying combinations of inflammation, alveolar epithelial injury, aberrant wound repair, and progressive interstitial fibrosis that impair gas exchange; major subtypes include idiopathic interstitial pneumonias such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis, connective tissue disease–associated ILD, pneumoconioses, and smoking-related ILDs. Pathobiology commonly involves TGF-β/SMAD, PDGF, VEGF, FGF, Wnt/β-catenin, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and chemokine signaling, with activation of fibroblasts, myofibroblast differentiation, macrophages, and type II alveolar epithelial cells. Genetic contributors are best defined in familial pulmonary fibrosis and include mutations in telomere-maintenance genes TERT, TERC, RTEL1, PARN, DKC1 and surfactant-related genes SFTPA1, SFTPA2, SFTPC, ABCA3, as well as the common MUC5B promoter variant; inheritance is often autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, though X-linked and recessive forms occur. Typical manifestations are progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, bibasilar crackles, fatigue, hypoxemia, and sometimes clubbing, while complications include pulmonary hypertension, acute exacerbations, respiratory failure, lung cancer, pneumothorax, and infections; common comorbidities include gastroesophageal reflux, emphysema, coronary disease, sleep apnea, and autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis. Diagnosis integrates exposure and family history, serologies, pulmonary function testing showing restriction and reduced DLCO, high-resolution CT patterns such as usual interstitial pneumonia, bronchoalveolar lavage in selected cases, and lung biopsy or cryobiopsy when imaging and clinical data are indeterminate. Treatment depends on subtype and includes antifibrotics for progressive fibrosing disease, notably nintedanib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor of PDGFR/FGFR/VEGFR, and pirfenidone, which suppresses TGF-β-driven fibrogenesis and inflammatory signaling, as well as corticosteroids such as prednisone and steroid-sparing immunosuppressants including mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine for inflammatory or autoimmune IL

Name: Cytomegalovirus Retinitis
Description: Cytomegalovirus retinitis is a necrotizing viral retinopathy caused by reactivation or, less often, primary infection with human cytomegalovirus (HHV-5), classically occurring in profoundly immunosuppressed patients, especially those with AIDS and CD4 counts below about 50 cells/µL, but also in solid-organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients and patients receiving corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants. The disease is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion; rather, host susceptibility is shaped by immune-related genetic factors and viral determinants, including CMV genes encoding phosphotransferase UL97 and DNA polymerase UL54, whose mutations confer resistance to ganciclovir and cidofovir/foscarnet, while host variation in HLA loci, IFNG, IL10, TLR2, and TLR9 has been associated with altered CMV control. Pathobiologically, CMV infects retinal vascular endothelium and neural retina, engaging immediate-early gene expression, viral DNA replication, and host innate and adaptive immune pathways involving TLR signaling, interferon-mediated JAK/STAT responses, NF-κB activation, NK cells, and CMV-specific CD4/CD8 T-cell surveillance. Patients typically present with painless floaters, blurred vision, scotomas, photopsias, and progressive visual field loss, and funduscopy shows yellow-white granular retinal necrosis with hemorrhage, vasculitis, and limited vitritis; fulminant/edematous and indolent granular peripheral forms are recognized. Diagnosis is usually clinical in the appropriate immunologic setting, supported by dilated retinal examination and optical coherence tomography or fundus photography, with aqueous or vitreous PCR for CMV DNA used in atypical cases and HIV/immunologic evaluation performed concurrently. Standard therapy includes valganciclovir or ganciclovir, guanosine analogs activated by UL97 that inhibit viral DNA polymerase, foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analog that directly inhibits polymerase without phosphorylation, and cidofovir, a nucleotide analog inhibiting viral DNA synthesis; intravitreal therapy is often added for sight-threatening lesions. Major complications include retinal detachment, immune recovery uveitis, optic nerve or macular involvement, bilateral blindness, and associations with HIV/AIDS, transplant status, and other opportunistic infections.

Name: Tuberculosis, Drug-Resistant
Description: Drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains with acquired resistance to one or more antituberculous agents, classically multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB; resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin), rifampin-resistant TB, pre-extensively drug-resistant TB, and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). Resistance is driven by bacterial, not Mendelian human, genetics, with representative mutations including rpoB in the RNA polymerase beta subunit conferring rifampin resistance, katG and inhA promoter mutations causing isoniazid resistance, embB for ethambutol, pncA for pyrazinamide, gyrA/gyrB for fluoroquinolones, and rrs or eis promoter changes for injectable aminoglycosides; relevant proteins include KatG catalase-peroxidase, InhA enoyl-ACP reductase, and ATP synthase targeted by bedaquiline. Pathobiology reflects macrophage infection, granuloma formation, and host TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-12, JAK-STAT, NF-kappaB, autophagy, and vitamin D-dependent antimicrobial pathways, while human susceptibility is influenced by variants affecting IFNG/IL12RB1 axis, SLC11A1, TLR2, and HLA, usually as complex/polygenic traits rather than a simple inheritance pattern. Clinical manifestations resemble drug-susceptible TB, including chronic cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, hemoptysis, chest pain, cavitary pulmonary disease, and extrapulmonary involvement. Major comorbidities and complications include HIV infection, diabetes, malnutrition, silicosis, chronic lung disease, hepatotoxicity from therapy, respiratory failure, massive hemoptysis, dissemination, relapse, and death. Treatment uses multidrug regimens guided by susceptibility testing, commonly including bedaquiline, which inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, linezolid, which blocks 50S ribosomal protein synthesis, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase, and sometimes delamanid or pretomanid, which impair mycolic acid synthesis and respiratory metabolism. Diagnosis requires microbiologic confirmation plus resistance testing by sputum smear and culture, phenotypic drug susceptibility testing, NAATs such as Xpert MTB/RIF

Name: Adenocarcinoma, Follicular
Description: Follicular adenocarcinoma most commonly denotes follicular thyroid carcinoma, a differentiated malignant epithelial neoplasm derived from thyroid follicular cells that shows follicular architecture and, unlike follicular adenoma, is defined by capsular and/or vascular invasion; major subtypes include minimally invasive, encapsulated angioinvasive, and widely invasive forms, with Hürthle cell carcinoma often considered a related oncocytic variant. It is driven by alterations in genes regulating MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling, especially RAS mutations in NRAS, HRAS, and KRAS, PAX8-PPARG fusion, and less often PTEN, TERT promoter, TP53, or EIF1AX abnormalities, with corresponding effects on follicular-cell differentiation, proliferation, angiogenesis, and iodine handling. Most cases are sporadic, but susceptibility may occur in familial thyroid cancer syndromes and inherited cancer predisposition disorders such as PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome/Cowden syndrome, DICER1 syndrome, and occasionally familial adenomatous polyposis or Carney complex. Patients typically present with a solitary painless thyroid nodule or enlarging neck mass, sometimes with hoarseness, dysphagia, or compressive symptoms; hematogenous spread may cause bone or lung metastases, while complications include recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, pathologic fracture, and postoperative or treatment-related hypothyroidism. Diagnosis relies on clinical examination, thyroid ultrasonography, thyroid function testing, and fine-needle aspiration, although cytology usually cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from carcinoma; definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic demonstration of capsular or vascular invasion after lobectomy or thyroidectomy, supplemented in selected cases by molecular testing for RAS, PAX8-PPARG, TERT, or other markers, and staging imaging such as radioiodine scanning, CT, or PET when advanced disease is suspected. Treatment centers on surgery and radioactive iodine, with levothyroxine used for TSH suppression, while systemic agents for recurrent or metastatic radioiodine-refractory disease include lenvatinib, a multikinase VEGFR/FGFR/RET/PDGFR inhibitor, sorafenib, a RAF/VEGFR/PDGFR inhibitor, and doxorubicin, a DNA-intercalating topoisomerase II inhibitor.

Name: Niemann-Pick Disease, Type C
Description: Niemann-Pick disease type C (MeSH D052556) is a rare, progressive lysosomal lipid-trafficking disorder caused predominantly by autosomal recessive biallelic pathogenic variants in NPC1, which encodes a late endosomal/lysosomal transmembrane cholesterol transporter, and less often NPC2, which encodes a soluble lysosomal cholesterol-binding protein; representative mutations include NPC1 p.I1061T and p.P1007A. Defective NPC1/NPC2 function disrupts intracellular egress of unesterified cholesterol and glycosphingolipids from late endosomes/lysosomes, leading to altered SREBP- and LXR-regulated sterol homeostasis, impaired autophagy, calcium signaling abnormalities, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and selective neuronal vulnerability, especially of cerebellar Purkinje cells. Clinical phenotypes are commonly stratified as perinatal/early infantile, late infantile, juvenile, and adolescent/adult-onset forms, and present with neonatal cholestatic jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia, gelastic cataplexy, seizures, dystonia, cognitive decline, psychosis, and progressive dementia. Major complications include aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, liver dysfunction, respiratory failure, and severe neurodegeneration; psychiatric illness and epilepsy are important comorbidities. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus laboratory and genetic confirmation using plasma oxysterols such as cholestane-3β,5α,6β-triol, lysosphingomyelin-509, filipin staining of cultured fibroblasts showing perinuclear cholesterol storage, and molecular testing of NPC1/NPC2, with supportive neuroimaging and neurophysiology as indicated. Treatment is largely disease-modifying and supportive: miglustat, an inhibitor of glucosylceramide synthase, reduces glycosphingolipid synthesis; arimoclomol amplifies heat-shock protein responses to improve lysosomal protein folding and function; and 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin mobilizes lysosomal cholesterol, while symptomatic agents such as antiepileptics, antidepressants/antipsychotics, and physical, nutritional, and respiratory support are commonly required.

Name: Hereditary Orotic Aciduria
Description: Hereditary orotic aciduria (UMLS C0220987) is a rare autosomal recessive inborn error of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis caused most often by biallelic pathogenic variants in UMPS, which encodes the bifunctional cytosolic enzyme uridine monophosphate synthase with orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine-5′-phosphate decarboxylase activities; representative loss-of-function missense, nonsense, splice-site, or truncating mutations impair conversion of orotic acid to UMP, leading to orotate accumulation and pyrimidine deficiency. The key affected pathway is the CAD-DHODH-UMPS pyrimidine synthesis axis, in which carbamoyl phosphate is converted through dihydroorotate and orotate to UMP; downstream deficits in UDP/UTP and CTP compromise DNA/RNA synthesis and erythroid maturation, while hyperammonemia is typically absent, helping distinguish this disorder from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Classic hereditary orotic aciduria includes type I deficiency of both UMPS activities and type II with isolated decarboxylase impairment, although many contemporary cases are described simply as UMPS deficiency. Patients usually present in infancy or childhood with failure to thrive, megaloblastic or refractory macrocytic anemia unresponsive to folate or vitamin B12, growth and developmental delay, feeding difficulty, recurrent infections, crystalluria, and marked urinary orotic acid excretion; complications include intellectual disability, severe anemia, urinary tract obstruction from orotate crystals, and chronic malnutrition. Diagnosis rests on elevated urine orotic acid, characteristic hematologic findings, normal ammonia in most cases, exclusion of urea-cycle defects, enzymatic assay of UMPS activity in erythrocytes or fibroblasts, and confirmatory molecular testing of UMPS. Treatment is based on pyrimidine replacement, especially uridine triacetate, uridine, or uridine monophosphate/cytidine preparations, which bypass the metabolic block and replenish UTP/CTP pools; supportive measures may include transfusions and hematinic supplementation when needed, though the latter do not correct the primary defect.

Name: Hyperammonemia
Description: Hyperammonemia is a metabolic disorder defined by pathologic elevation of სისხ ammonia, most often reflecting impaired hepatic detoxification or inherited defects of the urea cycle; major primary genetic causes include pathogenic variants in CPS1, OTC, ASS1, ASL, ARG1, NAGS, and the mitochondrial ornithine/citrulline transporter SLC25A15, with related hyperammonemic syndromes also seen in carbonic anhydrase VA deficiency (CA5A), citrin deficiency (SLC25A13), and lysinuric protein intolerance (SLC7A7). These defects disrupt the urea-cycle pathway spanning mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthesis and ornithine transport to cytosolic citrulline, argininosuccinate, and arginine metabolism, while excess ammonia drives astrocytic glutamine accumulation via glutamine synthetase, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, NMDA-receptor–mediated excitotoxicity, cerebral edema, and neuroinflammation. Disease subtypes include primary versus secondary hyperammonemia and neonatal-onset, late-onset, or episodic presentations; inheritance is usually autosomal recessive, except OTC deficiency, which is X-linked. Clinical manifestations range from vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, tachypnea from respiratory alkalosis, confusion, ataxia, and protein aversion to seizures, encephalopathy, coma, and death, with chronic cases causing developmental delay, intellectual disability, spasticity, and liver dysfunction. Important comorbidities and complications include cerebral edema, intracranial hypertension, hepatic failure, catabolism-triggered decompensation, and neuropsychiatric impairment. Treatment centers on nitrogen-scavenging drugs such as sodium benzoate, which conjugates glycine to form hippurate, sodium or glycerol phenylbutyrate/phenylacetate, which divert nitrogen through phenylacetylglutamine formation, and arginine or citrulline supplementation to support residual urea-cycle flux; carglumic acid, an N-acetylglutamate analogue, is used in NAGS deficiency. Diagnosis relies on elevated plasma ammonia, plasma amino acid and urinary orotic acid profiles, liver function assessment, molecular testing for causative variants, and in selected cases enzyme assays, with newborn screening detecting citrullinemia and argininosuccinic aciduria.

Name: Mastocytosis, Systemic
Description: Systemic mastocytosis is a clonal hematologic neoplasm characterized by pathologic accumulation of mast cells in bone marrow and other extracutaneous organs, most often driven by activating KIT mutations, particularly KIT D816V, which constitutively activates the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase and downstream PI3K/AKT, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, JAK/STAT, and PLCγ signaling pathways; additional mutations in SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1, TET2, DNMT3A, CBL, or JAK2 may occur in advanced disease and influence prognosis. The disorder is usually sporadic rather than Mendelian, although rare familial clustering and germline predisposition have been described; mast cells typically express KIT/CD117, tryptase, and aberrant CD25 and/or CD2 or CD30. Clinical manifestations reflect mediator release and tissue infiltration, including flushing, pruritus, urticaria pigmentosa or other cutaneous lesions, abdominal pain, diarrhea, peptic symptoms, hypotension, syncope, anaphylaxis, bone pain, osteoporosis, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, cytopenias, and malabsorption. Major subtypes include indolent systemic mastocytosis, smoldering systemic mastocytosis, systemic mastocytosis with an associated hematologic neoplasm, aggressive systemic mastocytosis, and mast cell leukemia. Important complications and comorbidities include severe anaphylaxis, especially with hymenoptera venom allergy, osteopenia/osteoporosis with fractures, portal hypertension, ascites, liver dysfunction, and transformation or coexistence with myeloid neoplasms. Diagnosis is based on WHO/ICC criteria using bone marrow or other tissue biopsy showing multifocal dense mast-cell aggregates plus minor criteria such as atypical spindle-shaped mast cells, KIT D816V or another activating KIT mutation, aberrant CD25/CD2/CD30 expression, and persistent serum tryptase elevation, supported by flow cytometry, high-sensitivity PCR or NGS, marrow histology, and imaging for organ damage. Treatment includes H1 and H2 antihistamines and cromolyn for mediator symptoms, epinephrine for anaphylaxis, bisphosphonates for bone disease, midostaurin, a multikinase inhibitor active against KIT D816V, avapritinib, a selective KIT D816V inhibitor,

Name: Hypertension, paroxysmal
Description: Paroxysmal hypertension is a clinical syndrome characterized by abrupt, episodic surges in blood pressure, often with severe sympathetic symptoms, occurring either secondary to catecholamine-secreting tumors or as pseudopheochromocytoma-like attacks without an identifiable tumor; patients typically present with sudden headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, tremor, anxiety, pallor or flushing, chest pain, dyspnea, and marked systolic and diastolic elevations that may resolve between episodes. A major biologic subtype is pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma-associated paroxysmal hypertension, driven by excess catecholamine synthesis and release through tyrosine hydroxylase and chromaffin-cell signaling, with genetic contributors including RET in MEN2, VHL, NF1, and succinate dehydrogenase complex genes such as SDHB, SDHD, and SDHC; less commonly TMEM127, MAX, FH, and EPAS1/HIF2A mutations are implicated. Key pathways include sympathetic-adrenal signaling, α1- and β-adrenergic receptor activation, cAMP/Ca2+-dependent exocytosis, and hypoxia-inducible factor/pseudohypoxia and MAPK/PI3K-related tumorigenic pathways in hereditary PPGL. Important comorbidities and complications include sustained hypertension, hypertensive emergency, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction, stroke, retinopathy, chronic kidney disease, panic disorder, and obstructive sleep apnea. Treatment depends on cause and severity: α-adrenergic blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin reduces catecholamine-mediated vasoconstriction; β-blockers such as propranolol or metoprolol control tachycardia only after adequate α-blockade; calcium-channel blockers such as nicardipine or amlodipine reduce vascular smooth muscle calcium influx; and clonidine decreases central sympathetic outflow, with adrenalectomy indicated for resectable pheochromocytoma. Diagnosis relies on documenting episodic hypertension, excluding common secondary causes, measuring plasma free or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines, imaging with CT/MRI and functional scans when indicated, and considering genetic testing in early-onset, multifocal, metastatic, or familial cases; inheritance in hereditary tumor syndromes is usually autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.

Name: Atrophic Vaginitis
Description: Atrophic vaginitis, now commonly encompassed within the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, is a chronic hypoestrogenic inflammatory-degenerative disorder of the vulvovaginal and lower urinary tract epithelium characterized by thinning of the stratified squamous mucosa, loss of rugae, reduced glycogen, diminished lactobacilli, elevated vaginal pH, and increased tissue fragility; it most often follows natural menopause but also occurs with lactation, surgical oophorectomy, chemotherapy, aromatase inhibitor use, or other states of estrogen deprivation. Molecularly, the condition is driven primarily by reduced estrogen signaling through ESR1 and ESR2 and altered downstream regulation of epithelial proliferation, angiogenesis, extracellular matrix turnover, and immune homeostasis, with representative implicated mediators including progesterone receptor, androgen receptor, collagen/elastin remodeling pathways, TGF-β, VEGF, and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF; no Mendelian inheritance pattern is established, but genetic susceptibility may be modulated by polymorphisms in ESR1, ESR2, CYP19A1, and steroid metabolism genes. Typical symptoms and signs include vaginal dryness, burning, irritation, dyspareunia, postcoital spotting, decreased lubrication, narrowing or shortening of the vagina, pallor, petechiae, friability, and urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria, or recurrent urinary tract infection. Subtypes are usually framed clinically as vulvovaginal-predominant, urinary-predominant, or mixed GSM. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by examination, vaginal pH usually greater than 5, microscopy showing reduced superficial cells and increased parabasal cells, and exclusion of infection, dermatoses, neoplasia, or sexually transmitted disease; biopsy is reserved for atypical lesions. Standard treatment includes estradiol, conjugated estrogens, or estriol, which restore ER-mediated epithelial maturation; prasterone, an intravaginal DHEA converted locally to estrogens and androgens; and ospemifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator that improves epithelial integrity, with moisturizers and lubricants as adjuncts. Important comorbidities and complications include menopause-related osteoporosis and sexual dysfunction, recurrent UTI, fissuring, bleeding, and impaired quality of life.

Name: Pituitary ACTH Hypersecretion
Description: Pituitary ACTH hypersecretion, most often the cause of Cushing disease, is a usually benign but hormonally active corticotroph pituitary adenoma that produces excess adrenocorticotropic hormone, driving bilateral adrenal cortisol overproduction; less commonly it reflects corticotroph hyperplasia or, rarely, aggressive pituitary neuroendocrine tumor behavior. Molecularly, recurrent USP8 gain-of-function mutations are the best-established genetic lesion, increasing EGFR signaling and POMC transcription, while USP48, BRAF V600E, TP53 alterations, and dysregulation of CABLES1, CDKN1B, and cell-cycle pathways are reported in subsets; rare familial cases occur with MEN1, AIP, CDKN1B/MEN4, or DICER1-related predisposition, although most cases are sporadic rather than classically inherited. Key signaling pathways include hypothalamic CRH-CRHR1 and vasopressin-V1b stimulation of corticotrophs, cAMP/PKA, MAPK/ERK, EGFR, and glucocorticoid receptor-mediated negative feedback, with aberrant POMC processing and ACTH secretion. Typical manifestations are central weight gain, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, proximal myopathy, purple striae, skin thinning, easy bruising, acne, hirsutism, menstrual disturbance, decreased libido, hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, osteoporosis, nephrolithiasis, mood and cognitive changes, infection risk, and hypokalemia in severe cases. Major complications and comorbidities include metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, venous thromboembolism, fractures, psychiatric illness, and persistent postoperative hypopituitarism or adrenal insufficiency. Diagnosis requires biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism with late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or low-dose dexamethasone suppression testing, demonstration of ACTH dependence, pituitary MRI, and often inferior petrosal sinus sampling when imaging is equivocal. First-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery; common drugs include pasireotide, a somatostatin receptor ligand that suppresses ACTH release, cabergoline, a dopamine D2 agonist, ketoconazole and metyrapone, which inhibit adrenal steroidogenesis, osilodrostat, an 11β-hydroxylase inhibitor, and mifeprist

Name: Chronic schizophrenia
Description: Chronic schizophrenia (UMLS C0221765) is a severe, usually lifelong psychotic disorder characterized by persistent or recurrent delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought and behavior, negative symptoms such as blunted affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia, and social withdrawal, often with cognitive deficits in attention, working memory, and executive function; traditional clinical subtypes include paranoid, disorganized, catatonic, undifferentiated, and residual forms, although current nosology emphasizes dimensional symptom domains. Its etiology is multifactorial and highly polygenic rather than Mendelian, with heritability around 70–80% and risk associated with variants in genes such as DRD2, COMT, DISC1, NRG1, AKT1, DTNBP1, CACNA1C, GRIN2A, and complement component C4, as well as rare copy-number variants including 22q11.2 deletion. Implicated pathways include dopaminergic dysregulation, especially mesolimbic D2 hyperactivity and mesocortical hypodopaminergia, glutamatergic NMDA-receptor hypofunction, GABAergic interneuron dysfunction, serotonin 5-HT2A signaling, calcium-channel signaling, synaptic pruning, neuroinflammation, and PI3K/AKT and neuregulin-ERBB pathways. Common treatments include antipsychotics such as haloperidol, a potent D2 receptor antagonist; risperidone and olanzapine, which block D2 and 5-HT2A receptors; and clozapine, used for treatment-resistant disease with broad serotonergic and dopaminergic receptor effects and superior anti-suicidal efficacy. Frequent comorbidities and complications include major depression, anxiety, substance use disorders, metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, cognitive and functional decline, homelessness, and elevated suicide risk. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 or ICD criteria requiring characteristic psychotic symptoms with functional impairment and duration of at least 6 months, supported by mental status examination, collateral history, cognitive assessment, toxicology and laboratory testing, and neuroimaging or other studies to exclude secondary psychosis.

Name: Severe anxiety (panic) (finding)
Description: Severe anxiety with panic refers to an episodic, often recurrent fear syndrome most closely aligned with panic attacks and panic disorder, characterized by abrupt surges of intense apprehension accompanied by palpitations, chest discomfort, dyspnea, tremor, diaphoresis, dizziness, paresthesias, gastrointestinal distress, derealization, fear of losing control, and anticipatory anxiety, frequently leading to avoidance behaviors or agoraphobia. It is a multifactorial neuropsychiatric condition with substantial but non-Mendelian heritability, typically polygenic, with susceptibility signals reported in serotonergic, catecholaminergic, and stress-response genes such as SLC6A4, HTR1A, COMT, MAOA, BDNF, NPY, CRHR1, TMEM132D, and RGS2; rare families show clustering rather than a single causal mutation. Pathobiology implicates dysregulation of amygdala-prefrontal-hippocampal circuits, locus coeruleus noradrenergic firing, serotonergic and GABAergic inhibition, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation with CRH and cortisol signaling, and downstream cAMP-CREB, BDNF-TrkB, glutamatergic, and autonomic/sympathoadrenal pathways. Common comorbidities include major depressive disorder, other anxiety disorders, substance use, insomnia, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pain, cardiovascular symptoms, and increased risk of functional impairment and suicidality. Clinical subtypes include panic disorder with or without agoraphobia and expected versus unexpected panic attacks. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria requiring recurrent unexpected panic attacks and persistent concern or maladaptive behavioral change, supported by structured psychiatric assessment and rating scales such as the Panic Disorder Severity Scale, while ECG, thyroid testing, toxicology, and other targeted studies help exclude arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, stimulant exposure, pheochromocytoma, or seizure disorders. First-line pharmacotherapy includes SSRIs such as sertraline and paroxetine, which inhibit serotonin reuptake, and SNRIs such as venlafaxine, which inhibit serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; benzodiazepines such as clonazepam or alprazolam potentiate GABAA receptor signaling for rapid symptomatic relief, though dependence limits long-term use.

Name: Myalgia
Description: Myalgia (UMLS C0231528) is a symptom-defined pain syndrome arising from skeletal muscle and occurring as acute or chronic, localized or diffuse, primary or secondary to inflammatory, metabolic, infectious, endocrine, toxic, neurologic, or inherited myopathic disorders. Clinically it presents with aching, cramping, stiffness, tenderness, fatigability, exercise intolerance, and sometimes weakness, swelling, or allodynia; major subtypes include exertional myalgia, fibromyalgia-associated myalgia, inflammatory myositis-related pain, drug-induced myalgia, and metabolic or mitochondrial myalgia. Molecular contributors vary by cause and include cytokine and nociceptive signaling through TNF, IL6, IL1B, COX-2/PTGS2, prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P, TRPV1, ASIC3, and NGF, with central sensitization involving serotoninergic and noradrenergic pathways in fibromyalgia; inherited forms may involve PYGM in McArdle disease, CPT2 in fatty-acid oxidation defects, RYR1 and CACNA1S in malignant hyperthermia/exertional rhabdomyolysis susceptibility, DMD, and mitochondrial DNA variants, while statin-associated myalgia may rarely reflect SLCO1B1 susceptibility or immune-mediated anti-HMGCR myopathy. Common treatments are acetaminophen, which inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2; and duloxetine, which inhibits serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake and reduces central pain amplification; additional options include pregabalin, which binds the alpha2delta calcium-channel subunit, and corticosteroids for inflammatory myopathies. Important comorbidities include viral illness, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, autoimmune disease, and statin exposure; complications can include reduced function, chronic pain, rhabdomyolysis, and renal injury when muscle breakdown is severe. Diagnosis is clinical but guided by history, examination, medication review, and targeted testing including creatine kinase, ESR/CRP, thyroid studies, vitamin D, autoantibodies, electromyography, muscle MRI, genetic testing, and occasionally muscle biopsy, with red flags being objective weakness, pigmenturia, fever, focal swelling, or progressive CK elevation.

Name: Lower Abdominal Pain
Description: Lower abdominal pain (UMLS C0232495) is a nonspecific clinical syndrome rather than a single inherited disease, arising from gastrointestinal, gynecologic, urologic, musculoskeletal, vascular, or neuropathic pathology; common subtypes include acute versus chronic pain and visceral, somatic, or referred pain, with representative causes such as appendicitis, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, cystitis, nephrolithiasis, pelvic inflammatory disease, dysmenorrhea, endometriosis, ovarian torsion, and ectopic pregnancy. Typical symptoms and signs include suprapubic or iliac fossa pain, cramping, bloating, altered bowel habits, dysuria, urinary frequency, vaginal bleeding or discharge, fever, nausea, guarding, rebound tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, or adnexal tenderness depending on etiology. Genetic components are cause-specific rather than universal: IBD is linked to NOD2, IL23R, and ATG16L1; endometriosis to ESR1, GREB1, WNT4, and inflammatory mediators; colorectal cancer presenting with pain may involve APC, KRAS, TP53, and mismatch-repair genes MLH1/MSH2; hereditary patterns include autosomal dominant Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis. Relevant pathways therefore include NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-6/IL-23/Th17 signaling, prostaglandin/COX pathways, Wnt/β-catenin, estrogen/progesterone signaling, smooth-muscle calcium signaling, and visceral nociceptive transmission via TRPV1, substance P, and CGRP. Treatment is etiology-directed and commonly includes acetaminophen, a central analgesic likely reducing CNS prostaglandin synthesis; ibuprofen or naproxen, nonselective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitors that suppress prostaglandin-mediated inflammation and uterine cramping; dicyclomine or hyoscyamine, antimuscarinic antispasmodics that reduce bowel smooth-muscle spasm; and when indicated antibiotics such as ceftriaxone plus doxycycline with or without metronidazole for pelvic inflammatory disease. Comorbidities and complications include infertility, abscess, bowel obstruction, sepsis, perforation, chronic pelvic pain, adhesions, anemia, and malignancy.
