Name: Bladder Pain
Description: Bladder pain, most often discussed clinically within the spectrum of bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis, is a chronic pelvic pain disorder characterized by perceived pain, pressure, or discomfort related to the urinary bladder accompanied by urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia, and pain worsened by bladder filling and relieved by voiding, sometimes with suprapubic tenderness, dyspareunia, and flares triggered by stress, infection, or diet. Its biology is heterogeneous and incompletely defined, but implicated molecular factors include urothelial barrier dysfunction with altered uroplakins, reduced tight-junction integrity, mast-cell activation, neurogenic sensitization, and inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL6, IL8, NGF, substance P, and TRPV1/P2X3 signaling; transcriptomic and candidate-gene studies have variably implicated cytokine, adrenergic, serotonergic, nitric oxide, and extracellular-matrix pathways, with examples including ADRB2, COMT, IL4, IL10, NOS3, HLA associations, and antiproliferative factor–related signaling, although no single causative mutation is established and inheritance is generally complex, polygenic, and non-Mendelian. Recognized phenotypes include Hunner lesion disease and non-Hunner bladder pain syndrome, often overlapping with central sensitization syndromes. Common comorbidities include irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, vulvodynia, endometriosis, anxiety, depression, migraine, and recurrent urinary tract symptoms; complications include sleep disturbance, sexual dysfunction, impaired quality of life, and opioid exposure. Treatment is multimodal: pentosan polysulfate sodium is used to help restore the glycosaminoglycan mucosal layer, amitriptyline reduces neuropathic pain via serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and antihistaminic effects, hydroxyzine blocks H1-mediated mast-cell activity, and other options include intravesical lidocaine for sodium-channel blockade and analgesia, dimethyl sulfoxide for anti-inflammatory and neuromodulatory effects, and cyclosporine A for refractory immune-mediated disease. Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion, supported by urinalysis and culture, symptom inventories, voiding diaries, cystoscopy with hydrodistension or biopsy when indicated to identify Hunner lesions or exclude malignancy, and selective use of urodynamics and pelvic evaluation.

Name: Secondary physiologic amenorrhoea
Description: Secondary physiologic amenorrhoea is a nonpathologic, reversible absence of menses occurring after previously established menstruation in normal life states such as pregnancy, lactation, and menopause, and is distinguished from pathologic secondary amenorrhoea by appropriate endocrine context and exclusion of disease. Its biology reflects coordinated suppression or cessation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis through GnRH, LH, FSH, estradiol, progesterone, prolactin, inhibin/activin, kisspeptin-KISS1/KISS1R, TAC3/TACR3, leptin, and estrogen receptor signaling; pregnancy is dominated by placental hCG maintaining luteal progesterone, lactational amenorrhoea by suckling-induced prolactin elevation with reduced pulsatile GnRH release, and menopause by ovarian follicle depletion with low estradiol/inhibin B and compensatory high FSH/LH. Although physiologic forms are not primarily genetic disorders, ovarian reserve and menopausal timing are influenced by genes such as FMR1 premutation, BMP15, GDF9, NOBOX, FOXL2, ESR1, and FSHR, while rare variants in KISS1R or TACR3 affect reproductive neuroendocrine signaling. Symptoms and signs include absent menses, pregnancy-related nausea and breast tenderness, lactation, vasomotor symptoms and urogenital atrophy in menopause, and infertility outside pregnancy; long-term hypoestrogenism may contribute to osteopenia, osteoporosis, dyslipidemia, and genitourinary syndrome, while important comorbid or confounding conditions include PCOS, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, hypothalamic amenorrhoea, and premature ovarian insufficiency. Subtypes are pregnancy-associated, lactational, and menopausal amenorrhoea. Diagnosis is clinical and laboratory based: pregnancy testing first, menstrual history, medication and breastfeeding review, pelvic examination when indicated, serum hCG, prolactin, TSH, FSH/LH, estradiol, and sometimes AMH, with pelvic ultrasonography reserved for uncertainty. Management is usually expectant, but commonly used therapies include combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives to suppress ovulation or regulate bleeding when desired, menopausal hormone therapy replacing estrogen with progestin endometrial protection, and dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine or cabergoline, which reduce

Name: Tense Feeling
Description: Tense feeling (UMLS C0233494) is best understood not as a discrete inherited disease but as a subjective symptom complex usually reflecting psychological stress, anxiety-spectrum illness, autonomic hyperarousal, or increased skeletal muscle tone; accordingly, no single causative gene is established, although susceptibility to anxiety-related tense states has been linked in some cohorts to variants affecting serotonergic, catecholaminergic, and stress-response systems, including SLC6A4, HTR1A, COMT, MAOA, BDNF, FKBP5, and CRHR1, with corresponding proteins such as the serotonin transporter, 5-HT1A receptor, catechol-O-methyltransferase, monoamine oxidase A, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and glucocorticoid-signaling regulators. Relevant pathways include serotonin and norepinephrine neurotransmission, GABA-A receptor signaling, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation involving CRH, ACTH, and cortisol, amygdala-limbic circuitry, and sympathetic adrenergic output. Clinically, patients describe inner tightness, nervousness, muscle tension, restlessness, jaw clenching, irritability, insomnia, palpitations, tremulousness, diaphoresis, impaired concentration, and sometimes chest or gastrointestinal discomfort; subtypes are contextual rather than nosologic, such as acute stress-related tension, generalized anxiety-associated tension, panic-related tension, and somatic muscle-tension states. Common comorbidities include generalized anxiety disorder, depression, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, insomnia, tension-type headache, temporomandibular dysfunction, hypertension, and substance misuse, while complications may include functional impairment and chronic pain. Treatment depends on cause and commonly includes SSRIs such as sertraline or escitalopram, which inhibit presynaptic serotonin reuptake; SNRIs such as venlafaxine, which inhibit serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; benzodiazepines such as lorazepam, which positively modulate GABA-A receptors; and occasionally buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history, mental-status examination, symptom duration and triggers, and exclusion of mimics such as hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, stimulant use, or medication effects using targeted laboratory testing, ECG, and validated scales such as GAD-7 or Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale.

Name: Behavior, Antisocial
Description: Behavior, Antisocial (UMLS C0233523) refers clinically to persistent antisocial behavior, most often conceptualized within conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder, characterized by recurrent violation of social norms and the rights of others, deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability, aggression, irresponsibility, and lack of remorse, often with childhood histories of truancy, cruelty, theft, or fire-setting and adult manifestations including criminality and interpersonal exploitation. Its biology is complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with heritability estimates typically moderate; implicated genes and variants include low-activity MAOA, SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR, DRD2, DRD4, COMT, OXTR, and FKBP5, with altered proteins involving monoamine oxidase A, serotonin transporter, dopamine receptors, catechol-O-methyltransferase, and stress-response mediators. Relevant pathways include serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission, noradrenergic arousal, HPA-axis regulation with CRH, ACTH, and cortisol, amygdala-prefrontal circuitry governing threat processing and impulse control, and inflammatory or neurodevelopmental pathways in some cohorts. Common comorbidities include substance use disorders, ADHD, mood and anxiety disorders, PTSD, traumatic brain injury, intermittent explosive symptoms, and increased risks of violence, incarceration, suicide, victimization, and medical morbidity. Subtypes include childhood-onset versus adolescent-onset antisocial behavior, aggressive versus nonaggressive forms, and callous-unemotional traits specifier in youth. There is no drug approved specifically for antisocial behavior, but treatment of target symptoms commonly uses risperidone, a D2/5-HT2A antagonist, lithium, which modulates second-messenger signaling and reduces impulsive aggression, and SSRIs such as fluoxetine or sertraline, which inhibit SLC6A4-mediated serotonin reuptake; mood stabilizers such as valproate and stimulants for comorbid ADHD are also used. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM or ICD criteria, collateral history, structured interviews such as the SCID, assessment for conduct disorder before age 15 in antisocial personality disorder, risk evaluation, neuropsychological testing when indicated, and exclusion of primary psychotic, manic, intoxication-related, or neurological causes.

Name: Memory Deficits
Description: Memory disorders comprise a heterogeneous group of acquired and hereditary conditions characterized by impaired encoding, consolidation, storage, or retrieval of information, most often affecting episodic memory and variably involving working, semantic, and procedural memory; major subtypes include amnestic mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer disease, vascular cognitive impairment, traumatic or hypoxic amnesia, transient global amnesia, alcohol-related Korsakoff syndrome, and memory-predominant disorders in frontotemporal, Lewy body, or temporal lobe epileptic syndromes. Key molecular associations are best defined in neurodegenerative forms and include APP, PSEN1, PSEN2, and APOE, especially APOE ε4, with tau/MAPT, amyloid-β, cholinergic deficits, and synaptic proteins such as BDNF also implicated; less commonly, prion protein PRNP and NOTCH3 are relevant in specific inherited dementing syndromes. Pathobiology centers on amyloid precursor protein processing, tau phosphorylation, glutamatergic excitotoxicity through NMDA receptors, cholinergic neurotransmission failure, hippocampal and limbic circuit dysfunction, neuroinflammation with microglial activation, mitochondrial injury, oxidative stress, and cerebrovascular small-vessel disease. Clinical features include forgetfulness, repetitive questioning, misplacing items, disorientation, impaired new learning, confabulation in diencephalic amnesia, and progression to executive, language, visuospatial, behavioral, or functional decline depending on cause. Common comorbidities and complications include depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, delirium, epilepsy, gait instability, falls, malnutrition, caregiver burden, and loss of independence. Inheritance is usually multifactorial, but autosomal dominant familial Alzheimer disease due to APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2 mutations and inherited prion or small-vessel disorders are recognized. Diagnosis relies on history with collateral informants, neuropsychological testing, mental status examination, medication and metabolic review, MRI or CT, and when indicated EEG, CSF biomarkers such as amyloid-β42 and phosphorylated tau, FDG or amyloid PET, and targeted genetic testing. Treatments are cause-specific; commonly used agents include donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, which inhibit acetylcholinesterase to enhance cholinergic signaling, and memantine, a low-affinity NMDA receptor antagonist that reduces excitotoxicity.

Name: Oily skin
Description: Oily skin, or seborrhea/sebostasis of the face, scalp, and upper trunk, is a common multifactorial cutaneous phenotype characterized by increased sebaceous gland activity and excess sebum production rather than a single Mendelian disease. Clinically it presents with a shiny or greasy appearance, enlarged pores, scalp oiliness, and frequent association with comedones, acneiform eruptions, and sometimes seborrheic dermatitis. Pathobiology is driven by androgen-dependent sebocyte stimulation, especially testosterone conversion to dihydrotestosterone by SRD5A1 and SRD5A2 acting through the androgen receptor; representative genetic contributors include AR, SRD5A2, IGF1/IGF1R, FGF receptor signaling, PPARG, and lipid-regulatory factors such as SREBF1, while acne-prone oily skin may overlap with inflammatory variants involving IL1A, TNF, and innate immune responses to Cutibacterium acnes. Key pathways include androgen receptor signaling, IGF-1–PI3K–AKT–mTORC1, PPAR/lipogenesis programs, and inflammatory NF-kB-mediated cytokine signaling. Oily skin commonly coexists with acne vulgaris, seborrheic dermatitis, folliculitis, enlarged pores, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, and occasionally scarring; it may also be accentuated in puberty, polycystic ovary syndrome, and endocrine hyperandrogenic states. Subtypes are often described pragmatically as facial, scalp, acne-associated, and endocrine-related seborrhea. Inheritance is usually complex/polygenic with familial clustering rather than simple dominant or recessive transmission, although rare syndromic or endocrine disorders with altered androgen signaling can contribute. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by sebumetry, lesion counts, dermoscopic assessment, and evaluation for secondary causes with androgen profile testing or ovarian/adrenal studies in women with hirsutism, irregular menses, or severe acne. Common treatments include topical retinoids such as tretinoin or adapalene, which normalize follicular keratinization and reduce microcomedone formation; topical or systemic antiandrogens such as spironolactone, which antagonizes androgen signaling; combined oral contraceptives, which reduce ovarian androgen production and increase sex hormone-binding globulin; isotretinoin, which markedly suppresses sebaceous gland size and sebum output;

Name: Partial Seizures, Simple
Description: Epilepsies, partial, now more commonly termed focal epilepsies, are disorders in which seizures arise from a localized cortical network and may remain focal or evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures; clinical manifestations depend on the involved lobe and include focal aware or impaired-awareness episodes with aura, automatisms, behavioral arrest, unilateral sensory or motor symptoms, autonomic or psychic phenomena, postictal confusion, and sometimes Todd paralysis. Etiologies are heterogeneous and include structural, infectious, immune, metabolic, and genetic causes; important genetic contributors include ion-channel and synaptic genes such as SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNQ3, KCNT1, DEPDC5, NPRL2, NPRL3, LGI1, GRIN2A, GABRA1, GABRG2, and CHRNA4, with pathogenic variants altering sodium, potassium, GABAergic, glutamatergic, cholinergic, or mTOR-related signaling. Key pathways involve excitation-inhibition imbalance, voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channel dysfunction, impaired GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition, NMDA/AMPA receptor hyperexcitability, synaptic vesicle release, neuroinflammation, and mTOR pathway activation, particularly in focal cortical dysplasia. Common subtypes include temporal, frontal, parietal, and occipital lobe epilepsy, mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis, sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy, and familial focal epilepsies; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or de novo depending on the gene, with examples including autosomal dominant CHRNA4- or LGI1-related focal epilepsy and DEPDC5-related familial focal epilepsy with variable foci. Treatment commonly uses antiseizure drugs such as carbamazepine or lamotrigine, which inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels, levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to modulate neurotransmitter release, and lacosamide, which enhances slow sodium-channel inactivation; valproate, topiramate, and oxcarbazepine are also used. Comorbidities and complications include depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, sleep disorders, injury, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Diagnosis requires history and witness description, focal epileptiform discharges or seizures on EEG or video-EEG

Name: Primary motor cortex frontal lobe epilepsy
Description: Primary motor cortex frontal lobe epilepsy is a focal epilepsy arising from the precentral gyrus and adjacent mesial or lateral frontal motor networks, characterized by brief, often nocturnal, stereotyped motor seizures with tonic posturing, clonic jerks, fencing or asymmetric tonic movements, speech arrest, vocalization, preserved awareness in some attacks, rapid secondary generalization, and postictal weakness or confusion. It is best viewed as a localization-related syndrome rather than a single molecular disease, but genetic contributions overlap with familial frontal lobe epilepsies, including pathogenic variants in CHRNA4, CHRNB2, and CHRNA2 encoding neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits, DEPDC5, NPRL2, and NPRL3 in the GATOR1 complex regulating mTOR signaling, and less commonly KCNT1, SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, GRIN2A, LGI1, and focal cortical dysplasia–associated somatic MTOR pathway mutations; implicated pathways include altered cholinergic neurotransmission, voltage-gated sodium and potassium channel excitability, glutamatergic NMDA signaling, GABAergic inhibitory failure, and mTOR-mediated cortical development and neuronal network hyperexcitability. Common comorbidities and complications include sleep disruption, cognitive or executive dysfunction, mood and anxiety disorders, injuries, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Subtypes include sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy, supplementary sensorimotor area epilepsy, and seizures due to focal cortical dysplasia, tumors, vascular malformations, trauma, or gliosis. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance in familial forms, whereas many cases are sporadic or structural. Diagnosis relies on seizure semiology, neurological examination, scalp EEG often with frontal or vertex interictal spikes but sometimes nondiagnostic, prolonged video-EEG, high-resolution epilepsy-protocol MRI, and when needed PET, SPECT, MEG, invasive stereo-EEG, and targeted genetic testing. Treatment commonly includes carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, which block voltage-gated sodium channels, lamotrigine, which inhibits sodium channels and glutamate release, levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to reduce synaptic vesicle neurotransmitter release, and lacosamide, which enhances slow sodium-channel inactivation; drug-resistant cases may require resective surgery or neuromodulation.

Name: Respiratory Depression
Description: Respiratory insufficiency is a clinical syndrome in which the respiratory system fails to maintain adequate oxygenation and/or carbon dioxide elimination, producing hypoxemic (type I), hypercapnic (type II), or mixed acute or chronic respiratory failure due to pulmonary, airway, neuromuscular, chest wall, or central ventilatory control disorders. Genetic contributors are usually disease-specific rather than primary to the syndrome itself and include CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis, SERPINA1 variants causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency emphysema, SFTPB, SFTPC, ABCA3, and NKX2-1 defects in surfactant dysfunction, PHOX2B mutations in congenital central hypoventilation, and SMN1 or DMD abnormalities in neuromuscular weakness; implicated proteins include surfactant proteins, alpha-1 antitrypsin, dystrophin, ion channels, and inflammatory mediators. Key pathways include alveolar-capillary gas exchange failure, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, intrapulmonary shunt, reduced respiratory drive, respiratory muscle fatigue, and inflammatory signaling involving TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, NF-kappaB, neutrophils, oxidative stress, hypoxia-inducible factor, and sometimes TGF-beta-driven remodeling. Common symptoms and signs are dyspnea, tachypnea, cyanosis, accessory muscle use, altered mental status, somnolence, headache, asterixis, and severe hypoxemia or hypercapnic acidosis on arterial blood gas testing. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment plus pulse oximetry, arterial blood gases, chest radiography or CT, spirometry and lung volumes when stable, and etiologic testing such as polysomnography, respiratory muscle testing, cultures, echocardiography, or genetic testing in suspected inherited disorders. Treatment is cause-directed and often includes oxygen to raise alveolar oxygen tension, bronchodilators such as albuterol, a beta2-agonist that relaxes airway smooth muscle, ipratropium, a muscarinic antagonist that reduces bronchoconstriction, and corticosteroids such as prednisone or methylprednisolone that suppress airway and parenchymal inflammation; antibiotics, diuretics, and noninvasive or invasive ventilation are also common. Frequent comorbidities and complications include COPD, asthma, pneumonia, ARDS, obesity hypoventilation, sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension,

Name: Cycloplegia
Description: Cycloplegia is the paralysis of the ciliary muscle causing loss of accommodation, most often acquired and pharmacologically induced rather than a primary monogenic disease, although congenital forms can occur with developmental or autonomic disorders. It reflects disruption of parasympathetic cholinergic signaling from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus through the ciliary ganglion to the sphincter and ciliary muscle, with key molecular components including acetylcholine, muscarinic M3 receptors, Gq/PLC/IP3-calcium signaling, and, less commonly, sympathetic or neuromuscular dysfunction; representative genetic associations are indirect and include PHOX2A/PHOX2B and other genes implicated in congenital cranial dysinnervation or autonomic neuropathy, while diabetic neuropathy and autoimmune ganglionopathy may produce secondary cycloplegia without Mendelian inheritance. Clinically, patients present with blurred near vision, loss of accommodation, photophobia, dilated or poorly reactive pupils when mydriasis coexists, asthenopia, and sometimes headache; subtypes include pharmacologic, traumatic, neuropathic, inflammatory, and congenital cycloplegia. Commonly used cycloplegic drugs are atropine, a long-acting nonselective muscarinic antagonist; cyclopentolate, an intermediate-acting antimuscarinic used for refraction and uveitis; and tropicamide, a shorter-acting antimuscarinic; homatropine and scopolamine are additional examples. These agents inhibit acetylcholine binding at muscarinic receptors in the iris sphincter and ciliary body, producing both mydriasis and accommodation paralysis. Important comorbidities and complications include anterior uveitis, Adie tonic pupil, third-nerve palsy, diabetes mellitus, orbital or ocular trauma, glaucoma risk from angle closure after mydriasis, and functional visual impairment. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on reduced accommodative amplitude and pupillary findings, supported by refraction before and after cycloplegia, slit-lamp and neurologic examination, pupillary pharmacologic testing, and targeted evaluation for underlying ocular inflammation, neuropathy, brainstem or cranial nerve lesions, or inherited autonomic syndromes.

Name: Red eye
Description: Red eye is a clinical sign rather than a single inherited disease, reflecting conjunctival, episcleral, scleral, corneal, uveal, or angle pathology caused by infection, allergy, inflammation, trauma, dryness, or acute glaucoma; common subtypes include conjunctivitis, keratitis, blepharoconjunctivitis, episcleritis, scleritis, anterior uveitis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and acute angle-closure glaucoma. Symptoms and signs typically include conjunctival injection, tearing, discharge, foreign-body sensation, pruritus, pain, photophobia, blurred vision, ciliary flush, corneal staining, elevated intraocular pressure, and sometimes hypopyon. Molecular mechanisms vary by cause but commonly involve innate and adaptive immune pathways, including TLR signaling, NF-κB activation, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, histamine-H1 receptor signaling, complement, matrix metalloproteinases, and VEGF-mediated vascular permeability; representative genetic associations are usually indirect through underlying disorders, such as HLA-B27 in acute anterior uveitis, HLA-DR and cytokine polymorphisms in allergic eye disease, NOD2 in Blau syndrome uveitis, and autoimmune susceptibility genes relevant to scleritis. Treatment depends on etiology: lubricating tears reduce tear-film hyperosmolarity and surface friction, topical antihistamines/mast-cell stabilizers such as olopatadine block H1 signaling and mast-cell degranulation, topical antibiotics such as erythromycin or fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial protein synthesis or DNA gyrase, corticosteroids such as prednisolone acetate suppress phospholipase A2 and NF-κB-driven inflammation, cycloplegics such as cyclopentolate relieve ciliary spasm, and antiglaucoma agents including timolol, acetazolamide, and latanoprost lower intraocular pressure via reduced aqueous production or increased uveoscleral outflow. Important comorbidities include atopy, dry eye, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis, herpes infection, and rosacea; complications include corneal ulceration, scarring, synechiae, cataract, glaucoma, scleral thinning, and permanent vision loss. Name: Atrial Fibrillation, Paroxysmal
Description: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, characterized by disorganized atrial electrical activity and ineffective atrial contraction, presenting as paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing persistent, or permanent disease and clinically causing palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse, dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, dizziness, chest discomfort, or sometimes no symptoms. It arises through electrical and structural atrial remodeling involving ion-channel dysfunction, abnormal calcium handling, fibrosis, inflammation, autonomic imbalance, and reentry/ectopic firing, especially from the pulmonary veins; implicated pathways include TGF-β/SMAD and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling promoting fibrosis, CaMKII- and calcium-handling networks involving RYR2 and ATP2A2/SERCA2a, and gap-junction and sodium/potassium channel components such as GJA5, SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNE2, and KCNA5. Genetic susceptibility is often complex and polygenic, but familial and monogenic forms occur, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance and variable penetrance; representative variants involve TTN, MYH7, LMNA, NPPA, PITX2, PRRX1, ZFHX3, SCN5A, KCNQ1, and GJA5, while RYR2 mutations may link atrial arrhythmia with catecholaminergic phenotypes. Major comorbidities and risk factors include hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, hyperthyroidism, chronic kidney disease, alcohol use, and aging; major complications are thromboembolic stroke, systemic embolism, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, heart failure exacerbation, and cognitive decline. Diagnosis is established by ECG showing absent discrete P waves and irregularly irregular RR intervals, supported by ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography, thyroid and electrolyte testing, and stroke-risk assessment. Treatment commonly includes rate control with beta-blockers such as metoprolol, nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as diltiazem, or digoxin via AV nodal slowing; rhythm control with amiodarone, flecainide, or dofetilide through potassium or sodium channel effects; and anticoagulation with apixaban, rivaroxaban, or

Name: Zinc deficiency
Description: Zinc deficiency is a nutritional and sometimes inherited trace-element disorder characterized by inadequate zinc-dependent enzymatic and transcriptional activity, causing impaired growth, epithelial integrity, immunity, and reproduction; it occurs as primary hereditary zinc malabsorption, classically acrodermatitis enteropathica due to biallelic SLC39A4 (ZIP4) variants with autosomal recessive inheritance, or as acquired deficiency from poor intake, malabsorption, alcoholism, chronic diarrhea, inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery, chronic kidney or liver disease, prematurity, prolonged parenteral nutrition, or excess phytate intake. Zinc homeostasis involves intestinal uptake and tissue trafficking by ZIP and ZnT transporters, metallothioneins, and zinc-dependent proteins regulating alkaline phosphatase, carbonic anhydrase, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase, thymulin, matrix metalloproteinases, and zinc-finger transcription factors; perturbed signaling affects immune-cell maturation, NF-kB, oxidative stress responses, wound healing, and epithelial barrier function. Typical findings include periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea, glossitis, angular cheilitis, impaired wound healing, dysgeusia, anorexia, growth retardation, delayed puberty, hypogonadism, recurrent infections, and in severe cases neurobehavioral changes. Important complications and comorbidities include protein-calorie malnutrition, anemia, secondary vitamin deficiencies, increased susceptibility to bacterial and fungal infections, poor pregnancy outcomes, and stunting. Treatment is zinc replacement, most commonly oral zinc sulfate, zinc gluconate, or zinc acetate, which dissociate to provide absorbable elemental zinc and restore zinc-dependent enzyme and signaling function; refractory or severe cases may require parenteral zinc. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical features and risk factors, low plasma or serum zinc, often low alkaline phosphatase, response to supplementation, and when hereditary disease is suspected, molecular testing of SLC39A4 and related zinc transporter genes; differential diagnosis includes biotin deficiency, essential fatty acid deficiency, and other causes of malabsorptive dermatitis.

Name: Alcohol withdrawal
Description: Alcohol withdrawal (UMLS C0236663) is an acute neuropsychiatric and autonomic hyperexcitability syndrome that occurs after reduction or cessation of prolonged heavy ethanol exposure, reflecting loss of ethanol’s chronic enhancement of GABAergic inhibition and suppression of glutamatergic excitation, with compensatory upregulation of NMDA/AMPA signaling, altered dopaminergic, noradrenergic, corticotropin-releasing factor, voltage-gated calcium-channel, and neurosteroid pathways; representative genetic contributors to vulnerability and severity, though not Mendelian or classically inherited, include variants in GABRA2 and other GABAA receptor genes, GRIN2A/GRIN2B, SLC6A4, DRD2, OPRM1, CRHR1, KCNJ6, CACNA1C, and alcohol-metabolizing genes ADH1B and ALDH2, with familial aggregation reflecting polygenic risk shared with alcohol use disorder. Clinically it ranges from uncomplicated withdrawal to alcoholic hallucinosis, withdrawal seizures, and delirium tremens, typically beginning within hours to days with tremor, anxiety, insomnia, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea, agitation, perceptual disturbance, fever, and, in severe cases, confusion and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Major comorbidities include alcohol use disorder, liver disease, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, electrolyte disturbances, malnutrition and thiamine deficiency, depression, anxiety, trauma, and infection; complications include arrhythmia, aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, status epilepticus, Wernicke encephalopathy, and death. Diagnosis is clinical, based on recent alcohol cessation in a dependent patient plus characteristic symptoms and signs, often quantified with CIWA-Ar or similar scales, while testing includes blood alcohol level, CBC, CMP with magnesium and phosphate, liver tests, glucose, toxicology, ECG, and targeted imaging or EEG when alternate causes of delirium or seizure are suspected. Treatment centers on benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam, and chlordiazepoxide, which are positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors; adjuncts may include phenobarbital, gabapentin, clonidine or dexmedetomidine for autonomic symptoms, and thiamine before glucose.

Name: Bipolar I disorder, most recent episode mixed
Description: Bipolar I disorder, most recent episode mixed, is a severe episodic mood disorder characterized by the coexistence or rapid alternation of manic and major depressive symptoms, producing marked functional impairment and high suicide risk; patients typically show elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, increased goal-directed activity, impulsivity, agitation, distractibility, alongside dysphoria, anhedonia, guilt, hopelessness, and sometimes psychosis. It is genetically complex and highly heritable, with risk influenced by polygenic variation in genes such as CACNA1C, ANK3, ODZ4/TENM4, TRANK1, and circadian genes including CLOCK and ARNTL, while BDNF, SLC6A4, COMT, and GSK3B are commonly implicated candidate genes rather than deterministic mutations; no simple Mendelian inheritance is typical, but familial aggregation is strong. Relevant biology involves calcium signaling, synaptic plasticity, monoaminergic neurotransmission, glutamatergic and GABAergic balance, circadian rhythm regulation, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial function, and intracellular cascades including GSK-3, PKC, cAMP-CREB, and BDNF-TrkB pathways. Standard treatment includes lithium, which modulates inositol signaling and inhibits GSK-3; valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and affects sodium channels and histone deacetylase activity; and atypical antipsychotics such as quetiapine, olanzapine, or risperidone, which primarily antagonize dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with lamotrigine or carbamazepine used in selected cases. Common comorbidities include anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, ADHD, migraine, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and thyroid dysfunction, while complications include relapse, psychosocial deterioration, treatment nonadherence, and suicide attempts. Subtypes include mixed episodes or mixed features specifiers across manic, hypomanic, or depressive episodes. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM criteria for bipolar I disorder with mixed features, supported by psychiatric interview, collateral history, rating scales, toxicology and laboratory testing to exclude substance-induced or medical causes, and assessment for psychosis and safety.

Name: Neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism
Description: Neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism (UMLS C0236830) is a secondary, usually reversible drug-induced movement disorder caused predominantly by dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway after exposure to antipsychotics and other dopamine-blocking agents; it typically presents with symmetric bradykinesia, rigidity, masked facies, hypophonia, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait, postural instability, and often tremor, usually emerging days to months after treatment initiation or dose escalation. The core pathobiology involves impaired basal ganglia signaling with reduced dopaminergic transmission, relative cholinergic overactivity, altered G protein-coupled D2 signaling, and downstream dysfunction in striatal medium spiny neurons, with implicated pathways including dopamine, acetylcholine, adenosine, glutamate, and oxidative stress/mitochondrial mechanisms. Although not a Mendelian disease, susceptibility is partly genetic, with reported associations involving DRD2, SLC6A3/DAT1, COMT, CYP2D6, RGS2, and parkinsonism genes such as SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN, and PINK1 as potential modifiers in some patients; inheritance is therefore generally non-Mendelian, polygenic, and pharmacogenetic rather than familial. Typical subtypes include acute versus persistent forms and tremor-dominant versus akinetic-rigid phenotypes, and an important distinction is unmasking of prodromal Parkinson disease. Commonly implicated treatments causing the syndrome include haloperidol, fluphenazine, risperidone, metoclopramide, and prochlorperazine, whereas management relies on dose reduction or withdrawal, switching to lower-risk agents such as quetiapine or clozapine, and symptomatic therapy with benztropine or trihexyphenidyl, which are central muscarinic antagonists, and amantadine, which enhances dopaminergic tone and weakly antagonizes NMDA receptors. Comorbidities and complications include schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, dementia, depression, falls, aspiration risk, functional decline, and tardive syndromes. Diagnosis is clinical, based on temporal association with dopamine-blocking drugs, parkinsonian examination findings, exclusion of idiopathic Parkinson disease, and, when needed, ancillary testing such as DAT-SPECT, which is typically normal in pure drug-induced cases.

Name: Poisoning caused by acetaminophen
Description: Poisoning caused by acetaminophen (UMLS C0237963) is an acute, dose-dependent toxic ingestion and a leading cause of drug-induced liver injury, classically resulting from single massive overdose or repeated supratherapeutic exposure; its major subtypes are acute, chronic/repeated-dose, and combination-product toxicity, with severity modified by age, fasting, alcohol use, and pre-existing liver disease. Toxicity reflects cytochrome P450 bioactivation, especially CYP2E1 with contributions from CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, generating the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which depletes glutathione and forms protein adducts, provoking mitochondrial oxidative stress, JNK/MAPK signaling, permeability transition, ATP depletion, centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis, and in some cases renal tubular injury; relevant genes/proteins include CYP2E1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4, UGT1A1/UGT1A6, SULT1A1, GSTs, NFE2L2/NRF2, and HLA-independent stress response mediators, although no Mendelian inheritance pattern is established and genetic susceptibility is typically polygenic, with representative variants reported in CYP, UGT, SULT, GST, and NRF2-related pathways. Patients often present within hours with nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, pallor, and abdominal pain, later developing right upper quadrant tenderness, marked AST/ALT elevation, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, jaundice, and possible acute liver failure. Important complications and comorbidities include alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, sepsis, chronic hepatic disease, acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, cerebral edema, and multiorgan failure. Diagnosis relies on exposure history, timed serum acetaminophen concentration interpreted by the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for acute ingestion, serial liver chemistries, INR, bilirubin, creatinine, blood gas/lactate, and occasionally acetaminophen-protein adduct assays. Treatment centers on N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione and improves mitochondrial redox balance; activated charcoal, which reduces gastrointestinal absorption when given early; fomepizole, which inhibits CYP2E1 and may limit NAPQI formation in massive overdose; and in selected severe cases hemodial

Name: Xanthomatosis, Cerebrotendinous
Description: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX; UMLS C0238052) is a rare autosomal recessive lipid-storage and bile-acid synthesis disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CYP27A1, which encodes the mitochondrial sterol 27-hydroxylase CYP27A1; representative mutations include missense, nonsense, splice-site, and frameshift alleles that reduce or abolish enzyme activity. The resulting defect in the acidic pathway of bile acid synthesis lowers chenodeoxycholic acid, disrupts feedback regulation of cholesterol 7alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7A1), and drives excess production and tissue deposition of cholestanol and abnormal bile alcohols in the brain, lenses, tendons, and other tissues, with neurodegeneration, mitochondrial dysfunction, macrophage foam-cell accumulation, and sterol trafficking abnormalities as key cellular features. CTX classically presents from childhood to adulthood with chronic diarrhea, juvenile cataracts, tendon xanthomas, progressive pyramidal and cerebellar signs, ataxia, spastic paraparesis, peripheral neuropathy, epilepsy, psychiatric or cognitive decline, parkinsonism, and premature osteoporosis; important complications and comorbidities include dementia, fractures, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, respiratory impairment, and severe disability. Phenotypic subtypes are often described as classic tendon-xanthoma/neuropsychiatric CTX and spinal or non-xanthomatous variants. Diagnosis relies on a compatible phenotype plus elevated plasma cholestanol, increased urinary bile alcohols, characteristic brain MRI abnormalities such as dentate nucleus or white-matter involvement, tendon imaging when indicated, and confirmatory CYP27A1 molecular testing; enzyme-based fibroblast studies may support ambiguous cases, and prenatal or family cascade testing is possible. Standard therapy is chenodeoxycholic acid, which restores feedback inhibition and suppresses cholestanol formation; cholic acid may also replace deficient bile acids, HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors such as simvastatin, pravastatin, or atorvastatin reduce cholesterol substrate flux, and symptomatic agents including antiepileptics or antiparkinsonian drugs are used adjunctively.

Name: Cyanide poisoning
Description: Cyanide poisoning (UMLS C0238080) is an acute toxicologic emergency rather than a primary inherited disease, caused by exposure to hydrogen cyanide gas or cyanide salts that rapidly bind the ferric iron of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV, encoded in part by mitochondrial and nuclear genes including MT-CO1, MT-CO2, MT-CO3 and assembly-related factors such as SCO1/SCO2), abruptly blocking oxidative phosphorylation, collapsing the electron transport chain, forcing anaerobic glycolysis, and producing histotoxic hypoxia with severe lactic acidosis; sulfur detoxification via mitochondrial thiosulfate sulfurtransferase/rhodanese (TST) and related sulfurtransferases is an important endogenous protective pathway. Clinically, patients develop headache, agitation, confusion, dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, hypotension, arrhythmias, coma, cardiovascular collapse, and sometimes bright red venous blood or soot exposure in smoke inhalation victims. Major forms include inhalational, ingestion-related, occupational/industrial, iatrogenic, and smoke-inhalation-associated poisoning, occurring as acute fulminant or less commonly chronic low-level exposure. Treatment centers on antidotes such as hydroxocobalamin, which chelates cyanide to form renally excreted cyanocobalamin; sodium thiosulfate, a sulfur donor that enhances rhodanese-mediated conversion of cyanide to thiocyanate; and nitrites such as sodium nitrite or amyl nitrite, which induce methemoglobin to sequester cyanide, though they may worsen hypoxemia; supportive oxygenation and source control are essential. Complications include profound metabolic acidosis, myocardial ischemia, aspiration, anoxic brain injury, Parkinsonian sequelae, and death, with common comorbid contexts including smoke inhalation, carbon monoxide poisoning, burns, renal impairment, and malnutrition. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for poisoning itself, but genetic variation affecting detoxification or mitochondrial vulnerability may modify susceptibility. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by exposure history, elevated lactate often greater than 8–10 mmol/L, high anion gap acidosis, venous hyperoxia, co-oximetry, and direct blood cyanide measurement when available, without delaying empiric therapy.

Name: Lennox Gastaut Syndrome
Description: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (MeSH D065768) is a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy of childhood characterized by multiple drug-resistant generalized seizure types, especially tonic seizures during sleep, atonic drop attacks, and atypical absences, with intellectual disability, behavioral disturbance, developmental regression or plateau, and a characteristic EEG showing slow spike-and-wave discharges around 1.5–2.5 Hz and paroxysmal fast activity in sleep. It is etiologically heterogeneous, arising from structural, metabolic, infectious, immune, and genetic causes; genetic contributors include de novo or inherited variants in SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, GABRB3, GABRA1, STXBP1, CHD2, DNM1, HNRNPU, SLC6A1, KCNT1, and mTOR-pathway genes such as DEPDC5, TSC1, and TSC2, implicating sodium-channel excitability, GABAergic inhibition, synaptic vesicle release, and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. Most cases are sporadic, though autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance, X-linked causes, and mosaicism are recognized depending on the gene. Common comorbidities include autism spectrum features, cerebral palsy, sleep disturbance, dysphagia, injury from falls, status epilepticus, and increased mortality including SUDEP. Treatment is usually symptomatic and polypharmacologic: valproate enhances GABAergic tone and reduces repetitive neuronal firing; lamotrigine inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and glutamate release; clobazam is a GABAA receptor positive allosteric modulator; rufinamide prolongs sodium-channel inactivation; topiramate blocks sodium channels, enhances GABA, and inhibits AMPA/kainate signaling; cannabidiol modulates endocannabinoid and other neuronal signaling; and felbamate inhibits NMDA receptors and potentiates GABAA receptors, with ketogenic diet, vagus nerve stimulation, or corpus callosotomy used in refractory drop attacks. Diagnosis is clinical-electrographic, supported by prolonged video-EEG, brain MRI, chromosomal microarray, epilepsy gene panels or exome sequencing, and selected metabolic tests; recognized forms include cryptogenic/unknown, symptomatic, and evolution from infantile epileptic spasms syndrome/West syndrome.

Name: Fallopian Tube Cancer
Description: Fallopian tube cancer is a rare, usually high-grade serous epithelial gynecologic malignancy now understood to overlap biologically with ovarian and primary peritoneal carcinoma, with many cases arising from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in the fimbria; less common subtypes include endometrioid, clear cell, mucinous, and transitional cell tumors, while nonepithelial forms such as carcinosarcoma are rare. It is commonly driven by TP53 mutation and homologous recombination deficiency, particularly germline or somatic BRCA1 and BRCA2 alterations, with additional abnormalities reported in PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, RB1, CCNE1, and mismatch repair genes in selected cases; implicated pathways include DNA damage repair/BRCA-PARP signaling, p53-cell cycle control, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, and angiogenic VEGF signaling. Most cases are sporadic, but hereditary predisposition is important, especially autosomal dominant hereditary breast-ovarian cancer due to BRCA1/2 and, less commonly, Lynch syndrome. Patients typically present with pelvic or abdominal pain, bloating, adnexal mass, abnormal vaginal bleeding or watery discharge, ascites, and occasionally the Latzko triad of pain, discharge, and a pelvic mass; complications include peritoneal carcinomatosis, bowel or ureteral obstruction, pleural effusion, venous thromboembolism, cachexia, and recurrence, and comorbid links include breast and ovarian cancer in hereditary syndromes. Diagnosis relies on pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasonography, CT or MRI for staging, CA-125 measurement, and definitive histopathology with FIGO staging after surgical exploration, supported by immunophenotyping such as WT1 and p53 and by germline/somatic testing for BRCA and other homologous recombination genes to guide therapy. Standard treatment uses cytoreductive surgery plus platinum-taxane chemotherapy, notably carboplatin, which forms DNA crosslinks, cisplatin with similar platinum-mediated cytotoxicity, and paclitaxel, a microtubule-stabilizing mitotic inhibitor; selected patients also receive bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody, or PARP inhibitors such as olaparib for BRCA-mutated or homologous recombination-deficient disease.

Name: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors
Description: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) are the most common mesenchymal neoplasms of the gastrointestinal tract, arising from or differentiating toward interstitial cells of Cajal, and range from indolent to highly malignant; they occur most often in the stomach and small intestine and are classified by site, spindle-cell, epithelioid, or mixed histology, and by molecular subtype. Most are driven by activating mutations in KIT, especially exon 11 and less often exons 9, 13, or 17, or in PDGFRA, particularly exon 18 including D842V; a minority are KIT/PDGFRA wild type and may show SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, or SDHD deficiency, NF1-associated alterations, BRAF V600E, or rare NTRK fusions. These lesions signal predominantly through constitutive KIT/PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinase activation with downstream PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, and JAK/STAT pathways. Clinical manifestations include occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, abdominal pain, early satiety, palpable mass, bowel obstruction, perforation, or incidental discovery, while metastases most often involve liver and peritoneum. Important associated syndromic settings include neurofibromatosis type 1, Carney-Stratakis syndrome with germline SDH mutations, and the nonhereditary Carney triad, with comorbid iron-deficiency anemia and complications such as rupture and recurrence. Treatment centers on tyrosine kinase inhibition: imatinib inhibits KIT, PDGFRA, and ABL and is standard in unresectable, metastatic, and adjuvant settings; sunitinib inhibits KIT, PDGFR, and VEGFR after imatinib resistance; regorafenib and ripretinib inhibit multiple KIT/PDGFRA resistance mutants; avapritinib is particularly active against PDGFRA D842V. Diagnosis relies on imaging and tissue biopsy with morphology plus immunohistochemistry, typically KIT (CD117) and DOG1 positive, molecular genotyping for predictive and prognostic stratification, and risk assessment based on tumor size, mitotic rate, and anatomic site.

Name: Myxedema coma
Description: Myxedema coma (UMLS C0238298) is a rare, life-threatening decompensation of severe hypothyroidism characterized by metabolic failure, impaired thermogenesis, and central nervous system depression, usually representing the extreme end of primary thyroid hormone deficiency rather than a distinct inherited disorder. Molecularly, it reflects deficient thyroid hormone synthesis, secretion, or action involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and thyroid hormone receptor signaling, with reduced T4/T3-dependent transcription through nuclear receptors THRA and THRB, diminished TSH receptor pathway activity, and downstream effects on mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, adrenergic responsiveness, sodium-water handling, and ventilatory drive; representative genetic causes of severe hypothyroidism that can predispose to this state include TSHR, TPO, TG, SLC5A5/NIS, DUOX2, IYD, PAX8, NKX2-1, FOXE1, THRB, and autoimmune susceptibility genes such as HLA-DR variants and CTLA4 in Hashimoto thyroiditis. It is most often triggered in older adults with long-standing hypothyroidism by infection, cold exposure, stroke, myocardial infarction, trauma, surgery, sedatives, opioids, lithium, amiodarone, or medication nonadherence. Typical findings include altered mental status progressing to stupor or coma, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, dry coarse skin, nonpitting edema, macroglossia, delayed reflex relaxation, and ileus. Major comorbidities and complications include sepsis, pneumonia, heart failure, pericardial effusion, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and adrenal insufficiency. Diagnosis is clinical and biochemical, supported by severe hypothyroidism with elevated TSH and low free T4 in primary disease or low/normal TSH with low free T4 in central hypothyroidism, plus characteristic labs, ECG, arterial blood gases, cortisol testing, and evaluation for precipitating illness; scoring systems may aid recognition. Treatment relies on intravenous levothyroxine, often with liothyronine for faster T3 replacement, empiric hydrocortisone to cover possible adrenal insufficiency, and comprehensive supportive care.

Name: Thyroid cancer, medullary
Description: Medullary thyroid cancer is a malignant neuroendocrine tumor arising from parafollicular C cells of the thyroid and characterized by calcitonin production; it occurs as sporadic disease or hereditary disease, most notably multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A, MEN2B, and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma, usually driven by activating RET proto-oncogene mutations such as M918T, C634R, or other cysteine substitutions, while a subset of RET-negative tumors harbor RAS mutations, especially HRAS or KRAS. Its biology is dominated by constitutive RET signaling through MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, with downstream effects on cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and neuroendocrine differentiation; relevant proteins include RET, RAS, ERK, AKT, mTOR, VEGFR, and calcitonin. Clinically, patients may present with a thyroid nodule, cervical lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, hoarseness, flushing, or secretory diarrhea, and advanced disease commonly metastasizes to cervical nodes, liver, lung, and bone. Important associated conditions include pheochromocytoma and primary hyperparathyroidism in MEN2, and complications include airway or esophageal compression, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, persistent calcitonin elevation, and distant metastatic progression. Diagnosis relies on neck ultrasonography, fine-needle aspiration with cytology and calcitonin immunostaining when needed, markedly elevated serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen, germline RET testing in all patients, and staging with cross-sectional or functional imaging for suspected metastatic disease. Histologic subtypes include sporadic and hereditary forms, often with amyloid-rich stroma. Standard treatment is total thyroidectomy with appropriate nodal dissection for localized disease; for advanced or progressive disease, vandetanib, a RET/VEGFR/EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, cabozantinib, a RET/MET/VEGFR2 inhibitor, and highly selective RET inhibitors such as selpercatinib or pralsetinib are commonly used, while external-beam radiotherapy and supportive management of hormone-mediated symptoms may also be required.

Name: Thyroid Cancer, Papillary
Description: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common differentiated thyroid malignancy, arising from follicular epithelial cells and typically exhibiting indolent behavior but a marked propensity for cervical lymphatic spread; classic, follicular variant, tall-cell, diffuse sclerosing, columnar-cell, and hobnail subtypes are recognized, with tall-cell and hobnail forms generally more aggressive. Its molecular pathogenesis is dominated by MAPK pathway activation through BRAF mutations, especially BRAF V600E, RAS mutations, and RET/PTC or NTRK fusions, with less frequent TERT promoter, TP53, PIK3CA, and EIF1AX alterations in advanced disease; key signaling networks include MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, and dysregulated iodine-handling programs involving NIS. Most cases are sporadic, but susceptibility may be inherited in familial nonmedullary thyroid cancer and tumor-predisposition syndromes such as PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis with APC variants, DICER1 syndrome, and Carney complex. Patients commonly present with an asymptomatic thyroid nodule, cervical lymphadenopathy, or incidentally detected lesion, while hoarseness, dysphagia, neck discomfort, extrathyroidal extension, pulmonary or osseous metastases, and postoperative or treatment-related hypoparathyroidism may complicate disease; associations include Hashimoto thyroiditis, multinodular goiter, and prior ionizing radiation exposure. Diagnosis relies on neck ultrasonography, fine-needle aspiration cytology interpreted by Bethesda criteria, histopathology showing papillary architecture and characteristic nuclear clearing, grooves, and pseudoinclusions, with immunohistochemistry and molecular testing for BRAF, RET, RAS, or NTRK aiding indeterminate cases; serum thyroglobulin is mainly used for surveillance. Treatment centers on surgery with selective radioactive iodine, while systemic therapy for recurrent, metastatic, or iodine-refractory disease includes levothyroxine for TSH suppression, sorafenib and lenvatinib, multikinase inhibitors targeting VEGFR and other kinases to inhibit tumor proliferation and angiogenesis, and mutation-directed agents such as selpercatinib for RET-altered tumors and larotrectinib for NTRK fusion-positive disease.

Name: Candidiasis of esophagus
Description: Candidiasis of the esophagus (UMLS C0239295) is an opportunistic fungal mucosal infection, usually caused by Candida albicans but also C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, and C. krusei, characterized by adherent white plaques and invasive inflammation of the esophageal squamous mucosa, most often in immunocompromised hosts. Pathobiology centers on fungal adhesion and hyphal invasion mediated by Candida genes and proteins such as ALS family adhesins, HWP1, SAP proteases, EFG1/CPH1-regulated filamentation programs, and ergosterol-biosynthetic enzymes including ERG11, while host susceptibility is influenced by impaired IL-17/Th17, CARD9, Dectin-1/CLEC7A-SYK, STAT3, AIRE, and HIV-related CD4 T-cell pathways; representative resistance mechanisms include ERG11 alteration or overexpression and efflux pumps CDR1/CDR2/MDR1, especially in azole-exposed isolates. Major signaling axes include fungal cAMP-PKA, MAPK, biofilm networks, and host innate recognition through Toll-like receptors and C-type lectin receptors driving neutrophil and epithelial antifungal responses. Typical symptoms are odynophagia, dysphagia, retrosternal pain, nausea, oral thrush, and occasionally bleeding or weight loss. Common settings and comorbidities include AIDS, hematologic malignancy, chemotherapy, corticosteroid use, transplant immunosuppression, diabetes mellitus, proton pump inhibitor exposure, and esophageal stasis or motility disorders; complications include ulceration, stricture, perforation, candidemia, and recurrent disease. Clinical subtypes include mild plaque-predominant disease, ulcerative or extensive disease, and infection due to azole-susceptible versus resistant non-albicans species. Most cases are acquired rather than inherited, but recurrent mucocutaneous candidiasis susceptibility may follow autosomal dominant STAT1 gain-of-function or STAT3 defects, autosomal recessive CARD9 or IL17RA/IL17RC pathway defects, and AIRE-related autoimmunity. Diagnosis is usually established by upper endoscopy showing characteristic plaques or ulcers with brushing/biopsy demonstrating budding yeast and pseudohyphae on PAS or GMS stains, with culture or susceptibility testing for refractory cases. Treatment commonly uses fluconazole, which inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-alpha

Name: Suprapubic pain
Description: Suprapubic pain is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease, usually reflecting pathology in pelvic structures centered on the bladder, distal ureters, uterus, adnexa, bowel, pelvic floor, or abdominal wall; common causes include acute cystitis, bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis, urinary retention, urolithiasis, prostatitis, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, irritable bowel disorders, and gynecologic or urologic malignancy. Clinically it presents as pressure, aching, cramping, or tenderness below the umbilicus, often accompanied by dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, hematuria, fever, pelvic fullness, pain with bladder filling relieved by voiding, dyspareunia, or bowel symptoms, with complications depending on cause such as recurrent UTI, hydronephrosis, sepsis, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and renal injury. Molecular associations are cause-specific rather than defining: recurrent UTI susceptibility has been linked to TLR4, CXCR1, IL6, and DEFB1; bladder pain syndrome has reported altered urothelial proteins and mediators including antiproliferative factor, nerve growth factor, mast-cell mediators, TNF, IL-6, TRPV1, P2X3, and epithelial barrier proteins such as uroplakins; endometriosis risk involves ESR1, PGR, WNT4, GREB1, and inflammatory and estrogen-signaling networks. Relevant pathways include innate immune TLR/NF-κB signaling, cytokine and chemokine cascades, mast-cell activation, neurogenic inflammation, sensory afferent signaling via TRPV1 and purinergic receptors, prostaglandin/COX pathways, estrogen signaling, and smooth-muscle contraction pathways. Treatment targets the underlying disorder and commonly includes nitrofurantoin, which damages bacterial ribosomal and DNA-related processes in lower UTI; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis; phenazopyridine, a urinary tract analgesic; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin production; antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin for bladder spasm via M3 blockade; and pentosan polysulfate, thought to restore the glycosaminoglycan bladder mucosal barrier in bladder pain syndrome. Name: Angiomyolipoma of kidney
Description: Renal angiomyolipoma is a usually benign mesenchymal perivascular epithelioid cell tumor composed of variable proportions of dysmorphic blood vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue, occurring as a sporadic lesion or in syndromic forms linked most classically to tuberous sclerosis complex and less often lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Its molecular basis most often involves inactivating alterations of TSC1 on 9q34 encoding hamartin or TSC2 on 16p13 encoding tuberin, with consequent disinhibition of RHEB and hyperactivation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling axis, promoting cell growth, angiogenesis, and abnormal melanocytic/smooth muscle differentiation; PEComa markers such as HMB45/gp100, Melan-A, smooth muscle actin, and often cathepsin K are typically expressed. Inheritance in syndromic disease is autosomal dominant for TSC1/TSC2, although many cases are de novo; sporadic tumors are generally non-inherited. Subtypes include classic triphasic angiomyolipoma, fat-poor or epithelioid angiomyolipoma, and multiple or bilateral lesions in TSC. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with flank pain, hematuria, palpable mass, anemia, hypertension, or life-threatening retroperitoneal hemorrhage from aneurysmal vessels, with chronic kidney disease possible after repeated bleeding or interventions. Important comorbidities include renal cysts, renal cell neoplasia, epilepsy, cortical tubers, skin angiofibromas, and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis in TSC-associated disease. Diagnosis is usually radiologic, with ultrasonography and especially CT or MRI demonstrating macroscopic fat; fat-poor and epithelioid lesions may require biopsy, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry, while TSC evaluation includes clinical criteria and germline TSC1/TSC2 testing. Management includes surveillance for small asymptomatic tumors, selective arterial embolization to control bleeding, nephron-sparing surgery when indicated, and mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus, sirolimus, and temsirolimus, which inhibit mTORC1 signaling and can shrink TSC-associated or unresectable lesions.

Name: Dyslipidemias
Description: Dyslipidemias are a heterogeneous group of metabolic disorders characterized by abnormal plasma concentrations or composition of lipoproteins, most commonly elevated LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and/or reduced HDL cholesterol, arising from polygenic susceptibility, secondary causes, or monogenic defects. Key genetic contributors include LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, LDLRAP1, APOE, LPL, APOC2, APOA5, GPIHBP1, ABCA1, CETP, and LCAT; representative mutations cause familial hypercholesterolemia, familial combined hyperlipidemia, dysbetalipoproteinemia, chylomicronemia, Tangier disease, and hypoalphalipoproteinemia, with autosomal dominant inheritance typical for LDLR/APOB/PCSK9-related familial hypercholesterolemia, autosomal recessive inheritance for LDLRAP1 deficiency, and complex polygenic inheritance common overall. Pathobiology centers on hepatic LDL receptor trafficking and clearance, apoB-containing lipoprotein production, lipoprotein lipase-mediated triglyceride hydrolysis, reverse cholesterol transport via ABCA1 and HDL, cholesterol ester transfer protein activity, and regulatory pathways involving SREBP, HMG-CoA reductase, PPAR-alpha, ANGPTL3, and bile acid signaling. Clinical manifestations may be absent until complications occur, but can include xanthomas, xanthelasma, corneal arcus, lipemia retinalis, hepatosplenomegaly, or recurrent abdominal pain and pancreatitis in severe hypertriglyceridemia. Major comorbidities and complications include premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral arterial disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, insulin resistance, diabetes, obesity, and acute pancreatitis. Diagnosis relies on fasting or nonfasting lipid profile, apolipoprotein B, lipoprotein(a), exclusion of secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, alcohol use, and medications, with genetic testing used selectively for familial syndromes and risk stratification aided by family history and physical findings. Name: Erectile Dysfunction
Description: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is a common, multifactorial disorder defined by the persistent inability to attain or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual activity, and it is broadly classified as vasculogenic, neurogenic, endocrinologic, psychogenic, medication-induced, structural/anatomic, or mixed. Clinically, patients report reduced penile rigidity, shortened erection duration, decreased nocturnal or morning erections, and impaired sexual performance, sometimes with decreased libido or ejaculatory symptoms depending on the cause. Its molecular basis centers on endothelial and cavernosal smooth-muscle signaling, especially the nitric oxide (NO)-soluble guanylate cyclase-cGMP-protein kinase G pathway, with contributions from PDE5-mediated cGMP degradation, RhoA/ROCK contractile signaling, autonomic cholinergic and adrenergic pathways, testosterone-androgen receptor signaling, and endothelial factors such as eNOS/NOS3, nNOS/NOS1, VEGF, TGF-β, and oxidative stress pathways; representative genetic associations include NOS3, NOS1, PDE5A, AR, ACE, VEGFA, and variants linked to diabetes, vascular disease, or hypogonadism, although most ED is complex rather than Mendelian. Inherited contributors may therefore be polygenic and familial rather than following a single clear inheritance pattern. Major comorbidities include atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obesity, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, depression, obstructive sleep apnea, Peyronie disease, hypogonadism, and neurologic disease, and ED may precede overt coronary disease as a marker of systemic endothelial dysfunction; complications include relationship distress, reduced quality of life, anxiety, and infertility in some contexts. Diagnosis is clinical, requiring symptom persistence for at least several months, with history, medication review, focused cardiovascular, neurologic and genitourinary examination, validated questionnaires such as the IIEF, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, testosterone and other endocrine tests when indicated, and selected studies including nocturnal penile tumescence testing, penile duplex Doppler ultrasonography after vasoactive injection, or specialized neurophysiologic evaluation. Name: Lung Cancer
Description: Lung neoplasms are predominantly malignant epithelial tumors of the lung, broadly divided into non-small cell lung cancer (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma) and small cell lung cancer, with less common neuroendocrine and mesenchymal subtypes; they arise through accumulated somatic alterations, most often smoking-related, although inherited susceptibility contributes in a minority of cases. Key molecular drivers include TP53 and RB1 loss, KRAS mutations, EGFR activating mutations, ALK, ROS1, and RET rearrangements, BRAF V600E, MET exon 14 skipping, ERBB2 alterations, and amplifications involving MYC or FGFR1, with proteins such as PD-L1, VEGF, and EGFR central to tumor behavior. Major dysregulated pathways include RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, p53 and RB cell-cycle control, apoptosis, angiogenesis, and immune-checkpoint pathways involving PD-1/PD-L1. Common symptoms are persistent cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, fatigue, recurrent pneumonia, and signs of metastatic or paraneoplastic disease such as bone pain, neurologic deficits, SIADH, or hypercalcemia. Important comorbidities include COPD, interstitial lung disease, cardiovascular disease, smoking-related illness, thromboembolism, cachexia, and metastatic complications to brain, bone, liver, or adrenal glands. Diagnosis relies on imaging with chest CT and often PET-CT, tissue confirmation by bronchoscopy, needle biopsy, or surgical sampling, histopathology with immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing by PCR or next-generation sequencing for actionable alterations; staging uses TNM for most cases and limited versus extensive classification for small cell disease. Treatment includes surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy such as cisplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum agent, paclitaxel, a microtubule stabilizer, pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, erlotinib or osimertinib, EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and alectinib, an ALK inhibitor.

Name: Macular Degeneration, Age-Related
Description: Macular degeneration, usually referring to age-related macular degeneration (AMD; MeSH D008268), is a progressive degenerative disorder of the central retina characterized by dysfunction and loss of retinal pigment epithelium, Bruch membrane, photoreceptors, and in some cases pathologic choroidal neovascularization, leading to central visual impairment; major subtypes are nonexudative/dry AMD, including early and intermediate stages with drusen and geographic atrophy, and exudative/wet AMD with neovascular membranes, hemorrhage, and fluid. Genetic susceptibility is strongly linked to complement and lipid/ECM pathways, with representative variants in CFH, ARMS2/HTRA1, C3, C2, CFB, APOE, CETP, TIMP3, and rare Mendelian macular dystrophy genes such as ABCA4 and EFEMP1 that can produce phenocopies; inheritance in typical AMD is complex multifactorial with polygenic risk and environmental interaction, whereas some inherited macular degenerations show autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked transmission. Pathobiology prominently involves complement activation, chronic para-inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, inflammasome signaling, lipid handling, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Clinically, patients develop blurred or distorted central vision, metamorphopsia, reduced contrast sensitivity, impaired reading, central scotoma, and delayed dark adaptation, while complications include subretinal fibrosis, disciform scarring, geographic atrophy progression, and legal blindness; common comorbid associations include smoking, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and cataract. Diagnosis is based on dilated fundus examination showing drusen or pigmentary change, optical coherence tomography, fluorescein or indocyanine green angiography for neovascular disease, fundus autofluorescence for atrophy, and Amsler grid or visual acuity testing, with genetic testing reserved mainly for atypical or inherited cases. Standard therapies include intravitreal anti-VEGF agents such as ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab, which inhibit VEGF-A signaling to suppress neovascular leakage and growth, and pegcetacoplan, a C3 inhibitor, for geographic atrophy; selected patients also benefit from photodynamic therapy with verteporfin and AREDS antioxidant-zinc supplementation to slow progression.

Name: Parkinsonian Disorders
Description: Parkinsonian disorders (MeSH D020734) are a heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative syndromes defined by parkinsonism, classically bradykinesia with rest tremor, rigidity, and postural instability, most often caused by degeneration of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons and, in synucleinopathies, misfolded alpha-synuclein aggregation. They include idiopathic Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal syndrome/degeneration, vascular and drug-induced parkinsonism, and rarer inherited forms. Genetic contributors include SNCA point mutations or multiplications, LRRK2 variants such as G2019S, PRKN/PARK2, PINK1, DJ-1/PARK7, VPS35, GBA1 risk variants, and MAPT in tau-related atypical parkinsonism; inheritance may be autosomal dominant (for example SNCA, LRRK2, VPS35), autosomal recessive (PRKN, PINK1, DJ-1), or complex/sporadic. Core pathogenic pathways involve dopamine synthesis and synaptic transmission, mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy, lysosomal-autophagic dysfunction, ubiquitin-proteasome impairment, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and in tauopathies abnormal tau phosphorylation and microtubule dysfunction. Common manifestations include hypomimia, shuffling gait, freezing, dysarthria, dysphagia, anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, depression, hallucinations, and cognitive decline; complications include falls, aspiration pneumonia, psychosis, dementia, and motor fluctuations with dyskinesias. Treatment is symptomatic and typically includes levodopa combined with carbidopa to replenish central dopamine, dopamine agonists such as pramipexole or ropinirole to stimulate dopamine receptors, MAO-B inhibitors such as rasagiline or selegiline to reduce dopamine breakdown, and often COMT inhibitors such as entacapone to prolong levodopa effect; amantadine, an NMDA receptor antagonist with dopaminergic effects, may reduce dyskinesia. Diagnosis is primarily clinical using parkinsonism criteria and red flags for atypical syndromes, supported by levodopa responsiveness, MRI, DAT-SPECT or PET to document presynaptic dopaminergic deficit, autonomic and neuropsychological

Name: Sore Throats
Description: Pharyngitis (MeSH D010612) is an acute or chronic inflammatory disorder of the pharyngeal mucosa, most often infectious and usually viral, but also caused by Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), Epstein–Barr virus, adenovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, Candida, irritants, allergy, or reflux; clinically it presents with sore throat, odynophagia, fever, pharyngeal erythema, tonsillar enlargement or exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and sometimes cough, coryza, hoarseness, palatal petechiae, or fatigue. Major subtypes include viral, streptococcal, non-streptococcal bacterial, fungal, chronic irritative/reflux-related, and ulcerative pharyngitis. Its biology is dominated by innate and adaptive immune activation, including epithelial toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB and MAPK pathway activation, inflammasome-mediated IL-1β release, and cytokines such as TNF, IL6, IFNG, CXCL8/IL-8, and C-reactive protein; in streptococcal disease, host-pathogen interactions involve streptococcal M protein encoded by emm genes, superantigen exotoxins such as SpeA/SpeC, and variable host susceptibility linked to HLA class II and other immune-response loci rather than a Mendelian inheritance pattern. Diagnosis is primarily clinical but is refined by Centor or McIsaac criteria, throat examination, rapid antigen detection testing for GAS, confirmatory throat culture when indicated, and selective nucleic acid amplification, viral testing, heterophile/EBV serology, or CBC/CRP in atypical cases. Treatment is usually supportive, with acetaminophen acting centrally to reduce pain and fever, ibuprofen inhibiting COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis, and topical benzocaine producing local sodium-channel blockade; confirmed streptococcal pharyngitis is treated with penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, or azithromycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor, in selected allergic patients. Name: Simple Pulmonary Eosinophilia
Description: Simple pulmonary eosinophilia, classically Löffler syndrome (UMLS C0242459), is a usually benign, transient eosinophilic lung disorder characterized by peripheral blood eosinophilia and migratory, nonsegmental pulmonary infiltrates, most often triggered by helminth larval migration, drug hypersensitivity, or atopic immune activation rather than a single monogenic cause. Its biology is dominated by type 2 inflammation, with Th2 lymphocytes, eosinophils, mast cells, and alveolar macrophages linked through IL-5–driven eosinophilopoiesis and survival, IL-4/IL-13 signaling, eotaxin/CCR3-mediated recruitment, IgE/FcεRI pathways, and JAK-STAT signaling; representative genes and proteins implicated in eosinophilic susceptibility or differential diagnosis include IL5, IL5RA, CCL11, CCR3, GATA2, STAT6, and, when clonal eosinophilic syndromes must be excluded, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, and JAK2 rearrangements or mutations. Symptoms are often mild or absent, but patients may develop dry cough, wheeze, low-grade fever, dyspnea, pleuritic discomfort, transient crackles, and occasionally urticaria or systemic allergic features. Recognized forms include parasitic, drug-induced, and idiopathic simple pulmonary eosinophilia, distinguished from chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and hypereosinophilic syndrome. Inheritance is generally not Mendelian, although atopic predisposition and rare variants affecting eosinophil/Th2 regulation may contribute. Diagnosis rests on compatible transient infiltrates on chest radiography or CT, blood eosinophilia, exposure history, exclusion of infection requiring other management, and selected testing such as stool ova and parasite examination, serologies, bronchoalveolar lavage showing eosinophilia, total IgE, and occasionally molecular studies for myeloid neoplasms in atypical or persistent cases.
