Name: Acute Lung Injury
Description: Acute lung injury (ALI), including its more severe subtype acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), is an acute, noncardiogenic inflammatory injury of the alveolar-capillary barrier that causes diffuse pulmonary edema, impaired gas exchange, and reduced lung compliance, most often triggered by sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, major trauma, pancreatitis, transfusion, or inhalational injury. Clinically it presents with rapid-onset dyspnea, tachypnea, refractory hypoxemia, bilateral crackles, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, often progressing to respiratory failure and multiorgan dysfunction; complications include ventilator-associated pneumonia, barotrauma, pulmonary fibrosis, right heart strain, and death, and common comorbidities include chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes, alcohol misuse, and immunosuppression. Pathobiology centers on dysregulated innate immunity, neutrophil-endothelial-epithelial activation, cytokine and chemokine release, and coagulation abnormalities involving TNF, IL1B, IL6, IL8, VEGFA, ANGPT2, ICAM1, selectins, TLR4, NF-kB, JAK/STAT, NLRP3 inflammasome, reactive oxygen species, complement, and surfactant dysfunction; representative susceptibility-associated genes or proteins include ACE, SFTPB, TNF, IL6, IL10, ANGPT2, NAMPT, FER, TLR4, and AGER/RAGE, although inheritance is generally complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian. Diagnosis is based on acute onset within 1 week of an inciting insult, bilateral opacities on chest radiograph or CT not fully explained by effusions, collapse, or heart failure, and impaired oxygenation by PaO2/FiO2 ratio as formalized in Berlin criteria for ARDS; testing includes arterial blood gas analysis, pulse oximetry, echocardiography or BNP to exclude cardiogenic edema, microbiologic studies for the precipitating cause, and inflammatory or organ-failure laboratory assessment. Treatment is primarily supportive and cause-directed, with oxygen and lung-protective ventilation, while commonly used drugs include dexamethasone or methylprednisolone, which suppress NF-kB-driven inflammation, neuromuscular blockers such as cisatracurium to improve ventilator synchrony, inhaled nitric oxide as selective pulmonary vasodilator rescue therapy, broad-spectrum antibiotics when

Name: Pulmonary Atresia
Description: Pulmonary atresia is a rare cyanotic congenital heart disease defined by complete atresia of the right ventricular outflow tract at the level of the pulmonary valve, producing absent antegrade flow from the right ventricle to the pulmonary arteries; major subtypes include pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum and pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect, often considered within the tetralogy of Fallot spectrum when VSD and major aortopulmonary collateral arteries are present. Its etiology is heterogeneous and frequently multifactorial, but pathogenic variants have been reported in cardiac developmental genes including TBX1, NKX2-5, GATA4, GATA6, JAG1, NOTCH1, ZFPM2/FOG2, and 22q11.2 deletion-associated genes, implicating second heart field, neural crest, Notch, BMP/TGF-β, VEGF, and SHH signaling pathways in conotruncal septation, valvulogenesis, and pulmonary artery development; inheritance may be sporadic, autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, or syndromic, as in DiGeorge or Alagille syndromes. Clinical manifestations typically include neonatal cyanosis, tachypnea, hypoxemia, single second heart sound, murmur from tricuspid regurgitation or collateral flow, poor feeding, and signs of ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow, with complications such as right ventricular hypoplasia, coronary sinusoids, arrhythmias, heart failure, polycythemia, infective endocarditis, and neurodevelopmental morbidity; associated anomalies include tricuspid valve dysplasia, atrial septal defect, VSD, MAPCAs, and other conotruncal defects. Diagnosis is based on echocardiographic demonstration of an imperforate pulmonary valve and right-sided anatomy, supported by pulse oximetry, ECG, chest radiography, fetal echocardiography, and CT, MRI, or cardiac catheterization for pulmonary artery, coronary, and collateral assessment; genetic testing with chromosomal microarray and targeted panels may identify syndromic or monogenic causes. Name: Abdominal Abscess
Description: Abdominal abscess is a localized collection of purulent material within the peritoneal, retroperitoneal, or visceral compartments, usually arising as a polymicrobial complication of perforated appendicitis, diverticulitis, bowel ischemia, postoperative anastomotic leak, penetrating trauma, or inflammatory bowel disease; major subtypes include intraperitoneal, subphrenic, pelvic, paracolic, retroperitoneal, hepatic, splenic, and psoas abscesses. It is fundamentally an acquired infectious-inflammatory disorder rather than a Mendelian disease, but host susceptibility can be influenced by genetic defects in innate and adaptive immunity, including CYBB and NCF1 mutations causing chronic granulomatous disease, ELANE-related neutropenia, and variants affecting TLR/NF-κB, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, and complement pathways; key molecular processes include pathogen recognition by TLRs and NOD receptors, neutrophil chemotaxis, macrophage activation, NF-κB-driven cytokine release, coagulation-fibrinolysis imbalance, biofilm formation, and, in sepsis, dysregulated endothelial and inflammasome signaling. Typical pathogens include Escherichia coli, Bacteroides fragilis, Enterococcus spp., streptococci, and sometimes Candida, with symptoms and signs of fever, abdominal pain, tenderness, guarding, ileus, anorexia, nausea, leukocytosis, elevated CRP, and occasionally sepsis or septic shock. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus laboratory inflammation markers and imaging, especially contrast-enhanced CT as the reference standard, with ultrasonography or MRI as alternatives; blood cultures and image-guided aspirate Gram stain/culture help define etiology. Management centers on source control by percutaneous or surgical drainage plus antimicrobials such as piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis and beta-lactamases, ceftriaxone combined with metronidazole, targeting bacterial cell-wall synthesis and anaerobic DNA damage, and carbapenems such as meropenem, which broadly inhibit cell-wall synthesis; vancomycin may be added for resistant gram-positive infection. Important comorbidities and complications include diabetes, malignancy, cirrhosis, immunosuppression, Crohn disease, fistula, recurrent infection, bowel obstruction, bacteremia, and multi-organ failure.

Name: Tricuspid Atresia
Description: Tricuspid atresia (MeSH D018785) is a cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by agenesis or imperforation of the tricuspid valve with absence of the direct right atrioventricular connection, producing a hypoplastic right ventricle and obligate right-to-left shunting across an atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale, usually with a ventricular septal defect and variably related great arteries; major anatomic subtypes are defined by the presence or absence of transposition of the great arteries and by pulmonary stenosis or atresia. Its pathogenesis reflects disturbed cardiac morphogenesis involving transcription-factor and laterality networks, with reported associations involving NKX2-5, GATA4, ZFPM2/FOG2, CITED2, HAND1, CFC1, and chromosomal syndromes such as 22q11.2 deletion, although many cases are sporadic and inheritance is typically multifactorial, with occasional autosomal dominant familial congenital heart disease patterns showing reduced penetrance. Relevant developmental pathways include NKX2-5/GATA/TBX cardiac transcriptional signaling, NODAL-CFC1 laterality signaling, BMP and Notch pathways, and hemodynamic remodeling processes affecting endocardial cushion and right ventricular development. Newborns commonly present with cyanosis, tachypnea, poor feeding, murmur, single second heart sound, and signs of heart failure when pulmonary blood flow is excessive; complications include severe hypoxemia, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, infective endocarditis, growth failure, paradoxical emboli, ventricular dysfunction, and late Fontan-associated liver disease. Diagnosis is established by pulse oximetry and echocardiography with Doppler demonstrating absent tricuspid inflow, interatrial shunt, right ventricular hypoplasia, and associated outflow lesions; ECG, chest radiography, cardiac MRI, CT, and catheterization further define anatomy and hemodynamics, while fetal ultrasound enables prenatal detection. Treatment is staged and palliative rather than curative: prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency by relaxing ductal smooth muscle, furosemide reduces preload via loop diuresis for heart failure, and milrinone, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor, augments inotropy and lowers afterload; additional agents include digoxin and anticoagulants, alongside surgical shunts, Glenn, and

Name: Superficial punctate keratitis
Description: Superficial punctate keratitis is a clinical corneal epithelial disorder characterized by multiple tiny punctate erosions or inflammatory lesions confined largely to the superficial cornea rather than a single genetically defined disease, and it commonly presents with foreign-body sensation, ցավ, photophobia, tearing, burning, reflex blepharospasm, fluctuating or blurred vision, and punctate fluorescein staining on slit-lamp examination. Major etiologic subtypes include infectious forms, especially adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis and herpes simplex keratitis; toxic or medicamentosa forms from preserved topical drugs; ultraviolet or exposure-related keratitis; dry-eye-associated disease; contact-lens-related keratopathy; and immune-mediated forms such as Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis. Molecular associations are therefore heterogeneous: HSV disease involves viral glycoproteins and host entry receptors with innate immune activation through TLR and interferon signaling; dry-eye-related punctate keratitis is linked to inflammatory mediators including IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6, MMP-9, MAPK and NF-κB pathways, mucins such as MUC1, MUC4, and MUC16, and tear-film proteins including lacritin; rare inherited predispositions may reflect disorders causing corneal fragility or dry eye, such as PAX6-related aniridia or ectodermal dysplasia genes, but most cases are non-Mendelian. Commonly used treatments target the cause and surface inflammation: preservative-free artificial tears lubricate and dilute inflammatory mediators; topical cyclosporine inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation; topical corticosteroids such as loteprednol suppress NF-κB-driven cytokine expression; ganciclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase in herpetic disease; and topical antibiotics such as erythromycin or fluoroquinolones are used when bacterial superinfection risk exists. Comorbidities include dry eye disease, blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, allergic conjunctivitis, autoimmune disorders including Sjögren syndrome, and viral conjunctivitis; complications include recurrent erosions, filamentary keratitis, infectious keratitis, subepithelial scarring, and reduced visual quality. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history, slit-lamp biomicroscopy with fluorescein or rose bengal/lissamine green staining, tear-breakup time and Schirmer testing when dryness is suspected, cor

Name: Accidental poisoning by methyl alcohol
Description: Accidental poisoning by methyl alcohol (methanol; UMLS C0261439) is an acute toxic exposure rather than a primary inherited disease, most often caused by ingestion of contaminated spirits, solvents, antifreeze, or industrial products; its pathobiology is driven by hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase ADH1B/ADH1C and aldehyde dehydrogenase-mediated oxidation of methanol to formaldehyde and then formic acid, with downstream inhibition of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), impaired oxidative phosphorylation, ATP depletion, oxidative stress, and selective injury to the retina, optic nerve, and basal ganglia. No single causative mutation defines the disorder, but polymorphisms in ADH, ALDH, and folate-pathway genes such as MTHFR may plausibly modify susceptibility to formate accumulation and toxicity; inheritance is therefore not Mendelian, though rare mitochondrial optic neuropathy predispositions, including LHON-associated MT-ND variants, may worsen visual outcomes. Hallmark manifestations include inebriation followed after a latent period by headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, confusion, visual blurring, photophobia, “snowfield” vision, mydriasis, dyspnea, and progression to severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis, coma, seizures, respiratory failure, blindness, or death. Clinically recognized forms are mild, moderate, and severe poisoning, with occasional inhalational or dermal occupational subtypes. Major complications and comorbidities include optic neuropathy, putaminal necrosis, pancreatitis, acute kidney injury, aspiration, and co-ingestion with ethanol or ethylene glycol, while alcohol use disorder and malnutrition may worsen prognosis. Diagnosis rests on exposure history plus anion-gap acidosis, elevated osmolar gap, low bicarbonate, arterial or venous blood gas abnormalities, and direct serum methanol measurement when available, supplemented by serum formate, ophthalmologic examination, neuroimaging, and exclusion of other toxic alcohols. Standard treatment includes fomepizole, a competitive alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor; ethanol, which acts as an alternative substrate for alcohol dehydrogenase; folinic acid or folic acid, which enhances formate metabolism to carbon dioxide and water; and hemodialysis to remove methanol and formate and correct acidosis.

Name: Accidental poisoning caused by lead and its compounds and fumes (disorder)
Description: Accidental poisoning caused by lead and its compounds and fumes is an acquired toxic disorder, usually from inhalational or ingestion exposure to inorganic lead, that may present as acute high-dose intoxication or more often chronic cumulative poisoning with multisystem injury. Lead has no Mendelian inheritance pattern, but susceptibility is modified by genes involved in heme synthesis, metal handling, and toxicant metabolism, including ALAD/ALAD2, VDR, HFE, SLC11A2/DMT1, and metallothionein-related pathways; functionally, lead binds sulfhydryl-containing proteins and inhibits key heme enzymes such as delta-aminolevulinate dehydratase and ferrochelatase, with secondary accumulation of aminolevulinic acid, impaired hemoglobin synthesis, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, calcium mimicry, altered NMDA receptor signaling, PKC-dependent neurotransmission, and disruption of vitamin D and nitric oxide signaling. Typical manifestations include abdominal colic, constipation, anorexia, fatigue, headache, irritability, cognitive slowing, peripheral neuropathy with wrist or foot drop, anemia with basophilic stippling, nephropathy, hypertension, gout, infertility, and in severe cases encephalopathy, seizures, coma, and a Burton gingival line; children are especially prone to neurodevelopmental delay and hearing impairment. Major complications and comorbidities include chronic kidney disease, neurocognitive and behavioral disorders, hypertensive cardiovascular disease, pregnancy loss, and iron deficiency, which can increase lead absorption. Treatment centers on exposure cessation and chelation, with calcium disodium edetate, which complexes extracellular lead for renal excretion, dimercaprol, a dithiol chelator used particularly with severe encephalopathy, succimer meso-2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid, an oral dithiol that enhances urinary lead elimination, and less commonly penicillamine. Diagnosis relies on a compatible exposure history plus elevated venous blood lead level, supported by zinc protoporphyrin or free erythrocyte protoporphyrin, CBC showing microcytic or normocytic anemia, renal and hepatic testing, radiographic lead lines in children or retained fragments, and in selected cases environmental assessment and electrophysiologic or neurodevelopmental evaluation.

Name: Bursitis of shoulder
Description: Bursitis of the shoulder, most often involving the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa and less commonly the subcoracoid or scapulothoracic bursae, is a usually nonhereditary inflammatory or degenerative periarticular disorder characterized by pain generated by friction, overuse, impingement, crystal deposition, trauma, or infection; it commonly presents with lateral shoulder pain, painful arc, tenderness over the greater tuberosity or bursa, night pain, reduced active abduction, and sometimes warmth or swelling, while septic cases may add fever and marked erythema. Molecularly, it is linked less to single-gene causation than to inflammatory mediators and tendon-bursa biology, with increased expression of cytokines and enzymes such as IL1B, IL6, TNF, PTGS2/COX-2, MMP1, MMP3, MMP9, VEGFA, TGFB1, and COL1A1/COL3A1 in rotator cuff–bursal disease; representative associated pathways include NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, prostaglandin-eicosanoid signaling, matrix-remodeling, angiogenesis, and calcium crystal–induced inflammasome activation. Genetic contribution is limited and typically polygenic or indirect through predisposition to calcific tendinopathy or rotator cuff disease rather than Mendelian inheritance, although variants in genes such as COL5A1, MMP3, and TGFB1 have been reported in related shoulder soft-tissue pathology. Common comorbidities include rotator cuff tendinopathy or tear, adhesive capsulitis, acromial impingement, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, calcium hydroxyapatite deposition disease, and occupational or athletic overuse, with complications including chronic pain, stiffness, weakness, reduced range of motion, and rarely abscess or osteomyelitis in infection. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by impingement maneuvers and pain with resisted abduction, with ultrasound or MRI demonstrating bursal fluid or synovial thickening, radiographs identifying calcifications or acromial morphology, laboratory tests and aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis when septic or crystal bursitis is suspected. Name: Contact dermatitis caused by urushiol from Pacific poison oak
Description: Contact dermatitis caused by urushiol from Pacific poison oak (UMLS C0263283) is an acquired, non-inherited allergic contact dermatitis in which pentadecylcatechol urushiol acts as a hapten, binds epidermal proteins, and triggers a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction after prior sensitization. Key molecular participants include keratinocyte danger signaling and innate cytokines such as TNF, IL1B, IL6, TSLP, and chemokines, followed by antigen presentation through HLA class I and II pathways, activation of Langerhans cells and dermal dendritic cells, and T-cell polarization involving NF-kB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, IFNG, IL17, and cytotoxic CD8+ effectors; representative susceptibility genes variably implicated in allergic contact dermatitis include HLA alleles, FLG, TLR2, TLR4, NFE2L2, GSTM1, GSTT1, NAT2, and cytokine-related loci, but no single mutation is diagnostic and inheritance is at most polygenic predisposition. Clinically, patients develop intensely pruritic erythematous papules, vesicles, bullae, edema, and often linear streaks at exposure sites, with severe facial or genital swelling in marked reactions; subtypes include acute vesicular, subacute eczematous, chronic lichenified, localized, and widespread secondary autoeczematization. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on a compatible exposure history, lesion distribution, and timing 12 to 72 hours after contact; patch testing may confirm urushiol sensitivity when needed, while biopsy shows spongiotic dermatitis and helps exclude mimics such as irritant dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, cellulitis, scabies, or herpes zoster. Standard therapy includes topical corticosteroids such as triamcinolone or clobetasol, which suppress glucocorticoid-responsive inflammatory gene transcription; oral prednisone for extensive disease, acting through systemic glucocorticoid receptor-mediated immunosuppression; and oral antihistamines such as hydroxyzine or diphenhydramine, which mainly reduce pruritus via H1 blockade. Comorbidities include atopy and occupational or recreational exposure risk, and complications include excoriation, secondary bacterial infection, sleep disturbance, postinflammatory pigment alteration, and rare severe generalized dermatitis.

Name: Chronic heart failure (disorder)
Description: Chronic heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which structural or functional cardiac impairment causes inadequate ventricular filling or ejection, producing chronic neurohormonal activation and end-organ congestion or hypoperfusion; it is commonly classified into heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, mildly reduced ejection fraction, preserved ejection fraction, and right-sided or biventricular failure. Major molecular pathways include maladaptive activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sympathetic nervous system, natriuretic peptide signaling, endothelin, nitric oxide-cGMP-PKG, inflammatory cytokines, calcium-handling defects, mitochondrial dysfunction, fibrosis mediated by TGF-beta, and ventricular remodeling. Genetic contributors are most evident in dilated or familial cardiomyopathy, with representative genes including TTN truncating variants, LMNA, MYH7, TNNT2, DSP, PLN, BAG3, RBM20, and SCN5A; inheritance is often autosomal dominant, though X-linked, mitochondrial, and syndromic forms occur. Typical symptoms and signs include exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, peripheral edema, elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary rales, hepatomegaly, and an S3 gallop. Common comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, sleep apnea, anemia, valvular disease, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, cardiorenal syndrome, recurrent hospitalization, and sudden cardiac death. Standard therapies include ACE inhibitors such as enalapril, which reduce angiotensin II generation; beta-blockers such as carvedilol or metoprolol succinate, which blunt adrenergic toxicity; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or eplerenone, which reduce aldosterone-mediated fibrosis; diuretics such as furosemide for symptomatic decongestion; SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin; and ARNI therapy with sacubitril/valsartan. Diagnosis relies on history and examination plus echocardiography to define structure and ejection fraction, natriuretic peptides, ECG, chest radiography, troponin and laboratory assessment, ischemic evaluation, and, when indicated, cardiac MRI

Name: Cerebral Vasospasm
Description: Intracranial vasospasm is a delayed, often reversible narrowing of the large basal cerebral arteries, classically arising 3–14 days after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and less often after traumatic SAH, surgery, or severe meningitis, and it is a major cause of delayed cerebral ischemia, infarction, and poor neurologic outcome. Its biology is multifactorial, involving oxyhemoglobin-driven endothelial injury, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, endothelin-1 excess acting through EDNRA, calcium-dependent smooth-muscle contraction via CACNA1C and RhoA/ROCK signaling, inflammation with IL6, TNF, TLR4, prostaglandins and leukocyte-endothelial adhesion, oxidative stress, and impaired vasodilation mediated by NOS3/eNOS, soluble guanylyl cyclase-cGMP, and prostacyclin pathways; representative genetic associations reported in susceptibility or severity include NOS3, EDN1, EDNRA, haptoglobin HP, APOE, inflammatory cytokine genes such as IL6 and TNF, and thrombophilia-related variants, although no Mendelian inheritance pattern is established because vasospasm is usually an acquired complication rather than a primary inherited disorder. Symptoms reflect cerebral hypoperfusion and include new headache, declining consciousness, confusion, aphasia, hemiparesis, cranial nerve deficits, and focal ischemic stroke; angiographic, clinical, and perfusion-defined subtypes are recognized. Diagnosis relies on the clinical setting plus serial neurologic examination, transcranial Doppler showing elevated flow velocities, CT or MR angiography, digital subtraction angiography as reference standard, and adjunctive CT/MR perfusion or multimodal monitoring to identify delayed cerebral ischemia. Standard therapy includes nimodipine, a dihydropyridine L-type calcium-channel blocker that improves outcome despite limited effect on vessel caliber; induced blood-pressure augmentation with vasopressors such as norepinephrine to raise cerebral perfusion; and endovascular rescue with intra-arterial vasodilators such as verapamil, nicardipine, or milrinone, the latter a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor increasing cAMP, as well as balloon angioplasty for proximal spasm. Name: Erosive oesophagitis
Description: Erosive oesophagitis (UMLS C0267055) is an inflammatory, acid-peptic injury of the oesophageal squamous mucosa, usually representing a mucosal-damaging form of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in which repeated exposure to gastric acid, pepsin, and sometimes bile salts disrupts epithelial tight junctions and barrier integrity, activates NF-κB-, IL-8-, COX-2-, TRPV1-, and oxidative stress–related pathways, and recruits neutrophilic and eosinophilic inflammation. It typically presents with heartburn, acid regurgitation, retrosternal pain, odynophagia, dysphagia, water brash, and sometimes upper gastrointestinal bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia. Endoscopic subtypes are commonly graded by the Los Angeles classification (A–D) and may be distinguished from non-erosive reflux disease, while severe chronic injury can progress to ulceration, stricture, haemorrhage, Barrett oesophagus, and ultimately oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Risk is increased by hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, delayed gastric emptying, smoking, alcohol use, connective tissue disease, and medications that reduce lower oesophageal sphincter tone or cause pill oesophagitis; common comorbidities include GERD, obesity, asthma, chronic cough, laryngitis, sleep disturbance, and Barrett metaplasia. The disorder is usually multifactorial rather than Mendelian, but genetic susceptibility has been linked to variants in inflammatory and epithelial barrier genes such as IL1B, IL10, IL8, COX2/PTGS2, and GNB3, with occasional overlap with inherited predisposition to Barrett oesophagus or obesity. Diagnosis is based on symptoms plus objective evidence of mucosal breaks on upper endoscopy, with biopsy when eosinophilic, infectious, caustic, or neoplastic causes are considered; ambulatory pH or pH-impedance monitoring and manometry help confirm reflux and exclude motility disorders. Standard treatment includes proton-pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, and pantoprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion; and alginate-antacids or sucralfate provide a protective barrier, alongside weight loss and reflux-reducing lifestyle

Name: Nonulcer dyspepsia
Description: Nonulcer dyspepsia, now usually classified within functional dyspepsia, is a chronic gastroduodenal disorder characterized by bothersome epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating, belching, nausea, and sometimes vomiting in the absence of peptic ulcer or other structural disease on routine evaluation. Clinically it is commonly divided into epigastric pain syndrome and postprandial distress syndrome, with overlap with irritable bowel syndrome and gastroesophageal reflux disease being frequent; anxiety, depression, Helicobacter pylori infection, delayed gastric emptying, visceral hypersensitivity, sleep disturbance, and reduced quality of life are important comorbidities or consequences. Pathobiology is multifactorial and includes abnormal brain-gut signaling, impaired gastric accommodation, low-grade duodenal inflammation with eosinophils and mast cells, altered mucosal permeability, vagal and enteric neural dysfunction, and dysregulated serotonergic, cholinergic, nitrergic, histaminergic, and acid-sensing pathways involving 5-HT receptors and transporter SLC6A4, TRPV1, nitric oxide synthase, cholecystokinin, ghrelin, and inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL6, and IL10; genetic susceptibility is modest and polygenic, with reported associations for GNB3 C825T, SLC6A4 5-HTTLPR, ADRA2A, SCN10A, TNF, IL10, and GNβ3-related signaling variants rather than a Mendelian inheritance pattern. Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion, typically using Rome IV criteria with symptom chronicity plus absence of alarm features and negative evaluation for organic disease; testing may include upper endoscopy, noninvasive H. pylori testing, basic laboratory studies, celiac testing when indicated, abdominal imaging, and gastric emptying studies in selected patients. Treatment commonly includes proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine, which reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion; and prokinetics such as metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist with 5-HT4 agonist activity that enhances gastric emptying, with additional options including acotiamide, a cholinesterase inhibitor that improves accommodation, and low-dose tricy

Name: Gastroparesis due to diabetes mellitus (disorder)
Description: Gastroparesis due to diabetes mellitus is a chronic diabetic autonomic neuropathic disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction, most often arising in long-standing type 1 or type 2 diabetes from hyperglycemia-driven injury to the vagus nerve, enteric neurons, interstitial cells of Cajal, and gastric smooth muscle. Its pathobiology involves oxidative stress, advanced glycation end products, microvascular ischemia, and impaired neuronal nitric oxide synthase signaling, with disruption of SCF/KIT-dependent pacemaker networks, altered acetylcholine, dopamine D2, serotonin 5-HT4, and motilin pathways, and inflammatory changes including macrophage dysfunction; representative molecular associations include NOS1, KIT, ANO1, SCF/KITLG, TNF, IL6, and HMOX1, although no single highly penetrant causal mutation is established and inheritance is generally not Mendelian, reflecting polygenic susceptibility linked to diabetes risk genes and variable host factors. Clinical manifestations include early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea, vomiting, bloating, epigastric pain, erratic glycemic control, weight loss, dehydration, and malnutrition; major complications include bezoars, recurrent hospitalization, aspiration, electrolyte disturbances, poor oral drug absorption, and comorbid diabetic neuropathy, retinopathy, nephropathy, and GERD. Subtypes are commonly diabetic versus idiopathic or postsurgical gastroparesis, and within diabetic disease may be acute hyperglycemia-related or chronic neuropathic forms. Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms, exclusion of obstruction by upper endoscopy or imaging, and objective delay on gastric emptying scintigraphy, with alternatives including 13C breath testing or wireless motility capsule; supportive evaluation includes glucose indices and nutritional assessment. Treatment emphasizes glycemic optimization plus prokinetic and antiemetic therapy, commonly metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist with 5-HT4 agonist activity; erythromycin, a motilin receptor agonist; domperidone, a peripheral D2 antagonist; and sometimes prucalopride, a selective 5-HT4 agonist, with refractory cases considered for gastric electrical stimulation or enteral feeding.

Name: Chronic ulcerative rectosigmoiditis
Description: Chronic ulcerative rectosigmoiditis is a distal form of ulcerative colitis, a chronic relapsing inflammatory bowel disease confined to the rectum and sigmoid colon and characterized by continuous superficial mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum; patients typically present with bloody diarrhea, urgency, tenesmus, mucus discharge, crampy left lower quadrant abdominal pain, nocturnal stools, anemia, and endoscopic friability or ulceration. Its pathobiology reflects polygenic susceptibility interacting with epithelial barrier defects, dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, and the gut microbiome; associated loci include HLA class II variants, IL23R, JAK2, ECM1, GNA12, NKX2-3, and genes shared with inflammatory bowel disease such as CARD9, with abnormal cytokine signaling through TNF, IL-13, IL-23/Th17, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, and integrin-mediated leukocyte trafficking pathways involving TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-17, IL-22, MAdCAM-1, and alpha4beta7. Inheritance is complex and non-Mendelian, with familial aggregation rather than a single causative mutation. Major subtypes are ulcerative proctitis, proctosigmoiditis, left-sided colitis, and extensive or pancolitis. Common comorbidities and complications include primary sclerosing cholangitis, peripheral arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, venous thromboembolism, severe bleeding, toxic megacolon, perforation, stricture, and increased colorectal dysplasia or carcinoma risk with chronic disease. Treatment commonly includes 5-aminosalicylates such as mesalamine, which inhibit cyclooxygenase/lipoxygenase pathways and mucosal inflammatory mediator production; corticosteroids such as prednisone or budesonide, which suppress NF-kB-dependent cytokine transcription; immunomodulators such as azathioprine, a purine synthesis inhibitor; and biologics including infliximab, an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody, vedolizumab, an alpha4beta7 integrin blocker, and ustekinumab, an IL-12/23 antagonist; tofacitinib, a JAK inhibitor, is also used. Name: Chronic idiopathic constipation
Description: Chronic idiopathic constipation (UMLS C0267509) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by persistently difficult, infrequent, or incomplete defecation without an identifiable structural, metabolic, or secondary drug-related cause, typically presenting with fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements weekly, hard or lumpy stools, straining, sensation of anorectal blockage, and incomplete evacuation. It is commonly classified into normal-transit constipation, slow-transit constipation, and defecatory disorders involving pelvic floor dyssynergia, with diagnosis usually based on Rome IV criteria, careful exclusion of alarm features, medication and metabolic review, digital rectal examination, and selected testing such as colonoscopy when indicated, colonic transit studies with radiopaque markers or scintigraphy, anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion testing, and defecography. Although usually sporadic and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, genetic contributions to motility, enteric neurotransmission, and epithelial secretion are implicated, with representative associations involving SCN5A sodium-channel variants, serotonin signaling genes such as SLC6A4 and HTR3-related pathways, and rare severe dysmotility phenotypes linked to enteric neuropathy genes including RET, EDNRB, and SOX10, while altered expression of aquaporins, CFTR-mediated chloride transport, and guanylate cyclase C signaling may influence stool hydration and transit. Key pathogenic pathways include enteric nervous system dysfunction, serotonergic 5-HT4 signaling, acetylcholine-mediated cholinergic transmission, nitric oxide and interstitial cells of Cajal pacemaker activity, bile acid signaling, and GC-C/cGMP-CFTR-dependent intestinal secretion. Common treatments include osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol, which retains luminal water; stimulant agents such as bisacodyl or senna, which increase colonic motility and secretion; secretagogues such as lubiprostone, a ClC-2 chloride channel activator, and linaclotide or plecanatide, guanylate cyclase C agonists that increase cGMP-driven chloride and bicarbonate secretion; and the 5-HT4 agonist prucalopride, which enhances propulsive motility. Frequent comorbidities include irritable bowel syndrome, anxiety, depression, pelvic floor dysfunction, hemorrhoids, anal fissures, rectal prolapse, and fecal impaction.

Name: Primary cholangitis
Description: Primary cholangitis, most commonly referring to primary biliary cholangitis and more rarely primary sclerosing cholangitis as a cholangitic subtype, is a chronic immune-mediated cholestatic liver disease characterized by progressive destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts, portal inflammation, fibrosis, and eventual cirrhosis; patients typically present with fatigue, pruritus, sicca symptoms, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, xanthelasma, hepatomegaly, and later portal hypertension, osteopenia, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with strong HLA class II associations and immune-regulatory loci such as IL12A, IL12RB2, STAT4, IRF5, SPIB, CTLA4, and TNFSF15 in primary biliary cholangitis, while primary sclerosing cholangitis is linked to HLA-B and DRB1 haplotypes; antimitochondrial reactivity against the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, and less often anti-gp210 or anti-sp100, implicates mitochondrial autoantigens and loss of tolerance. Key pathways include IL-12/Th1 and IL-23/Th17 signaling, TNF and interferon-mediated inflammation, T-cell and B-cell activation, cholangiocyte injury, bile acid toxicity, FXR-FGF19 signaling, and profibrotic TGF-β pathways. Diagnosis relies on persistent cholestatic liver tests, especially elevated alkaline phosphatase, positive antimitochondrial antibody or PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies, exclusion of extrahepatic obstruction, and liver biopsy when serology is negative or overlap with autoimmune hepatitis is suspected; ultrasound and MRCP help distinguish small-duct from large-duct disease and identify PSC-like stricturing. Standard therapy includes ursodeoxycholic acid, a hydrophilic bile acid that improves bile flow and reduces cholestatic injury; obeticholic acid, an FXR agonist that suppresses bile acid synthesis; and bezafibrate or fenofibrate, PPAR agonists that enhance bile acid metabolism and lower cholestatic enzymes, while cholestyramine is often used for pruritus. Name: Chronic arthritis due to gout
Description: Chronic arthritis due to gout is a crystal-induced inflammatory arthropathy caused by persistent hyperuricemia with deposition of monosodium urate crystals in synovium, cartilage, bone, and periarticular tissues, producing recurrent acute flares that may evolve into chronic tophaceous, erosive arthritis. Clinically it presents with intermittent or persistent joint pain, swelling, erythema, warmth, tenderness, reduced range of motion, tophi of the ears, olecranon, fingers, toes, or Achilles tendon, and in advanced disease deformity and radiographic erosions; common patterns include acute intermittent gout, chronic tophaceous gout, and axial or polyarticular forms. Core molecular drivers include urate transport and purine metabolism genes such as SLC2A9, ABCG2, SLC22A12/URAT1, SLC17A1, and less commonly HPRT1 or PRPS1 in purine overproduction states; familial risk is typically complex polygenic, although rare X-linked HPRT1 deficiency and PRPS1 gain-of-function can strongly predispose. Pathogenesis centers on phagocytosis of urate crystals, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1-mediated IL-1β and IL-18 release, neutrophil recruitment, TLR/MyD88 and NF-κB signaling, complement activation, and osteoclast-mediated bone damage. Major comorbidities include nephrolithiasis, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, obesity, insulin resistance, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidemia, and increased cardiovascular risk. Diagnosis relies on identification of negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid or tophus aspirate, supported by serum urate, inflammatory markers, ultrasound double-contour sign, or dual-energy CT, and classification commonly follows ACR/EULAR criteria. Treatment includes NSAIDs such as indomethacin or naproxen to inhibit cyclooxygenase, colchicine to block microtubule polymerization and neutrophil inflammasome responses, glucocorticoids to suppress cytokine transcription, and urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol or febuxostat as xanthine oxidase inhibitors, probenecid as a uricosuric URAT1 inhibitor, and pegloticase as recombinant uricase for refractory tophaceous disease.

Name: Molybdenum cofactor deficiency
Description: Molybdenum cofactor deficiency (MoCD; UMLS C0268119) is a rare, usually neonatal-onset autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder caused by failure of molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis, most commonly due to biallelic pathogenic variants in MOCS1 (type A), MOCS2 or rarely MOCS3 (type B), and GPHN/gephyrin (type C), leading to loss of activity of sulfite oxidase and also xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase and aldehyde oxidase; representative mutations include truncating, splice-site, and missense variants in MOCS1 or MOCS2. The central pathogenic pathway is accumulation of toxic sulfite and S-sulfocysteine with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, excitotoxic neuronal injury, and impaired purine metabolism characterized by low uric acid and elevated xanthine/hypoxanthine. Clinically, classic early-onset disease presents with intractable neonatal seizures, encephalopathy, poor feeding, axial hypotonia evolving to spasticity or dystonia, developmental arrest, microcephaly, exaggerated startle, and severe brain injury; later-onset attenuated forms also occur. Major complications include profound intellectual disability, cerebral atrophy, cystic encephalomalacia, lens dislocation, movement disorders, feeding failure, and early death, and comorbidities may include aspiration, recurrent infections, and epilepsy-related morbidity. Treatment is primarily disease-modifying replacement with fosdenopterin, a cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate substrate replacement for MoCD type A that restores downstream cofactor synthesis; supportive drugs commonly include antiseizure agents such as levetiracetam, which modulates synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, phenobarbital, a GABAA receptor positive allosteric modulator, and benzodiazepines such as midazolam or clonazepam, which enhance GABAergic inhibition, while dietary protein restriction may reduce sulfite precursor load. Diagnosis rests on compatible phenotype plus biochemical testing showing elevated urinary sulfite and S-sulfocysteine, low plasma urate, increased urinary xanthine/hypoxanthine, characteristic MRI changes, reduced enzyme/cofactor studies when available, and confirmatory molecular genetic testing.

Name: Immunoglobulin Light-chain Amyloidosis
Description: Immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL amyloidosis; UMLS C0268381) is an acquired systemic protein misfolding disorder caused by a usually small clonal plasma-cell or, less often, B-cell population that overproduces unstable monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains, most commonly lambda and less often kappa, which misfold into beta-pleated-sheet amyloid fibrils and deposit in tissues; representative genetic lesions are those of plasma-cell dyscrasias, including t(11;14)(CCND1-IGH), hyperdiploidy, and occasional NRAS, KRAS, BRAF, or del17p/TP53 abnormalities, while germline inheritance is not typical and familial transmission should instead prompt consideration of hereditary transthyretin or other non-AL amyloidoses. Pathobiology involves endoplasmic-reticulum stress, proteostasis failure, ubiquitin-proteasome dependence, NF-kB/IL-6-supported plasma-cell survival, and direct light-chain cardiotoxicity with oxidative stress, p38 MAPK activation, and apoptosis. Major subtypes are systemic AL, localized AL, and presentations associated with overt multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, or other lymphoplasmacytic neoplasms. Clinical manifestations reflect organ deposition, especially nephrotic-range proteinuria and renal insufficiency, restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy with increased wall thickness, heart failure, arrhythmias and orthostatic hypotension, plus hepatomegaly, peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, macroglossia, periorbital purpura, weight loss, diarrhea, and carpal tunnel syndrome; major complications include end-stage renal disease, sudden cardiac death, thromboembolism, and recurrent pleural effusions. Diagnosis requires demonstration of Congo-red-positive amyloid with apple-green birefringence and definitive typing, ideally by mass spectrometry or immunoelectron microscopy, combined with evidence of a monoclonal gammopathy by serum and urine immunofixation, serum free light-chain assay, bone-marrow biopsy with plasma-cell characterization, and organ assessment using cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography or cardiac MRI, and renal or hepatic testing. Name: Stiff heart syndrome
Description: Stiff heart syndrome generally refers to a restrictive cardiomyopathy phenotype characterized by impaired ventricular relaxation and markedly reduced diastolic compliance with relatively preserved systolic function early in the course, producing elevated filling pressures and biatrial enlargement. It may be idiopathic, familial, or secondary to infiltrative or fibrotic myocardial disease; genetic forms most often involve sarcomeric and cytoskeletal genes such as TNNI3, TNNT2, MYH7, MYBPC3, ACTC1, DES, FLNC, and LMNA, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance, although X-linked Fabry disease due to GLA and transthyretin amyloidosis from TTR variants are important specific causes. Pathobiology centers on myocyte stiffness, extracellular matrix remodeling, and fibrosis driven by altered calcium handling, titin-based passive tension, TGF-beta/SMAD, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, beta-adrenergic, and natriuretic peptide signaling, with infiltrative protein deposition or iron overload in some subtypes. Typical manifestations include exertional dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly, elevated jugular venous pressure, Kussmaul physiology, atrial fibrillation, and sometimes syncope or thromboembolism; major comorbidities and complications include pulmonary hypertension, right-sided heart failure, conduction disease, ventricular and atrial arrhythmias, stroke, sudden cardiac death, and progression to advanced heart failure. Subtypes include idiopathic/familial restrictive cardiomyopathy and secondary forms due to amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, radiation, or storage diseases. Treatment is largely supportive and etiology-directed: loop diuretics such as furosemide inhibit the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter to reduce congestion, spironolactone antagonizes the mineralocorticoid receptor to limit sodium retention and fibrosis, beta-blockers such as metoprolol reduce sympathetic drive and improve diastolic filling time, and anticoagulants may be used for atrial fibrillation; tafamidis stabilizes transthyretin in ATTR amyloidosis and enzyme replacement treats Fabry disease. Name: Type I Tyrosinemias
Description: Tyrosinemias are inherited disorders of tyrosine catabolism, classically transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner, that comprise tyrosinemia type I, II, and III, caused respectively by pathogenic variants in FAH encoding fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, TAT encoding tyrosine aminotransferase, and HPD encoding 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase; representative FAH mutations include missense, splice-site, and truncating alleles such as c.1062+5G>A in affected populations. The core pathogenic pathway is failure of hepatic and extrahepatic tyrosine degradation, leading to accumulation of toxic intermediates including fumarylacetoacetate, maleylacetoacetate, succinylacetoacetate, and succinylacetone in type I, with inhibition of porphobilinogen synthase by succinylacetone contributing to porphyria-like neurologic crises, oxidative stress, mitochondrial injury, hepatocyte apoptosis, renal tubular dysfunction, and carcinogenesis. Type I is the most severe form and presents in infancy or childhood with liver failure, jaundice, hepatomegaly, coagulopathy, failure to thrive, vomiting, rickets, Fanconi syndrome, nephromegaly, episodic neuropathic crises, and high risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; type II typically causes painful keratitis, corneal ulcers, photophobia, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, and variable developmental delay; type III is rare and may cause ataxia, seizures, and intellectual impairment. Treatment centers on nitisinone, which inhibits HPD upstream of toxic metabolite formation, combined with dietary phenylalanine and tyrosine restriction; supportive agents include phosphate and vitamin D for hypophosphatemic rickets and liver transplantation for refractory hepatic failure or malignancy. Diagnosis relies on elevated plasma tyrosine, characteristic urinary succinylacetone for type I, abnormal liver and renal indices, newborn screening by tandem mass spectrometry, enzyme or molecular genetic testing of FAH, TAT, or HPD, and imaging or biopsy when assessing cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.

Name: Disorders of fatty-acid metabolism
Description: Disorders of fatty-acid metabolism are a heterogeneous group of inborn errors of mitochondrial or peroxisomal fatty-acid transport and β-oxidation that impair energy production, especially during fasting, illness, or exercise, and include medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase/trifunctional protein deficiency, carnitine palmitoyltransferase I and II deficiencies, carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency, primary carnitine deficiency, multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, and peroxisomal disorders such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and Zellweger spectrum disease. Causative genes commonly include ACADM, ACADVL, HADHA, HADHB, CPT1A, CPT2, SLC25A20, SLC22A5, ETFA, ETFB, ETFDH, ABCD1, and PEX genes, usually with autosomal recessive inheritance, although X-linked inheritance occurs in ABCD1-related disease. Pathobiology centers on defective carnitine shuttle function, acyl-CoA dehydrogenation, electron transfer flavoprotein/ETF dehydrogenase signaling to the respiratory chain, and peroxisomal very-long-chain fatty-acid handling, leading to toxic acylcarnitine accumulation, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatic steatosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, and encephalopathy. Clinical manifestations range from neonatal metabolic decompensation, seizures, lethargy, vomiting, hepatomegaly, arrhythmia, and sudden death to later exercise intolerance, myalgia, weakness, pigmentary retinopathy, and recurrent myoglobinuria. Major complications include liver failure, developmental delay, peripheral neuropathy, retinopathy, maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy with fetal LCHAD deficiency, and adrenal insufficiency in adrenoleukodystrophy. Diagnosis relies on newborn screening and biochemical testing showing characteristic plasma acylcarnitine profiles, low free carnitine or elevated very-long-chain fatty acids, urine organic acids and acylglycines, enzyme assays, and confirmatory molecular testing. Name: Lower urinary tract infectious disease
Description: Lower urinary tract infectious disease, most commonly encompassing cystitis and urethritis, is usually an acute bacterial infection of the bladder or urethra caused predominantly by uropathogenic Escherichia coli, with Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, and in some cases sexually transmitted pathogens such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis contributing to specific subtypes including uncomplicated, complicated, catheter-associated, recurrent, and hemorrhagic lower UTI. Disease biology is driven by host-pathogen interactions involving urothelial Toll-like receptor and innate immune signaling, especially TLR4-CD14-LPS recognition, NF-κB activation, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, CXCR1, and antimicrobial peptides, while bacterial adherence factors such as type 1 fimbriae with FimH and other adhesins promote colonization. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, with reported associations involving TLR4, CXCR1, HSPA1B, DEFB1, and secretor status determined by FUT2; rare anatomic or vesicoureteral reflux predisposition may involve genes such as ROBO2 or PAX2. Typical symptoms and signs include dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy or malodorous urine, and sometimes hematuria, whereas fever, flank pain, or systemic toxicity suggest upper tract extension rather than isolated lower disease. Common comorbidities and risk factors include female sex, sexual activity, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, urinary obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia, neurogenic bladder, urolithiasis, catheterization, and postmenopausal estrogen deficiency; complications include recurrence, ascending pyelonephritis, prostatitis, bacteremia, renal scarring in susceptible patients, and struvite stone formation with urease-producing organisms. Diagnosis rests on compatible symptoms plus urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and microscopic bacteriuria, with urine culture and susceptibility testing used particularly for complicated or recurrent infection. Common treatments include nitrofurantoin, which is reduced intracellularly to reactive intermediates that damage bacterial DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis via dihydrofolate reductase and dihydropteroate synthase; and fosfomycin, which inhibits

Name: Endomyometritis
Description: Endomyometritis is an acute or subacute infectious-inflammatory disorder involving both the endometrium and adjacent myometrium, most often occurring postpartum, postabortal, or after uterine instrumentation, and is usually polymicrobial rather than a primary genetic disease; common pathogens include Streptococcus agalactiae, Enterococcus faecalis, Escherichia coli, Gardnerella vaginalis, anaerobes such as Bacteroides spp., and occasionally Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis. Its pathobiology is driven by microbial invasion with activation of innate immune pathways, especially Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-kB, inflammasome-associated cytokines such as IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, and IL-6, neutrophil and macrophage recruitment, prostaglandin synthesis via COX enzymes, and matrix-remodeling mediators including MMPs; while no monogenic inheritance pattern is established, host susceptibility may be modified by immune-response variants in genes such as TLR4, NOD2, TNF, IL6, and MBL2, and by altered expression of inflammatory proteins including CRP and procalcitonin. Typical features are postpartum or postprocedural fever, uterine tenderness, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, foul-smelling lochia or vaginal discharge, abnormal bleeding, tachycardia, and leukocytosis, with severe cases progressing to bacteremia, pelvic abscess, myometrial necrosis, peritonitis, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, infertility, or sepsis. Subtypes are commonly categorized as postpartum, postabortal, postcesarean, or procedure-associated disease. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by CBC, inflammatory markers, blood or endometrial cultures when indicated, pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound to detect retained products or abscess, and CT or MRI in complicated cases; differential diagnosis includes retained products of conception and pelvic inflammatory disease. Treatment relies on broad-spectrum antibiotics such as clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, gentamicin, which binds the 30S ribosomal subunit causing mistranslation, and ampicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, with alternatives including metronidazole for anaerobic DNA damage and doxycycline for intracellular pathogens; common comorbidities and risk factors include cesarean delivery, prolonged labor,

Name: Miscarriage with sepsis
Description: Miscarriage with sepsis is a severe obstetric emergency, usually corresponding to septic abortion, in which spontaneous or induced pregnancy loss is complicated by ascending polymicrobial infection of the uterus and products of conception; it is not a Mendelian disorder, but host susceptibility may be influenced by immune and coagulation genes such as TLR4, NOD2, TNF, IL6, and thrombophilia-associated F5 Leiden and F2 G20210A variants, while microbial virulence factors and, in rare recurrent pregnancy-loss settings, fetal or parental chromosomal abnormalities also contribute. Pathobiology centers on pathogen recognition and dysregulated innate immune signaling through Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, inflammasome, complement, and cytokine pathways, with TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, prostaglandins, tissue factor, endothelial activation, and coagulation cascades driving uterine infection, systemic inflammatory response, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and shock. Typical pathogens include Escherichia coli, streptococci including group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Clostridium species, anaerobes such as Bacteroides, and mixed genital tract flora. Clinical findings include fever or hypothermia, pelvic or abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, vaginal bleeding, foul discharge, retained products, tachycardia, hypotension, leukocytosis or leukopenia, and signs of organ dysfunction. Major subtypes are spontaneous versus induced septic abortion, early versus late gestation, and uncomplicated uterine infection versus infection with bacteremia, pelvic abscess, or septic shock. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound for retained tissue, CBC, metabolic panel, lactate, coagulation studies, blood and cervical cultures, urinalysis, and when indicated imaging for perforation or abscess. Treatment requires urgent uterine evacuation and broad-spectrum antibiotics, commonly clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit and suppresses toxin production, gentamicin, a 30S aminoglycoside causing bacterial mistranslation, and ampicillin, a beta-lactam that inhibits cell-wall synthesis; alternatives include piperacillin-tazobactam or metronidazole, with fluids, vasopressors, and source control. Important complications and linked comorbidities include anemia, retained placenta, pelvic inflammatory disease,

Name: Vomiting as reason for care in pregnancy
Description: Vomiting as a reason for care in pregnancy most commonly reflects the spectrum from nausea and vomiting of pregnancy to hyperemesis gravidarum, a multifactorial, usually non-Mendelian gestational disorder characterized by persistent nausea, recurrent vomiting, dehydration, ketonuria, electrolyte disturbance, and weight loss, typically beginning in the first trimester; severe cases may present with orthostasis, tachycardia, elevated liver enzymes, thiamine deficiency, and rarely Wernicke encephalopathy. Its biology is strongly linked to placental and hormonal signaling, particularly GDF15-GFRAL/RET and IGFBP7 pathways, with contributions from hCG, estrogen, progesterone, thyroid signaling, gastric dysmotility, central emetic circuits involving serotonin 5-HT3, dopamine D2, histamine H1, muscarinic, and neurokinin pathways, and inflammatory or placental stress responses. Genetic susceptibility is best supported for maternal and fetal variation near GDF15 and IGFBP7, with representative reports also implicating hormone and taste/olfaction-related loci, although inheritance is generally complex rather than classic Mendelian. Important comorbidities and complications include dehydration, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, starvation ketosis, malnutrition, venous thromboembolism risk from immobility, depression/anxiety, transient hyperthyroidism, preeclampsia associations in some cohorts, and adverse fetal outcomes such as low birth weight when severe and prolonged. Clinical subtypes include mild nausea/vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum, often defined by intractable symptoms causing more than 5% prepregnancy weight loss and objective metabolic disturbance. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by urinalysis for ketones, serum electrolytes, renal and liver tests, thyroid studies when indicated, and obstetric ultrasonography to confirm intrauterine pregnancy and exclude molar or multiple gestation, while ruling out gastroenteritis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, appendicitis, and urinary infection. Common treatments include doxylamine-pyridoxine, combining H1 antagonism with vitamin B6-mediated neurotransmitter support, metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist with prokinetic 5-HT4 activity, ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist, and promethazine, an H1 antagonist with antidopaminergic effects; refractory cases may require IV fluids,

Name: Nocturnal Enuresis
Description: Nocturnal enuresis is a common childhood voiding disorder defined by intermittent involuntary urinary incontinence during sleep, usually diagnosed after age 5 years, and classified as primary or secondary, and as monosymptomatic or non-monosymptomatic depending on the presence of daytime lower urinary tract symptoms. Its pathobiology is multifactorial, involving delayed maturation of arousal circuits, nocturnal polyuria from impaired circadian arginine vasopressin secretion, reduced functional bladder capacity, and detrusor overactivity; implicated pathways include vasopressin V2 receptor–aquaporin water reabsorption signaling in the kidney, circadian clock regulation of urine production, autonomic and pontine micturition circuitry, and cholinergic muscarinic signaling in the bladder. Familial clustering is strong, often consistent with complex polygenic inheritance and occasionally autosomal dominant transmission with reduced penetrance; linkage signals have been reported at loci such as 13q, 12q, and 22q, and candidate genes include AVPR2, AQP2, KCNJ10, and loci influencing sleep/arousal and bladder function, although no single mutation explains most cases. Typical features are bedwetting during sleep, often with large-volume nocturnal urine loss, deep sleep, difficult arousal, urgency, frequency, constipation, or daytime incontinence in non-monosymptomatic forms. Common comorbidities include constipation, urinary tract infection, sleep-disordered breathing, ADHD, developmental delay, anxiety, and psychosocial distress; complications are mainly reduced self-esteem and persistent symptoms into adolescence. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history, voiding and stooling patterns, physical examination, urinalysis, bladder diary, and screening for constipation, diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, renal disease, and obstructive sleep apnea, with ultrasound or uroflow/postvoid residual reserved for selected cases. Standard treatments include desmopressin, a vasopressin V2 receptor agonist that reduces nocturnal urine production; enuresis alarms that condition arousal to bladder fullness; imipramine, which likely increases arousal threshold and alters bladder contractility; and antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin or tolterodine, which inhibit M3-mediated detrusor overactivity.

Name: Bipolar disorder in remission
Description: Bipolar disorder in remission (UMLS C0270425) denotes a chronic, episodic mood disorder currently lacking full syndromal mania, hypomania, or major depression, but with ongoing vulnerability to relapse, residual cognitive or sleep disturbance, and psychosocial impairment; core subtypes include bipolar I disorder, bipolar II disorder, cyclothymic disorder, and mixed-feature specifiers. Typical lifetime manifestations include manic symptoms such as elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, increased goal-directed activity, impulsivity, and psychosis, and depressive symptoms such as anhedonia, low mood, fatigue, guilt, suicidality, and impaired concentration. The disorder is highly heritable, usually polygenic with complex, non-Mendelian inheritance, with representative risk genes including CACNA1C, ANK3, ODZ4/TENM4, SYNE1, TRANK1, and circadian genes such as CLOCK and ARNTL; implicated proteins and pathways include L-type voltage-gated calcium channels, sodium-channel anchoring at the axon initial segment, glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission, GSK3/inositol signaling, BDNF-TrkB neurotrophic signaling, mitochondrial and inflammatory pathways, circadian rhythm regulation, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction. Common treatments used to maintain remission include lithium, which modulates second-messenger signaling including inositol monophosphatase and GSK3 inhibition; valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and affects histone deacetylase and sodium-channel function; lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-sensitive sodium channels and reduces glutamate release; and atypical antipsychotics such as quetiapine or olanzapine, which primarily antagonize dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Frequent comorbidities include anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, ADHD, migraine, obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and thyroid dysfunction, while complications include suicide risk, treatment nonadherence, cognitive decline, occupational dysfunction, and recurrence. Diagnosis remains clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria and longitudinal history, supported by mental status examination, collateral history, mood rating scales, and exclusion of secondary causes with targeted laboratory testing, toxicology, and, when indicated, neuroimaging.

Name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
Description: Generalized anxiety disorder (UMLS C0270549) is a common, chronic psychiatric disorder characterized by excessive, difficult-to-control worry across multiple domains for at least 6 months, accompanied by restlessness, fatigue, impaired concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance, often with autonomic symptoms such as palpitations or gastrointestinal distress; DSM-5 diagnosis is clinical, requiring functional impairment and exclusion of substance-, medication-, or medical illness–induced anxiety, while assessment commonly uses structured interview and scales such as GAD-7, with targeted laboratory testing, thyroid studies, ECG, or toxicology used to rule out mimics. GAD is multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with moderate heritability and polygenic risk involving serotonergic, catecholaminergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, and stress-response genes; representative associations include SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR, HTR1A, COMT Val158Met, MAOA, BDNF Val66Met, CRHR1, FKBP5, and GABRA2, although effect sizes are small and non-diagnostic. Relevant pathways include amygdala-prefrontal-hippocampal fear circuitry, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation with CRH and cortisol signaling, altered serotonin and norepinephrine transmission, reduced inhibitory GABA-A signaling, glutamatergic plasticity, and neurotrophic mechanisms involving BDNF. Common treatments include SSRIs such as escitalopram or sertraline, which inhibit the serotonin transporter; SNRIs such as venlafaxine or duloxetine, which block serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake; buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist; benzodiazepines such as lorazepam, positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors for short-term relief; and pregabalin, which binds the alpha2delta calcium-channel subunit to reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release. Frequent comorbidities include major depressive disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, insomnia, substance use disorders, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pain, and cardiovascular disease risk, while complications include impaired occupational and social functioning, suicidality, medication dependence with sedatives, and chronic symptom persistence.

Name: Seizure, Atonic
Description: Seizures are paroxysmal episodes of abnormal, excessive, and hypersynchronous neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex, occurring as acute symptomatic events or as part of epilepsy, and are broadly classified as focal, generalized, or unknown onset, with subtypes such as absence, tonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonic, and focal impaired-awareness seizures. Clinical manifestations include transient loss or alteration of consciousness, convulsions, staring spells, automatisms, sensory phenomena, autonomic symptoms, tongue biting, urinary incontinence, and postictal confusion or focal neurologic deficits. Pathobiology reflects imbalance between excitation and inhibition, especially glutamatergic and GABAergic signaling, involving voltage-gated sodium, potassium, and calcium channels, synaptic vesicle release, and mTOR-related network hyperexcitability; representative genetic contributors include SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNQ3, CACNA1H, GABRA1, GABRG2, STXBP1, DEPDC5, TSC1, and TSC2, with mutations causing channelopathies, synaptic dysfunction, or cortical malformations. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial, or de novo, as seen in generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus, Dravet syndrome, tuberous sclerosis complex, and some developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Common comorbidities and complications include developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, depression, anxiety, migraine, sleep disturbance, injury, aspiration, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Diagnosis is based on careful history and semiology, eyewitness accounts, neurologic examination, EEG or video-EEG demonstrating epileptiform discharges, brain MRI to detect structural lesions, and targeted metabolic, infectious, toxicologic, or genetic testing when indicated. Treatment commonly includes levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to modulate neurotransmitter release, valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and affects sodium and calcium channels, lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and glutamate release, as well as carbamazepine, phenytoin, benzodiazepines, and ethosuximide for selected seizure types.

Name: Stargardt Disease
Description: Stargardt disease (UMLS C0271093) is an inherited juvenile-to-adult onset macular dystrophy and the most common hereditary macular degeneration, characterized by progressive loss of central vision due to lipofuscin accumulation in retinal pigment epithelium and secondary photoreceptor degeneration; it is most often caused by biallelic ABCA4 mutations in the ATP-binding cassette transporter ABCA4, with representative variants such as p.Gly1961Glu and p.Ala1038Val, while phenocopies or overlapping subtypes include dominant STGD3 from ELOVL4 mutations and rarer PROM1- or PRPH2-associated disease. Pathobiologically, defective ABCA4-mediated clearance of all-trans-retinal derivatives in photoreceptor outer segments promotes formation of toxic bisretinoids such as A2E, driving the visual cycle/retinoid pathway, oxidative stress, complement and inflammatory signaling, lysosomal dysfunction, and retinal pigment epithelial apoptosis. Clinically, patients present with bilateral blurred central vision, reduced reading ability, dyschromatopsia, central scotomas, delayed dark adaptation, and sometimes photophobia, with funduscopic pisciform yellow-white flecks and macular atrophy; complications include geographic atrophy, severe legal blindness, depression, and occasional choroidal neovascularization. Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive with substantial allelic heterogeneity in ABCA4, though dominant forms occur in ELOVL4-related disease. Diagnosis relies on phenotype plus molecular confirmation, supported by best-corrected visual acuity, dilated fundus examination, fundus autofluorescence showing hyperautofluorescent flecks and hypoautofluorescent atrophy, OCT demonstrating outer retinal/RPE loss, fluorescein angiography with a dark choroid in some cases, visual fields, ERG for cone or cone-rod involvement, and genetic testing panels or sequencing. No therapy is definitively disease-modifying, but management commonly includes low-vision rehabilitation and treatment of complications; examples include anti-VEGF agents such as ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab for choroidal neovascularization by inhibiting VEGF-A signaling, while investigational approaches include visual-cycle modulators such as emixustat or deuterated vitamin A to reduce toxic bisretinoid formation.

Name: Ciliary block glaucoma
Description: Ciliary block glaucoma, also termed aqueous misdirection or malignant glaucoma, is an uncommon but vision-threatening secondary angle-closure disorder characterized by misdirection of aqueous humor posteriorly into or behind the vitreous, causing anterior displacement of the lens–iris diaphragm, uniform shallowing of the anterior chamber, elevated intraocular pressure, and often a myopic shift despite a patent iridotomy. It usually occurs after intraocular surgery, especially in anatomically predisposed eyes with short axial length, nanophthalmos, hyperopia, plateau iris configuration, or primary angle-closure glaucoma, and may complicate cataract extraction, filtering surgery, laser procedures, or occur rarely spontaneously. The disorder is primarily mechanical rather than a classic monogenic disease, and no single causal mutation is established, although genes influencing anterior-segment development and angle-closure susceptibility, including PLEKHA7, COL11A1, PCMTD1-ST18, and rare nanophthalmos genes such as MFRP, PRSS56, BEST1, and TMEM98, may contribute in selected patients; inheritance therefore follows the underlying ocular phenotype, often complex/polygenic and occasionally autosomal recessive in nanophthalmos. Relevant pathways involve aqueous humor dynamics, ciliary body-choroid expansion, vitreous permeability, and biomechanical interactions among the ciliary processes, zonules, lens, hyaloid face, prostaglandin-mediated uveoscleral outflow, and adrenergic control of aqueous production. Symptoms and signs include acute ocular pain, headache, blurred vision, redness, corneal edema, a diffusely shallow or flat anterior chamber centrally and peripherally, closed or narrow angles, and ocular hypertension. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by slit-lamp examination, gonioscopy, tonometry, ultrasound biomicroscopy, B-scan ultrasonography, and anterior-segment OCT to exclude pupillary block, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, or choroidal effusion. Treatment commonly includes atropine to produce cycloplegia and posterior lens displacement, timolol and acetazolamide to reduce aqueous production, hyperosmotics such as mannitol to lower vitreous volume, and often laser hyaloidotomy/capsulotomy or pars plana vitrectomy. Complications include refractory glaucoma, peripheral anterior synechiae, optic neuropathy, and permanent vision loss.

Name: AOM - Acute otitis media
Description: Acute otitis media (AOM; UMLS C0271429) is an acute infectious and inflammatory disorder of the middle ear, usually following viral upper respiratory infection and eustachian tube dysfunction, characterized by rapid onset otalgia, fever, irritability, conductive hearing reduction, and otoscopic evidence of a bulging, erythematous, poorly mobile tympanic membrane with middle-ear effusion. Major pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis, and host susceptibility has genetic contributions involving innate and mucosal immune genes such as TLR4, TLR2, CD14, cytokine loci including IL6, IL10, TNF, and mucin-related genes; variants affecting FBXO11 and TGIF1 have also been linked to recurrent or chronic otitis phenotypes, although AOM is not usually a Mendelian disease and inheritance is typically complex, polygenic, and influenced by environmental exposures. Relevant pathways include Toll-like receptor/NF-κB signaling, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-8 inflammatory cascades, leukocyte recruitment, mucin production, and biofilm-associated responses in the nasopharynx and middle ear. Clinical subtypes include sporadic AOM, recurrent AOM, and AOM with perforation or otorrhea. Diagnosis is clinical, based on acute symptoms plus objective middle-ear effusion and inflammation, supported by pneumatic otoscopy and tympanometry; culture of otorrhea or, rarely, tympanocentesis is reserved for severe, refractory, or immunocompromised cases. First-line treatment commonly includes amoxicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation; amoxicillin-clavulanate, which adds beta-lactamase inhibition; and ceftriaxone, a parenteral cephalosporin blocking cell-wall synthesis, while azithromycin inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit in selected cases, and ibuprofen or acetaminophen provide symptomatic relief via cyclooxygenase inhibition or central analgesic effects. Important comorbidities and complications include viral respiratory infection, allergic rhinitis, adenoid hypertrophy, asthma, recurrent AOM, chronic otitis media with effusion, tympanic membrane perforation, mastoiditis, and rarely intracranial spread.

Name: Female hypogonadism syndrome
Description: Female hypogonadism syndrome is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by deficient ovarian sex-steroid production with impaired folliculogenesis or ovulation, arising from primary ovarian failure (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) or hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism). Genetic contributors include FMR1 premutations, Turner syndrome with X-chromosome monosomy or mosaicism, and pathogenic variants in BMP15, NOBOX, FOXL2, FIGLA, GDF9, FSHR, LHCGR, ESR1, NR5A1, AIRE, and steroidogenic genes such as CYP17A1 and HSD17B3; congenital hypogonadotropic forms may involve KAL1/ANOS1, FGFR1, GNRHR, KISS1R, TAC3, TACR3, and LEP/LEPR. Pathobiology centers on disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, including GnRH pulsatility, pituitary LH and FSH secretion, FSHR/LHCGR signaling in granulosa and theca cells, steroidogenesis via STAR, CYP11A1, CYP19A1, and aromatase activity, and modulatory pathways such as kisspeptin, inhibin/activin, AMH, and occasionally autoimmune ovarian injury. Clinical manifestations include delayed puberty, primary or secondary amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea, infertility, anovulation, low libido, vaginal dryness, hot flashes, sleep and mood disturbance, and reduced bone mineral density; complications include osteoporosis, cardiovascular risk, metabolic dysfunction, and in some etiologies autoimmune endocrinopathies. Subtypes include congenital versus acquired, isolated versus syndromic, and functional forms such as hypothalamic amenorrhea related to stress, weight loss, or excessive exercise. Inheritance may be X-linked, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, chromosomal, or mitochondrial depending on cause. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, repeated estradiol with LH/FSH, prolactin and TSH, pregnancy exclusion, AMH and inhibin B when useful, pelvic ultrasound, pituitary MRI if central disease is suspected, karyotype and targeted or panel genetic testing, and bone density assessment. Treatment commonly includes estradiol replacement to restore secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone, cyclic progesterone to prevent endometrial hyperplasia in women with a uterus,

Name: Hypogonadism, Hypogonadotropic
