Description: Hypogonadism is a clinical syndrome of deficient gonadal function causing impaired sex steroid production, gametogenesis, or both, and is classically divided into primary hypergonadotropic hypogonadism from testicular or ovarian failure and secondary/central hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, with congenital and acquired forms in both sexes. Genetic causes include defects in ANOS1/KAL1, FGFR1, FGF8, GNRHR, KISS1R, TAC3, TACR3, LEP, LEPR, PROP1, HESX1, DAX1/NR0B1, and CHD7 in congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism/Kallmann syndrome, and AR, Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY, CYP17A1, HSD17B3, SRD5A2, LHCGR, FSHR, and Turner syndrome in primary gonadal failure; inheritance may be X-linked, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, chromosomal, or sporadic. Key pathways involve hypothalamic kisspeptin-neurokinin B-GnRH pulsatility, pituitary LH/FSH secretion, gonadal steroidogenesis via StAR, CYP11A1, CYP17A1, aromatase/CYP19A1, androgen receptor and estrogen receptor signaling, inhibin-activin feedback, and Sertoli/Leydig or granulosa/theca cell function. Typical manifestations include delayed or absent puberty, infertility, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, amenorrhea, hot flashes, sparse body hair, gynecomastia, low muscle mass, fatigue, anemia, and reduced bone density. Diagnosis relies on symptoms plus repeatedly low morning total testosterone in men or low estradiol with menstrual dysfunction in women, interpreted with LH and FSH to distinguish primary from secondary disease, and supported by semen analysis, prolactin, iron studies, pituitary and thyroid testing, karyotype or targeted genetic testing, olfactory assessment, pelvic or testicular imaging, pituitary MRI, and bone densitometry. Common treatments include testosterone replacement, which activates androgen receptors; transdermal or injectable estradiol with cyclic progesterone in women, restoring estrogen receptor signaling and endometrial protection; gonadotropins such as hCG with FSH or pulsatile GnRH, which stimulate Leydig/Sertoli

Name: Hypercalcemia due to hyperthyroidism
Description: Hypercalcemia due to hyperthyroidism is a usually mild, PTH-independent metabolic complication of thyrotoxicosis in which excess thyroid hormone accelerates high-turnover bone resorption and, less prominently, intestinal calcium handling, leading to elevated serum calcium with suppressed parathyroid hormone; it is most often seen in Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, or toxic adenoma. Key molecular contributors include thyroid hormone receptor signaling, especially TRβ-mediated transcriptional effects, increased osteoclast activation through the RANK/RANKL/OPG axis, heightened sympathetic and cAMP signaling downstream of the TSH receptor, and, in autoimmune Graves disease, stimulatory TSHR antibodies; representative genetic associations therefore include TSHR, GNAS in autonomous nodules, and immune susceptibility genes such as HLA-DRB1, CTLA4, PTPN22, and TG or TPO-related autoimmunity backgrounds, although the hypercalcemia itself is generally acquired rather than inherited. Clinical features combine symptoms of thyrotoxicosis and hypercalcemia, including weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, proximal myopathy, polyuria, polydipsia, constipation, dehydration, and occasionally confusion or arrhythmia. Complications include osteoporosis, accelerated bone loss, fractures, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, nephrolithiasis, and rarely hypercalcemic crisis. Diagnosis rests on elevated calcium, suppressed or low-normal PTH, biochemical hyperthyroidism with low TSH and elevated free T4 and/or T3, exclusion of primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy, and etiologic testing with TSH-receptor antibodies, radioactive iodine uptake, thyroid scintigraphy, ultrasound, ECG, renal function, and bone density assessment when indicated. Treatment targets the thyrotoxicosis and calcium excess: methimazole or propylthiouracil inhibit thyroid peroxidase, radioactive iodine ablates hyperfunctioning tissue, beta-blockers such as propranolol provide adrenergic control and reduce peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, while acute significant hypercalcemia is managed with IV saline, calcitonin to inhibit osteoclasts, and bisphosphonates such as pamidronate or zoledronic acid to suppress bone resorption.

Name: Anemia of chronic renal failure
Description: Anemia of chronic renal failure, more broadly the anemia of chronic kidney disease, is typically a normocytic, normochromic hypoproliferative anemia caused primarily by inadequate renal erythropoietin production from peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells as nephron mass declines, compounded by inflammation-driven iron restriction, shortened erythrocyte survival, and occasional folate deficiency, blood loss, or marrow suppression. Key molecular features include reduced EPO expression, dysregulation of the hypoxia-inducible factor pathway involving HIF1A, HIF2A/EPAS1, EGLN prolyl hydroxylases, VHL, and the EPO receptor/JAK2-STAT5 axis, plus increased IL6-induced hepatic hepcidin (HAMP), which suppresses ferroportin-mediated iron export; iron handling genes and proteins such as HFE, HJV, TFR2, SLC40A1, transferrin, ferritin, and TMPRSS6 may modify severity, while hereditary nephropathies causing CKD, including PKD1/PKD2 or COL4A5-related disease, provide indirect genetic susceptibility rather than a classic inherited anemia pattern. Patients commonly present with fatigue, exertional dyspnea, pallor, reduced exercise tolerance, cognitive slowing, dizziness, tachycardia, and left ventricular hypertrophy, and the condition is linked to CKD complications including cardiovascular disease, heart failure, dialysis dependence, secondary hyperparathyroidism, malnutrition-inflammation syndrome, and increased transfusion burden. Subtypes are often stratified by dialysis status, iron deficiency, ESA responsiveness, or severity. Diagnosis rests on CKD with decreased hemoglobin, usually less than 13 g/dL in men or 12 g/dL in women, low reticulocyte response, CBC indices, ferritin and transferrin saturation, reticulocyte hemoglobin content, B12/folate testing, inflammatory markers, and exclusion of bleeding or hemolysis. Treatment commonly includes epoetin alfa or darbepoetin alfa, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents that activate EPO receptors; iron supplementation such as intravenous iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose to restore available iron; and HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors such as roxadustat, which stabilize HIF and increase endogenous EPO while improving iron utilization.

Name: Thrombocytopenia due to platelet alloimmunization
Description: Thrombocytopenia due to platelet alloimmunization is an immune-mediated disorder in which exposure to non-self platelet antigens, most classically during pregnancy or after transfusion, induces maternal or recipient IgG alloantibodies that opsonize platelets and accelerate Fc gamma receptor–mediated splenic and hepatic clearance, sometimes with complement participation; the major molecular targets are human platelet antigens on platelet glycoproteins, especially HPA-1a caused by the ITGB3 Leu33Pro polymorphism in integrin beta-3 on the GPIIb/IIIa complex, but also variants in ITGA2B, GP1BA, GP1BB, and CD109, with occasional contribution from anti-HLA class I antibodies. Clinically, this entity includes fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia and post-transfusion platelet refractoriness/alloimmune thrombocytopenia, presenting with isolated severe thrombocytopenia, petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding, and in severe fetal or neonatal cases intracranial hemorrhage and neurologic sequelae. It is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion, but genetic susceptibility reflects parental antigen mismatch and maternal HLA background, particularly HLA-DRB3*01:01 in anti-HPA-1a disease. Key pathobiologic pathways involve antigen presentation by maternal APCs, T-cell help to B cells, IgG production, placental FcRn-mediated transfer, and reticuloendothelial phagocytosis of antibody-coated platelets. Important complications and associations include anemia from bleeding, prematurity, hydrocephalus after hemorrhage, and coexistence with other causes of thrombocytopenia that must be excluded, such as sepsis, DIC, TTP, HELLP, and immune thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis relies on thrombocytopenia in the appropriate pregnancy or transfusion setting, platelet antibody testing, maternal/paternal or donor/recipient HPA genotyping or phenotyping, cross-matching, and exclusion of alternative etiologies; fetal imaging may assess hemorrhage. Treatment commonly includes IVIG, which saturates Fc receptors and modulates antibody-mediated clearance, corticosteroids, which suppress antibody production and macrophage activity, and transfusion of antigen-negative or washed maternal/HPA-compatible platelets; adjuncts may include plasma exchange or recombinant factor VIIa for refractory bleeding.

Name: Chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura
Description: Chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, now more commonly termed chronic immune thrombocytopenia, is an acquired autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia persisting for more than 12 months due to increased platelet destruction and impaired megakaryopoiesis. Its pathobiology centers on loss of immune tolerance with IgG autoantibodies, classically against platelet glycoproteins GPIIb/IIIa, GPIb/IX, and less often GPV, promoting Fc gamma receptor-mediated splenic macrophage clearance, complement activation, and T-cell dysregulation involving Th1/Th17 polarization, reduced regulatory T cells, cytotoxic CD8+ lymphocytes, B-cell activating factor, SYK- and BTK-dependent B-cell/Fc receptor signaling, and the thrombopoietin-MPL-JAK2-STAT pathway governing platelet production. Although usually non-Mendelian and sporadic, genetic susceptibility is supported by HLA class II associations and immune-regulatory variants such as FCGR2A, FCGR3A, CTLA4, TNFA, IL10, and rare familial thrombocytopenia genes including ANKRD26, ETV6, RUNX1, and MPL that are important in the differential diagnosis. Patients typically present with petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, easy bruising, and rarely life-threatening intracranial or gastrointestinal hemorrhage; common complications include iron deficiency from chronic blood loss, treatment toxicity, and associations with systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease, common variable immunodeficiency, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, lymphomas, HIV, hepatitis C, and Helicobacter pylori infection. Subtypes are usually categorized as newly diagnosed, persistent, or chronic, and as primary versus secondary immune thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion: isolated low platelet count on CBC, normal or increased marrow megakaryocytes when marrow is examined, peripheral smear excluding pseudothrombocytopenia or microangiopathy, and targeted testing for secondary causes, autoimmunity, viral infection, and occasionally antiplatelet antibodies. Treatment commonly includes corticosteroids, which broadly suppress autoantibody production and macrophage phagocytosis, intravenous immunoglobulin, which blocks Fc receptor-mediated platelet clearance, rituximab, which depletes CD20+

Name: Acute bacterial peritonitis (disorder)
Description: Acute bacterial peritonitis is an acute, usually nonhereditary infection-driven inflammation of the peritoneal cavity that most often occurs as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis with ascites or as secondary peritonitis after perforation, ischemia, appendicitis, diverticulitis, biliary or gynecologic infection, trauma, or peritoneal dialysis; primary cases are classically monomicrobial with enteric organisms such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or streptococci, whereas secondary disease is often polymicrobial and may include anaerobes. Its pathobiology is dominated by innate immune activation through pattern-recognition pathways, especially LPS-TLR4/CD14-MYD88-NF-κB signaling, inflammasome and complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokines including TNF, IL1B, IL6, CXCL8, and IFNG; representative host susceptibility factors described in related settings include TLR2/TLR4, NOD2, TNF, IL6, MBL2, and complement gene variants, although no Mendelian inheritance pattern defines the disorder. Typical manifestations are diffuse or localized abdominal pain and tenderness, guarding, rebound, fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, ileus, altered mental status, hypotension, and sepsis. Important comorbidities and complications include cirrhosis, portal hypertension, chronic liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, diabetes, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, and peritoneal dialysis, with progression to bacteremia, septic shock, hepatorenal syndrome, abscess, adhesions, multiorgan failure, and death. Diagnosis relies on urgent paracentesis or operative/peritoneal fluid sampling showing neutrophilic ascites, classically a polymorphonuclear count of at least 250 cells/µL for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, plus Gram stain and culture, blood cultures, CBC, CRP, lactate, renal and liver tests, and imaging such as ultrasound or CT to identify perforation or abscess. Treatment commonly includes cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, piperacillin-tazobactam, a β-lactam plus β-lactamase inhibitor with broad gram-negative and anaerobic coverage, or meropenem, a carbapenem cell

Name: Acute bacterial epiglottitis
Description: Acute bacterial epiglottitis is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening supraglottic infection and cellulitis of the epiglottis and adjacent aryepiglottic structures, classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b but also by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Staphylococcus aureus, in which host susceptibility is influenced more by immune and inflammatory biology than by Mendelian inheritance; representative genetic factors linked to severe invasive bacterial infection include variants affecting humoral or innate immunity such as TLR4, MYD88, IRAK4, NFKBIA, and complement pathway genes, while Hib virulence is strongly related to the capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis bexA-bexD locus and outer-membrane proteins rather than a single disease-defining host mutation. Pathobiologically, bacterial adherence and invasion trigger Toll-like receptor and NF-kB signaling, with IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and intense mucosal edema causing critical upper-airway narrowing. Patients typically present with abrupt fever, severe sore throat, odynophagia, dysphagia, muffled voice, drooling, stridor, tachypnea, tripod positioning, and anxiety, often with less dramatic oropharyngeal findings than expected; major complications include acute airway obstruction, respiratory failure, sepsis, pneumonia, cervical soft-tissue infection, and rarely abscess. Clinical subtypes include pediatric versus adult disease and Hib versus non-Hib bacterial epiglottitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical with urgent airway assessment, supported by flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showing an edematous cherry-red epiglottis; lateral neck radiography may show the thumb sign, and blood cultures, epiglottic cultures when safely obtained, CBC, inflammatory markers, and pulse oximetry help define etiology and severity. Treatment centers on airway stabilization plus empiric intravenous antibiotics such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, and vancomycin, a glycopeptide that blocks peptidoglycan polymerization, with ampicillin-sulbactam as another common option combining a beta-lactam with beta-lactamase inhibition; corticosteroids are sometimes added despite limited evidence.

Name: Acute bacterial sinusitis
Description: Acute bacterial sinusitis (UMLS C0275556) is an acute pyogenic infection of the paranasal sinus mucosa, usually arising after viral upper respiratory infection or allergic inflammation causes ostial obstruction and impaired mucociliary clearance; the main bacterial pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Molecularly, host susceptibility is linked more to innate-defense and mucociliary genes than to a Mendelian sinusitis gene, with representative associations involving CFTR dysfunction in cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia genes such as DNAH5 and DNAI1, and immune pathways involving TLR2, TLR4, NFKB, IL1B, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, and mucin genes including MUC5AC, which drive neutrophilic inflammation, epithelial barrier activation, biofilm formation, and impaired mucus transport. It is typically sporadic rather than inherited, although inherited disorders that impair airway defense predispose strongly. Clinically, patients develop purulent nasal drainage, nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, maxillary toothache, hyposmia, fever, cough, and sometimes headache; common subtypes include acute maxillary, ethmoidal, frontal, and sphenoidal sinusitis, and recurrent acute bacterial sinusitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by persistent symptoms for more than 10 days without improvement, severe fever with purulent discharge or facial pain for at least 3 to 4 consecutive days, or worsening after initial improvement; nasal endoscopy, sinus CT when complications or alternative diagnoses are suspected, and rarely sinus aspirate culture in refractory or immunocompromised cases are used. Standard treatment includes amoxicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis; amoxicillin-clavulanate, which adds beta-lactamase inhibition; doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor; and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Important comorbidities include allergic rhinitis, asthma, viral URI, dental infection, immunodeficiency, cystic fibrosis, and ciliary dyskinesia; complications include chronic rhinosinusitis, orbital cellulitis or abscess, osteomyelitis, meningitis, epidural or brain abscess, and cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Name: Pulmonary actinomycosis
Description: Pulmonary actinomycosis (UMLS C0275566) is a chronic, suppurative and granulomatous thoracic infection caused most often by Actinomyces israelii, with A. gerencseriae, A. meyeri, and A. odontolyticus as representative species, arising from aspiration of oropharyngeal flora rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder; accordingly, no disease-specific germline inheritance pattern is established, although host susceptibility may be influenced by immune-related pathways and defects affecting neutrophil and macrophage function, including IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6, TLR2/TLR4–NF-κB signaling, complement, and rare immunodeficiency-associated genes in selected patients. The disease typically presents as a subacute to indolent pulmonary infiltrative mass or cavitary process with fever, chronic cough, purulent sputum, chest pain, weight loss, fatigue, dyspnea, and hemoptysis, and may mimic lung cancer, tuberculosis, or nocardiosis; recognized patterns include parenchymal pulmonary disease, endobronchial disease, and extension to pleura or chest wall with sinus tract formation. Common comorbidities and predisposing conditions include poor dentition, alcohol use disorder, diabetes mellitus, chronic lung disease such as COPD or bronchiectasis, malignancy, aspiration risk, and immunosuppression, while complications include necrotizing pneumonia, abscess, empyema, rib or vertebral osteomyelitis, mediastinal spread, and bronchopleural fistula. Diagnosis relies on compatible radiology, usually consolidation, mass-like lesions, cavitation or pleural involvement, plus microbiologic or histopathologic confirmation by anaerobic culture or tissue biopsy showing branching filamentous Gram-positive organisms and sulfur granules, with species identification increasingly supported by 16S rRNA sequencing or MALDI-TOF; blood tests are nonspecific. Standard therapy is prolonged high-dose penicillin G followed by oral amoxicillin, both β-lactams that inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins; alternatives include doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit, clindamycin, which inhibits 50S-mediated protein synthesis, and ceftriaxone, another β-lactam, with drainage or surgical resection reserved for complicated or refractory disease.

Name: Acute gonococcal urethritis
Description: Acute gonococcal urethritis is an acute sexually transmitted mucosal infection of the urethra caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, usually presenting as uncomplicated anterior urethritis but also occurring as asymptomatic infection, persistent or recurrent urethritis, and coinfection-associated disease, particularly with Chlamydia trachomatis. Typical manifestations include dysuria, urethral pruritus, and a profuse purulent or mucopurulent urethral discharge, with examination showing urethral inflammation and, in some cases, epididymal tenderness or prostatitis; untreated infection may lead to epididymitis, periurethral abscess, urethral stricture, infertility, and dissemination causing septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, or dermatitis, and is epidemiologically linked to increased HIV acquisition and transmission. Pathobiology is driven mainly by bacterial rather than host inheritance factors: important gonococcal determinants include type IV pili encoded by pil genes, opacity proteins Opa, porin PorB, lipooligosaccharide biosynthesis genes, and iron-acquisition proteins, while antimicrobial resistance commonly involves penA mosaic variants encoding altered PBP2, mtrR and the MtrCDE efflux system, porB mutations, ponA, gyrA and parC for fluoroquinolone resistance, and 23S rRNA mutations affecting macrolide susceptibility. Host signaling involves epithelial adherence and invasion with TLR2/TLR4 activation, NF-kB and MAPK signaling, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-alpha, neutrophil recruitment, complement interactions, and IgA protease-mediated immune evasion; host susceptibility is not classically Mendelian, though variation in complement components and innate immune responses may influence risk. Diagnosis rests on compatible symptoms plus microbiologic confirmation, preferably nucleic acid amplification testing on first-catch urine or urethral swab, with Gram stain in symptomatic men showing intracellular gram-negative diplococci, and culture on selective media with susceptibility testing when resistance, treatment failure, or public health surveillance is relevant. Standard therapy includes ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis, cefixime when used as an alternative oral cephalosporin with the same mechanism, and doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor added when chlamydial coinfection has

Name: Gonorrhea of rectum
Description: Gonorrhea of the rectum is a sexually transmitted mucosal infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, usually acquired through receptive anal intercourse or contiguous spread, and may present as asymptomatic carriage or as acute proctitis with rectal pain, purulent or mucoid discharge, pruritus, tenesmus, bleeding, dyschezia, and erythematous friable anorectal mucosa. Disease forms are commonly described as uncomplicated rectal gonorrhea versus disseminated infection, and coinfection with urogenital or pharyngeal gonorrhea is frequent. Pathogenesis is driven largely by bacterial rather than host inherited genetics: key gonococcal virulence determinants include type IV pili encoded by pil genes, Opa outer-membrane adhesins, PorB porin, lipooligosaccharide, and the MtrCDE efflux pump regulated by mtrR; antimicrobial resistance can involve penA mosaic alleles affecting penicillin-binding protein 2, gyrA/parC mutations for fluoroquinolone resistance, 23S rRNA mutations for macrolide resistance, and penB/ponA changes. Host innate immune pathways implicated include TLR2/TLR4 recognition, NF-kB activation, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-alpha signaling, neutrophil recruitment, complement interactions, and CEACAM-mediated epithelial adherence; there is no Mendelian inheritance pattern, though susceptibility may be modified by host immune and complement-related variation. Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion plus microbiologic confirmation, with nucleic acid amplification testing of rectal swabs preferred, culture on selective media important for antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and Gram stain less sensitive than at urethral sites. Standard therapy is ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins; doxycycline is added when Chlamydia trachomatis has not been excluded and acts by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit; azithromycin, a 50S macrolide inhibitor formerly used in dual therapy, and ciprofloxacin, a DNA gyrase/topoisomerase inhibitor used only for susceptible isolates, are representative alternatives. Important comorbidities and complications include HIV infection, other STIs, pelvic inflammatory disease from concurrent cervical infection, epididymitis, disseminated gonococcal infection with arthritis-dermatitis syndrome,

Name: Pneumococcal pharyngitis
Description: Pneumococcal pharyngitis is an acute bacterial infection of the oropharynx caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, usually presenting as a localized mucosal infection but occasionally occurring as part of broader pneumococcal upper respiratory tract disease; patients typically develop sore throat, odynophagia, fever, pharyngeal erythema, tonsillar exudate, cervical lymphadenopathy, and sometimes concurrent otitis media, sinusitis, or cough. Its biology is driven primarily by microbial rather than host Mendelian genetics: major pneumococcal virulence determinants include the capsular polysaccharide synthesis cps locus, pneumolysin encoded by ply, autolysin lytA, surface adhesins such as pspA and pspC, neuraminidases nanA/nanB, and penicillin-binding proteins pbp1a, pbp2x, and pbp2b that mediate beta-lactam resistance; macrolide resistance commonly involves ermB or mefA/E. Relevant host-pathogen pathways include epithelial adherence and colonization, Toll-like receptor 2 and TLR4 signaling, MyD88–NF-kappaB activation, inflammasome engagement, complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, and IgA1 protease-mediated evasion of mucosal immunity. There is no classic inheritance pattern for the disease itself, but susceptibility is influenced by host immune genetics and comorbid states such as humoral immunodeficiency, asplenia, HIV infection, chronic lung disease, diabetes, smoking, and extremes of age. Important complications include peritonsillar extension, cervical adenitis, bacteremia, pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis media, and rarely meningitis or sepsis. Subtypes are not sharply defined clinically, but cases may be uncomplicated mucosal disease, recurrent infection, or infection due to antibiotic-resistant strains. Diagnosis relies on clinical pharyngitis assessment plus microbiologic confirmation by throat culture or PCR identifying S. pneumoniae, with susceptibility testing when needed; blood cultures are reserved for invasive disease. Common treatments include penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall transpeptidases; ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam with similar cell-wall inhibition; and macrolides such as azithromycin, which inhibit 50S ribosomal protein synthesis, although resistance patterns must guide therapy.

Name: Staphylococcal tonsillitis
Description: Staphylococcal tonsillitis (UMLS C0275793) is an acute or recurrent bacterial infection of the palatine tonsils, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-susceptible and occasionally methicillin-resistant strains, producing localized mucosal inflammation and sometimes suppurative disease. Bacterial virulence determinants commonly implicated include surface adhesins and biofilm-related proteins such as fibronectin-binding proteins and clumping factors, toxins including alpha-hemolysin, Panton-Valentine leukocidin in selected strains, and mecA-mediated altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a in MRSA; host susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with innate immune components such as TLR2, NOD2, IL1B, IL6, TNF, DEFB1, and HLA-linked variation influencing colonization, inflammatory tone, and recurrence. Relevant pathways include TLR2/MyD88/NF-kB signaling, inflammasome activation, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and cytokine networks centered on IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha. Clinical features typically include sore throat, odynophagia, fever, tonsillar erythema and swelling, purulent exudates, halitosis, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and occasionally dysphonia or referred otalgia; subtypes include acute, recurrent, chronic, exudative, ulcerative, and abscess-forming disease. Diagnosis is based on compatible pharyngotonsillar findings plus microbiologic confirmation when needed by throat swab culture, Gram stain, rapid molecular tests for S. aureus or mecA/MRSA targets, and selective susceptibility testing; CBC and inflammatory markers may support severity assessment, while imaging is reserved for suspected deep neck extension. Treatment commonly includes antistaphylococcal beta-lactams such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin, which inhibit cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins, clindamycin, which blocks 50S ribosomal protein synthesis and suppresses toxin production, and for resistant disease vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala to inhibit cell-wall synthesis; linezolid may be used in selected MRSA cases by inhibiting 50S initiation complex formation. Important comorbidities and complications include chronic tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess,

Name: Streptococcal tonsillitis
Description: Streptococcal tonsillitis (UMLS C0275804) is an acute infectious inflammation of the palatine tonsils most commonly caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and is best regarded as a non-Mendelian host–pathogen disease in which bacterial virulence determinants such as the emm gene encoding M protein, streptolysins O and S, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins SpeA/SpeC, hyaluronic acid capsule synthase hasA, and C5a peptidase ScpA interact with host immune pathways including Toll-like receptor–NF-kappaB signaling, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and superantigen-driven T-cell cytokine responses involving IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma. Host susceptibility is influenced by complex genetic factors rather than a simple inheritance pattern, with representative associations reported for HLA class II alleles and innate immune genes such as TLRs, TNF, IL6, and MBL2, potentially affecting recurrence and post-streptococcal sequelae. Clinically it presents with abrupt sore throat, fever, odynophagia, tonsillar erythema and exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, halitosis, palatal petechiae, and sometimes scarlatiniform rash; subtypes include acute, recurrent, exudative, and suppurative disease. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical findings, Centor or McIsaac criteria, rapid streptococcal antigen detection, and confirmatory throat culture, with nucleic acid amplification tests used in some settings; inflammatory markers are nonspecific. First-line treatment is penicillin or amoxicillin, beta-lactams that inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking by binding penicillin-binding proteins; alternatives include cephalexin with the same basic mechanism, azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis, and clindamycin, which also targets the 50S subunit and suppresses toxin production. Important complications and linked conditions include peritonsillar abscess, cervical adenitis, otitis media, sinusitis, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis,

Name: Latent early syphilis
Description: Latent early syphilis (UMLS C0275842) is an early, noncongenital stage of infection by the spirochete Treponema pallidum in which patients are seroreactive but lack clinical signs of primary or secondary syphilis at the time of assessment; it is usually defined as latent infection acquired within the preceding year and is classified within early latent versus late latent/unknown-duration disease. The disorder is infectious rather than inherited, and no host Mendelian genetic cause is established, although variability in innate and adaptive immune response genes and HLA background may influence susceptibility or serologic response; pathogen factors include T. pallidum outer membrane and adhesin-related proteins such as TpN15, TpN17, TpN47, and TprK antigenic variation. Pathobiology centers on spirochetal dissemination, endothelial attachment, and immune evasion, with activation of macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells through Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB, and Th1 cytokine pathways including TNF-α, IFN-γ, and IL-6. Patients are often asymptomatic, though a history of recent chancre, rash, mucous patches, condyloma lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, or alopecia may be elicited. Major comorbidities and complications include HIV coinfection, other sexually transmitted infections, neurosyphilis, ocular or otic syphilis, relapse to secondary syphilis, and vertical transmission in pregnancy causing congenital syphilis. Diagnosis relies on compatible exposure history and serology, typically a reactive nontreponemal test such as RPR or VDRL with confirmatory treponemal testing by FTA-ABS, TP-PA, or EIA/CIA, with staging based on documented seroconversion, a fourfold titer rise, recent symptoms, or known exposure; CSF VDRL and cell count/protein assessment are reserved for neurologic, ocular, or otic involvement. Standard therapy is benzathine penicillin G, a β-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking, while doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit, and ceftriaxone, a cephalosporin β-lactam with cell-wall inhibition, are alternatives in selected penicillin-allergic nonpregnant patients.

Name: Acute tuberculosis
Description: Acute tuberculosis (UMLS C0275959) is an active infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, most often presenting as primary progressive pulmonary infection or acute disseminated/miliary disease, and is characterized by granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis driven by macrophage–T cell interactions. Host susceptibility has important genetic components rather than simple Mendelian inheritance in most cases, with associations involving IL12B, IL12RB1, IFNGR1, IFNGR2, STAT1, TLR2, SLC11A1/NRAMP1, VDR, HLA class II alleles, and TNF-related pathways; rare monogenic defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ axis can confer marked vulnerability to mycobacterial infection. Key pathogenic pathways include TLR2/4 and NOD-like receptor sensing, macrophage phagolysosomal control, autophagy, vitamin D–dependent antimicrobial responses, TNF-α and IFN-γ signaling, Th1 polarization, granuloma formation, and immune-evasion mechanisms that permit intracellular persistence. Typical symptoms and signs include fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, persistent cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and in disseminated disease hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, meningismus, or sepsis-like illness. Major forms include pulmonary, extrapulmonary, miliary/disseminated, primary, and reactivation tuberculosis. Common comorbidities and risk modifiers include HIV/AIDS, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, silicosis, chronic kidney disease, alcoholism, smoking, and anti-TNF or corticosteroid therapy; complications include cavitation, massive hemoptysis, pleural effusion, respiratory failure, meningitis, pericarditis, vertebral osteomyelitis, adrenal involvement, and death. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical-radiologic findings, chest radiography or CT, microbiologic confirmation by sputum acid-fast smear, mycobacterial culture, and nucleic acid amplification testing such as Xpert MTB/RIF, with tuberculin skin test or interferon-γ release assay supporting infection status and biopsy showing necrotizing granulomas in extrapulmonary disease. Standard treatment uses isoniazid, which inhibits mycolic acid synthesis via KatG-activated InhA targeting; rifampin,

Name: Infection by Campylobacter fetus
Description: Infection by Campylobacter fetus is an acquired zoonotic bacterial disease, usually caused by C. fetus subsp. fetus and less often C. fetus subsp. venerealis, characterized by invasive gastrointestinal and systemic infection with tropism for the vascular endothelium; major virulence determinants include the surface-layer proteins encoded by sapA/sapB and related sap loci that mediate serum resistance and antigenic variation, lipooligosaccharide biosynthesis genes, flagellar proteins such as FlaA/FlaB, and adhesins including CadF, while host susceptibility is influenced more by immune status than by Mendelian inheritance, although defects in humoral immunity, hypogammaglobulinemia, complement dysfunction, and immunosuppressive states increase risk. Pathobiology centers on motility, epithelial adherence, complement evasion, and induction of innate immune signaling through TLR4/TLR2, NF-κB, IL-8, TNF-α, and neutrophil-rich inflammation, with possible bacteremic spread to endovascular sites. Typical manifestations include fever, diarrhea that may be bloody, abdominal pain, nausea, malaise, and in invasive disease, bacteremia, cellulitis, septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, mycotic aneurysm, meningitis, osteoarticular infection, or pregnancy-associated fetal loss. Important comorbidities include liver disease, diabetes, malignancy, HIV infection, advanced age, prosthetic vascular grafts, and other causes of immunocompromise. Diagnosis relies on blood or stool culture under microaerophilic conditions with species identification by biochemical methods, MALDI-TOF, or PCR/16S rRNA sequencing, supported by susceptibility testing because resistance can occur. Treatment typically uses macrolides such as azithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit; fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, which impair 30S-mediated protein synthesis; and often carbapenems or beta-lactams for severe bacteremia, with imipenem inhibiting penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis.

Name: Campylobacter Enteritis
Description: Campylobacter enteritis (UMLS C0275982) is an acute infectious inflammatory gastroenteritis caused predominantly by Campylobacter jejuni and less often C. coli, usually acquired from contaminated poultry, unpasteurized milk, or water; it is not a classic inherited disease, but host susceptibility and postinfectious sequelae are influenced by genetic factors including variation in innate immune and mucosal defense genes such as TLR4, NOD2, IL10, IFNG, and HLA class II alleles, while bacterial virulence determinants include flagellin FlaA/FlaB, cytolethal distending toxin subunits cdtA, cdtB, and cdtC, lipooligosaccharide biosynthesis genes linked to ganglioside mimicry, and adhesins such as CadF. Pathobiology involves intestinal epithelial adherence and invasion, activation of TLR4-NF-kB and MAPK signaling, inflammasome-related cytokine release, IL-8 driven neutrophil recruitment, and disruption of tight junctions, producing fever, crampy abdominal pain, watery or inflammatory diarrhea often with blood, nausea, vomiting, and fecal leukocytes; major subtypes include uncomplicated enteritis, inflammatory or dysenteric colitis, bacteremia, and postinfectious immune-mediated disease. Important complications and comorbid associations include dehydration, sepsis in immunocompromised hosts, toxic megacolon rarely, reactive arthritis, irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease flares, and especially Guillain-Barré syndrome or Miller Fisher syndrome due to anti-ganglioside antibodies. Diagnosis is based on compatible acute diarrheal illness plus stool testing by culture on selective microaerophilic media, multiplex PCR or NAAT, stool antigen assays, and blood cultures in severe disease; fecal lactoferrin or calprotectin may support inflammatory diarrhea. Treatment is primarily rehydration and electrolyte replacement, with azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, as a common first-line antibiotic; erythromycin acts similarly, ciprofloxacin inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV but resistance is frequent, and tetracycline or doxycycline inhibit the 30S ribosomal subunit in selected susceptible isolates.

Name: Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia
Description: Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia (UMLS C0276026) is an acute bacterial lower respiratory tract infection caused by encapsulated or, more often in adults, nontypeable H. influenzae, a Gram-negative coccobacillus that colonizes the nasopharynx and invades the bronchi and alveoli, producing community-acquired or healthcare-associated pneumonia. Major microbial virulence determinants include the polysaccharide capsule encoded by the cap locus, especially serotype b, lipooligosaccharide biosynthesis genes, outer-membrane adhesins and proteins such as P2, P5, protein D, HMW1/HMW2, Hia, Hap, IgA1 protease, and β-lactam resistance mechanisms mediated by blaTEM-1 or ROB-1 and altered penicillin-binding protein 3 due to ftsI mutations. Host response is driven by TLR2/TLR4 recognition of lipooligosaccharide, NF-κB and MAPK activation, inflammasome signaling, neutrophil recruitment, complement, and mucosal IgA-dependent defense. Typical manifestations include fever, cough, purulent sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, focal crackles, and radiographic lobar or bronchopneumonic infiltrates, with severe cases progressing to hypoxemia, sepsis, empyema, or respiratory failure. Important subtypes include invasive Hib pneumonia, non-type b encapsulated disease, and nontypeable H. influenzae pneumonia, particularly in older adults, smokers, and patients with COPD. Common comorbidities include COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, influenza, immunoglobulin or complement deficiency, asplenia, HIV, malignancy, and diabetes. Treatment commonly includes ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit cell-wall synthesis; amoxicillin-clavulanate, combining a β-lactam with β-lactamase inhibition; and azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, with fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin inhibiting DNA gyrase/topoisomerase also used. The disease itself is not inherited, but susceptibility may reflect host genetic variation in immune pathways, with examples including TLR4, MYD88, IRAK4, BTK, and complement component defects

Name: Sepsis caused by Bacteroides
Description: Sepsis caused by Bacteroides (UMLS C0276064) is a severe, usually polymicrobial, anaerobic gram-negative infection most often due to Bacteroides fragilis group organisms arising from intra-abdominal, pelvic, diabetic foot, or postoperative sources, and manifests as a dysregulated host response to infection with fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, lactic acidosis, and progression to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, ARDS, hepatic dysfunction, or metastatic abscesses. Major virulence factors include the capsular polysaccharide complex, lipopolysaccharide, fimbriae, superoxide dismutase, neuraminidase, and in some strains the B. fragilis toxin fragilysin encoded by bft; antimicrobial resistance determinants commonly include cepA and cfxA beta-lactamases, cfiA metallo-beta-lactamase, ermF-mediated ribosomal methylation causing clindamycin resistance, and tetQ for tetracycline resistance. Pathobiology centers on innate immune activation through TLR2/TLR4, CD14, MyD88, NF-kB, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, complement, coagulation, endothelial injury, and tissue-factor-driven microvascular thrombosis. Treatment requires prompt source control plus anaerobe-active antibiotics such as metronidazole, which generates DNA-damaging free radicals in anaerobes; piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibits cell-wall transpeptidation and beta-lactamases; carbapenems such as meropenem, which broadly block peptidoglycan synthesis; or beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as ampicillin-sulbactam. Important comorbidities include malignancy, bowel perforation, inflammatory bowel disease, cirrhosis, diabetes, neutropenia, and immunosuppression. Subtypes reflect source and severity, including bacteremic versus non-bacteremic disease, abdominal or pelvic sepsis, and sepsis versus septic shock. It is not an inherited disorder, although host susceptibility is influenced by genetic variation in inflammatory and innate immunity genes such as TLR4, TNF, IL6, NOD2, and coagulation-related loci

Name: Infection caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Description: Infection caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic, usually non-inherited Gram-negative bacterial disease that ranges from localized otitis externa, keratitis, folliculitis, urinary tract infection, and ventilator-associated pneumonia to chronic airway colonization in cystic fibrosis and fulminant bacteremia, sepsis, ecthyma gangrenosum, osteomyelitis, and burn-wound infection; typical manifestations include fever, purulent secretions, dyspnea, cough, pleuritic pain, dysuria, wound drainage, ear pain, or ocular pain, with severity shaped by host defense and bacterial virulence. Key microbial determinants include quorum-sensing regulators lasR, rhlR, and pqs systems; type III secretion toxins ExoS, ExoT, ExoU, and ExoY; alginate/biofilm genes such as algD and mucA; pili and flagellar proteins; elastase LasB; and resistance-related ampC, oprD, and mexAB-oprM, while host genetic susceptibility is best defined in disorders predisposing to infection such as CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis, as well as neutropenia or chronic granulomatous disease affecting phagocyte oxidative burst pathways. Major pathogenic pathways involve LPS-TLR4 and flagellin-TLR5 signaling, NF-kB-driven cytokine responses, inflammasome activation, iron acquisition, biofilm formation, quorum sensing, and c-di-GMP–regulated persistence. Commonly used therapies include piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibits cell-wall transpeptidation with beta-lactamase protection; ceftazidime or cefepime, antipseudomonal cephalosporins that bind penicillin-binding proteins; meropenem, a carbapenem blocking peptidoglycan synthesis; ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; and aminoglycosides such as tobramycin, which bind the 30S ribosomal subunit. Important comorbidities include cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, COPD, diabetes, malignancy, burns, immunosuppression, and indwelling devices. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical syndrome plus culture from blood or site-specific specimens with Gram stain and susceptibility testing, supported when needed by PCR or MALDI-TOF identification, imaging for deep infection

Name: Ecthyma gangrenosum
Description: Ecthyma gangrenosum (UMLS C0276085) is an acute, necrotizing cutaneous infection classically caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia, although similar lesions may arise from other Gram-negative bacteria and occasionally fungi in profoundly immunocompromised hosts; it is best regarded as an infectious vasculopathic syndrome rather than a primary inherited disease. Its pathobiology centers on microbial invasion of the media and adventitia of dermal and subcutaneous vessels with thrombosis, ischemic necrosis, and bacterial toxins and proteases, including elastase LasB, alkaline protease, phospholipase C, exotoxin A, and type III secretion effectors such as ExoS, ExoT, and ExoU, acting through quorum-sensing systems Las/Rhl/Pqs, LPS-TLR4–NF-kB inflammatory signaling, neutrophil dysfunction, and complement impairment. Representative host genetic contributors are usually indirect, involving inherited or acquired immunodeficiencies such as ELANE or HAX1 neutropenia, CYBB-related chronic granulomatous disease, BTK-associated agammaglobulinemia, or complement defects; inheritance therefore follows the underlying immune disorder, not the skin lesion itself. Typical findings are rapidly evolving painless or painful erythematous macules that become hemorrhagic bullae, pustules, or ulcers with a black eschar, often with fever, sepsis, and lesions in the axillae, groin, perineum, or extremities; bacteremic and non-bacteremic forms are recognized. Major comorbidities include hematologic malignancy, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, diabetes, burns, HIV infection, malnutrition, and intensive-care exposure, while complications include septic shock, multifocal necrosis, osteomyelitis, and death. Diagnosis is clinical plus microbiologic confirmation with blood cultures, tissue or wound culture, skin biopsy showing necrotizing vasculitis with organisms, CBC demonstrating neutropenia, and susceptibility testing; evaluation for occult immunodeficiency is often warranted. Treatment requires urgent antipseudomonal therapy such as piperacillin-tazobactam, a beta-lactam inhibiting cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; cefepime or ceftazidime, cephalosporins targeting penicillin-binding proteins; meropenem, a carbapenem inhibiting cell

Name: Septicaemic colibacillosis
Description: Septicaemic colibacillosis is an acute invasive extraintestinal Escherichia coli infection causing bacteremia and systemic inflammatory response, classically arising from urinary, gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, pulmonary, neonatal, or device-associated foci and presenting with fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, and potentially septic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation and multiorgan failure. Disease subtypes are commonly defined by source and host context, including urosepsis, neonatal sepsis/meningitis-associated disease, healthcare-associated bacteremia, and avian or veterinary septicemic colibacillosis; important comorbidities include diabetes, cirrhosis, malignancy, neutropenia, chronic kidney disease, urinary obstruction, prematurity, and immunosuppression, while complications include acute respiratory distress syndrome, renal failure, endocarditis, metastatic abscesses, and meningitis. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial virulence determinants rather than Mendelian inheritance: lipopolysaccharide endotoxin activates TLR4-CD14-MD2, triggering MyD88/TRIF, NF-kB, MAPK, TNF, IL-1, IL-6, complement, and coagulation pathways; representative microbial genes/proteins include fimH and pap adhesins, kpsM/kps capsule loci including the K1 capsule, siderophore systems such as iutA and iroN, hemolysin hlyA, ompA, iss, and LPS biosynthesis genes, with resistance determinants including blaCTX-M, blaTEM, blaSHV, carbapenemases such as blaNDM or blaKPC, and mcr-1. Host genetic susceptibility is polygenic and incompletely defined, with variants in TLR4, CD14, MBL2, and cytokine genes reported to influence sepsis risk or severity. Diagnosis requires compatible sepsis physiology plus microbiologic confirmation, chiefly blood cultures and culture of the primary focus with species identification and susceptibility testing, supported by CBC, chemistry panels, inflammatory markers, lactate, urinalysis, imaging for source control, and rapid PCR or MALDI-TOF when available. Treatment relies on prompt source control and empiric then susceptibility-guided antibiotics, commonly ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibit penicillin-binding

Name: Pneumonia caused by Escherichia coli
Description: Pneumonia caused by Escherichia coli is an acute bacterial lower respiratory tract infection, usually a severe gram-negative bacillary pneumonia acquired in the hospital, ventilator setting, or in frail neonates and older adults, and less often community acquired; it presents with fever, cough, purulent sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia, crackles, and radiographic lobar or bronchopneumonic infiltrates, with progression to sepsis, abscess, empyema, or acute respiratory distress syndrome in complicated cases. Pathogenesis is driven by virulence factors rather than a Mendelian host inheritance pattern: representative bacterial genes include fimH and papG adhesins, the capsule locus such as kpsM/K1, lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis genes, siderophore systems including iutA and fyuA, toxins such as hlyA and cnf1, and resistance determinants including blaTEM, blaCTX-M, blaSHV, and carbapenemases such as blaKPC or blaNDM; relevant proteins include type 1 fimbriae, P fimbriae, outer membrane proteins, beta-lactamases, and endotoxin. Key host-response pathways include TLR4-CD14-MD2 recognition of LPS, NF-kappaB and MAPK activation, inflammasome signaling, neutrophil recruitment via IL-8/CXCL8, and cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6, which underlie alveolar inflammation and capillary leak. Commonly used treatments include ceftriaxone or cefepime, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and peptidoglycan cross-linking; piperacillin-tazobactam, combining cell-wall inhibition with beta-lactamase blockade; meropenem for ESBL-producing strains, also inhibiting PBPs; and levofloxacin, which inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Important comorbidities include chronic lung disease, diabetes, alcoholism, aspiration risk, immunosuppression, renal failure, and prolonged ventilation. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms and imaging plus microbiologic confirmation by sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or blood culture with susceptibility testing, supported by CBC, inflammatory markers, and molecular resistance assays when needed; subtypes are commonly classified as community-acquired, hospital-ac

Name: Mpox, Monkeypox
Description: Mpox, formerly monkeypox, is an acute zoonotic and person-to-person transmissible orthopoxvirus infection caused by monkeypox virus, a large double-stranded DNA virus in the Poxviridae family, with two major genetic clades/subtypes historically recognized as Clade I (Congo Basin/Central African, generally more virulent) and Clade II (West African, including IIb linked to the 2022 global outbreak). Disease biology is driven largely by viral host-range and immune-evasion proteins rather than Mendelian inheritance; representative viral genes/proteins include B21/B22 glycoproteins, the envelope protein F13 targeted by tecovirimat, and DNA polymerase F8 targeted indirectly by cidofovir and brincidofovir, while host susceptibility and severity are influenced by immune pathways involving interferon signaling, TNF/NF-kB, JAK-STAT, chemokine networks, T-cell activation, and pattern-recognition receptors such as TLRs and cGAS-STING. Clinically, mpox typically presents after an incubation of about 5-21 days with fever, malaise, headache, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, and a characteristic centrifugal or anogenital mucocutaneous eruption that evolves from macules and papules to vesicles, pustules, umbilicated lesions, and crusts; proctitis, pharyngitis, and localized genital pain are common in recent outbreaks. Important complications include secondary bacterial infection, dehydration, bronchopneumonia, encephalitis, keratitis with vision loss, myocarditis, and severe disseminated disease, especially in people with HIV/AIDS, immunosuppression, pregnancy, eczema, or pediatric vulnerability, with coinfection with other sexually transmitted infections also frequent. Treatment is mainly supportive, but commonly used antivirals include tecovirimat, which inhibits the VP37/F13 envelope wrapping protein and blocks virion egress, cidofovir, a nucleotide analog inhibiting viral DNA polymerase, and brincidofovir, an oral lipid-conjugated cidofovir prodrug with similar polymerase inhibition; vaccinia immune globulin may be considered in select severe cases. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology and rash plus lesion swab real-time PCR for orthopoxvirus/MPXV DNA as the preferred confirmatory test, with sequencing for clade assignment and serology, histopathology, or electron microscopy as adjunct

Name: Encephalitis, Herpes Simplex
Description: Herpes simplex encephalitis is an acute, usually sporadic, necrotizing viral encephalitis caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 1 in older children and adults and by HSV-2 more often in neonates, involving hemorrhagic inflammation with temporal and inferior frontal lobe predilection. Host susceptibility is influenced by defects in innate antiviral immunity, especially the TLR3–TRIF–TBK1–IRF3/IRF7 type I interferon axis, with reported pathogenic variants in TLR3, TICAM1/TRIF, TBK1, IRF3, IRF7, UNC93B1, TRAF3, STAT1, and SNORA31; impaired IFN-α/β signaling and microglial/neuronal antiviral responses are central pathways, alongside NF-κB activation, cytokines such as TNF, IL-6, and CXCL10, and blood-brain barrier inflammatory injury. Typical manifestations include fever, headache, altered mental status, confusion, personality change, aphasia, focal neurologic deficits, seizures, hallucinations, and reduced consciousness, with complications including cerebral edema, status epilepticus, SIADH-related hyponatremia, respiratory failure, chronic epilepsy, cognitive impairment, and neuropsychiatric sequelae; comorbid immunosuppression, HIV infection, malignancy, or transplantation may worsen severity. Major forms include neonatal disseminated/CNS HSV-2 disease, pediatric disease, and adult sporadic HSV-1 encephalitis, with rare recurrent disease in genetically predisposed patients; inheritance of susceptibility can be autosomal dominant or recessive with incomplete penetrance in interferon-pathway disorders, although most cases are nonfamilial. Diagnosis rests on compatible encephalitic syndrome plus CSF pleocytosis, elevated protein, temporal lobe abnormalities on MRI, EEG periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges or focal slowing, and confirmation by CSF HSV PCR, with brain biopsy now rarely required. Treatment is urgent intravenous acyclovir, a guanosine analog activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibits viral DNA polymerase; alternatives or adjuncts include valacyclovir, the oral prodrug of acyclovir, famciclovir/penciclovir, guanosine analog polymerase inhibitors, and foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analog used for acyclovir-resistant thymidine-kinase-deficient HSV.

Name: Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis
Description: Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis is an ocular infection and immune-inflammatory disorder caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 1, involving the conjunctiva and cornea and presenting as primary epithelial disease, recurrent epithelial keratitis, stromal keratitis, endothelitis, or blepharoconjunctivitis. It typically manifests with unilateral red eye, pain, photophobia, tearing, foreign-body sensation, blurred vision, conjunctival injection, decreased corneal sensation, and characteristic dendritic or geographic epithelial ulcers that stain with fluorescein; stromal disease may produce edema, neovascularization, scarring, and vision loss. The disease reflects viral entry and latency biology rather than simple Mendelian inheritance: HSV-1 glycoproteins gB, gC, gD, gH/gL interact with host receptors such as NECTIN1/PVRL1, HVEM/TNFRSF14, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans, while viral replication engages thymidine kinase and DNA polymerase; host susceptibility and severity are influenced by innate immune genes and pathways including TLR3, IFNAR1, UNC93B1, TRAF3, STAT1, and interferon signaling, with rare defects predisposing to severe HSV disease. Key pathogenic pathways include trigeminal latency/reactivation, epithelial cytolysis, and corneal immunopathology driven by dendritic cells, CD4+ T cells, IL-1, TNF, VEGF, NF-κB, and type I interferon responses. Diagnosis is usually clinical by slit-lamp examination and fluorescein staining, supplemented when needed by corneal scraping PCR, viral culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing, or confocal microscopy; reduced corneal sensitivity and response to antivirals support diagnosis. Standard treatments include acyclovir and valacyclovir, guanosine analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit viral DNA polymerase, topical ganciclovir, a guanine analogue blocking viral DNA synthesis, and trifluridine, a fluorinated pyrimidine nucleoside analogue; topical corticosteroids are used cautiously for stromal disease with antiviral cover. Important complications and associations include recurrent keratitis, neurotrophic keratopathy, bacterial superinfection, corneal thinning or perforation, uveitis, glaucoma, and permanent corneal opacity with reduced visual acuity.

Name: Human immunodeficiency virus I infection
Description: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 infection is an acquired chronic retroviral disease caused by HIV-1, a lentivirus that infects CD4+ T lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells through gp120 binding to CD4 and the chemokine coreceptors CCR5 or CXCR4, followed by gp41-mediated fusion, reverse transcription, integrase-dependent proviral insertion, and protease-mediated virion maturation; major viral genes and proteins include gag, pol, and env, with accessory proteins tat, rev, nef, vif, vpr, and vpu, while representative host genetic factors include the CCR5-Δ32 loss-of-function variant, certain HLA class I alleles such as HLA-B*57/B*27 associated with slower progression, and APOBEC3G, TRIM5α, and tetherin-mediated restriction. Central pathogenic pathways involve chronic immune activation, NF-κB signaling, interferon responses, T-cell exhaustion, and progressive CD4 depletion. Clinical manifestations range from acute retroviral syndrome with fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and mucocutaneous ulcers to chronic infection with weight loss, diarrhea, night sweats, recurrent infections, and advanced AIDS marked by opportunistic infections and malignancies. Common subtypes include HIV-1 groups M, N, O, and P, with group M clades A-K predominating globally. Treatment relies on combination antiretroviral therapy, typically two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors such as tenofovir and emtricitabine, which inhibit viral DNA synthesis, plus an integrase strand transfer inhibitor such as dolutegravir, which blocks proviral integration; other key agents include protease inhibitors such as darunavir, preventing virion maturation, and entry inhibitors such as maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist. Important comorbidities and complications include tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, cardiovascular and renal disease, neurocognitive disorder, wasting, Kaposi sarcoma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The disorder is not inherited in a Mendelian manner, but host susceptibility and progression are genetically modified. Diagnosis is established by HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody immunoassay with confirmatory differentiation testing, HIV-1 RNA nucleic acid testing for acute infection, and disease monitoring with viral load, CD4 count, resistance genotyping, and opportunistic infection evaluation.

Name: Nutritional deficiency with AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome)
Description: Nutritional deficiency with AIDS is an acquired, non-Mendelian clinical state in which advanced HIV-1 or HIV-2 infection drives protein-energy malnutrition and multiple micronutrient deficiencies through reduced intake, malabsorption, chronic inflammation, opportunistic infection, and hypercatabolism; key viral and host genetic components include HIV gag, pol, and env, CCR5 and CXCR4 coreceptor usage, and representative host variants such as CCR5-Δ32, HLA-B alleles, and cytokine-related polymorphisms that can influence susceptibility, progression, and wasting severity, although they do not define inheritance of the syndrome itself. Central pathways involve CD4+ T-cell depletion, gp120-CD4/CCR5 or CXCR4 entry signaling, reverse transcription and integrase-mediated proviral insertion, NF-κB and JAK/STAT activation, TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6 mediated cachexia, microbial translocation, and mTOR/proteasome imbalance contributing to muscle loss. Typical manifestations include involuntary weight loss, low BMI, muscle wasting, weakness, chronic diarrhea, anorexia, oral candidiasis, glossitis, anemia, vitamin and trace-element deficiency signs, recurrent fever, night sweats, and frequent opportunistic infections. Common comorbidities and complications include tuberculosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, cryptococcosis, CMV disease, chronic hepatitis B or C, Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma, neuropathy, hypogonadism, and severe cachexia. Disease patterns may be described as HIV wasting syndrome, micronutrient-deficiency predominant disease, or enteropathy/malabsorption-associated deficiency. Diagnosis rests on confirmed HIV infection by fourth-generation antigen/antibody assay with differentiation testing and HIV RNA NAT, staging by CD4 count and viral load, nutritional assessment using weight history, BMI, anthropometrics, albumin or prealbumin, CBC, iron studies, B12, folate, vitamin D, zinc, and evaluation for diarrhea or malabsorption and opportunistic infection. Treatment centers on antiretroviral therapy such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, a nucleotide reverse-transcriptase inhibitor, emtricitabine, a nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor, and dolutegravir, an integrase strand-transfer inhibitor, with alternatives including protease inhibitors such as darunavir; these suppress viral replication, promote

Name: Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis
Description: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (UMLS C0276653) is a severe, usually non-hereditary opportunistic mold infection of the lung, most often caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and characterized by angioinvasive hyphal growth, tissue necrosis, hemorrhage, and potential hematogenous dissemination, especially in patients with prolonged neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, hematopoietic stem-cell or solid-organ transplantation, advanced corticosteroid or other immunosuppressive exposure, chronic granulomatous disease, and severe viral pneumonia. Host susceptibility is influenced by innate immune genes and proteins involved in fungal recognition and killing, including PTX3, TLR2, TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, MYD88, NADPH oxidase complex genes such as CYBB, CYBA, NCF1 and NCF2, and cytokine pathways involving IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and NF-κB; representative risk variants include PTX3 deficiency-associated polymorphisms, CLEC7A Y238X, and loss-of-function CARD9 defects. Pathobiology centers on conidial sensing by alveolar macrophages and neutrophils through pattern-recognition receptor signaling, ROS generation, inflammasome activation, Th1/Th17 responses, and fungal stress-response and ergosterol biosynthesis pathways. Clinical manifestations include persistent fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, hypoxemia, and nodular or cavitary pulmonary infiltrates; major forms include proven, probable, and possible invasive aspergillosis, with airway-invasive, angioinvasive, and chronic necrotizing/subacute invasive phenotypes. Diagnosis integrates host risk factors, compatible CT findings such as nodules with halo sign or air-crescent sign, bronchoscopy or biopsy showing septate acute-angle-branching hyphae, culture, serum or bronchoalveolar lavage galactomannan, β-D-glucan, and Aspergillus PCR. First-line therapy is typically voriconazole, a triazole that inhibits fungal 14-α-demethylase (CYP51) and ergosterol synthesis; alternatives include isavuconazole with the same mechanism, liposomal amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and disrupts membranes, and

Name: Pulmonary cryptococcosis
Description: Pulmonary cryptococcosis is an invasive fungal infection of the lung caused mainly by Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii, ranging from asymptomatic colonization-like nodules to severe pneumonia and potentially disseminated disease, especially with CNS spread. It occurs most often in immunocompromised hosts, particularly those with HIV/AIDS, solid-organ transplantation, hematologic malignancy, corticosteroid exposure, cirrhosis, diabetes, or sarcoidosis, but C. gattii disease may affect apparently immunocompetent individuals. Host susceptibility is linked to defects in cell-mediated immunity and innate fungal recognition, with representative genetic associations involving CD4 lymphopenia, GATA2 deficiency, anti-GM-CSF autoantibody syndrome, and variants or deficiencies affecting IL12RB1, IFNGR1, STAT1 gain-of-function, CARD9, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2/TLR4, FCGR, HLA loci, and mannose-binding lectin; these influence macrophage and dendritic-cell antifungal responses. Key pathways include Th1/Th17 immunity, IL-12/IFN-γ and TNF-α signaling, GM-CSF–dependent macrophage activation, pattern-recognition receptor pathways triggered by cryptococcal capsule and cell-wall components, NF-κB activation, and impaired phagolysosomal killing. Clinical manifestations include cough, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, weight loss, hemoptysis, and solitary or multiple pulmonary nodules, consolidation, cavitation, or diffuse infiltrates; complications include respiratory failure, fungemia, meningitis, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Subtypes are commonly classified by organism species and by localized versus disseminated disease or mild versus severe pulmonary involvement. Diagnosis relies on compatible imaging plus microbiologic or histopathologic confirmation by culture, biopsy showing encapsulated budding yeasts with mucicarmine or India ink, serum or BAL cryptococcal antigen testing, and evaluation for extrapulmonary spread, especially lumbar puncture in high-risk patients. Standard therapy includes fluconazole, which inhibits fungal 14-α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis, amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores, and flucytosine, a pyrimidine analog that inhibits fungal DNA and RNA synthesis.

Name: Disseminated sporotrichosis
Description: Disseminated sporotrichosis is an invasive, usually subacute to chronic fungal infection caused by dimorphic Sporothrix species, most often the Sporothrix schenckii complex and, in some regions, the more virulent S. brasiliensis, with spread beyond the primary cutaneous inoculation site to multiple skin lesions, osteoarticular structures, lungs, central nervous system, or other viscera; clinical forms include disseminated cutaneous and disseminated extracutaneous disease, often evolving from fixed cutaneous or lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. Typical manifestations are fever, weight loss, malaise, widespread papules, nodules, ulcers, verrucous plaques, lymphangitic lesions, arthritis or osteomyelitis, pulmonary infiltrates, and, in severe cases, meningitis. Host susceptibility is strongly shaped by cell-mediated immunity rather than Mendelian inheritance; important molecular components include fungal cell-wall glycoproteins such as gp70 and melanin, and host pattern-recognition and immune pathways involving TLR2/TLR4, dectin-1/CLEC7A, mannose receptor, macrophages, neutrophils, Th1/Th17 polarization, and cytokines including TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-12, IL-17, and IL-23. Rarely, impaired immunity from HIV/AIDS, alcoholism, diabetes mellitus, chronic lung disease, malignancy, transplantation, corticosteroid or TNF-inhibitor exposure, and other primary or secondary immunodeficiencies may reflect genetic contributors in IFN-gamma/IL-12 axis or CARD9-related antifungal defense, although no disease-specific inherited mutation is established. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology and examination plus culture of tissue, pus, sputum, synovial fluid, or CSF as the standard, supported by histopathology showing cigar-shaped yeasts or asteroid bodies, fungal PCR when available, imaging for visceral or osteoarticular involvement, and CSF analysis in suspected CNS disease. Treatment typically uses itraconazole, which inhibits fungal 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and disrupts membrane integrity, especially for severe disseminated or CNS infection; and terbinafine, a squalene epoxidase inhibitor, with posaconazole or saturated solution of potassium iodide used in selected cases.

Name: Onychomycosis caused by Trichophyton rubrum
Description: Onychomycosis caused by Trichophyton rubrum is a chronic superficial dermatophyte infection of the nail unit, usually involving the distal lateral subungual, superficial white, proximal subungual, or total dystrophic subtypes, in which fungal invasion of the nail plate, bed, and hyponychium produces yellow-white or brown discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, friability, thickening, and progressive nail dystrophy, often with concomitant tinea pedis. Its pathobiology reflects keratin adherence and digestion mediated by T. rubrum virulence factors including secreted subtilisin-like proteases Sub3 and Sub6, metalloproteases such as Mep4, keratinases, and cell-wall mannans, with host responses involving keratinocyte pattern-recognition receptors, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, Th1/Th17 cytokine pathways including IL-17 and IL-22, and innate antifungal signaling through the dectin/CARD9 axis; susceptibility is influenced by host genetic factors rather than Mendelian inheritance, with reported associations involving HLA class II variants, CARD9 defects in severe dermatophytosis, and polymorphisms in DEFB4, TLR2, or other epidermal barrier and immune genes. Major comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, psoriasis, advancing age, immunosuppression, trauma, and occlusive footwear; complications include pain, cellulitis, secondary bacterial infection, functional impairment, and recurrence. Diagnosis requires compatible nail changes plus mycologic confirmation by potassium hydroxide microscopy, fungal culture identifying T. rubrum, histopathology of nail clippings with PAS stain, and increasingly PCR-based assays when available. Standard therapy includes terbinafine, an allylamine that inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase and depletes ergosterol; itraconazole and fluconazole, triazoles that inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase; and topical efinaconazole, tavaborole, or ciclopirox, which respectively inhibit ergosterol synthesis, leucyl-tRNA synthetase, and metal-dependent fungal enzymes.

Name: Onychomycosis caused by Trichophyton mentagrophytes
Description: Onychomycosis caused by Trichophyton mentagrophytes (UMLS C0276755) is a contagious dermatophyte infection of the nail unit, usually producing distal-lateral subungual, superficial white, proximal subungual, or total dystrophic disease with nail discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, friability, thickening, and progressive dystrophy, often accompanied by tinea pedis. Its pathobiology depends on fungal adhesion and invasion of keratinized tissue through secreted keratinases, subtilisins, metalloproteases, and sulfite efflux systems, while host defense is shaped by innate and adaptive pathways including pattern-recognition receptors such as Dectin-1/CLEC7A and Toll-like receptors, CARD9-dependent NF-kB signaling, IL-17/Th17 and IL-22 responses, neutrophil recruitment, and antimicrobial peptides; rare host susceptibility variants reported for chronic dermatophytosis include CARD9, CLEC7A, STAT3, and other primary immunodeficiency-related genes rather than a Mendelian inheritance pattern for onychomycosis itself. Risk is increased by diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, psoriasis, advancing age, immunosuppression, trauma, hyperhidrosis, and occlusive footwear, and complications include pain, cellulitis, secondary bacterial infection, gait impairment, and recurrent spread to surrounding skin or household contacts. Diagnosis relies on compatible nail changes plus mycologic confirmation by potassium hydroxide microscopy, fungal culture identifying T. mentagrophytes/T. interdigitale complex, histopathology of clipped nail with PAS stain, and increasingly PCR or MALDI-TOF for species-level detection. Standard therapy includes terbinafine, which inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase and depletes ergosterol; itraconazole and fluconazole, azoles that inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase; and topical efinaconazole, tavaborole, or ciclopirox, which respectively inhibit ergosterol synthesis, leucyl-tRNA synthetase, or metal-dependent fungal enzymes, with treatment choice guided by extent of nail involvement and host comorbidity.

Name: Fusariosis
Description: Fusariosis (UMLS C0276758) is an opportunistic hyalohyphomycosis caused by filamentous Fusarium species, most often members of the Fusarium solani species complex, F. oxysporum, and F. verticillioides, producing localized disease such as keratitis or onychomycosis and, in profoundly immunocompromised hosts, invasive or disseminated infection. It is not a Mendelian inherited disorder; rather, host genetic susceptibility is polygenic and incompletely defined, with risk linked primarily to immune defects, including prolonged neutropenia, hematologic malignancy, hematopoietic stem-cell or solid-organ transplantation, corticosteroid exposure, burns, and indwelling catheters; representative immune-related genes/proteins implicated in antifungal defense include pattern-recognition and cytokine pathways such as TLR2, TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, IL-6, TNF, IFN-γ, and NADPH oxidase components, although no fusariosis-specific mutation is diagnostic. Pathobiology involves fungal adhesion, hyphal angioinvasion, biofilm formation, and innate immune signaling through C-type lectin/TLR pathways with downstream NF-κB activation, neutrophil oxidative killing, and Th1/Th17 cytokine responses. Typical manifestations include persistent fever, refractory neutropenic sepsis, painful erythematous or violaceous papules and nodules with central necrosis, sinusitis, pneumonia, fungemia, endophthalmitis, and osteoarticular or disseminated multiorgan disease; keratitis presents with pain, photophobia, corneal ulceration, and hypopyon. Major complications include metastatic skin lesions, pulmonary failure, endocarditis, renal or hepatic involvement, visual loss, and death. Diagnosis relies on clinical context plus microscopy and histopathology showing septate hyaline hyphae with tissue invasion, culture from blood or sterile sites, species identification by MALDI-TOF or sequencing, ophthalmic corneal scraping when relevant, and supportive fungal markers such as serum galactomannan or β-D-glucan, with imaging to define extent. Treatment commonly uses voriconazole, which inhibits fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51) and ergosterol synthesis, lipid amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol and disrupt

Name: Traveler's diarrhea
