Description: Traveler's diarrhea is an acute, usually self-limited infectious enteric syndrome acquired during travel, classically caused by ingestion of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli but also enteroaggregative E. coli, Campylobacter jejuni, Shigella, Salmonella, Vibrio, norovirus, rotavirus, Giardia, and Entamoeba; mechanistically, pathogen virulence factors such as ETEC heat-labile toxin encoded by eltAB and heat-stable toxin encoded by estA, Campylobacter cytolethal distending toxin, and Shigella invasion plasmid antigens activate cAMP-, cGMP-, CFTR-, inflammatory cytokine-, TLR/NF-kB-, prostaglandin-, and chloride secretion pathways, driving secretory diarrhea, epithelial injury, and mucosal inflammation. Host genetic contributions are modest and non-Mendelian, but susceptibility and severity have been linked to variants affecting innate and mucosal immunity or secretor status, including IL8, TNF, TLR4, lactoferrin, and FUT2, rather than a defined inheritance pattern. Typical manifestations are abrupt onset of loose stools, abdominal cramping, urgency, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and sometimes dysentery with blood or mucus; major subtypes are watery/noninflammatory, inflammatory/invasive, and persistent diarrhea, often stratified further by bacterial, viral, or protozoal etiology. Diagnosis is primarily clinical in a recent traveler with at least 3 unformed stools in 24 hours plus enteric symptoms, while stool culture, multiplex PCR panels, ova-and-parasite examination, fecal leukocytes or lactoferrin, and assessment of dehydration or electrolyte disturbance are reserved for severe, febrile, bloody, prolonged, immunocompromised, or outbreak-associated cases. Treatment centers on oral rehydration and, when indicated, antimicrobials such as azithromycin, a macrolide that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; and rifaximin, a nonabsorbed inhibitor of bacterial RNA polymerase, with loperamide as adjunctive peripheral mu-opioid antimotility therapy. Important comorbidities and complications include dehydration, acute kidney injury, electrolyte imbalance, postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome, reactive arthritis, Guillain-Barre syndrome after Camp

Name: Moderate pain (finding)
Description: Moderate pain (UMLS C0278139) is a clinical finding rather than a discrete inherited disease, denoting an intermediate-intensity nociceptive experience that typically impairs function but is not usually incapacitating, and it may arise in acute or chronic contexts from inflammatory, neuropathic, musculoskeletal, visceral, postoperative, or cancer-related etiologies. Its biology commonly involves peripheral transduction and central sensitization pathways, including TRPV1, SCN9A/Nav1.7, SCN10A/Nav1.8, CACNA2D1, OPRM1, COMT, and cytokine-related mediators such as TNF, IL1B, and IL6, with representative mutations in SCN9A causing altered pain sensitivity and variants in COMT or OPRM1 modulating pain perception and analgesic response. Key signaling mechanisms include prostaglandin-COX pathways, bradykinin and substance P signaling, glutamatergic NMDA receptor activation, voltage-gated sodium and calcium channel activity, and descending serotonergic and noradrenergic pain modulation. Common treatments include acetaminophen, which acts predominantly through central analgesic mechanisms; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and reduce prostaglandin synthesis; opioids such as morphine or oxycodone, which activate mu-opioid receptors; and, when neuropathic features are present, gabapentin or pregabalin, which bind the alpha-2-delta calcium-channel subunit, and duloxetine, an SNRI that enhances descending inhibitory pathways. Moderate pain is frequently linked with osteoarthritis, low back pain, migraine, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, cancer, depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbance, and complications include reduced mobility, impaired quality of life, opioid misuse, and transition to chronic pain. Symptoms typically include pain rated about 4-6/10, tenderness, guarding, reduced activity, and sometimes autonomic or neuropathic descriptors such as burning or paresthesia. Diagnosis is clinical, based on validated pain scales, history, physical examination, identification of cause, and selective testing such as imaging, inflammatory markers, nerve conduction studies, or quantitative sensory testing; no single inheritance pattern applies, although genetic predisposition to pain sensitivity and chronic pain vulnerability is often polygenic.

Name: Severe pain (finding)
Description: Severe pain is a clinical finding rather than a single disease entity, denoting intense nociceptive, neuropathic, inflammatory, or mixed pain that reflects heightened peripheral or central pain signaling; it commonly presents with marked spontaneous or provoked pain, hyperalgesia, allodynia, autonomic arousal, sleep disturbance, immobility, anxiety, and impaired function. Molecular contributors include ion-channel and neurotransmission genes such as SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A encoding Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9, TRPV1, CACNA2D1, OPRM1, COMT, and inflammatory mediators including PTGS2/COX-2, TNF, IL1B, and NGF; representative mutations in SCN9A can cause inherited erythromelalgia or paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, whereas loss-of-function variants cause congenital insensitivity to pain, illustrating the genetic architecture of pain susceptibility. Key pathways involve peripheral transduction and sensitization through prostaglandin, bradykinin, NGF-TrkA, cytokine, and TRP signaling; spinal and supraspinal transmission through glutamate, substance P, CGRP, NMDA receptor activation, microglial and astrocytic neuroinflammation, and descending serotonergic, noradrenergic, and endogenous opioid modulation. Treatment depends on etiology but commonly includes opioids such as morphine, a mu-opioid receptor agonist; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit COX enzymes and prostaglandin synthesis; acetaminophen, likely acting centrally on prostaglandin-related pathways; gabapentin or pregabalin, which bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels; and adjuvants such as duloxetine, an SNRI enhancing descending inhibition, or topical lidocaine, a sodium-channel blocker. Severe pain is frequently linked to cancer, trauma, postoperative states, osteoarthritis, sickle cell disease, diabetic neuropathy, radiculopathy, migraine, fibromyalgia, depression, and substance use disorder; complications include chronic pain chronification, disability, delirium, opioid tolerance, dependence, and respiratory depression. Subtypes include acute versus chronic, nociceptive versus neuropathic, visceral versus somatic, and centralized pain. Inheritance is usually multifactorial except for rare Mendelian channel

Name: Metastatic Renal Cell Cancer
Description: Metastatic renal cell cancer is an advanced malignant epithelial neoplasm of the kidney, most often arising from clear cell renal cell carcinoma but also including papillary, chromophobe, collecting duct, translocation-associated, and unclassified subtypes, defined by spread beyond the kidney to sites such as lung, bone, liver, brain, and lymph nodes. Its biology is commonly driven by loss of VHL on chromosome 3p in clear cell disease, causing HIF-1α/HIF-2α stabilization and upregulation of VEGF, PDGF, TGF-α, CAIX, and angiogenic signaling; other implicated genes include PBRM1, BAP1, SETD2, KDM5C, MTOR, PTEN, MET in hereditary papillary RCC, FH in hereditary leiomyomatosis-associated RCC, FLCN in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, and TSC1/TSC2. Key pathways include the VHL/HIF/VEGF axis, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MET, AXL, and immune checkpoint signaling involving PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4. Typical symptoms and signs include hematuria, flank pain, abdominal mass, weight loss, fever, fatigue, anemia, hypercalcemia, hypertension, and manifestations of metastases such as cough, pathologic fracture, or neurologic deficits; paraneoplastic syndromes and complications include venous thromboembolism, renal insufficiency, spinal cord compression, and brain edema. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited predisposition is usually autosomal dominant in VHL disease and other familial RCC syndromes. Diagnosis relies on cross-sectional imaging with contrast-enhanced CT or MRI for renal mass and staging, chest imaging, selective brain or bone evaluation, laboratory testing including CBC, renal function, calcium, and liver enzymes, and histopathologic confirmation with immunohistochemistry or biopsy when needed. Standard systemic therapies include sunitinib or pazopanib, VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors that block tumor angiogenesis; cabozantinib, which inhibits VEGFR, MET, and AXL; nivolumab, a PD-1 inhibitor; pembrolizumab plus axitinib; and lenvatinib plus everolimus, with mTOR inhibition by everolimus.

Name: Metastatic non-small cell lung cancer
Description: Metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is an advanced epithelial malignancy of the lung, usually comprising adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, or large cell carcinoma, defined by spread beyond the hemithorax and characterized by marked molecular heterogeneity. Common driver alterations include activating EGFR mutations such as exon 19 deletions and L858R, KRAS mutations, especially KRAS G12C, ALK, ROS1, and RET rearrangements, BRAF V600E, MET exon 14 skipping, ERBB2/HER2 alterations, and less commonly NTRK fusions; relevant proteins include EGFR, ALK, PD-L1, MET, and VEGF. Key dysregulated pathways include EGFR/RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, MET/HGF, ALK/ROS1 fusion signaling, angiogenesis via VEGF, and immune evasion through PD-1/PD-L1. Typical symptoms and signs include persistent cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, hoarseness, pleural effusion, and manifestations of distant spread such as bone pain, neurologic deficits, liver dysfunction, and adrenal metastases. Major complications include malignant pleural or pericardial effusions, venous thromboembolism, airway obstruction, brain and bone metastases, pathologic fractures, spinal cord compression, cachexia, and paraneoplastic syndromes. Although most cases are sporadic and strongly linked to tobacco exposure, inherited susceptibility can involve rare germline variants such as EGFR T790M, TP53 in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and DNA repair genes. Diagnosis relies on imaging with CT and PET-CT, brain MRI for staging, histopathologic confirmation from biopsy or cytology, and comprehensive molecular testing by PCR or next-generation sequencing with PD-L1 immunohistochemistry. Treatment commonly includes platinum-doublet chemotherapy, pembrolizumab or nivolumab as PD-1 blockade, osimertinib for mutant EGFR, alectinib for ALK-rearranged disease, sotorasib for KRAS G12C, and bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF antibody, selected by histology, biomarkers, and performance status.

Name: Cancer of Head and Neck
Description: Head and neck neoplasms (MeSH D006258) comprise a heterogeneous group of mostly epithelial malignancies arising in the oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, nasopharynx, nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, salivary glands, and related mucosal sites, with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma being the dominant subtype; major molecular lesions include TP53 mutation, CDKN2A/p16 loss, CCND1 amplification, EGFR overexpression or amplification, PIK3CA mutation, NOTCH1 alteration, HRAS mutation, FAT1 loss, and in HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers, viral E6/E7-mediated inactivation of p53 and RB, while EBV is linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Dysregulated pathways commonly involve EGFR-RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, p53/RB cell-cycle control, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, angiogenic VEGF signaling, and immune-checkpoint axes including PD-1/PD-L1. Risk factors are primarily environmental rather than Mendelian, especially tobacco, alcohol, betel quid, radiation, and oncogenic viruses, although inherited susceptibility is seen in syndromes such as Fanconi anemia, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and CDKN2A-related predisposition. Typical manifestations include a nonhealing oral ulcer, leukoplakia or erythroplakia, neck mass, odynophagia, dysphagia, hoarseness, otalgia, nasal obstruction or epistaxis, weight loss, pain, cranial neuropathies, and airway compromise. Important comorbidities and complications include malnutrition, dysphonia, aspiration, infection, osteoradionecrosis, fistula formation, carotid blowout, locoregional recurrence, nodal and distant metastases, and second primary tumors. Diagnosis relies on history and head and neck examination with endoscopy, tissue biopsy and histopathology, imaging by CT, MRI, or PET-CT for staging, HPV testing by p16 immunohistochemistry and/or HPV nucleic acid assays, EBV studies in nasopharyngeal disease, and molecular profiling in selected cases. Treatment commonly uses cisplatin, which forms DNA crosslinks; cetuximab, an EGFR-blocking monoclonal antibody; and pembrolizumab or nivolumab

Name: Leukemia, Myelogenous, Chronic, BCR-ABL Positive
Description: Chronic myelogenous leukemia, BCR-ABL positive, is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm of hematopoietic stem cells defined by the Philadelphia chromosome, usually t(9;22)(q34;q11.2), which creates the BCR::ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase, most often encoding p210, with rarer p190 or p230 isoforms; cooperating lesions such as ASXL1, RUNX1, IKZF1, TP53, or ABL1 kinase-domain mutations including T315I may emerge with progression or drug resistance. Constitutive BCR-ABL1 signaling drives proliferation and survival through RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, SRC-family kinases, MYC, and altered adhesion and DNA-damage responses. The disease typically presents in chronic phase, with accelerated and blast phases representing progression, and patients may be asymptomatic or have fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, low-grade fever, early satiety, abdominal fullness from splenomegaly, pallor, bleeding, or symptoms of leukostasis when counts are extreme; common findings include marked leukocytosis with left-shifted granulopoiesis, basophilia, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis or thrombocytopenia, anemia, and hypercellular marrow. It is generally acquired rather than inherited, with no Mendelian pattern, though somatic genomic instability underlies pathogenesis. Diagnosis relies on peripheral blood counts and smear, bone marrow examination, and definitive demonstration of BCR::ABL1 by conventional cytogenetics, FISH, or quantitative RT-PCR, which also establishes baseline transcript burden and is used for molecular monitoring; phase is assigned by blast percentage and other progression features. Standard therapy centers on tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib, and ponatinib, which inhibit BCR-ABL1 ATP-binding activity, with ponatinib retaining activity against T315I; omacetaxine, a protein-synthesis inhibitor, is used in select resistant cases, and allogeneic stem-cell transplantation remains an option for advanced or refractory disease. Important complications and comorbidities include anemia, infection, hemorrhage, thrombosis, gout or hyperuricemia, splenic infarction, transformation to acute leukemia, and treatment-related cardiovascular, pleural, hepatic, or metabolic

Name: Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma
Description: Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL; UMLS C0280803) is an aggressive extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma confined to the brain, leptomeninges, spinal cord, and/or vitreoretinal compartment, most often a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of activated B-cell phenotype, with rarer T-cell, low-grade, or lymphomatosis cerebri variants. Its biology is characterized by constitutive B-cell receptor, Toll-like receptor, and NF-kB signaling, with frequent MYD88 L265P and CD79B mutations, and additional alterations involving PIM1, CARD11, TBL1XR1, BTG2, PRDM1, BCL6, and immune-evasion loci such as CDKN2A loss and 9p24.1/PD-L1/PD-L2 copy gain; neoplastic cells typically express CD20, PAX5, MUM1/IRF4, BCL6 variably, and show a high Ki-67 index. Most cases are sporadic rather than inherited, although risk is increased by acquired or inherited immunodeficiency states, including HIV/AIDS, post-transplant immunosuppression, congenital immunodeficiency, and Epstein-Barr virus association in many immunocompromised patients. Patients commonly present with subacute focal neurologic deficits, neuropsychiatric or cognitive change, headache, seizures, gait disturbance, visual blurring or uveitis-like symptoms, and signs of raised intracranial pressure; complications include hydrocephalus, steroid-masked lesions, neurotoxicity, relapse, and ocular or leptomeningeal dissemination. Diagnosis relies on contrast-enhancing deep periventricular lesions on MRI, ophthalmologic evaluation when indicated, CSF cytology/flow cytometry and molecular studies, and definitive stereotactic brain or vitreous biopsy with immunophenotyping, while corticosteroids should ideally be deferred before biopsy because they can obscure histology. Standard therapy centers on high-dose methotrexate, a folate antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, often combined with rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, and cytarabine, a nucleoside analog inhibiting DNA polymerase; other active agents include temozolomide, an alkylating agent, ibrutinib, a BTK inhibitor targeting B-cell receptor signaling, lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory

Name: Adenocarcinoma of pancreas
Description: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, usually pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), is an aggressive malignant epithelial neoplasm arising most often from precursor lesions such as pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia, with major subtypes including conventional ductal adenocarcinoma and less common adenosquamous, colloid, and undifferentiated variants. Its molecular landscape is dominated by activating KRAS mutations and frequent inactivation of TP53, CDKN2A, and SMAD4, with additional alterations in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, STK11, and mismatch-repair genes in subsets; corresponding protein abnormalities involve mutant KRAS signaling, p53 loss, p16INK4A deficiency, and disrupted SMAD/TGF-β pathway function. Key pathways include RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, TGF-β/SMAD, cell-cycle checkpoint regulation, DNA damage repair, Hedgehog, Notch, and a dense stromal/inflammatory microenvironment involving CAFs, CXCL12, and immune suppression. Most cases are sporadic, but hereditary predisposition may be autosomal dominant in familial pancreatic cancer syndromes such as hereditary breast-ovarian cancer due to BRCA2 or BRCA1, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome due to STK11, Lynch syndrome, CDKN2A-associated melanoma-pancreatic cancer syndrome, and PALB2- or ATM-related susceptibility. Typical manifestations include painless obstructive jaundice, weight loss, epigastric pain radiating to the back, anorexia, new-onset diabetes, steatorrhea, fatigue, migratory thrombophlebitis, and occasionally pancreatitis. Common comorbidities and complications include diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, biliary obstruction, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, venous thromboembolism, cachexia, cholangitis, metastases to liver or peritoneum, and severe pain. Diagnosis relies on pancreatic-protocol contrast CT or MRI/MRCP for staging, endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration/biopsy for histology, CA19-9 as a supportive but nonspecific biomarker, and molecular/germline testing for actionable alterations. Name: Iron Overload
Description: Iron overload is a disorder of excessive total body iron accumulation causing parenchymal hemosiderosis and progressive oxidative tissue injury, classically affecting liver, pancreas, heart, joints, pituitary, and skin; it includes hereditary hemochromatosis and secondary iron overload from repeated transfusions, ineffective erythropoiesis, or chronic liver disease. The major molecular axis involves hepcidin–ferroportin signaling: HAMP-encoded hepcidin normally downregulates the iron exporter ferroportin (SLC40A1), while HFE, HJV, HAMP, TFR2, and BMP6/SMAD pathway components regulate hepcidin expression; representative pathogenic variants include HFE p.Cys282Tyr and p.His63Asp, HJV and HAMP mutations causing juvenile hemochromatosis, TFR2 mutations, and autosomal dominant SLC40A1-related ferroportin disease, with rarer aceruloplasminemia involving CP. Typical inheritance is autosomal recessive for HFE-, HJV-, HAMP-, and TFR2-related disease, and autosomal dominant for ferroportin disease. Clinical manifestations range from fatigue, arthralgia, decreased libido, hepatomegaly, skin hyperpigmentation, and diabetes mellitus to cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma; common comorbidities and complications include metabolic syndrome, osteoporosis, infection susceptibility, endocrinopathies, and chronic liver failure. Diagnosis relies on elevated transferrin saturation, increased serum ferritin, liver enzyme abnormalities, MRI quantification of hepatic or cardiac iron, HFE or broader genetic testing, and selected liver biopsy for iron quantification and fibrosis staging, interpreted with exclusion of inflammatory or alcohol-related ferritin elevation. Treatment centers on therapeutic phlebotomy, which removes iron-containing erythrocytes and induces negative iron balance, and iron chelation when phlebotomy is unsuitable or transfusional overload is present, including deferoxamine, a parenteral hexadentate chelator promoting urinary and biliary iron excretion, deferasirox, an oral tridentate chelator enhancing fecal excretion, and deferiprone, an oral bidentate chelator particularly useful for cardiac iron.

Name: Cystitis, Interstitial
Description: Interstitial cystitis, or bladder pain syndrome, is a chronic noninfectious inflammatory and sensory disorder of the bladder characterized by suprapubic pain related to bladder filling, urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia, pressure, and dyspareunia, often with sterile urine and cystoscopic or histologic evidence of urothelial dysfunction. It is clinically heterogeneous, with ulcerative or Hunner lesion disease and nonulcerative forms, and often reflects epithelial barrier failure, neurogenic inflammation, mast-cell activation, and central sensitization. Molecular studies implicate altered urothelial and inflammatory mediators including TNF, IL6, IL8, NGF, VEGF, COX-2, tryptase, E-cadherin, and antiproliferative factor pathways involving frizzled-8, as well as purinergic, TRPV1, substance P, histamine, and TLR-mediated signaling; representative genetic associations, generally complex and non-Mendelian rather than causal, include polymorphisms or differential expression in cytokine genes, ADRB2, COMT, HTR2A, and extracellular matrix or urothelial barrier genes, with familial clustering reported but no single established inheritance pattern. Common comorbidities include irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, vulvodynia, endometriosis, chronic fatigue, migraine, anxiety, depression, and autoimmune disorders, and complications include sleep disturbance, sexual dysfunction, reduced bladder capacity, and major quality-of-life impairment. Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion, typically requiring chronic bladder-centric pain with lower urinary tract symptoms for at least 6 weeks without infection or other identifiable cause, supported by urinalysis and culture, voiding diaries, symptom indices, pelvic examination, cystoscopy with hydrodistention and possible Hunner lesion identification, biopsy when malignancy or eosinophilic/carcinomatous processes must be excluded, and sometimes urodynamics. Treatments commonly include pentosan polysulfate sodium, which is thought to restore the glycosaminoglycan urothelial barrier; amitriptyline, which reduces neuropathic pain via serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and antihistaminic effects; hydroxyzine, an H1 antagonist that suppresses mast-cell mediated symptoms; and intravesical dimethyl sulfoxide, which provides anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and muscle-relaxant effects.

Name: Arsenic Poisoning
Description: Arsenic poisoning (UMLS C0311375) is a toxic, predominantly acquired metalloid intoxication caused by acute high-dose or chronic environmental, occupational, medicinal, or contaminated-water exposure to inorganic arsenic, producing multisystem injury rather than a Mendelian disease, although susceptibility is modified by genetic variation in arsenic biotransformation and oxidative-stress pathways, notably AS3MT, GSTT1, GSTM1, GSTP1, MTHFR, PNP, and DNA-repair genes such as XRCC1 and ERCC2; impaired methylation capacity can increase tissue retention and toxicity. Core molecular effects include glutathione depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, pyruvate dehydrogenase inhibition, endothelial injury, epigenetic dysregulation, reactive oxygen species generation, and altered Nrf2-Keap1, MAPK, NF-kB, p53, apoptotic, angiogenic, and DNA damage-response signaling. Clinical forms include acute poisoning with severe gastroenteritis, vomiting, abdominal pain, rice-water diarrhea, hypotension, QT prolongation, encephalopathy, hemolysis, and shock, and chronic poisoning with fatigue, sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, skin hyperpigmentation and raindrop depigmentation, palmar-plantar hyperkeratosis, Mee lines, anemia, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and vascular disease. Major complications and comorbidities include diabetes, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, bronchiectasis, peripheral arterial disease/blackfoot disease, and increased risks of skin, bladder, lung, liver, and kidney cancers. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus toxicologic testing, especially urinary total arsenic with speciation to distinguish inorganic arsenic and metabolites from seafood-derived organic arsenicals; blood arsenic may support recent exposure, while hair and nail analysis can document prior exposure, and ancillary studies include CBC, renal and liver panels, ECG, nerve conduction studies, and skin biopsy when indicated. Treatment centers on exposure cessation and supportive care, with chelation using dimercaprol, which complexes trivalent arsenic sulfhydryl-binding sites, succimer, an oral dithiol chelator that enhances urinary excretion, or DMPS, a water-soluble vicinal dithiol with similar chelating action.

Name: Urethritis, NOS
Description: Urethritis, NOS (UMLS C0311389) is a nonspecific inflammatory disorder of the urethral mucosa, most often infectious and sexually acquired, but also caused by mechanical irritation, chemicals, or trauma; major clinical forms include gonococcal urethritis and nongonococcal urethritis, the latter commonly linked to Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, and sometimes herpes simplex virus or adenovirus. Typical manifestations are dysuria, urethral burning or pruritus, frequency, meatal erythema, and urethral discharge ranging from purulent to mucoid, although asymptomatic infection is common. Pathobiology is driven largely by host innate and adaptive immune activation rather than a Mendelian genetic basis; implicated host susceptibility factors include cytokine and pattern-recognition pathways such as TLR2/TLR4, NOD signaling, NF-κB, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-α, and Th1/Th17 responses, while representative microbial virulence determinants include N. gonorrhoeae porins, pili, Opa proteins, and penA-mediated altered penicillin-binding protein 2, C. trachomatis major outer membrane protein and type III secretion machinery, and macrolide-resistance 23S rRNA mutations or parC/gyrA fluoroquinolone-resistance mutations in M. genitalium. No consistent inheritance pattern is recognized, though polymorphic variation in immune-response genes may modify risk and severity. Diagnosis rests on symptoms plus objective evidence of urethral inflammation, including urethral smear showing increased polymorphonuclear leukocytes, positive leukocyte esterase or pyuria on first-void urine, and nucleic acid amplification testing for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, with additional testing for M. genitalium, T. vaginalis, HIV, and syphilis as indicated. Standard treatment includes ceftriaxone, a β-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, for gonorrhea; doxycycline, a tetracycline blocking 30S ribosomal protein synthesis, for chlamydial NGU; azithromycin, a macrolide inhibiting 50S translocation, or moxifloxacin, a flu

Name: Lymphangiomatosis
Description: Lymphangiomatosis is a rare, usually nonhereditary congenital or sporadic lymphatic malformation characterized by diffuse multifocal proliferation and dilation of lymphatic channels that can involve bone, soft tissue, mediastinum, lung, spleen, liver, and skin, with localized, generalized, and complex forms that overlap clinically with generalized lymphatic anomaly and Gorham-Stout spectrum disorders. Molecular studies implicate dysregulated lymphangiogenesis driven by VEGF-C/VEGFR3 signaling, PI3K/AKT/mTOR and RAS/MAPK pathways, and lymphatic endothelial markers and regulators including FLT4/VEGFR3, PIK3CA, NRAS, KRAS, ARAF, CBL, PTEN, AKT1, TEK/TIE2, PROX1, SOX18, FOXC2, VEGFR2, podoplanin, LYVE1, and D2-40, with many lesions showing postzygotic somatic mosaic variants rather than germline inheritance; when inherited lymphatic dysplasia syndromes are considered in the differential, autosomal dominant examples include FLT4- and FOXC2-related disease. Clinical manifestations depend on organ burden and commonly include painless masses, lymphedema, chronic pain, pathologic fractures or osteolysis, chylothorax, pleural or pericardial effusions, cough, dyspnea, wheeze, ascites, protein-losing enteropathy, coagulopathy, and recurrent infection, with complications such as respiratory failure, malnutrition, bleeding, and skeletal deformity. Diagnosis is based on clinical-radiologic-pathologic correlation using MRI and CT to define extent, lymphoscintigraphy or dynamic contrast MR lymphangiography to assess flow abnormalities, plain radiographs for lytic bone lesions, and biopsy showing thin-walled endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces positive for podoplanin/D2-40, PROX1, and LYVE1 while excluding malignancy. Treatment is individualized and often multimodal: sirolimus inhibits mTOR to reduce aberrant lymphatic endothelial growth, alpelisib targets PI3K-alpha in PIK3CA-driven disease, trametinib inhibits MEK in RAS/MAPK-activated lesions, and adjunctive therapies such as propranolol, interferon-alpha, corticosteroids, bisphosphonates, sclerotherapy, drainage, or surgery may be

Name: Astrocytoma, Anaplastic
Description: Astrocytoma is a diffuse or circumscribed primary glial neoplasm derived from astrocytes, ranging from relatively indolent pilocytic astrocytoma to infiltrating WHO grade 2–4 tumors, including anaplastic astrocytoma and glioblastoma, and it typically presents with seizures, progressive headache, focal neurologic deficits, cognitive or personality change, nausea, papilledema, or signs of raised intracranial pressure. Molecularly, astrocytomas are defined by recurrent alterations in IDH1 or IDH2, TP53, ATRX, CDKN2A/B loss, PTEN, EGFR amplification or mutation, TERT promoter mutation, PDGFRA activation, BRAF alterations such as KIAA1549-BRAF fusion or BRAF V600E, and less commonly H3F3A or HIST1H3B mutations in pediatric high-grade disease; protein dysregulation involves p53, Rb, receptor tyrosine kinases, MGMT, and PI3K effectors. Key pathways include RTK/RAS/RAF/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53, RB cell-cycle control, hypoxia/VEGF-driven angiogenesis, and altered metabolic programs in IDH-mutant tumors with 2-hydroxyglutarate production. Most cases are sporadic, but predisposition occurs in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, Lynch syndrome/constitutional mismatch repair deficiency, and tuberous sclerosis complex, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance in the cancer-predisposition syndrome. Diagnosis relies on MRI with contrast, histopathology demonstrating astrocytic lineage and infiltrative growth where applicable, WHO integrated molecular classification with immunohistochemistry and sequencing for IDH, ATRX, p53, BRAF, H3, MGMT promoter methylation, and CDKN2A/B status, and selected use of MR spectroscopy or perfusion imaging. Standard treatment includes maximal safe resection, radiotherapy, temozolomide, an oral alkylating agent causing DNA methylation, lomustine, a nitrosourea alkylator, bevacizumab, a VEGF-neutralizing antibody that reduces angiogenesis and edema, and in selected BRAF-altered tumors dabrafenib plus trametinib targeting BRAF and MEK. Name: Meningitis, Escherichia coli
Description: Escherichia coli meningitis is an acute, usually pyogenic bacterial infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid, classically seen as neonatal meningitis but also occurring in adults after neurosurgery, trauma, bacteremia, or in immunocompromised states. Pathogenesis is strongly linked to extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli, especially K1-capsulated strains and sequence type ST131 in some adult invasive infections; representative virulence-associated genes and proteins include kpsM/kpsS and the K1 polysialic acid capsule, outer membrane protein A (ompA), type 1 fimbrial adhesin fimH, ibeA/ibeB involved in blood-brain barrier invasion, cnf1, aslA, and lipopolysaccharide-endotoxin determinants. These factors engage host inflammatory pathways dominated by TLR4-CD14-MD2 recognition of LPS, with NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL8, complement activation, endothelial injury, leukocyte trafficking, and blood-brain barrier disruption. Common therapies include third-generation cephalosporins such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and peptidoglycan cross-linking; meropenem, a carbapenem with broad β-lactam activity and good CNS penetration; and ampicillin, another cell-wall synthesis inhibitor, sometimes partnered with gentamicin, an aminoglycoside that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and impairs protein synthesis, with regimen choice guided by susceptibility and concern for ESBL-producing strains. Major complications include sepsis, ventriculitis, hydrocephalus, seizures, cerebral infarction, hearing loss, developmental delay, and death; linked comorbidities include prematurity, very low birth weight, urinary tract infection, gastrointestinal translocation, diabetes, cirrhosis, malignancy, and neurosurgical devices. Symptoms typically include fever, irritability, lethargy, poor feeding, apnea, bulging fontanelle, seizures, or in older patients headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. It is generally sporadic rather than inherited, although host susceptibility may be influenced by rare complement defects or polymorphisms in innate immune genes such as TLR4. Name: Proteus meningitis
Description: Proteus meningitis is an uncommon, usually acute bacterial meningitis caused most often by Proteus mirabilis and less commonly P. vulgaris or related Enterobacterales, typically arising as a sporadic, non-inherited infectious disease rather than a primary genetic disorder; host susceptibility may be influenced by innate immune defects involving complement components, TLR4-LPS signaling, MyD88/IRAK4, or neutrophil dysfunction, while bacterial virulence determinants include urease, flagellin, fimbrial adhesins such as MR/P fimbriae, hemolysin HpmA/HpmB, lipopolysaccharide, and biofilm-associated factors. Pathobiologically, meningitis follows bacteremia or contiguous spread and is driven by LPS-triggered TLR4/NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, complement, and neutrophil-mediated inflammatory pathways that increase blood-brain barrier permeability and produce purulent meningeal inflammation. Clinical features are those of gram-negative meningitis: fever, severe headache, vomiting, meningismus, photophobia, altered mental status, irritability or poor feeding in neonates, seizures, and signs of sepsis; recognized forms include neonatal and adult nosocomial disease, post-neurosurgical or trauma-associated infection, and secondary meningitis complicating urinary tract infection. Important comorbidities and risk factors include prematurity, urinary tract abnormalities, indwelling catheters, neurosurgical devices, immunosuppression, diabetes, and structural CNS defects, while complications include ventriculitis, hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, abscess, septic shock, hearing loss, and neurodevelopmental impairment. Diagnosis relies on blood and cerebrospinal fluid culture with species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose, Gram stain showing gram-negative rods, and neuroimaging when complications are suspected. Treatment generally uses intravenous antibiotics with CNS penetration such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins; meropenem, another cell-wall synthesis inhibitor with broad gram-negative activity; and gentamicin or amikacin, aminoglycosides that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and impair protein synthesis, tailored to resistance patterns and source control.

Name: Neurocysticercosis
Description: Neurocysticercosis (MeSH D020019) is an acquired parasitic infection of the central nervous system caused by larval Taenia solium, not a Mendelian disorder, although host genetic susceptibility and inflammatory severity have been linked to immune-response genes and proteins such as HLA class II alleles, TLR4, MMP-9, ICAM-1, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-10, which shape granulomatous inflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and seizure risk. Its pathobiology centers on host-parasite interactions involving innate immune signaling, NF-κB activation, Th1/Th2 and regulatory cytokine pathways, microglial and astrocytic activation, eosinophilic and macrophage responses, complement, and matrix remodeling during cyst degeneration. Major forms include parenchymal, ventricular, subarachnoid/racemose, spinal, and calcified neurocysticercosis, with viable, degenerating, and inactive stages. Typical manifestations are new-onset seizures, chronic headache, focal deficits, cognitive decline, raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, meningismus, visual symptoms, and psychiatric or gait disturbances depending on lesion burden and location. Frequent complications and comorbidities include epilepsy, ventriculitis, arachnoiditis, stroke from inflammatory vasculopathy, hydrocephalus, chronic calcific seizure disorders, and coinfection or systemic cysticercosis. Diagnosis relies on integration of epidemiologic exposure, neuroimaging with CT or MRI showing cysts, scolex, ring-enhancing or calcified lesions, supportive serology such as enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot or antigen assays, CSF analysis in selected extraparenchymal cases, and established radiologic, clinical, immunologic, and exposure-based diagnostic criteria. Treatment commonly uses albendazole, a benzimidazole that binds parasite β-tubulin and inhibits microtubule-dependent glucose uptake, praziquantel, which increases parasite calcium permeability causing spastic paralysis, and corticosteroids such as dexamethasone or prednisone to suppress cytokine-driven edema; antiepileptics including levetiracetam or phenytoin control seizures, and neurosurgical CSF diversion or endoscopic cyst removal is often required for obstructive ventricular or subarachnoid disease.

Name: Bipolar affective disorder, current episode manic
Description: Bipolar affective disorder, current episode manic (UMLS C0338873), is a severe episodic mood disorder in which the patient currently meets criteria for mania, characterized by abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, racing thoughts, distractibility, psychomotor agitation, impulsive high-risk behavior, and sometimes psychosis. It is usually classified within bipolar I disorder when full mania is present, with subtypes or specifiers including psychotic features, mixed features, rapid cycling, and severity-based distinctions. The disorder is multifactorial and highly heritable, with overall heritability commonly estimated around 60–80%; risk is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative susceptibility genes from psychiatric genomic studies including CACNA1C, ANK3, ODZ4/TENM4, SYNE1, TRANK1, NCAN, and circadian genes such as CLOCK and ARNTL, while BDNF and SLC6A4 have also been implicated, though without a single defining mutation in most cases. Relevant pathobiology involves dysregulation of dopaminergic, serotonergic, glutamatergic, GABAergic, and intracellular calcium signaling, abnormalities in cAMP, PKC, GSK3, inositol, mitochondrial and oxidative stress pathways, neurotrophin signaling including BDNF-TrkB, inflammatory cytokine networks, and circadian rhythm circuitry centered on the suprachiasmatic clock. Common treatments include lithium, which modulates inositol signaling and inhibits GSK3; valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and alters sodium-channel and histone deacetylase activity; and atypical antipsychotics such as olanzapine, quetiapine, or risperidone, which primarily antagonize dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors; carbamazepine is another option via sodium-channel blockade. Frequent comorbidities include anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, ADHD, migraine, obesity, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and thyroid dysfunction; complications include suicide, violence or accidental harm, financial and occupational impairment, relationship disruption, and treatment nonadherence. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 criteria, supported by psychiatric interview, collateral history, mental status examination, rating scales such as the Young Mania Rating Scale, and laboratory or toxicology testing to

Name: Mixed anxiety and depressive disorder
Description: Mixed anxiety and depressive disorder (UMLS C0338908) is a common, usually non-psychotic internalizing condition characterized by the co-occurrence of clinically significant anxious and depressive symptoms that do not fully meet criteria for a stand-alone anxiety disorder or major depressive episode, although nosologic boundaries vary across ICD and DSM frameworks and some cases evolve into major depression or generalized anxiety disorder. Clinical features typically include persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive worry, tension, irritability, fatigue, impaired concentration, insomnia or hypersomnia, autonomic arousal, and somatic complaints, with complications including functional impairment, substance misuse, suicidal ideation, chronic pain, and elevated cardiovascular and metabolic risk; frequent comorbidities include major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, PTSD, insomnia, and alcohol or other substance use disorders. The disorder is multifactorial rather than Mendelian, with modest polygenic liability and gene-by-environment effects involving stress-response, monoaminergic, and neurotrophic systems; representative associated genes include SLC6A4, HTR1A, HTR2A, COMT, MAOA, BDNF including the Val66Met variant, FKBP5, CRHR1, and NR3C1. Implicated pathways include serotonergic, noradrenergic, dopaminergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, HPA-axis, inflammatory, and neuroplasticity signaling, with key components such as 5-HT transporters and receptors, NET, COMT, glucocorticoid receptors, CRH signaling, cytokines including IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and BDNF-TrkB-mediated synaptic plasticity. Treatment commonly uses SSRIs such as sertraline or escitalopram, which inhibit SLC6A4 to increase synaptic serotonin, SNRIs such as venlafaxine or duloxetine, which inhibit serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, and buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist; benzodiazepines such as lorazepam may provide short-term GABA-A receptor–mediated anxiolysis. Diagnosis is clinical, based on structured history, mental status examination, symptom scales such as PHQ-9 and GAD-7 or HADS, exclusion of bipolar disorder, psychosis, thyroid disease, medication effects, and substance-induced states, while genetic testing is not routine.

Name: Fungal conjunctivitis
Description: Fungal conjunctivitis (UMLS C0339170) is an uncommon infectious conjunctival inflammation caused most often by Candida spp., Aspergillus spp., Fusarium spp., or Sporothrix schenckii, presenting as acute or chronic conjunctival hyperemia, irritation, pain or foreign-body sensation, tearing, mucopurulent or scant discharge, photophobia, lid edema, chemosis, and sometimes granulomatous nodules, pseudomembranes, or adjacent keratitis. It may occur as primary disease after trauma, contaminated topical medications, contact lens wear, agricultural exposure, or ocular surgery, or secondarily in immunocompromised hosts; important comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, HIV/AIDS, neutropenia, chronic ocular surface disease, dry eye, topical corticosteroid use, and systemic mycoses. Molecularly, host susceptibility is shaped more by innate immune signaling than Mendelian inheritance, with representative components including pattern-recognition receptors such as Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2, TLR4, CARD9, MYD88, NF-κB, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, TNF-α, complement, and neutrophil/macrophage antifungal responses; rare defects in CARD9 or related antifungal immunity pathways can predispose to invasive or refractory fungal infection, but no specific hereditary pattern is typical for isolated conjunctivitis. Subtypes are usually classified by pathogen and morphology, including candidal, filamentous mold, and granulomatous/sporotrichoid forms. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus slit-lamp examination and microbiologic confirmation by conjunctival scraping or biopsy for potassium hydroxide wet mount, calcofluor white stain, Gram stain, fungal culture, and histopathology, with PCR or sequencing used in difficult cases; differential diagnosis includes bacterial, viral, allergic, and chlamydial conjunctivitis. Treatment centers on topical or systemic antifungals: natamycin, a polyene that binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes; amphotericin B, another ergosterol-binding polyene; and azoles such as voriconazole, fluconazole, or itraconazole, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-α-demethylase (CYP51) and block ergosterol synthesis; severe disease may require debridement. Name: Corneal Perforation
Description: Corneal perforation (UMLS C0339293) is a vision-threatening full-thickness defect of the cornea that usually represents the end stage of severe infectious keratitis, sterile corneal melt, trauma, neurotrophic disease, or autoimmune ocular surface inflammation rather than a single inherited disorder; patients typically present with acute pain, redness, photophobia, tearing, blurred vision, shallow anterior chamber, positive Seidel test, iris prolapse, hypotony, and risk of endophthalmitis. Major etiologic subtypes include infectious perforation caused by bacteria, fungi, herpes simplex or zoster, and acanthamoeba; noninfectious inflammatory or melt-related perforation in rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sjögren syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and Mooren ulcer; traumatic or postsurgical perforation; and degenerative or ectatic forms such as keratoconus-associated hydrops with rupture. Molecularly, corneal stromal degradation commonly involves inflammatory cytokines and matrix-remodeling pathways, especially IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6, NF-κB, MMP-2, MMP-9, collagenases, neutrophil proteases, VEGF, TGF-β, and complement; representative genetic contributors are indirect and context dependent, including MMP9 and TIMP imbalance, HLA associations in autoimmune disease, TGFBI-related corneal dystrophies, COL5A1 and VSX1 in ectatic disease, and PAX6 in aniridia-related keratopathy, with inheritance patterns therefore varying from sporadic/acquired to autosomal dominant in some dystrophies. Treatment is cause directed and urgent: topical moxifloxacin inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase, fortified vancomycin inhibits gram-positive cell-wall synthesis, natamycin binds fungal ergosterol, acyclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase, doxycycline suppresses MMP activity and collagenolysis, and corticosteroids or systemic cyclophosphamide/rituximab reduce immune-mediated tissue destruction in selected sterile cases; cyanoacrylate glue, bandage contact lens, amniotic membrane graft, or keratoplasty are often required. Diagnosis relies on slit-lamp biomicroscopy, fluorescein Seidel testing, corneal scraping with Gram stain and culture or PCR, pachymetry

Name: Central retinal vein occlusion with macular edema
Description: Central retinal vein occlusion with macular edema is an acquired retinal vascular disorder in which thrombotic obstruction of the central retinal vein, classically at the lamina cribrosa, causes venous stasis, retinal hemorrhage, capillary nonperfusion, and breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier, leading to fluid accumulation in the macula and vision loss; it is usually classified as non-ischemic or ischemic CRVO, with the latter carrying greater risk of neovascular glaucoma and severe permanent visual impairment. Although not a Mendelian disease, genetic susceptibility has been linked to thrombophilia and vascular-risk variants, including factor V Leiden in F5, prothrombin G20210A in F2, MTHFR polymorphisms, SERPINE1/PAI-1, and occasionally protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, while key molecular mediators include VEGFA-driven angiogenic signaling through VEGFR2, inflammatory cytokines such as IL6, ICAM1, MCP-1/CCL2, and disruption of endothelial tight-junction proteins. Typical symptoms are sudden, painless unilateral blurred vision, metamorphopsia, central scotoma, and reduced acuity; signs include dilated tortuous veins, diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, optic disc edema, and cystoid macular edema on optical coherence tomography. Major comorbidities include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, glaucoma, smoking, atherosclerotic disease, and hypercoagulable states, while complications include retinal ischemia, neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, and tractional or neovascular glaucoma. Diagnosis is based on funduscopic examination supported by OCT to quantify macular edema, fluorescein angiography to assess delayed venous filling and capillary nonperfusion, OCT-angiography, intraocular pressure measurement, and selected thrombophilia or systemic vascular evaluation in younger or atypical patients. Standard treatment centers on intravitreal anti-VEGF agents such as aflibercept, ranibizumab, and bevacizumab, which inhibit VEGF-mediated vascular permeability and neovascularization, or corticosteroids such as dexamethasone implant or triamcinolone, which suppress inflammatory signaling and stabilize the blood-retinal barrier; laser photocoagulation is mainly reserved for neovascular complications rather than macular edema itself.

C0339507 corresponds to hereditary hemochromatosis, a systemic iron-overload disorder characterized by inappropriately increased intestinal iron absorption and progressive parenchymal iron deposition, most often in liver, pancreas, heart, joints, and endocrine organs. The classic genetic form is autosomal recessive HFE-related disease caused mainly by HFE mutations, especially C282Y homozygosity and, less penetrantly, compound heterozygosity for C282Y/H63D; rarer non-HFE forms involve HJV, HAMP, TFR2, or SLC40A1, with ferroportin disease due to SLC40A1 often showing autosomal dominant inheritance. Pathobiology centers on the hepcidin–ferroportin axis: deficient hepcidin signaling or ferroportin dysregulation increases iron export from enterocytes and macrophages, elevates transferrin saturation, and promotes non-transferrin-bound iron–mediated oxidative injury. Clinical manifestations range from fatigue, arthralgia of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, hepatomegaly, skin hyperpigmentation, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and diabetes mellitus to cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, hypogonadism, and arthropathy; major complications include hepatocellular carcinoma, portal hypertension, heart failure, osteoporosis, and susceptibility to certain infections such as Vibrio vulnificus. Disease subtypes include type 1 HFE hemochromatosis, juvenile hemochromatosis due to HJV or HAMP, type 3 due to TFR2, and ferroportin disease. Diagnosis relies on elevated transferrin saturation, increased serum ferritin, HFE or other genetic testing, exclusion of secondary iron overload, and assessment of organ injury by liver enzymes, MRI-based hepatic iron quantification, or occasionally liver biopsy. Treatment is primarily serial therapeutic phlebotomy, which removes iron directly; when phlebotomy is contraindicated, iron chelators such as deferasirox, deferoxamine, or deferiprone may be used, binding excess iron to enhance excretion, alongside management of cirrhosis, diabetes, and cardiac complications.

Name: Acute Moraxella catarrhalis bronchitis
Description: Acute Moraxella catarrhalis bronchitis is an acute bacterial lower-airway infection, usually a subtype of acute infectious bronchitis superimposed on viral mucosal injury or chronic airway disease, in which the gram-negative diplococcus M. catarrhalis triggers neutrophilic bronchial inflammation through epithelial adhesion and innate immune activation rather than through a Mendelian inherited disorder. Relevant microbial virulence determinants include UspA1/UspA2 adhesins, MID/Hag, outer-membrane proteins such as CopB and OMP CD, lipooligosaccharide biosynthesis genes, and BRO-1 or BRO-2 beta-lactamase, while host susceptibility is influenced by immune and inflammatory genes and proteins including TLR2, TLR4, CD14, MYD88, NF-κB, IL1B, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, mucins such as MUC5AC, and complement components; no single germline mutation is diagnostic, but predisposition is increased in COPD, immunoglobulin deficiency, complement defects, cystic fibrosis with CFTR mutations, primary ciliary dyskinesia, and smoking-related airway injury. Key pathways include TLR-mediated NF-κB and MAPK signaling, cytokine and chemokine recruitment of neutrophils, complement evasion, biofilm formation, and oxidative stress responses. Typical features are acute cough, purulent sputum, wheeze, dyspnea, chest discomfort, rhonchi, fever that is often low grade, and exacerbation of baseline airflow limitation; complications include COPD or asthma exacerbation, otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia, bacteremia rarely, and respiratory failure in frail patients. Diagnosis is clinical when acute bronchitic symptoms occur without focal pneumonia, supported when needed by sputum Gram stain and culture, nasopharyngeal or sputum PCR, chest radiography to exclude pneumonia, and inflammatory markers; susceptibility testing matters because beta-lactamase production is common. Common treatments include amoxicillin-clavulanate, in which amoxicillin inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamase; azithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; doxycycline, a 30S inhibitor; and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV

Name: Acute bacterial bronchitis
Description: Acute bacterial bronchitis (UMLS C0339933) is an acute infectious inflammation of the tracheobronchial tree caused by bacterial pathogens, most often secondary to viral mucosal injury or impaired host defense, and is characterized clinically by acute cough, purulent sputum, wheeze, rhonchi, chest discomfort, dyspnea, and sometimes fever, while lacking the parenchymal infiltrates that define pneumonia. Common bacterial agents include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphylococcus aureus, and atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Bordetella pertussis; relevant microbial genes and proteins include pneumococcal pneumolysin and capsule loci, H. influenzae lipooligosaccharide and adhesins, pertussis toxin, and macrolide-resistance determinants such as ermB and mefA, whereas host susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, involving innate and inflammatory mediators such as TLR2, TLR4, CD14, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, TNF, MUC5AC, CFTR, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in selected patients. Major pathways include Toll-like receptor, NF-kappaB, inflammasome, neutrophil chemotaxis, mucus hypersecretion, and oxidative-stress signaling in airway epithelium. Treatment, when bacterial infection is likely or confirmed, commonly uses amoxicillin-clavulanate, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis and beta-lactamases, azithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis, doxycycline, which binds the 30S subunit, and in selected cases levofloxacin, a DNA gyrase/topoisomerase inhibitor. Important comorbidities include asthma, COPD, smoking-related airway disease, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, diabetes, and immunosuppression; complications include persistent cough, bronchospasm, secondary pneumonia, respiratory failure in frail patients, and exacerbation of chronic lung disease. Subtypes are usually defined by pathogen class, including typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and pertussis-associated bronchitis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by history and examination, pulse oximetry, inflammatory markers when needed, sputum Gram stain/culture or PCR in selected cases, pertussis

Name: Chlamydial Pneumonia
Description: Chlamydial pneumonia (UMLS C0339959) is an infectious atypical pneumonia caused primarily by Chlamydia pneumoniae and less often by C. psittaci or neonatal C. trachomatis, characterized by intracellular replication in respiratory epithelium and macrophages with host inflammatory injury rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder. Disease biology involves bacterial attachment and endocytosis, transition between elementary and reticulate bodies, and activation of innate immune pathways including TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, MAPK, inflammasome signaling, and cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and IFN-γ; host susceptibility and severity have been variably linked to immune-response genes and proteins including HLA alleles, TLR2, TLR4, CD14, mannose-binding lectin, TNF, IL6, and IFNG, although no single mutation is diagnostic. Typical manifestations include subacute fever, dry cough, hoarseness, pharyngitis, malaise, headache, wheeze, and patchy interstitial or bronchopneumonic infiltrates, with neonatal C. trachomatis disease often presenting with afebrile staccato cough and eosinophilia. Common subtypes are C. pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia, psittacosis, and neonatal chlamydial pneumonia. Standard therapy includes azithromycin or erythromycin, which bind the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibit protein synthesis, doxycycline, which binds the 30S subunit to block tRNA attachment, and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Comorbidities and complications include asthma or COPD exacerbation, sinusitis, bronchitis, otitis, severe respiratory failure, ARDS, pleural effusion, and in psittacosis hepatitis, myocarditis, or encephalitis. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical and radiographic findings plus microbiologic evidence by NAAT/PCR from respiratory samples, paired serology showing rising antibody titers, culture in specialized laboratories, and in neonates testing conjunctival or nasopharyngeal specimens alongside maternal genital infection history.

Name: Neonatal pneumonia
Description: Neonatal pneumonia (UMLS C0339968) is an acute infectious inflammatory disease of the lung parenchyma occurring in the first 28 days of life, usually classified as congenital/intrauterine, early-onset peripartum or aspiration-associated, and late-onset nosocomial or community-acquired pneumonia. It is most often caused by Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, and gram-negative bacilli, with viral causes including RSV, influenza, and CMV in selected settings. Host susceptibility is influenced more by prematurity and impaired innate immunity than by simple Mendelian inheritance, but relevant genetic components include surfactant dysfunction genes SFTPB, SFTPC, and ABCA3, CFTR in cystic fibrosis, and primary immunodeficiency-related genes affecting TLR, MYD88, IRAK4, or neutrophil function; proteins central to pathobiology include surfactant proteins SP-A, SP-B, and SP-C, cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, and IL-8, and pattern-recognition receptors including TLR2 and TLR4. Key pathways involve pathogen recognition with TLR/NF-kappaB signaling, complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, inflammasome-mediated cytokine release, and disruption of alveolar-capillary barrier function causing impaired gas exchange. Typical signs are tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, apnea, cyanosis, temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, and hypoxemia, often overlapping with neonatal sepsis and respiratory distress syndrome. Diagnosis relies on clinical respiratory distress plus risk factors, chest radiography showing diffuse or focal infiltrates, blood culture and CBC/CRP or procalcitonin, blood gas assessment, and targeted viral PCR or tracheal aspirate culture when indicated. Standard treatment uses empiric ampicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, plus gentamicin, an aminoglycoside causing 30S ribosomal mistranslation; cefotaxime, a third-generation cephalosporin blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking, or vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala in resistant gram-positive infection, are common alternatives, with acyclovir added when neonatal HSV is suspected.
