Name: Q fever endocarditis
Description: Q fever endocarditis (UMLS C0340354) is a chronic, culture-negative infective endocarditis caused by persistent infection with Coxiella burnetii, typically involving previously abnormal or prosthetic valves and occasionally vascular grafts, and it most often presents subacutely with prolonged fever, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, new or changing murmurs, heart failure, and embolic or immunologic phenomena; major complications include valvular destruction, abscess, stroke, glomerulonephritis, and chronic vascular infection. The disease is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion, but host susceptibility and severity have been linked to immune-response genes and pathways, with representative associations involving HLA class II alleles, interferon-γ and IL-12 axis components, TLR2/TLR4, and cytokine variants in TNF, IL10, and IFNG; bacterial virulence is related to phase I lipopolysaccharide, type IV secretion system effectors, and intracellular survival in monocytes/macrophages within phagolysosome-like vacuoles. Pathobiologically, infection engages innate immune signaling through TLRs, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, interferon signaling, and granulomatous inflammatory pathways, while ineffective cellular immunity permits persistence. Recognized risk subgroups include native-valve, prosthetic-valve, and device- or vascular graft-associated disease, especially in patients with preexisting valvulopathy, congenital heart disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy exposure history, or renal disease. Diagnosis relies on high clinical suspicion, echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement, and characteristic serology showing markedly elevated phase I IgG antibodies, typically with indirect immunofluorescence, supported by PCR on blood or excised valve tissue and histopathology when available; routine blood cultures are usually negative. Standard therapy is prolonged doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit, combined with hydroxychloroquine, which alkalinizes the phagolysosome and enhances intracellular killing, often for 18 to 24 months, with alternatives or adjuncts such as rifampin, a DNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor, fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which

Name: Deficiency of pyruvate kinase
Description: Deficiency of pyruvate kinase is a hereditary erythrocyte enzymopathy causing chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia due most often to biallelic pathogenic variants in PKLR, which encodes the red-cell and liver pyruvate kinase isoforms; representative mutations include missense changes such as R510Q and R486W, as well as splice, nonsense, and deletion variants that reduce enzyme stability or catalytic activity, while rare differential considerations include other glycolytic defects rather than true locus heterogeneity. The core pathobiology is failure of the terminal glycolytic step converting phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate with ATP generation, leading to erythrocyte ATP depletion, membrane rigidity, impaired ion homeostasis, splenic sequestration, and compensatory elevations of upstream metabolites including 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate that alter oxygen affinity. It is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, with phenotypic severity ranging from severe neonatal disease to compensated adult hemolysis; recognized forms include classic congenital chronic hemolytic anemia and severe transfusion-dependent presentations. Typical findings are neonatal jaundice, pallor, fatigue, reticulocytosis, splenomegaly, scleral icterus, pigment gallstones, and iron overload, with complications including aplastic crises, leg ulcers, extramedullary hematopoiesis, osteoporosis, pulmonary hypertension, and post-splenectomy thrombosis or infection. Diagnosis rests on evidence of Coombs-negative hemolysis with elevated indirect bilirubin and LDH, low haptoglobin, exclusion of membrane and hemoglobin disorders, red-cell pyruvate kinase enzyme assay, and confirmatory molecular testing of PKLR, sometimes supported by next-generation sequencing panels. Treatment is supportive and targeted: transfusions correct symptomatic anemia by replacing enzyme-deficient erythrocytes, folic acid supports erythropoiesis, splenectomy reduces extravascular hemolysis, iron chelators such as deferasirox, deferiprone, and deferoxamine mitigate transfusional or disease-related iron overload, and mitapivat, an allosteric activator of pyruvate kinase-R, enhances residual enzyme activity and ATP production in selected adults.

Name: Bacterial Peritonitis
Description: Bacterial peritonitis is an acute infectious inflammation of the peritoneal cavity, classically presenting as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis with ascites or as secondary peritonitis after gastrointestinal perforation, ischemia, surgery, or dialysis-related contamination; patients typically develop fever, diffuse abdominal pain and tenderness, guarding, rebound, ileus, nausea, altered mental status, hypotension, and sepsis. Its pathobiology is driven less by single-gene causation than by host-defense and inflammatory pathways, notably bacterial lipopolysaccharide engagement of TLR4-CD14-MYD88, NF-κB activation, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokines such as TNF, IL1B, IL6, and CXCL8; representative susceptibility-associated genes or proteins discussed in the literature include NOD2, TLR2, TLR4, MBL2, and TNF promoter variants, especially in cirrhosis or peritoneal dialysis populations, but inheritance is not Mendelian and reflects complex polygenic and acquired risk. Common organisms include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, streptococci, enterococci, and in secondary disease mixed aerobes and anaerobes such as Bacteroides. Major comorbidities and complications include liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure, diabetes, peritoneal dialysis, bacteremia, septic shock, hepatorenal syndrome, abscess formation, adhesions, and multiorgan failure. Diagnosis relies on paracentesis or operative sampling with ascitic fluid neutrophils at least 250 cells/µL supporting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, plus Gram stain and culture, blood cultures, CBC, CRP, lactate, and imaging such as ultrasound or CT to identify perforation or loculated infection. Treatment centers on prompt antibiotics, including cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; piperacillin-tazobactam, a broad-spectrum β-lactam plus β-lactamase inhibitor; and metronidazole, which generates DNA-damaging radicals against anaerobes, with vancomycin added when resistant gram-positive infection is suspected, alongside source control and albumin in selected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Name: Epithelial tumor of ovary
Description: Epithelial tumor of the ovary is a heterogeneous group of neoplasms arising from ovarian surface epithelium or related müllerian-type epithelium, encompassing benign, borderline, and malignant forms, with major malignant subtypes including high-grade serous, low-grade serous, endometrioid, clear cell, and mucinous carcinoma. High-grade serous carcinoma, the commonest lethal subtype, is characterized by near-universal TP53 mutation, frequent homologous recombination deficiency due to BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51C, or RAD51D alterations, and genomic instability; other subtype-associated lesions include KRAS, BRAF, or ERBB2 in low-grade serous and mucinous tumors, CTNNB1, PTEN, PIK3CA, ARID1A, and mismatch repair genes in endometrioid tumors, and ARID1A and PIK3CA in clear cell carcinoma. Dysregulated pathways include p53, homologous recombination DNA repair, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, cell-cycle control, angiogenesis mediated by VEGF, and estrogen-related signaling. Clinically, patients often present insidiously with abdominal bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, early satiety, urinary frequency, increasing girth, adnexal mass, ascites, pleural effusion, bowel dysfunction, or weight loss, and complications include peritoneal carcinomatosis, malignant bowel obstruction, venous thromboembolism, cachexia, and recurrence; endometriosis is linked particularly to endometrioid and clear cell tumors, while hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome and Lynch syndrome are major genetic comorbid contexts. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited susceptibility is typically autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, especially involving BRCA1/2 and Lynch-associated MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, or PMS2. Diagnosis relies on pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasonography and cross-sectional imaging, serum CA-125 and sometimes HE4 with risk algorithms, and definitive histopathology with immunohistochemistry and molecular testing; treatment commonly includes cytoreductive surgery plus carboplatin or cisplatin, which form DNA crosslinks, paclitaxel, a microtubule stabilizer, bevacizumab, a VEGF inhibitor

Name: Severe pre-eclampsia
Description: Severe pre-eclampsia is a life-threatening hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, usually arising after 20 weeks’ gestation from abnormal placentation, defective spiral artery remodeling, placental ischemia, and widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction; it is often considered an early-onset/placental versus late-onset/maternal subtype, with severe disease defined by marked hypertension and end-organ injury. Genetic susceptibility is complex and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, involving maternal and fetal contributions; representative associations include variants or altered expression in FLT1/sFlt-1, ENG/endoglin, VEGFA, NOS3, ACE, AGT, F5 Leiden, MTHFR, STOX1, and HLA-C/KIR interactions, with abnormal proteins such as excess soluble Flt-1 and soluble endoglin antagonizing VEGF and TGF-β signaling. Key pathways include angiogenic imbalance, placental hypoxia with HIF-1α activation, oxidative stress, nitric oxide deficiency, endothelin signaling, complement and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, and coagulation pathway activation. Clinically, severe pre-eclampsia presents with severe hypertension, proteinuria or other evidence of renal injury, headache, visual symptoms, right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, edema, hyperreflexia, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, rising creatinine, and fetal growth restriction. Major complications and comorbid links include HELLP syndrome, eclampsia, placental abruption, acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, stroke, DIC, preterm delivery, stillbirth, and later maternal cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease; risk is increased with chronic hypertension, diabetes, obesity, antiphospholipid syndrome, lupus, and multifetal gestation. Diagnosis relies on blood pressure measurement plus proteinuria testing by urine protein/creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine, or in its absence severe features on CBC, creatinine, AST/ALT, LDH, and fetal surveillance with ultrasound and Doppler. Common treatments include magnesium sulfate, which blocks NMDA-mediated neuronal excitation to prevent seizures, antihypertensives such as labetalol, a combined α1/β-adrenergic blocker, hydralazine, a direct arteriolar vasodilator, and nifedipine, a calcium-channel blocker, with definitive treatment by delivery.

Name: Diabetes Complications
Description: Diabetes complications (UMLS C0342257) comprise the chronic microvascular and macrovascular sequelae of type 1, type 2, and monogenic diabetes, driven primarily by persistent hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, oxidative stress, and low-grade inflammation. Major pathogenic pathways include advanced glycation end-product formation with RAGE signaling, polyol flux via aldose reductase, protein kinase C activation, hexosamine pathway excess, mitochondrial ROS generation, endothelial nitric oxide dysregulation, RAAS activation, TGF-β–mediated fibrosis, VEGF-driven retinal neovascularization, and NF-κB cytokine signaling. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic and generally follows the inheritance of the underlying diabetes rather than a Mendelian pattern for complications themselves, although variants in AKR1B1, VEGFA, ACE, NOS3, CNDP1, APOE, SLC2A1, and RAGE/AGER have been associated with retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and vascular disease; monogenic diabetes genes such as HNF1A, GCK, and HNF4A influence risk indirectly through lifelong glycemic burden. Clinical manifestations include albuminuria, declining eGFR, edema, hypertension, visual blurring, retinal hemorrhages, sensory loss, burning pain, autonomic dysfunction, foot ulceration, poor wound healing, erectile dysfunction, and manifestations of coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral arterial disease. Key subtypes are diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy, peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, diabetic foot disease, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular complications; common comorbidities include obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, NAFLD, infection, depression, and heart failure. Diagnosis relies on established diabetes criteria plus complication screening with urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, serum creatinine/eGFR, dilated retinal examination or fundus photography/OCT, neurologic examination with monofilament and vibration testing, ankle-brachial index, and cardiovascular risk assessment. Treatment focuses on glycemic and risk-factor control, with metformin reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving insulin sensitivity, ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril lowering intraglomerular pressure and RAAS-mediated injury, statins such as atorvastatin inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase to reduce ASCVD risk, and SGLT2 inhibitors such as empag

Name: Deficiency of testosterone biosynthesis
Description: Deficiency of testosterone biosynthesis is a rare disorder of sex steroid production, usually presenting as 46,XY differences of sex development or hypogonadism caused by impaired testicular steroidogenesis; key genetic causes include biallelic pathogenic variants in CYP11A1, HSD3B2, CYP17A1, POR, HSD17B3, LHCGR, and STAR, with less common defects in SRD5A2 affecting conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone and causing overlapping phenotypes. The affected proteins participate in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and steroidogenic pathway, in which LH binds the LH receptor on Leydig cells, stimulates cAMP/PKA signaling, STAR-mediated cholesterol transport into mitochondria, CYP11A1 cleavage of cholesterol to pregnenolone, HSD3B2 and CYP17A1-mediated androgen precursor synthesis, and HSD17B3 conversion of androstenedione to testosterone, while androgen receptor signaling mediates downstream tissue effects. Clinical manifestations range from ambiguous genitalia, undervirilization, micropenis, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, delayed or absent puberty, low libido, infertility, reduced facial and body hair, gynecomastia, decreased muscle and bone mass, and osteoporosis to adrenal insufficiency in syndromic forms such as STAR, CYP11A1, or HSD3B2 deficiency. Subtypes are commonly defined by the specific enzymatic or receptor defect, and inheritance is most often autosomal recessive, although X-linked forms occur in broader DSD differentials. Diagnosis relies on clinical phenotype plus endocrine testing showing low testosterone with abnormal LH/FSH and steroid precursors, hCG stimulation testing, adrenal steroid profiling by LC-MS/MS, pelvic/testicular imaging, semen analysis when relevant, and confirmatory molecular testing. Treatment centers on testosterone replacement with testosterone enanthate or cypionate, transdermal testosterone gel, or testosterone undecanoate to restore androgen action, induce virilization, maintain bone and muscle, and improve sexual function; adjunctive hCG can stimulate Leydig-cell testosterone production via LHCGR, and fertility-directed gonadotropin therapy with hCG plus FSH may help selected patients.

Name: Neonatal hypocalcemia
Description: Neonatal hypocalcemia (UMLS C0342634) is a metabolic disorder of calcium homeostasis in the first weeks of life, classically divided into early-onset disease, usually within 72 hours and related to prematurity, intrauterine growth restriction, perinatal asphyxia, infant of diabetic mother status, or high phosphate load, and late-onset disease, often after day 3, commonly associated with high-phosphate formula feeding, hypomagnesemia, hypoparathyroidism, or vitamin D pathway defects. Genetic forms involve impaired parathyroid development or signaling and calcium-sensing abnormalities, with representative genes including CASR, GNA11, PTH, GCM2, TBCE, and 22q11.2 deletion involving TBX1 in DiGeorge spectrum; vitamin D-related cases may involve CYP27B1 or VDR. Key pathways include the PTH–PTH1R axis in kidney and bone, calcium-sensing receptor signaling via G protein pathways, renal tubular calcium and phosphate handling, magnesium-dependent PTH secretion, and vitamin D activation with 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D–mediated intestinal calcium absorption and skeletal mobilization. Clinical manifestations range from jitteriness, tremor, poor feeding, vomiting, apnea, stridor, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT to tetany and seizures, while complications include refractory seizures, cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia, and associations with prematurity, sepsis, hypoxic-ischemic injury, and syndromic congenital heart disease in 22q11.2 deletion. Inheritance depends on cause: CASR and GNA11 defects are often autosomal dominant, PTH, GCM2, CYP27B1, and TBCE disorders are commonly autosomal recessive, and chromosomal deletion syndromes are usually de novo. Diagnosis rests on age-appropriate low total or ionized calcium, often with hyperphosphatemia, plus PTH, magnesium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, creatinine, ECG, and targeted genetic testing when syndromic or familial disease is suspected. Treatment commonly includes intravenous calcium gluconate for acute membrane stabilization and calcium repletion, oral calcium carbonate for ongoing supplementation, calcitriol to bypass impaired vitamin D activation and raise intestinal calcium absorption, magnesium sulfate when hypomagnesemia suppresses PTH release

Name: Familial hypercholesterolemia - heterozygous
Description: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is a common autosomal dominant monogenic disorder of LDL metabolism characterized by lifelong elevation of LDL cholesterol and markedly increased premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, most often caused by pathogenic variants in LDLR, and less commonly APOB, PCSK9 gain-of-function, or rarely LDLRAP1-related phenocopies; representative defects include LDL receptor loss-of-function, apoB-100 impaired receptor binding, and PCSK9-mediated increased LDLR degradation. The core pathobiology involves the hepatic LDL receptor pathway, clathrin-mediated endocytosis of LDL particles, apoB-containing lipoprotein trafficking, intracellular cholesterol sensing through SREBP-SCAP, and PCSK9 regulation of receptor recycling, leading to reduced LDL clearance and cholesterol deposition in arterial walls. Clinically, patients typically have persistently high LDL-C from birth, often >190 mg/dL in adults, with tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, corneal arcus, and early coronary artery disease, while complications include myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral arterial disease, and aortic valvular disease; common comorbid associations include hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and elevated lipoprotein(a), which further amplify risk. Disease expression may be classified as receptor-negative versus receptor-defective, mutation-positive versus clinically defined FH, and distinguished from the more severe homozygous form. Diagnosis relies on lipid profile, family history of premature ASCVD or hypercholesterolemia, physical findings, and validated criteria such as Dutch Lipid Clinic Network, Simon Broome, or MEDPED, with confirmatory molecular testing of LDLR, APOB, and PCSK9, and cascade screening of relatives. Treatment centers on statins such as atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, or simvastatin, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and upregulate LDLR; ezetimibe, which blocks intestinal NPC1L1 cholesterol absorption; and PCSK9 inhibitors such as alirocumab or evolocumab, which prevent LDLR degradation, with bile acid sequestrants, inclisiran, or lipoprotein apheresis used in selected high-risk cases.

Name: Sitosterolemia
Description: Sitosterolemia (phytosterolemia; UMLS C0342907) is a rare autosomal recessive sterol storage disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in ABCG5 or ABCG8, which encode the ATP-binding cassette half-transporters sterolin-1 and sterolin-2 that heterodimerize at the apical enterocyte membrane and canalicular hepatocyte membrane to excrete plant sterols and limit intestinal sterol absorption; representative loss-of-function mutations in either gene impair this efflux pathway, causing marked accumulation of sitosterol, campesterol, and related non-cholesterol sterols. The core pathogenic pathway involves disrupted hepatobiliary and intestinal sterol trafficking, with altered NPC1L1-mediated uptake, reduced ABCG5/ABCG8-dependent export, and downstream foam-cell formation, xanthomatosis, hemolysis, and premature atherosclerosis. Clinically, disease severity ranges from classic childhood-onset xanthomatous disease to milder adult phenotypes; common findings include tendon or tuberous xanthomas, elevated LDL cholesterol that may mimic familial hypercholesterolemia, premature coronary or carotid vascular disease, arthralgia or arthritis, hepatosplenomegaly, and hematologic manifestations such as hemolytic anemia, macrothrombocytopenia, stomatocytosis, and abnormal liver tests. Important complications and comorbidities include accelerated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, valvular or supravalvular aortic involvement, pancreatitis, and liver dysfunction. Diagnosis rests on markedly elevated plasma plant sterols, especially sitosterol, by gas chromatography or mass spectrometry, supportive lipid phenotyping, and molecular confirmation of ABCG5 or ABCG8 variants; family screening is recommended. Treatment centers on dietary restriction of plant sterols and cholesterol plus drugs that reduce intestinal sterol entry, especially ezetimibe, an NPC1L1 inhibitor, with bile acid sequestrants such as cholestyramine or colesevelam decreasing enterohepatic sterol reabsorption, and statins such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin offering limited adjunctive LDL-lowering via HMG-CoA reductase inhibition; ileal bypass or LDL apheresis is reserved for refractory severe disease.

Name: Pantothenic acid deficiency
Description: Pantothenic acid deficiency (UMLS C0342938) is a rare nutritional deficiency disorder caused by inadequate intake, severe malabsorption, prolonged parenteral nutrition without vitamin supplementation, or increased metabolic demand, and only exceptionally reflects inherited defects affecting pantothenate handling or coenzyme A biosynthesis; relevant genes in the broader pathway include SLC5A6, which encodes the sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter for pantothenate uptake, and PANK1, PANK2, and PANK3, which encode pantothenate kinases catalyzing the first committed step of coenzyme A synthesis, although classic isolated deficiency is usually acquired rather than monogenic. Pathobiologically, reduced pantothenate impairs coenzyme A and 4-phosphopantetheine production, disrupting fatty-acid beta-oxidation, tricarboxylic-acid-cycle flux, acetylation reactions, cholesterol and steroid synthesis, and mitochondrial energy metabolism. Clinical manifestations are often nonspecific and include fatigue, irritability, anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, paresthesias, muscle cramps, weakness, sleep disturbance, and the characteristic burning feet syndrome; severe cases may show dermatitis, glossitis, enteritis, impaired wound healing, adrenal dysfunction, and peripheral neuropathy. Complications include malnutrition, secondary infections, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and worsening of concurrent alcohol use disorder, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, or generalized micronutrient deficiency states. Recognized forms are primary dietary deficiency and secondary deficiency due to malabsorption or iatrogenic deprivation; inheritance is generally not applicable, but when transporter or coenzyme A pathway defects are involved, inheritance is typically autosomal recessive, as with biallelic SLC5A6 or PANK2 variants. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical context, nutritional assessment, response to replacement, and supportive biochemical testing such as low plasma or urinary pantothenate, reduced erythrocyte coenzyme A-related metabolites, and exclusion of other B-vitamin deficiencies; genetic testing is reserved for suspected inherited transport or metabolic disorders. Treatment centers on pantothenic acid or dexpanthenol, which replenish intracellular pantothenate and restore coenzyme A synthesis, together with multivitamin supplementation and correction of the underlying cause; adjunctive agents such as gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic burning pain and topical emollients or corticosteroids for dermatitis may be

Name: Superficial bacterial infection of skin
Description: Superficial bacterial infection of skin (UMLS C0342985) comprises common epidermal and superficial dermal infections, classically impetigo, folliculitis, ecthyma, and secondary infection of eczematous or traumatized skin, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including strains carrying mecA-mediated methicillin resistance and virulence determinants such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin, or by Streptococcus pyogenes with emm/M-protein-associated pathogenicity; host susceptibility is influenced by barrier and innate immune genes including FLG, SPINK5, TLR2, DEFB4, IL1B, and cytokine pathway variants affecting cutaneous defense. Pathobiology centers on bacterial adhesion, biofilm formation, keratinocyte Toll-like receptor and NOD signaling, NF-kB and MAPK activation, neutrophil recruitment via IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and chemokines, and, in atopic skin, impaired barrier proteins and reduced antimicrobial peptides. Patients typically present with localized erythema, tenderness, pruritus, pustules, follicular papules, honey-colored crusts, erosions, or shallow ulcers; subtypes differ by morphology and depth, with nonbullous and bullous impetigo, superficial folliculitis, and ecthyma representing a spectrum. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by Gram stain, bacterial culture with susceptibility testing, MRSA screening, dermatoscopic assessment, and evaluation for predisposing disorders such as diabetes, atopic dermatitis, venous insufficiency, obesity, or immunodeficiency. Standard therapy includes topical mupirocin, which inhibits isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase, topical fusidic acid, which blocks elongation factor G, and oral beta-lactams such as cephalexin or dicloxacillin, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis; when MRSA is suspected, doxycycline inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit, clindamycin inhibits the 50S subunit, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole inhibits folate synthesis. Complications include recurrent infection, cellulitis, abscess formation, bacteremia, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and scarring; inheritance is generally non-Mendelian, reflecting polygenic predisposition to skin-barrier dysfunction and immune response abnormalities rather than

Name: dermographism
Description: Dermographism, or symptomatic dermographism/urticaria factitia, is the most common form of chronic inducible urticaria and is characterized by an exaggerated wheal-and-flare response minutes after stroking, চাপ, scratching, or friction of the skin, producing linear pruritic wheals, surrounding erythema, and sometimes burning; a simple, often asymptomatic form is distinguished from symptomatic dermographism, and delayed dermographism is a recognized but less common subtype. The disorder is usually acquired rather than monogenic, with no established single-gene cause, but it shares biologic overlap with mast-cell–driven urticarial disorders in which variants affecting KIT, TPSAB1/TPSB2, and, in rare syndromic or autoinflammatory differential diagnoses, NLRP3 or PLCG2 may influence mast-cell number or reactivity; autoimmune mechanisms with IgE or IgG against Fc epsilon RI or IgE have also been implicated in some chronic urticaria populations. Pathophysiology centers on mechanical triggering of cutaneous mast-cell degranulation with release of histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, tryptase, platelet-activating factor, and cytokines, activating H1/H2 receptor signaling, sensory nerves, endothelial adhesion, and vascular permeability pathways. It commonly coexists with other chronic urticarias, atopy, thyroid autoimmunity, anxiety, and occasionally mast cell activation disorders, while complications are usually limited to sleep disturbance, impaired quality of life, and excoriations rather than anaphylaxis. Diagnosis is clinical, based on reproducible linear whealing after provocation with a tongue blade, dermographometer, or FricTest, with lesion development typically within 10 minutes; evaluation may include urticaria activity assessment and selective laboratory testing to exclude mimics. Treatment relies on second-generation H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine, which block histamine H1 receptors; refractory disease may respond to dose escalation, H2 blockers such as famotidine, leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, or omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody that downregulates Fc epsilon RI signaling.

Name: Pseudomonas gastrointestinal tract infection
Description: Pseudomonas gastrointestinal tract infection, usually caused by the opportunistic Gram-negative bacillus Pseudomonas aeruginosa, is an acquired, non-Mendelian infectious disease ranging from asymptomatic colonization to antibiotic-associated diarrhea, enterocolitis, necrotizing enteritis, and bacteremia, particularly in neonates, intensive-care patients, and immunocompromised hosts. Bacterial virulence is linked to genes and proteins such as exoS, exoU, exoT, and exoY delivered by the type III secretion system, quorum-sensing regulators lasR and rhlR, alginate biosynthesis components including algD, lipopolysaccharide and flagellar proteins, elastase LasB, exotoxin A encoded by toxA, and multidrug-efflux and porin determinants such as mexAB-oprM and oprD; host susceptibility is increased in disorders affecting innate or epithelial defense, with representative genetic examples including CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis and, less specifically, neutrophil dysfunction states. Pathobiology involves biofilm formation, quorum sensing, type III secretion, inflammasome and NF-kappaB activation, epithelial barrier disruption, and cytokine signaling with IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha recruitment of neutrophils. Typical manifestations include fever, abdominal pain, watery or bloody diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, ileus, sepsis, and occasionally bowel necrosis or perforation. Important comorbidities and complications include prior broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, burns, neutropenia, transplantation, sepsis, toxic megacolon, perforation, and death. Diagnosis relies on stool or rectal cultures showing heavy growth of Pseudomonas in the appropriate clinical context, blood cultures when systemic illness is suspected, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and, in severe cases, imaging or endoscopy with histopathology to assess colitis or necrosis while excluding other enteric pathogens. Treatment is guided by susceptibilities and commonly includes piperacillin-tazobactam, a beta-lactam inhibiting cell-wall synthesis; ceftazidime or cefepime, antipseudomonal cephalosporins that bind penicillin-binding proteins; meropenem, a carbapenem cell-wall inhibitor; ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone blocking DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV;

Name: Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis
Description: Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis (UMLS C0343378) is a chronic infectious inflammatory disease of the gastric mucosa caused by colonization with H. pylori, typically presenting as antral-predominant, corpus-predominant, pangastritis, erosive, or atrophic gastritis, and clinically causing epigastric pain or burning, dyspepsia, nausea, bloating, early satiety, halitosis, and sometimes occult bleeding or iron deficiency, although many patients are asymptomatic. Pathogenesis reflects bacterial virulence factors and host susceptibility: representative microbial determinants include CagA, VacA, BabA, SabA, urease, and flagellins, while host genetic components associated with inflammation severity or cancer risk include polymorphisms in IL1B, IL1RN, TNF, IL10, TLR4, NOD1, and CDH1 in selected contexts; inheritance is therefore not Mendelian but multifactorial, with familial aggregation reflecting shared exposure and host immune-response variants. Major signaling pathways include adhesion-driven epithelial injury; cag pathogenicity island-mediated type IV secretion with CagA activation of SHP2/ERK-MAPK, beta-catenin, NF-kappaB, and JAK/STAT signaling; TLR/NOD recognition; and induction of IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, reactive oxygen species, and COX-2, leading to neutrophilic and mononuclear infiltration, mucosal damage, gland loss, and intestinal metaplasia. Important comorbidities and complications include peptic ulcer disease, gastric atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, MALT lymphoma, gastric adenocarcinoma, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, vitamin B12 deficiency, and refractory iron deficiency anemia. Diagnosis relies on endoscopic and histologic evidence of active chronic gastritis with H. pylori detection by biopsy urease testing, histology, culture, PCR, or noninvasive urea breath test and stool antigen assay, with serology used selectively. Standard treatment uses proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, which irreversibly inhibit gastric H+/K+-ATPase, combined with antibiotics such as amoxicillin, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, clarithromycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor, metronidazole, which causes DNA damage after reduction, tetracycline, a

Name: Bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae
Description: Bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae is an acquired, non-Mendelian Gram-negative opportunistic or community-acquired infection that most often presents as pneumonia, urinary tract infection, bloodstream infection, intra-abdominal infection, liver abscess, or device-associated disease, with subtypes including classical multidrug-resistant strains and hypervirulent K1/K2 capsular strains. Major bacterial virulence and resistance determinants include capsule polysaccharide genes in the cps locus with magA/wzy_K1 and K2-associated loci, the regulator rmpA/rmpA2 causing hypermucoviscosity, siderophore systems such as ybt, iuc, and iro, fimbrial adhesins fimH and mrkD, lipopolysaccharide-related genes, and beta-lactamase or carbapenemase genes including blaSHV, blaCTX-M, blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48, and porin alterations in OmpK35/OmpK36; host susceptibility is influenced by immune pathways rather than inheritance, with examples including diabetes predisposition and rare defects in TLR4-, MyD88-, neutrophil-, or complement-mediated antibacterial defense. Pathobiology centers on LPS-TLR4 signaling, NF-kB activation, inflammasome and cytokine responses involving TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6, IL-8, complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, biofilm formation, and iron acquisition. Typical features include fever, productive cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, currant-jelly sputum in severe pneumonia, dysuria, sepsis, and metastatic infection; complications include abscess formation, acute respiratory failure, bacteremia, septic shock, endophthalmitis, meningitis, and death, especially in alcoholism, chronic lung disease, diabetes, malignancy, cirrhosis, renal failure, and intensive-care exposure. Diagnosis relies on culture of blood, sputum, urine, or sterile-site specimens with susceptibility testing, Gram stain showing encapsulated Gram-negative bacilli, chest imaging when pulmonary, and molecular detection of resistance or virulence genes by PCR or sequencing. Common treatments include ceftriaxone or cefepime, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis; carbapenems such as meropenem for ESBL producers, also blocking cell-wall synthesis; and aminoglycosides such as gentamicin

Name: Erythema nodosum leprosum (disorder)
Description: Erythema nodosum leprosum is an immune-mediated inflammatory complication of multibacillary leprosy, especially lepromatous and borderline lepromatous disease, rather than a primary inherited disorder; it represents a type 2 lepra reaction driven by high Mycobacterium leprae antigen load, immune-complex formation, and exuberant innate and adaptive cytokine signaling. Key molecular associations include increased TNF, IFN-γ, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12, IL-17, and neutrophil recruitment, with involvement of TLR1/TLR2, NF-κB, complement, and inflammasome-related pathways; susceptibility or severity has been linked in some studies to polymorphisms in genes such as TLR1, TLR2, TNF, IL10, NOD2, HLA class I/II loci, and LTA4H, but there is no Mendelian inheritance pattern. Clinically, ENL presents in acute, recurrent, or chronic forms with crops of tender erythematous nodules, fever, malaise, edema, neuritis, lymphadenitis, arthritis, orchitis, iritis/uveitis, and sometimes hepatitis or nephritis, and may lead to nerve damage, ocular injury, infertility, amyloidosis, secondary infection, and disability; comorbidities include chronic neuropathic pain, anemia, and steroid-related diabetes or osteoporosis. Diagnosis is clinical in a patient with multibacillary leprosy who develops painful nodules and systemic inflammation, supported by slit-skin smear or biopsy showing abundant acid-fast bacilli, and skin histopathology with neutrophilic infiltrates superimposed on lepromatous granulomatous disease; inflammatory markers may be elevated, and nerve or eye assessment is important. Treatment commonly includes thalidomide, which suppresses TNF production and modulates T-cell cytokines; corticosteroids such as prednisone, which broadly inhibit NF-κB-dependent inflammation and are crucial for neuritis and organ involvement; and clofazimine, which has antimycobacterial and anti-inflammatory effects on macrophage and neutrophil responses; other steroid-sparing agents used in refractory cases include methotrexate, azathioprine, and TNF inhibitors in selected settings.

Name: Gas gangrene caused by clostridium perfringens
Description: Gas gangrene caused by Clostridium perfringens is an acute, rapidly progressive clostridial myonecrosis, usually an exogenous wound infection after trauma, surgery, injection drug use, or ischemic bowel contamination, characterized by massive toxin-mediated muscle necrosis, systemic toxicity, and high mortality. Its principal molecular determinants are bacterial toxin genes and proteins rather than inherited host mutations, especially plc/cpa encoding alpha-toxin phospholipase C (lecithinase), pfoA encoding perfringolysin O, and in some strains colA and nan genes, whose products promote membrane disruption, endothelial injury, hemolysis, platelet-leukocyte aggregation, and tissue spread; key pathogenic pathways include anaerobic fermentation with gas production, TLR-driven innate immune activation, microvascular thrombosis, cytokine surge, complement activation, and profound local hypoxia. Clinical findings typically include sudden severe pain out of proportion, tense edema, bronze to violaceous skin discoloration, hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, foul discharge, fever, tachycardia, shock, and rapid progression to compartment syndrome, hemolysis, acute kidney injury, DIC, multiorgan failure, and death. Major predispositions and comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, malignancy, neutropenia, bowel disease, major trauma, and postoperative wounds. Subtypes include traumatic/postoperative clostridial myonecrosis and spontaneous infection, more often linked to occult gastrointestinal lesions or hematologic malignancy. It is an infectious, non-Mendelian disease with no host inheritance pattern, although host susceptibility may be influenced by immune compromise rather than defined germline variants. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and surgical, supported by Gram stain and anaerobic culture of tissue showing large gram-positive rods with scant leukocytes, imaging demonstrating soft-tissue gas, laboratory evidence of hemolysis and sepsis, and histopathology showing myonecrosis with minimal inflammation. Treatment requires immediate radical debridement plus antibiotics such as high-dose penicillin G, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation, clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosome and suppresses toxin synthesis, and metronidazole, which causes anaerobic DNA strand damage; vancomycin or piperacillin-tazobactam may be added empirically when polymicrobial necrotizing infection is possible.

Name: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
Description: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (STSS; UMLS C0343532) is an acute, life-threatening invasive infection caused predominantly by toxigenic Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus), characterized by rapid-onset shock and multiorgan failure driven by bacterial superantigen-mediated immune dysregulation. Key microbial virulence determinants include the M protein encoded by emm genes, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins such as SpeA, SpeC, SpeG, and SpeJ, and other factors including streptolysin O, streptococcal inhibitor of complement, and DNases; host susceptibility has been linked to variation in HLA class II alleles and innate immune/inflammatory genes, although STSS is not a classical inherited disorder and shows no Mendelian pattern. Pathobiologically, superantigen binding to MHC class II and T-cell receptor Vbeta regions triggers massive T-cell activation, cytokine storm with TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IFN-gamma, and chemokine release, endothelial injury, capillary leak, coagulation activation, and NF-kappaB–dependent inflammatory signaling. Clinically, patients present with fever, severe pain often out of proportion to examination, hypotension, diffuse erythema or soft-tissue swelling, tachycardia, and progression to renal impairment, coagulopathy, acute respiratory distress syndrome, hepatic dysfunction, necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, and altered mental status; common associated conditions include skin or wound infection, varicella, diabetes, immunosuppression, and postpartum or postsurgical states. Subtypes are commonly described as STSS with or without a defined deep-tissue focus, especially necrotizing fasciitis-associated disease. Diagnosis relies on isolation of group A Streptococcus from a normally sterile site or severe clinical syndrome with hypotension plus multiorgan involvement, supported by blood or tissue cultures, rapid GAS tests or PCR, laboratory evidence of organ dysfunction, inflammatory markers, imaging for deep infection, and histopathology when indicated. Treatment centers on prompt source control and antibiotics, typically penicillin G, which inhibits cell-wall transpeptidation; clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosome and suppresses toxin production; and linezolid, another 50S inhibitor with antitoxin activity, with intravenous immunoglobulin often added to

Name: Tertiary lesion of yaws
Description: Tertiary lesion of yaws (UMLS C0343833) is a late, destructive manifestation of chronic nonvenereal treponemal infection caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, typically arising years after untreated primary and secondary yaws and characterized by granulomatous inflammation and tissue remodeling rather than a host inherited disorder. No validated human germline mutation or Mendelian inheritance pattern defines susceptibility, although host immune-response genes and inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IFNG, IL10, TLR2, and HLA class II loci are plausible modifiers, while pathogen-associated proteins including treponemal outer membrane antigens and flagellar proteins drive innate and adaptive responses through TLR signaling, macrophage activation, Th1-skewed cytokine pathways, endothelial activation, matrix metalloproteinases, and osteoclast-mediated bone injury. Clinically, tertiary yaws presents with gummatous nodules or ulcers, destructive nasopharyngeal and palatal lesions, gangosa, juxta-articular nodules, periostitis, osteitis, deformity, scarring, disability, and chronic pain; major subtypes are classically early infectious yaws, late noninfectious yaws, and tertiary destructive yaws. Important complications and linked comorbidities include secondary bacterial superinfection, chronic osteomyelitis-like damage, facial mutilation, contractures, anemia, malnutrition, and disability in impoverished endemic settings. Diagnosis relies on clinical recognition in an endemic context, treponemal and nontreponemal serology such as TPPA/TPHA with RPR or VDRL, dark-field or PCR testing from early lesions when available, radiography for osseous involvement, and exclusion of venereal syphilis, leprosy, tropical ulcers, and deep fungal infection; serology may remain reactive in late disease despite reduced infectivity. Treatment is primarily antibiotic, most commonly single-dose azithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis, or benzathine benzylpenicillin, whose beta-lactam activity inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and peptidoglycan cross-linking; alternatives include doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, and tetracycline or erythromycin in selected cases.

Name: Candidiasis of intestine
Description: Intestinal candidiasis (UMLS C0343886) is an opportunistic fungal infection of the gastrointestinal tract, usually caused by Candida albicans but also C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, or C. krusei, ranging from mucosal overgrowth to invasive disease; it is not classically inherited, yet host susceptibility is shaped by immune genetic factors, with representative defects in CARD9, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, STAT1 gain-of-function, STAT3 deficiency, IL17RA/IL17F, AIRE, and occasionally TLR-related pathways that impair antifungal mucosal defense. Pathobiology centers on fungal adhesion and hyphal invasion, biofilm formation, and host recognition through pattern-recognition receptors such as Dectin-1, TLR2/TLR4, and mannose receptor, activating CARD9–NF-κB, Syk, MAPK, NLRP3 inflammasome, and Th17/IL-17–IL-22 signaling; dysbiosis, antibiotic exposure, neutropenia, diabetes, HIV/AIDS, corticosteroid or chemotherapy use, organ transplantation, inflammatory bowel disease, and critical illness are major predisposing comorbidities. Clinical manifestations include abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, nausea, fever, oral or esophageal thrush, occult or overt GI bleeding, and in severe cases ulceration, necrotizing enterocolitis-like presentations, perforation, candidemia, and sepsis. Recognized forms include noninvasive luminal overgrowth, mucosal/ulcerative intestinal candidiasis, and invasive disseminated disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical context plus endoscopy with biopsy showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae invading tissue on PAS or GMS stains, fungal culture or species identification from tissue or sterile sites, blood cultures when systemic spread is suspected, and adjunctive serum β-D-glucan or molecular assays, while stool cultures alone are nonspecific for disease. Treatment commonly includes fluconazole, which inhibits fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase (ERG11) and ergosterol synthesis; echinocandins such as caspofungin or micafungin, which inhibit β-1,3-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall; and amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol to form membrane pores, with choice guided by severity, species, and azole susceptibility.

Name: Transplanted organ rejection
Description: Transplanted organ rejection is an acquired, immune-mediated disorder in which the recipient recognizes donor alloantigens, chiefly mismatched ABO and HLA class I and II molecules, leading to graft injury; major forms include hyperacute rejection driven by preformed anti-donor antibodies and complement, acute cellular rejection mediated predominantly by recipient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, acute antibody-mediated rejection characterized by donor-specific antibodies, and chronic rejection with progressive vasculopathy, interstitial fibrosis, and parenchymal atrophy. Key molecular pathways include direct and indirect alloantigen presentation through T-cell receptor signaling, CD28-B7 and CD40-CD40L costimulation, IL-2/JAK-STAT–dependent clonal expansion, calcineurin-NFAT activation, B-cell and plasma-cell differentiation, Fc receptor signaling, complement activation including C4d deposition, endothelial activation, and cytokines such as IFN-γ, TNF, and IL-17. Genetic susceptibility is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion, but risk is strongly influenced by donor-recipient immunogenetics, especially HLA-A, -B, -DR, and -DQ mismatch, donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies, ABO incompatibility, and polymorphisms affecting immune reactivity, with representative examples including variants in CTLA4, IL10, TNF, and CYP3A5 that also influence tacrolimus handling. Clinical manifestations vary by organ and timing, but commonly include graft dysfunction, tenderness, fever, edema, reduced urine output in kidney grafts, cholestatic or hepatocellular injury in liver grafts, dyspnea in lung grafts, and reduced ejection fraction or arrhythmias in heart grafts. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, organ function tests, donor-specific antibody assays, crossmatch testing, HLA typing, complement markers, imaging when relevant, and confirmatory biopsy using histopathology such as Banff criteria and C4d staining. Standard therapy includes tacrolimus or cyclosporine, calcineurin inhibitors that block NFAT-dependent IL-2 transcription; mycophenolate mofetil, an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor that suppresses lymphocyte purine synthesis; corticosteroids, which broadly inhibit inflammatory gene transcription; and in selected cases antithymocyte globulin, basiliximab, rituximab, plasmapheresis, IVIG, bortezomib, or e

Name: Cancer of Liver
Description: Liver neoplasms comprise a heterogeneous group of benign and malignant tumors, most importantly hepatocellular carcinoma, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma, with rarer entities such as hepatoblastoma, angiosarcoma, and hepatic adenoma; clinically they are usually sporadic but arise on a background of chronic liver disease, especially cirrhosis due to hepatitis B or C, alcohol-related liver disease, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, while inherited predisposition is seen with germline defects such as APC in familial adenomatous polyposis/hepatoblastoma risk, HFE in hemochromatosis, SERPINA1 in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and mismatch-repair genes in Lynch-associated cholangiocarcinoma. Key molecular alterations include TERT promoter activation, TP53 mutation, CTNNB1/β-catenin mutation, AXIN1, ARID1A/ARID2, and amplifications affecting MET or FGF19 in hepatocellular carcinoma, and IDH1/2, FGFR2 fusions, KRAS, BAP1, and SMAD4 abnormalities in cholangiocarcinoma; the major implicated pathways are Wnt/β-catenin, p53/cell-cycle control, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, JAK-STAT, TGF-β, Hippo-YAP, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, and immune-checkpoint signaling. Symptoms and signs include weight loss, fatigue, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites, fever, and decompensation of underlying cirrhosis, with complications such as portal vein invasion, biliary obstruction, hemorrhage, cachexia, metastases, and liver failure. Diagnosis relies on liver-function tests, alpha-fetoprotein and sometimes CA19-9, surveillance ultrasound in at-risk patients, multiphasic contrast CT or MRI showing arterial enhancement with washout for hepatocellular carcinoma, tissue biopsy when imaging is indeterminate or for cholangiocarcinoma, and staging by TNM/BCLC with molecular testing in selected cases. Treatment includes resection, ablation, transplantation, and systemic therapy such as sorafenib and lenvatinib, multikinase inhibitors targeting VEGFR/PDGFR/RAF, regor

Name: Malignant epithelial tumour of ovary
Description: Malignant epithelial tumour of the ovary is a heterogeneous group of primary ovarian carcinomas arising from müllerian-type epithelium, dominated by high-grade serous carcinoma but also including low-grade serous, endometrioid, mucinous, and clear cell subtypes, typically presenting with insidious abdominal bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, early satiety, increased abdominal girth, urinary urgency, adnexal mass, ascites, pleural effusion, weight loss, or bowel symptoms, and often complicated by peritoneal carcinomatosis, bowel obstruction, venous thromboembolism, cachexia, and recurrence. Molecularly, high-grade serous tumors commonly harbor TP53 mutations with homologous recombination defects involving BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51C, and RAD51D, while other subtypes may show KRAS, BRAF, ERBB2, CTNNB1, PIK3CA, PTEN, ARID1A, PPP2R1A, or mismatch-repair gene alterations; associated proteins and biomarkers include p53, WT1, PAX8, CA125/MUC16, HE4, folate receptor alpha, estrogen receptor, and VEGF. Key pathways include homologous recombination/DNA damage repair, p53-RB cell-cycle control, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, angiogenesis via VEGF, and Notch/Wnt signaling. Treatment usually combines cytoreductive surgery with platinum-taxane chemotherapy such as carboplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum agent, and paclitaxel, a microtubule-stabilizing taxane; additional agents include bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody, PARP inhibitors such as olaparib or niraparib causing synthetic lethality in HR-deficient tumors, and selected use of liposomal doxorubicin or gemcitabine. Hereditary predisposition is most often autosomal dominant through germline BRCA1/2 and other homologous-repair genes, and may occur in Lynch syndrome via MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2. Diagnosis relies on pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound and CT/MRI, serum CA125 and sometimes HE4, surgical-pathologic confirmation with histology and immunohistochemistry, FIGO staging

Name: Chronic Eosinophilic Leukemia
Description: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL; UMLS C0346421) is a rare clonal myeloid/hematologic neoplasm characterized by persistent eosinophilia with evidence of autonomous eosinophil proliferation, tissue infiltration, and organ damage, classically distinguished from reactive eosinophilia and from idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome. Molecularly, CEL is most often driven by constitutively activated tyrosine kinases, especially fusion lesions involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, or FGFR1, with FIP1L1-PDGFRA the prototypical cryptic deletion on 4q12; less commonly PCM1-JAK2, ETV6-PDGFRB, FLT3, KIT, JAK2, TET2, ASXL1, RUNX1, or SETBP1 abnormalities are identified, activating downstream JAK-STAT, RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, and SRC-related signaling pathways that promote eosinophil survival and myeloid proliferation. Clinical manifestations commonly include fatigue, weight loss, fever, pruritus, rash, cough, dyspnea, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and thromboembolic or constitutional symptoms, while major complications reflect eosinophilic tissue injury, particularly endomyocardial fibrosis, myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, and gastrointestinal involvement, with risk of progression to acute leukemia or myelofibrosis. Recognized disease subsets include CEL, not otherwise specified, and myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase fusions. Most cases are acquired rather than inherited, with no consistent Mendelian pattern, although the relevant genetic components are somatic rearrangements or mutations in hematopoietic progenitors. Diagnosis requires sustained eosinophilia, bone marrow and peripheral blood evaluation showing a clonal myeloid process or increased blasts, exclusion of secondary causes and BCR::ABL1-positive CML, and molecular/cytogenetic testing by karyotype, FISH, RT-PCR, or next-generation sequencing for PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, and related lesions. Treatment includes imatinib, a PDGFRA/PDGFRB/KIT/ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor and often dramatic first-line

Name: Metastatic malignant neoplasm to pancreas
Description: Metastatic malignant neoplasm to the pancreas is a secondary pancreatic malignancy produced by hematogenous, lymphatic, peritoneal, or direct spread from an extra-pancreatic primary tumor, most often renal cell carcinoma, lung carcinoma, colorectal carcinoma, melanoma, breast carcinoma, or gastric cancer, and it therefore reflects the molecular biology of the primary rather than a single inherited pancreatic cancer syndrome. Representative genetic and protein abnormalities include VHL loss and HIF/VEGF pathway activation in renal cell carcinoma, EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, or TP53 alterations in lung cancer, APC, KRAS, TP53, SMAD4, and mismatch-repair deficiency in colorectal cancer, and BRAF, NRAS, KIT, and MAPK pathway activation in melanoma; correspondingly, implicated signaling networks commonly include VEGF/angiogenesis, RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, EGFR/HER family, WNT/beta-catenin, TGF-beta/SMAD, and immune-checkpoint pathways involving PD-1/PD-L1. Clinical manifestations may be absent or include abdominal or back pain, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, pancreatitis, gastrointestinal bleeding, or new-onset diabetes, with complications such as biliary or gastric outlet obstruction, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, thromboembolism, cachexia, and widespread metastatic disease; common comorbidities derive from the primary cancer and treatment effects. Disease subtypes are defined by the primary site and pattern of spread, including solitary pancreatic metastasis versus multifocal or disseminated disease. Diagnosis relies on history of a known malignancy, cross-sectional imaging with pancreas-protocol CT or MRI, PET/CT in selected cases, and tissue confirmation by endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration or biopsy with histopathology and immunohistochemistry, often supplemented by molecular profiling to distinguish metastasis from primary pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma or neuroendocrine tumor. Treatment is directed by the primary tumor and extent of disease and may include fluorouracil, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor, oxaliplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum, gemcitabine, a nucleoside analog inhibiting DNA synthesis, pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, or sunitinib, a multitarget VEGFR/PDGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor

Name: Secondary malignant neoplasm of breast
Description: Secondary malignant neoplasm of the breast denotes metastatic involvement of breast tissue by a non-mammary primary cancer rather than a primary breast carcinoma; it is uncommon, clinically important because management follows the biology of the primary tumor, and may arise from melanoma, lung, ovarian, gastric, renal, thyroid, or hematologic malignancies. Its molecular features therefore mirror the source neoplasm, with representative alterations including EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, TP53, PIK3CA, PTEN, HER2/ERBB2, BRCA1/2, CDH1, VHL, or EWSR1-related fusions, and associated proteins such as estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, HER2, cytokeratins, S100, TTF1, PAX8, or GATA3 may aid lineage assignment. Relevant pathways include MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, HER2/EGFR signaling, hormone receptor signaling, WNT/beta-catenin, p53-mediated cell-cycle control, apoptosis, angiogenesis via VEGF, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Patients typically present with a rapidly growing painless breast mass, often superficial and well circumscribed, sometimes multiple or bilateral, with skin involvement, tenderness, axillary adenopathy, or symptoms of disseminated disease such as weight loss, bone pain, dyspnea, or neurologic deficits. Major subtypes are defined by the primary site and histology, including solid metastases and secondary involvement by lymphoma or leukemia. Comorbidities and complications include advanced systemic metastatic burden, pathologic fracture, pleural effusion, liver failure, CNS spread, lymphedema, infection, and treatment-related cardiotoxicity or myelosuppression. There is no specific inheritance pattern for the secondary breast lesion itself, but inherited cancer predisposition syndromes such as BRCA1/2, TP53 Li-Fraumeni, PTEN Cowden, CDH1, or VHL can underlie the primary malignancy. Diagnosis relies on history of prior cancer, breast imaging, core biopsy with histopathology and immunohistochemistry, molecular testing when needed to match the primary tumor, and staging studies such as CT, PET-CT, or MRI. Name: Carcinoma in situ of fallopian tube
Description: Carcinoma in situ of the fallopian tube, often corresponding in modern practice to serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), is a noninvasive epithelial precursor lesion of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma characterized by marked cytologic atypia, high proliferative activity, and confinement to the tubal epithelium without stromal invasion, most commonly arising in the fimbrial end. It is strongly associated with TP53 mutation and abnormal p53 protein expression, frequent genomic instability, and inherited defects in homologous recombination genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2; less commonly, alterations involving PALB2, RAD51C, RAD51D, and BRIP1 may confer susceptibility. Relevant pathways include p53-mediated DNA damage response, BRCA-dependent homologous recombination repair, cell-cycle checkpoint regulation, PI3K/AKT signaling, and apoptotic dysregulation. Many patients are asymptomatic, but possible manifestations include abnormal vaginal bleeding or watery discharge, pelvic pain, adnexal mass, and positive peritoneal cytology; important linked conditions include hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome, synchronous or subsequent ovarian or primary peritoneal high-grade serous carcinoma, and metastatic progression if occult invasion develops. Histologic subtypes are mainly serous in this in situ setting, although primary tubal carcinoma broadly includes endometrioid, clear cell, transitional, and mucinous forms. Diagnosis relies on prophylactic or surgical salpingo-oophorectomy specimens examined with extensive fimbrial sectioning protocols such as SEE-FIM, demonstrating severe atypia, mitotic activity, and a characteristic p53/Ki-67 immunophenotype, with correlation to pelvic imaging, CA-125, peritoneal washings, and germline genetic testing when hereditary risk is suspected. Management is primarily surgical staging and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy, while associated invasive or high-risk disease may be treated with carboplatin, a platinum DNA crosslinker, paclitaxel, a microtubule stabilizer, cisplatin, another DNA crosslinker, and in BRCA-mutated or homologous recombination-deficient cases PARP inhibitors such as olaparib, which exploit synthetic lethality.

Name: Asthma attack NOS
Description: Asthma attack NOS denotes an acute, nonspecific exacerbation of asthma, a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterized by variable expiratory airflow limitation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, mucus hypersecretion, and reversible bronchospasm, most often presenting with episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, tachypnea, prolonged expiration, accessory muscle use, and reduced peak expiratory flow or FEV1, with severe attacks causing hypoxemia, pulsus paradoxus, silent chest, respiratory failure, or death. Major biologic drivers include type 2 immune pathways involving epithelial alarmins TSLP, IL-33, and IL-25, Th2 cells and ILC2s, eosinophils, mast cells, IgE, and cytokines IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, alongside leukotriene, prostaglandin, cholinergic, and airway-remodeling pathways with smooth-muscle contraction, goblet-cell metaplasia, and subepithelial fibrosis; representative genetic associations include variants in IL4, IL13, IL4R, ADRB2, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, TSLP, ADAM33, FLG, and HLA loci, reflecting complex polygenic inheritance rather than Mendelian transmission, although familial aggregation and gene-environment interactions are well established. Common subtypes include allergic and nonallergic asthma, eosinophilic, neutrophilic, exercise-induced, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, cough-variant, occupational asthma, and severe therapy-resistant disease. Treatment of acute attacks commonly includes inhaled short-acting beta2-agonists such as albuterol, which activate beta2-adrenergic receptors to increase cAMP and relax airway smooth muscle; inhaled antimuscarinics such as ipratropium, which block M3-mediated bronchoconstriction; and systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone or methylprednisolone, which suppress NF-kB-driven airway inflammation; selected patients may also receive magnesium sulfate, oxygen, inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol, leukotriene modifiers, or biologics targeting IgE, IL-5, IL-5R, IL-4Ralpha, or TSLP. Comorbidities and complications include allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, GERD, obesity, anxiety, smoking-related

Name: Listerial endocarditis
Description: Listerial endocarditis is a rare, severe form of infective endocarditis caused predominantly by Listeria monocytogenes, a facultative intracellular Gram-positive bacillus, usually affecting older adults, immunocompromised hosts, pregnant patients, and individuals with prosthetic valves or prior valvular disease; native- and prosthetic-valve forms are recognized, with aortic and mitral valves most often involved. Its pathobiology reflects bacterial adhesion and intracellular survival rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder: key virulence determinants include internalins InlA and InlB, listeriolysin O encoded by hly, ActA-mediated actin polymerization, and phospholipases plcA/plcB, engaging host E-cadherin, c-Met, NF-kappaB, MAPK, PI3K/Akt, interferon-gamma, TNF-alpha, and cell-mediated immunity pathways. No specific inheritance pattern exists for the disease itself, but host susceptibility may be influenced by immune defects affecting IFNG/IL12 axis signaling or immunosuppressive states. Clinically, patients typically present with fever, chills, malaise, new or changing murmur, heart failure, embolic phenomena, and sometimes sepsis; complications include valvular destruction, abscess, conduction abnormalities, systemic emboli including stroke, and death. Common comorbidities include malignancy, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, transplantation, HIV infection, corticosteroid exposure, and iron overload. Diagnosis follows standard infective endocarditis principles, integrating repeated blood cultures yielding Listeria, echocardiographic evidence of vegetations or abscess by transthoracic or transesophageal imaging, and Duke criteria, with valve culture or molecular testing such as broad-range 16S rRNA PCR useful in culture-negative or surgically treated cases. Treatment relies on prolonged bactericidal therapy, most commonly ampicillin or penicillin G, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking by binding penicillin-binding proteins, often combined with gentamicin, an aminoglycoside that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit to enhance killing; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis via dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase inhibition, is an alternative, and vancomycin may be used in selected beta-lact

Name: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea
Description: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea (IBS-D; UMLS C0348898) is a functional disorder of gut–brain interaction characterized by chronic abdominal pain related to defecation and recurrent loose stools without structural pathology, typically presenting with urgency, increased stool frequency, bloating, borborygmi, mucus passage, and a sense of incomplete evacuation. Diagnosis is clinical using Rome IV criteria, supported by limited testing to exclude organic disease, including CBC, CRP or fecal calprotectin, celiac serologies, stool studies when indicated, and colonoscopy or imaging only for alarm features such as bleeding, weight loss, anemia, nocturnal symptoms, or family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. IBS-D is a subtype of IBS, alongside constipation-predominant, mixed, and unsubtyped forms, and commonly overlaps with functional dyspepsia, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue, anxiety, depression, GERD, pelvic pain disorders, and post-infectious states; complications are mainly impaired quality of life, work disability, dehydration from severe diarrhea, and risks from unnecessary procedures. Pathobiology is multifactorial, involving altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity, epithelial barrier dysfunction, bile acid malabsorption in a subset, immune activation with mast cells, enterochromaffin serotonin signaling, microbiome perturbation, and dysregulated gut–brain pathways involving 5-HT3/5-HT4, HPA-axis, cytokine, and enteric neural signaling. Genetic susceptibility is modest and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations reported for SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR, HTR3A and HTR3E, TNFSF15, SCN5A, NPSR1, IL10, and GNB3, sometimes influencing serotonin transport, ion channel function, or immune responses. Common treatments include loperamide, a peripheral mu-opioid receptor agonist that slows transit; rifaximin, a minimally absorbed antibiotic that modulates the intestinal microbiota; eluxadoline, a mixed mu-opioid receptor agonist and delta-opioid receptor antagonist that reduces motility and secretion; and alosetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist that decreases visceral pain and colonic transit in selected patients.

Name: Candidal septicemia (disorder)
Description: Candidal septicemia is an acute, life-threatening invasive fungal bloodstream infection caused predominantly by Candida albicans, but also by C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, and C. krusei, representing a major subtype within candidemia/invasive candidiasis and often arising as catheter-related, abdominal-source, or neutropenia-associated disease rather than a Mendelian disorder. Host susceptibility has recognized genetic components involving innate immune recognition and antifungal immunity, including variants in CARD9, CLEC7A encoding dectin-1, TLR2, TLR4, CX3CR1, IL10, IL17A/IL17RA, STAT1, and TYK2, which affect fungal sensing, Th17 signaling, cytokine production, and neutrophil/macrophage responses; fungal virulence factors include adhesins and biofilm-related proteins such as Als3, Hwp1, and secreted aspartyl proteinases. Key pathways include dectin-1/SYK/CARD9/NF-kB signaling, Toll-like receptor–MyD88 pathways, complement activation, inflammasome/IL-1 signaling, Th17/IL-17 axis, and biofilm-associated resistance mechanisms. Typical manifestations are persistent fever, chills, hypotension, sepsis, multiorgan dysfunction, and possible end-organ dissemination to retina, kidney, liver, spleen, heart, bone, or CNS. Major comorbidities and risk factors include central venous catheters, broad-spectrum antibiotics, total parenteral nutrition, ICU stay, recent surgery, abdominal perforation, malignancy, transplantation, diabetes, renal failure, neutropenia, corticosteroid exposure, and other immunosuppressive states; complications include septic shock, endocarditis, endophthalmitis, osteomyelitis, hepatosplenic candidiasis, and high mortality. Diagnosis relies on blood cultures with species identification and susceptibility testing, supported by beta-D-glucan, PCR or T2Candida assays, catheter or deep-site cultures, echocardiography or ophthalmologic examination when indicated, and fulfillment of sepsis criteria in the setting of Candida bloodstream isolation.
