Name: Korsakoff Syndrome
Description: Korsakoff syndrome (MeSH D020915) is a chronic amnestic neuropsychiatric disorder, usually the irreversible phase of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, caused predominantly by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency most often related to alcohol use disorder, but also seen with malnutrition, bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, cancer, and AIDS. Its molecular basis centers on impaired thiamine-dependent energy metabolism involving thiamine pyrophosphate-requiring enzymes and proteins such as transketolase (TKT), pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and the thiamine transporter SLC19A2, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier injury, and selective damage in mammillary bodies, thalamus, hippocampal circuits, and frontal-limbic memory pathways; genetic susceptibility has been proposed for variants affecting TKT affinity and other thiamine transport/metabolism genes, but inheritance is not Mendelian and most cases are acquired. Clinically, patients develop profound anterograde amnesia with variable retrograde amnesia, confabulation, executive dysfunction, apathy, disorientation, and poor insight, often following acute Wernicke encephalopathy marked by confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and gait ataxia. Major comorbidities and complications include alcohol dependence, liver disease, peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar degeneration, depression, infections, falls, and persistent disability requiring institutional care. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by a history of nutritional deficiency or alcoholism, neuropsychological evidence of disproportionate memory impairment, low thiamine or erythrocyte transketolase activity, magnesium assessment, and MRI showing mammillary body, medial thalamic, or periaqueductal abnormalities. Treatment relies on prompt parenteral thiamine replacement as cofactor repletion, magnesium supplementation to restore thiamine utilization, and management of alcohol use disorder with agents such as naltrexone, a mu-opioid receptor antagonist, acamprosate, a glutamatergic modulator, and disulfiram, an aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor, alongside nutritional rehabilitation and cognitive support.

Name: Photosensitization
Description: Photosensitivity disorders are a heterogeneous group of conditions in which ultraviolet or visible light provokes exaggerated cutaneous injury, encompassing primary photodermatoses such as polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria, chronic actinic dermatitis and actinic prurigo, as well as genetic and metabolic diseases including the porphyrias, xeroderma pigmentosum, lupus-associated photosensitivity and drug-induced photosensitivity. Clinically they present with rapid sun-induced erythema, burning, pruritus, edema, urticaria, vesicles, papules, eczematous or lichenified plaques, and in severe forms blistering, dyspigmentation, scarring or photoaging; systemic associations include fatigue or autoimmune features in lupus, and complications include recurrent secondary infection, chronic dermatitis, pigmentary change, ocular damage and markedly increased skin-cancer risk in DNA-repair disorders. Key molecular mechanisms include UV-induced DNA damage and defective nucleotide excision repair involving XPA, XPC, ERCC2/XPD, ERCC3/XPB and POLH in xeroderma pigmentosum, porphyrin accumulation from defects such as UROS, FECH, HMBS or PPOX causing photooxidative reactive oxygen species injury, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immune signaling with keratinocyte apoptosis, TNF-α, IL-1, type I interferon, mast-cell degranulation, histamine release and T-cell responses in idiopathic and autoimmune forms. Inheritance is often autosomal recessive in xeroderma pigmentosum and many porphyrias, though erythropoietic protoporphyria may involve FECH variants with low-expression alleles, while some forms are sporadic or medication triggered. Diagnosis relies on history of light-provoked eruptions, lesion morphology and timing, phototesting and photopatch testing, porphyrin studies in blood, urine and stool, ANA and lupus serologies when indicated, skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence in selected cases, and molecular genetic testing for suspected inherited syndromes. Treatment centers on strict photoprotection plus hydroxychloroquine, which dampens lysosomal antigen processing and toll-like receptor signaling in lupus and polymorphous light eruption; beta-carotene or afamelanotide, which increase photoprotection partly through antioxidant effects or MC1R-mediated eumelanin production in porphyrias; antihistamines, which block H1-mediated solar ur

Name: Glioblastoma multiforme of brain
Description: Glioblastoma multiforme of the brain is a highly aggressive, WHO grade 4 diffuse astrocytic glioma characterized by rapid proliferation, microvascular proliferation, necrosis, marked invasiveness, and profound intratumoral heterogeneity; it may arise as IDH-wildtype primary glioblastoma, the most common form, or less often as IDH-mutant secondary glioblastoma evolving from lower-grade diffuse glioma. Its molecular landscape commonly includes EGFR amplification or activating variants such as EGFRvIII, TERT promoter mutation, PTEN loss, CDKN2A/B deletion, TP53, ATRX, and PIK3CA/PIK3R1 alterations, chromosome 7 gain with chromosome 10 loss, and, in subsets, MGMT promoter methylation, which predicts relative sensitivity to alkylating therapy; dysregulated pathways prominently involve RTK/RAS/RAF/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53, RB, telomerase regulation, hypoxia/VEGF-driven angiogenesis, and DNA damage response networks. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited predisposition occurs in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, tuberous sclerosis complex, and rare constitutional mismatch-repair deficiency. Patients typically present with progressive headache, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, cognitive or personality change, aphasia, visual symptoms, or signs of raised intracranial pressure. Major complications include cerebral edema, mass effect, herniation, venous thromboembolism, seizures, neurocognitive decline, treatment-related myelosuppression, and recurrence. Diagnosis relies on MRI with contrast showing an irregular ring-enhancing, infiltrative, necrotic mass with edema, followed by histopathology and integrated molecular testing including IDH1/2, MGMT promoter methylation, TERT, ATRX, TP53, EGFR, and copy-number profiling. Standard treatment includes maximal safe surgical resection, radiotherapy, and temozolomide, an oral alkylating agent causing DNA methylation; additional agents include lomustine, a nitrosourea DNA cross-linker, bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody used particularly for recurrent disease and edema control, and tumor-treating fields, which disrupt mitotic spindle formation.

Name: Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Description: Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis is a rare, progressive cystic neoplasm of the lung that primarily affects women, characterized by proliferation of abnormal smooth muscle–like LAM cells within lung parenchyma, airways, blood vessels, and lymphatics; it occurs as sporadic LAM or in association with tuberous sclerosis complex, with pathogenic inactivation of TSC2 more commonly and TSC1 less commonly, leading to loss of hamartin-tuberin complex function, constitutive Rheb-dependent mTORC1 activation, dysregulated PI3K/AKT and ERK signaling, enhanced cell growth, lymphangiogenesis with VEGF-D, matrix remodeling via metalloproteinases, and expression of melanocytic/smooth muscle markers such as gp100/HMB-45, α-smooth muscle actin, estrogen and progesterone receptors. Disease manifestations include progressive exertional dyspnea, recurrent pneumothorax, cough, wheeze, chest pain, chylous pleural effusions or ascites, hemoptysis, and declining FEV1/DLCO, while common extrapulmonary associations and complications include renal angiomyolipomas, thoracic or abdominal lymphangioleiomyomas, TSC-related cortical and cutaneous lesions, pulmonary hypertension, respiratory failure, and complications of recurrent pleural disease. Inheritance is typically not Mendelian in sporadic cases but TSC-associated disease follows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity from germline TSC1 or TSC2 mutations followed by second-hit loss. Diagnosis rests on characteristic diffuse, thin-walled round cysts on high-resolution CT plus supportive evidence such as elevated serum VEGF-D, renal angiomyolipoma, chylous effusion, lymphangioleiomyoma, or definite/probable TSC; biopsy is reserved for uncertain cases and shows HMB-45-positive LAM cells, while pulmonary function testing and pleural fluid analysis aid assessment. Standard therapy centers on sirolimus and everolimus, mTOR inhibitors that suppress abnormal LAM-cell proliferation and stabilize lung function, with bronchodilators for airflow obstruction and pleurodesis for recurrent pneumothorax; oxygen, management of chylous complications, and lung transplantation are used in advanced disease.

Name: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial pneumonia
Description: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial pneumonia is a chronic, opportunistic pulmonary infection caused by environmental mycobacteria, most commonly Mycobacterium avium complex, Mycobacterium kansasii, and rapidly growing species such as M. abscessus, producing fibrocavitary disease or nodular-bronchiectatic disease with chronic cough, sputum production, fatigue, weight loss, fever, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and cavitary or multifocal nodular infiltrates on imaging. Host susceptibility is strongly shaped by impaired cell-mediated immunity and mucociliary clearance, with genetic associations involving the IL-12/IFN-γ axis and related defects in IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12RB1, STAT1, IRF8, GATA2, NEMO/IKBKG, and CFTR; neutralizing anti-IFN-γ autoantibodies and structural disorders such as primary ciliary dyskinesia also predispose, while M. abscessus macrolide resistance may reflect inducible erm(41) or rrl mutations. Core pathogenic pathways include macrophage phagocytosis, TLR2-mediated innate sensing, TNF-α, IL-12, IFN-γ, JAK-STAT signaling, granuloma formation, and dysregulated neutrophilic inflammation in damaged airways. Common comorbidities include bronchiectasis, COPD, prior tuberculosis, cystic fibrosis, HIV infection, connective tissue disease, gastroesophageal reflux, and malnutrition; complications include progressive cavitation, respiratory failure, recurrent hemoptysis, dissemination, and drug toxicities. Treatment usually requires prolonged multidrug therapy guided by species and susceptibility testing, typically a macrolide such as azithromycin or clarithromycin, which binds the 50S ribosome and inhibits protein synthesis, ethambutol, which impairs arabinosyl transferases and mycobacterial cell-wall arabinogalactan synthesis, and rifampin or rifabutin, which inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; additional agents may include amikacin, an aminoglycoside causing 30S mistranslation, or clofazimine, which disrupts mycobacterial membrane redox function. Diagnosis relies on ATS/IDSA-style integration of compatible symptoms, radiographic abnormalities on chest CT, and microbiologic confirmation by repeated sputum cultures or

Name: Female pelvic cellulitis
Description: Female pelvic cellulitis is an acute, usually non-hereditary bacterial soft-tissue infection of the female pelvis, often arising postpartum, postprocedurally, or by contiguous spread from pelvic inflammatory disease, involving polymicrobial flora such as Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, Enterobacterales, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and anaerobes including Bacteroides; accordingly, it is best understood as an infectious-inflammatory disorder rather than a primary genetic disease. Molecularly, host responses prominently engage Toll-like receptor and NF-κB signaling, with downstream TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, chemokine, complement, neutrophil, and macrophage pathways driving edema, pain, fever, and tissue injury; representative host susceptibility factors described in severe bacterial infection include variants affecting TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, MBL2, and cytokine genes, although no Mendelian inheritance pattern is established for pelvic cellulitis itself. Typical manifestations include pelvic or lower abdominal pain, uterine, parametrial, or adnexal tenderness, fever, chills, malodorous vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, dysuria, tachycardia, and leukocytosis, with subtypes ranging from superficial postoperative pelvic wound cellulitis to deeper parametrial cellulitis, pelvic abscess, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, and cellulitis associated with PID. Common comorbidities and risk factors include recent cesarean delivery or gynecologic surgery, retained products of conception, diabetes mellitus, obesity, immunosuppression, bacterial vaginosis, and sexually transmitted infections; major complications include abscess formation, bacteremia, sepsis, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, adhesions, peritonitis, and venous thrombosis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by CBC, CRP or ESR, blood cultures when febrile, cervical or vaginal NAAT testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia, and pelvic ultrasound or CT to exclude abscess or retained tissue. Treatment relies on broad-spectrum antibiotics such as clindamycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; gentamicin, which binds the 30S subunit; ampicillin or ampicillin-sulbactam, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, with metronidazole, acting through anaerobic DNA damage, often added

Name: Diverticulitis of gastrointestinal tract
Description: Diverticulitis of the gastrointestinal tract is an acquired inflammatory complication of diverticulosis, usually affecting colonic pseudodiverticula, in which microperforation of an obstructed diverticulum triggers mucosal injury, bacterial overgrowth, and a predominantly innate immune response; clinically it most often presents with acute localized abdominal pain, classically left lower quadrant, fever, leukocytosis, nausea, altered bowel habits, and focal tenderness, while severe disease may cause peritonitis, abscess, fistula, obstruction, or sepsis. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with heritability supported by twin studies and associations reported near genes involved in connective-tissue integrity, neuromuscular function, and immunity, including COL3A1, ELN, TNFSF15, LAMB4, and ARHGAP15; rare syndromic predisposition occurs in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and Williams-Beuren syndrome, reflecting extracellular matrix weakness. Relevant pathways include epithelial barrier dysfunction, dysbiosis, neutrophil recruitment, cytokine signaling through TNF, IL-1β, IL-6, NF-κB, prostaglandin/COX pathways, matrix remodeling by MMPs, and serotonin-mediated motility abnormalities. Disease subtypes include uncomplicated diverticulitis and complicated forms with abscess, perforation, phlegmon, fistula, bleeding, or stricture, often staged radiologically by Hinchey classification. Common comorbidities include obesity, low-fiber diet, constipation, smoking, NSAID exposure, chronic kidney disease, and cardiometabolic disease, with overlap with irritable bowel syndrome and segmental colitis associated with diverticulosis. Diagnosis is based on compatible symptoms plus inflammatory markers and is confirmed primarily by contrast-enhanced CT showing bowel-wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, diverticula, and possible extraluminal air or abscess; ultrasound or MRI are alternatives, while colonoscopy is deferred until recovery to exclude colorectal cancer. When antibiotics are indicated, typical agents include metronidazole, which disrupts anaerobic DNA synthesis, ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV, and amoxicillin-clavulanate, combining cell-wall synthesis inhibition with beta-lactamase inhibition.

Name: Asthma attack
Description: Asthma attack (UMLS C0349790) is an acute exacerbation of the chronic inflammatory airway disorder asthma, characterized by variable, usually reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness driven most often by type 2 immunity but also by non–type 2 neutrophilic mechanisms. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations involving IL4, IL13, IL4R, TSLP, ADAM33, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, ADRB2 variants influencing bronchodilator response, and FCER1B; relevant proteins include IgE, eosinophil cationic mediators, histamine, leukotrienes, thymic stromal lymphopoietin, and cytokines such as IL-5 and IL-13. Key pathways include allergen-induced dendritic-cell activation, Th2 polarization, IgE-dependent mast-cell degranulation, eosinophilic recruitment, leukotriene and prostaglandin synthesis, airway smooth-muscle contraction through cholinergic and beta2-adrenergic signaling, and epithelial alarmin pathways involving TSLP, IL-33, and IL-25; severe attacks may also involve neutrophils, IL-17, and airway remodeling. Clinically, attacks present with episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnea, tachypnea, prolonged expiration, accessory-muscle use, reduced peak expiratory flow, and in severe cases hypoxemia, silent chest, hypercapnia, or respiratory failure. Recognized phenotypes include allergic/extrinsic, nonallergic/intrinsic, eosinophilic, neutrophilic, exercise-induced, occupational, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and status asthmaticus. Diagnosis rests on compatible symptoms plus variable expiratory airflow limitation demonstrated by spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, serial peak-flow variability, or bronchoprovocation; pulse oximetry, arterial blood gases, chest imaging when alternative diagnoses are considered, and biomarkers such as eosinophils, total/specific IgE, or FeNO may support assessment. Name: Prostate Cancer
Description: Prostatic neoplasms, predominantly prostatic adenocarcinoma arising from glandular epithelium and less commonly including ductal adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine/small-cell carcinoma, and castration-resistant metastatic disease, are typically age-related malignant tumors driven by androgen receptor signaling and genomic alterations involving TMPRSS2-ERG fusion, PTEN loss with PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation, TP53 and RB1 inactivation, SPOP, FOXA1, ATM, CHEK2, CDK12, and DNA-repair defects such as BRCA1/2 mutations; inherited susceptibility is usually complex but is increased in familial cancer syndromes, especially autosomal dominant hereditary breast-ovarian/prostate cancer linked to BRCA2, and Lynch syndrome with mismatch-repair genes. Key pathways include androgen-AR transcriptional programs, PI3K/AKT, RAS/MAPK, WNT/beta-catenin, DNA-damage response, and neuroendocrine lineage plasticity. Common manifestations are often absent early, but may include urinary hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, hematuria, hematospermia, pelvic discomfort, erectile dysfunction, and, in advanced disease, weight loss, anemia, and bone pain from osteoblastic metastases. Major complications include bladder outlet obstruction, urinary retention, hydronephrosis, pathologic fractures, spinal cord compression, and thromboembolic disease; comorbidities commonly coexist with benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, and age-related cardiovascular or metabolic disease. Diagnosis relies on abnormal digital rectal examination, elevated or rising prostate-specific antigen, multiparametric MRI, and histopathologic confirmation by transrectal or transperineal biopsy with Gleason grade group/ISUP scoring, TNM staging, and immunohistochemistry; germline and somatic testing for homologous-recombination or mismatch-repair defects and PSMA-based PET imaging are increasingly used in advanced cases. Standard therapies include leuprolide, a GnRH agonist causing medical castration; enzalutamide, an androgen-receptor signaling inhibitor; docetaxel, a microtubule-stabilizing taxane; abiraterone, a CYP17 inhibitor that suppresses androgen synthesis; and in selected biomarker-defined tumors olaparib, a PARP inhibitor.

Name: Pulmonary Cystic Fibrosis
Description: Cystic fibrosis is a multisystem autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in CFTR on chromosome 7q31, encoding the ATP-binding cassette chloride and bicarbonate channel CFTR; representative mutations include F508del, G551D, G542X, and N1303K, with disease subtypes often defined by pancreatic sufficiency versus insufficiency and by mutation class causing defective protein production, processing, gating, conductance, or stability. Impaired CFTR function disrupts epithelial ion and water transport, with secondary ENaC hyperactivity, airway surface dehydration, defective mucociliary clearance, abnormal innate immune signaling, neutrophil-dominant inflammation, chronic biofilm infection, and progressive bronchiectatic lung injury. Typical manifestations include chronic cough, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, wheeze, nasal polyposis, failure to thrive, steatorrhea, meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstruction, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, male infertility from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, and later CF-related diabetes, liver disease, and osteoporosis. Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and especially Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Major complications and comorbidities include bronchiectasis, hemoptysis, pneumothorax, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, chronic rhinosinusitis, pancreatitis, and depression/anxiety. Treatment includes CFTR modulators such as ivacaftor, a potentiator that increases channel opening; lumacaftor or tezacaftor, correctors that improve folding and trafficking of F508del CFTR; and elexacaftor, a next-generation corrector used in triple therapy with tezacaftor/ivacaftor, plus dornase alfa, which cleaves extracellular DNA to reduce sputum viscosity, inhaled hypertonic saline to rehydrate airway secretions, azithromycin for anti-inflammatory and anti-biofilm effects, and inhaled tobramycin for antipseudomonal therapy. Diagnosis relies on compatible phenotype or newborn screening with elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen, confirmed by sweat chloride testing, CFTR genotyping, and when needed nasal potential difference or intestinal current measurements.

Name: Flu-Like Symptoms
Description: Flu-like symptoms (UMLS C0392171) describe a nonspecific clinical syndrome rather than a single inherited disease, most often reflecting acute viral infection such as influenza A or B, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, adenovirus, or EBV, but also occurring with bacterial infection, vaccination, interferon therapy, autoimmune disease, or malignancy. Its biology is driven predominantly by innate immune activation, with pattern-recognition receptors including TLR3, TLR7, RIG-I/DDX58, and MDA5/IFIH1 inducing type I and III interferon signaling through JAK-STAT pathways and inflammatory mediators such as NF-kB, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and prostaglandin E2; representative host susceptibility genes include IFITM3, TLR7, IFIH1, IRF7, STAT1, and HLA loci, while pathogen-specific proteins such as influenza hemagglutinin and neuraminidase shape infectivity and treatment response. Typical manifestations include fever, chills, myalgias, headache, malaise, fatigue, arthralgia, sore throat, rhinorrhea, and cough, with subtypes commonly divided into uncomplicated viral syndrome, influenza-like illness, medication-induced flu-like reaction, and severe systemic illness with pneumonia or sepsis. Important comorbidities and complications include asthma, COPD, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, pregnancy, immunosuppression, dehydration, viral or secondary bacterial pneumonia, myocarditis, encephalopathy, and acute respiratory failure. Inheritance is usually not Mendelian, but rare monogenic interferon-pathway defects or X-linked TLR7 deficiency can increase susceptibility to severe viral presentations. Diagnosis is clinical when influenza-like illness criteria are met, then refined by viral NAAT/PCR, rapid antigen testing, CBC, inflammatory markers, chest imaging when lower respiratory involvement is suspected, and cultures when bacterial superinfection is possible. Treatment is etiology-directed and supportive: acetaminophen inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis for fever and pain, ibuprofen reversibly inhibits COX-1/COX-2, oseltamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase, zanamivir and baloxavir similarly target influenza replication, and antibiotics are reserved for proven or strongly suspected bacterial causes.

Name: Necrobiosis Lipoidica Diabeticorum
Description: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum (UMLS C0392445) is a chronic granulomatous inflammatory microangiopathic dermatosis classically linked to diabetes mellitus, now often termed necrobiosis lipoidica because it also occurs without diabetes; it presents as well-demarcated yellow-brown, atrophic telangiectatic plaques, typically pretibial and often bilateral, with violaceous borders, reduced sensation, and a tendency to painful ulceration, secondary infection, and scarring, while rare long-standing lesions may develop squamous cell carcinoma. Its pathobiology is incompletely defined but implicates diabetic vasculopathy, endothelial injury, collagen degeneration, macrophage-rich granulomatous inflammation, and immune dysregulation involving TNF-alpha, IL-6, VEGF, TGF-beta, NF-kappaB, JAK/STAT signaling, and impaired wound-healing pathways; associated proteins and genes are therefore largely inferential rather than disease-specific, with representative examples including HLA class II immune susceptibility alleles, TNF, IL6, VEGFA, TGFB1, and genes predisposing to type 1 or type 2 diabetes and microvascular disease rather than a monogenic cause. Inheritance is not Mendelian, and no recurrent pathogenic mutation uniquely defines the disorder. Major comorbidities include type 1 and type 2 diabetes, retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, thyroid autoimmune disease, obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and smoking-related vascular impairment. Subtypes are commonly ulcerative versus non-ulcerative and diabetic-associated versus idiopathic. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by skin biopsy showing layered necrobiosis of collagen with palisading granulomatous inflammation, histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells, plasma cells, and vessel wall thickening; evaluation also includes glucose or HbA1c testing and exclusion of mimics such as granuloma annulare, sarcoidosis, xanthogranuloma, vasculitis, and necrobiotic xanthogranuloma. Treatments commonly include potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids, which suppress NF-kappaB-driven cytokine transcription; tacrolimus, a calcineurin inhibitor that reduces T-cell activation; pentoxifylline, which improves erythrocyte deformability and microcirculatory flow; and selected refractory cases may respond to TNF-alpha inhibitors such as infliximab

Name: Postoperative infection
Description: Postoperative infection (UMLS C0392618) is an acquired, non-Mendelian infectious complication arising after surgery, encompassing superficial incisional, deep incisional, organ/space surgical-site infection, and postoperative sepsis; it typically reflects microbial contamination of the wound or implanted material combined with host susceptibility and impaired tissue repair. Common manifestations include fever, incisional pain, erythema, warmth, edema, purulent drainage, wound dehiscence, malodor, delayed healing, leukocytosis, and in severe cases hypotension and organ dysfunction. Major pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Enterococcus spp., Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and anaerobes, with virulence determinants such as mecA in methicillin-resistant S. aureus and biofilm-associated proteins promoting device-related infection. Host genetic contributors are susceptibility modifiers rather than deterministic causes, with representative associations reported in innate and inflammatory genes such as TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, IL6, TNF, MBL2, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 variants that may influence pathogen recognition, cytokine response, and fibrinolysis. Relevant pathways include Toll-like receptor/NF-κB signaling, inflammasome activation, complement, IL-1/IL-6/TNF-mediated acute-phase responses, neutrophil recruitment, coagulation-fibrinolysis crosstalk, and biofilm quorum-sensing networks. Treatment depends on source control plus antimicrobials: cefazolin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall transpeptidases; vancomycin, a glycopeptide blocking peptidoglycan synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala; piperacillin-tazobactam, combining a broad-spectrum ureidopenicillin with beta-lactamase inhibition; and when indicated metronidazole, which causes anaerobic DNA damage. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes, obesity, malnutrition, smoking, immunosuppression, cancer, peripheral vascular disease, renal failure, prolonged operative time, foreign bodies, and prior colonization with resistant organisms. Diagnosis is based on clinical signs together with CDC surgical-site infection criteria, wound assessment, blood tests including CBC, CRP, and procalcitonin, Gram stain and culture of wound or fluid, blood cultures when systemic illness is suspected,

Name: Headache Disorders
Description: Headache disorders are a heterogeneous group of primary and secondary pain syndromes, dominated clinically by migraine, tension-type headache, and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias such as cluster headache, and characterized by recurrent or persistent head pain with variable nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, cranial autonomic symptoms, and focal neurologic aura in some patients. Their biology is polygenic and neurovascular, with representative genetic contributors including CACNA1A, ATP1A2, and SCN1A in familial hemiplegic migraine, KCNK18 in rare migraine susceptibility, and broader risk loci involving TRPM8, LRP1, PRDM16, and CGRP-related pathways; inheritance is usually complex multifactorial, although some migraine subtypes show autosomal dominant transmission. Key mechanisms include trigeminovascular activation, release of calcitonin gene-related peptide, substance P, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, cortical spreading depolarization in aura, altered serotonergic, dopaminergic, glutamatergic, and nitric oxide signaling, neurogenic inflammation, hypothalamic involvement, and brainstem pain-modulatory network dysfunction. Common treatments include triptans such as sumatriptan, 5-HT1B/1D agonists that inhibit trigeminal neurotransmitter release and promote cranial vasoconstriction; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, which inhibit cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin synthesis; topiramate, which modulates voltage-gated sodium channels, enhances GABAergic tone, and reduces glutamatergic transmission; beta-blockers such as propranolol for prevention; and CGRP-pathway agents including erenumab and gepants that block ligand or receptor signaling. Comorbidities include depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, epilepsy, obesity, temporomandibular dysfunction, cardiovascular disease, medication-overuse headache, and stroke risk in migraine with aura. Diagnosis is primarily clinical using ICHD criteria based on attack duration, pain features, associated symptoms, and frequency, supplemented when indicated by neurologic examination, headache diaries, neuroimaging, lumbar puncture, or laboratory testing to exclude secondary causes and identify complications.

Name: Initial Insomnia
Description: Initial insomnia (sleep-onset insomnia) is a symptom-defined subtype of insomnia disorder characterized by persistent difficulty initiating sleep despite adequate opportunity, typically presenting with prolonged sleep latency, bedtime arousal, frustration, daytime fatigue, impaired concentration, irritability, and reduced functioning; it may occur as acute/adjustment-related, chronic, psychophysiologic, paradoxical, comorbid, or circadian-related insomnia, particularly delayed sleep–wake phase disorder. Its biology is multifactorial and usually polygenic rather than Mendelian, with genetic susceptibility reported in circadian and arousal-related genes such as CLOCK, PER2, PER3, CRY1, ARNTL/BMAL1, adenosinergic and GABAergic signaling components, and orexin/hypocretin pathway genes, although no single mutation is diagnostic in most cases; familial clustering is recognized, with inheritance best viewed as complex and influenced by stress reactivity and environmental factors. Relevant pathways include the circadian clock network in the suprachiasmatic nucleus with melatonin signaling through MTNR1A/MTNR1B, hyperarousal systems involving orexin neurons, monoaminergic and HPA-axis activation, and sleep-promoting GABAergic pathways centered on GABAA receptor signaling. Common treatments include zolpidem, a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptors; ramelteon, an MT1/MT2 melatonin receptor agonist that shifts circadian/sleep-onset timing; low-dose doxepin, primarily an H1 histamine receptor antagonist at hypnotic doses; and, in selected patients, suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist. Initial insomnia is commonly linked to anxiety, major depressive disorder, ADHD, chronic pain, substance and caffeine use, restless legs syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, and cardiometabolic disease, and chronic cases increase risks of accidents, mood deterioration, hypertension, and impaired quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, based on ICSD-3/DSM-5-type criteria requiring recurrent sleep-initiation difficulty with daytime impairment despite adequate sleep opportunity, supported by sleep history, sleep diary, actigraphy when circadian disorder is suspected, polysomnography when another sleep disorder is suspected, and targeted psychiatric, medical, and medication review.

Name: Excessive daytime sleepiness - normal night sleep
Description: Excessive daytime sleepiness with apparently normal nocturnal sleep is a symptom-defined hypersomnolence phenotype rather than a single disease, most often encompassing central disorders of hypersomnolence such as idiopathic hypersomnia, narcolepsy type 2, and occasionally narcolepsy type 1 without obvious nocturnal disturbance; it is characterized by persistent sleepiness, unintended naps, sleep inertia, cognitive slowing, reduced vigilance, and impaired occupational and driving performance despite adequate or prolonged nighttime sleep. Its biology is heterogeneous: narcolepsy type 1 is strongly linked to HLA-DQB1*06:02 and loss of hypothalamic orexin/hypocretin neurons, with orexin peptides acting through HCRTR1 and HCRTR2 to regulate monoaminergic and cholinergic arousal networks, while familial and syndromic hypersomnolence may involve genes such as DNMT1, NALCN, ADA, PER2, CRY1, and occasionally GABA-A receptor–modulating mechanisms or circadian pathway abnormalities involving CLOCK-BMAL1 signaling. Associated pathways include orexin signaling, histaminergic, dopaminergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic, and GABAergic arousal circuits, as well as circadian pacemaker regulation in the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Common treatments include modafinil or armodafinil, which promote wakefulness partly via dopamine transporter inhibition; methylphenidate or amphetamines, which increase synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine; solriamfetol, a dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; pitolisant, an H3-receptor inverse agonist that enhances histaminergic transmission; and sodium oxybate, which consolidates sleep and improves daytime alertness through GABA-B–related mechanisms. Comorbidities include depression, anxiety, obesity, autonomic symptoms, headache, sleep paralysis or hypnagogic hallucinations in narcoleptic forms, and complications such as accidents and psychosocial dysfunction. Inheritance is usually complex or sporadic, though rare autosomal dominant familial forms exist. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, exclusion of sleep deprivation, medications, obstructive sleep apnea, circadian disorders, and medical causes, supported by polysomnography followed by multiple sleep latency testing, actigraphy/sleep logs, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, CSF orexin in selected cases, HLA testing, and targeted genetic testing when syndromic or

Name: Malignant otitis externa caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Description: Malignant otitis externa caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (UMLS C0395818), more accurately termed necrotizing otitis externa, is an aggressive invasive infection of the external auditory canal that extends to skull-base soft tissue and bone, typically affecting older adults with diabetes mellitus or other immunocompromising states. Its pathobiology is primarily infectious rather than inherited, but host susceptibility is influenced by impaired innate immunity, microangiopathy, and hyperglycemia-related defects in neutrophil function; representative host genes and proteins implicated in antibacterial defense include TLR4, MYD88, IL6, TNF, CFTR, neutrophil NADPH oxidase components such as CYBB, and antimicrobial peptides, while bacterial virulence determinants include exotoxin A, elastases LasA/LasB, alginate, quorum-sensing regulators LasR/RhlR, type III secretion effectors ExoS and ExoU, and biofilm-associated pathways involving Las, Rhl, and Pqs signaling. Clinically, patients present with severe otalgia often worse at night, persistent otorrhea, edema and erythema of the canal, granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction, conductive hearing loss, and in advanced disease cranial neuropathies, especially facial nerve palsy. Disease forms include localized necrotizing otitis externa, skull-base osteomyelitis, and refractory or recurrent biofilm-associated disease. Diagnosis rests on compatible symptoms in a high-risk host, otoscopic findings, elevated ESR or CRP, culture of ear drainage or tissue showing P. aeruginosa, and imaging with CT for bony erosion, MRI for soft-tissue spread, and radionuclide studies such as technetium or gallium scans to assess osteomyelitis and treatment response; biopsy may be required to exclude carcinoma. Standard therapy relies on antipseudomonal agents such as ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, ceftazidime or cefepime, beta-lactams that bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit cell-wall synthesis, and piperacillin-tazobactam, combining an antipseudomonal ureidopenicillin with beta-lactamase inhibition; resistant cases may require meropenem or aminoglycosides. Name: Laryngeal papillomatosis
Description: Laryngeal papillomatosis, most commonly recurrent respiratory papillomatosis of the larynx, is a benign but often chronic epithelial neoplasia caused predominantly by human papillomavirus infection, especially HPV-6 and HPV-11, with occasional detection of high-risk types such as HPV-16 or HPV-18 in dysplastic or malignant transformation; viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins functionally suppress TP53 and RB1 pathways, promote cell-cycle entry via CDK4/6-E2F signaling, and interact with EGFR, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, interferon-mediated immune responses, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, and matrix-remodeling programs. Disease is classically divided into juvenile-onset and adult-onset forms, is usually sporadic rather than Mendelian, and genetic susceptibility appears polygenic, with reported associations involving HLA class II alleles and immune-regulatory genes rather than a single inherited mutation. Patients typically present with progressive hoarseness, dysphonia, chronic cough, stridor, dyspnea, recurrent airway obstruction, and, when distal spread occurs, tracheobronchial or pulmonary papillomatosis; complications include frequent recurrence after excision, voice impairment, airway compromise, secondary infection, distal airway disease, and rare squamous cell carcinoma. Comorbidities may include asthma-like symptoms, gastroesophageal reflux, and immunosuppression or other states of impaired antiviral immunity. Diagnosis is based on laryngoscopy demonstrating exophytic papillomas, histopathology of squamous papillomas with koilocytic change, and HPV testing by PCR or in situ hybridization; imaging or bronchoscopy is used when lower-airway extension is suspected. Treatment is centered on repeated surgical debulking, often with microdebrider or laser, with adjuvant drugs in selected severe or recurrent cases, including bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody against VEGF-A that reduces angiogenesis; cidofovir, a cytosine nucleotide analog that inhibits viral DNA polymerase; and interferon-α, an immunomodulatory cytokine with antiviral and antiproliferative effects; additional agents used in some settings include celecoxib, an inhibitor of COX-2-mediated prostaglandin signaling, and PD-1 blockade in refractory disease.

Name: Postoperative ileus
Description: Postoperative ileus (UMLS C0400877) is a usually transient, acquired impairment of coordinated gastrointestinal propulsion after surgery, especially abdominal procedures, caused by a multifactorial interaction among neurogenic reflex inhibition, inflammatory activation, opioid-mediated dysmotility, and fluid-electrolyte disturbance rather than a classic inherited disorder. Clinically it presents with delayed passage of flatus and stool, abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, bloating, intolerance of oral intake, hypoactive or absent bowel sounds, and radiographic diffuse gaseous bowel dilation without a mechanical transition point; prolonged cases may lead to dehydration, aspiration, malnutrition, wound complications, pneumonia, venous thromboembolism, and longer hospitalization. Pathobiology prominently involves enteric and autonomic neural pathways, inhibitory sympathetic signaling, mu-opioid receptor signaling encoded by OPRM1, inflammatory cytokines such as IL6, TNF, and IL1B, prostaglandin pathways including PTGS2/COX-2, nitric oxide signaling through NOS isoforms, and leukocyte/macrophage recruitment in the muscularis externa; adrenergic, cholinergic, serotonergic 5-HT4, and ghrelin-related pathways also modulate motility. Genetic contribution is limited and non-Mendelian, but susceptibility may be influenced by common variants in OPRM1, COMT, ABCB1, IL6, TNF, and other inflammatory or analgesic-response genes, with no established inheritance pattern. Recognized subtypes include physiologic early postoperative ileus, prolonged postoperative ileus, and colonic-predominant forms often overlapping with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction. Management is mainly supportive and preventive, including alvimopan, a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist, methylnaltrexone or naloxegol with similar peripheral opioid antagonism in selected settings, and prokinetics such as metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist with weak 5-HT4 agonism, or neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor mainly for colonic pseudo-obstruction; opioid minimization, early ambulation, and electrolyte correction are essential. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by abdominal radiography or CT to exclude mechanical obstruction, plus laboratory testing for potassium, magnesium, calcium, infection, and other postoperative complications.

Name: Liver transplant rejection
Description: Liver transplant rejection is an immune-mediated allograft injury in which recipient recognition of donor alloantigens causes acute cellular, antibody-mediated, or chronic rejection, typically presenting with asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation or with fever, malaise, jaundice, pruritus, abdominal pain, cholestasis, and, in severe cases, graft dysfunction or failure. Its biology is driven by donor-recipient HLA mismatch and alloreactive T- and B-cell responses involving T-cell receptor signaling, antigen presentation by HLA class I/II molecules, CD28/CTLA4 costimulation, IL-2/JAK-STAT and calcineurin-NFAT pathways, TNF, IFN-γ, complement activation including C4d, endothelial injury, and fibrogenic signaling such as TGF-β in chronic ductopenic rejection. Genetic contributors are largely polygenic and non-Mendelian, with representative associations involving HLA loci, cytokine and immune-regulatory variants such as TNF, IL10, CTLA4, FOXP3, and pharmacogenes affecting immunosuppressant handling including CYP3A5 and ABCB1; rare donor-recipient mismatches in minor histocompatibility antigens may also contribute. Diagnosis relies on clinical context, serial AST, ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT abnormalities, exclusion of vascular thrombosis, biliary obstruction, recurrent viral hepatitis, drug toxicity, and infection, detection of donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies when antibody-mediated rejection is suspected, and confirmation by liver biopsy showing portal inflammation, bile duct injury, endothelitis, or chronic bile duct loss/obliterative arteriopathy. Standard treatment centers on corticosteroids such as methylprednisolone, which broadly suppress NF-κB-dependent inflammatory transcription; tacrolimus or cyclosporine, calcineurin inhibitors that block IL-2-driven T-cell activation; mycophenolate mofetil, an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor that impairs lymphocyte purine synthesis; and in selected refractory cases antithymocyte globulin, sirolimus, or rituximab/plasmapheresis for antibody-mediated disease. Important linked complications and comorbidities include opportunistic infection, renal dysfunction, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, recurrent primary liver disease, biliary strictures, chronic allograft fibrosis, and need for retransplantation.

Name: Constipation, chronic
Description: Chronic constipation is a heterogeneous gastrointestinal motility and defecatory disorder defined clinically by infrequent or difficult stool passage for at least 3 months, commonly classified into normal-transit constipation, slow-transit constipation, and defecatory disorders; typical symptoms include fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements weekly, hard stools, excessive straining, sensation of incomplete evacuation or anorectal blockage, abdominal bloating, and need for manual maneuvers. Pathobiology involves altered enteric neuromuscular function, colonic smooth-muscle activity, pelvic floor dyssynergia, epithelial secretion, and gut-brain signaling, with implicated pathways including serotonergic 5-HT4 signaling, guanylate cyclase C/cGMP/CFTR-mediated chloride and fluid secretion, prostaglandin E receptor EP4 signaling, bile acid-TGR5/FXR pathways, opioid receptor signaling, nitric oxide and acetylcholine neurotransmission, and interstitial cells of Cajal dysfunction. Genetic contributions are usually complex and polygenic, but rare monogenic forms and syndromic associations are known, including RET, EDNRB, EDN3, SOX10, PHOX2B, FLNA, ACTG2, and L1CAM variants in Hirschsprung disease, chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, or neuronal dysmotility; these are often autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked depending on the gene. Comorbidities include irritable bowel syndrome, pelvic floor disorders, hypothyroidism, diabetes, Parkinson disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, depression, and opioid exposure; complications include fecal impaction, hemorrhoids, anal fissures, rectal prolapse, stercoral ulceration, and overflow incontinence. Common treatments include polyethylene glycol, an osmotic laxative that retains water in the lumen; stimulant laxatives such as bisacodyl or senna, which enhance colonic motility and secretion; lubiprostone, a chloride channel activator; linaclotide and plecanatide, guanylate cyclase C agonists; prucalopride, a selective 5-HT4 agonist; and peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists such as naloxegol for opioid-induced disease. Name: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
Description: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV; UMLS C0401160) is an acute and delayed toxic syndrome caused by emetogenic anticancer therapy, rather than an inherited primary disease, characterized clinically by nausea, retching, vomiting, anorexia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, weight loss, and impaired adherence to chemotherapy; subtypes include acute CINV within 24 hours, delayed CINV after 24 hours, anticipatory CINV mediated by conditioned responses, breakthrough CINV despite prophylaxis, and refractory CINV after prior treatment failure. Its biology centers on peripheral enterochromaffin-cell release of serotonin activating 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents, and central substance P signaling through neurokinin-1 receptors in the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius, with additional contributions from dopamine D2, histamine H1, muscarinic, cannabinoid CB1, and glucocorticoid pathways. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic and non-Mendelian, with reported associations involving HTR3A/HTR3B, TACR1, DRD2, COMT, ABCB1, CYP2D6, CYP3A4, and CYP3A5 variants that may influence emesis risk or antiemetic pharmacokinetics; no single mutation is diagnostic. Common treatments include 5-HT3 receptor antagonists such as ondansetron or palonosetron, which block serotonin-mediated vagal and central signaling; NK1 receptor antagonists such as aprepitant or fosaprepitant, which inhibit substance P signaling; dexamethasone, which enhances antiemetic control through central anti-inflammatory and prostaglandin-modulating effects; and in selected cases olanzapine, a multi-receptor antagonist targeting dopaminergic and serotonergic pathways. Risk is shaped by regimen emetogenicity, especially cisplatin and anthracycline-cyclophosphamide, plus female sex, younger age, anxiety, motion sickness, pregnancy-related nausea, low alcohol use, and prior poor control. Diagnosis is clinical, based on temporal association with chemotherapy, symptom severity, and exclusion of alternative causes such as bowel obstruction, brain metastases, infection, metabolic derangement, or opioid toxicity, with supportive testing including history, examination, medication review, electrolytes, renal and hepatic panels, and imaging when indicated.

Name: Overactive bladder
Description: Overactive bladder (OAB; UMLS C0403643) is a symptom-defined syndrome of urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia and sometimes urgency urinary incontinence, in the absence of urinary tract infection or another obvious pathology; it is commonly classified as OAB-wet and OAB-dry and may be idiopathic or neurogenic. Its biology reflects disordered detrusor sensory-motor control involving parasympathetic cholinergic signaling through acetylcholine and muscarinic M3/M2 receptors, purinergic ATP-P2X3 pathways, β3-adrenergic relaxation signaling, urothelial afferent mediators, TRPV1/TRPV4 channels, and central inhibitory circuits; representative molecular associations reported in bladder dysfunction include CHRM3, ADRB3, TRPV1, TRPV4, P2RX3, NGF, BDNF, and genes linked to connective tissue or smooth-muscle regulation such as COL1A1 and ACTG2, although no single high-penetrance mutation explains most idiopathic OAB. Familial clustering and complex polygenic susceptibility are described, while rare neurogenic or syndromic contributors may follow the inheritance pattern of the underlying disorder rather than OAB itself. Typical signs include urgency, small voided volumes, increased daytime frequency, nocturia, and urge leakage, with complications including falls, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, skin breakdown, recurrent urinary infections, and reduced quality of life; common comorbidities include obesity, diabetes, constipation, pelvic organ prolapse, benign prostatic hyperplasia, menopause, and neurologic disease such as stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, or spinal cord injury. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history, bladder diary, urinalysis with culture when indicated, post-void residual assessment, pelvic or prostate evaluation, and exclusion of hematuria, stones, malignancy, and infection; questionnaires, urodynamics showing detrusor overactivity, cystoscopy, or imaging are reserved for selected cases. Common treatments include antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin, tolterodine, and solifenacin, which inhibit detrusor muscarinic receptors; the β3-agonist mirabegron, which promotes bladder relaxation; and onabotulinumtoxinA, which reduces acetylcholine release.

Name: Adrenal Insufficiency
Description: Adrenal insufficiency (UMLS C0405580) is a disorder of inadequate glucocorticoid production, often with mineralocorticoid and adrenal androgen deficiency, arising as primary adrenal failure, secondary pituitary ACTH deficiency, or tertiary hypothalamic CRH deficiency; primary disease is commonly autoimmune Addison disease but also results from infections, hemorrhage, metastases, or monogenic defects. Key genetic contributors include NR0B1/DAX1 mutations causing X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita, CYP21A2 defects in congenital adrenal hyperplasia, MC2R or MRAP mutations impairing ACTH signaling, STAR or CYP11A1 defects disrupting steroidogenesis, and AAAS mutations in Allgrove syndrome; autoimmune forms associate with AIRE mutations in APS-1 and HLA-linked susceptibility. Pathobiologically, disease involves the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, ACTH-MC2R-cAMP-PKA signaling, cholesterol transport by StAR, and steroidogenic enzymes including CYP11A1, CYP17A1, CYP21A2, and CYP11B1/B2, with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation in primary disease. Typical manifestations include fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, orthostatic hypotension, salt craving, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and in primary disease hyperpigmentation from elevated POMC-derived ACTH; adrenal crisis causes shock and electrolyte derangement. Comorbidities include autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, celiac disease, hypogonadism, and osteoporosis; complications include crisis, arrhythmia, and impaired growth in children. Inheritance may be autosomal recessive, X-linked, or syndromic depending on etiology. Diagnosis rests on low morning serum cortisol with elevated ACTH in primary disease or low/inappropriately normal ACTH in central forms, confirmation by cosyntropin stimulation testing, and adjunctive renin, aldosterone, adrenal autoantibodies, electrolytes, glucose, pituitary hormones, genetic testing, and adrenal or pituitary imaging. Treatment centers on glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone, prednisone, or dexamethasone, mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone, and emergency parenteral hydrocortisone, which act as glucocortico

Name: Chronic small plaque psoriasis
Description: Chronic small plaque psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory papulosquamous disorder, generally regarded as a limited plaque-type variant of psoriasis vulgaris, characterized by persistent, well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques that are typically smaller than classic large-plaque lesions and favor the trunk and proximal limbs, often with mild pruritus, waxing and waning activity, and occasional nail pitting. Its pathobiology reflects genetic susceptibility interacting with environmental triggers, with representative associations involving HLA-C*06:02 within PSORS1, IL23R, IL12B, TNFAIP3, TNIP1, TRAF3IP2, CARD14, and late cornified envelope genes such as LCE3B/LCE3C deletion; rare familial forms may show autosomal dominant clustering, but most disease is complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. Central pathways include dendritic-cell and keratinocyte activation, TNF-alpha, IL-23/Th17 and IL-17A/F signaling, NF-kappaB, JAK-STAT, and keratinocyte hyperproliferation with aberrant differentiation involving antimicrobial peptides such as beta-defensins and S100 proteins. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on chronic sharply bordered plaques with micaceous scale in a typical distribution, supported when needed by dermoscopy, skin biopsy showing psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with parakeratosis, diminished granular layer, and neutrophils in the stratum corneum, and severity assessment by body surface area, PASI, or physician global assessment; fungal studies may help exclude tinea. Common treatments include topical corticosteroids, which suppress inflammatory gene transcription; vitamin D analogues such as calcipotriene, which normalize keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation; retinoids such as tazarotene, which modulate retinoic acid receptors; phototherapy; methotrexate, which exerts antiproliferative and anti-inflammatory effects partly via adenosine signaling; cyclosporine, which inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation; and biologics targeting TNF-alpha, IL-17, or IL-23. Comorbidities include psoriatic arthritis, obesity, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, depression, and uveitis, while complications mainly relate to chronic inflammation, treatment toxicity, and impaired quality of life.

Name: Psoriasis of scalp
Description: Psoriasis of the scalp is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory dermatosis, usually representing plaque psoriasis localized to hair-bearing scalp but sometimes occurring with guttate, pustular, erythrodermic, or sebopsoriasis-like patterns; it is characterized clinically by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick micaceous or silvery scale, variable pruritus, burning, excoriations, and extension beyond the hairline, while alopecia is usually non-scarring and secondary to inflammation or scratching. Its pathobiology reflects genetic susceptibility and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity, especially the IL-23/Th17/TNF-α axis, with key mediators including TNF, IL23A/IL12B, IL17A, IL17F, IL22, NF-κB, STAT3, dendritic cells, and keratinocyte hyperproliferation; representative genetic associations include HLA-C*06:02 within PSORS1, plus variants in IL23R, IL12B, TNFAIP3, TRAF3IP2, CARD14, LCE3B/LCE3C deletion, and ERAP1, with mostly complex polygenic inheritance, though rare familial autosomal dominant forms related to CARD14 mutations are recognized. Comorbidities include psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, depression, anxiety, and secondary bacterial infection from excoriation. Diagnosis is primarily clinical based on scalp morphology and concomitant psoriasis elsewhere; dermoscopy may show regularly distributed red dots and white scale, and biopsy, when needed, demonstrates psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, parakeratosis with neutrophils, diminished granular layer, and dilated tortuous capillaries, helping distinguish it from seborrheic dermatitis, tinea capitis, lichen planopilaris, and atopic dermatitis. Treatment commonly includes potent topical corticosteroids such as clobetasol, which suppress inflammatory gene transcription; vitamin D analogues such as calcipotriene, which normalize keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation; and keratolytics such as salicylic acid to reduce scale, while more extensive or refractory disease may require methotrexate, a folate antagonist with antiproliferative and immunomodulatory effects, cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor that blocks T-cell activation, or biologics targeting TNF-α, IL-17

Name: Ocular Rosacea
Description: Rosacea is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory dermatosis of the centrofacial skin characterized by dysregulated innate immunity, neurovascular hyperreactivity, and epidermal barrier dysfunction, presenting with persistent erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, papules, pustules, burning, stinging, edema, and, in some patients, phymatous tissue hypertrophy or ocular disease with blepharitis, conjunctival injection, and keratitis. Major clinical subtypes include erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous, and ocular rosacea, although overlap is common. Pathobiology implicates increased cathelicidin processing with KLK5 serine protease activity, Toll-like receptor 2 signaling, NF-κB-driven cytokines, mast cells, matrix metalloproteinases, vascular endothelial growth factor, transient receptor potential channels such as TRPV1/TRPA1, and microbial triggers including Demodex-associated Bacillus antigens; representative associated genes/proteins include CAMP, KLK5, TLR2, MMP9, TNF, IL1B, VEGFA, GSTT1/GSTM1, and HLA class II loci, with genetic susceptibility typically complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, although family clustering is recognized. Diagnosis is clinical, based on persistent centrofacial erythema with periodic intensification or phymatous change as diagnostic features, supported by major features such as flushing, papules/pustules, telangiectasia, and ocular findings; dermoscopy may aid vascular assessment, biopsy is reserved for atypical cases, and ophthalmologic examination is indicated when ocular involvement is suspected. Common treatments include topical metronidazole, which reduces reactive oxygen species and inflammatory signaling; azelaic acid, which has anti-inflammatory and keratinocyte-normalizing effects; topical ivermectin, which is anti-Demodex and anti-inflammatory; oral doxycycline, especially subantimicrobial dose, which inhibits neutrophil-mediated inflammation and matrix metalloproteinases; and brimonidine or oxymetazoline, α-adrenergic agonists that vasoconstrict superficial vessels. Important comorbidities and complications include migraine, gastrointestinal disorders, cardiovascular risk associations, anxiety/depression, rhinophyma, and sight-threatening corneal involvement.

Name: Poisoning caused by opiate analgesic drug (disorder)
Description: Poisoning caused by an opiate analgesic drug is an acute toxicologic disorder resulting from excessive exposure to natural or semisynthetic opioid agonists such as morphine, codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone, and heroin, producing potentially fatal depression of the central nervous and respiratory systems through overstimulation of the mu-opioid receptor encoded by OPRM1, with additional contribution from delta and kappa opioid receptors encoded by OPRD1 and OPRK1. At the cellular level, opioid receptor activation engages Gi/o signaling, inhibits adenylyl cyclase and cAMP formation, reduces presynaptic calcium influx, increases postsynaptic GIRK potassium conductance, suppresses neurotransmitter release, and depresses brainstem respiratory drive; pharmacogenetic modifiers include CYP2D6 variants affecting codeine and tramadol bioactivation, CYP3A4 and UGT2B7 in oxycodone or morphine metabolism, and ABCB1 and COMT polymorphisms that may alter CNS exposure or sensitivity, although inheritance is not Mendelian and reflects complex susceptibility rather than a primary genetic disease. Hallmark findings are miosis, somnolence progressing to coma, bradypnea or apnea, hypoxemia, cyanosis, hypotension, bradycardia, decreased bowel motility, and occasionally noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, seizures in selected agents, and death; common subtypes include prescription opioid overdose, heroin toxicity, immediate-release versus sustained-release formulations, and single-agent versus mixed intoxication, especially with benzodiazepines or alcohol. Major comorbidities and complications include substance use disorder, chronic pain, depression, hepatitis C, HIV, aspiration pneumonia, anoxic brain injury, and recurrent overdose. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on exposure history and the opioid toxidrome, supported by pulse oximetry, arterial blood gas testing, serum chemistries, ECG, and urine or confirmatory toxicology testing. Treatment centers on naloxone, a competitive opioid receptor antagonist, with repeated dosing or infusion when needed; ventilatory support and oxygen; and adjunctive nalmefene, a longer-acting opioid antagonist, or methylnaltrexone, a peripheral mu-receptor antagonist, in selected settings.

Name: Meningococcus carrier
Description: Meningococcus carrier state (UMLS C0421162) denotes asymptomatic colonization of the human nasopharynx by Neisseria meningitidis, a Gram-negative encapsulated diplococcus that serves as the reservoir for transmission and the precursor state for invasive meningococcal disease. Carriage is usually transient and clinically silent, although mild pharyngitis or upper-respiratory symptoms may occur; important subtypes are defined by capsular serogroup, especially A, B, C, W, X, and Y, and by hyperinvasive clonal complexes. Host susceptibility to acquisition, persistence, or progression to disease is influenced more by immune genetics than classic Mendelian inheritance, with representative variants involving complement pathway genes such as C5, C6, C7, C8, C9, CFH and CFHR3/CFHR1, pattern-recognition and inflammatory loci including TLR4 and TNF, and immunoglobulin/Fc receptor pathways; bacterial virulence determinants relevant to carriage include capsule synthesis loci, factor H binding protein, PorA/PorB, Opc/Opa adhesins, pili, and lipooligosaccharide. Key pathways include nasopharyngeal epithelial adhesion and invasion, complement activation and evasion, TLR-triggered NF-κB signaling, and cytokine responses mediated by IL-6 and TNF-α. The main clinical concern is progression to meningitis, meningococcemia, septic shock, purpura fulminans, arthritis, pneumonia, or chronic complement-associated recurrent infection, with comorbidity risks increased by asplenia, complement deficiency, HIV, crowding, and concurrent viral respiratory infection. Diagnosis of carriage relies on oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal swab culture on selective media, PCR or NAAT for meningococcal targets, serogrouping, and genomic typing; evaluation for recurrent or invasive disease may include complement testing. Eradication therapy for carriers commonly uses rifampin, which inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, ciprofloxacin, which inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, and ceftriaxone, a β-lactam that blocks penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis; azithromycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor, is an alternative in some settings.

Name: Punctate keratopathy
Description: Punctate keratopathy is a clinical corneal disorder rather than a single etiologic disease, characterized by multiple small superficial epithelial or subepithelial corneal lesions that may be acute or chronic and include punctate epithelial keratitis, Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis, and punctate lesions secondary to dry eye, blepharitis, viral infection, contact lens wear, toxicity, or inherited corneal dystrophy. Patients typically present with foreign-body sensation, irritation, photophobia, tearing, burning, fluctuating or blurred vision, and fine punctate fluorescein-staining lesions on slit-lamp examination, sometimes with recurrent exacerbations. Molecularly, most cases reflect epithelial stress and inflammation involving tear-film instability, MAPK and NF-κB signaling, cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, matrix metalloproteinases, and, in dry-eye-associated disease, HLA-DR upregulation and T-cell-mediated ocular surface injury; infectious forms may involve viral replication pathways, especially adenoviral or herpes simplex infection. Genetic associations are limited for the common acquired forms, but punctate keratopathy can occur with inherited corneal disorders, with examples including TGFBI-related corneal dystrophies and KRT3 or KRT12 mutations in Meesmann epithelial corneal dystrophy, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance. Common treatments target lubrication, inflammation, infection, or epithelial healing: artificial tears such as carboxymethylcellulose act as tear substitutes; topical cyclosporine inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation; lifitegrast blocks LFA-1/ICAM-1-mediated lymphocyte adhesion; topical corticosteroids such as loteprednol suppress phospholipase A2-driven inflammatory gene expression; antivirals such as acyclovir or ganciclovir inhibit herpesviral DNA polymerase when HSV is implicated. Important comorbidities include dry eye disease, meibomian gland dysfunction, blepharitis, allergic conjunctivitis, autoimmune disorders including Sjögren syndrome, and contact-lens-related hypoxia or toxicity; complications include recurrent erosions, persistent epithelial defects, infectious keratitis, corneal scarring, and reduced visual acuity. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history, slit-lamp biomicroscopy with fluorescein or rose bengal/lissamine staining, tear testing, eyelid and meibomian assessment,

Name: Pain in spine
Description: Pain in the spine (back pain localized to the cervical, thoracic, or lumbar column) is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease, arising from degenerative, inflammatory, traumatic, infectious, neoplastic, or neuropathic disorders of vertebrae, intervertebral discs, facet joints, ligaments, paraspinal muscles, or nerve roots. Common subtypes include mechanical/nonspecific axial pain, radicular pain from disc herniation, spinal stenosis–related pain, myofascial pain, fracture-related pain, and inflammatory back pain as in axial spondyloarthritis. Molecular associations depend on etiology and include matrix and inflammatory mediators such as COL1A1, COL9A2/COL9A3, ACAN, MMPs, IL1B, IL6, TNF, and VDR in disc degeneration or osteoporotic vertebral pain, and HLA-B27 in inflammatory spinal pain; implicated pathways include TNF/NF-κB, IL-17/IL-23, prostaglandin-COX signaling, RANKL-mediated bone remodeling, nerve growth factor sensitization, and nociceptive transmission through peripheral and central glutamatergic pathways. Heritability is therefore disorder-specific: most mechanical back pain is multifactorial and polygenic, whereas ankylosing spondylitis shows strong HLA-B27 association and some vertebral fragility syndromes reflect Mendelian connective tissue or bone disorders. Symptoms include localized aching or stiffness, muscle spasm, reduced range of motion, tenderness, posture change, and, when neural structures are involved, radiating pain, paresthesias, weakness, neurogenic claudication, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Frequent comorbidities and complications include obesity, osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, depression, sleep disturbance, opioid dependence, falls, chronic disability, and neurologic deficit. Diagnosis is clinical, integrating pain pattern, inflammatory features, red flags, and neurologic examination, with testing tailored to cause: plain radiographs, MRI or CT for fracture, stenosis, tumor, or infection; ESR/CRP and HLA-B27 when inflammatory disease is suspected; and selective electrodiagnostic studies. Name: Pityriasis simplex
Description: Pityriasis simplex, usually corresponding clinically to dandruff or simple scalp scaling, is a common, chronic, non-scarring desquamative disorder of the scalp characterized by fine white or gray flaking, mild pruritus, and variable erythema without the thick plaques of psoriasis or the marked inflammation of seborrheic dermatitis; some authors distinguish dry and oily forms, although it exists on a spectrum with seborrheic dermatitis. Its pathobiology is multifactorial rather than Mendelian, involving Malassezia species overgrowth, altered sebaceous lipids, barrier dysfunction, and innate immune activation; no single causative gene is established, but susceptibility has been linked broadly to epidermal differentiation and inflammatory genes and proteins such as filaggrin, keratins, antimicrobial peptides, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and histamine-related pathways. Key signaling processes include keratinocyte hyperproliferation and abnormal cornification, Toll-like receptor and NF-κB signaling, cytokine-mediated inflammation, and disturbance of epidermal lipid homeostasis. Inheritance is therefore complex and likely polygenic with environmental modifiers rather than a defined monogenic pattern. Common comorbidities and mimics include seborrheic dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea capitis, contact dermatitis, and occasionally secondary excoriations or psychosocial distress from visible scaling. Diagnosis is clinical, based on diffuse scalp scaling with limited inflammation and absence of scarring; testing is reserved for atypical or refractory cases and may include potassium hydroxide preparation or fungal culture to exclude dermatophytosis, dermoscopy, patch testing when allergic contact dermatitis is suspected, and biopsy only rarely, showing nonspecific hyperkeratosis/parakeratosis. Treatment centers on topical agents such as ketoconazole, which reduces Malassezia by inhibiting fungal ergosterol synthesis; zinc pyrithione, which has antifungal and cytostatic effects; selenium sulfide, which suppresses epidermal turnover and fungal proliferation; and salicylic acid, a keratolytic that promotes scale removal, with topical corticosteroids used briefly when inflammation is more prominent.

Name: Excess subcutaneous fat
Description: Excess subcutaneous fat, often manifesting as overweight or obesity with preferential peripheral or truncal adipose accumulation, is a multifactorial metabolic trait rather than a single Mendelian disease, characterized by expansion of adipocyte number and size, chronic low-grade inflammation, altered adipokine secretion, and impaired energy homeostasis. Common clinical signs include increased skinfold thickness, elevated body mass index and waist circumference, body contour enlargement, reduced mobility, dyspnea on exertion, intertrigo, and, in severe cases, obesity-related lymphedema; subtypes include generalized obesity, central versus peripheral fat-predominant phenotypes, and rarer monogenic or syndromic forms. Genetic susceptibility is typically polygenic, with representative loci and proteins including FTO, MC4R, LEP, LEPR, POMC, PCSK1, PPARG, and ADIPOQ; rare pathogenic variants in LEP, LEPR, POMC, PCSK1, or MC4R can produce severe early-onset obesity, most often with autosomal recessive inheritance for leptin-melanocortin defects and autosomal dominant patterns in some MC4R-related disease. Key pathways involve hypothalamic leptin-melanocortin signaling, insulin/PI3K/AKT and mTOR nutrient sensing, AMPK-regulated energy balance, PPARγ-driven adipogenesis, sympathetic catecholamine and β-adrenergic lipolysis, and inflammatory TNF-α, IL-6, and NF-κB signaling within adipose tissue. Frequent comorbidities include insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, infertility, depression, cardiovascular disease, and increased risk of some cancers. Treatment commonly combines lifestyle therapy with anti-obesity drugs such as orlistat, a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor; liraglutide or semaglutide, GLP-1 receptor agonists that enhance satiety and delay gastric emptying; and phentermine/topiramate, which reduces appetite via sympathomimetic and central neuro-modulatory effects; naltrexone/bupropion is another option acting through hypothalamic POMC activation and reward-pathway modulation. Name: Incomplete passage of stool
Description: Incomplete passage of stool, a symptom complex often corresponding to tenesmus or a sensation of incomplete evacuation rather than a single disease entity, most commonly reflects functional constipation, dyssynergic defecation, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, or structural anorectal and colonic disorders such as rectocele, hemorrhoids, fissure, rectal prolapse, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal neoplasia, or Hirschsprung disease. Clinically it presents with persistent urge to defecate, straining, hard or fragmented stools, obstructed defecation, abdominal bloating, rectal discomfort, and reduced stool frequency, and may be complicated by fecal impaction, stercoral ulceration, hemorrhoidal bleeding, anal fissures, prolapse, megacolon, and psychosocial distress; common comorbidities include pelvic floor dysfunction, neurologic disease, diabetes, hypothyroidism, opioid exposure, anxiety, and depression. Molecular associations depend on etiology: Hirschsprung disease is linked to RET, EDNRB, EDN3, GDNF, SOX10, and PHOX2B variants affecting enteric neural crest migration, while motility and visceral sensitivity are influenced by serotonergic signaling through SLC6A4 and HTR3/HTR4 pathways, nitric oxide and cholinergic neuromuscular transmission, interstitial cells of Cajal, and ion channels such as SCN5A. Inheritance is therefore variable, including sporadic cases, multifactorial susceptibility, and Mendelian forms such as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or syndromic Hirschsprung disease. Diagnosis is based on history, medication review, Rome IV criteria when functional bowel disorders are suspected, digital rectal examination, and selective testing with colonoscopy, abdominal imaging, anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion testing, defecography, colonic transit studies, thyroid and metabolic panels, and rectal biopsy when aganglionosis is suspected. Treatment targets cause and includes polyethylene glycol, an osmotic laxative; senna or bisacodyl, stimulant laxatives that enhance colonic peristalsis; lubiprostone, a chloride channel activator; linaclotide or plecanatide, guanylate cyclase-C agonists that increase intestinal fluid secretion; prucalopride, a 5-HT4 agonist; and biofeedback therapy for dyssynergic

Name: Arrhythmias, supraventricular
Description: Supraventricular arrhythmias comprise a heterogeneous group of rhythm disorders arising above the His bundle, including atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, focal or multifocal atrial tachycardia, atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia, and atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia such as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome; they are characterized clinically by episodic or sustained palpitations, rapid regular or irregular pulse, dyspnea, chest discomfort, lightheadedness, fatigue, presyncope or syncope, and sometimes hemodynamic instability. Pathobiology involves abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, and re-entry mediated by atrial and AV nodal conduction properties, ion-channel dysfunction, calcium handling, autonomic signaling, and structural remodeling; key pathways include Na+, K+, and Ca2+ currents, fibrosis-promoting TGF-β signaling, adrenergic/cAMP-PKA pathways, and gap-junction/cell-cell coupling. Genetic contributors are most clearly defined in inherited pre-excitation and familial atrial arrhythmia syndromes, with examples including PRKAG2, MYH7, LMNA, NKX2-5, SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNE2, NPPA, GJA5 encoding connexin 40, and RYR2; accessory-pathway disease may occur in autosomal dominant settings, and supraventricular arrhythmias also accompany cardiomyopathies and channelopathies with variable penetrance. Important comorbidities and complications include hypertension, coronary or valvular heart disease, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, sleep apnea, obesity, congenital heart disease, tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, thromboembolism and stroke, especially with atrial fibrillation. Treatment commonly includes adenosine, which transiently blocks AV nodal conduction via A1 receptor activation; beta-blockers such as metoprolol, which reduce sympathetic drive and AV nodal conduction; non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil or diltiazem, which inhibit L-type Ca2+ current in nodal tissue; and class Ic or III antiarrhythmics such as flecainide or amiodarone for rhythm control.
