Name: Neonatal Sepsis
Description: Neonatal sepsis (UMLS C0456103) is a life-threatening systemic inflammatory syndrome caused by bacterial, and less often fungal or viral, infection in the first 28 days of life, classically divided into early-onset disease, usually vertically acquired from organisms such as group B Streptococcus or Escherichia coli, and late-onset disease, often nosocomial or community acquired, with coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negative bacilli, and Candida species prominent. Its pathobiology centers on innate immune dysregulation, including pathogen recognition through TLR2, TLR4, CD14, MYD88, NFKB, inflammasome signaling, complement activation, cytokines such as TNF, IL6, and IL1B, endothelial injury, coagulation cascade activation, and mitochondrial/metabolic dysfunction. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, with reported associations involving polymorphisms or altered expression in TLR4, TLR2, CD14, NOD2, BPI, MBL2, IL6, TNF, and FCGR2A, while rare primary immunodeficiencies may confer marked risk. Typical manifestations are nonspecific and include temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, apnea, respiratory distress, tachycardia or bradycardia, hypotension, jaundice, seizures, abdominal distension, and perfusion abnormalities. Major complications and comorbidities include prematurity, very low birth weight, meningitis, pneumonia, necrotizing enterocolitis, septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia, and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus microbiologic and laboratory evaluation, especially blood culture, with cerebrospinal fluid and urine studies when indicated, alongside CBC indices, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, blood gas and lactate assessment, and molecular pathogen detection in some settings. Empiric treatment commonly uses ampicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation, with gentamicin, an aminoglycoside causing 30S ribosomal mistranslation; cefotaxime, a third-generation cephalosporin blocking cell-wall synthesis, or vancomycin, a glycopeptide binding D-Ala-D-Ala, are used

Name: Neonatal meningitis
Description: Neonatal meningitis (UMLS C0456107) is an acute, usually life-threatening infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid occurring in the first 28 days of life, most often caused by Group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, especially K1 strains, and Listeria monocytogenes, and less commonly by other Gram-negative bacilli or viral pathogens; clinically it presents with fever or hypothermia, lethargy, poor feeding, irritability, apnea, respiratory distress, vomiting, bulging fontanelle, seizures, hypotonia or hypertonia, and signs of sepsis. Disease subtypes are commonly classified as early-onset versus late-onset, and by pathogen class, with frequent complications including septic shock, ventriculitis, hydrocephalus, cerebral infarction, hearing loss, epilepsy, neurodevelopmental impairment, and cerebral palsy; comorbid prematurity, low birth weight, maternal chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes, and neonatal bacteremia increase risk. Pathobiology involves microbial adhesion and blood-brain barrier invasion mediated by bacterial factors such as E. coli K1 capsule genes, ibeA, ompA, cnf1, fimH, and Group B Streptococcus surface proteins including HvgA, with host inflammatory signaling through TLR2/TLR4, CD14, MyD88, NF-kB, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, chemokines, complement, and neutrophil recruitment driving meningeal injury; rare host susceptibility may relate to innate immune defects such as IRAK4 or MyD88 deficiency, but inheritance is not typically Mendelian. Diagnosis rests on blood and CSF culture with lumbar puncture showing pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, supported by Gram stain, PCR or multiplex nucleic acid testing, inflammatory markers, neuroimaging, and hearing assessment. Empiric treatment commonly uses ampicillin, which inhibits bacterial cell wall transpeptidation, plus gentamicin, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, or cefotaxime, a beta-lactam blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking; pathogen-directed therapy may include penicillin G for susceptible streptococci or meropenem, a broad-spectrum carbapenem cell wall inhibitor, for resistant Gram-negative infection.

Name: Peripheral neuropathic pain
Description: Peripheral neuropathic pain is a chronic pain syndrome caused by a lesion or disease of the peripheral somatosensory nervous system, arising in conditions such as diabetic polyneuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, traumatic or postsurgical nerve injury, radiculopathy, chemotherapy-induced neuropathy, HIV neuropathy, and inherited small-fiber neuropathies; clinically it is characterized by spontaneous burning, shooting or electric-shock pain, hyperalgesia, allodynia, paresthesias, dysesthesias, numbness, sensory loss, and sometimes weakness or autonomic dysfunction. Mechanistically, it reflects peripheral and central sensitization driven by ectopic activity in injured nociceptors and dorsal root ganglion neurons, altered sodium and calcium channel function, neuroimmune activation, and signaling through TRPV1, Nav1.7/Nav1.8/Nav1.9, α2δ calcium-channel subunits, glutamatergic NMDA pathways, substance P, CGRP, inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and microglial and astrocytic responses. Genetic contributors are best defined in painful small-fiber neuropathy and channelopathies, including gain-of-function variants in SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A encoding Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9, with rarer associations involving TRPA1, NGF, and NTRK1; inheritance may be sporadic, but familial forms are often autosomal dominant, whereas causative neuropathies such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease may be dominant, recessive, or X-linked depending on genes such as PMP22, MFN2, and GJB1. Major comorbidities include diabetes, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, impaired mobility, falls, and reduced quality of life, with complications of chronic opioid exposure when used. Diagnosis requires a neuroanatomically plausible pain distribution plus history of relevant nerve lesion or disease, supported by sensory examination and confirmatory testing such as nerve conduction studies/electromyography for large-fiber disease, skin biopsy for reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density, quantitative sensory testing, autonomic testing, and targeted laboratory or genetic evaluation when hereditary or systemic causes are suspected. Common treatments include gabapentin and pregabalin, which bind the α2δ subunit of voltage-g

Name: Anemia of renal disease
Description: Anemia of renal disease is typically a hypoproliferative, usually normocytic and normochromic anemia caused by chronic kidney disease, especially advanced CKD and end-stage kidney disease, in which impaired renal erythropoietin production by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells is compounded by inflammation, reduced red-cell survival, blood loss, and functional or absolute iron deficiency. Key molecular contributors include EPO and the erythropoietin receptor–JAK2/STAT5 axis, iron-regulatory hepcidin encoded by HAMP, ferroportin SLC40A1, transferrin and ferritin pathways, hypoxia-inducible factors HIF1A and EPAS1/HIF2A regulated by EGLN/PHD enzymes and VHL, and inflammatory IL6–STAT3 signaling that increases hepcidin and restricts iron availability; rare inherited kidney disorders affecting these pathways may predispose indirectly, but the anemia itself is usually acquired rather than Mendelian. Common clinical manifestations are fatigue, weakness, pallor, dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, dizziness, tachycardia, cognitive slowing, and worsening angina or heart failure. Important comorbidities and complications include CKD-mineral bone disorder, diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, left ventricular hypertrophy, dialysis dependence, and increased hospitalization and mortality. Subtypes are often framed by CKD stage, dialysis versus non-dialysis status, and iron-deficient versus inflammation-driven or ESA-hyporesponsive anemia. Diagnosis relies on documenting anemia, typically low hemoglobin with inappropriately low or normal EPO for the degree of anemia, CBC indices, reticulocyte count, ferritin and transferrin saturation, renal function testing, CRP or other inflammatory markers, and exclusion of alternative causes such as B12 or folate deficiency, hemolysis, occult bleeding, or marrow disease. Standard treatments include epoetin alfa, darbepoetin alfa, and methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta, which activate EPO receptor signaling to stimulate erythropoiesis; iron supplementation such as iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose to restore iron availability; and HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitors such as roxadustat, which stabilize HIF and increase endogenous EPO while lowering hepcidin.

Name: Hypoalphalipoproteinemias
Description: Hypoalphalipoproteinemias are a heterogeneous group of disorders defined by abnormally low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), arising from primary monogenic defects or secondary acquired causes, and characterized by impaired reverse cholesterol transport with variable cardiovascular risk. Key genetic causes include APOA1 mutations or deletions causing apoA-I deficiency or dysfunctional apoA-I, ABCA1 loss-of-function variants causing Tangier disease, and LCAT mutations causing familial LCAT deficiency or fish-eye disease; less commonly, defects in APOA2, SCARB1 encoding SR-BI, CETP, or LPL-related pathways contribute. The core molecular pathways involve nascent HDL formation via apoA-I lipidation by ABCA1, HDL maturation through LCAT-mediated cholesterol esterification, remodeling by CETP, phospholipid transfer protein and hepatic lipase, and hepatic selective uptake through SR-BI, with regulation by PPAR, LXR, and related transcriptional networks. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic isolated low HDL to orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, corneal opacities, anemia, proteinuria, and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; common complications include coronary artery disease, stroke, chronic kidney disease in LCAT deficiency, and metabolic comorbidities such as hypertriglyceridemia, insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and fatty liver. Subtypes include familial apoA-I deficiency, Tangier disease, familial LCAT deficiency, fish-eye disease, and polygenic or secondary hypoalphalipoproteinemia. Inheritance is often autosomal codominant or dominant for APOA1-related disease and autosomal recessive for ABCA1 and LCAT disorders. Diagnosis is based on persistently very low HDL-C and apoA-I, lipid profile abnormalities, exclusion of secondary causes such as smoking, and confirmatory testing with apolipoprotein measurement, lipoprotein electrophoresis or ultracentrifugation, cholesterol efflux or LCAT activity assays, and molecular genetic testing. Treatment emphasizes aggressive risk-factor modification and treatment of secondary causes; representative drugs include statins, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase to reduce LDL-driven risk, fibrates, which activate PPAR-alpha to lower triglycerides and modestly raise HDL, and niacin, which reduces hepatic VLDL synthesis and can increase HDL, with omega-3 fatty acids also used in mixed

Name: Labor Pain
Description: Labor pain (UMLS C0474368) is an acute, physiologic nociceptive syndrome arising during parturition from uterine contractions, cervical effacement and dilation, distension of the lower uterine segment, vagina, and perineum; it is not a classic Mendelian disease, although interindividual pain sensitivity and labor timing show genetic influence. Key molecular contributors include oxytocin and its receptor OXTR, prostaglandin synthesis enzymes PTGS2/COX-2 and PTGES, prostaglandin receptors such as PTGER3, inflammatory cytokines including IL1B, IL6, and TNF, connexin-43 encoded by GJA1, nitric oxide signaling, and ion channels involved in nociception such as SCN9A and TRPV1; rare variation in pain-related genes like COMT and OPRM1 may modulate analgesic requirements rather than cause the condition. Central pathways include oxytocin receptor signaling, prostaglandin/arachidonic acid cascades, NF-kB-driven inflammatory activation, calcium-dependent myometrial contraction via MLCK, gap-junction coupling, and peripheral and spinal transmission through T10-L1 visceral afferents and S2-S4 somatic fibers. Clinically, labor pain presents as rhythmic painful contractions with increasing intensity, cervical change, pelvic pressure, back pain, and later perineal pain; major subtypes include first-stage visceral pain and second-stage somatic pain, and it may occur in term, preterm, spontaneous, or induced labor. Commonly used treatments include epidural local anesthetics such as bupivacaine, which block voltage-gated sodium channels; opioids such as fentanyl, acting as mu-opioid receptor agonists; and nitrous oxide, which provides analgesia through NMDA antagonism and endogenous opioid modulation; remifentanil PCA is another option. Important comorbidities and complications include preeclampsia, obesity, anxiety, depression, prolonged or obstructed labor, fetal malposition, postpartum hemorrhage, and maternal exhaustion, with poorly controlled pain linked to hyperventilation and catecholamine excess. Diagnosis is clinical, based on regular contractions with progressive cervical dilation and effacement, supported by pelvic examination, fetal and uterine monitoring, and, when needed, ultrasonography to assess labor progress and exclude alternative causes of pain.

Name: Disorder of keratinization
Description: Disorders of keratinization comprise a heterogeneous group of inherited or acquired cornification diseases characterized by abnormal epidermal differentiation and stratum corneum barrier formation, clinically presenting with xerosis, scaling, hyperkeratosis, palmoplantar thickening, fissuring, erythema, pruritus, and sometimes blistering, pain, secondary infection, or heat intolerance. Major genetic causes include mutations in keratin genes KRT1, KRT10, KRT2, KRT9, KRT5, and KRT14; cornified-envelope and desquamation genes such as FLG, LOR, TGM1, ABCA12, ALOX12B, ALOXE3, NIPAL4, CYP4F22, and CERS3; and connexin or protease-related genes including GJB2, SPINK5, and ST14, with corresponding protein defects in keratin intermediate filaments, filaggrin, transglutaminase 1, lipid transporters, lipoxygenases, and gap-junction proteins. Pathobiology centers on disruption of keratin filament assembly, epidermal calcium-regulated differentiation, lamellar-body lipid processing, corneodesmosome degradation, and inflammatory signaling through EGFR/MAPK, Notch, AP1, and NF-kB pathways, leading to barrier dysfunction and compensatory hyperproliferation. Recognized subtypes include ichthyoses, epidermolytic ichthyosis, ichthyosis vulgaris, lamellar ichthyosis, epidermolysis bullosa simplex with keratinization defects, palmoplantar keratodermas, Darier disease, and pityriasis rubra pilaris. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or sporadic, for example FLG-associated ichthyosis vulgaris often showing semidominant inheritance, TGM1-related lamellar ichthyosis being autosomal recessive, and KRT1/KRT10 disorders typically autosomal dominant. Common treatments include emollients and keratolytics such as urea or salicylic acid, which hydrate and soften hyperkeratotic scale, topical retinoids such as tazarotene, which normalize keratinocyte differentiation via retinoic acid receptors, and systemic retinoids such as acitretin or isotretinoin, which reduce hyperkeratosis by modulating epidermal gene

Name: Seizure, Tonic-Clonic
Description: Seizures are paroxysmal episodes of abnormal, excessive, and hypersynchronous neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex, occurring as acute symptomatic events or as part of epilepsy, and are broadly classified as focal, generalized, or unknown onset, with subtypes such as absence, tonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonic, and focal impaired-awareness seizures. Clinical manifestations include transient loss or alteration of consciousness, convulsions, staring spells, automatisms, sensory phenomena, autonomic symptoms, tongue biting, urinary incontinence, and postictal confusion or focal neurologic deficits. Pathobiology reflects imbalance between excitation and inhibition, especially glutamatergic and GABAergic signaling, involving voltage-gated sodium, potassium, and calcium channels, synaptic vesicle release, and mTOR-related network hyperexcitability; representative genetic contributors include SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNQ3, CACNA1H, GABRA1, GABRG2, STXBP1, DEPDC5, TSC1, and TSC2, with mutations causing channelopathies, synaptic dysfunction, or cortical malformations. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial, or de novo, as seen in generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus, Dravet syndrome, tuberous sclerosis complex, and some developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Common comorbidities and complications include developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, depression, anxiety, migraine, sleep disturbance, injury, aspiration, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Diagnosis is based on careful history and semiology, eyewitness accounts, neurologic examination, EEG or video-EEG demonstrating epileptiform discharges, brain MRI to detect structural lesions, and targeted metabolic, infectious, toxicologic, or genetic testing when indicated. Treatment commonly includes levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to modulate neurotransmitter release, valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and affects sodium and calcium channels, lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and glutamate release, as well as carbamazepine, phenytoin, benzodiazepines, and ethosuximide for selected seizure types.

Name: Dementia
Description: Dementia (MeSH D003704) is a clinical syndrome of acquired, usually progressive decline in memory and at least one other cognitive domain sufficient to impair independence, most commonly caused by neurodegenerative disease but also by vascular, mixed, infectious, inflammatory, toxic, or metabolic disorders; major subtypes include Alzheimer disease, vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, frontotemporal dementia, Parkinson disease dementia, and less commonly prion-related or Huntington-related dementias. Core molecular associations include APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2 mutations that increase amyloid-β production, APOE ε4 as a strong risk allele for late-onset Alzheimer disease, MAPT, GRN, and C9orf72 in frontotemporal degeneration, SNCA and GBA in Lewy body disease, and HTT in Huntington disease; implicated proteins include amyloid-β, tau, α-synuclein, TDP-43, and prion protein. Key pathways include amyloidogenic APP processing by β- and γ-secretases, tau hyperphosphorylation and microtubule destabilization, synaptic cholinergic deficit, glutamatergic excitotoxicity mediated by NMDA receptors, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired proteostasis/autophagy, neuroinflammation with activated microglia, complement, and cytokines, and cerebrovascular endothelial injury. Typical manifestations are insidious memory loss, executive and visuospatial dysfunction, aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, disorientation, behavioral and psychiatric symptoms, parkinsonism, hallucinations, gait disturbance, and later dysphagia, falls, and total functional dependence. Comorbidities and complications include depression, delirium, cerebrovascular disease, frailty, malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia, pressure injuries, sleep disorders, and caregiver burden. Treatment is largely symptomatic: donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine inhibit acetylcholinesterase to enhance central cholinergic transmission, while memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist that reduces excitotoxic signaling; selected patients with Alzheimer disease may receive anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies such as lecanemab. Most cases are sporadic and multifactorial, although autosomal dominant inheritance occurs in familial early-onset Alzheimer disease, some frontotemporal dementias, Huntington disease, and prion disorders. Name: Prostatitis/seminal vesiculitis
Description: Prostatitis/seminal vesiculitis is an inflammatory disorder of the prostate and/or seminal vesicles that is usually infectious but may also be chronic pelvic pain syndrome with nonbacterial, immune, neuromuscular, and pelvic floor contributions; recognized subtypes include acute bacterial prostatitis, chronic bacterial prostatitis, chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (inflammatory IIIA and noninflammatory IIIB), asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis, and seminal vesiculitis occurring alone or with prostatitis. Common pathogens include uropathogenic Escherichia coli and other Enterobacterales, with occasional Enterococcus, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma in selected cases. Molecularly, disease is linked more to host inflammatory response than Mendelian inheritance, with reported associations involving TLR4, TLR2, IL6, IL8, TNF, PTGS2/COX-2, NFKB1, and TGFB1, reflecting activation of innate immune, NF-κB, cytokine-chemokine, inflammasome, oxidative stress, and fibrosis pathways; no single high-penetrance mutation is established, but polymorphic variation in cytokine and pattern-recognition genes may influence susceptibility and chronicity. Typical symptoms include pelvic or perineal pain, dysuria, urinary frequency/urgency, painful ejaculation, hematospermia, low back pain, obstructive voiding symptoms, tender boggy prostate, and in acute infection fever and systemic illness. Comorbidities and complications include benign prostatic hyperplasia, recurrent urinary tract infection, epididymitis, infertility or impaired semen quality, sexual dysfunction, abscess, bacteremia/sepsis, and chronic pelvic pain syndromes with anxiety or depression. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, urinalysis and urine culture, pre- and post-prostatic massage localization tests or semen culture in chronic cases, STI nucleic acid testing when indicated, inflammatory markers, and selective use of transrectal ultrasound, CT, or MRI to detect abscess or seminal vesicle involvement; PSA may rise nonspecifically. Name: Pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae
Description: Pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae (UMLS C0519030) is an acute bacterial pneumonia, classically a severe necrotizing lobar or bronchopneumonic infection, caused by an encapsulated Gram-negative bacillus whose major virulence determinants include the capsular polysaccharide synthesis locus cps, hypermucoviscosity regulators rmpA/rmpA2, siderophore systems such as yersiniabactin, aerobactin and enterobactin, fimbrial adhesins fimH and mrkD, lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis genes, and resistance determinants including ESBL genes blaSHV, blaTEM, blaCTX-M and carbapenemases blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48; host susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with impaired innate immunity in variants affecting TLR4, CD14, NOD-like signaling, CFTR, neutrophil function or complement occasionally contributing to risk. Pathobiology is driven by TLR4/LPS-induced NF-kB and MAPK activation, inflammasome signaling, IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha release, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation and, in severe cases, dysregulated sepsis pathways. Typical manifestations include abrupt fever, chills, toxic appearance, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough with thick purulent or blood-tinged currant-jelly sputum, hypoxemia, crackles, consolidation, leukocytosis and multilobar infiltrates or cavitation. Important subtypes include community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration-related, hypervirulent invasive disease, and multidrug-resistant or carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae pneumonia. Common comorbidities include alcoholism, diabetes, COPD, chronic kidney or liver disease, malignancy, transplantation, advanced age and ICU exposure; complications include lung abscess, empyema, bacteremia, septic shock, ARDS and metastatic infection. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical and radiographic findings plus microbiologic confirmation by sputum, tracheal aspirate or bronchoalveolar lavage culture, blood cultures, Gram stain showing Gram-negative bacilli, susceptibility testing, and increasingly PCR or other molecular assays for resistance genes. Name: Urethral atrophy
Description: Urethral atrophy is generally an acquired, non-neoplastic degenerative thinning of the urethral mucosa and periurethral supportive tissues, most often recognized in postmenopausal women as part of the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, although it may also follow androgen-deprivation, pelvic radiation, chronic catheterization, prior urethral surgery, or inflammatory scarring. Its biology is dominated less by Mendelian inheritance than by hormonal and tissue-remodeling mechanisms: reduced estrogen signaling through ESR1 and ESR2 lowers epithelial proliferation, glycogenization, vascularity, and collagen support, while altered androgen receptor activity, transforming growth factor-β, matrix metalloproteinases, and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF contribute to extracellular-matrix loss, fibrosis, and impaired mucosal integrity; no specific recurrent mutation is established, though genetic variation in steroid-hormone pathways may influence susceptibility. Clinical features include urethral dryness, burning, dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, recurrent urinary tract infection, dyspareunia, spotting, stress incontinence, and sometimes a tender, friable, narrowed, or recessed meatus; subtypes are usually classified by etiology, such as hypoestrogenic/menopausal, post-radiation, postoperative/traumatic, and inflammatory-atrophic forms. Common comorbidities include vulvovaginal atrophy, pelvic floor dysfunction, overactive bladder, recurrent cystitis, urethral caruncle, stenosis, and sexual dysfunction, with complications including persistent lower urinary tract symptoms, infection, and urethral narrowing. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history, pelvic examination, and exclusion of mimics such as lichen sclerosus, urethral diverticulum, carcinoma, or active infection; supportive tests include urinalysis and culture, postvoid residual measurement, cystourethroscopy, uroflowmetry, pelvic imaging when indicated, and occasionally biopsy of suspicious lesions. Treatment is directed at restoration of trophic support and symptom control, commonly with topical estradiol or conjugated estrogens acting via estrogen receptor agonism to reverse mucosal atrophy, prasterone as an intratissue precursor of estrogens and androgens, and ospemifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator; adjunctive measures may include lubricants, moisturizers, treatment of infection, and management of coexistent

Name: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
Description: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD; UMLS C0520676) is a severe, cyclical, luteal-phase affective and somatic disorder regarded as a hormone-triggered mood disorder rather than a primary endocrine excess state, characterized by marked mood lability, irritability, anger, anxiety, depressed mood, anhedonia, impaired concentration, fatigue, sleep and appetite change, bloating, breast tenderness, and functional impairment, with remission shortly after menses onset. Its biology is linked to abnormal central nervous system sensitivity to normal ovarian steroid fluctuations, especially progesterone metabolites such as allopregnanolone acting at GABA-A receptors, with involvement of serotonergic signaling and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis regulation; implicated genes and molecular components include ESR1 and ESR2, PGR, BDNF, COMT, SLC6A4 including the 5-HTTLPR polymorphism, GABRB2/GABRA4, and variants in steroid-response transcriptional complexes, although no single causative mutation is established and inheritance is complex, polygenic, and familial rather than Mendelian. Relevant pathways include ovarian steroid signaling, neurosteroid modulation of GABAergic transmission, serotonin transporter and receptor pathways, and stress-response circuitry. Common comorbidities include major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, bipolar spectrum illness, migraine, dysmenorrhea, and increased risk of suicidality, social/occupational dysfunction, and relationship impairment. Clinical subtypes are often described as predominantly mood, somatic, or mixed presentations. Diagnosis is clinical under DSM-5 criteria, requiring at least five symptoms in the final week before menses, improvement within days after onset, minimal symptoms post-menses, and prospective confirmation across at least two symptomatic cycles using daily symptom ratings such as the DRSP; laboratory testing is mainly used to exclude mimics such as thyroid disease. Treatment commonly includes SSRIs such as fluoxetine, sertraline, and paroxetine, which enhance serotonergic neurotransmission and can be given continuously or luteally; combined oral contraceptives containing drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol that suppress ovulation; and GnRH agonists such as leuprolide, which induce ovarian suppression, with adjunctive cognitive-behavioral therapy and, in refractory cases, anxiolytics or ovulation-suppressing strategies.

Name: Sleep Apnea, Obstructive
Description: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA; UMLS C0520679) is a common, usually multifactorial sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by recurrent collapse of the pharyngeal upper airway during sleep, causing intermittent hypoxemia, hypercapnia, arousals, and sleep fragmentation; typical manifestations include loud habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, nocturnal choking or gasping, nonrestorative sleep, morning headache, excessive daytime sleepiness, impaired concentration, and resistant hypertension. Major subtypes include positional OSA, REM-predominant OSA, obesity-related OSA, and pediatric OSA, often linked to adenotonsillar hypertrophy, while severity is generally stratified by apnea-hypopnea index on polysomnography. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian in most cases, with familial aggregation involving variants influencing craniofacial anatomy, obesity, ventilatory control, and inflammation; representative associations include LEP and LEPR, TNF, IL6, PPARG, APOE, ADRB2, serotonin pathway genes such as SLC6A4 and HTR2A, and occasional syndromic contributors such as PHOX2B-related hypoventilation overlap or craniofacial disorders. Pathobiology centers on anatomically narrow airway plus impaired neuromuscular compensation, with intermittent hypoxia activating HIF-1, sympathetic catecholamine signaling, oxidative stress, NF-kB-mediated inflammatory pathways, endothelial dysfunction, and leptin/insulin-resistance networks. OSA is strongly linked to obesity, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, coronary disease, stroke, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, depression, cognitive impairment, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and motor vehicle accidents. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion supported by polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing documenting obstructive events, oxygen desaturation, and arousals, often supplemented by Epworth Sleepiness Scale, airway examination, and craniofacial or ENT assessment. Core treatment is positive airway pressure, but drugs used in selected patients include modafinil or armodafinil, wake-promoting agents that inhibit dopamine reuptake for residual sleepiness, solriamfetol, a dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, and intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which reduce upper-airway mucosal inflammation, especially in mild pediatric or rhinitic disease.

Name: Staphylococcal endocarditis
Description: Staphylococcal endocarditis is an acute, often destructive infective endocarditis caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus and less often coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis, involving native or prosthetic valves and increasingly linked to health care exposure and injection drug use. Its pathobiology is driven by bacterial adhesins and biofilm determinants, including clfA/clfB, fnbA/fnbB, cna, spa, icaADBC, and the mecA methicillin-resistance determinant, together with toxins and immune evasion factors such as agr-regulated virulence programs, alpha-toxin, Panton-Valentine leukocidin, and pathways centered on host endothelial injury, tissue factor induction, platelet activation, fibrin deposition, complement, TLR2-NF-kB signaling, and IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha mediated inflammation. It is not an inherited disease, but host susceptibility may be influenced by non-Mendelian risk factors and rare genetic components affecting innate immunity or valve biology; examples discussed in predisposition literature include TLR2, MBL2, and NOD2 variants, while major clinical risks include prosthetic valves, prior valve disease, intracardiac devices, hemodialysis, diabetes, and immunosuppression. Typical manifestations are fever, new or changing murmur, sepsis, persistent bacteremia, embolic phenomena, petechiae, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splenomegaly, heart failure, and conduction abnormalities; major complications include valvular destruction, perivalvular abscess, stroke, pulmonary septic emboli in right-sided disease, metastatic abscesses, glomerulonephritis, and shock. Subtypes include native-valve, prosthetic-valve, right-sided, left-sided, acute, and health care-associated disease. Diagnosis relies on Duke or modified Duke criteria using multiple blood cultures, echocardiography preferably transesophageal, and supportive inflammatory and microbiologic testing. Treatment commonly includes nafcillin or oxacillin for MSSA by binding penicillin-binding proteins and inhibiting cell-wall synthesis, cefazolin with the same core mechanism, vancomycin for MRSA by binding D-Ala-D-Ala termini, daptomycin by depolarizing the bacterial membrane, and rifampin or gentamicin in selected prosthetic-valve regimens for biofilm

Name: Klebsiella cystitis
Description: Klebsiella cystitis (UMLS C0520775) is a bacterial lower urinary tract infection of the bladder, most often caused by uropathogenic Klebsiella pneumoniae and less commonly K. oxytoca, presenting as uncomplicated community-acquired disease or complicated, catheter-associated, recurrent, emphysematous, and multidrug-resistant forms. Typical manifestations include dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy or malodorous urine, pyuria, and hematuria, with fever suggesting upper tract extension or complicated infection. Pathogenesis is driven less by host Mendelian inheritance than by microbial virulence determinants, including type 1 and type 3 fimbriae encoded by fim and mrk loci that mediate urothelial adherence and biofilm formation, capsular polysaccharide genes such as magA/wzy-K1 and rmpA, siderophore systems including enterobactin, yersiniabactin, and aerobactin, and resistance determinants such as blaSHV, blaTEM, blaCTX-M, carbapenemases blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48, and occasional porin alterations in OmpK35/OmpK36. Host inflammatory signaling commonly involves TLR4 recognition of lipopolysaccharide with NF-kB activation, cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8, neutrophil recruitment, and, in biofilm-associated disease, impaired bacterial clearance. Treatment depends on susceptibility testing and often includes nitrofurantoin, which is reduced intracellularly to reactive intermediates that damage bacterial DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which sequentially inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase; fosfomycin, which inhibits MurA and early peptidoglycan synthesis; and in susceptible or severe cases ceftriaxone or other beta-lactams that bind penicillin-binding proteins, fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin that inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, or carbapenems for ESBL-producing isolates. Name: Chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease
Description: Chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease (PID; UMLS C0520777) is an ascending infection of the upper female genital tract caused predominantly by Chlamydia trachomatis, especially genital serovars D–K, producing endometritis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian inflammation, and sometimes peritonitis; clinically it presents with lower abdominal or pelvic pain, cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, abnormal vaginal or mucopurulent cervical discharge, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, dyspareunia, fever, and occasionally subclinical disease. Its pathobiology is driven by epithelial infection and innate immune activation through Toll-like receptor and NF-κB signaling, MAPK cascades, inflammasome-related IL-1 responses, and Th1 cytokine pathways involving IFN-γ, TNF, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, and matrix metalloproteinases that contribute to tissue injury and scarring; chlamydial proteins such as major outer membrane protein, polymorphic membrane proteins, lipopolysaccharide, and heat-shock protein 60 have been implicated in persistence and immunopathology. Host susceptibility is not Mendelian, but polymorphisms in TLR2, TLR4, NOD1, IL10, TNFA, IFNG, HLA class II loci, and MMP genes have been associated with differential risk of infection, fibrosis, and tubal factor infertility. Recognized forms include acute, subacute, chronic, mild or subclinical PID, and complicated disease with tubo-ovarian abscess. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by evidence of lower genital tract inflammation and nucleic acid amplification testing for C. trachomatis from vaginal, cervical, or urine specimens, with pregnancy testing, gonorrhea testing, inflammatory markers, transvaginal ultrasound, and laparoscopy reserved for selected cases. Standard therapy includes doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor; azithromycin, a macrolide that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; ceftriaxone, a β-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis to cover possible gonococcal coinfection; and often metronidazole, which generates DNA-damaging radicals against anaerobes. Name: Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
Description: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is a common multifactorial perioperative complication, usually defined as nausea, retching, or vomiting within the first 24–48 hours after anesthesia and surgery, and is best viewed as a neurohumoral disorder of the emetic network rather than a primary inherited disease. It arises from activation of brainstem and vagal pathways involving the area postrema, nucleus tractus solitarius, vestibular system, and enterochromaffin cell–vagal afferent circuits, with key mediators including serotonin acting at 5-HT3 receptors, dopamine at D2 receptors, histamine at H1 receptors, acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, and substance P at NK1 receptors; opioid, cannabinoid, and inflammatory signaling may further modulate risk. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic and non-Mendelian, with reported associations involving HTR3A/HTR3B, TACR1, DRD2, COMT, OPRM1, ABCB1, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 variants that may influence emetic sensitivity or antiemetic pharmacokinetics, but no single mutation is diagnostic. Typical symptoms are nausea, pallor, diaphoresis, retching, and emesis, with complications including dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, delayed recovery, aspiration, wound dehiscence, esophageal injury, and increased unplanned admission. Common subtypes include early versus delayed PONV and post-discharge nausea and vomiting; major risk factors and linked conditions include female sex, prior PONV or motion sickness, nonsmoking status, opioid exposure, volatile anesthetics, laparoscopy, gynecologic surgery, and migraine or vestibular disorders. Diagnosis is clinical, based on postoperative symptom assessment and exclusion of ileus, bowel obstruction, intracranial events, myocardial ischemia, or drug toxicity, often guided by risk scores such as Apfel. Treatment and prophylaxis commonly include ondansetron, a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist; dexamethasone, which reduces central and peripheral inflammatory and emetic signaling; droperidol, a D2 receptor antagonist; and also aprepitant, an NK1 antagonist, or transdermal scopolamine, a muscarinic antagonist.

Name: Opioid Dependences
Description: Opioid-related disorders are chronic, relapsing substance-use conditions caused by maladaptive exposure to natural, semisynthetic, or synthetic opioids and include opioid use disorder, intoxication, withdrawal, opioid-induced mood or sleep disorders, and overdose. Core biology centers on mu-opioid receptor signaling encoded by OPRM1, with contributions from OPRK1 and OPRD1, dopaminergic and reward-pathway genes such as DRD2, SLC6A3, COMT, and BDNF, stress and cyclic-AMP pathways, and pharmacogenes affecting disposition, including CYP2D6 and CYP3A4; representative variants include OPRM1 A118G and COMT Val158Met, which may influence vulnerability, analgesic response, and treatment outcomes, although no single mutation is determinative. Pathophysiology involves Gi/o-coupled inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, reduced cAMP, altered calcium and potassium conductance, mesolimbic dopamine signaling in the ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens, glutamatergic plasticity, beta-arrestin signaling, and noradrenergic hyperactivity in the locus coeruleus during withdrawal. Typical features include craving, compulsive use, tolerance, withdrawal with mydriasis, piloerection, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, yawning, diarrhea, pain, anxiety, and insomnia, while intoxication causes euphoria, miosis, sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, and coma. Common comorbidities include depression, anxiety, PTSD, chronic pain, hepatitis C, HIV, endocarditis, constipation, hypogonadism, neonatal opioid withdrawal, and fatal overdose. Genetic risk is polygenic and multifactorial rather than Mendelian, arising from heritable susceptibility interacting with trauma, psychiatric illness, and social exposures. Diagnosis is clinical, primarily by DSM-5 criteria for opioid use disorder, supported by history, examination, prescription review, urine or serum toxicology, and assessment for overdose or withdrawal using pulse oximetry, arterial blood gases when needed, and scales such as COWS. Main treatments are methadone, a long-acting full mu-opioid receptor agonist; buprenorphine, a high-affinity partial mu agonist and kappa antagonist; naltrexone, a competitive opioid antagonist; and naloxone for acute

Name: Pneumonic Plague
Description: Plague (MeSH D010930) is an acute, often fulminant zoonotic infection caused by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Yersinia pestis, transmitted mainly by flea bites or exposure to infected animals and, in pneumonic plague, by respiratory droplets; major clinical forms are bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic plague. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial virulence genes and proteins rather than host Mendelian inheritance, notably the pCD1/type III secretion system with Yops such as YopH, YopE, YopJ/P, and LcrV, the plasminogen activator Pla, the F1 capsular antigen encoded by caf1, and iron-acquisition systems including yersiniabactin, which disable innate immunity, promote lymphatic and hematogenous spread, and trigger dysregulated host signaling involving TLR2/TLR4 recognition, NF-κB and MAPK modulation, inflammasome and complement activation, cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and profound coagulation-endothelial injury responses. Typical features include abrupt fever, chills, severe malaise, painful suppurative regional lymphadenitis (buboes), headache, myalgia, abdominal symptoms, and in advanced disease hypotension, delirium, acral necrosis, DIC, shock, hemoptysis, and rapidly progressive pneumonia or ARDS. Important complications and comorbid associations include bacteremia, meningitis, secondary pneumonia, multiorgan failure, and worse outcomes with delayed treatment, malnutrition, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, or immunocompromise. There is no recognized hereditary inheritance pattern for plague susceptibility, although host genetic variation in innate immune pathways may modify risk. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology plus clinical syndrome and confirmatory testing by culture or PCR from bubo aspirate, blood, or sputum, direct fluorescent antibody or F1 antigen detection, and paired serology to F1 antibody. First-line therapy includes streptomycin or gentamicin, aminoglycosides that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause mistranslation; doxycycline, a tetracycline that blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding at 30S; and ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; chloramphenicol, which inhibits the 50S pept

Name: Pulmonary Thromboembolisms
Description: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is an acute or chronic thromboembolic disorder in which thrombus, usually arising from deep venous thrombosis of the legs or pelvis, obstructs the pulmonary arterial tree, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxemia, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, right ventricular strain, and in severe cases obstructive shock; major forms include massive/high-risk, submassive/intermediate-risk, low-risk, recurrent, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, and septic or fat embolic variants. Genetic susceptibility is most clearly linked to inherited thrombophilia, especially F5 factor V Leiden, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1 antithrombin deficiency, PROC protein C deficiency, PROS1 protein S deficiency, and occasionally elevated factor VIII, ABO non-O blood group, or dysregulated fibrinolysis involving PLG and SERPINE1; these defects are typically autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and predispose through excess thrombin generation. Core molecular pathways include tissue factor-FVIIa activation of the coagulation cascade, factor Xa and thrombin signaling, platelet activation, impaired protein C/protein S and antithrombin anticoagulant pathways, fibrin formation and plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis, with endothelial injury, inflammation, and hypoxia-induced vasoconstriction contributing. Common symptoms and signs are sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, cough, hemoptysis, syncope, hypoxemia, accentuated P2, and signs of DVT; comorbidities and risk states include cancer, surgery, trauma, immobilization, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, obesity, heart failure, COPD, prior VTE, and antiphospholipid syndrome, while complications include recurrent VTE, pulmonary infarction, right heart failure, and death. Diagnosis integrates clinical probability scores such as Wells or Geneva, D-dimer testing in low/intermediate-risk patients, CT pulmonary angiography as the principal imaging test, ventilation-perfusion scanning when CT is unsuitable, lower-extremity venous ultrasonography, echocardiographic evidence of RV dysfunction, and cardiac biomarkers such as troponin and BNP for risk stratification. Name: Hepatitis B, Chronic
Description: Chronic hepatitis B (UMLS C0524909) is a persistent infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV), a partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus, defined clinically by persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for at least 6 months and characterized by variable phases including HBeAg-positive or HBeAg-negative chronic infection/hepatitis, inactive carrier state, and occult HBV infection. Viral determinants include HBV genes encoding HBsAg (S), core/precore proteins (C/preC), polymerase/reverse transcriptase (P), and HBx, with representative mutations such as precore G1896A and basal core promoter A1762T/G1764A linked to HBeAg negativity and disease progression; host genetic susceptibility and outcome are influenced by HLA class II loci, IFNL3/IL28B, TNF, TLR polymorphisms, and rare NTCP/SLC10A1 variation affecting viral entry. Pathobiology centers on covalently closed circular DNA persistence in hepatocytes, NTCP-mediated entry, reverse transcription, and immune-mediated liver injury involving interferon/JAK-STAT, TNF/NF-kB, T-cell exhaustion via PD-1, and fibrogenic TGF-beta signaling. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, malaise, right upper quadrant discomfort, hepatomegaly, jaundice, and stigmata of chronic liver disease. Major complications include cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, hepatocellular carcinoma, portal hypertension, and extrahepatic disease such as polyarteritis nodosa, membranous nephropathy, and glomerulonephritis; coinfection with HDV, HCV, or HIV worsens outcomes. Standard therapy includes tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafenamide, nucleotide reverse-transcriptase inhibitors that suppress HBV polymerase, entecavir, a nucleoside analog inhibiting viral DNA synthesis, and pegylated interferon alfa, an immunomodulator enhancing antiviral host responses. Diagnosis relies on serology including HBsAg, anti-HBc, HBeAg/anti-HBe, quantitative HBV DNA, liver enzymes, fibrosis assessment by elastography or biopsy, and surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma with ultrasound with or without alpha-fetoprotein.

Name: Hepatitis C, Chronic
Description: Chronic hepatitis C is a persistent hepatotropic RNA viral infection caused by hepatitis C virus, defined clinically by detectable HCV RNA for more than 6 months, that produces chronic necroinflammatory liver disease with variable progression from minimal hepatitis to advanced fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma; patients are often asymptomatic for years but may present with fatigue, malaise, right upper quadrant discomfort, nausea, arthralgia, pruritus, hepatomegaly, jaundice in advanced disease, and stigmata of portal hypertension or liver failure. Major disease subtypes include viral genotypes 1–6 and histologic stages by fibrosis severity. Pathogenesis involves viral entry through CD81, scavenger receptor class B type I, claudin-1, and occludin, replication by NS3/4A protease, NS5A, and NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and host innate immune, interferon/JAK-STAT, Toll-like receptor, TNF, TGF-β, and stellate-cell fibrogenic pathways; representative host genetic factors influencing clearance or treatment response include IFNL3/IL28B polymorphisms, HLA class I and II variation, PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 variants affecting steatosis/fibrosis risk, while the disorder is acquired rather than Mendelian inherited. Treatment is centered on direct-acting antivirals such as sofosbuvir, an NS5B polymerase inhibitor, ledipasvir or velpatasvir, NS5A inhibitors, and glecaprevir or grazoprevir, NS3/4A protease inhibitors, often in fixed-dose combinations; ribavirin, a guanosine analog with antiviral/immunomodulatory effects, and pegylated interferon-α, which augments antiviral interferon signaling, are older agents. Important comorbidities and complications include mixed cryoglobulinemia, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, insulin resistance and diabetes, hepatic steatosis, B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, depression, HIV or HBV coinfection, cirrhosis, decompensated liver disease, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis relies on anti-HCV serology followed by confirmatory nucleic acid testing for HCV RNA, with genotype testing when relevant, liver enzyme assessment, fibrosis staging by elastography or biopsy, and surveillance imaging

Name: Non-Q wave myocardial infarction (disorder)
Description: Non-Q wave myocardial infarction, now generally encompassed within non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, is an acute ischemic necrosis of myocardium usually caused by subtotal coronary artery occlusion, distal embolization, or severe supply-demand mismatch, classically presenting with prolonged retrosternal chest pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue, and sometimes heart failure, arrhythmia, or hemodynamic instability, but without diagnostic Q waves on ECG; common subtypes include type 1 infarction from plaque rupture/erosion and thrombosis and type 2 infarction from oxygen supply-demand imbalance. Its biology centers on atherosclerosis, endothelial dysfunction, platelet activation, coagulation, inflammation, and ischemia-reperfusion injury involving LDL handling and lipid pathways, thromboxane A2 and ADP-mediated platelet signaling, tissue factor-thrombin cascades, nitric oxide signaling, calcium overload, reactive oxygen species, NF-kB, cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF, and apoptosis pathways. Genetic contributors are typically complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations involving APOE, LDLR, PCSK9, LPA, CETP, APOB, ACE, NOS3, MTHFR, PAI-1/SERPINE1, and platelet receptor genes such as ITGB3; rare inherited dyslipidemias, especially familial hypercholesterolemia due to LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 variants, markedly increase risk. Diagnosis relies on ischemic symptoms plus a rise and/or fall in cardiac troponin I or T above the 99th percentile, supported by ECG showing ST depression or T-wave inversion rather than ST elevation, and supplemented by echocardiography, coronary angiography or CT coronary angiography, and risk scores. Major treatments include aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and thromboxane A2 synthesis; P2Y12 inhibitors such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor, which block ADP-mediated platelet aggregation; anticoagulants such as heparin or enoxaparin, which potentiate antithrombin inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa; plus beta-blockers, nitrates, statins, and ACE inhibitors. Frequent comorbidities and complications include hypertension, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease, peripheral vascular disease, recurrent ischemia, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, malignant

Name: Atherosclerotic occlusive disease
Description: Atherosclerotic occlusive disease is a chronic, progressive arterial disorder characterized by intimal lipid deposition, inflammation, fibrous cap formation, calcification, and eventual luminal narrowing or thrombosis in coronary, carotid, cerebral, mesenteric, renal, and peripheral arteries, producing subtypes such as coronary artery disease, carotid stenosis, peripheral arterial disease, and chronic limb-threatening ischemia. Its pathobiology centers on endothelial dysfunction, LDL retention and oxidation, macrophage foam-cell formation, smooth-muscle proliferation, platelet activation, and thromboinflammation mediated through LDL receptor and cholesterol-handling genes and proteins such as LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, APOE, LPA, CETP, ABCA1, NOS3, MTHFR, IL6, TNF, CRP, MMP9, and coagulation-related factors, with familial hypercholesterolemia due to pathogenic LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 variants being a representative inherited contributor; most cases, however, are multifactorial/polygenic rather than Mendelian. Major signaling pathways include oxidized-LDL scavenger receptor signaling, NF-kB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1/IL-6, TNF-alpha, TGF-beta, PDGF, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, nitric oxide/eNOS, renin-angiotensin, and platelet thromboxane A2/P2Y12 pathways. Typical manifestations include exertional angina, transient ischemic attack or stroke symptoms, intermittent claudication, diminished pulses, bruits, cool extremities, nonhealing ulcers, rest pain, or acute ischemia, while common comorbidities and complications include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, smoking-related vascular disease, obesity, chronic kidney disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, aneurysm, embolization, ulceration, gangrene, and limb loss. Diagnosis relies on clinical vascular examination plus risk profiling, fasting lipid and glucose testing, ankle-brachial index, duplex ultrasonography, CT or MR angiography, catheter angiography when intervention is considered, and disease-specific criteria such as hemodynamically significant stenosis or ABI of 0.90 or less. Name: Cutaneous larva migrans
Description: Larva migrans is a parasitic helminthic syndrome caused by migration of animal nematode larvae in human tissues, classically presenting as cutaneous larva migrans from dog or cat hookworms such as Ancylostoma braziliense and A. caninum, visceral larva migrans from Toxocara canis or T. cati, and less commonly ocular or neural forms; it is an acquired infectious disease rather than an inherited disorder, and no Mendelian pattern or recurrent host mutation defines susceptibility, although interindividual variation in immune-response genes regulating Th2 polarization, IgE production, and eosinophilic inflammation, including representative pathways involving IL4, IL5, IL13, STAT6, CCL11/eotaxin, FCER1, and eosinophil granule proteins such as major basic protein and eosinophil peroxidase, may influence severity. Pathobiology is driven by larval tissue invasion with epithelial injury, mast-cell activation, eosinophil recruitment, and granulomatous inflammation through Th2 cytokine signaling, IgE-mediated responses, and chemokine-dependent leukocyte trafficking. Typical manifestations include intensely pruritic, serpiginous, advancing erythematous tracks in cutaneous disease, while visceral disease causes fever, cough, wheeze, abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, marked eosinophilia, and hyper-IgE, and ocular disease may present with unilateral visual loss, uveitis, or retinal granuloma. Important complications include secondary bacterial skin infection, chronic eosinophilic pneumonitis, neurotoxocariasis, and permanent visual impairment; comorbid associations are strongest with atopy/asthma-like symptoms and eosinophilic syndromes. Diagnosis relies on characteristic exposure history and examination for cutaneous larva migrans, whereas visceral or ocular disease is supported by eosinophilia, elevated total IgE, Toxocara serology such as TES-ELISA with confirmatory immunoblot, ophthalmologic examination, and targeted imaging including liver ultrasound, chest imaging, or MRI; biopsy is uncommon but may show eosinophilic granulomas. Name: Hydatid mole
Description: Hydatid mole, or molar pregnancy, is a gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblast with hydropic chorionic villi and is divided into complete and partial forms; complete moles are usually androgenetic diploid conceptions caused by fertilization of an enucleate ovum by one sperm with duplication or by two sperm, whereas partial moles are typically diandric triploid, and rare familial recurrent cases are linked to maternal-effect genes such as NLRP7, KHDC3L, and PADI6 with autosomal recessive inheritance. Molecularly, trophoblastic overgrowth involves dysregulated genomic imprinting and overactivation of proliferative pathways including PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK/ERK, and Wnt/beta-catenin signaling, with high expression of trophoblastic proteins such as hCG and often p57 loss in complete moles because of absent maternal genome contribution. Patients commonly present in early pregnancy with vaginal bleeding, uterine size greater than dates, severe nausea and hyperemesis from markedly elevated beta-hCG, pelvic pain, passage of grape-like vesicles, and absent fetal cardiac activity in complete moles; complications include preeclampsia before 20 weeks, hyperthyroidism, anemia, theca-lutein ovarian cysts, hemorrhage, and progression to persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia or choriocarcinoma, with partial mole generally carrying lower malignant potential and sometimes fetal tissue. Diagnosis relies on quantitative beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasonography showing a diffuse snowstorm or cystic placental pattern, histopathology after evacuation, ploidy analysis, and immunohistochemistry such as p57 to distinguish complete from partial or nonmolar gestations. Treatment is primarily uterine evacuation by suction curettage with serial beta-hCG surveillance; chemotherapy is used for persistent or metastatic disease, commonly methotrexate, a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor, actinomycin D, a DNA intercalating transcription inhibitor, and multiagent EMA-CO including etoposide, a topoisomerase II inhibitor, cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent, and vincristine, a microtubule inhibitor.

Name: Meibomitis
Description: Meibomitis, commonly framed within meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) or posterior blepharitis, is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the eyelid meibomian glands characterized by terminal duct obstruction and/or altered meibum quality, leading to evaporative dry eye and ocular surface inflammation. It is typically non-Mendelian and multifactorial rather than a single-gene disease, but genetic susceptibility is suggested by associations with disorders affecting lipid metabolism, keratinization, and innate immunity; representative molecular players include PPARγ, SREBP-mediated lipogenesis, keratins, cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, matrix metalloproteinases, and antimicrobial pathways involving TLR signaling, while Demodex-associated and bacterial lipase-driven inflammation can amplify NF-κB and MAPK pathway activation. Clinically, patients develop lid-margin erythema, telangiectasia, capped gland orifices, turbid or toothpaste-like secretions, foreign-body sensation, burning, fluctuating vision, crusting, and signs of tear-film instability with punctate epithelial erosions. Subtypes include obstructive versus hyposecretory MGD, inflammatory posterior blepharitis, and forms associated with rosacea or seborrheic disease. Common comorbidities include dry eye disease, acne rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, atopy, Sjögren syndrome, chalazia, recurrent hordeola, and contact lens intolerance; complications include chronic keratoconjunctivitis, corneal staining, marginal keratitis, and visual fluctuation. Treatment commonly includes doxycycline, which suppresses bacterial lipases and matrix metalloproteinases while exerting anti-inflammatory effects; azithromycin, which reduces bacterial burden and modulates inflammatory cytokine production; and topical cyclosporine, which inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation and improves ocular surface inflammation; adjuncts may include lid hygiene, warm compresses, lubricants, and short courses of topical corticosteroids. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by slit-lamp examination, meibum expressibility and quality grading, tear breakup time, ocular surface staining, meibography, and, when needed, tear osmolarity or testing for associated dry eye and rosacea.

Name: Sarcoma, Ewing
Description: Ewing sarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant small round blue cell tumor of bone and soft tissue, typically arising in children, adolescents, and young adults, and belongs to the Ewing sarcoma family of tumors that includes classic osseous Ewing sarcoma, extraosseous Ewing sarcoma, peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor, and Askin tumor of the chest wall. Its defining genetic feature is a somatic chromosomal translocation involving EWSR1 on 22q12, most commonly t(11;22)(q24;q12) generating the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion, with less common fusions such as EWSR1-ERG, EWSR1-ETV1, EWSR1-ETV4, or FEV; these aberrant transcription factors dysregulate IGF1R/PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/MAPK, cell-cycle, and epigenetic programs, with expression of CD99 and NKX2.2 often serving as useful downstream markers. The disease is usually sporadic rather than inherited, with no classic Mendelian pattern, although rare germline susceptibility variants affecting TP53, DNA repair, or cancer predisposition syndromes may contribute. Patients commonly present with localized bone pain, swelling, a palpable mass, tenderness, fever, fatigue, weight loss, elevated ESR, or pathologic fracture, and pelvic, femoral, rib, and chest wall lesions are frequent; major complications include lung, bone, and marrow metastases, cord compression, pleural effusion, treatment-related cardiomyopathy, infertility, and secondary leukemia. Diagnosis relies on imaging with radiography, MRI, CT, and PET or bone scan, histology showing sheets of uniform small round cells, immunohistochemistry typically positive for membranous CD99 and FLI1, and molecular confirmation by FISH, RT-PCR, or next-generation sequencing for EWSR1 rearrangements. Standard therapy combines multiagent chemotherapy such as vincristine, which inhibits microtubule assembly, doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor and DNA intercalator, cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide, alkylating agents that cross-link DNA, and etoposide, another topoisomerase II inhibitor, together with surgery and/or radiotherapy for local control.

Name: Group A Streptococcal Infections
Description: Streptococcal infections are acute or invasive bacterial diseases caused by Gram-positive cocci of the genus Streptococcus, most commonly group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), and Streptococcus pneumoniae, producing syndromes ranging from pharyngitis, impetigo, cellulitis, erysipelas, pneumonia, otitis media, and neonatal sepsis to necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal toxic shock. Key microbial virulence determinants include the emm-encoded M protein, streptolysins O and S, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins SpeA/SpeC, hyaluronic acid capsule genes such as hasA, C5a peptidase ScpA, pneumococcal capsule loci, pneumolysin ply, and autolysin lytA; host susceptibility is partly influenced by variants in HLA class II, TLR2/TLR4, NOD2, complement components, and Fc-gamma receptor genes, but inheritance is not Mendelian and mainly reflects complex polygenic immune predisposition. Pathobiology centers on epithelial adherence, immune evasion, superantigen-driven T-cell activation, NF-kB and MAPK signaling, cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-17, complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, and, in post-streptococcal autoimmunity, molecular mimicry affecting heart, kidney, or CNS. Complications include scarlet fever, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, bacteremia, endocarditis, abscess, meningitis, and septic shock; important comorbid risks include diabetes, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy, and extremes of age. Diagnosis relies on syndrome-specific evaluation with throat culture or rapid antigen/PCR testing for pharyngitis, culture and susceptibility from blood, CSF, wounds, or sputum for invasive disease, urinary antigen for pneumococcus, imaging when deep infection is suspected, and serology such as ASO or anti-DNase B for recent infection. First-line treatment commonly includes penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking; ceftriaxone, another beta-lactam with

Name: Malignant Glioma
Description: Glioma is a primary neuroepithelial tumor of the central nervous system arising from glial-lineage cells and encompasses astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma, and highly aggressive glioblastoma, with diffuse gliomas now stratified by molecular features. Hallmark genetic alterations include IDH1 or IDH2 mutations in lower-grade diffuse gliomas and secondary glioblastomas, 1p/19q codeletion in oligodendroglioma, TP53 and ATRX mutations in astrocytoma, TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification or EGFRvIII, PTEN loss, CDKN2A/B deletion, PDGFRA amplification, NF1 alteration, MGMT promoter methylation as a predictive biomarker, and histone H3 K27M or G34 mutations in pediatric diffuse midline and hemispheric gliomas; inherited predisposition may occur in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, tuberous sclerosis, Lynch syndrome, and Turcot syndrome. Major dysregulated pathways include RTK/RAS/RAF/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53, RB-cell cycle control, hypoxia/HIF-VEGF angiogenesis, and epigenetic reprogramming related to IDH-associated 2-hydroxyglutarate. Patients typically present with headache, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, cognitive or personality change, aphasia, visual disturbance, gait impairment, nausea, and signs of raised intracranial pressure; complications include cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, endocrinopathy when hypothalamic-pituitary structures are involved, treatment-related neurocognitive decline, and recurrence. Diagnosis relies on MRI with contrast, advanced perfusion or spectroscopy when needed, histopathology and WHO grading, and integrated molecular testing by immunohistochemistry, FISH, PCR, or next-generation sequencing for IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion, ATRX, TP53, MGMT, TERT, and H3 alterations. Standard therapy includes maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy and temozolomide, an oral alkylating agent causing DNA methylation; lomustine or carmustine nitrosoureas that alkylate and crosslink DNA; bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody that reduces angi

Name: Uric acid nephrolithiasis
Description: Uric acid nephrolithiasis is a metabolic form of kidney stone disease characterized by precipitation of poorly soluble uric acid in persistently acidic, low-volume urine, often with hyperuricosuria, and includes mainly idiopathic uric acid stones but also secondary forms associated with gout, myeloproliferative states, tumor lysis, chronic diarrhea, ileostomy, and obesity-related insulin resistance. Clinically, patients present with renal colic, flank pain, hematuria, dysuria, nausea, urinary urgency, or recurrent stones, and may develop obstruction, hydronephrosis, recurrent urinary tract infection, acute kidney injury, or chronic kidney disease. Central pathogenic pathways involve purine metabolism and renal acid-base handling, including xanthine oxidoreductase-mediated urate production, proximal tubular urate transport through SLC22A12/URAT1, SLC2A9/GLUT9, and ABCG2, and ammoniagenesis defects linked to insulin resistance; representative genetic contributors include variants in SLC2A9, ABCG2, SLC22A12, UMOD, and monogenic disorders such as HPRT1 deficiency in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, PRPS1 superactivity, and renal hypouricemia due to SLC22A12 or SLC2A9 mutations, which are usually inherited in X-linked or autosomal dominant/recessive patterns depending on the gene. Diagnosis is based on stone analysis demonstrating uric acid composition, urine pH typically below 5.5, 24-hour urine showing low volume and/or hyperuricosuria, serum urate assessment, urinalysis revealing rhomboid or rosette uric acid crystals, and noncontrast CT or ultrasound, with radiolucency on plain radiography being suggestive. Treatment centers on urine alkalinization with potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate to raise urinary pH and dissolve/prevent stones, xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol and febuxostat to reduce uric acid production, and hydration; comorbidities commonly include gout, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and obesity.

Name: Antimetabolite overdose
Description: Antimetabolite overdose is an acquired toxicologic emergency caused by excessive exposure to antimetabolite drugs, most often methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil/capecitabine, cytarabine, gemcitabine, pemetrexed, mercaptopurine, or azathioprine, leading to exaggerated inhibition of nucleotide synthesis and DNA/RNA replication in rapidly dividing tissues. Molecular susceptibility is strongly influenced by pharmacogenetic variation, including DPYD deficiency for fluoropyrimidines, TPMT and NUDT15 variants for thiopurines, and reduced-function MTHFR, SLC19A1/RFC1, ABCB1, SLCO1B1, DHFR, and TYMS polymorphisms that alter methotrexate or folate-pathway handling; the disorder itself is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion, but these germline variants can show autosomal codominant or recessive pharmacogenetic risk patterns. Key pathways include folate metabolism and one-carbon transfer, thymidylate synthase inhibition, de novo purine synthesis blockade, pyrimidine metabolism, DNA damage response, apoptosis, and renal tubular transport affecting drug clearance. Typical manifestations include severe mucositis/stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, myelosuppression with neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and anemia, fever, sepsis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, dermatitis/hand-foot syndrome, and in severe cases multiorgan failure; common complications include pancytopenia, opportunistic infection, hemorrhage, acute kidney injury, and hepatic dysfunction, often in patients with cancer, renal impairment, folate deficiency, dehydration, drug interactions, or preexisting marrow suppression. Major clinical subtypes are high-dose methotrexate toxicity, fluoropyrimidine toxicity, thiopurine toxicity, and accidental oral or dosing-error overdose. Diagnosis rests on exposure history, dose and timing, serial CBC, renal and liver chemistries, drug concentrations when available such as plasma methotrexate, and pharmacogenetic or enzymatic testing including DPYD genotyping, DPD activity assays, TPMT/NUDT15 genotyping or phenotype, with supportive marrow and infectious evaluation as indicated. Name: Proteus septicemia (disorder)
Description: Proteus septicemia is an acute, life-threatening bloodstream infection caused most often by Proteus mirabilis and less commonly P. vulgaris or other Proteus species, typically arising from complicated urinary tract infection, catheter-associated infection, obstructive uropathy, infected stones, postoperative wounds, or intra-abdominal infection. It is not a Mendelian genetic disease and has no fixed inheritance pattern; rather, host susceptibility is influenced by immune and inflammatory genes and comorbid states, with representative implicated components including TLR4, CD14, NOD-like receptor signaling, cytokine genes such as TNF and IL6, and complement pathway defects, while bacterial virulence determinants include urease, flagellin, fimbriae/adhesins such as MR/P fimbriae, hemolysin HpmA, ZapA protease, lipopolysaccharide, and biofilm-associated factors. Pathobiology is dominated by endotoxin-triggered TLR4–MyD88–NF-κB and MAPK signaling, inflammasome activation, neutrophil and complement recruitment, coagulation cascade activation, and in severe cases dysregulated cytokine release leading to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction. Clinical features include fever or hypothermia, rigors, dysuria or flank pain when urinary in origin, altered mental status, tachycardia, hypotension, leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, lactic acidosis, acute kidney injury, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Important complications and linked conditions include pyelonephritis, struvite calculi, renal or perinephric abscess, pneumonia, endocarditis, respiratory failure, and death, especially in older adults, diabetics, immunocompromised patients, and those with indwelling catheters. Subtypes are usually categorized by causative Proteus species and source of sepsis, including urosepsis. Diagnosis rests on sepsis criteria with identification of a focus, blood cultures and urine cultures, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, CBC, chemistry panels, lactate, inflammatory markers, urinalysis, and imaging for obstruction or abscess. Treatment requires prompt source control and antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis; piperacillin-tazobactam, an antipseudomonal penicillin plus β-lactamase inhibitor; and ciprof

Name: Urinary tract infection caused by Escherichia coli
Description: Urinary tract infection caused by Escherichia coli is an acute bacterial infection of the urethra, bladder, and sometimes kidney, most often due to uropathogenic E. coli ascending from the periurethral area; major clinical forms include uncomplicated cystitis, complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated UTI, recurrent UTI, and, less often, urosepsis. Typical manifestations are dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy or malodorous urine, hematuria, and in upper-tract disease fever, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral-angle tenderness. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial virulence factors such as type 1 fimbriae encoded by fimH and pap/papG P fimbriae, toxins including hlyA, siderophore systems such as iroN and iutA, capsule-associated genes, and biofilm-related determinants; host susceptibility has genetic contributions rather than Mendelian inheritance, with reported associations involving TLR4, TLR5, CXCR1, CXCR2, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, DEFB1, and secretor-status gene FUT2. Key pathways include urothelial adherence and invasion, TLR4-MyD88-NF-κB signaling, cytokine and neutrophil recruitment through IL-6, IL-8, and CXCR1/2, inflammasome activation, and intracellular bacterial community formation. Common comorbidities and risk factors include female sex, sexual activity, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, nephrolithiasis, urinary obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, neurogenic bladder, benign prostatic hyperplasia, catheterization, and immunosuppression; complications include renal abscess, emphysematous infection, bacteremia, sepsis, renal scarring, and recurrent infection. Diagnosis rests on symptoms plus urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and bacteriuria, confirmed when needed by urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing; imaging is reserved for obstruction, stones, severe pyelonephritis, or recurrent/complicated disease. Treatment commonly includes nitrofurantoin, which is reduced in bacteria to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis via dihydrofolate reductase and dihydrop

Name: Proteus urinary tract infection
Description: Proteus urinary tract infection is a bacterial UTI caused predominantly by uropathogenic Proteus mirabilis, and less often P. vulgaris, characterized by ascending infection of the bladder and kidneys with a marked propensity for catheter-associated disease, alkaline urine, biofilm formation, and struvite stone production. It is not an inherited disorder in the classic sense, but pathogen virulence determinants and host susceptibility genes influence risk; representative bacterial factors include urease structural genes ureA, ureB, and ureC, flagellar regulators such as flhDC, fimbrial adhesins including MR/P fimbriae encoded by mrp genes and PMF/UCA fimbriae, hemolysin hpmA, and the zinc metalloprotease zapA, while host predisposition may reflect variants affecting innate immunity, vesicoureteral reflux, neurogenic bladder, or urinary tract obstruction rather than Mendelian transmission. Pathobiologically, disease involves adhesion to uroepithelium, swarming motility, quorum sensing, urease-driven hydrolysis of urea to ammonia with urinary alkalinization, crystal nucleation, and inflammatory activation through TLR4-NF-κB signaling with neutrophil recruitment and cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8. Typical symptoms and signs include dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, foul-smelling urine, hematuria, flank pain, fever, and in complicated cases sepsis; major subtypes are uncomplicated cystitis, complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated infection, and recurrent or stone-associated infection. Common comorbidities and complications include indwelling catheter use, diabetes, urinary retention, structural urinary abnormalities, staghorn calculi, hydronephrosis, renal abscess, bacteremia, and chronic kidney damage. Diagnosis rests on urinalysis showing pyuria, bacteriuria, and often alkaline pH, urine culture with speciation and susceptibility testing, and imaging such as ultrasound or CT when obstruction, stones, or upper-tract involvement is suspected.
