Name: Chronic Spontaneous Urticarias
Description: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU; UMLS C0578870) is a mast cell–driven inflammatory skin disease defined by the spontaneous appearance of pruritic wheals, angioedema, or both for more than 6 weeks without a consistent external trigger; major symptoms include recurrent transient hives, intense itch, erythema, swelling, and, in some patients, painful deeper angioedema. Pathobiologically, CSU is commonly linked to autoimmune and autoallergic mechanisms involving IgE, the high-affinity IgE receptor FcεRI, mast cells, basophils, histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, complement, and coagulation mediators, with signaling through FcεRI/Syk/Lyn, PI3K-AKT, MAPK, NF-κB, JAK-STAT, and Th2 cytokine axes including IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-31, and TSLP; representative associated genes or proteins include FCER1A, MS4A2/FCER1B, KIT, TPSAB1, HRH1, IL4, IL13, and autoantibodies to IgE or FcεRI, although most cases are polygenic and not monogenic. Subtypes include CSU with wheals only, CSU with angioedema, autoimmune type I and type IIb CSU, and overlap with chronic inducible urticarias. Inheritance is usually non-Mendelian, with familial clustering and rare hereditary angioedema due to SERPING1, F12, PLG, ANGPT1, or KNG1 serving as key differential diagnoses rather than classic CSU. Common comorbidities include autoimmune thyroid disease, asthma, atopy, chronic inducible urticarias, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, and reduced quality of life; complications are mainly refractory symptoms and medication adverse effects. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history and examination, exclusion of mimics, CBC and inflammatory markers, thyroid autoantibodies when indicated, and selected tests such as total IgE, autologous serum skin test, basophil activation testing, or skin biopsy for urticarial vasculitis. Name: Hyperhidrosis of axilla
Description: Axillary hyperhidrosis (UMLS C0580182) is a focal sweating disorder characterized by excessive, usually bilateral underarm perspiration beyond thermoregulatory needs, typically beginning in adolescence or early adulthood and causing visible sweat, maceration, malodor, clothing staining, and major psychosocial impairment; it is most often primary and idiopathic, but secondary forms occur with endocrine, neurologic, infectious, malignant, or drug-related causes. Primary disease reflects overactivity of sympathetic cholinergic innervation of otherwise histologically normal eccrine glands, with acetylcholine signaling through muscarinic receptors, especially CHRM3, promoting intracellular calcium flux and secretion; implicated biologic components include sympathetic ganglia, acetylcholine metabolism, aquaporin-mediated fluid transport, and stress-related central autonomic pathways, while genetic susceptibility is supported by frequent familial clustering, commonly consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance, although no single causative gene is established and candidate loci or genes involving cholinergic signaling and autonomic regulation remain incompletely validated. Subtypes include primary focal axillary hyperhidrosis, generalized hyperhidrosis, and secondary hyperhidrosis. Comorbidities include anxiety, depression, social phobia, bromhidrosis, contact dermatitis, intertrigo, superficial bacterial or fungal infection, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, based on focal visible excessive sweating for at least 6 months without apparent cause plus typical criteria such as bilateral symmetry, impairment of daily activities, onset before age 25, at least weekly episodes, positive family history, and absence during sleep; testing may include gravimetric sweat measurement, Minor starch-iodine testing for mapping, Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale scoring, and laboratory evaluation to exclude secondary causes such as thyrotoxicosis or diabetes. Common treatments include aluminum chloride hexahydrate, which obstructs eccrine ducts; topical or systemic anticholinergics such as glycopyrronium or oxybutynin, which inhibit muscarinic signaling; botulinum toxin A, which blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release; and, in refractory cases, microwave thermolysis, local surgery, or sympathectomy.

Name: Gastric spasm
Description: Gastric spasm is a largely clinical syndrome characterized by episodic, involuntary hypercontractility of the gastric smooth muscle, producing cramping epigastric pain, nausea, early satiety, bloating, retching, and occasionally vomiting; on examination, patients may have epigastric tenderness and symptoms provoked by meals or stress. It is usually a functional or secondary motility disorder rather than a distinct monogenic disease, and may occur as an acute transient phenomenon or as part of chronic gastric dysmotility, including pylorospasm and spastic disorders associated with gastroparesis or functional dyspepsia. Molecular mechanisms involve dysregulated enteric cholinergic signaling, vagal autonomic input, smooth-muscle calcium handling, nitric oxide–mediated inhibitory pathways involving neuronal nitric oxide synthase, interstitial cells of Cajal pacemaker activity with KIT/ANO1-related networks, and serotonin signaling, particularly through 5-HT3 and 5-HT4 receptors; in rare syndromic or visceral myopathy contexts, genes affecting smooth muscle contractility such as ACTG2 and ion-channel or pacemaker-related components may contribute, although no single recurrent mutation defines typical gastric spasm. Common treatments include anticholinergic antispasmodics such as dicyclomine or hyoscyamine, which reduce muscarinic receptor–mediated smooth-muscle contraction; papaverine, a phosphodiesterase-inhibiting smooth-muscle relaxant; calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine in selected refractory spastic states; and, when overlap with delayed emptying exists, prokinetics such as metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist with 5-HT4 agonist activity, or erythromycin, a motilin receptor agonist. Important comorbidities include functional dyspepsia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, anxiety, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, connective-tissue or visceral myopathy disorders, and postoperative states; complications include dehydration, poor oral intake, weight loss, and impaired quality of life. Diagnosis is based on symptom pattern and exclusion of structural disease using upper endoscopy, abdominal imaging when indicated, laboratory testing for metabolic causes, Helicobacter pylori assessment, and motility evaluation with gastric emptying scintigraphy, antroduodenal manometry, or electrogastrography in selected cases.

Name: Decompensated cardiac failure
Description: Decompensated cardiac failure is an acute or subacute deterioration of chronic or new-onset heart failure in which impaired ventricular filling or ejection causes elevated intracardiac pressures, pulmonary and/or systemic congestion, and reduced organ perfusion; it commonly presents as acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, preserved ejection fraction, right-sided failure, or cardiogenic shock. Clinical features include dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, peripheral edema, elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary rales, S3 gallop, hepatomegaly, ascites, cool extremities, and weight gain from fluid retention. Molecular contributors include pathogenic variants in cardiomyopathy genes such as TTN, MYH7, LMNA, MYBPC3, TNNT2, DSP, and PLN, with proteins affecting sarcomere integrity, cytoskeletal coupling, calcium handling, and nuclear structure; inheritance is often autosomal dominant in dilated, hypertrophic, or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy backgrounds, though decompensation itself is usually multifactorial and precipitated by ischemia, hypertension, arrhythmia, infection, renal dysfunction, or medication nonadherence. Key pathways include neurohormonal activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic beta-adrenergic signaling, natriuretic peptide signaling, inflammatory cytokines, endothelin, oxidative stress, calcium cycling abnormalities involving SERCA2a and phospholamban, and maladaptive remodeling through TGF-beta and MAPK pathways. Standard therapy includes loop diuretics such as furosemide, which inhibit the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter to relieve congestion; ACE inhibitors such as enalapril, which reduce angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and remodeling; beta-blockers such as carvedilol, which blunt sympathetic drive; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone; and SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin. Major comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, COPD, valvular disease, pulmonary hypertension, cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmias, thromboembolism, and sudden death. Diagnosis relies on history and examination, BNP or NT-proBNP elevation, troponin, renal and hepatic panels

Name: Osteosarcoma of Bone
Description: Osteosarcoma of bone is a high-grade malignant mesenchymal tumor in which neoplastic cells directly produce osteoid, arising most often in the metaphyses of long bones of adolescents and young adults, with conventional intramedullary osteosarcoma as the major subtype and recognized osteoblastic, chondroblastic, fibroblastic, telangiectatic, small-cell, parosteal, periosteal, and secondary forms. Its molecular pathogenesis is dominated by complex karyotypic instability rather than a single driver, with frequent disruption of TP53 and RB1, alterations in CDKN2A, MDM2, MYC, ATRX, PTEN, RECQL4, and occasional defects in DNA-helicase or chromatin-remodeling genes; inherited predisposition is usually autosomal dominant in cancer syndromes such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome due to germline TP53 variants and hereditary retinoblastoma due to RB1 mutations, and is also seen in Rothmund-Thomson syndrome with RECQL4 mutations. Dysregulated RB/E2F and p53 pathways, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, Wnt/beta-catenin, TGF-beta, IGF, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, and RANK/RANKL-related bone remodeling are commonly implicated. Patients typically present with progressive localized bone pain, swelling, tenderness, reduced joint motion, limp, and sometimes pathologic fracture; pulmonary metastases are the most common complication, with local recurrence and chemotherapy-related cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, and myelosuppression also important. Standard treatment combines multiagent chemotherapy and wide surgical resection, commonly using high-dose methotrexate, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor and DNA intercalator, cisplatin, which forms DNA crosslinks, and often ifosfamide, an alkylating agent. Diagnosis relies on characteristic imaging findings on radiograph, MRI, and CT, including aggressive bone destruction with periosteal reaction such as sunburst pattern or Codman triangle, elevated alkaline phosphatase or LDH in some cases, and definitive core biopsy demonstrating malignant osteoid production, with staging by chest CT and pathologic assessment of necrosis after neoadjuvant therapy.

Name: Sepsis caused by enterococcus
Description: Sepsis caused by Enterococcus is an invasive bacterial bloodstream infection, most often due to Enterococcus faecalis or Enterococcus faecium, that triggers a dysregulated host response leading to life-threatening organ dysfunction and, in severe forms, septic shock. Typical presentations include fever or hypothermia, rigors, hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, oliguria, and progressive renal, respiratory, or circulatory failure; common sources include urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, catheter-related infection, endocarditis, and postoperative or nosocomial infection. Major microbial determinants include adhesins and biofilm-associated proteins such as esp, aggregation substance, ace/acm, pili genes, cytolysin cyl, gelatinase gelE, and quorum-sensing fsr, while antibiotic resistance commonly involves vanA or vanB-mediated alteration of peptidoglycan termini causing vancomycin resistance, pbp5-linked beta-lactam resistance in E. faecium, and occasional linezolid resistance via 23S rRNA or optrA/cfr. Host signaling prominently involves TLR2-, NOD-, and NF-kappaB-dependent pathways, with TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6, complement, coagulation, endothelial activation, and neutrophil/monocyte responses driving systemic inflammation, capillary leak, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment relies on rapid source control and antibiotics such as ampicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting cell-wall transpeptidation; vancomycin, a glycopeptide blocking D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan synthesis when susceptible; linezolid, a 50S inhibitor; daptomycin, a membrane-depolarizing lipopeptide; and for selected severe E. faecalis infections, synergistic gentamicin or ceftriaxone combinations. Important comorbidities include diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, cirrhosis, immunosuppression, indwelling devices, and prior broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, with complications including infective endocarditis, metastatic abscesses, acute kidney injury, ARDS, and death. Name: Cystitis, Chronic Interstitial
Description: Interstitial cystitis, or bladder pain syndrome, is a chronic noninfectious inflammatory and sensory disorder of the bladder characterized by suprapubic pain related to bladder filling, urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia, pressure, and dyspareunia, often with sterile urine and cystoscopic or histologic evidence of urothelial dysfunction. It is clinically heterogeneous, with ulcerative or Hunner lesion disease and nonulcerative forms, and often reflects epithelial barrier failure, neurogenic inflammation, mast-cell activation, and central sensitization. Molecular studies implicate altered urothelial and inflammatory mediators including TNF, IL6, IL8, NGF, VEGF, COX-2, tryptase, E-cadherin, and antiproliferative factor pathways involving frizzled-8, as well as purinergic, TRPV1, substance P, histamine, and TLR-mediated signaling; representative genetic associations, generally complex and non-Mendelian rather than causal, include polymorphisms or differential expression in cytokine genes, ADRB2, COMT, HTR2A, and extracellular matrix or urothelial barrier genes, with familial clustering reported but no single established inheritance pattern. Common comorbidities include irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, vulvodynia, endometriosis, chronic fatigue, migraine, anxiety, depression, and autoimmune disorders, and complications include sleep disturbance, sexual dysfunction, reduced bladder capacity, and major quality-of-life impairment. Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion, typically requiring chronic bladder-centric pain with lower urinary tract symptoms for at least 6 weeks without infection or other identifiable cause, supported by urinalysis and culture, voiding diaries, symptom indices, pelvic examination, cystoscopy with hydrodistention and possible Hunner lesion identification, biopsy when malignancy or eosinophilic/carcinomatous processes must be excluded, and sometimes urodynamics. Treatments commonly include pentosan polysulfate sodium, which is thought to restore the glycosaminoglycan urothelial barrier; amitriptyline, which reduces neuropathic pain via serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and antihistaminic effects; hydroxyzine, an H1 antagonist that suppresses mast-cell mediated symptoms; and intravesical dimethyl sulfoxide, which provides anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and muscle-relaxant effects.

Name: Infection of bladder
Description: Infection of the bladder, usually acute bacterial cystitis, is a lower urinary tract infection most commonly caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli, with other pathogens including Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus; clinically it is characterized by dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy or malodorous urine, pyuria, and sometimes hematuria, while fever, flank pain, or systemic toxicity suggest extension beyond the bladder. Disease subtypes include uncomplicated cystitis, complicated cystitis associated with obstruction, stones, catheters, neurogenic bladder, male sex, pregnancy, or immunosuppression, as well as recurrent, catheter-associated, emphysematous, and interstitial forms, the last not being primarily infectious. Host susceptibility has no simple Mendelian inheritance, but genetic contributors include innate immune and epithelial defense genes such as TLR4, CXCR1/CXCR2, HSPA1B, DEFB1, IL6, and secretor status determined by FUT2; bacterial virulence factors include type 1 fimbriae with FimH adhesin, P fimbriae, hemolysin, and siderophore systems. Key pathogenic pathways involve adherence to uroplakin-coated urothelium, TLR4-mediated NF-kB activation, IL-6 and IL-8 signaling, neutrophil recruitment, inflammasome and complement activation, and in recurrent infection intracellular bacterial community formation and biofilm production, especially on catheters. Common treatments include nitrofurantoin, reduced by bacterial nitroreductases to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and ribosomal proteins; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis via dihydrofolate reductase and dihydropteroate synthase; fosfomycin, an inhibitor of MurA and early peptidoglycan synthesis; and beta-lactams or fluoroquinolones in selected cases. Diagnosis rests on symptoms plus urinalysis showing leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria, and bacteriuria, with urine culture and susceptibility testing recommended in complicated, recurrent, male, pregnant, or treatment-failure cases. Name: Hot Flashes
Description: Hot flashes, or vasomotor symptoms, are paroxysmal episodes of heat sensation with flushing, sweating, palpitations, anxiety, and sometimes chills or sleep disruption, most commonly arising during the menopausal transition from estrogen withdrawal but also occurring with androgen-deprivation therapy, antiestrogen treatment, premature ovarian insufficiency, and neuroendocrine states. The disorder is a nonmalignant neurovascular thermoregulatory syndrome in which reduced estradiol alters hypothalamic signaling and narrows the thermoneutral zone through KNDy neurons expressing kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin; implicated genes and proteins include TAC3 and TACR3, ESR1 and ESR2, KISS1/KISS1R, CYP19A1, and enzymes affecting catecholamine or serotonin tone such as COMT and SLC6A4, while IL-8/CXCL8 and CGRP have been linked as mediators or biomarkers in some studies. Key pathways include estrogen receptor signaling, hypothalamic neurokinin-3 receptor signaling, serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways, and peripheral vasodilation/sudomotor activation. Typical subtypes are menopausal versus secondary hot flashes and natural versus surgical or treatment-induced menopause. Genetic predisposition is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with familial clustering and variant associations in estrogen biosynthesis/receptor and thermoregulatory neurotransmission genes, but no single inheritance pattern is established. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on recurrent vasomotor episodes in the appropriate hormonal context, with menopause assessed by menstrual history and selective testing such as FSH/estradiol when uncertain, and secondary causes excluded by thyroid testing, medication review, pregnancy testing, or evaluation for carcinoid, pheochromocytoma, or infection when indicated; symptom diaries and validated severity scales may support assessment. Common comorbidities and complications include insomnia, fatigue, depression, anxiety, cognitive complaints, sexual dysfunction, reduced quality of life, and associations with cardiometabolic risk and bone loss. Treatments include menopausal hormone therapy with systemic estrogen, often with a progestogen if the uterus is present, fezolinetant, a neurokinin-3 receptor antagonist, and nonhormonal agents such as venlafaxine or paroxetine, which enhance serotonergic/noradrenergic modulation, and gabapentin, which reduces central neuronal excitability.

Name: Low Cardiac Output Syndrome
Description: Low cardiac output is a hemodynamic syndrome rather than a single disease, defined by inadequate cardiac pump function to meet systemic metabolic demand, most often arising in acute myocardial infarction, decompensated heart failure, cardiomyopathy, severe valvular disease, myocarditis, tamponade, or cardiogenic shock. Molecular contributors depend on the underlying disorder and include pathogenic variants in sarcomeric and cytoskeletal genes such as TTN, MYH7, MYBPC3, LMNA, TNNT2, and PLN in inherited dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, channelopathy-related genes in arrhythmic low-output states, and ischemia-driven neurohormonal activation involving the beta-adrenergic, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, natriuretic peptide, calcium-handling, nitric oxide-cGMP, endothelin, inflammatory cytokine, and mitochondrial energy pathways; key proteins include SERCA2a, phospholamban, troponins, BNP/NT-proBNP, ACE, angiotensin II, aldosterone, and catecholamine-responsive beta1 receptors. Typical manifestations are hypotension, narrow pulse pressure, cool extremities, oliguria, fatigue, dyspnea, altered mentation, elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary edema, and lactic acidosis. Major subtypes include acute versus chronic low-output states and left-, right-, or biventricular failure. Common comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, hepatic and renal hypoperfusion, multiorgan failure, and thromboembolism. Treatment targets cause and perfusion: dobutamine, a beta1-adrenergic agonist, increases inotropy; milrinone, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor, raises cAMP and reduces afterload; norepinephrine, an alpha1- and beta1-agonist, restores perfusion pressure in shock; additional therapy may include diuretics such as furosemide, vasodilators, or mechanical circulatory support. Inherited forms follow autosomal dominant patterns most commonly, though X-linked and mitochondrial causes occur. Name: Hashimoto Disease
Description: Hashimoto disease, or chronic autoimmune (lymphocytic) thyroiditis, is a common organ-specific autoimmune disorder and the leading cause of primary hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, characterized by progressive T-cell- and B-cell-mediated destruction of thyroid follicles with germinal center formation and autoantibodies to thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin; Graves-like stimulating TSH receptor antibodies are uncommon but may coexist. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with strong associations to HLA-DR3, DR4, and DR5, CTLA4, PTPN22, TG, TSHR, IL2RA, and FOXP3 variants, familial clustering, female predominance, and increased concordance in twins. Pathobiology involves loss of immune tolerance, enhanced antigen presentation, Th1/Th17 polarization, B-cell activation, cytokines such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-17, Fas/FasL-mediated apoptosis, and checkpoint dysregulation. Patients may have painless goiter or an atrophic thyroid and typically develop fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, menorrhagia, depression, cognitive slowing, delayed reflex relaxation, and sometimes a transient thyrotoxic hashitoxicosis phase; recognized forms include goitrous, atrophic, postpartum, juvenile, and fibrosing variants. Diagnosis rests on elevated TSH with low free T4 in overt disease, positive anti-TPO and often anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, characteristic hypoechoic heterogeneous ultrasound, and selected use of biopsy when nodules or lymphoma are suspected. Standard treatment is levothyroxine, a synthetic T4 replacement converted peripherally to T3 to normalize TSH; liothyronine, synthetic T3 acting directly at nuclear thyroid hormone receptors, is used selectively; and combination T4/T3 therapy is occasionally tried in persistent symptomatic patients. Comorbidities include other autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, pernicious anemia, Addison disease, vitiligo, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren syndrome, while complications include dyslipidemia, infertility, miscarriage, myxedema, and increased risk of primary thyroid lymphoma, with papillary thyroid carcinoma reported in some series.

Name: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with oesophagitis
Description: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with oesophagitis (UMLS C0677659) is an inflammatory mucosal injury syndrome caused by chronic retrograde exposure of the oesophagus to gastric acid, pepsin, and often duodenal bile, most commonly due to transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, hypotensive sphincter tone, hiatal hernia, impaired clearance, or delayed gastric emptying. Patients typically present with heartburn, acid regurgitation, retrosternal burning, chest pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, chronic cough, hoarseness, throat clearing, and dental enamel erosion; disease ranges from non-erosive reflux to erosive oesophagitis, with severity often graded endoscopically by the Los Angeles classification. Key molecular processes include epithelial barrier disruption with altered tight-junction proteins such as claudins and occludin, acid-sensing and inflammatory signaling through TRPV1, NF-kB, COX-2/prostaglandin pathways, and cytokines including IL-8, IL-1beta, IL-6, and TNF, with oxidative stress contributing to injury. Genetic susceptibility is modest and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with familial aggregation and representative associations reported near FOXF1, MHC/HLA loci, BARX1, GNB3, and genes influencing obesity or connective tissue traits, but no single mutation is diagnostic in routine practice. Common treatments include proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, and pantoprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase; H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine, which reduce histamine-mediated acid secretion; and alginate-antacid preparations or sucralfate, which form a protective barrier, while baclofen, a GABAB agonist, can reduce transient sphincter relaxations. Important comorbidities include obesity, pregnancy, diabetes, asthma, chronic cough, obstructive sleep apnoea, anxiety, and scleroderma; complications include ulceration, bleeding, peptic stricture, Barrett oesophagus, and oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis is based on typical symptoms plus response to acid suppression, upper endoscopy with biopsy when alarm features or refractory symptoms exist, and ambulatory pH or pH-impedance monitoring and manometry when confirmation or physiological characterization is needed.

Name: Breast Carcinomas
Description: Breast neoplasms are predominantly epithelial malignancies of the mammary gland, most commonly invasive ductal or invasive lobular carcinoma, with major biologic subtypes defined by estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 status, including luminal A/B, HER2-enriched, and triple-negative/basal-like disease. Their pathogenesis involves recurrent alterations in BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PIK3CA, ERBB2/HER2 amplification, PTEN loss, GATA3, CDH1, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, and occasionally ESR1 mutations, affecting proteins that regulate DNA repair, cell-cycle control, adhesion, and growth signaling. Key pathways include ER signaling, HER2/EGFR-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR cascades, TP53 and RB cell-cycle checkpoints, homologous recombination repair, and immune-related pathways in some triple-negative tumors. Clinically, patients may present with a painless breast mass, architectural distortion, skin dimpling, nipple inversion or discharge, erythema, peau d’orange, axillary adenopathy, or, in advanced disease, bone pain, dyspnea, or neurologic symptoms from metastases. Important comorbidities and complications include lymphedema, venous thromboembolism, osteoporosis, treatment-related cardiomyopathy, infection, local recurrence, and metastases to bone, liver, lung, or brain. Management commonly includes tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator; aromatase inhibitors such as letrozole, which suppress peripheral estrogen synthesis; trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody against HER2; and in selected settings CDK4/6 inhibitors, taxanes, anthracyclines, PARP inhibitors, or PI3K inhibitors. Inheritance is usually multifactorial, but 5-10% are hereditary, often autosomal dominant cancer-predisposition syndromes involving BRCA1/2, PALB2, TP53, PTEN, or CDH1. Diagnosis relies on clinical examination, mammography with adjunct ultrasound or MRI when indicated, followed by core needle biopsy for histopathology and immunohistochemistry or in situ hybridization for ER, PR, and HER2, with staging by TNM and selective germline or somatic molecular testing.

Name: Bacterial sepsis
Description: Bacterial sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to invasive bacterial infection, spanning community- and hospital-acquired forms and progressing from uncomplicated sepsis to septic shock, often originating from pneumonia, urinary, abdominal, skin, or catheter-related infections. Its pathobiology is driven by pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as lipopolysaccharide and peptidoglycan activating TLR4, TLR2, CD14, NOD-like receptors, NF-κB, MAPK, complement, inflammasome, and JAK/STAT signaling, with major mediators including TNF, IL1B, IL6, IL10, IFNG, HMGB1, nitric oxide synthase, coagulation pathways, and endothelial injury. Genetic susceptibility is complex and usually non-Mendelian, with polymorphisms reported in TLR4, CD14, TNF, IL6, IL10, FER, PAI1/SERPINE1, MBL2, and HLA-related immune genes influencing risk, severity, or outcome rather than causing classic inherited disease. Common signs include fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, oliguria, and evidence of organ dysfunction such as acute kidney injury, ARDS, coagulopathy, or hepatic injury. Important comorbidities and complications include diabetes, cirrhosis, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, disseminated intravascular coagulation, multiorgan failure, and secondary nosocomial infection. Diagnosis is based on suspected or proven bacterial infection plus organ dysfunction, commonly operationalized as an acute SOFA increase of at least 2 points; septic shock is defined by vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids. Testing includes blood and site-specific cultures before antibiotics when feasible, CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation studies, CRP, procalcitonin, arterial blood gas, serum lactate, urinalysis, and imaging for source control. Name: Metastatic malignant neoplasm to stomach
Description: Metastatic malignant neoplasm to the stomach is a secondary gastric cancer caused by hematogenous, lymphatic, transcoelomic, or direct spread from a distant primary tumor, most often breast carcinoma, melanoma, lung carcinoma, esophageal carcinoma, or renal cell carcinoma, and less commonly ovarian, colorectal, or pancreatic malignancies; histologic subtypes therefore mirror the primary disease, including metastatic adenocarcinoma, lobular breast carcinoma, squamous carcinoma, melanoma, and neuroendocrine tumors. Its molecular profile is usually determined by the primary tumor and may include TP53, KRAS, BRAF, EGFR, ERBB2/HER2, PIK3CA, CDH1, BRCA1/2, ALK, ROS1, RET, and MET alterations, with corresponding protein expression such as HER2, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, S100, HMB45, Melan-A, TTF-1, or GATA3; implicated pathways commonly include MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, WNT/beta-catenin, cell-cycle control, apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis via VEGF, and immune-checkpoint signaling through PD-1/PD-L1. Symptoms often include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, early satiety, anorexia, weight loss, occult or overt upper gastrointestinal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, and rarely perforation or obstruction. Major complications include hemorrhage, gastric outlet obstruction, malnutrition, cachexia, and widespread metastatic disease involving liver, peritoneum, lung, or bone, often with comorbidities related to the primary cancer. Inheritance is generally not specific to the gastric metastatic lesion itself, but familial cancer predisposition may underlie the primary tumor, for example BRCA1/2-associated breast or ovarian cancer, CDH1-related diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer susceptibility, or Lynch syndrome. Diagnosis relies on clinical history of prior malignancy, endoscopy with biopsy, histopathology and immunohistochemistry to distinguish metastasis from primary gastric carcinoma, cross-sectional imaging or PET, and selective molecular testing. Treatment is primarily directed by the primary tumor biology and disease burden and may include platinum agents such as cisplatin or carboplatin causing DNA crosslinking, fluoropyrimidines such as 5-fluorouracil inhib

Name: Tardive Dyskinesia
Description: Tardive dyskinesia (UMLS C0686347) is a usually persistent, often iatrogenic hyperkinetic movement disorder caused primarily by chronic exposure to dopamine receptor–blocking agents, especially antipsychotics and the antiemetic metoclopramide, and is characterized clinically by choreoathetoid or stereotypic involuntary movements of the tongue, lips, jaw, face, trunk, and limbs, including oro-buccal-lingual dyskinesia, grimacing, chewing motions, pelvic rocking, and, in some patients, tardive dystonia or akathisia. Its pathobiology is linked to maladaptive basal ganglia signaling involving dopamine D2 receptor supersensitivity, striatal medium spiny neurons, GABAergic and glutamatergic circuitry, serotonergic modulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and synaptic plasticity pathways; implicated genes and proteins include DRD2, DRD3, HTR2A, HTR2C, SLC6A3, COMT, CYP2D6, MnSOD/SOD2, and VMAT2/SLC18A2, with representative associations reported for DRD3 Ser9Gly and CYP2D6 poor-metabolizer variants, although inheritance is not Mendelian and genetic predisposition is polygenic and susceptibility-based. Important comorbidities and complications include schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, diabetes, older age, cognitive impairment, social disability, dysphagia, weight loss, aspiration, and reduced quality of life. Subtypes include classical oro-facial tardive dyskinesia, tardive dystonia, tardive akathisia, and tardive tremor. Diagnosis is clinical, based on delayed-onset involuntary movements after months of dopamine-blocking exposure and persistence beyond dose reduction or withdrawal, typically assessed with medication history, neurologic examination, the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale, and exclusion of mimics such as Huntington disease, Wilson disease, Parkinsonian syndromes, and primary dystonia through targeted laboratory tests or neuroimaging when indicated. Treatment centers on reducing or stopping the offending agent when feasible, switching to lower-risk antipsychotics such as clozapine or quetiapine, and using VMAT2 inhibitors including valbenazine and deutetrabenazine, which decrease presynaptic monoamine packaging and dopamine release, or tetrabenazine, a related VMAT

Name: Carcinoma in situ of adrenal cortex
Description: Carcinoma in situ of the adrenal cortex denotes a preinvasive neoplastic proliferation of adrenocortical epithelial cells confined above the basement membrane, an exceptionally rare and poorly characterized lesion generally considered within the spectrum of adrenocortical neoplasia that can precede invasive adrenocortical carcinoma. Molecularly, adrenal cortical tumorigenesis is linked to alterations in TP53, CTNNB1 (beta-catenin), ZNRF3, MEN1, PRKAR1A, RB1, and IGF2 overexpression, with occasional mismatch-repair defects and rare APC-associated Wnt activation; implicated pathways include Wnt/beta-catenin signaling, IGF2/IGF1R-PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling, p53/RB cell-cycle control, cAMP/PKA signaling, and steroidogenic programs mediated by SF1/NR5A1 and CYP11B1/CYP11B2. When clinically manifest, lesions may be nonfunctioning or hormone secreting, producing Cushing syndrome, virilization, feminization, hyperaldosteronism, or mixed steroid excess, with signs such as resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, weight gain, proximal myopathy, glucose intolerance, hirsutism, menstrual irregularity, or an incidentally discovered adrenal mass. Recognized related entities include functional versus nonfunctional tumors and progression to invasive low- or high-grade adrenocortical carcinoma; hereditary predisposition is uncommon but includes Li-Fraumeni syndrome with germline TP53 mutations, Lynch syndrome, MEN1, familial adenomatous polyposis, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome with 11p15/IGF2 dysregulation, and Carney complex with PRKAR1A variants, usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Diagnosis relies on endocrine evaluation with cortisol, ACTH, dexamethasone suppression, DHEAS, testosterone, estradiol, aldosterone-renin ratio, and steroid profiling, plus adrenal CT/MRI, and definitive pathologic assessment showing intraepithelial malignant cytology without stromal invasion, supported by Ki-67, p53, beta-catenin, SF1, inhibin, melan-A, and synaptophysin immunophenotyping. Name: Mineral deficiency
Description: Mineral deficiency is a heterogeneous nutritional and metabolic disorder characterized by inadequate body stores or impaired utilization of essential minerals such as iron, zinc, magnesium, calcium, phosphate, copper, selenium, and iodine, arising from poor intake, malabsorption, chronic disease, renal or gastrointestinal losses, or inherited transport defects. Genetic contributors are mineral-specific and include HFE, TMPRSS6, SLC11A2/DMT1, and TF for iron homeostasis; ATP7A and ATP7B for copper transport; SLC34A1, PHEX, FGF23, GALNT3, CYP27B1, VDR, CASR, and TRPM6 for phosphate, calcium, and magnesium balance; and SLC30A/ZIP transporter family genes for zinc handling, with representative mutations causing disorders such as iron-refractory iron deficiency anemia, Menkes disease, hypophosphatemic rickets, hereditary hypomagnesemia, and acrodermatitis enteropathica. Key pathways involve hepcidin–ferroportin signaling, erythropoietin-driven erythropoiesis, vitamin D–VDR, parathyroid hormone and calcium-sensing receptor signaling, FGF23–Klotho phosphate regulation, ATP7A/ATP7B copper trafficking, and redox and thyroid hormone pathways dependent on selenium and iodine. Clinical manifestations vary by mineral but commonly include fatigue, pallor, weakness, muscle cramps, paresthesias, bone pain, fractures, growth failure, glossitis, dermatitis, alopecia, impaired immunity, arrhythmias, and neurocognitive or endocrine dysfunction. Major subtypes are iron, zinc, magnesium, calcium/vitamin D-related, phosphate, copper, selenium, and iodine deficiency. Treatment is cause-specific and commonly includes ferrous sulfate, which replenishes elemental iron for hemoglobin synthesis; zinc sulfate, which restores zinc-dependent enzymatic and epithelial function; magnesium oxide or intravenous magnesium sulfate, which repletes intracellular magnesium; calcium carbonate, which supplies absorbable calcium; calcitriol, a vitamin D receptor agonist enhancing intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption; and potassium phosphate, which corrects phosphate depletion. Comorbidities and complications include anemia, osteoporosis/osteomalacia or rickets, cardiomyopathy, infertility, infection susceptibility, neuropathy, developmental delay, and thyroid disease. Diagnosis relies on history, diet and medication review, examination, and targeted testing such as CBC

Name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
Description: Community-acquired pneumonia (UMLS C0694549) is an acute infectious inflammation of the lung parenchyma acquired outside healthcare settings, most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, atypical bacteria such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, or respiratory viruses including influenza and SARS-CoV-2, and clinically presents with fever, cough with or without sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and crackles, sometimes with confusion or sepsis in older adults. Pathobiology is driven by innate and adaptive immune activation, particularly pattern-recognition receptor and Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, inflammasome, complement, and cytokine networks involving TNF, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, CXCL8, and interferons, with host susceptibility influenced by variants in genes such as TLR2, TLR4, TIRAP, MBL2, FCGR2A, CRP, IL6, TNF, HLA loci, CFTR, and mucin-related genes, although CAP is not typically a Mendelian disorder and inheritance is generally complex/polygenic rather than single-gene. Important microbial proteins include pneumococcal capsule polysaccharide and pneumolysin, staphylococcal Panton-Valentine leukocidin, and viral hemagglutinin or spike proteins. Major subtypes include typical versus atypical pneumonia, lobar versus bronchopneumonia, and severity strata such as nonsevere CAP versus severe CAP requiring ICU care. Common treatments include amoxicillin or ceftriaxone, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins; azithromycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit; doxycycline, which blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit; and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Frequent comorbidities include COPD, asthma, heart failure, diabetes, chronic kidney or liver disease, smoking, alcoholism, and immunosuppression; complications include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, acute respiratory distress syndrome, bacteremia, and septic shock. Name: Hypertrophic Subaortic Stenosis, Idiopathic
Description: Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a primary inherited myocardial disorder characterized by otherwise unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetric and involving the interventricular septum, with myocyte hypertrophy, disarray, and interstitial fibrosis; it most commonly follows an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance and expressivity and is caused predominantly by sarcomere gene mutations, especially in MYH7 encoding beta-myosin heavy chain and MYBPC3 encoding myosin-binding protein C, with additional cases involving TNNT2, TNNI3, TPM1, ACTC1, MYL2, and MYL3, while some phenocopies arise from PRKAG2, LAMP2, GLA, or mitochondrial defects. Pathobiology centers on abnormal sarcomeric force generation and calcium sensitivity, energetic inefficiency, and activation of hypertrophic and profibrotic signaling pathways including beta-adrenergic signaling, calcium/calmodulin-dependent pathways, calcineurin-NFAT, MAPK/ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, and TGF-beta-mediated fibrosis. Clinical expression ranges from nonobstructive to obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and less commonly apical, midventricular, or restrictive-like forms; typical manifestations include exertional dyspnea, angina, palpitations, presyncope or syncope, fatigue, harsh systolic murmur, and sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmia, with complications including atrial fibrillation, embolic stroke, heart failure, mitral regurgitation, myocardial ischemia, and progressive fibrosis. Treatment is largely symptom- and risk-directed: beta-blockers such as metoprolol reduce heart rate and contractility, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as verapamil improve diastolic filling and reduce inotropy, disopyramide provides negative inotropic sodium-channel blockade for obstructive disease, and cardiac myosin inhibition with mavacamten reduces excessive actin-myosin cross-bridge formation. Diagnosis relies on echocardiography or cardiac MRI showing unexplained wall thickness typically 15 mm or 13 mm in relatives, assessment of LVOT gradients, ECG abnormalities, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, family history, exclusion of secondary hypertrophy, and confirmatory or cascade genetic testing when a pathogenic variant is identified.

Name: Candidiasis, Vulvovaginal
Description: Vulvovaginal candidiasis is a common mucosal fungal infection, usually caused by Candida albicans but also by non-albicans species such as C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, and C. krusei, presenting with vulvar pruritus, burning, soreness, dyspareunia, dysuria, and thick adherent vaginal discharge with erythema and edema; complicated disease includes severe infection, recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, non-albicans infection, or disease in pregnancy or immunocompromised hosts. Pathogenesis reflects fungal adhesion and hyphal transformation mediated by adhesins and virulence proteins such as ALS family proteins, HWP1, SAP proteases, and candidalysin encoded by ECE1, interacting with host innate immune pathways involving TLR2/TLR4, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, CARD9, MyD88, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1β, IL-17/Th17 signaling, and epithelial neutrophil recruitment; genetic susceptibility is usually complex rather than Mendelian, but recurrent disease has been associated with variants in CLEC7A, CARD9, TLR2, TLR4, NLRP3, IL17A, IL17F, IL17RA, and mannose-binding lectin gene MBL2, while rare IL-17 pathway defects predispose to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use, estrogen exposure, HIV or other immunosuppression, obesity, and atopy; complications include recurrent infection, fissuring, excoriation, secondary bacterial infection, and impaired quality of life. Diagnosis is based on compatible symptoms plus demonstration of yeast, pseudohyphae, or hyphae by saline or 10 percent KOH microscopy, acidic to normal vaginal pH usually below 4.5, culture or speciation for recurrent or refractory cases, and increasingly nucleic acid amplification tests. Standard treatment includes azoles such as fluconazole, clotrimazole, and miconazole, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase to impair ergosterol synthesis, and for selected refractory or non-albicans cases boric acid, which exerts direct fungistatic and fungicidal intravaginal activity.

Name: Organophosphate Poisoning
Description: Organophosphate poisoning (UMLS C0700359) is an acute toxic cholinergic syndrome caused by inhibition of acetylcholinesterase and related esterases after exposure to agricultural insecticides or nerve agents, producing excess acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and central synapses. Core molecular targets include acetylcholinesterase encoded by ACHE, butyrylcholinesterase/BCHE, paraoxonase-1/PON1, and carboxylesterases such as CES1; genetic susceptibility is influenced by variants including PON1 Q192R and L55M and BCHE atypical alleles, which alter detoxification or bioscavenging capacity, although the disorder itself is acquired rather than inherited. Pathobiology centers on cholinergic signaling through muscarinic receptors, nicotinic receptor activation at the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, CNS excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and, after enzyme aging, irreversible phosphorylated AChE complexes. Clinical manifestations include miosis, diaphoresis, salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhea, urination, fasciculations, weakness, paralysis, seizures, coma, and respiratory failure; recognized forms include acute crisis, intermediate syndrome, organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy, and chronic neuropsychiatric sequelae. Major complications and comorbidities include aspiration pneumonia, acute respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmias, pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive impairment, depression, and prolonged ventilator dependence. Diagnosis relies on exposure history plus a cholinergic toxidrome, depressed erythrocyte AChE and plasma butyrylcholinesterase activity, supportive toxicology testing for parent compounds or urinary dialkyl phosphate metabolites, and cardiopulmonary and neurologic monitoring. Treatment includes atropine, a competitive muscarinic antagonist that reverses secretions and bronchoconstriction; pralidoxime or other oximes, which reactivate phosphorylated AChE before aging and improve nicotinic weakness; diazepam or other benzodiazepines for seizure control and neuroprotection; and aggressive decontamination, oxygenation, and ventilatory support.

Name: Adrenogenital disorder (disorder)
Description: Adrenogenital disorder most commonly refers to congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a group of inherited adrenal steroidogenesis disorders characterized by impaired cortisol biosynthesis with compensatory hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation, excess ACTH signaling through melanocortin 2 receptor, adrenal hyperplasia, and diversion of steroid precursors into androgen pathways; the classic molecular cause is biallelic CYP21A2 mutation encoding 21-hydroxylase, while less common forms involve CYP11B1, HSD3B2, CYP17A1, STAR, and POR, affecting proteins such as 11β-hydroxylase, 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase, steroidogenic acute regulatory protein, and P450 oxidoreductase. These defects disrupt cholesterol transport and adrenal mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid, and androgen biosynthetic pathways, involving cholesterol side-chain cleavage, cAMP-dependent ACTH signaling, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone regulation. The main subtypes are classic salt-wasting, classic simple virilizing, and nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, with genotype-phenotype correlation in many CYP21A2 variants. Clinical features include ambiguous genitalia or virilization in 46,XX infants, precocious pseudopuberty, rapid growth with advanced bone age, acne, hirsutism, menstrual dysfunction, infertility, dehydration, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and adrenal crisis; 11β-hydroxylase deficiency may cause hypertension. Comorbidities and complications include short adult stature, metabolic syndrome, testicular adrenal rest tumors, osteoporosis, psychosocial morbidity, and reduced fertility. Diagnosis relies on newborn screening and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, confirmatory ACTH stimulation testing, serum steroid panels, electrolytes, plasma renin, androgen measurements, urinary steroid profiling, genetic testing, and imaging when anatomy or tumors require clarification. Treatment commonly includes hydrocortisone, prednisone, or dexamethasone to replace glucocorticoids and suppress ACTH-driven androgen excess, fludrocortisone as a mineralocorticoid receptor agonist for salt-wasting disease, and sodium supplementation in infancy; stress-dose glucocort

Name: Bacterial urinary infection
Description: Bacterial urinary infection, encompassing lower urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis, is an acute infectious-inflammatory disorder of the urinary tract, most often caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli but also Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus; clinical subtypes include uncomplicated cystitis, complicated UTI, catheter-associated UTI, recurrent UTI, asymptomatic bacteriuria, and upper-tract infection. Symptoms typically include dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy or malodorous urine, and hematuria, while fever, flank pain, costovertebral-angle tenderness, nausea, and sepsis suggest pyelonephritis. Host susceptibility has a multifactorial rather than Mendelian basis, with representative genetic components involving innate defense and epithelial adherence pathways, including TLR4, TLR5, CXCR1/CXCR2, DEFB1, HSPA1B, and secretor-status FUT2 variation; bacterial virulence determinants include type 1 fimbriae FimH, P fimbriae PapG, hemolysin, and siderophore systems. Key pathways include urothelial TLR-mediated recognition of lipopolysaccharide and flagellin, NF-kB activation, IL-6/IL-8–driven neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and intracellular bacterial community formation within bladder epithelium. Important comorbidities and risk factors include female sex, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, urinary obstruction, nephrolithiasis, vesicoureteral reflux, neurogenic bladder, benign prostatic hyperplasia, catheterization, and spinal cord injury; complications include renal abscess, emphysematous infection, bacteremia, sepsis, recurrent scarring, and preterm birth in pregnancy. Diagnosis relies on symptoms plus urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and sometimes hematuria, with urine culture and susceptibility testing as the microbiologic standard, and blood cultures or renal imaging used in severe, recurrent, or obstructive cases. Name: Infective otitis media
Description: Infective otitis media is an infection-driven inflammatory disorder of the middle ear, usually classified as acute otitis media, otitis media with effusion, recurrent acute otitis media, or chronic suppurative otitis media, arising from eustachian tube dysfunction and microbial invasion, most commonly by Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and in chronic disease sometimes Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus. Host susceptibility has a polygenic, non-Mendelian basis, with representative associations involving cytokine and innate-immunity genes such as TNF, IL6, IL10, TLR4, TLR2, FBXO11, FUT2, and MUC5B/MUC2, which influence mucosal defense, biofilm formation, and middle-ear remodeling; rare syndromic predisposition occurs in disorders affecting ciliary or craniofacial development. Key pathways include Toll-like receptor, NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome, complement, and mucin-secretory signaling, with epithelial cells, neutrophils, macrophages, and bacterial biofilms central to persistence. Typical features are otalgia, fever, irritability, conductive hearing loss, aural fullness, otorrhea if tympanic membrane perforation is present, and on otoscopy a bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane with middle-ear effusion. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by pneumatic otoscopy and tympanometry demonstrating effusion; hearing assessment, culture of otorrhea in refractory or chronic cases, and occasionally imaging for suspected mastoiditis or intracranial spread are used. Standard therapy includes amoxicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation; amoxicillin-clavulanate, which adds beta-lactamase inhibition; azithromycin, a macrolide that blocks the 50S ribosomal subunit; and topical or systemic fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin in selected chronic or perforated cases, inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Name: Infective blepharitis
Description: Infective blepharitis (UMLS C0729587) is a common inflammatory disorder of the eyelid margins, usually caused by bacterial colonization, classically Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and less often streptococci, with anterior and posterior forms that overlap with seborrheic and meibomian gland dysfunction phenotypes. It is not a Mendelian disease and has no established inheritance pattern, but host susceptibility is influenced by genes regulating innate immunity and epithelial inflammation, with representative associations proposed for TLR2, TLR4, IL1B, TNF, DEFB4, MUC1, and HLA-linked immune response variation; relevant proteins include toll-like receptors, IL-1β, TNF-α, matrix metalloproteinases, mucins, and antimicrobial peptides. Pathobiology involves bacterial biofilm formation at the lid margin, lipase-mediated alteration of meibomian secretions, activation of TLR–NF-κB and MAPK signaling, neutrophilic and Th1/Th17 cytokine responses, complement activation, and tear-film instability that promotes chronic ocular surface inflammation. Typical symptoms are eyelid redness, burning, itching, foreign-body sensation, crusting on waking, photophobia, fluctuating vision, and dry-eye complaints; signs include collarettes, lid-margin hyperemia, ulceration, meibomian plugging, frothy tear film, conjunctival injection, and punctate keratopathy. Diagnosis is mainly clinical by slit-lamp examination, with selective use of lid-margin swab culture, meibomian secretion assessment, fluorescein staining, tear breakup time, and evaluation for Demodex or rosacea. Standard treatment combines lid hygiene with topical erythromycin or bacitracin, which inhibit bacterial protein synthesis and cell-wall synthesis respectively, azithromycin, a macrolide that suppresses ribosomal translation and reduces inflammation, and oral doxycycline, which inhibits the 30S ribosome and also suppresses bacterial lipases and MMP activity; fusidic acid or fluoroquinolone drops may be used in resistant cases. Important comorbidities and complications include seborrheic dermatitis, acne rosacea, chronic dry eye, recurrent hordeolum or chalazion, conjunctivitis, trichiasis, madarosis, marginal keratitis, corneal ulceration, and rarely vision-threatening scarring.

Name: Infective laryngitis
Description: Infective laryngitis (UMLS C0729772) is an acute or less commonly chronic inflammatory infection of the laryngeal mucosa, usually viral but also bacterial or fungal, producing edema and dysfunction of the vocal folds and adjacent supraglottic tissues. It most often presents with hoarseness or aphonia, throat pain, dry cough, odynophagia, fever, and laryngeal erythema/edema on examination, with severe cases causing stridor or airway compromise. Major infectious subtypes include viral laryngitis associated with rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, RSV, adenovirus, or SARS-CoV-2, bacterial disease due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, or less often Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and fungal laryngitis, especially Candida, in immunocompromised hosts or after inhaled corticosteroids. Molecularly, host defense is driven by innate immune pathways rather than a single disease gene, with viral sensing through TLR3, TLR7, RIG-I/DDX58, and MDA5/IFIH1 activating NF-kB, IRF3/7, type I interferons, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and chemokine-mediated leukocyte recruitment; representative susceptibility genes in severe respiratory infection biology include IFIH1, TLR3, IRF7, and ACE2/TMPRSS2 in SARS-CoV-2-related disease, but infective laryngitis itself has no established Mendelian inheritance pattern. Treatment is etiology-directed and supportive: acetaminophen inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis for pain/fever, ibuprofen inhibits COX-1/2, amoxicillin-clavulanate blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis and beta-lactamase activity when bacterial superinfection is suspected, azithromycin binds the 50S ribosome, and fluconazole inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis in candidal laryngitis. Important comorbidities include upper respiratory tract infection, sinusitis, GERD/laryngopharyngeal reflux, smoking, asthma, COPD, diabetes, and immunosuppression; complications include chronic dysphonia, secondary bacterial infection, epiglottic or subglottic extension, pneumonia, and rarely abscess or airway obstruction. Name: Severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Description: Severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is an advanced, largely smoking- and biomass-related heterogeneous airway and parenchymal lung disorder characterized by persistent, usually progressive airflow limitation caused by small-airway inflammation/remodeling and emphysematous alveolar destruction; major molecular drivers include protease-antiprotease imbalance, oxidative stress, and dysregulated innate immunity, with genetic contributors such as SERPINA1 mutations causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as the clearest Mendelian risk factor, and susceptibility loci in CHRNA3/5, HHIP, FAM13A, MMP12, TGFB1, GSTM1, and EPHX1, alongside proteins and mediators including neutrophil elastase, MMP-9, MMP-12, TNF, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, CRP, TGF-beta, and reduced HDAC2 activity. Key pathways include NF-kappaB, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, TGF-beta/SMAD, Nrf2 antioxidant signaling, and chemokine-mediated neutrophil and macrophage recruitment. Severe COPD commonly presents with exertional dyspnea, chronic cough, sputum production, wheeze, chest tightness, hyperinflation, exercise intolerance, hypoxemia, and frequent exacerbations, and major phenotypic subtypes include emphysema-predominant, chronic bronchitis-predominant, frequent-exacerbator, eosinophilic COPD, and alpha-1 antitrypsin-deficiency-associated disease. Diagnosis is based on compatible exposure history and symptoms plus post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1/FVC less than 0.70, with severity assessed by FEV1 reduction, symptom burden, exacerbation history, pulse oximetry or arterial blood gases, chest radiography or CT, diffusion capacity, and selected testing for eosinophils or SERPINA1 deficiency. Standard therapies include bronchodilators such as tiotropium, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist that inhibits M3-mediated bronchoconstriction, salmeterol or formoterol, long-acting beta2-agonists that increase cAMP, inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone that suppress inflammatory gene transcription, phosphodiesterase-4 inhibition with roflumilast, rescue albuterol, and in alpha-1 deficiency augmentation therapy

Name: Hyperuricemia
Description: Hyperuricemia (UMLS C0740394) is a biochemical disorder defined by persistently elevated serum urate, usually from impaired renal or intestinal urate excretion and less often from urate overproduction, and it may be asymptomatic or progress to monosodium urate crystal disease. Key genetic contributors include urate transport genes such as SLC2A9 (GLUT9), ABCG2, SLC22A12 (URAT1), SLC17A1, and SLC22A11, with rarer monogenic causes involving HPRT1 deficiency, PRPS1 superactivity, UMOD-related tubulointerstitial disease, and renal hypouricemia genes that alter handling pathways; familial clustering is typically complex polygenic, although X-linked HPRT1 and other Mendelian disorders occur. Pathobiology centers on purine catabolism via xanthine oxidoreductase generating uric acid, dysregulated proximal tubular transport through URAT1, GLUT9, OATs, and ABCG2, and downstream crystal-triggered inflammation through the NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1β, neutrophils, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction. Major clinical associations include gout, uric acid nephrolithiasis, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease; complications include recurrent arthritis, tophi, nephropathy, and stone obstruction. Symptoms and signs are often absent until complications develop, but may include episodic podagra or other acute inflammatory arthritis, tophi, renal colic, hematuria, and reduced kidney function. Subtypes include underexcretion versus overproduction hyperuricemia, primary versus secondary forms, and asymptomatic versus symptomatic disease. Diagnosis relies on elevated serum urate, typically above urate solubility thresholds, with assessment of renal function, urinary uric acid excretion or fractional excretion, stone analysis when relevant, medication and dietary review, and genetic testing in early-onset, familial, or syndromic cases; confirmation of gout requires identification of negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals. Common treatments include allopurinol and febuxostat, which inhibit xanthine oxidase, probenecid, which increases renal urate excretion by inhibiting URAT1, and pegloticase, a recombinant uricase that converts urate to allantoin

Name: Acute diarrhea
Description: Acute diarrhea is a usually self-limited syndrome defined clinically by the passage of increased-frequency, loose or watery stools for less than 14 days, most often caused by infectious gastroenteritis but also by toxin exposure, medications, inflammatory conditions, ischemia, or acute malabsorption; major subtypes include secretory, osmotic, inflammatory/exudative, and dysmotility-associated diarrhea, as well as viral, bacterial, and parasitic forms. Typical manifestations are abrupt watery or bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramping, urgency, nausea, vomiting, fever, dehydration, orthostasis, and electrolyte disturbances, with complications including hypovolemia, acute kidney injury, metabolic acidosis, hemolytic-uremic syndrome, sepsis, and post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome; common comorbid settings include malnutrition, immunosuppression, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes, and recent antibiotic exposure with Clostridioides difficile colitis. Although most acute diarrhea is not inherited, host susceptibility and specific syndromic forms have genetic components involving epithelial transport and innate immunity genes and proteins such as CFTR, SLC26A3, SCNN1B, NHE3/SLC9A3, aquaporins, TLR4, NOD2, IL8, TNF, and MUC2, while pathogen-host signaling often converges on cAMP-, cGMP-, calcium-, prostaglandin-, and NF-kappaB-mediated pathways; representative examples include cholera toxin ADP-ribosylation of GNAS-regulated adenylate cyclase causing CFTR-mediated chloride secretion and rotavirus NSP4 provoking calcium-dependent secretion. Treatment is primarily supportive with oral rehydration solution using sodium-glucose cotransport via SGLT1, intravenous crystalloids for severe dehydration, loperamide as a peripheral mu-opioid receptor agonist reducing intestinal motility, bismuth subsalicylate with antisecretory and antimicrobial effects, and when indicated antibiotics such as azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, rifaximin, oral vancomycin, or fidaxomicin depending on etiology. Diagnosis rests on acute symptom duration, exposure history, hydration assessment, and stool characteristics, supplemented selectively by stool culture, multiplex PCR panels, ova and parasite testing, C. difficile toxin/PCR assays, fecal leukocytes or calprotectin, serum electrolytes and creatinine, and rarely endoscopy in severe

Name: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
Description: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (UMLS C0740447) is a common, usually length-dependent, distal symmetric sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy caused by chronic diabetes-related metabolic and microvascular injury, with painful and painless forms and focal or multifocal variants such as mononeuropathies and radiculoplexus neuropathy. Its pathobiology centers on hyperglycemia-driven polyol flux via aldose reductase, advanced glycation end-product/RAGE signaling, oxidative and nitrosative stress, protein kinase C activation, PARP-mediated DNA damage responses, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation involving TNF, IL-6 and NF-kB, impaired PI3K-Akt insulin/neurotrophin signaling, and microvascular ischemia; representative susceptibility genes and proteins reported include AKR1B1, ACE, APOE, NOS3, VEGFA, MTHFR, SOD2, CAT, NGF, BDNF, SCN9A and TCF7L2, although inheritance is generally complex polygenic rather than Mendelian. Patients typically develop numbness, burning pain, paresthesias, allodynia, reduced vibration and pinprick sensation, distal weakness, gait imbalance, reduced ankle reflexes, and autonomic features such as orthostasis or gastroparesis. Diagnosis relies on established diabetes with compatible symptoms and signs, exclusion of alternative causes, bedside sensory testing with 10-g monofilament, vibration or temperature assessment, reflex examination, validated scores such as the Toronto criteria or Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument, and selected nerve conduction studies, quantitative sensory or autonomic testing, and skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density when small-fiber neuropathy is suspected. Major comorbidities and complications include poor glycemic control, obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, retinopathy, cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, foot ulceration, Charcot arthropathy, infection, falls and amputation. Treatment emphasizes glucose and risk-factor control plus symptomatic analgesia, commonly duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor enhancing descending inhibitory pain pathways, pregabalin or gabapentin, which bind the alpha2delta calcium-channel subunit to reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release, and tricyclics such as amitriptyline, which inhibit norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake and sodium channels; topical capsaicin and sodium-channel

Name: Paroxysmal atrial flutter
Description: Paroxysmal atrial flutter is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by abrupt, self-terminating episodes of rapid, organized atrial activity, most often due to a macroreentrant circuit in the right atrium involving the cavotricuspid isthmus in typical flutter, with atypical left- or right-atrial circuits occurring in the setting of prior ablation, surgery, or structural heart disease. It commonly presents with palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, lightheadedness, reduced exercise tolerance, or syncope, and examination may show a rapid regular pulse, tachycardia, and signs of heart failure. Although usually multifactorial rather than classically Mendelian, genetic susceptibility overlaps with atrial fibrillation and other atrial arrhythmias; reported associated genes include ion-channel and cardiac developmental genes such as SCN5A, KCNQ1, KCNA5, GJA5 connexin-40, NPPA, PITX2, TBX5, and NKX2-5, with rare familial clustering and mostly autosomal dominant inheritance of predisposing variants with incomplete penetrance. Relevant mechanisms include impaired atrial conduction, shortening or heterogeneity of atrial refractoriness, fibrosis, inflammation, stretch, and remodeling mediated by sodium, potassium, and calcium handling, gap-junction signaling, autonomic tone, and pathways involving TGF-β, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling, and oxidative stress. Major comorbidities include hypertension, coronary artery disease, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, heart failure, chronic lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea, hyperthyroidism, obesity, diabetes, and alcohol use; important complications are tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy and thromboembolism, especially stroke. Diagnosis is based on ECG showing sawtooth flutter waves, usually at 240-340 beats/min with commonly 2:1 AV conduction, supported by ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography, electrophysiology study, and laboratory evaluation for reversible triggers. Treatment includes rate control with beta-blockers such as metoprolol, nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as diltiazem or verapamil, rhythm control with ibutilide, dofetilide, amiodarone, or sotalol through potassium-channel blockade and action-potential prolongation, anticoag

Name: Bacterial cystitis
Description: Bacterial cystitis is an acute or recurrent bacterial infection of the urinary bladder, usually caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli but also Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus, and it is clinically characterized by dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy or malodorous urine, pyuria, and sometimes hematuria, with fever or flank pain suggesting upper tract extension rather than isolated cystitis. Pathogenesis centers on bacterial adherence and invasion of urothelial cells through adhesins such as type 1 fimbrial FimH and P fimbriae, activation of TLR4-, IL6-, IL8/CXCL8-, NF-kB-, and neutrophil-driven innate immune pathways, and epithelial antimicrobial responses involving defensins, uromodulin encoded by UMOD, and mucosal glycosaminoglycan barriers; host susceptibility has been associated with variants in TLR4, CXCR1, CXCR2, HSPA1B, VEGFA, and secretor status determined by FUT2, although inheritance is complex and non-Mendelian, with rare monogenic predisposition mainly in congenital urinary tract malformations or immunodeficiency states rather than cystitis itself. Subtypes include uncomplicated cystitis, complicated cystitis associated with catheterization, obstruction, stones, pregnancy, diabetes, neurogenic bladder, or male sex, as well as recurrent cystitis and emphysematous cystitis. Diagnosis is based on symptoms plus urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase, or nitrites, with urine culture and susceptibility testing, typically significant bacteriuria in the appropriate clinical context, used in complicated, recurrent, male, pregnant, or treatment-failure cases; imaging or cystoscopy is reserved for suspected obstruction, fistula, stones, abscess, or structural disease. Common therapies include nitrofurantoin, which is reduced intracellularly to reactive intermediates that damage bacterial DNA and ribosomal proteins, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which sequentially inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase, fosfomycin, which blocks MurA and peptidoglycan synthesis, and selected beta-lactams or fluoroquinolones, with complications including recurrent UTI, pyelonephritis, sepsis, and, rarely, renal injury.

Name: Hypertensive Emergency
Description: Hypertensive emergency is an acute, life-threatening syndrome of severe blood pressure elevation, typically systolic blood pressure at or above 180 mmHg and/or diastolic pressure at or above 120 mmHg, accompanied by rapidly progressive target-organ injury rather than defined by pressure alone. It most often arises in patients with chronic essential hypertension but may also occur in secondary forms driven by renal parenchymal disease, renovascular hypertension, endocrine disorders, pregnancy-related syndromes, sympathomimetic exposure, or catecholamine excess. Pathobiology centers on abrupt failure of vascular autoregulation, endothelial injury, oxidative stress, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation, sympathetic overactivity, nitric oxide depletion, endothelin signaling, calcium-dependent vasoconstriction, and inflammatory/thrombotic microvascular injury; implicated genetic contributors to hypertension susceptibility include ACE, AGT, AGTR1, REN, NOS3, CYP11B2, SCNN1B/SCNN1G, and WNK1/WNK4, with rare monogenic forms such as Liddle syndrome or glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism predisposing to severe hypertension, although hypertensive emergency itself is not usually inherited in a Mendelian fashion. Clinical manifestations reflect organ damage and include severe headache, visual disturbance, confusion, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, chest pain, dyspnea, pulmonary edema, oliguria, and retinal hemorrhages or papilledema; major subtypes include hypertensive encephalopathy, acute ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke with severe hypertension, acute aortic syndromes, acute left ventricular failure, eclampsia, pheochromocytoma crisis, and thrombotic microangiopathic presentations. Commonly used intravenous therapies include nicardipine or clevidipine, dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers that reduce arteriolar tone; labetalol, combined alpha1- and beta-adrenergic blockade; nitroprusside, a nitric oxide donor causing balanced vasodilation; nitroglycerin for coronary ischemia or pulmonary edema; hydralazine in selected pregnancy-related cases; and esmolol for aortic dissection.
