Name: Hypertensive Urgency
Description: Hypertensive urgency (UMLS C0745138) is an acute severe elevation of blood pressure, typically systolic at least 180 mmHg and/or diastolic at least 120 mmHg, without convincing evidence of ongoing acute target-organ injury, and is best regarded as a clinical syndrome rather than a single genetic disease; symptoms may include severe headache, dizziness, anxiety, palpitations, dyspnea, epistaxis, nausea, or chest discomfort, although some patients are minimally symptomatic, and the key distinction from hypertensive emergency is the absence of hypertensive encephalopathy, acute pulmonary edema, myocardial ischemia, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, or retinal hemorrhage/papilledema. Its biology overlaps with essential and secondary hypertension, involving dysregulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system, endothelial nitric oxide signaling, oxidative stress, vascular smooth-muscle calcium handling, and renal sodium transport; representative genetic contributors to hypertension susceptibility include ACE and AGT variants, AGTR1, REN, CYP11B2, NOS3, SCNN1B/SCNN1G in Liddle syndrome, WNK1/WNK4 in pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2, and CYP11B1/CYP17A1 or KCNJ5 in endocrine forms, with inheritance usually multifactorial/polygenic but occasionally monogenic, often autosomal dominant. Common comorbidities include chronic essential hypertension, chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, coronary artery disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, and medication nonadherence or withdrawal, as well as stimulant or cocaine use. Management relies on gradual blood-pressure reduction with oral agents such as captopril, an ACE inhibitor that reduces angiotensin II formation; clonidine, a central alpha2-agonist that lowers sympathetic outflow; and labetalol, a combined alpha1/beta-adrenergic blocker that decreases systemic vascular resistance and heart rate, with amlodipine or nifedipine acting via L-type calcium-channel blockade in selected settings. Diagnosis requires repeated validated blood-pressure measurements plus focused history, examination, fundoscopy, ECG, urinalysis, serum creatinine/electrolytes, and targeted troponin or imaging only when symptoms suggest end-organ injury; subtypes are usually primary versus secondary hypertension presenting with urgency.

Name: Erythrodermic psoriasis
Description: Erythrodermic psoriasis (UMLS C0748052) is a severe, potentially life-threatening inflammatory variant of psoriasis in which diffuse erythema and scaling involve most of the body surface area, often arising from plaque psoriasis but also occurring de novo; major subtypes are acute unstable and chronic stable forms. It is driven by dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity centered on the IL-23/Th17 and TNF-alpha axes, with contributions from IL-17A/F, IL-22, NF-kappaB, JAK-STAT signaling, dendritic cells, neutrophils, and keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Genetic susceptibility overlaps with psoriasis vulgaris, including PSORS1/HLA-C*06:02 and variants in IL23R, IL12B, TNIP1, TRAF3IP2, CARD14, and late cornified envelope genes such as LCE3B/LCE3C; rare pustular/erythrodermic overlap may involve IL36RN mutations, and inheritance is typically complex polygenic rather than Mendelian, although familial clustering is recognized. Clinically, patients develop generalized fiery erythema, exfoliative scale, pruritus, pain, edema, fever, chills, malaise, dehydration, thermoregulatory instability, and high-output cardiac stress, with complications including secondary infection, sepsis, electrolyte imbalance, protein loss, acute kidney injury, and hospitalization. Comorbidities parallel severe psoriasis and include psoriatic arthritis, obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, depression, and inflammatory bowel disease. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, usually requiring erythema and desquamation affecting more than 75 to 90 percent of the body surface area in a patient with personal or histologic evidence of psoriasis; skin biopsy shows psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with parakeratosis and diminished granular layer, while laboratory testing assesses CBC, albumin, renal and hepatic function, inflammatory markers, and infection, and helps exclude mimics such as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, drug eruption, and atopic erythroderma. Name: Biliary Tract Cancers
Description: Biliary tract cancers (UMLS C0750952) are aggressive epithelial malignancies arising from the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, gallbladder, and ampulla, classically grouped as cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma, with anatomic subtypes including intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. They are usually sporadic rather than inherited, but genetic susceptibility is increased in hereditary cancer syndromes such as Lynch syndrome and BRCA1/2- or PALB2-associated homologous recombination deficiency, while somatic alterations commonly involve KRAS, TP53, SMAD4, CDKN2A, ERBB2/HER2 amplification, BRAF V600E, FGFR2 fusions, and IDH1 mutations, with overexpression or dysregulation of proteins such as EGFR, VEGF, and PD-L1. These tumors are driven by MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, receptor tyrosine kinase, TGF-beta/SMAD, Wnt/beta-catenin, Notch, angiogenic, inflammatory IL-6/JAK/STAT, and immune-checkpoint pathways. Major risk factors and comorbid conditions include primary sclerosing cholangitis, choledochal cysts, hepatolithiasis, liver fluke infection, chronic viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, cholelithiasis, obesity, diabetes, and chronic cholangitis; complications include biliary obstruction, recurrent infection, hepatic failure, cachexia, and metastatic spread. Typical presentation includes painless jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, anorexia, fever, cholestatic liver test abnormalities, and sometimes a gallbladder mass. Diagnosis integrates liver biochemistry, CA 19-9 and CEA as adjunctive markers, multiphasic CT or MRI/MRCP, ERCP or EUS-guided brushings/biopsy, histopathology with immunophenotyping, staging, and increasingly next-generation sequencing to detect actionable alterations. Standard systemic therapy includes gemcitabine, a nucleoside analog inhibiting DNA synthesis, cisplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum agent, and 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine, thymidylate synthase inhibitors; selected patients may receive targeted agents such as pem

Name: Brain Neoplasms, Malignant, Primary
Description: Brain neoplasms comprise a heterogeneous group of primary and metastatic intracranial tumors arising from glial, meningeal, neuronal, embryonal, pituitary, or other CNS-associated cells, ranging from indolent lesions to highly aggressive malignancies; major subtypes include diffuse astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma, ependymoma, medulloblastoma, meningioma, schwannoma, and brain metastases. Their molecular landscape commonly involves alterations in IDH1/IDH2, TP53, ATRX, TERT promoter, EGFR amplification or EGFRvIII, PTEN loss, CDKN2A/B deletion, PDGFRA, BRAF V600E, H3 K27M, 1p/19q codeletion, MGMT promoter methylation, and NF2, with inherited predisposition in syndromes such as neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and APC-associated Turcot syndrome, although most cases are sporadic. Dysregulated signaling often centers on RTK/RAS/RAF/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, p53, RB cell-cycle, WNT/β-catenin, SHH, Notch, angiogenic VEGF, and epigenetic programs. Typical manifestations include headache, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, cognitive or personality change, aphasia, visual disturbance, gait imbalance, nausea/vomiting from raised intracranial pressure, and endocrine symptoms in sellar tumors. Common complications and comorbidities include cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, epilepsy, neurocognitive decline, endocrinopathies, depression, and treatment-related radionecrosis or myelosuppression. Diagnosis relies on contrast-enhanced MRI, sometimes CT for hemorrhage or calcification, advanced imaging such as perfusion or spectroscopy, histopathology integrated with molecular testing per WHO CNS classification, including immunohistochemistry, FISH, PCR, and next-generation sequencing; CSF cytology is useful in select leptomeningeal or embryonal tumors. Name: Epilepsy, Myoclonic, Infantile, Severe
Description: Myoclonic epilepsies are a heterogeneous group of epileptic disorders defined by brief, shock-like myoclonic jerks arising from cortical hyperexcitability, ranging from genetic generalized epilepsies such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies including Dravet syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut spectrum cases with myoclonus, progressive myoclonic epilepsies such as Unverricht-Lundborg disease, Lafora disease, and mitochondrial forms such as MERRF. Their molecular basis commonly involves ion-channel and synaptic genes, with representative examples including SCN1A, GABRA1, GABRD, CACNB4, EFHC1, CSTB, EPM2A, NHLRC1, SLC2A1, CHD2, and mitochondrial MT-TK mutations; implicated pathways include impaired GABAergic inhibition, altered voltage-gated sodium and calcium channel signaling, synaptic vesicle release, glutamatergic excitation, glycogen metabolism with polyglucosan accumulation in Lafora disease, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation dysfunction. Clinical features typically include myoclonic jerks, often after awakening, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, sometimes absence or atonic seizures, photosensitivity, and in severe forms developmental delay, ataxia, cognitive regression, and stimulus sensitivity. Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, mitochondrial, or complex/polygenic depending on subtype; for example, SCN1A-related disease is usually de novo dominant, CSTB and EPM2A/NHLRC1 disorders are recessive, and MERRF is maternally inherited. Common comorbidities and complications include intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, depression and anxiety, injuries, status epilepticus, SUDEP, gait impairment, and progressive neurodegeneration in PME. Diagnosis rests on seizure semiology, family history, neurologic examination, EEG showing generalized spike- or polyspike-wave discharges, photoparoxysmal response or background slowing, brain MRI to exclude structural causes, metabolic and mitochondrial testing when indicated, and targeted gene panels, exome sequencing, or specific assays such as skin biopsy for Lafora bodies. Name: Narcolepsy-Cataplexy Syndrome
Description: Narcolepsy (MeSH D009290) is a chronic central disorder of hypersomnolence characterized by instability of sleep–wake regulation, classically presenting with excessive daytime sleepiness, irresistible sleep attacks, fragmented nocturnal sleep, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, and, in type 1 disease, cataplexy. Its core biology centers on loss or dysfunction of hypothalamic orexin/hypocretin neurons, with deficient hypocretin-1 signaling through orexin receptors OX1R and OX2R and downstream arousal networks involving histaminergic, noradrenergic, dopaminergic, serotonergic, and cholinergic pathways; autoimmune mechanisms are strongly implicated, particularly in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02, often with associations at T-cell receptor loci such as TCRA and other immune-related genes including P2RY11 and CTSH. Rare familial or syndromic cases involve variants affecting hypocretin signaling, including HCRT, HCRTR2, or broader neurologic disorders, but most cases are sporadic with complex polygenic risk rather than Mendelian inheritance. Major subtypes are narcolepsy type 1, defined by cataplexy and/or low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1, and type 2, in which cataplexy is absent and hypocretin is usually normal or unmeasured. Diagnosis relies on clinical history plus polysomnography followed by multiple sleep latency testing showing mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with at least two sleep-onset REM periods; CSF hypocretin-1 measurement and HLA typing can support diagnosis. Common comorbidities include obesity, depression, anxiety, attention and cognitive difficulties, obstructive sleep apnea, REM sleep behavior phenomena, and accident risk. Treatment is symptomatic: modafinil or armodafinil promote wakefulness partly via dopaminergic catecholamine effects; solriamfetol inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake; pitolisant is an H3-receptor inverse agonist enhancing histaminergic arousal; and sodium oxybate or low-sodium oxybate, acting through GABA-B–related mechanisms, improve daytime sleepiness and cataplexy, while antidepressants such as venlafaxine or clomipramine suppress cataplexy via monoaminergic REM inhibition.

Name: Phenylketonuria, Classical
Description: Classical phenylketonuria (PKU; UMLS C0751434) is a severe autosomal recessive inborn error of phenylalanine metabolism caused predominantly by biallelic pathogenic variants in PAH on chromosome 12q23.2, which encodes hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase; representative missense mutations include p.Arg408Trp and p.Ile65Thr, among many alleles that reduce or abolish PAH activity. The biochemical consequence is failure of conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, leading to hyperphenylalaninemia, excess phenylketones, relative tyrosine deficiency, saturation of the LAT1 large neutral amino acid transporter at the blood-brain barrier, impaired cerebral uptake of tyrosine and tryptophan, reduced catecholamine and serotonin synthesis, defective melanogenesis, oxidative stress, and disturbed myelination. Classical PKU is the most severe PAH-deficiency subtype, distinct from milder hyperphenylalaninemia and from tetrahydrobiopterin-related disorders involving genes such as PTS, QDPR, GCH1, or PCBD1. Untreated infants typically develop progressive intellectual disability, developmental delay, microcephaly, seizures, eczema, hypopigmentation, musty body odor, behavioral and psychiatric disturbances, and later executive dysfunction; important complications include maternal PKU embryopathy, osteopenia, and nutritional deficiencies. Diagnosis is established by newborn screening showing markedly elevated blood phenylalanine, followed by quantitative plasma amino acid analysis, urine pterin studies and dihydropteridine reductase testing to exclude BH4 defects, PAH molecular testing, and in some cases BH4 responsiveness testing. Treatment centers on a lifelong phenylalanine-restricted diet with medical amino acid formula; sapropterin dihydrochloride, a synthetic tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor, enhances residual PAH activity in responsive genotypes; pegvaliase, a pegylated recombinant phenylalanine ammonia lyase, enzymatically degrades phenylalanine to trans-cinnamic acid and ammonia; and large neutral amino acid supplements competitively reduce brain phenylalanine influx.

Name: Hyperphenylalaninemia, Non Phenylketonuric
Description: Non-phenylketonuric hyperphenylalaninemia is a heterogeneous group of inherited disorders characterized by persistent elevation of blood phenylalanine without the classic severe phenotype of phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, most often reflecting defects in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis, recycling, or responsiveness; implicated genes include PTS encoding 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase, QDPR encoding dihydropteridine reductase, GCH1 encoding GTP cyclohydrolase I, PCBD1 encoding pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase, and rarely DNAJC12, with representative biallelic pathogenic variants causing autosomal recessive disease, although some GCH1-related states may be dominant. The core biochemical pathway involves phenylalanine hydroxylase and its BH4 cofactor, with related impairment of tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, reducing dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and serotonin synthesis; nitric oxide synthase function may also be affected. Clinical expression ranges from mild, transient, or benign hyperphenylalaninemia to neurologic disease with developmental delay, hypotonia, dystonia, parkinsonism, oculogyric crises, seizures, microcephaly, feeding difficulty, hypersalivation, irritability, and autonomic dysfunction. Important complications include intellectual disability and movement disorders if untreated, and comorbidities may include mood or sleep disturbance and growth impairment. Subtypes are commonly classified as BH4-deficient hyperphenylalaninemia, DHPR deficiency, PTPS deficiency, GTPCH deficiency, PCD deficiency, DNAJC12 deficiency, and mild PAH-related non-PKU hyperphenylalaninemia. Treatment commonly combines dietary phenylalanine restriction with sapropterin dihydrochloride, a synthetic BH4 that enhances residual hydroxylase activity; levodopa/carbidopa to replace deficient dopamine while limiting peripheral decarboxylation; and 5-hydroxytryptophan to restore serotonin synthesis, with folinic acid often added in DHPR deficiency. Diagnosis relies on newborn screening showing elevated phenylalanine with lower phenylalanine/tyrosine ratios than classic PKU in some cases, plasma amino acids, urinary or dried-blood pterin analysis, DHPR enzyme assay, BH4 loading tests,

Name: Carbamoyl-Phosphate Synthase I Deficiency Disease
Description: Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I deficiency disease is a rare urea-cycle disorder caused by deficient hepatic mitochondrial CPS1, the ammonia-detoxifying enzyme encoded by CPS1 on 2q35, most often due to autosomal recessive biallelic loss-of-function variants such as missense, nonsense, splice-site, small insertion-deletions, or compound heterozygous mutations that reduce enzyme abundance, stability, or activation by the essential allosteric cofactor N-acetylglutamate; functionally, the disorder disrupts the mitochondrial urea-cycle pathway linking NAGS-generated N-acetylglutamate, CPS1, ornithine transcarbamylase, citrulline production, and downstream argininosuccinate synthesis, leading to failure of nitrogen disposal, hyperammonemia, glutamine accumulation, cerebral astrocyte swelling, excitotoxicity, and encephalopathy. Classic neonatal-onset disease presents in the first days of life with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, tachypnea from respiratory alkalosis, hypotonia, seizures, coma, and potentially death, whereas partial or late-onset forms may cause episodic vomiting, protein intolerance, developmental delay, behavioral change, confusion, migraine-like episodes, ataxia, psychiatric symptoms, or liver dysfunction during catabolic stress, infection, fasting, postpartum stress, or high protein load. Major complications include recurrent hyperammonemic crises, cerebral edema, intellectual disability, epilepsy, spasticity, chronic neurocognitive impairment, and occasionally hepatic injury. Diagnosis rests on marked hyperammonemia with low citrulline, low or absent arginine, normal or low orotic acid unlike OTC deficiency, elevated glutamine, plasma amino-acid and urine organic-acid profiles, molecular confirmation of CPS1 variants, and sometimes enzyme assay in liver tissue. Treatment centers on nitrogen-scavenging drugs such as sodium benzoate, which conjugates glycine to hippurate, sodium phenylbutyrate or glycerol phenylbutyrate, which generate phenylacetate to conjugate glutamine as phenylacetylglutamine, and carglumic acid, an N-acetylglutamate analog that can enhance residual CPS1 activity in selected patients; adjuncts include arginine or citrulline supplementation, protein restriction, calories to prevent catabolism, emergency dialysis for severe crises, and liver transplantation in refractory

Name: Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting
Description: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS; UMLS C0751967) is the most common initial phenotype of multiple sclerosis, a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory demyelinating and neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system characterized by episodic neurologic dysfunction followed by partial or complete recovery; it is biologically associated with polygenic susceptibility, especially HLA-DRB1*15:01 within the MHC, and non-HLA loci such as IL2RA, IL7R, TYK2, TNFRSF1A, CD6, and CLEC16A, with effects mediated through immune proteins including HLA class II molecules, IL-2/IL-7 receptor signaling components, TNF/TNFR pathways, and B-cell and T-cell activation networks. Pathobiology involves Th1/Th17 polarization, B-cell antigen presentation, intrathecal immunoglobulin production, microglial activation, complement, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, and cytokines such as IFN-gamma, IL-17, GM-CSF, TNF-alpha, and CXCL13, leading to blood-brain barrier disruption, focal plaques, axonal injury, and brain/spinal cord atrophy. Typical symptoms include optic neuritis, diplopia, sensory loss, limb weakness, spasticity, ataxia, fatigue, pain, bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction, and cognitive or mood impairment; subtypes include clinically isolated syndrome, RRMS, secondary progressive, and primary progressive disease. Inheritance is not Mendelian but familial clustering and gene-environment interaction are recognized, with risks modified by Epstein-Barr virus exposure, smoking, vitamin D deficiency, and adolescent obesity. Diagnosis relies on 2017 McDonald criteria demonstrating dissemination in time and space by MRI and/or CSF oligoclonal bands, supported by spinal MRI, visual evoked potentials, and exclusion of mimics such as neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and MOG-associated disease. Common treatments include interferon beta, which reduces antigen presentation and inflammatory cytokine signaling; glatiramer acetate, which shifts T-cell responses toward anti-inflammatory phenotypes; fingolimod, an S1P receptor modulator that traps lymphocytes in lymph nodes; dimethyl fumarate, which activates Nrf2 and dampens oxidative/inflammatory stress; natalizumab, which blocks alpha4-integrin-mediated leukocyte trafficking; and ocrelizumab, which

Name: Lewy Body Disease
Description: Lewy body disease is a neurodegenerative synucleinopathy encompassing dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia, characterized pathologically by cortical and brainstem Lewy bodies and neurites composed largely of misfolded alpha-synuclein encoded by SNCA, with genetic risk or causal contributions also reported for GBA, LRRK2, APOE, MAPT, and less commonly VPS35 and PRKN; rare familial aggregation is usually autosomal dominant with SNCA duplication/triplication or point mutations and some LRRK2 variants, whereas most cases are sporadic and genetically complex. Core pathogenic pathways include alpha-synuclein misfolding, aggregation, and cell-to-cell propagation, impaired ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, cholinergic deficits, and dopaminergic nigrostriatal degeneration. Clinically, patients develop progressive cognitive fluctuations, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, spontaneous parkinsonism with bradykinesia and rigidity, visuospatial and executive impairment, autonomic failure, hypersomnia, depression, anxiety, falls, and marked antipsychotic sensitivity. Common comorbidities and complications include Parkinsonism, sleep disorders, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary dysfunction, aspiration pneumonia, delirium, fractures, and frequent concomitant Alzheimer-type amyloid-beta and tau pathology. Diagnosis is primarily clinical using consensus criteria that emphasize dementia plus core features and indicative biomarkers, with the one-year rule distinguishing dementia with Lewy bodies from Parkinson disease dementia; supportive testing includes neuropsychological assessment, polysomnography for REM sleep behavior disorder, dopamine transporter SPECT/PET showing reduced striatal uptake, cardiac MIBG scintigraphy, MRI to exclude alternatives, FDG-PET with occipital hypometabolism, and CSF or tissue biomarkers in selected settings, while definitive diagnosis remains neuropathologic. Treatment is symptomatic: rivastigmine, donepezil, or galantamine enhance central cholinergic transmission by acetylcholinesterase inhibition; levodopa augments dopamine after central conversion; memantine noncompetitively blocks NMDA receptors; pimavanserin antagonizes/inversely agonizes 5-HT2A receptors for psychosis; and clonazepam or melatonin are often used for REM sleep behavior disorder.

Name: Itching of ear
Description: Itching of the ear, corresponding clinically to pruritus auris, is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease and most often reflects inflammation or irritation of the external auditory canal from eczematous otitis externa, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, allergic contact dermatitis, fungal infection, cerumen disturbance, hearing-aid or topical-product irritation, and less commonly neuropathic or systemic pruritic disorders. Pathobiologically, itch is mediated by epidermal barrier dysfunction and neuroimmune signaling involving histamine, protease-activated receptors, TRPV1 and TRPA1 channels, substance P, IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, TSLP, and NF-kB/JAK-STAT signaling; representative genetic contributors are usually those of the underlying dermatosis, such as FLG loss-of-function variants in atopic dermatitis, and less commonly PSORS-associated loci including HLA-C*06:02 in psoriasis. Symptoms include persistent ear-canal itching, irritation, dryness, scaling, erythema, excoriations, flaking, aural fullness, and sometimes otorrhea, pain, conductive hearing reduction, or secondary infection. Important subtypes include eczematous, infectious, allergic, seborrheic, psoriatic, and neuropathic pruritus. Comorbidities commonly include atopy, asthma, allergic rhinitis, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, diabetes, fungal overgrowth, anxiety, and chronic otitis externa; complications include canal excoriation, lichenification, cellulitis, bacterial superinfection, fungal persistence, and rarely malignant otitis externa in immunocompromised patients. Treatment is cause-directed and commonly uses hydrocortisone or fluocinolone otic preparations, which suppress phospholipase A2-driven inflammatory transcription; acetic acid/aluminum acetate, which acidifies and dries the canal; and ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin otic drops, which inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase, often combined with dexamethasone. Clotrimazole, an ergosterol-synthesis inhibitor, is used for otomycosis, and oral antihistamines such as cetirizine may reduce histamine-mediated itch. Diagnosis is clinical, based on otoscopic evidence of dermatitis or infection, exposure history, and exclusion of middle-ear disease, with microscopy/culture for refractory discharge, patch testing for contact allergy, audiometry when hearing symptoms occur

Name: Dry Cough
Description: Dry cough (UMLS C0850149) is a symptom complex rather than a single inherited disease, characterized by non-productive coughing due to heightened cough-reflex sensitivity, airway irritation, or extrapulmonary triggers; common clinical features include frequent throat clearing, tickling or retrosternal irritation, nocturnal cough, cough triggered by talking, cold air, odors, viral illness, or exercise, and usually absence of sputum, fever, or focal consolidation unless another disorder is present. Major mechanistic pathways include vagal sensory nerve activation and neuroinflammation involving TRPV1, TRPA1, P2X3, neurokinin-1, and ATP-mediated signaling, with inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 contributing in asthma/eosinophilic bronchitis, and acid-pepsin or non-acid reflux activating esophagobronchial reflex pathways in gastroesophageal reflux disease. Genetic contributions are usually indirect and polygenic rather than Mendelian; representative associations include ACE variants influencing ACE-inhibitor cough susceptibility, polymorphisms affecting TRPV1, TACR1, P2RX3, ADRB2, IL13, and eosinophilic or asthmatic endotypes, while monogenic inheritance is not typical for isolated dry cough. Important subtypes include acute post-viral cough, subacute postinfectious cough, chronic refractory or unexplained cough, upper-airway cough syndrome, cough-variant asthma, nonasthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis, reflux-associated cough, and drug-induced cough, especially from ACE inhibitors. Commonly linked comorbidities and complications include asthma, allergic rhinitis/sinusitis, GERD, interstitial lung disease, pertussis, COVID-19, anxiety, insomnia, urinary incontinence, syncope, rib fracture, and impaired quality of life. Treatment targets the cause and symptom burden: dextromethorphan suppresses central NMDA/sigma-mediated cough pathways, benzonatate anesthetizes peripheral stretch receptors, inhaled corticosteroids reduce eosinophilic airway inflammation, bronchodilators such as albuterol activate β2 receptors, proton-pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid in reflux-associated cough, and gabapentin or pregabalin may reduce cough hypersensitivity. Name: Bipolar I disorder
Description: Bipolar I disorder (UMLS C0853193) is a severe, episodic mood disorder defined by at least one manic episode, usually with recurrent major depression, and is clinically heterogeneous, with subtypes such as bipolar I with psychotic features, mixed features, rapid cycling, melancholic or atypical depressive episodes, and catatonia. Core symptoms of mania include elevated or irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, increased goal-directed activity, distractibility, psychomotor agitation, impulsivity, and at times psychosis, while depressive phases feature low mood, anhedonia, guilt, fatigue, cognitive slowing, and suicidal ideation; complications include suicide, substance misuse, psychosocial and occupational impairment, and increased cardiometabolic disease. The disorder is highly heritable, typically showing complex polygenic rather than Mendelian inheritance, with risk enriched by variants in genes such as CACNA1C, ANK3, ODZ4/TENM4, TRANK1, and circadian regulators including CLOCK and ARNTL, and implicated proteins and pathways include L-type voltage-gated calcium channels, sodium channel-anchoring proteins, glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic signaling, dopaminergic and serotonergic neurotransmission, circadian-clock networks, neurotrophin/BDNF signaling, second-messenger systems including GSK3, PKC, cAMP-CREB, and mitochondrial, inflammatory, and oxidative stress pathways. Common comorbidities include anxiety disorders, ADHD, migraine, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and thyroid dysfunction. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 or ICD criteria and longitudinal history documenting a manic episode with functional impairment or hospitalization, supported by mental status examination, collateral history, and rating scales such as the YMRS and MADRS/PHQ-9, while laboratory testing, toxicology, and when indicated neuroimaging are used mainly to exclude secondary causes. Treatment commonly includes lithium, which modulates inositol signaling and inhibits GSK3; valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and affects ion-channel and histone deacetylase activity; quetiapine, a dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A antagonist; and lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and glutamate release.

Name: Bacterial keratitis
Description: Bacterial keratitis (UMLS C0854211) is an acute, vision-threatening infectious inflammation of the cornea, usually caused by epithelial barrier disruption and bacterial invasion, most commonly by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and coagulase-negative staphylococci; clinically it presents with rapid-onset ocular pain, redness, photophobia, tearing, mucopurulent discharge, decreased vision, and a corneal epithelial defect with stromal infiltrate, edema, and sometimes hypopyon. Disease subtypes are often classified by pathogen, contact-lens-associated disease, post-traumatic or postsurgical keratitis, and superficial versus deep stromal involvement. Host molecular determinants include innate immune genes and proteins such as TLR4, TLR2, NOD-like receptor components, IL1B, IL6, CXCL8/IL8, TNF, MMP9, DEFB4, and mucins including MUC1 and MUC16, while severe or recurrent susceptibility may reflect variants affecting corneal defense or immune regulation rather than a classic Mendelian inheritance pattern; rare predisposition also occurs in primary immunodeficiency or ocular surface disease with genetic bases. Key pathways include Toll-like receptor, NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome, complement, neutrophil recruitment, and matrix-remodeling cascades that mediate pathogen clearance but also stromal melting. Standard therapy relies on intensive topical antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones including moxifloxacin or ciprofloxacin, which inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, fortified vancomycin, which blocks cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis, and fortified tobramycin, an aminoglycoside that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; ceftazidime, a beta-lactam inhibiting cell-wall synthesis, is often used for gram-negative coverage. Important comorbidities and risk factors include contact lens wear, dry eye, blepharitis, diabetes, trauma, prior herpes simplex keratitis, corneal exposure, and topical corticosteroid use, while complications include corneal thinning, perforation, endophthalmitis, scarring, irregular astigmatism, and permanent vision loss. Diagnosis is based on slit-lamp evidence of infectious corneal ulceration, microbiologic confirmation by corneal scraping with Gram stain and culture

Name: Bacterial meningitis caused by gram-negative bacteria
Description: Bacterial meningitis caused by gram-negative bacteria is an acute, life-threatening purulent infection of the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid, most often due to Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Haemophilus influenzae, or Neisseria meningitidis, and may be classified as community-acquired, neonatal, nosocomial/post-neurosurgical, or meningococcal disease. Pathogenesis is driven less by a host inheritance pattern than by microbial virulence determinants and host inflammatory genetics: representative bacterial factors include the E. coli K1 capsule, lipooligosaccharide or lipopolysaccharide endotoxin, outer-membrane proteins, pili, and in meningococcus the capsule synthesis loci and factor H binding protein, while host susceptibility has been linked to variants in TLR4, TLR2, CD14, NOD2, CFH, MBL2, and cytokine genes such as TNF and IL6. Key pathways involve blood-brain barrier invasion and activation of TLR4/TLR2-NF-kappaB and inflammasome signaling, with TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, complement, neutrophil recruitment, matrix metalloproteinases, nitric oxide, and coagulation pathways contributing to edema, vasculitis, and neuronal injury. Typical manifestations include fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, petechiae in meningococcemia, and in neonates poor feeding, lethargy, apnea, and bulging fontanelle. Diagnosis relies on urgent lumbar puncture with CSF pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose, Gram stain, culture, and multiplex PCR, supported by blood cultures, inflammatory markers, and neuroimaging before LP when mass effect is suspected. Standard therapy uses prompt intravenous ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall cross-linking; meropenem, a carbapenem with broad bactericidal PBP inhibition; and vancomycin adjunctively for resistant empiric coverage, inhibiting peptidoglycan polymerization, with dexamethasone sometimes used to blunt inflammation. Name: Infection caused by anaerobic bacteria
Description: Infection caused by anaerobic bacteria (UMLS C0854328) is a usually endogenous, often polymicrobial infectious syndrome produced by obligate anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium perfringens, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, and Prevotella, typically arising in low-oxygen devitalized tissue after mucosal disruption, surgery, trauma, aspiration, or ischemia. Clinical manifestations vary by site but commonly include foul-smelling purulent discharge, abscess formation, tissue necrosis, crepitus, fever, pain, leukocytosis, and sepsis; major subtypes include intra-abdominal and pelvic infection, aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess, odontogenic and deep neck infection, diabetic foot and soft-tissue infection, brain abscess, and clostridial myonecrosis. Pathobiology reflects host inflammatory signaling through TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, inflammasome activation, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, together with microbial virulence factors including the B. fragilis capsular polysaccharide complex, fragilysin/BFT encoded by bft, clostridial alpha-toxin plc, perfringolysin O pfoA, and resistance determinants such as cfiA metallo-β-lactamase, cepA, and nim genes conferring reduced susceptibility to carbapenems, penicillins, and nitroimidazoles. Treatment relies on source control plus anti-anaerobic agents, commonly metronidazole, which is reductively activated in anaerobes to generate DNA-damaging radicals; β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibit cell-wall transpeptidation while clavulanate or tazobactam block many β-lactamases; and carbapenems such as meropenem, which broadly inhibit penicillin-binding proteins; clindamycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor, is also used selectively. Name: Bone marrow suppression
Description: Bone marrow suppression (UMLS C0854467) is a clinicopathologic state of reduced hematopoietic activity causing one or more cytopenias, most often acquired after cytotoxic chemotherapy, radiation, drugs, infection, autoimmune injury, nutritional deficiency, or marrow infiltration, but it may also reflect inherited marrow-failure syndromes. Key molecular associations include impaired hematopoietic stem-cell survival and DNA repair involving TP53, ATM, BRCA/Fanconi anemia genes such as FANCA and FANCC, telomere-maintenance genes TERT, TERC, and DKC1, ribosome biogenesis genes as in SBDS, and cytokine signaling through thrombopoietin-MPL-JAK2, stem-cell factor-KIT, erythropoietin-EPOR-JAK2-STAT5, and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor receptor CSF3R; inflammatory suppression may involve TNF, IFNG, Fas-mediated apoptosis, NF-kB, and TGF-beta/SMAD pathways. Clinically it presents with anemia, fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, neutropenia with recurrent or opportunistic infection and fever, and thrombocytopenia with petechiae, mucosal bleeding, or easy bruising; pancytopenia may lead to sepsis, hemorrhage, transfusion dependence, and progression to myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia in some inherited or clonal contexts. Subtypes include isolated lineage suppression, trilineage hypoplasia, aplastic anemia, chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression, radiation-induced suppression, and congenital marrow-failure disorders, with inheritance patterns varying from sporadic to autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked depending on the underlying gene defect. Diagnosis relies on complete blood count with differential and reticulocyte count, peripheral smear, marrow aspirate and biopsy showing hypocellularity or lineage-specific suppression, cytogenetics/flow cytometry when clonal disease is suspected, and targeted testing for vitamin deficiency, viral causes, and germline mutations. Common treatments include filgrastim or pegfilgrastim, G-CSF receptor agonists that stimulate neutrophil production; epoetin alfa or darbepoetin alfa, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents activating EPOR-JAK2 signaling; romiplostim or eltrombopag, thrombopoietin-receptor agonists promoting megakaryopoiesis; and

Name: Small lymphocytic lymphoma
Description: Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is an indolent mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that is the tissue-based counterpart of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, defined by lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly with a peripheral blood B-cell count below the CLL threshold, and it typically presents with painless generalized lymphadenopathy, fatigue, B symptoms, hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent infections, and sometimes autoimmune cytopenias. Biologically, SLL is driven by clonal CD5-positive, CD23-positive B cells with characteristic genetic lesions involving del(13q14) with loss of the miR-15a/miR-16-1 region, trisomy 12, del(11q) affecting ATM, del(17p) and TP53 mutation, and less commonly NOTCH1, SF3B1, BIRC3, MYD88, POT1, and XPO1 alterations; overexpression of BCL2 and surface immunoglobulin signaling are important protein-level features. Major pathogenic pathways include B-cell receptor signaling through SYK, LYN, BTK, and PI3K/AKT/mTOR, NF-kB activation, apoptotic dysregulation centered on BCL2, microenvironmental support via CXCR4/CXCL12, and p53 pathway disruption in high-risk disease. Most cases are sporadic, although familial clustering of CLL/SLL occurs, indicating inherited susceptibility without a simple Mendelian pattern. Diagnosis relies on lymph node, marrow, or other tissue showing diffuse small mature lymphocytes with proliferation centers, supported by flow cytometry demonstrating a monoclonal kappa- or lambda-restricted CD19-positive, CD20-dim, CD5-positive, CD23-positive phenotype, with FISH, karyotyping, IGHV mutation testing, and TP53 analysis used for risk stratification. Common treatments include anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab or obinutuzumab, BTK inhibitors such as ibrutinib or acalabrutinib that block B-cell receptor signaling, the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax that restores apoptosis, and selected chemoimmunotherapy such as bendamustine. Important complications include Richter transformation to aggressive lymphoma, progressive marrow failure, hypogammaglobulinemia, infection, and secondary malignancies.

Name: Refractory Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
Description: Refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL; UMLS C0855112) is an aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma defined by failure to achieve at least a partial response or by progression during or shortly after standard immunochemotherapy, most often arising within germinal center B-cell-like or activated B-cell-like/molecular high-grade subtypes. Its biology commonly involves dysregulation of B-cell receptor, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, apoptosis, and epigenetic control pathways, with representative alterations including BCL2, BCL6, and MYC rearrangements or overexpression, TP53 mutation, CD79A/CD79B, MYD88, EZH2, CREBBP, EP300, CARD11, and TNFAIP3 lesions; double-hit or triple-hit disease with MYC plus BCL2 and/or BCL6 is particularly chemo-refractory. The disease is usually sporadic rather than inherited, although rare predisposition may reflect germline defects causing immunodeficiency or DNA-repair dysfunction. Patients typically present with rapidly enlarging nodal or extranodal masses, B symptoms, elevated LDH, cytopenias, organ-specific pain or dysfunction, and complications such as bulky disease, bone marrow failure, CNS relapse, tumor lysis, infection, venous thromboembolism, and transformation-related treatment resistance; comorbidities often include immunosuppression, HIV infection, hepatitis B risk during anti-CD20 therapy, and cardiovascular or renal disease affecting treatment tolerance. Diagnosis requires excisional tissue biopsy showing diffuse sheets of large atypical CD20-positive B cells, immunophenotyping and cell-of-origin classification, Ki-67, FISH for MYC/BCL2/BCL6, targeted molecular testing, and staging with PET-CT, marrow evaluation, and laboratory prognostic assessment. Common treatments in refractory disease include rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody mediating complement and antibody-dependent cytotoxicity; polatuzumab vedotin, a CD79b-directed microtubule toxin conjugate; tafasitamab, an Fc-enhanced anti-CD19 antibody, often with lenalidomide, an immunomodulator; CAR T-cell therapies targeting CD19; and salvage agents such as cyclophosphamide or doxorubicin, which alkylate DNA or inhibit topoisomerase II

Name: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis
Description: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (UMLS C0856695) is an acute worsening of cough, sputum volume or purulence, and dyspnea occurring on a background of chronic bronchitis, usually within chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and is most often triggered by respiratory infection, pollution, or treatment nonadherence. Its biology is dominated by neutrophilic airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, oxidative stress, and airflow limitation mediated through NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TGF-β, EGFR, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, and protease-antiprotease imbalance involving MMP9 and neutrophil elastase, with oxidative injury amplified by NFE2L2/NRF2 dysfunction; genetic susceptibility is complex and usually non-Mendelian, but representative associated genes include SERPINA1 mutations causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, CHRNA3/5 and HHIP loci linked to COPD risk, and mucin-related genes such as MUC5AC. Common pathogens include Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and respiratory viruses. Typical findings are increased wheeze, chest tightness, tachypnea, prolonged expiration, hypoxemia, and sometimes hypercapnia; severe cases progress to acute respiratory failure. Clinical subtypes include infectious versus noninfectious exacerbations, eosinophilic versus neutrophilic phenotypes, and severity-based episodes requiring outpatient care, hospitalization, or ventilatory support. Treatment commonly includes short-acting bronchodilators such as albuterol, a β2-adrenergic agonist that increases cAMP and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, ipratropium, a muscarinic M3 antagonist that reduces vagally mediated bronchoconstriction, systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone that suppress inflammatory gene transcription, and when bacterial infection is suspected, antibiotics such as azithromycin, doxycycline, or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Major comorbidities and complications include emphysema, pneumonia, bronchiectasis, asthma overlap, pulmonary hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, anxiety/depression, respiratory acidosis, and recurrent hospitalization. Name: Malignant melanoma, metastatic
Description: Metastatic malignant melanoma is an aggressive malignancy of melanocytes in which tumor cells disseminate from a primary cutaneous, mucosal, acral, or uveal site to lymph nodes, lung, liver, brain, bone, or subcutaneous tissues, causing symptoms such as enlarging or changing pigmented lesions, bleeding, ulceration, palpable nodes, weight loss, fatigue, cough, dyspnea, pain, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits. Biologically, it is driven by constitutive MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling, most often through activating BRAF mutations, especially BRAF V600E/V600K, NRAS mutations, or KIT alterations, with additional recurrent abnormalities involving NF1, PTEN loss, CDKN2A, TP53, TERT promoter, GNAQ/GNA11 in uveal melanoma, and proteins such as MEK, ERK, PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 that shape tumor growth and immune escape. Major subtypes include superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous, mucosal, desmoplastic, and uveal melanoma, with metastases classified by stage IV burden and organ involvement. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited susceptibility occurs in familial melanoma, typically autosomal dominant, with pathogenic variants in CDKN2A, CDK4, BAP1, MITF, POT1, TERT, ACD, and TERF2IP; risk is increased by numerous atypical nevi, fair skin, and UV exposure. Diagnosis rests on excisional biopsy of the primary lesion with histopathology and immunohistochemistry such as S100, SOX10, Melan-A, and HMB-45, staging by sentinel node assessment and CT, PET-CT, or MRI, and molecular testing for BRAF, NRAS, KIT, and related alterations to guide therapy. Standard systemic treatments include immune checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab or nivolumab, which block PD-1, and ipilimumab, which blocks CTLA-4, as well as targeted therapy with dabrafenib plus trametinib or vemurafenib plus cobimetinib for BRAF-mutant disease by inhibiting mutant BRAF and MEK. Name: Superficial basal cell carcinoma
Description: Superficial basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a low-grade, locally invasive keratinocyte malignancy and a histologic subtype of basal cell carcinoma that typically presents as a slowly enlarging, thin erythematous scaly patch or plaque, often on the trunk or shoulders, with a shiny border, fine telangiectasias, and occasional erosion or crusting; aggressive metastatic spread is rare, but local recurrence, tissue destruction, and multiplicity are important complications. Its biology is driven predominantly by aberrant Hedgehog signaling, most often through loss-of-function PTCH1 or SUFU alterations or activating SMO mutations, with cooperating events in TP53, TERT promoter, MYCN, and less commonly RAS/PI3K-related pathways; pathway components include PTCH1, SMO, GLI transcription factors, and downstream cell-cycle and survival programs. Most cases are sporadic and strongly linked to cumulative or intermittent ultraviolet exposure, fair skin, immunosuppression, older age, and prior ionizing radiation, but inherited susceptibility occurs in autosomal dominant nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) due chiefly to germline PTCH1, and less often SUFU, mutations, often causing multiple early-onset BCCs with odontogenic keratocysts and skeletal anomalies. Superficial BCC is distinguished from nodular, infiltrative, micronodular, morpheaform/sclerosing, pigmented, and basosquamous variants. Diagnosis relies on clinical inspection and dermoscopy, typically showing fine arborizing or superficial telangiectatic vessels, shiny white-red structureless areas, and multiple small erosions, with confirmation by shave or punch biopsy demonstrating superficial buds of basaloid cells attached to the epidermis, peripheral palisading, and stromal retraction; adjunctive optical coherence tomography or reflectance confocal microscopy may assist selected cases. Standard therapies include surgical excision or curettage and electrodesiccation, while commonly used drugs include topical imiquimod, a TLR7 agonist that induces local interferon-mediated antitumor immunity; 5-fluorouracil, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor impairing DNA synthesis; and vismodegib or sonidegib, SMO inhibitors used for advanced or multiple lesions.

Name: Chronic graft-versus-host disease
Description: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD; UMLS C0867389) is a multisystem alloimmune and autoimmune-like complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in which donor-derived T cells, B cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts drive persistent inflammation, defective immune tolerance, and fibrosis rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder; genetic susceptibility is instead polygenic and transplant-related, with associations reported for donor-recipient HLA disparity and immune-regulatory variants or expression changes involving CTLA4, IL10, TGFB1, BAFF/TNFSF13B, CXCR5, PDCD1, and minor histocompatibility antigens, while elevated BAFF, autoantibodies, and aberrant B-cell reconstitution are common protein-level findings. Key pathogenic pathways include alloreactive T-cell receptor signaling, Th1/Th17 polarization, reduced regulatory T-cell function, B-cell receptor and BAFF signaling, germinal-center dysregulation, JAK/STAT activation, NF-kB, chemokine axes such as CXCL9/CXCL10-CXCR3, and profibrotic TGF-beta/PDGF-driven tissue remodeling. Clinically, cGVHD may be classic or overlap syndrome and commonly affects skin, mouth, eyes, liver, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, fascia, and genital tract, producing lichenoid or sclerotic rash, xerostomia, mucosal ulceration, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, cholestatic liver tests, bronchiolitis obliterans, dysphagia, diarrhea, weight loss, joint contractures, myositis, and recurrent infections. Major complications include severe functional impairment, opportunistic infection, pulmonary failure, malnutrition, osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome, and secondary malignancies. Diagnosis is based on NIH consensus criteria using characteristic or distinctive organ manifestations, severity scoring, exclusion of alternative causes, pulmonary function testing, liver chemistries, Schirmer testing, and when needed biopsy of skin, oral mucosa, liver, or lung. Treatment commonly includes corticosteroids such as prednisone, which broadly suppress NF-kB-dependent inflammatory transcription; calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus or cyclosporine, which block T-cell IL-2 transcription; ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor; belumosudil, a ROCK2 inhibitor that modulates Th17/Treg balance and fibrosis

Name: Excessive cornification
Description: Excessive cornification denotes a heterogeneous group of disorders of epidermal keratinization, most often represented clinically by ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, and related hyperkeratotic dermatoses, in which defective terminal differentiation of keratinocytes causes an abnormally thick stratum corneum with scaling, xerosis, fissuring, plaques, and variable erythema or pain. Key genetic causes include loss- or gain-of-function variants in filaggrin and the epidermal differentiation complex, keratins KRT1, KRT2, KRT9, and KRT10, transglutaminase 1 (TGM1), ABCA12, loricrin, involucrin, connexins such as GJB2 and GJB6, and desmosomal or protease-regulatory genes including SPINK5; representative protein defects disrupt the cornified envelope, intermediate filaments, lipid transport, or corneodesmosome turnover. Pathobiology centers on keratinocyte differentiation and cornified-envelope assembly, epidermal lipid metabolism and lamellar body secretion, calcium-gradient signaling, EGFR/MAPK and AP1 programs, Notch and p63 regulation, desmosomal adhesion, and inflammatory Th17/IL-23, IL-1, and TNF signaling in syndromic or inflamed forms. Subtypes include ichthyosis vulgaris, lamellar ichthyosis, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, epidermolytic ichthyosis, and focal or diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or sporadic depending on the gene, for example dominant KRT1/KRT10 disease, recessive TGM1 or ABCA12-related autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, and semidominant loricrin keratoderma. Common treatments are emollients and keratolytics such as urea, lactic acid, or salicylic acid, which hydrate and dissolve corneocyte cohesion; topical retinoids including tazarotene, which normalize keratinocyte differentiation via retinoic acid receptors; and systemic retinoids such as acitretin or isotretinoin, which reduce hyperkeratosis by modulating epidermal gene transcription. Name: Candidemia
Description: Candidemia (UMLS C0877445) is an invasive bloodstream infection caused by Candida species, most commonly C. albicans but also C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, and C. krusei, and it represents a severe opportunistic mycosis rather than a Mendelian disease; clinically it ranges from uncomplicated fungemia to persistent candidemia with deep-seated dissemination, septic shock, endocarditis, hepatosplenic candidiasis, endophthalmitis, osteomyelitis, and multiorgan failure. Typical manifestations are fever unresponsive to antibacterial therapy, chills, hypotension, sepsis, altered mental status, and signs of metastatic infection, especially in critically ill, neutropenic, postoperative, catheterized, parenterally fed, or broad-spectrum antibiotic-exposed patients. Host susceptibility is influenced by innate immune genes and pathways involved in fungal recognition and cytokine signaling, including CLEC7A/Dectin-1, CARD9, TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, IL17A, IL17RA, IL6, and CXCR1, while Candida virulence and drug response involve ERG11, FKS1/FKS2, CDR1/CDR2, and MDR1; key pathways include Dectin-1–CARD9–NF-kB signaling, Toll-like receptor pathways, Th17/IL-17 immunity, complement activation, neutrophil oxidative killing, fungal cell-wall beta-glucan and mannan sensing, ergosterol biosynthesis, and calcineurin- or Hsp90-associated stress responses. Treatment usually begins with an echinocandin such as caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin, which inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase; fluconazole inhibits lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase in ergosterol synthesis; amphotericin B binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores, with voriconazole or isavuconazole used selectively. Diagnosis relies on blood cultures from peripheral and catheter sources, species identification with susceptibility testing, beta-D-glucan assays, and increasingly PCR or T2Candida-based detection, together with evaluation for metastatic foci by ophthalmologic examination and echocardiography; inherited predisposition is usually complex or due to rare primary immunodeficiencies such as CARD9 deficiency rather than classic

Name: Erdheim-Chester Disease
Description: Erdheim-Chester disease (MeSH D031249) is a rare clonal non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterized by tissue infiltration by foamy CD68-positive, CD1a-negative, usually langerin-negative histiocytes within a fibrotic/xanthogranulomatous stroma, and it is now recognized as an inflammatory myeloid neoplasm driven in many cases by MAPK-pathway alterations, most commonly BRAF V600E, with other recurrent lesions in MAP2K1, KRAS, NRAS, ARAF, PIK3CA, and occasional ALK fusions, leading to constitutive RAF-MEK-ERK and sometimes PI3K-AKT signaling with cytokine activation including IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and interferon-mediated inflammation. The disease is typically sporadic rather than inherited, with no established Mendelian transmission, although somatic mutations in hematopoietic progenitors may coexist with clonal hematopoiesis or myeloid neoplasms. Classic manifestations include bilateral symmetric osteosclerosis of the long bones causing bone pain, retroperitoneal and perirenal infiltration producing the hairy kidney appearance, circumferential periaortic sheathing or coated aorta, cardiovascular involvement, pulmonary infiltrates, diabetes insipidus from pituitary involvement, exophthalmos, xanthelasma, and diverse neurologic deficits; major complications include renal obstruction, heart failure, arrhythmias, stroke, and progressive CNS dysfunction. Clinically recognized patterns include multisystem disease and organ-predominant variants, with overlap syndromes with Langerhans cell histiocytosis or Rosai-Dorfman disease reported. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical-radiologic findings, biopsy confirmation with characteristic immunophenotype and histology, molecular testing for targetable mutations by PCR or next-generation sequencing, and staging by PET-CT, MRI, CT, and bone scintigraphy. Treatment commonly includes interferon-alpha or peginterferon, which exerts antiproliferative and immunomodulatory effects; vemurafenib, a mutant BRAF inhibitor; cobimetinib or trametinib, MEK inhibitors for MAPK-activated disease; and selected use of anakinra, cladribine, corticosteroids, or infliximab for inflammatory or refractory manifestations.

Name: Optic Atrophy, Hereditary, Leber
Description: Leber hereditary optic atrophy, more commonly termed Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, is a primary mitochondrial neuro-ophthalmic disorder characterized by selective degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and the papillomacular bundle, causing subacute, usually painless central vision loss, dyschromatopsia, cecocentral scotomas, reduced visual acuity, and later optic disc pallor, often after a hyperemic disc with peripapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy and nerve fiber layer swelling. It is most often caused by maternally inherited pathogenic mitochondrial DNA mutations affecting complex I subunits of oxidative phosphorylation, classically MT-ND4 m.11778G>A, MT-ND1 m.3460G>A, and MT-ND6 m.14484T>C, with heteroplasmy, haplogroup background, and rare nuclear modifiers such as DNAJC30 influencing penetrance and phenotype; autosomal recessive LHON-like disease due to DNAJC30 variants has also been described. The core pathogenic pathway involves impaired mitochondrial electron transport, reduced ATP generation, excess reactive oxygen species, altered mitophagy and apoptosis signaling, and heightened vulnerability of retinal ganglion cells. Major subtypes include typical LHON and LHON-plus, the latter accompanied by neurologic or cardiac manifestations such as multiple-sclerosis-like illness, movement disorders, peripheral neuropathy, myopathy, arrhythmias, and occasionally Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Diagnosis rests on characteristic bilateral sequential optic neuropathy, ophthalmic examination, visual fields, optical coherence tomography, visual evoked responses, and confirmatory genetic testing for common mtDNA mutations, with broader mitochondrial or nuclear sequencing when initial tests are negative. Treatment is largely supportive, but idebenone, a short-chain benzoquinone that bypasses complex I to facilitate electron transfer and reduce oxidative stress, is commonly used; coenzyme Q10 and ubiquinol serve as electron carriers and antioxidant mitochondrial supports; and EPI-743/vatiquinone, an investigational para-benzoquinone, aims to enhance redox cycling. Management also includes low-vision rehabilitation and avoidance of smoking, alcohol excess, and mitochondrial toxins.

Name: Cerebral Ischemias
Description: Brain ischemia is an acute or chronic reduction in cerebral blood flow causing focal or global energy failure, excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and ultimately neuronal death; it includes thrombotic, embolic, lacunar, watershed, transient ischemic, and global hypoxic-ischemic forms. Clinical manifestations depend on vascular territory and severity, typically abrupt focal neurologic deficits such as hemiparesis, aphasia, dysarthria, hemisensory loss, visual field defects, ataxia, neglect, altered consciousness, and in severe cases coma, with complications including cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, seizures, recurrent stroke, cognitive impairment, and vascular dementia. Major comorbidities are hypertension, atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, dyslipidemia, smoking, carotid stenosis, obesity, chronic kidney disease, and coronary artery disease. Relevant molecular pathways include glutamate-NMDA receptor mediated calcium influx; nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species signaling; HIF-1/VEGF hypoxia responses; TNF, IL-1β, NF-κB, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation; apoptosis regulators such as caspase-3, BCL2, and BAX; and matrix remodeling via MMP9. Genetic contributors are usually polygenic and influence risk rather than simple inheritance, with representative associations in APOE, MTHFR, ACE, NOS3, PDE4D, HDAC9, PITX2 and ZFHX3 for cardioembolic risk through atrial fibrillation, while monogenic causes include NOTCH3 mutations in CADASIL, HTRA1 in CARASIL, COL4A1, GLA in Fabry disease, and mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS; inheritance may therefore be multifactorial, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or mitochondrial depending on etiology. Diagnosis rests on sudden neurologic deficit plus brain and vascular evaluation using noncontrast CT, diffusion-weighted MRI, CT or MR angiography, carotid ultrasonography, perfusion imaging in selected cases, ECG and echocardiography, and laboratory testing for glucose, coagulation, lipids, inflammatory or thrombophilia markers when indicated. Name: Hypersomnias
Description: Disorders of excessive somnolence, broadly termed hypersomnolence disorders, are sleep-wake conditions characterized by pathological daytime sleepiness despite adequate or prolonged nocturnal sleep, most prominently including narcolepsy type 1, narcolepsy type 2, idiopathic hypersomnia, Kleine-Levin syndrome, and secondary hypersomnolence due to neurologic, psychiatric, metabolic, medication-related, or sleep-disordered breathing causes. Core symptoms include irresistible sleep attacks, nonrestorative prolonged sleep, sleep drunkenness, cognitive slowing, impaired attention, and in narcolepsy, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis; complications include accidents, occupational impairment, depression, obesity, and cardiometabolic morbidity. A key molecular mechanism in narcolepsy type 1 is loss of hypothalamic orexin/hypocretin neurons, causing deficient hypocretin signaling through HCRTR1 and HCRTR2 and dysregulation of arousal circuits involving histamine, noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, and GABA; strong genetic association with HLA-DQB1*06:02 supports autoimmune susceptibility, and rare variants in HCRT, HCRTR2, and P2RY11 have been reported, while familial predisposition is usually complex rather than Mendelian, though rare canine narcolepsy reflects HCRTR2 mutations. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, exclusion of insufficient sleep and secondary causes, polysomnography followed by multiple sleep latency testing showing reduced mean sleep latency with sleep-onset REM periods, actigraphy or sleep logs, CSF hypocretin-1 measurement in suspected narcolepsy type 1, and targeted testing for comorbid obstructive sleep apnea or circadian disorders. Treatment is symptomatic and includes modafinil or armodafinil, which enhance wakefulness partly through dopamine transporter inhibition; methylphenidate or amphetamines, which increase synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine; solriamfetol, a dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; pitolisant, a histamine H3-receptor inverse agonist that augments histaminergic arousal; and sodium oxybate, a GABA-B receptor agonist that consolidates nocturnal sleep and reduces cataplexy.

Name: Insomnia
Description: Sleep initiation and maintenance disorders, broadly corresponding to chronic insomnia disorder and related phenotypes, are heterogeneous sleep-wake disorders characterized by persistent difficulty falling asleep, frequent nocturnal awakenings, early morning awakening, or nonrestorative sleep despite adequate opportunity for sleep, with resulting daytime fatigue, impaired attention, irritability, mood symptoms, and reduced function. Pathobiology is multifactorial, centering on hyperarousal and circadian dysregulation involving GABAergic inhibition, orexin/hypocretin signaling, melatonin pathways, and monoaminergic and HPA-axis activation; implicated molecular components include MTNR1A/MTNR1B, CLOCK, BMAL1/ARNTL, PER1-3, CRY1/2, ADA, COMT, SLC6A4, GABRA1, and orexin receptors HCRTR1/HCRTR2, with rare familial circadian-related sleep phenotypes linked to PER2 or CSNK1D variants and common insomnia susceptibility showing polygenic inheritance. Subtypes include short-term and chronic insomnia, psychophysiologic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, comorbid insomnia, and circadian-related sleep initiation complaints. Common comorbidities include depression, anxiety, PTSD, substance use disorders, chronic pain, cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes, GERD, and obstructive sleep apnea; complications include accidents, cognitive impairment, poorer cardiometabolic outcomes, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, typically using ICSD-3/DSM-5 criteria requiring nocturnal sleep difficulty with daytime consequences at least three times weekly for at least three months in chronic cases, supported by sleep history, sleep diary, actigraphy, insomnia severity scales, medication and psychiatric review, and polysomnography when sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder, parasomnia, or atypical features are suspected. Treatments include benzodiazepine receptor agonists such as zolpidem or eszopiclone, which positively modulate GABAA receptors; doxepin, which at low dose blocks histamine H1 receptors to improve sleep maintenance; melatonin agonists such as ramelteon acting at MT1/MT2 receptors to facilitate sleep onset; and dual orexin receptor antagonists such as suvorexant or lemborexant, which inhibit wake-promoting orexin signaling.

Name: Vitamin B 6 Deficiency
Description: Vitamin B6 deficiency is a nutritional and sometimes genetic disorder characterized by inadequate pyridoxine, pyridoxal, or the active cofactor pyridoxal-5′-phosphate (PLP), leading to impaired function of PLP-dependent enzymes in amino acid metabolism, neurotransmitter synthesis, one-carbon and transsulfuration pathways, glycogen phosphorylase activity, and heme synthesis. Although usually acquired from malnutrition, alcoholism, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy, or drug exposure, genetic forms include defects in ALPL causing hypophosphatasia with low PLP dephosphorylation, PDXK mutations impairing pyridoxal kinase, PNPO deficiency reducing conversion to PLP, and ALDH7A1 or PLPBP-related B6-responsive epilepsies; inheritance in these monogenic forms is typically autosomal recessive. Molecularly, deficiency disrupts GABA, serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine synthesis, elevates homocysteine through impaired cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase activity, and diminishes aminolevulinate synthase-dependent heme production, contributing to neurologic dysfunction and sideroblastic or microcytic anemia. Common manifestations include cheilosis, glossitis, seborrheic dermatitis, irritability, depression, confusion, peripheral neuropathy, seizures in infants, stomatitis, and anemia; complications include developmental delay, refractory epilepsy, immune dysfunction, and hyperhomocysteinemia-associated vascular risk. Clinically relevant subtypes include dietary deficiency, medication-induced deficiency, malabsorptive deficiency, and inherited B6-dependent epileptic or metabolic syndromes. Treatment centers on pyridoxine supplementation, which is converted to PLP to restore cofactor pools; pyridoxal-5′-phosphate is preferred in PNPO deficiency or selected refractory epilepsies because it bypasses impaired activation; and folic acid, iron, or multivitamin repletion may be co-administered to correct associated megaloblastic, sideroblastic, or mixed nutritional states, while withdrawal of causative agents such as isoniazid, hydralazine, penicillamine, or levodopa/carbidopa imbalance is essential. Name: Ischemic Stroke
Description: Ischemic stroke is an acute cerebrovascular syndrome caused by focal cerebral infarction from arterial occlusion, most commonly due to large-artery atherosclerotic thrombosis, cardioembolism, or small-vessel lipohyalinosis, and is clinically characterized by sudden focal deficits such as hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, aphasia, dysarthria, visual field defects, neglect, ataxia, or altered consciousness. Major molecular contributors include prothrombotic and vascular genes and proteins such as APOE, MTHFR, PDE4D, HDAC9, PITX2 and ZFHX3 in cardioembolic stroke, NOTCH3 in CADASIL, HTRA1 in hereditary small-vessel disease, and coagulation-related factors including factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1; most cases are multifactorial, although monogenic forms show autosomal dominant inheritance in disorders such as CADASIL. Pathobiology centers on atherosclerosis, platelet activation, thrombin generation, endothelial dysfunction, excitotoxic glutamate signaling, calcium overload, oxidative stress, mitochondrial injury, inflammation mediated by TNF-α, IL-1, NF-κB, complement, and matrix metalloproteinases, and ischemia-reperfusion pathways affecting the neurovascular unit and blood-brain barrier. Standard treatments include alteplase or tenecteplase, which promote fibrinolysis by converting plasminogen to plasmin; aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and thromboxane A2-dependent platelet aggregation; clopidogrel, a P2Y12 receptor antagonist; anticoagulants such as apixaban or warfarin for atrial fibrillation by inhibiting factor Xa or vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; and statins such as atorvastatin, which lower LDL and stabilize plaques. Common comorbidities and complications include hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, atrial fibrillation, carotid stenosis, smoking, coronary artery disease, recurrent stroke, cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, aspiration pneumonia, venous thromboembolism, seizures, dysphagia, depression, and vascular cognitive impairment. Diagnosis relies on abrupt onset of a compatible syndrome, exclusion of hemorrhage by noncontrast CT, confirmation with MRI diffusion-weighted imaging, vascular imaging by CTA

Name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
Description: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS; MeSH D054058) is an acute manifestation of atherosclerotic coronary artery disease caused most often by plaque rupture or erosion with superimposed platelet-rich thrombus and partial or complete coronary occlusion, encompassing unstable angina, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Its biology involves lipid handling, inflammation, thrombosis, endothelial dysfunction, and ischemia-reperfusion signaling, with associated genes and proteins including LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, LPA, APOE, CETP, NOS3, MTHFR, ACE, IL6, CRP, PAI-1/SERPINE1, F2, F5, and platelet receptors such as P2RY12 and ITGB3; rare monogenic dyslipidemias, especially familial hypercholesterolemia from LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 variants, confer strong inherited risk, whereas most ACS susceptibility is polygenic with gene-environment interaction. Key pathways include oxidized LDL uptake and foam-cell formation, NF-kB- and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated vascular inflammation, matrix metalloproteinase-driven fibrous cap weakening, tissue factor–thrombin–fibrin coagulation, platelet activation through thromboxane A2, ADP-P2Y12, and GP IIb/IIIa signaling, and endothelial nitric oxide dysregulation. Typical symptoms are pressure-like chest pain, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, radiation to arm, jaw, or back, and possible hypotension, arrhythmia, or heart failure. Diagnosis relies on history, serial ECG changes including ST elevation or depression and T-wave inversion, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin rise/fall, risk scores, echocardiography, and coronary angiography or CT coronary angiography. Standard therapies include aspirin, an irreversible COX-1 inhibitor; P2Y12 inhibitors such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor, which block ADP-mediated platelet activation; anticoagulants such as unfractionated heparin, which potentiates antithrombin; nitrates, beta-blockers, high-intensity statins, and reperfusion with PCI when indicated. Name: Infection caused by Citrobacter
Description: Infection caused by Citrobacter (UMLS C0948204) is an opportunistic Gram-negative Enterobacterales infection, most often due to Citrobacter freundii complex or C. koseri, producing urinary tract infection, bacteremia, intra-abdominal and hepatobiliary infection, pneumonia, wound infection, and in neonates meningitis with brain abscess. Pathogenesis reflects both host susceptibility and bacterial virulence: relevant bacterial genes and proteins include lipopolysaccharide, outer-membrane proteins, flagellar components, siderophore-mediated iron acquisition systems, adhesins, and resistance determinants such as chromosomal ampC beta-lactamase, ESBL genes including blaCTX-M, and carbapenemase genes such as blaKPC or blaNDM; host inflammatory signaling is driven largely through LPS-TLR4/CD14 activation, NF-kappaB and MAPK pathways, inflammasome-mediated cytokine release, neutrophil recruitment, complement, and in severe sepsis dysregulated TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6 responses. Common symptoms include fever, dysuria, flank pain, cough, abdominal pain, altered mental status, and signs of sepsis; neonates may present with lethargy, seizures, bulging fontanelle, or focal neurologic deficits. Major comorbidities and risk factors are prematurity, advanced age, diabetes, malignancy, chronic kidney or liver disease, urinary tract abnormalities, indwelling catheters, ICU exposure, and immunosuppression, while complications include septic shock, renal abscess, empyema, meningitis, ventriculitis, and permanent neurodevelopmental sequelae. Disease subtypes are commonly classified by species and by syndrome, especially uncomplicated or catheter-associated UTI, bloodstream infection, and neonatal CNS infection. It is not an inherited disease, but host genetics influencing innate immunity, such as rare TLR4 or MYD88 pathway defects, may alter susceptibility. Diagnosis relies on culture of urine, blood, CSF, or other sterile-site specimens with species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, supplemented when needed by PCR for resistance genes, inflammatory markers, and imaging such as renal ultrasound or brain MRI/CT to define complications. Name: Pneumonia, Hospital Acquired
Description: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (UMLS C0949083) is a nosocomial lower respiratory tract infection arising 48 hours or more after admission, typically caused by microaspiration of colonizing flora and characterized by alveolar inflammation, neutrophilic exudation, and impaired gas exchange; major subtypes include non-ventilator hospital-acquired pneumonia and ventilator-associated pneumonia. It is usually infectious rather than inherited, but host susceptibility is influenced by genetic and protein factors involved in innate immunity and inflammation, including TLR2, TLR4, CD14, NOD2, MBL2, TNF, IL6, IL10, CFTR, and surfactant proteins SFTPA1/SFTPD, while pathogen determinants such as mecA in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Panton-Valentine leukocidin, and resistance enzymes including ESBLs and carbapenemases in Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii shape phenotype and therapy. Key pathways include Toll-like receptor, NF-kB, inflammasome, complement, JAK/STAT cytokine signaling, and neutrophil recruitment, with epithelial injury, biofilm formation, and dysregulated macrophage responses central to pathogenesis. Common symptoms and signs are fever, purulent sputum, cough, dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, leukocytosis or leukopenia, new crackles, and in severe cases sepsis or acute respiratory distress syndrome. Frequent comorbidities include COPD, structural lung disease, heart failure, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, immunosuppression, recent surgery, and prolonged ventilation; complications include bacteremia, empyema, septic shock, multiorgan failure, and death. Diagnosis rests on a new or progressive infiltrate on chest radiography or CT plus compatible clinical features and microbiologic evaluation using sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or bronchoalveolar lavage with Gram stain and culture, blood cultures, and selected PCR-based resistance testing.
