Name: Peptostreptococcus infection
Description: Peptostreptococcus infection is an opportunistic, usually endogenous anaerobic gram-positive coccal infection caused by Peptostreptococcus species, now partly reclassified within anaerobic gram-positive cocci, and typically presents as polymicrobial disease involving oral, pleuropulmonary, intra-abdominal, pelvic, skin/soft-tissue, bone/joint, or central nervous system sites, often with abscess formation, foul-smelling drainage, fever, pain, swelling, tissue tenderness, and leukocytosis, with site-specific manifestations such as aspiration pneumonia, empyema, brain abscess, periodontal infection, or postoperative wound infection. It is not an inherited disorder and no pathogen-specific Mendelian pattern is recognized; rather, host susceptibility is influenced by immune and barrier-defect genes and comorbid states, with representative examples including neutrophil dysfunction, CYBB-related chronic granulomatous disease, TLR2/TLR4-NFKB pathway variation, and cytokine mediators such as TNF, IL1B, and IL6 that shape inflammatory response to anaerobes. Relevant molecular pathways include mucosal barrier disruption, biofilm formation, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and innate immune signaling through pattern-recognition receptors converging on NF-kB and inflammasome-associated responses. Common comorbidities and risk factors include periodontal disease, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunosuppression, aspiration risk, bowel perforation, pelvic inflammatory disease, trauma, surgery, and foreign bodies; complications include sepsis, bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis, and metastatic abscesses. Major subtypes are defined by anatomic syndrome rather than genotype, such as oral/dental, pleuropulmonary, intra-abdominal, pelvic, soft-tissue, and CNS infection. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion of anaerobic infection, imaging to define abscesses, aspiration or deep tissue sampling for anaerobic Gram stain and culture, increasingly MALDI-TOF or 16S rRNA identification, and blood cultures when invasive disease is suspected. Treatment usually combines source control with anaerobe-active agents such as metronidazole, which reduces nitro groups to DNA-damaging radicals; beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibit cell-wall synthesis while blocking beta-lactamases;

Name: Intraabdominal Infections
Description: Intraabdominal infections (UMLS C1112209) are usually acquired, polymicrobial infections arising from contamination of the peritoneal cavity or abdominal organs after perforation, ischemia, obstruction, surgery, trauma, or translocation of gut flora, rather than inherited disorders; they include uncomplicated infection confined to a viscus and complicated infection extending into the peritoneum with localized abscess or diffuse peritonitis, and may be community- or healthcare-associated. Typical pathogens include Enterobacterales such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis, enterococci, and sometimes Candida spp.; relevant microbial resistance determinants include ESBL genes such as blaCTX-M, carbapenemases including KPC and NDM, mecA in staphylococci, and vanA/vanB in enterococci. Host inflammatory signaling prominently involves pattern-recognition pathways triggered by LPS and other PAMPs through TLR4, TLR2, NOD-like receptors, NF-kB, complement, inflammasome activation, and downstream cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, and chemokine-driven neutrophil recruitment, with sepsis-related endothelial injury and coagulation activation in severe disease. Symptoms and signs commonly include abdominal pain, tenderness, guarding, fever, nausea, vomiting, ileus, leukocytosis, tachycardia, and in advanced cases hypotension, lactic acidosis, organ dysfunction, or septic shock. Important comorbidities and complications include appendicitis, diverticulitis, bowel perforation, pancreatitis, malignancy, cirrhosis, diabetes, immunosuppression, postoperative abscess, fistula, bacteremia, and multiorgan failure. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus CBC, inflammatory markers, blood cultures when septic, and especially contrast-enhanced CT to define source and abscess; ultrasound is useful for biliary or pelvic collections, and peritoneal or abscess cultures guide therapy. Treatment requires source control and antibiotics such as piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibits cell-wall synthesis with beta-lactamase inhibition; ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, targeting bacterial cell-wall synthesis and anaerobic DNA damage; and meropenem, a broad-spectrum carbapenem inhibiting penicillin-binding proteins.

Name: Aggressive Systemic Mastocytoses
Description: Aggressive systemic mastocytosis is a rare advanced form of systemic mastocytosis, a clonal hematologic neoplasm characterized by pathologic accumulation of neoplastic mast cells in bone marrow and extracutaneous organs, causing organ damage without meeting criteria for mast cell leukemia; related advanced subtypes include aggressive systemic mastocytosis, systemic mastocytosis with an associated hematologic neoplasm, and mast cell leukemia. It is driven most commonly by activating KIT mutations, especially KIT D816V, with aberrant expression of mast-cell proteins such as CD25, CD2, CD30, tryptase, and often additional somatic lesions in SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1, TET2, DNMT3A, EZH2, CBL, JAK2, or RAS pathway genes that worsen prognosis; inherited transmission is usually absent, as the disease is generally sporadic and acquired rather than Mendelian. Pathobiology centers on constitutive KIT receptor tyrosine kinase signaling through PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, and NF-κB pathways, promoting mast-cell survival, proliferation, cytokine release, and fibrosis. Clinical manifestations reflect mediator release and tissue infiltration, including flushing, pruritus, abdominal pain, diarrhea, peptic symptoms, anaphylaxis, weight loss, fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, malabsorption, ascites, portal hypertension, and osteolysis or severe osteoporosis with fractures; major complications include hepatic failure, hypersplenism, infections, and progression to leukemic disease. Diagnosis is based on WHO/ICC systemic mastocytosis criteria using bone marrow or other tissue histology with dense multifocal mast-cell infiltrates, atypical spindle-shaped mast cells, elevated serum tryptase, aberrant immunophenotype, and KIT mutation testing by sensitive PCR or next-generation sequencing, with imaging and organ-function studies used to document C-findings that define aggressiveness. Treatment commonly includes midostaurin, a multikinase inhibitor active against KIT D816V; avapritinib, a potent selective KIT D816V inhibitor; cladribine, a purine nucleoside analog cytoreductive agent; and selected interferon-α, corticosteroids, bisphosphonates, antihistamines, leukotriene antagonists, or ep

Name: NGU - Non-gonococcal urethritis
Description: Non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU; UMLS C1112709) is an inflammatory syndrome of the male urethra not caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, most commonly infectious and usually sexually transmitted, with major etiologic subtypes including chlamydial NGU, Mycoplasma genitalium-associated NGU, Ureaplasma-associated disease, Trichomonas vaginalis-related urethritis, and idiopathic or persistent/recurrent NGU. Its biology is driven more by pathogen and host inflammatory responses than by Mendelian genetics; representative microbial genes/proteins implicated in pathogenesis include Chlamydia trachomatis major outer membrane protein OmpA/MOMP and polymorphic membrane proteins, Mycoplasma genitalium adhesins MgPa/MgpB and MgpC, and Ureaplasma urease, which activate epithelial innate immune signaling through Toll-like receptors, NF-κB, MAPK, and cytokine networks involving IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-α, neutrophil recruitment, and in some cases inflammasome-related responses. There is no established inheritance pattern for NGU itself, although host susceptibility may be modified by common immune-response variants, for example in TLR or cytokine genes. Typical features are dysuria, urethral discomfort or pruritus, and mucoid, mucopurulent, or scant discharge, though asymptomatic infection is common. Diagnosis rests on compatible symptoms or signs plus objective urethral inflammation, such as urethral smear microscopy showing increased polymorphonuclear leukocytes or first-void urine positive leukocyte esterase/pyuria, with exclusion of gonorrhea by Gram stain and/or nucleic acid amplification testing; NAATs are preferred to identify C. trachomatis, M. genitalium, T. vaginalis, and sometimes Ureaplasma. Standard treatments include doxycycline, a tetracycline that inhibits 30S ribosomal protein synthesis; azithromycin, a macrolide acting at the 50S ribosome; and moxifloxacin, a fluoroquinolone inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with metronidazole used when trichomoniasis is suspected via nitro-radical mediated DNA damage. Name: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasm
Description: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasm (GTN; UMLS C1135868) is a malignant spectrum of pregnancy-related trophoblastic disorders arising from placental trophoblast, classically including invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumor, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumor, most often following a hydatidiform mole but also after miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or term gestation. Its biology is driven by abnormal paternal genomic contribution and disordered imprinting; complete moles are usually androgenetic diploid conceptions with overexpression of paternally expressed genes, while recurrent molar pregnancy is linked to maternal-effect variants in NLRP7, KHDC3L, and less commonly PADI6. Frequently reported molecular abnormalities include dysregulated p53, p57/KIP2 loss in complete mole, high hCG expression, and activation of proliferative PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK/ERK, TGF-β, Wnt/β-catenin, angiogenic VEGF, and immune checkpoint pathways including PD-1/PD-L1. Patients typically present with persistent or rising serum β-hCG after pregnancy, abnormal uterine bleeding, enlarged uterus, theca-lutein cysts, hyperemesis, pelvic pain, and symptoms from metastases, especially lung, vagina, brain, or liver. Major complications include hemorrhage, uterine perforation, anemia, preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism, respiratory compromise, and treatment-related infertility concerns. Diagnosis relies on serial quantitative β-hCG, pelvic ultrasonography, histopathology when available, chest imaging and cross-sectional staging for metastases, and FIGO anatomic staging with WHO risk scoring; p57 immunostaining and ploidy testing help classify molar antecedents. GTN is highly chemosensitive: methotrexate, a folate antagonist inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase; actinomycin D, an intercalating transcription inhibitor; and etoposide, a topoisomerase II inhibitor, are core agents, with cyclophosphamide DNA alkylation, vincristine microtubule inhibition, platinum compounds, and pembrolizumab PD-1 blockade used in selected resistant, high-risk, or refractory disease.

Name: Ovarian Cancer
Description: Ovarian neoplasms (MeSH D010051) comprise a heterogeneous group of benign, borderline, and malignant tumors arising from epithelial, germ-cell, sex cord-stromal, or metastatic sources, with epithelial ovarian carcinoma, especially high-grade serous carcinoma, being the most lethal subtype; other major subtypes include endometrioid, clear cell, mucinous, low-grade serous, granulosa-cell tumors, dysgerminoma, yolk-sac tumor, and teratoma. Clinically, patients often present insidiously with abdominal bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary urgency, increasing girth, adnexal mass, ascites, weight loss, or bowel symptoms, and complications include malignant ascites, bowel obstruction, pleural effusion, venous thromboembolism, cachexia, infertility, and recurrence. Key molecular alterations include TP53 mutations in most high-grade serous tumors; germline or somatic BRCA1/BRCA2 defects and broader homologous recombination deficiency; KRAS, BRAF, and ERBB2 in low-grade serous or mucinous tumors; PTEN, PIK3CA, ARID1A, and CTNNB1 in endometrioid and clear-cell tumors; mismatch repair genes in Lynch syndrome; and FOXL2 in adult granulosa-cell tumors. Pathways commonly implicated include homologous recombination/DNA repair, p53, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, cell-cycle dysregulation, and inflammatory or hormone-responsive signaling. Inheritance is usually sporadic, but hereditary predisposition is important, most notably autosomal dominant BRCA1/2-associated hereditary breast-ovarian cancer and Lynch syndrome due to MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2. Diagnosis relies on pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasonography, CT or MRI for staging, serum markers such as CA-125 and HE4 with ROMA in selected cases, and definitive histopathology with FIGO staging, supplemented by immunohistochemistry and germline/somatic molecular testing. Standard therapy includes cytoreductive surgery plus carboplatin or cisplatin, which form DNA crosslinks, and paclitaxel, which stabilizes microtubules; bevacizumab inhibits VEGF-A-mediated angiogenesis,

Name: Carnitine deficiency (disorder)
Description: Carnitine deficiency is a metabolic disorder in which impaired availability or transport of L-carnitine disrupts mitochondrial long-chain fatty acid oxidation, causing cellular energy failure, especially in heart, skeletal muscle, and liver; it includes primary systemic carnitine deficiency, usually due to autosomal recessive pathogenic variants in SLC22A5 encoding the high-affinity carnitine transporter OCTN2, and secondary forms associated with organic acidemias, fatty acid oxidation defects, renal tubular losses, malnutrition, liver disease, hemodialysis, or drugs such as valproate. The core pathobiology involves reduced intracellular carnitine, impaired CPT1/CPT2- and carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase–dependent transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria, diminished beta-oxidation, reduced ketogenesis, toxic acyl-CoA accumulation, and downstream energetic stress pathways affecting muscle and myocardium. Clinical manifestations range from infantile hypoketotic hypoglycemia, fasting intolerance, vomiting, encephalopathy, hepatomegaly, and hyperammonemia to childhood or adult skeletal myopathy, elevated CK, muscle weakness, fatigue, and dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with risks of arrhythmia, sudden death, recurrent rhabdomyolysis, and developmental delay; common comorbidities and complications include cardiomyopathy, heart failure, liver dysfunction, recurrent metabolic decompensation, and infection-triggered crises. Diagnosis relies on low plasma free carnitine, often markedly reduced in primary disease, acylcarnitine profiling, urine organic acids, reduced fibroblast carnitine transport, molecular confirmation of SLC22A5 variants, and supportive ECG, echocardiography, CK, liver enzymes, and newborn screening by tandem mass spectrometry. Treatment centers on oral levocarnitine replacement, which replenishes intracellular carnitine and facilitates acyl-group buffering and mitochondrial import; avoidance of fasting with high-carbohydrate support to reduce reliance on fatty acid oxidation; and acute intravenous dextrose, while medium-chain triglycerides may bypass the carnitine-dependent transport step and riboflavin or coenzyme Q10 are sometimes used adjunctively in selected secondary mitochondrial or fatty acid oxidation contexts.

Name: Rhinorrhea
Description: Rhinorrhea is a clinical sign rather than a single inherited disease, defined by excessive nasal discharge that may be serous, mucoid, purulent, allergic, vasomotor, infectious, medication induced, or due to cerebrospinal fluid leak; accordingly, most cases have no Mendelian inheritance, although genetic predisposition is recognized in atopic rhinorrhea through variants affecting type 2 immunity and epithelial barrier function, including IL4, IL13, IL4R, FCER1A, TSLP, FLG, and filaggrin-related pathways, while primary ciliary dyskinesia genes such as DNAH5 and DNAI1 can contribute to chronic rhinitis with rhinorrhea. Key pathways include IgE-mediated mast-cell activation, Th2 cytokine signaling through IL-4/IL-13 and JAK-STAT, eosinophilic inflammation, histamine H1 receptor signaling, leukotriene pathways, cholinergic parasympathetic stimulation of submucosal glands, neurogenic TRPV1-mediated responses, and in infectious forms, innate immune pathways involving TLRs, interferons, and neutrophilic cytokines. Common treatments include intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress NF-kB-driven inflammatory gene transcription; intranasal antihistamines such as azelastine, which block H1 receptors and reduce mast-cell mediator effects; and ipratropium bromide, a muscarinic antagonist that decreases glandular secretion; additional options include oral second-generation antihistamines such as cetirizine and leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast. Rhinorrhea commonly coexists with allergic rhinitis, acute viral upper respiratory infection, chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, nasal polyposis, adenoid hypertrophy, and, less commonly, skull-base trauma or spontaneous CSF leak, with complications including sinusitis, otitis media, sleep disturbance, dehydration in infants, and meningitis in CSF rhinorrhea. Diagnosis is clinical but guided by discharge quality, triggers, endoscopic findings, and associated sneezing, congestion, pruritus, facial pain, fever, or unilateral clear drainage; testing may include allergen-specific IgE or skin-prick testing, nasal endoscopy, sinus CT, viral testing when indicated, and beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein assay with CT/MR cisternography when

Name: Anemia, Diamond-Blackfan
Description: Diamond-Blackfan anemia is a rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by congenital pure red cell aplasia, usually presenting in infancy with severe macrocytic anemia, reticulocytopenia, and a normocellular marrow showing marked paucity or absence of erythroid precursors; many patients also have elevated erythrocyte adenosine deaminase and increased fetal hemoglobin. It is genetically heterogeneous but most often follows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance, although sporadic cases are common; causative variants typically affect ribosomal protein genes such as RPS19, RPL5, RPS26, RPL11, RPL35A, RPS24, and less commonly GATA1, TSR2, or ADA2, producing defective ribosome biogenesis, nucleolar stress, p53 activation, apoptosis of erythroid progenitors, and impaired erythropoietin-responsive erythropoiesis. Clinical manifestations include pallor, poor feeding, growth failure, congenital anomalies involving the craniofacial structures, thumb and upper limb, heart, and genitourinary tract, and later iron overload from transfusions; important complications include endocrine dysfunction, infection risk, osteoporosis, myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, colon cancer, and osteogenic sarcoma. Recognized forms include classic DBA, nonclassic or mild DBA, and transfusion-dependent versus steroid-responsive disease. Diagnosis rests on early-onset isolated anemia with macrocytosis, low reticulocytes, reduced marrow erythroblasts, exclusion of other inherited marrow failure disorders and transient erythroblastopenia, plus molecular confirmation by multigene panel or exome sequencing; supportive tests include eADA, HbF, and family evaluation. Treatment commonly uses prednisone or prednisolone, which stimulate erythropoiesis and reduce transfusion need; chronic red-cell transfusions with iron chelators such as deferasirox or deferoxamine to limit iron-mediated oxidative injury; and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only established curative therapy, often conditioned with busulfan-, fludarabine-, or cyclophosphamide-based regimens.

Name: Pasteurella multocida infectious disease
Description: Pasteurella multocida infectious disease is an acute zoonotic bacterial infection caused by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Pasteurella multocida, most often after cat or dog bites, scratches, or saliva exposure, and it ranges from localized skin and soft-tissue infection to invasive pneumonia, bacteremia, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, meningitis, or endocarditis. Major virulence determinants include the capsular biosynthesis loci associated with serogroups A, B, D, E, and F; lipopolysaccharide/lipooligosaccharide genes; adhesins and outer-membrane proteins such as OmpA and OmpH; iron-acquisition systems; and, in toxigenic strains, the dermonecrotic Pasteurella multocida toxin encoded by pmt, which activates Rho GTPase-dependent signaling through deamidation of G-protein alpha subunits, while host inflammatory responses prominently engage TLR4-, NF-kappaB-, MAPK-, and cytokine pathways including TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6. Disease subtypes are commonly classified as wound infection/cellulitis, respiratory infection, and systemic invasive disease. Typical findings include rapid-onset pain, erythema, swelling, purulence, lymphangitis, fever, and regional adenitis after animal exposure; respiratory disease may cause cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, and infiltrates, especially in patients with COPD or bronchiectasis. Important comorbidities and risk factors include chronic lung disease, cirrhosis, diabetes, malignancy, immunosuppression, and prosthetic joints or valves, which also predispose to complications such as abscess, sepsis, and metastatic infection. Inheritance is not Mendelian; known genetic components are chiefly microbial virulence genes rather than host pathogenic variants, although immunodeficiency states may increase susceptibility. Diagnosis relies on exposure history, compatible syndrome, culture of wound, blood, respiratory, or sterile-site specimens with species identification by biochemical methods, MALDI-TOF, or 16S rRNA/PCR, plus imaging when deep infection is suspected. First-line therapy includes amoxicillin-clavulanate, in which amoxicillin inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamases; intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam, with analogous mechanisms, for severe disease; and doxycycline

Name: Late latent syphilis
Description: Late latent syphilis is a sexually acquired, systemic chronic infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum, defined by serologic evidence of syphilis without clinical manifestations and with infection of more than 1 year’s duration or of unknown duration; it is often subclassified as early latent versus late latent/unknown-duration latent disease because this distinction guides therapy. The organism lacks a major culture system and disease risk is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion, but host susceptibility and immune response are influenced by genetic variation in innate and adaptive immunity, with reported associations involving HLA class II alleles and cytokine-related genes such as TLR1, TLR2, TLR6, TNF, IL10, and IFNG; key immunobiology includes treponemal lipoprotein activation of TLR1/2 signaling, NF-κB-mediated cytokine production, macrophage and dendritic-cell activation, Th1-predominant IFN-γ responses, and endothelial inflammation. Typical symptoms are absent in the latent stage, although history may reveal prior chancre, rash, mucous patches, condylomata lata, or lymphadenopathy; major complications of untreated infection include progression to tertiary syphilis with cardiovascular syphilis, gummatous disease, neurosyphilis, ocular or otic syphilis, and adverse pregnancy outcomes including congenital syphilis. Important comorbidities include HIV infection and other sexually transmitted infections. Diagnosis relies on compatible history and reactive serology, usually a nontreponemal test such as RPR or VDRL confirmed by a treponemal assay such as TP-PA, FTA-ABS, or EIA/CIA, with CSF examination reserved for neurologic, ocular, or otic findings; treatment is benzathine penicillin G, which releases penicillin slowly and inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking, typically given as 2.4 million units intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks, while doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor, and tetracycline, also a 30S inhibitor, are alternatives for nonpregnant penicillin-allergic patients, and ceftriaxone, a β-lactam cell-wall synthesis inhibitor, is sometimes used in selected situations.

Name: Proteus pneumonia
Description: Proteus pneumonia is a bacterial lower respiratory tract infection caused most often by Proteus mirabilis and less commonly P. vulgaris or other Proteus species, typically arising as a healthcare-associated, aspiration-related, or ventilator-associated pneumonia in debilitated hosts rather than an inherited disorder. Its pathobiology is driven by Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide engaging TLR4–MyD88–NF-κB signaling, with downstream TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and, in some strains, biofilm formation and urease, hemolysin HpmA, flagellar/swarming regulators flhDC, fimbrial adhesins such as MR/P fimbriae, and lipoprotein and capsule-associated factors that enhance colonization and tissue injury; resistance determinants may include ESBL genes such as blaTEM, blaSHV, and blaCTX-M, AmpC enzymes, or carbapenemases including blaNDM. Clinical manifestations resemble other Gram-negative pneumonias, with fever, cough, purulent sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest discomfort, hypoxemia, and radiographic lobar or bronchopneumonic infiltrates, and severe disease may progress to necrotizing pneumonia, abscess, empyema, sepsis, or ARDS. Important comorbidities include advanced age, chronic lung disease, neurologic dysphagia, diabetes, malignancy, renal failure, urinary tract colonization or infection, immunosuppression, and prolonged hospitalization or mechanical ventilation. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms plus chest imaging, microbiologic confirmation from sputum, tracheal aspirate, bronchoalveolar lavage, or blood cultures with species identification and susceptibility testing, while inflammatory markers and blood gases help assess severity. Treatment is guided by antibiogram and commonly includes ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins, fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, and carbapenems such as meropenem for ESBL-producing strains; aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, which bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, may be added in severe infection. Subtypes are best considered by clinical setting, including community-acquired rare cases versus hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated forms.

Name: Pelvic inflammatory disease caused by Metamycoplasma hominis
Description: Pelvic inflammatory disease caused by Metamycoplasma hominis (formerly Mycoplasma hominis; UMLS C1261256) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract in which this cell wall–deficient Mollicute contributes to endometritis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian infection, and postprocedural or postpartum pelvic sepsis, often in conjunction with anaerobes or other sexually transmitted pathogens. Disease manifestations typically include lower abdominal or pelvic pain, cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, fever, abnormal vaginal discharge or bleeding, dyspareunia, and, in severe cases, abscess, peritonitis, or sepsis. Major complications include infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, adhesions, Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and coinfection-associated bacterial vaginosis, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and postpartum endometritis. Pathobiology reflects mucosal adherence and immune activation rather than a single canonical virulence mutation; representative microbial factors include variable adherence/surface lipoproteins such as Vaa and OppA, membrane lipoproteins and antigenic variation systems, while host inflammatory pathways prominently involve TLR2/TLR6 recognition, NF-κB, MAPK, and cytokines including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, and TNF-α, driving neutrophilic and macrophage-rich inflammation. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for PID itself, but host susceptibility may be modified by immune-response variants, with examples reported in TLR2, TLR4, IL1B, IL6, TNF, and MBL2. Diagnosis is primarily clinical using PID criteria of pelvic/lower abdominal pain with cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness, supported by pregnancy testing, pelvic examination, leukocytosis or elevated CRP/ESR, imaging for hydrosalpinx or tubo-ovarian abscess, and microbiologic testing by culture or, more sensitively, nucleic acid amplification/PCR from cervical, vaginal, or endometrial specimens to detect M. hominis and exclude gonorrhea/chlamydia. Name: Sarcoma
Description: Sarcoma is a heterogeneous group of malignant mesenchymal neoplasms arising in soft tissue, bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, vascular, or fibrous connective tissues, with major subtypes including osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, liposarcoma, synovial sarcoma, angiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Its molecular basis varies by subtype and includes complex karyotypic tumors with TP53, RB1, ATRX, CDKN2A, PTEN, MDM2, and NF1 alterations, as well as translocation-driven sarcomas such as EWSR1-FLI1 in Ewing sarcoma, SS18-SSX in synovial sarcoma, FUS-DDIT3 in myxoid liposarcoma, and KIT or PDGFRA mutations in GIST; germline predisposition occurs in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, hereditary retinoblastoma, neurofibromatosis type 1, familial adenomatous polyposis, and SDH-deficient syndromes, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance. Key pathways include p53 and RB cell-cycle control, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-MAPK, IGF signaling, VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, Wnt/beta-catenin, and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling through KIT, PDGFRA, ALK, NTRK, and MET. Patients typically present with a painless enlarging mass, local pain, swelling, reduced function, pathologic fracture in bone sarcoma, constitutional symptoms in advanced disease, and pulmonary metastases as a common complication; treatment-related morbidity, local recurrence, thromboembolism, and cardiotoxicity may also occur. Diagnosis relies on imaging with MRI for soft tissue and CT or radiography for bone and staging, followed by core needle or incisional biopsy, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing by FISH, RT-PCR, or next-generation sequencing to define subtype and actionable alterations. Name: Uremic pruritus
Description: Uremic pruritus (CKD-associated pruritus; UMLS C1262019) is a chronic, multifactorial systemic itch syndrome occurring mainly in advanced chronic kidney disease, especially end-stage kidney disease on dialysis, characterized by generalized or symmetric intermittent or persistent pruritus, often worse at night, with excoriations, xerosis, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life, but usually without a primary inflammatory rash. Its pathobiology is incompletely defined and appears polygenic rather than Mendelian, with reported associations involving inflammatory and neuromodulatory genes and proteins such as IL6, TNF, IL31, OPRM1, OPRK1, TRPV1, PAR2/F2RL1, HRH1/HRH4, and mast-cell, eosinophil, and opioid-system mediators; inherited susceptibility is not established, but host genetic variation in cytokine and opioid receptor pathways may modify risk. Key implicated pathways include systemic microinflammation with elevated IL-6, CRP, TNF-α, and IL-31, dysregulated endogenous mu- and kappa-opioid signaling, peripheral neuropathy with C-fiber sensitization, mast-cell and eosinophil activation, xerosis-related skin barrier dysfunction, disordered calcium-phosphate-parathyroid hormone metabolism, and accumulation of poorly dialyzable uremic toxins. Common comorbidities and correlates include hyperparathyroidism, hyperphosphatemia, anemia, diabetes, neuropathy, cardiovascular disease, depression, insomnia, and secondary skin infection from scratching. Subtypes are usually described clinically as localized versus generalized and intermittent versus persistent CKD-associated pruritus. Diagnosis is clinical and one of exclusion in a patient with CKD and chronic itch, supported by severity scales such as the Worst Itch Numeric Rating Scale or 5-D Itch Scale, examination for xerosis and excoriations, and evaluation for alternative causes with CBC, liver and thyroid tests, iron studies, calcium, phosphate, PTH, and dialysis adequacy assessment. Frequently used treatments include difelikefalin, a peripheral kappa-opioid receptor agonist; gabapentin or pregabalin, which reduce neuronal excitability via the α2δ calcium-channel subunit; emollients to restore barrier function; narrowband UVB phototherapy with immunomodulatory and antipruritic effects; and, less

Name: Fungal keratitis
Description: Fungal keratitis is an infectious, vision-threatening corneal disease caused most often by filamentous fungi such as Fusarium and Aspergillus, and less commonly yeasts such as Candida, typically following corneal trauma with plant material, contact lens wear, ocular surface disease, or topical corticosteroid use. It is usually acquired rather than inherited, but host susceptibility has genetic components, with representative associations reported in innate immune genes and proteins including TLR4, TLR2, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, DC-SIGN/CD209, IL1B, IL6, TNF, MMP9, and MYD88, whose variants may alter risk or inflammatory severity. Pathobiologically, fungal cell-wall beta-glucans and mannans activate pattern-recognition pathways involving TLR2/TLR4, Dectin-1/Syk/CARD9, MyD88, NF-kappaB, MAPK, inflammasome signaling, neutrophil recruitment, reactive oxygen species, matrix metalloproteinases, and cytokines such as IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, IL-17, and TNF-alpha, driving corneal ulceration and stromal melt. Clinical features include severe ocular pain, redness, photophobia, tearing, blurred vision, discharge, a feathery-edged corneal infiltrate with epithelial defect, satellite lesions, endothelial plaque, and possible hypopyon; major subtypes are filamentous versus yeast keratitis, with superficial or deep stromal forms. Diagnosis rests on slit-lamp findings plus microbiologic confirmation by corneal scraping for KOH wet mount, Gram stain, calcofluor white, culture on fungal media, and increasingly PCR or in vivo confocal microscopy. Standard treatment includes topical natamycin, a polyene that binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes, especially for filamentous disease; amphotericin B, another ergosterol-binding polyene, often used for Candida; and voriconazole, a triazole that inhibits fungal 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis, with itraconazole or posaconazole as alternatives and therapeutic keratoplasty for refractory perforating cases. Important comorbidities and complications include diabetes, dry eye, prior herpetic keratitis, corneal scarring, descemetocele, perforation, endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, cataract, and permanent visual loss.

Name: Female genital tract infection
Description: Female genital tract infection is a predominantly acquired, polymicrobial or pathogen-specific inflammatory disorder involving the vulva, vagina, cervix, endometrium, fallopian tubes, or adjacent pelvic tissues, encompassing vulvovaginitis, bacterial vaginosis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, endometritis, and tubo-ovarian abscess; common symptoms and signs include vaginal discharge, malodor, pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, fever, mucopurulent cervicitis, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, and vulvovaginal erythema. Molecular pathobiology is driven largely by host-pathogen interaction rather than Mendelian inheritance, with representative host susceptibility genes including TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, IL1B, IL6, IL10, TNF, CXCL8, DEFB1, MBL2, and HLA variants, and pathogen-associated proteins or mutations such as Chlamydia trachomatis major outer membrane protein, Neisseria gonorrhoeae pili and porins, and Candida adhesins; key pathways include TLR/NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome, complement, Th17/IL-17, interferon, and estrogen-dependent epithelial barrier and microbiome regulation, with neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, Lactobacillus depletion, and biofilm formation central to disease expression. There is no classic inheritance pattern, but genetic predisposition to recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis or severe pelvic inflammatory disease is suggested by common immune-response polymorphisms. Major comorbidities and complications include sexually transmitted infections, HIV acquisition, urinary tract infection, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, preterm birth, chorioamnionitis, postpartum infection, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, and sepsis. Treatment depends on etiology and typically includes metronidazole, which generates nitro radical intermediates that damage anaerobic microbial DNA; doxycycline, a tetracycline that inhibits the 30S ribosomal subunit; ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis; azithromycin, a macrolide acting at the 50S ribosome; and fluconazole, an azole that inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase. Name: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity
Description: Attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity, now generally termed attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), is a common childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmentally inappropriate inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that often persist into adulthood and impair academic, occupational, and social functioning. Clinically, patients show distractibility, poor sustained attention, disorganization, forgetfulness, excessive motor activity, fidgeting, interrupting, and impaired inhibitory control; DSM-5 recognizes predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined presentations. ADHD is highly heritable, with twin-based estimates around 70–80%, and usually shows complex polygenic rather than Mendelian inheritance; implicated genes include dopaminergic and noradrenergic components such as DRD4, DRD5, SLC6A3/DAT1, SNAP25, ADRA2A, COMT, and SLC6A2, with rarer copy-number variants and occasional overlap with genes involved in autism and other neurodevelopmental disorders. Pathophysiology centers on dysregulation of catecholaminergic signaling in frontostriatal, frontocerebellar, and default mode networks, especially dopamine and norepinephrine pathways involving the prefrontal cortex, basal ganglia, synaptic vesicle release, transporter function, and cAMP-mediated intracellular signaling. Common comorbidities include oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder, anxiety, depression, learning disorders, substance use disorders, tic disorders, sleep disturbance, and autism spectrum disorder; complications include accidental injury, school failure, interpersonal dysfunction, and persistent emotional dysregulation. Diagnosis is clinical, based on persistent symptoms across at least two settings with functional impairment and onset in childhood, supported by standardized rating scales, developmental and psychiatric assessment, collateral reports, and exclusion of mimics; neuropsychological testing may characterize deficits but is not diagnostic, and genetic testing is not routine. Main pharmacotherapy includes methylphenidate and amphetamine preparations, which increase synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine by blocking and, for amphetamines, reversing monoamine transporters, as well as atomoxetine, a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; additional options include guanfacine and clonidine, central alpha2-adrenergic agonists that strengthen prefrontal cortical regulation.

Name: Major Depressive Disorder
Description: Major depressive disorder (MeSH D003865) is a common, typically recurrent mood disorder characterized by at least 2 weeks of depressed mood and/or anhedonia with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms such as sleep and appetite disturbance, fatigue, psychomotor change, impaired concentration, excessive guilt or worthlessness, and suicidal ideation; subtypes include melancholic, atypical, psychotic, seasonal, peripartum, and anxious-distress forms, with severity ranging from mild to severe and occasional catatonic features. Its pathobiology is multifactorial, involving moderate heritability of roughly 30–40% and polygenic risk rather than Mendelian inheritance, with representative susceptibility genes and variants including SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR, BDNF Val66Met, TPH2, HTR1A, FKBP5, CRHR1, COMT, MAOA, and circadian genes such as CLOCK and ARNTL; implicated proteins and pathways include monoaminergic serotonergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic signaling, glutamatergic NMDA/AMPA transmission, GABAergic tone, HPA-axis hyperactivity with cortisol dysregulation, neuroinflammatory cytokines, circadian networks, and reduced neuroplasticity mediated by BDNF, TrkB, cAMP-CREB, and mTOR signaling. Common treatments include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine and sertraline, which inhibit SLC6A4 to increase synaptic serotonin; serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors such as venlafaxine or duloxetine, which block SERT and NET; bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor; mirtazapine, an alpha2-adrenergic antagonist that enhances noradrenergic and serotonergic transmission; and ketamine/esketamine, NMDA receptor antagonists that promote rapid synaptic plasticity. Major depressive disorder is strongly associated with anxiety disorders, substance use, chronic pain, insomnia, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and increased risk of suicide and functional impairment. Diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 or ICD criteria, supported by structured interview and rating scales such as PHQ-9 or HAM-D, while laboratory testing is used mainly to exclude mimics such as thyroid disease, anemia, medication effects, or other medical and neurologic causes.

Name: FIGO stage finding for vulvar carcinoma
Description: FIGO stage finding for vulvar carcinoma refers to the anatomic staging assessment of a usually squamous cell malignancy of the vulva, less often melanoma, Paget disease, basal cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, or verrucous carcinoma, and reflects extent of local invasion, nodal spread, and distant metastasis rather than a hereditary disorder itself. Two major biologic subtypes are recognized: HPV-associated usual-type vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, often arising from high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and linked to HPV 16/18 with TP53 usually wild type, and HPV-independent keratinizing carcinoma, often developing in lichen sclerosus or differentiated VIN and enriched for TP53, CDKN2A, PIK3CA, HRAS, PTEN, TERT promoter, EGFR, and occasional NOTCH1 alterations; relevant proteins and pathways include p53 and p16INK4a/Rb cell-cycle control, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/MAPK, EGFR signaling, telomerase activation, angiogenesis via VEGF, and immune evasion through PD-1/PD-L1. Typical symptoms and signs include persistent vulvar pruritus, pain, burning, bleeding, discharge, exophytic or ulcerative mass, pigment change, and palpable inguinofemoral nodes. Common comorbidities and complications include cervical or anal HPV-related neoplasia, lichen sclerosus, smoking, immunosuppression, wound infection, lymphedema, urinary or sexual dysfunction, and metastatic recurrence. Diagnosis requires careful vulvar examination, biopsy for histopathology, FIGO staging based on tumor size, stromal invasion, spread to adjacent perineal structures, nodal metastases, and distant disease, with nodal assessment by sentinel lymph node mapping or lymphadenectomy and imaging such as MRI, CT, or PET/CT when indicated; HPV testing and p16 or p53 immunohistochemistry may help subtype tumors. Treatment commonly uses surgery with selective adjuvant or definitive chemoradiation; representative drugs include cisplatin, a DNA cross-linking platinum radiosensitizer, 5-fluorouracil, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor impairing DNA synthesis, mitomycin C, a bioreductive DNA cross-linker, and in advanced or biomarker-selected cases paclitaxel, carbop

Name: Asthma night-time symptoms
Description: Asthma night-time symptoms, a manifestation of nocturnal asthma rather than a distinct Mendelian disease, reflect circadian worsening of chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by reversible airflow limitation, airway hyperresponsiveness, mucus hypersecretion, and sleep disruption, typically presenting with nocturnal cough, wheeze, chest tightness, dyspnea, awakening from sleep, reduced peak expiratory flow overnight, and impaired daytime function. It commonly occurs in allergic/eosinophilic, nonallergic, exercise-associated, obesity-related, and severe corticosteroid-resistant asthma phenotypes, and is driven by type 2 immune signaling involving IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, IgE-FcεRI mast-cell activation, eosinophilic inflammation, leukotrienes, histamine, cholinergic bronchoconstriction, circadian clock influences, and airway-remodeling pathways including TSLP, IL-33, and epithelial EGFR signaling. Genetic susceptibility is complex and polygenic rather than following simple inheritance; representative associated genes include IL4, IL13, IL4R, ADRB2, FCER1B, ORMDL3/GSDMB at 17q21, TSLP, ADAM33, and FLG, with family clustering reflecting heritable atopy and asthma risk. Common comorbidities and aggravating factors include allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, gastroesophageal reflux, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, anxiety/depression, and recurrent exacerbations, with complications such as severe nocturnal bronchospasm, hypoxemia, emergency visits, and rarely respiratory failure. Diagnosis relies on clinical history of nighttime awakenings and variable symptoms, spirometry showing reversible obstruction after bronchodilator use, peak-flow variability, bronchoprovocation when needed, FeNO, allergy testing, blood or sputum eosinophils, and assessment of control by guideline criteria. Treatment centers on inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide or fluticasone, which suppress airway inflammation via glucocorticoid receptor-mediated transcriptional effects; β2-agonists such as albuterol or salmeterol, which increase cAMP to relax bronchial smooth muscle; leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, which block CysLT1 signaling; and, in selected severe type 2 disease, biologics including omalizumab, mepolizumab, or dup

Name: Recurrent herpes simplex labialis
Description: Recurrent herpes simplex labialis (UMLS C1274321) is a common mucocutaneous infection caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 1, characterized by lifelong latency in the trigeminal ganglion with episodic reactivation producing grouped painful vesicles on the vermilion border and perioral skin, often preceded by prodromal burning, tingling, pruritus, erythema, and followed by crusting and healing. Disease expression reflects viral and host factors, including HSV glycoproteins gB, gD, gH/gL mediating epithelial entry and spread, viral thymidine kinase and DNA polymerase required for replication, and host genetic susceptibility involving innate and antiviral immune genes such as TLR2, TLR3, IFNAR1, IRF7, and HLA class I/II variants, with most cases showing complex multifactorial rather than Mendelian inheritance. Key pathways include trigeminal neuronal latency-reactivation programs, interferon signaling, NF-κB activation, TLR-mediated pathogen sensing, and CD8+ T-cell/NK-cell control of infected keratinocytes. Subtypes include primary herpetic gingivostomatitis versus recurrent herpes labialis, with recurrent episodes triggered by fever, ultraviolet light, trauma, menstruation, or stress. Standard therapy includes acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, all guanosine analog prodrugs activated preferentially by viral thymidine kinase and then inhibiting viral DNA polymerase to terminate or suppress DNA synthesis; topical penciclovir and docosanol are additional options, the latter impairing viral-envelope fusion with host membranes. Comorbidities and complications include atopic dermatitis, immunosuppression, recurrent aphthous-like morbidity, secondary bacterial infection, eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow, keratitis, and rarely encephalitis or disseminated disease. Diagnosis is usually clinical based on recurrent stereotyped perioral vesicles, but confirmation may use lesion PCR as the most sensitive method, viral culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing, Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells, or type-specific serology when exposure history is uncertain.

Name: Recurrent genital herpes simplex
Description: Recurrent genital herpes simplex (UMLS C1274323) is a chronic, relapsing sexually transmitted mucocutaneous infection caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 2 and also HSV-1, characterized by primary infection of genital epithelium followed by lifelong latency in sacral sensory ganglia with periodic reactivation. Viral pathogenicity is driven by envelope glycoproteins gB, gD, gH/gL mediating attachment and entry via receptors such as nectin-1/PVRL1 and HVEM/TNFRSF14, while replication depends on viral thymidine kinase UL23 and DNA polymerase UL30, key therapeutic targets; immune control and recurrence susceptibility are influenced by host innate and adaptive pathways including TLR2/TLR3, type I interferon signaling, STING/TBK1/IRF3, JAK-STAT, NF-kB, CD8+ tissue-resident T cells, and HLA/KIR variation, with rare severe susceptibility linked to defects in TLR3-pathway genes such as UNC93B1, TRIF/TICAM1, TRAF3, TBK1, and IRF3. Typical manifestations are recurrent clusters of painful vesicles, pustules, or shallow ulcers on the genital or perianal skin and mucosa, burning, pruritus, dysuria, tender inguinal adenopathy, and prodromal tingling, with asymptomatic shedding common; recognized forms include primary, nonprimary first episode, recurrent disease, and localized versus disseminated presentations. Standard therapy includes acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, nucleoside analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit viral DNA polymerase and terminate or impair DNA elongation; foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analogue that directly inhibits polymerase, is used for resistant UL23-mutant or occasionally UL30-mutant strains. Important complications and comorbidities include HIV acquisition/transmission synergy, bacterial superinfection, aseptic meningitis, urinary retention, neonatal herpes, psychosocial distress, and increased severity in pregnancy or immunocompromise. Diagnosis is based on characteristic lesions plus laboratory confirmation by lesion HSV NAAT/PCR, preferred over culture, with type-specific serology for glycoprotein G antibodies when lesions are absent or history is unclear.

Name: Streptococcal infection of skin
Description: Streptococcal infection of skin (UMLS C1274355) is an acute bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus), producing clinical syndromes such as impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis, and, in severe cases, necrotizing fasciitis. It is not a classical inherited disease, but host susceptibility is influenced by genetic variation in innate and adaptive immunity, with representative associations involving HLA class II alleles, TLR2/TLR4, MBL2, NOD2, and cytokine genes such as TNF and IL6; bacterial virulence determinants are more clearly defined and include the emm-encoded M protein, streptolysins O and S, the hasABC hyaluronic acid capsule locus, streptokinase, DNases, and superantigen exotoxins SpeA, SpeB, and SpeC. Pathobiology centers on epithelial barrier disruption, adhesion and immune evasion, and activation of TLR/NF-κB, complement, inflammasome, and neutrophil-recruitment pathways, with superantigen-driven T-cell activation and cytokine release contributing to invasive disease. Typical findings include localized pain, warmth, erythema, edema, sharply demarcated plaques in erysipelas, crusted erosions in impetigo, lymphangitis, fever, and systemic toxicity when severe. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, obesity, chronic edema or lymphedema, venous insufficiency, peripheral vascular disease, eczema, tinea pedis, trauma, and immunosuppression; complications include abscess formation, bacteremia, sepsis, necrotizing fasciitis, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported when needed by wound or tissue culture, blood cultures in systemic illness, Gram stain, inflammatory markers, ultrasound or MRI for deep extension, and surgical exploration if necrotizing infection is suspected. Treatment usually includes penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit streptococcal cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins; cephalexin or cefazolin with the same core mechanism; and clindamycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis and

Name: Onychomycosis of fingernails
Description: Onychomycosis of the fingernails (UMLS C1274469) is a chronic fungal infection of the nail unit, usually caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum and T. interdigitale, but also by Candida spp. and nondermatophyte molds, producing distal-lateral subungual, superficial white, proximal subungual, endonyx, or total dystrophic patterns. Clinically it presents with nail discoloration ranging from white or yellow to brown, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, thickening, brittleness, crumbling, ridging, and periungual inflammation, with pain or impaired manual function in severe disease. Pathobiology involves fungal adhesion and keratin invasion mediated by secreted proteases and keratinases, host innate and adaptive immune signaling through pattern-recognition receptors including Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2 and TLR4, CARD9-dependent NF-kB activation, Th17/IL-17 and IL-22 pathways, and cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-1. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and non-Mendelian, but familial clustering is described; representative host risk genes include CARD9, CLEC7A, STAT1 gain-of-function, and other defects affecting IL-17 immunity, while fungal determinants include keratinolytic enzymes and efflux pumps rather than a single defining mutation. Diagnosis relies on compatible nail dystrophy plus mycologic confirmation by potassium hydroxide microscopy, fungal culture, histopathology of nail clippings with PAS stain, or PCR, while dermoscopy may support recognition and differential diagnosis from psoriasis, lichen planus, trauma, and tumors. Common treatments include terbinafine, an allylamine that inhibits squalene epoxidase; itraconazole and fluconazole, azoles that inhibit fungal 14-alpha-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis; and topical efinaconazole or ciclopirox, which disrupt membrane sterol synthesis or metal-dependent fungal enzymes. Important comorbidities and predisposing factors include tinea manuum or pedis, chronic paronychia, diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, psoriasis, immunosuppression, and occupational wet work, while complications include secondary bacterial infection, persistent dystrophy, recurrence, and reduced quality of life.

Name: Onychomycosis of toenails
Description: Onychomycosis of the toenails (UMLS C1274470) is a chronic fungal infection of the nail unit, usually caused by dermatophytes, especially Trichophyton rubrum and T. interdigitale, but also by nondermatophyte molds and Candida species, producing distal-lateral subungual, superficial white, proximal subungual, endonyx, or total dystrophic subtypes. It is not a classic Mendelian disorder, but host susceptibility has genetic contributors, including familial clustering and polymorphisms affecting innate and adaptive antifungal immunity, with representative examples involving HLA-associated predisposition and variants in pattern-recognition and cytokine pathways such as Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2/TLR4, CARD9, IL-17, and IL-22 signaling; fungal pathogenicity also depends on keratinases, subtilisins, and metalloproteases that facilitate nail keratin invasion. Relevant host-pathogen pathways include keratinocyte recognition of fungal cell-wall beta-glucans and mannans, activation of NF-kappaB, Th17-mediated immunity, neutrophil recruitment, and local inflammatory responses within the nail bed. Clinical features include nail discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, thickening, brittleness, friability, malodor, pain, and impaired ambulation or quality of life. Diagnosis relies on compatible morphology plus mycologic confirmation by potassium hydroxide microscopy, fungal culture, periodic acid-Schiff staining of nail clippings, and increasingly PCR-based assays; dermoscopy and histopathology may aid difficult cases. Common treatments include terbinafine, a squalene epoxidase inhibitor; itraconazole and fluconazole, azole inhibitors of fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase; and topical efinaconazole, tavaborole, or ciclopirox, which respectively inhibit ergosterol synthesis, leucyl-tRNA synthetase, and metal-dependent fungal enzymes. Important comorbidities and risk factors include tinea pedis, diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, psoriasis, immunosuppression, advanced age, trauma, and obesity, while complications include recurrent cellulitis, secondary bacterial infection, chronic pain, and persistent nail dystrophy.

Name: Meibomian Gland Dysfunction
Description: Meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD; UMLS C1275684) is a chronic, usually non-inherited disorder of the eyelid sebaceous glands characterized by terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative or quantitative changes in meibum, producing evaporative dry eye and ocular surface inflammation; major forms include low-delivery/obstructive posterior blepharitis, hypersecretory MGD, and less commonly hyposecretory or cicatricial variants. Symptoms and signs typically include աչքի burning, უცხო სხეულის sensation, fluctuating vision, photophobia, contact lens intolerance, lid margin telangiectasia, capped orifices, thickened toothpaste-like secretions, frothy tear film, reduced tear breakup time, and corneal or conjunctival punctate epitheliopathy. Pathobiology centers on abnormal meibocyte differentiation and keratinization, altered lipid synthesis, bacterial lipases, and inflammatory signaling involving IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, matrix metalloproteinases, NF-κB, MAPK, PPARγ, and androgen-receptor pathways; representative molecular associations include reduced PPARγ expression, altered keratinization markers such as KRT1/KRT10, and changes in lipogenic enzymes including elongases/desaturases such as ELOVL and SCD family members, while inherited contributors are usually indirect and syndromic, for example TP63-related ectodermal dysplasia, FOXC2 distichiasis-lymphedema, and EDA/EDAR pathway disorders that can impair meibomian gland development or function. Common comorbidities include acne rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, Demodex infestation, Sjögren syndrome, allergic eye disease, diabetes, and aging; complications include recurrent chalazia, hordeola, blepharokeratoconjunctivitis, corneal staining, filamentary keratitis, and visual fluctuation. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on symptoms plus lid margin and gland expressibility findings, aided by tear breakup time, ocular surface staining, meibography for gland dropout, interferometry or lipid-layer assessment, osmolarity testing, and occasional inflammatory markers such as tear MMP-9. Treatment commonly includes azithromycin, which suppresses bacterial protein synthesis and has anti-inflammatory effects; tetracyclines such as doxycycline, which inhibit bacterial ribosomes and reduce lipase activity and MMP-mediated inflammation

Name: HZV (herpes zoster virus) keratitis
Description: Herpes zoster virus keratitis, more accurately herpes zoster ophthalmicus–associated keratitis caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV; human herpesvirus 3), is an acquired infectious and immune-mediated corneal disease rather than a Mendelian disorder, typically arising when VZV in the trigeminal ganglion reactivates and spreads along the ophthalmic division, especially the nasociliary branch. Viral entry and replication involve envelope glycoproteins such as gE and gB, immediate-early/replication proteins including IE62 and the viral thymidine kinase/viral DNA polymerase axis, while host susceptibility and severity have been linked to cellular immunity genes and pathways, with representative associations reported for HLA class I/II alleles, TLR3, IFNAR1, IL10, and other interferon/NF-kappaB–related innate and T-cell response components, although no single causative germline mutation defines the disease. Key pathogenic pathways include viral replication, type I interferon signaling, TLR-mediated innate sensing, NF-kappaB activation, cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma, and T-cell–driven stromal inflammation and neurotrophic damage. Clinical forms include epithelial punctate or pseudodendriform keratitis, nummular anterior stromal keratitis, disciform/endothelial keratitis, neurotrophic keratopathy, and keratouveitis, presenting with dermatomal pain and vesicular rash, Hutchinson sign, red eye, photophobia, tearing, blurred vision, decreased corneal sensation, and sometimes elevated intraocular pressure. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining, corneal sensitivity testing, assessment for uveitis and IOP elevation, and, when uncertain, VZV PCR from corneal/tear/aqueous samples; differential diagnosis includes herpes simplex keratitis. Standard treatment includes acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, nucleoside analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase that inhibit viral DNA polymerase; topical or systemic corticosteroids are used for stromal or endothelial immune keratitis by suppressing inflammatory cytokine signaling, and adjuncts such as cycloplegics or lubricants address pain and neurotrophic disease.
