Name: Erysipeloid
Description: Erysipeloid is an acute localized zoonotic cutaneous infection, classically an occupational disease of butchers, fish handlers, farmers, and veterinarians, caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae rather than a primary genetic disorder, so no established Mendelian inheritance pattern, recurrent pathogenic human mutations, or disease-defining host genes are known; instead, pathogenesis is driven by bacterial virulence factors including surface protective antigens such as SpaA/SpaB, neuraminidase, hyaluronidase, and adhesive surface proteins that promote endothelial adherence, dermal invasion, and inflammatory signaling through innate immune pathways involving pattern-recognition receptors, macrophage and neutrophil activation, NF-kB, and cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6. The usual form is localized cutaneous erysipeloid, with less common diffuse cutaneous and invasive septicemic forms, the latter potentially complicated by bacteremia, endocarditis, and rarely osteoarticular infection; linked comorbidities that increase severity include immunosuppression, diabetes mellitus, chronic liver disease, alcoholism, valvular heart disease, and chronic skin barrier disruption. Clinically, patients typically develop after minor skin trauma a sharply demarcated, violaceous-red, nonpurulent, painful or burning cellulitis-like plaque, usually on the fingers or hands, with edema, tenderness, pruritus, and slow centrifugal spread; fever and systemic symptoms are often absent in localized disease but may occur in disseminated infection. Diagnosis is primarily clinical in the right exposure setting, supported when needed by tissue or blood culture, Gram stain showing slender Gram-positive rods, species identification by biochemical methods, MALDI-TOF, or PCR, and echocardiography if bacteremia suggests endocarditis. Treatment relies on antibiotics active against E. rhusiopathiae, especially penicillin G or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking via penicillin-binding proteins; ceftriaxone, another beta-lactam with the same core mechanism; and ciprofloxacin, which inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with clindamycin, blocking the 50S ribosomal subunit, as an alternative in selected patients.

Name: Postnatal infection
Description: Postnatal infection (UMLS C1278797) is an acquired infectious disorder arising after birth, spanning neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis, urinary tract, skin/soft-tissue, gastrointestinal, and viral or fungal infections, and is caused by organisms such as group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, respiratory syncytial virus, herpes simplex virus, and Candida species. Its pathobiology is dominated by innate and adaptive immune signaling, particularly pattern-recognition receptor pathways involving TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, CD14, MYD88, NF-κB, inflammasome/IL-1β signaling, and downstream cytokines including TNF, IL6, and IFN-γ, with complement, neutrophil, and endothelial activation contributing to tissue injury, shock, and organ dysfunction. Although most cases are not inherited, host susceptibility is influenced by genetic variants or inborn errors affecting immunity, with representative examples including TLR4 and CD14 polymorphisms, mannose-binding lectin deficiency due to MBL2 variants, and rare monogenic defects such as MYD88 or IRAK4 deficiency predisposing to recurrent pyogenic infection; these confer susceptibility rather than Mendelian transmission of the infection itself. Clinical manifestations vary by site and age but commonly include fever or hypothermia, poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, respiratory distress, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, jaundice, seizures, and hemodynamic instability. Major complications include bacteremia, sepsis, meningitis, pneumonia, abscess formation, necrotizing enterocolitis, neurodevelopmental impairment, hearing loss, and death, with prematurity, congenital anomalies, and immunodeficiency as important comorbid contexts. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment plus microbiologic testing, including blood, urine, or CSF culture, PCR/NAAT for viral or bacterial targets, CBC, CRP or procalcitonin, imaging when indicated, and CSF analysis for suspected meningitis. Treatment is etiology- and syndrome-specific but commonly includes ampicillin, a β-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, gentamicin, an aminoglycoside causing 30S ribosomal mistranslation, cefotaxime, a cephalosporin blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking, and, for selected viral or fungal disease, acyclovir

Name: Chlamydial urethritis
Description: Chlamydial urethritis (UMLS C1278807) is a sexually transmitted, usually non-gonococcal urethral infection caused predominantly by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D–K, an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium with a biphasic elementary body/reticulate body developmental cycle rather than a Mendelian inherited disorder; host susceptibility is influenced by immune-response genes and proteins, with reported associations involving HLA class II alleles, TLR2, TLR4, CD14, NOD1/NOD2, and cytokine pathway variants in TNF, IL10, IL6, IFNG, and CXCL8, while chlamydial virulence factors such as major outer membrane protein OmpA, polymorphic membrane proteins, type III secretion effectors, CPAF, and inclusion membrane proteins modulate pathogenesis. Disease biology centers on epithelial invasion and innate immune activation through TLR/NF-kB, MAPK, inflammasome, interferon-gamma, and chemokine signaling, driving neutrophilic urethritis and, in some hosts, persistent intracellular infection. Typical manifestations include dysuria, urethral pruritus, scant mucoid or clear discharge, meatal irritation, pyuria, and frequent asymptomatic infection; recognized forms include acute, persistent, recurrent, and coinfection-associated urethritis. Major complications and comorbidities include epididymitis, prostatitis, reactive arthritis, urethral stricture, facilitation of HIV acquisition/transmission, and in sexual partners cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Diagnosis is based on compatible symptoms or objective urethral inflammation, such as urethral smear showing at least 2 to 5 polymorphonuclear leukocytes per oil-immersion field or first-void urine leukocyte esterase/pyuria, with nucleic acid amplification testing on first-catch urine or urethral swab as the diagnostic standard; culture is rarely used, and testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and other STIs is recommended. First-line therapy commonly includes doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor; azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit; and levofloxacin or ofloxacin, fluoroquinolones that inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase

Name: Metastasis from malignant tumour of prostate
Description: Metastasis from malignant tumour of the prostate denotes advanced prostate adenocarcinoma, usually acinar type, that has spread beyond the gland, most often to bone, lymph nodes, liver, or lung, and is driven predominantly by androgen receptor signaling with frequent molecular alterations involving AR amplification or mutation, PTEN loss with PI3K/AKT/mTOR activation, TMPRSS2-ERG fusion, TP53 and RB1 loss, SPOP, FOXA1, BRCA2, BRCA1, ATM, CHEK2, and mismatch-repair genes; neuroendocrine or small-cell transdifferentiation may emerge in castration-resistant disease and is associated with TP53/RB1 disruption. Key pathways include androgen biosynthesis and AR transcriptional programs, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, DNA damage repair and homologous recombination, WNT/β-catenin, MAPK, TGF-β, and bone-metastatic interactions involving RANK/RANKL, endothelin, CXCL12/CXCR4, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts. Patients may present with urinary obstruction, hesitancy, hematuria, pelvic pain, weight loss, fatigue, elevated alkaline phosphatase, bone pain, pathologic fractures, spinal cord compression, or edema from nodal disease. Major clinical subtypes include metastatic hormone-sensitive and metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, with visceral, nodal, osseous, and neuroendocrine variants. Although most cases are sporadic, inherited susceptibility is recognized, particularly autosomal dominant predisposition linked to BRCA2, BRCA1, HOXB13, ATM, and Lynch-associated genes. Diagnosis relies on histologic confirmation of prostate carcinoma, PSA testing, testosterone level in castration-resistant assessment, and staging with CT, MRI, bone scan, or PSMA-PET; biopsy of metastatic sites and genomic testing for homologous recombination or MMR defects guide therapy. Common treatments include androgen deprivation with leuprolide or degarelix, abiraterone inhibiting CYP17 androgen synthesis, enzalutamide blocking AR signaling, docetaxel stabilizing microtubules, cabazitaxel after taxane resistance, and in selected patients olaparib as a PARP inhibitor; frequent complications include skeletal-related events, anemia, renal obstruction, thromboembolism, depression, and treatment-induced osteoporosis or metabolic syndrome.

Name: Metastasis from malignant tumor of colon (disorder)
Description: Metastasis from malignant tumor of the colon is advanced colorectal adenocarcinoma characterized by dissemination of the primary colonic epithelial malignancy, most often to liver, lung, peritoneum, and regional or distant lymph nodes, through a multistep process involving invasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, and immune evasion. Its molecular landscape commonly includes APC loss and WNT/β-catenin activation, KRAS or NRAS mutations driving MAPK signaling, BRAF V600E in a subset with aggressive biology, TP53 and SMAD4 alterations, PI3K/AKT pathway activation including PIK3CA mutations, TGF-β pathway dysregulation, and defects in DNA mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 causing microsatellite instability; overexpression of EGFR and VEGF-related angiogenic signaling are clinically relevant protein-level features. Clinically, patients may present with altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, abdominal pain, obstruction, fatigue, hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites, dyspnea, or symptoms referable to metastatic sites. Major subgroups include left- versus right-sided tumors, microsatellite-stable versus MSI-high disease, RAS-mutant, BRAF-mutant, HER2-amplified, and oligometastatic versus widely disseminated disease. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited susceptibility is important in Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis, with less frequent MUTYH-associated polyposis and other hereditary cancer syndromes. Diagnosis relies on histopathologic confirmation of colon adenocarcinoma and metastatic deposits, staging by contrast-enhanced CT or MRI, PET in selected cases, colonoscopy with biopsy, serum CEA monitoring, and molecular testing for KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, HER2, and MMR/MSI status to guide therapy. Treatment commonly includes 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine, which inhibit thymidylate synthase, oxaliplatin, a platinum DNA crosslinker, irinotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor, bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF antibody, and in selected RAS wild-type tumors cetuximab or panitumumab, anti-EGFR antibodies; complications include bowel perforation or obstruction, hepatic failure, venous thromboembolism

Name: Metastasis from malignant tumor of thyroid (disorder)
Description: Metastasis from a malignant thyroid tumor denotes advanced thyroid carcinoma, most often arising from papillary, follicular, medullary, poorly differentiated, or anaplastic subtypes, in which neoplastic cells spread to regional lymph nodes or distant sites such as lung, bone, liver, and brain. Its molecular basis commonly involves MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathway dysregulation, with representative alterations including BRAF V600E, RAS mutations, RET/PTC fusions, NTRK fusions, PAX8-PPARG rearrangement, TERT promoter mutations, TP53 in aggressive disease, and RET activating mutations in medullary thyroid carcinoma; relevant proteins include RET, BRAF, MEK, VEGFR, EGFR, and components of angiogenic signaling. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited susceptibility is important in medullary carcinoma, especially autosomal dominant MEN2 syndromes due to germline RET mutations; familial non-medullary thyroid cancer is less common. Clinical manifestations reflect both thyroid primary and metastatic burden, including thyroid nodule or neck mass, cervical adenopathy, hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, bone pain, pathologic fracture, neurologic deficits, and weight loss. Complications include airway compromise, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, spinal cord compression, malignant pleural disease, treatment-refractory progression, and endocrinopathies or hypocalcemia related to therapy. Diagnosis relies on ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging, radioiodine scanning for differentiated tumors, PET/CT in dedifferentiated disease, serum thyroglobulin or calcitonin/CEA as subtype-specific markers, fine-needle aspiration or tissue biopsy with histopathology and immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing for actionable alterations. Treatment commonly includes radioactive iodine for iodine-avid differentiated metastases, lenvatinib or sorafenib as multikinase inhibitors targeting VEGFR/FGFR/RET and angiogenesis, vandetanib or cabozantinib for metastatic medullary carcinoma through RET, VEGFR, and MET inhibition, and genotype-directed agents such as selpercatinib for RET-altered tumors, dabrafenib plus trametinib for BRAF V600E anaplastic carcinoma, or larotrectinib for NTRK fusion-positive disease.

Name: Malignant Neoplasm (Morphology)
Description: Malignant neoplasm is a morphologic designation for cancer characterized by clonal, autonomous proliferation of cells with the capacity for local tissue invasion, angiogenesis, immune evasion, and metastatic spread; it encompasses major subtypes such as carcinomas, sarcomas, hematologic malignancies, melanomas, and central nervous system tumors. Its molecular basis is heterogeneous but commonly involves activating alterations in oncogenes and loss of tumor suppressors, including TP53, KRAS, EGFR, BRAF, PIK3CA, MYC, ALK, HER2/ERBB2, APC, PTEN, RB1, BRCA1/2, and mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1 and MSH2, with corresponding protein dysregulation affecting cell-cycle checkpoints, DNA repair, apoptosis, and growth signaling. Core pathways include receptor tyrosine kinase/RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, WNT/β-catenin, p53, TGF-β, JAK/STAT, NF-κB, Hedgehog, Notch, and angiogenic VEGF signaling, together with alterations in the tumor microenvironment and immune checkpoints such as PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4. Clinical manifestations vary by site and stage but commonly include a mass lesion, pain, bleeding, weight loss, fatigue, anemia, cachexia, obstruction, neurologic deficits, or paraneoplastic syndromes. Comorbidities and complications include infection, venous thromboembolism, malnutrition, organ failure, pathologic fracture, metastases, and treatment-related toxicity. Inheritance is usually multifactorial or somatic, but hereditary predisposition is well established in syndromes such as hereditary breast-ovarian cancer due to BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome from mismatch-repair defects, familial adenomatous polyposis from APC mutations, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome from TP53 variants. Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation, imaging, histopathology confirming malignant cytology and invasion, immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry where relevant, and molecular testing including cytogenetics, FISH, PCR, and next-generation sequencing. Common therapies include cisplatin, which crosslinks DNA; doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor and free-radical generator; and pembrolizumab, a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor, with additional use

Name: Subacute bursitis
Description: Subacute bursitis (UMLS C1290159) is an inflammatory disorder of a synovial bursa, usually evolving over days to weeks between acute and chronic phases, most often caused by repetitive microtrauma, pressure, crystal deposition, inflammatory arthropathy, or less commonly low-grade infection. It commonly affects the olecranon, prepatellar, subacromial, trochanteric, and pes anserine bursae and presents with localized pain, tenderness, swelling or fluctuance, warmth, restricted motion of adjacent joints, and occasionally erythema; septic cases may add fever and marked inflammatory signs. Molecularly, bursitis is not a classic monogenic disease, but inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL1B, IL6, PTGS2/COX-2, NFKB, and matrix-remodeling enzymes including MMPs are implicated, with relevant pathways including innate immune/Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-kappaB, arachidonic acid–prostaglandin synthesis, inflammasome activation in crystal disease, and leukocyte recruitment. Genetic influences are usually indirect through predisposition to associated disorders, for example HLA-B27 in seronegative spondyloarthritis, HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles and PTPN22 in rheumatoid arthritis, and SLC2A9 or ABCG2 variants in gout; inheritance is therefore generally complex, multifactorial, and non-Mendelian. Important comorbidities include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, pseudogout, diabetes mellitus, obesity, occupational kneeling or leaning, and immunosuppression, while complications include chronic bursitis, bursal thickening or calcification, reduced function, recurrence, and septic bursitis, commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus. Treatment is directed at inflammation and cause: ibuprofen, naproxen, or diclofenac inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain and swelling; corticosteroids such as triamcinolone or methylprednisolone suppress glucocorticoid-responsive cytokine transcription; colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization and neutrophil activation in crystal-associated cases; and when infection is suspected, antibiotics such as dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or vancomycin target likely gram-positive pathogens. Name: Precursor T-Cell Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
Description: Precursor T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (UMLS C1292758) is an aggressive neoplasm of immature thymic T-lymphoblasts, biologically overlapping with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and distinguished mainly by a mass-forming presentation with limited marrow involvement; common molecular lesions include activating NOTCH1 and FBXW7 mutations, CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion, PTEN loss, TAL1, TLX1/HOX11, TLX3, LMO1/2, and MYC dysregulation, and aberrant expression of TdT, cytoplasmic/surface CD3, CD7, CD2, CD5, and variable CD1a, CD4, and CD8. Central pathogenic pathways include NOTCH signaling, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT, cell-cycle checkpoint disruption via RB and p16INK4A, and transcriptional programs governing thymocyte development. It typically presents in adolescents or young adults, often male, with a bulky anterior mediastinal/thymic mass, lymphadenopathy, pleural or pericardial effusions, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, wheeze, superior vena cava syndrome, fever, weight loss, and occasionally CNS or marrow dissemination. Immunophenotypic subtypes parallel cortical, early, or mature thymic T-cell differentiation, and early T-cell precursor-like biology may confer high risk. Most cases are sporadic rather than classically inherited, although rare predisposition is linked to constitutional variants affecting lymphoid development or tumor suppression, including TP53 or ATM pathway abnormalities. Diagnosis requires tissue biopsy showing lymphoblast morphology, high Ki-67, and T-lineage markers with TdT by immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry, plus bone marrow examination, CSF assessment, cytogenetic/molecular testing, and PET/CT or CT staging. Standard treatment uses intensive ALL-like multiagent chemotherapy such as vincristine, a microtubule inhibitor; prednisone or dexamethasone, lymphocytotoxic glucocorticoids; daunorubicin or doxorubicin, topoisomerase II inhibitors; cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent; cytarabine and methotrexate, antimetabolites, with intrathecal CNS prophylaxis; nelarabine, a guanosine analog, is active in T-lineage disease. Name: Early cirrhosis
Description: Early cirrhosis is an incipient, still potentially compensated stage of chronic liver fibrosis characterized by diffuse extracellular matrix deposition, architectural distortion, and regenerative nodule formation arising from persistent hepatocellular injury; major etiologic subtypes include alcohol-related cirrhosis, viral hepatitis B- or C-related cirrhosis, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis-related cirrhosis, cholestatic/autoimmune cirrhosis, and genetic/metabolic forms. Pathobiology centers on activation of hepatic stellate cells and portal fibroblasts through TGF-β/SMAD, PDGF, TNF-α, IL-6, NF-κB, Wnt/β-catenin, Hedgehog, oxidative stress, and apoptotic pathways, with matrix remodeling mediated by collagen I/III, TIMPs, and MMPs. Genetic contributors are usually disease-specific rather than cirrhosis-specific and include PNPLA3 I148M and TM6SF2 variants in steatotic liver disease, HFE mutations such as C282Y/H63D in hereditary hemochromatosis, SERPINA1 PiZZ in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, ATP7B in Wilson disease, and ABCB4 or JAG1 in cholestatic disorders; inheritance is therefore commonly multifactorial, but may be autosomal recessive, codominant, or autosomal dominant depending on the underlying cause. Early cirrhosis may be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, anorexia, right upper quadrant discomfort, hepatomegaly or a small firm liver, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, thrombocytopenia, and mild splenomegaly, and it is linked to portal hypertension, ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatocellular carcinoma, sarcopenia, osteoporosis, diabetes, renal dysfunction, and infections. Treatment targets cause and complications: nonselective beta-blockers such as propranolol, nadolol, or carvedilol reduce portal pressure via β-adrenergic blockade; spironolactone antagonizes mineralocorticoid receptors for ascites; furosemide promotes natriuresis; lactulose lowers ammonia by colonic acidification; and etiologic therapy includes antivirals such as tenofovir or entecavir for HBV and direct-acting antivirals for

Name: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (disorder)
Description: Acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction is an acute transmural ischemic necrosis syndrome, usually caused by abrupt thrombotic occlusion of an epicardial coronary artery after rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque, producing persistent ST elevation and biomarker release; common symptoms and signs include severe substernal chest pressure radiating to the arm, neck, or jaw, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, pallor, anxiety, hypotension, new heart failure, or malignant ventricular arrhythmias, although atypical presentations occur in older adults, women, and patients with diabetes. Molecular contributors include inherited and acquired determinants of atherothrombosis and ischemia-reperfusion injury, with representative genetic associations involving LDLR, APOE, PCSK9, LPA, APOA5, CETP, NOS3, MTHFR, ACE, F5 Leiden, F2, and platelet receptor variants such as ITGB3; these are generally complex polygenic risk factors rather than Mendelian causes, although familial hypercholesterolemia from LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 variants markedly increases risk. Key pathways include endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide signaling, oxidized LDL uptake, inflammation mediated by IL-1, TNF, NF-kB and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, platelet activation through thromboxane A2, ADP-P2Y12 and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, coagulation via tissue factor and thrombin, and reperfusion-associated calcium overload, reactive oxygen species, and apoptosis. Standard therapy combines urgent reperfusion by primary PCI or fibrinolysis with antithrombotic and secondary prevention drugs such as aspirin, an irreversible COX-1 inhibitor; ticagrelor or clopidogrel, P2Y12 antagonists; unfractionated heparin, which potentiates antithrombin; fibrinolytics such as tenecteplase, which converts plasminogen to plasmin; beta-blockers, statins, ACE inhibitors, and high-risk cases may receive GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors. Major comorbidities include hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, chronic kidney disease, obesity, and prior coronary disease; complications include cardiogenic shock, papillary muscle or septal rupture, acute mitral regurgitation, pericarditis, ventricular aneurysm, mural thrombus, recurrent ischemia,

Name: Primary malignant neoplasm of gastrointestinal tract
Description: Primary malignant neoplasm of the gastrointestinal tract is a heterogeneous group of epithelial and nonepithelial cancers arising anywhere from the esophagus to the anus, most commonly adenocarcinomas but also including gastrointestinal stromal tumors, neuroendocrine neoplasms, lymphomas, and squamous or small-cell variants depending on site. Its biology is driven by recurrent alterations in APC, TP53, KRAS, SMAD4, PIK3CA, BRAF, CDH1, mismatch-repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2, receptor tyrosine kinases such as ERBB2 and MET, and in selected tumors KIT, PDGFRA, and NTRK fusions; these lesions dysregulate WNT/β-catenin, EGFR/RAS/RAF/MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, TGF-β, p53, HER2, angiogenic VEGF, and DNA mismatch-repair/microsatellite-instability pathways. Inherited susceptibility is seen in Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis, MUTYH-associated polyposis, hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, and KIT/PDGFRA-related familial GIST. Symptoms vary by location but commonly include dysphagia, odynophagia, abdominal pain, early satiety, altered bowel habits, occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, obstruction, perforation, jaundice, and palpable mass. Frequent comorbidities and complications include malnutrition, cachexia, thromboembolism, bowel obstruction, perforation, fistula, metastatic spread to liver or peritoneum, and treatment-related cytopenias or neuropathy. Diagnosis relies on endoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy and histopathology, cross-sectional imaging and PET when indicated, TNM staging, immunohistochemistry and molecular testing for MMR/MSI, HER2, PD-L1, RAS/BRAF, KIT/PDGFRA, and NTRK, plus germline testing when hereditary cancer is suspected. Standard therapies include fluorouracil or capecitabine, antimetabolites that inhibit thymidylate synthase; oxaliplatin, a platinum DNA cross-linker; irinotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor; trastuzumab for HER2-positive

Name: Periarthritis of shoulder
Description: Periarthritis of the shoulder, commonly overlapping clinically with adhesive capsulitis and painful periarticular rotator-cuff–bursal disorders, is a non-neoplastic inflammatory and fibroproliferative condition of the glenohumeral capsule, synovium, subacromial bursa, and peri-tendinous soft tissues that causes progressive shoulder pain and restriction of both active and passive motion, especially external rotation, abduction, and elevation, often with night pain, stiffness, and functional limitation. It is usually classified into primary or idiopathic frozen shoulder and secondary forms related to trauma, surgery, immobilization, rotator-cuff disease, or systemic illness; clinically, freezing, frozen, and thawing phases are often recognized. Molecular studies implicate dysregulated fibrosis and inflammation rather than a single causative mutation, with increased expression of TGF-β1, CTGF, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, COX-2, MMPs/TIMPs, collagen types I and III, fibronectin, VEGF, and myofibroblast markers such as α-SMA, involving TGF-β/SMAD, NF-κB, MAPK, cytokine, and extracellular-matrix remodeling pathways; genetic susceptibility is limited but familial clustering and candidate associations in fibrotic/inflammatory genes have been reported, without a clear Mendelian inheritance pattern. Major comorbidities include diabetes mellitus, thyroid disease, dyslipidemia, Dupuytren contracture, cervical spondylosis, stroke, Parkinson disease, and prolonged immobilization; complications include chronic pain, persistent stiffness, capsular contracture, sleep disturbance, and disability. Treatment commonly includes NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and reduce prostaglandin synthesis, intra-articular corticosteroids such as triamcinolone or methylprednisolone, which suppress phospholipase A2–dependent inflammatory signaling and cytokine transcription, and analgesics such as acetaminophen for central pain modulation; refractory cases may require hydrodilatation, suprascapular nerve block, manipulation under anesthesia, or arthroscopic capsular release. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by restricted passive and active range of motion and exclusion of alternative pathology, with radiographs to exclude osteoarthritis or calcific tendinopathy and ultrasound or MRI to assess capsular thick

Name: Giant Cell Tumor of Tendon Sheath
Description: Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath (GCTTS), the localized form of tenosynovial giant cell tumor and closely related to diffuse-type pigmented villonodular synovitis, is a usually benign but locally aggressive synovial-like neoplasm arising from tendon sheath, bursa, or joint synovium, most often in the fingers and hand. A central molecular feature is CSF1 overexpression, commonly driven by chromosome 1p13 rearrangements such as COL6A3-CSF1 translocation, which recruits non-neoplastic CSF1R-expressing macrophages; additional reported alterations in some cases include FN1 fusions and occasional changes involving M-CSF/CSF1-CSF1R axis regulators rather than a classic inherited mutation pattern. Accordingly, key pathways include CSF1/CSF1R signaling, macrophage colony-stimulating networks, osteoclast-like giant cell differentiation via RANK/RANKL, MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT downstream signaling, and inflammatory mediators that contribute to hemosiderin deposition and bone erosion. Clinically, patients typically present with a slow-growing, firm, painless or mildly tender nodular mass, reduced range of motion, triggering, stiffness, swelling, and sometimes pressure erosion of adjacent bone; diffuse disease causes recurrent effusions and more destructive arthropathy. Important subtypes are localized and diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor. The condition is generally sporadic and not inherited in a Mendelian fashion. Diagnosis is based on clinical examination and imaging, especially MRI showing a lobulated soft-tissue mass with low T1/T2 signal from hemosiderin and blooming on gradient-echo sequences, followed by histopathology demonstrating mononuclear synovial-like cells, osteoclast-type giant cells, foamy macrophages, and hemosiderin, with immunohistochemistry or molecular testing such as FISH/RT-PCR for CSF1 rearrangement when needed. Standard treatment is surgical excision or synovectomy, while recurrent, unresectable, or diffuse disease may be treated with pexidartinib, a CSF1R tyrosine kinase inhibitor, imatinib, which inhibits CSF1R/KIT/PDGFR signaling, and nilotinib, another tyrosine kinase inhibitor with CSF1R activity; complications include local recurrence, joint damage, secondary osteoarthritis, tendon dysfunction

Name: Fusospirochetal pharyngitis (disorder)
Description: Fusospirochetal pharyngitis is an acute, usually nonhereditary, polymicrobial necrotizing infection of the tonsillopharyngeal mucosa classically caused by synergistic anaerobes, especially Fusobacterium necrophorum or other Fusobacterium species together with oral spirochetes such as Borrelia vincentii/Treponema species; unlike monogenic disorders, no specific germline mutation or Mendelian inheritance pattern is established, although host susceptibility may be influenced by immune-response genes and pathways governing neutrophil function and mucosal innate defense, including TLR2/TLR4-NF-kB signaling, cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, complement, and bacterial virulence factors including fusobacterial leukotoxin, endotoxin, hemagglutinins, and outer-membrane adhesins that promote tissue invasion and necrosis. It is considered within the spectrum of Vincent angina/necrotizing ulcerative pharyngotonsillitis and may overlap with necrotizing gingivitis or stomatitis. Typical findings include severe sore throat, fever, odynophagia, fetor oris, cervical lymphadenopathy, ulceronecrotic or pseudomembranous tonsillar lesions, gingival inflammation, and sometimes trismus. Important comorbidities or complications include poor oral hygiene, periodontal disease, smoking, malnutrition, immunosuppression, peritonsillar abscess, deep neck infection, septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with Lemierre syndrome, septic emboli, and rarely sepsis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by oropharyngeal examination, anaerobic culture when feasible, Gram stain showing fusiform bacilli and spirochetes, blood cultures in systemic illness, inflammatory markers, and imaging such as contrast CT neck if abscess or jugular vein thrombosis is suspected; differential diagnosis includes group A streptococcal pharyngitis, diphtheria, EBV, gonococcal infection, and malignancy. Treatment relies on antibiotics active against anaerobes, commonly metronidazole, which causes DNA strand breakage after anaerobic reduction, penicillin or amoxicillin, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall transpeptidation, and clindamycin, which binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to suppress protein synthesis; amoxicillin-clav

Name: Staphylococcus aureus Infection
Description: Staphylococcal infections are acute or chronic bacterial diseases caused primarily by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant strains, and less virulent coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis, producing syndromes that range from impetigo, cellulitis, folliculitis, abscesses, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, bacteremia, endocarditis, food poisoning, toxic shock syndrome, and scalded skin syndrome to device-associated biofilm infections. Major microbial determinants include mecA or mecC encoding the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a that mediates methicillin resistance, blaZ beta-lactamase, the accessory gene regulator agr quorum-sensing system, staphylococcal protein A encoded by spa, Panton-Valentine leukocidin genes lukS-PV/lukF-PV, alpha-toxin hla, and exfoliative toxins eta/etb. Host susceptibility has genetic components, particularly defects in neutrophil and Th17/IL-17 immunity, including CYBB in chronic granulomatous disease, STAT3 in hyper-IgE syndrome, and IL6ST, DOCK8, or CARD9-related immunodeficiency. Pathobiology centers on TLR2/NF-kB activation by peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, complement and opsonophagocytic killing, cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and the IL-17/IL-23 axis, together with biofilm pathways involving icaADBC polysaccharide matrix production. Typical findings include painful erythematous purulent skin lesions, fever, drainage, hypotension in invasive disease, respiratory symptoms in pneumonia, and positive blood or site cultures. Diagnosis relies on Gram stain and culture, susceptibility testing, PCR for mecA/mecC or toxin genes, blood cultures, imaging for deep foci, and echocardiography when endocarditis is suspected. Treatment commonly includes nafcillin or oxacillin, beta-lactams that inhibit cell-wall transpeptidation, vancomycin, a glycopeptide blocking peptidoglycan synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala, and linezolid, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor; daptomycin depolarizes the bacterial membrane,

Name: Infection caused by Enterococcus
Description: Infection caused by Enterococcus (most often Enterococcus faecalis or Enterococcus faecium) is an opportunistic, usually non-inherited bacterial disease that produces urinary tract infection, bacteremia, infective endocarditis, intra-abdominal and biliary infection, wound infection, and occasionally neonatal or device-associated disease, particularly in hospitalized, catheterized, immunocompromised, or antibiotic-exposed patients. Typical manifestations include fever, dysuria, urinary frequency, flank or abdominal pain, leukocytosis, sepsis, new murmur in endocarditis, and signs of metastatic embolic or deep-seated infection. Important microbial genetic determinants include intrinsic and acquired resistance genes such as pbp5, which contributes to reduced beta-lactam susceptibility in E. faecium, van operons including vanA and vanB mediating high-level glycopeptide resistance, aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme genes such as aac(6’)-Ie-aph(2”)-Ia causing loss of synergistic gentamicin activity, and virulence factors including esp, asa1, cylA, gelE, and the fsr quorum-sensing locus. Relevant pathways include peptidoglycan cell-wall biosynthesis targeted by beta-lactams and glycopeptides, D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac remodeling in vancomycin resistance, ribosomal protein synthesis, DNA replication, and biofilm formation regulated by quorum sensing and surface adhesins. Common treatments include ampicillin, a beta-lactam inhibiting penicillin-binding proteins; vancomycin, a glycopeptide that binds D-Ala-D-Ala; linezolid, an oxazolidinone blocking 50S initiation; daptomycin, which depolarizes the bacterial membrane; and nitrofurantoin for lower urinary infection via reactive intermediates that damage bacterial macromolecules. Major complications include persistent bacteremia, abscess, endocardial destruction, embolic stroke, osteomyelitis, and relapse. Disease subtypes are commonly classified by species, syndrome, and resistance phenotype, especially vancomycin-resistant enterococcal infection. Diagnosis relies on culture of urine, blood, or sterile-site specimens with speciation and susceptibility testing, echocardiography when endocarditis is suspected, and molecular detection of van genes or other resistance determinants when clinically needed.

Name: Allergic otitis externa
Description: Allergic otitis externa (UMLS C1320547) is a nonhereditary inflammatory disorder of the external auditory canal caused by hypersensitivity, most often allergic contact dermatitis to topical medications, hearing-aid molds, ear drops, shampoos, metals, or fragrances, and less commonly by atopic mechanisms; it presents with intense pruritus, erythema, edema, scaling, serous otorrhea, aural fullness, and variable conductive hearing loss, while pain is usually less prominent than in infectious otitis externa. Its molecular basis is primarily immune rather than monogenic, with relevant components including epidermal barrier proteins such as filaggrin (FLG) in atopic susceptibility, Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, epithelial alarmins such as TSLP, eosinophils, mast cells, IgE-mediated pathways in atopic cases, and hapten-specific type IV delayed hypersensitivity mediated by Langerhans cells and T lymphocytes with downstream NF-κB and JAK-STAT signaling. Common comorbidities include atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, and secondary bacterial or fungal superinfection; complications include canal stenosis, lichenification, chronic eczematous otitis externa, excoriation, and recurrent cerumen obstruction. Subtypes include allergic contact otitis externa, atopic/eczematous otitis externa, and chronic eczematoid forms. Treatment centers on allergen avoidance and topical therapy; representative drugs include hydrocortisone or dexamethasone, which suppress phospholipase A2-dependent inflammatory gene transcription, acetic acid, which acidifies the canal and inhibits microbial overgrowth, ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase when secondary infection is present, and clotrimazole, an azole that inhibits ergosterol synthesis for fungal superinfection. Diagnosis is clinical, based on otoscopic evidence of eczematous inflammation and exposure history, supported by patch testing for contact allergens, culture only when infection is suspected, audiometry if hearing loss is significant, and exclusion of mimics such as acute bacterial otitis externa, psoriasis, and neoplasia.

Name: Behçet disease affecting oral mucosa
Description: Behçet disease affecting the oral mucosa is a chronic, relapsing, multisystem variable-vessel vasculitis and autoinflammatory disorder in which recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers are the hallmark lesion, often accompanied by genital ulcers, erythema nodosum or papulopustular skin lesions, uveitis, arthritis, and less commonly neurologic, gastrointestinal, or vascular involvement; oral lesions may be minor, major, or herpetiform aphthae and can impair nutrition and quality of life. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with the strongest association to HLA-B*51, and additional implicated genes including ERAP1, IL10, IL23R-IL12RB2, STAT4, TNF, CCR1, KLRC4, and FUT2, supporting abnormal antigen processing, Th1/Th17 polarization, and dysregulated innate immunity; elevated TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-17, IL-23, IFN-γ, neutrophil hyperreactivity, endothelial activation, and NF-κB/JAK-STAT signaling are central pathogenic pathways. Diagnosis is clinical, commonly based on International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease or older ISG criteria, with supportive testing such as pathergy testing, slit-lamp examination for uveitis, biopsy showing nonspecific neutrophilic vasculitic inflammation, and laboratory studies mainly to exclude mimics, since no pathognomonic serologic test exists. Common treatments for mucocutaneous disease include topical or systemic corticosteroids, which suppress NF-κB-driven inflammatory gene transcription; colchicine, which inhibits microtubule polymerization and neutrophil chemotaxis; and azathioprine, a purine synthesis inhibitor that reduces lymphocyte proliferation; refractory disease may respond to TNF inhibitors such as infliximab or adalimumab, phosphodiesterase-4 inhibition with apremilast, or interferon-α. Important comorbidities and complications include vision loss from uveitis, venous thrombosis, arterial aneurysm, neuro-Behçet syndrome, bowel ulceration, chronic pain, and depression.

Name: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis
Description: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is a destructive metastatic form of tegumentary leishmaniasis caused predominantly by New World Leishmania (Viannia) species, especially L. braziliensis, and is characterized by chronic granulomatous inflammation of the nasal, oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal mucosa that usually follows a cutaneous lesion months to years earlier. Disease risk and severity reflect parasite virulence factors such as the surface metalloprotease GP63 and lipophosphoglycan, together with host immunogenetic susceptibility rather than Mendelian inheritance; implicated host genes and proteins include SLC11A1/NRAMP1, TNF, IL10, IFNG, IL6, HLA class II alleles, CXCL10, and TLR pathway components, with excessive TNF-α-, IFN-γ-, and cytotoxic CD8 T-cell–driven responses contributing to tissue injury. Key pathways include macrophage infection via complement receptors, TLR2/TLR4 signaling, IL-12/STAT4-mediated Th1 polarization, IFN-γ-induced nitric oxide killing, NF-κB activation, inflammasome signaling, and counterregulatory IL-10/TGF-β pathways. Typical findings are persistent nasal obstruction, epistaxis, crusting, septal perforation, oral or pharyngeal ulceration, hoarseness, dysphagia, facial disfigurement, and secondary bacterial infection; complications include airway compromise, malnutrition, stigma, and relapse, and comorbidities such as HIV infection, immunosuppression, and chronic bacterial superinfection worsen outcome. Clinical forms include localized cutaneous disease with later mucosal spread, concomitant mucocutaneous disease, and diffuse or recurrent variants. Diagnosis relies on compatible epidemiology and mucosal lesions plus demonstration of parasites or parasite DNA by biopsy histopathology, smear, culture, or PCR, with Montenegro skin testing and serology as supportive tests and endoscopic evaluation to define extent. Standard therapies include pentavalent antimonials such as sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate, which inhibit parasite bioenergetics and thiol metabolism; amphotericin B, which binds ergosterol-like membrane sterols causing pore formation; miltefosine, which disrupts membrane phospholipid metabolism and signaling; and, in selected cases, pentamidine, which impairs DNA

Name: Hormone refractory prostate cancer
Description: Hormone refractory prostate cancer, now commonly termed castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), is an advanced, biologically heterogeneous prostate adenocarcinoma that progresses despite castrate serum testosterone levels, usually evolving from androgen-deprivation-treated disease and manifesting as nonmetastatic CRPC, metastatic CRPC, or aggressive-variant/neuroendocrine-transdifferentiated subtypes. Its biology is driven by persistent androgen receptor signaling through AR amplification, point mutations, splice variants such as AR-V7, intratumoral androgen synthesis, and alterations in genes including PTEN, TP53, RB1, BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, SPOP, FOXA1, and TMPRSS2-ERG, with proteins and pathways involving PI3K-AKT-mTOR, DNA damage repair, WNT/beta-catenin, MAPK, cell-cycle regulators, and lineage plasticity programs. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited susceptibility is recognized, particularly with germline BRCA2, BRCA1, ATM, CHEK2, HOXB13, and mismatch-repair gene variants, which also influence prognosis and targeted therapy selection. Typical manifestations include rising prostate-specific antigen despite castration, urinary obstruction, hematuria, pelvic pain, weight loss, fatigue, anemia, and symptoms from metastases, especially osteoblastic bone lesions causing pain, fractures, spinal cord compression, and occasionally visceral spread. Important comorbidities and complications include skeletal-related events, cancer cachexia, thromboembolism, urinary retention, renal insufficiency, depression, and treatment-related metabolic and cardiovascular effects of long-term androgen suppression. Diagnosis requires evidence of progression by PSA rise, radiographic enlargement, or new metastases despite castrate testosterone, supported by serial PSA, serum testosterone, conventional imaging or PSMA PET, and biopsy of primary or metastatic sites when histologic transformation or molecular testing is needed; next-generation sequencing is increasingly used to identify homologous recombination repair or MSI-high disease. Standard treatments include docetaxel, a microtubule inhibitor; abiraterone, a CYP17A1 inhibitor that suppresses androgen synthesis; enzalutamide, an androgen receptor signaling inhibitor; as well as cabazitaxel, PARP inhibitors such as olaparib for HRR-mutated tumors, radium-223 for bone-predominant disease, and sipuleucel-T in selected patients.

Name: Marginal Zone B-Cell Lymphoma
Description: Marginal zone B-cell lymphoma (MZL) is an indolent mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising from post-germinal-center memory B cells and comprising extranodal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, splenic MZL, and nodal MZL. Its biology commonly involves chronic antigenic stimulation and dysregulation of NF-κB, B-cell receptor, Toll-like receptor, and NOTCH signaling, with recurrent genetic lesions including KLF2, NOTCH2, TNFAIP3, MYD88, BIRC3, TRAF3, and TP53 mutations, trisomies 3 and 18, and subtype-linked rearrangements such as t(11;18)(q21;q21) API2-MALT1, t(14;18)(q32;q21) IGH-MALT1, and t(1;14)(p22;q32) BCL10-IGH; relevant proteins include MALT1, BCL10, MYD88, and surface CD20. Most cases are sporadic rather than Mendelian, although inherited predisposition to lymphoid malignancy is occasionally suspected, and environmental or infectious drivers are important, especially Helicobacter pylori in gastric MALT lymphoma, and associations also occur with hepatitis C virus and autoimmune disease such as Sjögren syndrome or Hashimoto thyroiditis. Clinical presentation varies by subtype but often includes painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, cytopenias, fatigue, B symptoms, and organ-specific manifestations such as dyspepsia, GI bleeding, orbital swelling, salivary gland enlargement, or pulmonary lesions. Complications include marrow infiltration, hypersplenism, recurrent infection, transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and treatment-related cytopenias. Diagnosis relies on excisional or core biopsy with morphology and immunophenotype showing a clonal CD19-positive, CD20-positive, usually CD5-negative/CD10-negative B-cell population, supported by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, PCR for clonality, FISH or cytogenetics for MALT1/BCL10-associated abnormalities, bone marrow evaluation, and CT or PET/CT staging, with endoscopy for gastric disease. Name: Tinea Cruris
Description: Tinea cruris (UMLS C1384589) is a superficial dermatophyte infection of the groin, usually caused by Trichophyton rubrum, Trichophyton mentagrophytes/interdigitale, or Epidermophyton floccosum, in which fungal virulence is mediated less by host germline mutations than by keratinolytic proteins and secreted proteases, including fungal subtilisins and metalloproteases, that enable adherence to and digestion of stratum corneum keratin; host susceptibility is influenced by cutaneous innate and adaptive immune pathways, particularly pattern-recognition signaling through C-type lectin receptors and Toll-like receptors, downstream CARD9–NF-κB signaling, and IL-17/Th17 axis activity, with rare severe or recurrent dermatophytosis linked to inherited defects such as CARD9 deficiency and occasionally other immunogenetic abnormalities affecting antifungal immunity. Clinically, it presents as pruritic, erythematous, scaly, sharply marginated annular or arcuate plaques with central clearing and an active raised border on the inguinal folds and upper thighs, often bilateral and typically sparing the scrotum, and common subtypes include acute inflammatory, chronic recurrent, and extensive tinea cruris associated with concomitant tinea pedis or onychomycosis as reservoir sites. Major comorbidities and risk factors include obesity, diabetes mellitus, hyperhidrosis, occlusive clothing, humid environments, immunosuppression, and topical corticosteroid misuse, while complications include secondary bacterial infection, excoriation, lichenification, post-inflammatory pigment alteration, and tinea incognito. Diagnosis is usually clinical and confirmed by potassium hydroxide microscopy showing septate branching hyphae, fungal culture, dermoscopy, periodic acid-Schiff stain of scale, or PCR when needed, with differentiation from candidiasis, erythrasma, inverse psoriasis, and seborrheic dermatitis. Treatment relies on topical or systemic antifungals such as terbinafine, which inhibits squalene epoxidase; azoles including clotrimazole, miconazole, or itraconazole, which inhibit fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase; and butenafine, also targeting squalene epoxidase, alongside hygiene and treatment of coexistent fungal reservoirs.

Name: Dyspareunia
Description: Dyspareunia (UMLS C1384606) is a symptom-defined pain disorder characterized by recurrent or persistent genital or pelvic pain occurring before, during, or after intercourse, and is broadly divided into superficial or entry dyspareunia and deep dyspareunia; in contemporary nosology many cases overlap with genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder or vulvodynia. Its biology is heterogeneous and usually multifactorial rather than monogenic, but genetic susceptibility has been suggested through variants affecting pain sensitivity, inflammation, hormonal signaling, and connective tissue, with representative candidates including COMT, OPRM1, TRPV1, ESR1/ESR2, and inflammatory mediators such as IL1B, TNF, and NGF; disease-specific inherited patterns are not established, although dyspareunia may occur within heritable disorders such as endometriosis, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, or neuropathic pain syndromes. Relevant pathways include peripheral and central sensitization involving nociceptors, TRPV1 and sodium channels, neuroimmune signaling with cytokines and mast cells, estrogen-dependent maintenance of vulvovaginal epithelium, pelvic floor muscle hypertonicity, and in deep dyspareunia the prostaglandin-driven inflammatory and fibrotic pathways prominent in endometriosis. Common causes and comorbidities include vulvovaginal atrophy/genitourinary syndrome of menopause, vulvodynia, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, pelvic floor myalgia, vaginismus, dermatologic disorders such as lichen sclerosus, mood and anxiety disorders, sexual trauma, and infertility; complications include avoidance of intercourse, relationship distress, depression, and reduced quality of life. Typical findings are entry pain, burning, tearing, dryness, deep pelvic pain, levator tenderness, and occasionally allodynia or erythema. Treatment depends on etiology and commonly includes topical vaginal estrogen, which restores estrogen receptor-mediated epithelial maturation and lubrication; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, which inhibit COX-mediated prostaglandin synthesis; and tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline or anticonvulsants such as gabapentin, which reduce neuropathic pain signaling. Diagnosis is clinical, requiring characterization of pain location, timing, and triggers, focused pelvic examination with cotton-swab testing, assessment

Name: Arthropod bite wound
Description: Arthropod bite wound (UMLS C1444173) is an acquired, non-inherited cutaneous injury caused by hematophagous or defensive arthropods such as mosquitoes, fleas, bedbugs, ticks, spiders, and hymenoptera, producing a localized toxic, mechanical, and immune-inflammatory reaction rather than a primary genetic disease. Pathobiology is dominated by epidermal barrier disruption and innate/adaptive immune activation, with histamine-H1 receptor signaling, IgE–FcεRI mast-cell degranulation, arachidonic acid/prostaglandin and leukotriene pathways, complement, and cytokines such as TNF, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and IL-31; pruritic hypersensitivity phenotypes may show eosinophil-rich infiltrates and are influenced by atopy-associated genes or proteins such as FLG, IL4, IL13, FCER1A, TSLP, and histamine-related receptors, while severe venom anaphylaxis can be associated with KIT and TPSAB1-linked mast-cell disorders. Clinical manifestations typically include a punctum, erythematous papules, wheals, urticarial plaques, edema, burning or pain, intense pruritus, and occasionally vesicles, bullae, necrosis, or eschar; subtypes include simple papular bite reactions, exaggerated local reactions, papular urticaria, venom-induced immediate hypersensitivity, and secondarily infected bite wounds. Common treatments include oral antihistamines such as cetirizine or diphenhydramine, which block H1 receptors; topical corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone or triamcinolone, which suppress NF-κB-driven inflammatory gene transcription; antibiotics such as cephalexin or doxycycline when bacterial superinfection or tick-borne infection is suspected, inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis or the 30S ribosome, respectively; and epinephrine for anaphylaxis via alpha/beta-adrenergic vasoconstrictive and bronchodilatory effects. Important complications include secondary cellulitis or impetigo, abscess, scarring, postinflammatory pigment change, serum-sickness-like reactions, and vector-borne infections including Lyme disease or rickettsioses. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on exposure history, lesion morphology and distribution, with dermoscopy, skin biopsy, bacterial culture, allergy testing including venom-specific IgE

Name: Deficiencies, Vitamin
Description: Vitamin deficiencies are a heterogeneous group of nutritional disorders caused by inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased requirements, impaired transport, or genetic defects in vitamin metabolism, and they are often classified as fat-soluble deficiencies (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble deficiencies (B-complex, C). Molecularly, representative inherited forms implicate TCN2 and CUBN/AMN in cobalamin deficiency, SLC19A2 and SLC19A3 in thiamine transport disorders, ALPL and CYP27B1/VDR in vitamin B6- and D-related bone disease phenotypes, and genes affecting vitamin K recycling such as VKORC1; relevant proteins include transcobalamin, intrinsic factor-related uptake machinery, vitamin D receptor, 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X. Key pathways include one-carbon metabolism with methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in B12 deficiency, transketolase-dependent carbohydrate metabolism in thiamine deficiency, retinoid receptor signaling in vitamin A deficiency, gamma-carboxylation of clotting proteins in vitamin K deficiency, collagen hydroxylation in vitamin C deficiency, and calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 signaling in vitamin D deficiency. Clinical manifestations vary by subtype but commonly include fatigue, glossitis, dermatitis, neuropathy, cognitive change, anemia, bone pain, fractures or rickets/osteomalacia, night blindness, bleeding diathesis, and poor wound healing; complications include developmental delay, osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy, infection susceptibility, and irreversible neurologic injury. Comorbid settings include alcoholism, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, liver or renal disease, bariatric surgery, pregnancy, and strict dietary restriction. Treatment centers on replacement with cyanocobalamin or hydroxocobalamin, which restore cobalamin-dependent DNA synthesis and myelin metabolism; thiamine, a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase; ergocalciferol or cholecalciferol, replenishing vitamin D stores to normalize calcium absorption; phytonadione, which restores hepatic gamma-carboxylation; and ascorbic acid, which supports collagen synthesis. Name: Sjogren's Syndrome
Description: Sjogren's syndrome (MeSH D012859) is a chronic systemic autoimmune epithelitis characterized by lymphocytic destruction of exocrine glands, classically causing keratoconjunctivitis sicca and xerostomia, and occurring as primary disease or secondary disease in association with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or systemic sclerosis. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with strong associations to HLA class II alleles, especially HLA-DR and HLA-DQ haplotypes, and non-HLA risk variants involving IRF5, STAT4, BLK, IL12A, TNIP1, CXCR5, and TNFAIP3; hallmark autoantigens include Ro/SSA proteins (TRIM21/Ro52 and TROVE2/Ro60), La/SSB, alpha-fodrin, and muscarinic M3 receptor, while increased BAFF, type I interferons, IL-6, IL-17, B-cell receptor signaling, TLR7/TLR9 activation, NF-kB, JAK/STAT, CXCL13-CXCR5, and ectopic germinal-center pathways drive B-cell hyperactivity and glandular injury. Patients typically present with dry eyes, dry mouth, parotid enlargement, fatigue, arthralgia, dental caries, oral candidiasis, and vaginal dryness, with extraglandular manifestations including arthritis, interstitial lung disease, renal tubular acidosis or tubulointerstitial nephritis, peripheral neuropathy, vasculitis, autoimmune thyroid disease, and increased risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin, especially MALT, lymphoma. Diagnosis relies on sicca symptoms plus objective tests such as Schirmer test, ocular staining score, unstimulated salivary flow, anti-SSA/Ro with or without anti-SSB/La, ANA and rheumatoid factor, salivary gland ultrasonography, and minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, as reflected in ACR/EULAR classification criteria. Treatment is mainly symptomatic and immunomodulatory: artificial tears and saliva substitutes provide lubrication, pilocarpine and cevimeline are muscarinic agonists that stimulate residual exocrine secretion, hydroxychloroquine reduces antigen presentation and endosomal TLR signaling, glucocorticoids broadly suppress inflammation, and rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells

Name: Eosinophilic Pneumonias
Description: Eosinophilic pneumonias are a heterogeneous group of inflammatory lung disorders defined by eosinophil-rich infiltration of the alveoli and interstitium, encompassing acute eosinophilic pneumonia, chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, simple pulmonary eosinophilia/Löffler syndrome, secondary eosinophilic pneumonias due to drugs, parasites, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and rare familial or hypereosinophilic syndromes. Their biology is dominated by type 2 immune signaling, especially IL-5, IL-4, and IL-13 pathways, with eosinophilopoiesis and trafficking mediated by GATA2/GATA1-regulated myeloid differentiation, CCR3-eotaxin interactions, GM-CSF, TSLP, IgE-bearing mast cells, and STAT6 signaling; in clonal eosinophilic syndromes, recurrent lesions such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, or PCM1-JAK2 fusions may underlie pulmonary eosinophilia, while ANCA-associated disease may involve MPO autoimmunity. Symptoms typically include fever, cough, dyspnea, wheeze, pleuritic chest discomfort, night sweats, malaise, and hypoxemia, with acute forms progressing to respiratory failure and chronic forms often showing asthma and peripheral-predominant infiltrates. Common comorbidities and complications include asthma, atopy, chronic rhinosinusitis, vasculitis, parasitic infection, drug hypersensitivity, pulmonary fibrosis, relapse, and, in systemic eosinophilic disorders, cardiac or neurologic injury. Inheritance is usually absent or complex/polygenic, though familial eosinophilia linked to 5q31-q33 cytokine cluster variation including IL5 and rare hereditary predispositions to atopy have been described. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical-radiographic features plus eosinophilia in blood or bronchoalveolar lavage, exclusion of infection and secondary causes, chest imaging, CBC with differential, BAL, serologies including IgE, ANCA and parasite testing, and occasionally lung biopsy. Name: Granulomatosis infantisepticum (disorder)
Description: Granulomatosis infantisepticum is not a distinct inherited granulomatous syndrome but the classic disseminated fetal-neonatal form of listeriosis caused by transplacental or peripartum infection with Listeria monocytogenes, a facultative intracellular Gram-positive bacillus; thus no single causal human mutation defines the disorder, although susceptibility may be influenced by defects in cell-mediated immunity and, rarely, in IL12RB1, IFNGR1/2, STAT1, TYK2, NEMO/IKBKG, or GATA2, which impair macrophage activation and interferon-dependent antibacterial defense. Its pathobiology centers on bacterial internalins InlA and InlB mediating host-cell invasion, listeriolysin O enabling phagosomal escape, and ActA-driven actin-based intracellular spread, with host responses involving TLR2, MyD88, NF-kB, TNF, IL-12, IFN-gamma, and activated macrophages; placental infection leads to widespread fetal microabscesses and granulomatous lesions in liver, spleen, lung, skin, and sometimes CNS. Clinically it presents as early-onset neonatal sepsis with fever or hypothermia, respiratory distress, pneumonia, diffuse papular or pustular rash, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, lethargy, poor feeding, and often meningitis, and it is commonly categorized as early-onset congenital disease versus later neonatal meningitic disease. Major complications include septic shock, DIC, miscarriage, stillbirth, prematurity, hydrops, neurologic injury, and death; comorbid settings include maternal febrile gastroenteritis, chorioamnionitis, immunosuppression, pregnancy, and neonatal prematurity. Diagnosis rests on maternal-neonatal risk factors plus culture or PCR from blood, CSF, placenta, or amniotic fluid, histopathology showing disseminated granulomas or microabscesses, CSF analysis when meningitis is suspected, and standard sepsis evaluation. Treatment is antimicrobial rather than pathway-targeted: ampicillin or penicillin G inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins, gentamicin binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and is often added for synergistic bactericidal activity, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole blocks sequential folate synthesis and is used when beta-lactams

Name: Malignant neoplasm of common bile duct (& [carcinoma])
Description: Malignant neoplasm of the common bile duct, typically classified within extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, is an aggressive adenocarcinoma arising from the biliary epithelium and includes perihilar and distal subtypes with intestinal, pancreatobiliary, papillary, and mucinous histologic variants. It commonly presents with progressive obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, abdominal pain, weight loss, anorexia, cholangitis, and cholestatic liver enzyme elevation; complications include biliary obstruction, recurrent infection, hepatic failure, cachexia, and metastatic spread to lymph nodes, liver, and peritoneum. Molecularly, recurrent alterations involve KRAS, TP53, SMAD4, CDKN2A, ERBB2/HER2 amplification, EGFR, PIK3CA, ARID1A, BAP1, and less often IDH1/2 or FGFR2 fusions than in intrahepatic disease; abnormal proteins and pathways include EGFR/HER2-driven RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signaling, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, TGF-beta/SMAD, WNT/beta-catenin, Notch, and inflammatory IL-6/JAK-STAT signaling. Most cases are sporadic, but susceptibility is increased in hereditary cancer syndromes such as Lynch syndrome and BRCA-associated disease, and in disorders including primary sclerosing cholangitis, choledochal cysts, hepatolithiasis, liver fluke infection, chronic biliary inflammation, viral hepatitis, and cirrhosis. Diagnosis relies on cholestatic biochemistry, CA 19-9 and CEA as adjunctive markers, cross-sectional imaging with ultrasound, multiphasic CT, MRI/MRCP, ERCP or EUS-guided brushings/biopsy for histopathology, staging, and increasingly next-generation sequencing with MSI/MMR and HER2 testing. Name: Chronic Kidney Diseases
Description: Chronic kidney disease (CKD; UMLS C1561643) is a heterogeneous, usually progressive disorder defined by structural or functional kidney abnormalities persisting for at least 3 months, classically staged by estimated glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria, and encompassing diabetic kidney disease, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, glomerulonephritides, tubulointerstitial disease, obstructive nephropathy, and inherited cystic or basement membrane disorders. Its pathobiology converges on nephron loss, glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, inflammation, oxidative stress, and maladaptive repair driven by renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling, TGF-β/SMAD, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, endothelin, HIF, Wnt/β-catenin, and podocyte slit-diaphragm pathways involving nephrin and podocin. Genetic contributors are important in subsets, including PKD1/PKD2 in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, COL4A3/COL4A4/COL4A5 in Alport spectrum disease, UMOD and HNF1B in tubulointerstitial disease, APOL1 risk variants in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and hypertensive CKD, and NPHS1/NPHS2 mutations in hereditary nephrotic syndromes; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or complex/polygenic. Common manifestations include hypertension, edema, foamy urine/proteinuria, hematuria, nocturia, fatigue, pruritus, anorexia, cognitive changes, and later uremic symptoms. Major comorbidities and complications include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, heart failure, anemia from relative erythropoietin deficiency, CKD-mineral and bone disorder, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, dyslipidemia, infection risk, and progression to end-stage kidney disease. Diagnosis relies on persistent eGFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and/or markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria, abnormal urine sediment, imaging or histologic abnormalities; evaluation uses serum creatinine- or cystatin C-based eGFR, urine albumin-creatinine ratio, urinalysis, renal ultrasound, serologies, genetic testing when hereditary disease is suspected, and kidney biopsy in selected cases. Name: Anemia in chronic kidney disease
Description: Anemia in chronic kidney disease is typically a hypoproliferative, usually normocytic normochromic anemia caused primarily by impaired renal erythropoietin production and compounded by functional or absolute iron deficiency, chronic inflammation, reduced erythrocyte survival, blood loss, and uremic marrow suppression; it occurs across CKD stages, is often more severe in advanced non-dialysis CKD and end-stage kidney disease, and may be subclassified as iron-deficiency anemia, erythropoiesis-stimulating agent hyporesponsive anemia, or dialysis-associated anemia. Core molecular features involve the renal oxygen-sensing HIF-2α–prolyl hydroxylase–VHL pathway regulating EPO transcription, iron homeostasis through hepcidin encoded by HAMP and its target ferroportin SLC40A1, inflammatory IL-6/JAK-STAT signaling that increases hepcidin, and erythroid differentiation mediated by EPO receptor–JAK2–STAT5; representative genetic contributors include EPO, EPOR, HIF1A/EPAS1, EGLN1/PHD2, VHL, TMPRSS6, HFE, HAMP, TFR2, and SLC40A1, although classic Mendelian inheritance is not typical for CKD anemia itself and inherited components more often reflect susceptibility to CKD, iron handling defects, or rare familial erythrocytosis/anemia phenotypes. Common treatments include epoetin alfa or darbepoetin alfa, which activate the EPO receptor to stimulate erythropoiesis, iron replacement such as ferric carboxymaltose or iron sucrose to replenish iron stores, and HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors such as roxadustat or daprodustat, which stabilize HIF and increase endogenous EPO while improving iron utilization. Patients commonly present with fatigue, weakness, exertional dyspnea, pallor, reduced exercise tolerance, cognitive impairment, and tachycardia; major comorbidities and complications include cardiovascular disease, left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, diabetes, hypertension, frailty, hospitalization, and increased mortality. Name: Hormone receptor positive malignant neoplasm of breast
Description: Hormone receptor positive malignant neoplasm of the breast is a common invasive or in situ epithelial breast cancer defined by expression of estrogen receptor and/or progesterone receptor, most often corresponding to luminal A or luminal B molecular subtypes, and characterized biologically by dependence on ER signaling with cross-talk through PI3K/AKT/mTOR, cyclin D–CDK4/6–RB, MAPK, and growth factor pathways including HER2 and FGFR. Recurrent genetic alterations include ESR1 mutations in endocrine-resistant metastatic disease, PIK3CA mutations, GATA3, MAP3K1, PTEN loss, AKT1, CCND1 amplification, FGFR1 amplification, and less commonly ERBB2 alterations; inherited susceptibility is seen with BRCA2, BRCA1, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, and TP53 variants, usually in an autosomal dominant cancer predisposition pattern with incomplete penetrance. Patients typically present with a painless breast mass, mammographic calcifications or architectural distortion, nipple discharge or retraction, skin dimpling, or axillary adenopathy, while advanced disease may cause bone pain, dyspnea, liver dysfunction, or neurologic symptoms from metastases. Major complications include local recurrence, distant spread especially to bone, endocrine resistance, pathologic fractures, hypercalcemia, lymphedema, venous thromboembolism, and treatment-related osteoporosis or cardiotoxicity. Diagnosis relies on core biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry for ER, PR, HER2, and Ki-67, staging by imaging and nodal evaluation, and selected genomic assays such as Oncotype DX or MammaPrint to refine prognosis and chemotherapy benefit; germline testing is indicated by personal or family history risk. Treatment commonly includes tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator; aromatase inhibitors such as letrozole, anastrozole, or exemestane, which suppress estrogen synthesis; fulvestrant, an ER degrader; CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib; alpelisib for PIK3CA-mutant disease; and everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor.

Name: Muscle spasticity of spinal origin
Description: Muscle spasticity of spinal origin is a chronic upper motor neuron syndrome caused by lesions of the spinal cord or descending corticospinal pathways, most often after traumatic spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, transverse myelitis, hereditary spastic paraplegia, or less commonly amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; it is characterized clinically by velocity-dependent increased tone, hyperreflexia, clonus, extensor spasms, Babinski signs, stiffness, weakness, impaired dexterity and gait, pain, and bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction. Pathobiologically, loss of supraspinal inhibitory control with enhanced segmental reflex excitability, reduced GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition, glutamatergic overactivity, persistent inward sodium and calcium currents, altered chloride homeostasis via KCC2, and maladaptive plasticity involving interneurons, Ia afferents, and descending reticulospinal and vestibulospinal systems are central mechanisms. Genetic contributions are clearest in inherited spastic parapareses, with representative genes including SPAST/SPG4 encoding spastin, ATL1/SPG3A encoding atlastin-1, KIF5A, REEP1, CYP7B1, and HSPB1; inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or mitochondrial depending on the underlying disorder. Clinically recognized subtypes include flexor versus extensor spasticity, focal, segmental, or generalized forms, and acute versus chronic spinal spasticity. Common comorbidities and complications include contractures, pressure injuries, falls, sleep disturbance, neuropathic pain, urinary tract infection, constipation, depression, and reduced mobility. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by neurological examination, Modified Ashworth or Tardieu scales, assessment of spasms and functional impact, spinal MRI to define structural causes, electrophysiology in selected cases, and genetic testing when hereditary spastic paraplegia is suspected. Treatment commonly includes baclofen, a GABAB receptor agonist that suppresses excitatory neurotransmitter release and spinal reflexes; tizanidine, an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces presynaptic excitatory input; diazepam, a GABAA-positive allosteric modulator; dantrolene, which inhibits ryanodine receptor-mediated sarcoplasmic calcium release; and botulinum toxin for focal

Name: Leprosy, Multibacillary
Description: Multibacillary leprosy is a chronic infectious granulomatous neuropathy caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and less commonly M. lepromatosis, characterized by high bacillary burden, weak cell-mediated immunity, and clinical forms spanning borderline lepromatous to lepromatous disease in the Ridley-Jopling spectrum, broadly corresponding to WHO multibacillary classification when more than five skin lesions and/or slit-skin smear positivity are present. Host genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with representative associations involving HLA-DR/DQ alleles, LTA, TNF, TLR1, TLR2, NOD2, PARK2/PACRG, LRRK2, IL10, IFNG, SLC11A1, CCDC122, and RIPK2; implicated proteins and pathways include TLR1/2-MyD88-NF-κB signaling, NOD2/RIPK2 innate sensing, TNF-α, IFN-γ/IL-12, IL-10-mediated immunoregulation, complement, macrophage lipid metabolism, and Schwann-cell infection with demyelination. Patients typically develop numerous symmetric hypopigmented or erythematous infiltrated macules, papules, plaques, or nodules, diffuse skin thickening, madarosis, nasal stuffiness/epistaxis, glove-and-stocking sensory loss, peripheral nerve enlargement, and progressive motor deficits; complications include type 1 reversal and type 2 erythema nodosum leprosum reactions, neuritis, deformities, ulcers, secondary infection, orchitis, iridocyclitis, and chronic disability. Diagnosis relies on compatible skin and neurologic findings plus demonstration of acid-fast bacilli by slit-skin smear or biopsy, histopathology showing foamy macrophages packed with bacilli in lepromatous disease, and increasingly PCR-based detection, with nerve conduction studies used when neuropathy is prominent. Standard therapy is multidrug treatment with rifampicin, which inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; dapsone, a folate synthesis inhibitor targeting dihydropteroate synthase; and clofazimine, which binds mycobacterial DNA and has anti-inflammatory effects; alternatives or adjuncts in selected cases include ofloxacin, minocycline, and corticosteroids or thalidomide for reactions.

Name: Dapsone resistant leprosy
Description: Dapsone-resistant leprosy is a chronic infectious mycobacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and less commonly M. lepromatosis, in which bacilli are no longer inhibited by dapsone, classically through mutations in the bacterial folP1 gene encoding dihydropteroate synthase, especially at codons such as Thr53 and Pro55; resistance may coexist with rifampicin resistance from rpoB mutations and fluoroquinolone resistance from gyrA/gyrB alterations. Pathobiology reflects infection of macrophages and Schwann cells with host immune polarization across the tuberculoid-lepromatous spectrum, involving IFN-γ/IL-12/Th1 pathways in paucibacillary disease versus IL-4, IL-10, and Th2-skewed responses in multibacillary disease, together with TNF-α, TLR1/TLR2 signaling, macrophage activation, granuloma formation, and nerve injury. Treatment uses multidrug therapy to prevent further selection of resistance: rifampicin inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, clofazimine binds mycobacterial DNA and exerts redox/anti-inflammatory effects, and dapsone, when still active, inhibits folate synthesis; alternative or second-line agents include ofloxacin or moxifloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase, and minocycline, which blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit. Clinical manifestations include hypopigmented or erythematous anesthetic patches, plaques or nodules, peripheral neuropathy with sensory loss, nerve thickening, muscle weakness, madarosis, nasal involvement, and in advanced cases deformity, trophic ulcers, and blindness. Major subtypes are paucibacillary and multibacillary disease, with Ridley-Jopling forms from tuberculoid to lepromatous; complications include type 1 reversal reactions, erythema nodosum leprosum, secondary infection, disability, and social stigma, and comorbidities may include malnutrition, tuberculosis, and immunosuppression. The disease is not inherited in a Mendelian manner, but host susceptibility is influenced by variants in genes such as HLA, TLR1, NOD2, LTA, PARK2/PACRG, and SLC11A1.
