Name: Decompensated cirrhosis of liver
Description: Decompensated cirrhosis of the liver (UMLS C1619727) is the advanced, clinically unstable stage of chronic hepatic fibrosis and nodular regeneration in which portal hypertension and hepatocellular failure produce overt complications, most often arising from alcohol-related liver disease, chronic hepatitis B or C, and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease, while genetic causes include HFE-associated hemochromatosis, SERPINA1 alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, ATP7B Wilson disease, and less commonly PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 risk variants that modify susceptibility and progression. Its pathobiology is driven by chronic inflammation, hepatocyte death, stellate-cell activation, and extracellular matrix deposition mediated through TGF-beta/SMAD, PDGF, TNF-alpha, IL-6, NF-kappaB, oxidative stress, endothelin, nitric oxide dysregulation, RAAS activation, and gut-liver axis signaling involving LPS/TLR4, with reduced albumin synthesis, impaired ammonia detoxification, and circulatory dysfunction. Typical manifestations include jaundice, ascites, peripheral edema, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, fatigue, muscle wasting, pruritus, easy bruising, spider angiomata, splenomegaly, and infections. Major complications and comorbidities include spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome, portal vein thrombosis, hyponatremia, hepatocellular carcinoma, coagulopathy, malnutrition, sarcopenia, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder or viral hepatitis. Subtypes are commonly framed by etiology and by dominant decompensating event, including ascitic, variceal, encephalopathic, jaundiced, and acute-on-chronic liver failure phenotypes. Treatment is complication-directed: spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and furosemide, a loop diuretic, for ascites; lactulose, a nonabsorbable disaccharide that lowers colonic ammonia, and rifaximin, a gut-selective antibiotic, for encephalopathy; nonselective beta-blockers such as propranolol or carvedilol to reduce portal pressure; cefotaxime for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; terlipressin plus albumin for hepatorenal syndrome. Name: Breastfeeding mother
Description: Breastfeeding mother (UMLS C1623040) is not a disease but a physiologic maternal state of lactation in the postpartum period, characterized by milk synthesis, secretion, and transfer, and clinically recognized by breast fullness, milk let-down, nipple leakage, and infant milk intake; common complications include nipple pain or fissures, engorgement, plugged ducts, mastitis, breast abscess, low milk supply, and candidal or bacterial infection, with important comorbidities such as postpartum depression, thyroid disease, diabetes, obesity, and retained placental tissue that may impair lactation. Its biology is driven by endocrine and neuroendocrine pathways rather than a single inherited disorder: prolactin signaling through PRLR-JAK2-STAT5 promotes alveolar differentiation and milk protein gene expression, oxytocin acting via OXTR mediates myoepithelial contraction and milk ejection, while estrogen, progesterone, insulin, cortisol, and thyroid hormone regulate mammary gland development and secretory activation; representative lactation-related genes and proteins include PRL, PRLR, OXTR, STAT5A/STAT5B, ESR1, PGR, CSN2, LALBA, and SLC30A2/ZnT2, with SLC30A2 variants linked to low milk zinc and occasional lactation problems. Subtypes are generally physiologic stages such as colostral, transitional, and mature milk production, or disorders of insufficient versus excessive lactation. There is no classic Mendelian inheritance pattern, but genetic influences on milk production and composition are recognized through variants in hormone receptors and milk protein or transporter genes. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on postpartum status, direct observation of latch and milk transfer, infant weight gain and urine/stool output, and maternal breast examination; adjunct testing may include pre- and post-feed weights, milk culture when infection is suspected, breast ultrasound for abscess, and targeted endocrine studies such as TSH, prolactin, or glucose assessment when supply is poor. Commonly used drugs in breastfeeding mothers include ibuprofen, a cyclooxygenase inhibitor for pain and inflammation, acetaminophen for central analgesia, dicloxacillin or cephalexin for staphylococcal mastitis via bacterial cell-wall inhibition, and when indicated galactagogues such as metoclopramide, a dopamine D2 antagonist that raises prolactin.

Name: Complicated appendicitis
Description: Complicated appendicitis (UMLS C1632842) is an acute intra-abdominal inflammatory and infectious disorder in which luminal obstruction of the appendix progresses to gangrene, perforation, abscess, or phlegmon, representing severe subtypes of appendicitis rather than a distinct inherited disease. Its biology is dominated by innate immune and mucosal injury pathways, with activation of Toll-like receptor signaling, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, CXCL8/IL-8, cyclooxygenase-2, and neutrophil- and matrix metalloproteinase-mediated tissue destruction; studies have also implicated variants or differential expression in cytokine and inflammatory genes such as IL6, TNF, IL1B, TLR4, NOD2, and MMPs, but no single high-penetrance mutation or Mendelian inheritance pattern is established, although familial clustering of appendicitis suggests modest polygenic susceptibility. Patients typically present with migrating periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, rebound or guarding, leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, and in advanced cases sepsis or diffuse peritonitis. Commonly linked complications and comorbid contexts include perforation, generalized peritonitis, appendiceal abscess, small-bowel obstruction, pylephlebitis, postoperative wound infection, and higher risk in children, older adults, pregnancy, diabetes, and immunosuppression. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment integrated with laboratory inflammation markers and imaging, especially contrast-enhanced CT showing enlarged appendix, wall defect, extraluminal gas, abscess, or phlegmon; ultrasound is often first line in children and pregnancy, and MRI is an alternative when radiation should be avoided. Treatment centers on urgent appendectomy or image-guided drainage plus broad-spectrum antibiotics such as piperacillin-tazobactam, which inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and β-lactamases, ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking, and metronidazole, which generates free-radical metabolites that damage anaerobic bacterial DNA; carbapenems such as ertapenem are also used for severe polymicrobial infection.

Name: Arthritides, Bacterial
Description: Bacterial arthritides, most commonly manifesting as acute septic arthritis, comprise infectious inflammations of native or prosthetic joints caused by organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus spp., Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and gram-negative bacilli; they are fundamentally acquired rather than inherited disorders, although host susceptibility is influenced by immune-response genes and proteins including TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, HLA class II alleles, and cytokine mediators such as TNF, IL1B, IL6, CXCL8, matrix metalloproteinases, and complement components, with rare monogenic predispositions in immunodeficiency states affecting IRAK4, MYD88, CYBB, or BTK. Pathobiology centers on bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation, especially on prostheses, activation of TLR/NF-kB, inflammasome, complement, neutrophil-recruitment, and RANKL-mediated osteoclast pathways, producing synovitis, cartilage proteoglycan loss, and bone destruction. Typical features are abrupt monoarticular pain, warmth, swelling, erythema, effusion, restricted motion, and fever, most often in the knee, hip, shoulder, or ankle; polyarticular disease, gonococcal arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, prosthetic-joint infection, and hematogenous, postoperative, or contiguous-spread subtypes also occur. Major comorbidities and risk factors include rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, malignancy, HIV, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, skin infection, bacteremia, and prosthetic joints; complications include sepsis, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, growth-plate injury in children, chronic pain, ankylosis, and irreversible joint destruction. Diagnosis relies on urgent arthrocentesis with synovial leukocyte count typically above 50,000/µL with neutrophil predominance, Gram stain, culture, and increasingly PCR or 16S rRNA testing, plus blood cultures, inflammatory markers, and imaging such as ultrasound, radiography, or MRI. Name: Metastatic Malignant Neoplasm in the Leptomeninges
Description: Metastatic malignant neoplasm in the leptomeninges, or leptomeningeal metastasis/carcinomatosis, is a secondary dissemination of systemic cancer to the pia-arachnoid and cerebrospinal fluid, most often arising from breast cancer, lung adenocarcinoma, melanoma, and sometimes hematologic malignancies; its biology commonly reflects the driver landscape of the primary tumor, with representative alterations including EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS, HER2/ERBB2, PIK3CA, BRAF, NRAS, TP53, and less specifically MYC, with involvement of MAPK/ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, receptor tyrosine kinase, JAK-STAT, cell-cycle, adhesion/integrin, chemokine, and blood-CSF barrier trafficking pathways that facilitate CSF survival and neuroaxis spread. It is not an inherited disease per se, but inherited cancer-predisposition syndromes such as BRCA1/2-associated breast cancer, TP53/Li-Fraumeni syndrome, CDKN2A-associated melanoma, and EGFR- or other oncogene-defined familial susceptibility in lung cancer can indirectly increase risk through the primary malignancy. Clinical manifestations are typically multifocal and include headache, nausea, vomiting, encephalopathy, seizures, radiculopathies, back pain, cranial neuropathies, diplopia, hearing loss, cauda equina symptoms, weakness, sensory loss, gait impairment, and bowel or bladder dysfunction. Major complications include hydrocephalus, elevated intracranial pressure, ischemic events, severe pain, progressive neurologic disability, and frequent coexistence of parenchymal brain metastases or epidural/spinal disease. Diagnosis relies on compatible neurologic findings in a patient with cancer, contrast-enhanced MRI of brain and spine showing linear or nodular leptomeningeal enhancement, and CSF analysis with malignant cytology or flow cytometry, often supported by elevated protein, low glucose, pleocytosis, and increasingly CSF circulating tumor DNA. Recognized subtypes include nodular versus diffuse disease and tumor-specific forms such as leptomeningeal carcinomatosis, melanomatosis, or lymphomatous/leukemic meningitis. Name: Electrolyte disorders
Description: Electrolyte disorders are a heterogeneous group of acquired or inherited disturbances of sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, chloride, or acid-base balance that arise from altered intake, distribution, renal handling, gastrointestinal loss, or endocrine regulation; clinically important genetic contributors include AVPR2 and AQP2 in nephrogenic water-balance disorders causing hypernatremia, SLC12A3 in Gitelman syndrome, SLC12A1 and KCNJ1 in Bartter syndrome, SCNN1A/SCNN1B/SCNN1G and NR3C2 in pseudohypoaldosteronism, WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, and CUL3 in familial hyperkalemic hypertension, CASR and GNA11 in calcium-sensing defects, and PTH, CYP24A1, TRPM6, FGF23, and PHEX in calcium, magnesium, and phosphate disorders, with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, and de novo patterns all recognized. Key pathways include the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, vasopressin-V2 receptor-cAMP-AQP2 signaling, epithelial sodium channel and Na-K-2Cl/Na-Cl cotransporter transport systems, Na+/K+-ATPase, ROMK, acid-base buffering, PTH-vitamin D-CaSR signaling, and FGF23-klotho phosphate regulation. Common manifestations include weakness, cramps, paresthesias, polyuria, dehydration or edema, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, confusion, seizures, tetany, arrhythmias, blood pressure abnormalities, and in severe cases coma or sudden death. Major subtypes are hypo- and hypernatremia, hypo- and hyperkalemia, hypo- and hypercalcemia, hypo- and hypermagnesemia, and hypo- and hyperphosphatemia, often linked to chronic kidney disease, heart failure, cirrhosis, diabetes, adrenal or parathyroid disorders, malignancy, and drug exposure, with complications such as nephrolithiasis, rhabdomyolysis, osteoporosis, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Diagnosis relies on serum and urine electrolytes, osmolality, blood gases, ECG, renal function, endocrine testing, and targeted genetic testing when hereditary tubulopathy or endocrine disease is suspected. Name: Meningitis caused by Klebsiella aerogenes
Description: Meningitis caused by Klebsiella aerogenes (formerly Enterobacter aerogenes) is a rare, usually healthcare-associated Gram-negative bacillary meningitis that typically follows neurosurgery, ventricular shunting, head trauma, or bacteremia in immunocompromised hosts, and is characterized by acute fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, photophobia, seizures, and sometimes focal neurologic deficits or signs of raised intracranial pressure. The organism’s pathogenicity is mediated by lipopolysaccharide, outer-membrane porins, capsule, siderophore iron-acquisition systems such as enterobactin, and biofilm-related factors, which activate TLR4–MyD88–NF-κB, inflammasome, complement, and cytokine pathways including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, driving neutrophilic meningeal inflammation and blood-brain barrier injury. Important microbial genetic determinants include chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase genes, porin alterations, and acquired resistance elements such as ESBL genes blaTEM, blaSHV, and blaCTX-M, carbapenemase genes including blaKPC, blaNDM, and blaOXA-48-like, plus quinolone-resistance loci such as gyrA and parC mutations and plasmid-mediated qnr genes; these affect treatment rather than conferring Mendelian inheritance, as the disease itself is infectious and non-inherited, although host susceptibility is increased by diabetes, malignancy, cirrhosis, prematurity, neurosurgical devices, and other causes of immune dysfunction. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical syndrome with cerebrospinal fluid showing neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose, and positive CSF Gram stain and culture, supported by blood cultures, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and increasingly PCR or metagenomic sequencing; imaging helps identify ventriculitis, abscess, hydrocephalus, or device infection. Major complications include sepsis, ventriculitis, brain abscess, stroke, hydrocephalus, hearing loss, cognitive impairment, and death. Clinical subtypes include postoperative, post-traumatic, shunt-associated, neonatal, and hematogenous meningitis. Commonly used therapies are cefepime, a fourth-generation cephalosporin that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis; meropenem, a carbapenem with broad beta-lactam activity

Name: Gastrointestinal infection caused by Klebsiella aerogenes
Description: Gastrointestinal infection caused by Klebsiella aerogenes (formerly Enterobacter aerogenes; UMLS C1720135) is an opportunistic, usually non-inherited Gram-negative enteric infection ranging from self-limited gastroenteritis to severe healthcare-associated enterocolitis and bacteremic intra-abdominal disease, particularly in hospitalized, immunocompromised, antibiotic-exposed, neonate, or critically ill patients. Clinical manifestations typically include diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, and sometimes hematochezia, with severe cases progressing to dehydration, sepsis, peritonitis, or shock. Disease presentations may be community-acquired or nosocomial and may occur as uncomplicated infectious gastroenteritis, antibiotic-associated colitis, or invasive gastrointestinal infection with translocation into blood or other sterile sites. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial adhesins, lipopolysaccharide endotoxin, capsule polysaccharide, siderophore-mediated iron acquisition, porins, and resistance determinants such as AmpC beta-lactamase, ESBL enzymes including CTX-M, SHV, and TEM variants, and occasionally carbapenemases such as KPC or NDM; these activate host innate immune pathways centered on TLR4 recognition of LPS, NF-kB signaling, inflammasome activation, and cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6, with neutrophil recruitment and epithelial barrier injury. There is no Mendelian inheritance pattern for the infection itself, but host susceptibility is influenced by genetic and acquired factors affecting mucosal immunity, such as variants in TLR4, NOD2, or CFTR, alongside comorbid diabetes, malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, liver disease, malnutrition, and prior microbiome disruption. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms plus stool culture or multiplex PCR identifying K. aerogenes, blood cultures in systemic illness, susceptibility testing, inflammatory markers, and imaging or endoscopy when complications are suspected. Treatment is guided by antibiogram and commonly includes ciprofloxacin, which inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, cefepime, a fourth-generation beta-lactam inhibiting penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis, piperacillin-tazobactam, combining a ureidopenicillin with beta-lactamase inhibition, and for multidrug-resistant strains carbapenems such as meropenem, which also block cell-wall synthesis.

Name: Toxoplasmosis associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (disorder)
Description: Toxoplasmosis associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome is an opportunistic, usually reactivation disease caused by the intracellular protozoan Toxoplasma gondii in the setting of advanced HIV-related cellular immunodeficiency, classically when CD4+ T-cell counts fall below 100/µL. Its pathobiology centers on failure of IL-12/IFN-γ–driven Th1 immunity, impaired CD8+ T-cell and macrophage control, and parasite invasion pathways involving microneme/rhoptry proteins and host signaling through JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and nitric oxide–dependent antimicrobial responses; host susceptibility has been linked to polymorphisms in immune genes such as IFNG, IL12B, IL12RB1, TLR2, TLR4, TLR9, HLA loci, and CCR5, although inheritance is not Mendelian and reflects complex polygenic predisposition rather than a defined hereditary syndrome. The major clinical subtype is cerebral toxoplasmosis, but ocular, pulmonary, and disseminated forms also occur; common manifestations include subacute fever, headache, confusion, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, altered mental status, ataxia, and sometimes chorioretinitis. Frequent comorbidities include HIV/AIDS itself and other opportunistic infections, while complications include cerebral edema, mass effect, coma, relapse, and death. Diagnosis is typically based on compatible syndrome in an immunocompromised host, positive Toxoplasma IgG indicating prior exposure, characteristic multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia or corticomedullary lesions on CT/MRI, and clinical-radiologic response to empiric therapy; CSF PCR for T. gondii, ocular examination, and, when needed, brain biopsy help distinguish it from primary CNS lymphoma, tuberculosis, cryptococcosis, or pyogenic abscess. Standard treatment includes pyrimethamine, a parasitic dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor, plus sulfadiazine, which inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, with leucovorin rescue to limit marrow toxicity; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole provides sequential folate antagonism and is also used for prophylaxis, while atovaquone inhibits mitochondrial electron transport and clindamycin inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit as alternatives or adjuncts, alongside antiretroviral therapy–guided immune reconstitution.

Name: Persistent erythema of skin
Description: Persistent erythema of skin is a chronic clinical sign rather than a single disease entity, reflecting sustained cutaneous vasodilation and/or inflammation, most commonly in erythematotelangiectatic rosacea, photosensitivity disorders, chronic dermatitis, connective-tissue disease, and mast-cell or autonomic dysregulation; patients typically present with fixed or recurrent facial or acral redness, flushing, warmth or burning, telangiectasia, edema, pruritus, and sometimes scaling, papules, or pustules depending on the subtype. Molecular associations vary by cause but include dysregulated innate immunity and neurovascular signaling, with representative involvement of TLR2, KLK5, cathelicidin/LL37, TRPV1, VEGFA, TNF, IL1B, IL6, and matrix metalloproteinases in rosacea-like erythema, while autoimmune erythema may involve type I interferon, JAK-STAT, NF-κB, complement, and Th1/Th17 pathways; hereditary vascular or inflammatory contributors can include RASA1 or EPHB4 mutations in capillary-malformation syndromes, ATP2A2 in keratinization disorders with erythematous plaques, and rare familial flushing traits, although most persistent erythema is multifactorial rather than Mendelian. Important comorbidities include ocular rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis, migraine, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis, hypertension, anxiety, and secondary infection or disfigurement. Treatment is directed at etiology and commonly includes topical brimonidine or oxymetazoline, alpha-adrenergic agonists that reduce erythema by vasoconstriction; metronidazole, which has anti-inflammatory and reactive-oxygen-species-modulating effects; azelaic acid, which suppresses keratinocyte inflammation and microbial stimuli; doxycycline, which inhibits neutrophil-driven inflammation and matrix metalloproteinases; and topical calcineurin inhibitors or corticosteroids in selected inflammatory dermatoses. Diagnosis is clinical but supported by morphology, trigger history, distribution, dermoscopy, patch testing, autoantibodies such as ANA when connective-tissue disease is suspected, skin biopsy for interface dermatitis, vasculitis, mastocytosis, or neoplasia, and occasionally phototesting or genetic testing in syndromic vascular lesions.

Name: Hypertrophies, Prostatic
Description: Prostatic hyperplasia, usually benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), is a common age-related, nonmalignant enlargement of the periurethral/transition zone prostate caused by nodular hyperplasia of both stromal and epithelial elements, producing bladder outlet obstruction and lower urinary tract symptoms such as hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining, incomplete emptying, frequency, urgency, nocturia, and sometimes acute urinary retention, hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infection, bladder stones, hydronephrosis, or obstructive renal insufficiency. Its biology is driven chiefly by androgen signaling, especially testosterone conversion by steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 encoded by SRD5A2 to dihydrotestosterone acting through the androgen receptor, with contributions from estrogen receptor pathways, stromal-epithelial paracrine signaling, adrenergic smooth-muscle tone via alpha-1A adrenergic receptors, and proliferative/inflammatory pathways involving TGF-beta, FGF, EGF, IGF, PI3K-AKT, MAPK, NF-kappaB, cytokines such as IL-6, and apoptosis regulators including BCL2; representative associated genes or proteins include AR, SRD5A2, ESR1/ESR2, KLK3 (PSA), FGFs, TGFB1, and adrenergic receptor ADRA1A, while inherited susceptibility is complex and polygenic rather than Mendelian, with familial clustering and reported associations in AR CAG-repeat length, SRD5A2 variants, and loci affecting steroid metabolism and inflammation. Clinical subtypes include microscopic versus macroscopic BPH and symptom-based bladder-outlet-obstructive versus storage-predominant disease. Diagnosis relies on history and digital rectal examination, symptom quantification with the International Prostate Symptom Score, urinalysis, serum creatinine when indicated, PSA testing to assess prostate biology and exclude cancer risk, and selective use of postvoid residual measurement, uroflowmetry, ultrasound, cystoscopy, or urodynamics. Standard therapy includes alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin, alfuzosin, and doxazosin, which relax prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride and dutasteride, which lower dihydrotestosterone and shrink prostate volume; and tadalafil, a PDE5 inhibitor that enhances nitric oxide-cGMP

Name: Aspiration Pneumonitis
Description: Aspiration pneumonitis (UMLS C1761609) is an acute chemical lung injury caused by inhalation of sterile but acidic gastric contents, distinct from aspiration pneumonia by its primarily inflammatory rather than initially infectious nature, and it typically presents after impaired airway protection from anesthesia, sedation, stroke, seizures, dysphagia, gastroesophageal reflux, vomiting, or neuromuscular disease with abrupt dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, cough, wheeze, fever, diffuse crackles, and radiographic dependent infiltrates that can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome. Its pathobiology is dominated by epithelial and endothelial injury, surfactant dysfunction, alveolar-capillary leak, and neutrophil-rich innate immune activation involving TNF, IL1B, IL6, CXCL8/IL8, TLR4, NFKB, complement, reactive oxygen species, and coagulation pathways; no single causative mutation defines the disease, but genetic susceptibility may be modified by variants in inflammatory or mucosal defense genes such as TNF, IL6, TLR4, MUC5B, and surfactant-related genes including SFTPA1, SFTPB, and SFTPC, although inheritance is not Mendelian and risk is usually acquired. Important subtypes include witnessed macroaspiration pneumonitis, occult recurrent microaspiration injury, and mixed aspiration pneumonitis with secondary bacterial superinfection. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by aspiration history, pulse oximetry or arterial blood gases, chest radiography or CT, bronchoscopy when particulate aspiration or an alternative diagnosis is suspected, and microbiologic testing mainly to distinguish superimposed infection. Management is largely supportive with supplemental oxygen, airway protection, suctioning, bronchodilators such as albuterol, a beta2-adrenergic agonist that reverses bronchospasm, and mechanical ventilation when needed; antibiotics are not routine for pure chemical pneumonitis but are used when infection is suspected, commonly ampicillin-sulbactam, a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor blocking bacterial cell-wall synthesis, piperacillin-tazobactam with similar broad anaerobic and gram-negative coverage, or clindamycin, a 50S ribosomal inhibitor. Name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
Description: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF; UMLS C1800706) is a chronic, progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause, usually occurring in older adults and pathologically characterized by usual interstitial pneumonia, with temporal and spatial heterogeneity, fibroblastic foci, and irreversible extracellular matrix deposition leading to restrictive lung disease and respiratory failure. Patients typically present with insidious exertional dyspnea, persistent dry cough, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, digital clubbing, reduced diffusion capacity, and progressive hypoxemia. Disease biology reflects repeated alveolar epithelial injury and aberrant repair involving TGF-β/SMAD, PDGF, VEGF, FGF, Wnt/β-catenin, integrin-mediated mechanotransduction, telomere maintenance, ER-stress, and MUC5B-related mucociliary dysfunction, with activated epithelial cells, fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, and macrophages as key effectors. Genetic susceptibility is supported by familial and sporadic cases associated with the MUC5B promoter variant rs35705950, telomere-related genes such as TERT, TERC, RTEL1, PARN, DKC1, and surfactant genes SFTPA1, SFTPA2, and SFTPC; inheritance in familial pulmonary fibrosis is often autosomal dominant with age-dependent penetrance, although many cases are sporadic. Major comorbidities and complications include pulmonary hypertension, acute exacerbations, gastroesophageal reflux, emphysema, obstructive sleep apnea, lung cancer, venous thromboembolism, cachexia, and secondary infections. Recognized forms include sporadic IPF and familial pulmonary fibrosis within the broader idiopathic interstitial pneumonias. Diagnosis requires exclusion of alternative causes of interstitial lung disease, multidisciplinary assessment, high-resolution CT showing a definite or probable usual interstitial pneumonia pattern with subpleural basal-predominant reticulation and honeycombing, pulmonary function testing, serologic evaluation for connective tissue disease, and selected bronchoalveolar lavage or surgical/cryobiopsy when imaging is indeterminate. Name: Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis
Description: Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB; UMLS C1827301) is a severe, transmissible form of pulmonary or extrapulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection defined by resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin plus any fluoroquinolone and at least one additional key second-line agent, historically amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin, and more recently framed around resistance to core Group A drugs; it arises through acquired bacterial genetic mutations rather than Mendelian inheritance in the host, with representative resistance determinants including katG and inhA promoter mutations for isoniazid, rpoB for rifampin, gyrA/gyrB for fluoroquinolones, and rrs, eis promoter, or tlyA for injectable drugs, while host susceptibility is influenced by immune-related genes such as SLC11A1/NRAMP1, TLR2, IFNG, and IL12B. Pathobiology centers on macrophage infection, granuloma formation, and Th1/IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-12, autophagy, and reactive nitrogen/oxygen pathways, with immune dysregulation facilitating persistence and cavitary disease. Patients typically present with chronic cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and radiographic upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or disseminated lesions; major subtypes are pulmonary versus extrapulmonary and primary transmitted versus acquired XDR-TB. Important comorbidities and complications include HIV infection, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, chronic lung disease, substance use, treatment toxicities, respiratory failure, massive hemoptysis, bronchiectasis, and death. Diagnosis requires microbiologic confirmation with culture or nucleic acid amplification, demonstration of M. tuberculosis, and phenotypic or molecular drug-susceptibility testing, including line-probe assays and targeted or whole-genome sequencing for resistance mutations, supported by smear microscopy, chest imaging, and evaluation for extrapulmonary involvement. Treatment uses multidrug regimens guided by susceptibility testing, commonly including bedaquiline, which inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, linezolid, which blocks 50S ribosomal protein synthesis, and fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase when active, with additional agents such as pretomanid disrupting

Name: Dementia associated with Parkinson's Disease
Description: Dementia associated with Parkinson’s disease, commonly termed Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD), is a progressive neurodegenerative synucleinopathy characterized by cognitive decline arising in established Parkinson’s disease, usually after at least 1 year of motor symptoms, and is closely related to dementia with Lewy bodies within the Lewy body disease spectrum. Its pathology centers on misfolded alpha-synuclein encoded by SNCA, with important genetic contributors including GBA1 variants that impair lysosomal glucocerebrosidase function, LRRK2 mutations affecting kinase signaling and vesicular trafficking, and less commonly PARK2, PINK1, DJ-1/PARK7, APOE, and MAPT risk effects; inheritance is most often sporadic, but autosomal dominant SNCA and LRRK2 forms and recessive PRKN/PARK2, PINK1, and DJ-1 forms are recognized. Key pathogenic pathways include alpha-synuclein aggregation, ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosome dysfunction, mitochondrial impairment and oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, cholinergic deficits, and dopaminergic denervation involving basal ganglia-cortical and limbic networks. Clinically, patients develop executive and visuospatial dysfunction, impaired attention, memory retrieval deficits, fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, apathy, depression, REM sleep behavior disorder, autonomic dysfunction, gait instability, falls, and worsening bradykinesia and rigidity; common comorbidities and complications include depression, psychosis, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, dysphagia, sleep disorders, fractures, aspiration pneumonia, and caregiver burden. Diagnosis is clinical, based on established Parkinson’s disease with later-onset dementia causing functional impairment, supported by neuropsychological testing, exclusion of delirium and major alternative causes, MRI or CT to exclude structural lesions, and supportive DAT-SPECT, FDG-PET, polysomnography, or CSF/experimental biomarker assessment in selected cases. Treatment is symptomatic: rivastigmine, a central acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is most established; donepezil and galantamine also enhance cholinergic transmission; levodopa replenishes dopamine for motor symptoms; pimavanserin, a 5-HT2A inverse agonist, or quetiapine may be used for psychosis, with careful avoidance of antidopaminergic agents.

Name: VITILIGO
Description: Vitiligo (UMLS C1847835) is a chronic acquired depigmenting disorder caused by selective autoimmune destruction of epidermal melanocytes, producing well-demarcated chalk-white macules and patches, often symmetric, accentuated under Wood lamp, and commonly involving the face, hands, body folds, and periorificial sites, with leukotrichia and Koebnerization in some patients. It is clinically classified into nonsegmental forms, including generalized, acrofacial, mucosal, and universal vitiligo, and segmental vitiligo, which is typically unilateral and more stable. Pathogenesis is polygenic and multifactorial, integrating genetic susceptibility, oxidative stress, and adaptive and innate immune activation; associated genes include HLA class I/II loci, PTPN22, NLRP1, TYR, CTLA4, IL2RA, IFIH1, and XBP1, while melanocyte proteins such as tyrosinase, MART1, and gp100 can serve as autoantigens. Key pathways include IFN-gamma/CXCL9-CXCL10/CXCR3 signaling with JAK1/JAK2-STAT1 activation, cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell recruitment, TNF-alpha and IL-15-mediated resident memory T-cell persistence, and oxidative stress pathways involving reactive oxygen species and impaired antioxidant defenses. Vitiligo often coexists with autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, alopecia areata, Addison disease, and other autoimmune polyglandular syndromes, and complications are mainly psychosocial distress, stigmatization, and sun sensitivity rather than systemic organ damage. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by Wood lamp examination, dermoscopy showing depigmentation with perifollicular changes, and biopsy when needed demonstrating loss of melanocytes with variable lymphocytic interface change; laboratory testing commonly screens for associated autoimmunity, especially thyroid dysfunction. Treatment commonly includes topical corticosteroids, which broadly suppress cutaneous inflammation; topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, which inhibit T-cell activation via calcineurin-NFAT blockade; narrowband UVB phototherapy, which promotes melanocyte regeneration and immunomodulation; and ruxolitinib cream, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor that interrupts IFN-gamma signaling.

Name: Proopiomelanocortin Deficiency
Description: Proopiomelanocortin deficiency is a rare, usually autosomal recessive monogenic disorder of energy balance and adrenal function caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in POMC, which encodes the prohormone precursor of adrenocorticotropic hormone, alpha-, beta-, and gamma-melanocyte-stimulating hormones, and beta-endorphin; representative pathogenic changes include nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and exon-deleting mutations that abolish peptide production or processing. The core pathobiology involves failure of hypothalamic leptin-melanocortin signaling, with impaired POMC neuron output to melanocortin receptors, especially loss of alpha-MSH activation of MC4R in the paraventricular nucleus causing hyperphagia and severe early-onset obesity, and loss of ACTH signaling through MC2R in the adrenal cortex causing secondary-like primary adrenal insufficiency with low cortisol; altered MC1R stimulation also contributes to pale skin and red hair in some patients. Clinically, affected infants present with neonatal hypoglycemia, cholestatic jaundice, seizures or shock from adrenal crisis, followed by intense hyperphagia, rapid weight gain, severe childhood obesity, and variable pigmentary abnormalities; complications include metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, fatty liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, and psychosocial morbidity. Classic complete POMC deficiency contrasts with partial or atypical phenotypes, sometimes due to hypomorphic alleles or defects in related genes such as PCSK1 that impair POMC processing. Diagnosis rests on characteristic phenotype plus biochemical evidence of adrenal insufficiency with very low ACTH and cortisol, obesity/hyperphagia, and confirmatory molecular testing by targeted sequencing, multigene obesity panels, or exome sequencing; endocrine evaluation, pigment assessment, and family segregation testing are useful. Treatment includes lifelong glucocorticoid replacement such as hydrocortisone, prednisolone, or dexamethasone to replace cortisol, and setmelanotide, an MC4R agonist that restores downstream melanocortin signaling and reduces hunger and weight; supportive anti-obesity measures may include lifestyle therapy and, less specifically, agents such as orlistat, a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor.

Name: Irritable bowel syndrome characterized by constipation
Description: Irritable bowel syndrome characterized by constipation (IBS-C; UMLS C1868889) is a chronic functional disorder of gut–brain interaction defined by recurrent abdominal pain associated with defecation or change in stool frequency/form, with constipation-predominant bowel habits and no structural explanation; typical symptoms include hard or infrequent stools, straining, bloating, abdominal distension, sensation of incomplete evacuation, and pain often relieved by bowel movements. Diagnosis is clinical, usually by Rome IV criteria, supported by normal basic evaluation and selective testing to exclude mimics such as celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal neoplasia, pelvic floor dyssynergia, or hypothyroidism; testing may include CBC, CRP or fecal calprotectin, celiac serologies, colonoscopy when alarm features are present, anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion testing, or colonic transit studies. IBS-C overlaps with functional constipation but is distinguished by pain prominence; recognized subtypes include IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M, and IBS-U. Pathobiology is multifactorial, involving altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity, psychosocial stress, mucosal immune activation, epithelial barrier dysfunction, bile acid and serotonin signaling, enteric nervous system dysregulation, and microbiome perturbation; implicated pathways include 5-HT/TPH1-SLC6A4 signaling, guanylate cyclase C–cGMP–CFTR chloride/fluid secretion, chloride channel and sodium-hydrogen exchange transport, and brain-gut neuroimmune pathways. Genetic contribution is complex and generally non-Mendelian, with modest associations reported for SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR, HTR3A/HTR3E, SCN5A, TNFSF15, NPSR1, FAAH, and GNβ3 variants; rare SCN5A channelopathy may influence motility in select patients. Common treatments include linaclotide and plecanatide, guanylate cyclase C agonists that increase intestinal secretion and reduce pain signaling; lubiprostone, a chloride channel activator enhancing fluid secretion; tenapanor, an NHE3 inhibitor reducing sodium absorption; osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol; and sometimes tegaserod, a 5-HT4 agonist that stimulates motility. Name: Human Herpesvirus 6 encephalitis
Description: Human herpesvirus 6 encephalitis is an acute viral inflammatory disease of the central nervous system, usually caused by reactivation of latent HHV-6B, less often HHV-6A, with marked tropism for limbic structures and a predominance in immunocompromised hosts, especially allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipients. Viral entry and persistence involve host factors such as CD46 for HHV-6A and CD134/TNFRSF4 for HHV-6B, while chromosomally integrated HHV-6 can reflect inherited germline integration with autosomal dominant transmission, complicating interpretation of high blood HHV-6 DNA; impaired T-cell immunity and cytokine dysregulation, including NF-kB, JAK/STAT-interferon signaling, TNF-alpha, IL-6, and microglial/astrocytic activation, are implicated in pathogenesis. Clinically, patients typically present with fever, confusion, short-term memory loss, personality change, reduced consciousness, and prominent seizures or nonconvulsive status epilepticus, often with hyponatremia; complications include limbic encephalitis, hippocampal injury, persistent cognitive deficits, epilepsy, SIADH, and death, and comorbidities commonly include graft-versus-host disease, hematologic malignancy, solid-organ transplantation, HIV infection, and other opportunistic infections. Diagnosis rests on compatible encephalopathy plus detection of HHV-6 DNA, preferably in cerebrospinal fluid by quantitative PCR interpreted alongside blood viral load to exclude inherited chromosomal integration, supported by mesial temporal T2/FLAIR MRI abnormalities, EEG slowing or epileptiform activity, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis or elevated protein, and occasionally tissue methods or droplet-digital PCR for integration status. Treatment relies on antivirals active against the viral DNA polymerase U38 and related replication machinery: ganciclovir, a guanosine analog causing chain termination after phosphorylation; foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analog directly inhibiting viral DNA polymerase; and cidofovir, a nucleotide analog inhibiting viral DNA synthesis, with valganciclovir used orally in selected cases.

Name: Calcium renal calculus
Description: Calcium renal calculus, the most common form of nephrolithiasis, is a multifactorial disorder characterized by formation of calcium oxalate and/or calcium phosphate stones within the kidney due to urinary supersaturation, crystal nucleation, growth, and retention, often on Randall plaques. Clinical manifestations typically include acute colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, dysuria, urgency, nausea/vomiting, and, when complicated, fever, obstruction, hydronephrosis, or recurrent urinary tract infection; chronic consequences include recurrent stones, chronic kidney disease, and rare loss of renal function. Major subtypes are calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones, including brushite-predominant disease. Pathobiology involves hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia, low urine volume, altered urinary pH, and tubular handling of calcium and phosphate, with important roles for the calcium-sensing receptor, vitamin D receptor signaling, parathyroid hormone, claudin-mediated tight-junction transport, sodium-phosphate cotransport, and inhibitors of crystallization such as osteopontin and uromodulin. Genetic contributors are usually polygenic, but representative monogenic or strong susceptibility genes include SLC34A1, CLDN14, CASR, CYP24A1, ADCY10, ALPL, SLC26A1, UMOD, and OCRL; APRT and AGXT are relevant inherited mimics or mixed stone disorders, and inheritance may be autosomal dominant, recessive, or complex depending on cause. Comorbidities include primary hyperparathyroidism, distal renal tubular acidosis, medullary sponge kidney, obesity, diabetes, gout, osteoporosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and bariatric surgery. Diagnosis rests on imaging, usually noncontrast CT or ultrasound, urinalysis showing hematuria/crystals, stone analysis, and metabolic evaluation with serum calcium, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid, creatinine, PTH when indicated, and 24-hour urine for calcium, oxalate, citrate, sodium, uric acid, pH, and volume; genetic testing is considered in early-onset, familial, recurrent, or syndromic disease. Name: HER2-positive carcinoma of breast
Description: HER2-positive carcinoma of the breast is an aggressive molecular subtype of invasive breast cancer defined by amplification of ERBB2 on chromosome 17q12 and consequent overexpression of the HER2/neu receptor tyrosine kinase, often with co-alterations involving TP53, PIK3CA, PTEN loss, CCND1, MYC, and variable expression of ESR1 and PGR; it may arise as HER2-enriched, hormone receptor-positive/HER2-positive, or less commonly inflammatory or metastatic phenotypes. HER2 signaling drives receptor homo- and heterodimerization, especially with HER3, activating PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-RAF-MAPK, SRC, and PLCγ pathways to promote proliferation, survival, invasion, and resistance. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited susceptibility may coexist, particularly with germline BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, TP53, CHEK2, or ATM variants, although HER2 amplification itself is a somatic event and not usually inherited. Patients commonly present with a palpable breast mass, asymmetric breast thickening, skin or nipple retraction, peau d’orange, axillary adenopathy, or less commonly pain, nipple discharge, or metastatic symptoms involving bone, liver, lung, or brain. Major complications include locoregional recurrence, distant metastasis, CNS spread, treatment resistance, cancer-associated thrombosis, and cardiomyopathy related either to disease therapy or comorbid hypertension and coronary disease. Diagnosis relies on core biopsy showing invasive carcinoma, usually ductal type, with HER2 status established by immunohistochemistry showing 3+ membranous staining or by in situ hybridization demonstrating ERBB2 amplification in equivocal cases, alongside ER/PR testing, staging imaging as indicated, and increasingly next-generation sequencing for actionable mutations. Standard therapy combines anti-HER2 agents such as trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks HER2 signaling and mediates antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, pertuzumab, which inhibits HER2 dimerization, lapatinib, a small-molecule HER2/EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and antibody-drug conjugates such as ado-trastuzumab emtansine or trastuzumab deruxtecan, used with surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and endocrine therapy when hormone receptor positive.

Name: At increased risk of venous thromboembolus
Description: At increased risk of venous thromboembolus denotes a prothrombotic state predisposing to deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism through interaction of inherited thrombophilia, acquired hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and endothelial injury. Important genetic contributors include F5 factor V Leiden causing activated protein C resistance, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1 antithrombin deficiency, PROC and PROS1 deficiencies, and less commonly elevated factor VIII, non-O blood group, and variants affecting fibrinogen or platelet-endothelial interactions; inheritance is often autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance for classic thrombophilias, while risk may also be polygenic. Core pathways involve tissue factor–factor VIIa initiation, factor Xa and thrombin generation, fibrin formation, impairment of the protein C/protein S/antithrombin anticoagulant systems, reduced fibrinolysis via plasminogen and PAI-1, and inflammatory and neutrophil extracellular trap–mediated endothelial activation. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic risk status to calf pain, unilateral leg swelling, warmth, erythema, superficial venous dilation, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis, or syncope when embolization occurs. Subtypes include inherited versus acquired thrombophilia, provoked versus unprovoked VTE risk, and special settings such as cancer-associated, pregnancy-related, postoperative, estrogen-related, antiphospholipid-associated, and recurrent VTE. Major comorbidities and complications include malignancy, obesity, immobility, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, myeloproliferative neoplasms, antiphospholipid syndrome, post-thrombotic syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, and death from massive PE. Diagnosis relies on clinical probability assessment and confirmation with duplex ultrasonography for DVT, CT pulmonary angiography or ventilation-perfusion scanning for PE, D-dimer testing in low-risk patients, and selective thrombophilia testing using APC resistance assays, factor V Leiden and prothrombin genotyping, and antithrombin, protein C, and protein S measurement. Common treatments include heparins that potentiate antithrombin against factor Xa and thrombin, warfarin that inhibits vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis, and direct oral anticoagulants such as apix

Name: Long-chain fatty acid transport deficiency
Description: Long-chain fatty acid transport deficiency, usually classified within long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders, is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disease most often caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC27A4/FATP4, although clinically overlapping long-chain transport or utilization phenotypes may also involve CPT1A, SLC22A5, CPT2, SLC25A20, or ACADVL; representative mutations include missense, nonsense, splice-site, and truncating alleles that reduce expression or function of the encoded transport or mitochondrial entry proteins. The core pathobiology is impaired cellular uptake and/or mitochondrial import and β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, disrupting the carnitine shuttle pathway involving FATP proteins, carnitine, CPT1, CACT, CPT2, acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, PPAR signaling, and energy production during fasting or physiologic stress. Clinical manifestations typically include fasting intolerance, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, recurrent rhabdomyolysis, myalgia, exercise intolerance, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, skeletal muscle weakness, lethargy, vomiting, and, in severe infantile cases, liver dysfunction or sudden decompensation. Subtypes are generally described by age and organ involvement as neonatal/infantile severe multisystem forms, childhood hepatic forms, and later-onset myopathic forms. Important complications and comorbidities include recurrent metabolic crises, heart failure, peripheral neuropathy, pancreatitis, developmental delay, and chronic liver disease. Treatment relies on avoidance of fasting and a low-long-chain-fat/high-carbohydrate diet, together with triheptanoin, an odd-chain medium triglyceride that provides anaplerotic substrates and bypasses defective long-chain oxidation, medium-chain triglycerides such as octanoate-containing formulations that supply oxidizable fuel independent of long-chain transport, and L-carnitine in selected patients to replenish carnitine stores and facilitate acyl-group transport; acute episodes may require intravenous dextrose to suppress lipolysis. Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion, plasma acylcarnitine profiling, low free carnitine in some forms, urine organic acids, CK and transaminases, newborn screening, confirmatory enzyme studies, and molecular genetic testing demonstrating pathogenic variants.

Name: Epidermal growth factor receptor positive non-small cell lung cancer
Description: Epidermal growth factor receptor positive non-small cell lung cancer is a molecularly defined subtype of NSCLC, most often adenocarcinoma, characterized by activating EGFR alterations that drive oncogenesis, classically exon 19 deletions and exon 21 L858R substitutions, with less common G719X, L861Q, S768I, exon 20 insertions, and resistance mutations such as T790M and C797S; related genes and proteins that may modify biology or confer resistance include ERBB2/HER2, MET, KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, ALK, ROS1, RET, and TP53. EGFR activation stimulates the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, JAK-STAT, and PLCgamma-PKC pathways, promoting proliferation, survival, invasion, angiogenesis, and metastatic spread. Typical therapies include gefitinib and erlotinib, reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors that block the ATP-binding site of mutant EGFR; afatinib, an irreversible ErbB family inhibitor; osimertinib, a third-generation irreversible inhibitor active against sensitizing EGFR mutations and T790M with central nervous system activity; and, in selected settings, amivantamab, a bispecific EGFR-MET antibody, or mobocertinib for some exon 20 insertion tumors. Patients commonly present with cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, recurrent pneumonia, pleural effusion, and symptoms from brain, bone, or liver metastases; complications include malignant effusions, respiratory failure, thromboembolism, pathologic fractures, and acquired drug resistance. EGFR-positive NSCLC is usually sporadic rather than classically inherited, though somatic genetic drivers are central and rare germline EGFR variants such as T790M can confer familial susceptibility. Diagnosis requires histologic confirmation of NSCLC with molecular testing by PCR, Sanger or next-generation sequencing, and sometimes liquid biopsy circulating tumor DNA analysis, complemented by immunohistochemistry, FISH when needed for alternative drivers, and CT, PET, and brain MRI for staging.

Name: Precursor T-Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma
Description: Precursor T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia-lymphoma is an aggressive neoplasm of immature thymic T-lineage lymphoblasts that presents along a spectrum from T-acute lymphoblastic leukemia with predominant marrow and blood involvement to T-lymphoblastic lymphoma with a bulky mediastinal/thymic mass and limited marrow disease; common molecular lesions involve NOTCH1 activating mutations, CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletions, FBXW7, PTEN, IL7R, JAK1/JAK3, PHF6, WT1, TAL1, TLX1, TLX3, LMO1/2, LEF1, MYC, and occasional NUP214-ABL1 or MLL/KMT2A rearrangements, leading to dysregulation of NOTCH, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, JAK-STAT, RAS-MAPK, cell-cycle, and T-cell receptor/developmental transcriptional programs. It is usually sporadic rather than classically inherited, although rare predisposition occurs in cancer susceptibility syndromes such as ataxia-telangiectasia, constitutional mismatch-repair deficiency, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and germline RUNX1, ETV6, or PAX5-related predisposition. Patients often present with fever, fatigue, pallor, bleeding, infections, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and especially cough, dyspnea, superior vena cava syndrome, or pleural/pericardial effusions from mediastinal disease; central nervous system and testicular involvement may occur. Diagnosis relies on blood counts, marrow aspirate/biopsy or tissue biopsy showing lymphoblasts, flow cytometry demonstrating immature T-cell markers such as cytoplasmic/surface CD3, CD7, CD2, CD5, TdT and variable CD1a/CD4/CD8, cytogenetics/FISH, and molecular testing, with leukemia generally defined by at least 25% marrow blasts. Treatment uses intensive ALL-type multiagent chemotherapy including vincristine, a microtubule polymerization inhibitor, prednisone or dexamethasone, glucocorticoids that induce lymphoblast apoptosis, daunorubicin or doxorubicin, topoisomerase II-interacting anthracyclines, and L-asparaginase/pegaspargase, which depletes extracellular asparagine; meth

Name: Chlamydia trachomatis infection of genital structure
Description: Chlamydia trachomatis infection of genital structures is a common sexually transmitted bacterial disease caused by obligate intracellular C. trachomatis, most often urogenital serovars D–K, producing cervicitis, urethritis, endometritis, salpingitis, epididymitis, and proctitis; many cases are asymptomatic, but typical findings include dysuria, mucopurulent cervical or urethral discharge, postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, pelvic or testicular pain, dyspareunia, and adnexal or cervical motion tenderness. Pathogenesis depends on bacterial major outer membrane protein OmpA/MOMP, polymorphic membrane proteins, type III secretion effectors, lipopolysaccharide, and heat-shock protein 60, which drive epithelial entry and persistence, with host signaling involving TLR2/TLR4, NF-kappaB, MAPK, interferon-gamma, TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, and adaptive Th1 responses; fibrosis and tubal injury reflect chronic inflammation and matrix-remodeling pathways. Human susceptibility is not Mendelian, but host genetic components have been associated, including variants in TLR2, TLR4, NOD1, HLA class II alleles, IL10, TNFA, IFNG, MMP9, and CCR5, while bacterial ompA genovariants contribute to tissue tropism. Major complications include pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, reactive arthritis, adverse pregnancy outcomes, neonatal conjunctivitis or pneumonia, and coinfection with gonorrhea, HIV, bacterial vaginosis, and Mycoplasma genitalium. Diagnosis is established primarily by nucleic acid amplification testing on vaginal or endocervical swabs, first-catch urine, or rectal/pharyngeal specimens, with culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing, and serology used selectively; clinical criteria support PID when pelvic pain is accompanied by cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness. Standard treatment includes doxycycline, a 30S ribosomal inhibitor; azithromycin, a macrolide that blocks 50S-mediated protein synthesis; and levofloxacin or ofloxacin, fluoroquinolones that inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with partner treatment and retesting important to prevent reinfection.

Name: Left ventricular cardiac dysfunction
Description: Left ventricular cardiac dysfunction is a clinical syndrome in which impaired left ventricular systolic and/or diastolic performance reduces forward cardiac output and/or elevates filling pressures, most commonly manifesting as heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, preserved ejection fraction, or mildly reduced ejection fraction, and arising from ischemic heart disease, hypertension, valvular disease, myocarditis, toxic injury, or primary cardiomyopathy. Genetic contributors are best established in inherited dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies and include TTN truncating variants, LMNA, MYH7, MYBPC3, TNNT2, PLN, DSP, DES, and SCN5A mutations, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance, although X-linked dystrophin-related and mitochondrial forms occur. Pathobiology involves maladaptive neurohormonal and cellular signaling, especially renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, sympathetic beta-adrenergic, natriuretic peptide-cGMP, calcium-handling, inflammatory cytokine, oxidative stress, TGF-beta fibrotic, and apoptosis/remodeling pathways, with key mediators including ACE, angiotensin II, aldosterone, beta1-receptors, neprilysin, SERCA2a, phospholamban, TNF-alpha, and collagen-producing fibroblasts. Typical symptoms and signs include exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, edema, pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pressure, displaced apical impulse, and an S3 or S4. Major comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension, functional mitral regurgitation, ventricular arrhythmias, thromboembolism, cardiogenic shock, and sudden cardiac death. Standard therapy includes ACE inhibitors such as enalapril, which reduce angiotensin II formation; beta-blockers such as carvedilol or metoprolol succinate, which blunt sympathetic signaling; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone, which inhibit aldosterone; plus loop diuretics, SGLT2 inhibitors, and sacubitril/valsartan, a neprilysin inhibitor-ARB combination. Name: Thromboembolism of vein
Description: Thromboembolism of vein, most commonly presenting as deep venous thrombosis with or without pulmonary embolism, is a multifactorial thrombotic disorder characterized by pathologic clot formation in the venous circulation driven by Virchow triad mechanisms of stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Genetic susceptibility is well established, especially inherited thrombophilias involving F5 factor V Leiden causing activated protein C resistance, F2 prothrombin G20210A, and deficiencies or pathogenic variants in SERPINC1 antithrombin, PROC protein C, and PROS1 protein S; less commonly ABO non-O blood group, elevated VWF, FGG, and MTHFR-related hyperhomocysteinemia have been implicated, typically with autosomal dominant inheritance and incomplete penetrance. Key molecular pathways include tissue factor–factor VIIa initiation, thrombin generation, factor Xa amplification, fibrin formation, platelet–leukocyte interactions, NETosis, inflammatory cytokine signaling, and impaired natural anticoagulant and fibrinolytic pathways involving antithrombin, protein C/protein S, plasmin, and PAI-1. Clinical manifestations include unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, erythema, edema, superficial venous distention, and, when embolization occurs, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, or syncope. Major subtypes include proximal or distal lower-extremity DVT, upper-extremity DVT, catheter-associated thrombosis, portal or cerebral venous thrombosis, and provoked versus unprovoked events. Important comorbidities and risk settings include cancer, surgery, trauma, immobility, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, obesity, heart failure, antiphospholipid syndrome, myeloproliferative neoplasms, and COVID-19; complications include pulmonary embolism, recurrence, post-thrombotic syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, and venous insufficiency. Diagnosis relies on pretest probability tools such as Wells score, D-dimer testing, compression duplex ultrasonography, and CT pulmonary angiography or ventilation-perfusion scanning when PE is suspected, with thrombophilia testing reserved for selected patients. Name: Osteomyelitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus
Description: Osteomyelitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus (UMLS C1997728) is a pyogenic bacterial infection of bone and marrow, typically arising hematogenously, by contiguous spread from skin or soft tissue, or after trauma, surgery, or prosthetic implantation, and is broadly classified as acute or chronic, native-bone or implant-associated, and methicillin-susceptible versus methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MSSA/MRSA). Disease pathogenesis reflects bacterial adhesins and toxins, including fibronectin-binding proteins fnbA/fnbB, clumping factors clfA/clfB, protein A spa, alpha-toxin hla, Panton-Valentine leukocidin lukS/F-PV, and biofilm-associated loci such as icaADBC, with methicillin resistance mediated by mecA or mecC encoding the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a; host susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with reported influences in innate immune and inflammatory genes such as TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, IL6, TNF, and VDR. Key pathways include TLR2/NF-kB, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha and RANK/RANKL/OPG signaling, driving neutrophilic inflammation, osteoclast activation, bone resorption, and intracellular persistence in osteoblasts. Typical features are localized bone pain, tenderness, swelling, erythema, warmth, reduced limb function, fever, draining sinus tracts in chronic disease, and elevated ESR/CRP, with complications including abscess, bacteremia, sepsis, pathologic fracture, avascular necrosis, chronic osteomyelitis, and adjacent septic arthritis; common comorbidities include diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, sickle cell disease, immunosuppression, and orthopedic hardware. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical and imaging findings, especially MRI, supported by inflammatory markers and microbiology, with bone biopsy and culture plus histopathology as the diagnostic standard, and blood cultures often positive in hematogenous cases. Treatment commonly includes nafcillin or cefazolin for MSSA, vancomycin for MRSA via cell-wall inhibition, and linezolid, daptomycin, or clindamycin in selected cases, with rifampin often added for biofilm-associated hardware infections because it inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase.

Name: Acute pyelonephritis caused by bacterium
Description: Acute pyelonephritis caused by bacterium is an acute, usually ascending bacterial infection of the renal pelvis and parenchyma, most commonly due to uropathogenic Escherichia coli, with Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and occasionally Staphylococcus saprophyticus or hematogenous S. aureus as other causes; it presents with fever, chills, flank pain, costovertebral-angle tenderness, dysuria, frequency, urgency, nausea or vomiting, and pyuria or bacteriuria, and may be classified as uncomplicated or complicated, community- or healthcare-associated, emphysematous, xanthogranulomatous, or recurrent. Host susceptibility has a polygenic, non-Mendelian pattern rather than a single inherited cause, with representative associations involving innate immune and epithelial defense genes and proteins such as TLR4, TLR5, CXCR1/CXCR2, IL6, IL8/CXCL8, ICAM1, HSPA1B, DEFB1, UMOD, and secretor-status FUT2 variants; bacterial virulence determinants include type 1 and P fimbriae and hemolysin. Key pathways include urothelial TLR4-LPS recognition, MyD88/NF-κB and MAPK signaling, IL-6/IL-8-driven neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and vesicoureteral reflux or obstruction–facilitated ascent of organisms. Important comorbidities and predisposing conditions include urinary tract obstruction, nephrolithiasis, vesicoureteral reflux, neurogenic bladder, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, indwelling catheters, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and immunosuppression; complications include renal abscess, papillary necrosis, emphysematous pyelonephritis, acute kidney injury, bacteremia, sepsis, and renal scarring. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical features plus urinalysis showing pyuria, leukocyte esterase and nitrites, urine culture with organism identification and susceptibilities, blood cultures in severe cases, inflammatory markers, renal function testing, and imaging, usually CT or ultrasound, when obstruction, abscess, stones, atypical presentation, or treatment failure is suspected. Name: Acute Postoperative Pain
Description: Postoperative pain is an acute nociceptive and inflammatory pain state arising after tissue injury from surgery, often with neuropathic features when nerves are stretched, transected, or inflamed; clinically it is characterized by incisional or deep visceral pain, tenderness, hyperalgesia, allodynia, guarding, impaired mobilization, tachycardia, hypertension, sleep disruption, and reduced pulmonary effort, and may be classified as somatic, visceral, neuropathic, acute versus persistent postsurgical pain, and procedure-specific syndromes. Its biology involves peripheral sensitization driven by prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P, CGRP, NGF, TNF, IL-1β, and IL-6, and central sensitization through glutamatergic NMDA receptor signaling, microglial activation, descending serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways, and ion channels including SCN9A/NaV1.7, SCN10A/NaV1.8, TRPV1, OPRM1, COMT, and CACNA2D1; representative genetic influences on pain sensitivity or analgesic response include OPRM1 A118G, COMT Val158Met, CYP2D6 variation affecting codeine or tramadol bioactivation, and rare SCN9A variants altering nociception, although postoperative pain itself is not inherited in a Mendelian pattern. Common treatments include acetaminophen, which acts centrally to reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or ketorolac, which inhibit COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis; opioids such as morphine, fentanyl, or oxycodone, which activate μ-opioid receptors; and adjuvants including local anesthetics such as bupivacaine, which block voltage-gated sodium channels, and gabapentin, which binds the α2δ calcium-channel subunit. Important comorbidities and complications include anxiety, depression, catastrophizing, sleep disturbance, obesity, diabetes, chronic pain disorders, opioid-related respiratory depression, ileus, nausea, delirium, infection risk from immobility, thromboembolism, and transition to chronic postsurgical pain. Name: menstrual periods stopped for over 6 months
Description: Menstrual periods stopped for over 6 months corresponds clinically to secondary amenorrhea, a sign rather than a single disease, defined in a previously menstruating person by absence of menses for at least 3 cycles or 6 months and arising from hypothalamic, pituitary, ovarian, uterine, or outflow-tract dysfunction. Common symptoms and signs include absent bleeding, infertility, decreased libido, vasomotor symptoms, galactorrhea, hirsutism, acne, weight change, stress/exercise-related energy deficit, pelvic pain, or hot flashes. Major subtypes include functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea, polycystic ovary syndrome-related amenorrhea, primary ovarian insufficiency, thyroid- or adrenal-related amenorrhea, and uterine causes such as Asherman syndrome. Molecular associations vary by subtype: GnRH/KISS1/KISS1R/TAC3/TACR3 and leptin signaling in hypothalamic forms; FSHR, LHCGR, CYP17A1, CYP19A1, ESR1, and steroidogenic pathways in ovarian dysfunction; FMR1 premutation, BMP15, NOBOX, FOXL2, NR5A1, and Turner syndrome-related X-chromosome abnormalities in primary ovarian insufficiency; and dopamine D2 receptor–prolactin and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis signaling in hyperprolactinemia. Relevant pathways include pulsatile GnRH release, pituitary LH/FSH secretion, ovarian folliculogenesis, prolactin inhibition of GnRH, insulin/PI3K-AKT and androgen excess in PCOS, and thyroid hormone regulation. Comorbidities and complications include infertility, osteopenia/osteoporosis, endometrial hyperplasia from chronic anovulation, cardiovascular risk, anxiety/depression, metabolic syndrome, and hypoestrogenic genitourinary symptoms. Treatment is cause-specific and includes cabergoline or bromocriptine, dopamine D2 agonists that suppress prolactin; combined estrogen-progestin therapy to replace estrogen and protect the endometrium; cyclic progesterone to induce withdrawal bleeding; metformin, which improves insulin sensitivity and ovulatory function in PCOS; and pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins for fertility induction. Name: Carcinoma, Hepatocellular
Description: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a primary malignant epithelial tumor of hepatocytes, usually arising in chronically injured, cirrhotic liver due to hepatitis B or C infection, alcohol-related liver disease, or nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, and less often in hemochromatosis, aflatoxin exposure, or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Molecularly, HCC commonly shows TERT promoter activation, TP53 loss, CTNNB1/β-catenin mutations, AXIN1 alterations, chromatin-remodeling gene defects such as ARID1A/ARID2, and less frequently amplifications involving MET, FGF19, or VEGFA; serum alpha-fetoprotein, des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin, glypican-3, and heat-shock proteins may be informative protein markers. Key dysregulated pathways include Wnt/β-catenin, p53/cell-cycle control, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, JAK-STAT, TGF-β, MET/HGF, and VEGF-driven angiogenesis, with strong contributions from inflammation, fibrosis, and immune evasion. Typical manifestations include weight loss, fatigue, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, jaundice, decompensated cirrhosis, portal hypertension, ascites, and occasionally paraneoplastic hypoglycemia or erythrocytosis; major complications include portal vein invasion, intrahepatic spread, rupture, and metastases to lung or bone. Histologic subtypes include conventional, fibrolamellar, steatohepatitic, clear cell, and macrotrabecular-massive forms. Most HCC is sporadic rather than Mendelian, although inherited risk occurs through disorders such as hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE), Wilson disease (ATP7B), familial adenomatous polyposis, and rare germline TP53 predisposition. Diagnosis relies on surveillance in high-risk patients with ultrasound with or without alpha-fetoprotein, followed by multiphasic CT or MRI showing arterial phase hyperenhancement with portal/delayed washout in cirrhosis, or biopsy with histopathology and immunohistochemistry when imaging is nonclassic. Name: Bone infection
Description: Bone infection, most commonly osteomyelitis and less often septic osteitis of the jaw, vertebrae, or prosthetic-associated bone, is an infectious inflammatory disorder of bone caused predominantly by hematogenous spread, contiguous soft-tissue infection, trauma, or implanted hardware; Staphylococcus aureus is the leading pathogen, with virulence factors and resistance determinants such as mecA in MRSA and biofilm-associated proteins, while host susceptibility and severity are influenced by genes regulating innate immunity and bone remodeling, including TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, IL6, TNF, IL1B, RANK/RANKL/OPG, MMPs, and variants affecting neutrophil or NADPH oxidase function in rare primary immunodeficiencies. Pathobiology centers on TLR–NF-κB, JAK/STAT, MAPK, inflammasome, and RANKL-mediated osteoclast activation pathways, with cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6 driving marrow edema, cortical destruction, and sequestrum formation. Typical manifestations include localized bone pain, tenderness, swelling, warmth, erythema, fever, reduced limb use or limp, draining sinus tracts in chronic disease, and back pain with neurologic deficits in vertebral infection. Major subtypes include acute, subacute, and chronic osteomyelitis, hematogenous versus contiguous-focus disease, diabetic foot osteomyelitis, vertebral osteomyelitis, and prosthetic-joint or hardware-associated infection. Common treatments include vancomycin, a glycopeptide that inhibits cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis; cefazolin or other β-lactams, which bind penicillin-binding proteins to block bacterial cell-wall cross-linking; and fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with rifampin often added for staphylococcal biofilm infection by inhibiting DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Comorbidities and complications include diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, pressure ulcers, sickle cell disease, immunosuppression, bacteremia, abscess, pathologic fracture, chronic draining sinus, growth disturbance in children, epidural extension, and sepsis. Name: Human epidermal growth factor 2 negative carcinoma of breast
Description: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2/ERBB2)-negative breast carcinoma is a malignant epithelial neoplasm of the breast defined by absence of HER2 overexpression or ERBB2 gene amplification on immunohistochemistry and/or in situ hybridization, and it encompasses hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative cancers and triple-negative breast cancers. Its biology commonly involves alterations in TP53, PIK3CA, GATA3, ESR1, PTEN, AKT1, RB1, and BRCA1/BRCA2, with proteins and pathways centered on estrogen receptor signaling, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, DNA damage repair and homologous recombination, cell-cycle regulation through cyclin D-CDK4/6-RB, and in triple-negative disease EGFR, MYC, immune checkpoint, and basal-like programs. Clinical manifestations typically include a palpable breast mass, mammographic density or calcifications, breast pain, skin or nipple retraction, nipple discharge, axillary lymphadenopathy, and in advanced disease weight loss or metastasis to bone, liver, lung, or brain. Major subtypes include luminal A, luminal B, and triple-negative/basal-like carcinomas, with inherited susceptibility most often autosomal dominant through germline BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, or TP53 variants, while most tumors are sporadic. Diagnosis relies on core biopsy with histopathology, ER/PR immunohistochemistry, HER2 testing by IHC with reflex ISH when equivocal, grading, TNM staging, and adjunctive mammography, ultrasound, MRI, and when appropriate genomic assays or germline testing. Standard treatments include endocrine therapy such as tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, and aromatase inhibitors such as letrozole or anastrozole, which suppress estrogen synthesis; cytotoxics such as doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, paclitaxel, and capecitabine; CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib; PI3K inhibition with alpelisib for PIK3CA-mutant disease; PARP inhibitors such as olaparib in BRCA-associated tumors; and immune checkpoint blockade with pembrolizumab in selected triple-negative cases.
