Name: Pseudobulbar Affect
Description: Pseudobulbar affect (PBA; UMLS C2316460) is a neurologic disorder of emotional expression characterized by involuntary, sudden, and disproportionate episodes of laughing and/or crying that are incongruent with or excessive relative to underlying mood, reflecting disinhibition of corticobulbar and cerebellar-limbic circuits rather than a primary affective illness. It is usually secondary to structural or neurodegenerative disease, most commonly amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, stroke, traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer disease, Parkinsonian disorders, and other dementias, and may be complicated by social dysfunction, depression, anxiety, caregiver burden, and reduced quality of life. Although PBA itself is not a classic inherited monogenic disease, genetic contributors are largely those of the underlying disorders, with representative examples including C9orf72 expansions and SOD1, TARDBP, and FUS mutations in ALS and susceptibility loci in multiple sclerosis; molecularly, implicated pathways include glutamatergic excitotoxicity, serotonergic and sigma-1 receptor signaling, frontopontine-cerebellar network dysregulation, and altered neurotransmission involving NMDA receptors, monoamines, and cerebellar modulation of affective output. Symptoms include brief, stereotyped crying or laughing spells, emotional lability, poor voluntary control, and a mismatch between expressed affect and internal mood; subtypes are commonly described as predominantly laughing, predominantly crying, or mixed forms. Diagnosis is clinical, based on inappropriate or exaggerated emotional outbursts occurring in the context of neurologic disease and distinguished from major depression, bipolar disorder, and gelastic phenomena by history and examination; supportive tools include the Center for Neurologic Study-Lability Scale and the Pathological Laughing and Crying Scale, with neuroimaging used to define the underlying lesion. Treatment includes dextromethorphan/quinidine, in which dextromethorphan acts as an NMDA antagonist and sigma-1 agonist while quinidine inhibits CYP2D6 to raise dextromethorphan exposure, as well as SSRIs such as sertraline or fluoxetine and tricyclics such as amitriptyline, which enhance serotonergic and/or noradrenergic neurotransmission and reduce episode frequency.

Name: Microscopic Polyarteritis
Description: Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing, pauci-immune small-vessel vasculitis in the ANCA-associated vasculitis spectrum, classically affecting capillaries, venules, arterioles, and small arteries and most often presenting as a renal-pulmonary syndrome. It is usually sporadic rather than Mendelian, but genetic susceptibility is linked to immune-regulatory loci including HLA-DQ, HLA-DP, PTPN22, SERPINA1, CTLA4, and genes influencing autoantigen expression such as MPO and PRTN3; MPO encodes myeloperoxidase, the dominant target antigen in MPA, and rare alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency variants may amplify neutrophil protease injury. Pathogenesis centers on loss of tolerance to MPO-ANCA, neutrophil priming by TNF-α, IL-1, and C5a, ANCA-mediated Fc receptor engagement, NET formation, endothelial adhesion, and alternative complement pathway activation, especially the C5a-C5aR axis, with downstream oxidative burst and fibrinoid necrosis. Typical manifestations include constitutional symptoms, palpable purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, arthralgia, myalgia, rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis with hematuria and proteinuria, and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage causing hemoptysis and dyspnea; gastrointestinal, ocular, and cutaneous involvement also occur. Major complications include chronic kidney disease, end-stage kidney failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, infection, venous thromboembolism, and treatment toxicity; comorbid interstitial lung disease, especially MPO-ANCA-associated fibrosis, is increasingly recognized. Subtypes are commonly defined clinically as renal-limited MPA, pulmonary-renal disease, or systemic MPA. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical features, elevated MPO-ANCA/p-ANCA by immunoassay with immunofluorescence support, urinalysis, inflammatory markers, chest imaging, and confirmatory tissue biopsy showing pauci-immune necrotizing vasculitis or crescentic glomerulonephritis, while excluding granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, anti-GBM disease, and infection. Name: Relapse multiple myeloma
Description: Relapse multiple myeloma (UMLS C2349261) is the return or progression of a clonal plasma-cell malignancy after prior response, biologically marked by re-expansion of genetically heterogeneous myeloma subclones and clinically by renewed marrow and end-organ injury. Recurrent genomic lesions include immunoglobulin heavy-chain translocations such as t(11;14)(CCND1), t(4;14)(FGFR3/MMSET), and t(14;16)(MAF), hyperdiploidy, 1q gain/amplification, del(17p) with TP53 loss, and mutations in KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, FAM46C, DIS3, and cereblon-pathway genes that can influence drug sensitivity. Central signaling networks include IL-6/JAK/STAT3, NF-kB, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, unfolded-protein response/proteasome dependence, cyclin D dysregulation, and bone-marrow microenvironment interactions involving CXCR4, VLA-4, RANKL, osteoclast activation, and angiogenic mediators such as VEGF. Patients typically present with recurrent CRAB manifestations and related findings: bone pain, lytic lesions or fractures, anemia, fatigue, renal insufficiency, hypercalcemia, recurrent infections, neuropathy, and rising monoclonal protein or free light chains; complications include spinal cord compression, amyloidosis, hyperviscosity, venous thromboembolism, and treatment-related cytopenias. Major clinical forms include biochemical versus clinical relapse, oligosecretory/nonsecretory relapse, extramedullary disease, and high-risk relapsed/refractory myeloma. Therapy commonly uses proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib or carfilzomib, which block the 26S proteasome and trigger plasma-cell apoptosis; immunomodulatory drugs such as lenalidomide or pomalidomide, which bind cereblon to induce IKZF1/3 degradation and enhance immune cytotoxicity; dexamethasone; anti-CD38 antibodies such as daratumumab; and selected targeted agents including venetoclax for t(11;14) disease. Name: Pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus
Description: Pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus is an acute bacterial lower respiratory tract infection, often severe and either community acquired, post-influenza necrotizing, ventilator-associated, or hospital acquired, characterized by alveolar infection, intense neutrophilic inflammation, and in some cases abscess formation or empyema. Major microbial determinants include mecA or mecC encoding the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), blaZ beta-lactamase, and virulence factors such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin genes lukS-PV/lukF-PV, alpha-toxin hla, protein A spa, agr quorum-sensing regulators, and adhesins including fnbA/fnbB; host susceptibility is not classically Mendelian, but risk is increased by immunodeficiency or variants affecting innate immunity, with representative examples in TLR2, MYD88, IRAK4, NCF1/NCF2 in chronic granulomatous disease, and STAT3 in hyper-IgE syndrome. Key pathogenic pathways include TLR2-NF-kB signaling, inflammasome activation with IL-1 and IL-18 release, neutrophil recruitment via IL-8/CXCL8, complement activation, epithelial injury from alpha-toxin pore formation, and agr-mediated toxin regulation. Typical symptoms and signs are high fever, productive cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxemia, tachypnea, and multilobar or cavitary infiltrates, sometimes with hemoptysis and rapid septic deterioration. Frequent comorbidities include influenza, COPD, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, alcoholism, cystic fibrosis, mechanical ventilation, and injection drug use; complications include bacteremia, sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, empyema, and metastatic infection such as endocarditis. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical and radiographic findings plus microbiologic confirmation by sputum, tracheal aspirate, bronchoalveolar lavage, or blood culture, Gram stain showing gram-positive cocci in clusters, susceptibility testing, and rapid molecular detection of S. aureus and mecA. Name: tinea barbae
Description: Tinea barbae (UMLS C2349994) is a contagious dermatophyte infection of the beard and moustache region, usually an inflammatory ectothrix folliculitis caused by zoophilic fungi such as Trichophyton verrucosum and T. mentagrophytes, with less frequent involvement of Microsporum canis or anthropophilic Trichophyton rubrum; it is an acquired infectious disorder rather than a classic inherited disease, and no specific Mendelian susceptibility gene is established, although host-defense variation affecting epidermal barrier and antifungal immunity, including pathways involving CARD9, Dectin-1/CLEC7A, IL-17, Toll-like receptors, keratinocyte cytokines, neutrophils, macrophages, and Th17 signaling, may influence severity or chronicity. The disease reflects fungal adherence to keratinized hair shafts and follicles, secretion of keratinases and other proteases, and activation of innate and cell-mediated inflammatory pathways. Clinically, patients develop erythematous follicular papules, pustules, nodules, crusting, scaling, broken hairs, painful boggy kerion-like plaques, regional lymphadenopathy, and sometimes patchy alopecia; less inflammatory superficial variants also occur. Major subtypes are inflammatory deep folliculitis/kerion and more superficial non-kerion tinea of beard hair. Important comorbidities or risk settings include diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, topical corticosteroid use causing tinea incognito, occupational animal exposure, and secondary bacterial infection, with complications such as scarring alopecia or abscess formation. Diagnosis is based on characteristic beard-area folliculitis plus direct microscopy of plucked hairs or skin scrapings with potassium hydroxide, fungal culture, and increasingly PCR-based dermatophyte testing; biopsy shows perifollicular inflammation and fungal elements when needed. Treatment generally requires systemic antifungals, most commonly terbinafine, which inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, itraconazole, which inhibits lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis, and griseofulvin, which disrupts fungal microtubules and mitosis; fluconazole is an alternative azole, and adjunctive topical antifungals and antibacterial measures may be used.

Name: Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension
Description: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH; UMLS C2363973) is a rare, potentially curable form of precapillary pulmonary hypertension caused by incomplete resolution and fibrotic organization of pulmonary thromboemboli, leading to chronic mechanical obstruction of proximal elastic pulmonary arteries together with secondary small-vessel arteriopathy. It is usually sporadic rather than classically inherited, but genetic susceptibility overlaps with venous thromboembolism and pulmonary arterial hypertension, with reported associations involving BMPR2, ACVRL1, ENG, SMAD9, CAV1, KCNK3, and thrombophilia-related variants such as F5 Leiden, F2 prothrombin G20210A, SERPINC1, PROC, PROS1, and non-O blood group; dysregulated proteins may include endothelin-1, nitric oxide synthase, prostacyclin synthase, von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, and inflammatory mediators. Key pathways include coagulation and fibrinolysis, endothelial dysfunction, endothelin, nitric oxide–soluble guanylate cyclase–cGMP, prostacyclin–cAMP, BMP/TGF-β signaling, platelet activation, and vascular remodeling involving smooth-muscle proliferation and inflammation. Typical manifestations are progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, exercise intolerance, chest discomfort, syncope, palpitations, and signs of right-heart strain or failure such as loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation, edema, hepatomegaly, and jugular venous distention. Important comorbidities and risk factors include prior acute pulmonary embolism or deep venous thrombosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, splenectomy, infected shunts or pacemaker leads, chronic inflammatory disease, malignancy, thyroid disease, elevated factor VIII, chronic thrombotic disorders, and complications such as right ventricular failure, hemoptysis, arrhythmias, and death. Disease patterns include operable proximal CTEPH, inoperable distal/microvascular CTEPH, and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease without resting pulmonary hypertension. Diagnosis requires at least 3 months of effective anticoagulation plus mismatched perfusion defects on V/Q scanning and confirmation by right-heart catheterization and imaging, typically mean pulmonary artery pressure greater than 20 mmHg, pulmonary arterial wedge pressure 15 mmHg or less, elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, and

Name: Rhinitis, Allergic
Description: Allergic rhinitis is a common, predominantly IgE-mediated inflammatory disease of the nasal mucosa triggered by aeroallergens such as pollens, dust mites, animal dander, and molds, and is classically classified as seasonal, perennial, or occupational, and by ARIA criteria as intermittent or persistent, mild or moderate-severe. It presents with paroxysmal sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, nasal pruritus, congestion, postnasal drip, and often conjunctival itching/tearing, with pale edematous turbinates on examination; complications include sleep disturbance, impaired quality of life, sinusitis, otitis media with effusion, and exacerbation of asthma. Pathobiology centers on allergen presentation to Th2 cells with IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 signaling, class switching to IgE, FcεRI-mediated mast-cell and basophil activation, eosinophilic recruitment, and epithelial alarmins such as TSLP, IL-25, and IL-33, with chemokines including CCL11 and leukotriene and histamine pathways contributing to early- and late-phase responses. Genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian, with heritable atopy risk and representative associations in IL4, IL13, IL4RA, FCER1A, TSLP, HLA class II loci, ORMDL3/GSDMB, ADAM33, FLG, and filaggrin-barrier variants, although no single mutation is diagnostic. Diagnosis is based on compatible symptom patterns temporally linked to exposures, physical findings, and demonstration of sensitization by skin-prick testing or serum allergen-specific IgE; adjunctive tests may include nasal eosinophils, total IgE, endoscopy, or sinus imaging when alternative diagnoses are suspected. Standard therapy includes intranasal corticosteroids such as fluticasone, which suppress cytokine transcription and eosinophilic inflammation; second-generation H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine or loratadine, which block histamine H1 receptors; and leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast, which inhibit cysteinyl leukotriene signaling; additional options include intranasal azelastine, ipratropium for rhinorrhea, and allergen immunotherapy to induce immune tolerance.

Name: Influenza caused by Influenza A virus
Description: Influenza caused by Influenza A virus (UMLS C2711180) is an acute, contagious orthomyxoviral respiratory disease characterized by infection of airway epithelial cells by enveloped, negative-sense segmented RNA viruses classified by hemagglutinin and neuraminidase subtypes, most commonly seasonal H1N1 and H3N2, with avian or zoonotic forms such as H5N1 and H7N9 causing more severe disease. Viral pathogenicity is shaped by proteins and mutations including hemagglutinin, neuraminidase, matrix protein M2, nucleoprotein, NS1, and polymerase subunits PB1, PB2, and PA; representative adaptive or resistance-associated changes include PB2 E627K, HA receptor-binding alterations, M2 S31N conferring adamantane resistance, and NA H275Y reducing oseltamivir susceptibility. Host response involves sialic acid receptor-mediated entry, endosomal acidification, RIG-I/MAVS and TLR7 sensing, interferon/JAK-STAT signaling, NF-kB activation, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, and cytokine and chemokine networks that can drive lung injury. Illness typically presents after a short incubation with abrupt fever, chills, myalgias, headache, malaise, nonproductive cough, sore throat, and rhinorrhea, and may progress to viral pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, myocarditis, encephalopathy, myositis, or exacerbations of asthma, COPD, heart failure, and diabetes; pregnancy, advanced age, immunosuppression, obesity, and chronic cardiopulmonary disease increase risk. Treatment commonly includes oseltamivir and zanamivir, neuraminidase inhibitors that block virion release, peramivir, an intravenous neuraminidase inhibitor, and baloxavir marboxil, a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor targeting PA; amantadine and rimantadine inhibit M2 but are now rarely useful because of resistance. The disease is not inherited in a Mendelian manner, but host genetic susceptibility has been linked to variants in IFITM3, TLR3, IRF7, GATA2, TMPRSS2, and related innate immune genes. Diagnosis relies on compatible influenza-like illness plus laboratory confirmation by RT-PCR or other nucleic acid amplification testing, with rapid antigen tests, viral culture

Name: Ischemic priapism
Description: Ischemic priapism (UMLS C2711256) is the common, painful low-flow subtype of priapism and represents a compartment syndrome of the corpora cavernosa caused by impaired venous outflow and progressive corporal hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis; clinically it presents with a rigid tender penile shaft, typically with a softer glans, erection persisting longer than 4 hours, and increasing risk of fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction as duration lengthens. Important molecular associations include dysregulation of nitric oxide–cGMP–phosphodiesterase type 5 signaling, adenosine excess, RhoA/Rho-kinase smooth-muscle contractile pathways, and endothelial dysfunction; representative genetic contributors are HBB mutations in sickle cell disease, the major inherited risk factor, as well as variants affecting G6PD, PDE5A, NOS3, adenosine signaling, or coagulation/thrombophilia pathways in selected cases. It may be idiopathic, recurrent/stuttering, or secondary to hematologic disease, trauma, malignancy, spinal cord injury, or drugs such as trazodone, antipsychotics, cocaine, and intracavernosal vasoactive agents. Key comorbidities include sickle cell disease, other hemoglobinopathies, leukemia, thalassemia, hypercoagulable states, and substance use; complications include corporal necrosis, infection, penile deformity, and severe erectile dysfunction. Diagnosis is based on history and examination, corporal blood gas showing dark hypoxic acidotic blood, penile Doppler ultrasonography demonstrating minimal or absent cavernosal arterial inflow, and selective laboratory testing for CBC, reticulocyte count, hemoglobin electrophoresis, toxicology, and coagulation or malignancy evaluation when indicated. Standard treatment is urgent corporal aspiration and irrigation plus intracavernosal phenylephrine, an alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that contracts cavernosal smooth muscle; adjuncts or alternatives include pseudoephedrine, another sympathomimetic alpha-agonist, terbutaline, a beta-2 agonist historically used to promote detumescence, and in recurrent disease preventive hydroxyurea in sickle cell disease or PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil/paradoxical tadalafil to normalize aberrant NO-cGMP signaling.

Name: Epilepsy characterized by intractable complex partial seizures
Description: Epilepsy characterized by intractable complex partial seizures is a focal epilepsy syndrome, often centered in the temporal or frontal lobe, in which impaired-awareness seizures persist despite appropriate trials of antiseizure medications; it may be structural, genetic, metabolic, infectious, immune, or cryptogenic in origin. Patients typically have recurrent stereotyped episodes with aura, behavioral arrest, staring, oral or manual automatisms, altered consciousness, postictal confusion, and sometimes secondary generalization, with chronic complications including injury, status epilepticus, sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, cognitive decline, depression, anxiety, and psychosocial disability; common comorbidities also include hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, traumatic brain injury, stroke, brain tumors, and neurodevelopmental disorders. Genetic contributors are heterogeneous and include ion-channel and synaptic genes such as SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, DEPDC5, LGI1, GRIN2A, GABRA1, GABRG2, RELN, and mTOR-pathway genes including TSC1, TSC2, and MTOR, with pathogenic variants causing autosomal dominant, de novo, or less often recessive forms; mechanisms converge on impaired GABAergic inhibition, excess glutamatergic transmission, altered sodium, potassium, and calcium channel excitability, synaptic vesicle dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. Major subtypes include mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, lesional focal epilepsy, familial focal epilepsies, and focal cortical dysplasia-associated epilepsy. Diagnosis rests on clinical history plus EEG or prolonged video-EEG showing focal epileptiform discharges or ictal onset, brain MRI with epilepsy protocol to detect hippocampal sclerosis or other lesions, and selected PET, SPECT, MEG, neuropsychological testing, autoimmune studies, and genetic testing. Common treatments include carbamazepine and lamotrigine, which inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels, levetiracetam, which binds SV2A to reduce neurotransmitter release, lacosamide, which enhances slow sodium-channel inactivation, and adjunctive options such as valproate or topiramate; drug-resistant cases may require surgery, vagus nerve stimulation, responsive neurostimulation, or dietary therapy.

Name: Breakthrough cancer pain
Description: Breakthrough cancer pain (UMLS C2721580) is a transient, severe flare of pain occurring despite otherwise stable, adequately controlled background cancer pain, most often in patients with advanced malignancy, and it is typically classified as incident pain triggered by movement or procedures, spontaneous or idiopathic pain, and end-of-dose failure when baseline analgesia wanes. Its biology reflects the underlying tumor and tissue injury rather than a single inherited disorder, with nociceptive and neuropathic mechanisms involving inflammatory mediators and signaling through prostaglandin-COX pathways, cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, nerve growth factor-TrkA, glutamatergic NMDA receptor activation, voltage-gated sodium channels, TRPV1, and central sensitization; when directly driven by tumor, representative molecular correlates may include bone-metastatic or invasive cancers with alterations such as TP53, KRAS, EGFR, PIK3CA, or HER2 depending on the primary site, but no specific germline inheritance pattern is defined for breakthrough pain itself, although pharmacogenetic contributors such as CYP2D6, CYP3A4/5, OPRM1, COMT, and ABCB1 can influence opioid response. Clinically, episodes are rapid in onset, intense, short in duration, and may present as stabbing, aching, burning, or cramping pain with functional limitation, distress, tachycardia, and sleep disruption. Common comorbidities and complications include bone metastases, mucositis, neuropathy, depression, anxiety, cachexia, opioid tolerance, constipation, sedation, falls, and reduced quality of life. Diagnosis is clinical, based on documentation of controlled baseline pain with transient exacerbations, pain diaries, numerical rating scales, and assessment of temporal pattern, triggers, and opioid timing, supplemented by imaging or neurologic evaluation to define the cause. Treatment commonly uses rapid-onset opioids such as transmucosal fentanyl, a μ-opioid receptor agonist, immediate-release morphine, another μ-opioid agonist, and oxycodone, a μ-opioid agonist with some κ activity, with adjuvant NSAIDs that inhibit COX enzymes and gabapentinoids that reduce α2δ-mediated calcium-channel neurotransmission in selected patients.

Name: Pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection
Description: Pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection is a chronic nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease, usually caused by Mycobacterium avium or M. intracellulare, that occurs in structurally abnormal lungs or in hosts with impaired antimycobacterial immunity. Genetic susceptibility is classically linked to defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ axis and related macrophage activation pathways, including IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, STAT1, IRF8, ISG15, NEMO/IKBKG, GATA2, and sometimes CFTR variants, while proteins such as TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-12, and macrophage Toll-like receptor signaling are central to granuloma formation and intracellular mycobacterial control. Disease phenotypes include fibrocavitary disease, often in older male smokers with COPD, and nodular bronchiectatic disease, often involving the right middle lobe and lingula; Lady Windermere syndrome is a recognized clinical pattern. Common symptoms are chronic cough, sputum production, fatigue, weight loss, dyspnea, low-grade fever, hemoptysis, and malaise. Major comorbidities include bronchiectasis, COPD, prior tuberculosis, cystic fibrosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, thoracic skeletal abnormalities, rheumatoid arthritis, and immunosuppression from corticosteroids, anti-TNF biologics, transplantation, or HIV; complications include progressive cavitation, respiratory failure, recurrent infections, and disseminated MAC in severe immune defects. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical and radiographic findings plus microbiologic confirmation, typically at least two positive sputum cultures, one positive bronchial wash/lavage, or histopathologic granulomatous inflammation or acid-fast bacilli with a positive culture; chest CT usually shows bronchiectasis, nodules, tree-in-bud opacities, or cavities, and species identification is made by culture and molecular assays. Standard therapy is multidrug, centered on a macrolide such as azithromycin or clarithromycin, which inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit, ethambutol, which impairs arabinosyl transferases and cell-wall arabinogalactan synthesis, and rifampin or rifabutin, which inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; amikacin, a 30S inhibitor,

Name: Sepsis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (disorder)
Description: Sepsis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae is an acute, life-threatening invasive pneumococcal disease in which bloodstream infection triggers a dysregulated host inflammatory and coagulation response leading to organ dysfunction, septic shock, and death if untreated. Major bacterial virulence determinants include the capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis locus, pneumolysin encoded by ply, autolysin lytA, surface adhesins such as pspA and pspC/cbpA, and neuraminidases, while host susceptibility is influenced by variants affecting innate and humoral immunity, including TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, IRAK4, NFKBIA, complement components and regulators such as C3, CFH and MBL2, FCGR2A, and asplenia or antibody deficiency states; inheritance is not Mendelian for most cases but reflects complex polygenic risk, although rare primary immunodeficiencies can be autosomal recessive or dominant. Pathobiology centers on pattern-recognition signaling through TLR2/TLR4, NOD and inflammasome pathways, NF-κB, TNF, IL-1, IL-6, complement activation, endothelial injury, platelet activation, and tissue-factor-driven coagulation. Typical findings include fever or hypothermia, chills, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, and signs of a pulmonary focus such as cough, pleuritic pain, dyspnea, and lobar pneumonia; subtypes include uncomplicated bacteremic sepsis, severe sepsis with organ dysfunction, septic shock, and focal invasive disease with meningitis or empyema. Common comorbidities and complications include chronic lung disease, influenza coinfection, diabetes, alcoholism, cirrhosis, renal disease, HIV, malignancy, splenectomy, acute respiratory distress syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, myocardial dysfunction, meningitis, and multiorgan failure. Diagnosis relies on sepsis criteria with confirmed or suspected pneumococcal infection using blood cultures, cultures from sterile sites, Gram stain, urinary pneumococcal antigen testing, PCR-based detection including lytA targets, susceptibility testing, inflammatory markers, imaging, and organ dysfunction assessment. Treatment commonly includes ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, which inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins

Name: Sepsis caused by Staphylococcus aureus
Description: Sepsis caused by Staphylococcus aureus (UMLS C2887088) is an acute, life-threatening dysregulated host response to invasive S. aureus bloodstream or deep-tissue infection, ranging from methicillin-susceptible to methicillin-resistant disease and often progressing to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction. Bacterial virulence determinants commonly implicated include mecA or mecC encoding the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a in MRSA, accessory gene regulator agr, staphylococcal protein A spa, alpha-toxin hla, Panton-Valentine leukocidin genes lukS/lukF, coagulase, and biofilm-associated genes such as ica; host susceptibility and severity are influenced by variants in innate immune and inflammatory genes including TLR2, TLR4, NOD2, TNF, IL6, IL1B, and coagulation-related pathways, although the disorder itself is not inherited in a Mendelian pattern. Core signaling involves TLR2/TLR6 recognition of peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid, activation of MyD88, NF-kB and MAPK cascades, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, complement, neutrophil and endothelial activation, cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6, and downstream coagulation and microvascular injury. Typical features include fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, and organ dysfunction; common foci include skin and soft tissue infection, pneumonia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and catheter-related bacteremia. Major comorbidities and complications include diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, malignancy, immunosuppression, prosthetic devices, infective endocarditis, disseminated abscesses, ARDS, DIC, acute kidney injury, and death. Diagnosis rests on suspected or confirmed infection plus organ dysfunction, supported by blood cultures, culture or PCR from source sites, susceptibility testing for MSSA versus MRSA, inflammatory markers, lactate, and imaging for metastatic infection. Treatment typically includes vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala and inhibits cell-wall synthesis; daptomycin, which depolarizes the bacterial membrane; and linezolid, which blocks 50S initiation of protein synthesis,

Name: Severe sepsis with acute organ dysfunction caused by Haemophilus influenzae
Description: Severe sepsis with acute organ dysfunction caused by Haemophilus influenzae is a fulminant invasive bacterial infection, usually due to encapsulated type b or nontypeable strains, in which bloodstream or deep-site infection triggers a dysregulated host response leading to hypotension, tissue hypoperfusion, and failure of organs such as the lungs, kidneys, liver, or brain. Key molecular drivers include bacterial lipooligosaccharide and, in type b disease, the polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule, which activate TLR4-, MyD88-, NF-κB-, TNF-, IL-1-, IL-6-, complement-, neutrophil-, endothelial-, and coagulation pathways, promoting capillary leak, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and septic shock. Host susceptibility is influenced by genetic variation in innate immunity and splenic function, with representative associations involving TLR4, CD14, NFKB1, MBL2, CFH, C2/C3, IRAK4, MYD88, and BTK defects, as well as sickle cell disease or anatomic/functional asplenia; these are generally complex or primary immunodeficiency traits rather than a Mendelian inheritance pattern for sepsis itself. Clinical features typically include high fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, oliguria, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, and focal syndromes such as pneumonia, meningitis, epiglottitis, cellulitis, or septic arthritis. Important complications and comorbidities include ARDS, acute kidney injury, DIC, adrenal dysfunction, meningitis-related neurologic sequelae, chronic lung disease, immunodeficiency, extremes of age, alcoholism, and COPD. Diagnosis rests on sepsis criteria with acute organ dysfunction, microbiologic confirmation by blood, CSF, or respiratory culture and PCR, Gram stain, inflammatory markers, organ function testing, coagulation studies, and imaging to define source. Treatment commonly includes ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, third-generation cephalosporins that inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins, or ampicillin-sulbactam, which combines a beta-lactam with beta-lactamase inhibition; meropenem is used for severe resistant infection by the same cell-wall mechanism, and dexamethasone may be added in Hib meningitis

Name: Sepsis caused by Pseudomonas
Description: Sepsis caused by Pseudomonas, usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa, is an acute life-threatening dysregulated host response to invasive Gram-negative infection that most often arises in hospitalized, immunocompromised, neutropenic, burn, ventilated, catheterized, cystic fibrosis, diabetic, or chronically lung-diseased patients and may present as primary bacteremia, pneumonia-associated sepsis, urinary-source sepsis, wound sepsis, or ecthyma gangrenosum–associated disease. Its pathobiology is driven by bacterial virulence determinants including lipopolysaccharide, flagellin, alginate, elastase LasB, exotoxin A, phospholipase C, pyocyanin, and type III secretion effectors ExoS, ExoT, ExoU, and ExoY, with resistance-associated genes or mutations such as ampC derepression, oprD loss, and mexAB-oprM efflux upregulation; host susceptibility is influenced by variants affecting TLR4, TLR5, CD14, NOD2, CFTR, mannose-binding lectin, and cytokine genes. Major pathways include TLR4/CD14/MD2 recognition of LPS, TLR5 sensing of flagellin, NF-kB and MAPK activation, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, complement and coagulation cascades, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, interferon, and neutrophil extracellular trap responses, culminating in endothelial injury, capillary leak, mitochondrial dysfunction, and shock. Typical findings are fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, organ dysfunction, and sometimes necrotic skin lesions. Diagnosis relies on Sepsis-3 criteria with suspected infection plus organ dysfunction, blood and source cultures with antimicrobial susceptibility testing, rapid molecular resistance assays when available, inflammatory markers, arterial blood gas and lactate, and imaging to define the source. Treatment centers on prompt source control and antipseudomonal drugs such as piperacillin-tazobactam, a cell-wall active ureidopenicillin plus beta-lactamase inhibitor, cefepime or ceftazidime, cephalosporins that inhibit penicillin-binding proteins, meropenem, a carbapenem blocking peptidoglycan

Name: Severe sepsis with acute organ dysfunction caused by Serratia
Description: Severe sepsis with acute organ dysfunction caused by Serratia, most often Serratia marcescens, is a life-threatening Gram-negative bacterial infection in which invasive Serratia triggers a dysregulated host response leading to hypotension, microvascular injury, and dysfunction of organs such as the lungs, kidneys, liver, brain, and coagulation system. Pathobiology is dominated by lipopolysaccharide activation of TLR4-CD14-MD2, NF-κB, MAPK, NLRP3 inflammasome, complement, endothelial adhesion molecules, and tissue-factor/coagulation pathways, with cytokines including TNF, IL1B, IL6, IL8, and anti-inflammatory IL10 contributing to shock and immune paralysis; host susceptibility and outcome have been associated with variants in TLR4, CD14, NOD2, TNF, IL6, FER, and SERPINE1/PAI-1, but the disorder is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion. Serratia virulence factors include LPS, hemolysin ShlA, phospholipase, siderophores, fimbriae, and biofilm formation, and resistance determinants may include chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase and acquired ESBL or carbapenemase genes such as blaKPC or blaNDM. Typical features include fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated lactate, oliguria, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, acute kidney injury, ARDS, and septic shock. Important subtypes include catheter-related bloodstream infection, hospital-acquired pneumonia, urinary tract source, intra-abdominal sepsis, and neonatal or immunocompromised host sepsis. Common comorbidities are malignancy, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, neutropenia, mechanical ventilation, indwelling catheters, burns, and recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure; complications include DIC, multiorgan failure, and death. Diagnosis relies on Sepsis-3 criteria with documented or strongly suspected Serratia infection, blood or site cultures with species identification and susceptibility testing, CBC, metabolic panel, lactate, CRP/procalcitonin, coagulation studies, urinalysis, imaging for source control, and sometimes PCR or MALDI-TOF. Treatment is urgent source control plus active antibiotics such as cefepime, a fourth-generation

Name: Post traumatic osteoarthritis
Description: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis (UMLS C2894027) is a secondary, mechanically initiated but biologically mediated degenerative joint disease that develops after intra-articular fracture, ligament or meniscal injury, cartilage impact, or chronic post-injury instability, most often affecting the knee, ankle, hip, or shoulder and presenting with activity-related pain, stiffness, swelling, crepitus, reduced range of motion, intermittent effusions, malalignment, and progressive functional limitation. Its pathobiology involves chondrocyte injury and synovial activation with upregulation of inflammatory and catabolic pathways, notably IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, NF-kappaB, MAPK, TGF-beta, Wnt/beta-catenin, COX-2/PGE2, reactive oxygen species signaling, and matrix-remodeling enzymes such as MMP-13 and ADAMTS-4/5, with extracellular matrix proteins including type II collagen encoded by COL2A1 and aggrecan encoded by ACAN being major targets; genetic susceptibility is complex and usually non-Mendelian, but representative associations include variants in GDF5, SMAD3, FRZB, ASPN, DOT1L, and inflammatory mediators, while rare cartilage disorders due to COL2A1 or COMP mutations may predispose to earlier osteoarthritis phenotypes. Common subtypes are defined by inciting injury, such as post-fracture, post-meniscectomy, post-ligamentous, and chronic instability-associated disease. Diagnosis rests on a history of antecedent joint trauma plus clinical findings and imaging evidence of joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, cysts, cartilage loss, bone marrow lesions, or malalignment on radiography, MRI, or CT, with arthroscopy used selectively and synovial fluid analysis mainly to exclude crystal or septic arthritis. Treatment is symptomatic and function-directed, commonly using acetaminophen for central analgesia, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen via COX inhibition to reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain and inflammation, and intra-articular corticosteroids such as triamcinolone through glucocorticoid receptor-mediated suppression of cytokine signaling; hyaluronic acid viscosupplementation is also used in some patients. Frequent comorbidities and complications include obesity, metabolic syndrome, osteoporosis risk after immobilization, chronic synovitis, recurrent effusions, gait impairment, muscle weakness,

Name: Cystinosis, Nephropathic
Description: Cystinosis is a rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused predominantly by biallelic pathogenic variants in CTNS on chromosome 17p13, which encodes the lysosomal cystine/proton symporter cystinosin; representative mutations include the common 57-kb deletion, nonsense, missense, and splice-site variants that reduce or abolish cystine export from lysosomes, leading to intralysosomal cystine crystal accumulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis, and disturbed lysosomal-autophagy, mTOR-TFEB, and proximal tubular endocytic pathways involving megalin/cubilin. The major clinical subtypes are infantile nephropathic cystinosis, juvenile/intermediate cystinosis, and adult ocular non-nephropathic cystinosis. Infantile disease typically presents in the first year with renal Fanconi syndrome, failure to thrive, polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, vomiting, rickets, metabolic acidosis, hypophosphatemia, and growth retardation, followed by corneal photophobia from crystal deposition and progression to chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease; later complications and comorbidities include hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism/infertility, myopathy, dysphagia, hepatosplenomegaly, pulmonary and neurologic involvement, osteopenia, and retinal damage. Diagnosis relies on elevated leukocyte cystine levels, slit-lamp demonstration of corneal crystals, and confirmatory molecular testing of CTNS, with supportive findings from renal tubular studies, prenatal testing, or family screening when indicated. Treatment centers on cysteamine bitartrate orally, which enters lysosomes and converts cystine to cysteine and a cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide that can exit via alternative transporters, and topical cysteamine eye drops for corneal crystals; adjunctive therapy commonly includes potassium citrate or bicarbonate to correct acidosis, phosphate and active vitamin D such as calcitriol for hypophosphatemic rickets, indomethacin to reduce polyuria in selected patients, hormone replacement such as levothyroxine, and ultimately renal transplantation for kidney failure.

Name: Thomsen Generalized Myotonia
Description: Thomsen generalized myotonia (UMLS C2936781) is the autosomal dominant form of nondystrophic myotonia, classically caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in CLCN1 encoding the skeletal muscle chloride channel ClC-1; representative missense mutations such as p.Gly230Glu, p.Phe307Ser, and p.Ile556Asn reduce sarcolemmal chloride conductance and impair membrane repolarization, producing muscle fiber hyperexcitability. The core pathophysiology centers on altered ClC-1 channel gating in the sarcolemma/T-tubule system, with secondary involvement of voltage-gated sodium channels, especially NaV1.4 encoded by SCN4A, in repetitive action potential firing, although SCN4A mutations more typically define sodium-channel myotonias rather than classic Thomsen disease. Clinically, patients present from infancy or childhood with generalized stiffness, delayed relaxation after voluntary contraction, percussion myotonia, transient weakness, muscle hypertrophy, and a warm-up phenomenon, usually without progressive muscle degeneration. Subtypes are primarily distinguished as dominant Thomsen disease versus recessive Becker myotonia, the latter generally more severe and more often associated with transient weakness. Comorbidities and complications include painful cramps, falls, exercise limitation, laryngospasm or dysphagia in some patients, anesthetic sensitivity, and occasional psychosocial burden from chronic symptoms. Diagnosis is based on characteristic history and examination, electromyography showing diffuse myotonic discharges, normal or mildly elevated creatine kinase, exclusion of myotonic dystrophy and paramyotonia congenita, and confirmatory molecular testing of CLCN1, sometimes with broader channelopathy panels; family history strongly supports dominant inheritance. Treatment is symptomatic and often uses mexiletine, a use-dependent sodium-channel blocker that reduces repetitive firing, with alternatives including lamotrigine, which inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels, acetazolamide, which alters membrane excitability partly through carbonic anhydrase inhibition, and sometimes carbamazepine or flecainide in selected refractory cases.

Name: UC - Ulcerative colitis confined to rectum
Description: Ulcerative colitis confined to the rectum, or ulcerative proctitis, is a localized subtype of ulcerative colitis characterized by chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated inflammation limited to the rectal mucosa, producing continuous superficial ulceration rather than transmural disease. Patients typically present with rectal bleeding, urgency, tenesmus, mucus discharge, frequent small-volume stools, and mild diarrhea, while systemic symptoms are often limited unless disease extends proximally. Its pathobiology reflects polygenic susceptibility and dysregulated epithelial-immune signaling rather than Mendelian inheritance; representative genetic associations include HLA class II alleles, ECM1, IL23R, JAK2, CARD9, and loci affecting epithelial barrier and innate immunity, with altered expression of TNF, IL-13, IL-17, IL-23, NF-kB, JAK-STAT, T-cell receptor, and integrin-mediated leukocyte trafficking pathways, alongside epithelial junctional defects and microbiome perturbation. Diagnosis rests on clinical features, exclusion of infection, elevated inflammatory markers such as fecal calprotectin in many cases, and endoscopy showing continuous inflammation confined to the rectum with erythema, friability, granularity, erosions, and biopsy evidence of chronic active colitis with crypt distortion, cryptitis, and crypt abscesses. Standard therapy includes topical or oral 5-aminosalicylates such as mesalamine, which inhibit cyclooxygenase/lipoxygenase pathways and reduce mucosal prostaglandin- and leukotriene-driven inflammation; corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone or budesonide, which suppress NF-kB-dependent cytokine transcription; and, for refractory disease, biologics or small molecules including infliximab or adalimumab targeting TNF-alpha, vedolizumab blocking alpha4beta7-mediated gut lymphocyte trafficking, and tofacitinib inhibiting JAK signaling. Important complications and comorbidities include anemia, extension to left-sided or extensive colitis, severe bleeding, corticosteroid dependence, colorectal neoplasia risk with longstanding broader disease, primary sclerosing cholangitis, venous thromboembolism, and extraintestinal manifestations such as arthritis, uveitis, episcleritis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum.

UMLS C2960008 corresponds to Cornelia de Lange syndrome, a multisystem developmental disorder and cohesinopathy characterized by prenatal-onset growth restriction, distinctive craniofacial dysmorphism, limb anomalies, neurodevelopmental impairment, and variable visceral malformations. The disorder is most often caused by pathogenic variants in NIPBL, with additional cases due to SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21, BRD4, and HDAC8; these genes encode components or regulators of the cohesin complex, leading to disturbed sister chromatid cohesion, transcriptional regulation, chromatin organization, DNA damage responses, and altered developmental signaling including WNT, Notch, and Sonic hedgehog-related pathways. Most cases are de novo; inheritance is usually autosomal dominant for NIPBL, SMC3, RAD21, and BRD4, X-linked for SMC1A and HDAC8, and mosaicism can occur, contributing to variable expressivity. Clinical features include synophrys, long eyelashes, short upturned nose, thin upper lip, microcephaly, short stature, hirsutism, feeding difficulty, gastroesophageal reflux, intellectual disability, autism-spectrum behaviors, hearing loss, upper-limb reduction defects, and congenital heart, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, or diaphragmatic anomalies; phenotypes range from classic severe to milder atypical forms. Common comorbidities and complications include recurrent aspiration, failure to thrive, seizures, scoliosis, self-injurious behavior, constipation, and delayed puberty. There is no disease-specific curative pharmacotherapy; treatment is supportive and complication-directed, commonly including proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole or lansoprazole, which irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase for reflux; baclofen, a GABAB agonist that can reduce transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations and spasticity; and antiepileptics such as levetiracetam, which modulates synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, or valproate, which increases GABAergic tone. Diagnosis is based on consensus clinical scoring using cardinal and suggestive features, complemented by chromosomal microarray, targeted gene panels, exome sequencing, and mosaicism-aware testing; echocardiography, audiology, ophthalmologic assessment, and swallow or gastrointestinal studies help define associated complications.

Name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
Description: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH; WHO group 1) is a progressive vasculopathy of the small pulmonary arteries characterized by endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, smooth-muscle proliferation, inflammation, and in situ thrombosis, leading to elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, right ventricular failure, and premature death; major subtypes include idiopathic, heritable, drug- and toxin-induced, and PAH associated with connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease, portal hypertension, HIV infection, and schistosomiasis. Germline pathogenic variants most often involve BMPR2 with autosomal dominant inheritance and incomplete penetrance, while ACVRL1/ALK1, ENG, SMAD9, CAV1, KCNK3, SOX17, TBX4, and EIF2AK4 are also implicated; biallelic EIF2AK4 mutations cause pulmonary veno-occlusive disease/pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, typically autosomal recessive. Core dysregulated pathways include reduced BMPR2-TGF-beta-SMAD signaling, excess endothelin-1 activity, impaired nitric oxide-soluble guanylate cyclase-cGMP signaling, reduced prostacyclin synthesis with altered cAMP signaling, serotonin and Rho kinase activation, and metabolic and inflammatory remodeling. Symptoms usually include exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, palpitations, presyncope or syncope, and edema, with exam findings such as loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, and peripheral cyanosis in advanced disease. Common complications and comorbidities include right heart failure, arrhythmias, hemoptysis, thromboembolism, connective tissue disease, sleep-disordered breathing, and pregnancy-associated decompensation. Diagnosis requires right heart catheterization showing mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mmHg, pulmonary arterial wedge pressure 15 mmHg or less, and pulmonary vascular resistance greater than 2 Wood units, supported by echocardiography, ECG, chest imaging, pulmonary function testing, V/Q scanning to exclude chronic thromboembolic disease, serologies, and genetic testing in idiopathic, familial, or early-onset cases. Treatment commonly targets the endothelin, nitric oxide, and prostacyclin pathways with endothelin receptor antagonists such as bosentan, ambrisentan, and macitentan, phosphodiesterase-

Name: Refractory anemia
Description: Refractory anemia (UMLS C2981142) is classically a lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome characterized by persistent anemia due to ineffective clonal hematopoiesis, usually involving dysplastic erythropoiesis with a hypercellular marrow and, depending on classification, variable ring sideroblasts or multilineage dysplasia; older FAB categories included refractory anemia and refractory anemia with ring sideroblasts, whereas WHO frameworks place many cases within MDS with single-lineage dysplasia, multilineage dysplasia, or ring sideroblast–associated subtypes. Its molecular basis commonly includes somatic lesions in RNA-splicing and epigenetic regulators such as SF3B1, TET2, ASXL1, DNMT3A, SRSF2, U2AF1, and TP53, with SF3B1 particularly associated with ring sideroblasts, while disordered heme synthesis, mitochondrial iron handling, apoptosis, and inflammatory signaling involving TGF-β/SMAD, JAK-STAT, NF-κB, p53, and erythropoietin receptor pathways contribute to ineffective erythropoiesis. It is generally acquired rather than inherited, although germline predisposition can occur in syndromes involving DDX41, GATA2, RUNX1, or telomere biology genes. Patients typically present with fatigue, pallor, weakness, exertional dyspnea, tachycardia, and sometimes macrocytosis; neutropenia or thrombocytopenia may coexist, increasing infection or bleeding risk. Important complications include transfusion dependence, iron overload, cardiac and hepatic injury, recurrent infection, progression to higher-grade MDS or acute myeloid leukemia, and comorbid chronic kidney disease, inflammatory disorders, or nutritional deficiency states that complicate evaluation. Diagnosis requires persistent cytopenia, CBC and smear review, marrow aspirate/biopsy showing dysplasia, blast quantification, iron stain for ring sideroblasts, cytogenetics/FISH, and increasingly next-generation sequencing; secondary causes such as B12, folate, copper deficiency, hemolysis, bleeding, renal disease, and drugs must be excluded. Common treatments include erythropoiesis-stimulating agents such as epoetin alfa or darbepoetin alfa acting via erythropoietin receptor–JAK2 signaling, luspatercept which traps TGF-β superfamily ligands to enhance late erythroid

Name: Carcinoma of female breast
Description: Carcinoma of the female breast is a heterogeneous malignant epithelial neoplasm, usually arising from ductal or lobular units, whose major clinicopathologic subtypes include hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative disease, HER2-positive tumors, and triple-negative breast cancer, with histologies such as invasive ductal carcinoma, invasive lobular carcinoma, and in situ lesions including ductal carcinoma in situ. Its biology commonly involves alterations in ERBB2/HER2 amplification, PIK3CA, TP53, GATA3, MAP3K1, PTEN loss, ESR1 mutation in endocrine-resistant disease, and germline or somatic defects in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, and less often TP53, linked to dysregulation of estrogen receptor signaling, HER2/EGFR-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways, cell-cycle control through cyclin D-CDK4/6-RB, DNA repair by homologous recombination, and apoptosis. Typical presentation includes a palpable breast mass, mammographic abnormality, skin or nipple retraction, nipple discharge, peau d’orange, axillary adenopathy, or metastatic symptoms involving bone, liver, lung, or brain. Diagnosis rests on triple assessment with clinical examination, mammography and/or ultrasound, often breast MRI in selected patients, and core-needle biopsy with histopathology plus immunohistochemistry for ER, PR, and HER2, with ISH for equivocal HER2, and genomic assays or germline testing when hereditary risk is suspected; staging uses TNM and appropriate systemic imaging. Standard therapies include tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator; aromatase inhibitors such as letrozole, which suppress peripheral estrogen synthesis; trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting HER2; pertuzumab, which blocks HER2 dimerization; CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib; PARP inhibitors such as olaparib for BRCA-associated disease; and cytotoxics including anthracyclines and taxanes. Important comorbidities and complications include lymphedema, venous thromboembolism, treatment-related cardiomyopathy, osteoporosis, neuropathy, local recurrence, and distant metastasis; inheritance is usually multifactorial, but autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndromes are well established.

Name: Severe sepsis with acute organ dysfunction caused by Gram-negative bacteria
Description: Severe sepsis with acute organ dysfunction caused by Gram-negative bacteria (UMLS C3163829) is a fulminant, life-threatening infection syndrome in which lipopolysaccharide-bearing organisms such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Neisseria meningitidis trigger dysregulated host inflammation, endothelial injury, microvascular thrombosis, and tissue hypoperfusion leading to acute kidney injury, acute respiratory distress syndrome, hepatic dysfunction, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and shock. Core molecular pathways include LPS binding to LBP-CD14-MD2-TLR4, activation of MyD88/TRIF, NF-kB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, NLRP3 inflammasome, complement, tissue factor-coagulation, and nitric oxide signaling, with mediators such as TNF, IL1B, IL6, IFNG, CXCL8, HMGB1, protein C, and angiopoietin-Tie2 contributing to capillary leak and organ failure. Genetic susceptibility is complex and non-Mendelian rather than a classic inherited disorder; representative host variants reported in TLR4, CD14, NOD2, TNF, IL6, FER, PAI1/SERPINE1, MBL2, and complement genes may influence infection risk, inflammatory intensity, coagulopathy, or outcome. Clinical findings typically include fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated creatinine, and raised serum lactate. It may be classified by source or syndrome, including urosepsis, abdominal sepsis, pneumonia-associated sepsis, bacteremia without focus, septic shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation-predominant disease. Diagnosis relies on suspected or proven Gram-negative infection plus acute organ dysfunction, using blood and site cultures, CBC, chemistry, coagulation testing, lactate, arterial blood gases, procalcitonin or CRP, urinalysis, and imaging, with qSOFA/SOFA often used to quantify severity. Treatment centers on rapid source control and antimicrobials such as piperacillin-tazobactam, a beta-lactam inhibiting cell-wall transpeptidation; cefep

Name: Carcinoma of thyroid
Description: Carcinoma of the thyroid is a malignant epithelial neoplasm arising from follicular or parafollicular thyroid cells, most commonly presenting as differentiated thyroid carcinoma, including papillary and follicular types, with less common medullary and highly aggressive anaplastic subtypes. Its molecular landscape is dominated by MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathway activation, with representative alterations including BRAF V600E, RAS mutations, RET/PTC and NTRK fusions in papillary carcinoma, RAS and PAX8-PPARG in follicular carcinoma, RET activating mutations in hereditary or sporadic medullary carcinoma, and TP53, TERT promoter, CTNNB1, and additional PI3K-pathway lesions in poorly differentiated or anaplastic tumors; relevant proteins include RET, BRAF, RAS, VEGFR, EGFR, and thyroglobulin. Most cases are sporadic, but inherited forms occur, especially autosomal dominant MEN2A and MEN2B due to germline RET mutations causing medullary carcinoma, and familial nonmedullary thyroid cancer is also recognized. Typical manifestations include a painless thyroid nodule, cervical lymphadenopathy, hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea, and, in advanced disease, local invasion or distant metastases; medullary carcinoma may produce diarrhea or flushing via calcitonin-related secretion. Common comorbidities and complications include multinodular goiter, autoimmune thyroid disease, postoperative hypoparathyroidism or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, airway compromise, and pulmonary or osseous metastases. Diagnosis relies on neck ultrasonography with risk stratification, fine-needle aspiration cytology, histopathology, serum TSH, thyroglobulin for differentiated cancers, calcitonin and CEA for medullary carcinoma, molecular testing for BRAF, RET, RAS, or fusion drivers, and radioiodine imaging or cross-sectional imaging when indicated. Treatment commonly includes surgery and, depending on subtype, levothyroxine suppression and radioactive iodine; systemic agents include sorafenib and lenvatinib, multikinase inhibitors targeting VEGFR and RAF-related signaling, vandetanib and cabozantinib for RET-driven medullary disease, and selective RET or NTRK inhibitors such as selpercatinib or larotrectinib when actionable fusions or mutations are present.

Name: Prothrombin deficiency
Description: Prothrombin deficiency is a rare inherited bleeding disorder caused primarily by pathogenic variants in F2 on chromosome 11, leading either to quantitative hypoprothrombinemia (type I) or qualitative dysprothrombinemia (type II), usually with autosomal recessive inheritance, although heterozygous carriers may show mild abnormalities and specific missense variants have been described, including defects affecting prothrombin biosynthesis, secretion, or activation. The disorder involves the coagulation cascade, particularly the tissue factor–factor VIIa and intrinsic tenase pathways converging on factor Xa, which with factor Va, calcium, and phospholipid forms the prothrombinase complex that converts prothrombin (factor II) to thrombin; impaired thrombin generation reduces fibrin formation, platelet activation through PAR receptors, and amplification of factors V, VIII, XI, and XIII. Clinical manifestations typically include easy bruising, epistaxis, mucosal bleeding, menorrhagia, prolonged bleeding after trauma, surgery, dental extraction, umbilical stump bleeding, hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, and in severe cases intracranial or gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Important complications include chronic iron deficiency anemia, hemorrhagic shock, disability from recurrent joint bleeding, and adverse pregnancy outcomes or postpartum hemorrhage. Diagnosis relies on bleeding history, family history or consanguinity, prolonged PT and usually aPTT with normal thrombin time, low factor II activity, antigen studies to distinguish type I from type II, mixing studies, and confirmatory molecular testing of F2; differential diagnosis includes vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, and acquired inhibitors. Treatment is mainly replacement and supportive: fresh frozen plasma supplies factor II and other clotting factors, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate directly replenishes vitamin K–dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X, recombinant activated factor VII can bypass deficient thrombin generation by enhancing factor X activation on activated platelets, and adjunctive tranexamic acid inhibits plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis; vitamin K is useful only when deficiency is acquired rather than congenital.

Name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
Description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly Wegener granulomatosis) is a necrotizing, granulomatous, ANCA-associated small-to-medium vessel vasculitis that predominantly affects the upper and lower respiratory tract and kidneys, with limited and generalized phenotypes. Its strongest molecular association is with anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, especially PR3-ANCA directed against proteinase 3 encoded by PRTN3, and less often MPO-ANCA against myeloperoxidase; genetic susceptibility is polygenic rather than Mendelian and includes HLA-DP and other HLA class II loci, SERPINA1 variants affecting alpha-1 antitrypsin, and genes influencing immune regulation such as PRTN3 and CTLA4. Pathobiology centers on loss of tolerance to neutrophil granule antigens, B-cell and T-cell dysregulation, complement alternative pathway activation, especially C5a-C5aR signaling, cytokines including TNF, IL-6, IL-17, and BAFF, neutrophil priming, endothelial injury, and formation of granulomatous inflammation and pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. Typical manifestations include chronic sinusitis, epistaxis, nasal crusting or saddle-nose deformity, otitis, cough, hemoptysis, pulmonary nodules or cavitation, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, arthralgia, palpable purpura, scleritis, mononeuritis multiplex, and hematuria with rapidly progressive renal failure. Major complications and comorbidities include chronic kidney disease, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, subglottic stenosis, hearing loss, venous thromboembolism, accelerated cardiovascular disease, severe infection, and treatment-related malignancy or infertility. Diagnosis integrates compatible clinical features, PR3-ANCA or MPO-ANCA serology by immunoassay, inflammatory markers, urinalysis and renal function, CT chest/sinus imaging, and biopsy of kidney, lung, or upper airway showing necrotizing pauci-immune vasculitis and granulomas. Standard therapy includes glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, methotrexate, azathioprine, and avacopan; cyclophosphamide alkylates DNA, rituximab depletes CD20-positive

Name: Perioperative hypertension
Description: Perioperative hypertension is an acute or subacute elevation of arterial blood pressure occurring before, during, or after surgery, usually reflecting sympathetic overactivity, pain, anxiety, hypothermia, hypercarbia, hypoxemia, volume overload, medication withdrawal, or preexisting essential or secondary hypertension rather than a single inherited disorder. Its biology is dominated by catecholamine and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling, with key components including alpha1-adrenergic receptor-mediated vasoconstriction, beta1-adrenergic cardiac stimulation, angiotensin II acting through AGTR1, endothelial nitric oxide pathways involving NOS3, and vascular smooth muscle calcium influx through L-type calcium channels; representative genetic contributors to baseline hypertension susceptibility include variants in ACE, AGT, AGTR1, ADD1, NOS3, and CYP11B2, while rare perioperative hypertensive crises may accompany catecholamine-secreting tumors linked to RET, VHL, NF1, or SDHB/SDHD mutations. Clinically, patients may show severe blood pressure lability, tachycardia, headache, chest pain, dyspnea, agitation, epistaxis, or may be asymptomatic, but complications include myocardial ischemia or infarction, stroke, heart failure, arrhythmia, bleeding, aortic syndromes, and acute kidney injury; common comorbidities are chronic hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and pheochromocytoma. Subtypes are often described as preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative hypertension, or as urgency versus emergency when end-organ injury is present. Treatment commonly uses titratable intravenous agents such as nicardipine or clevidipine, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers that reduce arteriolar smooth muscle contraction; labetalol, a combined alpha1- and beta-adrenergic antagonist; and esmolol, an ultra-short-acting beta1-selective blocker, with nitroglycerin donating nitric oxide and sodium nitroprusside causing direct arterial and venous vasodilation in selected cases. Diagnosis relies on repeated or invasive blood pressure measurement, assessment for precipitating causes and end-organ damage, medication review, ECG, troponin, renal function tests, and targeted evaluation for secondary etiologies when suggested clinically.

Name: Dyslipidemia due to type 2 diabetes mellitus
Description: Dyslipidemia due to type 2 diabetes mellitus is an acquired, multifactorial metabolic disorder in which insulin resistance and relative beta-cell failure drive a characteristic atherogenic lipid pattern, typically elevated triglycerides, increased very-low-density lipoprotein, reduced HDL cholesterol, and a predominance of small dense LDL particles, often with few symptoms until vascular disease emerges; clinical signs may include central obesity, hypertension, xanthomas or pancreatitis when hypertriglyceridemia is severe, and it is commonly classified as diabetic mixed dyslipidemia, predominant hypertriglyceridemia, low-HDL dyslipidemia, or combined forms. Its molecular basis involves impaired insulin signaling through the insulin receptor–IRS1/PI3K/AKT pathway, increased adipose lipolysis and hepatic free-fatty-acid flux, overproduction of APOB-containing lipoproteins, reduced lipoprotein lipase activity, altered CETP-mediated lipoprotein remodeling, and inflammatory signaling via PPAR, AMPK, SREBP-1c, ChREBP, and TNF-α/NF-κB pathways; associated genes and proteins include APOE, APOA5, APOC3, LPL, CETP, LDLR, PPARG, GCKR, TCF7L2, and PCSK9, with variants in APOA5, APOC3, LPL, or LDLR modulating severity on a polygenic background rather than a simple Mendelian inheritance pattern, though familial dyslipidemias may coexist. Diagnosis rests on established type 2 diabetes plus fasting or nonfasting lipid profile abnormalities, often supported by HbA1c, apolipoprotein B, non-HDL cholesterol, remnant indices, liver and thyroid testing, urine albumin, and occasionally genetic testing when familial hyperlipidemia is suspected. Major comorbidities and complications include metabolic syndrome, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, obesity, chronic kidney disease, diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy, peripheral neuropathy, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease, and hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis. Treatment commonly includes statins such as atorvastatin, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and upregulate LDL receptors; fenofibrate, a PPAR-alpha agonist that lowers triglycerides and raises HDL; ezetimibe, which blocks intestinal NPC

Name: Chronic kidney disease due to type 2 diabetes mellitus
Description: Chronic kidney disease due to type 2 diabetes mellitus, commonly termed diabetic kidney disease, is a progressive microvascular and tubulointerstitial complication of T2DM characterized by persistent albuminuria and/or reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate due to chronic hyperglycemia-driven renal injury; major pathogenic mechanisms include activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, TGF-β/SMAD and CTGF-mediated fibrosis, PKC, AGE-RAGE, oxidative stress, NF-κB inflammatory signaling, glomerular hyperfiltration, podocyte loss, and altered SGLT2-dependent tubular glucose-sodium handling. Genetic susceptibility is complex and usually polygenic rather than Mendelian, with associated variants reported in ACE, AGTR1, APOE, CNDP1, ELMO1, SLC2A1, NOS3, TGFB1, UMOD, and APOL1 in some ancestries, while altered expression of proteins such as nephrin, podocin, collagen IV, fibronectin, VEGFA, and KIM-1 reflects glomerular and tubular damage. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic microalbuminuria to edema, hypertension, foamy urine, declining eGFR, and later uremic symptoms, often accompanied by diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy, and cardiovascular disease; complications include nephrotic-range proteinuria, hyperkalemia, anemia, mineral-bone disorder, heart failure, and end-stage kidney disease. Phenotypes include albuminuric classical diabetic nephropathy and nonalbuminuric DKD. Diagnosis relies on diabetes history, repeated urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio elevation, sustained eGFR reduction for at least 3 months, urinalysis, serum creatinine, electrolytes, blood pressure assessment, retinal examination, and renal ultrasound, with kidney biopsy reserved for atypical features such as rapid decline, active urine sediment, or absent retinopathy. Core treatments include ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril or ARBs such as losartan, which reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria via RAAS blockade; SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin, which lower proximal tubular glucose-sodium reabsorption and hyperfiltration; and finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that attenuates inflammation and fibrosis.

Name: Ulcerative colitis in remission
Description: Ulcerative colitis in remission refers to a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory bowel disease confined to the colonic mucosa in which prior active continuous inflammation, typically beginning in the rectum, is clinically and endoscopically quiescent; patients may be asymptomatic or have only mild residual urgency, increased stool frequency, tenesmus, or intermittent rectal bleeding, while persistent fatigue, anemia, and extraintestinal manifestations can still occur. Disease extent and subtypes include ulcerative proctitis, left-sided colitis, and extensive or pancolitis, with remission defined clinically and ideally by endoscopic and increasingly histologic healing. Its pathobiology reflects polygenic susceptibility and barrier-immune dysregulation involving epithelial junction and mucin defects, altered microbiota, and activation of TNF, IL-23/Th17, JAK-STAT, NF-κB, integrin-mediated leukocyte trafficking, and regulatory T-cell pathways; representative associated genes include HLA class II variants, IL23R, JAK2, ECM1, HNF4A, GNA12, MUC2, and loci near TNFRSF14, with complex non-Mendelian inheritance and familial aggregation rather than a single inherited mutation. Common maintenance therapies include mesalamine or other 5-aminosalicylates, which inhibit cyclooxygenase/lipoxygenase signaling and reduce mucosal prostaglandin- and leukotriene-mediated inflammation; thiopurines such as azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, which suppress purine synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation; and biologics including infliximab or adalimumab, monoclonal antibodies against TNF-α, vedolizumab, an α4β7 integrin antagonist that blocks gut-selective lymphocyte homing, ustekinumab, which inhibits IL-12/23 p40, and tofacitinib, a JAK inhibitor. Important comorbidities and complications include primary sclerosing cholangitis, venous thromboembolism, osteoporosis, colorectal dysplasia and carcinoma, severe flare, toxic megacolon, stricture, and pouchitis after colectomy. Diagnosis relies on history, exclusion of infectious colitis, elevated inflammatory markers or fecal calprotectin during activity, colonoscopy with continuous colitis and biopsies showing chronic mucosal architectural distortion and basal plasmacytosis, with remission monitored by symptom scores

Name: Asymptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction
Description: Asymptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ALVSD; often Stage B heart failure) is a preclinical disorder defined by impaired left ventricular contractility, typically a reduced ejection fraction or abnormal global longitudinal strain, in the absence of overt heart failure symptoms; it commonly reflects ischemic injury, longstanding hypertension, valvular disease, toxic cardiomyopathy, or genetic dilated cardiomyopathy. Molecular contributors include pathogenic variants in TTN, LMNA, MYH7, TNNT2, PLN, DSP, SCN5A, and RBM20, with corresponding sarcomeric, nuclear-envelope, desmosomal, calcium-handling, and ion-channel protein abnormalities that promote adverse remodeling; inheritance is most often autosomal dominant in familial dilated cardiomyopathy, though X-linked and mitochondrial forms occur. Key pathways include neurohormonal activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sympathetic nervous system, maladaptive beta-adrenergic signaling, TGF-beta and inflammatory/fibrotic signaling, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, calcium-cycling defects involving SERCA2a and phospholamban, and natriuretic peptide counter-regulation. Typical symptoms are absent by definition, but subtle reduced exercise tolerance, fatigue, an S3, displaced apical impulse, or ECG abnormalities may be found, and subtypes include ischemic versus nonischemic, genetic/familial, post-myocardial infarction, hypertensive, valvular, and chemotherapy-related LV dysfunction. Major comorbidities and complications include coronary artery disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, functional mitral regurgitation, progressive symptomatic heart failure, and sudden cardiac death. Diagnosis relies on echocardiography showing reduced LVEF, ventricular dilation, or impaired strain, supported by cardiac MRI for scar/fibrosis, ECG, natriuretic peptides, stress or ischemia testing, and selected genetic testing with family screening when inherited cardiomyopathy is suspected. Common treatments include ACE inhibitors such as enalapril, which reduce angiotensin II-mediated remodeling; beta-blockers such as carvedilol or metoprolol succinate, which blunt sympathetic toxicity; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or eplerenone, which inhibit aldosterone-driven fibrosis; and in appropriate patients ARNI therapy with sacubitr

Name: Post-polycythemia vera myelofibrosis
Description: Post-polycythemia vera myelofibrosis (PPV-MF) is a chronic clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm representing fibrotic progression of polycythemia vera, characterized by marrow stromal reaction with reticulin/collagen fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, progressive cytopenias, and risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukemia. It is driven most often by acquired somatic JAK2 mutations, especially JAK2 V617F and less commonly exon 12 variants, with cooperating mutations in epigenetic/spliceosome or tumor suppressor genes such as TET2, ASXL1, DNMT3A, EZH2, SRSF2, IDH1/2, TP53, and occasionally MPL or CALR in related MPN biology; these are generally non-Mendelian, though familial predisposition to MPN can occur. Central pathogenic pathways include constitutive JAK-STAT signaling downstream of cytokine receptors, with contributions from MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT, inflammatory cytokines including TGF-β, TNF-α, and IL-6, and abnormal megakaryocyte-driven fibroblast activation promoting fibrosis and osteosclerosis. Typical manifestations include fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, pruritus, bone pain, symptomatic splenomegaly or hepatomegaly, anemia, leukoerythroblastosis, thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis, constitutional symptoms, and thrombotic or hemorrhagic events. Major complications and comorbidities include portal hypertension, infections, gout/hyperuricemia, cachexia, iron overload from transfusions, thrombosis, and leukemic transformation. Diagnosis is based on prior polycythemia vera plus IWG-MRT/WHO-type evidence of marrow fibrosis progression, anemia or loss of erythrocytosis, increasing splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, leukoerythroblastic blood smear, elevated LDH, and molecular testing for driver mutations, supported by bone marrow biopsy, CBC, peripheral smear, cytogenetics, and next-generation sequencing. Treatment commonly includes ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor; fedratinib, a selective JAK2 inhibitor; hydroxyurea, a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor for cytoreduction; and in selected patients interferon-α

Name: Myelofibrosis due to and following essential thrombocythaemia
Description: Myelofibrosis due to and following essential thrombocythaemia, also termed post-essential thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis, is a clonal Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm that arises from antecedent essential thrombocythaemia through progressive marrow stromal reaction, cytokine-driven fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and risk of leukemic transformation. It is most often associated with driver mutations in JAK2, particularly JAK2 V617F, CALR exon 9 frameshift mutations, or MPL W515 variants, while additional adverse mutations such as ASXL1, EZH2, TET2, DNMT3A, IDH1/2, SRSF2, SF3B1, U2AF1, and TP53 may influence progression, phenotype, and prognosis. Pathobiology centers on constitutive JAK-STAT signaling downstream of mutant JAK2/MPL/CALR, with involvement of STAT3/5, MAPK, and PI3K-AKT pathways, megakaryocytic proliferation, and profibrotic mediators including TGF-beta, PDGF, and inflammatory cytokines.
