Patients typically develop constitutional symptoms, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, pruritus, bone pain, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, early satiety, anemia, thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis, leukoerythroblastosis, and teardrop cells. Common complications include portal hypertension, thrombosis, bleeding, transfusion dependence, infection, cachexia, and progression to acute myeloid leukemia. Disease may be prefibrotic/fibrotic in the antecedent ET phase and is diagnosed as post-ET myelofibrosis using WHO/ICC criteria that require a prior ET diagnosis, bone marrow fibrosis grade 2-3, and supportive features such as anemia, splenomegaly, elevated LDH, constitutional symptoms, or leukoerythroblastosis; testing includes CBC, smear, marrow biopsy with reticulin/collagen staining, molecular testing for driver and high-risk mutations, cytogenetics, and imaging for splenomegaly. Most cases are sporadic rather than Mendelian, though inherited predisposition can occur through familial MPN susceptibility and the JAK2 46/1 haplotype. Treatment commonly includes ruxolitinib

Name: Lipodystrophy due to HIV and antiretroviral therapy
Description: Lipodystrophy due to HIV and antiretroviral therapy is an acquired, non-Mendelian fat-distribution and metabolic disorder seen in treated HIV infection, characterized by lipoatrophy, lipohypertrophy, or mixed forms; patients typically develop loss of subcutaneous fat in the face, limbs, and buttocks together with central adiposity, dorsocervical fat pad enlargement, breast enlargement, or visceral fat accumulation, often accompanied by insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hepatic steatosis, and increased cardiovascular risk. Its pathobiology reflects interaction between HIV-related inflammation and drug toxicity, especially from older thymidine analogue NRTIs and some protease inhibitors, involving mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA depletion through POLG/TWINKLE-related pathways, impaired adipogenesis and lipid storage with reduced PPARG, CEBPA, SREBF1, adiponectin, and leptin signaling, GLUT4 dysregulation, and altered TNF-alpha, IL-6, cortisol, and GH/IGF-1 axes; representative host genetic susceptibility factors include variants in PPARG, LMNA, LEPR, ADIPOQ, TNF, APOC3, APOE, and mitochondrial haplogroups, which modify risk rather than confer simple inheritance. Important drug associations include stavudine and zidovudine, which inhibit mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma and promote adipocyte apoptosis and lipoatrophy; indinavir or lopinavir/ritonavir, which impair GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake and adipocyte differentiation; and therapeutic agents such as tesamorelin, a GHRH analog that reduces visceral adipose tissue, metformin, which improves insulin sensitivity via AMPK, and recombinant leptin in selected hypoleptinemic patients. Comorbidities include type 2 diabetes, pancreatitis with severe hypertriglyceridemia, NAFLD, polycystic-appearing gonadal dysfunction, depression, and body-image distress. Diagnosis is clinical and metabolic, integrating ART exposure history, anthropometry or waist-hip ratio, fasting glucose and lipid testing, lactate when mitochondrial toxicity is suspected, and body-composition assessment by DEXA, CT, or MRI, while excluding inherited lipodystrophies such as LMNA- or PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy.

Name: Recurrent candidiasis of vagina
Description: Recurrent candidiasis of vagina, more commonly termed recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, is a chronic mucosal fungal disorder defined clinically by at least 3 to 4 symptomatic, microbiologically documented episodes within 12 months, usually caused by Candida albicans but also non-albicans species such as C. glabrata, and characterized by vulvovaginal pruritus, burning, soreness, dyspareunia, dysuria, erythema, edema, fissuring, and a thick white discharge, although discharge may be minimal. Pathobiology reflects dysregulated host-fungal interactions rather than simple immunodeficiency, involving fungal adhesins and biofilm programs and host innate and adaptive pathways including Dectin-1/CLEC7A, TLR2 and TLR4, CARD9, NLRP3 inflammasome, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, Th17 signaling, neutrophil recruitment, and epithelial pattern-recognition responses; representative susceptibility genes or variants reported in some patients include CLEC7A, CARD9, TLR2, TLR4, NLRP3, IL17A, IL17F, IL22, and mannose-binding lectin gene MBL2, while familial clustering is described but most disease is complex/polygenic rather than Mendelian, with rare primary immunodeficiencies affecting IL-17 immunity conferring increased mucocutaneous candidiasis risk. Important comorbidities and risk factors include diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, estrogen use, corticosteroid or other immunosuppressive therapy, HIV infection, obesity, and atopy; complications include marked quality-of-life impairment, sexual dysfunction, vulvar excoriation, and azole-refractory disease. Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms plus microscopy with budding yeast or pseudohyphae, vaginal pH typically less than 4.5, fungal culture or PCR/speciation for recurrent or refractory cases, and susceptibility testing when non-albicans species or resistance are suspected. Treatment commonly includes fluconazole, a triazole inhibiting fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase and ergosterol synthesis, topical azoles such as clotrimazole or miconazole with the same target, and nystatin, a polyene that binds ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes; boric acid is also used intravaginally for

Name: Therapeutic opioid induced constipation
Description: Therapeutic opioid induced constipation (UMLS C3874358) is a secondary, usually noninherited gastrointestinal motility disorder caused by exposure to opioid analgesics, in which activation of peripheral mu-opioid receptors encoded by OPRM1 in the enteric nervous system inhibits acetylcholine and vasoactive intestinal peptide release, decreases propulsive peristalsis, increases nonpropulsive segmenting contractions, enhances anal sphincter tone, reduces intestinal secretion, and prolongs colonic transit; relevant biologic pathways therefore include mu-opioid receptor Gi/o-coupled signaling with inhibition of adenylate cyclase, reduced cAMP, modulation of calcium and potassium channels, and downstream effects on enteric neurons, epithelial transport, and gut-brain neuroimmune signaling. Genetic contributors are modest and not determinative, but polymorphisms in OPRM1, COMT, ABCB1, UGT2B7, and CYP2D6 may influence opioid exposure, receptor sensitivity, and susceptibility. Clinical features include reduced stool frequency, hard stools, excessive straining, incomplete evacuation, bloating, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and occasionally fecal impaction or overflow diarrhea; complications include hemorrhoids, anal fissures, ileus, bowel obstruction, urinary retention, pain-related functional decline, and impaired adherence to analgesia. It commonly coexists with chronic pain, cancer, palliative-care states, postsurgical opioid use, and other constipation-promoting conditions or drugs. Subtypes are generally defined by context, such as cancer-related versus noncancer chronic opioid therapy, and by severity or refractory disease. Diagnosis is clinical, based on new or worsening constipation after opioid initiation or dose escalation, supported by Rome IV criteria for opioid-induced constipation, medication review, bowel habit assessment, digital rectal examination, and selective testing such as abdominal imaging, colonoscopy, thyroid or calcium studies, or transit and anorectal testing when alarm features or alternative causes are suspected. Treatment includes stimulant or osmotic laxatives such as senna, bisacodyl, and polyethylene glycol, and targeted peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists including methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, and naldemedine, which reverse opioid effects in the gut while largely preserving central analgesia; lubiprostone, a chloride channel activator, is also used to increase intestinal fluid secretion.

Name: Inflammatory dermatosis (disorder)
Description: Inflammatory dermatosis is a broad, predominantly immune-mediated category of skin disorders characterized by epidermal and dermal inflammation that may be acute, relapsing, or chronic, and includes major subtypes such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, hidradenitis suppurativa, and interface or neutrophilic dermatoses. Typical manifestations include pruritus, erythema, scaling, papules, plaques, vesicles, lichenification, fissuring, pain, excoriations, and sometimes pustules or nodules, with complications including secondary bacterial or viral infection, sleep disturbance, scarring, pigment alteration, erythroderma, and impaired quality of life; common comorbidities include asthma, allergic rhinitis, psoriatic arthritis, obesity, metabolic syndrome, anxiety, and depression. Genetic susceptibility is usually complex and polygenic, although monogenic forms exist; representative associations include FLG loss-of-function variants in atopic dermatitis, HLA-C*06:02, IL23R, IL12B, TNFAIP3, CARD14, and TRAF3IP2 in psoriasis, and NCSTN, PSENEN, and PSEN1 mutations in familial hidradenitis suppurativa, with inheritance often multifactorial but sometimes autosomal dominant in syndromic or familial forms. Key pathogenic pathways include epidermal barrier dysfunction, keratinocyte activation, Th2 cytokine signaling via IL-4, IL-13, and JAK-STAT in eczema, the TNF, IL-23, and IL-17 axis in psoriasiform disease, NF-kB activation, complement, inflammasome signaling, and recruitment of dendritic cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, and T cells. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by morphology and distribution, exposure history, family history, and disease scores; testing may include skin biopsy with histopathology, patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis, bacterial or fungal studies, serum IgE or eosinophils in selected cases, and genetic testing when hereditary disease is suspected. Name: Interstitial fibrosis
Description: Interstitial fibrosis is a pathologic process rather than a single inherited disorder, defined by excess extracellular matrix deposition, especially collagen I/III and fibronectin, within organ interstitium, most commonly the kidney or lung, leading to progressive architectural distortion and organ dysfunction. Central molecular drivers include TGF-β/SMAD signaling, connective tissue growth factor, PDGF, Wnt/β-catenin, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, NF-κB, endothelin-1, oxidative stress, and epithelial/endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, with myofibroblast activation marked by α-SMA; representative implicated genes/proteins include TGFB1, CTGF, COL1A1, MMPs/TIMPs, ACE, AGT, TNF, IL6, and in familial fibrosing syndromes telomerase-related TERT and TERC, surfactant genes SFTPA1/SFTPA2 and SFTPC, and MUC5B risk variation. Inheritance is usually non-Mendelian and reflects secondary injury from diabetes, hypertension, autoimmune disease, toxins, ischemia, infection, radiation, or chronic rejection, although familial pulmonary or syndromic fibroses may show autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance. Symptoms depend on organ involved: renal interstitial fibrosis commonly presents with chronic kidney disease, proteinuria, reduced eGFR, hypertension, edema, and small echogenic kidneys, whereas pulmonary interstitial fibrosis causes exertional dyspnea, dry cough, bibasilar crackles, clubbing, restrictive physiology, and impaired diffusion. Major subtypes include renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, fibrosing nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, and secondary fibroses related to connective tissue disease or environmental exposure. Common comorbidities and complications include diabetes, systemic sclerosis, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, progressive renal failure, respiratory failure, and increased mortality. Diagnosis relies on clinical context, serologies, renal function testing or pulmonary function tests, high-resolution CT in lung disease, ultrasound or MRI when relevant, biomarkers such as KL-6 or surfactant proteins in select settings, and histopathology demonstrating interstitial matrix expansion and fibroblast/myofibroblast accumulation. Name: Congenital Hyperinsulinism
Description: Congenital hyperinsulinism (UMLS C3888018) is a heterogeneous group of genetic disorders of inappropriate pancreatic β-cell insulin secretion causing persistent hypoketotic hypoglycemia, typically presenting in neonates or infancy with jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, apnea, seizures, cyanosis, or coma, and risking neuroglycopenic brain injury, developmental delay, epilepsy, and focal neurologic deficits. The core pathophysiology is dysregulated stimulus-secretion coupling in β cells, most commonly involving the ATP-sensitive potassium channel pathway, in which biallelic or dominant mutations in ABCC8 or KCNJ11 impair SUR1/Kir6.2 channel function, producing membrane depolarization, calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels, and constitutive insulin exocytosis; other causes include GLUD1 activating variants with hyperinsulinism-hyperammonemia, GCK activating mutations, HADH deficiency, HNF4A or HNF1A variants, UCP2, SLC16A1 promoter defects causing exercise-induced disease, and less commonly HK1, PGM1, PMM2, CACNA1D, FOXA2, or EIF2S3 abnormalities. Disease subtypes include transient versus persistent forms and focal, diffuse, and atypical histologic forms; focal lesions often reflect a paternally inherited ABCC8/KCNJ11 mutation plus somatic maternal 11p15 loss, whereas diffuse disease is commonly autosomal recessive, though autosomal dominant and syndromic forms occur. Diagnosis relies on critical-sample biochemistry during hypoglycemia showing inappropriately detectable insulin or C-peptide, suppressed β-hydroxybutyrate and free fatty acids, glycemic response to glucagon, exclusion of endocrine/metabolic mimics, genetic testing, and localization with 18F-DOPA PET/CT for focal disease. Name: Asthma-Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Overlap Syndrome
Description: Asthma–chronic obstructive pulmonary disease overlap syndrome (ACOS, also termed ACO) is a heterogeneous obstructive airway disorder in which patients exhibit persistent airflow limitation together with clinical, inflammatory, and physiologic features of both asthma and COPD, typically presenting with exertional dyspnea, chronic cough, wheeze, chest tightness, sputum production, variable symptoms, bronchodilator responsiveness, and frequent exacerbations. Its biology reflects mixed type 2 and non–type 2 inflammation, with implicated genes and proteins including IL4, IL13, IL4R, TSLP, ADAM33, ORMDL3/GSDMB, TGFB1, MMP9, CHRNA3/5, HHIP, and SERPINA1, the latter relevant when alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency contributes to emphysematous change; eosinophilia, IgE, periostin, neutrophil elastase, TNF, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, and matrix-remodeling proteins are representative biomarkers. Key pathways include Th2/IL-4–IL-5–IL-13 and IgE signaling, epithelial alarmin pathways driven by TSLP, IL-33, and IL-25, NF-kB and inflammasome-mediated innate inflammation, oxidative stress, cholinergic bronchomotor tone, protease-antiprotease imbalance, and TGF-beta remodeling with mucus hypersecretion. Treatment usually combines inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide or fluticasone, which suppress glucocorticoid-responsive inflammatory gene transcription; long-acting beta2-agonists such as formoterol or salmeterol, which activate beta2-adrenergic receptors to relax airway smooth muscle; and long-acting muscarinic antagonists such as tiotropium, which block M3-mediated bronchoconstriction, with rescue albuterol, leukotriene antagonists, roflumilast, biologics such as omalizumab or anti-IL-5 agents, smoking cessation, and pulmonary rehabilitation used selectively. Common comorbidities and complications include allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, gastroesophageal reflux, obesity, anxiety/depression, obstructive sleep apnea, cardiovascular disease, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, respiratory failure, and accelerated lung-function decline. Name: Bronchopneumonia caused by Haemophilus influenzae
Description: Bronchopneumonia caused by Haemophilus influenzae (UMLS C4040491) is an acute bacterial lower respiratory tract infection, usually due to nontypeable H. influenzae in adults and encapsulated type b strains less commonly where vaccination is incomplete, characterized pathobiologically by bronchocentric suppurative inflammation with patchy alveolar consolidation. Major microbial virulence determinants include the polysaccharide capsule encoded by the cap operon, lipooligosaccharide biosynthesis genes, outer-membrane adhesins such as P2, P5 and HMW proteins, IgA1 protease, and beta-lactamase genes blaTEM-1 and less often ROB-1; host susceptibility is influenced by immune and airway-defense genes including TLR4, TLR2, MYD88, NFKB-related signaling, complement components, immunoglobulin deficiency states, and CFTR or primary ciliary dyskinesia genes in predisposed patients, but the disease itself is not classically inherited. Key pathways involve epithelial adherence and invasion, TLR2/TLR4 recognition of lipooligosaccharide, NF-kB activation, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha and CXCL8/IL-8 signaling, neutrophil recruitment, complement activation, and impaired mucociliary clearance. Typical symptoms and signs include fever, productive cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest discomfort, tachypnea, hypoxemia, crackles, and radiographic multifocal patchy infiltrates; severe cases may progress to sepsis or respiratory failure. Clinically relevant subtypes include community-acquired versus nosocomial disease, bronchopneumonia from nontypeable versus encapsulated strains, and beta-lactamase-positive or BLNAR isolates. Common treatments include amoxicillin-clavulanate, in which amoxicillin inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamases; ceftriaxone or cefuroxime, beta-lactams that block peptidoglycan cross-linking; and azithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Name: Urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella
Description: Urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella, most often uropathogenic Klebsiella pneumoniae and less commonly K. oxytoca, is a bacterial infection of the lower or upper urinary tract that may present as uncomplicated cystitis, complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated UTI, prostatitis, or urosepsis, typically causing dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, foul-smelling or cloudy urine, hematuria, and, in upper-tract disease, fever, flank pain, nausea, leukocytosis, and systemic inflammatory response. Pathogenesis is driven by bacterial adhesins and virulence determinants including type 1 and type 3 fimbriae genes fimH and mrkD, capsule polysaccharide loci such as cps, siderophore systems including entB, ybtS, iroB, and iucA, urease genes, lipopolysaccharide, and biofilm formation; clinically important resistance genes include ESBL and carbapenemase determinants such as blaSHV, blaTEM, blaCTX-M, blaKPC, blaNDM, and blaOXA-48. Host-pathogen signaling prominently involves TLR4 recognition of LPS, NF-kB activation, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF-alpha, neutrophil recruitment, complement, and in some strains cAMP/PKA-linked regulation of fimbrial expression and quorum-sensing-associated biofilm pathways. Major risk factors and comorbidities include diabetes, urinary obstruction, nephrolithiasis, vesicoureteral reflux, neurogenic bladder, pregnancy, indwelling catheters, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression, and structural urinary tract abnormalities; complications include renal abscess, emphysematous infection, bacteremia, septic shock, and recurrent multidrug-resistant infection. Treatment commonly includes ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam that inhibits penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall synthesis; ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which blocks sequential folate synthesis; nitrofurantoin, which damages bacterial DNA in lower UTI; and, for resistant strains, carbapenems such as meropenem. Name: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma (disorder)
Description: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma is an advanced malignant epithelial neoplasm arising most often from the bladder urothelium and spreading to lymph nodes, bone, liver, lung, or peritoneum; it is biologically heterogeneous, with luminal and basal/squamous-like molecular subtypes and occasional plasmacytoid or micropapillary variants that influence prognosis and therapy. Common genomic alterations include FGFR3 activating mutations or fusions, TP53 and RB1 loss, CDKN2A deletion, ERBB2 amplification, PIK3CA, TERT promoter, KDM6A, ARID1A, and DNA damage repair gene defects such as ERCC2, ATM, BRCA1/2, and FANCC, with frequent protein dysregulation involving PD-L1, HER2, and cell-cycle regulators. Major pathways implicated include RTK-RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling, p53/RB cell-cycle control, chromatin remodeling, DNA repair, angiogenesis via VEGF, and immune-evasion through the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. Typical symptoms and signs include gross or microscopic hematuria, irritative voiding symptoms, pelvic pain, weight loss, fatigue, anemia, and manifestations of metastases such as bone pain, pathologic fracture, or hepatic dysfunction. Diagnosis relies on cystoscopy with biopsy or transurethral resection for histology, CT or MRI and often PET/CT for staging, urine cytology, immunohistochemistry including GATA3, p63, uroplakin, and PD-L1 in selected settings, and molecular testing for FGFR2/3 alterations, HER2, or other actionable changes. Standard systemic therapies include cisplatin or carboplatin plus gemcitabine, in which platinum agents form DNA crosslinks and gemcitabine inhibits DNA synthesis; pembrolizumab, nivolumab, or avelumab, which block PD-1/PD-L1 signaling; enfortumab vedotin, a nectin-4-directed antibody-drug conjugate delivering monomethyl auristatin E; sacituzumab govitecan, a Trop-2-directed SN-38 conjugate; and erdafitinib, an FGFR inhibitor. Name: Primary thymic carcinoma
Description: Primary thymic carcinoma is a rare, aggressive epithelial malignancy of the thymus, usually arising sporadically rather than through a defined inherited syndrome, and includes histologic subtypes such as squamous cell carcinoma, lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma, basaloid, mucoepidermoid, sarcomatoid, and undifferentiated forms. Molecularly, recurrent but heterogeneous alterations have been described in TP53, CDKN2A/CDKN2B loss, KIT overexpression or occasional activating mutation, PIK3CA, FGFR3, CYLD, BAP1, and less often EGFR, with protein markers including c-KIT (CD117), p63/p40, and frequent PD-L1 expression; these abnormalities implicate PI3K/AKT/mTOR, cell-cycle dysregulation via p16-RB, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, and immune-checkpoint pathways involving PD-1/PD-L1. Patients commonly present with cough, chest pain, dyspnea, hoarseness, superior vena cava syndrome, weight loss, or an anterior mediastinal mass, while local invasion can cause pleural/pericardial effusions and metastases to lymph nodes, lung, liver, or bone; unlike thymoma, paraneoplastic myasthenia gravis is less common, but autoimmune disease, infection, and treatment-related cardiopulmonary complications may occur. Diagnosis relies on CT or MRI and often PET imaging, followed by core biopsy or surgical pathology showing overt cytologic atypia and invasive growth, with immunohistochemistry to distinguish it from thymoma and metastatic carcinoma; staging commonly uses Masaoka-Koga or TNM systems. Standard treatment for localized disease is surgical resection with consideration of radiotherapy, whereas advanced disease is typically treated with platinum-based chemotherapy such as cisplatin plus paclitaxel or carboplatin plus paclitaxel, in which platinum agents form DNA cross-links and paclitaxel stabilizes microtubules; other agents include doxorubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor and DNA intercalator, and cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent. Name: Reactive oxygen species 1 positive non-small cell lung cancer
Description: Reactive oxygen species 1 positive non-small cell lung cancer is a molecularly defined subset of NSCLC, usually adenocarcinoma, driven by oncogenic rearrangements of ROS1 on chromosome 6q22 that create constitutively active fusion kinases, most commonly CD74-ROS1, with other partners including SLC34A2, EZR, TPM3, and FIG/GOPC; the ROS1 receptor tyrosine kinase protein activates downstream MAPK/ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, JAK-STAT, and PLCγ signaling, promoting proliferation, survival, invasion, and metastatic spread. It is not an inherited cancer syndrome in most cases, but rather a sporadic somatic alteration, typically mutually exclusive with other major drivers such as EGFR, KRAS, and ALK, although co-alterations such as TP53 may occur. Clinically, patients present with manifestations typical of lung cancer, including cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, and sometimes malignant pleural effusion or brain metastases; complications include respiratory failure, thromboembolism, post-obstructive infection, and widespread metastatic disease involving brain, bone, liver, or adrenal glands, often in the setting of comorbid COPD, smoking-related lung disease, and cardiovascular illness, though ROS1-positive tumors are enriched in never-smokers or light smokers. Major subtypes are defined by histology, predominantly lung adenocarcinoma, and by fusion partner. Diagnosis requires pathologic confirmation of NSCLC with molecular testing for ROS1 rearrangement by FISH break-apart assay, next-generation sequencing, RT-PCR, or validated immunohistochemistry, interpreted alongside imaging and staging studies. Treatment centers on ROS1 tyrosine kinase inhibitors: crizotinib, which inhibits ROS1, ALK, and MET; entrectinib, a ROS1/TRK/ALK inhibitor with CNS activity; ceritinib or lorlatinib, more potent kinase inhibitors used in selected settings, particularly after resistance; and chemotherapy or immunotherapy may be considered depending on stage and molecular context.

Name: Extensive stage primary small cell carcinoma of lung
Description: Extensive stage primary small cell carcinoma of the lung is a high-grade pulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma defined by disease that has spread beyond a single hemithorax and tolerable radiation field, typically with rapid growth, early hematogenous dissemination, and frequent metastases to liver, bone, brain, adrenal glands, and contralateral lung. It is strongly linked to tobacco exposure rather than Mendelian inheritance, although molecular pathogenesis commonly includes near-universal loss-of-function alterations in TP53 and RB1, frequent MYC family amplification, and changes in NOTCH pathway genes, CREBBP, EP300, PTEN, and BCL2-related survival programs; tumor cells characteristically express neuroendocrine proteins such as ASCL1, synaptophysin, chromogranin A, CD56, and often TTF-1. Relevant signaling networks include TP53/RB cell-cycle control, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, DLL3/NOTCH neuroendocrine differentiation, DNA damage response pathways, and antiapoptotic BCL2 signaling. Patients commonly present with cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, or symptoms from metastatic disease, and may develop paraneoplastic SIADH, ectopic ACTH production, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome, recurrent pneumonia, pleural effusion, and respiratory failure. Major clinicopathologic categories include limited-stage versus extensive-stage disease, with molecular subtypes described by ASCL1-, NEUROD1-, POU2F3-, or YAP1-dominant expression. Standard therapy for extensive-stage disease includes platinum agents such as cisplatin or carboplatin, which form DNA crosslinks, plus etoposide, a topoisomerase II inhibitor, often combined with PD-L1 inhibitors such as atezolizumab or durvalumab that restore antitumor T-cell activity; irinotecan, another topoisomerase I inhibitor, and lurbinectedin, a transcription inhibitor causing DNA damage, are additional options. Diagnosis relies on imaging with chest CT and PET/CT, brain MRI, histologic confirmation from bronchoscopic or needle biopsy, immunohistochemistry for neuroendocrine markers, and staging by TNM and Veterans Administration systems, with molecular testing used selectively rather than routinely for targeted treatment selection.

Name: Influenza caused by pandemic influenza virus
Description: Influenza caused by pandemic influenza virus is an acute, contagious zoonotic-to-human respiratory infection produced by novel influenza A strains with sustained human transmission, classically pandemic subtypes such as A(H1N1), A(H2N2), and A(H3N2), whose virulence and host range are shaped by viral genes and proteins including hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, the M2 ion channel, nucleoprotein, polymerase subunits PB1, PB2, and PA, and nonstructural protein NS1; representative adaptive or resistance-associated mutations include PB2 E627K or D701N, HA receptor-binding changes, M2 S31N causing adamantane resistance, and neuraminidase H275Y conferring oseltamivir resistance. Pathobiology involves viral binding to sialylated airway epithelium, endosomal entry and uncoating, replication through host-dependent MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT signaling, activation of RIG-I, TLR3/7, JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and interferon pathways, and in severe disease exuberant cytokine and chemokine responses with diffuse alveolar damage. Typical manifestations are abrupt fever, cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, myalgias, headache, malaise, and dyspnea, with signs ranging from uncomplicated upper respiratory illness to viral pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, myocarditis, encephalopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and secondary bacterial pneumonia. Important comorbidities and risk states include chronic lung or cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, pregnancy, immunosuppression, extremes of age, and coinfection. Treatment commonly uses neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir, and peramivir, which block release of progeny virions, and the cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir marboxil, which inhibits PA-mediated viral mRNA transcription; adamantanes such as amantadine inhibit M2 but are usually ineffective because of resistance. The disease is not inherited, but host susceptibility and severity are influenced by genetic variation in genes such as IFITM3, TLR3, IRF7, MX1, and HLA loci. Name: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of pancreas / Neuroendocrine tumor of pancreas
Description: Well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is a usually slow-growing epithelial neoplasm arising from pancreatic islet endocrine cells, encompassing functional and nonfunctional tumors and graded G1 to G3 by mitotic count and Ki-67 index; major clinical subtypes include insulinoma, gastrinoma, glucagonoma, VIPoma, and somatostatinoma. Its molecular profile commonly includes alterations in MEN1, DAXX, ATRX, and genes in the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway such as TSC2 and PTEN, with less frequent MUTYH, VHL, NF1, or CDKN1B involvement in inherited syndromes; relevant proteins include menin, ATRX/DAXX chromatin-remodeling complex components, somatostatin receptors, especially SSTR2, and mTOR pathway effectors. Key pathogenic pathways include chromatin remodeling, telomere maintenance with alternative lengthening of telomeres, angiogenesis driven by VEGF, and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. Most cases are sporadic, but autosomal dominant predisposition occurs in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 and can also be seen with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, and tuberous sclerosis complex. Symptoms vary by hormone secretion and tumor burden: nonfunctional tumors often present with abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice, GI bleeding, or liver metastasis, whereas functional tumors cause hypoglycemia, peptic ulcer disease and diarrhea, necrolytic migratory erythema, watery diarrhea with hypokalemia, or diabetes and cholelithiasis. Important comorbidities and complications include multiple endocrine tumors, malnutrition, biliary obstruction, thromboembolism, carcinoid-like symptoms rarely, and metastatic spread, particularly to liver and lymph nodes. Diagnosis relies on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI, endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy, histopathology showing neuroendocrine markers chromogranin A and synaptophysin, Ki-67-based grading, hormone assays, and somatostatin receptor imaging such as 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT. Name: Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia pneumoniae
Description: Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia pneumoniae (UMLS C4510691) is an atypical, usually community-acquired respiratory infection produced by the obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium C. pneumoniae, classically presenting as mild to moderate tracheobronchitis or pneumonia but ranging from subclinical infection to severe lower respiratory tract disease, especially in older adults and immunocompromised hosts. The organism alternates between infectious elementary bodies and replicative reticulate bodies and exploits host-cell endocytosis, inhibition of phagolysosomal fusion, and inflammatory signaling pathways including NF-kB, MAPK/ERK, PI3K-Akt, TLR2/TLR4-mediated innate immune responses, and cytokine networks involving IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma; implicated host susceptibility genes are not Mendelian but include polymorphic immune-response loci such as TLR2, TLR4, HLA variants, and cytokine genes including TNF and IL6. Clinical features commonly include gradual-onset fever, dry cough, sore throat, hoarseness, malaise, headache, wheeze, and patchy interstitial or bronchopneumonic infiltrates on chest imaging; subtypes are best considered upper respiratory infection, bronchitis, and atypical pneumonia, with severity stratified by host risk factors rather than discrete inherited forms. Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical and radiographic findings plus laboratory confirmation, preferably nucleic acid amplification testing or PCR from respiratory specimens, with serology using microimmunofluorescence or paired titers as supportive but less specific, and culture being difficult and rarely used. Standard therapy includes macrolides such as azithromycin or clarithromycin, which bind the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis; tetracyclines such as doxycycline, which bind the 30S subunit and block aminoacyl-tRNA attachment; and respiratory fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, which inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Important comorbidities and complications include asthma or COPD exacerbation, chronic bronchitis, sinusitis, otitis, respiratory failure, and rarely severe systemic inflammatory complications.

Name: Acute myeloid leukemia with FMS-like tyrosine kinase-3 mutation
Description: Acute myeloid leukemia with FMS-like tyrosine kinase-3 mutation is an aggressive molecular subtype of AML defined by somatic activating alterations of FLT3, most commonly internal tandem duplications in the juxtamembrane domain (FLT3-ITD) and less often tyrosine kinase domain point mutations such as D835 or I836, leading to constitutive FLT3 receptor signaling in myeloid progenitors; cooperating lesions frequently involve NPM1, DNMT3A, WT1, TET2, IDH1/2, RUNX1, CEBPA, NRAS/KRAS, and genes regulating epigenetic control or hematopoietic differentiation. Pathobiologically, aberrant FLT3 activates JAK/STAT5, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK, and anti-apoptotic programs including BCL2, promoting proliferation, survival, blocked differentiation, and high leukemic burden. Clinically it presents as de novo or secondary AML with fatigue, pallor, fever, infections, easy bruising or bleeding, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, leukostasis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and sometimes CNS involvement; complications include severe cytopenias, sepsis, tumor lysis syndrome, relapse, and poor overall prognosis, particularly with high-allelic-ratio FLT3-ITD. Major disease subsets are FLT3-ITD AML and FLT3-TKD AML, often further risk-stratified by allelic burden and co-mutations such as NPM1. Inheritance is generally not Mendelian because FLT3 mutations are acquired somatic events, although germline predisposition to AML may occur through other genes such as CEBPA, DDX41, RUNX1, GATA2, or TP53. Diagnosis requires standard AML criteria, typically 20% or more marrow or blood blasts or defining recurrent genetic lesions, plus molecular confirmation of FLT3 mutation by PCR fragment analysis, allele-specific PCR, or next-generation sequencing, alongside bone marrow morphology, flow cytometry immunophenotyping, cytogenetics, and comprehensive molecular profiling. Treatment commonly combines intensive chemotherapy with the multikinase/FLT3 inhibitor midostaurin, the selective FLT3 inhibitor gilteritinib for relapsed or refractory disease, or quizartinib targeting FLT3-ITD

Name: Myeloid and/or lymphoid neoplasm associated with platelet derived growth factor receptor alpha rearrangement
Description: Myeloid and/or lymphoid neoplasm associated with platelet derived growth factor receptor alpha rearrangement is a rare clonal hematologic malignancy in the WHO/ICC category of myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase fusion genes, usually driven by somatic PDGFRA rearrangements on 4q12, most commonly the cryptic FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion created by CHIC2 deletion, with less frequent partners such as BCR, KIF5B, CDK5RAP2, ETV6, or STRN; these lesions generate constitutively active PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinase protein that signals through JAK/STAT, RAS/MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and PLCγ pathways, promoting eosinophilopoiesis, myeloproliferation, and occasionally lymphoid transformation. The disease is usually sporadic rather than inherited, with no consistent germline transmission, although additional cooperating mutations may occur in some cases. It most often presents as chronic eosinophilic leukemia or another myeloproliferative neoplasm with persistent hypereosinophilia, but may also manifest as acute myeloid leukemia, T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, or mixed phenotype disease. Typical findings include leukocytosis, marked eosinophilia, anemia, thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis, splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, rash, cough, dyspnea, thrombosis, and organ damage from eosinophilic infiltration, especially endomyocardial fibrosis, heart failure, neuropathy, pulmonary infiltrates, and gastrointestinal or hepatic involvement. Diagnosis rests on blood counts and smear, bone marrow morphology showing eosinophil-rich myeloid neoplasm, and demonstration of PDGFRA rearrangement by FISH for CHIC2 deletion/PDGFRA break-apart, RT-PCR or next-generation sequencing for fusion transcripts, with cytogenetics and exclusion of reactive eosinophilia. Treatment is centered on tyrosine kinase inhibition: imatinib, which potently inhibits PDGFRA kinase and induces rapid hematologic and molecular remissions; nilotinib and ponatinib, alternative ATP-competitive TKIs with activity in selected cases, especially some imatinib-resistant disease, whereas the PDGFRA T674I gatekeeper mutation confers

Name: Chromaffin paraganglioma
Description: Chromaffin paraganglioma is a neuroendocrine tumor of extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglia derived from neural crest chromaffin cells and is closely related to pheochromocytoma; it may be functional, secreting catecholamines, or nonfunctional, and can be sporadic or hereditary. The strongest genetic associations involve SDHx complex genes, especially SDHB, SDHD, SDHC, SDHA, and SDHAF2, with additional susceptibility genes including VHL, RET, NF1, TMEM127, MAX, FH, EPAS1/HIF2A, EGLN1/PHD2, and occasionally HRAS; corresponding protein defects converge on mitochondrial complex II dysfunction, pseudohypoxia, and dysregulated HIF signaling, while kinase-signaling tumors activate RAS/RAF/MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways. Typical symptoms reflect catecholamine excess and mass effect, including paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, tremor, pallor, anxiety, weight loss, orthostatic changes, and pain from local compression; complications include hypertensive crisis, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, stroke, metastatic spread, and associations with MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, renal cell carcinoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and polycythemia in EPAS1-related disease. Subtypes are often defined by location, secretory status, molecular cluster, and metastatic behavior, with SDHB-linked tumors carrying higher metastatic risk. Inheritance is commonly autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, including parent-of-origin effects for SDHD and SDHAF2. Diagnosis relies on elevated plasma free or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines, anatomic localization by CT or MRI, and functional imaging such as 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT, 18F-FDG PET, or 123I-MIBG scintigraphy, supplemented by histopathology, immunohistochemistry including SDHB loss, and germline genetic testing. Treatment commonly includes preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin to prevent catecholamine-mediated crises, beta-blockers such as propranolol only after alpha blockade for tachyarrhythmia control, surgical resection when feasible, and for advanced disease radiopharmaceutical 131

Name: Chronic refractory cough
Description: Chronic refractory cough (UMLS C4552486) is a chronic cough hypersensitivity syndrome defined by cough persisting for more than 8 weeks despite appropriate evaluation and treatment of common causes such as asthma, eosinophilic bronchitis, upper airway cough syndrome, and gastroesophageal reflux, and is characterized by neuronal sensitization of vagal afferents and central cough networks rather than a simple inherited Mendelian disorder. Molecular studies implicate sensory ion channels and neuroinflammatory mediators including P2X3 encoded by P2RX3, TRPV1, TRPA1, neurokinin signaling with substance P/TAC1 and NK1 receptor pathways, ATP release from injured airway epithelium, and eosinophilic/type 2 inflammatory components involving IL4, IL5, IL13, TSLP, and prostaglandins in selected patients; rare pathogenic mutations are not established, but genetic susceptibility has been suggested by polymorphisms affecting TRP channels, neurokinin, and inflammatory pathways, without a clear inheritance pattern. Typical symptoms are a dry or minimally productive cough, throat tickle, laryngeal irritation, urge-to-cough, allotussia and hypertussia, often triggered by talking, სიცest? Wait.

Name: Germline BRCA-mutated, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer
Description: Germline BRCA-mutated, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer is an advanced breast carcinoma defined by distant spread and the presence of an inherited pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 alteration, most often inactivating truncating or splice-site mutations that impair BRCA protein function in homologous recombination DNA repair; related genomic features can include TP53, PIK3CA, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, and PTEN abnormalities, while HER2 negativity denotes lack of ERBB2 amplification/overexpression. The disease is biologically driven by defective double-strand break repair, genomic instability, PARP-dependent DNA damage responses, and crosstalk with PI3K/AKT/mTOR, cell-cycle, apoptosis, and estrogen-receptor signaling pathways; clinically it comprises hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative and triple-negative/HER2-negative subtypes, the latter enriched in BRCA1 carriers. Inheritance is typically autosomal dominant cancer predisposition with variable penetrance, often accompanied by family histories of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, or male breast cancer. Patients usually present with a breast mass, skin or nipple changes, axillary adenopathy, and metastatic symptoms such as bone pain, pathologic fractures, dyspnea, cough, pleural effusion, jaundice, hepatomegaly, headache, seizures, or weight loss; common complications include visceral crisis, marrow suppression, skeletal-related events, venous thromboembolism, treatment resistance, and increased risk of second primary ovarian or pancreatic malignancies. Diagnosis requires histologic confirmation of metastatic breast cancer, immunohistochemical or in situ hybridization demonstration of HER2-negative status, staging with CT, PET/CT, bone scan, or MRI, and germline testing for BRCA1/2 by blood or saliva using targeted sequencing with deletion-duplication analysis; tumor next-generation sequencing may complement this and identify homologous recombination deficiency. Common treatments include olaparib and talazoparib, PARP inhibitors that exploit synthetic lethality in BRCA-deficient cells, platinum agents such as carboplatin that induce DNA crosslinks, capecitabine or taxanes as cytotoxic therapy, and in hormone receptor-positive disease endocrine therapy with CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib to block cell-cycle progression.

Name: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 deficiency
Description: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 deficiency (CDKL5 deficiency disorder; UMLS C4750718) is a severe X-linked developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused by pathogenic variants in CDKL5 on Xp22, which encodes the serine-threonine kinase CDKL5, a protein highly expressed in developing neurons and involved in dendritic growth, synapse formation, microtubule dynamics, and activity-dependent nuclear signaling; representative disease-causing lesions include nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, missense, and exon-level deletions or duplications that produce loss of function, with occasional mosaicism. The disorder is usually de novo and X-linked dominant, affecting females more often, although hemizygous males are often more severely affected; phenotype may vary with X-inactivation. CDKL5 intersects with pathways regulating neuronal maturation and excitability, including MECP2/BDNF-related transcriptional networks, AKT-mTOR and ERK signaling, and cytoskeletal and synaptic vesicle components. Clinically, onset is typically in the first weeks to months of life with refractory epileptic spasms or tonic, tonic-clonic, myoclonic, or focal seizures, followed by profound global developmental delay, severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, cortical visual impairment, poor eye contact, autistic features, hand stereotypies, limited or absent speech, feeding difficulty, reflux, constipation, sleep disturbance, scoliosis, and impaired mobility. Common complications and comorbidities include status epilepticus, aspiration, failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory infections, and movement disorders. Recognized phenotypic patterns include infantile spasm-predominant, early-onset seizure variant, and rare later-onset or milder forms. Treatment is symptomatic, especially antiseizure therapy, with commonly used agents including vigabatrin, which irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase to raise brain GABA; valproate, which enhances GABAergic tone and modulates sodium and calcium channels; clobazam, a GABAA receptor positive allosteric modulator; and often topiramate, levetiracetam, corticosteroids, or ketogenic diet. Diagnosis relies on characteristic early-onset epilepsy with developmental impairment, EEG abnormalities such as hypsarrhythmia or multifocal epileptiform discharges, brain MRI often normal or nonspecific, and confirmation by targeted sequencing, multigene epilepsy panels, chromosomal microarray for copy

Name: Abnormal uterine bleeding due to uterine fibroid
Description: Abnormal uterine bleeding due to uterine fibroid (AUB-L; UMLS C5190725) is a structural cause of heavy, prolonged, or irregular uterine bleeding arising from leiomyomas, benign monoclonal smooth-muscle tumors of the myometrium, most often submucosal or other cavity-distorting FIGO types, with symptoms including menorrhagia, intermenstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, dysmenorrhea, bulk-related urinary or bowel complaints, infertility, and anemia. Molecularly, leiomyomas commonly harbor somatic MED12 mutations, HMGA2 overexpression or rearrangement, biallelic FH inactivation in a minority, and less often COL4A5-COL4A6 or chromatin-remodeling alterations; associated proteins and pathways include estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor signaling, TGF-β/SMAD-driven extracellular matrix deposition, WNT/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, IGF, angiogenic mediators such as VEGF, and inflammatory/prostaglandin pathways that contribute to abnormal bleeding and growth. Most fibroids are sporadic, but genetic predisposition is supported by familial clustering, higher concordance in first-degree relatives, and syndromic associations such as hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer due to germline FH mutations, which is typically autosomal dominant. Important comorbidities and complications include iron-deficiency anemia, reduced quality of life, subfertility, adverse pregnancy outcomes, hydronephrosis in severe bulk disease, and coexistence with adenomyosis or endometriosis. Diagnosis follows PALM-COEIN classification after excluding pregnancy and nonstructural causes, using history, pelvic examination, CBC and ferritin, pregnancy testing, and often TSH as indicated; transvaginal ultrasonography is first-line, with saline infusion sonography or hysteroscopy for submucosal lesions, MRI for mapping or procedural planning, and endometrial sampling when age, risk factors, or bleeding pattern raise concern for hyperplasia or malignancy. Common treatments include tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic that inhibits plasminogen activation; levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system or other progestins, which suppress endometrial proliferation; combined hormonal contraceptives, which stabilize the endometrium; GnRH agonists such as leuprolide

Name: Obesity due to leptin receptor gene deficiency
Description: Obesity due to leptin receptor gene deficiency (UMLS C5191640) is a rare monogenic, usually autosomal recessive form of severe early-onset obesity caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in LEPR, which encodes the long signaling isoform of the leptin receptor (Ob-Rb/LEPRb); representative loss-of-function changes include nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and deleterious missense variants that impair receptor expression, ligand binding, trafficking, or downstream signaling. The disorder is characterized by disruption of leptin-dependent hypothalamic energy homeostasis, principally the JAK2-STAT3 pathway, with additional effects on PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MAPK/ERK, and SOCS3-mediated feedback signaling in POMC/CART and NPY/AgRP neurons, leading to hyperphagia, reduced satiety, diminished energy expenditure, and neuroendocrine dysfunction. Typical manifestations begin in infancy with marked hyperphagia, rapid weight gain, severe obesity, increased fat mass, and often hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed or absent puberty, infertility, and sometimes immune dysfunction; common complications include insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, and psychosocial morbidity. Disease subtypes are generally defined by the specific LEPR variant and residual receptor function rather than distinct clinical classes. Diagnosis is suspected in a child with severe obesity before 5 years of age and intense hyperphagia, especially with consanguinity or affected siblings, and is supported by serum leptin concentrations that are normal or elevated for fat mass, then confirmed by molecular testing of LEPR using targeted sequencing, multigene obesity panels, or exome sequencing; endocrine and metabolic evaluation helps define complications. Treatment combines intensive nutritional and behavioral care with anti-obesity pharmacotherapy, including setmelanotide, an MC4R agonist that bypasses defective leptin signaling, GLP-1 receptor agonists such as liraglutide and semaglutide that enhance satiety and delay gastric emptying, and orlistat, a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor reducing fat absorption.

Name: Solid neoplasm with neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase gene fusion
Description: Solid neoplasm with neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase gene fusion is a molecularly defined group of malignant or occasionally locally aggressive solid tumors driven by oncogenic rearrangements involving NTRK1, NTRK2, or NTRK3, which encode the TRKA, TRKB, and TRKC receptor tyrosine kinases; representative fusions include ETV6-NTRK3, TPM3-NTRK1, LMNA-NTRK1, TPR-NTRK1, and SQSTM1-NTRK3. These chimeric proteins constitutively activate downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, PLCgamma-PKC, and JAK-STAT signaling, promoting proliferation, survival, invasion, and resistance to apoptosis. NTRK fusions occur across diverse histologies, including infantile fibrosarcoma, secretory carcinoma of breast or salivary gland, thyroid carcinoma, lung adenocarcinoma, sarcoma, glioma, and colorectal and other rare cancers, so the clinical phenotype depends largely on tumor site and stage; common manifestations include a growing mass, pain, organ-specific dysfunction, bleeding, weight loss, fatigue, and symptoms of metastatic spread such as dyspnea, neurologic deficits, or pathologic fracture. Important complications include local tissue destruction, recurrence, metastasis, treatment resistance, and organ failure, with comorbidities reflecting disease burden and therapy effects. Most cases are sporadic somatic events rather than inherited cancer syndromes, although rare germline predisposition may coexist in individual tumors through unrelated genes; the defining genetic component is the acquired NTRK fusion itself. Diagnosis requires integration of histopathology with molecular testing, using pan-TRK immunohistochemistry as a screening tool and confirmation by RNA-based next-generation sequencing, targeted DNA sequencing, reverse-transcription PCR for known fusions, or break-apart FISH in selected settings. Targeted therapy is central: larotrectinib and entrectinib inhibit TRK kinase activity and produce tumor-agnostic responses, while repotrectinib has activity against some solvent-front or resistance mutations; multikinase inhibitors such as crizotinib or cabozantinib may have limited off-target TRK activity in select contexts.

Name: COVID-19
Description: COVID-19 (UMLS C5203670) is an acute viral respiratory and systemic infectious disease caused by SARS-CoV-2, with clinical phenotypes ranging from asymptomatic infection and mild upper respiratory illness to severe viral pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, thromboinflammatory multiorgan failure, and post-acute sequelae; major variants/subtypes are defined by viral lineages and spike mutations, including D614G, N501Y, E484K, L452R, T478K, and P681R/H, which can alter transmissibility, immune escape, and occasionally disease severity. Viral entry depends on the spike protein binding ACE2 and priming by TMPRSS2, with host factors and severity-associated genes including IFNAR2, OAS1, TYK2, DPP9, ABO, and HLA loci, while rare inborn errors of type I interferon immunity and autoantibodies to interferons predispose to critical illness; inheritance is therefore not Mendelian for the disease itself but reflects complex polygenic susceptibility and rare monogenic immune defects. Key pathogenic pathways include ACE2-TMPRSS2-mediated entry, innate sensing with type I/III interferon signaling, NF-kB and JAK-STAT activation, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, complement activation, endothelial injury, and IL-6/TNF-alpha-driven hyperinflammation with immunothrombosis. Typical symptoms and signs include fever, cough, sore throat, dyspnea, anosmia, ageusia, fatigue, myalgia, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, with hypoxemia, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, lymphopenia, and elevated CRP, ferritin, D-dimer, and transaminases in severe disease. Common comorbidities and complications include advanced age, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular and chronic lung disease, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy, venous thromboembolism, myocarditis, acute kidney injury, stroke, and secondary infection. Diagnosis is based on compatible clinical and epidemiologic features plus detection of viral RNA by NAAT/RT-PCR, rapid antigen testing, or less commonly sequencing, with chest imaging and laboratory markers used for severity stratification and serology indicating prior exposure. Common treatments include nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, a SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitor boosted by CYP3A inhibition; remdesivir, an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor; dexameth

Name: Pneumonia caused by SARS-CoV-2
Description: Pneumonia caused by SARS-CoV-2 is an acute viral lower respiratory tract infection, usually manifesting as COVID-19 viral pneumonia and ranging from mild interstitial disease to severe bilateral diffuse alveolar damage, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and multiorgan failure; common symptoms and signs include fever, cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, fatigue, myalgias, anosmia, and radiographic ground-glass opacities or consolidations. The disease is initiated by viral spike protein binding to ACE2 with priming by TMPRSS2, and host susceptibility and severity have been linked to variants or differential expression in genes such as ACE2, TMPRSS2, IFNAR2, OAS1, DPP9, TYK2, TLR7, and loci in the HLA region, while viral evolution is shaped by spike mutations such as D614G and receptor-binding domain substitutions in major variants. Key pathogenic pathways include ACE2–angiotensin signaling imbalance, innate immune sensing, type I and III interferon pathways, NF-kB and JAK-STAT activation, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, endothelial injury, complement and coagulation cascades, and cytokine-mediated hyperinflammation involving IL-6, TNF, and chemokines. Major comorbidities associated with severe disease include advanced age, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease, cancer, and immunosuppression; complications include ARDS, venous thromboembolism, secondary bacterial infection, myocarditis, acute kidney injury, and post-acute sequelae. Subtypes are often defined clinically by severity, oxygen requirement, imaging pattern, and viral variant. Inheritance is not Mendelian, but host genetic predisposition is polygenic, with rare inborn errors of interferon immunity and X-linked TLR7 deficiency predisposing to severe pneumonia. Diagnosis relies on compatible symptoms plus detection of SARS-CoV-2 by NAAT or antigen testing, supported by chest imaging, pulse oximetry, inflammatory and coagulation markers, and microbiologic exclusion of alternative causes. Common treatments include remdesivir, an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor; dexamethasone, a glucocorticoid that suppresses inflammatory gene transcription; and tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist, with anticoagulation often used to mitigate thrombotic risk.

Name: Malignant melanoma with BRAF V600E mutation
Description: Malignant melanoma with BRAF V600E mutation is an aggressive cutaneous melanocytic neoplasm defined by constitutive activation of the serine-threonine kinase BRAF, most commonly the c.1799T>A p.Val600Glu substitution, which drives MAPK signaling; related genetic events may include NRAS, NF1, PTEN, CDKN2A, TERT promoter, TP53, KIT, and MITF alterations, while the principal protein and pathway consequences involve aberrant RAF-MEK-ERK signaling with crosstalk to PI3K-AKT-mTOR, cell-cycle regulators such as CDK4/6, and apoptosis control. Clinically, it typically arises de novo or from a dysplastic nevus and presents as an asymmetric pigmented lesion with border irregularity, color variegation, diameter enlargement, evolution, bleeding, pruritus, ulceration, or nodal and visceral metastases; histologic subtypes include superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, and acral lentiginous melanoma, and advanced disease may involve brain, lung, liver, or bone. Treatment commonly includes BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib, dabrafenib, and encorafenib, which selectively inhibit mutant BRAF V600 signaling, often combined with MEK inhibitors such as trametinib, cobimetinib, or binimetinib to suppress downstream ERK activation and delay resistance; immune checkpoint inhibitors including pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and ipilimumab are also widely used by enhancing antitumor T-cell responses through PD-1 or CTLA-4 blockade. Important complications include rapid metastasis, treatment resistance via MAPK reactivation or PI3K pathway escape, secondary cutaneous squamous neoplasms with BRAF inhibitor monotherapy, and comorbid UV damage, multiple atypical nevi, and familial melanoma syndromes. Most cases are sporadic and multifactorial, but inherited susceptibility is seen with germline CDKN2A, CDK4, BAP1, POT1, TERT, MITF, and PTEN variants, usually in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance. Diagnosis relies on clinical ABCDE assessment and dermoscopy, confirmatory excisional biopsy with histopathology and Breslow depth, ulceration and mitotic evaluation, staging by sentinel lymph node biopsy and imaging when indicated, and molecular testing for B

Name: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase fusion oncogene positive non-small cell lung cancer
Description: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase fusion oncogene positive non-small cell lung cancer is a molecularly defined subtype of NSCLC, usually adenocarcinoma, driven by activating rearrangements of ALK on chromosome 2p23 that create constitutively active fusion kinases, most commonly EML4-ALK, with less frequent partners such as KIF5B, TFG, and KLC1; these alterations are somatic rather than inherited, arise in tumor tissue, and typically occur in younger patients with little or no smoking history, often mutually exclusive with EGFR and KRAS driver mutations, although TP53 co-mutation and secondary ALK kinase-domain resistance mutations such as L1196M, G1202R, and F1174C may emerge under therapy. ALK signaling promotes tumorigenesis through MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, JAK/STAT3, PLCγ, and RAS-mediated pathways, enhancing proliferation, survival, invasion, and metastatic spread. Clinically, patients present with features of lung cancer including persistent cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, and recurrent pneumonia, and the disease has a strong propensity for brain, pleural, liver, bone, and lymph node metastases, leading to complications such as malignant pleural effusion, respiratory failure, pathologic fractures, pain, and neurologic deficits. Diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation of NSCLC and demonstration of an ALK rearrangement by immunohistochemistry screening, fluorescence in situ hybridization, reverse-transcription PCR, or increasingly next-generation sequencing of tissue or plasma; staging imaging and CNS evaluation are important because of frequent intracranial disease. Treatment centers on ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including crizotinib, which inhibits ALK, ROS1, and MET; alectinib, a potent CNS-active ALK inhibitor; ceritinib and brigatinib, next-generation ALK inhibitors active against several resistance variants; and lorlatinib, a third-generation ALK/ROS1 inhibitor with broad activity against resistant mutations and brain metastases.
